Similarly, "That which is devoid of the nature of consciousness is devoid of the state of being composed of pleasure and so forth," for example, the Puruṣa. "And sound and the others are devoid of the nature of consciousness"—this is a non-perception of the pervader. Thus, the proof is established. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the word "manifestation" (*vyakti*) here refers to the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*). Because it is a manifestation, it is its own consciousness. Why is that nature of being consciousness established for pleasure and the rest?
Because the self-cognition, the self-awareness, of pleasure and the rest is manifest.

This self-cognition—characterized by its own self-luminous nature, independent of any other illumination—is extremely clear in the form of pleasure, joy, pain, and so forth, whether there is proximity to objects such as sound or not.

For that which is established by itself through its own nature as pleasure (*sātā*) and so forth, independent of any other illumination, is designated by such synonyms as "consciousness" (*caitanya*), "happiness" (*sukha*), "experience" (*saṃvedana*), and "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

If the manifestation of experience for pleasure and the like were due to their being experienced by another consciousness, then their experience would take the form of non-pleasure (*asātā*) and so forth, because they themselves would not consist of that [pleasure] by nature—
just as when a yogi or an inferer experiences the pleasure and so forth belonging to another.
Otherwise, even those such as Yogins would be like the sick and others who directly experience pleasure and so forth;
or else, just as with the Yogins, there would be no benefit or harm for others either, since there would be no distinction between them.
Furthermore, if it is admitted that consciousness has the nature of pleasure and so on, then it is established that pleasure and the rest have the very nature of cognition.
For this alone is our pleasure and pain, namely, the experience of the agreeable and the disagreeable.
Therefore, there is neither inconclusiveness nor lack of proof regarding the reason;
for among all proponents of external objects, it is established that sounds and other phenomena are devoid of the nature of consciousness.

Otherwise, the position of the Vijñānavādins themselves would have to be accepted, and that is indeed desired [by us]. Nor is there any contradiction in the reason, because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa).

It might be argued: "Just as a cognition, though not having the nature of blue and so forth, appears in the form of blue and so forth due to the proximity of external blue objects and the like, so too, by the influence of external adjuncts such as pleasure, that which is not of the nature of pleasure appears as if it were of the nature of pleasure. Therefore, even if cognition possesses the nature of pleasure and so forth, it does not follow that pleasure and the like have the nature of consciousness; thus, the primary reason is not inconclusive. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And in one and the same [object]," and so forth.
"In one and the same [object], such as sound, due to the difference in mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and genus (*jāti*..."
Attachment and the others, which are possible, are clearly indicated as being determinate.
Regarding the phrase "due to the difference between cultivation and birth":
*bhāvanā* refers to repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), while *jāti* refers to one's innate nature (*nijā prakṛtiḥ*); the "difference" (*bheda*) between these two is their distinction (*viśeṣa*).
This refers to attachment and so forth.

"Attachment" (*saṅga*) means longing (*abhilāṣa*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are included the groups of effects of the three qualities (*guṇa*), such as affection and the like, aversion and agitation and the like, and dejection and obscuration and the like.
They are "determined" (*niyata*) in the sense that they are of a uniform nature.

For instance, due to specific mental cultivations (*bhāvanāviśeṣa*), affection and the like arise only for certain individuals—such as those who have cultivated the notions of beauty or ugliness regarding wine, women, and so forth, namely the lustful and others—and due to their specific biological species, such as deer, young elephants, and so forth.
Furthermore, this [argument] is not tenable if sound and the other objects were to possess the nature of pleasure and so forth for everyone.
He asks "Why? and says: "In the case of being subsumed under a single entity," and so forth.
If [consciousness] were subsumed under a single entity, a variegated consciousness would follow as an absurd consequence.
If you say this is not so because of the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) and other factors, then it would not be something that conforms to the object.

For indeed, since all of those [cognitions] have as their object a single undivided entity, it would follow that each individual cognition would be variegated (*citrā*), just like the perception of an object such as blue.

One might argue: "Even though the entity consists of three natures, nevertheless, by the power of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) characterized as merit (*dharma*) and so forth—such as past karma (*adṛṣṭa*)—only a certain form appears to someone, and not every form to everyone.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), differences in genus (*jāti*), the desire to apprehend (*jighṛkṣā*), and other such factors.
The point is that if this were not so, that cognition would not follow after the object nor have the object as its support, because it would be devoid of the object's form.
Demonstrating that very emptiness of those forms, he says: "The form of the object has three aspects, whereas the cognitions of it have only one aspect;
how can those [cognitions] be applicable to that [object], since they are future and possess characteristics different from it?"
This is the nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

And "those who know them are of a single form" means that the cognitions (*vidas*)— the consciousnesses— of those persons are experienced as being of a single form, because each is restricted to a single nature consisting merely of attachment and so forth.
The phrase "those cognitions" refers to [cognitions] regarding objects such as sound; "about to arise" means they are ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).
To the question "Why are they not tenable?", he says: "because they are of a different character from that.
This means they are of a different character from the object which serves as their objective support.
The formal argument is as follows: whatever does not have the cognition of a particular form is not of that object, just as visual cognition is not of the object sound;

and the aforementioned cognitions are devoid of the forms of the three-natured reality. Thus, the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the opposite position, which would otherwise lead to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

It might be argued that just as, even when an object such as sound is apprehended by perception in its entirety, a determinate cognition (*niścaya*) arises only with respect to certain aspects like momentariness due to the force of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, and not with respect to everything—likewise, a consciousness of a single form will arise due to the force of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors.
This is incorrect;
for we do not maintain that, in the ultimate sense, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "momentary" have a real entity (*vastu*) as their object.
Because the real entity transcends all conceptual construction,
its validity consists in its being the cause for attaining such an entity through an indirect connection with that entity.
However, others maintain that, in the ultimate sense, joy and the other [mental states] have the real entity itself as their object.

For otherwise, if there were no objective support (*anālambanatva*), then the manifestation of the experience of pleasure and so forth—arising from the experience of sounds and other objects which are themselves of the nature of pleasure and so forth—would not occur.

Furthermore, since those [states] such as joy (*prīti*) are conceptual (*savikalpaka*), they would lack any determinate form; thus, there would be a manifestation of an experience of them in their entirety.
For this indeed is the comprehension of an object by determinate cognitions (*niścaya*): namely, that which is called "ascertainment" (*niścayana*).
Regarding what was stated— that the accompaniment of sound and other objects by pleasure and so forth is established because one perceives effects such as serenity, agitation, and dejection—
he says "serenity, agitation," etc., showing that this is inconclusive: "Serenity, agitation, and obstruction [occur] in a single person for yogins..."
They are born, yet a person of that same nature is not accepted by the opponents.

For instance, among the followers of Kapila who practice yoga, those who meditate upon the *puruṣa* as distinct from *prakṛti* and have well-practiced their yoga by taking the *puruṣa* as their object experience clarity and joy;
however, for those whose yoga is unmastered and who do not perceive it quickly, agitation arises, and for those whose intellects are dull by nature, a state of obstruction occurs.
Yet, that *puruṣa* is not accepted by others as being of such a nature, consisting of the three *guṇas*.
Therefore, because effects such as serenity, distress, and dejection are observed, this [argument] is inconclusive.
If it is argued that those states of pleasure and so forth arise from mental volition (saṅkalpa) and not from the Person (puruṣa),
this is equally applicable to sound and other objects.
Furthermore, if [pleasure and so forth] were produced by mere conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*), external pleasure and the like would not be established,
because conceptualization is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*).
For this very reason, the claim that "consciousness takes on the form of pleasure and so forth by virtue of the presence of external pleasure and the like" is also fallacious.
For it is observed that joy and the like arise even without the presence of external objects, by taking the *puruṣa* as their objective support.

Furthermore, how could that well-known experience of pleasure and so forth—which occurs through the conceptualization of the desirable and undesirable without depending on the proximity of external objects—be due to the influence of something else?
This is because the nature of consciousness has been established [by the author] in the passage beginning with "The mind is also established," and so on.
Therefore, the reason "because of [the presence of] concomitance" is unestablished (asiddha).

Now, having for the sake of argument accepted the establishment of the reason, he states "Even if [the manifest] were established... and so forth, in order to demonstrate its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*):
"Even if the manifest (*vyakta*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) were established, the Pradhāna is not proven;
for that single, eternal cause is not indeed endowed with the same genus."
Even if it were established that the manifest is indeed composed of the three guṇas, nevertheless, its desired cause—termed *pradhāna*—is not established.
The point is that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason with such a cause is not established anywhere.
For instance, its cause is intended to be proven as being likewise composed of the three guṇas, eternal, and all-pervading.
Nor is the connection of a reason established anywhere by such a cause;
nor is it the case that whatever nature an effect is observed to have must necessarily be possessed by its cause in that same nature,
because of the difference between cause and effect.

For you maintain that the effect called the "manifest" (vyakta) is endowed with properties such as having a cause, impermanence, and non-pervasiveness; yet you do not accept that its cause possesses those same characteristics. Therefore, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Furthermore, showing that it is also contradictory (viruddha) because it establishes the opposite of the specific property intended, he says: "That cause is one," and so forth.
The intended property to be proven is a single, eternal cause consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa); however, such a thing is not established, but rather the opposite—this is the meaning.
He asks "Why? and replies: "For that is not endowed with a single genus. The word "hi" indicates the reason.
Therefore, that effect called the "manifest" is not established as being endowed with a single genus consisting of the three *guṇas* which constitutes its own essence.
Rather, it is perceived as being endowed with properties such as multiplicity and impermanence.
For if the manifest were endowed with a single genus as previously described, then its cause would also be established as characterized by those same aforementioned properties.
However, since the effect is observed to be associated with the properties of impermanence and multiplicity, its cause is likewise inferred to be exactly so.
Because for that which is eternal, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is incompatible with both successive and simultaneous action;
and because the diversity of effects is produced by differences in their causes,
otherwise it would follow that they are causeless.
Therefore, there is no proof for a *pradhāna* that is eternal and of a single nature.
Furthermore, the point is that if the designation "pradhāna" were applied to a cause that is simply impermanent and manifold in nature, then there would be no dispute.
But why is it that the manifest does not possess a single genus? To this he says: "Like iron rods," and so forth.
For all manifest individuals are seen to have forms that are joined in succession like iron rods, and their nature is intermingled with conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

For just as iron needles do not adhere to one another, so too these manifestations of sound and other objects—being established in their own respective natures—do not interpenetrate one another due to differences in place, time, capacity, appearance, and so forth.
By this, their plurality has been established.
To establish their impermanence, he says: "having forms that occur in succession."
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose forms are conjoined with, that is, embraced by, the process of arising.

To the question, "How then are entities determined to be followed by a single form such as earth and so forth, and by a stable nature such that one thinks 'this is that very same thing'? he says: "having a nature mixed with conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
The meaning is that this apprehension of a single identity among objects is a false conceptualization (*mithyāvikalpa*).
And this will be demonstrated later, in the section on momentary destruction and so forth.

Thus, the fallacies of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) regarding the reason "because of concomitance" (*samanvayāt*) have been demonstrated. Now, demonstrating that the example "like the various differences such as jars" possesses the property of the concomitance between the probandum and the probans, he says: "The various modifications of clay, etc. and so forth.

"Just so, the various differences such as the modifications of clay are not endowed with a single genus, nor are they established as having a single cause, because of their distinction from the lump of clay and other such factors."
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), modifications such as gold and so forth are included.
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) serves either to aggregate another refutation or to indicate similarity.
By the phrase "not endowed with a single genus," the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) is demonstrated.
"And they do not have multiple causes"—
this connects with the word "established" from the context. By this, the absence of concomitance with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is demonstrated.

But surely, a single cause such as a lump of clay or gold is already established for those [products], and likewise, a universal such as "clay-ness" or "gold-ness" is observed to follow them; so how can there be a lack of both? To this he says: "because of the difference from the lump of clay and so forth. For there is no single composite whole (avayavin) such as a lump of clay, because if it were to cover one part, it would follow that it covers the whole.
Nor is there a single universal, because there is a difference in appearance for each individual instance.
Furthermore, demonstrating that the reason "because of concomitance" (*samanvayāt*) is inherently inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says "caitanya... and so forth:
"Even though they are accompanied by consciousness (*caitanya*) and other qualities, it is not accepted that they have a single prior cause."
If it is argued that [the self] is not primary among persons, then why is this not the same in this case as well?

For indeed, persons are held by you to be endowed with immeasurable attributes such as consciousness (*caitanya*), the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), and so forth; yet you do not accept that they are preceded by a single cause of that nature.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the possession of consciousness and other qualities by persons is not intended in a primary sense, but rather in a secondary sense;

for since all persons are excluded from non-consciousness and the like, "consciousness" is postulated as a universal (*jāti*) consisting in the exclusion of other things (*arthāntara-vyāvṛtti*) which follows after them, but there is no single real entity of that kind.

If that is so, then why is it not equally postulated here in the case of the manifest (vyakta) as well—that its possession of pleasure and so forth is secondary—even in the absence of such a single preceding cause, just as in the case of the Puruṣas?
Therefore, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
The mention of "of the Puruṣas" is merely illustrative.

Likewise, pleasure and the other qualities, which exist in the state of the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti), are endowed with properties such as being attributes (guṇatva), insentience (acetanatva), and non-enjoyership (abhoktṛtva); and the Pradhāna and the Puruṣas are joined with properties such as eternality (nityatva). Yet, these are not preceded by a single cause of that same nature; therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is indeed inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Thus, first of all, this reason "because of concomitance" has been refuted.

Now, under the guise of a conclusion, he states a mere indication for the purpose of refuting the remaining reasons, beginning with the words: "Even in the absence of a primal cause (pradhāna), everything is produced from that [nature]," and so forth.
Even in the absence of a primal cause, everything is conceptualized from that.
Through the differentiation of power, there arises diversity, such as the relationship between cause and effect.
In this regard, as for what was stated— that the Pradhāna exists because of finite magnitude, because of activity proceeding from power, and because of the relationship between cause and effect—
these three reasons are inconclusive with respect to the opposite of the thesis,
since no subverting evidence has been presented.
Because there is no contradiction among these [reasons], such as limited magnitude (*parimāṇa*) and so forth, even in the absence of a cause designated as "Primal Matter" (*pradhāna*).

To explain: if one were to prove merely the existence of a cause in general, then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), for we do not maintain that the production of an effect occurs without a cause; and if one applies the name "Primal Matter" to a mere cause, nothing is undermined.

However, if it is argued in this way—that there exists an intelligent cause which produces this manifest world of fixed dimensions and proceeds from a specific capacity—[then the reasons are indeed contradictory].

In that case, there is inconclusiveness [of the reason], for even without an intelligent creator, there is no contradiction in the arising of something endowed with specific dimensions and other qualities due to the specific determination of the capacity of its own causes.
Furthermore, it is not logical for *pradhāna* to be intelligent, because it is insentient,
and because "intelligence" (*prekṣā*) is a synonym for sentience (*caitanya*).

Furthermore, regarding the argument "because activity proceeds from power" (*śaktitaḥ pravṛtteḥ*): if by this you seek to prove merely that the cause possesses non-distinct powers (*avyatirikta-śakti*), then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
If, however, you mean to prove a single, eternal cause endowed with distinct and diverse powers (*vyatirikta-vicitra-śakti*), then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Such a [cause] is unestablished (*asiddha*) because a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with such a thing is not established anywhere; for it is not proven that the activity of any cause toward an effect occurs by virtue of distinct powers, since powers are essentially identical with the nature of the cause itself (*svātmabhūtatvāt*).
As for what was stated—that "due to the non-differentiation of the manifold form"—that is unproven;

because all entities possess the nature of destruction without residue, dissolution is not established anywhere. For instance, if dissolution were to occur, it would have to take place either upon the loss of the prior intrinsic nature or without such loss. If it were upon the loss of that nature, then the consequence of destruction without residue follows.

Furthermore, if [the cause] were not subject to transformation, then dissolution would be impossible; for dissolution is not logical for anyone who experiences the nature of the self in its entirety, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Therefore, this [Sāṃkhya position]—that there is both non-distinction and a manifold variety—is mutually contradictory.

Thus, even in the absence of *pradhāna* as a cause, the diversity of the effect in the form of limited dimensions and so forth, as well as the distinction between cause and effect, arise due to the differentiation of the powers of the cause; consequently, the [Sāṃkhya] arguments are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the phrase "because of activity according to capacity" (*śaktitaḥ pravṛtteḥ*) is included.
Alternatively, in the expression "even in the absence of a primary cause" (*pradhānahetvabhāve 'pi*), the particle "even" (*api*) functions as a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇe*).
By this, the meaning becomes as follows:

The reasons [put forward by the Sāṃkhya] are contradictory because the diversity of the effect—consisting in its limited dimensions and so forth—is established through the very cause that is the differentiation of causal potencies, which is precisely the absence of a primal cause (*pradhāna*).

For instance, if *pradhāna* were the cause of the manifest (*vyakta*), then, since everything would have that as its essence, the entire universe would be a single substance identical to its own nature.
Consequently, there would be no division of limited dimensions such as "one intellect," "ego," or "the five subtle elements."
And this being the case, the world would indeed be without measure.

Furthermore, the activity of potters and others in producing jars and such things is possible through their capacity even in the absence of a primary cause (*pradhāna*), but not when such a cause exists.
As was stated previously: "There is neither capacity nor action."
Furthermore, the distinction between cause and effect is only logical if there is an absence of a primary cause (pradhāna).
Moreover, the previously mentioned manifold diversity (vaiśvarūpya) is simply not tenable if a pradhāna exists;
for it has been stated that because the entire world consists of that [pradhāna], it would follow that everything is one, just like its own nature.
And therefore, since manifoldness does not exist from the very beginning, how could there be its non-differentiation?
Thus concludes the examination of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Chapter: Examination of Horses.
Now, demonstrating the absence of the activity of a Lord (Īśvara), he says "of all things that have an origin," and so forth:
"Others declare the Lord to be the cause of all things that have an origin."
For it is said that that which lacks consciousness does not, of its own accord, initiate its own effects.
Since non-originated things such as atoms and space are eternal, they have no cause; therefore, [the author] specified "of those that possess origination.
"Īśam" means the Lord (Īśvara).
"Others" refers to the Naiyāyikas and so forth.
Regarding this, some maintain that the creator of the entire world is a distinct self (ātman) possessing special qualities, namely the omniscient Lord (īśvara).

Others hold that he is a separate substance (dravyāntara), distinct from the self, because he possesses different qualities by virtue of being endowed with an eternal, unitary consciousness whose object is all things.

[Page 41] Now, one might ask: since merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), atoms, and so forth already exist as causes of the world, for what purpose do they postulate another cause in the form of a Lord? To this, he replies with the words "not insentient," and so on.

Although merit (*dharma*) and the other causes exist, nevertheless, because they are insentient, they are not capable of initiating their own effects by themselves without a supervisor; therefore, there must be some agent who supervises them. For no insentient thing is ever observed to be an independent supervisor. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is insentient does not initiate its own effect without a supervisor, just as a lump of clay, water, thread, and so forth [cannot produce] a jar when devoid of a potter; and merit and the rest are insentient. This is an observation of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Therefore, it is established that he who is the presiding agent is God (Īśvara).
And this being so, there is no futility regarding merit, demerit, and the like, because God is their efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*).
It might be argued: "The very self in whom merit and demerit inhere will be the presiding agent of that self."
"Therefore, why postulate a Lord?
This is incorrect;

for at that time, that self is ignorant. Indeed, as long as its aggregate of effects and causes—such as the body and sense organs—has not arisen, this ignorant being does not perceive even perceptible objects such as form; how then could it perceive dharma and adharma, which are imperceptible?
As it has been said:
"This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain;
impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed into the abyss."
Thus [it is said].

In that regard, he states the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) presented by Aviruddhakarṇa for the proof of God (*īśvara*), beginning with the words "that which possesses a particular arrangement of its own constituent parts," etc.: "That which possesses a particular arrangement of its own constituent parts is to be understood as having an intelligent cause, just like a jar and so forth."
Such a subject of dispute, which is perceptible by two sense organs and yet not [universally] perceptible, is preceded by an intelligent agent; by contrast, atoms are considered to be otherwise.

As it has been stated: "That which is perceptible by two sense organs and that which is not perceptible [by them], when taken as the subject of dispute, is preceded by an intelligent cause, because it possesses a specific configuration of its own constituent parts, like a jar; by way of contrast, atoms [are not].

In this context, the three kinds of substance known as earth, water, and fire—which are perceptible by two sense organs (sight and touch) and are endowed with the causes for perceiving magnitude, multiplicity of constituent substances, color, and so forth—are what is meant by "perceptible by two sense organs."

Air and the like are ungraspable because the causes of perception—namely, magnitude (*mahattva*), the state of being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyavatva*), and inherence of color (*rūpasamavāya*) and so forth—are held to be necessary, yet these do not exist in air and the like.
As it has been stated: "Perception occurs due to magnitude, the state of being composed of multiple substances, and color;
atoms are imperceptible because they are not composed of [multiple] substances."
Air is not perceived because it lacks the formation of color (*rūpa-saṃskāra*);
"formation of color" means the inherence of color.
Furthermore, dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth are not perceived because they lack magnitude (*amahattva*).

In this context, when proving in general that whatever is perceptible by two sense-faculties or imperceptible is preceded by an intelligent cause, there is the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) with respect to jars and the like,
because both [proponent and opponent] accept it and there is no dispute.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with what is accepted, because atoms, space, and so forth are not accepted as being such [i.e., produced].
Moreover, their eternality is contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition.
Therefore, for that purpose, the term "those who have entered into the state of being subjects of dispute" is included.
"Vividhā matiḥ," "vimatiḥ," and "vipratipattiḥ"—that is to say, that which has become the locus (*adhikaraṇabhāvāpanna*) of these, meaning that which has become the subject of dispute.
Such being the case, only the body, the sense organs, the worlds, and so forth, are made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*); thus there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to atoms and the like.

Even if the probandum were merely "having a cause as its antecedent," the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) would occur; therefore, the term "intelligent cause" (*buddhimatkāraṇa*) is employed.

With respect to the Sāṃkhya, there is no proof of what is already established [by us], because the existence of the intellect (*buddhi*) as a distinct entity is untenable; for the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the intellect is not separate from primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
And a thing cannot possess a quality by means of itself alone.
Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the arrangement of the constituent parts that originate it, consisting of an accumulation.
That which is distinguished and delimited by that [quality]—the state of being so distinguished—is what is meant by "from that.

Since being distinguished by the arrangement of constituent parts (*avayavasanniveśa*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like, the term "its own constituent parts" (*svārambhaka*) is employed.
For while "cowness" and the like are qualified by the arrangement of parts that originate the substance (*dravya*), they are not qualified by the arrangement of parts that originate themselves.
Therefore, that which is intelligent is God;
this very proof has been indicated by the two verses beginning with "That which... and so forth.
The term "tadviśeṣavat" means that which possesses a particularity (*viśeṣa*), namely, the specific arrangement of its own constituent parts (*svārambhakāvayavasaṃniveśa*). Thus it is so described.
The meaning is that [the object] is distinguished by that.
By this, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason is shown.
Demonstrating the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, he says "dvīndriya" and so on.

"Subject of dispute" (vivādapada) means that which has become the basis for a dispute. Second, in order to make known the aforementioned means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he says "of reality, etc. and so forth.
The appropriation of the principles (tattva) and so forth is presided over by an intelligent being,
because they possess form and other qualities, just as we observe that threads and the like, which produce their own effects, do so [when supervised].

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: the material causes (upādāna) of the principles (tattva) and so forth, such as the body and so forth—namely, atoms and the like—are the performers of their own effects when presided over by a conscious cause.
"Because they possess color and other qualities" is the logical reason (hetu);
"such as threads" is the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).

As it has been stated: we maintain the thesis that the material causes of the body, the world, and the instruments are presided over by an intelligent being when they produce their own effects, because they possess form and other qualities, like threads and the like.

Uddyotakara, however, offers this proof: "The causes of the world—namely *pradhāna*, atoms, and *adṛṣṭa*—require a controller who possesses superior intelligence for the production of their own effects, because they act after having remained inactive, like threads, a shuttle, and so forth.
He demonstrates this very point with the verse beginning "Dharma, adharma, and atoms," etc.:
"All dharma, adharma, and atoms are presided over by an intelligent being."
Having remained as the initiators of their own effects, they proceed like a weaver's shuttle.
This is easily understood.

Praśastamati, however, says: At the beginning of creation, the linguistic usage of persons must have been preceded by the instruction of another, because it is restricted to specific objects for those who have subsequently awakened to it.

Just as the linguistic usage of children—who have not yet established their own linguistic conventions—is restricted to specific objects such as cows and so forth, and is preceded by the instruction of their mothers and others.
"Because for the awakened ones there is a determination toward each respective object.
This means: because for those who are awakened, there is a determination toward each respective object.

He demonstrates that the Lord—who is established as the one whose worldly activity at the beginning of creation is preceded by instruction, and whose excellence of knowledge remains unimpaired even at the time of dissolution—is indeed the Lord, by stating "at the beginning of creation," and so forth.
Furthermore, at the very beginning, the linguistic usage of persons arises from the instruction of others,
because it is fixed, like the linguistic usage of children among adults.
*Sarga* means creation, that is to say, origination;
its *ādi* is the first moment.
The remainder, however, is easy to understand.

Likewise, the other proofs stated by Uddyotakāra are as follows: "The manifest world, consisting of the great elements and so forth, is presided over by an intelligent cause, because it serves as the cause of pleasure and pain, because it is insentient, because it is an effect, because it is perishable, and because it possesses form and other qualities, like a shuttle and other such objects.
He demonstrates these [arguments] with the words "the great elements and so forth," etc.
The manifest world, beginning with the great elements, being presided over by an intelligent cause,
serves as the occasion for the pleasure and pain of the entire world.

Because of reasons such as its lack of consciousness, being an effect, and being subject to destruction— just like an axe or similar tools— it is clearly understood that everything [pertaining to it] is of that [insentient] nature.
"Presided over by an intelligent cause" means governed by a conscious being.
"Therefore" refers to the aforementioned collection of reasons.
Regarding the word "tasya" (of him):
it refers to Īśvara, the cause of the entire world.

Now, how is his omniscience established, by virtue of which he might become an object of devotion for those desiring both the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*)? To this, he says: "And when the status of being the creator of all is established," and so forth.

And once his status as the creator of all things is established, his omniscience is proven without effort; for he who is the creator must be the knower of the nature, form, and other qualities of every effect.
And thus Praśastamati and others have said: "His omniscience is established precisely because he is the cause of the entire universe;
for a creator possesses complete knowledge of the material cause, the instruments, the purpose, and the recipient of his work.
For in this world, whoever is the creator of something knows its material cause and so forth."

Just as it is well known that a potter, the maker of jars and the like, knows their material cause—the lump of clay—as well as the instruments such as the wheel, the purpose—such as the fetching of water—and the recipient, namely the householder; so too does the Lord, the creator of all worlds, know their material causes characterized by atoms and the like, their instruments characterized by merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), space (dik), time (kāla), and so forth, the instruments of worldly transaction characterized by generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya), the purpose—which is experience—and the persons designated as recipients.
Therefore, it is established that he is omniscient.
Regarding the phrase "the knower of effects, forms, and so forth":

the compound means the knower (*vedaka*) of those things which are the effects—namely, their forms (*rūpa*), intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and so on; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of material causes (*upādāna*) and other factors is intended.

Since [the word] *yājaka* belongs to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa*, one may either apply the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇyaṇ*) or apply the suffix *ka* as a self-referential (*svārthika*) suffix. The rest is easily understood.
Furthermore, another collection of proofs has been stated by them:

"That which is the locus of diverse arisings and movements, yet is not their locus— that which has become the subject of dispute— is delimited by another means of valid cognition distinct from the five [other] means of valid cognition,
because it possesses the nature of being a real entity (*vastutva*) and so forth, just like color-form (*rūpa*) and the like."
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), [the examples] are "tortoise-hair" and so forth.

In that context, the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*) is said to have a manifold arising (*vicitrodaya*), based on the analysis "that which has a manifold arising. Motion (*prasyanda*) is the category of action (*karmapadārtha*). Substance (*dravya*) is the locus (*āspada*) of those two, being their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); the five categories beginning with quality and ending with inherence (*samavāya*) are non-loci (*anāspada*). As for the second through the fifth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), starting from inference (*anumāna*) and ending with non-existence (*abhāva*), there is another means of valid cognition distinct from them, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*). The rest is easily understood. This is another reason stated by them.

That which is either pervaded by the six non-distinctive properties beginning with "existence" (sat) or not so pervaded, and which has become the subject of dispute, is perceptible to someone because it exists, like color-form (rūpa) and so forth. In this context, the "six non-distinctive properties" are: existence, impermanence, possession of substance, being an effect, being a cause, and possessing generality and particularity; these are the distinctive properties of substances, qualities, and motions. That which is "pervaded" or "overcome" by them consists, as the case may be, of the three categories—substance, quality, and motion. That which is "not pervaded" [by them] is the category of generality (sāmānya). The rest is easy to understand.
He demonstrates this collection of proofs with the verse beginning "vimata" (the object of dispute), and so forth:
"The object that is the locus of dispute is clearly perceived by someone,
because it is a real entity and so on, just like the various states of pleasure, pain, and the like."
Thus, he begins the refutation with the words "In this case, the reason is unestablished," and so forth:
"In this regard, the reason is unestablished in the first proof,
because neither that which is called 'configuration' nor the 'composite whole' is established in that manner."

In this regard, the meaning is that in the initial formal argument—"that which is insentient does not begin its own effect without a controller"—the reason is inconclusive because there is no subverting proof against the opposite of the probandum, and thus its exclusion from the heterologue is doubtful.

Furthermore, as for this reason in the first formal proof—namely, "because it possesses a specific arrangement of its constituent parts"—he explains how it is unestablished by saying "since," and so forth.

For by the term "arrangement of parts" (*avayava-saṃniveśa*), a particular kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) is intended; and since the substance called the "whole" (*avayavin*) is qualified by that [conjunction], there is a twofold non-establishment of the reason (*hetu-asiddhi*) because both of those—the qualifier and the qualified—are unestablished.
But how is it that both are unestablished? To this he says: "Because of the non-perception of the two, which are accepted as being perceptible," and so forth.
45] This is because the two, which are asserted to be objects of perception, are not perceived.
Therefore, this example as well is devoid of a means of proof.
In this regard, he states briefly that the subverting proof is precisely that which is called the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*).
A detailed refutation of both of these will be set forth in the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*.
[This refers to] that which is accepted as the arrangement and the whole (*avayavin*).

For it is stated that "configuration (*saṃniveśa*), as well as number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and action, are visible because they are inherent in color (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, the whole (*avayavin*) is intended to be visible, according to the statement: "Perception [of a substance] occurs because it is large, possesses multiple substances, and possesses color.
Yet, no other entity such as conjunction or a whole, apart from color and the rest, appears in the cognition as something intended to be visible.
Therefore, because that which has reached the conditions for perception is not perceived, it is the object of the conventional designation "non-existent," like the horn of a hare.

Nor does it follow that color and other qualities would be unperceivable simply because atoms are beyond the senses; for since we accept that these [qualities] in their specific state are sensory objects, their being beyond the senses is unproven.

For this very reason, he shows that the pot—which is cited as a homogeneous example—is devoid of the probans (sādhanadharmavikala) due to the non-existence of both conjunction and the whole, by stating "not connected with the probans" and so forth.

Thus far, the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*) by way of its own nature has been demonstrated through the non-establishment of the qualifier and the qualified; now, he shows that it is also unestablished by way of the non-establishment of a portion of its locus (*āśrayaikadeśāsiddhi*), beginning with the words "The eye... and so forth:
"The visual and tactile consciousnesses arise with distinct appearances;
there is no single objective support (*ekālambanatā*) for the two, just as in the case of the cognitions of odor and so forth."
For here, two kinds of subjects (*dharmin*) are indicated: that which is perceptible by two sense-faculties and that which is imperceptible.
Among these, no subject that is perceptible by two sense-faculties is established.

This is because visual cognition and tactile cognition arise as distinct from one another, respectively, because they manifest only the form of blue and so forth, and because they are established as manifesting only the specific tangible qualities of hardness and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no single object for those two cognitions—visual and tactile—because they have different appearances, just like the cognitions of odor, taste, and so forth.

This formal argument is as follows: two cognitions with different appearances do not have a single object, as in the case of the cognitions of odor and taste; and the visual and tactile cognitions have different appearances. This is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi).

If there were a single object despite a difference in appearance, it would follow that the cognitions of color, sound, and so forth would also have a single object; this is the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) in this case.

If, then, these two do not have a single object, how can there be this synthetic cognition (*pratisandhānajñāna*)—namely, "The very jar that was seen by me in the light is now being touched in the dark"? Therefore, this proposition is sublated by inference. Regarding this, Uddyotakara has stated the following inference: "The cognitions of seeing and touching, which are the subject of dispute, have a single object because they are synthesized, like the cognitions of blue and yellow. To this, he replies with the words beginning "tatsāmarthya" [on page 46].
The synthesizing consciousness, whose nature is accompanied by conceptual construction arising from that capacity,
determines the aggregate.
Therefore, water, fire, and so forth do not exist as this [object], because they are not perceivable by two sense-faculties;
thus, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) for the subject as it has been stated.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *sāmarthya* means the capacity of those two—visual and tactile consciousnesses—which manifest merely color-form (*varṇa*) and the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*); that from which [the cognition] arises has a nature (*ātmā*) followed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

By this, it is established that the synthesizing cognition (*pratisandhāna-pratyaya*) is not direct perception (*apratyakṣatva*), because it is an error due to its determination of unity in what is manifold, and because its nature is followed by conceptual construction.

Nor is there another means of valid cognition [to establish this], because it would involve apprehending what has already been apprehended by determining an object already delimited by a prior cognition, and because it would be erroneous.
Therefore, the reason "because of being connected" (*pratisaṃdhīyamānatvāt*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For if the validity of the cognition that synthesizes [past and present perceptions] were established, then the reason would not be inconclusive; however, in the case of those things such as form (*rūpa*) for which the conventional designations "pot" and so forth are common [to multiple senses] in order to manifest their functional capacity—when these have been experienced by both sight and touch according to their respective natures—a memory-cognition arises at a later time. This cognition, which is essentially erroneous, determines a unity with respect to the object as it was previously perceived, and it is produced through a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*) instilled by a corresponding convention.
For indeed, when one attends to it in that manner, even the color—blue and so forth—is manifested therein.
And it is not logical for a manifestation of color to occur in tactile consciousness, because that [color] is the object of visual consciousness.

Therefore, what was stated by the Teachers—that having perceived their respective distinct objects through sight and touch, there subsequently arises a distinct memory-based cognition of the aggregate as a whole which is associated with them—is alone reasonable.

Now, if the collection (*samudāya*) had been previously experienced, then this [cognition] would appropriately be a memory (*smārta*); however, for you, a collection distinct from color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest is not accepted, such that it could be experienced. And when color-form and the rest are experienced, there would be the cognition "color-form" and so on, but not "pot. Furthermore, memory is not possible regarding what has not been experienced. So how does this memory-cognition, which has the collection as its object, arise? This is not so.

For it is not said that a "collection" (*samudāya*) distinct from form and the other [sensory objects] was previously experienced, such that this [recollection] could occur; rather, those very forms and so forth, which perform the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of holding water and so on, are designated as the "pot," which is the collection.
And when these have been individually experienced by sensory cognitions, it is explained that a memory arises—according to the established convention—that "this is a pot.

Alternatively, since the imagined collection consists of the nature of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), it is indeed experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*); so why should a memory of it not arise?

Therefore, he asks why the reason "because of being characterized by a specific arrangement of its own constituent parts" suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*). He replies: "Because of the non-establishment [of the subject], in the case of the subject as previously described.

This means that because the subject as previously described—that which is perceptible by two sense organs—is not established, the reason is unestablished due to the non-establishment of a portion of its locus.

Thus, since the qualified object, the qualifier, and their substratum are unestablished, the threefold non-establishment of the reason has been stated; now he states the fourth type of non-establishment indicated by the Teacher, beginning with "sanniveśa" (structure): "Whatever kind of distinctness of structure is seen in temples and the like, which leads to the cognition of an intelligent agent even when no agent is perceived..."
If that very same [property] were observed in the subjects, such as bodies and so forth,
then it would be logical for this means of proof to establish what is intended.

For that specific configuration which is well-known in the world—such as in temples and the like—as being preceded by the activity of an intelligent person, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and upon seeing which one understands an intelligent cause even when the actual maker is not seen; if such a configuration were adduced as the reason (*hetu*) in the case of the subjects of proof (*sādhyadharmin*), such as those minute trees, mountains, and so forth, then there would be the establishment of your desired probandum (*sādhya*).
Indeed, an effect that has been clearly distinguished through positive and negative concomitance does not deviate from its cause, for if it did, it would follow that it is causeless.
Furthermore, no such specific configuration (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*) is established in trees, mountains, and so forth; rather, it is merely the empty chatter that "configuration" alone is established.

Nor is a property (*dharma*), which by its very nature is established as distinct from others, sufficient for establishing the intended probandum when it is employed as a reason based solely on the non-difference of the word, because there is no contradiction in its existence even in the opposite of the probandum.
The collective meaning is as follows: just as when one seeks to establish that an anthill is the work of a potter, the mere fact of being a modification of clay is adduced as the reason.
Now, the meaning of the individual parts is stated: "in the perception of which, there is the cognition of an intelligent agent."
The meaning is that when the arrangement of something is perceived, there occurs an inference—that is, a cognition—of an intelligent cause.
Regarding the phrase "in bodies, mountains, etc.": *tanu* means the body; *agāḥ* means mountains or trees; and by the word "etc.," oceans and so forth are included.
"Of that which is desired" means of the state of being preceded by an intelligent agent;
"proof" (sādhana) means its establishment (siddhi). //61–//

To explain how this is logical, he says "by positive and negative concomitance," and so forth: "That which is determined to be the effect of something by means of positive and negative concomitance—its determination [occurs] upon seeing that [cause]; such is the established principle."
However, no such specific arrangement exists among these [atoms];
rather, in the case of the differences between trees and so forth, there is only the word itself.
When stated in such a manner, however, it incurs the fallacy of doubtful negative concomitance (sandigdhavyatirekatā) in cases such as a potter's work found upon an anthill.
"That which is the effect" refers to smoke and so forth;
"of which" refers to fire and so forth;
"the ascertainment of that" refers precisely to fire and so forth.
"In the perception of that" means when there is the perception of an effect such as smoke and so forth.
If it is argued that the same will apply here as well, he says: "But the specific arrangement," and so on.
If it is then argued that the very arrangement which is established through the generality of the term "arrangement" shall serve as the reason, he says: "Of such a kind," and so on.
Such [an object] is non-different merely by way of its name,
just like those made by a potter; the remainder of the sense is "merely being a modification of clay."
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the specific arrangement [of parts] is unestablished, whereas the mere fact of being an arrangement is inconclusive. //63–66//
With the words "nanu" and so forth, the opponent raises a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*):
"Is this not a futile rejoinder, because of the conceptualization of a difference in properties?
For it has been established that the proof consists of the effect and so forth, which are merely universals."
This is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) that obstructs the accomplishment of the intended purpose.

For instance, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," the proponent of the futile rejoinder objects: "Is this 'being produced' (kṛtakatva) adduced as the reason insofar as it resides in things such as a jar, or insofar as it resides in sound, or does it reside in both?
In the first case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*)."
For a property belonging to one thing does not exist elsewhere.
In the second case as well, the example lacks the probans.
In the third case too, these same two faults apply.
And this has been established as the futile rejoinder (jātyuttara) called "balancing the effect" (kāryasama).
As it has been stated:
"That demonstration of the non-establishment of the probandum based on a mere slight difference in the nature of the effect is 'balancing the effect'."
Since it is accepted that the inference of impermanence is intended by grasping only the generality (*sāmānya*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), and not its particularity (*viśeṣa*),

it is established that when such a generality is the intended means of proof, any rejoinder based on a conceptual distinction regarding the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) known as "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*). And because this is a conceptualization based on a difference in properties, it is therefore a futile rejoinder.
Regarding verse 67,
he provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "not having that nature" (*atadrūpa*): "The mere entity, as excluded from what does not have that nature, is impermanence."
Because of identity, this [reason] establishes [the probandum]; there is no other logical principle for proof here.
This is logical.
For, in the case where mere "being produced" (kṛtakatva) establishes impermanence,
this is because of the existence of a necessary connection (pratibandha) characterized by identity (tādātmya);
however, in this present case, when establishing merely the specific arrangement of its own constituent parts, this logical principle does not apply.

The meaning is this: because there is no subverting evidence against the possibility that the commonality of arrangement might be otherwise, the necessary connection (pratibandha) is not established; for that connection characterized by "origination from that" (tadutpatti), by the perception of which even one who does not see an agent would have the cognition that it was made, is unestablished.
Regarding verse 68:

Now, showing that if one sets aside the specific characteristic of the non-obstruction of the production of that [effect] and asserts the universal alone as the logical mark (*liṅga*), then it would be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), he says "dhūma... and so forth: "The white substance that is smoke is seen to be invariably concomitant with fire."
Nor can that [snow] be understood from the word "white" alone, even though it is derived from the Himalayas.
Regarding verse 69 [p.49], he says "sāmānya... and so forth, asking: "How then is *kāryasama* cited as a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*)?
[The answer is: "But when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with respect to the general, yet one resorts to a particular..."
An objection is raised there; that is cited as a futile rejoinder (jātyuttara).

Even when the connection of the probans-property with the subject through its general form has been established by the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), if an objection is raised by resorting to a specific property of that [subject], that is a "futile rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*).

However, in this case, no such connection has been established in a general sense; rather, that which possesses a connection to a specific configuration (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Therefore, this is not a futile rejoinder.
Now, showing that if even an unconnected universal were to be a signifier, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says "gośabda... and so forth:
"From the mere fact of being denotable by the word 'cow,' there would follow the possession of horns for [objects such as] the directions (*dig*) and so on."
Otherwise, this [result] would not be accomplished, for this logical principle would not be accepted.

For in this way, there would follow the absurd consequence that even heaven, the quarters of space, speech, the eye, rays, thunderbolts, and water—merely because they are denoted by the word *go*—would be inferred to possess horns, just like Bāhuleya and other such cows.
Regarding verse 71:

it might be argued that, just as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, there indeed exists a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for this [arrangement] as well—namely, its being preceded by an intelligent cause characterized by a specific configuration. To this, he says: "But if," and so forth.
That is, if such a necessary connection is not established in this proof (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, since this is established through reasoning, there is no dispute regarding it for anyone.
Regarding verse 72:
however, showing that this very [logical] connection is not established, he says "But rather," and so forth:
"But rather, [the subject] has as its basis one who is eternal, unitary, omniscient, and whose cognition is eternal."
Due to the deficiency of the probandum and because of non-pervasion, it does not attain proof.

For it is not merely the fact of being preceded by an intelligent agent that you wish to prove; rather, what you wish to prove is that this world is preceded by that entity designated as "God" (Īśvara)—an intelligent being who is the cause of the entire universe, a single, eternal, and omniscient substratum for eternal cognition.
It is precisely that [entity] which is the subject of dispute, and such a being does not attain proof.
Why?

Because of the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and because of the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*); for the pot and other such examples of similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*) are deficient in the aforementioned similarity, and thus the pervasion of the reason (*hetu*) by such a probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*) is not established.
That is to say, there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the reason with the aforementioned probandum-property in any example whatsoever.
Demonstrating this very point, he says "for instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth:
"For instance, palaces, staircases, gate-towers, watchtowers, and the like..."
They are ascertained by virtue of being preceded by manifold and impermanent cognitions.

Furthermore, he shows that the reason is not only unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), but also contradictory (*viruddha*) as well, by saying "for this very reason," and so forth: "For this very reason, this [reason] is also regarded as a subverter of what is desired,
because it establishes that [the world] is preceded by multiple, non-eternal cognitions."
"From this very [reason]" means because it is pervaded by a property contrary to the probandum (*sādhyaviparītadharma*).
By the word "also" (*api*), he indicates that it is not only unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) according to the method previously stated, but [is also contradictory].

But surely, a contradictory [reason] would occur only when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in the case of the opposite; yet there is no such connection even for the mere fact of being preceded by an intelligent agent—so how could it exist for that specific [case]? To this he says: "For you have stated the connection only with respect to the mere cause consisting of an intelligent agent," and so forth. For you have indeed asserted the connection only with respect to the mere cause consisting of an intelligent agent.
In the second [chapter], however, it is stated by us very clearly.
By you, who propound a creator god, a necessary connection has been described only with respect to an intelligent cause;
otherwise, if no connection were established even in a general sense, how could the fact that entities have God as their cause be proven?

Therefore, having accepted for the sake of argument that the mere fact of being preceded by an intelligent agent—which you yourself have already established—is indeed proven, we shall now clearly state the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of our reason with a second specific property of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣa*) that you intend, namely, that it is preceded by multiple impermanent cognitions; this second specific property of the probandum is one that proves the opposite of what you desire.
To explain how this is clearly stated, he says:
"By the contradiction of succession and non-succession, eternal things do not produce effects;
and because objects possess succession, there is also succession in the cognitions of them."
For God and other such eternal entities are not performers of causal action, because for that which is eternal, purposeful activity (arthakriyā) is contradicted by both succession and simultaneity.
Therefore, only impermanent things are performers of purposeful activity.
And since these [impermanent things] possess different natures at every moment, it is established that the intelligent creator is both impermanent and manifold.
Furthermore, demonstrating that the thesis asserting that Īśvara is endowed with a single, eternal cognition is also contradicted by inference, he says: "Of objects," and so forth.
He provides proof with the verse beginning "occurring in succession," etc.:
"The cognition of God occurs in succession because it is connected with objects of cognition that occur in succession,
just like the cognition of Devadatta and others directed toward a flame and so forth."

[Page 51] Knowledge whose object is to be cognized in a sequence occurs sequentially, just like the cognition of Devadatta and others directed toward a flame and so forth; and the cognition of Īśvara has as its object that which is to be cognized in a sequence. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, this is a proof by reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*); therefore, one should not suspect that the reason is unestablished with respect to its locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).

The cognition of Devadatta and others, which has as its object categories such as "generality" (sāmānya), is cited as an example because it is devoid of the probans-property; likewise, that which has a flame and so forth as its object is cited.
But what here is the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa)?
It is said: if that cognition of God were produced with a self-manifestation by means of an object that possesses succession, then its successive nature is already established.

If, on the other hand, it is not produced [at that time], then, due to the absence of a basis for proximity, it would not cognize that [object]. Furthermore, your accepted validity (*prāmāṇya*)—which occurs even in the absence of an object—would be lost;
and there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [cognition] is without an object (*nirviṣayatva*) regarding an object that has perished or not yet been born.
This is the subverting proof in this case.

Regarding what was stated by way of dissimilarity—that "atoms are held [to be eternal]"—demonstrating that this example of dissimilarity also lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), he says: "It is merely an aggregation of atoms," and so forth.
We maintain that jars and the like are merely aggregations of atoms;
therefore, the potter and other such agents are agents of the atoms themselves.
The property intended as the probandum is not excluded from that [subject],
as is revealed by this example of atoms presented through negative concomitance (vaidharmya).

Since the possessor of parts (*avayavin*) will be refuted in detail and has already been refuted, it is established that the potter and others are merely the agents of the atoms. Therefore, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), namely "having an intelligent precursor," is not excluded from the atoms—which have been presented as the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Thus, the example by way of dissimilarity suffers from the fault of having a property to be proven that is not excluded (*avyāvṛttasādhyadharmatā*). //78–79//

It might be argued as follows: "If we intended to prove a specific [creator], then the previously mentioned deficiency of the example in terms of the property to be proven (sādhyavikalatā) would apply; however, since we are proving merely that things are preceded by an intelligent agent in a general sense, once that is established, it follows by implication that God is their creator. For it is not possible for them to have a potter or similar craftsman as their creator in the same way as jars and the like. Therefore, because the general property is qualified by a specific [agent], and because no other creator is conceivable in the case of trees and such, it is established by implication—even without explicitly grasping the specific—that God alone is their creator. To this, he says: "preceded by an intelligent agent," and so forth.
And if it is generally accepted that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent being, we have no dispute at all; for the manifold diversity of forms is indeed born of karma.

For in this way, there is the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Why? He says: "Because the manifoldness (*vaiśvarūpya*)... and so forth. "Manifoldness" refers to the diversity of the world of sentient beings and the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*), which is born of karma;
that is, produced by common and uncommon virtuous and non-virtuous karma.
Therefore, since intelligent persons who perform auspicious and inauspicious actions become the cause of this [world], the argument is one of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
If it is argued that [the probandum] is established specifically [as a particular], he says "eternal," etc.:
"In establishing that [the world] is preceded by a single eternal intellect, there is a lack of the probandum."
And there is deviation [from the rule] because palaces and the like are seen to be produced by many [causes].
And although this was stated previously, it is mentioned again for the sake of a conclusion.
The analysis of the compound is: "one whose cognition is single" (*ekabuddhiḥ*), and he is both eternal and such a one with a single cognition;
or alternatively, it is a compound meaning "one whose cognition is eternal and single."
"Emptiness of the probandum" (sādhyaśūnyatā) refers to the homologue (sādharmyadṛṣṭānta); the word "of" is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
"And deviation" (vyabhicāra) [is also mentioned].
The word "from the reason" (*hetoh*) is to be supplied.
To the question "How so?", he says "saudha," etc.
Regarding what was stated, "of trees and so forth," he says "this very [refutation]," and so on:
"This very refutation, as appropriate, should be applied to the remaining reasons; furthermore, some slight [additional] point is being revealed."

For even in those cases where [the opponent] offers proofs such as "because it possesses form and so forth," this very same refutation should be stated according to the circumstances. "This very same" refers to: [the reason being] unestablished (*asiddha*); [the reason being] inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) due to the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*); [the reason being] contradictory (*viruddha*) when a connection does exist; [the example being] deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*); or [the argument being] proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) by way of generality, and so forth.

For even in that case, the kind of possession of form and so forth that is controlled by a conscious agent is not established in trees and the like. Since a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established for the mere possession of form and so forth, there is an inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*). If a necessary connection were admitted, there would be a contradiction (*viruddhatva*) because it would prove the opposite of what is intended. The example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the property to be proven—namely, being controlled by a single, eternal conscious agent—is not established. There is proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in a general sense, while there is inconclusiveness in a specific sense, because the opposite is observed in the case of jars and other things. This same reasoning should be applied to the other reasons as well.
Regarding the proof stated as "because [the atom] acts after having remained stationary," he states a further refutation beginning with "sthitvā" (having remained):
"The acting after having remained stationary is not established for atoms and the like, because of their momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Furthermore, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by that very [reason], since even that [atom] possesses successive activity."

Since all entities perish immediately upon their arising, there is no stability even for a single moment; how, then, can there be activity after having remained? Therefore, the reason [adduced by you] is unestablished for the opponent.
Furthermore, it is inconclusive because of that very Lord (Īśvara), since the Lord, like those possessing succession, acts after having remained [in a state] with respect to his successive effects;
yet he is not presided over by another conscious being, as that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.

Now, if a qualified reason is formulated as "being insentient," as was done by Praśastamati, even so, its inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) remains unavoidable because its exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa) is doubtful.

For only that qualification which actually excludes the reason from the counter-example is logical; however, that which does not remove doubt regarding the counter-example is as good as non-existent, even if it is included.
Furthermore, the previously mentioned defects such as being unestablished (asiddha) remain exactly as they were, even when the reason is qualified.
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "And at the beginning of creation, there is conventional usage," he says "In dissolution," and so forth:
"In our view, persons do not have their consciousness and memory destroyed during dissolution."
Because of arising from the Ābhāsvara heaven and so forth, and because of arising right here from that very same source.

The qualification "of those who have awakened at a later time" is unestablished; for, according to our view, it is not the case that at the time of dissolution persons remain with their knowledge and memory destroyed and devoid of body and sense organs. Rather, they are reborn among the classes of gods in the Ābhāsvara and other realms who possess an excellence of clear knowledge. However, those whose karma is conducive to the ripening of specific hells and so forth are reborn in other world-systems. Thus, even at the time of evolution, they arise here having descended from the Ābhāsvara realm with their knowledge and memory entirely undestroyed.
Therefore, the qualification "of those awakened at a later time" is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.

Moreover, if the probandum (*sādhya*) is merely "being preceded by the instruction of another," it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhya*), since it is accepted by all that beginningless worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is indeed preceded by the instruction of another.

If it is being proven that [the Vedic tradition] is preceded by the instruction of a person possessing the characteristics of a Lord (īśvara), then there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva), because linguistic usage is possible even otherwise. Furthermore, the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikalatā).
And this general refutation has already been stated previously.

Showing that the reason is contradictory and that the thesis is sublated by what has been accepted, he says: "The teaching of one who is averse," and so forth: "If the status of being a teacher for one who is averse is to be understood solely through faith, then his aversion arises from the lack of discrimination between dharma and adharma due to the absence of discernment."

If it were possible for worldly activity to be preceded by the instruction of Īśvara, then the reason [for his non-existence] would not be contradictory; however, because he is devoid of a mouth, he cannot logically be an instructor. And that state of being devoid of a mouth is due to his bodilessness—this is the meaning.
To the question, "How is this bodilessness of his established? he says: "Because of the absence of dharma and adharma."
The meaning is that this is due to the absence of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the causes of a body.
Thus, Uddyotakara has stated:

"Just as there is proof for the existence of the Lord's intellect, there is no such proof for the existence of [His] merit and so forth. Therefore, since it is impossible for the Lord to be a teacher, His being the instructor of conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is not established; rather, it must have been preceded by the instruction of another person distinct from the Lord. Consequently, because it results in the subversion of what is desired, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*).

If the status of the Lord as a teacher is accepted, then the [previously] admitted quality of being faceless (vimukhatva) is abandoned; thus, there is a contradiction with what was previously accepted (abhyupetabādhā).

Furthermore, regarding the argument beginning with "the manifest consists of the great elements and so forth," the reasons are, as before, inconclusive (anaikāntika) because there is no subverting proof (bādhakapramāṇa) against the counter-example (vipakṣa). One should apply the following: in a general sense, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā), while in a specific sense, the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikalatā).

[Page 54] Having thus refuted in detail the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish an *īśvara*, he now says "contradiction with inference," etc., in order to demonstrate a means of valid cognition that subverts that [position] by way of pointing out defects in its pervasion (*vyāpti*), for the sake of establishing his own thesis:
"And there is contradiction with inference in every proof of pervasion."
The pervasion of the reason by a contradictory property is not possible.

In every case, when the stated means of proof (sādhana) is present, there is a pervasion (vyāpti) between that and the probandum (sādhya); the contradiction of that [pervasion] by inference will be explained below.
Now, why is a contradiction of the thesis (pratijñā) by inference not pointed out?

If the thesis (*pratijñā*) were a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*), then its defects would have to be pointed out; however, since it—either directly or indirectly—does not function as a factor for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), the pointing out of a defect in the thesis when the context is the statement of defects in the proof would constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent due to the pointing out of a non-defect. Therefore, no defect of the thesis should be mentioned in the employment of proofs. But where a contradiction of the thesis is occasionally pointed out, it should be understood that by means of that [contradiction], the pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself is being undermined.
Alternatively, this should be understood as referring to cases other than the application of the proof (*sādhana*).
Now, [the author] asks: "How does there come to be a contradiction with inference even at the time of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*)? To this he says: "Not by the contradictory," and so forth.
Regarding the term "by the contradictory":

Since that [subject] is impossible because it is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), pervasion (vyāpti) is not tenable; for, in short, pervasion cannot be conceived with something non-existent.
