"What is that inference by which the pervasion (vyāpti) is sublated? To this he says: "God is not the cause of living beings," and so forth:
"God is not the cause of those who are born, because He is devoid of origination, like a sky-lotus; otherwise, everything would come into being simultaneously."

That which is devoid of origination is not the cause of anything, just as a lotus in the sky; and since Īśvara is devoid of origination, this is an observation of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
This is a proof by reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*), and therefore one should not raise the objection that it suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).
Otherwise, everything would arise simultaneously.
The meaning is that, because the cause possesses unimpeded causal capacity, everything would arise simultaneously, like a collection of effects intended to occur at one and the same time.

This is either the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in this context, or it is merely an exposition of the sense. However, the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*) should be formulated as follows:
Whatever possesses its complete cause necessarily comes into being,

just as a sprout, when its causes are complete upon reaching the final stage of the causal complex, does indeed arise. And since the entire world has God as its cause, it would all come into being simultaneously, as its causes are complete.

It might be argued: "The Lord alone is not the sole cause; rather, He acts in dependence upon other auxiliary causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, since the Lord is a causal condition (*nimittakāraṇa*). Therefore, because of the deficiency of these other causes like merit, the claim that the cause is 'unimpaired' (*avikalakāraṇatva*) is unestablished. This is incorrect.

For if some benefit were to be produced for that [permanent entity] by its auxiliaries through some assistance, then it would have a dependence upon those auxiliaries; however, since it is eternal and its excellence cannot be imparted by others, there is nothing for it to obtain from its auxiliaries—so why would it depend upon such unbeneficial auxiliaries?

Furthermore, even those auxiliaries, all having their birth dependent upon Īśvara, are always already present together with him; thus, how can the reason [of the opponent] be considered unestablished?

Nor is there any inconclusiveness [in the reason], because it would entail the loss of the status of having complete causes; for if that which has complete causes were not to arise, it would follow that nothing would ever arise, since there is no difference [between one case and another]. Uddyotakara says: "Even though the eternal cause called God is always present and complete for all entities, nevertheless, they do not arise simultaneously, because God acts with prior intelligence."
If he were the producer of entities without prior intelligence (abuddhipūrva) merely by the existence of God himself, then this objection would hold;
but when he acts with prior intelligence, there is no fault, because his engagement in effects proceeds through his own volition.
Therefore, the reason is indeed inconclusive.
This is incorrect.

For the activity or cessation of effects does not depend upon the presence or absence of the will of their cause, such that one could claim that although the cause called Īśvara is always present with unimpeded power, the effects do not proceed because of the absence of his will.
What, then, is the case?
Entities conform to the presence or absence of the capacity residing in their causes.

For instance, even for a creator who possesses the desire [to produce], things do not arise from what lacks capacity; yet they do arise from seeds and the like that possess capacity, even when the creator lacks the desire.

In this regard, if the cause called "God" remains forever with its power unimpeded—just as it is at the time of producing an effect—why would entities depend upon His desire, which renders no assistance, such that they would all arise simultaneously, just as they do at the time of production?
For in this way, they would demonstrate that the self possesses its causes in their entirety only if [all effects] were to arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, since God cannot be assisted by others, He has no dependence whatsoever such that He would have to depend on desire.

Moreover, apart from intellect (*buddhi*), there is no other desire; and you maintain that God’s intellect is eternally of a single form. Consequently, even if God acts preceded by intellect, why do entities not arise simultaneously?
Because, like Īśvara, his intellect (*buddhi*) is also eternally present.
Even if it is admitted that his intellect is impermanent, since it arises solely from the mere existence of Īśvara, it must likewise exist eternally just like Īśvara; thus, the same fault remains.
Therefore, the qualification "because of being intelligent" (*buddhimattvāt*) is entirely ineffective, and the reason (*hetu*) is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Nor is there contradiction [of the reason], because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*); nor does it follow that the opposite is the case. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whenever something does not exist, its causes are not complete at that time, just as a sprout that is not produced while remaining in the state of a seed inside a granary.
And at the time when one particular entity arises, the entire universe does not arise; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established, because it has been demonstrated that when God is the cause, it is impossible for him to be a deficient cause.

He states another proof as well, beginning with "Or those which arise in succession," etc.: "Those things which arise in succession do not have God as their cause, just like the cognitions of insentient beings produced by the aforementioned means."
Even for those [auxiliaries], the statement of a means toward their production is futile;
because it is eternal and thus incurable, that [means] can never be a cooperative cause.

The meaning is that the cognitions—meaning certainties—of the dull-witted who are intent upon God as the cause, which arise from the aforementioned proofs such as "being characterized by a specific arrangement of their own constituent parts," have as their object the desired subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).

Now, one might object: "Since these [proofs] are tainted by the aforementioned defects, no cognitions regarding the desired probandum arise from them; thus, the property of the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) is not established.
This is true.

For this very reason, it was said "of the insentient" (*jaḍānām*). For indeed, because the insentient are incapable of discriminating between a valid means of proof and its semblance, cognitions arise for them even from fallacious proofs. [Objection: Even so, the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), since even those cognitions of the insentient are accepted as having God as their efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). To this, he says: "Of those too," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the arising of those [effects] which are insentient cognitions":

if it is maintained that they arise from Īśvara, then the statement of the proof would be fruitless; that is, the formulation of the proof would be useless because they would originate from Īśvara alone. This is the intended meaning.

[Objection: "Surely, by depending on the expression of the means [of proof] as a cooperative cause, God will be their producer, not [God] alone; therefore, He will not be fruitless. To this, he says: "Because of eternality," and so forth. If that expression of the means were to remove the incapable nature of that God and bestow upon Him a capable one, then it would be His cooperative cause. However, because God is eternal, His nature is unproduced and irreversible; thus, nothing can be effected by anything. Therefore, it is not logical for that expression of the means to be His cooperative cause. (88)

Furthermore, if you postulate that God is a cause even though his causal capacity is unperceived—distinct from causes such as the means of accomplishment whose capacities are clearly perceived—an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) follows for you; for, having postulated that God, one would likewise have to postulate another [cause], such as a *ḍeṭkaṣaka* (a type of artisan), since there is no distinction [between them]. Demonstrating this, he says "In those which... and so forth: "But for those things which are seen by you to occur when [other causes] are present, and never when they are absent—if you postulate that these have another cause [in the form of God], how is it that you do not fall into an infinite regress?"* *This verse points out that if every effect requires a further cause beyond its manifest conditions, one must posit an endless chain of causes.*
The phrase "that which has been seen by you" is an addition [to the text].

Regarding the expression "in the postulation of another cause": the analysis of the compound is as follows: "another cause" (*anyahetu*) refers to a cause other than those whose causal capacity is already observed; "the state of being another cause" (*anyahetutā*) is the condition of being such a cause; and "postulation" (*klṛpti*) means the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of that state. Thus, it refers to the conceptualization of the existence of a cause other than those whose efficacy has been perceived.
Regarding what was stated in the passage beginning with "And in establishing [his] being the creator of all," etc., he says "kartṛtva" and so forth:
"By the negation of agency, omniscience is also refuted;
for it must be understood that the establishment of omniscience depends precisely upon that [agency]."

Since you maintain that he is omniscient by virtue of his power as the creator of all things, the refutation of that [creatorship] automatically refutes his omniscience as well, without further effort.

Having conceded that the means of proof (*sādhana*) are unperceived, he states another refutation with the words "yathokta" and so forth: "Even if the means of proof were not vitiated by the aforementioned defects,
nevertheless, the oneness of the agent is not established, because of the demonstration of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)."
And if a single creator is not established, upon what could omniscience be based?
The aforementioned faults, extending up to the contradiction with inference, [apply here].

This is the collective meaning here: although an intelligent creator is established by these proofs for [the production of] bodies, mountains, and so forth, nevertheless, it is not certain that he who is the cause of one is the very same as the cause of another, because a different creator is possible for each individual effect; furthermore, since even a single structure such as a palace is seen to be built by many people, a single creator cannot be established. And as long as a single creator is not established, how can omniscience be proven?

Here, Praśastamati provides a proof to establish that there is a single creator: "Brahmā and the others, down to the Piśācas, have a single supervisor because they exist in a state of mutual superiority. In this world, it is observed that those who exist in a state of mutual superiority are dependent upon one [authority], just as in this world the lords of households, villages, towns, and regions are all subordinate to a single sovereign king. Likewise, since serpents, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and so forth exist in a state of mutual superiority, we conclude that they too are subject to dependence upon a single Lord."
In this regard, if the intended point to be proven is that these [entities] are presided over by that which is called "God," then the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika),
because there is no subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the contrary and because the necessary connection (pratibandha) is not established.

Furthermore, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*). If, on the other hand, it is argued that [the world] is "possessed of a presiding agent" merely by virtue of having a presider, then this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); for we ourselves accept that the entire world is presided over by the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the crest-jewel of all the worlds, out of his compassion—by whose power virtuous people even today attain the excellence of worldly prosperity and the ultimate good.
And this further proof was stated by that same [author]:
"The seven worlds are created by a single intellect, because they are contained within a single entity,
like the rooms contained within a single house."
Just as it is observed that the chambers situated within a single dwelling are the product of the intellect of a single architect, so too are the seven worlds contained within this one world.
Therefore, it is determined that they, too, are the product of a single intellect;
and the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, by whose intellect these are fashioned, is the sole architect of all the worlds.

Therefore, the reason (hetu) here is unestablished (asiddha), for there exists no single world, dwelling, or the like; rather, this designation was applied to many things for the sake of linguistic convenience.
For this very reason, the example is also devoid of the probans (sādhanavikala).
Furthermore, because one observes that even rooms and such situated within a single mansion are constructed by many architects, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
In this same way, refutations should be stated as appropriate for other proofs as well.
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "the object that is the locus of dispute," he says:
"In establishing that, the means of proof... and so forth.
"In establishing that, the means of proof proclaimed among the followers of Jaimini shines forth."
Thus ends the examination of the Lord (Īśvara).

If it is being proven that "there exists someone who is omniscient" in a general sense, then this proof of yours does not shine before us, because of the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). However, it is only appropriate against those followers of Jaimini (*jaiminīya*) who deny the existence of an omniscient being.

If, on the other hand, an omniscient being named Īśvara is what is to be proven, then because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Therefore, the sense is that this proof does not appear valid against us.
Furthermore, as for the qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaṇa*) introduced in the phrase "the arising of diverse [effects]" and so forth, it serves no purpose whatsoever.
This proclamation of your own system is made by you solely for the purpose of deluding others.

For instance, if the proof (*sādhana*) is free from defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) even without such specific qualifications as "possessing the property" (*dharmī*), then the establishment of the intended probandum (*sādhya*) certainly occurs.

However, if the proof is corrupted by defects such as being unestablished, then even with the inclusion of such qualifications, there is no establishment of the probandum; thus, the qualification is entirely useless in every respect.
Furthermore, that qualification alone which excludes the reason from the counter-position (vipakṣa) is logical.
Moreover, the reason is unestablished with respect to its locus (āśrayāsiddha);
for the subject (dharmin) qualified by the aforementioned qualification is not established for the opponent. Therefore, it is not [established] by what is renowned in the treatise (śāstra).
The subject (dharmin) must be established.
Thus concludes the examination of the Lord (Īśvara).
Chapter: Examination of Both (Ubhayaparīkṣā).
In order to demonstrate that [the two] are devoid of causal activity, he says "of primordial matter and God," and so forth.
This is because the status of being the cause belongs exclusively to primordial matter and God [and is thus negated].
For living beings, neither of these two, taken individually nor together, can be the agent.
In this regard, some Sāṅkhyas say: "These various effects do not proceed from the *pradhāna* alone, because it is insentient (*acetana*).
For an insentient entity is never observed to initiate its own effect without a directing agent.
Nor is it logical that the *puruṣa* is the director, because at that time he is devoid of knowledge."

For it is thus: the *puruṣa* perceives only that object which has been determined by the intellect (*buddhi*). Prior to its association with the intellect, it is indeed unconscious and never cognizes any object whatsoever. And since no one is capable of acting upon an object that has not been cognized, the *puruṣa* is not the agent.
Therefore, it is God alone, in dependence upon primordial matter (*pradhāna*), who is the agent of the various effects, not [God] alone.
For Devadatta and others do not produce a son alone, nor does a potter make a jar alone.

Thus, since the causality of both primordial matter and God has been individually refuted, it is established that even when combined, this pair called God and primordial matter is not the creator or progenitor of living beings.

Now, one might object: "Even if the agency of these two individually has been refuted, their agency when combined is certainly not refuted; for it is not the case that because the eyes and other organs lack the capacity to produce visual cognition individually, they likewise lack it when combined. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As for their combination," and so forth.
"As for the combination of these two which is imagined due to their being cooperative causes... [p.59]
That [cognition] would arise either from the imparting of an excellence or from the performance of a single purposeful action.
The conceptualization of the first [cause] is not tenable because it is immutable;
nor is that of the second, because it would entail the simultaneous production of all effects.

What is called "association" (*sāhitya*) is the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*), and that is of two kinds: either through the conferring of mutual excellence or through the performance of a single purpose.
In this regard, first of all, the postulation of the first kind of cooperation—characterized by the conferring of excellence—is not logical;
why? Because those two, namely Īśvara and Pradhāna, being eternal, are devoid of modification.
Nor is the second alternative logically tenable; this is the connection with the subject at hand.
Why?
Because it would entail the absurd consequence of all effects occurring simultaneously.
Because the causes known as Īśvara and Pradhāna possess unimpaired and unobstructed capacity and are always present, [the effect] arises from a complete cause.
In this regard, as before, the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*) beginning with "that which has a complete cause" and so forth should be stated.
(95) Then, with the words "If it is said," etc., he points out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason "that which has a complete cause" according to the opponent's view.
Now it is said: the threefold nature of the Pradhāna is established;
therein, Maheśvara, joined with Rajas, is the cause of creation.
But when it again takes recourse to sattva, whose function has become manifest, then it becomes the cause for the continued existence of the entire world.
When it is joined with *tamas* in the form of emergent power (*udbhūta-śakti*),
then indeed this [Prakṛti] brings about the dissolution of the entire world.

Thus, the qualities such as *rajas* and *sattva*, as well as form and so forth, function as its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) in a strictly sequential manner; therefore, there is no simultaneity among its effects.

Although these two causes are eternally present, nevertheless, these various effects will proceed only in succession; for the three qualities—sattva and the others—residing in *pradhāna* are the auxiliary factors of Īśvara, and since they function successively, there is succession even in their effects. To illustrate: when Maheśvara is joined with *rajas*, whose activity has become manifest, he then becomes the cause of creation for living beings, because *rajas* has the effect of procreation as its nature.
When, however, it resorts to *sattva* with its function fully aroused, then it becomes the cause of the stability of the worlds, because *sattva* is the cause of stability.

But when it is joined with *tamas*, whose power has been aroused, then it effects the dissolution and destruction of the entire universe, because *tamas* is the cause of such conditions. As it has been said:
"To him who partakes of *rajas* at birth, who abides in the function of *sattva* for the maintenance of creatures, and who touches upon *tamas* at their dissolution."
Salutation to the Unborn One, who brings about the maintenance and destruction of all things, who consists of the three Vedas, and whose nature is the three *guṇas*.
Thus;
the word *kila* indicates impossibility.
He provides the rebuttal with the words "Here it is said," and so forth:
"It is said here: at the time of their single action, does that capacity for the accomplishment of other effects exist or not?"
If even at the time of creation both [subject and object] were to exist as something other [than each other], then,
given the existence of one, the other two would necessarily follow.
"Of those two" refers to primordial matter (prakṛti) and the Lord (īśvara).
"At the time of a single action" means:
There are two alternatives: at the time of the operation of any one of the three—creation, maintenance, or dissolution—does it possess the capacity to produce the other two effects, or does it not?

In that regard, if it does possess such capacity, then at the times of creation, because the causes would be complete, the other two effects consisting of maintenance and dissolution would come into being just like the effect of creation.
Likewise, during the time of maintenance, both creation and destruction would likewise occur.
Furthermore, at the time of dissolution, both persistence and origination would occur;
yet this is not logical.
For it is not reasonable that things existing in mutual exclusion should simultaneously exist within a single substratum. //101–102//

It might be argued: "At the time when those two—Prakṛti and Īśvara—are producing that single effect, no other form for them exists to produce another pair of effects; therefore, there is no such contingency for them at that time. To this he says "na hi" and so forth:
"For it does not become the producer of another thing again by means of its other form;
and since its own nature is precisely that [same], how could there be a cessation of that activity?"
The word "that" refers to the cause known as Primordial Matter (prakṛti) and God (īśvara); "of another" means of the two subsequent effects.
The meaning is that it is not by way of another's form, but rather that the cause exists precisely by way of its own form.

It might be argued: "Even if that [cause] is not a cause by way of its other form, nevertheless, at the time of producing one effect, it lacks the capacity to produce the remaining two effects; therefore, those two effects do not arise at that time. To this he says, "tatsāmarthya... and so forth:
"But if it were deprived of that capacity, it would not be a producer of them at all."
Because at other times it lacks causal capacity, like a sky-lotus and the like.
"At another time" means at the time of beginning the desired effect.

It might be argued: "Even though all power is present in the Pradhāna, nevertheless, only that whose activity has become manifest attains the status of being a cause, and no other; therefore, there will be no simultaneity of effects. To this he says, "If the predominant," and so forth:
"And if that which is of the nature of a predominant power were the sole cause..."
That [effect] would exist at all times, because of the constant presence of its cause, which is eternal in nature.
For this intense form of passion and the other afflictions cannot reasonably be said to be eternal, because it occurs only occasionally.
Consequently, its existence must arise—on occasion—from one of three possibilities: either from causes such as *prakṛti* and *Īśvara*, or from some other cause, or independently.
Regarding the first position, that intense form would have to exist at all times, because the cause known as *prakṛti* and *Īśvara*, being eternal in nature, is always present.
Regarding the second position as well, he says: "And not another," and so forth.
"Nor is another [cause] accepted; therefore, that [arising] does not come from anything else either.
Nor is this [arising] independent, because its occurrence is only occasional."
For no other cause apart from primordial matter (prakṛti) and God (īśvara) is accepted, by which [the world] might arise from something else;
nor is the third position tenable, as he says with the words "nor also," and so forth.
Now, [the author] states "svataḥ" and so forth, asking: "If there is independence, what is the contradiction with occasional occurrence?
For if existence were from itself, there would be causelessness, because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself.
Indeed, the possibility of occasional occurrence for entities arises through dependence.
If an entity (*bhāva*) were to arise from its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would necessarily be causeless. [Objection:

But how can that which arises from its own intrinsic nature be causeless, given that its very intrinsic nature is understood to be its cause? [Response: It is because of the contradiction in an action directed toward itself (*svakriyā-virodhataḥ*); for there is a contradiction in the causal status of an action directed toward its own essential form (*svarūpa*). [Objection: This may be so; let it be causeless, but even so, why is its occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*) not tenable? [Response: He says: "For by dependence," and so forth.
For entities whose occurrence depends upon another nature are logically occasional,
because their existence and non-existence are tied to the presence or absence of that other nature.
However, as for those whose occurrence does not depend on anything else, since there is nothing for them to depend upon, why would they exist only at certain times?
Now, he explains how the contradiction with its own activity is indeed established, beginning with "For thus" (tathā hi):
"For indeed, no operation upon itself is admitted for non-existence;
because even for that which has come into being, its self-nature is already established in this state."
For when producing itself, is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) already established or not?
It cannot be that it is already established;

because at that stage, since the self would also be established by virtue of being non-different from the established form, it would follow that the self is established just like the intrinsic nature.
And consequently, since there is no produced effect, where could this entity exercise its causal efficiency?
Nor is it unestablished; this is shown by the passage beginning with "unestablished" (*aniṣpanna*).
For that which has not established its own nature does not function at all, because it is devoid of all causal capacity, like a sky-lotus and the like.
Thus ends the examination of both.
"In some cases" is a general statement;
the meaning is that [the action] exists neither as its own nature nor as something other than it.
If there were an activity, it would necessarily be of an already accomplished nature.
The meaning is that this is because the perfected [nature] has precisely this much as its defining characteristic.
Thus concludes the examination of both.
Chapter: Examination of the Doctrine of Essential Nature (Svabhāvikavāda).

Without following the sequential order—since the doctrine of those who maintain the existence of an essential nature (svabhāva), which is included by the word "etcetera," requires little to be said—the author refutes it, saying "all," and so forth:
"The birth of entities is described as being independent of all causes."
For those proponents of intrinsic nature do not say that even themselves are a cause.

Although the doctrine of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavāda) is not explicitly mentioned by the word "etcetera," it is nonetheless indicated by the inclusion of the proponents of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavādins).
Among them, those who describe how entities arise from themselves alone [are included].

They have already been refuted by the passage beginning with "due to the contradiction with their own activity," and so forth; now, the proponents of the theory of inherent nature (*svabhāvavādins*) are being refuted. They argue as follows: "The birth of entities does not arise from themselves, nor does it arise from another; rather, it is independent of all causes—meaning it is indifferent to any cause, whether its own or another's. One might ask: "What is the difference between these [proponents] and those who describe how entities arise from themselves alone? To this, he says: "For they... and so forth.
Those proponents of intrinsic nature [say] "its own," meaning its own-form; by the word "also," they mean that it is also the form of another.
The former, however, maintain that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the cause; these [latter] do not accept even that—this is the distinction.

And here they set forth the reasoning: that which meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) but whose existence is not perceived is, for discerning persons, an object of the conventional usage of "non-existent," just like a rabbit's horn.
And since the cause of entities is not perceived to exist, this is a non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
To show that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says "rājīva" and so forth.
For who indeed creates the variegation of the lotus filaments and so forth? Or by whom was the multicolored eye of the peacock's tail fashioned?
The analysis of the compound is: "rājīva" means "lotus," and "tasya kesarādayaḥ" means "its filaments and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of the stalk, petals, pericarp, and so on, as well as the sharpness of the thorns and the like.
This is what is meant by "variety" (vaicitryam).
Who creates the distinctions of shape, color, hardness, and so forth? No one at all.
The meaning is that this is because a cause such as Īśvara (God) is not perceived.

This might be the case: even if the lack of a cause for external entities is established because no cause is perceived, how is it established for internal ones? To this he says "just as," and so forth: "Just as the sharpness and other qualities of thorns and the like are without a cause, because they occur only occasionally, in the same way, suffering and the rest are without a cause."
[63] Even if the causelessness of suffering and so forth is not established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is nonetheless established by inference (*anumāna*).

For instance, whatever is occasional is determined to be without a cause, just as the sharpness of a thorn and the like; and since suffering and so forth are occasional, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that "that whose presence or absence necessarily results in the presence or absence of another is the cause of that other," because such a rule is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
For instance, when contact exists, visual consciousness arises, and when it does not exist, it does not arise;
yet that contact is not the cause of the visual consciousness.
Therefore, this characteristic of the relationship between cause and effect is inconstant; thus, it is established that the arising of entities is independent of all causes.

He offers a rebuttal with the words "of the lotus filaments, etc.": "The seeds, mud, water, and so forth, which undergo a succession of states characterized by excellence, possess positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with respect to the lotus filaments and other parts."
When a cause has been ascertained through both perception and non-perception,
why then is another cause asked for regarding these [effects]?
By this, he demonstrates both the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*) and the contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

As for what was stated—that no cause for the lotus petals, filaments, and so forth is perceived—that is unestablished; for by means of perception and non-perception, the causality of seeds, mud, water, and so on has been determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
For instance, that in the presence of which alone something arises, and the modification of which results in the modification of another, is called its cause.
Furthermore, since such seeds and so forth are ascertained to have reached specific states characterized by swelling and the like, the reason [you have provided] is unestablished (*asiddha*).
As for what was also said—that the definition of cause and effect is subject to deviation—that too is unestablished;
for it is accepted that even tangibility (*sparśa*) serves as a causal condition (*nimitta*) for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) by way of being a cause for form (*rūpa*).
For instance, "contact" refers to the primary elements;
and since form exists by depending upon them again and again, contact indeed possesses the status of a causal condition for visual consciousness.
The only distinction lies in whether it is produced directly or through a succession.
Nor is it merely negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that we accept as the cause for determining the causal relationship;
rather,
it is specifically qualified [negative concomitance].
For it is described that when other causes are present and capable, if something does not occur due to the absence of one specific factor, that factor is its cause;
however, it is not merely the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the sense that "if X is absent, Y does not occur.
Otherwise, [one would have to consider as a cause] even the birth in a region where the marriage of one's mother is customary.
For if there were no marriage of the mother of the *piṇḍakharjūra* fruit, it would follow that the fruit itself does not exist.
Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding such a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the case of touch.

To explain: if, after demonstrating the presence of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it were shown that visual consciousness does not arise solely due to the absence of touch, then there would be a deviation; however, this cannot be demonstrated.
Therefore, there is no deviation from the definition of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
Not only is the seed and so forth ascertained as the cause of entities, but space and time as well are ascertained as being restricted; this is shown by the words "restricted" (*niyatau*) and so on.
How could space and time be restricted for entities? [p.64]
If these [causes] were not the cause of those [effects], then those [effects] would exist everywhere and at all times.
At some time, in some place, and in some respect, these [entities] are indeed determinate;
they become dependent upon that very thing by way of excluding its opposite.

For if lotuses and other such things did not have that causality—that is, causality restricted to specific places and times—then their occurrence only in specific locations such as water while avoiding places like stones, and their occurrence during seasons such as summer while avoiding seasons such as winter, would not be possible.
Instead, those entities such as lotuses would exist in all places and at all times, because they would be independent of those [specific conditions].
However, since they occur with necessity only in specific places and so forth by excluding other places and times, it is certain that they are dependent upon them. //115–116//

Now, one might ask: "What is this 'dependence' (apekṣā) of entities that are devoid of intentionality? To this he says: "Dependence on that is such an occurrence. Dependence on that, which is such an occurrence, is called dependence; it is called being an effect. And such an occurrence is directly perceived; therefore, in this context, these are established as reasons (hetus).
The occurrence [of a thing] in a restricted place and so forth, by way of excluding other places and so forth, is precisely what is called "dependence" (*apekṣā*);
it is not, however, of the nature of intention.
One might object: "Even if they indeed have that dependence, how is their status as its effect (*kāryatā*) determined? To this he says: "Dependence is said to be the state of being an effect."
For there is no other such "being its effect";
rather, that very dependence characterized by such a mode of functioning is what is called "being its effect.
If it is asked how this such mode of functioning of these [causes] is established, he says: "perception," and so forth.
This doctrine of intrinsic nature is sublated by direct perception,
because the nature of the cause is ascertained through both perception and non-perception.
The word *tat* means "therefore" (*tasmāt*),
or it is a compound meaning "the doctrine of inherent nature (*svābhāvikavāda*) regarding those [things], such as lotuses and so forth."

"It is sublated by perception" [is said] because non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), too, has the nature of perception since it consists in the apprehension of something else. Furthermore, as for the argument stated— that pleasure and so forth are causeless because they are occasional— that is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of what is to be proven.

The meaning is that for that which is independent of causes, occasional occurrence is logically impossible; furthermore, the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikala).
[65] Thus far, it has been demonstrated that the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Now, while provisionally accepting the establishment of the reason, he says "mā vā" and so forth, in order to demonstrate its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
Or let there be no existence of means of valid cognition for the sake of establishing the existence of the reason;
nevertheless, the non-existence of an object is not ascertained simply by the absence of a means of valid cognition.
If mere non-apprehension is taken as the reason, then it is inconclusive;
for by the absence of means of knowledge—that is, by the mere absence of valid cognition as a reason—there can be no certain determination of the non-existence of an object's reality.

To the question "Why does it not exist?", he says "Because," and so forth: Because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is neither the pervader nor the cause of the existence of an object, due to the presence of diversity, due to deviation, and because [the cognition] arises from that [object].
For when an inclusive nature (svabhāva) is excluded, it excludes its own included (vyāpya), or [excludes] the cause [when the effect is excluded],
because the included and the effect are necessarily connected [to the former] through identity (tādātmya) and origination (tadutpatti) respectively.
Furthermore, there is no non-difference between the object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the existence of the thing, because they appear as distinct.
Nor is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) the cause of an object, because of the possibility of deviation;
for an object may exist even in the absence of a means of valid cognition.
Thus, it is not at all contradictory for objects that are remote in terms of space, time, or intrinsic nature to exist even when they have not been made into objects by a means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, it is not logical for something to be the cause of another when it can exist even without that [cause], because this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Or, if one were to accept its status as a cause, one would be abandoning one's own position.
Moreover, because it arises from that [object], the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not the cause of the existence of the object.

For it is from the object itself, which serves as the objective domain, that the means of valid cognition arises; it is not, however, from the means of valid cognition that the object of cognition arises.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is not [logically] connected could exclude the existence of an object; to this he says "And that which... and so forth:
"And for that entity which is not of such a nature, the exclusion of another is by no means understood with certainty through its own absence, because there is no necessary connection."
"It is not of such a kind" means it is neither the cause nor the pervader.
For it is not logical that the necessary cessation of one thing follows from the cessation of another that is not related to it, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For in this way, upon the exclusion of the horse, there would also be the exclusion of the cow.
Non-perception by everyone is doubtful, while non-perception by oneself is inconclusive;
for even though [certain things] such as dūrvā grass in the hollows of the Vindhya mountains are not perceived, they nonetheless exist.

Furthermore, when non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is adduced as a logical reason (*hetu*), it must be characterized either by the cessation of apprehension by all persons or by the cessation of one's own apprehension. It cannot be the former, because that is doubtful, being impossible for one with limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) to ascertain.

[66] It is not the case that there is any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) available to those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*) to establish that no unperceived cause exists for the eye-like spots on a peacock’s tail and so forth simply because it has not been perceived by all persons. Furthermore, one's own non-perception is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*); why?

Because even though things such as blades of *dūrvā* grass, sprouts, or fragments of stone located within mountain caves are not perceived, they nonetheless exist; thus, non-perception does not contradict existence—this is the meaning.
Therefore, non-existence is certainly not established, because of doubt.
If a reason is not employed for the sake of establishing causelessness, then there is no establishment without a means of valid cognition; therefore, the thesis is not established.
And even if a reason were employed for the sake of establishing that [subject], it would still not be so;
because the subject is already established through being produced by that very reason, your position is already proven.
Moreover, you should be questioned as follows:
In order to establish your own position—that entities are without cause—do you put forward some reason, or not?
In that regard, if no reason is put forward, then your position is not established.
For there is no establishment of an object without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even if one were to accept [the existence of such a means], nevertheless, your thesis (*pakṣa*) will not be established; this is the connection with what is to be stated hereafter.
Why?
Because success (*siddhi*)—that is, the ascertainment (*niścaya*) whose object is the thing to be proven—is produced by that cause; for it is produced by that very cause.
And so it has been said by the venerable teacher Sūri:
"One who says 'there is no cause' surely destroys his own thesis by making it possess a cause."
"Moreover, even if the reason (hetu) were to be reluctant to exert itself, what would be gained for him by a mere thesis (pratijñā) alone?
[Verse 123] It might be argued: "I employ a reason that is indicative (jñāpaka), not a productive one (kāraka).
Why, then, should my position (pakṣa) not be established? To this he says: "For thus... and so forth.
For indeed, whether it be a logical reason (*hetu*) or a statement, that which makes [the object] known is called a "knower" (*jñāpaka*) of the probandum (*sādhya*),
because it serves as the instrumental cause for its establishment.
"A probans that makes known" refers either to the three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*) at the time of inference for oneself,
or to the verbal expression [of it].
"At the time of inference for the sake of others" means that which illuminates it; that is,
that which illuminates the reason (hetu).
"From accomplishment" means from the ascertainment of the object of cognition (*prameya*).
Otherwise, if it did not even serve as the cause for accomplishment, how could it not be a communicator (*jñāpaka*)?
For in this way, it would follow that everything is a means of making everything known.
If this is so, why do the teachers make this distinction between the causal (kāraka) and the indicative (jñāpaka)?
And here, the designation of the object is by virtue of cognition, not by virtue of the actual existence of the object as in the case of a producer;
therefore, he says that this very cause is called "indicative" while remaining a "causal" factor.
But because it does not produce the object to be accomplished, the agent is not manifested.

Because it does not produce the probandum (*sādhya*), this [reason] is called "indicative" (*jñāpaka*) and not "productive" (*kāraka*); however, that which produces the probandum, such as a sprout and so forth, is called "productive"—thus there is no fault.
By all of this, the objection that arises against the refutation stated by the Master Sūrya is countered.
For instance, the following objection occurs there:
Even one who asserts that "there is no cause" while nevertheless speaking with a reason—why would such a person undermine their own thesis?

For he speaks of a reason as a communicator (*jñāpaka*), yet rejects it as a producer (*kāraka*). To this, the reply is: even a communicator is indeed a producer, because it is a cause of cognition (*jñāna*).
By this, a contradiction with one's own words is pointed out;
however, there is no reason whatsoever that establishes the absence of a cause, because such a pervasion (vyāpti) is sublated by perception and other means of valid cognition.
By means of the conclusion beginning with "Therefore," he demonstrates that the meaning of the proposition is also sublated by inference:
"Therefore, other entities as well have causes and arise in a restricted manner,
just like the cognition produced by the means of proof which has the object to be proven as its domain."
"Others as well" refers to the lotus filaments and so forth, which are distinct from the cognition whose object is the thing to be proven.
"Of restricted birth" means:
The phrase "when there is the presence of fixed objects" is to be understood as the ellipsis [to be supplied].

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which have a fixed birth when there is the presence of fixed objects are possessed of a cause; for example, the cognition whose object is the thing to be proven (*sādhya*), which arises upon the presence of your means of proof (*sādhana*); and likewise, entities such as lotuses and the like [arise only when their specific conditions are present]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Thus concludes the examination of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikavāda*).
Chapter: Examination of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahmaparīkṣā).
Proponents of the doctrine of the Word-Brahman state: "The supreme Brahman, consisting of sound, is untouched by destruction or origination."
That this collection of entities is perceived as its transformation.

This collection of entities consisting of form and so forth is perceived as the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of that Brahman which consists of sound, is devoid of distinctions such as prior and posterior, unarisen, and indestructible—as it has been said:
"Brahman, the reality of sound, which is without beginning or end and imperishable, evolves (*vivartate*) into the nature of objects; from it proceeds the process of the world."
Thus:
therein, "beginning" (ādi) means origination; "end" (nidhana) means destruction; because of the absence of these two, it is "without beginning or end.
It is called "the imperishable" (akṣara).
Because the letters beginning with 'a' serve as the cause [of manifestation],

by this it is shown that there is a manifestation (vivarta) in the form of the denotator. Furthermore, by the phrase "in the form of the object" and so forth, the manifestation of the denoted is shown.
"Prakriyā" refers to the various distinctions;
"Brahman" is the proclamation of its name.
He explains the meaning of this very verse with the words: "untouched by destruction or origination."
The mention of destruction and arising is illustrative;
this too should be understood here: that it is devoid of the distinction between prior and posterior locations.
For indeed, its being without beginning or end, as well as its being devoid of the distinction between prior and posterior locations, has been specified therein.
"Consisting of sound" means that because its intrinsic nature is sound, sound itself is its reality; thus it is called "the reality of sound.
The meaning is that sound is its non-erroneous form.
"Supreme" means consisting of the *praṇava*.
For the *praṇava* is indeed the source of all words and all meanings, and it is the Veda.
But this Veda, established through the sequence of phonemes and words, is the means for its comprehension; it stands as a reflection (*praticchabdaka*) of that [Veda].
Those whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are graced by the dharma that has the fruits of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) perceive that Supreme Brahman.
And here they provide the following proof:

Whatever things are permeated by a certain form are composed of that [form], just as objects such as pots, bowls, and water-jars, which are modifications of clay, are well known to be made of clay because they follow the form of clay.
And since all entities are permeated by the form of the word (*śabda*), this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
For it is established through direct perception itself that all objects follow the form of the word.
For indeed, a cognition arising with respect to objects arises as being accompanied by the verbal expression of the word itself;
as it has been said:
"There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words."
All knowledge occurs as if permeated by sound.
Thus, the designation of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things is based on the forms of cognition.

Therefore, it is established that these [things] are permeated by the forms of words; and once that is established, their being composed of those [forms] is also necessarily established, because "being composed of them" consists in nothing but that.
With the words "they are to be addressed," etc., he refutes the meaning of the proposition:
"Those who also say this must be asked: what is this [nature] of theirs that is innate?"
Having abandoned its form as sound, it attains the state of being blue and so forth.
Or rather, "not so. If the first position is adopted, then there would be a loss of its imperishability due to the destruction of its prior nature.
Furthermore, in that case, according to the immediately following position regarding the cognition of blue and so forth,
there would clearly be a cognition of the nature of sound even for one who has not heard it.
In this context, it might be intended that the world consists of sound either because it is of the nature of a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of sound, or because it arises from sound—
just as in the expression "the vital breaths consist of food" (*annamaya*), where the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed in the sense of a cause.
Here, the first position is not tenable, because transformation itself is logically untenable.
For instance, Brahman, whose nature is sound, when assuming the form of blue and so forth, must either abandon its own innate, natural form of sound or not abandon it.

In that regard, if the first position—that it abandons it—is adopted, then there would be a loss of that imperishability and indestructibility which was accepted by the statement "without beginning or end," because its prior nature would have been destroyed.

If, on the other hand, the latter position—that it does not abandon it—is adopted, then even at the time of perceiving blue and so forth, sound would be perceived by one who is deaf and lacks hearing.

Because it is non-different from that, just like the cognition of blue and so forth. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is non-different from something else is cognized when that thing is being cognized; for example, the self-nature of that very blue object is cognized during the state of the cognition of blue. And sound is non-different from blue. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Otherwise, because they would have different fates (*bhinnayogakṣema*), its being of that very nature would not be established; this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in this case. [p.69]
Explaining this very point in detail, he says "by which," and so forth:
"By which [power] everything consisting of sound is established in its primary sense,
without abandoning its nature as sound, because there is no designation of transformation."
"By which" means "for which reason"; for you describe the very primacy of sound as the nature of the world.
He asks "Why? and says: "Because it does not abandon its form as sound."
If it is indeed established that [the object] consists primarily of sound, then what follows? He says:

"And when such non-figurative unity of blue and so forth is established," and so on. When such non-figurative unity of blue and so forth is established, why is there no cognition of this [unity] at the time of its cognition?
"In the case of the identity of blue and so forth"— the phrase "with the word" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "At the time of the cognition thereof."
Regarding those [objects] such as blue and so forth, at the time of their cognition:
how could it be that there is no cognition of this [cognition] itself?
The intention is that, just like the intrinsic nature of blue and so forth, its cognition is indeed logical because it has attained the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
For if this [consciousness] were not cognized, there would be no cognition even of blue and the like;
for if they were of a single nature, yet possessed distinct attributes, an absolute duality would result.
If its cognition is not admitted, then it follows that even blue and the like would be uncognized, just like the nature of the word itself;
the meaning is that because of their identity, blue and the like share the same intrinsic nature as the word.
Otherwise, if it were accepted that blue and the like possess properties distinct from the word, then an absolute difference between them would have to be admitted.
Why is this so? He says:

"For the association with contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of the difference among many things; otherwise, that [difference] would not exist even if it were imagined for individual instances."
For it is not logical for a single entity to be both perceived and not perceived at one and the same time from the perspective of a single cognizer;
this would entail the loss of its unity.

Otherwise, if unity were to persist even when contradictory properties are superimposed, then even the imagined distinction between individual instances (vyakti) that is accepted for jars and the like would no longer exist.
The word "also" (api) indicates that not only is there no difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman;
for the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that since it is established within its own self, there is no difference in it, because difference pertains to modifications (*vikāra*).
For instance, its state of being without beginning or end is not asserted in the form of things such as jars.
What then?
For jars and other such things, which possess visible arising and passing away and are perceived as having limited spatial extent, are [perceived] by means of the Supreme Self.

Furthermore, regarding the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) stated—that if Brahman were not heard, there would clearly be a perception of sound—that consequence should be considered only if the form of Brahman is held to have reached the conditions for perceptibility.
If, on the other hand, it is described as being extremely subtle and beyond the senses, then this fault does not apply;
however, one must state the following fault: since blue and other colors would also possess that same nature, they too would necessarily fail to be perceived, just like its own essential nature.
Consequently, this established rule is untenable.
Those of inferior vision perceive only the object as possessing arising and passing away.

It might be argued that, just as for you [the Yogācārins], momentariness is not distinct from blue and so forth, yet it is not perceived even when blue and so forth are experienced—so too is the nature of sound.
This, however, is incorrect.

For it is not the case that momentariness is not perceived in the cognition of blue and so forth; rather, it is said that although it is grasped by a non-conceptual mind, it is not ascertained because other qualities are superimposed due to the causes of error. Therefore, with respect to direct experience (*anubhava*), it is indeed grasped, but with respect to determinate cognition (*niścayajñāna*), it is ungrasped. Thus, through the distinction between types of cognition, the state of being both grasped and ungrasped regarding a single object is entirely non-contradictory.
Moreover, in your view, the apprehension and non-apprehension of a sound are not tenable;
for you admit that all cognitions are conceptual,
and thus that sound would be determined in its entirety by a single cognition alone.
Because it is impossible for there to be another nature that has not been apprehended.
As it has been said regarding certainty:
"How can that form which is not ascertained be an object for them?"
Now, if it is admitted that there is some cognition even that is free from conceptual construction, then it should not be said:
"There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words."
Thus,
the reason "because they are permeated by the form of sound" would not be established;
and consequently, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the determination that entities have the nature of sound would be entirely without foundation.
Furthermore, since the momentariness of entities is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is described as being "not determined" even though it has been experienced.
But from what source is the nature of entities as consisting of sound established, such that it too could be established in this same manner?
He states another line of criticism, beginning with "And for every object," and so forth:
"If a single nature of the word is held to be distinct for each individual object,
then all [words] would occupy the same location and possess a single form."
For that essence of sound, undergoing transformation, either attains differentiation with respect to each object or does not.

In that regard, if the position is taken that it is not differentiated, then it follows that all [qualities] such as blue and so forth would occupy the same location. "Occupying the same location" is an illustrative term.
The specific distinctions of time, transformation, activity, and state should also be understood as objects of apprehension.
Furthermore, cognition would result in a single form of appearance;
this follows because all things such as blue and so forth are not distinct from a single word-form.
If, however, this [Brahman] were distinct with respect to each individual, it would follow that Brahman is manifold,
because its nature would consist of a plurality of distinct entities, just like the distinction between individuals.

Now, if a difference in this word-essence (*śabdātman*) is admitted for each individual instance, then it follows that Brahman is manifold. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that whose form—its nature—is a distinct, manifold state of being," meaning its nature consists of the essence of many distinct entities. The abstract state of being that is the condition of having such a nature. Thus, because it possesses the nature of many distinct entities, multiplicity results for Brahman.
And one [Brahman] is desired as the Supreme Brahman;
therefore, the meaning is that the thesis is undermined by what has been accepted.
He states another refutation as well, beginning with "And if [the world] consists of eternal sound," and so forth:
"And if entities consist of eternal sound, they too would be eternal;
since their existence is established simultaneously, transformation is not tenable."

Regarding "being of the nature of eternal sound" (*nityaśabdamayatve*) and "having eternal sound as its intrinsic nature" (*nityaśabdasvabhāvatve*): if sound were the essential form (*svarūpa*) of the world, then even existing entities (*bhāva*) would necessarily be eternal. Consequently, since entities would be established as coexistent with sound at all times, transformation (*pariṇāma*)—which consists in change—would not apply to them. The word *tad* (in the phrase *tat... na prāpnoti*) means "therefore. Alternatively, the compound *tadyaugapadyam* is analyzed as: "the simultaneity (*yaugapadyam*) of those [entities], such as blue and so forth, is 'tadyaugapadyam'."

Now, as to why transformation does not occur even for that which is established simultaneously, he says "ekarūpa" and so forth: "For transformation would be established in the case of clay and the like when one form disappears upon the emergence of another form; but it is not possible in the absence of succession."
But transformation cannot be established in an unchanging entity; thus, the word "tu" (but) is placed out of its logical order.
In this way, first of all, it is not tenable that things consist of sound by virtue of transformation.
Showing that the second position is also not tenable, he says "athāpi" and so forth:
"Even if the world consists of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) in the form of an effect,
nevertheless, because it is changeless, there can be no gradual emergence from it."
Even so, because sound is eternal and thus unchanging, effects and the like could not arise from it sequentially;
rather, all things would have to arise simultaneously, since their causes possess complete and unimpeded capacity.
For effects depend upon the deficiency of their causes; if that cause is non-deficient, what else would they require?
By which [means] they would not exist simultaneously.
Since they arise from one another's forms, how indeed can that which is of a single nature be said to have evolved into the form of an object?

Furthermore, if it is admitted that from that single-natured essence of sound there arises another and yet another nature, then the claim that "that Brahman has evolved in the form of objects" would not be established; for when a different object is produced, it is not logical for something else to evolve into that [new] form without entering into its own nature.
Therefore, in every respect, the meaning of the proposition is untenable.
Demonstrating that the reason "because of being permeated by the form of sound" is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says:
"Because of the perception of the nature of clay as excluded from what is not that form," and so forth.
In the case of various distinctions such as jars, vases, and so forth, a single entity consisting of clay is conceived here.
But such [a nature] is not perceived in the case of entities such as blue or yellow;
even the conceptual construction, which is the seed for the exclusion of what is other than its own non-verbal nature, is likewise absent there.
For there is no following after a single form among entities from the perspective of ultimate reality;
because all things are established in their own respective intrinsic natures, they possess natures that are excluded from those of their own kind.
However, a conceptual continuity of a single form is established for them based on their exclusion from what is of a different class.

Just as, although jars, bowls, buckets, and so forth are ultimately distinct, the nature of "clay" is conceptually imputed therein based on their exclusion from things that do not have clay as their essence;
even so, this conceptual continuity of blue and other [colors] with the form of sound is not possible.
For we do not perceive the nature of sound within blue, yellow, and the like.
And since we do not perceive [such a thing], how can we imagine that the state of being permeated by the form of sound is produced by the exclusion of what is non-sound in nature?
Therefore, this conceptualization is without foundation, and the reason [adduced] is unestablished.

Regarding what was stated—that "all [sounds] would occupy the same location and cognition would have a single form"—the author anticipates the opponent's view with the words beginning "Now, [if it were] indeed indivisible," and so forth.
Now, this reality of Brahman remains eternally undivided;
yet, due to the affliction of ignorance, the world conceives of it as manifold.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the reality whose essence is Brahman is always undivided, changeless, and established as such in the ultimate sense;

it does not undergo transformation in reality, but rather those whose eyes of intellect are struck by the cataracts of ignorance perceive it as if it were diverse through distinctions such as blue and so forth.
As it has been said:
Just as a person afflicted by cataracts perceives the pure sky as if it were filled with various diverse forms, so too does one falsely imagine [the mind].
In the same way, this immortal Brahman, though changeless, appears through ignorance to have attained impurity and manifests in the form of diversity through illusory transformation (*vivarta*).
Thus, because they are not of the nature of real entities (avasturūpa), there will be no consequence of all [cognitions] occupying the same location;
and there will be a distinction between cognitions, because that [distinction] is produced by the affliction of ignorance (avidyopaplava). This is the intended meaning.
To this, it is replied with the words "tatrāpi" and so forth:
"Even there, form is perceived by people overwhelmed by ignorance in the manner of blue and so on, which serves as the basis for rejection and acquisition."
Apart from that form, how could the nature of Brahman, which is unperceived,
be recognized as existing by those whose minds have emerged [from meditative absorption]?

[73] For the existence of an object of cognition (*prameya*) is established by virtue of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); yet, there is no such means of valid cognition for establishing Brahman as having such a form (*rūpa*). To explain: first of all, perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not establish it.
Indeed, no other form of Brahman appears distinct from blue and so forth, which serve as the basis for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful.
And how could that which does not appear be perceived as existing by those whose minds have emerged [from meditative absorption] and who abide on the path of logic?
It is not established through direct perception, because it does not appear as something undivided;
nor is there an inferential mark consisting of an effect, since production from an eternal entity is impossible. (145)
But since the subject (dharmin) is not established, an essential nature (svabhāva) cannot be a prover;
nor, apart from this, is there any logical mark (liṅga) that can establish existence.
It might be argued as follows:
that [sound] is established by the very perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), because its nature is that of cognition;
for light is indeed that [same thing], since it consists of sound and has the nature of consciousness (*caitanya*).
This is contradicted by one's own experience (*svasaṃvedana*).

For instance, even when the mind is directed elsewhere, one who perceives a form with the eye experiences the cognition of blue and so forth as being entirely devoid of verbal designation (*anabhilāpa*).
This will be demonstrated in detail later.

By this, that which was stated— namely, "There is no such cognition in the world," and so forth— is also refuted. Therefore, Brahman, which is undivided and consists of sound, is not established through direct perception,
because it does not appear in that manner.
Nor [is it established] through inference;
for inference must be based either on an effect as its logical mark (*kāryaliṅga*) or on an essential nature as its logical mark (*svabhāvaliṅga*).
However, since non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) has negation as its object, it has no role whatsoever in affirmation (*vidhi*).

In that regard, first of all, there is no effect-as-evidence (*kāryaliṅga*), because no effect whatsoever can arise from an eternal [entity], since for an eternal thing, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradictory with both succession and simultaneity.
Nor is there any essence-as-evidence (*svabhāvaliṅga*).
Because that very subject (dharmin) called "Brahman" is unestablished;
for when a subject is unestablished, a property (dharma) that constitutes its very nature cannot be established independently.
To the objection that there might then be some other logical mark (liṅga), he says: "And this [is not so]," and so forth.
Because there is no connection with the object to be proven for anything other than its own nature (*svabhāva*) or its effect (*kārya*),
and it is not logical for a mark (*liṅga*) that lacks such a connection to be [valid], as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, as for what was said regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of entities with the form of words:
Because that [word] is unestablished and unreal, it is not capable of proving that Brahman possesses the nature of sound in an ultimate sense;
nor can its establishment be derived from scripture, because that [scripture] is itself unstable.
Even though there exists a logical mark (liṅga) called non-perception (anupalambha),...
The point is that this [reason] is actually included within the *svabhāvahetu* (essential identity reason).
Alternatively, because it is intended to establish existence (*sattā*), he says for that very reason: "establishing existence.
Furthermore, let it be understood that Brahman is incapable even of performing the function of being a mere object of cognition.
Because of its unsuitability for that [purpose], form is characterized by its lack of reality;
demonstrating this, he says: "Cognition is established through the sequence of the cognizable," and so forth.
Cognition is established through the sequence of the cognizable; otherwise, everything would be sequential.
That effect, consciousness, is produced simultaneously.
Even if it were mere cognition, no form of Śakra could exist beyond that;
consequently, it would follow that this [cognition] is equal to the son of a barren woman.

And this has already been established previously in the examination of the Lord (*īśvaraparīkṣā*). "Beyond that" means something other than blue and so forth, which are the basis for rejection and acquisition.
Alternatively, "from that" (*tataḥ*) is the conclusion.
"Other than" (*param*) means something else, distinct from blue and so forth, which serves as the basis for their rejection or acquisition.
Alternatively, "from that" (*tataḥ*) is the conclusion.

"Param" means ultimate or real. "Similarity to the son of a barren woman" is used because, in establishing the non-substantiality of the son of a barren woman, there is no basis other than the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). //149-

Now, this is said: "But that supreme Brahman, the Self, is perceived only by yogis whose internal organs are favored by dharma that results in worldly prosperity and the highest good"—this too is untenable, as shown by the verse beginning with *viśuddha*.
"Even yogis, whose stream of consciousness is purified, do not perceive that form of Brahman, because [their] cognition, being engaged [with objects], is conjoined [with them]."
For if he were to have an activity with respect to the knowledge born of yoga, then it would be possible to say that "the yogins see his form.
However, since there is no activity of his with respect to the knowledge in the manner already described, this is untenable.
It might be argued: "The yogins do not see him by means of the arising of a cognition having him as its object."
Because there is no yogi or yogic cognition distinct from that [consciousness], it is said:
rather, in the state of being a yogi, yogis perceive their own self as the nature of light, shining forth as such. It is replied: [this is so].
If this is so, it must be stated what its nature is prior to the state of non-yoga.
If it is always of the nature of light, then there would never be a state of non-yoga, because Brahman is eternally of the nature of the light of the Self;
consequently, it would follow that liberation occurs effortlessly for everyone.

Now, it might be argued: "Just as for you, cognition—even though it is non-dual—appears in the states of dreaming and so forth by assuming various forms, so too that non-dual reality appears in such a way due to the power of ignorance to those whose mental continuums are impure.
That is incorrect;
for there are no others with impure continuums apart from that [reality] to whom it could appear in such a manner.
If it is argued that [Brahman] appears as such by itself, then it follows that liberation is impossible;
for Brahman would always consist of the appearance of a non-dual form.
For us, however, liberation is indeed logical, because it arises from the emergence of another, purified cognition.

Furthermore, for you, there is no ignorance distinct from that [consciousness] by virtue of which it could appear in such a manner. And if ignorance were not distinct, then to say that "by virtue of that [ignorance], that very [consciousness] appears in such a manner" is a most ill-spoken statement.
Now, it might be argued that by the statement "it appears through the power of ignorance," its very nature as ignorance is being demonstrated.

If this were so, it would rather demonstrate all the more the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation; for liberation cannot occur while Brahman—eternal and uniform in nature—is established as being of the nature of ignorance.
The disappearance of ignorance (avidyā), which is of the nature of that [Brahman], is possible;

through the disappearance of ignorance, liberation would occur. Now, if it is accepted that ignorance is distinct [from Brahman], even so, because Brahman is eternal and incapable of having any excellence added to it, it is not logical that ignorance should effect anything whatsoever upon it. Consequently, since there would be no manifestation [of the world] as such due to the power of ignorance, and because there would be no connection between Brahman and ignorance, it follows that saṃsāra could never exist.
Nor can it be said that it cannot be described as either identical to or different from that [reality], because there is no other possible mode for the nature of a real entity;
otherwise, it would not even be a real entity.
Furthermore, it cannot be [described] by way of being a non-entity, for such a distinction would lead to an over-extension of the argument.
There is no dispute among us regarding the designation of "abiding" for such a nature that performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
For us, however, ignorance (*avidyā*) is simply the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for false attachment; and that predisposition is called a "capacity" (*śakti*).
Furthermore, this capacity is essentially identical with the cognition that constitutes its cause.

Therefore, because the subsequent cognition of an effect—which clings to a false form—arises from the preceding cognition that constitutes ignorance as its cause, such a manifestation [of the world] is logical due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, since that ignorance is removed through the sequence of producing increasingly more incapable moments by means of the practice of yoga, the arising of a continuum of purified cognition leads to the attainment of liberation (*apavarga*); thus, the distinction between bondage and liberation is logically consistent.
However, this is not possible for you [the Vedāntins], because Brahman is eternal and of a single nature, and therefore the two states [of bondage and liberation] are impossible.
Furthermore, because that Brahman is one, it follows unavoidably that when one is liberated, all are liberated, and when one is not liberated, all are not liberated.
Moreover, there is no proof whatsoever for its being of the nature of self-luminosity during the state of non-yoga;
for it is only the establishing cognition that is established by self-awareness through its luminous nature.
However, it has already been demonstrated that the essence of sound (*śabdātmā*) is not perceived everywhere within the nature of cognition.

Now, if you do not accept its nature as the light of the self (*ātmajyotiṣṭva*) during the state of unfitness, then you must explain from where this nature as the light of the self—which did not previously exist—arises later for Brahman, which has not abandoned its prior form, during the state of fitness.
Therefore, this doctrine of yours regarding the *Śabdabrahma* (the Word-Brahman) is a false proclamation; enough of this prolixity.
With the words "the primal matter" (*pradhāna*) and so forth, he extends the previously stated method of refutation here as well:
"The view of Brahman is equal to the transformation of the primal matter;
the refutation here should be understood according to that [previous] refutation."
Thus concludes the examination of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahma).
In that very case, the refutation should be stated:
"That effect is not produced by sound, because it exists, like the cognition of the reason;
therefore, the intended reason is not a valid reason, because it is not something to be proven, like the self of another."
And so forth.
Thus ends the examination of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahma).
Chapter: Examination of the Person (Puruṣaparīkṣā).
