With the words "Others [say... and so forth, he introduces the view of the proponents of the Veda:
"But others [hold that] the Person, who possesses the same nature as the Lord, is the cause of the world."
Those whose intellects follow doctrines poorly expounded construct [false] conceptualizations.
Even during the dissolution of all things, he possesses the power of unimpaired cognition; indeed,
like a spider to its threads, he is the cause of all living beings.

They say this: "The Puruṣa alone is the cause of the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the entire world; even at the time of dissolution, his excellence of knowledge and power remain undiminished.
And so it has been said:
"Like a spider with its threads, like a moonstone with its waters..."
He is the cause of all living beings, just as the Plakṣa tree is the source of its shoots.
Thus [it is said]:
"The Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be.
This is because both possess the attributes of a Lord—that is, attributes equal to those of Īśvara—and both serve as the cause for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.

However, this is the distinction: for those who accept God as the cause, other factors such as the Self (ātman) and so forth are also accepted as inherent causes (samavāyi-kāraṇa) and the like, alongside God;

whereas for the proponents of the Puruṣa, the Puruṣa alone is the cause. Nevertheless, both schools are identical in their view that the Puruṣa serves as the instrumental cause (nimitta-bhāva) for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. Thus, they are said to be "those whose intellects follow doctrines that are far removed from [the truth]."

The analysis of the compound is: "those whose intellect follows poorly expounded doctrines. For this [theory] as well, everything that must be said by way of refutation regarding the Lord applies;
and for what purpose does he perform such an activity?
The suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
Here too, the following refutation should be stated:
"A person is not the cause of living beings, because he is devoid of birth."
Otherwise, the world would arise simultaneously, like a lotus in the sky.
As stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 87,
and so forth: "And if, for the sake of establishing Īśvara, proofs have been stated by others as follows..."
In the same way, when [reasons] are employed by those who claim the existence of the *puruṣa* for the sake of establishing the *puruṣa*,
then, just like that [previous case], defects such as being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) must be stated.
He also states another mode of refutation, beginning with "And for what purpose," and so forth.
Since the activity of one who acts with foresight is necessarily pervaded by a purpose, it must be stated for what purpose this Person performs such an operation as the creation of the world.
If, because it is impelled by another, he were not independent,
then, out of compassion, he would make the world exclusively happy.
But what compassion is perceived in him as he creates beings tormented by various anxieties such as mental anguish, poverty, and grief?
If he acts even against his will because he is impelled by another, such as Īśvara, then that independence (*svātantrya*) which was admitted of him would be lost.

Alternatively, if he acts out of compassion for the sake of favoring others, then he should not create beings who suffer in the hells and so forth; he should create only those who are exclusively happy.
[For] prior to creation, the existence of compassionate ones is not possible.
If even compassion is imagined as this creator, then it too would be subject to destruction.
Furthermore, because there were no sentient beings to be pitied prior to creation— that is, before the act of creating—
on account of which compassion this Creator (dhātṛ) might be postulated as the one who creates?
Moreover, He would not bring about the dissolution of those who are always engaged in spiritual progress;
for if His action were dependent on that unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), His sovereignty would be lost.
If he acts out of compassion, then why does he bring about the destruction of those humans who are always endowed with prosperity?
The sense is: let him rather bring about the destruction of those very beings who belong to the miserable realms and possess a continuum of suffering.

Furthermore, it might be argued that he creates a world endowed with pleasure and pain in dependence upon the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) characterized as dharma and adharma belonging to those whom he intends to show compassion for.
This is not the case;
for in this way, the independence [of the capacity] that has been accepted would be lost,
nor is there any dependence on a capacity whatsoever.
Alternatively, if it lacks causal capacity, its status as a cause is lost, because the world arises from that very thing upon which it depends.
And for what purpose would he regard that unseen cause of suffering?
On the contrary, in the presence of such compassion, equanimity alone is appropriate for him in that situation.

Granted that there may be a dependence on the unseen (adṛṣṭa) for that [suffering]; nevertheless, it is not fitting for us who possess compassion to depend upon that unseen force—consisting of merit and demerit—which is the cause of affliction. Rather, it is appropriate for one who is governed by compassion to simply disregard it.
For those who are compassionate do not seek out the very causes of others' suffering, since their engagement [in the world] proceeds solely from the desire to separate others from suffering.
If his activity were for the sake of play, he would not be the master of that play,
because of his dependence on various means of play, just like a child.
Now, if he acts not out of compassion,
but rather for the sake of sport,
this too is incorrect.
In this way, he would lack independence in the production of play, because he would have to depend upon various means of play consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
And whatever pleasure is to be accomplished through play, and whatever means there may be for that [pleasure],
he would perform all of them simultaneously, provided he were capable of performing them.
Even gradually, he would not be capable [of action] unless he were already capable at the outset;
for it is not logical that a single entity should possess both capacity and incapacity simultaneously.
Furthermore, regarding those various means of play, if he possesses the power for their cause, then he would produce them all simultaneously;
if, however, he lacks that power at the outset, then he would not produce them even sequentially,
because his state of incapacity remains unchanged.
For it is not possible for two mutually contradictory properties—capacity and incapacity—to belong to a single entity in respect to a single object.
Furthermore, every such conceptual inquiry as "for what purpose does he undertake such an activity? is common to the case of God as well.
Therefore, as Praśastamati has said: "God acts for the sake of favoring others."

Just as a certain sage who has accomplished his own purpose gives instruction for the sake of others' welfare— even though there is no possibility of his own attainment of benefit or avoidance of harm—

so too does Īśvara proceed to manifest His own sovereign power and majesty, intending to take hold of living beings. Or else, it is due to the very nature of His power, just as the production of transformations in the stationary and moving worlds occurs by their own nature through the successive manifestation of seasons such as spring and so forth.

Likewise, [the claim] that even for Īśvara, his powers of manifestation (*āvirbhāva*), grace (*anugraha*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) become causes for the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of living beings through their successive manifestation—
this too has been refuted by the very same [argument]. For instance, regarding the statement "he acts for the sake of favoring others," this is precisely the refutation.
"He would bring about the highest favor, making the world exclusively happy," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "due to the nature of his power" (*śaktisvābhāvyāt*), this very same refutation applies here as well:
[If he were] one whose power is manifest, he would simultaneously perform creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
If he were not possessed of unmanifest power, he could not create the world simultaneously.
This Lord is not established as manifest even through a sequence;
therefore, since his power is distinct from anything else, how could there be a single manifestation?
Thus, even regarding time (*kāla*), this same fault applies if it functions sequentially in the manifestation of spring and so forth.

For it will be demonstrated later that what we call "time" is actually nothing other than entities (*bhāva*) themselves, which perish at every moment and possess the distinctions of following upon cold and heat. (162)
Now, he raises the objection representing the view of Uddyotakara, beginning with "If its activity is by way of its own nature," etc.:
"If its activity at the beginning of creation is described as being by way of its own nature,
just as fire and the like [act] by their very nature in the act of burning and so forth."
If all things were thus to exist simultaneously,
then [they would do so] because of the presence of causes endowed with the capacity to produce them.
For he says: "The activity of the Blessed Lord is not for the sake of play;
rather, it is just as the nature of the great elements such as earth is such that they engage in their own effects, so too is it with the Lord.
This is incorrect.

For if all entities were to arise solely through the operation of that [efficient cause], they would necessarily arise simultaneously, since their capable and unimpaired causes would be present at once.
Furthermore, we have already demonstrated previously that being "intelligent" is not a valid differentiator. [Objection:
If this is so, why do the effects of fire and the like not also occur simultaneously? To this he replies: "Produced by the power of their own causes," and so forth.
The powers produced by the force of their own causes are indeed restricted;
they do not exist at all times in things such as fire and the like.
Otherwise, all effects would arise simultaneously,
if this restriction is not admitted even for those [causes].
"Of them" means of fire and so forth.
The word "also" (api) indicates that this applies not only to Īśvara.
"This is the rule" means it is produced by the power of its own causes. [Objection:
It might be asked, "Why does the spider, though active by its very nature, not produce its effects such as webs simultaneously? To this he says, "By its very nature," and so forth.
Even in the case of the spider, its status as the cause of its threads is not accepted as being due to its own nature alone,
since it produces the web of saliva out of a craving for devouring living beings.
The spider, too, does not act by way of its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
Rather, the intention is that it acts due to an occasional craving for devouring living beings, which arises from specific causes.
For it is not eternally uniform in form; its power is occasional, as it is produced by the force of its own causes.
Furthermore, it might be argued:

"It is neither out of compassion nor for sport, but rather it proceeds somehow quite unintentionally. To this he says, "In whatever way," and so forth: "If its activity is in whatever way [unintentional], what kind of intelligence does it possess?"
For even a dog does not undertake an action without first considering it.
For in this way, since he is utterly ignorant even of common people such as fishermen and the like, how could his words be worthy of attention by discerning persons?
"Buddhimattā" means "prekṣāvattā" (the state of being discerning).
Śanaka was a fisherman.

By this very refutation of the human [agency of creation], it should be understood that those such as Śauri and others who are imagined by others to be the creators of the world are likewise rejected; thus he demonstrates.
"Śauryātmaja and the others," and so forth:
even those who are imagined to be creators, such as Śauryātmaja and the rest,
are in reality refuted by this very same method.
In that context, Śauri is Viṣṇu;
Ātmaja is Brahmā;
and by the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of Time (kāla), which is held by others to be the intelligent principle.
As it has been said:
Thus concludes the examination of persons.

Chapter: Examination of the Self (Ātmaparīkṣā). Now, others here [propound] an examination of the self as conceived by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, who maintain that the self is the substratum of desire and so forth.
They maintain that it is by its own nature insentient, eternal, and likewise all-pervading.
It is the agent of wholesome and unwholesome actions and the experiencer of their fruit; it is conscious because of its association with consciousness, not by its own nature.
The connection with the instruments of knowledge and so forth is called its agency;
however, the inherence in the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so on constitutes its state as an enjoyer.
Birth is said to be his association with a specific group, as well as with unprecedented cognitions and sensations.
Separation from those [elements] previously acquired is death; life, moreover, is the conjunction of the mind with the body, consecrated by merit and demerit.
For violence is attributed to him [the self] due to the destruction of the body, eyes, and so forth;
thus, even though the person is eternal, this process is observed in its pure form.

The specific types of cognition—namely, perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, knowledge of established facts, clairvoyance, and intuitive knowledge; as well as doubt, error, dream, and dream-within-a-dream—are cognizable by a conscious perceiver distinct from my own body and so forth. This is because they possess the properties of having an origin dependent on their own causes, being of the nature of consciousness, being subject to rapid destruction, producing mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and being of the nature of cognition, just like the cognitions of another person. By contrast, objects such as jars, as defined by Praśasta, are [insentient].
Among these, the six non-specific categories beginning with "existence" (*sat*) have been explained previously.
The objects of these six, beginning with "being," are substance, quality, and action;
their non-objects are generality, particularity, and inherence.
Thus, this twofold knowable is the object of the specific cognitions such as perception and the rest; they are described in that manner.
The expression "perception, inference, analogy," and so forth, is a copulative compound (*dvandva*).

"Vision of the perfected ones" (*siddhadarśana*) refers to that which is set forth in the *jyotiḥśāstra* (astronomy/astrology) and other sciences; for it is called the "vision of the perfected ones" because it is either the vision of those who have attained perfection (*siddha*) or it is a vision that has been perfected.
Intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*), however, is that of the sages (*ārṣa*), such as [the thought], "My brother, the horse, will go.
It is called *ārṣa* because it generally occurs among the sages (*ṛṣi*).
*Āreka* means doubt (*saṃśaya*).
Perversion (*viparyāsa*) is error (*viparyaya*).
A cognition occurring during the initial stage of sleep is "dream" (*svapna*).
Furthermore, any subsequent cognition that has that dream as its object is "the state following a dream" (*svapnāntika*).
These alone are the specific types of wisdom (*prajñāna*);
the rest is easily understood.
Pointing out this very validity in terms of its meaning, he says "and the cognitions," and so forth.
And my cognitions are to be known by an experiential subject distinct from the objects of knowledge and so forth, because they are cognitions, like anything other than them.
In the phrase "from reality, etc.," the word "etc. includes the sense-faculties and sensations.
"Because they are conditioned" is an illustration; other reasons, such as having an origin dependent upon their own causes, are also to be understood.

Śaṅkarasvāmin, however, proves it otherwise: "Desire and the rest are supported by something, because, while being entities, they are effects, like color and so forth. He shows this in the passage beginning with "And desire and the rest," etc.:
"And all these, beginning with desire, are supported by something."
Since it exists as a real entity and is an effect, it is like color; and that [entity] for us is the Person (puruṣa).
Because it apprehends [the object] as a real entity (*vastu*), this [reason] is not subject to deviation regarding destruction;
for even though destruction possesses a cause, it does not possess the nature of a real entity.

With the words "because of the apprehension of being a real entity" (*vastutva-grahaṇāt*), etc., he demonstrates the efficacy of the qualification "provided that there is being a real entity" (*vastutve sati*). However, Udyotakara proves [the existence of the self] as follows: "The cognitions of Devadatta regarding color, taste, smell, and touch have a single and manifold cause, because they are synthesized by the cognition 'by me,' just like the simultaneous cognitions of several men when a single dancer makes a movement with her eyebrows after a signal has been given."

This is the meaning: just as, for example, among many people who have made an agreement that "the garments must be thrown [to us] immediately after the dancer’s brow-flicker," there arise various cognitions produced by various agents, so too here, various object-cognitions will be synthesized because of the unity of the cause. And that which is the single cause is the Self.
Furthermore, synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) is the unification of such cognitions as "seen by me" and "heard by me" by virtue of having a single knower as their cause.
In the case of a dancer’s movement of the eyebrows, however, it is the bringing about of a single object for the cognitions;
in every respect, "synthesis" (pratisandhāna) is said to be the connection of cognitions by taking a single object as their basis.
Demonstrating this very means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he says: "the cognitions of form and so forth."
All cognitions of form and so forth have both single and multiple causes,
because they exist through the synthesis [of these causes] by means of the cognition "by me."
Just as there is a single cognition of many [individuals] in the movement of a dancer’s creeper-like eyebrows,
otherwise, the synthesis [of experiences] would not occur, being without a basis.
This is easily understood.

//180// This is another formulation of his [argument]: "The word 'self' (ātman) denotes something distinct from the aggregate of body, sense-faculties, mind, intellect, and feelings; because, while being distinct from well-known synonyms, it is a single word, like the word 'pot' and so forth.
He states this as: "Intellect, sense-faculties," etc.
Because this word "ātman" is considered a single term, it denotes something distinct from the aggregate of the intellect, the sense organs, and so forth.
Whatever is thus ascertained as being distinct from the synonyms of "established" is endowed with the property as specified, just like the word "cloth."
Regarding the phrase "being distinct from the established synonyms":
the meaning is that it exists as something different from those established synonyms for the intellect, sense faculties, and so forth, such as *dhī* (intellect) and the like.
And regarding the phrase "that which is thus definitively determined": [it refers to that which is ascertained in this manner].
Because, while being distinct from the synonyms of "accomplished" (siddha), it consists of a single word;
and because it denotes an object distinct from cognition and so forth, according to the property as specified [in the definition]. //182–183//
Furthermore, he himself employed a negative (vyatirekin) reason for the sake of establishing his own position:
"This living body is not soulless, because [if it were] it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth, like a jar.
He shows this by saying, "by means of breath and so forth."
Furthermore, this living body would be devoid of breath and the other vital functions due to its lack of a self, like a jar; therefore, it is not the case that it lacks a self.
"Of this, there is no selflessness" refers to the living body;
or alternatively, the meaning is that for this self, there is no selflessness— that is, no lack of intrinsic nature— but rather its existence is established.

Now, regarding how its permanence and omnipresence are to be understood, Aviddhakarṇa first provides the proof: "My cognitions occurring at times other than [the present], which are perceivable by the same perceiver who perceives my first cognition immediately after emerging from my mother's womb, are my cognitions because they are my cognitions, just like my first cognition.
In this way, suffering and the other [mental factors] are also to be made the subject of the argument.
This is the inference for permanence; he demonstrates this with the words "sadyojātādya" and so forth.
Every subsequent cognition is known by that very same cognition which knows the immediately preceding unarisen [cognition] and so forth, because it is a cognition, just like that first one.
Regarding the phrase "tadādyavat": "tadādya" means that which is the first (ādya) of that [subsequent] knowledge which occurs at a later time.
He provides a proof for the sake of establishing [his] sovereign power (*vibhutva*):
"Earth, water, air, and mind, which have become objects of dispute and exist at a great distance, are connected with my own self;
because they possess corporeality, velocity, priority, mutual conjunction, and disjunction, just like my own body and so forth."
He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "madīya" (my own):
"Even though it resides in a distant place, [the earth and so forth] are joined with my self,
because they possess form and other qualities, just like our own body."
He concludes with the words "Thus" and so forth:
"And thus, when the permanence, omnipresence, and existence of sentient beings have been definitively established,
it remains that all phenomena are not without a self."
He refutes this with the passage beginning "That [fault]... and so forth.
First, regarding the first proof, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For it is accepted that your knowledge is to be understood as "omniscient" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the first proof" (*prathame sādhane*),
it refers to the argument beginning with "and my cognitions" (*jñānāni ca madīyāni*) and so forth.

In that case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because we admit that your cognitions are known by an omniscient being— who is distinct from your body and other such factors— as well as by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others who possess knowledge of the thoughts of others.

Furthermore, demonstrating that the concordant example (sādharmyadṛṣṭānta) "just like the cognition of another person" is deficient in the probandum (sādhyavikala), he says: "And independent of an illuminator," and so forth.
"And its own cognitive form arises independent of an illuminator;
likewise, the cognition of another is [adduced as] an illustration, yet it is devoid of the probandum."
Since even the cognition belonging to another person arises as a self-cognizing form that does not depend on another illuminator,
this example is devoid of the probandum, which is the state of being cognizable by a cognizer distinct from [the object] such as "thatness" (tattva) and so forth.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "It is not another's mind alone that is intended as the example; rather, the object in relation to which consciousness arises having assumed its form is the example here. To this, [the author] says: "By that which is colored by its form," and so forth: "Even if that which is cognized by another [consciousness] colored by its form were the example, there would still be doubt regarding it being [cognized] by another."

Even so, since cognition arises as having the nature of self-awareness alone, devoid of being cognized by another cognition, there would be doubt; that is to say, the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Now, if it is held that even that [cognition] is cognizable by a cognizer distinct from itself—on the grounds of its possessing the properties of arising and passing away, its being an object of knowledge (prameyatva), and its being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) when being remembered, just like an external object—then here too, because there is no subverting argument (bādhaka) against the opposite of the probandum (sādhyaviparyaya), the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not certain.
Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress regarding the experience of successive cognitions;
for an object cannot be established if it is not manifested by a cognition.
Consequently, for one who follows a succession of cognitions in order to establish a single object, an entire human lifespan would be consumed.
Furthermore, if it is argued that some cognition arises as something whose nature is already self-known for fear of an infinite regress,
then by that very fact, the reasons such as "having the nature of arising and passing away" are rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Likewise, what aversion can there be toward accepting the self-cognizing nature (*svasaṃvedanatva*) of other cognitions as well?
Now, if it is maintained that this [manifestation] is indeed of an unperceived nature,
even so, since it is unestablished, there would be a lack of establishment for all preceding cognitions, because their manifestation would not have been made manifest.
Consequently, the object as well would not be established.

However, for those Vijñānavādins whose view is that all cognition manifests by itself alone due to the absence of the distinction between apprehended object and apprehending subject, and is not known by another cognition, the fault of the "lack of the probandum" (sādhyavikalatā) remains absolutely unshakable.

In the same way, regarding other proofs such as "having an origin dependent on causes," one should state faults such as "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhyatā). Furthermore, the qualification of the subject (dharmin) made as "existent" and so forth is useless, as before; for it has no role in establishing the probandum under discussion.
For instance, what is not already established by this much: that my cognitions, such as perception and so forth, are cognized by a cognizer distinct from my body and other such things?
Even with the distinction between perception, inference, and so on, the differentiation of the subject (*dharmin*) is entirely useless, since it is already understood simply by saying "my cognitions.

Furthermore, the subject characterized by the aforementioned qualifications is not established for the opponent; thus, the reasons (*hetu*) suffer from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).
Furthermore, if, having employed a useless qualification, another proof altogether is stated for the sake of establishing that [original] point,
then— since it is unrelated to the subject under discussion— an "irrelevant matter" (arthāntara) would constitute a ground for defeat (nigrahasthāna).
If it is being proved that desire and so forth have a locus in some respect,
and if that locus is conceived as merely a cause;
If you maintain that the substratum of that [consciousness] is its support,
even so, the postulation of a support for that which lacks movement is fruitless.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "desire and so forth," if it is being proven that the mere cause is the substratum (*āśraya*) of desire and the rest, then this is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), for we do not maintain that desire and the rest are without a cause, since it is said: "Mind and mental factors [arise] from four [conditions].
Thus it is conceptualized.
The meaning is that it is being described.

Now, if the substratum characterized as the locus (*āśraya*) is established, even then, because the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is sublated by inference, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*) by that [proposition] is not established; this he demonstrates with the words "tadādhāra" and so forth.
"Tadādhāraḥ" means the substratum (*ādhāra*) of those [qualities], such as desire and the rest.
For material entities that possess the property of movement, one may postulate a substratum to prevent their downward fall;
however, since pleasure and the like are devoid of motion, they cannot possibly fall downward—so what could the self or other such things do to serve as their substratum?

(vv. 191–) [Objection: Just as jars and the like are substrata for jujube fruits and so forth even though they perform no service for them, so too the self will be the substratum for pleasure and the like. To this he says: "The support," etc.
A vessel or similar object is established as the support for jujube fruits and the like,
either by obstructing their movement or by producing a specific transformation.
"In the case of the non-momentary position, [it acts] by obstructing the movement;
or in the case of the momentary position, by producing a specific change. That [action] consists in the production [of an effect] in the same location as its material cause."
Since neither of these two types is possible for desire and the other mental factors, it is not logical for them to have any substratum whatsoever.

Furthermore, demonstrating that the qualification "provided it is a real entity" (vastutve sati) is indeed purposeless because there is nothing to be excluded, he says: "Of that which is formless," and so forth:
"And it is not at all logical for destruction, being formless, to possess the nature of an effect;
therefore, the qualification stated here by the opponents in their reason is redundant."

For if destruction could possibly be an effect, then the qualification "while being a real entity" would be meaningful for the purpose of excluding it. However, since it is a non-entity, nothing can be produced by causes; how, then, could it possess causality? The formal argument is as follows: that which is a non-entity is not the effect of anything, just like a rabbit's horn.
Furthermore, since destruction is a non-entity (*avastu*), there is the perception of something contrary to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
If it were an effect, it would follow that it is an entity, like pleasure and so forth; this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) here.
Moreover, there is a contradiction with your own tenets.
For it is thus: the designation and cognition "effect" arise from its own cause through the acquisition of self-nature (ātmalābha), that is, through inherence in existence (sattā-samavāya).
However, there is no inherence of destruction—which is devoid of the nature of substance and so forth—either in its own cause or in existence.
Because it lacks form (nīrūpa);
for otherwise, even though it is dependent on substances and so forth, it would still be a real entity (vastu), and thus it could not be excluded by the qualification of the reason.
Therefore, the qualification "provided it is a real entity" is redundant.

Regarding the passage beginning with "having form and so forth as their conditions," he says "by me" and so on: "By me" is a synthesis [of experiences] arising from the affliction of ignorance; for even though all things are momentary, there appears a unity of agent and so forth.
Furthermore, because it arises from false conceptualization, the establishment of reality is not tenable [from that perspective];
yet, even though things are distinct due to differences in their capacities, they can share a single basis.
The synthesis characterized by the unification of cognitions—such as "I have seen" and "I have heard"—on the basis of a single knower, is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

This is because such synthesis is possible even among momentary entities due to the deluded conceit of a single agent. Therefore, the determination of the nature of things based on such synthesis is not tenable.
But how do your moments (kṣaṇas) come to serve as the cause for reconnection? To this he says: "Due to the distinction of capacity," and so forth.
"Due to the distinction of capacity" means due to a specific capacity.

Even though an object is manifold, it is the basis—that is, the cause—of a single effect such as a conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*) in a single form; just as *guḍūcī* and other herbs are the cause for the alleviation of fever and so on, as he will demonstrate in detail later. //195–196//

Now, he asks: "How is its very state of being erroneous determined? and replies with the verse beginning "ekānugāmī" (following a single [object]): "If there were a single, persisting causal efficacy, the sequence of priority and posteriority would be contradicted for cognitions of form, sound, and so forth, because of the presence of their capable causes."

For if these cognitions of blue and so forth were the effects of a single, permanent entity such as a self that persists through prior and subsequent times, then their occurrence in succession would be contradicted;
for, since their cause would be unimpaired, it would follow that they must arise simultaneously. Furthermore, a permanent entity has no dependence upon anything else.
Because it cannot be assisted by anything whatsoever.

Furthermore, he shows that if one were to establish merely the general fact that [cognition] is preceded by a cause, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), by means of the verse beginning with "from the immediately preceding cognition" (*ekānantara-vijñānāt*). "The arising of the six cognitions occurs from the immediately preceding cognition."
It is clearly perceived simultaneously; in this case, the desired conclusion is established.

For it is clearly experienced that from a single immediate consciousness acting as the *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition), the arising of all six consciousnesses—visual and the rest—occurs.

For instance, at the very moment one sees the form of a dancer, one simultaneously hears the sound of drums and other instruments, smells the scent of blue lotuses and so forth, tastes the flavor of camphor and the like, experiences the touch of fans, breezes, and so on, and thinks with the mind of taking hold of garments and such.
Nor is it correct to say that this perception is like the sight of a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*), resulting from rapid succession.
Because it would follow that [the object] appears indistinctly.
For you describe this conceit of simultaneous apprehension as resulting from the synthesis of visual perceptions;
and such synthesis is performed by memory.
Furthermore, that [cognition] is indistinct because its object is past;
yet this simultaneous manifestation of color-form and so forth is experienced as distinct.
Moreover, in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, there is the arising of cognitions grasping the phonemes *sa* and so forth with extreme speed.
In this case as well, there would be the conceit of simultaneous apprehension;
consequently, no sequence whatsoever could be determined.
This will be demonstrated in detail later.
But here, by the statement "it is manifest," the direction of the refutation has indeed been shown.

Now, if it is sought to establish that these [effects] have a single cause because they are caused by an entity that is eternal and of a single nature, then he shows that this is subverted by inference through the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the verse beginning with "of successive [effects]," and so forth.
It was just stated that successive effects cannot possibly have a single cause;
therefore, the subversion of this [position] by inference is clearly observed through the pervasion.
Regarding the phrase "immediately after" (*anantaram*), it refers to [the definition] beginning with "following a single [cause]" (*ekānugāmī*) and so forth.
In this regard, the following is the refutation: those things which are present and whose causal capacities are unimpeded necessarily arise simultaneously.

Just as sprouts and the like, which possess a complete causal complex, arise simultaneously; and just as Devadatta’s cognitions of objects such as form have causes whose capacities are present and unimpeded—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
But this is not possible [in the case of the opponent's position].
Therefore, there is a reversal.
He shows that the example is also devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) with the verse beginning "nartakī" and so forth:
"The movement of the dancer’s creeper-like eyebrows is not truly one;
because it is a collection of many atoms, its oneness is merely imagined."
For there is no single entity such as the creeper-like brow of a dancer, because it is a collection of many atoms.
If this is so, how can it be the object of a single word? To this he says: "Its unity is imagined."
[87] Now, as to what the basis for conceptual construction is, he says: "Because of their utility for a single effect," and so forth.
Because they are useful for a single effect, they fall within the scope of a single word.
If even such a thing as this is intended as the probandum, then it would be the proving of what is already established.

Because this contraction of the creeper-like eyebrows is employed for a single effect, such as visual consciousness and so forth, it therefore becomes the object of a single word despite being distinct [in its parts].

Now, one might argue: "We intend to prove precisely such a unity as imagined; therefore, the example does not suffer from the fallacy of lacking the property to be proven (sādhyavikalatā). To this he says, "The property to be proven also... and so forth.

For in this way, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā), because conditioned phenomena existing in prior and posterior moments are the objects of a designation as a single entity based on a single cognition.
Regarding what was said, "the sense-faculties of cognition," and so forth, he replies with "cognition, mind," and so forth: "For us,
words such as 'cognition' (buddhi) and 'mind' (citta) do not denote something distinct [from consciousness],
even though they are different terms."
Therefore, the reason is inconclusive; has it not been stated that there is a qualification for it?
It is replied: no, for that [qualification] is certainly not established, since the state of being synonyms is maintained.
The mind is called the "self" because it is the locus of the ego-sense; this is according to conventional truth, but in terms of the actual nature of reality, no such object exists for it.

The reason "because it consists of a single word" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, although terms such as *buddhi*, *citta*, *jñāna*, *indriya*, *akṣa*, *vedanā*, *cittanu*, *kāya*, *śarīra*, and so forth—which are synonyms for intellect, sense-faculty, sensation, and body—are single words, they do not, in our view, denote a category of entities distinct [from those they name]. Therefore, because its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is unestablished, the reason is inconclusive. Now, one might object: "Anticipating this very doubt, the qualification 'provided that it is distinct from established synonyms' was stated for that reason; so how can there still be inconclusiveness? To this, it is replied: [The response follows: ... [the full argument continues] ... [it is] not so. Why? Because even if a word is distinct from established synonyms, it may still be used to denote a meaning other than that which has been previously established. For example, the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), though distinct from established synonyms such as "śimśapā," "palāśa," and "khadira," is used to denote a meaning other than those [specific trees], namely, the general class of trees. Furthermore, the word "tree" is indeed distinct from the synonym "forest" (*vana*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from forest-trees. Thus, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "fire" (*tejas*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from fire. Therefore, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "air" (*vāyu*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from air. Hence, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "space" (*ākāśa*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from space. Thus, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "time" (*kāla*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from time. Therefore, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Consequently, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "self" (*ātman*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from the self. Thus, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "person" (*pudgala*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from the person. Therefore, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "sentient being" (*sattva*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from sentient beings. Hence, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "life-force" (*jīva*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from life-forces. Thus, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "nourishment" (*āhāra*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from nourishment. Therefore, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "birth" (*jāti*), yet it does not denote a category of entities distinct from birth. Consequently, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Thus, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Hence, because the reason is not excluded from the counter-example, it is inconclusive. Furthermore, the word "tree" is distinct from the synonym "suffering" (*duḥkha

This qualification of the reason is unestablished. Why? Because of the established fact that "mind" (*cetas*) is a synonym for "self" (*ātman*); for this term "self" is determined to be a synonym for "mind."

As it has been said: "Mind alone is metaphorically designated as the 'self' because it is the locus of the notion of 'I'. The meaning is that it is metaphorically designated, that is, it is so used in conventional discourse.

Therefore, what was stated by Uddyotakara—that metaphorical designation is not tenable because a primary sense exists—should be understood as resulting from a failure to comprehend his intended meaning.
He clarifies this by saying, "this very thing is sung.
Therefore, the reason has an unestablished qualification.

Furthermore, having provisionally accepted that [the cognition] possesses an object from the perspective of conventional reality (saṃvṛtti), the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) of this reason has been stated.

But if it is sought to establish, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that [words] denote objects distinct from cognition and so forth, then this reason is indeed untenable because its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is sublated by inference. Demonstrating this, he says "in terms of the actual nature of things" (*vastuvṛttyā*) and so on. This is because all linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) has as its object only superimposed entities; this will be demonstrated later.
The point is this: since there is no object for this word "self" at all, how could there be a pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason by the probandum?
Showing that even with its qualification, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika), he says: "In the case of the sky-lotus and so forth," etc.
"Whatever single thing is applied to the sky-lotus and so forth..."
Therefore, because of such terms as "agent" (kāraka) and so forth, even deviation is observed.

For just as in the case of "sky-flowers" and the like, where because of their absolute non-existence no term such as "agent" (kāraka) can be applied, yet that [term]—being established for both parties—is a single word while being distinct from words denoting the body and so forth, and yet does not have as its object a real entity distinct from the body and so forth; thus, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
But how can words such as "agent" and so forth be applied to that which lacks any defining characteristic? To this he says: "Existing solely through convention," and so on.
Where are words not applicable, since they exist merely through convention? Nor do words such as "self" and the like possess an inherent capacity to manifest an object by their very nature.
For convention arises solely from independent desire, and words denote only that [convention]; how then could there be any obstruction to the flow of their application anywhere?

Furthermore, if it were argued that the intended meaning of the reason is "because of being a single word not based on convention," and thus there would be no deviation, the author says "not at all" and so forth.

Indeed, there is no manifestation of meaning by words through their own nature (*prakṛti*) without convention, because it would follow that even one who has not learned the language would understand the meaning from them.
Furthermore, because it would follow that there is no necessity [of convention] by one's own will, and because it would follow that linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) is useless;
therefore, it is not established that words such as "self" (*ātman*) reveal their meaning through their primary form (*prakṛti*). Thus, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Now, if another qualification is added—namely, "while having as its object a knowable that is included within a category that is not the locus of any distinction"—as stated by Bhāvivikta:
even so, because the aforementioned qualification is unestablished, the reason (hetu) is unestablished; and due to the absence of pervasion (vyāpti), it is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Regarding what was said, namely "separated from the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth," he replies with the words "And of the vital breaths and so forth," etc.: "If the connection of the vital breaths and so forth with the self were established, then this [absurd] consequence would be appropriate; otherwise, it is not."
If [the body] were empty due to the absence of a barren woman’s son, it would follow that a living body [is likewise empty];
for in this way, even according to your own view, this consequence follows because of the absence of breath and so forth.

For if some relationship—characterized either by identity (*tādātmya*) or by origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—were established between the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth and the self (*ātman*), then the consequence that the vital breaths and so forth must cease when the self ceases would be logical.

Otherwise, the consequence that the cessation of one thing entails the cessation of another that is unrelated to it would be entirely inconsistent, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Indeed, upon the cessation of the son of a barren woman, there is no cessation of the vital breaths and so forth, which are not related to him.

Therefore, just as when the son of a barren woman ceases to exist, the cessation of [attributes] such as breath—which are not connected to him—would follow [as they would cease] like a jar or similar objects; thus, a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) being advanced by someone in this manner is inconclusive (anaikāntika). Likewise, your own attempt to entail the cessation of breath and so forth upon the cessation of this self is also strictly inconclusive, because no connection has been established. This is the intended meaning. But how is it that the connection is unestablished? He says: "First of all, there is no identity here," because their difference is admitted.
Nor is there a relationship of cause and effect, because that would entail the consequence of simultaneity.
For when that self has ceased, do these vital breaths— exhalation and inhalation— along with the body, cease as well, being entirely devoid of connection to it?
"Because their difference is admitted"— that is, between those two,
the self and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, there exists no relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), because a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) is accepted.
For instance, the vital breaths and so forth are impermanent, non-pervasive, and corporeal, whereas the self is the opposite of that.

Nor is it characterized by origination from that [the body], because since the causes of the vital breaths and so forth are unimpaired, their simultaneous occurrence would follow as a logical consequence.
Furthermore, there exists no other relation apart from these two.
Therefore, being devoid of any relation, why do the vital breaths and so forth cease from the body when it is distinguished by life?
Not at all;
the meaning is that, for this reason, the logical reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

By this, those [qualities] such as desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition which have been asserted by others to be marks of the self (ātman-liṅga) should be understood as refuted, because the relationship [between them and the self] is unestablished.

The formal argument is as follows: those things which are not invariably concomitant with something else cannot be indicators of that thing, just as cranes and the like are not indicators of sesame seeds and so forth; and vital functions (prāṇa) and the like are not invariably concomitant with the self. This is a non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi).
Nor is the reason unestablished, because both types of relationship have already been refuted.
Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because that would entail the absurd consequence that everything could prove everything.
Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Furthermore, as for the one who says, "The establishment of the agent follows from the establishment of the instrument," that is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For the status of the eye and so forth as instruments is not established from the perspective of ultimate reality;
this is because all [factors] are equal in their causal role regarding the arising of consciousness,
and because the conventional distinction between agent and instrument is merely imagined through the power of one's own whim.
If the proof is for agency in general, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because that which is merely imagined has not been refuted.

If the proof is for ultimate agency, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), because no connection whatsoever has been established between the eyes and other sense organs and such an agent. //209–210//
Regarding what was said [in the verse] beginning with "because [the self] is not known through the Sadyojāta-mantra and so forth," he says "And thus" and so on:
"And thus, since the existence of the self is not established by any of these proofs,
the example cited for its eternity and omnipresence is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyahīna*)."

Like the initial cognition; like my own body—this illustration which has been stated is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) as described, because the self (*ātman*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
With the words "anair" and so forth, [the author] again raises the objection of Uddyotakara, Bhāvivikta, and others:
"Others have postulated that the self is established by perception;
for the 'I-notion' (ahaṅkāra) is self-cognized, and it is held that the self is its object."

For they say this: the self is established by direct perception itself; for thus, the cognition "I," which does not depend on the recollection of the relationship between a mark and the bearer of the mark, is a direct perception, like the cognition of color and so forth.
And its object is not color and so forth, because it appears as distinct from the cognition of those [objects].
Therefore, the object must be something else entirely.
He refutes this with the words "That is incorrect," and so forth:
"That is incorrect because that form does not appear in the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
for the manifestation of permanence, omnipresence, and so on is not observed therein."
The appearance of a white color and so forth is clearly present therein;
however, the self is not accepted as having that nature, and therefore this [self] is not the object of that [appearance].

The fact that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) has the self as its object is unestablished, because it is devoid of the form of that [self]. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is devoid of the form of something does not have that thing as its object;
for example, visual cognition does not have sound as its object.
"The cognition 'I' is empty of the form of a self" is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

He shows that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*) with the words "for indeed," and so forth. For instance, the self is held to be endowed with qualities such as permanence, omnipresence, and consciousness.
Furthermore, in this notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya), no manifestation of permanence or similar qualities is observed.

Rather, because it arises in contact with the states of the body—such as "I am fair," "I have weak eyes," "I am emaciated," or "I am pierced by intense pain"—the manifestation characterized by a fair complexion and so forth is perceived.
Therefore, it is understood that the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), arising in contact with the states of the body and so on, has the body and such as its very objective support.
"Manifestly" means clearly, because its operation is unerring. Consequently,

as for what was stated by Uddyotakara and others— that this is a metaphorical designation of the self (*ātma-upacāra*) with respect to the body, which is the locus of experience— just as one says of a compliant servant, "He who is I, he is this very servant of mine."
That [objection] is refuted.
For if this were secondary (gauṇa), then its application would be faltering;
for in the world, when both "lion" and "boy"—the primary and the superimposed—are present, the cognition "lion" does not arise unfalteringly with respect to both.
If it is argued that the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) has a faltering application toward the body and so forth because of the perception of their difference— expressed as "the body and so forth are mine"—
we say no; for then it would follow that it must also have a faltering application toward the self (*ātman*).
For even there, the distinction "this is my self" is observed.
If you argue that the difference in this case is merely imagined,
let it be the same in the other case as well.

If that is so, then the cognition "I am fair-complexioned" and so forth is primary; nevertheless, why is the self not its object? To this he says: "Because it has that as its nature. That is, it has the nature of being fair-complexioned and so forth, because the qualities such as color and form are impossible for the self. //213-1//
Thus, it has first been described that the notion of "I" (ahaṅkāra) cannot have the self as its object because the self lacks any form;
furthermore, he shows that it is not tenable [as an object] because it would follow that there could be no dispute regarding it, starting with the words "If," and so forth:
"If the person were truly accessible through direct perception..."
Therefore, for what purpose does this dispute proceed regarding that existence and so forth?
Regarding that self's existence, permanence, omnipresence, and so forth.

It might be argued: "Just as for you [Buddhists], even though blue and so forth are directly perceived, a dispute still arises regarding their momentariness and other qualities that are not distinct from their own nature, so it will be with respect to the self as well. To this he says, "For thus," and so forth: "For this very reason, this ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) proceeds as having the nature of ascertainment (*niścaya*)."
And the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is established between the cognitions of certainty and superimposition.

For it is indeed reasonable that there should be dispute regarding momentariness and other such qualities—which are non-different from the blue and so forth—even when they have been apprehended by perception; this is because that perception, being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), is not determinative, and thus momentariness and the like remain undetermined. But in your position, such dispute is not reasonable, because the notion of "I" (*ahampratyaya*) is conceptual and thus determinative in nature, whereby the self is determined. Furthermore, once an object has been made the content of a cognition through determination, there can be no occurrence of a superimposing cognition (*samāropa-pratyaya*) that grasps a form contrary to it, such that a dispute could arise.

Because these two exist simultaneously, they stand in a relationship of the sublated and the sublator. For this indeed is the comprehension of their own objects by determinations: namely, that they determine them. If they do not determine [them], it follows that they do not apprehend them at all.
Having thus refuted the opposing position and establishing his own, he says "therefore," and so forth:
"Therefore, desire and all the rest do not inhere in a self,
because they arise sequentially, like seeds, sprouts, creepers, and so on."
Alternatively, all internal [phenomena] have their forms overcome by selflessness,
because of reasons such as being real entities and so forth, just like external things such as jars.

The formal argument is as follows: those things which arise sequentially do not inhere in a self, just like seeds, sprouts, creepers, and so forth; and pleasure and other such states arise sequentially. This is because of the perception of a pervasion by the opposite [of the probandum]. Since sequential arising is pervaded by non-inherence in a self—which is the opposite of inherence in a self—the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the contrary position is the undesirable consequence that they would have to arise simultaneously, given that their complete causes are present.

Alternatively, whatever things are endowed with properties such as substantiality (*vastutva*), being produced (*kṛtakatva*), or having an origin (*utpattimattva*), all those are devoid of a self (*nirātman*), just like external objects such as jars; and internal entities such as the living body, mind, intellect, pain, and pleasure are likewise endowed with properties such as substantiality. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
To explain how the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in this case is established, he says "sātmakatva" and so forth.

For if they possessed a self, it would follow that their causes are eternal; and since eternal things lack the capacity for causal efficiency, existence and other such properties cannot arise from them.
If the body and so forth were possessed of a self—that is, if they were presided over by a self—then the self would be their cause.
For it is not logical that a non-cause should be a presider, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Consequently, since the causes of those things such as the body which have the self as their cause would possess unimpaired causal conditions, it would follow that they are eternal and lack succession.

It might be argued: "Even if their permanence were to follow as a consequence, nevertheless, their status as real entities (*vastutva*) and so forth would still persist. To this he replies with the words "And being permanent," and so on.

The phrase "being permanent, they would consequently be incapable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) regarding the body and other things" connects to the subject at hand by means of an implied change in the verbal construction. The underlying intention is that for a permanent entity, purposeful action is contradictory whether it occurs successively or simultaneously.

And when the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya) ceases, the status of being a real entity (vastutva) also ceases, because the definition of a real entity is precisely the capacity for causal efficiency.
When the status of being a real entity ceases, there is also the cessation of existence and other such properties that belong to real entities; thus, the pervasion (vyāpti) is established.
Uddyotakara, however, says: "Now, what is the meaning intended as the probandum by the term 'selflessness' (*nirātmakatva*)?
If it means that [the self] is not assisted by anything, then there is no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), for nothing whatsoever exists that does not assist the self."

Now, regarding the negation of the self (*ātman*): [the statement] "the self is not the body" implies whose self is the body? Furthermore, because the negative particle *nis-* has the subsequent word as its scope, one must state what it is that possesses a self (*sātmaka*).
For we do not observe the use of *nis-* when there is no subsequent word, such as in the case of *nirmakṣika* ("free from flies").
Now, if you are refuting the body as the self, you are proving what is already established.
Or for whom does the body exist as a self?
Or [if you mean that] the body exists through its connection with a self?
Furthermore, there is no further example;
all these are negations of specific attributes, and from the negation of specific attributes, the general is understood.
This being the case, that which was intended to be negated becomes effectively admitted.
Now, if it is argued that the word "self" (ātman) has an impermanent object because it is a word,
even so, this reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to the existence of eternal words.
Furthermore, since the body and so forth are designated by the term "self" through figurative usage (upacāra), the argument results in proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).

Now, if it is argued that the word "self" (ātman) is established as having impermanent objects because its referent is an impermanent entity distinct from the body and so forth, even so, there is a contradiction because one must admit that its object is something distinct from form (rūpa) and the other aggregates. He refutes this with the passage beginning "In the case of jars, etc. (ghaṭādiṣu).
And that very selflessness which is denied by others in the case of jars and the like is established by those who identify with the self in this body.

This same objection applies equally to you as well. For instance, you also certainly accept that external objects such as jars are devoid of self (*nairātmya*), either because they are not presided over by a self or because they are not the locus for its enjoyment. Otherwise, they could not be employed as examples in the following reductio argument: "This living body is not devoid of a self, for if it were, it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth, like a jar. Thus, their inclusion as examples in that argument would be impossible.
Consequently, the same objection applies even in that case regarding jars and so forth: "How can these be selfless (nairātmya) if the self does not benefit them," and so on.

Therefore, in whatever manner it may be—whether by way of not being presided over by a self or by not being a locus for its enjoyment—the property of selflessness is established as common to all those external things, such as jars, even according to your own [position].

And as for that which you deny regarding the living body—namely, "this living body is not soulless"—and by the denial of which the living body alone is accepted as possessing a self, while dead bodies, jars, and so forth are not, that very point is what we are establishing: that the living body is soulless because of its being a functional entity (*vastu*) and so on.
Therefore, the alternative arguments such as "it provides no benefit to the self" are entirely baseless even for you, since the absence of a self (*nairātmya*) is already established.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that there is no illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for proving that the self receives no benefit—that is incorrect.

For it is indeed possible to establish this: that which does not bestow a specific excellence of nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) upon another is not a benefactor of that other, just as the Vindhya mountains are not a benefactor of the Himalayas; and since the body and so forth do not bestow a specific excellence of nature upon the self—which is eternal and of a single form—there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because a specific excellence of nature is not distinct from the self itself.
If that [quality] were to be produced, it would be the production of the self itself;
and from that, the consequence of impermanence would follow.

Furthermore, if there were a distinction [between the self and the quality], since there would be no basis for a relation between the essential nature and the excellence [of the quality], the relation "this belongs to that" could not be established.
Therefore, no benefactor can exist for that which is eternal, because such a benefactor would have no effect upon it.
Furthermore, as for what was said—"Whose body is the self?"—that too is incorrect;
for there are indeed some who describe the body and so forth as being of the nature of transformations of the self.
This is as in the case of the followers of the Upaniṣads;
therefore, they are refuted.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that because the negative particle *nis-* has as its object the meaning of the subsequent word, one must state "Is it with a self?"—[that is now addressed].
That too is inconsistent;
for it is not the actually existing referent of the second member of the compound that is negated,
but rather that which has been superimposed.
Because that which exists cannot be negated,
that very object which has been superimposed by the other [opponent] through delusion becomes the referent of the subsequent word;
for it is precisely by restating that [object] that the negation is performed in order to demonstrate the erroneous nature of the other's cognition.

Otherwise, when you negate the momentariness imagined by the Buddhists in such statements as "lamps and the like are non-momentary," this very objection would indeed apply: "For we do not see the use of the word *naṭa* (actor) when the subsequent term [to be negated] is absent.
Furthermore, what was said—"In whose body does the self exist?"—is also incorrect.

For according to those whose view is that the self is the size of half a thumb-joint or the fruit of the *śyāmāka* grain, the self possesses form (*mūrtatva*); thus, for them, its residence in the body certainly exists, and therefore a negation directed at them is entirely appropriate.
As for what was said—that there is no illustrative example for the negation of the body’s relation to the self—that is unproven;

for it can be established, as before, that there is no relation between the self and the body, just as there is none between the Vindhya and Himalaya mountains, because they lack the mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary.
Furthermore, the claim that a general principle is implied by the negation of specific instances is inconclusive.
Even if you were to refute the momentariness of lamps and such things, you would still not accept the general property of momentariness for anything at all.

Now, it might be argued: "We certainly do accept that the application of the word 'momentary' to lamps and the like is based on their persisting for only a short time; therefore, momentariness is indeed established in a general sense.

If this is so, then we too certainly accept the application of the word 'self' (ātman) to the mind when it is conjoined with the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); thus, the self is established in a general sense.
Furthermore, as for the two positions previously stated— that the word "self" (ātman) has impermanence as its referent, and so forth— that too is entirely inconsistent,
because it is not accepted.
For no referent of the word "self" is accepted as existing in an ultimate sense.
Nor is it distinct from form and the other aggregates.
Furthermore, the application of the word "eternal" to any eternal entity in an ultimate sense is not established such that there would be a deviation [from the rule].

Nor is it the case that the word "self" applies metaphorically to the body and so forth because its usage is unerring; this has already been stated. Therefore, this is not a proof of what is already established.
And thus, since the self is not established, every process that has been formulated regarding it stands entirely without foundation, like the son of a barren woman.

Thus, since the substratum (dharmin) called the "self" is unestablished because it is contradicted by valid cognition (pramāṇa), the framework of agency, enjoyership, and so forth that you have metaphorically attributed to it is baseless like the son of a barren woman; therefore, no separate refutation of this framework is made here.
It has already been rejected by the refutation of its very locus.

Furthermore, as to how the faults of the loss of what was done (kṛtanāśa) and the acquisition of what was not done (akṛtābhyāgama) do not occur, that will be demonstrated in the examination of the connection between action and its fruit.
Thus concludes the examination of the self as conceived by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas.
The examination of the self as conceived by the Mīmāṃsakas,

which is the refutation of the self imagined by the Mīmāṃsakas, is stated beginning with the words "having the nature of exclusion and inclusion," etc.: "Furthermore, others [assert] a self that has the nature of exclusion and inclusion."
They maintain that consciousness is of the nature of sentience, and that sentience is characterized by the intellect (buddhi).

*Vyāvṛtti* refers to the mutual distinctions between states such as pleasure and pain; *anugama* refers to the persistence of [qualities] such as consciousness (*caitanya*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and existence (*sattva*). The analysis of the compound is: "that whose nature (*ātman*) or essence consists of these two, exclusion and persistence. What is meant is this: others, namely the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas), describe the self (*ātman*) as being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), excluded in the form of pleasure and so forth, yet persisting in the form of existence and so forth. Furthermore, they maintain that this consciousness is not something other than the intellect (*buddhi*), as is asserted by the Sāṅkhyas; rather, it shows that consciousness is nothing but the intellect itself, stating: "consciousness has the intellect as its defining characteristic."
The meaning is that the "characteristic of cognition" (buddhilakṣaṇam) is the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of cognition;
the intention is that nothing other than cognition is perceived as having the nature of consciousness (cidrūpatva).

But how is it possible for a single self to possess two mutually contradictory natures—one characterized by exclusion (vyāvṛtti) and the other by inclusion (anugama)? To this he says: "Just as of a snake," and so forth.
Just as the coiled state of a snake disappears immediately thereafter, [so too does its previous form].
The state of straightness arises, yet the nature of being a serpent persists.
In the same way, for the self whose nature is eternal consciousness,
there is neither a total disappearance of its form nor a universal pervasion of it.
However, its states characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth, cease and arise; yet consciousness persists throughout.

Just as, for instance, in the case of a single serpent, when its coiled state ceases there is the manifestation of a straightened state, yet its nature as a serpent persists through both states; so too, although the Self is a single entity whose nature is eternal consciousness, there is neither a total disappearance of its nature nor—like the self imagined by the Naiyāyikas and others—a persistence of every [transient] attribute. Rather, states such as pleasure cease and arise, while the form of consciousness persists throughout all of them. Therefore, there is no contradiction; this is the collective meaning.
The meaning of the individual components is now stated: "of that whose nature is eternal consciousness.
The analysis of the compound is: "that of which eternal consciousness is the nature.
Regarding the word "of all": [it refers to all objects].
The word "of form" (rūpasya) is to be supplied as the remainder. As for the phrase "or even following," it is connected with the preceding "no" (na).
"And those" refers to the states of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

Now, why is the position of absolute exclusion alone not adopted—as is desired by the Buddhists who propound non-concomitant destruction—or why is absolute persistence not adopted—as is resorted to by the Naiyāyikas and others? To this he says: "They would both be," and so on.
For if there were absolute destruction, there would be the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done;
furthermore, the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth could not occur for that which is of a single, unchanging nature.
For if destruction were without any continuity (niranvaya), then there would be the destruction of performed karma, because the agent would have no connection with the fruit.
Furthermore, there would be the acquisition of what was not done, because one who did not perform the action would be connected with its fruit.
Moreover, if the self were of a single uniform nature, there could be no experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, just as in the case of space.
Because there is no distinction between the state of being a non-experiencer and the state of being an experiencer.
And so it has been said by Kumārila:
"Therefore, by the abandonment of both [extremes], [the self] consists of exclusion and inclusion."
A person must be admitted [as the underlying reality], just as a snake is [admitted] in the case of its coils and so forth.
Thus it is said in the *Ślokavārttika*.

But surely, if the person possesses both natures, that state which is the agent is not the experiencer; thus, even here, the faults of the destruction of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) would follow. To this he says "And not," and so forth:
"And agency and experience do not depend upon a state of the person. Therefore, because the person is identical [to itself] throughout the states, the agent alone obtains that fruit."
For agency and enjoyership do not depend upon a state, but rather upon the person (*puruṣa*) alone.

Since it is the person himself who acts and enjoys, and not the state, therefore—because the person who possesses the state remains identical in essence and does not abandon his prior nature—it is the agent alone who obtains the fruit of that action; thus there is no fault.

Furthermore, what is the proof that establishes the existence of this self? He says: "A person"—for such a person is established by the existence of recognition; and indeed, by this very same [recognition], the doctrine of no-self is refuted.

The self is established because of the existence of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) directed toward a single agent, such as "I myself have known" and "I myself know. Furthermore, by this very recognition, the refutation of the doctrine of no-self (*nairātmya*) imagined by the Buddhists and others is also established, as it has been said: "Therefore, the self [is proven] from recognition, which is determined by all the world."
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the doctrine of selflessness.
But how, then, is this pair established through the cognition of recognition? To this he says, "I," and so forth:
"The notion of 'I' in the form 'I know' refers to a knower;
and that [knower] must be either the self or a cognition that is absolutely perishable."
If the self were the object of that [cognition], then everything would be consistent;
however, on the view that cognition is momentary, everything is utterly untenable.
For instance, there arises the cognition: "I myself knew [it] previously, and now I myself perceive it."
What object, indeed, is conceived for that moment of cognition:
is it the past, or the present, or perhaps the continuum itself?
In that case, when the first object has been known, it is appropriate to say "I have known it"; however, it is not appropriate to say "I know it," because he does not know it at this present moment.
Regarding a present object, it is appropriate to say "I perceive";
however, to say "I have known" is untrue, because this [object] did not exist previously.
For this very reason, a duality of objects of apprehension is not at all postulated for that [cognition];
for neither have both [the subject and object] already known it, nor do they know it now.
The continuum, moreover, is not external to those [two], because both [an external entity and its cognition] are impossible;
for it did not know [the object] previously due to its non-substantiality, nor does it know it now.
Therefore, that object-sphere in which this ego-conception operates—
distinct from what has been previously described— is established as a self possessing an eternal nature.

There is no dispute at all regarding the point that this "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), expressed as "I know," refers to a knower, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the agentive suffix in "I know.
