And as for that knower, there are only two possible conceptualizations: either it is the Self (*ātman*), or it is the cognition (*jñāna*) imagined by you to be exclusively perishable and momentary.
In that regard, if the position is that it is the Self, then everything is perfectly consistent, since the desired object is thereby established.

Now, if the position is that [the object] is cognition (*jñāna*), then everything becomes extremely difficult to establish. To explain: regarding this "I-consciousness" (*ahambuddhi*) which arises through the recognition of a single agent in the form, "I have known" and "I myself now know," if one considers the moment of cognition as its object, there are four possible positions: it may be conceived as (1) past, or (2) present, or (3) both past and present, or (4) a continuum (*santati*).

Among these, in the first case, when a past cognition is conceived as the object, the determination of the form "I have known" is logical, because [the object] was previously known by that [past cognition].

However, it is not tenable to say "I know [it] now," for this [cognition] does not know [the object] at the present time, since that moment of cognition has already ceased. If, on the other hand, the second position is taken—that the object is present—then it is appropriate to say "I know [it]," because it is currently performing the act of knowing.
But to grasp the form of the cognition as "I have known" is not tenable.
Why? Because this did not exist previously;
"this" refers to present cognition.

For this very reason, since this intellect functions by turning away [from the past], it is established that the two types of consciousness—the past and the present—are not its objects of apprehension.

For it is not the case that both the present and the past possess the characteristic of cognition such that they have known [the object], nor do they know it at the present moment. Rather, one has known it and the other knows it. For this very reason, even the continuum (*santāna*) cannot be grasped by that notion of "I," because the two-fold activity of cognition—the past and the present—is impossible for a single entity.

For this reason, that continuum did not know [the object] previously, nor does it know it now, because, being conceptually constructed, it lacks substantial reality; and a non-substantial entity cannot possess the quality of knowing, since knowing is a property of a real entity. Therefore, it is established that the "self" is that object upon which this ego-conception operates, distinct from the aforementioned cognition. Now, he explains how its eternal nature is established with the words beginning "vyatīta... (passed away, etc.).
And the primordial knower, though its egoity has passed away, continues even now,
because it is accessible through the notion of "I," just like the cognizer of the present moment.
Or rather, this present knower is indeed the same as the knower of yesterday because he possesses the quality of being a knower;
for that very reason, those cognitions [of yesterday] are established as having the same status as the present ones.
That which is accessible through the notion of "I" continues even today, just like the cognizer of the present moment.
And this present cognizer is accessible through the notion of "I"; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Or rather, it is as follows:
The present cognizer [is known] from that very [source],
because he is accessible through the notion of "I."

Having thus presented the formal argument by taking the cognizer as the subject (dharmin), he now states "of those" and so forth, showing another formal argument by taking the "I-notions" themselves as the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmitā).
"Of those" refers to the various "I-notions" belonging to the past and so on; [the phrase] "the state of being the thesis" [refers to their being the subject].
The meaning is "having the property-possessor that is the subject of the thesis" (sādhyadharmin).
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because they are cognitions of 'I' belonging to a knower connected to a single continuum,
all [cognitions] of yesterday and today have the same object, like a single cognition."
"All [cognitions] of yesterday and today are 'I-notions'—this is the statement of the subject (*sādhyadharmin*).
'Having the same object' is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). 'Having a single object' is the meaning."

The state of being that [nature] (*tattva*) belongs to those notions of "I" (*ahampratyaya*) which are connected to a single continuum—that is, to the cognizer who is linked to a single continuum such as Devadatta—or to the cognizer himself;
this is the indication of the reason (*hetu*).

Since the mere quality of being a notion of "I" (*ahampratyayatvamātra*) also occurs in the ego-notions of other persons, the qualification "having as its object a cognizer connected to a single continuum" is added to the reason in order to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
"Like a single cognition" is the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).
The meaning is: "like one specific cognition intended among those very same cognitions of 'I'."
With the words "Therefore, in this regard," etc., he begins the refutation:
"In this matter, it is considered that consciousness is held to be eternal and unitary;
if that were so, then even the intellect would necessarily be of that same nature."

For if consciousness (*caitanya*) is admitted to be eternal and of a single uniform nature, then cognition (*buddhi*)—being non-different from the nature of consciousness—would necessarily follow as being eternal and of a single uniform nature. This is not desired; therefore, there is a contradiction with the initial proposition (*pratijñā*).
Thus, it has been stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "For that [cognition] is momentary; it does not persist until the time of another cognition."
Likewise, Jaimini also stated: "When there is contact of a person's sense-faculties with an existing object, the arising of cognition is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Since arising is incompatible with eternity, Kumārila’s own statement contradicts himself, as he himself has said: [as stated by him].
For that [cognition] does not remain even for a moment, nor is it produced as something non-cognitive,
such that it might subsequently function in the apprehension of an object like the sense organs and so forth.
Thus, because cognition is unitary, there is a contradiction with the acceptance of six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Likewise, there is also a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because when one reflects on various kinds of objects presented in immediate succession, cognitions that are associated with arising and passing away are experienced with extreme clarity.
But Kumārila, seeing no such mass of contradictions, says "of cognitions," and so forth:
"Since both cognitions and the person possess the nature of consciousness, they are held to be eternal and unitary; if there is any distinction, it is based on their objects."

The eternity and unity of cognitions (*buddhi*) and the Person (*puruṣa*) are asserted because their essential nature is consciousness (*caitanya-svābhāvya*); that is to say, according to our view, the essential nature of the Person is consciousness characterized as cognition. If one asks, "In that case, how is a distinction perceived, such as 'the cognition of form' or 'the cognition of taste'? he replies: "If the distinction is based on the objects. The word "if" (*cet*) indicates an acceptance of the opponent's position.
The meaning is: "if it is conceived in this way."

It might be argued: "If cognition is eternal and unitary, then why does it apprehend color and other objects sequentially? It should rather apprehend them all at once, since there is no difference [in its nature]. To this he says: "By its own nature," and so forth. Just as fire is eternally characterized by the property of burning by its very nature...
It burns the fuel that has been brought near; it does not burn anything else, nor does it fail to burn when other [fuel] is present.
Just as fire, although its nature is eternally that of burning, does not burn at all times, but rather burns only what is brought near or presented;
and even there, it burns only that which is combustible and capable of being burned, and not things such as clouds—therefore, he says "the combustible."
With the words "Or just as," etc., he states another example:
"Just as a mirror that is clear, or just as a crystal stone,
assumes the reflection of whatever is placed before it."
In the same way, the person, who is eternally conscious, perceives forms and other objects brought by the instruments through the functions of the body; and this, O wise one, is our view.
It is said to be "clear" because there is no perception of a reflection in what is turbid.
"Is placed" (ādhīyate) means "is brought near" (ḍhaukyate).
The phrase "in that very way" indicates the application of the example.

Although individual souls (*puruṣa*) are all-pervading, nevertheless, by the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), they reside only within the body and perceive objects brought to them by the instruments such as the eyes, and not elsewhere.
As for this eternal consciousness, that is our *dhī* (intellect); it is *buddhi*, but unlike the Sāṅkhya school, it is not a *buddhi* distinct from that [consciousness].

Anticipating the objection, "If this is so, how is it well-known that this cognition is transitory?", he demonstrates the very reason indicated by the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, thereby establishing the transitoriness of cognition: "Because of the transitoriness of the exertion of the agent who brings [the object] near, the cognition is transitory; just as fire is not always a burner when the fuel to be burned is absent."

The "conveyors" (*upanetāraḥ*) are the eyes and other sense organs, which bring about the objects such as form and so forth. Their "activity" (*saṃrambhaḥ*) is their functional operation; because that activity is "transient" (*bhaṅgitvāt*), meaning perishable, the cognition is observed to be transient. However, this [cognition] is not perishable by its own nature.

If it were not perishable by its own nature, then it would perceive every object simultaneously, and thus the objection remains exactly as before. To this, he says: "It does not burn eternally," and so forth.
Likewise, the intellect does not perceive every object permanently; the point is that at all times, every object is not present.
Now, as to how its permanence is understood, he says "In that regard" and so forth:
"In that regard, cognition is recognized through its nature as consciousness;
its status as the cognition of a jar, an elephant, and so on, is considered by the world to be due to its differentiation [by objects]."
The word "therein" (*tatra*) is used to introduce the statement.
Cognition (*buddhi*) is called "cognition" because its essence is awareness; since it is recognized as such [across time], cognition is eternal, like sound.

If this is so, one might ask: how is it that this distinction among cognitions—such as "this is the cognition of a jar" and "this is the cognition of a cloth"—is accepted by those who perceive them in the world? To this, he says "the jar," and so forth.
"Due to its differentiation" means due to the differentiation of jars, elephants, and so forth.
With the words "That very [cognition]," and so forth, he clarifies this very point:
"Those who follow the distinction between objects do not say that the cognition is that very same [one];
nor is there a lack of recognition when a distinction between objects is relied upon."
"By those who follow the distinctions of objects" means by the cognizers.
By this, he demonstrates through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the distinction in cognition is produced solely by the distinction of objects.
"And there is no non-recognition" means that recognition certainly exists.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely): "But surely,
on a ground devoid of elephants and the like, what is the basis for the distinction among those cognitions that arise as superimpositions?"

For if the difference in cognition were caused solely by a difference in the object, then in those cognitions which arise by sequentially superimposing elephants, horses, and so forth upon a ground that is actually devoid of them—on what basis would their difference be perceived?
The point is that there is no basis whatsoever for establishing a difference.
This is because there is no difference [in the cognitions] in themselves.
This is because the Śrāvakas accept the oneness [of consciousness],
nor is it due to the diversity of objects acting as conditions, since there is no separate entity whatsoever that could act as such a condition.
It might be argued that [the claim] "it is devoid of an object" is unestablished; for it has been stated by Kumārila:
"In cognitions such as dreams, an external object is by no means denied;
in every case, the external is the objective support (ālambana), though its nature differs according to place and time."
Thus, he raises this very doubt with the words "occurring in another place," and so forth:
"If individual instances occurring in other places and so on are the basis [of cognition],
then everything would be the objective support (ālambana), because [the object] consists of different places, times, and natures."
"Grounding cause" (*nibandhana*) means the cause for the determination of distinctions by the intellect.
That which has space and time as its contrary nature—that is, having different modes—is so described; or, the analysis of the compound is "that whose nature is otherwise due to space and time."
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely):
"But surely, those [cognitions] do not have a connection with that place in that manner;
why then do they appear there in that form?"

For in whatever place and by whatever sequence those individuals were superimposed, they appear [now] with that same place and sequence; yet, for those [individuals] which have moved to other places and other times, such a connection with that place and sequence does not exist. So why do they appear in that form superimposed according to one's own whim?
Indeed, it is not logical for one thing to appear in the form of another, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For if this were so, it would follow that every cognition would have everything as its object.
And consequently, there would be the total destruction of the established order of specific objects.
For in your view, no form belongs to the cognition itself; rather, it is described as external.
Furthermore, elephants, pillars, and so forth do not exist in the specific location intended [by the cognition].
Furthermore, in your view as a Mīmāṃsaka, that form which appears does not belong to the cognition; rather, it is described as having the nature of an external object, according to the statement:
"The external object possesses form, while cognition is formless.
If this is indeed the case, what follows? To this he says: "Not intended," and so forth.
The location intended is that where the superimposition has been made;
consequently, those elephants and so forth, being connected to that specific place and time, would appear as being connected to that very place.
But why do they appear in another place and at another time, which are devoid of themselves?

Therefore, it is established that these conditions (*pratyaya*) are indeed without objective support (*nirālambana*), possessing in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) unmixed natures and a mobile essence, because they are occasional (*kādācitkatva*). Furthermore, once it is established that the person (*puruṣa*) has as its nature [these conditions] and is thus impermanent and manifold, one might think: "The condition is a property (*dharma*) of that person; therefore, even though there is a difference in that [property], there is no difference in the person, because it is the substratum (*dharmin*) of that [property]."
That is incorrect, because "cognition" (*pratyaya*), "consciousness" (*caitanya*), "intellect" (*buddhi*), and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) are not different in meaning.
For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things does not differ merely by a difference in names.
Furthermore, even though there is a difference in names, it is indeed accepted that those cognitions possess a single, underlying form whose essence is consciousness (*caitanyātmaka*).
And since that consciousness is non-different, there is likewise no division among the cognitions, which have that as their intrinsic nature;
for otherwise, due to the imposition of contradictory properties, there would necessarily be a total difference.
By this very demonstration that cognitions are without external objects, the non-perceptibility of cognition has been refuted.

For it has been established that this manifest form is not an external object such as an elephant; therefore, cognitions which apprehend that manifest form as being their very own nature are proven to be of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), because they are self-luminous in essence.

Regarding what was stated [at p. 102], "Just as [it exists] externally in its own form," and so forth; in order to refute that, he says here, beginning with "sarvārtha... (if cognition, whose nature is the awareness of all objects, were always present):
"If cognition, whose nature is the awareness of all objects, were always present,"
Since there is always the cognition of everything, for what reason is it not perceived?
If cognition were always established as having the nature of perceiving all objects, then it would follow that there would be perception of all objects at all times.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"That cognition which has sound as its adjunct and has taste, color, and so forth as its object-domain—
it is that very same [cognition]," provided that no difference [between them] has been established by you.

For instance, the cognition that has sound as its adjunct and sound as its object is itself the cognition that has taste, form, and so forth as its objects, and not another. Consequently, at the time of experiencing one object, there would follow the undesirable consequence of experiencing all objects, because the cognition whose nature is the apprehension of those [other] objects is always present.
As it has been said:
"If multiple cognitions were produced by a single [cause], then that [cognition] would perceive them all simultaneously."
Since there is no distinction [between them], let it not be that even in succession there is no such distinction.
Thus [it is said]:

"If not" means that if the cognition conditioned by sound is not admitted to be the very same cognition whose object is taste and so forth, then the distinction between cognitions would be established by your own words.
Showing that this example of fire is also unestablished (*asiddha*), he says "samasta" and so forth:
"Even fire does not eternally have the nature of burning all combustible forms;
otherwise, it would be reduced to ashes without remainder."

For fire, whose nature is to burn all combustible things, does not remain eternally established [in its burning state]; otherwise, every combustible object would be reduced to ashes, because—just like a combustible object currently in contact with the flames of fire—it would have its own burner perpetually present.
By the word "also" (api), he shows that it is not only cognition that does not have the nature of cognizing all objects.
If fire were thus not eternally of the nature of burning, how then could it burn an object even when brought near? To this he says: "In the proximity of the object to be burned," and so forth.
Only in the presence of an object to be burned does its nature as a burner of that object occur;
for otherwise, the burning of all objects would logically happen all at once, which is not observed.
"Thus" means:
when the meaning just stated is accepted, the burning of all objects does not occur, nor is it entailed, simultaneously—this is the meaning.
And as for what was said, beginning with "or as in the case of a mirror," and so forth.
Showing that even this is not tenable if the mirror and so forth possess a permanent, unitary nature, he says:
"Due to connection with a blue lotus," and so forth:
due to connection with a blue lotus and the like, mirrors, crystals, and other such objects [assume that color].
They are momentary perishing entities, which serve as the causes for the arising of the illusion of their own shadow.
Since it is always one and the same, whether in a state with a support or otherwise, it would either always appear as having that shadow or as being devoid of it; otherwise, it could not be so.

A crystal, a mirror, and the like, being subject to destruction at every moment, exercise a dominant influence (*ādhipatya*) in the production of erroneous cognition through contact with objects such as a blue lotus.

Otherwise, if they were non-momentary and yet were to receive a reflection, then—given that the very same entity exists both in the state of having an adjunct (*sopadhāna*) and in the state of lacking an adjunct (*anupadhāna*)—the reflection of blue and so forth would be perceived even when separated from the adjunct of blue and so on, because it has not abandoned its previous form.
Alternatively, even in the state of having an adjunct, it would be seen devoid of the form of blue and so forth, because there is no difference from its previous form.
By this, the perception of reflections by all things whatsoever—such as crystals, mirrors, and the like—is generally refuted under the non-momentary position.
Now, he refutes the perception of reflections individually for both the momentary and non-momentary positions, beginning with the words "Because of stability," and so forth:
"Because of stability, because of being partless, and because material objects cannot coexist..."
It never reflects an image upon the surface of a mirror.
Because it is stable, it is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*); the connection is that the surface of the mirror bears the previous reflection.
Even if it were momentary, one must connect [the argument] by saying it does not bear [the reflection] because it is partless (*nirvibhāga*).

For instance, like water inside a well, the reflection is perceived as being situated within the surface of the mirror; yet there is no division or cavity in the mirror's surface, because its constituent parts are arranged in an extremely dense manner. Therefore, this is an illusion.
Alternatively, "being without division" means the absence of difference between the prior and subsequent states;
the reason for this is "because of stability. By this, the following meaning is established:
The meaning is that because it is stable and indivisible, it is devoid of prior and subsequent states.
Furthermore, since corporeal things cannot coexist, it follows that the surface of the mirror does not actually bear a reflection.

For indeed, on the surface of the mirror, reflections of mountains and so forth are perceived as occupying that very same space; yet corporeal objects never attain the state of occupying a single location, for that would entail the consequence of their becoming one and the same entity (*aikātmya*).
And this is a refutation common to both the positions of momentariness and non-momentariness.

He shows that even for crystal, there is no actual apprehension of the reflection of an adjacent object by means of the verse beginning with "pārśva" and so forth: "And when two sides of a very white crystal stone are observed, it [is not truly colored], because this too does not actually apprehend the reflection."

For instance, if a perceiver standing in front perceives a crystal as red due to contact with a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*), at that very moment those standing on both sides perceive the entire crystal stone as purely white, not in parts.

Consequently, if there were a perception of a shadow [of the color], then for those standing on both sides, just as for the person standing in front, there would have been a perception appearing as red.
And this is a defect common to both the position that [the entity] is momentary and the position that it is non-momentary.
With the words "Difference [and] with each substrate," etc., he states the fault specifically in the case of non-momentariness:
"Difference would follow for the crystal and so forth with each substrate;
if its cognition of that reflection were real."

For if, in ultimate reality, there were an apprehension of the coloring [imposed] by an adjunct upon a crystal or similar object, then—just as the successive reflections produced by various adjuncts would lack a single nature due to the difference in their own natures—it would follow that the crystal itself, being identical with those [reflections], would also undergo differentiation with respect to each successive adjunct. However, if it is admitted that this is an illusion, then this fault does not arise; it is for the purpose of making this known that he says "real" (*tātvikī*).
Therefore, this is an illusion regarding those [objects] which possess diverse and inconceivable powers.
Since, in this way, the perception of a reflection is not tenable in either of the two positions, it is established that "this is an illusion.
If this is so, why does that illusion occur only in the case of crystal and the like, and not in the case of a wall and so forth? To this he says: "possessing diverse and inconceivable powers."
"Variegated" means of various kinds; those whose powers are "inconceivable" are so described.

Indeed, the specific determination of the powers of entities does not admit of questioning, because that [determination] is produced by a succession of their own causes. Furthermore, you yourselves have no dispute on this point.
As it has been said: "Fire burns, but space does not; who can be questioned about this?

If that is so, then even in the case of cognition (*buddhi*), let the apprehension of the reflection of an object be merely an error; let there be no actual apprehension of a reflection. To this he replies:
"Even the existence of error in cognition is not logical, because of the absence of differentiation."
The existence of error within cognition is not tenable;
the word "also" implies that it is not only the perception of a reflection that is untenable.
Why?
"Due to the absence of differentiation," that is, because of the non-existence of difference.

For an error is possible in the case of crystals and the like, since an erroneous cognition distinct from them can occur; however, there is no other cognition in the form of an error within cognition itself, because cognition is held to be unitary. Nor is it reasonable to say that cognition arises as an error by its own nature, because cognition is admitted to be eternal.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated—that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) occurs there by way of having cognition as its essence in order to establish unity and permanence—he replies with the verse beginning "But the distinction of non-cognition... and so forth: "But having superimposed a distinction consisting of non-cognition, which is common to all cognitions, recognition proceeds even though there is multiplicity."

This recognition is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for it is not contradictory that recognition proceeds even when there is diversity among all cognitions, provided that one superimposes a distinction—that is, an exclusion—from jars and other objects which consist of the nature of awareness.

Indeed, this must necessarily be understood: that this recognition is based on the exclusion of heterogeneous things (*vijātīya-vyāvṛtti*) precisely when there is diversity, and not when there is non-diversity.

For instance, in the case of superimposing cognitions that lack a real objective basis (*nirālambana*), non-recognition (*apratyabhijñāna*) certainly occurs even when no difference in object is resorted to; for it does not occur there that "the very cognition that was of an elephant is the same as the cognition of a horse or a chariot.
Furthermore, since the lack of an objective basis for these cognitions has already been established, it will not be stated again.
Therefore, what was asserted—that "there is no non-recognition when no difference in object is resorted to"—must be understood as unproven (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, if you maintain that the self is eternal and of a single uniform nature, then the distinction between states such as pleasure and so forth would not be possible.
If, however, the distinction between states such as pleasure and so forth is admitted, then its being eternal and of a single uniform nature must not be accepted.
For it is not logical for a single entity to possess two mutually contradictory intrinsic natures, namely difference and non-difference.
In order to refute what Kumārila has said for the purpose of answering this objection, [the author] introduces it for the sake of criticism, saying:
"Even though the self remains absolutely devoid of any distinction caused by the difference of states,
this [objection] which is imagined by others regarding that stable self..."

The "distinction" (*bheda*) refers to the diversity (*nānātva*) of states such as pleasure and so forth; by that distinction, there is indeed a multiplicity of the person (*puruṣa*), and thus it is "empty" of that.
The meaning is that even though there is a plurality of states, [the person] remains of a single nature.
He states the reason for this: "in its stable essence" (*sthirātmani*).
"Stable" means eternal; that whose nature (ātman-svabhāva) is such is so described.

Alternatively, "distinctions of state" refers to specific states such as pleasure and the like; "absolute difference" from these means being separate from them, and by that [difference] it is "empty," meaning it is not distinct from them either.
To the question "What is that which is being conceptualized?", he says "pleasure," and so forth:
"Even while passing through states such as pleasure and pain, my person does not at all relinquish its nature as consciousness, substance, existence, and so on."
"Even while going" means even while proceeding;
"a person" (nara) refers to...
The term "ātman" [is used];

by the word "etcetera" in "sattva etc.," there is the inclusion of general properties such as being knowable (*jñeyatva*), being cognizable (*prameyatva*), being an agent (*kartṛtva*), and being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).
Furthermore, demonstrating that even specific attributes are not absolutely annihilated, he says "na ca" and so forth:
"And upon the arising of another state, the previous one does not perish utterly."
But for the sake of conforming to what follows, it dissolves into the universal self.
Regarding the word "prior":
it refers to states such as pleasure.
If this is so, one might ask why a state of suffering is not perceived even during a state of pleasure; to this, he says, "for the sake of conforming to what follows," and so forth.

For when the state of happiness remains in its own essential nature, the subsequent state of suffering does not arise; therefore, as it dissolves, it merges into the general essence—which permeates all states and is characterized by consciousness, substantiality, and so forth—becoming conducive to the production of the subsequent state of suffering, and for that purpose, it dissolves therein.

If this is so, one might suspect that just as with the different states, dissolution into the universal self is also untenable due to contradiction; anticipating this, he says: "For by their own nature," and so forth.
"For it is by their own nature that the states are mutually contradictory, whereas the universal self is perceived as non-contradictory in all of them."

Because states existing in their own forms as pleasure and so forth are mutually contradictory, their mutual dissolution is not logical; however, what contradiction could there be in a dissolution into another state that consists of a universal nature, such that it would not occur therein? For that universal nature is observed to be non-contradictory and pervasive across all states, since consciousness and the like are perceived in every state.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "In that case," and so forth: "In that regard,
if the states were not absolutely distinct from the person,
then upon their arising separately from him, those two [properties] would belong to him as well."

For if an absolute difference between the person (*puruṣa*) and the states (*avasthā*) were not accepted, then upon the destruction and arising of those states, this person too would undergo that same destruction and arising.

The inclusion of the word "absolutely" (*ekāntena*) is for the purpose of making it known that if there were no distinction whatsoever [between them], the consequence of arising and destruction following the states would be unavoidable.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: whenever there is the arising or destruction of something from which another is non-different, the arising and destruction of that other also occur; just as, for example, the nature (*svarūpa*) of those very things such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth.
And since the person has a nature that is not distinct from pleasure and so forth, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
And showing that this reason is not inconclusive, he says "viruddha" and so forth:
"But when there is a connection with contradictory properties, there would be an absolute difference,
just as among men, due to their nature which is restricted to each individual."

For if it is accepted that only the states (avasthās) possess arising and passing away, while the person (puruṣa) does not—and thus a locus of contradictory properties characterized by arising and non-arising is admitted—then the consequence of difference (bheda) follows. Just as among many persons there is mutual difference due to their respective, individually determined natures (svabhāva), so too would it be here; for the conventional usage of "difference" is based solely on this much. This is the intended meaning.

Since even in the case of the self (puṃs), there is no mutual difference in terms of their nature as entities and so forth, the phrase "restricted to each" was stated in order to eliminate the fallacy of the example being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*). The form of these [mental states] is absolutely distinct for each individual; otherwise, because there would be an absence of specific restriction regarding recollection and so forth, a confusion of established order (*vyavasthā*) would result. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not share the same acquisition and preservation (*ekayogakṣema*) is not non-different from that [other thing]; for example, the selves are mutually distinct in terms of acquisition and preservation due to forms restricted to each individual self.
Furthermore, states such as pleasure and so forth do not share the same acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema) as the person, because their pervading concomitance is unperceived.
Regarding what was said— that upon the arising of another state, the preceding one does not utterly perish— he replies with the words "by its very nature," and so forth:
"If, according to you, the states dissolve into the person by their very own nature,
then suffering and the rest would also be experienced at the time of the arising of pleasure and the rest."
For when states dissolve into the universal self, they must dissolve either in their own form or in the form of another.

If the first alternative is held, then even upon the arising of pleasure and so forth—and even during the experience of those states of pleasure and so forth—that pain would also be experienced, because it has reached the conditions for perception.
Now, regarding the position that [transmigration occurs] "by means of another form," he says "na ca" and so forth:
"Nor is there the possibility of the transmigration of one thing when there is a transmigration of another form;
and since transmigration would have to occur through identity, it would follow that the self possesses arising."
Furthermore, the transition of pleasure and so forth into the person is accepted as occurring through identity alone;
consequently, because it is non-different from them—just like pain and so forth—the self, which is the person, would be subject to arising, that is, it would possess origination.
Regarding what was stated— "Nor do agency and enjoyership depend upon a state of the person"— he says "yadi" and so forth:
If agency and enjoyership did not depend at all upon a state, then,
because they would be identical to that which possesses the state, the occurrence of agency and so forth would be impossible.
For if agency and so forth were dependent solely upon the person (puruṣa), they could not belong to the Self (ātman) which has not abandoned its prior nature.

The formal argument is as follows: that which has not abandoned the state of being neither agent nor enjoyer does neither act nor enjoy, just like space; and the person is always such that it has not abandoned the state of being neither agent nor enjoyer. This is the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi).
If the birth of cognition in a person constitutes a modification, then there is impermanence;
if, on the other hand, that which is called the self is unmodified, it is not tenable for it to be the cognizer.
Regarding this which was stated by the venerable teacher Dignāga, Kumārila said therein: "The fact that the self is denotable by the word 'impermanent' is not being denied."
Since it denotes merely the occurrence of modification, its cessation occurs by that much alone.
Thus, under the guise of a conclusion, he states the fault with the words beginning with "that":
"That state of being denotable by the word 'eternal' is not denied of the self;
however, because it possesses modifications of its own nature, its cessation does occur."

Therefore, we do not deny that consciousness is denotable by the word "eternal," because consciousness—which is preceded by its own material cause and perishes at every moment—continues without interruption throughout the duration of saṃsāra.

However, since its essential nature (svarūpa) or intrinsic character (svabhāva) is subject to modification, involving the necessary abandonment of its prior nature and the manifestation of another nature, it follows most clearly that there is "interruption" (vyuccheda), that is, destruction (vināśa).

Furthermore, demonstrating that even the example of the snake and so forth cited [by the opponent] does not establish a permanent, unitary nature, he says "The snake too," and so on: "The snake too, because of its momentary destruction, undergoes states such as crookedness; for if it were of a stable nature, there could be no transition to another state, just as in the case of a person."
For just as it is not logical for a person to undergo the occurrence of different states because of their stable and uniform nature, so it is for a snake as well.

If this [snake] were subject to momentary destruction, then the occurrence of different states would be logical, since the manifestation of a different state is characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding what was said—that the notion of "I" (ahaṃbuddhi) in the form "I know" refers to a knower—that is unproven; demonstrating this, he says: "This 'I'-conceit proceeds entirely without an objective support," and so forth.

Indeed, this 'I'-conceit proceeds as something entirely without an objective support, due to the power of the seed of the vision of sentient beings from beginningless time, occurring only in certain instances.
For this ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*) has, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), no objective support whatsoever by which its object could be known.
If this is so, what is the cause for its arising? To this he says "beginningless," and so forth.
"View of a self" (*sattvadṛk*) means the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); its "seed" means its latent predisposition (*vāsanāśakti*). This is the meaning.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which is beginningless and is the seed of the vision of sentient beings.
Its power is its sovereign influence (*ādhipatya*).
[The phrase] "only in certain cases" means:
It is restricted solely to the six sense bases within the internal self.
Now, as to why [this] does not occur everywhere, he says: "For only certain... and so forth.
For only certain conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) exercise sovereignty over that which determines such a form; therefore, it does not occur everywhere.
"Apprehending that form" means apprehending the form of the knower which persists through preceding and succeeding moments; it does not apply to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) in all cases.
In other continua, such as a jar and so forth.

This same objection applies equally [to you] regarding the person (puruṣa) as well; otherwise, because of the existence of a distinction in its powers, everything for you would be entirely free from confusion.
Furthermore, even if the *ahaṃkāra* has the self as its object, the same objection applies: why does it not also operate with respect to another self?

If you argue that this is not so because of the specific restriction of its power (*śakti*), then for us as well, there is a systematic determination that—due to the restriction of power—it operates with respect to certain internal objects such as the deity, but not everywhere; thus, everything is entirely free from confusion.
It might be argued: "Let this distinction be granted; however, how is its lack of an objective support (*nirālambanatva*) established? To this he says, beginning with "nitya":
"But if there were the position of an eternal object, then all instances of ego-conception would arise simultaneously, because a potent cause is established [as being always present]."
Even though they have impermanent things as their objects, subsequent cognitions would still possess clear appearances;
therefore, [the opponent] fruitlessly questions the actual existence of the object of cognition.
For its object must be either permanent or impermanent.
If it were permanent, then all instances of "I-making" (*ahaṅkṛti*) and ego-conceptions (*ahaṅkāra*) would arise simultaneously, because their cause would be complete.
Indeed, it is not logical for an object to be a cause that is non-existent, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, it has been repeatedly demonstrated that a potent cause does not require auxiliary causes.

Nor can it be said that this *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense) is a single entity, because its multiplicity is established by its occasional nature. For instance, the *ahaṅkāra* is not perceived during deep sleep, intoxication, or fainting, yet it is perceived again at other times; thus, its occasional nature is established by the fact that it is not perceived at all times.

Furthermore, since they are occasional, their multiplicity is also established; thus, all instances of ego-grasping (*ahaṅkṛti*), which arise solely in dependence upon its existence, would have to be produced simultaneously.

Alternatively, if the position is that the objective support (*ālambana*) is impermanent, then, like visual and other sensory cognitions, all instances of ego-grasping would necessarily appear with extreme clarity, because they would directly apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the real entity.
Therefore, for that reason, other outsiders such as Kumārila and others fruitlessly interrogate its objective support, asking things such as:
"What indeed is the imagined object characterized by ignorance? and so forth.

In this regard, concerning what was stated— that this *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) is indeed without an object and proceeds as an error through the force of the beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—
the author anticipates the objection raised by Kumārila, beginning with the words "jñātari" and so forth:
"The recognition [of the self] as the knower can be produced by latent impressions."
Therefore, there is no cognition of "that" in this, for this [latter] is not the cause of error.
If it is claimed that the cognition of "I" is not an error because it is free from sublation, [then...
281ab

For a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is capable of producing a recognition whose object is the knower; it is not, however, capable of producing the cognition or knowledge that "he is the knower" with respect to one who is not the knower. This is the connection [of the words]. Why? Because this [impression] is not a cause of error; rather, the meaning is that it generates a cognition whose object is precisely the thing as it was experienced, and not an erroneous one.

Therefore, since this ego-conception (ahaṅkāra) arises from latent impressions (vāsanā) and because there is an absence of any subverting means of valid cognition (bādhaka-pramāṇa), it is not logical to consider it an error.
The word "if" (cet) is displaced; it should be understood as following immediately after the phrase "due to the avoidance of subversion" (bādhavarjanāt).
He refutes this with the words "no," and so forth,
because the invalidation of that [position] has been demonstrated by the reasoning just stated.
The reasoning just mentioned, beginning with "But in the case of the position that [cognition] has a permanent object," and so forth.

Showing that the statement "habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not the cause of error" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "Among those devoted to Īśvara and others," and so forth: "How could various delusions regarding [Īśvara] as being the cause [of the world] and so forth arise among those devoted to Īśvara and others, if they were produced solely from habitual tendencies?"
When non-referentiality is thus established regarding the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra),
then no cognizer exists who is graspable by the notion of "I."

Consequently, among all means of valid cognition, there exists no corroborative instance that possesses established validity; and the logical reasons are shown to be unestablished in their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*), as the case may be.
An Examination of the Self as Conceptualized by the Mīmāṃsakas.

For if habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) were not the cause of error, then how could such delusions as "the Lord is the cause of all things that arise," "He is omniscient," and "He is the substratum of eternal cognition" ever emerge, given that they can only arise from habitual tendencies?
Indeed, even Kumārila has refuted the Lord and others as the creator of the world.

Furthermore, in the phrase "because of the existence of [error] through habitual tendencies alone" (*vāsanāmātrabhāvāt*), the inclusion of the word "alone" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding an object that exists in such a manner [as the Lord].

Therefore, since the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is without a real objective basis, there exists no well-established knower who could be its object; thus, the self (*ātman*) is not established on that basis.

Regarding the argument for permanence previously stated—that [the self] is the object of a past ego-sense and so forth—he replies with the words beginning "that" (*tat*), etc., and "anyone" (*kaścana*).
Whether the cognizer is eternal or non-eternal, there is no subject (dharmin) in the example; thus, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For in the first and second formulations, the non-establishment of the subject is a fault of the example, because there exists no cognizer whatsoever—whether present or past—who is accessible through the notion of "I" (*ahampratyaya*). In the third formulation, however, the example "like a single cognition" is deficient in both the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*).

Because it is unestablished that the single cognition under discussion possesses the nature of an "I-notion" belonging to a cognizer connected to a single continuum, and because its having a single object is also unestablished;
therefore, its lack of establishment has been stated by way of the non-establishment of these two properties.
They have been cited according to their respective applications.
The reasons (hetu) previously mentioned and set forth— according to their respective applications and possibilities—
are [classified as] "unestablished in their locus" (āśrayāsiddha).
For instance, the reasons in the first and second formal arguments are unestablished in their locus because no subject (dharmin)— namely, a cognizer graspable by the notion of "I"— is established.

In the third formulation, however, there is no "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because the subjects (*dharmin*), namely the conditions (*pratyaya*), are established; yet, they remain unestablished with respect to a specific cognizer connected to a single continuum (*ekasantāna*).
Since the state of being without an objective support (*nirālambanatva*) is well-established,
it was therefore stated "according to what is appropriate.
Thus ends the examination of the self as conceived by the Mīmāṃsakas.
Now, for the purpose of refuting the self (ātman) as conceived by the Sāṃkhya school, he says "consciousness" and so forth:
"Others consider consciousness to be distinct from the nature of the intellect (buddhi)."
And they imagine consciousness to be the innate nature of the self.
He merely enjoys the fruit presented by Pradhāna;
he possesses no agency at all, for that is held to belong to Prakṛti alone.
"Others" refers to the Sāṃkhyas;
for they postulate that consciousness (*caitanya*) is the innate nature of the self (*ātman*), distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*).
This is because, according to their doctrine, the intellect is of the nature of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), whereas consciousness is the very essence of the person (*puruṣa*).

And that person is the enjoyer of the fruits of good and evil actions as brought about by primordial matter (*pradhāna*), but not the agent of those actions; for it is accepted that agency belongs solely to *prakṛti*, which takes the form of the transformation of the entire world.

And here they provide the proof: whatever object is of a composite nature is seen to exist for the sake of another, just like a bed and so forth; and since the eyes and other organs are of a composite nature, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
And that "other" [for whose sake they exist] is, by implication, established to be the Self (*ātman*).
Such is the opponent's position.
With the words "In that case as well" (*tatrāpi*) and so forth, [the author] first refutes the meaning of the proposition:
"In that case as well, how could forms, sounds, and other objects be experienced by cognitions?"
If a single consciousness is asserted to have a clearly manifest form that possesses differentiation, [it would follow that it is manifold].

For instance, by one who asserts that consciousness (*caitanya*) is the innate nature of the person (*puruṣa*), it is effectively proposed that consciousness is eternal and of a single form, since it is non-different from the person who is eternal and of a single form.

And this contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the distinct forms and diverse natures of cognitions regarding color, sound, and so forth, are very clearly and vividly experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) as being differentiated.
This [differentiation] would not be possible if consciousness were a unity.
Demonstrating the contradiction with his own accepted position, he says "ekarūpe" and so forth:
"And while consciousness, being of a single form, remains constant at all times..."
How indeed can the state of being an enjoyer of various kinds of objects be logically established?
Furthermore, it is mutually contradictory that the self is of a single form and yet the enjoyer of manifold objects;
for [the self] would be indistinguishable from its state as a non-enjoyer.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of the presence of the desire to see (*didṛkṣā*) and so forth, he says "no" and so on:
"The desire to see and the rest, being distinct [from the Self], are not the cause of its experience;
for if they were so, the person would be subject to birth."

If the desires to see, to hear, and so forth regarding form and the other sense-objects— which are conceived as the basis for his experience— are distinct from one another, they do not belong to this self, nor do they arise [as its attributes]. For if they were to arise, then, given their existence as such distinct entities, the person would be subject to birth, because he is non-different from them, just like the desire to see and the rest.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "For there exists nothing such as the desire to see that is distinct from consciousness," and so forth. Indeed, since there is no desire to see or the like apart from consciousness, if its arising and passing away were admitted, that [change] would be unavoidable for the person (puruṣa) as well.
For if there were a difference between them, the relation expressed by "his" would be untenable,
because there would be no basis for a relationship consisting of mutual benefit.
[The word] "this" refers to that.
The convergence of arising and passing away.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that for which there is no basis for establishing its existence is not to be established by a discerning person as having that nature, just as space is not [established] as being corporeal.

And there is no basis for establishing the existence of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), such as the Puruṣa or the desire to see (*dṛkṣā*) and so forth; this is because the cause [for such establishment] is not perceived (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).
And it has been demonstrated that this reason is not unestablished.
Furthermore, because he lacks agency, it is shown that his being an enjoyer is also untenable; thus [the author] says "And auspicious and inauspicious," and so forth:
"If auspicious and inauspicious karma were not at all performed by the self, then from what source would this variety of experience arise for him?"
For no one experiences the fruit of an action not performed, because that would entail the logical fault of the occurrence of what was not done (akṛtābhyāgama) and other such defects.
Here, he anticipates the opponent's reply with the words "In accordance with desire," and so forth:
"If Nature bestows [results] in accordance with desire,
then this relationship between the two is established like that of the lame man and the blind man."

Although the *puruṣa* is not the agent of actions, there is no fault in this, for *prakṛti* brings about for him the object according to his desire, which he then experiences. Now, one might ask: since *prakṛti* is insentient, how can she be the agent of virtuous and other such actions, by which she accomplishes for the *puruṣa* the fruit of action as intended? To this he says: "Like the lame man and the blind man," and so forth.

Just as it is said that a blind man’s engagement with objects occurs through his connection with a sighted person, so too the subtle body (*liṅga*), consisting of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, performs determination regarding effects such as merit (*dharma*) and the like—as if it were conscious—due to its contact with the conscious Puruṣa; thus there is no fault. And so it has been said: "For the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception, and likewise for the sake of the isolation (*kaivalya*) of Pradhāna, the union of both occurs like that of the lame and the blind; from that [union] proceeds creation."
He replies with the words "If this were so," and so forth:
"If this were the case, then even when there is a desire for what is desired, [the result] would not be established;
why then does primordial nature (prakṛti) not depend on anything else at all?"

For if it were the case that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) brings about the desired fruit even of an action not performed, then why would the desired object not be accomplished for every person at all times whenever there is a longing for what is wished for? It might be thought: "It is not accomplished because of the absence of its cause, namely *dharma*. To this he says: "Primordial nature is not [the cause]," and so forth.
For *dharma* is an effect of primordial nature; and since that [effect] is non-different from it, it would exist at all times, and thus the desired fruit would necessarily come to be.
For it is thus: all this is simply Nature (prakṛti) and Spirit (puruṣa), and these two are eternally present. Therefore, the fruit [of action] would necessarily be eternal.
Furthermore, if Nature bestows the desired object, why would she bestow what is undesired? For no one desires what is undesired.

Moreover, even if nature (*prakṛti*) were to present objects to it, its status as an enjoyer would still be untenable because it is unchanging; this is shown in the passage beginning with "And at the time of enjoying objects," and so forth:
"And if, at the time of enjoying objects, there is no modification (*vikriyā*) in it at all, then it could not be an enjoyer, nor would nature be a benefactor."
Furthermore, if transformation truly exists, its permanence is lost;
for transformation is indeed a change of state, and how could that exist if there were persistence in the same condition?
For if [the Self] were not brought into a modification consisting of joy, distress, and so forth by means of pleasure, pain, and the like, it would be a non-experiencer (*abhoktṛ*) just like space;
furthermore, Nature (*prakṛti*) would not be a benefactor. This is the connection [of the argument], because it is impossible to effect a benefit for a Self that is unchanging.
If, on the other hand, its state of being subject to modification is admitted, then there follows the undesirable consequence of the loss of its permanence;
for we define impermanence precisely as the lack of remaining in the same state (atādavasthya).
Since that [lack of remaining in the same state] exists when there is modification, how could it possess permanence?
Because eternity consists in remaining in that very state. [p.

114] He raises another objection regarding the nature of the enjoyer according to the view of others, beginning with "It might be thought," etc.: "It might be thought that first the cognition in the form of the object undergoes a transformation (*vivartate*)."
And a person attains the purpose determined by that [intellect].
And thus, through the emergence of reflections, this [Puruṣa] possesses the state of being an enjoyer;
yet this Puruṣa never abandons its own essential nature.
For its state as an enjoyer is not intended to arise through undergoing a transformation;
rather, it occurs by way of the emergence of a reflection of the object determined by the intellect (*buddhi*).

To explain: the reflection of the object mounted upon the mirror of the intellect is transferred to the *puruṣa*, who is like a second mirror. That alone constitutes its state as an enjoyer, and not the occurrence of a transformation.
Moreover, even when a mere reflection is transferred, the person (puruṣa) does not abandon its own nature, because it remains as it is, like a mirror;
therefore, in the argument that "it is indistinguishable from the state of being a non-experiencer," the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said," etc.:
"It is said that when the reflection arises through identity [with the original], that very thing possesses the state of arising; but if there is a distinction, there is no status as an enjoyer."

If that reflection of an object which has mounted upon the mirror of the intellect is held to be transferred to the *puruṣa*, who is like a second mirror, then if it is non-different from the *puruṣa*, it follows—just as was stated immediately above—that it would be subject to arising and passing away;
for it would be non-different from that which possesses the nature of a reflection subject to arising and passing away.

On the other hand, if the position is that it is different, then the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*) does not obtain, because there is no distinction whatsoever from its state of being a non-enjoyer.

Nor is it logical for a person to possess the status of an enjoyer by virtue of a connection with the reflection of an object, because a relationship cannot be established between two things that do not mutually benefit one another.
Primal Matter (pradhāna) proceeds in accordance with the desire to see [the Puruṣa] and other such factors;
how could it produce such a variety of diverse arrangements if it were insentient by nature?

Furthermore, if the *pradhāna* were to know the desire to see and so forth of the *puruṣa*, then its activity toward the goal of that *puruṣa* would be appropriate as a form of compliance; however, because it is insentient by nature, even though there is a connection with a sentient being—as in the case of the lame man and the blind man—such activity is not logical. For instance, although the blind man may not perceive the path himself, he nevertheless perceives the intention of the lame man because the latter possesses sentience. But the *pradhāna* does not know the *puruṣa*'s desire to see and so forth, because, being composed of non-sentience, it is insentient in form.
Nor is there a relationship between these two, who do not assist one another, such as that which exists between a cripple and a blind man.
He indeed knows how to prepare the primary dishes, the condiments, and so forth;
yet he does not know how to eat them—what could be more improper than this?
Now, if it is maintained that the *pradhāna* knows the desire to see and so forth of the person (*puruṣa*),
then, this being the case, it would follow that it must also be an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).
For how could one who indeed understands how to act not also understand how to enjoy?

Therefore, the meaning is: what could be more unreasonable than this, that he knows how to act but not how to enjoy? For it is not the case that a cook, who is the maker of sauces and the like, does not know how to eat them.
The word *iti* should be supplied here [at the end of the sentence].
With the words "Because it possesses intelligence," etc., he anticipates the opponent's reply:
"If [you argue] that because the *pradhāna* possesses intelligence, everything is consistent for it, then by virtue of possessing intelligence,
it would follow that it has consciousness, just as in the case of the *puruṣas*."

For intellect (*buddhi*) is indeed determination (*adhyavasāya*), as well as consciousness (*saṃvit*), the act of cognizing (*saṃvedana*), perception (*saṃvitti*), and sentience (*cetanā*); all these are designations for consciousness (*caitanya*).
"Everything" means the instigation [of activity] in accordance with the desire to see and so forth.
"Of this" refers to the primary cause (pradhāna).

This is what is meant: even if the *pradhāna* is not of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), nevertheless, because it is endowed with the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by determination, it will act after having fully understood the desire to see and so forth residing in the *puruṣa*; therefore, everything is consistent.
To this, he states the reply beginning with "by being possessed of intellect" (*buddhimattvena*).
For if the possession of intellect were admitted for the *pradhāna*, then it would follow that it possesses consciousness (*caitanya*), just like the *puruṣa*.
This is because terms such as "intellect" (*buddhi*) are synonyms for "consciousness.

For instance, that which, by its nature of luminosity, has a self-cognized form and shines forth entirely independent of anything else is called consciousness (*caitanya*). Since this essential nature also belongs to the intellect, why should it not be of the nature of consciousness?
Nor do we perceive any other form of consciousness apart from the intellect.
By which the existence of a person distinct from that [aggregate] would be established.

In this context, in order to establish the difference between the intellect (*buddhi*) and that which is of the nature of consciousness (*pariścit*), he says: "The intellect is insentient by nature," and so forth.
If it is thought: "The intellect is insentient by nature, like sound, smell, taste, and so on, because of the two reasons of having an origin and being subject to destruction."

The formal argument is as follows: whatever possesses properties such as having an origin and being subject to destruction is insentient, just like taste and so forth; and the intellect likewise possesses these properties—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

He replies with the words beginning "Not these two," etc.: "These two reasons are not established for both parties when an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*) is intended; nor is there a sublation of the opposite [position] even when a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is being asserted."
This might be either an independent proof (*svātantryeṇa sādhana*) or a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*).
If it were an independent proof, then the reason would be unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*).

For instance, the kind of "possessing origination" (*utpattimattva*) characterized by the production of what was previously non-existent, or the kind of "perishability" (*nāśitva*) consisting of absolute annihilation, which is well-known to the Buddhist, is not of that same kind for you, the Sāṅkhya.

Because you accept that these two consist in transformation and concealment, just as they are for you, so they are not established for the Buddhist; thus, the reason is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*).

Nor is the reason established merely by the establishment of the word, for the establishment of a thing follows from the establishment of the actual entity, since the reason exists only as a real entity.
As it has been said:

"Even when the word itself is non-deviant, if its object is deviant and so forth, the means of proof should be known as defective; for the establishment of a real entity depends upon the real entity."
Thus [he says].

Now, even if the position is that this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum), nevertheless, because no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been shown against the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya-viparyaya*), the two reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For what necessary connection exists here such that consciousness must not possess the properties of being produced and being perishable?
This conception— that the activity of the Pradhāna proceeds for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa, just as the activity of the insentient milk proceeds for the sake of the growth of the calf—
is itself merely an unfounded imagination.

For milk does not function independently as the cause for the growth of the calf; rather, it arises from its own specific causes and conditions that occur at particular times. Once produced, it becomes the cause for the calf’s growth; thus, it is described as "functioning" even though it is insentient.
Furthermore, such an activity of the Pradhāna is not logical.
For, because it is eternal and because there is no other cause for it, its occasional power cannot reasonably depend on the occasional proximity of causes.

Nor can it be inherent, for since its complete causes would be constantly present, it would follow that all human goals—characterized by worldly prosperity and the ultimate good—would arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let there be non-difference between cognition and consciousness; nevertheless, its status as the self remains unrefuted. To this he says, "In consciousness," and so forth:
"Even if the term 'self' were applied to consciousness, there would be no harm to our position.
However, its permanence is difficult to prove, because the eyes and other sense organs possess efficacy [which would otherwise be inexplicable]."
If consciousness were eternal, it would be useless for the sake of the eyes and other sense organs;
if fire were eternal, there would be no need for fuel.
For we do not deny consciousness merely because of the application of the word "self"; rather, that superimposed property characterized by permanence which is attributed to it is what is denied.
Why? Because of the efficacy of the eye, light, mental attention, and so forth.
Otherwise, if consciousness were eternal and permanent, then the eye and other such factors would be entirely fruitless.
Because those [causes] exist for the purpose of producing that [effect],
and because production is impossible for that which is eternal;
regarding this very point, he states an example, beginning with "it would not be," and so forth.
If fire were eternal, then people would never fetch fuel for the sake of fire; therefore, it is not logical that consciousness is of a single, permanent nature.
"That which is composite in nature is seen to exist for the sake of another," and so forth.
In this regard, seeking to determine who that "other" intended by the author is, he says: "The state of being for the sake of another," and so on.
Furthermore, the fact that the eyes and other [senses] exist for the sake of another is established by the reason of their being composite entities,
just like beds, seats, and so forth.
If it is established that these [faculties] possess the property of having a superadded excellence (atiśaya) deposited in them,
then our desired conclusion is proven, since we maintain that they are benefactors of cognition.

In proving that what is unchanging is incapable of being an auxiliary cause, the example is devoid of the probandum; for it is only those things which are mobile that are logically capable of being auxiliaries.
But if their being for the sake of another is established only in a general sense,
even then the proof is useless, since they are already established as serving the mind.

There are three possible alternatives: either the intended "other" (para) is one to whom an excellence can be imparted; or it is unchanging because its nature is such that no excellence can be imparted to it; or, in a general sense, mere "being for the sake of another" (pārārthya) is being proved as something merely pleasing when left unexamined.

Regarding these, in the first position, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā), because we ourselves accept that the eyes and so forth are benefactors of consciousness.

This is because of the scriptural statement: "Dependent upon the eye and visible forms, visual consciousness arises," up to "dependent upon the body and tangible objects, tactile consciousness arises."
Now, showing that the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddhatā*) if the second position is held, he says: "Because of being a benefactor to the unchangeable," and so forth.

"Being a benefactor to the unchangeable" (*avikāry-upakāritva*) means the state of being a benefactor to that which is permanent (*nitya*). When this is established for the eyes and other [senses] by means of an example, the reason is contradictory because it is pervaded (*vyāpta*) precisely by the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyaviparyaya*). This is because those things such as beds and the like are logically benefactors only of that which is mobile and impermanent (*anitya*); for it is impossible to produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in that which is unchangeable.

Now, if the third position is taken— that having set aside the alternatives such as "possessing an excellence to be produced" (*ādheyātiśaya*) and so forth, one proves merely "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*)— even then, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the eyes and other [faculties] are accepted by you as being beneficial to the mind (*citta*).

If, on the other hand, the mind itself is also accepted as the subject of the proposition (*sādhyadharmin*), as is accepted by the Naiyāyikas, even so, your desired conclusion is not established, because the self (*ātman*) is not accepted by you as being distinct from the mind.

Nor is the object desired by the Naiyāyikas established; for since the eyes and so forth arise through mutual assistance and by way of supporting others, their state of being a composite (saṃghātatva) is indeed postulated. Thus, the reason [adduced] is not unestablished.
Thus concludes the examination of the self as conceived by the followers of Kapila.
[118] For the purpose of refuting the self (ātman) as conceived by the Digambaras, he says "like the Jaiminīyas," and so forth.
Like the Jaiminīyas, the Jainas assert that the person, characterized by consciousness,
consists of substance and modes, having the nature of both exclusion and inclusion.

Regarding the term "Jainas": the Digambaras speak as follows: the self (ātman) is characterized by consciousness (cillakṣaṇa). In its aspect as substance (dravya), it is of the nature of persistence (anugamātmaka) because it remains identical across all states; however, in its aspect as modification (paryāya), it is of the nature of exclusion (vyāvṛttyātmaka) because it differs in each state.
And this twofold nature of the self is established through direct perception itself; thus, it need not be proven by any other means of valid cognition.

For instance, the opponent's position is as follows: that which remains constant through the various states such as pleasure and so forth, and which is perceived as consciousness throughout all those states, is the substance (*dravya*);
whereas the modifications (*paryāya*) are the distinct states of pleasure and so forth that occur in succession, and these are established by direct perception itself.

He responds with the words "tatrāpi" and so forth: "If, even in that case, the unmodified substance were conjoined with its modes, there would be no distinction in it; thus, it would not be subject to transformation."

In this regard, there are two positions: that substance whose nature is consciousness is at some time connected with its modifications (paryāyas) while remaining unmodified and not abandoning its prior form of consciousness and so forth; or else, it has abandoned its prior form.
If the latter position were held, then the consequence would be the loss of its permanence, because there would be no persisting entity whatsoever.

If, on the other hand, the first position—that it remains unmodified—is accepted, then there would be no distinction between the prior and subsequent states; since there would be no "otherness" (anyathātva), that consciousness would not be, nor could it become, transformative (pariṇāmin).

Because transformation is characterized by the quality of becoming otherwise (*anyathātva*), and consciousness (*caitanya*) is accepted as being subject to transformation; the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is not differentiated across its prior and subsequent states does not undergo transformation, just like space (*ākāśa*); and consciousness is not differentiated across all its states—this is established through the non-perception of a counter-example (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
With the words "of place, time, and intrinsic nature," and so forth, he raises the objection that the reason is unestablished according to the opponent's view:
"Oneness is asserted because there is no difference in place, time, and intrinsic nature;
however, difference is described due to differences in number, characteristic, name, and purpose."
"Form and so forth, and the jar"—this is the distinction of number and designation;
"the persistence and exclusion of effects"—this is the distinction of characteristic and purpose.
Thus, substance and mode are not entirely without distinction;
for the substance itself undergoes differentiation through the form of its modes.

For if substance were absolutely distinct from its modes, then it would possess a separate identity; however, since substance and mode are held to be identical due to the non-difference of their location, time, and intrinsic nature, they are one.
Their distinction, however, arises from differences in number and so forth.
In this context, "number" refers to oneness, plurality, and the like.
For instance, substance is characterized by the number one, whereas the modes, such as pleasure and so forth, are distinguished by multiple numbers;
their characteristics are also distinct.
This is because substance has the characteristic of persistence (*anuvṛtti*), while the modes have the characteristics of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), namely: name, designation, object, and function.

And so it has been said: "There is non-difference between a property (*dharma*) and its substratum (*dharmin*) due to the non-difference of place, time, and intrinsic nature; however, there is difference due to the difference in number, designation, characteristic, and function, as in the case of a jar and its color and other qualities.

For instance, there is non-difference of the jar and its color and other qualities with respect to place and so forth; for whatever is the place, time, and intrinsic nature of the jar, that same is the place, time, and intrinsic nature of the color and other qualities. Yet, there is a difference of these [qualities] from the jar due to number and so forth. Thus, there is a difference in number, since the jar is one while the color and other qualities are many.
The distinction in designation is that there is the term "jar" and the terms "color-form" and so forth.

The distinction in characteristic is that the substance, such as a jar, has the characteristic of persistence (*anuvṛtti*), whereas the modes (*paryāya*), such as color-form and so forth, have the characteristic of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
The distinction in function is that the task of fetching water is performed by the jar, whereas the dyeing of cloth and so forth are performed by color-form and the rest.

In this same way, the principle should be extended to the self-substance (*ātman-dravya*), which is of the nature of consciousness (*caitanya*), and to its successive states (*paryāya*) such as pleasure, pain, and so forth.

However, the distinction between their effects should be understood as follows: through consciousness, the experience of objects is produced; whereas through pleasure, pain, and the like, there is affliction, favor, and so on.
He demonstrates this with the words "form and so forth," etc.
"Divided by number and designation" refers to substance and mode, as will be stated later.
"Divided by characteristic, purpose, and function" refers to the persistence and exclusion of effects.
The connection is according to what is appropriate.
