The connection is as follows: "the difference in effects" means the differentiation of objects, characterized by the differentiation of inclusion and exclusion; this applies to "substance and mode. There is a pause (or separation) at the word "dravyaparyāyoḥ."
With the words "In this way," and so forth, he concludes the argument regarding the unestablished nature of the reason (*asiddhi*).
And having established this, substance (*dravya*) is not absolutely undifferentiated; rather, it attains distinction through the differentiation of the forms of its modes (*paryāya*).
Therefore, because there is no absolute difference of the substance from its modes, the reason is unestablished.

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "non-difference of intrinsic nature" and so forth: "If there is non-difference of intrinsic nature, that constitutes oneness; and while that [oneness] exists, difference would be difficult to establish in any way whatsoever, just like the essential nature of synonymous terms."

For if identity between substance and mode is also admitted, then this identity would have to be in its entirety; and how could difference, which is the opposite of that, exist? Indeed, it is not logical for affirmation and negation, which are mutually contradictory, to apply to one and the same thing at the same time. Thus, by the term "one," an absence of difference in intrinsic nature—which is inseparable from the negation of difference—is expressed; and when such an absence of difference in intrinsic nature exists, how could there be difference at that very same time, since difference consists in the negation of that [identity]?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: where there is non-difference (*abheda*), its opposite, difference (*bheda*), finds no room; for example, in the case of those very modes (*paryāya*) and the substance (*dravya*), there is no difference from their own respective, specific, and unique essential nature (*ātmarūpa*). And since non-difference between substance and mode is established, [difference is excluded] by the perception of a contradictory [property].

And therefore, since substance and mode are non-different in the ultimate sense, he demonstrates that even a difference in their characteristics would not obtain, by stating "And thus, when there is no figurative [distinction]," and so forth: "And thus, when the non-figurative oneness of substance and mode is established,
the substance would be subject to exclusion, just like the intrinsic nature of the modes."
Alternatively, if all those modes were also of a pervasive nature,
they would result in being substantial entities, because their identity with the substance would remain constant.

That which has a nature non-different from a form possessing exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is itself possessed of exclusion; for example, the intrinsic nature of the modes (paryāya). And substance (dravya) is not distinct from the form possessing exclusion. This is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu). Alternatively, that which is not distinct from a nature consisting of inclusion (anugata) is necessarily inclusive in nature; for example, the nature of substance. And the modes, such as pleasure and so forth, have a nature non-different from a nature consisting of inclusion. This is likewise a reason based on essential nature. Otherwise, because their acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema) would be distinct, there would be nothing but difference.

If there were unity even for that which is characterized by contradictory properties, then the conventional usage of difference would be utterly destroyed; this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the opposite position.
He concludes with the words "tataḥ" and so forth: Therefore, no substance such as the self exists as something persisting;
because it is not distinct from its modes, just like the nature of the modes themselves.
Regarding the phrase "the self, etc.":
by the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of jars, rice grains, and so forth.
With the words "And not," etc., he states the result of the second reductio ad absurdum:
"Nor are even any of the modes (paryāyas) subject to arising and passing away,
because they are non-different from the substance (dravya), like the fixed nature of that very substance."

Since that substance is also accepted as being subject to arising and passing away in the form of its modes (paryāya), the phrase "like a fixed self" (niyatātmavat) was stated so that there might not be the undesirable consequence of the probandum being deficient.
It is a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa): "fixed" (niyata) and this "self" (ātman), meaning its own nature (svabhāva), in the form of substance and so forth.
Then, he concludes with the words "therefore, [it would be] a destruction without continuity," and so forth:
"Therefore, either destruction must be admitted as being without continuity, or everything must be accepted as permanent;
for within a single self, these two—exclusion and inclusion—cannot both exist."

Not only is there no proof for a substantial entity (dravya) that possesses a nature non-different from its modes (paryāya) and persists through them, but for this reason as well: since such an entity, if it met the conditions for perception, is not perceived apart from its modes, it must be the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent. Demonstrating this, he says: "And not... and so forth.
"And not [is there proof] of a perceptible form whose nature persists through the modes."
The appearance of a substance exists, yet it does not exist, like a lotus in the sky.
Therefore, what was stated—that the substance-soul (*dravyātman*) is established as being perceived through direct perception itself—is unproven.
For nowhere in any cognition admitted to be perceptual is a substance-soul observed appearing as a single, persisting form, distinct from its modes (*paryāya*).
If this is so, and if there is no substantial essence (dravyātman) apart from its modes (paryāya), then how is the distinction of number and so forth established? To this, he says:

"Capable of various purposeful actions," and so on: "Those [entities] which are capable of various purposeful actions, which are the causes of cognitions such as 'equal' and so forth, and which are the objects of words and cognitions based on conventions regarding such objects."

There are various and manifold causal functions (*arthakriyā*) of the constituents (*paryāya*), such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, distinguished by being common or uncommon. Among these, the common ones are characterized by functions such as holding water, while the uncommon ones are characterized by the production of cognitions such as the coloring of cloth or the perception of the eye. The analysis of the compound is: "those which are capable" (*yogya*) or "efficacious" (*samartha*) therein. In that regard, since all [constituents] contribute simultaneously to a common effect, this is for the purpose of making known their status as causes in their totality; thus, even though there is no single, undivided substantial form (*dravyarūpa*), those very constituents, despite being distinct, are expressed by a single term such as "jar" as qualified by a singular number.

However, when there is an intention to express their utility for distinct effects, they are said to have various numbers; thus, both a difference in number and a difference in function are established among them.
To the question, "In that case, how is there a difference in their defining characteristics? he replies: "They are the causes of cognitions such as 'similar' and so forth.

Although [the atoms] perish at every moment in states such as raw or cooked, these very particulars, arising with similar configurations, become the objects of non-conceptual experience; being experienced as such, they serve as the causes for similar cognitions—such as "a jar, a jar"—in all their states.

Arising with distinct colors such as dark-blue, red, and so forth, they are the causes of dissimilar cognitions; thus, even without the persistence of a single form, they are established in the form of the inclusive and the exclusive by being the causes of similar and dissimilar cognitions. This is how the distinction of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) is established. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "similar, etc.," the dissimilar cognition is included. To the question, "What then is the difference in designation? he says: "In that manner," and so forth.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "of such a kind" means that which is capable of various purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) and is the cause of cognitions such as [the notion of] similarity; "object" (*artha*) refers to the referent (*viṣaya*), such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) such as "this is a jar" or "these are color-forms and so forth"—that is what is called "of such a kind. Those words and cognitions whose conventions have such objects are called "of such a kind"; they are the "objects of experience" (*gocara*). This is the grammatical analysis.
He demonstrates through a conclusion that the selflessness of entities is established by direct perception itself, beginning with the words "arising" and so forth:
"Only mere successions characterized by the nature of arising and passing away are perceived;
therefore, selflessness is clearly and most purely evident."
"Synonyms" refers to form and so forth, as well as suffering and so forth, which have the nature of being self-cognized. "Exclusively" means:

Because they lack the nature of a single, indivisible substance, and because for that which is eternal, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradictory whether it occurs successively or simultaneously; and because the capacity for causal efficiency is only possible when these things possess the character of arising and passing away— therefore, through inference as well, their selflessness (*nairātmya*) is established by the mark (*liṅga*) of existence (*sat*), which consists in being causally efficient.
Regarding what was stated, "And not for that which has a perceptible form," and so forth, the opponent here anticipates a reply with the words "the object" (*artha*), etc.:
"Now, the form of substance and its modes exists as a unified whole;
for that, though dual in nature, is held to be partless, like Narasiṃha."
The meaning is that because it has become "coalesced"—that is, merged into a single unity—the nature of the substance does not appear through discernment, even though it exists.
He states the reason for this coalescence in the passage beginning with "for that is of two forms" (*taddvirūpaṃ hi*).
"That" refers to the entity consisting of the self and so forth.
Since that [entity], although possessing two forms, is held to be partless—just like Narasiṃha—it is therefore, due to its partlessness, a conjoined dual form and is not perceived separately.
Showing that this which you state is mutually contradictory, he says "nanu" and so forth:
"Is it not the case that the designation 'of two forms' is based on multiple meanings,
since the word 'form' (rūpa) denotes intrinsic nature (svabhāva)?"

For if it were partless, then the claim that it "has two forms" would be contradicted, because this designation is based on multiple objects. Why? Because by the word *rūpa*, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is denoted. Thus, that which has two forms—that is, two intrinsic natures—is called "two-formed. And it is not logical for a single thing to have two intrinsic natures, as that would entail the loss of its unity.
You have merely demonstrated two separate intrinsic natures; however, a single entity cannot possess two forms, because unity and plurality are characterized by mutual exclusion.
And he shows by the words "Even Narasiṃha... and so forth that even Narasiṃha, while being one, is not established as having a dual nature:
"Even Narasiṃha is certainly not one, nor is it logically possible for him to have a dual nature;
for he is perceived as being composed of a collection of many atoms."
The word "also" (api) indicates that not only is that which has become the subject of dispute untenable;
"he" refers to Narasiṃha.
"So be it.
[This refers to] its diversity of parts and its occupation of a more extensive space;
otherwise, it would not appear in such a manner.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that even by covering it with something the size of a fly's foot, such an object would be completely concealed.
By this, colors and other qualities that are like a dark-blue gem (mecakamaṇi) are also refuted.
The intention is that we shall establish this in detail during the refutation of the "whole" (avayavin).
Thus concludes the examination of the self as conceived by the Digambaras.
[Examination of the Upaniṣadic Self] [p.

123]: Others, the followers of the Upaniṣads who rely on the doctrine of non-duality (advaitadarśana), postulate a self whose nature is eternal, unitary cognition, and which consists of the transformation of earth and the other elements.
Therefore, presenting their very view, he says "eternal," and so forth.
Others, moreover, maintain that this world, consisting of earth, fire, water, and so forth, is an evolution of eternal consciousness, and that the Self is of the same nature as that.
"Consisting of that" means having as its essence a single, eternal consciousness whose form is the transformation of earth and the other elements.
"The other" [refers to the following].
Those pertaining to the Upaniṣads.
"What is the proof for this? he says: "Nothing here exists that is endowed with the characteristics of an object of apprehension;
therefore, all this is observed as a transformation of consciousness."
For earth and the other elements do not exist apart from cognition as things possessing the characteristic of being perceivable, such that they could appear as composite wholes;
moreover, atoms are non-existent.
Therefore, by implication, it is determined that these [elements] such as earth are nothing but forms appearing to consciousness.
"This" refers to earth and the other [elements].
He offers a rebuttal with the words "Of these," and so forth:
"However, their view is only slightly erroneous because of the assertion of permanence;
for the cognitions of form, sound, and so on, clearly exhibit difference."

If, however, [the self] were of the nature of a single cognition, then form, sound, taste, and so forth would necessarily be cognized simultaneously; moreover, there could be no change of state in that which is eternal.
Regarding the phrase "a minor fault":
this is because one accepts mere cognition accompanied by reasoning.
If that is so, why is even a slight fault said to exist therein? To this he replies with the words "because of the assertion of permanence," and so forth.

Why, then, is the acceptance of permanence not logical? To this he says: "The cognition appearing as form, sound, etc. and so forth. Permanence indeed means remaining in the same state (*tādavasthya*); impermanence, however, is the lack of remaining in that same state. Furthermore, the cognition appearing as form, sound, and so on, is never experienced as being in a single, constant state; rather, it appears successively—sometimes appearing as form and at other times appearing as sound and so forth. If these [objects] such as sound and the rest were of the nature of appearances within a single, permanent cognition, then they would appear all at once, like the appearance of a variegated carpet.
Because cognition, whose nature consists in the appearance of those [objects], exists at all times.

Now, it might be argued that this is a different state of cognition which arises sequentially as the appearance of sound and so forth; therefore, there will be no simultaneous perception of sound and the rest. To this, he says: "And if there is no different state in the eternal [cognition]."
Since the states are not distinct from the substratum of the states, the substratum itself would likewise undergo destruction and origination, just like the states.
Alternatively, if the states were identical to the substratum, it would follow that the substratum is eternal, just like the states.
Furthermore, if the states were distinct from the substratum, the relationship expressed as "these belong to that" could not be established, because there would be no mutual benefit.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the admission that [the self] is eternally nothing more than a single consciousness.

Furthermore, the proof of an eternal self consisting of cognition must occur either through perception or through inference; it is not, however, through perception, as shown by the verse beginning with "rūpa" (form).
"Cognition distinct from the awareness of form and so forth is not perceived.
Since that [awareness] differs at every moment, what remains established as non-different?"

Indeed, apart from the cognitions of form and so forth which appear in succession, no cognition is experienced that is permanent, unitary in nature, and abiding, by virtue of which its establishment through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) might occur.
Since it is established that this cognition of form and so forth, being experienced in succession, perishes at every moment, one must state what else remains that is non-different [from it].

Therefore, the meaning is that because such a self consisting of cognition—which has reached the moment of apprehension—is not perceived, it is simply an object of the conventional usage of "non-existent."
Nor is it thought that [the existence of eternal cognition] is established through inference;

for inference must have either absence as its logical mark (*liṅga*) or an effect as its mark. First of all, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes such a nature of cognition itself, whereas subverting evidence such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does exist; thus, the transformation (*vivarta*) of eternal cognition is untenable.

Furthermore, he demonstrates that on this view, the systematic distinction between bondage and liberation is not possible, beginning with the words "viparyasta" and so forth: "In a person who consists of a single cognition, no distinction exists between erroneous and non-erroneous knowledge; therefore, how could there be bondage and liberation?"

For one who holds the position that consciousness—which perishes at every moment—is indeed manifold for each person and proceeds as a distinct continuum, it is logical to establish the distinction between bondage and liberation based on the arising of a series of cognitions, whether erroneous or non-erroneous.

Furthermore, through the gradual practice of yoga, by the arising of increasingly pure knowledge, the cessation of the impure stream of cognition occurs, whereby liberation is attained; thus, the exertion for the sake of attaining liberation is fruitful.

Furthermore, for you who hold the position that the self (*ātman*) has the nature of a single, eternal cognition, how can bondage and liberation occur within a person whose essence is that single cognition?

For instance, if that single cognition were always of a distorted nature, then because there would be no other state, there could be no establishment of liberation. On the other hand, if it were undistorted, then because its nature would be eternally pure, there could be no bondage.

For us, however, representation (vijñapti) is held to be either afflicted or pure according to the distinction between individual mental continua; thus, the established order of bondage and liberation is logical.
As it has been said:
"It is both afflicted and purified, with stains and without stains."
If it were not defiled, all embodied beings would be liberated.
If this [mind] were not pure, then effort would be fruitless.
Thus [it is said].

[Page 125] Furthermore, it might be argued that bondage and liberation are merely conceptual constructs (*kalpita*) and not ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). To this, one must state the basis for even such a conceptual construction. However, in the case of the view that cognition is impermanent (*anityajñāna*), the basis has already been demonstrated. Consequently, this effort of yours toward the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*) for the sake of attaining liberation (*apavarga*) and transcending cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) results in nothing but mere exhaustion; this is what [the author] shows with the words "What indeed... and so forth.
What indeed would the yogi turn away from, or what would he accomplish through the practice of yoga?
For how could that which is of the nature of perversion ever be abandoned?
The knowledge of reality is not something to be produced, because it exists eternally through identity;
therefore, this entire practice of yoga is likewise fruitless.

For if the yogin were to cause anything to cease or to arise through the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*), then his effort would be fruitful; however, he does not so far remove error (*viparyāsa*), because that error is of the nature of that [Self], being of the nature of eternal consciousness (*nityajñāna*). Therefore, it cannot be abandoned, since abandonment is impossible for that which is eternal due to its indestructibility.
Nor does he accomplish the knowledge of reality through cultivation, because the knowledge of reality is already present at all times by virtue of being of the nature of eternal consciousness.
Therefore, this is not tenable.
Thus concludes the examination of the self according to the Upaniṣads.
The Examination of the Self according to the Vātsīputrīyas is stated, beginning with "But some," for the purpose of refuting the *pudgala* as conceived by the Vātsīputrīyas:
"But some, though considering themselves followers of the Sugata, nevertheless proclaim a self."
By means of the designation "person" (pudgala), it is devoid of being identical to or different from [the aggregates] and so forth.
"Some" refers to the Vātsīputrīyas.

For although they consider themselves sons of the Sugata, under the guise of the *pudgala*, they postulate a self that is inexpressible as either identical to or different from the aggregates (*skandhas*).

To show how those who have indeed accepted the status of being sons of the Blessed One—the Sugata, the proponent of selflessness—could possibly be so deeply attached to a false view of self, [the author] says, "even those who consider themselves followers of the Sugata," providing a ground for derision.

For this is the definition of a self: that which is the agent of the various types of wholesome and unwholesome actions, the experiencer of the desired and undesired fruits of its own performed actions, and that which transmigrates by abandoning the previous aggregates and taking up other subsequent aggregates, and is the enjoyer—that is the self.
And since all of this is also accepted [as true] regarding the person (pudgala), there is merely a dispute over a name.
Now, as to what the reasoning is for the ineffability of the person (*pudgala*), he says "from the aggregates," and so forth:
The person is not other than the aggregates, because that would entail the views of the non-Buddhists;
nor is it non-other, because that would entail [the faults of] multiplicity and so on. Therefore, its ineffability is correct.

If the person (*pudgala*) were other than the aggregates (*skandhas*), then there would be the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) imagined by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and consequently, the consequence of an eternal self would follow.
Furthermore, it is not logical for an eternal self to possess agency, enjoyership, and so forth, because—like space—it remains forever without distinction.
Moreover, the Blessed One has refuted an eternal self, and thus the teaching that "all phenomena are selfless" (*nirātman*) would be contradicted.
If it is argued that "then let [the person] be non-different [from the aggregates]," he says, "it is not non-different," and so forth.

For if the person were merely the aggregates, such as form and the rest, then because it would be non-different from the many aggregates, the person would necessarily possess multiplicity, just like their own nature;
yet it is held to be one.
As it has been said: "Just as a single person (pudgala) arises when arising in the world, so too does the Tathāgata.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), qualities such as impermanence are included.
And this being the case, the person (pudgala), like the aggregates (skandhas), would also be subject to annihilation.

Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the destruction of performed karma, and for you, this would result in the doctrine of nihilism which has been refuted; therefore, it is established that the *pudgala* exists as something inexpressible.

By the words "they are to be described," and so forth, he demonstrates that you yourselves have established—by your own very statement—that the person (*pudgala*) does not exist as a real entity because it is inexpressible:
"Those [elements] are expressible, but the person does not exist at all in an ultimate sense;
because it is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from them, like a sky-lotus and the like."

The formal argument is as follows: that which cannot be expressed in terms of being either identical to or different from a given entity is not a real entity, just like a sky-lotus; and the person (pudgala) is not expressible [in those terms]. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), [the examples are] feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, he states "otherness," and so forth, to show how pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established here:
"A real entity (*vastu*) never transcends either otherness or non-otherness;
however, that which is in reality formless is conceived as inexpressible."
For an entity cannot, in relation to another entity, transcend being either identical to it or different from it, as there is no other possible mode of existence.
Otherwise, even form and the other [sensory objects] would be inexpressible in relation to one another.
Therefore, it is only that which is formless and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is conceived as inexpressible, and not a real entity (*vastu*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because the conceptual construction of difference and non-difference has a real entity as its basis,
the inability to designate [an object] as either identical to or different from [it], and so forth, is appropriate only in the case of things that lack intrinsic nature."
For that negation which says "this is not that" with respect to a real entity is,
like another entity, clearly stated to be a distinctness [from it].
The negation of its being otherwise is itself designated as reality;
that entity does not transcend either reality or the differentiation of the entity.
For it is only a real entity (*vastu*), and not a non-entity (*avastu*), that serves as the basis for the conceptual alternatives of identity and difference.

Therefore, the inability to designate [an object] as being either identical to or different from [something else] is appropriate only in the case of things that lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), that is, those devoid of self-nature (*svabhāva*).
The connection [of the sentence] is: "The inability to designate identity, difference, and so forth is not appropriate in the case of a real entity."
In this regard, because there is no other possible alternative between difference and non-difference, he asks:

"How, then, is there no other alternative? and replies with the words beginning "That which is this... and so forth. For instance, when it is said that the person (*pudgala*) does not have the nature of form (*rūpa*) and the rest, that negation expresses precisely its distinctness from those [factors] such as form.

Because the nature of a thing is inseparable from the affirmation of its own intrinsic nature, the entity called "person" (pudgala) is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form and so forth; this is thus a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, this negation of a thing being something other than itself—the negation of its not having that nature—is expressed as being non-different from its true reality (*tattva*), because the negation of a thing's existence as a separate entity is inseparable from the affirmation of its true reality.
Otherwise, if no intrinsic nature whatsoever were established for it, then, due to the negation of all intrinsic natures, it would necessarily be a non-entity;

for non-entity is characterized by the negation of all intrinsic natures. The formal argument is as follows: whatever entity has its essential reality negated as being distinct from something else, that is precisely that [non-entity], just as form has its essential reality negated as being distinct from its own intrinsic nature.
And since the person (*pudgala*) has been refuted as being the self-nature (*ātmatattva*), the reason "because it is a distinct entity from form and so forth" is a *svabhāvahetu*.
Therefore, because a real entity does not transcend being either identical to or different from that given thing, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the fundamental reason is established.
Thus, it has first been demonstrated that if one accepts the inexpressibility [of the person], it follows that the person is merely a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*).

Now, considering that if one accepts the person as a real entity (*vastu*), its inexpressibility is untenable—otherwise there would be a contradiction with one's own words regarding the thesis—the author concludes with the verse beginning "from the aggregates" (*skandhebhyaḥ*) and so forth.
The statement "the person is not other than the aggregates" is an indication of its non-difference.
"The aggregates are not the person"—this clearly demonstrates its distinctness from them.

Furthermore, by asserting that the person (*pudgala*) is inexpressible, you have most clearly and loudly proclaimed the distinctness of the person from the aggregates (*skandha*); this is shown in the passage beginning with "for the association with contradictory properties," and so forth.
For the association with contradictory properties is said to be the difference between entities;
why then is there no such distinctness between the aggregates and the person?

The formal argument is as follows: those two things which are characterized by properties existing through mutual exclusion are mutually distinct, just like form and sensation, or like that which is possessed of corporeality and that which is possessed of incorporeality; and since the aggregates (skandhas) and the person (pudgala) are characterized by such mutually contradictory properties as "expressibility" and "inexpressibility," this is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
Showing that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says "For thus," and so forth:
"For in this way, the person (*pudgala*) is said to be inexpressible in relation to feeling and the other aggregates;
however, form, perception, and the rest are expressible in terms of identity or difference."
For instance, the person (pudgala) is held to be inexpressible in terms of identity or difference from feeling, perception, and so forth;
however, form, feeling, and the rest are expressible as being mutually different from one another—such as from feeling and the rest—and therefore the reason is not unestablished (asiddha).
He demonstrates that the imposition of contradictory properties is established here as well, with the words "by impermanence," and so forth:
"The aggregates such as form and the rest are held to be expressible as impermanent, but the person (pudgala) is not so; therefore, their difference is perfectly clear."

Because of the statement "all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent," form and the other aggregates must indeed be described as impermanent; however, the person (pudgala) is not intended to be described as impermanent in that same way, because it is held to be inexpressible in every respect. Furthermore, the reason [for its non-permanence] is not inconclusive, since the conventional usage of distinction is based solely on this much [i.e., the nature of the phenomena themselves]. Otherwise, the entire universe would become a single entity, and consequently, there would follow the absurd consequence of simultaneous arising and destruction.

It has been established that this person (pudgala) is not a real entity because it cannot be described as either identical to or different from [the aggregates]. To establish further that it is not a real entity precisely because it cannot be described as impermanent, he says: "The capacity for causal efficiency is the defining characteristic of existence; it is restricted to things that are momentary. Thus, that which is indescribable lacks the nature of a real entity. The capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) is the very definition of existence. This capacity is necessarily restricted to things that are momentary. Therefore, that which is indescribable [in terms of permanence or impermanence] cannot possess the nature of a real entity.

For this alone is the defining characteristic of existence and the intrinsic nature of a thing, namely, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); since the nature of a non-entity is the absence of all capacity, it follows by implication that the nature of a real entity is defined solely by its capacity for causal efficiency. Furthermore, that causal efficiency is restricted exclusively to momentary things;
that is to say, it is pervaded by momentariness itself.
Because for that which is permanent, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is incompatible with both successive and simultaneous action,
there is no reality (*vastutā*) in a person (*pudgala*) that cannot be described as momentary.
This is because its pervader, momentariness, is absent therein— just as when "treeness" is absent, "being a *śiṃśapā* tree" and so forth are necessarily absent.
As it has been said: "That which is inexpressible as impermanent cannot be the cause of anything. It might be argued:

"If the person (*pudgala*) were permanent, then there would be a contradiction regarding its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity; however, since it is inexpressible as impermanent, it is likewise [inexpressible] as permanent. Therefore, its capacity for causal efficiency is not at all contradictory. This is incorrect, for it is not logical that a thing (*vastu*) as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) could be devoid of both these modes; this is because permanence and impermanence are defined by their mutual exclusion.
Because, regarding a single entity, the abandonment or acceptance of one aspect is necessarily concomitant with the acceptance or abandonment of its other aspects.

For we do not here prohibit the application of the term "ineffable" (*avācya*) to the person (*pudgala*), since it is impossible for anyone to prohibit that which is introduced merely by one's own independent whim; rather, what is being examined here is the actual nature of the entity.

Is this intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity called the "person" (*pudgala*) always existent, or is it non-existent? If it exists, then it is necessarily eternal; for that which is called "eternal" is nothing other than that intrinsic nature which remains forever and does not perish.
As it has been said: "The wise call that eternal whose intrinsic nature does not perish.
On the other hand, if the position is that it does not exist, then it is likewise impermanent, because the characteristic of the impermanent is to have a non-abiding intrinsic nature.

Therefore, since there is no other alternative besides being momentary or non-momentary, and since for that which is non-momentary there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—whether occurring successively or simultaneously—existence, characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency, is pervaded by momentariness; thus, it is established that when momentariness ceases in the person (*pudgala*), existence also ceases.

If this is so, and if the person (*pudgala*) does not exist at all, why did the Blessed One, when asked whether the soul is the same as the body or the soul is different from the body, not say "this is undeclared" (*avyākṛta*), but instead simply say "it does not exist"? To this he says: "But regarding the contradiction with the meaning of the scriptures... and so forth.
"But regarding the contradiction with the meaning of the scriptures, the Great Beings have exerted themselves;
the various words of the Compassionate One were intended to refute nihilism."

For if the person (*pudgala*) were established as a real entity (*dharmin*), then its properties—such as identity with or difference from [the aggregates]—would deserve to be declared as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
However, since that very entity is not established, how could a property of it be specified when it is non-existent?
For sharpness and such qualities cannot belong to a non-existent thing like a donkey's horn, by virtue of which it might be declared.
Therefore, demonstrating that the person (*pudgala*) exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisattva*), the Blessed One stated, "This [person] is undeclared.
However, he did not say "it does not exist," because the opponent had not asked about the actual nature (*svarūpa*) of the subject (*dharmin*).

Alternatively, even though it exists as a designation, he did not say "it does not exist" out of consideration for the disposition of disciples who are unfit for the teaching of emptiness, in order to avoid their adherence to the notion of non-existence even regarding what exists as a designation.
And as it has been said:
"Having regard for the injury from the fangs of [wrong] views and the ruin of [wholesome] actions,
the Jinas teach the Dharma like a man who carries off a cub of a tiger."

Thus, since masters such as Vasubandhu have exerted themselves in elucidating this intention in works such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Paramārthasaptatikā*, it should be understood from those very sources.
The point here is that it is not written out due to the fear of excessive prolixity.
To the question, "If this is so, how is the statement 'there exists a being who undergoes rebirth' to be interpreted? he says: "Because of [the fear of] nihilism," and so forth.
The ellipsis of the sentence is: "For the various teachings of the Compassionate One, which assert the existence of sentient beings, are not contradictory.

For when there is the designation of a "sentient being" within a continuum of consciousness, the Blessed One said, "A sentient being exists," with the underlying intention that this [continuum] is not annihilated.
Otherwise, one would understand the non-existence of even those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) whose succession of causal moments has not ceased.
Because there is no being in the next world, the non-existence of the next world is established; thus, those with nihilistic views would be the ones to be converted.
As for that which was said: "O monks, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the bearer of the burden.

Therein, the burden is the five aggregates of clinging; the taking up of the burden is craving; the laying down of the burden is liberation; and the bearer of the burden is the person (pudgala). How is this to be understood? For it is not logical that the burden itself should be the bearer of the burden. To this he says: "By means of a mind [concerned with] the collection and so forth, there is the teaching of the bearer of the burden and so forth."
And the specific negation shines forth for those who hold such views.

In this context, the aggregates (*skandhas*) themselves, existing at the same time and intended as a totality, receive the designation "collection" (*samudāya*); these very same [aggregates], existing simultaneously as cause and effect, are designated as a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*). And when they exist as the basis for a single conceptual apprehension (*ekākāra-parāmarśa*), they are indicated by the two terms "possessor of the continuum" (*saṃtānin*) and "constituent of the collection" (*samudāyin*). Therefore, the remainder of the argument is that the teaching concerning the bearer of the burden (*bhārahāra*) and so forth is not contradictory, because it is based on the intention of a "collection" and so forth, with the mind directed toward a collection and so forth. By the first word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of "continuum" and so forth is intended; by the second, the inclusion of "burden" and so forth.
In that context, those very aggregates (*skandhas*), when intended in the form of a collection, a continuum, and so forth, are designated as the "person" (*pudgala*) who "carries the burden.
This is because in common worldly usage, the term "person" is applied precisely to that [collection].

For this very reason, after the Blessed One asked, "Who is the carrier of the burden? It is the person," he explained the person by saying: "O Venerable One, he who has such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a long life," and so on.

This [person], being thus characterized as a collection of aggregates (*skandha-samudāya-lakṣaṇa*), exists as a mere designation (*prajñapti*); it is for the purpose of demonstrating that he should not be understood otherwise—as something else that is permanent or a substantial entity (*dravya*) as imagined by others—that this must necessarily be understood in this way. Otherwise, since the burden (*bhāra*) and so forth are also taught separately from the aggregates, they would likewise not be included within the aggregates, just like the person (*pudgala*).
Therefore, those very same preceding aggregates which function toward the arising of subsequent aggregates are spoken of as "the burden."

However, those who are designated as having attained the fruit are called "bearers of the burden"; thus, this [scriptural passage] is not a proof [for the existence of a self]. Uddyotakara says: For one who does not accept a self, it is impossible to establish that this word of the Tathāgata possesses meaning, because this was said:

"Venerable sir, form is not I; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, venerable sir, are not I. Likewise, it is said: "O monk, form is not you; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not you."
For by this, the aggregates such as form and the rest are refuted as being objects of the notion of "I.
Furthermore, this is a specific refutation and not a general refutation;
and one who does not accept a self ought to refute [the aggregates] only in a general sense.

"But you are not [that]"— such a specific negation is invariably concomitant with the affirmation of something else. For example, when it is said, "I do not see with my left eye," it is understood that one does see with the right.
Even by that non-perception, the mention of "either" would be useless; one should simply say, "I do not see [it].
Likewise here as well, when it is said, "Form is not the self," up to "Consciousness is not the self," it is indicated that there exists a self distinct from those [aggregates].
Whether that [self] is inexpressible or something else, in any case, the self exists.
Regarding this, it is said: "And there is the negation of specific [attributes]," and so forth.
What is meant by this is as follows: this mountain of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), rising with twenty peaks, prevails among those of poor intellect.
Namely: form is the self, up to consciousness is the self; the self possesses form, up to the self possesses consciousness; form is in the self, up to consciousness is in the self.
In that regard, for the purpose of refuting the first five views, a specific refutation directed at those who hold such views is appropriate.
Those for whom there is a view such as "form is the self" are called "those who hold such views.
Indeed, precisely that which is a point of doubt for one of deluded intellect is restated and then negated.
However, no injunction for anyone is intended here;
otherwise, a proponent who utters a statement that does not refine the listener would indeed be an unwise person.
Thus concludes the examination of the self according to the Vātsīputrīyas.

In order to justify this qualification "perishable," he says "Alternatively," and so forth: "Alternatively, this effort is made in vain, because by the very establishment of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the rest are already refuted."

Therefore, in order to negate without distinction the categories already mentioned and those yet to be discussed, such as genus and so forth, the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is clearly established.

The sense is this: since the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) pervading all things without exception has been established, the entire mass of entities postulated by others—such as *prakṛti*, *Īśvara*, and so forth—is already being cast aside with a single blow; therefore, our undertaking of refutations by articulating [the faults] at every step through an excessively extensive composition of text results in nothing but mere exhaustion, for that [mass of entities] has already been refuted by a very brief means.

For indeed, all [categories] such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth are not accepted by others as perishing immediately after arising, nor are they held by some to have the property of ceasing without leaving a trace (*niranvayanirodha*).

Therefore, considering that this [objection] is already refuted by the very proof of the momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) which pervades all things, we establish momentariness specifically in order to refute: (1) the [categories] beginning with "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) and ending with the "person" (*pudgala*) as stated by us; (2) the genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), substance (*dravya*), and so forth to be discussed hereafter; (3) the referent of words (*śabdārtha*); (4) the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*); (5) the variegated entity resembling a multi-colored gem; (6) the entity persisting through the three times; (7) the four elements accepted by the Cārvākas and others; and (8) the collection of Vedic words desired by the followers of Jaimini. [The word] "clearly" (*spaṣṭam*) [is used].

Because that [reason] is demonstrated by means of the three-fold characteristic of the probans for the sake of the practitioner, it follows that the entire meaning of the treatise is fully completed within this very examination of the permanence of entities; thus it is said.
How is this established? To this he says: "By way of being produced or unproduced," and so forth.
Some maintain that there is a twofold division by way of being produced or unproduced;
others hold that the division of entities is by way of being momentary or non-momentary.
For here, the Naiyāyikas and others, maintaining that not even a single entity is momentary, establish a twofold classification of things based on their being produced or unproduced:
some are produced, such as jars and the like; some are unproduced, such as atoms, space, and so forth.
However, others, such as the Vātsīputrīyas and others, also accept a twofold classification of things based on their being momentary or non-momentary.
For, according to his view, cognitions, words, flames, and so forth are momentary, whereas earth, space, and the like are non-momentary.

Thus, the division of views having been established, [the author], demonstrating that those things which are accepted as being produced are first taken as the subject (*pakṣa*) and then proven by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), says "In that regard," and so forth:
"In that regard, whatever entities are produced, all of them are subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgin*),
because they exist independently with respect to their own destruction."

By the statement, "Because all things remain independent of other causes with respect to their destruction," the three-fold logical reason (*trilakṣaṇa-hetu*) is indicated; explaining that very point, he says:
"That which, with respect to a certain state, does not depend at all on another cause, is to be known as certain in that regard, because it arises in that manner from its own causes."
For just as a causal complex is independent in producing its own effect,
so too all things that are born are independent with respect to their destruction.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which are independent with respect to a certain state are necessarily restricted to that state.
For example, a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) whose fruit is immediately subsequent is restricted to the production of its own effect.
And all produced (*janmin*) or conditioned (*kṛtaka*) entities are independent with respect to their destruction; this is thus a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
"Another cause" means distinct from the producer. Regarding the term "determined," he states the reason: "from its own causes."
The meaning is: because they have arisen with that very determined form.

Furthermore, those things which are not determined in a particular respect do not at all become independent in that respect, just as unbaked jars and the like [are not independent] with regard to baking and so forth; this is the example here by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).

But is the reason not inconclusive? For even if entities do not depend on other causes for their destruction, since it is possible for an entity to be destroyed after having endured at another place or at another time, it cannot be established that they must perish immediately upon arising. To this he says: "Even though independent," and so forth.
Even though independent, if this [destruction] were to occur at another place or time...
Because it depends upon that, it does not follow that this [entity] is independent.
"This" refers to destruction. "By virtue of depending upon that" means...
Because it depends on other places and times:

for if that which is independent of something were to exist at some place or at some time, then, by virtue of depending on that place and time, it would not be independent at all; so how could there be any deviation? To explain: how can that which exists in another place or time by excluding one particular place or time be called "independent"? For its very existence [there] is its dependence, and not an intentional effort, since it is devoid of intentionality.
If, then, the intended meaning of the reason is "because of being entirely independent," then the reason is not established;
for instance, some things are seen to depend upon hammers and the like for their destruction,
such as jars and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that even those things such as cognitions and sounds, which are well-known to be independent, do not depend on a hammer or the like, yet still depend on place and time—and thus the reason is unestablished (asiddha)—the author replies with the words "In all cases indeed," etc.:
"All produced things whatsoever are entirely independent regarding their destruction;
for in every respect, the causes of destruction are incapable of acting upon them."
"Everywhere indeed" means that produced things are independent of all causes of destruction, such as place, time, and so forth.

Since those [causes] accepted as being the causes of destruction are incapable of acting and provide no assistance, it is not logical for [a thing] to depend on what provides no assistance, as that would lead to an absurdity.
To explain how [the cause of destruction] is ineffective, he says "tathāhi" and so forth:
"For thus, a cause of destruction is not logically the producer of a destruction that is not distinct from the entity itself,
because the entity is born from its own cause."

For destruction, when being produced, must be either a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*). In that regard, if it were a real entity, then that destruction would be produced by a cause of destruction as either non-different from the object or different from it.
Since there are no two possible alternatives for something that exists as a real entity, the positions of "both" or "neither" are indeed untenable;
for in the case of a real entity, the abandonment or acceptance of one aspect is necessarily concomitant with the acceptance or abandonment of its other aspects.
It has been stated that the application of affirmation and negation belongs to a single entity.
In that regard, first of all, the position that [negation] is not a distinct entity is untenable; for the nature of an existent arises from its own cause alone at the very moment of its production.
Furthermore, because it is non-different from that [existent], it must likewise be already established, just like the existent itself.
Furthermore, a cause for that which has already been produced is not logical, because it would entail the consequence of the cause never ceasing.

It might be argued that this entity is not produced from its own cause in its entirety; therefore, it acquires another nature called "destruction" from another cause. To this he says: "And not when the partless has arisen," and so forth. When the partless self of the entity has arisen from its own cause—
Therefore, destruction is indeed identical to that [entity] itself; it cannot be produced again by others.

For a single entity does not possess two intrinsic natures (svabhāva) by which there could be a partial production; rather, an entity is partless, and since it arises from its own causes as produced in its entirety, how could another nature be imparted to it at a later time by other causes?

For it is not logical that something which is not established when another is being established should be its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because non-difference is characterized by a single destiny (ekayogakṣema). Therefore, that entity which arises at a later time and has destruction as its nature is a different intrinsic nature; and how could that which is different belong to it? Thus, this [argument] is trivial.

Now, as for the position that destruction is a distinct entity, he shows that even in that case, the cause of destruction does nothing at all for the entity, in the verse beginning with "padārthavyatirikte":
"But when a name called 'destruction' is applied as something distinct from the entity,
nothing at all is produced in that entity by other causes."
Therefore, as before, the consequences regarding perception and so forth follow;
and because it remains in that same state, its practice is not at all logical.
For it is not the case that by the production of one thing another is assisted, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor is it reasonable to say that an entity is assisted by the production of its destruction, because no relationship between them is established. To explain: since their difference is admitted, there is no relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*); nor is there one characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*), because the destruction arises solely from its own cause; and there exists no other real relationship whatsoever.

Alternatively, even if a relationship [between cause and effect] were to exist, because the entity would remain in its state, there would follow the consequence that it would be perceived in exactly that same way;
"perception" is the effect, and by the word "etcetera," the holding of water, the breaking of a thigh, and so forth are included.

If it is argued that [the entity] does not perform its effects, such as perception, because it is covered or obstructed by that distinct destruction, he replies with the words "because of remaining in the same state" (*tādavasthyāt*), and so forth.

For it is not logical that something which neither impairs nor produces a specific excellence (*svabhāvātiśaya*) in the nature of an entity should be its coverer or its obstructor, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, since its previous nature remains unobscured and unobstructed, both its covering and its obstruction are untenable.

It might be argued that the consequence of [the entity] being perceived as before does not arise, because the entity is destroyed by that destruction which is distinct from it; to this he says: "By the entity named 'destruction,' etc.
It is false that an entity is destroyed by an entity called "destruction," because the same alternatives regarding its difference and so forth apply there as well.

For when destruction destroys an entity, does it destroy something other than itself or not? Or, in the case where destruction characterized by annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa-lakṣaṇa*) is produced, the same alternatives recur here as well— just as with a hammer or similar instruments— and the fault already stated applies there too,
and will be stated again in that context as well regarding this "other destruction" which is produced under the name of destruction.
"By way of following after the object" means by way of following after conceptual constructions such as otherness and so forth.
Thus, it has first been demonstrated that [the effect] is not produced as a real entity.
Showing that [destruction] is also not a non-entity, he says "consisting of existence and non-existence," and so forth:
"If destruction— which consists of existence and non-existence and is known by another name as 'annihilation' (pradhvaṃsa)— is produced,
its production is not logically consistent."
And if non-existence were an effect, it would necessarily follow that it is produced by the power of a cause— just like a sprout or other such things— since it would then possess a generated nature.

For there is the production of an existent (*bhāva*), not of a non-existent (*abhāva*), because the latter is characterized by the absence of all inherent nature that could be made its cause; thus, there is no form whatsoever to be produced.

Therefore, destruction—which consists of both the existent and the non-existent, and which is essentially the negation of existence—is not produced by anything, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), like the horn of a donkey.
Otherwise, due to being an effect, it would necessarily be a real entity (*vastu*), just like a sprout or similar things.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is an effect is a real entity (*vastu*), just like sprouts and so forth; and destruction is an effect. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
To establish its pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "because it arises through the power of a cause. For that alone is called an effect.

By virtue of the power of its cause, a thing attains a specific excellence of its own nature; and it is precisely that thing which has attained this excellence of its own nature [that is the effect]. On this point, there is no disagreement even with the Naiyāyikas and others.
For instance, "being an effect" is defined as either inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*) or inherence in its own cause (*svakāraṇa-samavāya*).

However, neither inherence in existence nor inherence in its own cause can apply to destruction, because that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that destruction, like substances and so forth, would be a substratum for existence.

If this is so, let there be substantiality for destruction; what fault is there in that? To this he says: "By affirmation alone," and so forth: "And thus non-existence is established by way of affirmation, because it relies upon exclusion (paryudāsa).
Yet, the conceptual construction regarding difference and so forth continues to operate therein."

Furthermore, when the question arises as to how there can be the production of a non-entity (abhāva) through a positive injunction (vidhi), this was stated: "by resorting to exclusion" (paryudāsāśrayāt).
The meaning is: by relying upon exclusion (paryudāsa).

For, by the force of intention, a very real entity (bhāva) that is distinct from some other entity is designated as a "non-entity" (abhāva); and in that case, the previously mentioned fault recurs regarding the conceptual alternatives such as difference (vyatireka) and so forth.

Now, fearing this fault, if it is accepted that negation (*abhāva*) as destruction is not produced by causes of destruction in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), but rather in the form of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*),
[the author] says "Now," etc., demonstrating that even in that case, the utter lack of efficacy of the cause of destruction has been established most clearly.
Now, this negation of action certainly does not produce an entity;
nevertheless, the lack of causality is established for the agent because his status as a cause is abandoned.

For instance, in the case of a simple negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha), because the word "actor" (naṭaḥ) is connected with the verb "does" (karotinā), the phrase "he does non-existence" means "he does not do existence. Thus, through the negation of an action, the causality of the cause of destruction is shown to be non-existent; and since that which is a non-agent cannot be a cause, there is no such thing as a cause of destruction.
Desiring here to point out the proofs stated by Aviddhakarṇa for establishing that destruction has a cause, he says "nanu" and so forth:
"Now, this destruction does not exist at the time of the entity's existence;
it is neither prior nor long after; rather, it occurs immediately following the entity."
And thus, this [cause] is properly characterized as possessing a cause because it is restricted by time;
for the connection with occasional occurrence is refuted in the case of that which is independent [of causes].

For instance, destruction does not occur at the time of a thing’s existence, because that would entail the non-existence [of the thing] even for a single moment; nor does it occur prior to its arising, because it is impossible for that which has not yet been born to be destroyed—indeed, the sons of barren women and the like do not perish while still unproduced. Furthermore, even if it were to occur later, it could not happen immediately in the third or subsequent moments, because it is impossible for that which has already perished to perish again, just as fire cannot be burned once it has been reduced to ashes. Rather, destruction occurs in the second moment immediately following the existence of the thing.
Consequently, it is established that destruction possesses a cause, because it is restricted in time, just like a sprout and the like.
This is what is meant by "because it is restricted in time."
The meaning is "because of being occasional.
Establishing the pervasion (vyāpti) of this, he says: "For the connection with being occasional," and so forth.
Indeed, being occasional is not logical for that which is independent, because it would follow that such a thing must exist eternally.
Therefore, because it occurs only occasionally, its possession of a cause is established.
He shows that [the point] is established from this as well, with the words "and because of its existence immediately after the entity," and so forth.
And because it exists immediately after the entity, it is logical that it is indeed an effect;
furthermore, because it comes into being after having not existed, it is regarded as just like any other subsequent moment.
Thus, these three reasons have been stated:

destruction has a cause because it is occasional; because it is accepted by the Buddhists as occurring immediately after the production of a thing; and because it acquires its own nature having previously not existed, just like any other moment.
By way of contrast, [the absence of a cause applies to] things such as a rabbit's horn.
He also states the reasoning set forth by Uddyotakara, beginning with "because of being causeless," and so on:
"Furthermore, because it is causeless, this [non-existence] is non-existent, like the son of a barren woman;
or else it is eternal, like space, since there is no other alternative."
If all things were non-existent, they would be eternal because they would not perish; furthermore,
the cognition that all conditioned phenomena are subject to destruction would be without a cause.
Even if [the entity] were eternal, its coexistence with destruction would not be contradictory; furthermore, the assertion that the unborn perishes does not follow reason at all.

For he who says thus, asserting that there is no cause for destruction, must be questioned: "Is destruction non-existent because it lacks a cause, like a lotus in the sky? Or is it eternal because it lacks a cause, like space? For in your own system, that which is causeless is seen to be of two kinds: eternal or non-existent; indeed, there is no other category apart from existence and non-existence.

In that regard, if destruction were non-existent because it lacks a cause, then it would follow that all entities are eternal, since there would be no destruction. Furthermore, the cognition that "all conditioned phenomena perish" would become baseless; for one does not say "he goes" when there is no going. Alternatively, if it were eternal, then an entity would have to coexist with its own destruction, because it would persist at all times.
And this is not logical, because existence and non-existence are characterized by being mutually exclusive.
Now, if coexistence is not admitted, then the arising of an effect would not be possible, because its opposite, destruction, would be eternally present.

Consequently, even the destruction of that which has not arisen is not tenable; for it is well known in the world that things such as a rabbit’s horn, which have not arisen, do not perish. Therefore, the statement that "there is destruction of the unarisen" does not at all conform to reason.
With the words "In this regard," and so forth, he refutes everything:
"In this matter, what kind of destruction are they questioning as being ultimate? Is it the entity itself, which has the nature of existing for only a moment, that has arisen in such a way?"
Now, regarding the cessation of the nature of an entity,
which is designated as "destruction," there is indeed no contradiction whatsoever when one first subjects it to critical inquiry.

For destruction is of two kinds, characterized as either affirmation or negation. To explain: first, an entity itself, which by its very nature abides for only a moment, is designated as "destruction" on the grounds that it perishes while in motion;
or second, destruction is the act of perishing, also known by the name *pradhvaṃsa* (annihilation), which is characterized by the falling away from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity.

In that regard, if an inquiry is made concerning the proof of the state of having a cause for the former alternative by means of the reasons already stated, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
He demonstrates that very state of being established and to-be-established with the words "For that which... and so forth:
"For whatever entity, lasting for only a moment, is called 'destruction,' we maintain that it possesses a cause; however, because of the absence of anything else, it is without a cause."

If this is so, how is it that you accept destruction to be causeless? To this he says: "But because of the absence of another, it is causeless. The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: we maintain that it is causeless because of the non-existence of "another"—that is, a destroyer such as a hammer occurring at a later time—which is distinct from its own causes.

And in this case, regarding destruction (*vināśa*) as the subject (*dharmin*) characterized in such a way, these two reasons—namely, "because of its occasional nature" and "because of its acquisition of self-existence after not having existed before"—are unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, if "occurring immediately after another entity" is intended in a general sense, then it is indeed established, since it is well-known that its existence occurs immediately after a causal entity.

However, if what is intended is its occurring immediately after an entity that is essentially perishable, then the reason is unestablished; this he demonstrates with the words "occurring immediately after another entity," and so forth.
In such a case, there is no absence of the state of occurring immediately after an object;
for that which has the nature of a mobile entity arises together with existence itself.

Regarding the phrase "of such a kind": since [destruction] is not distinct from the nature of the moving entity, there is no part of an impartite entity by which its state of occurring immediately after that [entity] could be established. This is because destruction, being non-distinct from that nature, is established at the very moment that [the entity] is established, just like that nature itself.
Otherwise, as has been stated, that very nature of his would not exist.
He shows that what was stated—that the cognition of the perishability of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is itself causeless—is also refuted by this very same reasoning, saying: "Therefore":
because destruction exists, all conditioned things are not eternal;
nor does it follow that the cognition "they are perishable" is without a cause.

For precisely because things have the nature of momentary existence and are thus determined as having such forms, they serve as the cause for that cognition; therefore, there is no consequence of [the cognition] being without a cause.

Now, if destruction characterized by total annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*) is intended as the subject (*dharmin*), then he shows that all three reasons are unestablished (*asiddha*) with the words "But of annihilation," and so forth:
"But because annihilation is devoid of self-nature (*nairātmya*), it has no state of existing immediately after [the cause];
for it lacks the connection of coming into being after not having existed, like a sky-lotus and the like."

For properties such as "occurring immediately after" (anantarabhāvitva) and so forth are based only on existent things (vastu), not on non-existent things, as in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like. Furthermore, destruction (pradhvaṃsa) is without self (nirātman) and without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva); how, then, could properties such as "occurring immediately after" be possible for it? And [the phrase] "not being a connection with existence after having been non-existent" (nābhūtvā bhāvayoga)—by the word "and" (ca), the inclusion of "occasional occurrence" (kādācitkatva) is intended.

If this is so, one might raise the objection: "If destruction does not exist as something that occurs immediately after [the entity], then how can it be said that 'the destruction of the entity occurs'? For it cannot be the case that something which simply does not exist can be said to 'occur'. Anticipating this, he says "pradhvaṃsa" and so forth.
The meaning conveyed here is simply that "destruction occurs," not that "an entity occurs";
no positive injunction of anything is intended in this case.

Although destruction is indicated as something being enjoined, nevertheless, what is perceived is merely the negation of an entity; it is not, in the ultimate sense, the injunction of any positive thing.

One might object: "Since the word 'becomes' (bhavati) is employed here just as in the expression 'he becomes his son' and so forth, it follows that becoming itself is being enjoined here. To this he replies with "For not," and so on:
"For when a man is merely given the name 'bāleya,' no property whatsoever belonging to a donkey attaches to him."
For the existence or non-existence of things does not conform merely to the application of words, because the application [of words] is dependent solely upon one's own will.
Otherwise, if a certain person were to apply the name "bāleya" to someone by the force of his own desire, it would follow that all the properties of a donkey would apply to that person.
The words *bāleya* and *rāsabha* are synonyms for "donkey."

This must necessarily be understood: namely, that there is only a negation of the intrinsic nature of a thing, and nothing at all is being affirmed. For if an entity called "destruction" were itself affirmed, then what would be removed by the statement, "nothing whatsoever arises from this thing"?
Otherwise, if a distinct category called "destruction" (dhvaṃsa) were postulated, nothing at all would have happened to the entity; so why would that entity cease to exist?

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "if all things were non-existent," he says: "And thus, for destruction whose nature is the cessation of an entity," and so forth. "And thus, for destruction whose nature is the cessation of an entity, non-existence is accepted because of its separation from the form of a real thing (*vastu*), not because it has the nature of the absence of an entity (*bhāvābhāva*)."
Thus it is said:

because [non-existence] consists in the dissociation from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, and not in the cessation of the essential form of an existing entity, how could all things be eternal? For if their destruction—characterized by the negation of intrinsic nature—were non-existent, then they would be eternal. However, since destruction, characterized by the negation of intrinsic nature, exists for them as something itself of a non-existent form, how could they be eternal?
However, the cause for the cognition that all conditioned phenomena are subject to destruction has indeed already been stated.
Regarding what was stated—that even if [the entity] were eternal, there would be co-existence, and so forth—he replies with the verse beginning "nivṛttirūpatā":
"In this case, its nature as a cessation is not expressed by way of a positive injunction (vidhi);
rather, the persistence of its substantial form beyond a single moment is what is negated."
Therefore, since no established form whatsoever has been prescribed for this,
the conceptualization of it as permanent is groundless when applied to it.

Even by this statement, "cessation occurs," the nature of cessation is not expressed as a positive injunction (*vidhi*) regarding this destruction, because it possesses no form that could be enjoined.
Rather, what is negated is the persistence of the entity's own nature beyond a single moment.

Therefore, this [destruction] is exclusively of the nature of non-existence; thus, the conceptualization of it as permanent is entirely without foundation, since, due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), it cannot possess a form that remains established at all times.
Because [the property] is tied to its own nature, it is tied to the nature of being either eternal or non-eternal.

As for what was stated by you—that that which is causeless is twofold, namely eternal or non-existent—that is due to your ignorance of the tenets of others; for according to the Buddhist logicians (*nyāyavādin*), that which is causeless is simply non-existent.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "A Bodhisattva dwelling in the contemplation of phenomena among all phenomena does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon."
Regarding the phrase "that which is devoid of dependent origination":

those Vaibhāṣikas who conceptualize entities such as space (*ākāśa*) as existing substances are relegated solely to your own [non-Buddhist] position and are not followers of the Son of the Śākya; therefore, the citation of their opinion would be irrelevant.
Thus, since all causes of destruction are incapable of producing any effect, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
For this reason as well, it must be stated that the causes of destruction are ineffective.
To explain: an entity, when arising from its own cause, arises either by nature as something inherently perishable or as something inherently imperishable.
If it is perishable, there is no role for a cause of destruction, because it perishes by virtue of its very own nature.
For whatever is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of something, that very thing, arising from its own cause, becomes such; it does not, however, depend on another cause for its existence.
Just as luminosity, fluidity, heat, hardness, and so forth, having arisen with those as their very essence, do not depend on another cause for their state of being luminous and so on.

It might be argued: "Just as seeds and the like, although possessing the intrinsic nature of producing sprouts and so forth, do not produce them alone because they depend on other causes such as water, in the same way, an entity—even if its intrinsic nature is non-perishing—will require another cause for its destruction."
This is incorrect;
for it is only that which has reached its final state that is admitted to have the nature of a producer, and nothing else.
Therefore, whatever possesses that nature necessarily produces [the effect] and does not depend on anything else.
That which, while situated in a granary or similar location, does not produce [the effect], is not of that [productive] nature;
however, because it is the cause of the cause, it is designated as a "cause" only figuratively, and thus there is no deviation [from the rule].
Furthermore, if the position is taken that the self is imperishable, then even the cause of destruction would be entirely ineffective.
Because it is impossible for anyone to effect a change in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

For instance, if the intrinsic nature were not to perish immediately after arising, then even later that very same nature would remain its established characteristic; being in that state, what could a cause of destruction do to it such that it would perish?
Alternatively, one might argue that just as copper and other substances, though possessing a solid form, undergo a transformation through contact with fire and so forth.
Likewise, even though an entity possesses an indestructible intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is argued that its alteration is produced by a cause of destruction;
thus, having encountered the cause of destruction, it perishes.
This is incorrect.

In this case, that very same thing does not become otherwise, because "becoming otherwise" is characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). To explain: as for this so-called "becoming otherwise," is it something distinct from the entity, or is it the entity itself? It cannot be the entity itself, because that has already been established previously by its own causes.

If, on the other hand, it is a different entity, then in that case the entity would possess the quality of being non-perishable and would remain exactly as it was; thus, there would be no change in its state.

Furthermore, the example of copper and so forth is also unestablished.
