For instance, when the preceding moment of hardness in copper and such things ceases due to its own inherent nature of cessation, another entirely distinct entity called "liquidity" arises from a different causal complex consisting of fire and other auxiliary causes, as well as its own material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

Furthermore, when that which has the nature of fluidity and so forth perishes due to its spontaneous cessation (*svarasanirodha*), another distinct nature called "solidity" arises from both auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*) and its own material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). Thus, there is no alteration (*anyathātva*) of a single entity.

Therefore, the cause of destruction is in every respect ineffective; hence, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists within one's own position.
Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it has already been established previously.

It might be argued: "Just as space does not depend on anything else for its corporeality (*mūrtatva*) and yet is not invariably present therein, so too there may be a produced entity (*bhāva*) which, though created, is not accepted by the opponent as impermanent;
for [the opponent] accepts that everything possessing a cause is impermanent."
Since only those [entities] are here made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*) and no others, how could there be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*)?

As for those which, despite being produced (*kṛtaka*), might be thought to be eternal because they are indestructible, they are in reality included within the category of the unproduced (*akṛtaka*); therefore, it should be understood that by the very refutation of the latter, the former is also refuted—thus there is no fault.

Nor is it established that space and the like are independent with respect to properties such as corporeality; for whatever property a thing lacks, it is necessarily dependent with respect to that property. Indeed, no dependence of entities is postulated with respect to a property already possessed; rather, it is only with respect to what is not yet attained. Thus, the example is unestablished.

Now, with reference to the category of unproduced things, he says "But those," and so forth: "But those entities such as space which are accepted as being unproduced do not exist at all in reality, because they are devoid of causal capacity."
At that time, conceptual constructions such as momentariness or non-momentariness have no footing in those [entities];
for it is the entity itself by which one might [predicate] it as momentary or otherwise.

For if entities such as space were established as having real existence, then only then could an investigation into properties such as momentariness apply to them; for properties do not have establishment independently. Otherwise, their very status as properties would be lost.

Furthermore, space and the like are not unconditioned subjects (dharmin), because, being devoid of all causal capacity, they fall within the scope of conventional discourse as non-existent, like the son of a barren woman. The formal argument is: whatever is devoid of all causal capacity is a non-entity, just like the son of a barren woman; and space and the like are devoid of all causal capacity. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
In reality, it is either a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the conventional usage of "non-existent" is based solely on this much; nor is it unestablished (*asiddha*), as we shall demonstrate later. Furthermore, because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory (*viruddha*).
But why does the conceptual distinction between momentary and non-momentary not apply to a non-entity? To this he says: "For that which has a form persisting for a moment," and so forth.
For an entity whose form persists for a moment is called momentary;
conversely, an entity that is pervaded by a stable form is called non-momentary.
This is easily understood.

Uddyotakara, however, says: "The suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*) is untenable in the word *kṣaṇika*. For, if—according to the etymological rule—the moment (*kṣaṇa*) is defined as destruction (*kṣaya*), and it is understood that something is *kṣaṇika* because it possesses such a moment, then this is not logical due to the difference in time; for when there is destruction, the thing undergoing destruction is not present, and a possessive suffix is not observed between two things existing at different times. Furthermore, if it is said that a 'moment' is a state characterized by destruction immediately following existence, even then, since the thing is identical with that [characteristic], the possessive suffix is not appropriate."

Now, as for the claim that "momentary" refers to things that abide for the duration of a moment— since a moment is the ultimate limit of time, those which abide for it are called "momentary"— this too is not tenable.
This is because time is accepted as a mere designation (*saṃjñāmātra*), and it is not logical for a mere designation to serve as a qualification of a real entity.
Regarding this, he says: "That which does not endure beyond its arising," and so forth.
That intrinsic nature of a thing which does not endure beyond its arising is called a *kṣaṇa* (moment). That which possesses such [a nature] is considered momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
The moment (*kṣaṇa*) of a thing is said to be its nature of perishing immediately after arising; that which possesses this [nature] is called "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).
Thus it has been said: "A moment is that which perishes immediately after attaining its own existence; that which possesses this [nature] is momentary."

[Objection: "Even so, since the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not a different entity [from the thing itself], the cognition ‘this belongs to that’—which is based on a distinction—is not tenable. To this, he says: "Even though there is no difference in the object," and so forth. Even when there is no difference in the object, the expression ‘this belongs to that’ is not contradicted;
for a denotative word arises merely through a convention established by desire.

Just as in expressions such as "the nature of itself" (*svasya svabhāvaḥ*) or "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*), the genitive case of separation (*vyatireka-ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) occurs by relying on a distinction conceptually constructed by the intellect even though no real distinction exists, so too will it be here; for words do not conform to the actual nature of things, but rather follow the speaker's intention.

Furthermore, to whatever extent a sound is employed by speakers for a particular meaning, to that same extent it conveys that meaning through the power of convention; however, in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a "base" (prakṛti) or an "affix" (pratyaya).
And this word "momentary" (kṣaṇika) has been applied by the learned to any entity whatsoever that does not persist beyond its moment of arising.

And regarding such a thing intended by the term "momentary," whether the word "momentary" (kṣaṇika) be employed with its suffix or without its suffix, we show that there is no great regard for this conventional expression which follows our mere whim, by saying "that which lasts only after its arising," and so forth:
"But what is intended here is a thing that lasts only after its arising;
in that case, let the word be used either with its suffix or without its suffix."
"Thus" means by the term "momentary.
It is "with a suffix" (sapratyaya) because it occurs together with a suffix that expresses possession.

Thus, it has been demonstrated that if one accepts space and so forth as being uncreated, they necessarily fall within the scope of the conventional designation "non-existent. Now, demonstrating that if one instead accepts their existence, momentariness inevitably follows for them, he says: "But if," and so on.
"But if space, time, and the rest were existent, then in that case, even they would not escape this momentary destruction, just like created things."
"Like things produced" means "as if they were produced.
By this, the reason (*hetu*) "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) is indicated.
Clarifying that very point, he says "For instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth:
"For indeed, whatever things are called 'existent,' they are all subject to momentary destruction;
just as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-bhāva*) have been established immediately prior."
Moreover, these entities such as space, time, and the Lord are accepted by you as being existent;
however, if they were devoid of momentariness, their existence would not logically follow.
Since causal efficiency is performed neither successively nor simultaneously, stable entities do not exist; therefore, they are considered to be devoid of intrinsic reality.

The formal argument is as follows: whatever exists is momentary, just like the momentary entities established immediately prior; and you yourself accept that entities such as space and so forth exist. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Thus, they are established as being momentary.

By this, he shows that one should not suspect the example of being deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*), because it has already been established. By the phrase "are intended by you," he shows that this is a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) proof;
otherwise, the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished for at least one of the two parties.

But how is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason established? To this he says: "If, however, there were a lack of momentariness," and so forth. Here, existence is intended as the reason, characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). And that [existence] ceases when momentariness ceases. For things, while performing causal efficiency, must do so either successively or simultaneously; indeed, no other mode besides succession and simultaneity is possible, because those two consist in mutual exclusion.
And this is established by direct perception itself.

For instance, a jar, gradually bringing honey, water, and so forth—which are distinct from other substances—and performing its own cognition and the fetching of water not simultaneously, is determined by direct perception alone.

In that regard, whatever distinct effects the jar or the potter is observed to bring about sequentially, such as bowls, jars, and the like, it is not capable of producing those very same things simultaneously at that same time.

Or rather, a jar is perceived as producing cognitions and so forth regarding its own object simultaneously, and not at that very same time producing them successively; all of this is established by direct perception.

Therefore, since succession is determined precisely by the exclusion of simultaneity, and simultaneity is determined precisely by the exclusion of succession, the operation of a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) determines one of the two while excluding its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) and indicating the absence of any other alternative mode. Thus, the contradiction between these two—characterized by their existence through the mutual exclusion of each other's occurrence—is established solely by the means of direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Consequently, because there is no third possibility, causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is pervaded by both succession and simultaneity.

And since that [succession] ceases when its pervader [simultaneity] ceases among stable entities, it causes the cessation of existence (*sattva*), which is characterized by that [succession]; thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.
Nor can it be argued that succession and simultaneity are not established for entities because a distinct category of time (*kāla*) is not accepted;
for we do not claim that the succession and simultaneity of entities are produced by a category of time that is a separate entity (*arthāntara*).
Rather, it is produced by arising in such and such a manner.

For instance, if one being experiences existence at the very same time that others experience it in exactly the same way, then all of them, arising in this manner, become the basis for the designation of simultaneity (*akrama*),
just as many sprouts arise together when their respective causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) are complete.

By contrast, those things that possess a sequential designation, such as the sprout, the stalk, and the leaf, are established through direct perception and are designated by people in exactly that way. Therefore, even though the operation of a cause has as its object entities of such a nature, it is designated according to the sequence or simultaneity pertaining to those objects; thus, this objection is not valid.
Now, if a stable entity were established, then, upon the exclusion of succession and simultaneity therein, the exclusion of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would be established—
just as, in a certain locus, the absence of a *śiṃśapā* tree is established when trees are excluded.
Otherwise, if the locus as a factual subject (*dharmin*) were not established, where could the absence of a *śiṃśapā* be cognized?
And that [subject] is not established, because it is precisely what one intends to negate.
Furthermore, if its establishment is accepted, then its rejection is not logical, since the essential nature of that subject (dharmin) is admitted as being established.
Consequently, even the reason "because of existence" (*sattva*) and so forth is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it occurs in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
This is not the case;

for we do not independently employ this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Rather, what is done is the application of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) against the opponent.

If you were to accept their stable nature, then you would also have to accept their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*); however, this cannot be accepted because the presence of succession and simultaneity—which pervade that capacity—is absent therein.
For when the pervader is absent, the pervaded cannot possibly remain;
otherwise, the very relationship of pervader and pervaded between the two would not exist.
Therefore, since the capacity for causal efficiency has ceased, their existence also must not be admitted, because existence is defined by the capacity for causal efficiency.

By this means, their non-existence alone is established. Furthermore, in a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), it is not necessary to rely on a real entity as the locus (dharmin), because what is intended to be proven there is merely the cessation of the probans when the probandum has ceased.

And this is understood from the mere statement that, once the relationship of pervaded and pervader has been established between two properties, even without specifying a particular locus (*dharmī*), the pervaded does not exist in the absence of the pervader in a general sense;
just as it is said, "In the absence of a tree, there is no *śiṃśapā*. As it has been stated:
"Therefore, in the case of a negative example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), a substratum is not necessarily required here."
Moreover, because it is understood from the statement, "In the absence of that, however, there is not that," [the nature of the object] is apprehended.
Thus [it is said].
He demonstrates that it is not logical for a stable entity to perform causal efficiency (arthakriyā) sequentially by stating "the effects," and so forth:
"For effects are delayed due to the absence of their causes;
when a capable cause is present, what could possibly cause their delay?"
For the arising or non-arising of an effect does not occur by its own will; rather, its existence or non-existence conforms to the presence or absence of its cause.

In that regard, if this entity were stable and of a single nature, existing at all times as the cause of all effects, then why would all effects—which require nothing more than its mere existence—not arise simultaneously, such that they would instead occur in a sequence?
This is what is meant by "delay."
There would be a delay; therefore, even his subsequent task would occur beforehand,
because its causal capacity is unimpeded, just like the desired task— this is the intended meaning.

With the words "But even so" (*athāpi*) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's reply: "Even so, there exist successive auxiliary causes for the eternal [entity]; depending upon these, it produces the collection of effects that rely on succession."
Although a permanent entity is always present, its auxiliary conditions (sahakārīṇi) nevertheless approach it in succession;
therefore, depending upon them, it will produce its effects sequentially.
He responds with "Well said," and so forth:
"This is well; however, do those [conditions] become its auxiliaries by virtue of being causes of a suitable nature, or by virtue of producing a single effect?"
If that which is capable were the cause, then that entity would be produced by them;
yet it cannot be produced, because its own nature was already established at that time.
Or, if it were produced, its own essential nature would lose its permanence.
If this excellence is distinct from it, how can it be the agent?
For no auxiliary cause whatsoever is possible for that which is eternal.

To explain: an auxiliary cause would have to function either by imparting an excellence (*atiśaya*), as the earth and other factors are auxiliaries to a seed by imparting specific states such as swelling;
or by performing a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*), as color and other factors are to the eye in the perception of form merely upon its opening.

In this regard, the first position is not tenable. For instance, when this excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced in that [entity] by its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), it must be either non-different from its own nature, different from it, or of a nature that is both or neither—these being the four positions as stated by the Ājīvikas. Among these, the first position is not tenable; because, like the entity's own nature, it would be eternally present due to its non-distinction from it, and it is impossible to produce what already exists. Alternatively, if it were produced, it would follow that the entity itself is also produced, just like that excellence.
And consequently, there would be a loss of its permanence.
Now, if the second alternative is accepted, then since the effect arises solely from that excellence (*atiśaya*), it follows that the entity itself is not the agent.
As for the word "this" (*asau*): [it refers to the excellence].
An eternal category.
This very point is clarified by the passage beginning with "tasmin sati" (when that exists), and so forth:
"For when that exists, there is the arising of effects; due to its absence, they do not arise. Thus, it alone is established as the cause."
"In that" means "when there is an excellence.
"In this way" means:
Because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) residing therein.

Now, with the words "athāpi" and so forth, [the author] anticipates the opponent's response to this very point: "Even so, because of its connection with that [object], it (the cognition) indeed possesses the status of a cause.
What kind of connection between those two is intended, since they are distinct by virtue of their different natures?"
Nor does that [effect] arise from it, because that would entail simultaneity;
and consequently, there would be the simultaneous emergence of all effects.
"Teneti" means "excessively.
"Tasyāpi" means "of that too."
Regarding the question "What is the connection of that which is eternal? and so forth, he provides the answer: "What is the connection? None at all. This is the meaning.
For there are only two kinds of connection: identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*).
In that regard, it cannot first be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), because difference has already been accepted;

nor can it be characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*), because that [difference] arises solely from auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). If its origination were accepted [from those very causes], then, since the excellences (*atiśaya*) would be produced by those alone, they would necessarily arise all at once.
Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that all effects arise simultaneously,
because a cause possessing excellence (atiśaya) would be present at all times.
In that case as well, if there were dependence on another, an infinite regress would result; consequently, the effect could not be established even once, because of the lack of a connection.

Now, if it is argued that even in that case, because an excellence (*atiśaya*) arises through dependence on auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*), the effects do not occur simultaneously because the excellence arises sequentially—that is simply untenable. For in this way, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To explain: even in that case, the status of being an auxiliary cause must be asserted by virtue of producing another excellence; and since that excellence is distinct [from the primary cause], its connection [to the effect] is unestablished. Furthermore, if that excellence were produced, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the effect being produced all at once. If one again resorts to dependence on auxiliary causes for that too, then this very same inquiry recurs.
Furthermore, in the case of an infinite regress, its connection with the excellence would never be established;
and if that is not established, there can be no production of the effect from it, because the effect arises solely from the excellence itself.
If the relation is inherence (*samavāya*), then this must also be considered there:
is that [inherence] accepted as being inherent in it by becoming a benefactor (*upakārī*)?
If the first alternative—that it is not so—is accepted, then that very production [of the effect] which was previously refuted would follow; yet that too has just been rejected.

Furthermore, it might be argued that its relation with the excellence (*atiśaya*) is not characterized by "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*), but rather is characterized by "inherence" (*samavāya*), because that excellence inheres in that eternal substratum (*dharmin*). To show that this is incorrect, he says: "In that case also," and so forth.
Or rather, it is not so;
the connection is that "being a benefactor, it is not intended to be the inherent cause (samavāyin) of that.

In that regard, according to the first position, since the benefit is non-different from the object being benefited, that very relationship characterized by origination (tadutpatti-lakṣaṇa) would be admitted.
And that has been refuted immediately following [the previous point].
Now, if the second position were held, then, because there would be no distinction, everything would be inherent in everything.
He demonstrates this with the words "others also," and so forth:
"All other entities as well would likewise be inherent."
If it is argued that this [agent] is not considered a benefactor of that [action] because there is no distinction [between them], then...
"It is exactly so," because,
like the desired object, it is not distinguished [from others] by virtue of providing no assistance.
With reference to both the positions of difference and non-difference, he says "difference-and-non-difference," and so forth:
because the conceptual construction of difference and non-difference is individually negated,
the two-fold excellence of that entity becomes excluded.
By the very refutation of each individual position, the position that it possesses both natures is also refuted, because there exists no position possessing both natures apart from those two.

Furthermore, since the abandonment or acceptance of one aspect is inseparable from the acceptance or abandonment of the other aspect, it is illogical for a real entity to have the nature of being both [existent and non-existent] or neither; for it is not possible for affirmation and negation, which are mutually contradictory, to apply to a single thing at the same time, as that would entail the loss of its unity.

And this has been established in the examination of the person (*pudgala*) and so forth; he demonstrates that with the words "the person and so forth," etc.: "Because the two-fold alternative is refuted in the examinations of the person and so forth, there is no excellence of two forms, nor is there one that is neither."

Now, if the second position is adopted—that the causal factors are its auxiliaries by virtue of performing a single purposeful action—as some have said: "It does not depend on auxiliaries, nor is it a producer of the effect when separated from them; for its nature is established by its very essence such that it is a producer only when all auxiliary causes are present, like the final cause, and not alone.
Therefore, even though it exists, there is no consequence of the effect being produced at all times."
He demonstrates this with the words "atha" and so forth: "Now,
if the eternal [cause] does not depend upon auxiliary conditions,
nevertheless, being devoid of them, it is not a producer [of the effect], like the final cause."
This is indeed its own inherent nature when those [causes] are present;
therefore, it acts as a producer, and thus the effect does not occur at all times even when that [nature] exists.
"No," [it is said].
This should be connected with the word "agent" (*kāraka*).

The phrase "like the final cause" (*antyahetuvat*) is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṭānta*). Alternatively, it is connected with the subsequent term "agency" (*kārakatva*) as an example by way of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
And the suffix *vati* should be applied after a word ending in the sixth case;
"even in the presence of that" means even when that eternal category (*padārtha*) exists.
He responds with the words "Let it be so," and so forth:
"Let it be so; however, if that very nature which is considered its own when complete is also held to be present when there is deficiency, then the auxiliary factors would have to be eternal."

Let this be such a conceptual construction; however, this is what is being examined here: is that very nature which belongs to it in the state where there is a completeness of auxiliary causes (sahakārin) also present in the state of their deficiency, or is it something else? If it is the same, then it follows that the auxiliary causes themselves must also be eternal.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because when that which has a nature connected to them exists, they too persist;
otherwise, if the form were different, oneness would be lost."
And for this reason, even by virtue of dependence, there is no sequential arising of effects.
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose nature is connected with those auxiliary causes.
[The phrase] "of those too" refers to the auxiliaries.
Regarding the auxiliary causes:
just as when pulling a man bound by shackles, the shackles themselves are also pulled along, so too do these [auxiliaries] follow along;
for in this way, that very [entity] continues to exist without abandoning its prior intrinsic nature.
For if it does not abandon its nature as connected with the auxiliary cause, then by virtue of not abandoning that connected nature, it necessarily does not abandon the auxiliary causes either;
this is because being related is dependent upon the counter-correlate.
Otherwise, that very nature would not belong to it.
Now, regarding the position that it is "other," he says "and other" and so forth.

For if it is maintained that its form, when devoid of auxiliary causes, is something else, then there follows the consequence of the loss of its permanence, because the form is not distinct from the entity itself.
Therefore, even with regard to the dependence on auxiliary causes, it is not logical for permanent things to perform causal efficiency sequentially.
Nor does it occur simultaneously; this is shown by the passage beginning, "And simultaneity is certainly not accepted," and so forth:
"And simultaneity is certainly not accepted, because those effects are seen to perish."
Even by others, simultaneity is not at all accepted for the effects of eternal entities;
for these effects are described as being eternal in the following ways:

pleasure, pain, and so forth of the self; sounds of space; successive cognitions of the mind; gross objects produced from atoms through the sequence of dyads and so on; and all things produced from time, direction, the Lord (Īśvara), and the like.
And the sequential arising of these is established through direct perception itself.
Thus, by accepting simultaneity, both contradiction with perception and contradiction with one's own tenets have been stated.
Now, demonstrating the contradiction with inference, he says "niḥśeṣāṇi" and so forth:
"And having performed all effects at once, it ceases."
If that object consists essentially of causal efficiency, its momentary destruction is established.
For instance, having performed all its effects simultaneously, does that nature capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā-samartha) of his cease or does it persist? These are the two alternatives.
In that regard, if the position is that it ceases, then its momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgitva) is established;
for there is the arising of successive distinct natures at every moment, and because each preceding nature perishes by its own inherent tendency (svarasa-vināśa).
If that same nature persists, it would produce the effect once again;
how can efficacy be attributed to a nature that is incapable of acting?
Because they are devoid of all causal efficacy, like a lotus in the sky, all non-momentary things are non-existent; for efficacy is the defining characteristic of a real entity.

Now, if the second position is adopted, then, since its nature remains capable and the mind continues to follow it, it would produce the effect once again, because it has not abandoned its prior form, just as it was in its previous state.

Consequently, that same sequence has arisen; thus, the acceptance of simultaneity is contradicted by inference. Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let there be no causal efficiency for it through either sequence or simultaneity, yet it certainly possesses capacity. To this he says: "Of that which has a nature incapable of acting," and so forth. For the capacity of entities is established on the basis of their producing an effect.
And how could that which performs no action whatsoever be capable?
Otherwise, why would one not establish the capability even of things such as a sky-lotus?
This might be argued: "Even if its capability has indeed ceased, its existence (*sattva*) remains unceased."
And therefore, the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) is indeed inconclusive; thus he says, "they are non-existent," and so forth.

For this alone is the defining characteristic of a real entity (*vastu*), namely, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). If that [capacity] has ceased, how can the nature of being a real entity—which is defined by that [capacity]—maintain its status among them?

Thus, it is established that space and the like, which are intended to be non-momentary, are fit for conventional treatment as non-existent—just like the son of a barren woman—because they are devoid of the capacity for causal efficiency through either successive or simultaneous action.
Now, if this definition of reality as "potency" (śakti) were not accepted,
then some other characteristic of real entities would have to be pointed out by the opponents.
Moreover, it might be argued: "If the definition of a real entity were solely characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), then all this would be acceptable.
But if that is so, what other definition of a real entity must be stated?
For instance, the reason why non-reality is attributed to things such as a rabbit's horn is precisely the absence of the capacity for causal efficiency."

Since the existent and the non-existent are defined by their mutual exclusion, it follows by implication that the definition of the existent is precisely the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), which is the opposite of the characteristics of the non-existent; this is the intended meaning.

Here, the author anticipates the opponent's reply with the words "sattā" and so forth: "If the connection with existence (*sattā*) is intended as the definition of entities, that is not [correct], because inherence (*samavāya*) and the like are unestablished; or else, how could they be mutual definitions?"

For the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is not the defining characteristic of a real entity; rather, it is the connection with existence (*sattāsambandha*), that is to say, inherence in existence (*sattāsamavāya*).
"Not that" means that [causal efficiency] is not logically the defining characteristic of a real entity; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Because inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth are unestablished;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), existence (*sattā*) is included.
If inherence and the rest were established, then inherence would be the defining characteristic of a real entity (*vastu*).
This is because those very [entities] are introduced as the objects to be proven (*sādhya*),
and because there exists the subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) that will be stated hereafter;
or else, because existence (*sattā*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are unestablished by the very same subverting evidence mentioned previously.
Because existence has no established relation with anything else, as it cannot be assisted [by anything];
for it has been stated that there can be no mutual relation between two things that do not assist one another, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, it must be explained what the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is of those two—existence and inherence—as well as of the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*), if they are indeed real entities (*vastu*).
For existence (sattā) does not inhere in inherence (samavāya) or in the ultimate particulars (viśeṣas), nor does it inhere in existence itself;
rather, according to the established doctrine, existence is that which causes the three categories—substance, quality, and action—to be existent.
Therefore, this definition of a real entity (vastulakṣaṇa) is non-pervasive (avyāpin). Let it be granted, for the sake of argument, that existence and so forth are established.
Nevertheless, it is not logical that inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*) is the definition, because it is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*).
For a distinct entity cannot be the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of another entity such that it could serve as its definition.

Thus, when a definition is being formulated for someone of dull intellect who lacks knowledge of the true nature of a thing, it must be stated that the very essence of that thing—perceived through its exclusion from something else—is the definition, by means of which one determines that very thing to be the nature of the object; as, for example, earth is defined by its solid hardness (*kharakaṭatva*).
Furthermore, one entity cannot have the nature of another entity, because that would entail the loss of its distinctness.
How, then, could it be the definition [of that other]? For the word "definition" (lakṣaṇa) is being used here in the sense of "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva).

Some say: "What subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is there against the existence of such an object which, even for an omniscient one, does not produce cognition? For it is by means of such a proof that this pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that whatever exists is momentary—is established through universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*). Furthermore, the lack of knowledge regarding that [object] does not entail the loss of omniscience, because his authority extends only over knowable things (*jñeya*).
Indeed, one would be non-omniscient only if he failed to cognize an object capable of being known; but that [object] is not knowable."
"Because it is also unfit for the production of knowledge"—
in response to those [objections], he says "And all," and so forth:
"And every activity, such as the investigation of objects and the like, belongs to one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)."
One whose mind is undisturbed should practice with diligence, and not again with the state of a madman.
In that regard, since the name of certain things is useful in some way,
in some place, and at some time, it is precisely there that the establishment of their existence is appropriate.
And it is precisely the momentariness of an object of such a nature that is established;
the universal concomitance (vyāpti) is stated with reference to that very [object] by way of a complete induction (sarvopasaṃhāra).
For this investigation into the existence or non-existence of a mere thing is undertaken entirely by one who seeks causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), not out of mere habit;
otherwise, he would be a madman.

Therefore, it is only with respect to that collection of objects which is somehow—either directly or indirectly, at some place or at some time—of use to certain seekers of causal efficacy, that a determination of "real entity" (*vastu*) is appropriate for a discerning person.
The sense is that [it is not established] elsewhere because there is no basis [for it] and because it would be purposeless.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the investigation of specific objects such as fire, water, and so forth is intended.

Consequently, we establish the momentariness of that very thing which is well-known among those who act with foresight—that is, of that nature which performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—as being of the form of performing causal efficiency.
Since that which is characterized by the capacity for causal efficacy is intended as the reason (*hetu*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
This is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of such a reason with the probandum (*sādhya*) is established through a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāra*).
For that pervasion which is demonstrated generally, without making a distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), is the pervasion of universal induction. (419)

[Page 152] Now, as to why the status of being a real entity (*vastutva*) is not accepted even for that which is devoid of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), he says "niḥśeṣa... and so forth:
"But that which is devoid of all powers, resembling the son of a barren woman,"
It never becomes the cause even for the mind of an omniscient one.
In that case, since this [existence] is not perceived as having the form of an effect and so forth,
the wise do not establish its existence without a basis.
No purpose whatsoever is served by proving momentariness in that regard;
and any further inquiry made concerning it is likewise fruitless.
Regarding the phrase "even of the mind of the Omniscient One":
the word "even" (api) indicates that this applies not only to a moment of the same kind [as its cause] and to effects such as the holding of water, but also to others.
This is because the form and other qualities of the effect are not perceived.

Its effect, its fruit, its form, and its intrinsic nature (svabhāva)— by the word "etcetera" (ādi), its location, time, and specific state are included— the point is that for such a thing, there is no distinction whatsoever from things like a rabbit's horn. Furthermore, once such an entity has been established as momentary, there is no purpose whatsoever for one who seeks causal efficiency (arthakriyā) in it.
Because it is incapable of attaining the beneficial or avoiding the harmful regarding both the seen and the unseen;
as it has been said:
"What is the use of investigations for one who seeks that which is capable of purposeful action?"
What is the use of examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch for a woman who desires a lover?
As it is said in *Pramāṇavārttika* 2.211:

"For this very reason, the opponent's objection—asking 'How is it understood that this is momentary? and so forth—is entirely fruitless, because the proponent does not intend to prove [the subject] as being momentary. (vv. 422–)

Now, [the author] demonstrates that the opponent's definition of a real entity (*vastu*) as "that which possesses causal efficiency" (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is also incorrect because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpi*), starting with the words "But surely," and so forth:
"But surely, sky-lotuses and the like possess the capacity for causal efficiency;
yet, by virtue of being causes of their own cognition, these do not exist as real entities (*bhāvika*)."

For instance, things such as "sky-lotuses" are capable of performing causal functions characterized by the production of cognitions such as "sky-lotus, sky-lotus," yet they do not exist in an ultimate sense; therefore, this definition—"capacity is the defining characteristic of an entity"—is over-extensive (*ativyāpin*).
Regarding this, he states the rebuttal: "It is indeed without an objective basis," and so forth.

"In the case of [non-existent things] such as a sky-lotus and the like, this cognition proceeds entirely without an objective basis, arising solely from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of verbal expressions regarding them."

The capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) in things such as the sky-lotus and the like is unestablished; for their conceptual cognitions arise solely through the maturation of the latencies of one's own conceptualization, since they lack any objective basis (*nirālambanatva*).

[Page 153] Now, he states "But if non-existence were the cause," etc., to address the question: what is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the arising [of things] from such things as space or a lotus?
However, if non-existence were the cause, [things] would arise continuously;
for non-existence, being devoid of any distinction, never requires anything else.

That which has as its cause a non-entity, such as a lotus in the sky and so forth, is described as "tathokta" (so-called); the state of being that is its "tattva" (reality). If that were the case, the cognition of that non-existent lotus in the sky and so forth would arise at all times, because its cause would be eternally present and unimpaired.

Furthermore, it is not logical for that [cause], which cannot be assisted by others, to depend on them, such that it might produce the effect only occasionally due to a deficiency in auxiliary factors (sahakārin).
With the words "Even in the case of momentary things," etc., he raises the objection of the Venerable Yogasena:
"Indeed, how can there be causal efficiency (arthakriyā) even in things that are momentary?
For the initial auxiliary causes do not produce any mutual distinction [in one another]."
If [the cause] were established as existing in its entirety at the time of production, then since the non-existent thing would not exist at the time of non-production,
and because there would be no distinction between these two states, why would the effect not arise even when there is no distinction?
Nor are they distinguished from anything else, because the same objection applies equally; furthermore, there would be an infinite regress for you regarding the collection of auxiliary causes.
Since they do not perform causal efficiency either successively or simultaneously,
their reliance on momentariness is therefore futile.
And since no excellence whatsoever is produced by auxiliary conditions in this way,
the continuum is therefore held to be always without distinction.
If destruction were without cause, this [destruction] would exist at the very beginning;
if its origination did not exist at the beginning, how could it come to be at the end?
If it is maintained that there is no cause for the destruction of entities other than their own causes,
how could they ever be subject to contradiction in certain cases?
For he says that even if things are momentary, there is indeed a contradiction regarding their causal efficiency (arthakriyā) with respect to both succession and simultaneity.
For they must either be inherently capable or incapable; if they are capable, then they would not depend upon auxiliary causes (sahakārikāraṇa).
Indeed, no dependence whatsoever is logical for that which is already capable.
Furthermore, even if they were incapable [of acting upon one another], their mutual dependence would be all the more illogical.
For those factors that exist within the first complex do not acquire any distinction from one another;
because they exist in states both arisen and unarisen, they stand in a relationship of neither being assisted nor assisting, due to their respective existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, since they are indistinguishable in the first moment, there could be no production of a subsequent distinct moment from them.
And if a distinct subsequent moment were produced from those indistinguishable [moments], why would the effect itself not also be produced?

Nor is it tenable to say that they have arisen from a preceding complex (kalāpa) that was distinct, because for that very reason, there is likewise an absence of distinction among the members within that complex through their mutual succession.
If a further distinction were to arise even for those [distinctions], there would be an infinite regress.
Thus, in the absence of such distinctions, how could an effect arise from a causal complex that is itself undifferentiated?
If it were to arise from what is undifferentiated, then everything would arise from everything.

Furthermore, even if there is such a contradiction regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) with respect to succession and simultaneity, it might be argued that just as these [entities] are indeed performers of causal efficiency, so too will permanent things be; thus, their reliance on momentariness would be useless.
The implication is that the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) is therefore inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Nor is it reasonable to say that the production of an effect will occur from a continuum that has reached a particular state, and not at all times.
According to the principle already stated, because there is no specific quality produced by auxiliary causes, the continuum would always remain undifferentiated.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to say that the continuum is a specific quality dependent solely upon its own material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*),
for that would contradict what is observed.
For it is observed that the manifestation or cessation of an effect depends upon the presence or absence of auxiliary causes.
If the specific quality [of the cause] were dependent solely on its own material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), then it would possess the capacity to produce the effect independently of any auxiliaries.
Furthermore, according to the principle already stated, the continuum (*santati*) remains forever without distinction [in its nature].
Since it is impossible for jars and the like to produce specific effects such as shards,
if destruction— characterized by the cessation of a continuum of homogeneous moments— were causeless, then, being independent [of causes], it would have to occur even prior [to the object].
If, however, it does not occur at first, it would not occur later either, because there is no difference [in the object] compared to its previous state.

Furthermore, if one does not accept that, apart from their own causes, there is another distinct continuum acting as the cause for the destruction of entities, then how could fire and the like be the opposites of cold and the like? For it is not logical that something which performs no function can be an opposite, as this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); indeed, in that case, everything would follow as being the opposite of everything.

Consequently, the application of non-perception by way of opposition, as well as the establishment of [the prohibitions against] killing living beings and so forth, would become extremely difficult to maintain—this is the intended meaning.
He provides the rebuttal with the words "It is said," and so on.
It is said: in the initial stage, they do not assist one another;
rather, it is through the performance of a single purposeful action that these become cooperative causes.
Even though they do not assist one another, these [causes] are not undifferentiated,
because they arise from the power of their own respective material causes and produce the aggregate individually.
For the production of an effect occurs only from that which is capable; yet there is no futility regarding auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
To explain: there are two kinds of auxiliary causality—namely, by performing a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritā*) and by mutual assistance (*parasparopakāritā*).
In this context, with respect to an immediate effect, there is only the performance of a single purposeful action, not mutual assistance.
Because it is impossible to impart a distinction [to a thing] in a single moment due to its indivisibility;

however, with respect to a mediated effect, since a subsequent, more distinguished moment arises from each other, there is a production of the mediated effect through mutual assistance in relation to the continuum. Thus, "cooperation" is characterized by mutual assistance.

In that regard, although there is no distinction among those existing in the initial state relative to one another, their cooperation is not at all contradictory, because they perform a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*).

Nor are they indistinguishable with respect to the production of a subsequent moment that is distinguished from the preceding one, because each of them has arisen as individually capable of producing such a collection of subsequent effects from their own respective causes and conditions.

Furthermore, since those causes and conditions also arise from other causes and conditions, and those others from yet others—this being accepted as an beginningless succession of causes—an infinite regress is not a fault.
And even though each is individually capable, there is no pointlessness for the others, because they have arisen in that manner through the power of their own causes.
Nor is their separate existence possible, because there is no such cause for it; nor can they exist separately afterwards, because of their momentariness.
Thus, those that produce the aggregate are not separate [from it].
The meaning is that each [moment] is capable of producing its own collection of parts (*kalāpa*) occurring in the second moment.
The mention of "its own material cause" (*svopādāna*) should be understood as intended to negate the utility provided by auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) occurring in the first state;
however, no effect can arise from its material cause alone, because everything arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
As it has been said: "Nothing arises from a single cause; everything arises from a causal complex.
From that point onward, whatever specific qualities arise are produced by that [complex], because they possess that nature and are thus dependent upon it.
"From that time forward" means beginning from the moment immediately following the second instant.
"Produced by that" means produced by the specific causes brought about by the auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).

Why? Because they have that as their nature (*tadrūpaprakṛtitvāt*). Those whose nature (*prakṛti*), that is, their intrinsic being (*svabhāva*), is produced by specific causes consisting of particular auxiliary conditions (*viśiṣṭasahakārikṛtaviśeṣakāraṇa*) of that form, are described as such. [The phrase] "of those things which are conducive to that" (*teṣāṃ tadupayoginām*) is to be connected with "because they have that as their nature."
In the phrase "useful for that" (*tadupayoginam*), the letter *c* is indicated as elided; therefore, the meaning is as follows:

regarding the effect that occurs in the third moment, those specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) existing in the second moment which are employed as causes—since those qualities useful for that [effect] possess a nature capable of producing an effect generated by a cause consisting of specific qualities produced by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), the specific qualities occurring in the third and subsequent moments are produced by them.

To the question of how this restriction also applies to these [entities], he says "restricted," and so forth: "Entities with restricted and inconceivable powers come into being at every moment; they are not to be questioned, just as the power to burn resides in fire."

Indeed, the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities do not admit of questioning, because their differentiation of intrinsic nature results from their being brought about by a succession of their own causes and conditions. Just as fire possesses the property of burning, these [entities] arise at every moment with distinct capacities through the application of successive and antecedent conditions. Therefore, even if they are perceived as having an identical form due to some similarity, their intrinsic nature remains strictly distinct.
Therefore, this [notion] that something is the cause of only a certain thing and not of everything else is trivial.
"They come into being" (bhavanti) means "they are born" (jāyante).

Regarding what was said—that if destruction were causeless—he replies with the words "But that destruction which consists in the cessation of the continuum," and so forth: "But for that destruction which consists in the cessation of the continuum and which possesses no cause, there is no existence even at its end; likewise, [its] arising is prevented."
The production of dissimilar shards and the like, however, is caused;
yet even that does not arise at the very beginning, because at that time the cause is impossible.

For destruction is of two kinds: that consisting in the cessation of the continuum, and that characterized by the arising of a dissimilar continuum. In this regard, if it is with reference to destruction in the form of the cessation of the continuum that [the objection] is stated, then that is incorrect; for its existence does not arise from that [destruction], because it is devoid of any nature (nīrūpatva). Therefore, since it is not admitted that it ever comes into being at any time, the consequence that there would be existence at the beginning and non-existence at the end is entirely inconsistent.
In this context, only birth—that is, arising through the reconnection with another similar moment—is negated;
the meaning is that for a jar or the like, "destruction" simply means that it does not come into being again.
Nothing else is affirmed therein.
Now, if the second kind of destruction, characterized by the arising of a dissimilar moment, is intended, its lack of a cause is unestablished;
for it is admitted that, as a real entity (*vastu*), it arises through the power of causes such as a hammer.
For this very reason, it does not arise at the beginning, because its own causes, such as the hammer, are absent at that time. (439)
In order to establish the resolution of this contradiction, he says "of two kinds" and so forth:
"Momentary entities are of two kinds: some are causes of diminution, such as fire and the like for cold and so forth; others are not of that nature."
But the world, not having perceived the true nature of reality, conceives of contradictions in many ways even regarding the relationship of cause and effect as previously described.
The relationship between the sublated and the sublator, however, does not exist as something real in an entity;
for that very reason, it is also said that there is only the "cognition of contradiction."
For some entities, there occurs a diminution in certain others through a sequence of arising with increasingly slower moments; in that case, things such as fire and the like serve as causes.
Other things are not of such a kind—that is, they are not causes of diminution—just as those same things like fire are not causes of smoke and the like.

Regarding the first-mentioned causes of diminution, although the causal relationship exists, people, whose light of knowledge is obscured by the cataract of ignorance, mistakenly perceive them as contradictory.
"In many ways" means by way of distinctions such as fire being the opposite of cold, wind of a lamp, and light of darkness, and so forth.

However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no relationship of sublated and sublator among things, because that which exists is established in its entirety; it is impossible to effect a change in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), since—given the dilemma of whether such a change is distinct or non-distinct from the thing—it cannot be effected in either case.
Since even that which is non-existent lacks reality, nothing at all can be produced by it; thus, in both cases, the contradictory is ineffective.

For this very reason, the Teacher stated: "The cognition of contradiction arises because there is an absence [of the effect] when another [contradictory factor] is present, despite the cause being complete.
The meaning is that "the cognition of contradiction" refers to the determination of contradiction, and not to a real, ontological contradiction.
The word *api* has the sense of *ca* (and). It is displaced [from its usual position] and should be understood immediately after the word *eva*. //441–442//
With the words "But surely... and so forth, [the author] raises an objection from the perspective of the Jaiminīyas and others, that the thesis of momentary flux is contradicted by direct perception:
"But surely, when the operation of the senses is present, there arises an unshakeable and uncontradicted recognition in the form 'this is that very same thing'."
Consequently, this sublation by direct perception (pratyakṣabādha) becomes unavoidable in all reasons adduced for the purpose of establishing momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga).

For instance, immediately following the operation of the sense organ with respect to such things as mountains, bodies, and diamonds, there arises a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which takes the form "this is that very same thing. This recognition refutes the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of entities.

Although it is true that recognition is indeed observed in the case of nails, hair, grass, and so forth, which have clearly grown back again, nevertheless, there is no lack of validity in the two recognitions whose objects are diamonds and the like, because their objects are not sublated.

For this very reason, he says "unwavering" and "unsublated. The point is that it is not reasonable for one with clear vision to declare that because a cognition of hair produced by eyes impaired by cataracts is found to be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), therefore an eye-cognition produced by clear eyes regarding real hair must also be non-authoritative. In that context, by the term "unwavering," he expresses its nature as being free from doubt, since there is an absence of such doubt as "Is this the same [object] or is it another?"
By the phrase "unsublated," its non-erroneousness is indicated.
He refutes this with the words beginning "certainly not" (*na khalu*):
"Indeed, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) cannot be established as being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
For the nature of an entity is inexpressible, yet it is accompanied by verbal designation.
And recognition is erroneous, for each instance is distinct from the others;
it functions by determining non-difference even with respect to that which has a differentiated form.

In that regard, its status as perception (*pratyakṣatva*) is first of all unestablished; for since the characteristic of being a real entity (*vastutva*) lacks concomitance (*ananvaya*), it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (*asaṃketa*) for it.
The cognition that grasps it is nothing other than mental discourse (*manojalpa*).
Because it is impossible to grasp an object whose relation [to a word] has already been apprehended by conjoining it with a word,
that which exists as perception must necessarily be free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), since its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
and because it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), it must be non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
Consequently, the experts declare that this definition of perception—namely, "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous"—is in accordance with logic.
However, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not free from conceptual construction, because it is experienced as having the form of verbal expression, such as "this is that very same thing.
Nor is it non-erroneous, because it functions by determining non-difference among things that are actually distinct. (vv. 446–)

To the question "How so?", he says: "If this were to have as its object a form previously prepared," then this [cognition] would indeed arise previously, because it has that [form] as its purpose, just like the previous cognition.

For if this [cognition] had as its object a thing already previously perceived, it would have arisen at that very time, because its causes would be complete insofar as they have that thing as their object, just like the previous cognition. "Tādarthyāt" means: that which has as its object (artha) the thing (bhāva) previously known—that is its object—and the state of having that as its object is "tādarthya."
And it is not thus; he states the reversal of the reductio (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*) as follows:
"It is not thus; therefore, this is not considered to be the grasper of that object, because it arises at the time of that [other] cognition, like the cognition of another object."
Because it functions by determining as non-different even that which has a differentiated form,
this [cognition] stands as an error, like the cognition of a magical ball.

The formal arguments are as follows: if a cognition does not arise even when a certain object is present in its entirety, that cognition does not have that object as its domain. For example, even when form (*rūpa*) is present in its entirety, auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) does not arise with respect to it. Likewise, at the time of perceiving a diamond (*vajra*) and such objects, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) does not arise even though they are present in their entirety. This is a case of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Thus, if a diamond and the like were eternal and independent of other factors, recognition having them as its object would have occurred previously, since its causes would be unimpaired; yet it does not occur. Therefore, its impermanence is established.

Furthermore, because activity proceeds by determining non-difference among things that are actually distinct—just like the cognition of a magical sphere (māyāgola)—this [cognition] is erroneous; thus, this point remains entirely intact.

For this very reason, the claim that its object is uncontradicted is also unestablished, since its object is contradicted by the very same reason that proves its erroneous nature as previously stated. //449–450//

Furthermore, showing that this [subsequent cognition] lacks validity because it apprehends what has already been apprehended—just like memory—he says: "Because it operates upon an object for which the action has already been accomplished," and so forth.
159] Because it operates upon an object for which the action has already been accomplished, just like memory and the like.
This is not a valid means of knowledge, because it lacks the function of an instrument.

For that alone which is the most excellent instrument for the accomplishment of the act of valid cognition is called the *sādhakatama* (most effective) factor, namely, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And if recognition were to have as its object a thing already grasped by a previous means of valid cognition, then, because it would operate upon an object for which the act of cognition has already been accomplished, it would lack the status of being the *sādhakatama*; how, then, could it attain the status of a means of valid cognition?
Otherwise, even memory would possess the status of a means of valid cognition.
Nor can that which has not attained the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) serve as a sublater (*bādhaka*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It might be argued: "Let it be that this [subsequent cognition] lacks independent validity; nevertheless, by having the same object as the previous one, it certainly sublates momentary destruction.
That is incorrect.

For this [recognition] does not, in the ultimate sense, have a previously perceived object as its domain, because it is a form of conceptual verbalization (*mābhijalpa*). Rather, although it is actually devoid of an object, it arises through the power of error as something that determines a previously seen object; thus, by virtue of this determination, it is said to have a previously seen object as its domain. Therefore, how could the refutation of momentary destruction be established on the basis of such recognition, which is inherently erroneous?

With the words "Now, [the existence] of the interval," and so forth, he raises the objection regarding the unestablished nature of the non-apprehension of what has been apprehended, according to the opinion of Kumārila: "The existence of the interval is certainly not grasped by the preceding cognition;
if it is argued that this [interval] is a specific feature of the object which is not present in the memory."
For memory arises as "that" with respect to merely what was previously cognized;
however, this recognition, "this is that very same thing," is something distinct from memory.

For he says: "Indeed, the existence of the object at the present time was not apprehended by the previous perception, because that [previous perception] did not arise with the form of grasping [the object] as 'this is that very same thing.
Therefore, this recognition has a distinction from memory.
To the question "How so?", he says "pūrva... and so forth.
For memory functions by grasping only the form of a previous cognition,
whereas recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) grasps an object-form that is additional [to that]. The meaning is that it is distinct and superior to memory.
Therefore, having sublated both doubt and error, recognition attains the status of a valid means of knowledge.
Regarding the question "Why does it sublate those two?", he states the reason: "Because they do not exist once [the object] is known.
Since doubt and error do not exist once [the object] is known, recognition, having sublated them, certainly attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Because those two do not exist when the object is known, it is like coldness in a place surrounded by a mass of thick, blazing flames.

[Page 160] One might object: "Just as a property such as the dark complexion of a son, which was established by inference, may later be sublated by perception and thus undergo change, so too here, even if the permanence of an object is established through recognition, its change is nonetheless established because its successive effects are subsequently proven to be sequential through inference. Therefore, how can momentariness be sublated? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even though it is known," and so forth.

Even if an object has been cognized by other means, it may turn out otherwise through direct perception; however, when an object is already determined by direct perception, there is no possibility for another [cognition] to arise.
"By other [means]" means by inference and so forth;
for example, as in the [fallacious] argument: "He must be dark-complexioned because he is that man's son, like his currently visible sons," and so on.

"By means of perception it would be otherwise" means that by means of perception acting as the instrument, it would be otherwise— that is, contrary to the form established by inference and other means of valid cognition.
"Obstructed" (avaruddha) [is the meaning].
The meaning is "made an object.
"The possibility of the arising of another [cognition] is not" means that the arising of something other than perception— namely, inference and so forth— is not possible as a sublater.

To the question "Why?", he says "For who," and so forth: "For who, once an object has been determined by the eldest and firm means of valid cognition, would later determine its opposite by means of other, weaker [means]?"
For it is logical that an object established by inference should be shown to be otherwise by means of perception,
because perception is the most senior of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
However, inference and the other means do not seek to alter what is established by perception, because they are weaker than it.
"By means of that which is firm" means by that which is free from doubt and error. "Error" refers to...
Alteration.

He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely): "But surely, if you maintain that present non-existence is distinct from prior existence, then the distinction [between the two] has been established by you yourself."

As for this present existence which is the object of recognition, is it different from the existence previously grasped by perception, or is it that very same one? If it were different, then since the difference would have been established by your own words, you would be guilty of abandoning your own tenet; for us, however, it is the establishment of our desired position.
Even if existence is non-different [from the object], how could it be apprehended by a previous cognition?
For if that [existence] were not apprehended, it would follow that the object itself is unperceived.

Now, if the position is that [the object] is not different [from the cognition], then how could it be that the previous cognition did not apprehend it, such that one could say, "It was indeed not apprehended by the previous cognition"? It might be argued: "Just as momentariness, though non-different from sound and so forth, is said to be unapprehended even when those [sounds] are apprehended, so too will this be the case here.
That is incorrect.
For it is not established that, even when the subject (dharmin) "sound" has been apprehended, its non-different property of momentariness remains unapprehended.
Rather, although it has been apprehended, it is said to be "unascertained" due to the absence of a cause for the arising of ascertainment;
for ascertainment does not arise from mere experience alone.
This is because that [inference] depends upon factors such as the subject's desire to know, repeated practice, and excellence [of the means];
however, this is not possible for you,
since even prior perception possesses the nature of determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*).
And when the nature of the object is being ascertained by that [cognition], its existence at the present time—which is non-different from it—is necessarily ascertained as well.
If that were not ascertained, it would follow that the very nature of the object is also unascertained, because it is non-different from that [existence] which is likewise unascertained.
This also refutes those who claim that the authority of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is based on the determination of a doubtful object.

Furthermore, there is no determination here of the existence of a doubtful object, because doubt persists due to the observation of recognition even when similar [moments] arise one after another, as in the case of hair and the like.

Regarding what was said, namely, "even when an object is known by others," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "And by perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa ca*): "And when there is sublation by perception regarding the domain of inference and the like,
there would be no validity for inference and the rest because of that sublation, just as in the case of [cognition affected by] ophthalmia and so forth."

However, for an inference such as "because he is your son" and the like, if there were a sublation by perception regarding its object—that is, its domain—then it would possess no validity at all, because, having a sublated object, it lacks correspondence with reality, like the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia.
Therefore, what was stated—that even an object known by others might be otherwise according to perception—is entirely inconsistent, as such a thing is impossible.
Showing that even the claim regarding the primacy of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is likewise unreal, he says: "And when there is the cognition of the object," and so forth.
When the capacity for correspondence with the object is equal, why should this [perception] be held in contempt?
But in the absence of that [correspondence], inference and the other means of knowledge would not be valid at all.
For this indeed is the very nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely: their capacity for the cognition of objects.
If that [capacity] is admitted for all means of valid cognition, then by what means would this perception (*pratyakṣa*) possess primacy?
Furthermore, if it were argued that only perception—and not inference (*anumāna*) and so forth—possesses the quality of correspondence with the object, he says: "In the absence of that," and so on.
In the absence of that correspondence with the object and so forth, it would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even as an inference;
for the conventional usage of "valid means of knowledge" is based on non-discrepancy with the object, and that [non-discrepancy] exists here.
With the words "But not by this," etc., [the author] raises the objections stated by Bhāvivikta:
"But surely, by this inference, the universal concomitance (vyāpti) in all reasons is sublated,
or else there is a destruction of the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā) through its universal application."
"What is that inference? To this he says: "That which pertains to the intended sun, moon, and so forth," and so on.
"The cognition that arises regarding the intended objects such as the sun and moon has as its object the sun and other bodies connected with that very time."
For, since it is designated as a cognition of that [object] despite the object not being within the range of the earth-dweller (pārthiva),
it is just like the first cognition which has the sun at that time and so forth as its object.

As it has been stated: "The cognitions of the moon, sun, planets, constellations (*nakṣatra*), and so forth, which have become the subjects of dispute, [must] have as their objects precisely the moon, sun, planets, stars, and so forth as delimited by time—namely, that cognition of Devadatta and others regarding the intended moon, sun, planets, stars, and so forth—because, while not being perceived as connected with the earth, they are denotable by the words 'cognition of the moon, sun, planets, constellations, and so forth,' just like the cognition of Devadatta’s stars and so forth occurring at the first moment. [The phrase] "having as their object the intended sun, moon, and so forth" means having as their object a luminous substance (*taijasa-dravya*).

The qualification "while not being perceived as connected with the earth" is intended to avoid a logical fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to cognitions whose objects are the sun and so forth located in paintings and the like.
The word "other" (*param*) means different from that [earth].
The meaning is "at a time other than that."
This is another authority belonging to him alone.

Those which are the substrata of universals such as "form-ness" (*rūpatva*), those which are the substrata of those [universals], and those specific cognitions (*prajñānaviśe�ṣa*)—namely perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, memory, recognition, the cognition of established objects, doubt, error, subsequent reflection (*anuvyavasāya*), dream, and the state following a dream—all these do not perish immediately after their own acquisition of self-nature, because they possess the properties of being knowable (*jñeyatva*), being cognizable (*prameyatva*), being nameable (*abhidheyatva*), being either existent or non-existent, being delimited by a cognition whose object is knowable as distinct from both existent and non-existent, being neither graspable nor ungraspable with respect to its object, being neither nameable nor non-nameable, and being nameable by a sound produced by conjunction and disjunction of substances of the same or different classes. This is because [these properties] belong to them even prior to their destruction, just like prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

In that context, "form and so forth" (rūpādayaḥ) are the substrata of universals such as "form-ness" (rūpatva); and the "substrata of those" (tadāśrayāḥ) are the substrata of those form and so forth. What are they? They are jars and so forth. "Vision of the accomplished" (siddhadarśana) is the cognition of a yogin. The rest has already been explained.
"Being either existent or non-existent" (sadasadanyataratva) means either existence or non-existence.

Since there is no object of knowledge distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, there is no cognition having that as its object; and because of its very non-existence, its incapacity to be delimited by such cognition is established.
Likewise, since there is no apprehension of an ungraspable object, its state of being ungraspable is established precisely from the absence of such apprehension.
Similarly, that which has no denotable referent is "inexpressible" (anabhidheya); and because it lacks a referent, its inexpressibility by any denoter is established simply from its meaninglessness.

Substances of the same class, such as the lower teeth and so forth, [are distinguished] by the generality of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so on, while those of a different class are space (*ākāśa*) and so forth. From the mutual conjunction and disjunction of these two types, a first sound is produced; that which is its successive effect, having entered the path of hearing, is what constitutes the denotability [of the word]. For this is their process: the first sound indeed has conjunction and disjunction as its source, and from that sound, other sounds manifest according to the analogy of the *kadamba* flower bud.
In this regard, that which reaches the space within the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) is perceived, and nothing else.
He demonstrates that very collection of proofs with the words "all [qualities] having color-form (*rūpa*) as their basis," and so forth:
"All those things having color-form as their basis, and whatever their common substrata may be."
