And whatever cognitions arise that have those as their objects, likewise [are not produced].
They do not perish immediately after their arising,
because they possess the properties of being knowable and nameable, just like a sky-lotus.
The mention of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*) is illustrative;
other reasons (*hetu*) should also be understood as applicable.
[The example is: "In the sky (*khe*), that is, in the ether (*nabhasi*), there is a lotus (*aravinda*), meaning an ethereal lotus."

Uddyotakara, however, says: "The cognitions that are under dispute—though occurring at non-simultaneous times—are directed toward a single object, because, while there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the cognitions that does not cease, they are denoted by a common term, like the various cognitions of many persons regarding an object characterized as being present."

In this context, "non-deviating" (*avyutthāyi*) means that its nature is not subject to deviation—that is, becoming otherwise—due to the force of subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*). The co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of those cognitions, such as "jar" and so forth, is non-deviating; thus it is described as "that co-referentiality of those cognitions which is non-deviating. The meaning is: "when there is uncontradicted co-referentiality.
And this qualification is intended to avoid the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) based on cognitions such as those of a lamp and the like.
And there is the state of being denotable by the same term, such as "Caitra’s cognition, Caitra’s cognition," and so forth.
This very point he demonstrates with the words "those which are the objects of dispute," and so on:
"Those cognitions which are the objects of dispute and which occur in succession..."
It is proclaimed that all of them as well have a single object as their domain.
For, since they are established as having a common designation based on their sharing a single undivided substratum,
just as various cognitions do not occur simultaneously in a single present moment.
"Proclamation" (avaghoṣaṇā) refers to the thesis (pratijñā).

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "having a common substratum" (sāmānādhikaraṇya) means having a single locus; and "unsublated" (abādha) means being without sublation; thus, it is "that which has a single locus and is unsublated."
To this, he offers a rebuttal beginning with "sādhyena" and so forth:
First of all, the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) in the first reason is deficient in respect to the probandum (*sādhya*);
for not every object [of a cognition] is co-temporal with its own cognition, since it is an object by virtue of being a cause.
"In the first reason" refers to the statement "because of the designation as that cognition.
For even the initial cognition of the moon and so forth does not have as its object a moon and so forth delimited by its own [present] time.

Because that which has become a cause is precisely what constitutes the object; and because the relationship of cause and effect is untenable between things that exist at the same time—as it has been said: "Because that which is non-existent lacks capacity beforehand, and because that which exists afterwards is of no use."
The priority of all causes [is established]; therefore, an object does not exist simultaneously with its own cognition.

With the words "When... and so forth, he demonstrates that even when the reason is qualified by the condition "while not being perceived as connected with the earth," it remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
When words such as "sun" and so on—which arise solely from the speaker's intention—are applied to things like lamps, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāritā*) due to those cognitions.

In the second set of reasons as well, since the subject (*dharmin*)—namely, birth and so forth—is existent, momentary destruction is not desired for it; thus, in proving its absence therein, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). This is shown by the verse beginning with "jātyādeḥ": "Because birth and so forth lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), momentary destruction is not at all desired for them. Therefore, the proof adduced to establish their absence is futile."
By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of the forms, jars, and so forth which serve as its substrata, as well as the cognitions which have them as their objects.

For these too, being characterized by the aforementioned qualifications, are indeed non-existent; therefore, the proof stated for the purpose of establishing the absence of that momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitā*) in them is useless, because there is no dispute regarding it—this is the intended meaning. Here too, no subtle investigation has been made.
If that [reason] were employed, then a vast web of faults would descend here.

For instance, this reason stated as "being either existent or non-existent" is unestablished (*asiddha*) both with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), because the word "either one" (*anyatara*) has conceptualization (*vikalpa*) as its object; and conceptualization occurs only when multiple things are possible, not when there is only one.
Furthermore, the possibility of both existence and non-existence does not exist within the subject of the thesis.
Because existence is possible only as a real entity (*vastu*),
and because non-existence is possible only as a non-entity (*avastu*), neither of the two [existence and non-existence] can possibly occur in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).
Furthermore, the reason is accompanied by a useless qualification.
For instance, even the formulation "because it is denotable by words" is not appropriate here, since the fact that it is a word is already established simply by the statement that it is "denotable.
Moreover, the qualification by means of terms such as "belonging to the same class" and so forth is utterly trivial.
In this way, it should be understood that any other qualification of the reason (*hetu*) is likewise useless;
furthermore, all these reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
because no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been shown against their opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*).
And this will indeed be explained later.

Regarding what was stated, "those which are the objects of dispute," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "samāna" (common): "The state of being denotable by a common term also exists in cognitions such as those of a lamp; therefore, this reason is inconclusive."

Regarding the term "lamp-cognition": since one observes the application of a common word even when the cognitions of a lamp and so forth have distinct objects, the reason—"because it is denotable by the same word precisely as that which is denotable by the word whose object is the cognition of a lamp and so forth"—is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*). Alternatively, there is a reading with an interrogative intonation (*kākvā*): "Is it not the case that, because it exists in those very instances, the reason is not inconclusive for you? On the contrary, it *is* indeed [inconclusive]"—this is the meaning.
"If it is argued that there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)," he says, raising the opponent's position; "if coreferentiality is postulated despite being sublated,
then why is this very same sublation not clearly perceived even when [the latter] is intended to be expressed?"

The qualification "provided there is co-referentiality with a cognition that does not undergo sublation" has been added to the reason in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of cognitions such as those of a lamp; for the single-objectness of these cognitions of a lamp and so forth is contradicted.
To explain: at that very moment, a lamp is perceived as having a long flame and a short flame, or as being bright and more intensely bright.
Thus, the opponent's thought is: "How, then, can there be deviation from the reason?"
Showing that this qualification is also unestablished, he says: "Even in the intended [subject]," and so forth.
"Why is sublation not observed even there, in the case of the property to be proven as intended?

For instance, even in the case of Caitra and others, a cognition arises with a changing form due to the distinctions of infancy, childhood, youth, and so on; and in the case of mountains and the like, due to the distinctions of cold, heat, and so on. Therefore, their state of being otherwise is more clearly established than that of a lamp and such."

Otherwise, if that very same thing which was previously connected with cold were later connected with heat, then both cold and heat would be perceived in both states; for it would follow that when the entity possessing that [dual] nature exists, both [properties] must also exist— just as, as has already been stated, when a man bound in shackles is pulled, the shackles are also pulled along.
Therefore, even with its qualification, the reason is unestablished (asiddha).
He also states the sublation by inference (*anumānabādhā*) in the passage beginning with "the subject of dispute" (*vivādapada*), etc.:
"Cognitions directed toward the objects of dispute do not have a single object as their domain,
because they arise successively, like the cognitions of lightning, a lamp, and so forth."
For there is a contradiction in the sequential existence [of cognitions] when they arise from a single object;
because for those [cognitions] whose difference is not caused by other factors, dependence upon that [object] is contradictory.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever occurs successively does not have its complete cause always present, just like the cognitions of lightning, lamps, and so forth; and the cognitions under dispute occur successively. This is an observation of the contrary of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because when [cognitions] have a single object, it is impossible for them to occur successively if their causes are complete.
Furthermore, there can be no dependence on other causes for that which is eternal, since such a thing cannot be assisted by them.
Furthermore, dependence upon that which provides no assistance is not logical, as it would lead to an over-extension;
or, if there were assistance, it would entail the loss of its permanence—this has been discussed hundreds of times.

And he demonstrates that in all these applications, the reasons (*hetu*) are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because there is an absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), by stating "doubtful," and so forth:
"In all these reasons, there is a doubtful exclusion (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*),
because no subverting proof has been shown for those [reasons] that exist in the counter-example."
This is easily understood.
Thus concludes the examination of the permanence of entities.

Now, in order to establish the foundation for the systematic arrangement of the relationship between action and its fruit, he says "momentary," etc., beginning with an objection: "If every entity is touched by momentary impermanence, then how [can there be] the relationship between action and its fruit, causality, and so forth?"
The mention of "momentary impermanence" (*kṣaṇikānityatā*) is for the purpose of excluding impermanence that persists over a period of time.

If you assert that the entire range of entities is permeated—that is, pervaded—by that impermanence of things which exist only momentarily, then how could these well-known relations between actions and their fruits, as recognized in both the world and the treatises, be established?

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there are included such categories as the means of valid cognition that apprehends cause and effect, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding experience, the desire for another object when one object has been seen, bondage and liberation, memory, determination preceded by doubt, the searching for something previously hidden by oneself, and the cessation of curiosity regarding objects already seen—all of which are imagined by those of poor intellect.

The sense is that a proposition (*pratijñā*) does not attain establishment if it is asserted in contradiction to what is recognized in common worldly experience or in the treatises; thus, this is the fault of the proposition known as "contradiction of what is accepted and recognized" (*abhyupetapratītabādhā*).
For it is well-known in the world that the very person by whom an action, such as a virtuous one, was performed is the one who experiences its fruit;
indeed, it is not established in common experience that when an action, such as a virtuous one, has been performed by Devadatta, Yajñadatta experiences its fruit, whether desirable or undesirable.
Nor is this so in the scriptures, as it is said: "Who else shall experience the fruit of the action performed by this very person?"
And this [position] is contradicted by the doctrine of momentariness,

because, in the absence of a single agent who appropriates both the action and its fruit, it would entail the faults of the destruction of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
To the question "How so?", he says "That which," and so forth:
That moment which is conceived as the agent of wholesome states and the like does not persist at all at the time when the fruit is produced.
The moment that is described as the experiencer at the time of the production of the fruit has not performed that action, because it did not exist previously.
Thus, because the action and its fruit are grasped as having a single agent,
the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done follow, which is deeply contradictory.
Nor does it persist,
because it ceases immediately after its arising;
and because there is no appropriation by a single agent.
The meaning is that because those two—the action and its fruit—are not grasped by a single agent.

Due to the lack of connection between the agent and the fruit, there is the "destruction of what was done" (*kṛtanāśa*); and due to the connection of the fruit with one who was not the agent, there is the "acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
Thus, [the doctrine] is highly contradictory.
The meaning is that this is because such a thing is not observed in either worldly practice or in the treatises.
Thus, having first accepted the process of activity, the consequence of the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done has been stated.
Now, he demonstrates that activity itself is impossible by presenting the view of Kumārila, beginning with the words "In the doctrine of selflessness," and so forth:
"But in the position of the doctrine of selflessness, [the agent] understands [the result] beforehand."
If I were destroyed, the fruit would not come to pass; or else it might belong to someone other than me.
Thus, a discerning person would not engage in the undertaking of auspicious or inauspicious actions out of a desire for results, for the result remains far off.
For if one accepts the momentariness of all phenomena, one must necessarily accept their selflessness (*nairātmya*),
because everything is dependent on causes and thus lacks independence.
When that [selflessness] exists, a discerning person understands and ascertains it even before engaging in any activity.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "Because of my destruction," and so forth.
After my destruction, the fruit would not belong to me, because at the time the fruit arises, I am no longer present.

Even if the fruit were to arise, it would then belong to another moment distinct from me; knowing this, engagement itself is impossible for a discerning person, let alone the attainment of a fruit produced by an action preceded by such engagement.
Because it remains at a great distance, such that its occurrence is impossible to conceive.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the connection between action and its fruit is not tenable.
Now, demonstrating the untenability of the relationship between cause and effect according to the view of Kumārila himself, he says:
"Neither the future nor the past entity is capable of performing an action," and so forth.
Even while existing, it does not remain for even that much time.
The phrase "for that long" means that once it has arisen, it does not persist for as much time as it takes to accomplish its effect, because of its momentariness; such is the intended meaning.
He provides the justification for the passage beginning with "not future," etc., in due order, stating: "For that which has not attained its own nature," and so forth.
For an entity that has not attained its own nature is not capable of becoming an auxiliary to another;
nor is that which is destroyed, nor its persistence, capable of performing a function.
Furthermore, if the destruction of the preceding moment is conceived as being without any continuity,
its subsequent arising would be untenable because it would lack a cause.

For that which is called "the future" has not yet attained its own essential nature (*ātmatattva*). And that which has not attained its own essential nature is non-existent; and that which is non-existent is devoid of all causal capacity (*sāmarthya*). How, then, can that which is devoid of all causal capacity be fit for being a constituent part of another—that is to say, how can it function as a cause for another? This is the meaning, because only that which is capable is recognized as having the status of a cause. In the same way, even that which has perished is not fit for being a constituent part of another, because it is devoid of all causal capacity; such is the connection [of the argument].
Furthermore, there is no duration for that which is present such that it would be capable of performing an action;
moreover, if it is imagined that the preceding moment perishes without leaving a trace, then the subsequent moment could not arise due to the absence of a cause.

It might be argued: "Just as the lowering and raising of the two ends of a scale occur simultaneously, so too the destruction of the cause and the arising of the effect are accepted [as simultaneous]; therefore, since the production of an effect from that which is present and not yet destroyed is accepted, its production will not be without a cause. To this, he says: "Even though destruction and arising are simultaneous," and so forth: "Even though destruction and arising are simultaneous, there is no mutual dependence;
causality does not exist [between them] because they do not assist one another's operation."

Even if one were to assume the equality of destruction and arising, it is not possible for destruction and arising—or for their possessors—to stand in the relation of cause and effect, because they are mutually independent.
To the question "How are they independent? he says: "Because there is no assistance from its operation.
This means that the effect is not assisted—that is, not benefited—by the operation of that [destruction] or of its possessor.

For destruction, being devoid of form (nīrūpa), lacks any activity; and even for that entity which is considered a cause, there is an absence of activity because it is not present at the time when the effect is capable [of arising].
It might be argued that even without an intervening operation, the relation of cause and effect will exist by mere immediate succession; to this he says: "And while being born," and so forth.
Just as a smell and other qualities arising while the form of a jar is perishing are not accepted as its effects, so it is with other forms as well.

If it were the case that whatever arises immediately after something else is its effect, then, since a moment of odor and so forth arising within that same complex arises immediately after a moment of form belonging to a jar or the like—just as a moment of form of the same kind [arises]—that odor and so forth would also have to be its effect. Yet, even though such immediate succession exists, that odor is not accepted as being its effect.

For there is no mutual relationship of cause and effect among derived forms (*bhautika*) as there is among the primary elements (*bhūta*), because they belong to different continua; such is the opponent's view. Likewise, other instances of form—namely, subsequent moments of form belonging to the same class—should not be apprehended as its effects merely by virtue of their immediate succession, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is the intended meaning.

Having thus demonstrated that it is not logical for mere immediate succession alone to be the basis for establishing the absence of a cause, he presents his own position by way of a conclusion, beginning with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt):
"Therefore, that whose activity is observed prior to the production of the effect is indeed its cause, and not mere immediate succession."
"But not merely immediate succession"— the remainder of the sentence is "it is based on the established relation between cause and effect."

Showing the very same point in brief, he says: "This is the summary," and so forth: "If this is the summary—that an effect arises from a cause that has perished—then because that which is destroyed is indefinable, this [effect] would be without a cause."
And since that which is produced from what has not perished can persist for many moments,
how then would the momentariness of entities not be contradicted?
In this regard, there are two possible alternatives:
either the effect arises from a cause that has perished, or from one that has not perished;
for there exists no entity that is distinct from both the perished and the unperished.

In this regard, the first position is not tenable; for if one accepts production from that which has perished, since the perished thing is non-existent, it would follow that the effect is causeless. And consequently, its eternal existence and so forth would be untenable. Nor is the second position tenable, because if things were to persist through multiple moments, it would entail the loss of their momentariness.
"How could it not be contradicted?
means that it is indeed contradicted.

For instance, an entity first arises, then exerts activity, then produces an effect, and finally perishes; thus, for a single entity to be present at more than one moment would constitute a contradiction of its momentariness.

Having thus established the impossibility of the relation between cause and effect, he says "kṣaṇasthāyī" and so forth, demonstrating the impossibility of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that could apprehend it:
"If a jar or the like were to exist for only a single moment, it would not be perceived by the eye;
for things that have perished are not cognized, just like objects that have long since passed away."
The causal relation as well is not established through perception and non-perception,
because the intrinsic nature of entities is not perceived.

For the causal relation is established through perception and non-perception; however, since entities are momentary, they do not persist at the time of their own cognition and thus are simply not perceived.
This is because a causal relation is impossible between simultaneous entities.
Consequently, there is an absolute absence of both perception and non-perception.

Since non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is itself a specific form of perception (*pratyakṣa*), by virtue of its nature being the apprehension of an object that is not mixed with anything else, it follows that when there is an absence of the apprehension of a thing, that [non-apprehension] is likewise impossible. Therefore, how could the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) be established through perception and non-apprehension?

Granted that there may be perception of an object, nevertheless, because there is no single persisting agent who connects the preceding and succeeding moments, the relationship [between them] is not established; showing this, he says "Who indeed," and so forth:
"Or rather, what persisting agent connects the sequential course?
When this is seen, that is seen; but when this is not seen, it is not perceived."
"Going" (gati) means apprehension;
and since this going is successive, it is "successive going.
Who connects—that is, joins together—that [going]?
Not at all.

For if someone were to connect this sequential process—namely, that "this smoke and so forth was perceived because of the perception of this fire, and it is not perceived when that [fire] is not perceived"—as having a single agent, then the establishment of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) would occur. But according to your view, such a connector does not exist; therefore, the meaning is that the causal relationship cannot be established.
Now, demonstrating the impossibility of recognition, he says "In things subject to momentary destruction," and so forth:
"Recognition is difficult to establish in entities that are subject to momentary destruction;
for an object seen by one person is not recognized by others."

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the synthesis of two cognitions—the former and the latter—by way of their having a single object and a single knower, such that one thinks: "That very same object which was previously seen by me is now being seen.
And this [recognition] is not possible if all things are subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*), because there would be no single knower or single known object whatsoever.

For Viṣṇumitra does not recognize an object seen by Devadatta. The mention of "one or the other" is an illustration; it should also be understood that no other object whatsoever is recognized [by another].

Now, one might object: "Even though there is a difference—as in the case of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back again—recognition will still occur because of similarity. Anticipating this, he says "from similarity," and so forth: "Recognition based on similarity may occur in the case of hair and the like, even when they are different, because a single cognizer exists; but in the case of a twofold difference, [recognition] would be without basis."
And if no single entity exists that performs the act of synthesis,
then how could there be desire and so forth for taste and other qualities when only form has been seen?
For if there were indeed a single knower, then, by virtue of that unifying subject, there could be recognition based on similarity even when the objects of knowledge are distinct.
But in the case of a "twofold distinction"—that is, a distinction between both the knower and the object of knowledge—recognition would be entirely without foundation.

Furthermore, if there were no single person acting as a unifier, then how could there arise, upon seeing the form of a citron fruit or the like, a desire preceded by memory for its taste and other qualities which are invariably concomitant with that form, and an engagement toward its consumption?
For indeed, when something has been seen by one person, another person cannot have desire or similar mental states toward it.

Showing that even bondage and liberation are not attained [by moments], he says "rāgādi" and so forth: "One moment is bound by the shackles of passion and the like within the prison of existence, while another is unbound and liberated; this fact is not understood."
For one moment is bound by passion and the like, while another is liberated; this is not understood, meaning it is not even conceivable.
Regarding the term *bhavavāraka*: "existence" (*bhava*) is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), and that itself is the prison (*vāraka*).
Showing that effort for the sake of liberation is futile because liberation would be impossible, he says: "Liberation is not at all," and so forth.
For liberation is never possible for one who is bound, because of the absolute destruction [of the self]; therefore, the momentary existence [of the self] is useless for those seeking liberation.
[Objection: "Surely liberation will belong to one who is not bound; what contradiction is there in this? To this, he says "mokṣam" and so forth:
"One who has attained liberation is seen to have been bound by shackles and the like;
that one who is unbound attains liberation—such a thing contradicts what is observed."
For it is both commonly recognized and observed in the world that "he who is bound is the very one who is liberated.

However, the proposition that one who is unbound is liberated is contradicted by common worldly recognition and by direct perception; thus, the meaning is that the proposition is in conflict with direct perception and common experience.
He also states the sublation by inference [as follows]: "These two, bondage and liberation, have a single locus, because they exist in such a manner;
like those [states] found in the world, therefore everything is established most beautifully."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those two, bondage and liberation, have a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*), just like worldly bondage and liberation; and these two, which are the subjects of dispute, characterized by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and their dissociation (*tadvisaṃyoga*), are indeed bondage and liberation. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Likewise, "because they exist" means because they exist in the form of bondage and liberation, that is, because they possess the nature of bondage and liberation.
“Those two” refers to bondage and liberation.

And thus, because a single substratum—the self—is established, the connection with the fruits of all actions and so forth remains more beautiful; that is to say, it is established in a more excellent manner, because the aforementioned defects are absent.
"By this very [method]" means that in this very manner, there is the impossibility of memory and so forth,
because of the absence of a single substratum among things that perish moment by moment.
Because there is no single agent,

one must understand that the previously mentioned acts— such as memory, ascertainment, searching for what was hidden by oneself, and so forth— are impossible. For even in those cases, if they were located in different substrata, it would entail contradictions such as those observed in the case of [different] persons.

For when Caitra—the experiencer, the one who deposited [the object], or the one who desires it—is in a state of doubt, it is impossible for Maitra to experience recollection, certainty, the search for the object, curiosity, cessation, and so forth.
To this, he replies with the words "In this regard, it is said," and so forth:
"In this matter, it is said that when the existence of the causal relationship between all effects and causes is established,
these [properties] are proven to be unimpeded even in things that are devoid of a self."

For even though there is selflessness (nairātmya) regarding all phenomena, this systematic arrangement of the relationship between actions and their results and so forth is brought about by the principle of cause and effect; and since the causal relationship exists, everything is entirely consistent, and thus nothing is lost.
It might be argued that this very restriction of the causal relationship would not be possible without a self (ātman). To this he says, "Just as," and so forth:
"Just as the restricted capacity of seeds and the like toward sprouts and the like exists even in the absence of a persisting self, so too is the situation regarding internal [phenomena]."
For just as the power of seeds and the like toward sprouts and so forth is determined even without a self as a presiding controller, so it will be with respect to internal entities as well.
Indeed, seeds and the like are not presided over by a self as a locus of experience in the manner that the body is;
otherwise, the argument that "this living body is not devoid of a self, because [if it were] it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth" would not be tenable.

For it is indeed observed that when the self is absent in things such as a jar, the vital breaths and so forth are seen to cease; thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason would be established.
However, if even a jar and the like were possessed of a self, how could this reason be one characterized by negative concomitance?
[The phrase] "even in the absence of a self" refers to positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
The meaning is: "even in the absence of some persisting intrinsic nature."
What, then, is this "stability"? He says: "By way of succession," and so forth.
For something is indeed capable [of producing an effect] either indirectly or directly in some cases;
therefore, the relationship between actions, their fruits, and so on, is established.

For just as the fixed determination of cause and effect exists externally, so too does it exist within this internal aggregate of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra-rāśi*), due to the restriction of causal capacity.

Indeed, from a specific pure or impure karma, a restricted desired or undesired fruit manifests through a succession of moments; from the experience of form and so forth comes recollection; from deliberation comes ascertainment; from a location comes searching; for one who desires, there is the sight of the object; and from that, the cessation of curiosity—all of this is entirely consistent.
For nowhere are recollection and so forth established for the Buddhist as being associated with a single substantial entity.
What then? This is merely a cognition (*pratyayamātra*).

As it has been said: "Karma exists, its fruit exists, but an agent is not perceived—one who casts off these aggregates and takes up other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṅketa*)."
In this regard, this is the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṅketa*): namely, "when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "of karma, its fruit, etc.," there is the inclusion of memory and so forth.
The relationship, however, is that of the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*).

If this is so, how then is it that in the world and in the treatises, with reference to such and such a person (pudgala), it is said: "By this very person was the karma performed; who else shall experience its result? To this he says: "The establishment of agency and so forth," and so on.

"The establishment of agency and so forth is intended [only] by way of the unity of the continuum (santāna); it is accepted as being merely superimposed through conceptual construction (kalpanā). It is not a factor in the actual state of reality (tattva)."

The world, whose light of knowledge is impaired by a dense mass of the darkness of abundant ignorance, disregards the investigation into whether [the self] is identical to or different from the [constituents], or even non-existent; rather, having determined the continuity of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)—which possess a nature fixed by specific causes and effects—to be a unity, it engages in the conventional usage "I myself am the one who acts," and it exerts itself for the sake of liberation.

And in accordance with that conceit, the Blessed Tathāgatas, desiring to protect those to be trained from falling into the abyss of the view of annihilation, demonstrate the unity of the continuum and thereby establish [conventions such as] agency.
If it is argued that the establishment of a real entity follows from such a conventional arrangement, he replies with the words "That [arrangement] is not a factor," and so forth.

For it is impossible to establish reality by the force of the attachment of ordinary people—those who have fallen into the conventional and whose minds are averse to the investigation of ultimate truth—because that attachment is sublated by the valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) established through selflessness and momentary destruction.

Anticipating the objection of an opponent who considers the example to be unestablished—on the grounds that the dissociation of the persisting self (*anvayyātman*) from seeds and so forth is unproven—the author says: "In the absence of continuity, that very same causal relation would be possible, as it is appropriately [distinguished] from those occurring in other continua. "In the absence of continuity, that very same causal relation would be possible, as it is appropriately [distinguished] from those occurring in other continua. This means that if there were no persisting entity, the causal relationship itself would be established as distinct from those things belonging to other continua.
Now, is it not observed that the causal relationship between seeds, sprouts, and so forth is fixed? In that case, there is no part whatsoever that possesses a nature of persistence.
"Concomitance" (anvaya) means "following after" (anugama); the remainder of the sense is "of some intrinsic nature" (svabhāva).
It might be argued that there is indeed continuity (*anvaya*) even in the case of seeds and the like.

As Uddyotakara has stated: "In that case as well, those parts of the seed, upon abandoning their previous configuration, attain another configuration. And when another configuration is attained, the earth element, being moistened by the water element and cooked by internal fire, produces the substance of sap (*rasadravya*). That sap, together with the preceding parts, attains the state of a sprout and so forth."
To the question, "How then can it be said that not even a subtle part exists there? he says: "Of earth and the rest," and so forth.

"If earth and the rest were not distinct [from one another] in seeds, sprouts, creepers, and so on, then no differentiation would be logical because of their identity; thus, it is established that [destruction] is without residue."

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the existence or non-existence of karma, its fruits, and so forth, it is sufficient that the relationship of cause and effect be established; what need is there for others?

This is what is meant: if earth and the other elements, while existing in a subsequent arrangement, continue to exist without abandoning their prior intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then it would not be possible for them to abandon their former configuration (*vyūha*) and undergo a transition to another configuration, because of their identity with that [prior nature], just as before. Consequently, the mutual distinction between seeds, sprouts, and so forth would not be established.
Because they possess a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāva*).

If, on the other hand, a distinction among the sprout and so forth is admitted, then, since their previous intrinsic nature must necessarily be abandoned, one must admit that the earth and the other elements abandon their former configuration (*vyūha*) and undergo a transition to another configuration;
otherwise, as has been stated, there would be no distinction at all.
Furthermore, since things arise with successive and distinct natures, how could there be any continuity?

Thus, when the relationship between cause and effect is established in this way, everything—including the connection between actions and their fruits—becomes coherent; yet when it is refuted, it falls apart. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the existence of actions, fruits, and so forth, one must exert effort toward establishing the causal relationship.
This is by others—the followers of the supreme vision, that is to say, the excellent Buddhists.

And for the sake of establishing their non-existence, an effort must be made by the opponents—the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika)—to establish the non-existence of that very causal relation; this is the meaning. The phrase "in the establishment of causal relation" should be repeated twice, with the vowel 'ā' elided in one instance.

In this regard, setting aside the two alternatives—whether [the cause] has perished or not perished—which were raised by the opponent, he says "To this it is replied," and so forth, in order to establish the causal relation as the very foundation of all systematic arrangements:
"To this it is replied: for the effect is produced in the second moment, while the cause was born and remains unperished in the first, at which time that [effect] exists."
But because it is momentary, that effect does not exist at the time of its own moment;
or, if it were to exist, the effect would be fruitless, since it has already been accomplished by that time.
Our position is that the effect arises from a cause that has not yet perished; nor does this entail the consequence of simultaneity.
For, depending upon the cause—which has acquired its own existence through its causal status in the first moment and remains unperished—the effect is produced in the second moment.
And that effect, being thus produced, arises precisely from that which has not yet perished.
Because it has not yet perished at the first moment;
and the cause does not persist until the time of the effect’s existence,
since it does not remain due to its momentariness.
Moreover, even if it persists, it cannot be the cause at that time, because once the effect has been accomplished, it can no longer perform any function.
He demonstrates that very point of its being ineffective with the words "And not," and so forth:
"Nor can that which has already arisen previously be produced again by it;
because production consists in the coming into being of what was non-existent, there is no other state [for it]."
"Not otherwise is there stability" means that otherwise there would be no fixed rule (niyama),
which is to say, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā).

For if that which has already been produced were to be produced again, then, because there would be no distinction [between its states], it would follow that it must be produced yet again; consequently, there would be an infinite regress of births,
and the causal factors would never cease their activity, as there would be no difference [in the cause] itself due to the absence of any distinguishing feature.
Consequently, there would be no established distinction such that "this is the cause" and "this is the effect."
Having concluded with the words "Therefore," etc., he demonstrates that the position of the proponent (sthitapakṣa) is faultless:
"Therefore, from that non-perished cause existing in the first moment,
the effect arises from the potent [cause] at the very second moment."
If, however, an effect were to arise from what has perished in the third or subsequent moments,
it would be like the effect that will be explained as arising from a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) once it has been destroyed.
If that [simultaneity] were to occur in the first [moment], there would be the consequence of simultaneity;
however, that is not tenable through reasoning, just as in the case of co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*).
The [position that the cause] has perished is untenable precisely because it is not accepted.
For if it were accepted that the effect arises in the third or subsequent moments— as the Vaibhāṣikas maintain when they assert that "one past [moment] bestows [the fruit]"—
then one would be accepting the production of an effect from a cause that has already perished.
And this position is not ours,
because it is devoid of reason;
furthermore, the consequence of simultaneity might occasionally occur if the effect were held to arise in the very first moment.
Just as that very same Vaibhāṣika school maintains that there is a coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*),
this is also untenable.
He asks "Why? and says: "Because of the non-existence [of the effect] prior [to its production], because of the lack of capacity; and because when there is capacity, the effect is possible.
Thus, a clear simultaneity of cause and effect is contradicted."
For a cause that produces an effect existing simultaneously with it must produce it either while being unarisen or while being arisen.
It cannot be the case that it produces it while unarisen, because it does not exist prior to the arising of the effect,
and because that which is non-existent is devoid of all causal capacity.

If it is argued that when [the cause] has arisen, it will produce [the effect] because it possesses efficacy, [the author] replies: "Because the effect is impossible when there is efficacy. For when its efficacy exists in its state of having already arisen, then the effect must also exist; thus, like its own nature, it has already arisen. In what way, then, could its efficacy be of any use?
Therefore, the acceptance of the simultaneity of cause and effect is contradicted by the means of valid cognition known as inference.
[Objection: But surely the relationship of cause and effect is the relationship of object and agent, and that is contradicted when they exist at different times;
for the relationship of object and agent is not observed between a jar and a potter when they are not simultaneous. To this, [the author] says "na hi" and so forth:
For that effect does not grasp its own cause like a pair of tongs.
Having grasped these, it produces them; from this, simultaneity would arise.
Nor does a result arise by embracing its own nature tightly,
such that there would be a single state between the two, as occurs between a lover and his beloved.

For if the cause were to operate toward the production of the effect according to the logic of grasping with tongs, or if the effect were to attain an operation toward its own birth through contact with its own cause—like an embrace by a woman—then co-existence would necessarily follow.

However, this entire world is indeed devoid of activity; for in ultimate reality, there is no agent nor any object of action, except as a conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṅketa*). This is the collective meaning.
[The word] "prakṛtim" [is used].
The cause.

If this is so, and if both the effect and the cause are indeed devoid of activity, then how can speakers say that "fire produces smoke" or "smoke arises depending upon fire"? To this he says: "Because of necessity," and so forth.
[This is] because of the necessity arising from its own cause, which exists at the first moment.
Whatever is produced immediately after something else is the presence of the second moment.
Those who follow conventions produced by mere intention say that "it produces that," even though the entity is devoid of activity.

Due to the specific determination of the capacity of a cause—which arises from its own causes and conditions—that particular effect which is produced from a cause existing in the first moment is said to be "produced" by that cause when it is present in the second moment; this is the analysis of the compound *dvitīye kṣaṇe sannidhiḥ* (that which has presence in the second moment).
To say that "it produces" is an elliptical expression;
it should also be understood as meaning that "it arises depending upon that."
"But who are those who speak thus? and so forth.

The meaning is that it is the speakers themselves—who engage in linguistic usage according to conventions arising from their intention to express [something] independently of external objects—who speak in this way.

Now, one might object: "How could that which, having arisen, does not enter into an activity for the sake of producing a specific effect be a cause? To this he says: "janmātiriktetyādi" (What result is there here from an activity at a time distinct from its birth?). [p.177] What fruit is there here from an activity occurring at a time other than its own arising?
Existence itself is its activity, since it is only when that exists that the effect arises.

Since the effect is already accomplished immediately after the existence of the cause, the operation that occurs at a time subsequent to the birth of the effect is entirely ineffective with respect to that effect. For what indeed is called the "operation" (vyāpāra) of a cause? It is that immediately following which the effect attains its arising; and since the effect arises immediately after the existence of the cause, let "existence" itself be what is denoted by the word "operation. What is the point of postulating an operation distinct from birth?

If this is so, and there is no activity on the part of entities, how is it that one studies [the following]: "the effect has a dependence upon the cause, and the cause has an activity toward the effect"? To this he says: "That which is the restriction of immediate succession," and so forth.
That very restriction of immediate succession is designated as "dependence";
and the constant presence [of the cause] at the time of the arising of the effect is the "activity" of the cause.

For this indeed is the dependence of the effect upon the cause: namely, its state of occurring immediately after that [cause]; and this alone is the operation of the cause upon the effect: namely, its state of being constantly present at the time of the effect's arising.

Furthermore, you must accept that the causal status of either an activity or an entity possessing an activity toward an effect arises solely from the principle of "existence when that exists" (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*). For there is no means other than positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) for apprehending the relationship between cause and effect. This being the case, why is the causal status not attributed even to a mere entity? Indeed, it is well known that an effect follows the positive and negative concomitance residing in a mere entity; therefore, it is better that the mere entity itself—within which the following of the effect’s positive and negative concomitance is established—be the cause. This is what [the author] demonstrates with the words beginning "tadbhāva... (from existence...).
Since the causal operation is merely postulated on the basis of its existence being contingent upon that [cause],
it is better that either the possessor of that operation attains the status of cause, or that the operation itself be the cause.

"Imagined" (avakalpita) means that which has been conceptually constructed by you as an activity (vyāpāra) that is either other [than the agent], or of the nature of both, or of neither. "Possessing that" (tadvān) means possessing that activity.
The connection with the context is: "it becomes a cause merely by being permeated by that.
"That very thing" means: let the mere entity, devoid of any distinct operation, be the cause.
"What excellence is there in that by which it is called 'better'? To this he says, "When there is existence," and so forth:
"For when existence is present, the emergence of sprouts from seeds and so on is observed; but when [mere] activity is present, nothing at all is seen to come into being."
"In an entity" means in a mere entity, that is to say, when the seed or other such causes are devoid of the entry of any further operation.

By this, it is shown that it is established that effects follow only the positive and negative concomitance residing in the mere entity, and not the positive and negative concomitance residing in an operation.

It might be argued: "Even if the effect's conformity to the positive and negative concomitance residing in the operation is not established, nevertheless, that [operation] will still possess the status of a cause. To this, he says: "adṛṣṭaśakteḥ" and so forth.
Even if the status of being a cause is postulated for something whose causal power is unperceived, it is not accepted.
Why would anything else also have the status of a cause? Or what is its distinction from that [unperceived power]?
For if one were to thus postulate even an operation (*vyāpāra*) as the cause, another [operation] would likewise have to be postulated;
since there is no distinction because its power is unperceived, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.

If, on the other hand, another is not postulated due to a lack of basis (*nibandhana*), then let there be no postulation of an operation either, for the absence of a basis is equal in that case as well.

Furthermore, as for that activity which produces an effect, does it do so by entering into another activity, or rather by its mere existence? If it were by entering into another activity, then that other activity alone would be the cause, not the [original] activity; and regarding that other activity’s status as a cause, the same objection applies.
For if its causal nature were likewise imagined to result from the entry into yet another activity, there would be an infinite regress.

Now, if the position is that [the cause acts] by its mere existence, then even a thing (padārtha) would produce the effect by its mere existence alone, just like an operation; thus, the postulation of an operation is useless. This is shown by the words "And by another," and so forth: "And just as an operation is accepted as the cause of an effect even without anything else, why then are other things not also causes?"

For just as an activity is accepted as a cause for an effect such as a sprout even without another distinct activity, why are other entities not likewise accepted as causes while being entirely devoid of any distinct activity?

Furthermore, it might be argued that the operation does not directly assist the effect, but rather assists the entity itself as something possessing an operation. To this he says, "Or else, the entity," and so forth.
This is to be connected with the context: "is intended as the cause."

For even in your case, this reason, while being active, exists as something devoid of the entry of any other activity; thus, that very [example] will serve as the illustration—this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, there is no operation of an entity apart from its existence;
for that which meets the conditions for perception is not perceived. This is shown by the passage beginning with "that which is considered visible," and so forth.
We do not perceive that which is claimed to be visible;
how then can we accept its relationship as the basis [for inference]?
For you maintain that activity (*vyāpāra*) is perceptible, as Kumārila has stated: "That whose activity is perceived prior to the production of the effect," and so forth.

Furthermore, that entity consisting of activity must be either distinct from the active thing or non-distinct from it, since there is no other possible mode for a real entity; the alternatives of being both or neither are simply impossible. If it were distinct, then the active thing would not possess causality.
Because only the operation distinct from that [entity] possesses the status of being a cause.
If it is argued that the entity also possesses the status of being a cause because of its connection with the operation, we say no;
for a connection between two things that do not mutually assist one another is not established.
Now, it might be argued that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is indeed assisted by the entity (*padārtha*).
That too is incorrect;

for it has no further operation by which it could assist an [other] operation. Otherwise, due to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of operations alone being joined to one another, a connection between the operation and the entity would never be established.

Now, if it were argued that an entity assists an operation even without another intervening operation, then why would the effect not also assist by its mere existence, just as an operation does, while itself being devoid of an operation—such that one would postulate an operation as a distinct entity? For there is nothing to prevent it from serving its purpose toward the effect through its mere existence.
Therefore, it is not logical for an operation to be a distinct entity.
Now, if the position is that [the operation] is not a distinct entity [from the thing itself], then it is established that existence (*sattā*) alone is the operation;
for it is the very nature of the object (*padārtha-svabhāva*) that is denoted by the word "existence.
Consequently, the operation does not prove to be something additional to birth (*janman*).

Moreover, just as cognition, in the act of apprehending an object, functions by its mere existence even while devoid of any further operation, so too will the causality of all entities exist without an operation occurring at a subsequent time; this is what [the author] demonstrates with the words "of cognition," and so forth:
"Just as the very birth of cognition is established as its status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), why is it not likewise accepted that the same applies to the causality of all entities?"

For there is no operation of the intellect distinct from its birth. Thus, Kumārila, while explaining the purpose of the inclusion of the term "birth" (*janman*) in the sūtra—"When there is contact of a person's sense organs with an existing object, the birth of cognition is perception"—stated: "And by saying 'the birth of cognition,' he [the author] asserts that the cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely as it is being born."
For the activity of causes is indeed observed to be distinct from their arising.
"In order that it may not be so even in the case of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its birth is intended to be expressed.
Thus,
[it refers to] its being the cause of that.
Those for whom that birth from causes is the cause are so described;
the state of being that is their reality (*tattva*).

It might be argued that an activity (*vyāpāra*) is logically possible for a cognition, but not for an entity (*bhāva*), because the latter does not persist beyond its own moment due to its momentariness; to this he says, "For they are momentary," and so forth.
For just as cognition is momentary, so too are all other things that are born.
Therefore, it has been established that this world is likewise devoid of activity.
"Established": because, in the *Sthirabhāvaparīkṣā* (Examination of Permanent Entities), momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), which pervades all things, has been established;
"just like that."
It is just like the intellect;
"therefore" means because of momentariness.

The formal argument is as follows: those things which are momentary are devoid of any operation distinct from their birth, just like cognition; and seeds and other such things have been previously established as being momentary—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is that since there is no persistence [of the cause] at a later time, an operation without a substratum is impossible. Therefore, it is established that the mere immediate succession alone is the basis for determining the causal relationship, and not an operation.

Regarding what was said, "And that which is being born, such as odor," and so forth—he says "By way of a continuous series" (*prabandha*) etc., demonstrating that even there there is no deviation [from the rule].
"By way of a continuous series, the mutual causality of odor and the rest is indeed accepted;
therefore, this [objection] which results in their being causes is not at all a subverter of that."
For it is indeed accepted that color, taste, and so forth stand in a relationship of auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*) with respect to one another in terms of their continuity;
as it has been said:
"Without the operation of a capacity, there is no other cause for taste itself."
Thus, the movement of those [beings] belonging to a single past time is known through the inferential mark of its effects.
Thus it is said.

But surely, since [an effect] such as a cow or a horse sometimes occurs on the ground immediately after fire as well, how is it that immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not subject to deviation? To this he says: "Even when occurring immediately after another," and so forth. "Even when occurring immediately after another, only a specific thing is accepted as the cause, precisely because of such a restriction; and this is equally the case even with regard to permanent things."

For we do not say that mere immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is the basis for understanding the relation of cause and effect; rather, it is that which is necessary (*niyata*). For instance, whatever arises immediately after something else is accepted as the cause of that thing. And smoke does not arise immediately after cows and the like, because it exists even in the absence of cows and such.

Furthermore, this objection applies to you as well, who maintain the doctrine of permanence: why is it that smoke, even though it arises immediately after a cow or other such things, is not their effect?
Regarding this, the opponent says:
"If it is held that whatever is engaged in a particular effect is not its cause,
then let it be accepted that whatever has a restricted existence in relation to something is the cause of that thing."
With the words beginning "In which," he states the rebuttal even for his own position.
Thus, the causal relationship between entities has been established even given their momentariness;
now, in order to establish the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends this, he says "existence and non-existence," and so forth.
If it is held that the object is to be known by consciousness possessing a form (sākāra-vijñāna), then these two— existence and non-existence— are established through perception and non-perception.
When you maintain that an object is cognizable by a cognition devoid of aspects,
that same [objection] applies equally even to the position that it consists of moments and so forth.
For indeed, every single consciousness arises from its own preceding causes as a form of awareness, possessing equal portions of time, form, and so forth.

For just as your perception of a stable entity is established, so too will our perception of the momentary be established. To explain: when there is a perception of an object, it must occur either through a cognition possessing a form (*sākāra*) or through one devoid of form (*anākāra*). In that regard, if it occurs through a cognition with a form, then the experience of the cognition’s own form is itself the experience of the object; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever between the positions of the stable and the unstable.
Furthermore, even if it were without an aspect (*anākāra*), there would still be no distinction [between the cognition and its object].
For that cognition arises from its own preceding causes in such a way that it perceives only the color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth existing at the same time as itself, and nothing else;
this is because it has arisen as having precisely that perception as its nature.

Therefore, if it is admitted that cognition has as its intrinsic nature the awareness of form and so forth arising at the same time [as those objects], there is no distinction whatsoever regarding whether an object is stable or unstable.

Furthermore, you must necessarily admit that the intrinsic nature of cognition—which apprehends specific form and so forth occurring at the same time—is produced solely by a prior cause; for only in this way could it be the case that, although the simultaneity is equal, cognition determines only the form and so forth, and not the sense organ.
And since that [prior causality] is exactly the same even if entities are momentary, this [objection of yours] is trivial.
With the words "sākāra" and so forth, the opponent raises an objection against both [positions]: "If consciousness possesses an aspect (sākāra), then there would indeed be a variety of the mind;
but if it were not marked by an aspect (anākārānaṅkitatva), there would be no basis for the connection [between object and cognition]."
If cognition possesses an aspect (*sākāra*), then in the case of a multicolored carpet and the like, the cognition itself would have to be multicolored;
yet it is not logical for a single entity to be multicolored, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
On the other hand, if it is without an aspect (*anākāra*), then the determination that "this is the experience of blue" and not "of yellow" could not be established.
Because there is no distinction [between them] insofar as they all consist of the nature of consciousness, there is an absence of any basis for proximity.
He responds with the words "By you as well" and so forth:
"Even by you, something must be said as a reply to this;
and whatever solution you have in this matter, that shall be ours as well."

This objection applies equally to both positions, since you too must necessarily accept one of the two alternatives— either with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*anākāra*)— otherwise, cognition that apprehends an object could not be established. Furthermore, there is no other mode apart from these two positions by which cognition would apprehend an object.
And when a fault applies to both parties, it is not proper for one side alone to be challenged;
therefore, whatever answer you have in this matter will also be ours.

For instance, in the case of the theory of mental aspects (sākārapakṣa), you must necessarily provide an answer such as: "The aspects are unreal," or "Because they are necessarily perceived together, they are non-different from a single cognition even though they appear distinct."

"That very [explanation] shall be ours as well; even in the case of the position that [cognition] is formless (*nirākāra*), it must be described that the nature of cognition, which causes the apprehension of specific objects, is produced solely by prior causes.

This response—that "this will also serve as an answer for us Buddhists who maintain the doctrine of formless consciousness (*nirākāra-vijñānavāda*)," and thus this solution is not subject to objection—is the rebuttal.

Having thus established the means of valid cognition that apprehends the relationship between cause and effect, [the author], while refuting the faults of the destruction of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done, says "the destruction of what has been done," and so forth:
"The destruction of what has been done would indeed occur if the cause did not produce the effect;
however, this is not accepted, because causality does not exist in a [static] continuum."
Furthermore, there would be the arrival of what was not produced, if an effect were ever to arise without its cause; this is not so, because of the necessity of causal power.

For if, from the perspective of ultimate reality, some agent or enjoyer were intended, then by accepting the doctrine of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgitva), there would follow the undesirable consequence of the loss of what has been done (kṛtanāśa) and so forth. However, since this entire world is merely a matter of conditioned causality (idaṃpratyayatāmātra), nothing whatsoever is created or enjoyed by any agent;
how then could the consequence of the loss of what has been done and so forth be leveled against us?

Now, it is argued that because the capacity to produce desired and undesired fruits—established by the volitions of prior wholesome actions and so forth—is lost, and because the fruit arises from a specific capacity not instilled by prior karma, there follows, respectively, the faults of the destruction of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
This is incorrect; for there is no contradiction whatsoever between the continuity of the capacity instilled by prior karma and the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

For instance, just as in the case of seeds sprinkled with the juice of lac and other substances, specific capacities (sāmarthya-viśeṣa) deposited by prior karma continue through the continuum (saṃtāna); from these, when they have reached maturation at a later time, a desirable or undesirable fruit arises.

Nor is it accepted that the production of a fruit occurs from a continuum that has not been infused with the impressions (saṃskāra) of prior karma; therefore, how could there be the fault of "the arrival of what was not done" (akṛtābhyāgama)?
Uddyotakara, however, says: "Because the mind is unstable, the infusion (vāsana) by karmas is not possible."

That is incorrect; for there can be no perfuming (*vāsanā*) of that which is stable and has not abandoned its prior nature. Rather, perfuming is simply the production of a distinct, qualified state in that which is unstable. Furthermore, when it is stated in the treatise that "the stable and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) are to be perfumed," this is said with reference to the stability of the continuum (*prabandha*).

For that continuum which is subject to annihilation lacks presence at the time when the fruit arises after a very long period; therefore, it cannot function as a cause. Consequently, it is illogical for such a continuum to serve as the substratum for the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that produces such a fruit—this is the intended meaning.
Thus, what has been stated by this author deserves to be disregarded, as it was said out of ignorance regarding the established doctrines of others.

Kumārila, however, says: "We do not assert the loss of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) or the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) due to the destruction of an action performed by some agent, for in your own view no such agent exists. Rather, since you admit the destruction of an action and the arising of its fruit without any continuity (*niranvaya*), it follows that *kṛtanāśa* and *akṛtābhyāgama* would result. To show that this is not a valid reductio (*aniṣṭāpādana*), because such a loss of what is done and acquisition of what is not done is actually desired [by us], he says: "By means of the conceptualization of momentary difference (*kṣaṇabhedavikalpena*), the objection regarding the destruction of moments and so forth is raised.
[This means: By means of the conceptualization of the distinction between moments, the objection concerning the destruction of moments and so forth is urged.
And furthermore, nothing undesirable whatsoever has been brought about by others.

Because the preceding moment of karma perishes without leaving a trace, there is the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*); and because a previously non-existent moment of the fruit arises, there is the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Thus, whatever objection is raised regarding the loss of what was done and so forth based on the conceptual distinction between moments is precisely what we accept. For we shall demonstrate that there is no persistence (*anvaya*) of even the slightest portion of any entity whatsoever.
Regarding what was said— that a discerning person would not act at all— he replies with the verse beginning "ahīnasattva":
"For those whose resolve and views are unimpaired, the conceptualization of momentary differences does not lead to action in any way, due to the conceit of a single continuum."
But those who have realized reality, having understood the necessity of causes that perish at every moment, undertake auspicious actions.
First, for those who have not yet abandoned the innate and acquired views of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, this conceptualization of momentary differentiation does not exist at all.
For they, having determined the continuum to be a unity, engage in actions with a sense of satisfaction, thinking, "We shall become happy.

Furthermore, even those virtuous ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-kalyāṇa*) who, through both reasoning and scripture, have correctly understood momentariness and selflessness and have thus awakened to reality, likewise realize the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*).

From acts such as giving, preceded by compassion and the like, there arise momentary mental formations (*saṃskāra*)—one after another in succession—that result in the welfare of oneself and others; however, this does not occur from acts such as violence. Therefore, having ascertained this specific determination of cause and effect, people engage in virtuous actions and the like.

As it has been said: "As long as the loss of love for oneself does not perish, one remains established in well-being without imposing suffering upon others; thus, effort is made to eliminate false imputations, even though there is no experiencer."
How the relationship of cause and effect and the means of valid cognition that apprehends it are established has already been demonstrated.
Regarding what was said— that recognition is difficult to establish among entities that are subject to momentary destruction—
the author replies with the words "of only some," and so forth:
"Only for certain mental states is there a specific capacity for being cause and effect."
Therefore, memory and the other [cognitions] are everywhere determined and uncontradicted.
Regarding the term "causal efficiency" (*kāryakāritā*): that which possesses an effect is "possessing-an-effect" (*kāryin*), meaning a cause.
The state of being between the effect and that which possesses the effect is "causal efficiency."
The meaning is that there is a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
For in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there exists neither one who remembers nor one who experiences;
therefore, it would follow that only he by whom something was experienced is the one who remembers it.

What, then, is the concise meaning? Memory and so forth arise only in that continuum where the seed of memory and so on has been deposited through the production of successively more distinguished moments by means of a powerful experience; they do not arise elsewhere, because the relationship between cause and effect is strictly determined.
As it has been said:
"The consequence of [memory] occurring in another [continuum], or of [another] experiencing [the result], does not constitute a refutation."
For memory arises regarding something that has been experienced by that [consciousness] which was not itself remembered.
Thus, since recognition and other such cognitions arise preceded by memory and so forth, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, it is not established anywhere that recognition and the like are based on a single cognizer, such that one could say, "But if there were duality [of cognizers], there would be no basis [for them]"; for it is accepted that in all cases there is only a relationship of cause and effect between distinct entities.

Regarding what was stated—that the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation is untenable because [the self] is bound by the shackles of passion and so forth—the author replies with the verse beginning "kāryakāraṇabhūtāś ca" and so on:
"In that context, ignorance and the rest are considered to exist as cause and effect;
bondage is held to be their presence, while liberation is the stainlessness of the intellect resulting from their disappearance."
For nowhere is bondage and liberation established for us as having a single person as their locus, since no one who is being bound and simultaneously being liberated is established.

Rather, the formative factors (saṃskāra) beginning with ignorance and ending with old age and death are conventionally designated as "bondage" because they are the causes for the arising of suffering.
Thus it has been said: "In this way, there occurs the origination of this entire mass of suffering."
And when those [factors] beginning with ignorance have ceased through the knowledge of reality, that purity of the intellect is called liberation (*nirmukti*).
As it has been said:
"The mind itself, when permeated by the afflictions such as passion and the like, is indeed *saṃsāra*."
That very same thing, when freed from those [defilements], is called the end of existence.
Thus.

Regarding what was stated, namely that "they have a single substratum" and so forth, [the author] says "Even in common worldly experience, these two— bondage and liberation— are not established as having a single substratum," and so on, demonstrating that even the example cited is devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikala). For everything is indeed established as momentary.

For it has been established that every entity indeed perishes immediately after its arising; therefore, since the coexistence of bondage and liberation within a single substratum is not established anywhere, the example is unestablished.

[185] Having thus established his own position, he refutes the opposing position with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*), and so forth: "Otherwise, because no excellence exists in any way, such an arrangement of agency, enjoyment, bondage, and so on, would be contradicted within its own nature."

For if some excellence were produced in the self by means of the afflictions such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, or by means of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, then there would be a systematic distinction of its bondage, liberation, and so on.

However, since no excellence can be imparted to it because of its eternity, this systematic distinction of bondage, liberation, and so forth—characterized by the fixed limits of cause and effect—is not possible for it, just as it is not possible for space (*ākāśa*); such is the intended meaning.
"Otherwise" [means]: [if it were otherwise].
If an excellence were produced in the self, then because that excellence would be identical with the self, the self itself—being non-different from it—would, like the excellence, be impermanent.
However, it is not logical for the excellence to be something other than the self, because no relationship could be established; this has been discussed at length a hundred times.
Thus concludes the examination of the relationship between action and its fruit.

Now, in order to establish that [the world] is empty of adventitious designations such as quality, substance, action, genus, and inherence, he introduces an examination of the six categories (ṣaṭpadārtha), saying "of genus, etc. and so forth;
it was previously demonstrated that it is illogical for genus and the rest to possess intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva).
The six categories, beginning with substance, which exist as ultimate realities;
Thus say the followers of Akṣapāda and Kaṇāda, who rely solely on scripture;
this refutation of substance and the other categories is now stated in brief.

In the previous examination of the permanence of entities, it was stated that "because birth and so forth lack intrinsic nature, momentary destruction is not at all accepted. By this, the fact that birth and so forth were previously shown to lack intrinsic nature is [alleged to be] incorrect. For the followers of Akṣapāda and others assert that the six categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—are ultimately real.
They are called *ākṣapādāḥ* because they are disciples of Akṣapāda; that is, the Naiyāyikas.

The disciples of Kaṇāda, however, are called Vaiśeṣikas or Kāṇādas. They are called "those who rely on scripture alone" (āgamamātrakas) because they possess only scripture, devoid of reasoning; thus they are "those who rely on scripture alone."
In this regard, beginning with the words "earth and so forth," he first states its classification for the purpose of refuting the category of substance (*dravya-padārtha*):
