Therefore, the inference of the mind is made through the successive production of cognitions by means of the genus of cognition.
And thus says the Sūtra: "The non-simultaneous production of cognitions is the mark (liṅga) of the mind.

The formal argument is as follows: this apprehension of form and so forth depends upon a cause distinct from the eye and other [senses], because it arises successively, like a chariot and such things.
He offers a rebuttal with the words beginning "upāttādibhiḥ":

"Since it is accepted that sound has as its cause the primary elements (mahābhūta) such as those that are appropriated (upātta), sounds are already established as being dependent upon them; therefore, the first [argument] is not a proof."
If it is being proved in a general sense that these sounds merely possess the quality of being dependent, then the reason is one whose probandum is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For it is accepted that sounds have as their cause the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), both those currently appropriated [by a living being] and those not so appropriated;
and since they are effects of those elements, they are indeed dependent upon them.
Because effects depend upon causes, they obtain their own existence (*ātmalābha*) by being bound to them.

"Appropriated" means taken possession of by the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). By the word "etcetera," the inclusion of those caused by non-appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is intended.
"In them" means in the appropriated and other primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
"Thus" means as follows.
"Therefore" means for this reason.

Regarding the phrase "the first," the sense is that what was stated in the passage beginning with "words are sometimes dependent on something" is not a valid proof, because it suffers from the fault of attempting to prove what is already established.

Now, if it is intended to prove that these [qualities] possess a specific kind of dependence by virtue of being inherent in a substance that is formless, eternal, unitary, and all-pervading, then—because there is no example endowed with the property to be proven—the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is what is shown in the verse beginning with "eka... and so forth:

"But the inherence in a sky that is unitary, all-pervasive, and eternal is established for these [qualities], because of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and because they [the qualities] are pervaded by such properties as non-succession."
"Of these" refers to the connection with the preceding word "is established.
He demonstrates that the thesis is contradicted by inference by stating, "likewise, because of the pervasion by non-succession and so forth."
The connection is as follows: it has been stated that the inherence of these [sounds] in space is not established.

For if these were inherent in the single, eternal substance of space, then—just like multiple sounds produced at once—even sounds belonging to other times would exist at the very time intended, because their cause would be unchanging and they would share a single substratum.
Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated that an eternal entity has no dependence on anything else.
Nor is it logical for that which provides no assistance to be an inherent cause (*samavāyin*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Thus, there follows the consequence of [the qualities] being non-successive;
by the word "etcetera," there is also the consequence of the faults of being perceived by all persons and so forth.

For the auditory organ is indeed of the nature of space, and space is one and the same; consequently, there would be hearing of all sounds reaching it. Indeed, because it is partless, such a restriction—that "this is my own auditory organ" and "this is another's"—is not logical.

It might be thought: "The auditory organ (*śrotra*) is that very portion of space delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), which has been conditioned by the person's own unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); for this reason alone, the perception of sound does not occur through other apertures such as the mouth or nose, and it is precisely due to an injury to that ear-cavity that deafness and so forth are established.
This is entirely untenable, because since space is partless (*niraṃśa*), such a division is impossible.
Furthermore, imagined divisions of parts cannot, by virtue of mere conceptual superimposition, bring about the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that is accomplished by the divisions of a real entity.
For water, when metaphorically designated as "fire," does not actually burn or consume.
Now, if it is thought that [the term] refers to a single part of space— [this is] said because conjunction is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti)—
this too has already been refuted.
Furthermore, objects such as a jar, the ear, and the auditory canal would also occupy the same location, because they are all in contact with the same single space (*vyoman*).

For by that very nature of space through which one object is conjoined, others too are conjoined; consequently, other jars and so forth would also exist in the very location intended for the first, since they are conjoined with the space whose nature is conjoined with that [first object], just like a jar situated in that same place.

For this very reason, even sounds would have to occupy the same location; consequently, the well-attested distinction between objects situated at distant or near locations—which is perceived in the case of certain things—would be contradicted. In this way, many such defects proliferate.

He demonstrates that even regarding the proofs for time and space, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established in a general sense, while in a specific sense, the logical reason lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the thesis is sublated by inference, by stating "viśiṣṭa" and so forth:
"The cognition of priority, posteriority, and so on, is based on mental attention (*manaskāra*) arising from a particular convention; it does not [arise] from time nor from space."
Because it possesses a single, partless nature, the occurrence of priority and posteriority is impossible.
If it is argued that this is due to the difference between the two related entities, then surely those two [entities] are themselves fruitless.

A "distinct convention" (*viśiṣṭasamaya*) is the designation of priority, posteriority, and so forth, applied specifically to objects that have arisen in a temporal sequence such as before and after; the mental impression (*manaskāra*) produced from that is the "mental application" (*ābhoga*), and since this [cognition] has that as its basis, it is described as such.

For this very reason, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), because this cognition is based on the convention regarding distinct entities. Thus, he shows that if one were to prove merely that [cognition] is caused, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); if one were to prove it with a specific qualification, it would be sublated by inference (*anumānabādhā*) and suffer from the fault of lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*), as previously stated. Furthermore, he demonstrates that the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of what is intended, by stating "partless," and so forth.
The phrase "of those two" refers to space and time.
It is intended to establish that the cognition of priority, posteriority, and so forth is based on a single, partless category of entities called space and time; however, this is not proven.
For instance, a thing becomes an object [of cognition] only by producing a cognition that conforms to its own form.

Furthermore, for that which is partless, a division such as priority and posteriority is not possible, by means of which there could arise a cognition of priority, posteriority, and so forth produced by that [division].
Therefore, because it proves the opposite of what is intended, the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*).
With the words "if [it is argued] due to the difference of related entities," the author anticipates the opponent's reply.

Now, if it is thought that external and internal entities—such as lamps, bodies, and so forth—which are related to space and time, possess priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*), and therefore this priority and posteriority belonging to their relata is attributed to those two, space and time, and thus there is no contradiction in the reason (*hetu*)—to this he replies: "In that case, surely those two would be fruitless.
For if they are conceived in this way, those two, space and time, would indeed be useless.
This is because the effect intended as the probandum has already been produced by those very same related factors.

For instance, time is accepted as the cause for the production of cognitions such as "prior" and "subsequent," as well as moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), twinklings (*nimeṣa*), units of time (*kāṣṭhā*), minutes (*kalā*), hours (*muhūrta*), days and nights, fortnights, and so forth.
Likewise, space is held to be the cause for the determination of directions such as "east" and "north."

Moreover, this entire distinction does not exist within those two [universals] themselves; yet it exists among the individuals. Thus, the conceptual construction of that [distinction] is utterly futile.

He shows that even when the mind is intended as the probandum, if it is established merely as a cause in general, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), by means of the verse beginning with "the eye, etc. [The verse reads: "But we also accept a mind distinct from the eye and so forth; for that which is the cognition immediately following the six [sensory cognitions] is the mind. [The commentary continues: We also accept a mind that is distinct from the eye and other [senses]. For that cognition which arises immediately after the six [sensory cognitions] is indeed the mind. Thus, since this is accepted by us as well, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established. Furthermore, if one were to argue that the mind is something distinct from the aggregate of the senses and their objects, that too would result in proving what is already established, because we also accept such a mind. Alternatively, if one argues that the mind is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) distinct from the external organs, that too is proving what is already established, because we also accept an internal organ consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Moreover, if one argues that the mind is the agent of the activity of thinking, that too is proving what is already established, because we also accept the intellect (*buddhi*) as the agent of the activity of thinking. Furthermore, if one argues that the mind is the substratum of the activity of thinking, that too is proving what is already established, because we also accept the intellect as the substratum of the activity of thinking. Thus, the reason is inconclusive. Finally, if one argues that the mind is the instrument of the activity of thinking, that too is proving what is already established, because we also accept the intellect as the instrument of the activity of thinking. Therefore, the reason is inconclusive. Consequently, the reason is not established. Therefore, the reason is inconclusive. Consequently, the reason is not established. Furthermore,
But if the mind were eternal, cognitions would occur simultaneously;
therefore, the reason stated here results in the subversion of your own desired position.

Specifically, regarding the proof of a single eternal mind, [the author] demonstrates the lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), the subversion of the proposition by inference, and the contradictory nature of the reason (*hetu*) in the passage beginning with "But if it were eternal" (*nitye tu*).

The phrase "it would destroy what is desired" (*iṣṭavidhātakṛt*) means that because one is proving dependence on impermanent causes distinct from the eyes and so forth, otherwise— if there were an eternal cause— the successive arising of cognitions would be contradicted, since the cause would be complete and unimpaired.

And confirming that very same contradiction in the reason by way of mockery, he says "saugata" and so forth: "For the sake of establishing or disproving the mind as designated by the other Sugatas... [p.210]
I consider this sutra to have been composed with a specific intention and in a different manner.

I consider this very point to be the meaning of the sūtra, "The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind," intended for the sake of establishing or disproving the mind as desired by both the Buddhists and the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
The collective sense is that, in one view, the negative particle *a-* is elided.
As for the analysis of the individual parts: it is a compound (*vigraha*) consisting of those [Buddhists] and the other outsiders, and the two minds indicated by them.
For those two, there are respectively accomplishment (*saṃsiddhi*) and non-accomplishment (*asiddhi*), or non-accomplishment accompanied by accomplishment; for that purpose, with that as the cause.
But how can a single sūtra convey two contradictory meanings? To this he says: "with form" (*sākāra*), and so forth. It exists together with a companion (*sahakāreṇa*).
The instruction "aliṅgam" (without a mark) is a reading with the vowel *ā* elided (*praśliṣṭākāra*) for the purpose of proving that the mind of another is not established [as a separate substance].
For the sake of establishing the mind of the Sugatas, it is otherwise; the meaning is that it is "anakāram" (without the letter *a*).
To the question of how both having a form (*sākāratva*) and being without the letter *a* (*anakāratva*) can be established for one and the same thing, he says: "āvṛttam" (repeated).
In that case, it follows that repetition is the proper course.
Thus concludes the examination of substance as a category.
He states the negation of qualities and so forth with the words "of substances," etc.:
"By the negation of substances, all those things dependent upon them—qualities, actions, and the rest—are indeed discarded; such is the intended view."
Qualities, actions, and so forth, up to the particularities (*viśeṣa*), are already discarded by the very refutation of substances, because these [categories] are dependent upon them;
for in the absence of a substratum, it is impossible for dependents to exist, as they lack independent status.
Thus it is held.
Likewise, they are held to be dependent on substance either directly or through a succession.
For instance, quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*) are intended to be dependent on substance directly;
and thus the Sūtra provides the definition of quality: "That which resides in substance, is devoid of qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent."
"The definition of action (karman) is: 'that which resides in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is an independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions.
The term "residing in a single substance" means that it is dependent upon a single substance.
As for qualities (guṇas), some exist in multiple substances, such as conjunction, disjunction, and so forth.
Furthermore, some universals and particulars reside only in substances, such as "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*) and the like;

while "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), "action-ness" (*karmatva*), and so forth, reside in the categories of quality and action which are connected to substances; and the great universal called "Being" (*sattā*) resides in the three categories beginning with substance.
Therefore, when substance is refuted, qualities and the rest are also refuted without any further effort.
It is thus shown that the fruit of the examination of the remaining categories is completed within the examination of substance itself.
If it is argued that the refutation of inherence (samavāya) must therefore be undertaken separately, he replies with the words "Where, of what," and so forth:
"And where, when the related entities have been discarded, could there be inherence of one thing in another? [p.211]
This is a specific negation; nevertheless, it is stated once again.
For inherence is described as having the nature of subsisting in the five categories.

Since the fivefold types of related entities, such as substance and the rest, have been refuted, where could there be inherence of what? The meaning is that it would be of nothing anywhere, because all bases and dependents have been negated. Among these, the specific negation of qualities is now stated.

"In this regard, the qualities (guṇas) are color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognitions, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort"—this is the aphorism.
By the word "and" (ca), heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, mental impressions (saṃskāra), merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), and sound are also included.
Among these, color is perceptible by the eye and resides in earth, water, and fire.
Taste is that which is perceivable by the gustatory faculty; it functions in earth and water. Odor is that which is perceivable by the olfactory faculty; it functions in earth.
Touch is that which is perceivable by the tactile faculty; it functions in earth, water, fire, and air.
He states the negation of these first four— form and so forth— in the verse beginning with "In a large substance" (*dravye mahati*).
"If it is maintained that blue and so forth are a single [entity] in a large substance,
then when that [substance] is manifested by light through an aperture, why is there no manifestation or perception of this [color]?"

For [the qualities] inherent in a large substance possess the conditions for perception; therefore, he says "large. Now, if it is maintained that in that substance there is only one partless [quality], such as blue and so forth, of four kinds, then even when a subtle light from a lamp or similar source passing through a crack in a keyhole illuminates the color blue and so forth inherent in a larger substance like a jar situated in a room, it would follow that there is illumination and perception of the entire color and other qualities residing in the whole substance, because it is partless.
For there are no parts in a single [entity] by which there could be a manifestation in one part;
the phrase "by means of light through a hole" is an illustration.
[This is shown by] the manifestation of fragrance by water in one region of the earth, and the perception of its manifestation in another region as well.
It would follow that,
upon touching or tasting a single part of a flame or a mango fruit, there would be a perception of the entire extent of the touch or taste inherent in that substance.
It might be argued that for you [the opponent], there is indeed the manifestation of the apprehension of the entire blue object and so forth; to this he says "na ca" and so on:
"Nor is it accepted that the blue object and so forth exist as spatially divided;
since it is manifested by that [apprehension] at that time, it follows that it is therefore composed of atoms."
"At that time" means at that moment. "By that" means by the light entering through the aperture.
"Of that" refers to the blue object and so forth.

If their own division into atoms is admitted, then—just like the substance of the atoms of earth and so forth—they would possess the nature of a substance (*dravya*) because they are endowed with atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*), and thus would not be qualities (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, for such things that are divided atomically, applying the designation "quality" results in a mere dispute over names.
Nor is it logical that they should be qualities simply because they are dependent (*āśrita*), even though they possess atomicity.
Because a substratum for both the existent and the non-existent is untenable, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For in that case, since a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) rests upon its constituent parts (*avayavadravya*), the latter too would consequently become a quality (*guṇa*); such is the sense.

In that regard, number—characterized by oneness and so forth—is the cause for certain linguistic usages. Furthermore, it resides in either a single substance or multiple substances. Among these, the number one resides in a single substance; however, numbers such as duality and the rest reside in multiple substances.
In this context, the eternality and production of the number residing in a single substance should be understood to be like those of color and other qualities belonging to water-atoms and the like.

However, for that which consists of multiple substances, its production arises from unities accompanied by a cognition of multiple objects; its destruction occurs through the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), and in some cases, through the destruction of its substratum.
This twofold number is indeed established through perception alone;
yet the opponent maintains that it is also established through inference, because specific cognitions depend upon other causes.

Regarding this, he states its refutation with the words "atadrūpa" and so forth: "Number, which is distinct from elephants and the like excluded from what is not that [number], does not appear in cognition; since it is not perceived, it is not accepted as existing. Thus, it does not exist.

For in those elephants and so forth, upon which the designations "collection" and the like have been applied, no number is perceived apart from them that meets the criteria for its existence; thus, it is an object of the conventional usage of non-existence, like the horn of a hare.
This is because it is intended to be perceptible.
And so says the Sūtra: "Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and action are visible because they inhere in things possessing color."

Furthermore, showing that number is not established by means of a cognition of specific difference, he says: "But this cognition of 'one' and so forth regarding jars follows from mental attention to conventions fashioned by desire, just as it occurs in the case of cognitions and the like."
Because they lack substantial reality, there is no differentiating number among them;
therefore, it is not logical that cognition of them should be figurative, since it is unerring.

For just as in cases such as "one cognition" or "two cognitions," the cognition of "one" and so forth occurs even without a [real] number, so too in the case of objects like jars and the like when they are unaccompanied, the cognition of "one" and so forth will arise following upon the mental attention (manaskāra) or application (ābhoga) toward whatever convention (saṅketa) has been established by one's own will. Therefore, this [argument] is inconclusive (anaikāntika). For there is no number in those things such as cognitions, because they are not substances (adravyatva);
and since number is a quality (guṇa), it must reside in a substance.

Now, if it is thought that this cognition regarding them is figurative—that there is a single similarity here, such as being "without a companion," and thus it is called "that cognition"—this is not at all appropriate, for this cognition is not metaphorical because its application is unerring (*askhalad-gati*).

For instance, while the cognition "the Vāhīka is an ox" is erroneous—since he is like an ox but not actually an ox due to the absence of a dewlap and so forth—this cognition is not erroneous; it is as if it were one, such as a single cognition, yet it is not literally one.
Rather, just as the cognition regarding jars and the like is unshakable, such is the cognition regarding knowledge and the like as well.
It might be argued: "This cognition is not described as being dependent upon similarity;

rather, because the substance which serves as their substratum possesses oneness and so forth, and because of the inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), this cognition of 'one' and so forth arises with respect to these qualities, actions, and inherence. Anticipating this objection, he says: "If it is postulated from the oneness inherent in that substance," and so forth. *If it is postulated from the oneness inherent in that substance,* [then...]
There is a single cognition regarding qualities and so forth, because of their inherence in a single object.
To this, he states the following reply, beginning with "Let it be so" (*astu nāma*):

"Let it be so that there is a cognition of pervasion in a single [instance]; however, what need does the cognition of pervasion have for these [other factors], such as a logical reason (*hetu*) or the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*)?"
This cognition is secondary (gauṇa), arising from such relations as inherence in a single object;
and thus it is erroneous, because it occurs with respect to a boy [while perceiving fire], just like the cognition of fire [when mistaking a boy for one].

If this cognition [of number] arises from a unity (ekatva) and so forth inherent in that substance, then let it be granted that there is the cognition "one, one" regarding a single cognition or pleasure and so forth, as these are inherent in a single self-substance.
But what is the cause for the cognitions "two cognitions," "three," "four," and so on? For in those cases, duality and the like do not exist within a single self.

And as for what is said—namely, "the six categories; pleasure and pain; desire and aversion; fivefold action; generality is twofold, higher and lower; existence is one; inherence is one"—what is the cause for that?
For in that case, there is no number inherent in a single object; therefore, this conceptualization is also untenable because it lacks pervasion (*avyāpin*).

Furthermore, whether you state as the reason "inherence in a single object" or some other cause imagined by your own intellect, even so, this cognition arising from such inherence in a single object would have to be figurative (*gauṇa*), because of the absence of any other distinct entity.

Consequently, however, there would be a lapse [of the cognition], just as there is no cognition of fire in a boy because the ground for its application (pravṛttinimitta) is absent; yet this is not the case, and therefore the previously mentioned fault remains unremoved.

He raises an objection regarding the authority for establishing number as stated by Aviddhakarṇa, beginning with "gajādityādi": "And because it is distinct from cognitions such as 'elephant' [and so on], the cognition of number is proven to arise from something other than those, like the cognition of blue cloth and the like."

For he says: "The cognition of number has a basis distinct from elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, because it is different in character from the cognitions of elephants and the like, just like the cognition of a blue cloth.

Regarding the phrase *tadanyotthā* (arising from something other than that): the analysis of the compound is *tasmād gajaturagasyandanāder anyaḥ tadanyaḥ*, meaning "other than those [elephants, horses, and chariots]," and *tata utthānam yasyāḥ* means "that from which its arising occurs."

He replies with the verse beginning "icchā" (desire): "Through means such as the mental attention to conventions established by desire, there is the accomplishment of what is intended in that regard; or else, [the property of] number would exist in cognition and so forth by this very same [reasoning]."

Since internal factors such as the mental attention (*manaskāra*) toward a convention, which are distinct from the elephant and so forth, are accepted as the cause, the argument merely proves what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the recollection of the convention and other such factors are included.

Now, if it is intended to prove that [the cognition] is based on an object distinct from the application of the convention and so forth, then there is the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*); this he demonstrates under the guise of raising an objection: "In the case of cognition and so forth, it would be by means of this very number."

By this very [reasoning], namely "because of being distinct from that cognition," even in cases such as "one cognition," "two cognitions," or "five actions," number would follow—that is, it would obtain.

Yet, in those instances as well, because the single cognition and so forth are distinct from that [corresponding] cognition, [number] does not occur; therefore, the sense is that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, regarding that number— duality and so forth— which resides in multiple substances and whose production from unities accompanied by a non-unitary cognition is described by you, he shows that this is without foundation in the verse beginning with "And dependent on cognition" (*buddhyapekṣā ca*).
If the production of number is described as being dependent on cognition,
why is it not accepted that the cognition of that [number] arises merely through the mental engagement (*ābhoga*) with the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*)?

The inclusion of the term "measure" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding the cognitions of unity, duality, and so forth, as well as the cognitions of their universals and the relations between them.
Regarding the phrase "the cognition of that":
is the cognition such as "two," "three," or "four" with respect to the objects to be numbered not accepted [as a number], being merely a conventional usage? No, it is not.
For in this way, the causality of that whose capacity is unperceived would not be postulated; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress of causes.

Thus, since [the effect] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance residing in that [mental cognition] when the mental cognition exists, it is that very [cognition] which is rightly to be postulated as the cause.
Otherwise, one might as well have to postulate that a deity causes purging upon reaching a myrobalan fruit (*harītakī*).

Furthermore, dualities and so forth—which are intended to meet the criteria for perception—are neither observed nor logically consistent apart from the categories excluded by [the concept of] conjunction and the like; this is because the occurrence of a single entity in multiple locations has been refuted, and because universals and inherence will also be rejected later. This is the underlying sense.
With the words beginning with "not" (na hi), he states the negation of dimension: "That which is called dimension through the distinctions of 'large,' 'long,' and so forth—
is that not also considered to be non-existent in the object, precisely because of the same [reasoning] as in the case of color-form?"
Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the cause for the conventional usage of measurement; it is fourfold: large (*mahat*), small (*aṇu*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*).
Among these, the large is of two kinds: eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*).
The eternal [large dimension] is the state of supreme largeness (*paramamahattva*) existing in space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), and the self (*ātman*).
Impermanence resides in substances such as triads (tryaṇuka) and so forth.
Furthermore, it is of two kinds: permanent and impermanent.
The permanent is characterized by the extreme spherical form of atoms (paramāṇu) and the mind (manas).
The non-eternal [dimension] exists only in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
Even in large objects such as the *kuvala*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits, this conventional usage is figurative, in consideration of the absence of the excellence [of that dimension].
For the magnitude found in an *āmalaka* fruit is not the same as that found in a *kuvala*.
The same should be applied elsewhere as well.

Here, what is the distinction between the largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) existing in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, and the minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) existing in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*)?
It is said: in that case, there is a mutual distinction between largeness and length.
"Let the long be brought among the large, and let the large be brought among the long"—from such observations of differences in usage [it follows that these are distinct].
However, the distinction between minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) is perceptible only to yogins who perceive them; this is the system of the opponents.

Furthermore, the opponents maintain that "this [quality] such as largeness (*mahat*) is established as a different entity from color (*rūpa*) and so forth, because it is apprehended by a cognition distinct from the cognition of those [colors], just like pleasure (*sukha*) and the like."

In this regard, if the intended meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is apprehended by a perceptual cognition that is distinct from the cognitions of the sense organs regarding objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth," then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For apart from the entities such as form existing in their respective states, no dimension (*parimāṇa*) such as "large" (*mahat*) or the like is observed appearing in sensory cognition.

Alternatively, if what is intended is that conceptual cognition (*vikalpikā buddhi*) which takes the form "minute" (*aṇu*), "large" (*mahat*), and so on, is a cognition distinct from that [sensory] cognition; [then the following applies].
Even so, the reason remains inconclusive because there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
For this [cognition], in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is not even the slightest thing to be grasped, since it is accompanied by verbal expression (*sābhijalpatvāt*).

Rather, when those things such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are seen occurring in a single direction and so on, the cognition arises—determined as "large" and so forth—in accordance with conventional designations (*samaya*) made for the purpose of demonstrating their difference from other forms and so forth that possess different characteristics. Therefore, the existence of a separate entity is not established from this.
For this very reason, there is no object of cognition to be apprehended as distinct from color and so forth; thus, the logical reason (hetu) is also unestablished (asiddha).

Furthermore, the thesis is contradicted by direct perception (pratyakṣabādhā), because the "large" and so forth—which are intended to be perceived—are not observed apart from their nature as color and so forth.

Therefore, why is that dimension (parimāṇa) not accepted as being identical with the object, such as color, when it occurs in a single direction and so forth, based on its distinction from the object as it appears otherwise?
For by the word "eva" (only/just), he shows that no assumption of unobserved and irrational entities has been made.
Thus, when many visible or tangible forms and so forth are perceived as proceeding in a single direction, people employ the convention "long";
and in relation to that, when fewer [forms] arise, they employ the convention "short."
The same should be applied to the "Great One" (mahat) and the other principles as well.
Just as there was the negation of form and so forth, the negation of the Great One and the rest should be stated by means of the two alternatives of being one or many.
Furthermore, demonstrating that the inconclusiveness [of the reason] is even more evident because its presence is observed even in the absence of the probandum, he says "dīrghā" and so forth:
"Just as a long garland of palaces is perceived as large,
yet no dimension corresponding to that [perceived] form is actually postulated there."
If it is designated in that way by virtue of inherence in a single object,
then neither magnitude nor length exists as intended within the substratum itself.

For instance, even in the absence of "largeness" (*mahattva*) and so forth as imagined by you, the arising of cognitions such as "large" with respect to things like rows of palaces is actually experienced.
Nor can it be argued as follows:

"In those very palaces and so forth where the quality called 'row' (*mālā*) inheres, largeness and the like also inhere; and by virtue of their inhering in the same object (*ekārthasamavāya*), that row and so forth is designated as 'large' and so on."
Showing that this too is contrary to one's own tenets, he says "not greatness," and so forth. "In the abodes" means in the palaces. "Intended" [means...]
The measurement consists of half a krośa, one krośa, and so forth.
He asks, "Why does it not exist? and replies: "Because a palace is intended [as the referent].
A palace is intended as a conjunction (*yoga*) of qualities (*guṇa*), and that [conjunction] possesses immeasurable [parts].
It has no further series (*mālā*), nor is it the basis for metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

For instance, you maintain that a palace (*prāsāda*) is a quality (*guṇa*) consisting of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and not a composite substance (*avayavidravya*), because it does not originate from substances of different classes (*vijātīyadravya*).
Furthermore, that quality cannot possess dimension (*parimāṇa*), according to the established tenet (*samaya*) that "qualities are devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇā guṇāḥ*).
Consequently, since qualities such as palaces lack another quality called a "row" (*mālā*), the very expression "a row of palaces" (*prāsādamālā*) would be impossible.
How could there be such things as "large" or "small," and so forth?
For a garland (*mālā*) is intended to have the nature of a number (*saṃkhyā*), and since number is a quality (*guṇa*), it must reside in a substance (*dravya*) and not in a quality.

Even if a garland is considered to have the nature of a whole (*avayavin*), even then a substance can only have another substance as its substratum, not a quality; therefore, it is not logical for a garland to have palaces as its substratum.
Now, if it is accepted that the universal (jāti) is the nature of the garland,
even so, because the universal is entirely present in each individual substratum, even a single palace would be called a "garland," just like a "tree.
As it has been said:
"Even if a house is a conjunction, how could a collection of them be that [conjunction]? If it were a genus (*jāti*), then even a single house would be called a 'garland,' just like a tree."
Thus,

the impossibility of designations such as "one," "long," or "great" remains exactly the same in the case of a garland and its substratum, such as a palace, because the qualities of oneness and so forth do not exist there;
furthermore, in the case of pieces of wood and the like, the intended length and other such qualities are simply non-existent.
Furthermore, in the case of many rows of palaces, there would be no recurring designation such as "a row, a row," because a genus (jāti) cannot itself possess a genus.
As it has been said: "If there is a plurality of rows, how can that word [be applied] since a genus cannot have a genus?"
Therefore, the meaning is that it is not logical for there to be a basis or a substratum for this metaphorical designation;
nor is this cognition of "largeness" and so forth with respect to garlands and the like one whose application falters.
Consequently, it is not tenable as being merely figurative.
For a figurative [usage] is not tenable if it is indistinguishable from the primary [usage], because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
As it has been said: "In the case of a garland and the like, greatness and so forth are desired as both primary and figurative."
Because it is apprehended by a cognition that is primary and undifferentiated, it is not figurative.
Thus [it is said].

In this regard, the opponent’s intention is as follows: that by virtue of which even a conjoined substance is separated out—namely, the cause of such separation called *pṛthaktva* (separateness)—is a distinct entity from things like a jar, because it is apprehended by a cognition distinct from the cognition [of those things], just as in the previous case.
Having kept in mind that here too, as with the case of dimension (*parimāṇa*), the reason is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says:
"But the conventional usage of separation (*apoddhāra-vyavahṛti*) which is postulated as separateness (*pṛthaktva*)... and so forth.
For that reason, why is it not considered to be established upon a distinct nature?

For even here, no other distinct entity called "separateness" (pṛthaktva) appears in perceptual cognition apart from form and the rest; thus, its being graspable by a cognition distinct from the cognition of those [objects] is not established. For this very reason, since it is not perceived despite being intended to have reached the conditions for perception, it is simply non-existent. Nor is its establishment possible on the basis of a conceptual cognition such as "it is separate."

For those very entities, such as color and so forth, by virtue of their abiding in their own intrinsic nature, are perceived as having an essence that is excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes; thus, they will serve as the basis for the conventional usage of "distinct. Therefore, no separate entity [such as "separateness"] is established. Consequently, regarding this conventional practice of abstraction (*apoddhāra*) which is described as being caused by "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), why is it not accepted as residing in the distinct natures of things belonging to the same or different classes?
The sense is that it is logical that it resides precisely in those [natures].
By this, the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) of the reason is demonstrated.
Those whose self-nature (svabhāva), or essence, is distinct are described as such.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has its culmination (niṣṭhā), or completion, in those entities (bhāva)."
Showing that the presence of the reason (hetu) might even be observed in the counter-example of the probandum (sādhyavipakṣa), he says: "For [things] mutually distinct," and so forth.
"For just as cognition, pleasure, and the like are mutually distinct and are expressed separately, so too are others [distinct] without any other [common factor] being their constituent part."
For there is no quality of separateness (*pṛthaktva*) among qualities such as pleasure and the like, because qualities themselves are devoid of qualities;
nevertheless, they must be called "distinct" by virtue of having mutually exclusive natures,
and they serve as the basis for that linguistic usage of abstraction (*apoddhāra*).

Likewise, other things such as jars and the like, which are considered substances, will exist even without a quality called "separateness" (pṛthaktva) distinct from themselves. Nor can this cognition regarding them be considered figurative, because it is no different from a primary (non-figurative) cognition; such is the meaning.

Alternatively, by demonstrating that the practice of analytical abstraction (apoddhāra-vyavahṛti) is based on entities that possess distinct natures, he states the sublation of the proposition by inference with the words beginning "paraspara... and so forth.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things whose natures are mutually exclusive do not serve as the substrata for a distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) separate from themselves, just like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth.
And jars and other such things have mutually exclusive natures; this is thus a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

The impossibility of a single [entity] residing in many, and the impossibility of a relation because inherence (*samavāya*) will be refuted, as well as the undesirable consequence that the conventional usage of that [inherence] would be absent in the case of pleasure and so forth, constitute the subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
In that regard, for the purpose of refuting conjunction and disjunction, he says "yau" and so forth:
"And those two, conjunction and disjunction, which are held by others to be restricted to substances..."
The two causes postulated for cognitions such as those of conjunction are, for their part, purposeless.

The system of others [the Vaiśeṣikas] is as follows: conjunction and disjunction are, respectively, the causes of the notions of "conjoined" and "disjoined" regarding substances; they consist in the attainment and non-attainment of what was previously unattained; they are produced by the action of either one or both [of the two things involved]; and they are produced by [prior] conjunction and disjunction. However, this is merely a theoretical construction. There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever that establishes the real existence of these two; therefore, these two are fruitlessly imagined by others.

The formal argument is as follows: That for which there exists no valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) establishing it is not an object of the practical activity of the discerning, just like the son of a barren woman and so forth; and for the opponents, there is no valid means of cognition establishing conjunction and disjunction. This is [an inference] based on the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi).
By means of the passage beginning with "seeds, water, earth," etc., he raises the objection that the reason [adduced] for demonstrating the view of Udyotakara is unestablished (asiddha):

"Seeds, water, earth, and so forth would necessarily follow as being productive of effects at all times, because they lack any distinction; however, this is not the case due to the impossibility of their conjunction."
It is understood that the field, seed, water, and so forth are dependent [on other factors],
because they constantly produce their own effects, like a staff, a wheel, water, and so on.
That entity which is depended upon by them will be conjunction;
and because it possesses qualifiers, it is understood to be indeed distinct [from its constituents].
When it is said, "Bring the conjoined," one looks for that conjunction between two things;
indeed, setting aside everything else, one brings those two alone.

For he [the opponent] says: if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) were not a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), then the field, the seed, and so forth, being indistinguishable [from their previous states], would always produce sprouts and the like; yet this is not the case. Therefore, because they do not initiate the effect at all times, the field and other factors depend upon another factor for the production of the effect, such as the sprout; just as the lump of clay, the staff, water, thread, and so forth, depend upon the potter and others for the making of a jar. That which is thus depended upon is established as conjunction.

Furthermore, that conjunction which exists between two substances is established by direct perception itself as being a distinct entity from them, because it is perceived as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).
For instance, when someone is told by another, "Bring those two substances that are conjoined," he brings only those two substances in which he perceives the conjunction;
he does not bring just any substance at random. Otherwise, he might bring anything whatsoever.
And all of this should also be applied to the proof of distinction through the opposite [of the previous arguments].
By what is this distinction in cognition established— that "this object is continuous" and "this is discontinuous"— if both of these [objects] exist here?

Furthermore, even when there is no difference in the object itself, how could the distinction in cognition—namely, "this object is contiguous" and "this object is separated"—be logically possible if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) were not here distinct entities (*arthāntara*) within the object? For a specific cognition cannot possibly arise without a specific quality in the object, as that would entail the absurd consequence of such a cognition occurring at all times and in all places.
This cognition which perceives continuity despite there being intervals,
and that other cognition which perceives continuity even where there is no interval— this twofold cognition is erroneous.
And every false cognition conforms to the primary object;
therefore, that primary object must be stated here, for when it is stated, those two [the cognition and its object] are established.

Furthermore, this cognition which arises for a person situated at a distance as one that perceives trees such as the *dhava* and *khadira*—though they are located very far away—as being without any intervening space; and this other cognition which arises regarding a flight of cranes perched on the top of a tree, though they are actually contiguous, as if there were an interval between them—both of these types of cognition are false, because they function toward an object that is not of that nature. Moreover, a false cognition never arises anywhere without the prior experience of a primary (real) object.
For one who has not previously experienced the sight of a cow, the delusion "this is a cow" does not arise from seeing the object that is a gavaya.
Therefore, some primary referent must necessarily be stated as the basis for this delusive cognition.
And when that [basis] is stated, conjunction and disjunction are established.
For apart from that, no other basis for this cognition can be established.
If this cognition "this is a earring" arises, what is its cause? It does not arise from the nature of the man and the earring, because that would entail [the cognition] occurring at all times.
The negation of a thing observed in one place is appropriate in another;
since conjunction is indeed observed, how can it be denied?
Therefore, Caitra who is "without earrings" exists as a real entity;
for it is precisely because of him that the application of negation and affirmation proceeds through such distinctions.
Furthermore, regarding the cognition "Devadatta is wearing earrings," one must state upon what basis this cognition arises.
It cannot be produced by the mere existence of the person and the earrings,
for if it were, it would follow that such a cognition would always exist whenever Devadatta and his earrings are present.
Furthermore, it is observed that worldly linguistic usage proceeds by means of affirmation and negation only with respect to that whose existence has been perceived somewhere by someone;
if conjunction were never perceived by you, how could there be such a differentiated linguistic usage as "Caitra is without earrings" or "he is with earrings"?

For instance, in this case, by the statement "Caitra is not wearing earrings," it is not the earring that is being negated, because its existence at a different time and place cannot be negated, as its form is established through superimposition (*adhyāsita*). Nor is it Caitra who is negated, for he shares the same logical status (*tulyayogakṣema*) as the earring. Therefore, what is negated is the conjunction of Caitra with the earring. Similarly, by the affirmative sentence "Caitra is wearing earrings" (*caitraḥ kuṇḍalī*), neither Caitra nor the earring is being enjoined, since both are already established.
By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is understood that the injunction refers solely to the conjunction, which was previously unperceived.

Therefore, conjunction and the like must indeed exist as real entities, on account of which the distinctions such as "this person is not a coiled one" and so forth are perceived as being strictly differentiated.
By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the previously mentioned [categories] such as "being taken up as a qualifier" are included.
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said":
It is said that water and the other elements are not non-distinct by virtue of their momentariness;
even though they exist, they depend upon another state, such as the absence of obstruction.

As for what was stated—that because there is no distinction, seeds and so forth would always produce their effect—that lack of distinction in seeds and so forth is unestablished (*asiddha*), because all things, being subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitā*), are productive only when they exist in a specific state. Furthermore, regarding what was said about "the field, seed, and so forth," he shows that even there, if one intends to prove merely a general dependence, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). He says, "Even though [they] exist," and so on: we ourselves indeed accept that seeds and so forth, while existing, are capable of accomplishing effects such as sprouts only by depending on other states such as the absence of obstruction; thus, it is a case of proving the already established.
In this context, "where there are no intervening factors and so forth" refers to that particular location or specific state in another place;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), obstructing conditions, resistance, and the like are included.

The meaning is that in that other state, there exists no intervention, no remaining at a great distance, no obstruction by a contrary factor, or any such thing that would hinder the production of the effect.
Furthermore, since a state is not distinct from its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva), the existence of conjunction as a separate entity is not established.

Now, if it is intended to prove dependence upon another category called "conjunction" as you define it, then the reason lacks positive concomitance (anvaya) with such a property; thus, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika), and the example is deficient in the probandum (sādhyavikala). This is the sense.

It might be argued: "How is this understood—that earth and other factors are causes for the production of effects such as sprouts by depending on a specific difference in their own state, and not rather by depending on a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), such that you would fall into the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) when you seek to prove mere dependence through a general property? Anticipating this objection, he says: "If water and the rest were dependent merely upon conjunction," and so forth: "If water and the rest were dependent merely upon conjunction, then the effect would either arise immediately after the conjunction, or it would arise even without it."

For if they were dependent solely upon conjunction, then the effect, such as a sprout, would necessarily arise from the earth and other factors at the very first moment of their encounter, because the causes would subsequently remain no different.

Alternatively, if it does not arise at the first encounter, there would be the consequence that it never arises later either, since the state of the causes being incomplete— just as in the prior non-productive stage— remains indistinguishable.
Furthermore, it is not logical for earth and the other elements to depend upon conjunction, which provides them no assistance, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Nor is it reasonable that conjunctions should be occasional, since their causes—earth and the other elements—are eternally present.
If it is argued that even in the production of that conjunction, earth and the others are held to depend upon action (*karman*) and so forth;
No;
for even in that case, the same objection applies.
For instance, when one objects, "Why does that action not produce [the result]?", what could possibly be said in reply?

If it is argued that [the effect does not arise] because of the absence of an impelling cause for it, then the question "Why is there an absence of that [impelling cause]? applies equally everywhere if one accepts eternal causes.

However, for one for whom every entity is indeed impermanent, the consequence of all things arising simultaneously does not occur, because the succession of causes is beginningless and subsequent effects are dependent upon their respective preceding causes.

And because all of them are simultaneously absent due to the deficiency of their causes, it follows that in your own view, earth and the other factors would always be the cause for the production of effects such as sprouts; therefore, it is established that earth and the others do not depend on conjunction as a distinct entity.
Regarding what was stated, "And because of the state of having qualifiers," and so forth, he replies with "The state of reaching," and so on:
"For when two objects are produced in immediate succession,
this [cognition] perceives and grasps them as being of such a kind."

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), as a distinct entity separate from the conjoined objects, does not enter the range of perception for the cognizer, such that one would take up a substance distinguished by its observation.

Rather, it is those two things which previously existed in a state of being separated by an interval, and which subsequently arise in a state of being without interval, that are denoted by the word "conjoined"; for this is established because the term "conjunction" refers to a specific state (*avasthāviśeṣa*).

Therefore, when one perceives such objects as having become the referents of the word "conjunction," one brings only those and no others; for a discerning person does not act upon the basis of a word regarding an object that has not been made known by that word.

Regarding what was stated as "without interval" and so forth, he says in response: "Separated or otherwise arisen, it becomes a cause," as in the case of cognitions with intervals or without intervals, like a house, the Vindhya mountains, and the Himalayas.

The collective meaning is this: it is precisely another distinct entity arising in such a manner that serves as the basis for the differentiation of cognition; therefore, this [object] is not a single [unitary] thing.
In that context, the connection is as follows: that object which has arisen as discrete becomes the cause for the cognition of having intervals [between objects].
"Otherwise" means...
The connection is that "whatever has arisen is uninterrupted. "Like a house, the Vindhya, and the Himalaya" refers to the respective examples for these two cases.

For even according to the opponent’s own view, there is no further conjunction that serves as the basis for the cognition of "immediacy" between two houses that have arisen without interval and are themselves of the nature of conjunction. Nor is there, for those same two houses that have arisen with an interval, a disjunction that is the cause of the cognition of "separation," because it has already been stated that qualities are devoid of further qualities;

indeed, there is no disjunction between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains that could be the cause of a cognition of separation, according to the established rule that disjunction is non-attainment preceded by attainment.
Regarding what was said—that "this cognition which occurs with an interval," and so forth—he replies with the verse beginning "false" (mithyā):
"Not every false cognition follows the primary object;
some [cognitions] do so even without regard for similarity, due to an internal derangement."
Just as the cognition of two moons and so forth occurs for one whose mind is directed elsewhere,
or as that which arises from an uninterrupted [stream] exists here as the primary cause (pradhāna).

It is unproven that all false cognition arises from the apprehension of similarity (*sādharmya*), for we observe that some [false cognitions] arise even without depending on similarity, solely through a defect of the sense organ (*indriyavaiguṇya*). For example,

even for one whose mind is occupied with a conceptualization of something else, there arises a cognition permeated by the form of two moons— clearly manifest and untouched by the stain of conceptual construction— due to a defect of the sense organ produced by cataracts (*timira*), triggered merely by the non-apprehension of the single moon standing before them.
By the phrase "of one whose mind has gone elsewhere," he demonstrates that the cognition of two moons is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
For there is no grasping of similarity in a non-conceptual mind;
because such a mind consists of the ascertainment of the identity between objects seen previously and subsequently, it consists of the verbalization (*abhijalpa*) of an object previously experienced.

Alternatively, even if we grant that the preceding false cognition conforms to the primary object, nevertheless, your desired conclusion is not established; this is what [the author] demonstrates with the words "or that which is produced as uninterrupted, etc.
By the inclusion of the word "etc.," an object produced as interrupted is also included.

For that very same object, whether arising as interrupted or uninterrupted, exists primarily as that which has first been assigned a distinct designation such as "division" for the sake of activity by excluding what is of a different kind; thus, your desired conclusion is not established.
Regarding what was said, "And this cognition 'the earring-possessor' (kuṇḍalī)," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "The cognition 'the earring-possessor'":
This cognition "the earring-possessor" arises only between Caitra and the earring during their two specific states of being born, just like a conjunction [between two things].

For just as the conjunction between Caitra and the earring arises only when a specific state has been attained and not at all times, so too this cognition "he is the one with the earring," being based on a particular state, why should it occur at all times?
Those two, Caitra and the earring, for whom a specific state has arisen, are described as such.

Regarding what was stated elsewhere, beginning with "of a thing seen in another place," he says: "That excellence of state. That excellence of state, being of such a kind as has been observed elsewhere, is denied [in the case of Caitra].
In expressions such as "the earring is on Caitra," conjunction is not [denied] because it is not perceived by you.

This cognition has been described as being based on a specific state; since that [object], which meets the conditions for perceptibility, is not perceived in another state, its negation is established. However, this does not apply to the *saṃyoga* (conjunction) imagined by you, because such a conjunction never appears in the intellect when the objects it would connect are separated.
Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

It might be argued: "Even if a proof for conjunction has not arisen for us, what subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) do you have? To this he says: "Not from the conjunction postulated by others," and so forth:

"A cognition of things as conjoined does not arise from a conjunction postulated by others, because it is a cognition of being conjoined, just like the cognition of being conjoined in the case of palaces and the like."
Alternatively, because it arises when multiple entities are present,
these cognitions are like those whose objects are distinct and multiple, such as threads and the like.
Even in the case of division, these two types of invalidity should be stated as applicable;
moreover, the objection that "the existence of one thing in many [locations] is not logical" serves as a subverting argument.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is a cognition of conjunction (*saṃyuktabuddhi*) arises solely with respect to objects that lack the locus of the conjunction imagined by you, just as in the case of "two palaces are joined" and so forth; and this cognition of conjunction in cases such as "Caitra is wearing an earring" is likewise [a cognition of conjunction]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Alternatively: whatever arises when multiple things are brought together arises solely with respect to those multiple things devoid of the conjunction imagined by you, just as the cognitions whose objects are multiple threads situated at a distance; and this cognition of being joined is likewise [such a cognition]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Thus, it is called "the cognition of the joined."
The meaning is that it is a cognition of conjunction (*saṃyuktabuddhi*).
These two very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should be stated in the refutation of disjunction (*vibhāga*).

For the cognition of disjunction in respect to rams and the like is based solely on specific objects that lack the disjunction postulated by opponents—either because it is a cognition of distinctness, or because its arising depends upon the non-proximity of multiple objects—just as the cognition whose objects are two rams situated at a great distance, or the cognition whose objects are the Vindhya and Himavat mountains.

Now, what is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) for the reason (*hetu*), by which the suspicion of the reason's occurrence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is removed? To this he says "of one," and so forth.

Just as the existence of one thing in many places is not logical, so too has this been elaborated upon in the refutation of the composite whole (*avayavin*) [in the passage beginning] "by means of that very form which possesses occurrence in one," and thus it is not elaborated upon again here.
He states the refutation of "remoteness" (*paratva*) and "nearness" (*aparatva*) with the verse beginning "parāpara... and so forth:
"That which is postulated as the cause for the designations 'remote' and 'near,' namely remoteness and nearness, does not have space and time as its limiting conditions."

Just as forms such as blue and so forth are designated according to their established sequential existence— even when distinguished from other limiting conditions— so too are others described in that same way.

Since the designations and cognitions "this is distant" and "this is near" occur, distance (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are established as the respective causes for the mental reflections of being distant and near.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the cognition is included.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: this consciousness of "distant" and "near" is based on a distinct object other than the jar and so forth, because it is of a different character from the cognition of those [objects], just like the cognition of pleasure and so forth.
For instance, when two masses are situated in a single direction, the mental application of "prior" and "posterior" does not arise based on direction;

nor does it arise based on time, because even when time is the same, the distinction between "prior" and "posterior" occurs through the differentiation of a youth and an elder who exist at the present time but are joined with indefinite directions and locations—since there is a difference [in their cognition] despite the lack of difference in that [time].
Furthermore, no other basis for this cognition can be stated.
Therefore, it is established that this "priority" (*paratva*) and "posteriority" (*aparatva*) have a specific basis;
they do not have space and time as their limit.
This means that they do not have as their limit objects that are merely conjoined with or proximate and remote from a location in space or a point in time.
For by the terms "space" (dik) and "time" (kāla), there is an indication, through metaphorical usage, of those things conjoined with the spatial and temporal locations [of the objects].
Thus, it has been described by the opponent that both types of this priority and posteriority—namely, that produced by space and that produced by time—are twofold.
Among these, the production of that which is produced by space occurs as follows.

When two masses are situated in a single direction, for an observer, taking one as the proximate limit, the cognition arises in the substratum of "remoteness" that "this is distant from that"; then, depending on that [cognition], remoteness (*paratva*) is produced through conjunction with a more remote spatial region (*dikpradeśa*).

Taking the distant object as the limit, the cognition arises in the substratum of "nearness" that "this is near to that"; depending on that [cognition], nearness (*aparatva*) is produced through conjunction with a more proximate spatial region.
This, however, is the sequence of production for those [qualities] produced by time (*kāla*).

For instance, between two persons—one young and one old—who exist at the present time and are conjoined with indefinite directions and locations, that one among them who is inferred to have experienced a great number of sunrises and sunsets by means of such signs as wrinkles, grey hair, and a grown beard, becomes the object of a cognition of "remoteness" (viprakṛṣṭa) for a single observer who takes the younger person as the limit (avadhi). Depending upon that [cognition], the quality of "priority" (paratva) arises from the conjunction with a more distant point of time.

Taking the elder as the limit, when one infers from the growth of his beard and so forth that the number of sunrises and sunsets has been small, a cognition of proximity arises toward that youth; with respect to that [cognition], another [quality] arises from conjunction with another point of time.

This proof for priority and posteriority is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it shows that the reason (*hetu*) also occurs in the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhyavipakṣe*). This is shown by the passage beginning "just as blue and other forms," and so on.

The analysis of the compound is: *bhāva* is arising (*utpāda*); *vyavasthiti* is that which is accompanied by that; thus, "the sequential establishment of existence" (*bhāvavyavasthiti*) means the establishment [of things] in succession through arising.

This is what is meant: just as in the case of blue and other colors, because they arise sequentially, there is a sequential determination based on the limiting condition of time, and not based on a quality; and just as the designations "prior" and "posterior"—such as "this blue is prior" and "that blue is posterior"—occur even in the absence of a quality characterized by priority and posteriority (since qualities themselves lack qualities), why is this not accepted for jars and other objects as well?

By this, he demonstrates that if one merely wishes to prove here that [the designation] has a cause distinct from the object itself, then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it occurs even in the opposite of the probandum.

Now, if it is intended to prove that this cognition is based on a specific quality caused by the categories of eternal space and time (*dikkāla*), then there is an absence of an example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*) is sublated by inference (*anumānabādhā*). For it can be argued as follows: "Whatever cognition is 'prior' or 'posterior' is based on a temporal sequence produced solely from objects devoid of the qualities imagined by others, because it is a 'prior' or 'posterior' cognition, just like the cognition of priority and posteriority regarding color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; and this [cognition] is a cognition of priority and posteriority regarding jars and so forth. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

If it is argued that this cognition of "priority" and so forth with respect to blue and other qualities is merely metaphorical due to their inherence in the same object, and therefore the reason is inconclusive—since priority and the like are admitted to be causes for blue and so forth through a mediated succession—and that the example lacks the property to be proven, we say no.
This has already been refuted by the fact that because the cognition proceeds without faltering, it is not reasonable to regard it as metaphorical.
Furthermore, since those two (priority and posteriority) are not perceived even in their own substratum, a cognition based on their power is not tenable.
Therefore, how could that [distinction] be based upon form and so forth?
Or rather, what could be postulated regarding pleasure and so forth, which exist at earlier and later times, since there is no inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) therein?

Furthermore, since space and time have already been refuted and thus do not exist, the properties of priority and posteriority—which are caused by them—also do not exist; so how can there be any suspicion that they are the cause of it?
By which [reason] the cause would become inconclusive?

Furthermore, space and time do not possess parts such that, through their conjunction accompanied by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there could arise "priority" (*paratva*) and so forth; for they are unitary in nature and partless.

Nor is it logical to attribute a figurative distinction of parts to them in accordance with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), because such efficiency is tied to the actual intrinsic nature (*vastusvabhāva*) of things, and what is figurative is unreal. Thus, there is no inconclusiveness.
Furthermore, regarding the opponent's reason, its unestablished nature (asiddhatva) should be stated as before.

With the words beginning "number" (saṅkhyā), he raises the objection of the opponent's proof for the category of qualities such as number under discussion: "If it is thought that all [qualities] such as conjunction with number are not non-different from substance,
because they serve to differentiate it, just like a staff and so forth."
For them, the description [of things] as conventional entities establishes what is desired;
however, because they are conventional existents, they cannot be defined as being either identical to or different from reality.

All these aforementioned qualities, such as number and the rest, are not non-different from the substance, because they serve as the cause for the differentiation of that substance. For whatever differentiates something is not non-different from it, just as a staff and so forth are not non-different from Devadatta.
In this case, if the thesis merely intends to negate the non-difference of qualities from the substance, there is the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
This is because all things that exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*) are accepted as being inexpressible in terms of identity or difference due to their lack of substantial reality (*avastutā*).
With the words "Now," and so forth, he anticipates the response of Aviddhakarṇa:
"Now, the indeterminability of a collection and the like is denied,
because it possesses determinate properties, just like color, sound, taste, and so on."

He said: The specific states of the collection and the continuum of the aggregates are not inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different from [the aggregates], because they possess determinate properties, just like form, taste, and so forth.
He refutes this with the passage beginning "by way of its lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatayā*), stating:
"Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it does not exist in reality, like a lotus in the sky."
Phenomena are neither established nor fixed; rather, they are superimposed by conceptual construction.
In that very case, the reason is inconclusive because of [the examples of] the sky-lotus and so forth;
for non-difference and difference are established only with respect to real entities.
For if the reason is intended to be the possession of ultimate, fixed properties (*pāramārthika-niyata-dharmatva*), then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*);
for it is not established, from the perspective of a Buddhist, that things such as the continuum (*saṃtāna*)—which are conventionally existent (*saṃvṛti-sat*)—possess ultimate, fixed properties.

On the other hand, if the reason is stated in a general sense, then there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), since even [non-existent things] such as a sky-lotus possess imagined fixed properties, such as non-existence and incorporeality (*amūrta*).
"Stated in the same way" means that when they are stated by abandoning those properties that have been conceptually constructed as existing in general yet are inexpressible [as real entities].
Furthermore, for this reason, this logical reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Since non-difference (*abheda*) is identity (*ananyatva*) and difference (*vyatireka*) is otherness (*anyatva*), these two are established only in relation to real entities (*vastu*), not elsewhere.

Since continua (*santāna*) and so forth do not exist as real entities because they exist only as designations (*prajñaptisattva*), how can their difference or non-difference from a real entity be established?

Thus, it has been demonstrated that in the aforementioned formal argument, if the mere negation of the non-distinction of number and so forth from the substance is the probandum, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
If it is argued that number and so forth are indeed distinct from substance,
then the reason [adduced] suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*), because number and the rest themselves are unestablished.

Now, it might be argued: "It is not merely the negation of non-distinction that is being established; rather, two negations lead to an affirmation. Thus, by means of the double negation, it is precisely the non-distinction from substance that is being established.

This [objection] is refuted by the passage beginning with "of number and so forth" and "the unestablished nature of the substratum," etc., as follows: "In this way, [they are] not non-distinct from substance."
What, then, is the meaning? It means "of those that are distinct."
That very point—the unestablished nature of the substratum such as number—is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "samuccayādi" (and so forth):
"But that which is distinct from conjunction and the rest is indeed a substance;
and if difference were established as arising from its own nature alone, it would be contradictory."
"It is said thus" refers to [expressions] such as "one," "two," or "many," and so forth.
One might object: "Even for that which exists as a substantial entity (*dravya*), the distinction of number and so on is being established. To this, he says: "From its own nature alone," and so on.
For in reality, there is no difference from its own nature, because that would entail the consequence of it being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
"Contradictory" means mutually opposed.
Because difference and non-difference are mutually exclusive by their very nature, they are contradictory when existing simultaneously in a single locus.
In this way, first, the qualities ending with remoteness (*paratva*) have been refuted.
However, the qualities beginning with cognition (*buddhi*) and ending with effort (*prayatna*) are accepted as qualities of the self (*ātman*) because they are dependent upon it.
These [qualities] should be understood as being refuted by the very refutation of the self (*ātman*).
