Furthermore, it is not logical for these to have the self as their substratum; for the self would be their substratum either as the cause of their production or as the cause of their persistence.

It cannot first be the cause of their production, because that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that pleasure and the other qualities would be produced at all times, since their causes would always be complete.
Furthermore, it has been discussed hundreds of times that there can be no dependence upon auxiliary causes for that which cannot have any excellence added to it by others.

Nor does a permanent entity possess the capacity to produce an effect, because such capacity is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity; and it has already been established that for a permanent entity, purposeful activity (arthakriyā) is incompatible with both succession and simultaneity.
Nor is it logical [for staying] to be the cause of staying, because staying does not have a nature distinct from the stayer;
if it were the cause of that, it would simply be called the cause of the stayer,
and that has just been refuted.
And for that endurer, because its own essential nature is already fully established, no cause whatsoever is possible; for no cause can effect anything in it.
Even if endurance were distinct [from the endurer], nothing would be produced by that cause for the endurer, since it would merely produce an endurance that is a separate entity.
Furthermore, how could that which is ineffective be its substratum?
Nor is it logical for this [substratum] to be a benefactor by producing a persistence related to that [entity], because such a relationship is unestablished.
Moreover, it is not logical for it to be the cause of persistence.
It has already been stated that for that which is eternal, causal efficacy is impossible in any respect.
Furthermore, this entity being established must be either inherently unstable by nature or stable by nature.
If it is of an unstable form, how could it be made stable by another?
Because that would entail the loss of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Even if it were of a stable nature, the sustainer (*sthāpaka*) would still be entirely ineffective, since its stability is established by its very own nature.

Furthermore, as for those entities that possess form (*mūrta*), one might indeed postulate a substratum (*āśraya*) insofar as it prevents their downward movement; however, as for these [mental states] such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, since they are formless (*amūrta*), there is no downward movement—what, then, could a substratum do for them?
Furthermore, because both the existent and the non-existent lack expectation (*nirāśaṃsatā*) and are indefinable (*anupākhyatva*), it is impossible for them to serve as a substratum.

Thus, since the status of being dependent cannot be established for pleasure and other such qualities, as well as for others, according to their respective cases, the point is that there is no such thing as a "quality" (*guṇa*).
Moreover, by others, intellect (*buddhi*) is accepted as having the nature of cognition (*jñāna*).
As it has been said: "Intellect (*buddhi*), apprehension (*upalabdhi*), and cognition (*jñāna*) are not different in meaning.
Yet, even though it is of such a nature, its self-cognizing form is not accepted by others;
rather, they maintain that it is accessible only through another cognition.
And since such a thing, like form and so forth, is not established by itself, its very status as "cognition" is untenable; this he will demonstrate.
It is also accepted that pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are of the nature of non-cognition (*ajñāna*);
this too shall be refuted during the examination of the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

However, considering that the negation of heaviness, fluidity, and viscidity must be established just like [the negation of] form and so forth, he states the negation of *saṃskāra*—beginning with "that which is called velocity" (*vegākhyo*) and so on—without explicitly negating these [other qualities].

Impression (*saṃskāra*) is said to be of three kinds: that called momentum (*vega*), that termed cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and that characterized as elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*). None of these [three] is entirely consistent [with the Buddhist position].
Because all things are momentary, no action whatsoever exists that could serve as the cause for a continuum; such would be the conditioning force known as velocity (*vega*).
Momentum (*saṃskāra*) is threefold: velocity (*vega*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*).
Among these, that which is called velocity arises from action dependent upon specific effort or impact within five corporeal substances—earth, water, fire, air, and mind.
It is the cause of a continuous series of actions in a fixed direction and is opposed by conjunction with a substance possessing touch.

For instance, in the case of arrows and the like, [the upward motion] is caused solely by a specific action produced by a specific effort, by virtue of which there occurs the non-falling of the head even while in mid-air; this [action] is established as existing because its presence is inferred from the occurrence of such regulated and other actions. In the case of branches and the like, however, it is born from an action produced by the impact of a clod of earth.
The quality called *bhāvanā* (mental impression) is a quality of the self (*ātman*).

That which is said to be born of knowledge and to be the cause of knowledge is established as existing because its presence is inferred from its effects, namely memory and recognition regarding things seen, heard, or experienced.

On the other hand, *sthitasthāpaka* (elasticity) is a quality of material substances. It is that which, when its own substrate—a solid object with a specific arrangement of parts—is altered by effort and persists for a period of time, restores it to its former state exactly as it was.
Just as a palm leaf or similar object that has been folded for a long time returns to its original state when unfolded and released;
and just as the functional capacity is indeed observed in bows, branches, horns, tusks, and so forth, as well as in cloth and other items when they are rolled up;
[this applies to] "the entire" (akhila).
It is also threefold.
Among these, the effect called "conjunction with action" for that which is termed "velocity" is unestablished,
because momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga), which pervades the entire class of entities, has been proven.

Furthermore, since all entities are non-existent after the acquisition of their own nature (*svabhāva*), there is no action whatsoever of which this [momentary entity] could be the cause of a continuum.

Now, if it is intended that the "continuum of action" is simply the arising of entities perceived as occurring by abandoning the location of their own material causes (*upādāna*), even so, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is because it is the preceding causes and conditions themselves that are inferred from the continuum of such actions constituting the very essence of the entities as they arise in various ways, and not the aforementioned *saṃskāra*.
Because no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with that [cause] is established anywhere.

Furthermore, if the non-falling of arrows and the like were due to the force of such a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), then they would never fall at all, since the velocity—which is the cause obstructing their falling—would persist everywhere.
Consequently, how could this falling of an arrow, which is observed to occur suddenly as it traverses regions of space that are otherwise indistinguishable, be logically accounted for?

Nor can it be said that the falling [of an arrow] occurs because its momentum is destroyed due to the impairment of its power through conjunction with material entities such as air; for in that case, falling would follow immediately, since air-conjunction, which is its opposite, exists everywhere. If it were argued that, because the momentum is extremely powerful at first, it carries the arrow to another location by overcoming even the opposing air-conjunction, then why would its power not remain so at the end, such that it would not carry it even to a very distant place?
For it is observed that even in the case of an arrow gliding through the expanse of space—which everywhere possesses an undifferentiated conjunction with air—it falls midway;
nor can it be said that the velocity becomes something else later on, because otherwise there would be no cause for its production.
For in all cases, the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), such as the arrow itself, remains exactly the same.

Nor is it reasonable to assert that the cause called "action" (karma) becomes modified later, for that [cause] is subject to the same objection. Or, even if there were a difference, since there would be no cause for the destruction of the preceding velocity, it would remain in that very state, and the arrow would simply not fall.

Nor can contact with air be the cause of its destruction, because it would follow that the arrow would fall prematurely; this has already been stated, as such contact is likewise indistinguishable everywhere due to the lack of distinction in the air itself—thus, this [argument] is trivial.
He states the refutation of that which is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā) with the words "But that which is called cultivation," and so forth:
"But that formation (saṃskāra) called cultivation, which consists of the mental impression (vāsanā) of the mind, is logical; it is not a quality of the self, because this [self] has been refuted."
For if, on the basis of effects such as memory, one were to establish merely a general cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For indeed, a cultivation that is essentially identical with the mind—characterized by a capacity deposited by a prior experience—is accepted as the cause of memory and so forth;
this is precisely what is well known as "latent predisposition" (*vāsanā*).

Now, if it is intended to prove that cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has the nature of being a quality of the self (*ātman*), then, because a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of memory and the other [mental states] with such [cultivation] is not established anywhere, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, the thesis (*pratijñā*) is contradicted by inference (*anumāna-bādhā*);
since the self, which would be its substratum, has already been refuted and is therefore non-existent, the non-existence of that [cultivation] is also established.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which are dependent upon something else do not maintain their existence when that [basis] is absent, just as a painting does not exist in the absence of a wall or similar support. Furthermore, according to the opponent's own view, the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) is dependent upon the self (*ātman*). Thus, because there is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*), the desired conclusion is not established;

for that self has already been refuted previously. Therefore, it is logical that the mental formation consists solely of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the mind, and is not a quality of the self. This is the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
The meaning is that one [of the two] is established by valid cognition, while the other is the opposite.
The refutation of the third [type of cause] as well begins with "sthitetyādi":
"However, that which has the nature of a stabilizer (sthitasthāpaka) is not tenable because of the doctrine of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga).
Since a persisting object is impossible, its stability exists only through the very nature of the entity itself."
For instance, regarding the object that he [the stabilizer] establishes as remaining, there are two possible positions: either he himself is inherently unstable, or he is inherently stable.
If he is inherently unstable, then since that object ceases to exist after a single moment, of what would he be the stabilizer?

If, on the other hand, it is the second position—that he is inherently stable—then, because objects that exist while remaining are already of such a nature (tādrūpya) that they do not fall away from their established state, they are already "remaining. Thus, one must state the refutation as before: what is the use of postulating a stabilizer who performs no function at all?

[Page 230] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even though all things are momentary, their causal capacity is said to consist in their abiding for a single moment and their persistence through a continuum. To this, he says: "But a single moment's duration," and so forth:
"A single moment's duration arises from its own cause alone;
and persistence through a continuum occurs due to the influence of each preceding [moment]."

Thus, being produced from their own causes, they are established as lasting for only a single moment. For their "staying" is said to consist solely in the acquisition of their own self-nature; it does not consist in the maintenance of their own form at a later time once their existence has been acquired, because that which is by nature unstable cannot persist at a later time.
Alternatively, if it were to persist, there would follow the undesirable consequence of its never ceasing, just as before.
Because it would follow that [the subsequent moment] is no different [from the preceding one], and because it would entail that it lacks the nature [of being a cause],

and because the production of each subsequent effect is brought about by the capacity of each preceding cause, even in a continuous series, the capacity of a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) is not established.
[The opponent objects: "In that case, let this [cause] be the sustainer of that which is non-momentary. To this he replies: "Not otherwise," and so forth.
"Since this [entity] does not arise in any other way, of what would it be the sustainer?
Furthermore, its status as a cause is not observed; it might be either a conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*) or something else."
This quality that is claimed to be the stabilizer of cloth and so forth only for what has already arisen—
this very thing called a "qualitative embellishment" (guṇasaṃskāra) is impossible in every respect.

For it has been stated that since that which is non-momentary cannot undergo change, its persistence is due to itself alone; therefore, what could this [cause] do to be its sustainer? Furthermore, one might argue: "Let it not be a sustainer, but rather let it be the producer of the moment itself. To this, he says: "And not... and so forth.

For the determination of the reality of an object of cognition depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, apart from well-known causes, its status as a cause—established through perception and non-perception in the case of cloth and the like, or through the non-occurrence of the effect as in the case of the eye and so forth—is not observed or certain, such that it could justify its conventional usage.

If, however, one were to postulate its causality despite its potency being unobserved, then either a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) or even something else, such as a parrot or a crane, would have to be postulated as a cause of production.
(The word "to be postulated" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.)

For there is no distinction whatsoever based on having an unperceived power (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*) by which you might find satisfaction in the mere conceptualization of a single entity, such as the nature of a *saṃskāra*, whose capacity remains undetermined.
Furthermore, this [impression] is not accepted by you as the cause of production; rather, it is held to be a quality that stabilizes things like cloth after they have already been produced.
And it has already been explained previously that such a thing is utterly ineffective in that regard.
However, this refutation was stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's view] that [the universal] is the cause of production.
The intention is that someone might occasionally even overstep the boundaries of their own system and imagine such a thing.
He concludes the previous argument with the words "guṇasaṃskāranāmna" and so forth.
Regarding the refutation of the characteristics and qualities of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), he says "the mind," and so forth:
Because the mind, its conjunction, and the self have already been examined in detail previously,
the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) endowed with the characteristics stated by others is not tenable.
Adṛṣṭa is a quality of the self that bestows the fruit upon the agent, is produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind, and is opposed to its own effect.
It is of two kinds, distinguished as dharma and adharma. Among these, dharma is the cause of the agent’s pleasure, welfare, and liberation.
"Adharma, moreover, is the cause of what is unpleasant, harmful, and sinful"—this is the definition of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) stated by the opponent.

This [definition] is established as non-existent precisely because of the absence of a cause, since the self, the mind, and their conjunction—which were intended as its causes—have already been refuted.

Furthermore, sound is held to be a quality of space; however, that has already been rejected previously by such arguments as "because it would follow that it lacks succession," and so forth; therefore, no further refutation of it is stated here.
Thus concludes the examination of the category of quality.
In order to refute the category of karma, he says "momentary," and so forth: "In entities that perish moment by moment, actions such as lifting [an object] are impossible;
because there is only a falling away at the very place where it was born, it is impossible for it to reach another location."

"Throwing upwards, throwing downwards, contraction, expansion, and going—these are the actions," so says the Sūtra. Among these, throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) is that action which arises as the cause of conjunction with and disjunction from regions above and below. For example, when an action is produced in a limb of the body or in a corporeal substance connected to it, such as a clod of earth, by virtue of effort and other factors, that action which causes conjunction with points of space delimited by the limiting adjuncts of the upward direction and disjunction from those delimited by the downward direction is called throwing upwards.
The opposite of this is the action of throwing (*avakṣepaṇa*), which is the cause of conjunction and disjunction.

Curving (*ākuñcana*) is the cause of the crookedness of a straight substance. As it has been stated: when there is disjunction of the parts at the extremity—such as the fingers—of a straight substance like an arm from their respective conjuncts such as space, and there is conjunction with the parts at the base—such as the shoulder—by means of that action through which the whole characterized as the arm and so forth arises as crooked, that is curving.
Conversely, regarding the production of conjunction and disjunction: that action by which a whole object becomes straightened is *prasāraṇa* (extension).
That which causes conjunctions and disjunctions with objects such as pots located in indefinite directions and places is *gamana* (locomotion).
The fourfold action beginning with upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with fixed spatial points, such as the sky and the quarters of space.
Motion, however, produces conjunctions and disjunctions with points of space in all directions through its various directional aspects;
for this very reason, only five types of action are possible,
since whirling, flowing, scattering, and so forth are included within motion itself.
And this fivefold action is established as existing because its presence is inferred from the effects of conjunction and disjunction occurring in corporeal substances.
Since every particular conjunction and disjunction is its common effect, its existence is established through its effects;
likewise, it is also established through perception.
As it has been said: "Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and action are perceptible by the eye due to their inherence in substances possessing color.
Thus, this system of others has been stated in brief.
In this regard, since conjunction and disjunction have already been refuted, they are established as effects [of motion].

Now, if it is argued that conjunction and disjunction—characterized merely by arising in immediate succession—are stated as the cause because they are the effects [of action], even so, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This is because the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of such actions with those two [conjunction and disjunction] is not established anywhere.
Furthermore, since the reason is pervaded by the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*), it is also contradictory (*viruddha*).

Furthermore, if the mere existence of a cause is what is to be proven, then the argument commits the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because air and other such elements are already accepted as causes of conjunction and disjunction of that kind. Moreover, if a specific [cause] is to be proven, the thesis itself is sublated by inference. For instance, the occurrence of the entry of action must belong either to a momentary entity or a non-momentary one.
First of all, for that which is momentary, there can be no reaching of another location because it perishes—that is, is destroyed—at the very place of its birth.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever perishes at a certain location does not reach another location subsequent to that time, just like a lamp or the like.
And all intended entities perish at the very location of their birth; thus, this is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Showing that the reason is not inconclusive, he says "birth," and so forth:
"For others have asserted that the time of action is a time distinct from birth,
even in the case of things such as lamps, which are admitted to perish very rapidly."
Those whose destruction is accepted as being extremely rapid are "thus" [referred to].

For even in the case of a lamp and the like—which are accepted as having a destruction occurring at a very swift time—the action exists only at a time subsequent to their birth; for, by virtue of persisting for six moments, it would follow that they are not momentary.
"How so? and so forth; "For instance," and so forth.
For instance, the contact with its cause is the manifestation of the universal;
from that, motion arises in its own parts, and immediately after that, disjunction.
The destruction of the conjunction follows, and from that comes the dissolution of the substance;
thus, even in an object such as a lamp-flame, a duration of exactly six moments is accepted.
For instance, first there occurs the moment of connection with its own cause;

after that, the moment of the manifestation of its own universal (sāmānya); then the moment of action in the parts; immediately following that, the moment of disjunction of the parts; then the destruction of the conjunction of the parts that constitute it; and finally, the destruction of the substance. Thus, even for an entity such as a lamp, a duration of exactly six moments is accepted.
Therefore, since there is no such thing as a moving object that exists for even a single moment, for all things possessing motion, the action occurs only at a time subsequent to their birth.
Nor is the reason unestablished, because it is impossible for anything else to be momentary.

[Page 233] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even if we indeed accept the momentariness of entities, why does their activity not occur precisely at the time of their birth? To this he says "paścima" and so forth:
"When there is the possibility of separation from and contact with the posterior and anterior locations..."
Or another goer, and everything that serves as the substratum for action, is postulated.
For that person who remains seated for even a single moment,
there is no possibility of moving to another location, even by the measure of a single atom.

For that which is capable of separation from a western location and conjunction with a location situated in front of it is either a mover or else a substratum for extension and so forth; but nothing else, such as space and the like.
Furthermore, for that which exists for only a single moment, there is no such duration by which it could abandon the previous location and occupy another location.
Because it is brought to its end at the very time of its existence, it is incapable of traversing another location.
Therefore, action occurring even at the time of birth is not tenable;
nor is it possible during the preceding or succeeding limits, because at those times the entity is non-existent.
Thus, for that which does not endure for even a single moment, let alone the impossibility of traversing to another very distant place, [it is impossible].
Moreover, since there is not even a transition to a location the size of a single atom, how can there be action in that which is momentary?
Nor does it belong to that which is non-momentary; this he shows with the words "But if there were stability," and so forth:
"But if a thing were stable, all [actions] such as going and the like would be impossible, especially since it would remain without distinction across all states."

For an entity that is always of a single form is said to be non-momentary; in such a case, the occurrence of activity is absolutely impossible, because, like space, it remains forever without distinction. The formal argument is as follows: whatever is always without distinction cannot possess activity, just as in the case of space; and the entity held to be non-momentary is always without distinction—this is the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

One might object: "Even if the non-momentary entity is indeed indistinguishable [from the momentary], nevertheless, because its nature is inherently that of a mover and so forth, it will possess activity; thus, the reason is inconclusive. Anticipating this, he says "yadi" and so on:
"If that [entity] were by nature of the form of a mover and so forth, then motion and the rest would exist at all times; it could not remain motionless for even a single moment."
Because, even in the absence of motion and so forth, those [properties] necessarily belong to this [entity],
since it has not abandoned its prior nature, just as at the time when motion and so forth arise.

For if these [entities], such as Devadatta and others, which are considered to be momentary, were by their very nature possessed of movement, upward throwing, and so forth, then they would never remain motionless at any time, because they would always possess the form of a mover and so on. Consequently, for this Devadatta and others who possess movement and the like, those [actions] such as going would occur even during a state of immobility when movement is absent,
because they have not abandoned their previous nature, just as at the time when movement and the like actually arise.
Furthermore, if that [self] were by nature of the form of coming and so forth, then coming and the rest would exist at all times;
it would not remain motionless for even a single moment.
Because, even when there is movement and so forth, it remains essentially immobile,
since it has not abandoned its prior nature, just like a period of time that is essentially immobile.
Now, if— out of fear of these defects— it is accepted that this [substance] has the nature of not moving and so forth,
then, being of a single uniform nature like space, it would follow that non-movement and the rest would exist at all times;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), throwing upwards and other such actions are included.

Consequently, even when motion and the like exist, it follows that [the substance] must be entirely immobile, because it has not abandoned its nature of being without motion and so forth, just as it is in its immobile state.
"Praspandavat" means "possessing vibration," which is action (*karman*);
the suffix *vati* is applied here after a locative case-ending, as in the expression "like time, whose nature is immobile."

Furthermore, it might be argued: "He does not have a single uniform nature; rather, because he possesses both the nature of a non-goer and a goer, the aforementioned fault does not follow, and the reason is unestablished. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "But if," and so forth.
"But if he were a non-goer at one time and otherwise at another, there would be a difference [in his nature] due to the association with mutually distinct essences."
Regarding the phrase "and at one time" (*ekadā ca*):
the particle *ca* is displaced in order; it should be understood as following the word *punaḥ*.
Its meaning is "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) and "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
For in this way, due to the superimposition of contradictory properties such as being a goer and a non-goer, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the loss of oneness.
Therefore, demonstrating that its momentariness is established, he says:
"The two selves are determined to be absolutely distinct," and so forth.
"Because they possess contradictory properties, like a moving object and a stationary object."
"Those two" refers to those existing in the states of moving and non-moving;
it is like the objects that are moving and stationary.
The meaning is: "like a creeper, a mountain, and so forth."
Having thus established the sublation of the proposition by means of inference, he now states the following—beginning with "dṛśyatva" (visibility)—while also establishing its sublation by perception:
Action, which is held to be perceptible, is not distinct from the substance;
nor is it perceived [as such], and its existence does not withstand logical scrutiny.

Whatever, being characterized by perceptibility, is not perceived, enters into the conventional usage of non-existence for those who are discerning, just as a cloth not being perceived in a certain place. And action (*karman*) is not perceived apart from entities such as form (*rūpa*); this is a non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
For action is never observed appearing in sensory cognition as something distinct from form and so forth when they arise occupying another location.

Furthermore, this cognition that arises in connection with verbal expression, such as "throwing upward" or "throwing downward," is not perception because it is accompanied by conceptualization (*sābhijalpatvāt*). Nor is it reasonable to claim that this [cognition] arises from the experience of the category of action (*karmapadārtha*), since we observe that form and other [sensory objects] arise in various ways precisely as they appear. This is because [the cognition] functions by determining those very objects according to convention.
This has been established immediately prior [in the argument]: "Because motion and so forth do not exist in things that are either eternal or non-eternal.
Therefore, the statement that action is established through perception itself is unproven.
Summarizing the very point already stated, he says:
"Whether [the object] be unstable or stable, in this way there is no possibility of motion and so forth,
because separation from and arrival at a former and another location are impossible."

The word "thus" (evam) refers to the fact that [the opponent's position] has been refuted by the two means of valid cognition—perception and inference—just mentioned. Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of reaching a division":
the connection is to be understood respectively as "because of the impossibility of a division with the former [space]" and "because of the impossibility of reaching it with another location."

If this is so, how then does the conventional usage of "motion" occur in the world? To this he says: "Due to the perception [of an object] in another location," and so forth. "But because of the continuous arising of similar and dissimilar entities, there is the illusion of motion, as in the case of a lamp."

Regarding the phrase "of similar and other things" (*samānāparavastūnām*): the analysis (*vigraha*) should be performed by first compounding *samānāni* and *aparāṇi* as *samānāparāṇi*, and then compounding that with *vastūni* to form *samānāparavastūni*.

Because of the perception of the arising—meaning the coming into existence—of those similar and other things in immediate succession, while abandoning the location of their own material cause (*svopādānakāraṇadeśa*), there arises the cognition "this very same thing is moving," just as a lamp being carried by someone serves as the cause for the cognition that it is "going to another place."
It occurs thus: for it is not the very same lamp that moves to another location,
since it is held to endure for six moments.
For it is precisely the intrinsic nature of an entity (*bhāvasvabhāva*), which is empty of prior and posterior limits, that is designated as "birth.
Therefore, its perception is indeed logical.
Alternatively, this term *janmanaḥ* ends in the ablative case.
The connection [of the sentence] is: because similar and subsequent entities arise in uninterrupted succession, they are perceived in another location.
Thus concludes the examination of the category of action.
With the words "In substances, etc.," he begins the refutation of universals and particulars:
"When substances and the rest have been negated, the universals are also rejected;
for all those [universals] are postulated as subsisting in the three categories."
"Universals" refers to generalities.
And since these are dependent upon the three categories consisting of substance, quality, and action, they are discarded simply by the refutation of those [three categories].
For there can be no existence anywhere for things that depend [on a substratum] without a substratum, as that would entail the consequence of their being non-dependent.

The mention of "universals" (jāti) is illustrative; particulars (viśeṣas) are also accepted as being dependent because they reside in ultimate substances, and thus they too are discarded by the very refutation of the substratum.

Nevertheless, wishing to state a further specific refutation—and because it is impossible to refute that whose essential nature is not known—he says "In this regard," etc., demonstrating first the essential nature of the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*):
"In this regard, this genus (*jāti*) is accepted by others as being twofold:
[first] the universal alone, called 'Being' (*sattā*), because it persists through all [entities];"
But substance-ness and the like are called both universals and particulars,
because they serve as the cause for a cognition that persists across their own substrates.
And because they differentiate their own substratum from all things of a different class,
it is established that they alone are the causes of the cognition of exclusion (vyāvṛtti).

In that regard, generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). The higher is called "Being" (*sattā*); and because it is the sole cause of the inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttipratyaya*) across all three categories—substance, quality, and action—it is generality alone and not a particularity (*viśeṣa*). The lower, however, is characterized by such [universals] as substantiality (*dravyatva*), actionhood (*karmatva*), and so forth. Because it is the cause of the inclusive cognition among its own substrata, such as substances and the like, it is called "generality"; yet, because it also serves as the cause of the exclusive cognition (*vyāvṛttipratyaya*) of its own substratum from heterogeneous things by way of differentiation, it is designated as a "particularized generality" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).

For instance, regarding this exclusionary cognition (*vyāvṛttabuddhi*) that arises with respect to qualities and so forth—such as "it is not a substance" or "it is without quality"—the causality for this [cognition] is established solely in these [universals] such as quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and substance-ness (*dravyatva*), and not in anything else; for there exists no other [universal] such as "non-substance-ness" (*adravyatva*).
Furthermore, the sense is that the relationship of both generality and particularity does not contradict itself in a single entity due to a difference in perspective (*apekṣābheda*).
He states the definition of the particularities (*viśeṣa*) for others: "The particularities themselves," and so forth.
However, some particularities are indeed the causes of differentiation alone;
these are described as the ultimate particularities residing in eternal substances.
Some maintain that only particulars (viśeṣa) are intended, and not universals (sāmānya);
the meaning is that this is because exclusion itself is the cause of the cognition of exclusion.
To the question "What, then, are those [particulars]? he says: "eternal," and so forth.
And thus it has been said: "The ultimate particulars (antyaviśeṣas) reside in eternal substances.
Regarding the phrase "residing in eternal substances":
this is because they reside in atoms, space, time, ether, self, and mind.

Because atoms constitute the limit of both the destruction and the origination of the world, and because liberated selves and liberated minds represent the ultimate limit of saṃsāra, they are called "ultimate" (*antya*) since they exist at that end;
this is because [the universal] is perceived most clearly in them.
Furthermore, their occurrence (*vṛtti*) is in all eternal substances, beginning with atoms.
For this very reason, both [terms] are employed: they are "ultimate" (*antyāḥ*) because they reside in eternal substances.
In that regard, they are called "particularities" (*viśeṣāḥ*) because, by being the cause of mutually exclusive cognitions, they distinguish their own substrata from all others.
But from what [source] are these perfected beings (siddhas) established? To this he says: "By whose power," and so forth.
"By whose power cognitions arise for yogins regarding atoms and the like, they each rely on [the existence of] this [object], thinking: 'This [atom] is distinct from that [other atom].'"

For just as in the case of people like us, a cognition regarding cows and the like—which is distinguished from the cognitions of horses and so forth—is observed to be caused by the configuration (ākṛti), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), and the conjunction of parts (avayavasamyoga), such as: "This is a cow," "It is white," "It moves swiftly," or "It has a thick hump."

Regarding the term "mahāghaṇṭa" (the great bell), it is as follows: for yogins superior to us, with respect to eternal atoms that are identical in form, quality, and activity, as well as with respect to liberated souls—for whom no other cause [for differentiation] is possible—it is by the power of these [particulars] that there occurs the exclusion of the cognition "this is distinct from that," and the recognition "this is that very same one" regarding what is perceived at a distance in space and time. Therefore, those ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*), whose existence is inferred from the specific cognitions of yogins, are established.
And they, each residing in their respective substratum, are established for yogins through direct perception itself.
Now, as to how universals (*jāti*) are established, he says: "By perception," and so forth.

Universals such as "existence" (*sattva*) and "cowness" (*gotva*) are indeed established through perception, because cognitions such as "existent" (*sat*) arise whenever the operation of the sense faculties is present.
Whatever arises in conformity with the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of something else is established as being produced from that;

and since the production of cognitions such as "existent" regarding substances and the like follows the positive and negative concomitance residing in the sense organs, why should it not receive the designation of being "produced by the senses," just like other sensory cognitions? Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Establishing their existence through inference as well, he says "by inference," and so forth:
"Their existence is also understood by the force of inference,
because the cognition of specific [features] arises from another cause."
"A cognition of distinction" (*viśeṣapratyaya*) means a cognition whose form is distinct from substances and other such entities.
It is "produced by another cause" (*nimittāntarabhāvika*); that is, having in mind that it possesses an arising (*bhāva*)—meaning production—from another cause.

The formal argument is as follows: whatever cognition is distinct from the form of a given object arises from another cause distinct from that object, just as the cognition of "red" and so forth regarding cloth, leather, or woolen blankets; and likewise, this cognition of "existent" and so forth regarding substances and other categories [is such]. Thus, the opponent considers this to be a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
He demonstrates this very point regarding the nature of the means of valid cognition by presenting the arguments composed by Bhāvivikta and others, beginning with the words "gavādi" (cows, etc.):
"The specific cognitions of words such as 'cow' with respect to cows, elephants, and so forth,
have as their cause an object distinct from convention, shape, the individual body, and other such factors."

For if [the cognition] has cows and so forth as its object, it must be distinct from the word and the cognition [of them], just as, in the case of these very same objects, there are distinct cognitions and words such as "with calf" or "with goad."
The qualification [of the definition] is for the sake of avoiding deviation (vyabhicāra) through cognitions such as that of a hare's horn;
and the mention of its own nature (svarūpa) serves as an illustration by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya).
And the cognition that persists across cows and other such objects arises as distinct from the individual bodies [of those objects],
because it is a qualifier, just like the cognition of blue and so forth.

Cowness is a different entity from the individual cow, because it is the object of a distinct cognition, just like color, touch, and so forth; and because it is spoken of as "its" (the cow's), just like a horse.

Regarding this, Bhāvivikta declared: "The specific designations and cognitions of 'cow' and so forth with respect to cows, horses, buffaloes, boars, elephants, and the like, are based on other causes that are related to and conform to a nature distinct from convention (*samaya*), configuration (*ākṛti*), the individual body (*piṇḍa*), and so on. This is his proclamation.

For, while having as their object cows and the like, these are designations and cognitions distinct from the designations and cognitions of the nature of the individual body and so forth; they are like the specific designations and cognitions such as "a cow with its calf," "a buffalo burdened by a load," "a boar with a thorn," or "an elephant with a goad" applied to those very same cows and others.
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), there are the specific designations and cognitions of the essential natures of lumps of clay and so forth;
and those other causes (*nimitta*) are established as being "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like.
In this context, "designation" (*abhidhāna*) means the word (*śabda*), and "cognition" (*prajñāna*) means the conceptualization (*pratyaya*) or knowledge (*jñāna*).

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "designation" (*abhidhāna*) and "cognition" (*prajñāna*) themselves are the "particulars" (*viśeṣa*); thus, it is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśe�ṣaṇasamāsa*). "Convention" (*samaya*) means linguistic agreement (*saṅketa*); "form" (*ākṛti*) means configuration (*saṃsthāna*); "mass" (*piṇḍa*) means substance (*dravya*); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of [the categories] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth is intended. The analysis of the full compound is: those things whose own nature (*svarūpa*) is distinct from these [convention, form, mass, etc.]—which serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) corresponding to their respective designations and cognitions—and which are the causes (*nimitta*) for other associated factors; those [things] have these as their basis. Alternatively, the analysis should be made as: those things which are distinct from convention and so forth, and which are associated with a nature that corresponds to the cognitions and designations of "existence" (*sat*) and so on.
The remainder is as before.
"Proclamation" refers to the formal proposition (*pratijñā*).
The qualification "provided that it has as its object a cow or the like" is added to exclude the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the cognition of things such as a rabbit's horn.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *tattva* (the true nature) is that state of those for whom the designation (*abhidhāna*) and cognition (*prajñāna*) are distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the lump (*piṇḍa*) and so forth.
By way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), [the examples] are "the specific designations and cognitions of the lump and so forth.
For in those cases, since there is an absence of dependence on another cause distinct from the lump and so forth, the aforementioned reason is also absent.

Uddyotakara, however, says: "The cognition of recurrence (anuvṛttipratyaya) regarding cows and the like arises from a cause distinct from the individual bodies (piṇḍa), because it is a qualifier, like the cognition of blue and so forth.

Likewise, 'cowness' (gotva) is an entity different from the cow, because it is the object of a distinct cognition, like color, touch, and so forth; and because it is the object of a designation such as 'its,' just as in the case of 'Caitra’s horse,' which is designated as distinct from Caitra.
He demonstrates this [objection] with the words "regarding cows and the like," etc.
This is easily understood.
He offers a rebuttal with the words "asāram" and so forth: "This effect is without essence; it is merely a description of a process.
However, no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists here that could indicate its existence."
For the cognitions of "existent" and so forth are not established as occurring immediately after the operation of the senses;
rather, they arise from the mental application of linguistic convention.
Regarding what was stated— that because of the presence of the operation of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*), cognitions such as "existent" and so forth are dependent upon the sense-faculties—

if the intended meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is "because they arise immediately after the operation of the sense-faculties," then that reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), since [cognitions like "existent"] are mediated by conceptualization (*savikalpatva*), the application of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), mental engagement (*ābhoga*), recollection (*smaraṇa*), and so on.

Nor can it be said that this is impossible—namely, how entities whose natures are mutually exclusive could, even through a succession [of causes], serve as the basis for a cognition of a non-different form without a single underlying commonality. Anticipating this objection, he says "Just as," and so forth:
"Just as the individual or collective power of the *dhātrī*, *abhaya*, and other [medicines] to eliminate various diseases is observed, even though they are diverse."
In those [remedies], there exists no commonality whatsoever that possesses efficacy,
since the alleviation of disease is observed through distinctions such as being slow or quick.
There is no excellence whatsoever in a universal due to differences such as the field and so forth;
however, such excellence exists eternally in the case of a nurse and the like, because they possess a uniform nature.
Thus, even though there is absolute difference, some things, by virtue of their restricted capacity,
become the cause of a uniform reflective awareness and so forth, while others do not.

For just as the *āmalaka* and other fruits, though their forms are utterly distinct from one another, each individually or collectively possess the capacity to eliminate various kinds of diseases even without a recurring commonality— since it is not tenable to say that a universal (*sāmānya*) alone performs such a purposeful action (arthakriyā)—
because there exists no universal among them that is capable of accomplishing those diverse purposeful actions.
If it were so, then this observed capacity of certain nurses and others to pacify diseases—sometimes slowly and sometimes quickly—would not exist, because a universal (sāmānya) is uniform in nature.
Nor is it logical to claim that the universal itself, having attained excellence through specific refinements such as the field, milk, or irrigation, performs these diverse causal functions;
for since it is eternal and its modifications cannot be produced by others, no excellence whatsoever can arise from differences in the field and so forth, owing to its uniform nature.

However, that excellence of impermanent things such as nurses and the like varies according to differences in the field (*kṣetra*) and other factors; therefore, they alone are endowed with the capacity to pacify diseases and so forth.

Consequently, there is no fault in the view that other entities, such as jars and the like, will likewise—by virtue of arising from their own causes and conditions in such a manner—be by their very nature the causes for a single uniform conceptual reflection (*pratyavamarśa*) and so on.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "uniform conceptual reflection and so forth," the inclusion of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), such as holding water, is intended.
But how is it established that these [words] are intervened by convention, mental effort, and so forth? To this he says "kārya" and so on:

"And when there is the intention to express the mere utility [of a word] for its effect, a convention is made regarding those [words] upon hearing the sound 'sat' (existent), or rather, regarding another [word], according to one's preference."
Users of language establish linguistic conventions such as "cow" and so forth for things that are useful for various functions, such as carrying loads or yielding milk.
These cognitions of "existent" and so forth are observed to arise from the mental attention to conventions; they do not occur immediately after the operation of the sense faculties.
For those who have not grasped the convention (*samaya*), the cognition of "existence" and so forth would not arise; otherwise, the establishment of conventions would be rendered useless.

Therefore, when makers of conventions apply the term "existent" by referring to that non-difference which is indicated solely by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*) established through a single uniform conceptual determination (*ekākāra-parāmarśa*), it is in respect to that [capacity] that the cognition of "existence" and so forth occurs.
Or, as it is said: "or of another."
This applies to the scriptural statement "the thing" (*vastu*).

In the same way, it should be understood that even for specific scriptural statements such as "cow" and so forth, a convention is established when there is a desire to know specific capacities, such as the ability to carry a load.

Consequently, at the time of linguistic usage following the establishment of the convention, even when cows and the like are perceived, the recollection of the previously made convention occurs; from that, the memory of the name arises; and subsequently, the cognition of "being" (*sat*) and so forth emerges—this is indeed clearly observed.

In some cases, due to extreme familiarity, these [cognitions] arise so rapidly that their sequence cannot be discerned; however, those with less practice clearly perceive that sequence. He concludes: "Therefore, because they are intervened by factors such as time and mental effort (*ābhoga*), they do not arise directly, and thus their status as perception (*pratyakṣatva*) is unestablished. Furthermore, it is not logical for that which arises through a succession of steps to be considered perception, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, showing that because it is based on memory (*smārta*), the cognition of "being" and so forth is improperly considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—just like other types of memory—he says "without verbalization," and so on:
"At first, however, a cognition arises that has a non-verbalized form;
thereafter follows the application of linguistic convention (*samaya*); therefore, for you, that [cognition] is also derived from memory."

Because a convention is not established for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and because one conceptualizes after having seen [the object], first of all there arises a cognition dependent on the sense organs which, having as its object the particular characteristic of the thing, is free from association with verbal expression. Subsequently, regarding that very same perceived thing, there occurs the application of a convention; immediately thereafter, cognitions such as "existent" arise, taking as their object the perceived thing according to the convention, and by way of determining it. How could these cognitions—which express that very perceived object—not attain the status of being recollective (*smārta*)?
Therefore, [it follows] from this as well...
"From the determination of what has been perceived," namely,
the cognitions of existence and so forth.
But from where is this sequence of the arising of cognitions observed? To this he says "elsewhere," and so forth:
"In one whose mind has gone elsewhere, there is the perception of the mere object;
from that very [object], [the subsequent cognition] proceeds by way of the exclusion of all adjuncts."

Since those cognitions of "existent" and so forth arise in this sequence, for that very reason, when one whose mind has gone elsewhere toward another object and whose attention is distracted sees an object standing before him, the first [cognition]—which is the perception of the mere object devoid of all adjuncts—occurs because the mental application (*manaskāra*) regarding the conventional designation of the object present before him has not yet arisen. Otherwise, if every cognition were accompanied by verbal expression (*sābhijalpa*), how could one whose mind is directed elsewhere perceive the object standing before him as it is, stripped of all adjuncts?
For two expressions are not experienced simultaneously at one and the same time;
thus, in this way, the fact that [the cognition] directly follows the positive and negative concomitance of the sense organ is unestablished.

Regarding that which was stated, beginning with "cows and so forth," he says: "Even in the case of the first reason, there is futility; for those [words], it is indeed accepted that their manifestation is produced through the application of convention (*samaya*); that [convention] is the concomitant factor, possessing both positive and negative concomitance."

If it is being proved in a general sense that these [cognitions] are based solely on some other cause that is a corresponding correlate (*anurūpa-saṃsargi-nimitta-antara*), then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For the very apprehension of the convention (*saṅketa*) regarding "cow" and so forth is itself the corresponding correlate for the cognition and verbal designation of "cow" and so forth. To explain: when that [apprehension of the convention] exists, [the cognitions] occur; and when it does not exist—even if there is a mental attention (*manaskāra*) toward a different class [of objects]—they do not occur. Therefore, it is established that this [convention] alone is the cause possessing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because [the cognitions] strictly follow its own positive and negative concomitance. Consequently, the effort of employing a formal reason [to prove this] is futile.
If that [example] were excluded from the subject class (*pakṣa*), the illustration would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
It is not so with its causes— such as the goad and so forth— which, like external things, are directly [the cause].
The operation of designations and conceptual constructions does not exist within the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
because the particular characteristic has a form that transcends the entire range of speech.

Now, if this mental attention to convention (*saṅketamanaskāra*) is included within the very category [of the subject], and it is then sought to prove that these [cognitions] are based on a connection with a so-called "universal" (*sāmānya*)—which is distinct from that [subject], eternal, unitary, and pervasive—then the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); for no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has ever been established with such a thing anywhere.

Furthermore, those things such as the calf and the goad, which were described as being the causes for the naming and cognition of the cow and so forth, are themselves not established as such causes. For these [particulars], having attained their own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), do not possess the capacity to be the direct cause of naming and cognition, because the specific nature transcends the domain of all speech and conceptualization. Consequently, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

If, however, one imagines that they are causes through a mediated succession (*pāramparya*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since everything is potentially useful for everything else in some indirect way.

If this is so, how then does the world determine external things such as the goad to be the cause of that [perception]? To this he says: "Antarmātra... and so forth. Relying upon that which is merely internal and conventional, they proceed by determining it to have an external form, such as the goad.
It has already been stated that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the basis for the designation "hook" and so forth, is not touched by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

As for that which is conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), because its nature is produced by the artisan of imagination, it is established solely within the internal [mind] and is not external. However, due to a lack of discernment between the perceived object and the conceptual construction, people imagine that form to be as if external and thus rush toward it as an external entity. Therefore, the existence of an external form for things such as hooks is not established. The phrase "relying on the hook and so forth" should be connected with what precedes it.

The meaning is that, having taken as their object conventional things such as goads and so forth—which have ascended into the internal measure alone and are determined as external forms—they proceed toward the external.
"Internal measure" refers to the intellect (*buddhi*).

Furthermore, the qualification "provided that it has as its object a cow or the like" is also entirely improper, because there is nothing to be excluded [by it]. Demonstrating this, he says: "The absence of action, quality, and designation is described as the reason for the cognition of non-existence; thus, the qualification is meaningless."

That too is incorrect; for if it were a cause, it would possess substantiality by virtue of its causal capacity, and consequently, the cognition of "non-existence" would apply even to [categories] such as "Being," since there is no distinction [in that regard].
[Page 243] You also describe the very absence of action, quality, and designation as the cause for the cognition of non-existence;
that too is incorrect.
This refers to the description of the absence of action and so forth as being the cause.

For it is precisely the capacity to produce an effect that is called "causality," and that capacity has a real entity as its substrate, because that is the defining characteristic of a real entity (*vastu*).

If even a non-entity (*abhāva*) were to be endowed with such a capacity, how could it not then attain the status of a real entity? Since the status of a real entity is based solely on this [capacity], it would consequently abandon its very nature as a non-entity.
This is because non-existence consists in the departure from the intrinsic nature of a real entity (*vastu*).

Furthermore, if the absence of action, quality, and designation were the cause for the cognition of non-existence, then the cognition of non-existence would also apply to [categories such as] "Being" (*sattā*) and so forth; for there too, as in the case of a rabbit's horn, there is no difference in the absence of action, quality, and designation.
Showing that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "Dissimilarity.
Dissimilarity is unestablished with respect to the cognition of the lump, the shape, and so forth;
therefore, this [reason] is also unestablished for those cognitions.

For there is no other object distinct from the individual body and so forth that can be determined by the cognitions of "cow" and the like, by virtue of which those [cognitions] would be different from the cognition of that [individual].
Showing that the thesis is contradicted by inference, he says "anvayī" and so forth:
"Since the inclusive cognition (*anvayī pratyaya*) manifests as the individual word (*śabdavyakti*),
the universal (*jāti*) is described as being devoid of the forms of color (*varṇa*), shape (*ākṛti*), and syllables (*akṣara*)."

This is what is meant: you wish to establish that for the following cognitions there exists a cause (nimitta) distinct from the collection [of parts] and so forth, which serves as their objective support (ālambana); however, that is untenable, because such a thing does not appear [in cognition], and because what appears is rather the color, shape, and so forth, which are of a different nature than that [postulated cause].

For you describe the universal such as "cowness" as being entirely devoid of color, shape, syllables, and form; yet cognition is experienced as following after the appearance of color and so forth. How, then, could its objective support (ālambana) be something devoid of color and the rest? Indeed, it is not logical for a cognition having one form to have an objective support of a different nature, as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition has the appearance of an object distinct from [the universal] does not apprehend that [universal], just as the cognition of sound does not apprehend form; and the continuous cognition (*anvayī-pratyaya*) has the appearance of something distinct from the genus (*jāti*) and so forth. This is because of the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*). "Manifesting the individuality of the word" (*śabda-vyakty-avabhāsavān*): "word" (*śabda*) refers to designations such as "cow" and so forth; "individuality" (*vyakti*) consists of the phonemes and the configuration (*saṃsthāna*); that which possesses the manifestation of these two is "possessing that" (*tadvān*).
The syllables are the letter *ga*, the letter *au*, the visarga, and so forth.

But Śaṅkarasvāmin says: "Even a universal, such as blueness and so forth, has the very form of blue and so on; otherwise, there would be no recurring cognition in the form 'this is blue. Therefore, because the reason is unestablished, there is no sublation by inference.
To this, he replies with the words "Even of the universal," and so forth:
"If the universal also had the nature of blue and so forth, what difference would there be between it and a quality?"
A single, non-pervasive particularity, such as blue and so forth, is perceived.
If this [universal], though appearing, is not perceived through its distinction [from the particular],
then how could the cognition and the word apply to the individual by virtue of that [universal]?
This cognition of a universal is accepted by others as being determinate in nature;
and since it has been apprehended, it is not logical to claim that it is unperceived.
This being the case, no distinction between a quality such as blue and its universal, "blueness," would be possible, because there is no difference in their form (*ākāra*).

It might be argued that a quality such as blue is not pervasive (*anugata*), whereas a universal follows after individuals existing in different places and times; therefore, there is a difference in form. To this, he says: "And that which is pervasive is one," and so forth.

Indeed, no other entity such as "blueness" (nīlatva), which is distinct from the quality of blue and so forth, is observed to appear as a persisting factor that conforms to the forms of blue and so on;
for, through direct perception, only a single, unique blue or similar object appears.

Nor does a second property such as "blueness" appear in the conceptualizing mind, because that mind determines only what has been perceived [in the preceding sensory perception]. It might be argued: "Just as for you [Buddhists], momentariness, though appearing, is not discerned by the dull-witted due to its distinctness, so too is this universal. That too is incorrect;
for it is precisely through the power of perceiving that [universal] that non-distinct cognition and verbal expression arise with respect to individual entities, even though they are distinct.

What has been described here is untenable; for indeed, when the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not perceived, no cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) arises—just as the notion "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) does not occur when the staff is not perceived, so it would be in this case as well.
This is because you describe particulars (*bheda*) as transcending by their very nature the range of words and cognitions.

And how could a cognizer, perceiving those particulars whose forms transcend by nature the objects of intellect and speech through the power of observing a commonality (*sāmānya*), be said not to perceive them?

Furthermore, it is appropriate for one for whom perception is exclusively non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) to say that "even though something appears, it is not perceived," because perceiving consists in the operation of a determinative cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*). However, for you, whose position is that all perception is indeed conceptual (*savikalpaka*), such non-perception is untenable, as it would entail the consequence of total non-apprehension. For this is precisely how determinations apprehend their own objects: by determining them; if they do not determine them, it follows that they do not apprehend them at all.

Even granting the establishment of another entity distinct from blue and so forth, your desired conclusion is not established, because the object you intend to prove is sublated by inference, and thus the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with it is unestablished. Showing this, he says: "Even if [it were] established," and so on.

"Even if its having another cause were established, a universal (*sāmānya*) is not proven; for it would have to be a single, persisting entity, yet it arises sequentially and is distinguished by non-permanence."
"Distinct from non-duration" means distinct from impermanence; that is to say, eternal.
Why is it not established? Because it would arise in succession.
The phrase "of the designations and cognitions of 'cow' and so forth" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

For if these were caused by such a universal property (*sāmānyadharma*), then they would not arise sequentially; rather, because their causes would be complete, they would arise simultaneously, like multiple objects that arise at once.
For that which is not to be assisted by another has no dependence whatsoever.
Now, having for the sake of argument conceded the establishment of the reason, he states the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words "the word *padārtha*":
"To what other reason does the word *padārtha* refer? And that cognition which persists even in the case of *sattā* (existence) and the like?"
For there is no further category called "padārthatva" (categoriness) among the six categories by which a recurring cognition "this is a category, this is a category" could arise;

likewise, existence (*sattā*) does not reside in universals, particulars, or inherence, such that there would be a cognition "it exists" regarding them, since existence is established only in substances, qualities, and actions.

Furthermore, for others [the Vaiśeṣikas], the designation [of "existence"] regarding substances and so forth is held to be based solely on a universal; therefore, no deviation [from the rule] is alleged on that account.

It might be argued: "Even in that case, there exists the property of being an object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends existence and so forth; therefore, this designation here too is caused by something else, and thus there is indeed no deviation. To this, he says: "If [the cognition] has another property as its cause," and so on. "If the cognition of 'existence' regarding that [object] were also caused by another property, then, because that [second property] would likewise require a cause in the form of yet another property, there would be an infinite regress, resulting in the absence of any property-possessor (dharmin)."
Therefore, this reason is held by them to be inconclusive;
moreover, its pervasion has not been established through a universal induction.

Even if it is admitted that [the existence of] another property serves as its characteristic (nimitta), the fault of deviation remains exactly as it was; for even in that case, there would be the notion of existence regarding this property itself, such as "this existent property exists.
If another property were further admitted in that case as well, it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress.
Moreover, since those other properties would also depend upon yet other properties, they too would face the consequence of being [mere] subjects (dharmin).

Consequently, there would be no restriction to the number six, as the six categories alone would not necessarily be the subjects (*dharmin*). Alternatively, if—out of fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—no further properties are admitted, then the reason (*hetu*) becomes inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) due to those cognitions which occur with respect to these categories or with respect to properties such as existence (*sattā*). Or, even if its being "inconclusive by being over-common" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) is avoided, by what means is its "uncertainty of negative concomitance" (*saṃdigdhavyatirekitā*) refuted? To this he says: "And not because of a universal application," and so forth.

The demonstration of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the probandum across every locus (*dharmī*) constitutes a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāra*). It may be argued that pervasion is indeed appropriate here; for if there were no other cause, how could the difference between cognitions of those very objects be established? Indeed, there is no difference among many cognitions even when they have a single object. If there were such a difference, then even the cognitions of color, taste, and so forth would not be established as having distinct objects, because the determination of the distinction between objects is produced by the distinction between the cognitions themselves.
That too is incorrect;
for it is not logically tenable, from the perspective of ultimate reality, that a cognition of a universal has the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity as its object,
because a cognition permeated by verbal expression does not take the specific characteristic as its object.

However, if conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and denoters (*vācaka*), which are based on the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of even a single object from this or that [other thing], were to proceed—through the medium of the experience of that object—in accordance with the habituation to linguistic conventions (*saṅketābhyāsa*), even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), then what contradiction would there be? It is for this reason that the lack of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*) is stated.
Regarding what was said, namely that [the universal] "subsists in cows and so forth," and so on, he says immediately thereafter:
"That which was pointed out immediately after that has been refuted by this very [argument].
In proving a universal, the same [faults] such as the establishment of what is already accepted apply."
"By this very [reasoning]" means by the refutation of the reason just stated,
because the same fault applies there as well;
for in this case too, the [undesirable consequences] such as the establishment of what is already accepted are identical.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the following are included: the example being devoid of the probandum (sādhya-śūnyatā), the non-establishment of the reason (hetu-asiddhi), and the deviation of the reason (vyabhicāra).
He states another form of deviation with the words "In the case of cooks, etc. and so forth:
"And in the case of cooks and the like, a specific cognition arises;
and there is the cognition of absence in the case of an absence, even without a single recurring [entity]."
Therefore, because of all these aforementioned cases— such as forms created by desire, or those that have perished or not yet arisen— the reason is inconclusive.
For in those cases, there is no single, recurring cause—such as "cook-ness" or "reader-ness"—by virtue of which the recurring cognition "cook," "reader," and so on, could arise.

Likewise, regarding the four types of non-existence, such as antecedent non-existence and the rest, how could there be a recurring cognition of "non-existence, non-existence"? For even here, there is no universal (sāmānya), because a universal must reside in a real entity (vastu). Furthermore, in the case of forms created by the will, such as Candrāpīḍa and others; in palatial mansions and the like imagined in the sky; and in those who have perished or not yet been born, such as Mahāsammata, Śaṅkha, and so forth—how could cognition occur without a single, recurring [cause]?
For even there, a universal does not exist, because it must depend upon an individual instance.
With the words "not in the case of 'cook' and so forth," he establishes the cognition regarding cooks and the like:
"There is no basis whatsoever for the cognitions of 'cook' and so forth;
if it is argued that the action is the basis, then surely that action differs with each individual instance."
Since there is no persisting entity in things that are distinct, a persisting cognition is not tenable;
therefore, a single universal is accepted as that which conforms to all individual instances.
If a cause is postulated that is impoverished of its connection with action,
then why are the individual manifestations themselves not accepted as its causes?
In that case, there would be no cognition of "the cooker" and so forth when the action has ceased;
for others do not maintain that the agent is always present like a universal (jāti).
If the cognition and the term "cook" and so forth are applied to those [beings] by taking past or future karma as the basis, that is not a valid reason, because [the karma] is non-existent.

It is not reasonable to say that the cognition [of "cook" and so forth] is based on action (*karman*), because that action, too, is admitted to be distinct for each individual, just like the individuals themselves. For, given that a recurring cognition cannot be explained among distinct things without a single underlying factor that persists through them, you postulate a universal (*sāmānya*) that conforms to all individuals.

If, however, action—even though devoid of such persistence—could be the cause of a non-differentiated designation and cognition, then why this aversion toward individuals? Why reject them and instead postulate a universal as the cause of that [cognition]?

Furthermore, if the cognition [of "cook" and so forth] regarding cooks and the like were based on action, then when the action has ceased and one is no longer performing the cooking, the cognition "cook" would not occur.
For you do not accept that action is always present—like a universal (jāti)—such that the cognition would persist even when the action has stopped.
Indeed, whatever is based on something cannot exist in the absence of that thing, for otherwise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); in that case, everything would be based on everything.

Nor is it logical that past or future karma should be the basis for those conditions, because that which is past and so forth does not exist, and it is impossible for what is non-existent to function as a cause.

Śaṅkarasvāmin said: "The recurring cognition of 'cook' and so forth arises from a connection with an action that is linked to the universal (jāti) of that [specific] action; therefore, even when the action has ceased, the cognition of 'cook' and so forth is to be understood as occurring because the action serves as a constant indicator (upalakṣaṇa) of the underlying cause. He demonstrates this in the verse beginning with "kriyā" and so on:
"If the cognition [arises] from a connection with an action that is linked to the universal of action-ness..."
And even when the action has perished, [the result arises] because that [action] serves as the indicator of the cause for its inevitable occurrence.
By "that" (tayā) is meant the action;
the universal of action-ness (kriyātvajāti) is the constant cause (dhruvanimitta).
He provides the rebuttal with the words "But not," and so forth: "But it is not the case that even though it is characterized there, it does not exist when the action has perished;
for a genus that is permanent is perceived [as such] because its own substratum has ceased to exist."
The very action is the substratum of its own genus of action;
for there is no perception or persistence of a genus in isolation without the apprehension of its locus, as that would entail the consequence of it being non-dependent.

It might be argued: "Since the universal (*jāti*) has been perceived at some point, even when the action has ceased, the cognition based upon it continues to function toward its substratum. To this he says, "The staff," and so forth:

"For when universals such as 'staff' or 'club' have been perceived even once, the cognition of 'one with a staff' and so on does not continue to apply to them even when they are separated from those objects."
