Moreover, if the universal such as "cook-ness" were something distinct [from the individual],
then even in one just born, the cognition of being a "cook" and so forth would arise due to its connection with that universal.
If you claim that the cognition of "existence" and so forth always exists as an inherent property (samavāyinī),
then it could not exist there even later, because there is no difference in the circumstances.
Because of the deficiency in the nature of that which is connected, this inherence does not exist between those two;
likewise, how could it exist later, even if there were identity?

For in this way, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for it is not the case that because the universals (*jāti*) such as "staff-bearer" and so forth have been perceived once, the cognition "Devadatta is staff-bearing" or "he is earring-wearing" would arise even with respect to those same persons after they have discarded the staff or earrings.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that a universal such as "cook-ness" exists here as well; for since the universal would exist even in one who has just been born, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cognition "he is a cook" arising [immediately].

It might be argued as follows: just as the cognition "existent" (sat), though based on existence (*sattā*), does not occur at all times, so too the universal (*jāti*), though inhering in its specific substratum, will not exist at all times; therefore, in the state of being just born, the universal will simply not be inherent. [Note that "inhering" is an elliptical expression; it should be understood as "not manifested" as well. If this were the case, then it would follow that the universal would never be inherent in it at all.

For instance, first of all, because of the deficiency in the nature of those two—the universal (*jāti*) and the substance (*dravya*)—there is no inherence (*samavāya*) of the universal; and since that deficiency remains exactly as it was even afterwards, how could it possibly inhere? For according to your own view, the substance is not momentary (*kṣaṇika*), such that it might later acquire some distinctness. "In that way" means as one which has come to inhere. "Of those two" refers to the universal and the substance.
"Tādātmya" (identity) means [the state] when the previous nature characterized by defects has not been abandoned.
Furthermore, showing that there is a fault even if one accepts that the substance is impermanent, he says "yadi nāma" and so forth:
"Even if the individual manifestation were unstable and were to acquire an excellence,
the deficient nature of the universal would never cease."

If an individual (vyakti), by virtue of its instability, acquires a superior state later on, the universal (jāti), however, because of its stability, possesses that same form characterized by the excellence of inherence even as it did before; how then could it come to inhere later on? Nor can it be said that the universal remains eternally present with a form whose excellence consists in inherence in a substance existing at a later time, for that would entail the consequence that the substance itself is eternal, since the universal—whose very nature is to be connected with it—would then exist at all times.
For in the absence of a second related entity, it is not logical for that which has a related nature to remain unimpaired.
With the words "cooking, etc.," he anticipates the rebuttal formulated by Uddyotakara:
"And cooking and other such actions are considered to have a primary instrument (sādhana), namely the 'cook' and so forth; and that primacy exists even when there is another cook."
For he said: "This is stated because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason [given].
Just as words such as 'cook' (pācaka) are applied recurrently even though there is no universal (sāmānya) called 'cook-ness,' so too are there recurrent cognitions regarding cows and the like.
This is the meaning of the reason: "because particular cognitions are not without cause."

The claim that a cognition distinct from the cognition of the individual object arises from another cause does not mean, however, that every inclusive cognition (anuvṛttipratyaya) arises solely from a universal (sāmānya).
This being the case, the primary instrument of the act of cooking is denoted by the word "cook" (pācaka); and since that primacy exists in other cooks as well, there is no fault.
He offers a rebuttal with the words "This primacy... and so forth:

"What indeed is this so-called 'primacy'? It is not power, because there is no logical connection; for this very reason, it cannot be conceived as having the nature of substance, action, quality, and so on."
What is this so-called "predominance"? If it is power (*śakti*), that is incorrect, because power is restricted to each respective substratum and thus does not connect with other individuals.
Nor is it the self-nature or essence of substance and the rest, for its independence would likewise preclude such connection.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), a property (*dharma*) intended to be distinct from the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) is included.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the meaning of [the claim] 'arising from another cause' is as follows," it has already been countered there: if one attempts to prove generally that "there exists some other cause," this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the mental attention to linguistic convention (*saṅketamanaskāra*) is accepted as being the cause. However, in terms of a specific [cause], there is a lack of positive concomitance (*anvayavaikalya*) and a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as seen in the case of cognitions such as "cook" (*pācaka*).

He concludes with the verse beginning "tad" and so forth: "The cognition regarding [terms] such as 'cook' and the like— which terminates in a mere form distinguished from what is heterogeneous— depends upon the distinction of linguistic convention."
Therefore, words and cognitions function according to convention alone;
they do not operate in their differentiation unless there is a single underlying commonality.
Therefore, since no other cause can be established for the cognition of "cook" and so forth, there arises— conforming to convention— a mental state (*śemuṣī*) such as "cook,

cook" with respect to distinct objects like cooks, which determines a mere object excluded from those of a different class (*vijātīya*), even though it appears as non-differentiated. This is because the exclusion of the heterogeneous is present in all cases.

Since cognitions and words that determine a non-differentiated form will likewise function with respect to cows and other such things according to convention—even in the absence of a universal—the reason [you have provided] is inconclusive.
With the words "And likewise," etc., he establishes that there is a cognition of absence in the case of an absence;
thus, the cognition of non-existence is not contradictory regarding absences,
just as a word is pervasive because it follows the convention for its referent in both cases.

For this alone is the pervasive basis for the cognition of a universal, namely, the mental application (*ābhoga*) of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); otherwise, by what would the corresponding cognition and the vocal sound "non-existence" (*abhāva*) in regard to non-existent things not be contradicted? For in this case there is no genus (*jāti*), because [a genus] must inhere in a real entity (*vastu*). He states the reason why they are not contradicted with the words: "Because those two follow a convention whose object is non-existent. That convention in which an object such as a genus is non-existent is so described; because of that following—that is, the concomitance (*anvaya*)—of those two, namely the vocal sound and the cognition.
That is to say, because both sound and cognition follow the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of mere convention (saṅketa).
With the words "of the jar," etc., he anticipates the response of Śaṅkarasvāmin:
"This is the prior non-existence of the jar; this is its destruction"—it is only by means of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of those very objects that cognition apprehends non-existences.

If it is argued that its recurrence everywhere is due solely to the power of a universal residing in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), this is not so, because of the distinctness [of those adjuncts] and because they are the substrata thereof.
The cognition "jar" and so forth follows logically from those [atoms];
however, the cognition "non-existence" is of a different character from that cognition of existence.
For it is not accepted that the cognitions "cow" and "horse" arise by virtue of [their respective] existence;
rather, a single universal must be postulated as the means for establishing all [such cognitions].

For he says: "Indeed, in those absences, no cognitions are observed that are devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Rather, in every case—such as 'the prior absence of the jar' or 'the posterior absence of the jar'—the cognition of absence relies exclusively upon absences that have a real entity as their limiting adjunct.
Therefore, in all instances, the recurrence of that cognition occurs solely by virtue of the universal residing in the limiting adjunct; thus, there is no deviation.
The word "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) refers to the cognition (*dhiyaḥ*), as it is the subject under discussion.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "not so" (*naivam*) and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which is accompanied by dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) and does not have that as its substratum (*atadāśraya*).
Alternatively, it is a collective *dvandva* compound.
The meaning is that [the existence of a universal] is not at all tenable because of dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) and because it does not have that as its substratum.
Regarding this, he provides a detailed justification for the point "because of dissimilarity" with the words beginning "a jar," and so forth.

For it is not logical that cognitions of different forms should be based upon a single limiting condition (*upādhi*), because if the effects of all universals were accomplished by that one alone, it would follow as an absurd consequence that the postulation of multiple universals is useless.

Therefore, let cognitions such as "jar" arise by virtue of universals such as "jarness"; but how could cognitions such as "non-existence," which are entirely distinct in character, be logically based upon that [universal], for a cognition of "cowness" and the like does not arise by virtue of "existence."
Bhāvivikta, however, says: "The meaning is that not everywhere is the cognition conformable to its cause.

For instance, the number 'plurality' inherent in elephants, horses, dhavas, khadiras, and so forth, is the cause for the cognitions of an 'army,' a 'forest,' and the like; whereas the conjunction of heterogeneous substances is the cause for the cognitions of 'beverage' (*pānaka*), 'sour gruel' (*kāñjika*), and so forth. Otherwise, there would arise the cognition 'many [things] conjoined. Having raised this objection with the words 'This is not the cause,' etc., he provides the rebuttal with the words 'If it were so,' etc."
If it is maintained that cognition in all cases does not conform to its objective mark (nimitta),
then since number and so forth are accepted as the basis for cognitions such as "an army" and the like.
If this is so, why is this cognition not accepted as having its application follow the distinctions of conventions fashioned by desire, even with respect to these very particulars?
"This" refers to the cognition of a universal;
"distinction" refers to the particularity of the convention.

"What excellence is there here by virtue of which this is said? To this he replies with the words beginning "bhedajñāne": "For when there is cognition of difference, there arises the desire to establish a convention;
from that comes its creation, then the hearing of it, then the mental application toward it, and from that, the cognition of it."
Through positive and negative concomitance, it is ascertained that this alone is the efficient cause; for there would be an infinite regress if other factors were required.

The causal relation is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance; and that [relation] is ascertained with respect to a cognition of universals, which consists merely in the application of a convention fashioned by intention.

For instance, first of all, an experiential cognition whose object is a particular difference arises; once that has arisen, the desire to establish a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) is born; from that desire follows the making or performance of that convention; then, at the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), there is the hearing of that very [word] which constitutes the convention; and following upon this hearing, there occurs an "enjoyment" (*ābhoga*) directed toward the object of the convention as it was heard; and from that enjoyment, through the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of those very same differences, the cognition "this is a jar," and so forth, comes into being because of the engagement [of the person] with those differences.
From the cowherds downwards, it is determined that only this much is the cause in this cognition.

However, if one were to postulate a universal (*sāmānya*) whose causal capacity is unobserved as being the cause, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for even after postulating that, why should something else not also be postulated, since it is equal in having its capacity unobserved?
In that very context, he states the reinforcement with the words "for [it would be] concordant," and so forth:
"For a correlate must be concordant; thus one might imagine another object.
But since cognitions are dissimilar, it is better to rely on this much alone."
For in this case, a restriction of capacity must indeed be postulated;
and it is better that such a restriction be postulated among those whose capacities are known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

For in this way, while you are determining a cause called an "objective support" (ālambana) that corresponds to universal cognitions (*sāmānyabuddhi*), you have postulated a universal for a multitude of distinct individuals. And if even that postulated universal produces cognitions of other forms, then it would be better if only this much were postulated—namely, that which has been described as having a perceived efficacy.
For in this manner, no postulation of an unperceived object would be made.

Furthermore, when asked how a non-different universal can produce cognitions that are of different characteristics, one must necessarily say this: namely, that there is a specific restriction of power (*śaktipratiniyama*) among entities such that even a single thing is capable of generating cognitions of multiple forms.

If this is so, then since the capacity-restricting factor would reside in the differences themselves—whose powers are already known and whose efficacy is certain—it would not be postulated [in the universal]. For in this way, one would not be acting in contradiction to experience.

It might be argued that the causal efficacy of a universal is indeed ascertained through positive and negative concomitance; to this, he says "anvaya... and so forth: "And positive concomitance is not found in universals, because they are always present; nor is negative concomitance possible for eternal things."
Since cognitions such as "existent" (sat) and so forth never arise—due to their non-existence—it is not logical for them to conform to a positive concomitance (anvaya) residing in that [universal].

For if these were to conform to a universal, then, since the universal would be present at all times, why would they not exist at all times? Indeed, the universal has no dependence whatsoever, because according to the opponents it cannot have any adventitious particularity (viśeṣa) imposed upon it; therefore, these cognitions do not conform to a positive concomitance residing in it.

Nor is there a conformity with their absence; for when these cognitions such as "existent" do not arise, one cannot say that the absence of the universal (*sāmānya*) is the cause there, because since eternal things persist at all times, an absence [of them] is impossible. Therefore, these [cognitions] also do not conform to the absence residing in those [universals].

Since there is thus a fault in the admission of other causes for the cognitions of universals and so forth, that which is asserted by others—that "the universal-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) such as *guṇatva* (the property of being a quality) itself is the cause of the cognition of 'non-substance,' 'non-action,' and so on, with respect to qualities and the like; and with respect to universals such as *sattā*, the cause of the inclusive cognition 'universal' is inherence in multiple objects"—is thereby refuted. This is what he states in the verse beginning with *adravyādi*.
"It is not logical that *guṇatva* and the like are the cause of the cognitions of non-substances and so forth."
Furthermore, because there is no single inherent collection [of individuals], there can be no cognition of a universal from that.

Showing that this conceptualization also leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), he says "aneka" and so forth: "And inherence in many is also found in numbers and the like; therefore, just as with universals, there would arise cognitions [of them] as 'universals'."

If the inherence of multiple objects were the basis for the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) in universals, then since the state of being dependent on multiple substances exists in number, conjunction, disjunction, composite substances, and so forth, there would likewise arise the cognition that these too are "universals," as the cause [of such a cognition] would be no different. Furthermore, the fact that [universals] such as *sattā* (existence) are the cause of a single cognition is restricted to their own nature in the form of "existent" and so on; it does not extend to another universal. Consequently, even by virtue of that, a recurring cognition in the form "universal, universal" regarding universals is not tenable. Therefore, what was stated by Kumārila is incoherent.

Therefore, the word for a universal (sāmānyaśabda) is based either on the occurrence of a single [entity] across diverse [particulars], or on the production of a single cognition regarding existence (sattā) and so forth.
Thus [it is said].

Thus, first, the point "due to dissimilarity" has been explained. Now, wishing to explain the point "because it does not reside in that," he says: "And [universals] such as 'pot-ness'... and so forth.
A universal such as pot-ness resides only in things like pots; its occurrence in absences, however, does not exist. Therefore, how indeed could there be a cognition [of it] in those [absences]?

For it is not logical that a cognition or a verbal expression occurring in one substratum should apply to another— just as the term "elephant" does not apply to a white horse— and in this case, there is not even a single common substratum.
The cognition that "taste is cold" and "heavy" arises because they reside in a single object;
however, even this [cognition] does not exist here [in the case of non-existence], for non-existence never exists anywhere.
A universal inheres only in things such as jars and the like, not in absences, because the latter are non-entities.
Therefore, how could there arise with respect to those absences a cognition that conforms to and follows a universal—such as "jar-ness" and so forth—which inheres in something else?
For instance, "elephant-ness" and the like do not serve as the basis for a uniform cognition regarding white horses (*karka*) and other such animals.
But is it not observed elsewhere that a cognition [of co-referentiality] occurs even when things are inherent in different loci? For example, "the sweet taste is viscous, cold, and heavy.
To this he replies: "Nor does it occur when they have a single substratum.

For in whatever substance sweetness is inherent, coldness and the other qualities are inherent in that very same substance; thus, co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arises here by virtue of their inherence in a single object. However, non-existence (*abhāva*) does not inhere in any single substance whatsoever along with universals such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
Because that which is formless cannot be inherent in anything whatsoever.
With the words beginning "viśeṣaṇa," he anticipates Uddyotakara’s rebuttal here:
"If the relationship of qualifier and qualified also exists in this case..."
Indeed, this [relation] is postulated only when another relation exists.
Based on the proximity between those two, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is postulated;
in the absence of that [proximity], however, it cannot be established as it would lack a basis.

For he (the proponent of the jar) says that for universals such as "jar-ness," the relation with jars and so forth is characterized by inherence (*samavāya*), whereas for absences, it is characterized by the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*); and therefore, even in this case, there certainly exists a relation between the universal and the absence within a single object, which serves as the basis for the designation.
To this, he states the rebuttal beginning with "sambandhāntara... and so forth.

For the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) among entities arises from another underlying relation; for example, the state of being qualifier and qualified between a staff and Devadatta, or between a king and his servant, occurs by depending on relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or the master-servant relationship (*svasvāmibhāva*). But in the absence of that other relation which serves as the cause for the qualifier-qualified relationship, how could that state of being qualifier and qualified possibly exist? Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
for in that case, everything would become a qualifier of everything.

To the question, "How is it that in the world the relation of qualifier and qualified—such as 'the prior non-existence of a jar'—is perceived without an actual [intrinsic] connection?", he says: "The jar's," and so forth. Furthermore, an expression such as "this is the prior non-existence of the jar" is a construction produced by mere conceptualization (kalpanā), imagined like [qualities such as] bravery and the like.
Where the relationship between qualifier and qualified is based on a real entity,
the existence of another underlying relation must necessarily be postulated.

When there is a desire to know merely the meaning that "having not existed previously, it comes to be," this conceptualizing cognition arises by presenting prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as if it were a distinct entity from the existent thing (*bhāva*), through the medium of a relation.
It is by virtue of that intention that the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) exists here, but it is not real.
Just as qualities such as bravery are taken as qualifiers for a person fashioned by the art of imagination.

But where you have grasped the relation of qualifier and qualified as being based on real entities, there another relation must necessarily be sought; otherwise, there would be no fixed rule for their determination.
Furthermore, demonstrating that the response stated by Śaṅkarasvāmin is not even appropriate to the objection raised, he says: "Non-existence, non-existence," and so forth.
Here, the cognition "non-existence, non-existence" itself has been challenged;
moreover, a universal residing in a limiting adjunct (upādhi) exists only in its own substrata.

[Page 255] Regarding this: when a recurring cognition (*anugāmijñāna*) arises—such as "absence," "absence"—in the case of the absence of a jar, the absence of a cloth, or the absence of a rabbit’s horn, we have argued that since such a recurring conceptualization is observed even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), the postulation of a universal elsewhere is futile. This was said with respect to the cognition of those prior absences (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth belonging to many similar things, such as jars.
If that is so, what follows? To this he says: "And residing in a limiting condition (*upādhistha*)," and so on.

The meaning is this: the universal such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva), which resides in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as pots, exists only in its own substrata—the pots and so forth—and not in other substrata such as cloth. Therefore, how could there be a cognition [of that universal] with respect to the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and so on residing in heterogeneous things like cloth? This is the intended sense.

If it is argued that there exists a single, pervasive universal (*sāmānya*) in all things, he replies with the words "And not," and so forth: "Nor is another existence (*sattva*) accepted as following through them; for if such were desired, cognitions of non-existence would not arise apart from the six categories."
Indeed, there exists no higher universal that pervades multiple heterogeneous entities such as cloth and the like, from which this cognition could arise.

It might be argued that the "Great Universal" (mahāsāmānya) called *sattā* (existence) exists, and by its power the cognition of non-existence will occur; but that is incorrect, because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

For instance, since there is no other category of entity—such as *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* and so forth—apart from the six categories, those cognitions of non-existence that arise in you regarding them, as well as the notions that entities such as *kapiñjala* (the partridge) described in fictional narratives lack existence in the ultimate sense—in these cases, what universal (*sāmānya*) residing in a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) could serve as their objective cause?
For, according to your own view, these things such as *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* have no real existence.
By this, that which was stated by Kumārila is also refuted.

"But surely, in the case of antecedent non-existence and the like, a universal (sāmānya) is not accepted as a real entity; for here it is existence itself (sattā) that is the universal, characterized by the nature of non-arising and so forth."
Thus,
"having the nature of non-arising and so forth" means being characterized by non-arising and so on;
for here too, this very same fault applies.
For there is no existence of the categories belonging to other schools nor of the objects of narratives to be produced, by virtue of which their non-existence could be cognized.
If it is argued that what is cognized therein is the existence of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) determining those [objects], which is devoid of an external referent,
then why is it not accepted that every word-meaning consists solely of conceptual construction, being devoid of any eternal or unitary existence?

Otherwise, if one were to accept universals such as existence (*sattā*) and personhood (*puruṣatva*) as being eternal, unitary, and so forth in nature, then since these would lack any internal differentiation across all their instances, the objection—namely, how there could be a cognition of distinct forms—would indeed be impossible to resolve.
Now, regarding objects whose forms are fashioned by the will—such as those that have perished or are yet to be born—he states this justification beginning with "icchāracita" and so forth:

"In an object such as a form fashioned by the will, there is no universal (jāti), because the manifestation (vyakti) itself is impossible; thus, the [universal's] deviation from its locus remains established."
If cognition regarding things past and those not yet arisen has only the eternal universal as its object,
then this universal alone would be apprehended, and not [the particular].
Or, if it were perceived independently, this would not belong to the individuals;
nor could that universal be manifested by them, just as the Himalaya is not manifested by the Vindhya.
For this [cognition] is bound to those [objects] by way of dependence on their production;
it is not, however, dependent on cognition, because [the object] is eternal and is apprehended in its entirety.
Since dependence on its own substratum, the sense faculty, and so forth, is impossible,
that [cognition] would either always be perceived or never at all.
Whether it is capable or indeed incapable of producing cognition within itself,
if its nature were fixed at one time, it would certainly remain that way forever.
Whether its form be fit or unfit, that which exists as its very nature is indeed unshakable due to its permanence; for who could possibly cause it to waver?

The analysis of the compound is as follows: that whose nature (*svabhāva*) is a form fashioned by desire (*icchā*) is so designated; "that which has this as its beginning" (*yasya sa ādiḥ*) is the analysis.
By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the destroyed and the unborn are included.
For there is no universal (*sāmānya*) in those [categories] such as the imagined (*kalpita*), by means of which a cognition based upon it could arise regarding them.

It might be argued: "Let there be no universal (*sāmānya*) in imagined things; however, with respect to the past and the unborn, cognition based upon it will still occur. This is false. For this is not the nature of dependent entities that they exist even in the absence of their substratum; yet even so, the fault remains, because the apprehension of a universal in isolation is not admitted. Thus it has been said: "A universal is that whose cognition depends upon contact between its own substratum and the sense organ. If there were apprehension of a universal in isolation, the determination of the particular (*vyakti*) by the cognition of the universal would not occur, because the particular is absent at that time.
Furthermore, there would be no connection such that "this is the universal of these individuals," because of the absence of a basis for it.

For if there were a basis for the relation, it would have to be either the universal's being manifested by them, its being produced by them, or its being perceived in dependence upon their perception.

Among these, the universal cannot first be connected to them by way of being manifested, because since it is eternal, it cannot be assisted by others and thus lacks any specific change, making manifestation impossible.
For that which does not provide assistance to something cannot be its manifestor, just as the Himalayas are not the manifestor of the Vindhya mountains.
And so it is with individuals (vyakti) in relation to the universal (sāmānya); this is because of the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi).
If that which provides no assistance could nonetheless be a manifestor, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), such that everything would be the manifestor of everything.
Precisely because it is accepted as being eternal, it is logical that universals do not possess dependence on production (*utpatti-pāratantrya*).
Furthermore, since they are perceived even when solitary, they do not possess dependence on cognition (*jñāna-pāratantrya*). Thus, all three positions are untenable.

Consequently, the claim that "a universal is apprehended in dependence upon contact with the sense organ of its own substratum" is incorrect, because the very existence of a substratum is impossible; how then could there be dependence upon contact with a sense organ residing therein?
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-sannikarṣa*) and so forth are encompassed.
Since it is eternal, no particularity can be imparted to it by others; therefore, it has no dependence on anything whatsoever.
Consequently, if it were capable of producing a cognition of its own object, it would produce it at all times.

Furthermore, if it were incapable [of producing], then it would never produce at all; for its nature—whether capable or incapable—cannot be altered in any way, because that would entail the loss of its permanence.
As it has been said:
"Its capacity or incapacity, which is established by its very nature..."
Since it is incurable due to its permanence, who is capable of exhausting it?
Thus it is said.
Regarding what was stated— that "cowness" is a different entity from the cow, and so forth—
he shows that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by means of examples such as "the cook," etc., in the passage beginning with "from the cow":
"Cowness is a different entity from the cow, because it is the object of a distinct cognition."
And because it is said to "belong to him," like color, touch, and so forth, or like Caitra’s horse.
Thus, in this case, there is the statement of deviation by means of "being a cook" and so forth; and in this same manner, all other fallacious reasons (kuhetu) are also to be refuted.

For instance, even though there is no existence of "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) as a separate entity distinct from the cook (*pācaka*), the cognition "the cook, the cook" indeed occurs as having distinct objects; furthermore, the case-ending of separation (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) occurs in such expressions as "Devadatta’s cook-ness. Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive due to being common (*sādhāraṇānaikāntikatā*). The same applies to other fallacious reasons (*kuhetu*) mentioned by Kumārila.
In this regard, he has stated these fallacious reasons (*kuhetu*):
"The cognition of 'cow' that arises with respect to various individual cows is based on a single *gotva* (cowness), because it appears as a cow and because it has a single form,
just like a cognition whose object is a single individual cow."

Alternatively, this cognition of "cow" does not arise from the brindled cow (*sābaleya*), or rather, it has as its objective support an entity distinct from that [individual], because it occurs even in the absence of that [individual], just like the cognition of "earthen" with respect to a jar.
If it is asked how its omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) is established, it is said:

this cognition of "cowness" has as its object an entity inherent in each individual, because it possesses the form of the entire category in every single instance, like a cognition whose object is each individual manifestation.

Unity is also established; for instance, although the universal is fully present in its entirety within each individual, it is nevertheless one, because it is apprehended by a cognition of a single form—just as, for example, the exclusion of non-Brahmins and so forth is [one] when applied to various actors.

Nor can it be said that this non-differentiated cognition regarding distinct things is erroneous, and therefore that establishing the reality of things on its basis is untenable; for there is no defect in its cause.
Nor does there arise a subverting cognition; therefore, since there is no basis for its falsity, this [position] is untenable.
And it has been said:
"The cognition of a cow with respect to various individual bodies is based on a single *gotva* (cowness)."
"Just as there is a single cognition of a cow-individual based on the two [factors] of the appearance of a cow and its uniform form."
The cognition of a cow does not arise from the black-spotted [cow], nor does it have something else as its objective support;
for it exists even in the absence of that [particular], just like the cognition of "earthen" with respect to a jar.
Alternatively, the cognition of "cow" has as its object meanings inherent in each individual;
for it possesses the complete form in each [individual], just like the cognition of an individual entity.

Even though a genus is inherent in each individual, it appears as a single unit through a single cognition, just as the exclusion of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth occurs in sentences uttered by different actors.
Nor can it be said that the cognition of various forms regarding the universal *gotva* is erroneous;
for in this case, there is neither a defect in the cause nor a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*).
Thus [it is said].

Here, first of all, in the first proof, the example is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*); since a single "cowness" (*gotva*) is unestablished, the fact that the cognition of a single cow is based upon it is likewise unestablished.

If, on the other hand, it is being proved in a general sense that [the cognition] has a single basis, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because it is accepted that [the cognition] is based on the exclusion of non-cows (*go-vyāvṛtti*), which is a single conceptual construct through the differentiation from heterogeneous things.

Even in the case of [the argument] "the cognition of a cow does not arise from a black cow," if what is to be proven is the direct negation of its arising from that, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because that [cognition] is mediated by the perception of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), mental attention (*manaskāra*), and so forth. If, on the other hand, it is being proven that it does not arise from that even through a causal succession (*paramparayā*), then the thesis (*pratijñā*) is contradicted by experience, and the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). Furthermore, if the property to be proven is that it has a different object (*anyālambanatva*), and it is argued that the cognition which arises when a black cow is present—namely, "this is a cow"—has an object other than that [black cow], then here too there is a contradiction with experience.
For it functions precisely through the determination of a proximate individual;
thus, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).

Alternatively, if it is argued that the cognition which functions in that manner when a brindled cow (*bāhuleya*) or similar animal is present—despite the absence of that [specific] individual—is proven to have a different objective basis (*anyālambana*), then this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

If, however, it is sought to be proven that [the cognition] has a directly existing real entity as its object (*sākṣād-vastu-sad-ālambana*), then there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).
For it has already been demonstrated that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), this [cognition] does not have any existing real entity whatsoever as its object.

Furthermore, regarding the proof that [the cognition] has as its object a thing that is complete in each individual instance: even in that case, if the probandum is stated in general terms, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because [the cognition] functions by determining the nature of a real entity as being excluded from what is not of that form (*atadrūpa-parāvṛtta*) with respect to each individual object.

Now, if it is being proved that [the universal] has as its object a category called "universal" (sāmānya) which is eternal, unitary, and fully present in each individual, then the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikalatā), and the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntikatā), because a concomitance (anvaya) with such a property is not established anywhere. Furthermore, if one [universal] were fully present in many [individuals] by its entire essence, then all the distinct individuals would result in having an identical form, because they would be touched by the category of the universal whose nature is fully established in a single individual, and thus they would take on the form of that single individual.

Alternatively, there is the logical fallacy of contradicting inference (*anumāna-bādhā*), because the universal would result in being multiple, since its essential nature is such that it must be fully present in many distinct objects—just like bilva fruits and the like contained within several vessels situated in distant locations.

Therefore, the claim made previously that "there is no subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) here" is unestablished; for a subverting cognition has already been stated and will be further explained below.

Furthermore, regarding the proof of the unity of the universal (*jāti*), since the universal—being inherent in each individual—is unestablished, the reason "being grasped by a single cognition" is unestablished; thus, it is a fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Moreover, the exclusion of [non-Brāhmaṇas] such as Brāhmaṇas and so forth is not ultimately one, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*); therefore, the example is deficient in its probandum (*sādhyavikala*).

And if the unity to be proven is merely conceptual, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because that which is conceptualized is accepted as being of the nature of *apoha*.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "there is no defect in the cause here," that too is unproven, because a causal defect characterized by the beginningless latencies of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*) does indeed exist. Thus, in this manner, these fallacious arguments (*kuhetu*) are to be refuted.

Having thus stated in detail the refutation of the proofs for the universal (sāmānya) as propounded by others, [the author], desiring to state the valid cognition that sublates the universal, says "Moreover" (apica) and so forth:
"Moreover, regarding that which is called 'subsisting in many' (anekavṛttitva) of the universal:
what is this 'subsistence' (vṛtti) considered to be there—is it 'abiding' (sthiti), or is it simply 'manifestation' (vyakti)?"
Its stability consists in its non-deviation from its own nature by virtue of its very essence;
there is no external substratum capable of producing that [stability], by which it could possess the status of a stabilizer.
Nor is there any obstruction to its movement, as is the case with jujube fruits and the like;
because it is devoid of action, no substratum is therefore postulated for it.
If it is argued that subsistence is their inherence (*samavāya*), it is not examined in that same manner;
for that [inherence] is held to consist in the relationship of substratum and superstratum among things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*).
The subsistence of a universal in its particulars must necessarily be accepted;
otherwise, how could a uniform cognition restricted to those particulars be established as having that [universal] as its basis?

And its subsistence therein must be characterized either as "staying" (sthiti) or as "manifestation" (abhivyakti). Furthermore, staying is twofold: characterized either by the non-deviation from one's own nature, or by the prevention of downward movement.
In this regard, the first [position] is not tenable because, being eternal, it is established by its very nature as never deviating from its own essence.

Nor is the second [position] tenable, because due to its incorporeality and omnipresence, it is inactive and thus incapable of downward motion; therefore, its status as an obstacle is not logically consistent.
Furthermore, the claim that the "subsistence" of a universal in its particulars is its inherence (*samavāya*) is no answer at all, since that very inherence is currently under investigation.

For it is said that *samavāya* (inherence) is the relation characterized by the status of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) among things that are not established separately; and this state of being dependent (*āśritatva*) must belong to the universal either because its existence is restricted to that [substratum] or because it is manifested by it—this is precisely what has begun to be examined.

Indeed, it is not logical for *samavāya* to be a separate entity (*arthāntara*) that performs no function toward entities whose natures are mutually unmixed, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For in that case, everything would be the inherence of everything, since *samavāya* is conceived as that which joins together entities whose forms are mutually distinct.

Furthermore, even if another entity exists, things established in their own nature do not enter into one another's essence, for that would entail the loss of their own form. Thus, there is no dispute regarding the naming of that other entity as "inherence" (samavāya); therefore, it is incorrect to say that "abiding" (sthitih) is a distinct entity.
With the words "It might be," etc., he demonstrates the absolute lack of connection between a universal and the postulation of a substratum.
[p.260] It might be that water and so forth are substrata because they obstruct motion; but what is the use of postulated substrata for universals, which are devoid of motion?
If it is already capable of producing its own cognition, what is the use of causes for manifestation? If it is incapable of producing its own cognition, what is the use of causes for manifestation?
If that which was incapable yesterday were made capable today by manifesting agents,
then the entity would necessarily be unstable, like a jar manifested by a lamp.
"Of those without motion" means of those devoid of movement; for there is an absence of motion due to their being formless and all-pervading.

Furthermore, stability characterized by manifestation is also untenable; for its manifestation consists solely in the production of a cognition having it as its object, rather than being characterized by the nourishment of its own nature, since a change in the nature of a permanent entity is impossible. Consequently, if it possesses the capacity to produce cognition by itself, why would it depend on a cause of manifestation?
On the other hand, if it lacks such capacity, then dependence on that cause is not logical, because its nature cannot be imparted by others.

If it were admitted that [the universal] possesses specific qualities produced by others, the consequence would be its impermanence; and consequently, like an individual, it would not be a universal because of its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*).
Regarding the term "existence" (*bhāva*):
since both the designation and the cognition arise from that which exists, the entire category of the universal is so designated.

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: that for which there exists no basis for occurrence in something does not occur in that thing, just as the Himavat mountain does not exist in the Vindhya range. And there exists no basis for the occurrence of a universal (sāmānya) in its particulars (bheda); this is a non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi).
With the words "the jar and so forth," he states another refutation: "Furthermore, the specific universals (jāti-bheda) such as 'jar' must either exist only in their own substrata,
or they must subsist everywhere like a higher universal (parajāti)."
Regarding the distinctions among universals such as "jar-ness" and so forth:

there are two possible positions concerning universals like "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva) and "earth-ness" (pārthivatva), which are described as being all-pervasive—either they are described as pervading only their own substrata, or else because they exist everywhere even in places devoid of individual instances.
This is "like a higher universal" (parajātivat).
Existence (*sattā*) is designated as "other" because it has a vast scope (*mahāviṣayatva*);
and this [existence] is used as an illustration solely on the basis of the similarity consisting in having a vast scope alone.
It is not [used as an illustration] because it pervades the space situated between other individuals, for even that [space] is not perceived to possess that property [of existence].
Regarding that, he states the fault in the first position with the words "tatra" and so forth:
"In that case, when an object appears in another location, how indeed are they perceived as possessing activity therein? This is not understood."

When an object such as a jar appears in a place devoid of the manifestation of jars and the like, it is not understood—that is to say, it is not comprehended—how those specific universals, such as "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva) and so forth, are seen or exist within that jar and other objects.
He asks "How so? and replies with "For not," and so forth:
"For they do not arise together with it because of its eternity, nor do they abide therein;
furthermore, since they lack prior pervasiveness and are inactive, they do not come from elsewhere."

For instance, if those [universals] were to arise simultaneously with the particular individuals such as jars, or if they were already present there beforehand, or if they were to come from another location, then they would either be perceived or exist therein.

However, since they are eternal, they have no arising; since they are all-pervading, they cannot have existed there previously; and since they are inactive, they cannot come from another place. Therefore, how could their existence or perception occur within those individuals?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which have not arisen in a certain place, nor existed there previously, nor arrived from another location afterwards, are neither perceived nor present in that place—just as a horn on the head of a hare. And such is the case with a universal (*sāmānya*) in relation to an object such as a jar that has arisen in a place devoid of it. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Nor is this reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because there is no other possible mode for its existence or perception therein.
Regarding the second position as well, he states the fault with the words "svāśraya" and so forth: "If,
when there is a connection with the sense organ that is its own substratum and so on, there is the apprehension of that [universal] in one [locus],
it would be perceived everywhere, because there is no differentiation in its essential nature."
From the cause of perception— namely, the contact of [the object] with its own substratum and the sense organ—
the word "etcetera" (ādi) including the contact between the self and the mind and so forth—

if there were a perception of those various universals (jāti) within a single individual instance, then they would be perceived everywhere, even in other instances of a different class and in the intervening space; for each of them, by virtue of having a single uniform nature, would not differ from the form already grasped.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"If [the object] were non-different from what is known, then that [knowledge] too would be apprehended;
or else, like that [object], it would not be apprehended, or there would indeed be a difference."

For instance, if the universal form existing between two individuals were non-different from the universal form perceived as inherent in the observed individual, then that [intervening] universal form would also be apprehended, because it is not distinct from what has been apprehended, just like the nature of the apprehended [individual].

On the other hand, if there is no apprehension of it, then, due to its non-distinction from the unapprehended form, there would likewise be no apprehension of that which inheres in the observed individual.
If, however, both forms are admitted, then a difference in essential nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) follows, owing to the imposition of mutually contradictory properties.

For it is not logical for one of pure intellect to assert that something existing is a single unity when it is characterized by the properties of mutual opposition, such as being perceived and not being perceived; for this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

For in this way, the entire universe would become a single substance, and consequently, there would follow the absurdity of its simultaneous arising and destruction. Otherwise, "one" would be a mere name, and there is no dispute regarding a name.
Having thus refuted "universal" (jāti) in every respect, he sets forth a formal argument (prayoga), saying:
"These cognitions of 'tree' and so forth do not arise from universals postulated by others,
because they possess succession, concomitance, and so on, just like the cognitions of 'cook' and the like."
Furthermore, the fact that what is eternal cannot be a producer is recognized as a subverting argument;
everything that was stated in the refutation of conjunction serves as a subversion here as well.

Those things which possess properties such as succession, concomitance, substantiality, and having an origin do not exist as a universal that is eternal, unitary, and all-pervasive as imagined by others; for example, just like the cognitions of "cook" and so forth, these cognitions of "tree" and so forth are likewise [non-eternal]. This is an instance of the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (viruddhavyāptopalabdhi). Since succession and the other properties are pervaded by non-eternality—which is the opposite of the absence of eternality—and since for an eternal entity there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (arthakriyā) whether it occurs successively or simultaneously, the reason is not inconclusive.
Furthermore, since it has already been established in detail that the example is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyāvikalatā*), the example is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
He also states another refutation beginning with "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.
In that regard, the refutation concerning the critique of conjunction was stated by the words: "And the subsistence of one [entity] in many is not tenable; thus there is a sublation."

Just as the existence of a single entity in multiple locations is not logical, so too has it been demonstrated in the refutation of the composite whole (*avayavin*) by the passage beginning with "for that [whole] would have to occupy a single location," and so forth.
He concludes with the words "Thus" and so forth:
"In this way, the view that this [universal] belongs to an entirely distinct genus has been refuted; however, that which is accepted by the followers of Jaimini will be rejected in the *Syādvāda*."

This refutation has been stated for those Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain that the universal (*jāti*) is absolutely distinct from the individual (*vyakti*). However, as for those such as the Jains, the followers of Jaimini (Mīmāṃsakas), and the Sāṅkhyas who assert a universal that is non-distinct or of a dual nature, the universal described by them will be refuted in the context of the *syād-vāda*.

Here, however, since the universal conceived by the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas is the subject at hand, it is not being refuted here; the point is that there is no occasion for its refutation in this specific context.
Thus concludes the examination of the universal.
He states the refutation of the specific qualities with the words "But those which," and so forth:
"Furthermore, these imagined specific qualities that occur at the end—
by the exclusion of eternal substances— they too are impossible moments."

As for the definition of particulars (viśeṣas) stated—that they reside in eternal substances and exist only in the ultimate substances—that is indeed no definition at all, because it is vitiated by the fault of impossibility. For there is no such thing as an eternal substance, since that was already refuted previously during the examination of substances; how then could their residence in such [substances] be established?

Furthermore, regarding the argument that the existence of these [entities] is established by the power of the yogis' specific cognition, he shows that even there the reason is inconclusive with the words "of atoms, space, direction, and so forth," etc.: "When the unmixed nature of atoms, space, direction, and so forth is established,
then from this [nature] the perception of their distinctness [is derived]."
If those [entities] were again to become mixed with another self,
then even when there is no otherness, there would be no unerring perception of their distinct characteristics.
How is the perception of differentiation among those particularities [established]?
If you say it is "by themselves" (*svata eva*), then why is this not also accepted in the case of atoms and so forth?

Likewise, the form of atoms and so forth must either be mutually unmixed due to their abiding in their own respective natures, or it must be mixed. If the first alternative is held, then since things that are inherently unmixed would be perceived, yogins would possess a cognition of their mutual distinctness on its own; thus, the postulation of further "particularities" (viśeṣa) would be useless.

Now, as for the second position: how could a non-erroneous, distinct cognition arise for yogins even when those [entities], which possess mutually distinct natures, are in proximity with another category of entity called "particularity" (viśeṣa)? That [cognition] would indeed be erroneous, because it occurs in that manner toward what is not that [object]. Consequently, they would be no different from non-yogins, due to being associated with erroneous cognition; such is the sense.

Furthermore, if a distinct cognition does not arise without another category called "particularity" (viśeṣa), then how can a distinct cognition arise with respect to those very particularities themselves? For there are no further particularities residing in them, as that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress;
moreover, it would entail the abandonment of your own tenet that particularities reside only in eternal substances, since they would also reside in [other] particularities.

Therefore, if it is accepted that their mutual distinctness and their status as causes [of cognition] exist by themselves (*svata eva*), then let atoms and the like also have that causal status by themselves. For what reason is there here for this prejudice against them, such that the causal status of producing the cognition of mutual distinctness is not admitted for atoms and the like—which, though existing with forms mutually excluded from one another by themselves—while it is nevertheless admitted for the *viśeṣas*?
We perceive no reason for this other than sheer stupidity.
With the words "by itself alone" (*svata eva*), etc., Praśastamati raises an objection here:

"Just as the impurity of dog-meat and the like is established by its very nature, if it is likewise maintained in this case that the impurity of other things arises through association with that [impure thing]."
Just as a lamp, which is inherently present, illuminates objects such as a jar,
so too is this [consciousness] necessarily fixed in its nature as illumination.

For he has said: just as dog-meat and the like are impure by their very nature, while other things become so through association with them, so too here, because of that identity (*tādātmya*), the quality of being the cause of the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) belongs to the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) by their very nature, and to atoms (*paramāṇu*) through association with them.

Furthermore, even in cases where something does not possess that nature, a cognition [of exclusion] certainly arises due to another cause; for example, in the case of jars and the like, it arises from a lamp, but not in the case of lamps, which arise from jars and the like.
Thus, this [distinction] is restricted.
"A pot and so forth.
"This is such" is the characterization of their distinctness; the meaning is that the particularity of atoms and so on arises from their own particularities alone, by themselves.
He replies with the words beginning "But surely," etc.:
"But surely this state of impurity is merely conventional (sāṃvṛta) and not ultimate (tāttvika);
how then could it possibly arise either by itself or from another?"

Alternatively, even if they were real entities, these impure things would arise due to [the consumption of] dog-meat and so forth; they could not be eternal, because that which is unborn is not eternal.
Indeed, momentary objects such as jars and ornaments acquire the nature of producing cognition through the power of lamps and other such factors.
The cognition of distinctness among those [atoms] does not arise from the power of a specific property that is the subject of dispute,
because it arises sequentially, like pleasure and so forth.

Indeed, the impurity of entities is merely constructed by conceptualization and is not ultimate, because it is unstable. For instance, that very substance which appears as impure to someone such as a Vedic scholar (śrotriya) appears as pure to another, such as a hunter (kauṭika); and it is not logical for two mutually contradictory forms to coexist in a single thing, as that would entail the loss of its unity.
Even if the impurity of entities were real, even so, this is not the same as the example [adduced].
For instance, when substances such as food come into contact with impure things like dog meat, they abandon their previous pure nature and arise as something entirely different—impure.

Therefore, it is logical that their impurity is adventitious (paropādhika). However, there is no such basis for atoms and the like by which they could possess such adventitious distinctness; this is because, being eternal, they are unproduced and do not undergo origination.

In this way, even in the example of the lamp, the fact that jars and other objects serve as causes for the arising of cognition must be understood as being contingent upon external conditions (*paropādhika*).

With the words beginning with "no" (*na*), he states the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the specific qualities; its essential nature and its logical connection (*pratibandha*) must also be stated, just as before.
Thus concludes the examination of particulars.
In order to refute inherence (*samavāya*), he says "in the threads," and so forth:
"The cloth is in these very threads; the mat, moreover, is in the *vīraṇa* grasses"—since such notions as "it is here" exist, inherence is understood.

Inherence (*samavāya*) is that relation which serves as the cause for the cognition "it is here" regarding things that are inseparable and stand in the relationship of the supported and the support; and this is understood to be a distinct entity from substances and the rest, by virtue of the specific cognition "the cloth is here in these threads," and so forth.

For just as existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth, because they produce cognitions corresponding to themselves in their own substrates, are distinct from their own supports and from one another, so too inherence (*samavāya*) is understood to be a distinct entity from the five categories, since we observe such cognitions as: "the cloth is here in these threads," "quality and action are here in this substance," "existence is here in substances, qualities, and actions," "substantiality is here in this substance," "quality-ness is here in these qualities," "action-ness is here in this action," and "ultimate particularities are here in these substances. Thus, its status as a separate entity from the five categories is established.

The formal argument is as follows: whatever cognition regarding certain things is distinct from their own forms must be based on an object other than those things, just like the cognition "the staff-bearer" with respect to Devadatta; and such is this cognition of "here" (ihapratyaya) regarding the five categories. This is considered a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Showing the obstacle to this [position], he says: "In its absence," and so forth.
If that [object] were absent, what indeed would be the basis for this cognition?
A cognition of a particular [quality] is never observed to be devoid of another cause.
And because there is no difference in the cognition of "this-ness," it is not divided like [the cognition of] a conjunction;
rather, this [universal] is perceived as one alone throughout all its instances.
And because its cause is not perceived, it is eternal, just like [other] entities;
for no cause whatsoever of this is perceived by any means of valid cognition.

The subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against you is that, in the absence of an underlying relation (*nibandhana*), there would follow the consequence of [the cloth] existing eternally and so forth.

Thus, first according to the view of the Vaiśeṣikas, inherence (*samavāya*) is to be inferred from the mark of the cognition "here" (*ihabuddhi*); however, according to the view of the Naiyāyikas, it is indeed directly perceivable through the cognition "here.
For they declare it to be perceptible because, when the operation of the senses is present, there arises the cognition, "The cloth is here in these threads," and so on.

And this inherence (*samavāya*), unlike conjunction (*saṃyoga*) which differs among various relations, does not differ in this way. Rather, like existence (*bhāva*)—that is, like the universal existence (*sattā*)—inherence is one and the same everywhere because its defining mark is non-distinct and there is no specific mark to differentiate it.
The phrase "like conjunction" is an example by contrast (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Furthermore, because it is not a cause, inherence is established as eternal just like existence; and its lack of causality is established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by the non-perception of any cause.
With the words "This very [point]" and so forth, he begins the refutation:
"This very cognition here belongs only to others;
through attachment to their own tenets, they have failed to see that it is indeed worldly."

By this, he states that the reason (hetu) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished substratum (āśrayāsiddhatā). For cognitions such as "the cloth is in these threads" are merely fabricated through attachment to one's own philosophical tenets;
they are not experienced as arising in that manner in common worldly experience. Therefore, the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) is not established.
With the words "nānātva" (diversity) and so forth, he supports that very same lack of establishment of the substratum (*dharmin*): "For if there were diversity as their defining characteristic,
there would arise the cognition 'this is here' regarding the locus and the located, as in the case of bilva fruits and the like in a bowl."
There is no perception of multiplicity in the case of threads, cloth, and so forth,
by virtue of which the cognitions "this is here" would arise with respect to them.

For in this world, the cognition "here" arises only when a relationship of locus and located exists between two things whose distinctness has been perceived, as seen in the case, for example, of "mangoes here in the bowl. However, no distinctness is perceived between the threads and the cloth; so how could the cognition "here" occur in that case?

It might be argued: "Even if this mental construction (*ihamati*) has been devised by us on the strength of our own tenets, you must still state its basis. To this he says, "By one's own will," and so forth: "Whether this [cognition] is produced by one's own will or is like things imagined, this demand for a cause does not hold against an opponent."

For how can one who does not even accept that something is a cause be questioned about its effect by having that effect itself postulated? Indeed, you yourself must be questioned as to why you have postulated this effect according to the force of your own desire; for desires do not conform to the intrinsic nature of things, since even an object postulated by you could be postulated otherwise by others.

Furthermore, demonstrating that not only are cognitions such as "the cloth is here in these threads" unestablished in the world, but rather their opposites are what are well-known, he says "tree," and so forth:
"Branches on a tree, stones on a goat— this is the worldly understanding."
Because of the perception of the uninterrupted succession of the parts of the body known as "the house" (agākhya).
Furthermore, the cognition that "those [qualities] are in those [substances]" is said to transcend the world;
however, one understands identity in the form "the color and action are in the jar."
For words such as "form" (rūpa) and "jar" denote all states;
they are applied in that manner in order to denote specific instances of those states.
Having perceived those [individuals], consciousness functions toward them in that form;
for, due to inherence, no distinction among any of them is observed.
In the world, one observes that "branches are on the tree" and "rocks are on the mountain," but not that "the tree is in the branches" or "the mountain is in the rocks.

Furthermore, this cognition—that branches are on a tree and so forth—is not due to inherence (*samavāya*), but rather because of the perception of the uninterrupted proximity of those remaining parts called "limbs" (*aga*), such as the trunk and so on, which are distinct from the intended branch or rock and are situated below.
Here, by the word *aga*, trees and mountains are intended in the sense of "that which does not move" (*na gacchanti*).
"Those two" refers to the cow and the tree;
"in those" refers to the stone and the branches.

To the question, "What then is the object of that well-known worldly cognition—such as 'there is color, taste, smell, touch, and motion in this jar'—if one sets aside its inherence (samavāya)? he says "the jar," and so forth.

The meaning is that identity (*tādātmya*) consists in the nature of the jar being its form (*rūpa*), and not in [the jar] having the nature of the form and so forth. With the desire to indicate a specific common power among the many [qualities] such as form and so on, the term "jar" is applied by way of excluding other forms and so forth; however, the term "form" and so on is applied to illuminate the capacity for producing individual, non-common effects such as visual consciousness. Therefore, since the term "jar" does not imply the distinctions of form and so on, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); rather, identity is established through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
He asks: for what purpose is the employment of both [terms]? He replies with the words "rūpakumbha" and so forth.

For words such as *rūpa* (form) and the like are denoters of form and so forth in all their states. To explain: just as form and the like that exist in the nature of a jar are called "form and the like," so too are those existing in the nature of a cloth and so forth. Consequently, from the mere words "form and the like," no specific distinction is understood—namely, in what state the forms and so forth are. However, when used in the expression "the forms and so forth in a jar," they are understood through the exclusion of cloth and other things as being of the nature of a jar.

Likewise, the word "jar" also denotes the jar in all its states—whether white, yellow, moving, or stationary—and so forth; therefore, from the word alone, there is no cognition of a specific attribute. However, in an expression such as "the white color in the jar," comprehension occurs through the exclusion of other colors and so on. Consequently, in order to denote such a specific attribute, those words were employed in the form "color in the jar. The word "words" (*śabdāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Relying on those words, cognition proceeds with respect to these things such as jars in that form—such as "color in the jar" and so forth—but it does not proceed by relying on inherence (*samavāya*); this is the connection [of the sentence].
He states the reason for this in the passage beginning with "of the difference" (*bhedasya*), etc.
For no mutual difference is perceived among all these factors: inherence, the jar, color, and so forth.

By this, it is stated that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and that the thesis is sublated by inference and other means of valid cognition, since there would otherwise be a cognition based on a causal complex (*samavāya*).
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "because there is no difference in the cognition of 'here'," he says: "If inherence were one... and so forth.
If inherence were a single entity existing in all things, then the cognition of "cloth" and so on would necessarily follow even in relation to potsherds and the like.
It follows that the nature of "cowness" and so forth also exists in elephants and other animals;
therefore, these possess the form of a cow and the like, just as a brindled cow does.
That which exists in the threads of a cloth is perceived through inherence;
since that same [inherence] exists in the potsherds as well, why is it not so [perceived] there?
If it is argued that [the jar] does not reside in the potsherds, surely it is held to reside even in the threads;
why then does it not also reside in the potsherds by way of inherence (*samavāya*)?
For that which is called the "inherence" of the cloth in its threads would likewise exist in the potsherds of a jar; thus, the cognition of that [inherence] would be without limit.
If there were a single collection (samavāya) throughout the three worlds, then cognitions such as "a cloth in potsherds" would also arise;
furthermore, it would follow that "cowness" and so forth exist in horses and other animals.
Consequently, just as there is a cognition of "cow" in variegated cows and the like, such a cognition would also occur in relation to elephants and other creatures.

For instance, regarding the cognition "the cloth is in the threads" which is described as arising through the power of inherence (*samavāya*), that very inherence exists in the potsherds and so forth with respect to that same cloth; yet such a cognition does not occur.
This too is false.

For why should that inherence—which is described as existing by virtue of its power in the case of the cloth being supported in the threads—not exist in the potsherds, such that the cognition "the cloth is there" would not arise in them just as it does in the threads?
But that very inherence which is designated as the inherence of the cloth in the threads is the same as the inherence of the cloth in the potsherds; how then could there not be confusion?

Therefore, the cognition would be without limit—that is, devoid of any restriction—because the relation of substances, qualities, and actions with their qualifiers such as "substance-ness," "quality-ness," and "action-ness" is one and the same.
The classification of the five categories would not be possible.
With the words "In this way," and so forth, he establishes the consequence that there would be the cognition of cows and the like with respect to elephants and the like.

"In this way, that very same inherence of elephant-ness and so forth which exists in elephants and the like, belongs to the distinct universals such as cow-ness and so forth, even in their own respective substrata."
With the words beginning "ādhāra" (the substratum), Praśastamati here raises an objection, providing the following answer:
"The restriction of the substratum and the superstratum exists even when there is identity;
for it is indeed observed among substances, as well as among universals and actions, that they possess the nature of being an action."
For he says: although inherence (*samavāya*) is one, nevertheless there is no confusion among the five categories, because of the restriction between locus and located.

For instance, "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) exists only in substances, "qualityness" (*guṇatva*) only in qualities, and "actionness" (*karmatva*) only in actions; thus, the cognition of substanceness and the other [categories] arises through the delimitation of their respective restricted loci. If this is so, then it follows that inherence must be different for each category; to this he replies with the words "here" (*iha*), etc.
[The word] "here" is used because one observes the persistence of the cognition arising from inherence.
It is understood that this inherence is one and the same everywhere.
Because the exclusion of the causes such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva) is observed,
the restriction of cognitions regarding the universals such as "substance" is determined.

Because the cognition whose cause is inherence (*samavāya*) is observed everywhere to have an identical form—expressed as "it is here"—it is understood that inherence is one and the same in all cases.

Furthermore, even though it is unitary, because cognitions caused by "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth arise only with respect to their respective limited substrates, the exclusion (*vyatireka*) characterized by non-occurrence elsewhere is observed; thus, the distinctness of the universals such as "substanceness" is known.
Consequently, there is no confusion among the five categories.

But how is it that, even though there is no difference in their relationship, this specific restriction of container and contained is logical for these [elements]? To this he says: "Just as," and so forth.
Just as in the case of a bowl and its curd, although their conjunction is one and the same, a restriction of container and contained is observed; so too here, such a restriction is held to exist.

If it is argued that, although inherence (samavāya) is a single entity, there is no contradiction [in its being manifold] due to the difference in the capacities of the manifested and the manifestor among the universals such as substance and so forth; |||

Just as there is a fixed relationship between substratum and superstratum despite the unity of the conjunction between a bowl and curd, so too, despite the unity of inherence (*samavāya*) in the case of substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the like, there is a fixed relationship between locus and located due to the distinction between the powers of the manifestor and the manifested.
This refers to the restriction of locus and located.
[Page 270] He offers a rebuttal beginning with "the locus and the located" (*ādhārādheya*):
"The restriction of locus and located is difficult to establish if there is identity between them.
Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is held to reside only in a substance; how could that be so by way of inherence (*samavāya*)?"
And that inherence of his is also found in qualities and so forth;
for this [inherence] is indeed one and the same for both, due to its connection with qualities, universals, and so on.

For us, a restriction regarding the inherence of "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth within "form" (*rūpa*) and the like is not established; rather, it is for you alone. And that [restriction] is difficult to maintain for those who admit only a single, universal inherence (*samavāya*), as we shall demonstrate through such reductio arguments (*prasaṅga*).
