To explain: the restriction that "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) resides only in substance is held to be due to the power of inherence; yet that very same inherence which belongs to "substance-ness" and the like exists even in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, because they are related to them by way of universals such as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*).

Even if there were such a relation, how could it be established that "that very same inherence (samavāya) exists therein"? To this he says, "only one," and so forth. "Of those two" refers to the universals (jāti) such as substance-ness and quality-ness.
Therefore, because they would have an identical cause, the consequence of their confusion (saṅkara) would be unavoidable; this is the intended meaning.
Otherwise, this [Yoga] would be distinct [from itself] due to differences in qualities, genus, and so forth,
just as Yoga is differentiated with respect to each individual according to the difference between practitioners.

"Otherwise" means that if the inherence of "substance-ness" (dravyatva) in a substance were not the very same as the inherence of "quality-ness" (guṇatva) and so forth in qualities and the like, then—inherence would differ with each substratum, just as conjunction does.
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "of the causes such as substantiality," he says:

"Of the causes such as substantiality, etc."—the exclusion [of these causes] from cognitions is not tenable because the causes do exist; therefore, their restriction [to specific objects] is also not possible.

For when the cause is unimpaired, it is not logical for there to be an absence—i.e., a non-existence—of the effect, because that would entail the consequence that the effect is not produced by that cause.
Consequently, since an absence of cognitions is impossible, a restriction regarding that relationship of locus and located is also not tenable.

[Objection: "Surely, the restriction will be established through such designations as 'substantiality (dravyatva) is supported by and resides in substance (dravya) itself'. [Reply: To this, he says "tadāśritatva... and so forth: "Being supported by that, residing in it, and so on, are designated as originating from that very [substance] due to inherence (samavāya); therefore, this [inherence] is not a suitable regulator of that [restriction]."

For it is precisely from that very inherence (*samavāya*) that you describe the determination of such things as "being supported" (*āśritatva*); yet, since that [inherence] is indistinguishable everywhere, how can this restriction be justified?

Therefore, even this "being supported" and so forth is not logically the regulator of that relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), because these [properties] share the same fate as the relationship of container and contained itself.

[Page 271] If it is argued that the restriction will then arise from the specific determination of the powers of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), he says "of the manifested," etc.:
"Even the distinction between the capacities of the manifested and the manifestor arises from inherence (*samavāya*);
it does not arise from anything else, because production is impossible for eternal things."
The statement that substances and so forth are the manifestors of universals such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) occurs solely by virtue of inherence (*samavāya*).
For it is precisely because substantiality inheres in a substance that it is said to be manifested by it;
not otherwise.
Because [the Samkhya] maintains that it arises from the production of a nature capable of generating cognition as described by the Sugatas;
since inherence (*samavāya*) is also accepted for eternal things such as existence (*sattā*), the production of eternal things is not logical.
He supports this very point with the words beginning with "na hi" (for not):
"For jars and other such classes of things do not become capable of producing consciousness merely through the presence of lamps and the like, in the same way as these [atoms] are."

Furthermore, he shows that even the example cited—the conjunction of the bowl and the curd—is unestablished for us, in the passage beginning with "of the bowl and the curd. The single conjunction of the bowl and the curd has already been refuted;
moreover, it is not restricted [to those two alone], because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Regarding the word "previously":
this refers to the refutation of the category of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
He shows that even if conjunction were to exist as a single entity, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would apply there as well, by stating "and that [conjunction]... and so forth.
"Therefore" means because of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
The "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*) refers to the undesirable consequence that cognitions such as "the bowl is in the curd" would arise;
this is because the cause, namely conjunction, is indistinguishable [in all cases].
Regarding what was stated—that inherence is eternal because no cause for its production is perceived—the author replies with the verse beginning "By virtue of its eternity," and so forth:
"By virtue of its being eternal, all things [such as jars and the like] would necessarily become eternal;
for their inherence in their substrata would exist at all times, since it does not depend on [any further] establishment."

For if inherence were eternal, it would follow that jars and other such things would also be eternal, because they would exist at all times within their own substrata. To explain: it is precisely because of the existence of inherence that these things are held to abide in their substrata; and since that inherence is eternal, why should these things not remain so forever?

With the words "svārambhaka" and so forth, he anticipates the opponent’s reply: "If it is argued that those [qualities], such as action and the rest, perish either through the disjunction of their own constituent parts or through their destruction— just as [action perishes] through conjunction and so forth— that is not so."
For their inherence in their own substrata is also held to be eternal;
however, if those [substrata] were subject to destruction, its [inherence’s] perishability would be certain as well.
It might be argued as follows: the destruction of jars and the like occurs through the disjunction or the destruction of their own constituent parts.
For example, in the states of being wound up or baked, the motions and other qualities of a jar perish due to contact with a substance possessing touch, and so forth.
As it has been stated: "Motion perishes from contact with a substance possessing touch, and motion is also opposed by its effect."
Likewise, according to the system of others, the destruction of one cognition occurs through another cognition, and that of a sound through another sound.

Thus, even though inherence exists as the cause of subsistence, because of the absence of other auxiliary causes and due to the encounter with a contrary condition, there is no consequence of permanence for jars and the like; such is the position of the opponent.
[The author replies: That is not so; since inherence always exists in the other constituent parts that originate it, how could there be destruction or disjunction?
By the word "also" (api), he indicates that this applies not only to the substances initiated by it, but also to their actions and so forth.
For if the destruction of its own constituent parts were admitted, then the destruction of this inherence (samavāya) would necessarily follow as well.
He asks "Why? and replies with the words "For when the related term has ceased," and so forth.
For when the related term has ceased, it is difficult to maintain that the relation still exists;
indeed, even when the conjoined [substances] have perished, the conjunction does not fail to persist [as a non-entity].
Just as there is the persistence of conjoined things when conjunction exists,
so too would there be [the persistence] of inherent things when inherence exists.
Demonstrating this very point, he says "nahi" and so forth.
Consequently, because its relata have perished, it follows that inherence would be impermanent—just like a conjunction whose conjuncts have perished;
or else, the persistence of the relata would follow, because their connection has not perished, just like two substances whose conjunction has not ceased.
Otherwise, for both [parties], there would follow the loss of the very nature of that relation.
With the words "Even upon the destruction of one relation," etc., the opponent objects:

"Even when one related member is destroyed, inherence (samavāya) persists because of the existence of the other related member; if you say it does not, that is not so, because [inherence] is non-different [from the relation]."

He thinks as follows: if, in the first reason, the intended meaning of the reason is "because all related things have perished," then the reason is unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*).
For the destruction of all related things does not occur anywhere.

Because even at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), atoms and so forth remain. Now, if the reason is stated with reference to a connection consisting in having some kind of destroyed relatum, then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*); for even if one relatum has perished somewhere, its persistence will still be based on another relatum. Anticipating the objection that "if this were the case, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would also consequently become eternal," the opponent replies: "Not because of difference" (*na bhedataḥ*).
For conjunction (*saṃyoga*) differs according to its correlates;
therefore, its impermanence is logical. Inherence (*samavāya*), however, is one and the same throughout the world, because the basis for the cognition "here" (*iha-pratyaya*) is undifferentiated.
Therefore, its impermanence is illogical, since it is perceived even in other related objects elsewhere.
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "If this is so" (*yadyevam*):
"If this is so, then regarding those inherent entities such as jars that perish, that inherence which has been postulated as consisting of their subsistence [in a substrate]— "
Would that very [conjunction] itself remain fixed because of its existence in another related object, or is it something else entirely,
like plurality and so forth?
Not the first [alternative], because if inherence, which has that very characteristic, were established,
then jars and other such things would necessarily remain exactly as they were before.
If those [qualities] do not persist, then their inherence (samavāya), which consists in their functioning, could not subsist anywhere;
or rather, it would exist as such merely by name.

Therefore, because they exist even prior [to the arising of their support], those [properties] would not have occurred in the support, just as they do afterwards; for thus, their occurrence is unreal.

For instance, regarding those things such as jars that perish—which are inherent in their own causes—is it the very same inherence (samavāya), conceived as consisting in their existence within their own causes, that remains when they have perished but relates to other relata; or is it something else entirely, just as conjunction or plurality differs with each respective relatum?
By the word "etcetera," disjunction and so forth are included.

In that regard, if the first position is held, then because their activity has not ceased—just as in their prior state—it follows that jars and so forth must remain exactly as they were; or else, if those jars and so forth do not remain, then because their activity is non-abiding, it follows that there can be no abiding of the inherence (*samavāya*), for otherwise it would not consist of "subsistence" (*vṛtti*).

And if such a thing, being independent and providing no assistance, is given the name "inherence" merely as a designation for its subsistence, then there is no actual reality corresponding to that designation.
"Consisting of that function"— thus he demonstrates the fault of its being a mere conventional designation by the words "therefore" and so forth.
"Even before the destruction of the relata" means even in the state where the relata have not yet been destroyed.
Those things, such as jars and the like,
which reside in their own substratum, would not be established by the existence of that inherence due to the power of its presence;
for, ultimately, there is no actual residence [of the effect] in it, just as in the case of a destroyed inherent cause.
With the words "For it is thus" and so forth, he demonstrates the meaning of the reason.
Alternatively, like conjunction, disjunction, plurality, and so forth,
inherence persists only when another related entity exists.
For in this way, like conjunction and so forth, there would indeed be a multiplicity of this; if such an original entity were to exist, much that is inconsistent would follow.

If the second position—that it is indeed something else—is maintained, then, like conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, there would follow a multiplicity of inherences (*samavāya*). Consequently, the unity of inherence would be lost, and there would be an abandonment of the accepted doctrine of its eternity.

By the phrase "and so forth" (*evam-ādi*), other defects are included: the futility of causes, contradiction with numerous sūtras, contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition, and the simultaneous production of all categories of entities.

For instance, birth (*janman*) is said to be either inherence in its own cause (*svakāraṇasamavāya*) or inherence in existence (*sattāsamavāya*), and since inherence is eternal, causes would have no efficacy whatsoever in the production of any effect; thus, there would be a futility of causes.

Furthermore, this contradicts those sūtras that establish the production [of effects], such as "conjunction is born from the action of one [of two things], from the action of both, or from conjunction," and "knowledge produced by the contact of the sense-organ with the object.
Likewise, it contradicts the eyes and other organs which are the causes for the cognition of perception and so forth.
Likewise, since birth—characterized as inherence—is eternal, there can be no sequence; thus, the sequential arising of perceived entities would be contradicted.
Consequently, the statement that "the non-simultaneous production of cognitions is the mark of the mind" would contradict one's own established tenet.

Furthermore, because birth is eternal, the world would consist of things that neither benefit nor harm one another, rendering the composition of the scriptures useless; thus, many other such inconsistencies would result in a doctrine that is torn asunder and shattered.
Thus concludes the examination of the category of inherence.

In order to establish that the objects of verbal and conceptual cognitions consist of superimposed forms, [the author], setting forth the introductory context, says: "If," and so on. "If no limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) whatsoever exist in an ultimate sense, [then how could there be] such cognitions and words as 'the man with a staff,' 'white,' 'he moves,' 'it exists,' or 'a cow here'?"
What could be the objects of these two? They are not considered to be without an object; for their functioning toward everything without distinction is impossible.
For it is the thing (*vastu*) itself that is ultimately graspable by words and cognitions.

Therefore, because the nature of a thing is directly communicated through affirmation and negation by means of words, the view of those who maintain that the word-meaning is positive (*vidhi-śabdārtha-vādin*) is that the word-meaning is indeed an affirmation.
For the proponents of exclusion (*apoha-vādin*), however, there is in reality no objective form whatsoever that constitutes the denotation of words.
For every verbal cognition is indeed erroneous, because it functions by determining a non-differentiated form with respect to objects that are actually distinct.
However, it is observed that where there is an indirect connection to a real entity (*vastu*), there is correspondence with the object despite the cognition being erroneous.
In that case, that non-differentiated form which is superimposed upon objects by the conceptualizing mind is [the universal]. 1.
1. Because it arises through the force of experiencing an object as excluded from others;
2. because it itself appears as being excluded from others;
3. and because it is determined by those under delusion to be one with an object that is excluded from others.
And because its fruit is the comprehension of an object as excluded from others, it is called "excluded from others" (*anyāpoḍha*).
By this, it is well established that exclusion (*apoha*) is the meaning of a word.

In this regard, the proponents of the theory of positive affirmation (vidhivādins) raise an objection: "If, according to you, the adjuncts (*upādhi*)—characterized as substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—which serve as the causes for verbal cognition and conceptualization do not exist in ultimate reality, then how is it that in the world there proceed designations and cognitions such as 'the man with a staff' (*daṇḍin*), which are caused by adjuncts such as substance and the rest? For instance, in common usage, the cognition and expression 'the man with a staff' or 'the one with horns' are well known to have substance as their adjunct; 'white' or 'black' have quality as their adjunct; 'he moves' or 'he wanders' have action as their cause; 'it exists' or 'it is found' have existence (*sattā*) as the cause of their application; 'cow', 'horse', or 'elephant' have generality and particularity as their adjuncts; and 'the cloth is here in these threads' proceeds by virtue of inherence (*samavāya*)."
In that regard, if these [factors] such as substance were non-existent, the cognition and verbal expression "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth would be without an object.
The inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is connected to each [term].
By this, there is the inclusion of cognitions and verbal expressions of the same class for each [case], such as "one with an umbrella" (*chatrin*) and "one with horns" (*viṣāṇin*).
The final particularities (*viśeṣas*), however, are perceivable only by yogins; therefore, they are not included by the word "beginning" (*ādi*).
Nor is it logical for these two [the universal and the particular] to be without a cause (*animitta*), because that would entail their functioning everywhere, at all times, and without distinction.
Furthermore, there is no functioning of these two without differentiation.

Therefore, the opponent [argues] that substance and so forth do exist. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those [cognitions] whose occurrences are mutually non-confounded possess a basis; for example, the cognitions of the ear and other [senses]. And the word-cognitions such as "the one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) have non-confounded occurrences; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
The subverting proof [against the opponent's position] is that if there were signlessness (*animittatva*), it would follow that activity would occur everywhere without distinction.
To this, he replies with the verse beginning "It is said," etc. (TS 868).
It is said that there is no object whatsoever for these cognitions and words;
rather, their basis is the seed residing within the internal dimension alone.

In this regard, if it is intended to establish that these [cognitions] possess an objective cause (*sanimittatva*) primarily by means of an external object, then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the opposite of the thesis (*sādhyaviparyaya*).
Alternatively, if it is intended that they possess an objective cause by means of any cause whatsoever, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

For we indeed accept that the awakening of the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for internal verbal discourse is their cause, but not an external object; since the former, being erroneous, lacks an external object as its referent.
"Residing within the internal measure" means residing in consciousness—that is to say, as a latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Having thus [explained it], he says "of whatever... and so forth, in order to corroborate this very point with scripture (TS 869).
For whatever object is expressed by whichever word, that [object] does not at all coalesce [with it]; for such is the true nature (dharmatā) of things.
"Whichever object" refers to the particular (svalakṣaṇa), the universal (sāmānya), and so forth.

"For that is the true nature of phenomena" (dharmatā) means that it is the primordial nature (prakṛti); in other words, the fact that things transcend all paths of speech is their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
As it has been said:
"By whatever name each and every phenomenon is expressed, that phenomenon does not exist therein; for such is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena."
Thus [it is said].

[p.276] (2p.340) Now, if it is asked what is the proof for the fact that verbal cognition is both erroneous (*bhrāntatva*) and lacks a real object (*aviṣayatva*), we have already stated the proof here: because it proceeds by determining non-difference among things that are actually different, this entire verbal cognition is erroneous.
For indeed, whatever cognition takes one thing to be another when it is not that thing is erroneous, just like the cognition of water in a mirage.
Thus, this verbal cognition, which determines non-difference among distinct objects, is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Nor can it be argued that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) because there exists no real entity (*vastubhūta*) as a universal (*sāmānya*) to be apprehended by it, for such a thing has already been refuted at length.
Or, let there be a universal; even so, if it were an entity distinct from the particulars, then the determination of non-difference among distinct things would be nothing but an error.
For it is not logical that distinct things could be identical by virtue of something else [a universal], such that they might be called "possessors of that" (*tadvant*);
even if the universal were not a separate entity, the entire universe would in reality be a single object, and thus the cognition of a universal therein would be nothing but an error.
Indeed, the cognition of a universal does not have a single object as its domain, because it is preceded by the apprehension of difference.
Once error is established, objectlessness is also established,
because there is no external object— capable of imparting its own form to the cognition— that could satisfy the definition of an objective support (*ālambana*).
Alternatively, objectlessness is proven in another way.
For that alone which has been the object of convention for words is their proper referent, and nothing else, because [otherwise] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And since no convention regarding these [words] exists in reality with respect to any entity whatsoever, cognitions and words are devoid of objects. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which have not been conventionally established in relation to something do not, in ultimate reality, denote it—just as the word "horse," when its convention has not been established, does not denote an individual possessing a dewlap and so forth; and all words have not been conventionally established in relation to any entity in reality. This is a proof by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Because the status of being a denoter is pervaded by having a conventional agreement (*kṛtasamaya*), and that [agreement] is absent here;
and showing that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says "since," and so forth:
"Since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the universal (*jāti*), the connection with that [universal], and likewise the possessor of the universal..."
In reality, the form of the cognition does not fit with the meaning of the word.

For instance, when an object for which a convention has been grasped is established as the referent of a word, it may be established as either the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), or the universal (*jāti*), or the connection with that universal—where "connection" (*yoga*) means a relation—or else as the possessor of the universal, or as the mental image (*ākāra*) of the cognition of the object; these are the alternatives.
Since a convention is impossible in all of these cases, it is not logical for them to be the referents of words.
By the phrase "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*), he shows that there is no negation of the conventional referent of words.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with one's own words;
for otherwise, there would be a contradiction between the thesis and one's own statement.

This is because it is impossible to demonstrate that these [categories], such as specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, are not the referents of words without first having communicated them through words.

Furthermore, by intending to explain that very point and thereby indicating the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth through words, one would necessarily admit that these are the referents of words.
Yet, that same point is subsequently negated by the formal proposition (*pratijñā*); thus, there is a contradiction with one's own statement (*svavacanavyāghāta*).

By this, the argument stated by Uddyotakara—"If words lack denotative power, there is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason"—is also refuted; for we do not deny the existence of word-referents altogether, since that is recognized even by cowherds.
However, it is the property of reality that others have superimposed upon that [subject] which is negated;
but not the subject itself.

In that regard, demonstrating first that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) cannot be the referent of words by showing the impossibility of establishing a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) with respect to it, he says "tatra" and so forth: "In that case, the particular characteristic is not at all communicated by words,
because it lacks the pervasion [necessary] between the time of the convention and the time of practical usage."
"It is not expressed by words" means that there is an absence of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) in that regard.
To the question "How is there an absence of convention?", he says "convention," and so forth.

The time that is reached or attained through convention (*saṅketa*) and linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*); because of its separation from the pervasion—that is, the encompassing—of that [time], there is no convention regarding that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). This is the remainder [of the sense].

What is meant is this: for a convention is established for the sake of linguistic usage, not out of mere whim; therefore, it is only with respect to that which possesses the quality of pervading the time reached by convention and linguistic usage that a convention is appropriate for speakers, and not elsewhere.

Furthermore, a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not possess the quality of pervading the times of convention and linguistic usage; therefore, no linguistic convention (samaya) can apply to it.

But why is it that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) cannot pervade the times of convention and linguistic usage? To this he says: "The individuals themselves," and so forth: "The individuals themselves do not follow one another in their mutual form, due to differences in place, time, action, capacity, appearance, and so on."
Therefore, the object perceived through convention is not seen in actual usage;
nor can one who has not grasped the convention be awakened by a sound, just like another person.
For individual instances such as brindled cows and the like, whose forms are entirely excluded from one another due to differences in location and so forth, do not interpenetrate each other.
Consequently, for a person who has established a linguistic convention regarding one instance, there would be no practical usage with respect to others.
By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "appearance and so forth," the inclusion of specific colors, shapes, states, and other particularities is intended.
"The conventional usage is not observed.
The meaning is that because there is no linguistic convention (*samaya*) regarding that [object] there, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, demonstrating that it is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "And not 'unapprehended,'" and so forth.
That in which a convention has been grasped is "one for whom the convention is grasped"; one for whom it has not been grasped is "one for whom the convention is not grasped.
"As if other" means like an object of a different class (*vijātīya*).
"Of the sound" means of the word (*śabda*).
This is what is meant: if a word were to convey an object for which no convention has been established, then even the word "cow" would convey a horse.
Furthermore, the establishment of conventions would be rendered useless.
Therefore, the occurrence of such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and thus the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.

This very reason—that "because it is not subject to convention" (*akṛtasamayatvāt*)—was indicated by the teacher Dignāga in the passage: "A genus-term (*jātiśabda*) is not a denoter of particulars because of their infinity (*ānantyāt*).
For, by the phrase "because of their infinity," the impossibility of convention itself is demonstrated.

Consequently, what was stated by Uddyotakara—"If you take words as the subject (*pakṣa*), then the reason 'because of their infinity' is misplaced (*vyadhikaraṇa*), since it is a property of real entities (*vastudharma*)"—is refuted.

Now, if the particulars themselves (*bheda*) are made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), then there exists neither a positive nor a negative example; thus, "infinite variety" (*ānantya*) is not a valid reason (*ahetu*). That [objection] has been answered. Again, he says: "This fault applies to one for whom particulars are denoted by words without qualifications (*nirviśeṣaṇa*); but for us, substances, qualities, and actions are denoted as qualified by existence (*sattā*) and so forth.
For instance, wherever one perceives a universal such as existence, there one employs a word such as 'existent' (*sat*)."

"And there is only one universal, such as 'existence' (sattā), and therefore, since the establishment of linguistic convention (*samaya*) is possible with respect to particulars characterized by that universal, their infinity is not an obstacle.
This is incorrect;
for it has already been established that no real entity (*vastubhūta*) called a universal, such as "existence," exists as either distinct from or identical to those [particulars].

Or, let there be a universal; even so, because multiple universals can coexist within a single particular, the application of words such as "existent" (*sat*) and so forth would not serve their purpose through non-confusion.

Furthermore, the author of the convention (*samayakāra*) would not be able to cause others to indirectly indicate (*upalakṣayituṃ*) particulars by means of that existence and so forth without first presenting existence and the rest through the word.
Nor is there the application of words for existence and so forth in cases where no convention has been established.
Consequently, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Suppose it were argued that the cognizer himself, through the observation of linguistic usage and by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), understands the convention (*samaya*) regarding words such as "existent" (*sat*) and so forth.
This is incorrect.
For no one perceives a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) that encompasses every single particular (*bheda*) without exception.

If it is argued that, having perceived a repeated linguistic usage once with respect to particulars that possess existence (*sattā*) and so forth, one then applies that same terminology even to unperceived particulars of that same class, we say no; because they have not been perceived.
For a linguistic convention (*samaya*) is impossible regarding infinite particulars—divided by past and future—that have never been perceived, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that one indeed engages with those [particulars] after having designated them through a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), then it follows that the application of words has as its object only a thing superimposed by conceptualization, and not particulars in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

For, since the past and the future are non-existent and thus not present, the conceptualizing cognition occurring with respect to them is entirely without an objective referent; therefore, what is designated by it is simply non-existent. Consequently, how could a convention (*samaya*) established therein be ultimately a real entity? Enough of this prolixity.
Since it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa), the reason is not contradictory; thus, it is established that words do not have particular characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as their object.

It might be argued: "Since entities such as the Himalayas possess a stable and uniform nature, no differentiation based on distinctions of place, time, and so forth is possible for them; therefore, because they pervade the time of convention and linguistic usage, a linguistic agreement (*samaya*) is possible regarding them. Thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddhatā*). To this, he says: "The Himalayas and so forth," etc.:
"Even those things such as the Himalayas that appear undifferentiated by place, time, and so forth—atoms within them have been shown to be distinct and momentary."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), places such as Malaya are included.

For these are by nature an accumulation of many atoms; therefore, no convention exists that encompasses all their constituent parts. Furthermore, it has been established that they perish immediately after arising.
Therefore, even in these cases, the nature observed at the time of the convention does not persist through the times of linguistic usage; thus, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

Thus far, it has been demonstrated that a linguistic convention (samaya) is not possible regarding a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), because conventional usage would be untenable and it would follow that the convention is useless.
Now, demonstrating that it is impossible precisely because it cannot be established, he says: "It is impossible," and so forth.
"It is impossible to conceive this convention [either] with respect to what has arisen or what has not yet arisen."
A real convention is not possible for that which has not arisen, just like a horse's horn.
Furthermore, when words previously uttered have been grasped and later recollected,
how indeed can a convention be established regarding that which has long since passed away?

All entities have been previously established as perishing immediately after their arising; regarding these, a convention (*samaya*) being made would have to be made either when they have not yet arisen or when they have already arisen.

In that regard, first of all, a convention is not logically possible for things that have not yet arisen from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). However, there is no contradiction with observed experience because conventions are seen even in the case of an unborn son and so forth, since such [conventions] do not pertain to actual reality, having as their object a thing constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), like the "horn of a horse."
The suffix *vati* is applied to a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*).

Nor is it logical for a convention (*samaya*) to be established regarding something already arisen; for a convention must be formed when there is the arising of an experience and the subsequent recollection of the distinction of names based on that [experience], and not otherwise, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Consequently, at the time of recollecting the distinction of names, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has long since ceased due to its momentary destruction. Thus, just as with the unborn, there is no real convention even regarding the born, because both [the object and the name] are absent at the time the convention is being made.
For even during the state of direct experience, that particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), as the cause of that [experience], being momentary, does not possess a present existence;
how much less will it exist at the time when the recollection arises, which occurs after the experience and consists of the enjoyment of non-differentiation?

Furthermore, it might be argued: "A convention will be established for that subsequent moment which arises by the force of its capacity within the same class [as the first], occurring at the time of the performance of the convention. To this, he says:
"And as for that other [moment] which is of the same class through the force of that [first]," and so forth:
"In that case, there is no application of a convention, and similarity is merely conceptualized."

Even though there exists another moment present at the time of making a convention (*samaya*), nevertheless, because it is impossible to have the mental application (*ābhoga*) toward that [other moment], a convention is not tenable. For no one, having perceived a horse, while making a convention preceded by the recollection of its name, would apply the convention "horse" to a cow or the like present at that time which has not been made an object of mental application.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Since there is similarity among all particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), a convention will be made by determining them as one. To this he says: "And similarity is conceptualized (*vikalpita*)."

For similarity is superimposed by a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), and its communication by means of sounds would mean that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself remains inexpressible.
Thus, in this way, a convention (*samaya*) is not possible regarding the specific characteristic;
nor is it possible regarding the specific characteristic of the sound itself, because the author of the convention applies a distinct name to the object only as it is presented by memory.
Furthermore, memory is not able to bring forth an expression for that which has been experienced as a real entity, because that [experience] has long since ceased.
And there can be no memory regarding that which one utters, because it was not previously experienced; nor can that which has not been made an object of cognition be brought forth by memory.

Therefore, that which is brought forth by memory and subsequently connected is, by virtue of being constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), nothing but a non-particular (*asvalakṣaṇa*); thus, there can be no linguistic convention (*samaya*) with respect to a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is established that the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is inexpressible.

Right here, for the sake of establishing that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible, he states another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), beginning with "the perception of heat," and so forth:
"The clear perception of heat and so on, which arises from words such as 'name' and the like,
does not appear [as the object itself], just like the sensory cognition of those objects."

For just as the sensory cognition whose object is a thing such as heat is experienced with a clear manifestation, it is not so [experienced] when arising from words such as "heat. Indeed, those whose eyes, tongues, or noses are impaired do not experience the color, taste, and so forth of a citron or similar fruit upon hearing the word for it, in the way that those with unimpaired eyes and other senses experience them through sensory cognition.
As it has been said:
"One who is burned perceives the burning quite differently from the connection with fire [as it actually exists]."
Otherwise, the meaning of burning would not be revealed by the word "burning."
Thus:
"like the sense-cognition of that object" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). The analysis of the compound is: "this is both that object and a sense-cognition."

Even if that were not the case, why would the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word not be its object? To this he says: "That [connection] is not his," and so forth. That connection is not logical for that word;
the object does not appear when the cognition produced by it exists, just as taste does not appear in a cognition of form.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not appear in a cognition produced by something is not the object of that [thing], just as taste is not the object of a cognition produced by visible form. And the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear in the cognition of a word; this is a non-apprehension of the establishing factor (*sthāpakānupalabdhi*). Here, the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For it is said that a word’s status as a designator of an object consists precisely in its producing a cognition having that object as its content, and nothing else. Furthermore, it is not logical for a cognition to have something as its object when it is devoid of the aspect (*ākāra*) of that thing, because that would lead to an over-extension.
Furthermore, a single entity cannot possess two forms—one clear and one unclear—by virtue of which it could be said that the indistinct form inherent in the object itself is expressed by words.
This is because it is contradictory for a single thing to have duality, and because those existing at different times would be establishing mutually contradictory natures.
The Naiyāyikas, however, state: "The individual, the configuration, and the genus are the referents of a word" (*padārtha*).
The referent of a word (*padārtha*) means the meaning of a word (*śabdārtha*). Among these, by the term "individual" (*vyakti*), substances, qualities, particularities, and actions are denoted.
And so the Sūtra states: "Manifestation (vyakti) is form (mūrti), which is the substratum of specific qualities (guṇaviśeṣa).

First, its meaning is explained according to the view of the Vārttikakāra: that which is distinguished is a "specific" (viśeṣa); a "specific quality" (guṇaviśeṣa) is action (karman), distinguished from [other] qualities.
Furthermore, the second term "quality-specific" (guṇaviśeṣaṇa) is indicated here by means of a *ekaśeṣa* compound; by this, the category of quality (guṇapadārtha) [is intended].
It is apprehended.

"Qualities and those particulars" (guṇaviśeṣāḥ) means that these qualities are the particulars; the inclusion of the term "particulars" (viśeṣa) is for the purpose of excluding the generic form (ākṛti).

For the generic form is a particular conjunction, and conjunction by its very nature is included within the category of quality (guṇapadārtha); therefore, if the term "particulars" were not included, the generic form would also be apprehended.
Nor is its inclusion within "manifest" (vyakta) intended, because it is mentioned separately by means of a distinct word.
By the word "substratum" (āśraya), substance (dravya) is denoted; the meaning is that the substratum of those specific qualities is the substance which serves as their support.
In the aphorism, the instruction was given by omitting the pronoun *tat*.

The compound should be analyzed as follows: "particular qualities" (*guṇaviśeṣāḥ*) refers to both [the individual] particular qualities and [their collective]; "the substratum of particular qualities" (*guṇaviśeṣāśrayaḥ*) refers to those particular qualities together with their substratum. This is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*), and because gender depends on common usage, it is designated in the neuter gender.
Therefore, the meaning is this: that which is the substratum of particular qualities is called both "individual" (*vyakti*) and "form" (*mūrti*).

In that context, when the word *mūrti* is applied to a substance (*dravya*), it should be understood as having a locative derivation (*adhikaraṇasādhana*): "form" (*mūrti*) is so called because its constituent parts coalesce (*mūrcchanti*) therein.

But when [the term *mūrti*] refers to color and so forth, it is derived with the agent as the efficient cause (*kartṛ-sādhana*): color and the rest are "form" (*mūrti*) because they coalesce and inhere in a substance.

However, the word *vyakti* (individual manifestation) is derived with the object as the efficient cause (*karma-sādhana*) when referring to a substance, and with the instrument as the efficient cause (*karaṇa-sādhana*) when referring to color and the rest.

According to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, however, the meaning of the Sūtra follows the literal reading: it is his view that the substance alone, which is the substratum of specific qualities, is both the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) and the form (*mūrti*).

As it has been said: "That substance is that which, as the case may be, is the substratum of specific qualities—namely color, taste, smell, touch, gravity, fluidity, density, and the latent impressions (saṃskāra)—as well as of non-pervasive specific dimensions; it is characterized by its parts being massed together.
By the word *ākṛti* (configuration), the conjunction of the limbs of living beings, such as the hands and so forth, and their further subdivisions, such as the fingers and so forth, is denoted.
Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "*Ākṛti* is the designation of the marks of a genus (*jāti*)."

The commentary on this states: "One should know that *ākṛti* (form) is that by which the genus (*jāti*) and the gender-marks (*liṅga*) of the genus are expressed; and it is nothing other than the fixed arrangement (*vyūha*) of the parts of a living being and their own constituent parts.
By the word *vyūha*, a specific kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is meant. By the inclusion of the term "fixed" (*niyata*), artificial conjunctions are excluded.

In this context, the "marks of the genus" (*jātiliṅga*) are the limbs of living beings, such as the head, hands, and so forth; for by means of these, the genus characterized as "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like is indicated.

However, sometimes the genus is manifested directly through the configuration (*ākṛti*); that is, when cowness is manifested upon seeing the particular arrangement of the head, hands, and other parts.

At other times, it is the marks of the genus themselves [that manifest it], as when cowness and the like are manifested by individual parts such as horns, which are revealed through their own specific arrangements.
Therefore, the *ākṛti* (form) serves to manifest that genus (*jāti*) and its characteristics.
By the word "genus," there is denoted a real entity called a "universal" (*sāmānya*), which is the cause for the production of a single designation and a single cognition.
Thus, the statement in the *Sūtra*, "Genus is that whose nature is to produce a common [cognition]," means that genus is the cause for the arising of a common cognition.

In this regard, showing that the refutation of the individual (vyakti) and the configuration (ākṛti) as the meaning of a word should be understood through this very same refutation of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) being the word-meaning, he says "by this very [method]," and so forth: "By this very method, there is the refutation of the individual and the configuration;
for their nature as particulars is also accepted by the opponents."
The intention is that the refutation of "birth" (jāti) will follow later;
the phrase "as the meaning of the word 'refutation'" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because its very nature is that of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)," and so forth.
The phrase "of those two" refers to the individual (vyakti) and the form (ākṛti).

The point is that, just as the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not the referent of a word because no linguistic convention has been established for it, so too it is with those two; therefore, the reason "because no convention has been established" is neither unestablished (asiddha) nor inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Furthermore, he demonstrates that it is not logical for these two—individual essence (*vyakti*) and configuration (*ākṛti*)—to be the meaning of a word because they do not exist, by stating "dravyādi" and so forth. Individual essence is characterized by substance, quality, particularity, and action, while configuration consists of conjunction; and since these [categories], such as substance and the rest, have already been refuted, it follows that their status as the word-meaning is untenable.
This is shown by the passage beginning with "dravyādi," which states:
"But because the refutation of substance and the rest, as well as of conjunction, has already been set forth."
Therefore, the establishment of those two as being the word and its meaning is not ultimately real.

Having thus established the impossibility of linguistic convention (*samaya*) with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), he says "of genus and relation," etc., while establishing the impossibility of convention with respect to the three [categories] beginning with genus:
"Because genus and relation have already been refuted at length previously,
other threefold word-meanings are not postulated as being distinct from these."

Regarding the term "immediate" (*anantara*): since the universal (*jāti*) has already been refuted as being distinct from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and since the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*) is defined by its connection with that universal, it follows that because neither the universal nor its connection exists, the possessor of the universal is likewise impossible. This is because the designation of it is produced by those two, and the possessor of the universal is essentially identical to the specific characteristic itself. The point is that the fault inherent in that position remains exactly the same.
Vājātakāyana [Vājapyāyana] maintains that the word-meaning is the universal (jāti), Vyāḍi holds it to be the substance (dravya), and Pāṇini asserts it to be both.

This too has been refuted by the very same [argument]: because the universal is untenable and the substance consists of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), the defects inherent in those respective positions do not cease.
Introducing [the following], he says:
"That which is called the status of being a word-meaning (*padārthatva*) for those individuals, forms, and universals," and so forth. [p.283]
Therefore, the formlessness of all things is impossible, since [form] exists.
The word "tad" means "therefore";
"nīrūpatā" means the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The form of the cognition, residing within the cognition itself, does not follow from the object nor from another cognition;
furthermore, since it does not produce the intended object, it cannot be said to be [the object] in reality.

For the form of the cognition (buddhyākāra), by virtue of its identity with it, resides only within that very cognition; thus, like the nature of that cognition itself, it does not follow after the object to be communicated nor another cognition. Consequently, because it does not pervade the time of the convention and the time of practical usage, no linguistic convention (*samaya*) is possible there, just as in the case of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Or, even if it were to persist until the time of practical usage, nevertheless, it is not logical for users to establish a convention regarding it.

For instance, users of language apply expressive words with the thought that "perhaps a person seeking purposeful action (arthakriyā), having cognized objects capable of such action through this word, will engage with them. This is not done out of mere whim; nor is the form of the conceptual cognition itself able to accomplish the intended effect, such as the removal of cold, for one who seeks it, because even when that [conceptual] experience arises, the [actual] effect is absent.
Therefore, since there is no convention regarding that [conceptual form], the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because no convention has been made with respect to it.

It might be argued: "There are other word-meanings, such as 'existence' (asti) and so forth; therefore, because a convention (*samaya*) is possible with respect to those, the reason is simply unestablished (*asiddha*). To this, he says: "Those others who explain the word-meaning in quite another way than 'existence' and so forth," and so on.
Those others who explain the meaning of words in a manner entirely different from "existence" and the like—
These [objections] have already been refuted by these [arguments]; nevertheless, it is stated once more.

"By these" means by the negations of the referents of words such as "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) and so forth; the sense is that those [other categories] are already included within the specific characteristic and the rest.
Showing what those objects denoted by "existence" (astyartha) and so forth are, he says:

"The meaning of 'is' (astyartha), etc. The definition of that which is to be conveyed by all words is as follows: they say that in the case of words such as "cow" and so on, [the object] is identical to [the objects denoted by] "unprecedented power" (apūrva), "deity," and "heaven."
The word *iti* is displaced; it is connected immediately after the phrase "the meaning of 'is'.
By this, the following sense is established: that which is perceived as "the meaning of 'is'" is the defining characteristic of the referent—that is, the denotable object—of all words.
This means that it is the definition of the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*).
Therefore, they say that among objects such as cows which have become the domain [of cognition], that which is conveyed by words such as "cow" is equal to the *apūrva*, the deity, and heaven;
the meaning is that they say it is equal to the referents of words such as *apūrva* and so forth.

For just as words such as "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) do not instill a specific form of an object within cognitions—wherein only this much is understood, namely, that there exist certain objects to which words like "unprecedented" are applied—in the same way, it is identical even for words with perceptible referents, such as "cow" and so on.
Because from these too, one understands in this manner: "there exists some object denoted by the word 'cow' and the like, or something connected with universals such as cowness.
As for the apprehension of a specific form that arises for some people in that regard, that occurs due to the force of their own established tenets (*siddhānta*).

Showing the meanings of words included by the word "etcetera," he says: "The aggregate," and so forth: "Some say that the meaning of a word is either an aggregate whose components are not distinct or which is a mere collection, or else it is an unreal relation."

Some say that by words such as "brāhmaṇa" and so forth, a collection of austerity, birth, learning, and the like is denoted without either alternative (vikalpa) or conjunction (samuccaya), just as by words such as "forest" (vana) the dhava and other trees are denoted.

For instance, when "forest" is said, there is no cognition through alternative—such as "is it a dhava, or a khadira, or a palāśa?"—nor is there cognition through conjunction—such as "the dhava, the khadira, and the palāśa"; rather, the dhava and others are cognized through a generality.

Similarly, when "brāhmaṇa" is uttered, there is no cognition of [the word] as referring to asceticism (*tapas*), or caste (*jāti*), or learning (*śruta*), or as "asceticism, caste, and learning" taken together.
Rather, what is cognized is a collection of asceticism and the rest, in their entirety, as distinguished from other related things.

In that context, *vikalpa* (option) is the determination of one specific member from among many undetermined members of a collection; whereas *samuccaya* (conjunction) is the determination of the distinct natures of several fixed factors that are simultaneously connected to a single thing.
That in which both conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) and synthesis (*samuccaya*) are non-existent is so described.

Others, however, maintain that the meaning of a word is the relation of substances and the like with their forms undetermined by [categories such as] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth; and because that relation is unreal due to the unreality of the relata as word-meanings, it is called "unreal.
Alternatively, because austerity, learning, and so forth appear as a unity—like the color black (*mecakavarṇa*)—their mutual connection itself is unreal.
For in this way, these [elements], whether individually or collectively, are not perceived in their own form; rather, their aggregate appears by transcending its own nature, like a firebrand-circle.

Either that reality which is qualified by the unreal is the basis for words, or else it is the word itself— having attained the state of being associated with mental discourse— that becomes the denotable object.

Others, however, say: that which is real by virtue of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is the meaning of a word. In this context, the meaning of a word is that reality—such as gold or the like—which, being of a universal nature (*sāmānyātman*), persists through all particular differences, and whose unreal limiting adjuncts—the specific forms such as bracelets, rings, and so forth—are the basis for verbal expression; that is to say, they are the grounds for the application of words and their denotable objects.
Others, however, say that the word itself, having attained the state of being expressed, is the meaning of the word.
Regarding that, what is this "discursive talk" (*abhijalpa*)? He says: "When this form is unified through the connection 'this is that,' etc.
285] When this form is unified through the connection "this is that," etc.
The internal verbalization of that word with its object is called *abhijalpa*.

The superimposition of the object upon the word—namely, the connection "this is that" in the form "the word itself is the object"—is the cause; therefore, when the form of the word becomes unified with the object, they call that word, which has assumed the form of the object, "abhijalpya."

Others, however, maintain that the meaning of a word is the mental form itself, which has an external object as its referent, which is apprehended as an external thing, and which is manifested as having the nature of cognition. He shows this with the verse beginning "Or else...
(yo vā): "Or else, that object which is the domain of the intellect, which is based on an external thing, and which is known as an external thing—that is held by some to be the meaning of a word."
"An object of the intellect" means revolving within the intellect; that is to say, residing in the intellect.
"Based on an external thing" means...
That which has for its basis an external object— real or unreal— that serves as the support for its own nature, like a written sign, is "based on an external object.
The phrase "the external object is known" means that [the object],
having manifested in the form of cognition, is determined (adhyavasita) as being external.

For as long as the form of the cognition, which has not been projected onto external objects, is apprehended through the cultivation of its true nature as being merely the form of cognition itself, so long its status as the meaning of a word is not determined, because there is an absence of connection with specific actions therein.
Indeed, actions such as "bring the cow" or "eat the curd" are not possible in relation to such a form of cognition; and it is an object capable of connection with action that is denoted by words.
Therefore, when it is apprehended as the form of cognition, it is not the meaning of a word.

But when [the word] is projected onto an external object, then the cognizer imagines that the capacity to accomplish an action—which actually belongs to the [cognition itself]—belongs to that [external object] by way of its being external; thus, it becomes the meaning of the word.
Now, what is the distinction between this [view] and the position of the proponent of Apoha?
For even by the proponent of Apoha, the form of the cognition is grasped as having the nature of an external object as the meaning of the word.
This is indeed stated in the *Bhāṣya*:
as it has been said,
"Furthermore, because [the object] is understood through the exclusion of others by means of the cognition that superimposes that form [upon it]..."
"Therefore, it is not contradictory to state that the object [of the word] is indeed that very [object]."
Thus [it is said].

This is not so; for this proponent of the theory that the form of cognition is the object (buddhyākāravādin) maintains that the form of cognition—which is non-erroneous with respect to an external object and superimposed upon substances and other categories that are ultimately real—is the ultimate referent of words.

Indeed, he maintains that [cognition] is without a [real] objective support (nirālambana), erroneous because it functions by determining non-difference among things that are different, and is based upon mutual exclusion (itaretara-bheda).
But if it is as we say: "All this false appearance is the apprehension of objects as having a single nature;
the seed of this is mutual differentiation, for which purpose designations exist."
Thus,
[the reason] would be proving what is already established; and so he will state later.
"If mutual difference is its seed, then this is our own position.
Furthermore, for the proponent of apoha, nothing whatsoever is accepted as the ultimate denotation of words, whether it be the form of a cognition or something else.
For indeed, that alone which appears in a verbal cognition by way of being determined is the word-meaning.

Furthermore, the form of the cognition is not determined by the verbal cognition; rather, it is the external object itself that performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Nor is the external object determined in its ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) by that [verbal cognition], because it is not determined according to its true nature, and because it does not exist according to how it is determined.
Therefore, the referent of a word is purely superimposed (*samāropita*).
And that which is superimposed is nothing at all; thus, nothing is denoted by words in terms of its actual existence.
As for what was said—"the referent of a word is that very [object]"—that was intended with reference only to a superimposed object.
However, there is a great difference in that the proponent of the mental aspect (buddhyākāravādin) maintains that the mental aspect is the ultimate denotable object.

But others say that, due to habituation (*abhyāsa*), a word is the cause of intuition (*pratibhā*) and not a communicator of an external object; he demonstrates this with the verse beginning "Due to habituation" and so forth:
"In brief, every word is, through habituation, the cause of intuition for children and even for animals, in the communication of objects as they truly are."
Practice (*abhyāsa*) is the observation of a word’s repeated application toward a particular object.
Intuition (*pratibhā*) is the wisdom conducive to the comprehension of an action as delimited by its specific means;
it is produced by a word accompanied by the repetition of observing its usage.

That [conventional usage] differs with every word and every person; however, because its divisions are immeasurable due to the infinity of linguistic usage, it is impossible to prescribe them all. Therefore, he says, "And for children and for animals," and so forth.

For just as the strikes of a goad and the like, when employed to bring about the comprehension of an object by elephants and such creatures, serve only as causes for the gathering of intuition (*pratibhā*) and do not directly convey the object itself.

Otherwise, how could the various divisions of the teachings, which are mutually contradictory, as well as the compositions of fictional narratives, manifest distinct categories of entities constructed by one's own conceptual imagination?

He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "In that regard" (*tatra*): "In that case, is this denotable object 'existent' intended to be the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or a universal (*jāti*), or a connection (*yoga*), or something else, or perhaps a reflection (*pratibimbaka*) of the cognition?"
These aforementioned faults apply even when the mere existence [of an object] is to be established;
in that case, linguistic usage cannot be conceived through differentiation.
If the referent "exists" is held to have the nature of the specifically characterized (svalakṣaṇa) and so forth as previously stated, then the aforementioned faults necessarily follow.

Furthermore, because the specific form of the referent "exists" is undetermined, when that alone is apprehended by words, there would be no conventional usage based on distinctions such as "cow," "gavaya," or "elephant," since those distinctions would not be conveyed by the words.
With the words "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, the author anticipates the opponent's reply: "The cognition of the mere existence of an object qualified by the word 'cowness' may occur;
however, that [opponent's] view is that there is no manifestation of distinctions such as horns, shape, or blue color."

It might be argued: "Since the mere existence of an object, qualified by the [universals] *gotva* (cowness) and [the word] ‘cow’, and devoid of particulars such as *sāvaleyatva* (the quality of being a brindled cow), is understood from the word ‘cow’, there will be linguistic usage through differentiation. If this is so, then how can it be maintained that the meaning of a word is the mere entity (*astyartha-mātra*), given that specific particulars such as cows are indeed conveyed? Anticipating this objection, the opponent offers a rebuttal beginning with the words “viṣāṇākṛti” (the form of a horn), and so forth.

Because a specific [object] such as a horn is not perceived due to the non-apprehension of what is called "the word," it is correct to say that there exists some object to be signified; however, this is not a fault, for it is not because the qualifiers—namely *gotva* (cowness) and so forth—are not perceived in relation to the words *gotva* and so forth.
He replies with the words "nanvevam" and so forth:
"But in that case, there would be the denotation of both the object possessing those [qualities] and of the particulars;
and if those were present, the same fault would apply there, and no other object is perceived."
If it is held that only the object qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth is expressed, then the denotation of the object as possessing that [universal] would have to be accepted.
In that case, since the universal and its inherence (*samavāya*) have been refuted, the object possessing it is impossible; thus, the previously mentioned fault remains.

Furthermore, because the object possessing that [universal] consists of a specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), the same difficulties as before necessarily follow: the impossibility of establishing a linguistic convention (*asaṃketatva*), the impossibility of conventional usage (*avyavahāryatva*), and the consequence of an indistinct appearance (*aspaṣṭāvabhāsa*).
If it is argued that there exists a distinct object of existence apart from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, he replies: "No other object of existence is seen.
When examined, no object of existence other than the specific characteristic and so forth enters the range of the intellect.
He states the fault in the position that [the word] denotes a collection, beginning with "Even in the denotation of a collection," and so forth:
"Even in the denotation of a collection, the denotation of distinct universals (jāti) is evident,
because austerity, caste, action, and so on, are denoted in their totality."

In the view that the word denotes the aggregate (*samudāya*), it is even more clearly accepted that both the universal (*jāti*) and the particulars (*bheda*), such as austerity (*tapas*) and so forth, are denoted; thus, all the defects that arise in the view of denoting each individual member occur simultaneously in the case of denoting the aggregate.

He states the fault in the two positions beginning with "or [the universal] is unreal" by means of the verse beginning with "nirddhārita": "Furthermore, the connection of substances and so forth, whose own natures have been determined through association, and that universal which is real— both of these have already been refuted previously."
Since it is logically untenable for the meaning of a word to take on forms such as particularity or genus,
a form of the word that has been unified with the object is not possible.
This verbal discourse exists only within the mind, due to its differentiation from external objects;
therefore, what difference is there between this and the immediately preceding position that [the object] is fragmented?
The view that the form of cognition is the meaning of a word has already been refuted,
because that which is not distinct from cognition lacks pervasiveness.

Since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*), characterized as such, have already been refuted previously during the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*); and since a real generality (*sāmānya*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), whether non-distinct or distinct [from its substratum], has been rejected during the examination of the Sāṅkhya system and during the examination of the six categories respectively; therefore, one must not assert a generality that is either a false conjunction or a false limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Regarding the position of "verbal association" (*abhijalpa*), he says: if some object of a word were possible, then there might be an identification with it; however, since it has already been established that a word-meaning in the form of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth is impossible, how could there be an identification with it? Furthermore, this verbal association exists only within the mind; for, since the difference between external word and meaning is established by such factors as their being apprehended by different sense organs, any production of identity between them is simply not real.
Therefore, it is logical that the unification of word and object occurs only when they reside within a single cognition, because they have entered into one and the same mental state.

For instance, the nature of the word—which has assumed the form of the denoted object, has its own verbal essence obscured, and revolves within the intellect—places the object internally according to its own form by means of a conceptual differentiation; this is called "internal discourse" (*abhijalpa*).
And it is logical that this form belongs exclusively to the self of the cognition and is not external, because external objects are absolutely distinct from one another in their intrinsic natures.
And so, what is the difference between this [position] and the one just mentioned regarding the object being a mental construct (*buddhy-artha*)?
None at all.
In both cases, the object is purely mental.
Only this much differs: that the word and the object are treated as one.
But the fault remains exactly the same: "And how can that which is non-different from cognition become another object?
He demonstrates that very point with the words beginning, "The form of the cognition as well... (verse 898).
Regarding the position that intuition (*pratibhā*) is the meaning of words, he states the fault: "If intuition, which is the meaning of words, has external objects as its domain,
then how could there be diverse intuitions regarding an external object that is restricted to a single nature?"
Now, if these [cognitions] are devoid of objects because they exist as mere latent impressions (vāsanā),
how could there be any comprehension or activity regarding external objects?
If you maintain that [the cognition] has its own form through the mental resolve upon external form,
then it follows that the word-meaning is unreal, because it functions through such an error.
Nor is it logical that it should be seedless, for that would lead to an over-extension in all cases;
if its seed is mutual difference, then this is our own position.

If cognition (*pratibhā*) were, in the ultimate sense, to have external objects as its domain, then diverse cognitions would not arise for those abiding in contradictory conventions regarding a single entity such as a word, because it is impossible for a single thing to possess multiple natures.
If, on the other hand, it were without an object, then activity and comprehension with respect to the object would not occur, since the word would not have that object as its domain.

If, finally, those activities and comprehensions occur through the error of determining a non-object—namely, one's own internal reflection—to be an object, then it follows that the referent of a word is erroneous.
Furthermore, the seed—that is, the cause—of that error must be stated; otherwise, if error were to arise without a seed, it would occur from everything at all times.

If, on the other hand, the mutual difference between entities itself is accepted as its seed, then you are merely proving our own position, which results in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Now, he states a refutation that applies equally to all positions, beginning with "yadi vā" (or if):
"Or if all this were indeed momentary, or not so;
if it were momentary, there would be no logical connection for persistence, and sequential cognition would not be possible otherwise."
All this—whether it be the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the universal (*jāti*), and so forth—is either momentary or non-momentary.

Regarding the first position, because there is no persistence (*anvaya*) at the time of linguistic usage of that which was perceived at the time of the convention, no linguistic agreement (*samaya*) can apply to it.

And in the case of the non-momentary position, since a successive entity cannot arise from what is non-successive, it follows that there would be an absence of successive cognition regarding the object of the word’s meaning.
"Otherwise" means in the case of non-momentariness.
Others, however, say that the word leads one to infer the speaker’s intention to express a meaning, as it has been said: "Inference of the intention to speak does not exist apart from the word.
To this, he says: "By this very [reasoning]," and so forth.
By this very [argument], the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) as being cognizable through words is also refuted;
for if there is no connection between word and object, where could there be intention to speak, and where could there be hearing?

If it is maintained that from the ultimate standpoint (pāramārthataḥ) there is an intention to speak regarding objects that are ultimate word-meanings, that is unestablished, because no word-meaning whatsoever—such as a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) and so forth—is possible.
Therefore, there is no intention to speak from the ultimate standpoint with respect to any object, because of the absence of any recurring (anvayin) object.
Nor is there any word that expresses such [an object]; thus he says: "Or where is the scripture? (kva vā śrutiḥ).
*Śruti* means "word.

And when the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is what is to be communicated, it follows that the operation of *śruti*— that is, of the word— does not extend to an external object, because that [intention] is not directly expressed by it, just like any other distinct meaning.

Now, if it is thought that there is a similarity between the object such as form (rūpa) which follows from the speaker’s intention and the external object, and that because of this similarity, activity toward the unexpressed external object will occur—just as in the case of twins—then [the author] says: "Because of similarity" (*sārūpyāt*).
"And if the operation of the word were due to similarity, how could there be activity toward what is not expressed by the word?
By this, the [theory of] names and so forth, based on similarity like that of twins, is refuted. (PV 1.206)

This being the case, activity directed toward external objects would never occur; even when something is uttered that is intended to be changed by the speaker's desire, activity might still arise, as in the case of twin trees. Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika position—which maintains that there exists a dissociated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) called "name" (*nāman*), which has sound as its object, and another called "sign" (*nimitta*), which consists of the mark of an object—should also be understood as refuted by this very same argument.

For instance, if that name and so forth were momentary, then there would be no logical connection (anvaya); if it were non-momentary, successive cognitions would be impossible; and if it were external, there would be the consequence of an absence of engagement [with it]. Furthermore, because of its similarity [to the object], it would not exist at all times. Thus, every aforementioned refutation applies entirely and without exception. Alternatively, by the phrase "by this," it refers to the refutation of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) and so forth, as applicable.
For in this case as well, it should be stated thus:
"The essence of names and so forth cannot be conventionally designated, as it does not partake of anything else;
since it is held to be such, its expressibility is in no way possible."
Thus [it is said].
Regarding what was said— that if words illuminate an object as it has ascended into the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), their application to the external object would not be possible—
the author, anticipating the opponent's response, says "the intention" (*vivakṣā*) and so forth: "[The form] conjoined with the inference of the intention [is grasped] as an external entity."
If it is argued that activity occurs for those who are making a resolve, then that is precisely our own position once again.
