Therefore, under the view that the word-meaning is exclusion, the cognition of it as something to be accomplished and the cognition of it as a past entity (*bhūta*) and so forth would result in being without a basis; thus, there is a contradiction with empirical experience (*pratītibādhā*).
This refers to the "representation in the form of a past entity" and so on.
The determination of the primary elements and so forth is what is meant by "condition" (pratyaya).
Furthermore, demonstrating that [the theory] is non-pervasive, he shows the contradiction with common experience (pratītibādhā) in the verse beginning with "vidhyādau" and so forth:
"In a category of objects such as injunctions (vidhi) and the like, there is no determination of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).
Moreover, since 'actor' and 'actorhood' are not distinct, what kind of exclusion could there be?"
Since particles such as "ca" (and) also lack connection with a verb, they do not involve exclusion;
furthermore, the exclusion of others cannot be designated as the meaning of a sentence.
Furthermore, in the case of words such as "non-exclusion of others" (ananyāpoha), no denotable object can be determined;
how much less, then, could there be an object to be excluded (apohya) for words such as "knowable" (prameya) or "cognizable" (jñeya)?

By the word "etcetera," the inclusion of invitation (*nimintrana*), addressing (*āmantraṇa*), and so forth is intended. There is no determination or apprehension of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), that is, the differentiation from others (*anyavyavaccheda*). The meaning is that the reason for this is precisely what was stated previously: "For in that case, there exists nothing to be negated in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*). When there is a connection with another negative particle (*na*) in the phrase "Devadatta does not cook" (*na na pacati devadattaḥ*), what kind of exclusion (*apoha*) could there be?
It is not at all [the case that there is no connection], because even in a double negation, there is indeed contact with a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

Furthermore, it is accepted that particles (*nipāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and prepositions (*karmapravacanīya*)—such as *ca* and others—are words (*pada*); yet these have no connection with the negative particle *naṭ*, because they denote non-substantiality (*asattvavacana*).

For instance, in cases such as *aghaṭa* ("non-pot") and so forth, when the word *ghaṭa* ("pot") is connected with the negative particle *naṭ*, another object such as a cloth (*paṭa*) is apprehended; thus, by means of that exclusion, the meaning of the word *ghaṭa*—as devoid of the negative—is determined. However, there is no such connection of the particles *ca* and so forth with the negative particle *naṭ* in expressions such as *na ca*. Nor is it logical for there to be an exclusion (*apohana*) by the negative of that which is not being connected with it.
Therefore, there is no exclusion in the case of the particles *ca* and so forth.

The meaning is that there is an absence of exclusion (apoha). Furthermore, the meaning of a sentence is held to be a single variegated form, like a mottled color; therefore, in that case, the exclusion of others cannot be designated, because no counter-correlative (pratiyogin) with a completed form is perceived.

Furthermore, in cases such as "Caitra, bring the cow," where the exclusion of others (anyanivṛtti)—in the form of the exclusion of non-Caitras and so forth—is described by means of grasping the individual parts [of the sentence], that would be the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) alone, not the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).

This is because it is impossible to analyze in this way that which is partless. Thus, the established rule regarding the meaning of words is not all-pervasive. Moreover, in expressions such as "the exclusion of others is not the exclusion of non-others," the sense is that no denotable object other than a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) can be defined or perceived.

For indeed, by means of two negations, it is not merely the form of an exclusion (*apoha*) that is understood as the denotable object, since there is the determination of a positive entity (*vidhi*) itself.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), synonyms such as "exclusion from others" (*ananyavyāvṛtti*) and "differentiation from others" (*ananyavyavaccheda*) are included. [Objection:
But is this not a redundant statement, since it has already been covered by the phrase "even a negation is joined with a negation"?
This is true;

however, it is stated once again for the purpose of making it known that even by the very words of one who asserts that "the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others" (anyāpoha), a positive affirmation (vidhi) is intended.
For indeed, the object to be excluded by the word "exclusion of others" is the meaning of the word "non-exclusion of others," and that is not perceived as anything other than a positive affirmation.

Furthermore, regarding words such as "the cognizable," "the knowable," and "the expressible," there is nothing whatsoever that can be excluded (apohya), because everything possesses the very nature of being cognizable and so forth.

For instance, whatever is imagined to be excluded by these [terms], all of it, when apprehended in the form of an exclusion, remains nothing other than having the nature of the "knowable" and so on; for it is impossible to exclude that which has not been made an object of cognition.
Consequently, because there is no object to be excluded for these [terms], their systematic arrangement would be non-pervasive.
[Objection: But was it not stated in the *Hetumukha* that, having designated "the unknowable" as a conceptual construct, inference regarding "the knowable" occurs by means of its exclusion?
How then can it be said that the determination of the referent of a word lacks pervasiveness? To this he says: "apohya... and so forth.
And rather than postulating an object of exclusion (*apohya*), it is better to postulate the real entity itself.
And because the form of cognition is denied, no internal object is denoted.

Furthermore, because there is nothing to be excluded from them, exclusion (apoha) is not established for those [words] such as "thus" and so forth; nor can an object of exclusion be determined for words like these.

If even all that is knowable is conceived as being excluded by this [conceptual cognition] on the grounds of its being an object of knowledge, then it would be better if the entity itself were conceptualized as the meaning of a word in its positive form (*vidhirūpa*), just as it is determined by worldly convention.
For in this way, neither the superimposition of the unperceived nor the denial of the perceived object would be committed; such is the intended sense.
It is for this very reason that the word "better" (*varam*) was used.

Regarding those who say that the object of all words is nothing other than the conceptual reflection (*vikalpapratibimbaka*), and that this very thing is what is "denoted" (*abhidhīyate*) and what is "excluded" (*vyavacchidyate*), [the author] says this in response to them: "Because the form of cognition is negated," and so forth. We have negated the form of cognition on the grounds that cognition is formless, while the external object possesses form; moreover, that [external object], which is connected to external space, is clearly perceived. Therefore, since an internal form mounted upon the intellect does not exist, it is untenable for words to denote such a form.
Nor is it logical for that intermediate object to be the thing to be excluded (*apohya*), precisely because it does not exist.
Regarding those words such as "knowable" (*prameya*) and so forth,

and also words such as "thus" (*evam*) or "in this way" (*ittham*), nothing at all is found to be excluded, because there exists no counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) in the form of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Now, it might be argued that what is to be negated is not of this kind, but rather a negation in the form of a prasajya (non-presuppositional).
This is not so, as has been stated here.

For even in this case, when there is the instruction "not not thus," there is a negation of a negation; however, that which is "thus" remains in its own nature as non-negated. Thus, the very same principle mentioned previously applies here.

All of this has been set forth as stated by Kumārila; now, beginning with the words "of the word 'all'," he raises the objection against Apoha stated by Uddyotakara: "And what object is conceived as being excluded by the word 'all'? For there would be nothing that is not a name [i.e., not a universal] which could be negated."
If it is argued that "one and so forth" means "not all," then the exclusion of the object (arthāpoha) follows as a consequence;
for the parts are negated, and the whole is not desired as something separate from them.

In this way, regarding the meaning of a word denoting a collection, all [words] would become meaningless, because the individuals that constitute the collection are excluded and no other [referent] is desired.
Furthermore, words such as "two" and so forth, which are intended here to have the scope of conjunction (*samuccaya*),
would not be of that nature if there were a negation of "one" and the rest.
Furthermore, as for that which is called the meaning of the word "cow" through the exclusion of the non-cow (*apoha*), is it a positive entity or a negative absence?
If it is a positive entity, is it a cow or a non-cow?

If there is no dispute regarding the cow itself, then this matter must be characterized as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). If, however, the non-cow were the denotation of the word "cow," that would indeed be a great skill in understanding the meaning of words!
This non-existence is also not tenable, because injunctions and the like are impossible;
for no one understands non-existence from the word "cow."

He says: "The claim that exclusion (apoha) is the meaning of a word is incorrect, because it is not universally applicable. Where there is a duality of categories, one thing is understood through the negation of the other, as in the case of the word 'cow,' where the cow is understood while the non-cow is being excluded. However, this is not the case for every word."

For there is nothing whatsoever called "not-all" that could be excluded by the word "all. If you think that "not-all," such as the number one and so forth, is excluded by the word "all," that is not so, because it would entail the fallacy of negating the very meaning of its own term.

For in this way, the word "all" (*sarva*), functioning by excluding one and so forth, would become meaningless because it negates the parts (*aṅga*) and no whole (*aṅgin*) distinct from the parts is admitted.
By the word "part" (*aṅga*), a single constituent element is expressed.

Similarly, all collective terms (*samudāya-śabda*), functioning by way of negating a single constituent, would result in being meaningless because no other collective distinct from the constituents is admitted.

Furthermore, since words such as "two" and so forth denote a collection of objects (*viṣaya-samuccaya*), when "one" and so on are negated, the objects being negated cannot form a collection; thus, [the word] would be meaningless. He demonstrates this by saying, "they would not be of such a kind. The meaning is: those intended objects, which are the domain of a collection, would not be of such a kind [if they were merely the absence of one]. And as for this exclusion of the non-cow (*ago'poha*), which is the referent of the word "cow" in the sense that "it is not a non-cow," is that a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a non-entity (*abhāva*)?
If that entity exists, is it the cow or the non-cow?
If it is the cow, there is no dispute. But if it is the non-cow, then for the word "cow" to have the non-cow as its referent is a remarkable skill in the meaning of words!
Now, if it is non-existence, that is not tenable, because it cannot be the object of either an injunction or a comprehension [of its meaning].
For neither an injunction nor a comprehension can occur regarding non-existence upon hearing a word.
This very point he demonstrates with the words: "This non-existence is also not tenable," and so forth.

*Praiṣaṇa* (commanding) is *praiṣa*; it is the application [of an action] for the sake of the hearer by the speaker, and this is a property of the speaker. *Sampratipatti* (comprehension) is a property of the hearer.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), all properties of the entity (*bhāva*), such as carrying, milking, and the like, are included.
Moreover, the meaning of a word is understood through cognition; yet no one understands non-existence from the word "cow."

Furthermore, since exclusion (*apoha*) is of the nature of an action, its object must be stated: in this regard, regarding the exclusion "it is not a non-cow," is this exclusion directed toward the cow as its object, or is it directed toward the non-cow?
If the cow is the object, how can there be the absence of a cow in the cow itself?

If the non-cow is the object, how can there be a cognition of something else based on an exclusion whose object is something else? For when a *khadira* tree is being cut, the cutting does not occur in a *palāśa* tree.

Now, regarding the negation of "non-cow" with respect to a cow—namely, that "a cow is not a non-cow"—by what means was the state of being a non-cow (*agotva*) previously established so that it might be negated?
Considering that the first two alternatives here are incoherent, [the author], demonstrating only the third, says: "A cow is not a non-cow," etc.
Why is the meaning of the word "a cow is not a non-cow" accepted as an exclusion (*apoha*)?
For by whom has "non-cowness" been attached to a cow, such that it must be excluded?
Furthermore, as for this "exclusion of the non-cow" (agaurapoha) which is said to be the meaning of the word "cow"— is it held to be distinct from the cow, or non-distinct?
Even if it were distinct, it would either be dependent or independent.
If it were dependent, it would follow that it is a quality (*guṇa*), and therefore it could not be denoted as a substance (*dravya*).

Therefore, because the word "cow" denotes only a quality (guṇa), there would be grammatical coreferentiality [with other qualities]; however, there would be no such coreferentiality in expressions such as "the cow goes" or "the cow stands."
Now, if this object were indeed without any basis,
what would it be by which it is designated as "cow" for the purpose of negation?
Moreover, if this "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is held by you to be non-different from the cow itself, then it follows that this is simply the cow; what more has been said beyond that?
The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction.
The meaning of the sentence is: why do you not state that the referent of the word "cow" is the exclusion (apoha), characterized as "not non-cow"?
Furthermore, to the question "Why should it not be stated?", he says "by what," and so forth.
For this reason as well, exclusion (*apoha*) is untenable, because conceptual construction is impossible. To explain:
regarding this exclusion of the non-cow (*agoh*) in the cow, is it distinct from the cow or non-distinct? If it is distinct, is it dependent or independent?

If it is dependent, then by virtue of being dependent, it follows that it is a quality (*guṇa*); consequently, the word "cow" would denote only a quality and not the non-cow, and thus grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in "the cow stands" or "the cow walks"—would be impossible.
If it is not dependent [on the cow], then for what reason would there be a genitive case in the expression "the exclusion of the non-cow" (*agorapoha*)?
If, on the other hand, it is not distinct [from the cow], then that is just the cow itself, and nothing at all has been accomplished.
This exclusion (apoha) of each individual entity may be either one or many;
if it were one, being connected with many cows, it would simply be "cowness" itself.
Even if there were multiplicity, infinity would apply just as it does to a physical aggregate;
therefore, its being expressible by words is not applicable, precisely because it possesses differentiation.
Furthermore, it must be stated whether this *apoha* is one or many with respect to each individual object.

If it were one, then, being related to multiple individual cows (*godravya*), it would simply be "cowness" (*gotva*). If, on the other hand, it were many, then—due to its infinity like that of individual bodies—it would be impossible to designate it, and thus it would be truly inexpressible.
And is this exclusion of others (anyāpoha) intended to be denotable or undenotable? If it is denotable, is it so by way of a positive form or through the negation of another?
If this [object] were denotable by way of its nature as a positive injunction (*vidhi*), then the view of exclusivity (*ekānta-darśana*) would have to be abandoned;
for it has been described that the meaning of a word consists everywhere in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
[Page 316] Now, if exclusion (apoha) is expressed by means of the exclusion of exclusions, then, if one desires it in each such case, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā). Thus:
Moreover, if you maintain that this [exclusion] is indeed inexpressible, then your statement that "a word effects the exclusion of others" would be contradicted by that very position.
First, you must be asked this: is apoha expressible or inexpressible?

If it is expressible, is it expressed as a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) or by the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*)? In that regard, if it were expressed as a positive form, then the word-meaning would not be exclusively "the exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). Thus, the claim that "the word-meaning is the exclusion of others" would be inconclusive.

If the position is that [the word functions] by means of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), then that exclusion of others would also have to be denoted by another exclusion of others, and that too by yet another; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*avyavasthā*). Alternatively, if it were inexpressible, then the claim that "a word effects the exclusion of the referents of other words" would be contradicted.

All of this was stated and presented by Uddyotakara; regarding that, Ācārya Dignāga said: "Because the substratum is everywhere undifferentiated, because it is not subject to destruction, and because it is fully present in its entirety, the properties of a universal—namely, unity, eternity, and complete presence in each individual—reside in *apoha* alone, according to the respective order. Therefore, due to the excellence of these qualities, it is established that the meaning of a word is indeed *antarāpoha* (internal exclusion). Anticipating this objection, Kumārila, concluding his argument, says: "Moreover, [the properties of] unity, eternity, and inherence in each individual... and so forth. Furthermore, those [properties] which consist of unity, eternity, and inherence in each [individual]...
When both [the proponent and the opponent] are operating upon exclusions (apohas) that are devoid of any defining characteristics, who among them is superior?
Therefore, only in those words where there is a connection with negation does there occur the aspect of the exclusion of others; elsewhere, one's own nature alone is understood.
"In those very words where there is no connection with *naṭ*," as in "the village pig (*grāmasūkara*) is not to be eaten," and so forth;
[this refers to] "one's own self" (*svātmaiva*).
The very essential nature [of the word] is what is characterized by the injunction;
"elsewhere" means in cases devoid of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Having thus raised the opponent's view according to its primary points, he begins the refutation with the words "because of the lack of understanding of the exclusion of others" (*anyāpohāparijñānāt*), and so forth:
"Because they do not understand the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), these people of wrong views are satisfied with themselves; being evil-natured, they destroy others as well."
For exclusion (apoha) is twofold, by way of relative negation (paryudāsa) and absolute negation (niṣedha);
and relative negation is also twofold, through the distinction between that which is of the nature of cognition and that which is of the nature of an object.
"By way of exclusion and negation" means:
by way of both exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and negation (*niṣedha*), that is to say, the characteristic of exclusion and the absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
"By way of the distinction between the nature of cognition and the nature of the object" means: [as follows].
The meaning is: "due to the difference between the nature of cognition and the nature of the object.

In this context, the "nature of cognition" (*buddhyātman*) refers to the appearance of cognition as determined (*adhyavasita*) through a single, pervasive form across various objects; the "nature of the object" (*arthātman*) refers to the intrinsic essence of the object, namely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is excluded from what is dissimilar. The compound [buddhyātma-artha-ātma-bheda] means the distinction or separation between these two.
In this regard, showing the essential nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), he says "one" and so forth: "The causes previously stated for a single reflective awareness—
objects such as fearlessness and the like— are by their very nature distinct from others."
Relying upon those [mental constructs], when knowledge arises, the reflection of an object appears;
even though the nature of the object is absent in the conceptualizing mind, it is ascertained simply as "objects."

This was stated previously in the examination of the universal (*sāmānyaparīkṣā*) in the passage beginning, "Just as in the case of the *dhātrī*, *abhaya*, and so forth. There it was said: just as many things such as the *harītakī* produce a single effect characterized by the alleviation of fever and the like even without a single universal, so too will objects such as the brindled cow (*sāvaleyādi*)—despite their difference—be the causes of a reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśa*) of a single form by their very nature, even without a real entity (*vastubhūta*) that is a universal.
"Equal to *abhayā* and so forth" means they are equivalent to *harītakī* and the like;
their equality consists in their performing the same function.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Depending upon them" means depending upon those objects that have a common purpose, such as fearlessness and so forth, and taking them as the cause; then, by the power of experiencing them, there arises a conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-jñāna*). Within that [cognition], there appears an image of the object (*arthapratibimbaka*), which is a manifestation of the object (*arthābhāsa*) in the form of the object itself.
It is this [image] that is designated by the term "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) because it exists through identity (*tādātmya*) with that [object]. This is the syntactic connection.
"Kalpaka" means that which conceptualizes; that is to say, "savikalpa.
And this [term] is in grammatical apposition with "jñāna" (cognition).
"[Even though there is an absence of the nature of the object]"—that is to say:
Even though there is an absence of the nature of external objects,
"ascertained" means determined through conceptual construction (*adhyavasita*).
Now, as to how this designation "its exclusion" (apoha) is applied, he says: "Because of the difference from other appearances," and so forth.

[It is called exclusion] because of its difference from other appearances—that is, from the entity excluded from others—and also because it is understood by way of a real entity associated with it, through its being the cause of apprehension.
That result, which is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), is excluded from what is of a different class;
or rather, it is due to the deluded [cognition] determining that [particular characteristic] as being identical with this [conceptual object].
In this context, the designation "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) has been stated along with its basis;
the term "exclusion" (apoha) is applied to it for four reasons:
primarily, because it manifests itself as distinct from other manifestations superimposed by other conceptual constructions (vikalpa).

It is called *apoha* because it is excluded (*apohyate*); thus, based on its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), it is "the exclusion from others" (*anyasmād apohaḥ*) or "the exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).

However, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), there are three reasons: either through the attribution of the properties of the effect to the cause, as he says, "because it is the cause for the cognition of the object excluded from others";
or through the attribution of the properties of the cause to the effect, which he demonstrates by saying, "also because it proceeds by means of the door of the non-adherent object."
"Unattached" (aśliṣṭa) means not connected with anything else; that is to say, it is excluded from others.

That very thing is the door to the real entity (vastu), which is the means (upāya), because a conceptual construction of that kind arises through the power of experiencing it. Furthermore, it is the fourth cause [for its being a means], because it is determined by deluded cognizers as being one with the referent of the term "exclusion of the dissimilar" (vijātīyāpoha); this he demonstrates with the words "vijātīya... and so forth.
"Of this" refers to the reflection of an object mounted upon the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*).

"With its basis" (*sanibandhanā*) means that it exists together with its basis—the fourfold [basis] previously mentioned, such as the distinction from other appearances and so forth. Thus, it is "with its basis."
Showing the nature of exclusion (apoha) as having the essence of the object, he says: "Even in the case of the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)," and so forth:
"Even in the case of the particular characteristic, which is its cause, because of the existence of the exclusion of others."
The connection with the subject at hand is that this designation "anyāpoha" (exclusion of others) has been stated as being based on a foundation.
Regarding that, he states the foundation: "because of the state of being distinct from others.
This means because of the existence of distinction—that is, exclusion—from "others," namely from those of a different class.
This means that because there exists a separation from what is of a different class;
by this, it is stated that, primarily, the designation "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) applies to the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) itself.

He shows the essential nature of apoha, characterized as a non-presuppositional negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha), with the words beginning "prasajya": "And this non-presuppositional negation is: 'This cow is not a non-cow.
This exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is indeed understood most clearly."

Having thus demonstrated the threefold nature of exclusion (apoha), [the author], applying it to the subject at hand— the referent of words— says "tatrāyam" and so forth: "In that regard, this first type of exclusion is conveyed by words,
because a cognition that determines an external object arises from the word."
Regarding the term "the first":
it consists of the reflection of the object as previously described.
He states the reason for this in the passage beginning with "of that which determines an external object," and so forth.

For that alone which appears in verbal cognition is rightly the meaning of the word; nor is there here a determination of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), nor is there an appearance of the characteristics of a real object as in sensory cognition. What then?
A purely verbal cognition arises merely as a determination of an external object.

Therefore, it is that very reflection of the object which is rightly the meaning of the word in verbal cognition, because it appears directly in that cognition as having its own nature, and not anything else—this is the sense.

Furthermore, he demonstrates that the well-known relationship between a word and its object, characterized as the relation of the signifier and the signified, does not exist apart from the relation of cause and effect; rather, it consists essentially of the relation of cause and effect, by means of the passage beginning with "of the reflection of that form" [p.
When a cognition arises from a word through the appearance of that [object's] form as a reflection,
this relationship of signifier and signified is produced, consisting of the nature of cause and effect.

That which has as its nature (*rūpa*) or essence (*svabhāva*) the characteristic of having an externalized form determined by conceptualization is described as such; the compound *tadrūpapratibimba* means "that reflection which has that form. When there is the arising or production of that reflection belonging to the cognition from a word, this relationship characterized as signifier and signified (*vācyavācakalakṣaṇa*), when examined, turns out to consist solely of the relation of cause and effect.
For instance, the word is called the "signifier" because it generates the reflection of the word, and that reflection is the "signified" because it is produced by the word.
Therefore, what was stated—namely, "mere negation does not appear here in verbal cognition"—is inconsistent; the point is that mere negation is not accepted as the meaning of a word.

Thus, it has first been shown that exclusion (*apoha*) characterized as a reflected image (*pratibimba*) is the primary meaning of a word, because it is directly produced by words. Now, demonstrating that for the remaining two types of exclusion as well, the status of being the word-meaning in a secondary sense is described as entirely uncontradicted, he says "sākṣāt" and so forth:
"When this [reflected image] has been established in this way as the direct form, even the non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is understood by implication."

When there is a relation with entities such that "this is not its self" or "this is another's self," the comprehension of the excluded entity also occurs by implication; therefore, [the exclusion is established].
Therefore, this too is metaphorically designated as the word's own meaning;
however, this twofold apoha is not said to be directly denoted by the word.
"And thus" means by way of being produced.
Furthermore, showing why a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*), he says:
"It is not of that nature."
This is because the nature (ātman) of that reflection of a cow and so forth does not constitute the nature (svabhāva) of another reflection, such as that of a horse.

Having thus established that the status of the word-meaning is secondary (*gauṇa*) because exclusion (*apoha*) characterized by negation (*prasajya*) is understood as being inseparable from it, [the author], now demonstrating this even for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), says: "When there is a connection," and so forth.
In this context, the "connection" is a causal bond (*pratibandha*) between the word and the real entity, characterized by a causal relationship through a mediated succession.

First there is the experience of the object as it exists; from that, the desire to speak arises; from that, the movement of the palate and other vocal organs; and from that, the sound. When the word is thus connected with external objects such as fire through this sequence, then—given that connection—the object, even though it is excluded from things of a different class, becomes apprehended through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Therefore, the nature of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is twofold;
by the use of the word "also" (*api*), it is also of the nature of a simple negation (*prasajya*).

Regarding what was stated by Uddyotakara against the teacher Diṅnāga: "If the exclusion (apoha) of other objects is the denoted meaning of a word, then its own meaning must be stated as distinct from that denoted object; or, if that [exclusion] itself is its own meaning, even so, this statement—that 'a word denotes while effecting the exclusion of the meanings of other words within its own meaning'—is contradictory. For the meaning of this sentence at that time would be: "while denoting, it denotes."

Showing that this was stated due to a lack of understanding of the meaning of the sentence, [the author] demonstrates the absence of contradiction with the Master’s statement by saying "of another object," and so forth.
When a word is said to perform the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaravyavaccheda*),
it is not contradictory to say that it "denotes its own object" (*abhidhatte*).

For it has been established that even the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), the word’s own referent (*svārtha*). Therefore, when a word expresses its own referent consisting of the specific characteristic, it is said to "denote" (*abhidhatte*) by producing—i.e., generating—an exclusion (*apoha*) of other referents, which consists of a reflection excluded from other reflections. This statement of the Teacher (Dharmakīrti) is thus free from contradiction.
With the words "bāhyārtha" and so forth, he explains this very statement of the Teacher:
"Because it produces a reflection that functions through the determination of an external object,
it is designated as 'it speaks'."
But this [denotation] does not touch the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) which is the distinct [part];
apart from that portion consisting of the mere [universal], it has no act of denotation.
This is the Master’s intention:
apart from the production of a conceptual reflection that determines an external object, no other activity of denoting an external object is possible for a word,
because all phenomena are devoid of activity.
Therefore, it is said that by producing a conceptual reflection through the determination of an external object, the word expresses its own meaning;

however, it does not touch upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as differentiated—namely, as excluded from similar and dissimilar things—because such contact would be ineffective. This is because [the word] functions only insofar as it exceeds the mere portion [of the object].
The meaning is that, apart from the production of such a reflection, there is no other denotative function (*abhidhākriyā*) belonging to the Veda.
Having thus stated the essential nature of apoha, he now begins to refute the objections raised by others.
Regarding what was said, "If the word 'cow' [is applied]," and so forth, he replies with the words "And of that," and so on:
"And it is only when that reflection is apprehended that [the exclusion] is followed."
By implication, there is no separation from another, because there is no identity with another.

For a word produces only the cognition of a cow; however, the exclusion of others is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*), not from the word itself, because that reflection of a cow lacks the nature of any other appearance. Otherwise, there would be no apprehension of it as having a determinate form. Therefore, another sound need not be sought as the producer of the cognition of a cow, since the cognition of a cow is produced by that very word "cow."
To the objection that "words have cognition as their fruit," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "divābhojana" (eating by day):
"Like the sentence regarding eating by day, this [sentence] also has two fruits;
for its connection, whether direct or through implication, is not devoid of negative concomitance."

For example, in the sentence "Devadatta is fat because he does not eat during the day," the direct expression of its own meaning is the prohibition of eating during the day; however, the injunction to eat at night is what is understood, not directly. In the same way, for a word such as "cow" which conveys positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the knowledge of that concomitance is the direct result, whereas the comprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) follows by implication.
He states the reason for this with the words "because," and so forth:
because there is no positive concomitance of an injunction that is devoid of negative concomitance.

What then? It is precisely that which is non-deviant through the exclusion of dissimilar instances (*vijātīya-vyavaccheda*). For there is no possibility of anything existing that is not excluded from what is dissimilar.
Therefore, it is entirely non-contradictory for a single word to have two results.

He asks "Why? and replies with the words "Not by way of direct presence," and so forth: "Because, in reality, a word does not perform these two functions directly: the denotation of its own object and the exclusion of another."

If it were intended that a single word directly produce two simultaneous results— namely, the injunction and the cognition of a prohibition— then there would be a contradiction. However, if— as in the case of the sentence regarding daytime fasting— it is accepted that one result is direct while the other is obtained through implication, then there is no contradiction.
As for what was stated previously— that "the cognition 'it is not a cow' [is non-perceptual]" and so forth—
that too is refuted,
because it is not accepted.
For we do not maintain that the word "cow" directly intends the negation of the non-cow;
rather, it has been demonstrated that this occurs through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*).
Regarding what was stated— that the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*) is the universal (*sāmānya*), and so forth— he replies with the verse beginning "tādṛśa" and so on:
"And such a manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) is accepted as the universal 'cow-ness' (*gotva*),
because it is determined to be the same in all cases, such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others."
"Such" means superimposed as an external form and mounted upon the intellect.
He states the justification for this with the words "in all cases," and so forth.
Because there is a determination of them as having an identical form—namely, "cow, cow"—in all instances such as the brindled cow and others, that [form] is called their universal (sāmānya).

He shows that even its status as an external object is designated by virtue of the cognition of a deluded perceiver, and not from the perspective of ultimate reality, by stating: "and because of the determination that it is a real entity" (*vastvityadhyavasāyāt*).
And because of the determination that it is a real entity, it is also called a "real entity."
For that cognition has indeed arisen instantly as an error from its own seed.

One might object: "If at some time a primary entity, namely a universal (*sāmānya*), were perceived as residing in an external object, then a delusion regarding that universal might arise there through the observation of similarity; however, since no such primary object exists, this very delusion of a universal is untenable for you. Anticipating this objection, he says: "For it arises instantaneously," and so forth. This cognition arises—without depending on the observation of a universal and the like—due to an internal disturbance, just like the first moment of perception and so on. Indeed, not all delusions arise solely from the observation of similarity.
What then? There is no fault, because [the cognition] arises even from an internal disturbance.
Showing that, for this reason, the fault of proving what is already established does not occur, he says "sa eva" and so forth:
"That very thing, which is the object of the word in its [exclusion] form, is called apoha;
and it is [also termed] a universal (sāmānya) and a real entity (vasturūpa), because it is determined as such through error."
That very form of cognition, superimposed as something external, is called "exclusion" (*apoha*), the "meaning of a word," and a "universal" (*sāmānya*) that exists as an external entity.
He states the reason for this: "because it is determined through such an error.
This is because it is determined as having the nature of a universal and as having the nature of a real object.
The reason why [the object] is both the meaning of a word and of the nature of exclusion (apoha) has already been stated [in the verse]:
"Because the cognition that determines an external object arises from the word itself,
and because it is distinct from other appearances," and so forth.
But why is it that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, that [universal] is not a universal? To this he says "sāmānya... and so forth:
"It is not logical for its nature as a real entity to be a universal;
for how could that which has no form other than the cognition itself become a different object?"

For, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this [universal] is not distinct from cognition; how then could it become a separate entity, such that it would exist as a real universal (*sāmānya*) of objects?
As it has been said: "And how could that which is not distinct from cognition become a separate entity?

Therefore, there is no fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), for you do not accept that the universal called "cowness" (*gotva*), which is the form of cognition, is of an unreal nature; what then [do you accept]?

The point is that since a single, recurring, ultimate universal such as "cowness" (gotva) has been postulated as residing in external individuals like Śābaleya and others, there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).
Furthermore, regarding what was stated—"if it were of the nature of a mere negation," etc.—there is no fault because that [position] is simply not accepted.
Regarding what was said— "And in that [cognition], the cognitions of horses and so forth," etc.— he says "Even though," and so on:
"Even though this form is not distinct from the nature of the cognition, nevertheless its status as an external object is determined by those who are deluded."
This is easily understood.

Regarding what was stated—that "the meaning of a word is independent of [external] objects"—he says "of that," and so forth: "That [word-meaning] is not independent of objects, because it is derived from them through a traditional lineage; moreover, it has been demonstrated that it possesses no reality as such [an external object]."

For where there is a connection to a real entity through a causal lineage, even though that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is erroneous, it does not lack dependence on an external object—just as the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel [depends on the jewel].
Therefore, the claim that it is independent of an external object is unestablished.
Regarding what was stated—"And that cognition has the nature of a real entity," and so forth—he replies with "By that," and so on.

Although that cognition has the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), it has nevertheless been established by such statements as "it is not of that nature, nor of another nature" that its status as a real entity does not exist in the form of an external object or in the form of another cognition.
Therefore, the point is that it is not unestablished to say that the exclusion of one cognition by another is not perceived, because it is perceived through implication (*sāmarthya*).

Regarding the statement, "And even though an external object does not exist," he says "consisting of a reflection," and so forth: "Apoha consisting of a reflection arises even from a word; this very thing, called intuition (*pratibhā*), is for us the meaning of the word as well."

For just as we have described *apoha*—which consists of a reflection (*pratibimba*) and is termed "manifestation" (*pratibhā*)—as the external object (*bāhyārtha*), so too is it in the case of the word-meaning (*padārtha*). Since from a word (*pada*) as well, *apoha* consisting of a reflection indeed arises, for us this very *apoha* consisting of a reflection is considered to be the word-meaning as well; the word "also" (*api*) indicates that it is not merely the external object.
Therefore, the sense is that because there is no disagreement [on this point], a censure is not appropriate.
Regarding the statement that "the exclusion from another cognition is not perceived by the cognition," he says: "Because it arises merely as its own nature," and so forth.
For, arising merely as its own nature, it does not possess any other part;
therefore, the exclusion of the cognition from another cognition is perceived.

For precisely because that cognition does not possess any part other than the mere production of its own nature, it is therefore—by virtue of being established in its own essential character—that the exclusion of that cognition from another cognition is perceived; otherwise, if it were bearing the form of something else, how could it be perceived as excluded from that?
"By that" means by the non-determination of the nature of objects distinct from itself.
Regarding the passage beginning with "words denoting distinct universals," he says "just as," and so forth:
"Just as there is no ultimate difference for that which does not exist, so too is there no non-difference; therefore, they would be synonyms."

For just as it is said that because exclusion (*apoha*) lacks intrinsic nature and has no existing form, there is no mutual difference between them, so too there is no non-difference. Therefore, how can the consequence of synonymy be leveled against them when there is no distinct object?
Clarifying this very point, he says: "For non-difference [results] from having a single form.
Indeed, non-difference is the state of having a single form; and how could that exist in things that are formless?
Furthermore, if the object were a single entity, its various expressive words would become synonyms.

If it is argued: "Even if there is no single uniform nature among things that lack form, why should synonymy not still occur? [the author] replies with the words beginning "ekatve 'rthasya" (if the object were one).

It might be argued: "Even if there is no real identity among formless things, nevertheless, a conceptual identity exists; therefore, it is perfectly logical to entail their synonymy. To this, he says: "Even in the absence of form," and so forth.
"Just as unity is constructed by conceptualization even in the absence of form, so too is diversity. How, then, can synonymy follow from that?"
"Even in the absence of form" means even in the absence of intrinsic nature.
If this is so, how is the distinction between synonyms and non-synonyms established for words? To this he says: "In reality, however," and so forth.
"In reality, however, expressive words are neither synonyms nor non-synonyms;
for it has been explained that there is no single external object for them, nor is there a plurality."
For if there were some denotable object for words that was, in ultimate reality, either different or non-different [from its attributes], then there would be either synonymy or non-synonymy.

However, since it has been described—through such [categories] as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the universal (*jāti*), the connection with that [universal] (*tadyoga*), and the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*)—that none of these is a denotable object at all, [the distinction between synonyms and non-synonyms does not apply].

How, then, is the systematic arrangement of synonyms and so forth established? To this he says "But rather," and so on: "But even if that which is manifold is observed to perform a single function, a single verbal expression is applied to it by superimposing a single property."

In this regard, even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), the basis for establishing the status of a word as a "universal-term" is this: the fact that many things perform a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*).
For by their very nature, certain entities, though many, are performers of a single purposeful action.
To convey their capacity for such a single purposeful action, speakers, for the sake of brevity, apply a single form through superimposition and assign a single term to them.

Just as the designation "jar" is applied to many things such as forms and so forth, which are capable of performing a single purposeful action characterized by the fetching of honey, water, and the like.
But how is it possible for there to be a single term for many things without a single accompanying factor? To this he says: "In the case of the eye, etc. and so forth.
Just as in some cases, such as the eye and so on, which have the single result of visual consciousness...
If someone were to compose a scripture without a single follower, [it would not be authoritative].

For the application of words to their objects is dependent solely upon one's own will; for instance, even though the eye, visible form, light, and mental attention have the single result of visual consciousness, if someone, by the force of their will, were to apply a scriptural expression such as "there is a commonality" [or "a universal"] even without a single underlying entity, who could possibly prevent them?

Indeed, there is no such thing as a universal called "the state of being a producer of visual consciousness" existing in those factors like the eye and so forth, since you yourselves maintain that universals, particulars, and inherence are also producers of visual consciousness.
In these [universals], there is no inherence of a universal, because a universal is itself devoid of further universals, and because inherence lacks a second inherence.

But how can it be said that a jar and so forth produce a single effect, given that their effects—such as the holding of water—and the cognitions apprehending them are indeed distinct due to the difference in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)? To this, he says: "And of jars and so forth," etc.
And the effect of jars and so forth is the holding of water and the like.
And although that cognition which has that as its object is distinct, those two are nevertheless [not different].

Because it is the cause of a single unifying cognition, it is called "one"; likewise, although the cognitions are thus [multiple], the objects are non-different because they serve as the cause for that [unifying cognition].

Although that effect differs due to the difference in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, the effect known as cognition is said to be "one" because it is the cause of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśajñāna*) which determines a single object. And because they are the causes of that cognition, objects—such as those characterized by the fetching of honey, water, and so forth, as well as those characterized as individual jars and the like—are also said to be "non-different. He demonstrates this with the words: "Nevertheless, because they are its causes, the objects are non-different.
The word "is said" (*ucyate*), which is the subject under discussion, is connected here in the plural form through a modification of the verbal expression.
The word "api" (also/even) is displaced in its order and is connected immediately after the word "arthāḥ" (objects/purposes).
By this, the capacity to perform a single purposeful action is indeed established.
But would this not result in an infinite regress?

For instance, that very conceptual cognition (*pratyavamarśapratyaya*) is itself differentiated by the differentiation of its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, its unity is unestablished.
Consequently, for one who pursues a further effect of a single-form conceptual cognition in order to establish its unity, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
And because of this lack of a stable single effect, the application of a single term to anything whatsoever could never be established.
This is not so;

for we do not assert the unity of the reflective cognition (pratyavamarśapratyaya) on the basis of its having a single effect. Rather, it is due to its determining a single object; therefore, there will be no infinite regress.
Because it is established by its very nature that all reflective cognitions (*pratyavamarśa-pratyaya*) possess the determination of a single object;
therefore, this is the meaning:

because they are the cause of a single-form reflective cognition, the effect called "cognition" is said to be one, and because they are the cause of that [cognition], objects such as jars and the like also partake in the designation of unity.

Concluding that even without a real entity as a universal (*sāmānya*), words such as "jar" and so forth are established as denoting universals, he says "tatra" and so on: "In this regard, the words 'jar' and so forth, which were stated to be denoters of universals,
have as their sole cause a reflected image (*pratibimba*) excluded from those of a different class."

Demonstrating that even with respect to a single entity, there indeed occurs the application of multiple unmixed terms even without a universal-particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa), he says "tathā" and so forth:

"Likewise, because it performs multiple functions, a single [entity] is spoken of as if it were not one; it is conceptually constructed based on the multiplicity of exclusions (parāvṛtti) from those things that do not perform those functions."
Even a single entity, by its very nature, performs multiple purposeful actions due to its inclusion within various causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).

In that regard, even in the absence of a distinction between properties such as a real universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, a manifold designation is applied through the superimposition of multiple properties, owing to the multiplicity of distinctions among the objects that are the results of those actions.
Regarding this, he states an example, beginning with "just as": "Just as visible form is characterized by resistance,
or likewise, sound is known to arise immediately after an effort, so too is [the subject] inaudible."
Visible form (*rūpa*) is said to be "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) because it acts as an obstacle to the arising of another [form] in its own location.

It is "with demonstration" (*sanidarśana*) because visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arises with respect to it; since it exists together with that [consciousness], it is called "with demonstration.
He provides a second example as well, beginning with "effort" (*prayatna*), and so forth.
For just as a sound, although being a single entity, is said to be "known after effort" because its cognition results from an effort that follows [upon another],
and it is said to be "audible" (*śrāvaṇa*) because its cognition results from auditory perception;
for "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) means "audition," which is to say, auditory cognition.
It is "audible" (*śrāvaṇa*) because it exists therein by way of appearing as such;
or else, it is "audible" because it is apprehended by hearing.

Thus it has been shown that, through the distinction of non-causal effects, multiple designations are applied even to a single thing; now, he shows that in some cases a designation is applied even through the distinction of non-causal causes, stating:
"Through the distinction of non-causal causes, in some cases a word is applied, as for example the word 'sound' which arises from effort, or as for example 'honey' which is produced by bees."
"Bhrāmaram" means produced by bees; it is distinguished from honey made by small insects and the like.
Thus, it has been shown how there is a difference in verbal designation for a single entity due to the distinction between categories that are neither its effect nor its cause.

Now, with the desire to demonstrate the mere exclusion of categories that are its effect or cause, he says "tat-kārya" and so forth, showing how verbal designations are applied differently even in the absence of a universal (sāmānya).
Therefore, due to the absence of the reason of being an effect, a scriptural statement is sometimes made here [to the contrary],
such as "form is inaudible" or "lightning is not produced by effort."
Those two previously mentioned are the effect and the cause; those things which possess these are so described.
"Exclusion from them" means their differentiation.
To the question, "What then is this [word] *śruti*? he says: "Inaudible," and so forth.
Form is said to be "inaudible" by way of its exclusion from sound, which is the result of auditory cognition;
likewise, lightning is designated as "not produced by effort" by way of its exclusion from objects such as pots, which have effort as their cause.

Having thus demonstrated that even in the absence of a real entity such as a universal (*sāmānya*), the application of words according to their distinctions is produced solely by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), he says "ityādinā" and so forth, showing the absence of the consequence that [synonymous] words would be interchangeable: "By means of such distinctions, exclusions based on different objects are conceptualized; likewise, the linguistic expressions (*śruti*) are grounded in those [exclusions]."
Therefore, since words function according to convention alone to express unmixed objects,
they do not, for us, become synonyms by virtue of their distinct modes of operation.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), words such as "child" and so forth, which denote specific states, as well as words such as "selflessness" and so forth, are included.

Regarding the phrase "based on distinct referents" (vibhinnārthanibandhanā): those exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) for which the basis (*nibandhana*) is a referent (*artha*) that is distinct—that is, excluded from this or that [other thing]—are described in that way.
"Likewise" means like the exclusion [itself].
"Established in that" means established in the object as excluded,
because they are, by way of a causal series, the cause for the comprehension of such objects.
The term "śrutayaḥ" refers to words.

It might be argued: "Let it be that these [words] are not synonyms, since their difference in meaning is merely imagined; however, how can the established status of denoting a universal and a particular be proven for them without actual universals and particulars? To this, he says: "By virtue of having many or few objects," and so forth:
"Because they have many or few objects, and because of the inference based on linguistic convention (saṅketa), it is not contradictory that these [words] denote both universals and particulars."
For the word "tree" produces a reflection that infers the mere exclusion of non-trees with respect to all [trees] such as the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa*.
Because it has many objects, its denotable meaning is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*).

However, because the word "dhava" and so forth produce a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines only a few trees by excluding the *khadira* and others, its denotable meaning is called a "particular" (*viśeṣa*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "But surely, by means of the difference of the excluded objects," he says "And those," and so forth:
"And those exclusions (vyāvṛttayaḥ) of objects are constructed solely by conceptualization."
They do not, in the ultimate sense, become differentiated by means of the differentiation of their substrates through exclusion.

For if a real distinction between exclusions (apoha) based on the distinction of the objects to be excluded or the distinction of their substrata were intended, then this objection would apply; however, it is only through conceptual construction that distinct exclusions—based on the differentiation of homogeneous and heterogeneous entities—are imagined, not in ultimate reality.
And he shows that these [appearances] appear as if distinct from the real entity due to the power of conceptual construction, but not in ultimate reality, by saying "tāsāṃ hi" and so forth:
"For their status as external forms is imagined; it is not real.
Furthermore, difference and non-difference are established in reality only with respect to the real entity."
Or why is it real? To this he says: "And difference and non-difference," and so forth.

However, [the author] shows that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is only conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that differ, by stating "from their own seeds, manifold," and so forth: "But conceptual constructions, which determine those forms, differ on account of the power of conventions regarding objects that are distinct from their own manifold seeds."

Objects, which consist of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), do not attain a single nature, nor are they divided into fragments; rather, it is this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that fluctuates.

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "one's own seed" refers to the latencies (*vāsanā*) of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as wind and so forth; "the object" refers to that which is distinct from many [particulars]; and "convention" (*saṅketa*) is the linguistic agreement. Their "power" (*śakti*) is their efficacy. Consequently, conceptual constructions—which determine an object as being excluded from many heterogeneous things—are differentiated [from one another], but the objects themselves are not. For instance, the *dhava* tree and others do not attain a single nature through a universal form such as "treeness," nor are they divided into fragments by way of distinctions in properties such as momentariness.
It is only conceptual construction that fluctuates in such a manner, but not the object itself;
as it has been said:
"Ultimately real objects are neither conjoined nor divided by their own nature."
Form is both one and many; [the notion of these] is a cognitive distortion.
Thus it is said.
Regarding what was stated—"There are no [exclusions] with unestablished similarity," and so forth—he replies: "Even in the absence of the persistence of a single property," and so on.

"Even in the absence of the persistence of a single property, those which are the objects of the exclusion and the excluded are understood through their distinctness by means of a differentiated reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)."
The analysis [of the compound] is: "those which are to be excluded (apohya) and those which are the objects of exclusion (apohagocara).
Among these, the things to be excluded are horses and so forth, because the word "cow" functions by excluding them.
The objects of exclusion are the brindled cow and so forth, because the exclusion of non-cows has them as its domain.

Therefore, although there is no persistence (*anvaya*) of any single universal form, nevertheless, those things which are the causes of a non-differentiated reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) possess well-known similarity (*sārūpya*), whereas those that are the opposite are the opposite.

It might be argued: "Without a single universal, how can distinct objects be established as the causes of that single reflective awareness? To this, he says: "For in the case of a single reflective awareness," and so forth.
For it has been demonstrated that even though they possess difference by their very nature, only certain things are conducive to a single reflective awareness, while others are not.

This has been established in the *Sāmānyaparīkṣā*: just as a nurse and other such things perform a single purposeful action even without a universal (*sāmānya*), so too certain distinct entities will become the causes of a reflective judgment (*pratyavamarśa*) despite being different from one another.
Regarding the passage beginning with "nor [is it] devoid of positive concomitance" (nacānvayavinirmukta), he says "of a different nature" (atadrūpa) and so forth:
"The particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is the mere thing (vastumātra) excluded from what is not of that nature;
this positive concomitance (anvaya), being produced through effort, is not contradictory."

Although a universal does not exist as a real entity, nevertheless, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not contradicted when it is established solely on the basis of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as excluded from dissimilar instances.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"In that [which] exists as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinct from non-smoke,
there exists a particular characteristic excluded from non-fire."
Just as in a kitchen here there exists that which distinguishes [it] from non-smoke,
therefore the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) exists here as distinguished from non-fire.
"In which" refers to the location; and "here there exists a specific characteristic distinct from non-smoke" is the demonstration of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
With the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, he demonstrates the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*);

or rather, he shows that even when the five-membered syllogism is formulated through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by way of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it serves as a demonstration of the [subject].
And this has been stated regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
Regarding the essential-reason (*svabhāvahetu*), he says "of the non-existent," and so forth:
"That which is the distinct specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of non-existent things such as a human horn..."
Like the lamp of the intellect and other such things, all that is excluded even from the permanent.
Likewise, this [object] does not have the nature of a non-existent form, such as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound and so forth;
thus, through the distinction specified in this way, there is indeed a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with that.

That which is excluded from the non-existent by virtue of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— because it is not of that nature— is also excluded from everything permanent, just like cognitions, lamps, and so forth.
And since this specific characteristic of sound and the rest is not of the nature of the non-existent,
therefore, by this reasoning, a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) established through the specific characteristic is not contradicted, as it does not touch upon particularities (*viśeṣa*).
And this demonstrates the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the reason "because of being an entity" (sattvāt).

If, in this way, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established by the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone, how then is inference, which has the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object, established? To this he says: "And that very [specific characteristic], when its differences are not intended to be expressed," and so forth. It is proclaimed as being the general characteristic because no other [object] is desired.

For that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), when its internal distinctions are not intended to be expressed, is called the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). It is a "universal characteristic" because it is characterized—that is, determined—by way of a generality, through non-reflection upon its specific differences. Nor is there another [kind of universal], such as that postulated by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), because that is not accepted [by us].
As it has been said: "Because that very [cognition] apprehends both its own form and the form of another, two objects of cognition are recognized.
Likewise, another [author] has stated:
"On the basis of the mere entity that is excluded from what possesses a different nature..."
"The inferential mark (liṅga) is said to have a universal as its object, because it is not established in particular instances."
Thus,
even the concomitance of the mark (liṅga) and the word is stated by means of the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) alone;
nor do we determine the absence of the mark in the counter-example (vipakṣa) merely on the basis of non-perception.
What, then, is the meaning? It is that [the distinction] arises from a specific kind of non-apprehension; such is the intention.

Regarding what was stated, "The difference from the brindled one," and so forth, he replies with "Because of being the offspring of Śabalā," and so on: If the difference from the offspring of Śabalā is equal in both the Bāhuleya cow and the horse, then why does "cowness" (gotva) reside there [in the Bāhuleya] while excluding the horse?

For you ought to explain this: although the difference between a *sābaleya* (a brindled cow) and a *bāhuleya* (a black cow) is equal [to that between them and other cows], why is it that "cowness" (*gotva*) resides only in those such as the *sābaleya* and not in a horse?

It might be argued: "What is there to say here? For it is only the *sābaleya* cow and others that are capable of manifesting that universal of cowness (*gotva*), not horses and the like; therefore, it resides only in them and not elsewhere. Nor is this objection appropriate: 'Why is only that *sābaleya* cow and so forth capable of manifesting it?'—because this is a restriction based on the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things. Indeed, the intrinsic nature of things does not admit of questioning, since the restriction of their distinct natures is produced by a succession of their own causes. To this, he says: "In its manifestation," and so forth.
If it is maintained that the very same entity is capable of manifesting [the universal] there,
then even when there is an identical reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), that [cow] alone is capable [of producing it], and not the horse.
"Of that" refers to "cowness.
"That very thing" refers to the *sāvaleyādi* (the brindled cow and so forth), and not the horse.

If this is so, then even though there is a difference [between individuals], the fact that only the *sāvaleyādi*—and not the horse—is capable of producing a uniform conceptual reflection (*tulyapratyavamarśa*) even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), does not contradict our position at all.
And what follows from this? He says: "tādṛk" and so forth.
"In whatever object such a reflective awareness exists, even in the absence of the universal 'cow,' the exclusion of the non-cow (agopoha) proceeds."
In whatever object, such as a brindled cow and the like, there arises a reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśa*) in the form "this is a cow,
this is a cow," it is precisely therein that the exclusion of the non-cow (*agopoha*), though unreal, functions as a reflection within the real entity belonging to the cow-class.
Showing that what was stated beginning with "by the sense organs" (*indriyaiḥ*) and so forth is unestablished, he says: "And that entity which is non-different from the non-cow," and so on.
That entity which is non-different from the non-cow is determined by the senses;
however, the reflection superimposed upon it is understood through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).
Having perceived this, the word is employed by people in that regard;
thus, its experience of the relationship [with its meaning] is clearly established thereby.
In this regard, exclusion (*apoha*) as having the nature of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is indeed apprehended by the sense faculties.

As for exclusion whose nature is the reflection of its own object, that is established through the very perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), because it is ultimately of the nature of cognition.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to collect meanings not explicitly mentioned.
By this, it is shown that even the self-nature (*svātmā*) is indeed understood through implication, and not as "that nature" being "another nature.

Therefore, it is precisely this exclusion (*apoha*), in the form of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, which people perceive and employ words for; it is not a universal (*sāmānya*) that exists as a real entity, because such a thing does not exist and does not appear [in cognition].

And only with respect to that which people perceive when they employ a word is its relationship [with the word] understood, and not with anything else, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Regarding what was asked, "And how, moreover, is there the state of not being denotable by the word 'non-cow'?", he says here, beginning with "tādṛk" (of such a kind):
"In whatever entity there is no such reflective awareness at all,
the state of not being denotable by the word 'non-cow' is clearly understood therein."
Regarding what was said—that "the cow would be excluded as something already established," and so forth—he replies with the verse beginning "Cows and non-cows":
"Cows and non-cows are well-established through distinct conceptual cognitions;
however, the word alone is not established [independently] and is employed according to one's wish."
For the apprehension of one thing does not depend upon a distinct object for its cognition;
therefore, this fault of mutual dependence has no basis in this case.
For entities such as cows and the like, by their very nature, produce distinct conceptual cognitions and are thus correctly determined in their differentiation.

For the sake of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), speakers employ words as they please toward these objects, even though the words themselves are not inherently established [as denoting those distinctions].

That is to say, if the apprehension of another object were required for the sake of understanding the specific nature of a distinct entity, then there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*); however, [in reality], the distinct [entity] is [apprehended] even without the apprehension of another.

The object is perceived; once it is established through differentiation by virtue of being the cause for the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of distinct forms, a convention such as "cow, cow" is made according to one's will. Thus, how could there be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*)?
The word "in cognition" (*vittau*) is used for the sake of making it known.
Regarding what was stated— "there is no relation of substratum and superstratum, etc."— he replies with the verse beginning "Even though its external reality is unperceived," and so forth:
"Even though its external reality is unperceived and it is subject to intense cognitive distortion, this verbal cognition determines its own internal representation as having an external form."
This much is accomplished by words; words do not even touch the object itself.
Nor is any object qualified by exclusion (apoha) denoted [by them].
Indeed, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), no object qualified by exclusion (*apoha*) is denoted by words;
for it has already been established that not even the slightest real entity (*vastu*) is touched by words, because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for such contact is absent anywhere.

Thus, although verbal cognition has no external object as its domain, it arises by determining its own internal reflection—its own form—as being an external object; it does not, in reality, touch the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing, because it does not determine [the object] according to its true state (*yathātattvam*).
If this is so, how is it that the Master stated: "Words such as 'blue lotus' express objects qualified by the exclusion of other objects"? To this he says:
"By the exclusion of other objects, they express [objects] as qualified"—as for what was further stated by the author of the *Lakṣaṇa*, therein this is the intended meaning.

To the question "What is this intended meaning?", he says: "By way of mutual difference," and so forth. Those entities which, by means of a cause or an instrument, are distinguished as being of different classes, are determined to be unmixed with others.
Because sound, when striking trees and the like,
produces a cognition that determines their existence, this constitutes the refutation of [the reality of] universals and so forth.
For there are two kinds of objects: the external and that which is mounted upon the intellect.

Among these, with respect to the external, there is no denotation by words in an ultimate sense; rather, it is said figuratively that "word expresses the object" solely because it produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines that [external object]. And the purpose of this figurative usage is the refutation of the theory that the universal (*jāti*) is what is expressed. This is the general meaning [of the passage].
The meaning of the individual members [of the compound] is now stated: "by way of otherness from others" (*anyānyatvena*).
Otherness from another is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); by that reason or instrument, namely otherness from others, entities such as trees are distinguished—that is, determined.
This means they are determined as excluded from others.
By this, the meaning of the instrumental case in the word "nivṛttyā" (by means of exclusion) in the phrase "distinguished by the exclusion of other objects" has been explained.
"Dhvani" refers to sound.

He shows that an object which has ascended into the intellect is denoted by words primarily through the verse beginning with "in the intellect" (*buddhau*), etc.: "Those which revolve in the intellect, these he calls internal;
and their distinction by exclusion (*nivṛtti*) has been stated immediately after."
"This" refers to the sound (*dhvāna*).
Now, as to how these [words] are to be understood as being qualified by the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaranivṛtti*), he says: "by means of exclusion" (*nivṛttyā*).
And so forth.

"Immediately thereafter" means that by [the passage] beginning with "by way of being distinct from one another," even those objects established as the Buddha are demonstrated to be excluded from other things.

Now, if no part of an entity whatsoever is expressed by a word, how is it that the Teacher stated: "By the exclusion of other referents, some part of the entity is understood"? To this he says: "Exclusion of other referents," and so forth. "It is said that by the exclusion of other referents, some part of that entity is understood; that very thing is the reflection."
Now, one might object: "Since the reflection is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), how can it be established as a portion of the real entity (*vastubhāga*)?
To this he says: "By means of the exclusion of other objects," and so forth:
"Because it relies upon the perception of a real entity as excluded from other objects."
And because it is superimposed upon that which has arrived there, a portion of it is designated.

Because it is brought about through the perception of a real entity as excluded from other objects, and because that very reflected image is superimposed by the deluded as being identical with that real entity excluded from other objects, it is metaphorically designated as a "part" of the real entity.
Applying the meaning of the instrumental case here as "by means of the exclusion of other objects," he says: "The meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument, as before, by that very nature;
if a thing were not different from those of a dissimilar class, it would not be so [distinguished]."
