"‘As before’ means that just as it was shown in the passage ‘they state [them] as qualified by the exclusion of other objects’ by means of the phrase ‘as being distinct from one another,’ etc., so too should it be applied here; this is the meaning.
Alternatively, he shows that in every case this is a third case ending used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇā*), as in the expression ‘by that very nature’ (*tena vātmanā*).”

Now, one might object: "The exclusion of other [contrary] things is a property residing in the external object; how then can that serve as the cause or the instrument for the apprehension of a reflection? To this he says: "If the object were not excluded from heterogeneous things," and so forth.

For if the object were not excluded from heterogeneous entities, then it would not be determined as having the nature of a reflection through its essence as an object excluded from the heterogeneous; therefore, the status of being the cause and the status of being the instrument belong to the exclusion of other objects—this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the passage beginning with, “Knowledge cannot produce a distinguishing characteristic that is of a different form or of a different nature,” he says:
“The exclusion of the non-cow is otherness, and that [otherness] resides in its own self.
Even when difference is expressed, the mere absence does not cease [to exist].
Even when there is the state of being a qualifier for that [object], the cognition of the thing itself is not lost;
for this qualifier is constructed by conceptualization, even though there is no actual difference [between the object and its qualities].
Then, having extracted it, Dharma was established as if possessing differentiation,
by which it indeed acquires a qualifier, just like a staff or other such attributes.

For if the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) were intended as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) serving as a qualifier of a thing, then all these objections would be valid; however, since the exclusion of others is taken as a qualifier precisely as the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the thing itself, the cognition of the qualified object necessarily conforms to that qualifier. To illustrate: the "exclusion of the non-cow" which is expressed by the word "cow" is nothing other than the cow's own nature, namely its difference from horses and so forth. It is not something else.

And therefore, although this exclusion of the non-cow (*agonivṛtti*) is designated as "cow" by way of distinction when there is a desire to know merely the rejection of other differences, nevertheless, in the ultimate sense, that [exclusion] belongs to the very nature of that cow itself. Just as "otherness" (*anyatva*)—for "otherness" is not something other than the other entity, but rather that [entity] itself;
otherwise, that entity would not be established as distinct from that other thing.
Therefore, even though it is a qualifier, the cognition of the entity as the qualified object indeed occurs through the exclusion of others.

It might be argued: "In the world, a qualifier is well known to be distinct from the qualified, as for example a staff is [distinct] from a man; yet exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is non-distinct from the entity. Therefore, how is it logical for that [exclusion] to be its qualifier? To this, he says: "Conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*), and so forth.

In the ultimate sense, it is not logical for anything to be a qualifier of anything else, because that which provides no assistance cannot function as a qualifier. Furthermore, if one were to admit that it does provide assistance, then since the cause does not persist at the time of the effect, a relationship of qualifier and qualified is not logical between two things that do not exist simultaneously. On the other hand, if they were to exist simultaneously, then because both are already fully established in their entirety at that time, there can be no mutual assistance; thus, a relationship of qualifier and qualified is not tenable.
Therefore, because all entities abide in their own respective natures and are like iron rods [standing independently], their mixing occurs only within conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

Thus, although in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) there is no distinct exclusion (*vyāvṛtta-bheda*), nevertheless, by relying on a distinction fashioned by conceptual construction, the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) will come to be.
Regarding what was stated— "Since [the universal] is denotable by words and cognitions, individuals are not excluded"— and so forth,
he replies with "And the manifestation," etc.:
"The thinkers of reality say that the manifestation is the meaning of a word."
One who does not understand the non-differentiation between the object of perception and its conceptual construction considers it to be external.
Therefore, by virtue of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), it is only individuals that are denoted;
and it has been established that, in reality, there is nothing denotable for words.
The reason "because individuals are inexpressible" is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For the inexpressibility of individuals that we have described pertains to the investigation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and not even to conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*); for in conventional reality, it is well known—though only as long as one does not subject it to analysis—that individuals themselves are expressible. Thus, the reason is unestablished.

The "perceptible" (*dṛśya*) is the external thing whose nature is its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); the "conceptualizable" (*kalpya*) is the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) that revolves within conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*).

Now, if ultimate ineffability is adduced as the reason, then since the exclusion [of individuals] is also not accepted as being ultimately real, he shows that this results in proving what is already established by saying "tattvataśca" and so forth.
With the words "In this way" (*ittham*) and so forth, he concludes the very point that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*):
"And thus, because individuals are denotable by words, they possess the quality of being excluded (*apohyatā*);
but for the universal (*sāmānya*), there is no exclusion, nor does it possess the nature of a real entity (*vastutā*) even if it were excluded."

Regarding what was stated— "That [exclusion] has no universal as its object of exclusion, and because it is excluded, it possesses the nature of a real entity"— the author demonstrates through the words "of the universal," etc., that the reason "because it is an object of exclusion" is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This is because it has been established that exclusion (*apoha*) belongs only to individual instances (*vyakti*).

And "even in the case of an apoha, it is not a real entity" means that there is an absence of a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the reason when its opposite of the probandum is asserted. This is the intended sense.
Regarding what was stated—"Exclusion does not apply to non-entities," and so forth—he replies with "It is not a non-entity," and so on:
"For in this way, a non-entity is not excluded [by the thought] 'this is a non-entity, a non-entity';
rather, since a positive entity (bhāva) does not have that as its nature, it is precisely for that reason that its status as an object of exclusion is accepted."
If one were to say "non-existence is not non-existence," then non-existence would not be excluded in such a way that its nature as non-existence would be abandoned.
What then? That which is existence, because it has a positive form, stands apart from the nature of non-existence; therefore, by implication, the exclusion of that non-existence is intended.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "That which is called 'name' is not its own nature; that is said to be its exclusion (apoha). It is neither an entity nor of the nature of non-existence, and in the absence of such exclusion, there is no reality."
Regarding the phrase "the exclusion of that":
when there is such an exclusion of that very non-existence, it does not attain the status of a real entity.

Clarifying the inconclusiveness [of the reason] by demonstrating examples established for both sides, he says: "The state of being produced by primordial matter (prakṛti), God (īśa), and so forth," and so on.

When it is urged that things do not have the state of being produced by primordial matter, God, and so forth, indeed, the state of being produced by primordial matter, God, and so forth is not established as a real entity.
For indeed, even you Mīmāṃsakas do not accept that the existence of entities is produced by primordial matter (prakṛti), God (īśvara), time (kāla), or the like.

Just as those [entities] do not attain the status of real things (vastutva) despite their being negated, so too, even if non-existence (abhāva) is the object of exclusion (apohya), it will not incur the status of a real thing; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).
Regarding what was said—"In that case, even for that which is non-existent, there would be substantiality;
thus, a great difficulty would arise"—he shows that this too has been refuted by the very same demonstration of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), stating:
"Therefore, even for the non-existent, there is no being-ness; thus, there is no difficulty whatsoever."
And when that [non-existence] is established, existence exists; and that non-existence is thereby established.
Regarding the statement, "If that is not established, there is no existence, nor is non-existence established," he says: "And when that is established, existence exists," and so forth.
When that non-existence is established by the manner already described, the existence of the entity is indeed established, because it is established in its own intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, that very establishment of non-existence by the manner already described is what is known as non-existence.
And this has been refuted right here on the grounds that the rebuttal is the same.
Now, he states the rebuttal in its proper sequence. Regarding what was said—"the non-existence of non-existence," and so forth—he says "non-cow," and so on:
"The cow is held to be the exclusion of the non-cow and to possess a distinct characteristic;
therefore, this [cow] is indeed a positive entity (bhāva), and my position does not entail the consequence that it is a non-cow."

If it is argued that "it would indeed be a positive entity (bhāva)," this does not entail an undesirable consequence, because it is actually desired. For instance, the horse and so forth, which possess the nature of a non-cow, are held to be distinct from the cow precisely as a specific kind of positive entity, and not as a non-entity; therefore, it remains a positive entity. Furthermore, since the non-cow is held to be distinct from the cow, there is no consequence of the non-cow being the essence of "cowness" (gotva).

Regarding what was stated—"For it is not held [to exist] in the case of a non-entity"—the author says "Even with respect to a non-entity... and so forth, demonstrating that this [reason] is unestablished and inconclusive:
"Even with respect to a non-entity, there exists a latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) produced by the mind alone, as if fashioned from the various distinctions of conceptual construction."

And thus, due to the difference in latent impressions (vāsanā), both differentiation and the nature of existence are attributed to exclusions (apoha), just as they are to things constructed by conceptualization.
The claim that the mind has no object consisting of a non-entity is unproven;
for indeed, the mind does function precisely through the superimposition of the form of an entity arising from an object produced by its own limited capacity.
And that [mind] certainly deposits a latent impression (*vāsanā*) in the immediately succeeding moment of consciousness for the sake of producing a subsequent conceptualization of the same kind.

Since, however, by the power of the further ripening of the mental continuum, that very same kind of cognition arises again upon encountering an awakening condition, so too will the mutual distinction and the positive nature (*sadrūpatā*) of exclusions (*apoha*) come about through the force of conceptual construction; thus, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*).
As for the meaning of the individual members [of the compound], they have not been analyzed because they are easily understood.
Regarding what was stated by you— "the distinction between words is also not found to be caused by that"— he says "of such a kind," and so forth:
"Just as this exclusion of other objects (arthāntarāpoha) has been established as the denoted meaning, let the exclusion of other words (śabdāntaravyapoha) be understood to be exactly the same."
"Of what kind? means having the nature of a reflection; and its distinction from another reflection is indeed perceived most clearly.
Therefore, the sense is that everything which was stated at length is entirely inconsistent.
Regarding the argument that "there would be no relationship between the signified and the signifier," etc., he provides the following rebuttal beginning with the word *vastu*:
"Because the two exclusions (*apoha*) are determined as real entities (*vastu*), they are not non-entities;
this is established on the conventional path, while on the ultimate level, it proves what is already accepted."

If "because of being non-entities" is stated as a general reason, then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because the two—namely, the reflected image and the self [of the cognition], or the excluded referent (*apoha*) and the denoter—are determined by the deluded as external entities; thus, they indeed possess conventional reality (*sāṃvṛta-vastutva*).
Now, if the reason is stated by relying on ultimate non-substantiality, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For we do not, from the perspective of ultimate reality, admit the existence of anything that is denotable or denotative.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "nor is there anything denotable," and so forth.
In the ultimate sense, there is nothing whatsoever that is either the signified or the signifier,
because among entities that are subject to momentary destruction, there is an absence of pervasiveness.
"Because of the lack of pervasiveness" means that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) lacks pervasion over the time required for convention and linguistic usage due to its momentariness.
It might be argued: "We do not deny a real relationship between the signified and the signifier."

What then? Relying on the fact that both exclusions (*apoha*) are ultimately non-entities, it is only their conventional status as the cognized and the cognizer (*gamyagamakatva*) that is negated, not their real existence; therefore, there will be neither the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhatā*), nor the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in the thesis.

If both [the object to be understood and the means of understanding] were assumed to be either conventional or ultimate, these two faults would indeed arise; therefore, he says: "And if the state of being the understood and the understander is negated as conventional, having relied upon their ultimate non-substantiality in the case of cessation."
Nevertheless, the charge of deviation remains unavoidable,
because of objects constructed by conceptual thought and the words that denote them as well.

This being the case, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because in objects such as Mahāśvetā and the like—which are constructed by conceptualization—as well as in the words that denote them, a conventional relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is observed even though, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), they lack the status of real entities.
He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "by those constructed by conceptualization" (*vikalparacitaiḥ*).

It might be argued: "Even in those cases such as Mahāśvetā and others, the universal (sāmānya) exists in the ultimate sense as both the denoted and the denoter; therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule] by means of them. Anticipating this objection, he says "For not... and so forth:
"For in those cases, there is no universal that is the denoted, nor is there a denoter of it."
The unique particular (svalakṣaṇa) of a word, being momentary, does not possess the capacity to denote [an object].

Since the universal (*sāmānya*) has been refuted in detail during the examination of the universal, there exists neither a universal that is denoted nor one that denotes among those [particulars]; thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The word "of that" (*tasya*) refers to the universal.
Furthermore, in the phrase "denoting," the word "universal" is also connected with the subject under discussion.

It might be argued: "Even if there is no real entity (*vastubhūta*) there to be denoted, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word ‘Mahāśvetā’ and so forth, which is the denoter, certainly exists. To this he says: "The word does not possess the nature of a denoter," and so on.

Since it has been established that momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) pervades all things, the specific characteristic of a word cannot be a denoter; for, due to its momentariness, it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) for it, and it has also been established that it does not persist until the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra*).
He concludes with the words "Therefore" and so forth:
Therefore, those two—the reflection and the rest—must be accepted as conventional;
their deviation from [the object] remains unavoidable among them.
"Two things" refers to the signified and the signifier.

By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "reflected images, etc.," he shows that even when one accepts a cognition devoid of an objective form (*nirākārajñāna*), one must necessarily admit some other specific internal factor belonging to consciousness itself—one which, though lacking an object, determines an object within those [images]. This is what is indicated by the words "in them."
The word "tad" means "therefore," or it refers to the fact that the reason is inconclusive (vyabhicāritva).
Regarding the statement, "And by whom the word-meaning as a positive form is not accepted," he says:
"And by whom the word-meaning as a positive form is not accepted,
then the mind arises bearing its appearance, for it is indeed a determination of the object from the word."
When words express their own meanings, the exclusion of others follows by implication;
that [exclusion] is also a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for me, for it is preceded by that [expression of the positive meaning].

For it is not the case that we do not accept the referent of a word as having a positive form (vidhirūpa) in every respect, such that you would be able to level this charge of an undesired consequence against us.
To the extent that a word produces a cognition which determines an object, the referent of the word is indeed accepted as being conventionally positive in form.
In reality, however, there is nothing at all that is denotable by words; thus, it is the real existence of an affirmative form that is being negated.

Therefore, since a conventional word-meaning in the form of an affirmation is accepted, and because the exclusion of others (anyavyatireka) is understood through the force of implication when the word denotes its own object in an affirmative form, it is indeed logical for exclusion to be preceded by affirmation.

This might be the case if the meaning of a word were accepted as having a positive form; how then is it that the author of the *Lakṣaṇa* stated in the section on the "Reason" (*hetumukha*) that there is no possibility of a positive [referent]? To this he says: "There is no possibility," and so forth. "There is no possibility of a positive [referent] because universals (*sāmānya*) and the like are impossible, and because words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have real entities (*vastu*) as their objects."

Since the denoted—such as the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—and the denoter are ultimately non-existent, and since words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) lack an object in reality from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the Master stated that affirmation (*vidhi*) is impossible when relying on the ultimate truth; thus, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the state of being denotable as mere exclusion" (*apohamātravācyatva*), he says "nīlotpalādi" and so forth: From words such as "blue lotus," only a single reflection is apprehended— one that is excluded from the non-blue, the non-lotus, and so on.

The word "blue lotus" denotes a single reflection that is excluded from what is non-blue and non-lotus; it possesses the form of the object and has the nature of both [the word and the thing], and does not denote a mere absence. Therefore, by virtue of the force of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), words such as "blue lotus" indeed possess the capacity to express a real object. Consequently, based on that [determination], grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is perfectly justified.

Regarding what was stated—"Now, if it is asserted that the object denoted is a thing possessing the exclusion of others"—to this he replies with "But not as possessing the exclusion of others," and so forth:
We do not maintain that the denotable object is a thing possessing the exclusion of others;
because there is no absence of anything other than that which is excluded, for us there is no exclusion from something else.
Therefore, this fault of dependence is not applicable here as it is in the case of [words denoting] birth;
for when the meaning of a word is stated as "pure," there is no distinction [between the word and its referent].
Therefore, since the relation of qualifier and qualified and co-referentiality [are possible], the systematic arrangement [of linguistic usage] is not contradicted when the word-meaning is *apoha*.

For if exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were indeed something other than that which is excluded (*vyāvṛtta*), then the aforementioned faults regarding that [position] would follow. However, for us, there is no exclusion other than the entity itself as it is excluded from others; rather, it is the excluded entity itself that is designated in such a way when there is a desire to know merely the exclusion of other differences. Therefore, just as when a universal (*jāti*) is the primary object of expression, its possessor (*tadvat*) is expressed through dependence [upon it].

It was stated that because the distinctions residing in that [object] are not implied, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with it; however, this does not apply to the theory of exclusion (apoha), because that which possesses the exclusion of others (anyāpohavat) is not denoted as distinct [from the exclusion].
He demonstrates this with the words "Therefore, this fault of dependence... and so forth.
"Tat" means "therefore" (tasmāt).
Regarding the phrase "it is declared to be pure":
this refers to the definition of the meaning of a word as *apoha* (exclusion) as propounded by the teacher Diṅnāga, who possessed purified intellect.
He states the reason for this here: "because of non-separateness."
Because that word-meaning, characterized as the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), is not distinct from— and indeed does not differ from— the referent (padārtha) which is excluded from others;
that is to say, [the relation of] qualifier and qualified, and so forth, is easily understood.
Showing how grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth are not contradicted, he says "from the isolated," and so on:
"From the isolated word 'blue' and the like, a distinguished reflection proceeds,
hovering over the cuckoo, the blue lotus, the bee, and so forth."
Furthermore, by the exclusion (*apoha*) of the *pika*, the *añjana*, and so forth,
that object qualified [by those exclusions] is definitively established by the word "blue lotus" (*indīvara*).
Thus, grammatical coreferentiality and other such relations remain uncontradicted in this [view];
however, in the opposing position, the systematic establishment of all these is extremely difficult to maintain.

For instance, when "blue" is uttered, there arises a conceptual reflection whose form is subject to doubt regarding bees, cuckoos, collyrium, and so forth—other objects excluded from "yellow" and the like.

That reflection, being established by the word "lotus" as having for its object a thing excluded from non-lotuses (i.e., distinguished from *kikilā* and the rest), is perceived as having a definitively determined nature.

Therefore, because of the relationship between the excluded and the excluder (*vyavacchedya-vyavacchedaka-bhāva*) with respect to these mutually related conceptual reflections as described, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) between the words "blue" and "lotus" is not contradictory.

The collective meaning is that because the two [terms] establish a single entity whose nature is a reflection distinguished from both the non-blue and the non-lotus, they possess grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by virtue of referring to one and the same object.
As for the meaning of the individual parts, it is said: "floating" (*plavamāna*) means not finding a firm footing; that is to say, being of the nature of doubt.
The word *pika* is a synonym for the cuckoo (*kokila*).
The rest is easily understood.

One might argue that even in our own position, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth are not at all contradictory; therefore, he says: "But in the case of the opponent's position," and so on.
"Tadvyavasthā" means the establishment (*vyavasthā*) of that [relationship], such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth; thus, it is "the establishment of that."
To explain how it is difficult to establish, he says "For instance" (*tathā hi*) and so forth:
"For in this way, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is expressed in its entirety by a single word;
and since it has been thus denoted, why would there be no cognition of other particulars?"
If another word were to be employed here for some purpose in reality,
then it would follow that [the object] is manifold, unless it has been expressed in every respect.

In the view of those who maintain that the meaning of words consists solely in injunctions (*vidhi*), once the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a lotus or the like has been denoted by a single word such as "blue," there can be no ignorance regarding other particulars—such as whether it is a lotus or perhaps collyrium—because that object would have been presented in its entirety.
This is because it is contradictory for a single thing to be both known and unknown simultaneously from the perspective of a single cognizer.
He demonstrates this by asking: "Why is there no cognition of other distinctions?"
Ignorance is the lack of knowledge;
"amati" is a contemptible form of cognition,
meaning doubt and error.

And thus, because there is an absence of doubt and error, he shows that the speaker would have no need for the employment of other words such as "lotus" (*utpala*) by saying "for which purpose," and so forth.
"For which purpose" means:
for the sake of removing that particular ignorance.

Now, it might be argued: "That object is expressed only by one part, not in its entirety; therefore, another word must indeed be sought to express its other intrinsic natures. To this, he says "in every way" (*sarvathā*) and so forth.
For a single object does not possess parts by which there could be an expression of only one part, because unity and multiplicity are defined by their mutual exclusion.
Consequently, as many parts as you may propose, you have merely established that many distinct objects; thus, neither a single entity nor a multiple entity would be established.

It might be argued as follows: "The word 'blue' does not denote a substance; rather, it denotes either the quality called blue or the universal 'blueness' inherent in it. Likewise, by the word 'lotus,' only the universal 'lotus-ness' is expressed, not the substance. Therefore, because they denote different objects, the requirement for another word, such as 'lotus,' is indeed appropriate. To this, he replies with the words beginning "the universal of blueness," etc.
If the blue universal or the quality blue is already apprehended by the word "blue," then the other lotus universal must be determined through the auditory perception of the word "lotus."

This being the case, because there is a distinction between the two, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth are all the more appropriately established, just as in the case of the words "bakula" and "utpala."
"Anyendīvarajātiḥ" means "another lotus-species";
it is a compound (samāsa) consisting of "anyā" (another) and "indīvarajātiḥ" (lotus-species).
"Vyavasya" means having determined.
It is to be understood [as such]. The term "utpalaśruteḥ" ends in the ablative case.

On this view, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is even more untenable, because—just as in the case of the words "bakula" and "utpala"—there is no occurrence of the two words "blue" and "lotus" in reference to a single object.
For it is not the case that a *bakula* is an *utpala*.

It might be argued as follows: "Even though the word *nīla* denotes a specific universal (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*), nevertheless, by means of those two, the substance connected with that blue quality and its universal is also denoted by it; likewise, the word *utpala* also denotes that very same substance by means of its universal.

Therefore, because it is possible for those two to refer to a single object, there will be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), but this is not the case for the words *bakula* and *utpala*. To this, he says: "If the substance connected with the quality and its universal... and so forth. If the substance connected with the quality and its universal is what is being conveyed, [then...]
If it were so by means of the word "blue," then the mention of "lotus" would be redundant.
Whatever is connected with those two is precisely that which possesses the universal "lotus-ness";
since that is already expressed there by the word "blue" alone, the expression "blue lotus" is redundant.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "guṇa" is that which is called blue (*nīla*), and "tajjāti" is that which is called blueness (*nīlatva*); thus, it means "connected with those two.
[The opponent argues: "The word 'lotus' would be redundant," because that substance has already been conveyed by the word "blue" alone.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "by those two," and so forth.
"By those two" means by the quality and its corresponding universal.

It might be argued: "Even though the word *nīla* denotes a substance that possesses both the quality [blueness] and its genus, nevertheless, because it is observed to apply to multiple referents, a cognition of a determinate form does not arise in the hearer regarding the object *utpala* (blue lotus), since things such as *kiṅkirāta* are also blue.
Therefore, because the hearing of the word *utpala* excludes doubt regarding other objects, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is indeed meaningful.
This is incorrect, because it is stated by one who is ignorant of the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛtārtha*).

For in this context, the subject at hand is that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth are not tenable under the view that the meaning of a word is a positive injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, if the word "lotus" functions solely for the purpose of excluding doubt and not for the cognition of a substance, then the word-meaning could no longer be a positive injunction; for the word "lotus" would merely convey the exclusion of a form superimposed by error. Moreover, it is contradictory to assert that the word "blue" denotes a substance such as a lotus, yet no certainty arises in the cognizer regarding it.
For it is not logical that a word’s referent be something regarding which doubt arises, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor can doubt find any room in an object that has been made the objective domain of a certain cognition (*niścaya*),
because there exists a relationship of sublation between certainty and superimposition (*āropa*).

It might be argued: "Even if the words *nīla* (blue) and *utpala* (lotus) do not apply to a single object, their referents—the quality (*guṇa*) and the universal (*jāti*)—do indeed apply to a single substance;
therefore, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) will occur by way of their referents. This is incorrect, because it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For in that case, even the words *rūpa* (color/form) and *rasa* (taste) would possess coreferentiality, since their referents, color and taste, both reside in a single substance such as earth.

Furthermore, the cognition whose object is a single referent, such as "a blue lotus," would not arise, because two qualities and two universals inhering in a single substance are denoted separately by the two words; and if a cognition whose object is a single referent does not arise, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words—enough of this prolixity!

It might be argued: "The object connected with the quality blue and its universal is not the very same thing denoted by the word 'lotus' (utpala); rather, it is something else entirely. Thus, the term 'lotus' will not be redundant. To this, he says: "From that which is connected with the quality and its universal," and so forth. "If the word 'blue' and the word 'lotus' were to have different substrata [referring to two distinct things], then [the lotus] would be something other than what is connected with the quality and its universal, yet possessing the universal of the lotus."
The word "yadi" (if) serves as a restriction.
"They would have different loci" means that they would exist in different substrata.

Now, it might be argued: "Even though that very same substance is denoted by the word 'blue' (*nīla*), it is also denoted by the word 'lotus' (*utpala*). Nevertheless, the word 'blue' does not denote the substance by way of its form as connected to the universal 'lotus-ness' (*utpalatva*); rather, it denotes it precisely by way of its form as connected to the quality 'blueness' (*nīlaguṇa*) and its universal. Therefore, the application of the term 'lotus' to denote this [substance]’s form as connected to the universal 'lotus-ness' will not be purposeless. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words beginning "But if [it were] by way of being connected to lotus-ness... (*athotpalatva-sambandhi-rūpatvena*). "But if [it were] by way of being connected to lotus-ness, one would not raise the objection."
The word "blue" denotes a substance connected with a quality and its genus.
Now, the connection is as follows: the word "blue" would not denote a substance related to a quality and its universal by way of having a form connected to the state of being a blue lotus (utpala).
Granted that the form of the possessor of the lotus-ness may be non-identical with it [the lotus],
yet that which is connected with "lotus-ness" is indeed connected with both of those.
And that [blue thing] is expressed by the word "blue" and is made the object here by verbal cognition in its entirety, not by parts; therefore, the word "lotus" is meaningless [in that context].
This is correct.

For the form related to the lotus-genus (*utpalajāti*) is not something other than the form related to the quality blue (*nīlaguṇa*) and its genus; for if it were so, then when the form related to "blue lotus" and so forth is denoted, the denotation of the substance's form related to the lotus-genus would not occur.

Since the two [properties], namely the state of being a relation and the state of being non-different from that [substance], are not distinct from a single substance, it is illogical for there to be a lack of expression of the other form when one form is expressed; for even if it were granted that the nature of "lotus-ness" consists in its being related [to a substance], because it is related to the universal through its connection with "blue-ness"—just as in the case of "blue"—the term "lotus" would still be redundant. For indeed, that very partless entity which is connected with the universal "lotus-ness" is the same one that is connected with these two, namely the quality "blue" and the universal [itself]; nothing else is involved.

And since that [universal] is a part [of the individual], it is expressed in its entirety by the word "blue" alone; and since it is made an object of the verbal cognition consisting of determinate judgment (*vyavasāyātmikā*), what further unexpressed nature remains for it such that the word "lotus" would have a purpose in denoting it?

Uddyotakara, however, says: "In the case of a partless entity, this conceptual distinction—that it is apprehended in its entirety and not in parts—does not apply; for the word 'all' has multiple things as its object, whereas the word 'one' functions with respect to a part.
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "And if... and so forth:
"And if there is no conceptualization of 'entirety' or 'part' in that which is devoid of differentiation..."
This is not because of a complete understanding of the meaning of the sentence; for this is what is intended here.
By the very first word, that [self] has been revealed in every respect;
no aspect of it has been omitted, exactly as it is, so it has been described.
"Free from division" means in an entity that is partless. "The conceptualization of division as a whole" [is what follows].
The conceptualization that [the word] makes its object known either "in its entirety" or "only in part" is stated because of a failure to understand the meaning of the sentence.

For, by the very first word *nīla* (blue), it is intended to convey that the object is revealed in its entirety; that is to say, the thing is expressed exactly as it is, and no aspect of its nature remains unexpressed for which the word *utpala* (lotus) would have to function. Since that entity is partless (*niraṃśatvāt*), this is merely a quibble of words (*vākchalam*). //1115//

Thus, just as the mention of the word "lotus" (utpala) would be purposeless, so too the employment of other words such as "impermanent" (anitya) and so forth would result in being purposeless. Since their employment would merely constitute synonyms, like the words "taru" and "pādapa," he makes this extension [of the argument] by saying "by this very same method," and so on:
"By this very same method, the utterance of other words is not fruitful; in that case, when these words are spoken, they are certainly synonyms."
"Udīraṇa" means application;
"in speech" means in utterance.
Regarding the act of utterance,
it has been said: "Otherwise, if a single object were pervaded by one word, or by a cognition, there would be no other object [for another word], and thus they would be synonyms."

It might be argued: "Even in your own position, when a single object has been denoted by one word, why does it not follow that there is an absence of doubt and error regarding other distinctions, and why does it not follow that other words would fail to apply? To this, he says: "But for us," and so forth. "But for us, an external object is not communicated by a word.
It is held that from a word, cognition arises which has the universal (jāti) as its object, not the external object."
Since, after they have been made objects by those two [the senses] in their entirety,
a subsequent verbal cognition arises regarding them, it will result in synonymy.
"By those two" means by word and cognition. "Beyond" means—
At a later time. //1118//

Now, if the referent of a word is conventional (sāṃvṛta), why does this fault—the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—not arise? To this he says, "But the reflection," and so forth:
"But the reflection is produced by the word only successively;
yet it appears as a unity and as something external due to delusion."
Grammatical coreferentiality and the like exist by way of conformity with reflections;
however, in ultimate reality, these words are considered to be without an object.

For, by the word "blue" (nīla), there is first produced a conceptual reflection which—by way of its form floating over lotuses and so forth as excluded from non-blue objects—is not a rejection of those [objects], yet is determined as having an external form. Then, by the auditory perception of the word "lotus" (utpala), that very same [reflection] is produced as excluded from non-lotuses, with the nature of a single superimposed external entity. Thus, in this sequence, a mistaken conceptual reflection is produced which is excluded from both the non-blue and the non-lotus, and is determined as a single external form; in accordance with that, conventional coreferentiality and so forth are indeed tenable.
But why is it not tenable from the perspective of ultimate reality? To this he says: "From the perspective of ultimate reality," and so forth.
Regarding what was stated—"There exists no connection with gender, number, and so forth for the exclusion (apoha)"—he says here, beginning with "liṅgasaṅkhyādi":
"But this connection with gender, number, and so forth does not belong even to individual entities (vyakti);
for it is caused by conventions fashioned by human will, and is not real."
It is unestablished that these— gender, number, and so forth— are properties of real entities (vastu),
because they exist merely through conventions fashioned by independent whim;
the word "also" implies that this applies to individuals as well as to the exclusion (apoha).

The formal argument is as follows: whatever does not conform to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of something is not a property of that thing, just as coldness is not a property of fire; and gender, number, and so forth do not conform to the actual positive and negative concomitances—this is a non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi).
Showing that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "The bank, the slope, and the bank"— there is no lack of form (*nairūpya*) in the object,
because all cognitions of it attain a variegated appearance (*śabalābhāsatā*).

For if gender were a property inherent in the thing itself, then in the case of a single entity called a "bank" (*taṭa*), where words associated with the three genders—*taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*—are applied, it would follow that a single entity possesses three forms.
Yet, it is not logical for a single thing to possess a triple nature consisting of female, male, and neuter, because that would entail the loss of its unity.
If even that which is superposed with contradictory properties were to remain one, then the entire universe would be a single entity.
Consequently, there would follow the absurdity of their arising and perishing simultaneously.

Furthermore, since it is observed that every single object—whether by means of a single word or another word—is perceived as possessing the three genders, it would follow that all cognitions directed toward those objects would possess a variegated appearance, like a multi-colored gem.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even though all things possess the three genders, those cognitions will—by the force of the speaker's intention—manifest only that specific form which the speaker wishes to express, and not as having a variegated manifestation. To this, he says: "Or, if they were to follow the speaker's intention," and so forth. "Or, if they were to follow the speaker's intention, they would not have those [external objects] as their objects; by virtue of that [intention], they would take on a single form, yet the object is not of a single form."
Or, [the phrase] "in accordance with the intention to speak" (*vivakṣānugatatve*) is to be understood as referring to "of cognitions" (*cetasām*).

For if it is admitted that cognitions take on a single form by the power of the intention to speak, then those cognitions would not have as their object a thing consisting of the three natures (*tryātmaka-vastu*), because they would be devoid of those [three] forms, just as visual consciousness has sound as its object.
"By the power of that" (*tadvaśāt*) [means by the power of the intention to speak].
By virtue of the intention to speak.

To demonstrate that the view of one who thinks that the established distinction of femininity, masculinity, and neuter-ness occurs respectively in contraction (*saṃstyāna*), production (*prasava*), and persistence (*sthiti*) is also not tenable, he says "persistence," etc.: "If the establishment of gender were dependent upon persistence, production, and contraction, then the consequence would follow that there is a state of being all three genders simultaneously, since they are inseparable."
The punctuation here should be after "yadi syāt" (if it were).

For if the establishment of gender (*liṅgasthiti*)—that is, the determination of gender (*liṅgavyavasthā*)—were based on [universal properties] such as persistence (*sthiti*), then all three genders would apply to all things without distinction, like the case of a riverbank (*taṭa*) or a chain (*śṛṅkhala*), because persistence and the other properties exist everywhere, just as they do in the case of a bank.
Otherwise, even in instances such as *taṭas*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*, there would not be three genders, since there would be no distinguishing factor.
Therefore, over-extension is a defect of the definition.
Showing that [the definition] is non-pervasive because deviation is observed, he says "non-existence" and so forth:
"That which is called non-existence, the state of being indefinable, or voidness—
what kind of connection with persistence and so forth could possibly be imagined for that?"

For even in the absence of [the characteristics] such as duration, since non-existence—such as that of a hare's horn and the like—is observed to be conveyed by words such as "being of an unreal nature," "indefinability," and "insubstantiality" through the apprehension of all three genders, this grammatical rule regarding gender is not universally applicable.
The arising and production of these [entities] is held to be their destruction,
while their own inherent form is designated as their persistence.
In that [reality], there is no destruction in arising; so why is it called "origination"?
Nor is there a persistence characterized by a self-nature; so how is it proclaimed as "birth"?

In the case of contraction (*saṃstyāna*), there is neither of the other two; how then can it be designated as "disappearance" (*tirobhāva*), "destruction" (*nāśa*), or even "the act of making disappear" (*tirobhāvana*)?
If stability is [itself] stable, by what cause is its intrinsic nature said to exist?
Or else, their form would be entirely undifferentiated, resulting in a single characteristic.
For this reason as well, [the theory] is non-pervasive, because we observe the application of words endowed with all three genders to each of those very states—origination and so forth.
To explain: *prasava* is said to be origination (*utpāda*), *saṃstyāna* is destruction (*vināśa*), and the essential nature of the self is persistence (*sthiti*).
In that context, since persistence and destruction are absent in origination, how could feminine and neuter gendered terms such as *utpattiḥ* (feminine) and *janma* (neuter) apply to origination?

Likewise, since there is an absence of persistence and production during contraction (*saṃstyāna*), how could it be designated by such terms as "concealment" (*tirobhāva*), "destruction" (*vināśa*), or "the act of concealing" (*tirobhāvana*)?
By the word "also" (*api*), he shows how even "contraction" itself would be designated by its own specific term.

Similarly, since contraction and production are impossible during persistence, it must be explained by what reason that persistence is called "having the nature of persistence" (*sthitisvabhāva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, it might be argued that because these [states]—stability and so forth—are mutually inseparable in form, each one among them will possess the suitability for all three genders; to this he says, "Now, if they were inseparable," and so on.
For if their forms were mutually inseparable, then there would be only one gender in the ultimate sense, not three genders.
But another says: "Femininity and the like are general-particulars (sāmānya-viśeṣa), just like cowness and the like. To him, he replies with the words beginning "just like cowness and the like":
"If these [qualities] such as femininity are considered to be just like cowness and the like..."
By the refutation of the universal, those [particulars] of that kind are already discarded.

Since universals and particulars were previously refuted in the examination of the universal (*sāmānyaparīkṣā*), it is impossible for those forms such as femininity (*strītva*) and so forth to exist; therefore, this is a definition that is impossible.

Furthermore, he demonstrates that the definition [of universals] is non-pervasive (*avyāpitā*) because we observe the application of words with feminine, masculine, and neuter genders—such as *jātiḥ*, *bhāvaḥ*, and *sāmānyam*—even in the absence of another universal within those very same general and particular entities (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). Thus he says: "The universal (*jāti*), the state of being (*bhāva*), and the commonality (*sāmānya*) are accepted as such among them; for other universals are not logically applicable to universals.

The universal (*jāti*), the state of being (*bhāva*), and the commonality (*sāmānya*) are agreed upon by you as residing in those [particulars]. However, other universals cannot be joined to universals themselves.
It is not tenable for universals to possess further universals,
because the established doctrine (siddhānta) is that universals are devoid of further universals.
And this has been stated on the basis of the Vaiśeṣika school's doctrine.
However, when grammarians maintain that there are further universals within universals— as it has been said:
"Even when the meaning is a universal, all [words] denote universals, because word-meanings are established as being characterized by activity."

For the classification of universals (jāti) observed in other treatises need not necessarily be accepted by grammarians. Indeed, universals have their forms inferred from the effects of the operations of suffixes, denotations, and syntactic concomitance; there is no fixed limit to them. Therefore, since a universal existing as the substratum of a commonality is established through the observation of the enjoined effect, this serves as the basis for the scriptural statement "universals" (jātayaḥ).
The phrase "characterized by function" (vyāpāralakṣaṇā) means that their characteristics are established through the functions of designation and cognition.
The refutation of this has already been stated immediately prior: "By the rejection of the universal, such [entities] are likewise discarded."
And he states this common refutation beginning with "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
How could [the three genders] be non-existence, the state of being indefinable, or mere nothingness?
Therefore, this establishment of the three genders is merely conventional.

For there is no universal (*jāti*) in non-entities such as a hare’s horn and the like, because it is a property of real things; therefore, the application of words such as "non-existence" to them would not be possible.
Consequently, the formal arrangement of logical marks (*liṅga*) is not all-pervasive.
Thus, it is established that this arrangement of the three types of logical marks exists solely by virtue of conventions fashioned by human desire.
Demonstrating that number, too, does not follow the presence or absence of an objective reality, he says "Number, also," and so forth:
"Number, indeed, is conceptualized even regarding things that are conventionally uniform, according to the speaker's intention;
this occurs despite the distinction between difference and non-difference, as in the cases of 'wife' (*dārā*) and 'forest' (*vipina*)."
Number, too, is merely conventional and not real;
for even in the case of "wife" and so forth, although no real distinction exists, it is constructed by the force of intention (*vivakṣā*).
Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

For instance, numbers such as plurality and singularity do not have as their defining characteristic the difference or non-difference residing in the object itself; for in cases such as *dārāḥ* (wife), *sikatāḥ* (sand), and *varṣāḥ* (rainy season), the number of plurality occurs even though there is no actual difference in the objects.

Likewise, in cases such as *vanaṃ* (forest), *tribhuvanaṃ* (the three worlds), *jagat* (the world), and *ṣaṇṇagarī* (the city of the six), the number of singularity is designated even though there is no non-difference of the referent.
Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Nor is it inconclusive, because that would entail the absurd consequence that everything would possess the nature of all things;
nor is it contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa).
With the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely), he raises an objection regarding the unestablished nature of the reason according to the view of Kumārila:
"But surely, [words] such as *dāra* (wife) are applied to both the individual and the genus;
they function by taking up either the number of the individual or the number of its constituent parts."
Furthermore, the word "forest" (vana) denotes either many individuals qualified by a genus and a number,
or it denotes the genus itself as residing in many individuals.

He said: The word *dāra* (wife) sometimes applies to the genus (*jāti*) and sometimes to the individual (*vyakti*). When it applies to the genus, it functions by taking on the number residing in the individuals; and since there are many female individuals, [the plural form is used]. When it is applied to the individuals, it functions by taking on the plurality of the parts of those individuals, such as hands and feet. However, by the word *vana* (forest), distinct individuals—such as mango, khadira, and palāśa trees—are conveyed as qualified by the number belonging to the genus "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva-jāti*) inherent in them; therefore, the singular form *vanam* occurs.
This is because the word denotes a substance qualified by the singular number belonging to the genus (*jāti*).

Alternatively, it is the genus itself, as residing in individual trees such as *dhava* and others, that is expressed by the word "forest" (*vana*); therefore, the singular number occurs because the genus is one.
He offers a rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely):
"But surely, by this method, the entire [theory of] speech as a single unit is destroyed.
If there is no intention to speak in other cases, let that very [intention] be its basis."
By this aforementioned method, the entire singular number, such as "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), would be destroyed or abolished, because this same logic applies equally in all cases.
For here too, it can be argued in this way: if [the word] "tree" and so forth [applies] both to the individual (*vyakti*) and to the universal (*jāti*).
"Is applied," and so forth. Now,

if it is thought that in other cases, such as trees and the like, there is no intention to express the number of the individual or its parts— if this were so, then number would not conform to the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and other relations existing in the real entity (*vastu*), because it would instead conform solely to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

Consequently, let that very intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) be the basis for this plural number in cases such as *dārāḥ* (wife/wives) and so forth; since even a single entity may be intended to be expressed as a plurality despite the absence of actual difference, the reason [adduced] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Regarding what was said—that the word "forest" denotes individuals qualified by a genus and a number—he replies with the verse beginning "Of the genus," and so forth:

Even for a genus there is no number; or, even if it were present, how could the individuals be qualified by it? Is it through a connection with that which is connected [to them], or even through a direct connection?

For there is no number belonging to a genus, because number resides in a substance. Now, if this Vaiśeṣika system is not accepted, then how could those individual entities such as *dhava* trees be established as being qualified by that number, whether it exists in the genus or in the substance?
It might be argued that they are established through a relation with a relation, or through a direct relation.

For instance, when number is distinct from the universal (jāti), then, because the individuals such as *dhava* trees are connected to the universal which is itself connected to the number one, those individuals are qualified by that number through a mediated relationship; however, when number is indeed distinct from the universal, then they are qualified by it through a direct relationship. Therefore, they are established as being qualified by the number of the universal.
He replies with the words "If this were so," and so forth:
"If it were stated in this way that even a single tree is a forest,
then many [trees] would indeed be called so because of their connection, and that [connection] exists."

If the application of the word "forest" (*vana*) to individual *dhava* trees and the like occurs either through a connection with a connection or through a direct connection, then even a single tree would have to be called a "forest," because the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) exists there as well.

For instance, many *dhava* trees and others are called a "forest" solely due to their connection with the number associated with the genus (*jāti*), and not for any other reason; since that same connection exists even in a single tree, why should it not be called so?
Alternatively, regarding the statement "the genus is based on many individuals," he says:
"That which is based on many individuals is also present in a single one;
because its cause is the same, the cognition of 'forest' would occur there as well."

For even on this view, there would be the designation "forest" for even a single tree. To explain: by that word "forest," a genus (jāti) residing in many individuals is denoted; and that very same [genus] is established in even a single individual, such as a dhava tree. Consequently, since the cause for the cognition of a "forest" is identical everywhere, why should the cognition of a forest not occur even with respect to that one tree?
With the words "by means of positive and negative concomitance" and so forth, he concludes the discussion on causality: "Therefore,

by means of positive and negative concomitance, this restriction regarding words such as 'one' and so on arises from the speaker's intention, not from the object itself, because [the word] deviates from the object."
"Because of its deviation from that" means because of the deviation of that object.

Regarding the statement, "The connection with gender, number, and so forth does not exist for the exclusion (apoha)," the author addresses the connection with action, time, and so on, which was indicated by the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi). He says "action," etc.:
"The connection with action, time, and so forth has already been refuted previously.
Therefore, these [connections] are merely conventional; they do not even exist in [particular] individuals."

Since the connection with action and so forth has already been refuted by the negation of categories such as the time of action and so on, it is improper for these [categories] to be properties of real entities (*vastu*).
Those which exist in convention are "conventional" (*sāṅketika*).

Or, let it be granted that these [exclusions] possess the nature of real entities (*vastudharmatva*); nevertheless, because the exclusion characterized as a reflection (*pratibimba*) is determined by those under delusion to have the form of external individuals, there will—by virtue of such conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*)—be a connection with gender, number, and so forth, mediated through the individual. Thus, he demonstrates that what was stated—"Since the individual is inexpressible, this [exclusion] exists even through it"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and unestablished (*asiddha*) from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), by means of the passage beginning "by the determination of the form of the individual.
Alternatively, if the exclusion is said to be expressed by way of the determination of the form of the individual:
Its connection with tallness, gender, and so forth exists by way of the individual instance.
"It is called apoha" means "by means of a word"— this is the ellipsis. "Tat" means "therefore."
"Of this" refers to the exclusion (apoha).

Regarding the passage beginning with "And not for another in the case of verbs," he says: "For the sake of establishing [the meaning] in what is intended," and so forth. A word is employed for the purpose of directing the intellect toward what is intended;
therefore, the exclusion of what is unintended is established by implication alone.

It is unproven that the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is not perceived in verbal expressions (*ākhyāta*). For instance, a word is employed by speakers to direct the listener’s intellect toward some intended object, not out of mere habit; therefore, when the intended object is understood, the exclusion of what is unintended is necessarily perceived through implication (*sāmarthyāt*), because the intended and the unintended consist in mutual exclusion.
If it is argued that "everything is indeed desired," he replies with the words beginning "everything indeed":
"Everything indeed is not desired, because it would follow that there is no restriction regarding all objects;
therefore, that which is to be excluded by words such as 'cooks' is perfectly clear."

If everything were indeed intended, then a specific word-meaning would not be established; consequently, the listener’s engagement with a particular object through a word—while excluding other objects—would not occur. Therefore, the claim that "everything is intended" is untenable.
Thus, by implication, the exclusion of what is unintended is clearly understood from words such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and the like.

With the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth, he demonstrates that very exclusion of what is unintended, which is understood through implication: "For instance, when it is said 'he cooks,' it is understood that he does not remain indifferent; rather, it is understood as the exclusion of others, namely: 'he does not eat' or 'he does not gamble.'"
Therefore, there is indeed this state of indifference, and yet there is another distinct action;
for whatever is intended as the object of exclusion, it must necessarily be of the nature of a relative negation (paryudāsa).

Therefore, for the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*), there exists that which is to be excluded by way of preclusion (*paryudāsa*), namely indifference (*audāsīnya*) and other actions such as "he eats" or "he plays. Consequently, the claim that "the object of negation in the form of a preclusion does not exist" is unestablished;
for the analysis of the compound *paryudāsātmakāpohyam* is:
"that which is of the nature of a preclusion (*paryudāsātmaka*) and that which is to be excluded (*apohya*)."
The connection is as follows: for whatever is intended as "certainly," there exists a corresponding object of exclusion (*apohya*) consisting in the negation of indifference and so forth.
Regarding what was stated— "but that which is 'cooking' remains unprevented, abiding by its very own nature"— the author, demonstrating the opponent's self-contradiction, says "pacati" and so forth:
"But that which is 'cooking' remains unprevented, abiding by its very own nature."
And this statement of yours is mutually contradictory.
"This is the negation of other forms while abiding by its own nature alone;
otherwise, the emphatic particle used would be meaningless."
But how is this mutually contradictory? To this he says: "This is the negation of another form," and so forth.

By the restriction "it remains in its own essential nature" (*svarūpeṇaiva tiṣṭhati*), which demonstrates the form as it has been performed, it is shown that the existence of the word "cooks" (*pacati*) consists in the negation of another form.
Otherwise, the very restriction "in its own essential nature" (*svarūpeṇaiva*) employed by you would be meaningless, because there would be nothing to be excluded.
Regarding what was stated—"And here there is the cognition of being a probandum," etc.—he replies with "The state of being accomplished," etc.:
"What kind of 'accomplishment' can there be for an exclusion (apoha) that is indefinable?
For there is no accomplishment whatsoever of things such as a sky-lotus."

If it is argued that this [cognition] appears as something possessing a defining characteristic because of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "it is a real entity," then what follows? Is its possession of properties identical to those of real entities thereby established?

If you have apprehended apoha as being devoid of any defining characteristic (*nirupākhyasvabhāva*), how can it be said that it is "established" (*niṣpanna*)? For there is no establishment whatsoever of things such as a sky-lotus, since they are characterized by the absence of all defining characteristics. To this one might reply: although this apoha is indeed devoid of defining characteristics from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), nevertheless, because it is determined as having the nature of an external object by deluded cognizers, this apoha appears as if it possessed defining characteristics.

To this, he asks: "What follows from that? [The opponent replies: "Even if it indeed appears as possessing a designation (*sopākhyatva*), what has occurred here that is favorable to the subject at hand?
To this, the other says: "Its similarity in properties with real entities (*vastu*) is thereby understood."

Therefore, just as a real entity is perceived as having an established form, so too exclusion (apoha) is perceived as if established, appearing as though it possesses the same properties as real entities; thus, the statement "because of its established nature" is proven.

If it is argued that you yourself have thus demonstrated the cause for the cognition of being "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) and the cognition of "past" (bhūta) and so forth, and that it should not be said that this [cognition] results in being causeless—showing this very point, he says: "Therefore, the cognition of being to-be-accomplished... and so on.

"Therefore, the cognition of being to-be-accomplished, as well as the representation of 'past' and so forth, results in having that [accomplishment] as its cause, because it possesses a form identical to real entities."
"Having that as its cause" means having as its cause the determination that [the object] possesses the same nature as the real entities.

Regarding what was stated— "In the mass of objects such as injunctions (*vidhi*), there is no determination of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)"— he replies with the verse beginning "In injunctions, etc. In the mass of objects such as injunctions, non-existence and so forth are negated by implication (*sāmarthya*), but not by the word itself, since that which is not intended to be expressed [by the word] is not [directly negated].

Since the meaning of an injunction and so forth exists as being excluded from what is prohibited and so forth, when that [meaning] is understood, non-existence and the like—which are not intended to be expressed—are precluded by implication; thus, even here, the determination of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) certainly occurs.

Regarding the statement, "And the actor is also joined with actors," he says "And the actor... and so forth: "And the actor is also joined with actors; exclusion (apoha) would be of such a kind as is perceived when those four are present."
In the case of a verb (*naṭ*), the meaning of "acting" is understood; by some [auxiliary], an injunction is conveyed, and by a third [auxiliary], the absence of that [injunction] is established.
When another [word] is employed for the purpose of negating that [which was previously mentioned],
then, while that [negation] is intended to be expressed, the exclusion of other [possibilities] is made known by it.

Regarding the phrase "the existence of that tetrad": this refers to the existence of four negatives. To the question, "What kind of thing is perceived in that case?", he says: "The connection with *naṭ*," and so forth.
The word *artha* (meaning/purpose) is to be connected with the word *vidhi* (injunction). "Its absence" (*tasya viraha*) means the negation of that injunction.
"For the sake of the negation of another" means for the sake of negating that which is presented by the third case-ending and the suffix -anaṭ, and which is devoid of a positive injunction.
"The fourth" [refers to this].
The fourth [case ending]:
because the suffix *yat* is prescribed for the purpose of ordinal numbering by the rule "caturasthayatāvādyakṣaralopaśca" (Pāṇini 5.2.51),
it is said "when that [ordinal] is intended."
The meaning is that when that fourth actor has been employed;
"by him" means by the fourth actor;
"it is made known" refers to the exclusion of others.
Because, through the exclusion (*viveka*) of the negation presented by the third actor, there is the presentation of an object-reflection in the form of an affirmation (*vidhi*).
Making this very point clear by means of an illustration, he says: "He does not not cook," and so forth.
For when it is said, "He does not not cook," it is understood that "he cooks";
indeed, the connection with indifference and so on is understood by the third [negation].
But in the fourth [state], it is determined that he is distinct from those [states] as one who "cooks";
therefore, by this injunctive statement, there is likewise the cessation of other [notions].
"Distinct from that" means distinct from indifference and so forth. "The exclusion of others is equal to an affirmative sentence" means [the same].

Just as in an injunctive sentence such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), the cessation of indifference (*audāsīnya*) is intended by implication, so too in the second case, "he does not" (*naṭi*), its cessation is established here as well;
however, the example of the fourfold *nañ* is given for the sake of clarity.
To the objection that even for words such as *ca* (and), there is no connection with a negation, he says: "The conjunction and so forth," etc.

Whatever meaning, such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) and the like, is intended by the word *ca* and others, by that [meaning] there occurs the exclusion of its opposite, such as disjunction (*vikalpa*) and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such [meanings] as: the meaning of option (*vikalpa*) for the particle *vā*; for the particle *api*, the meanings of possibility (*sambhāvanā*), connection with a word-meaning (*padārtha*), concession (*anvavasarga*), and so forth; for the particle *tu*, the meaning of distinction (*viśeṣaṇa*); and for the particle *eva*, the meaning of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "other than that":
it means other than that [group], namely, other than conjunction (*samuccaya*) and the rest.
And by that first one.
Regarding the statement, "And the exclusion of others cannot be designated as the sentence-meaning," he says "vākyārthe" and so forth:
"The exclusion of others in the sentence-meaning is indeed well-known;
for it is said that certain word-meanings themselves, when combined, constitute the sentence-meaning."
And those things which are of a different class from them must be clearly excluded;
for they alone constitute the meaning of the sentence, since there is indeed nothing else that exists apart from them.
"Accompanied" means being connected to one another by way of the relationship of cause and effect.
"Of them" refers to those categories (padārthas).

Now, it might be objected: "The word-meaning is one thing, while the sentence-meaning is another; so how can it be said that those very things which are the objects of exclusion for the word-meanings are also the objects of exclusion for the sentence-meaning? To this he says: "That [sentence-meaning] does not exist as something other than them. The point is that there is no sentence-meaning distinct from the word-meanings—whether it be partless, variegated in nature, or resembling a mottled color—because such a thing, even if it met the conditions for perception, is not perceived.

Clarifying this very point by means of an example, he says "Caitra" and so forth: "When the meaning of a sentence such as 'Caitra, bring the cow' has been understood, the exclusion (apoha) of other agents, objects, and so forth is understood by implication."

For in this sentence, no object other than the referents of "Caitra" and so forth appears to the intellect. Indeed, when the meaning of "Caitra" is understood, the exclusion of non-Caitras and the like is understood by implication;
otherwise, if the exclusion of other agents and so forth were not intended, the mention of Caitra and the others would be entirely purposeless.
And consequently, since nothing would be expressed by anyone, the world would be entirely devoid of activity.
Regarding the statement that "in the case of words such as *ananyāpoha* (exclusion of others), no denotable object is determined," he says:
"In the case of words such as *ananyāpoha*, no positive entity (*vidhi*) is ascertained,
because [such a positive entity] previously [was shown to be] intended by others [as being] a universal (*jāti*) and so forth, and has been refuted."

For here, the meaning of a word in the form of a positive affirmation characterized by universals (*jāti*) and so forth—such as you intend—is not established in an ultimate sense, because such things as universals have already been refuted at length previously in the "Examination of the Universal" (*Sāmānyaparīkṣā*) and other sections.
To the question, "What then is determined? he says "But... and so forth:
"However, from this sound, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises that determines a positive injunction;
subsequently, when there is a negation of the word-meaning as exclusion (*apoha*), cognition arises."

If it is maintained that a cognition arises when there is the negation of the word-meaning "exclusion" (apoha), then the word-meaning "exclusion" should not be accepted, because it has been negated; to this he says: "But that [cognition] is non-correspondent, being of such a kind. "But that [cognition] is non-correspondent, because of its loss of connection with a real entity. Not all verbal cognitions determine a real object."
"Sa" refers to words and so forth that do not exclude other things (*ananyāpoha*).
"Non-corroborative" (*asaṃvādaka*) means that which does not correspond (*na saṃvadati*), or that for which no correspondence exists; thus it is non-corroborative.
Why?
Because of the loss of connection with a real entity (*vastu*), since there is no such connection with a real entity as previously [described].
For it has been refuted earlier that the meaning of a word is a real entity characterized by genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

If this is so, how then does the cognition that negates the word-meaning of "exclusion" (apoha) arise from words such as "non-exclusion of others" (ananyāpoha)? To this he says: "[They are] not verbal.

For certain verbal cognitions indeed arise—due to being produced by the latencies of the habituation of false conceptualization—as adhering to objects that do not truly exist; therefore, the existence or non-existence of things is not established on the basis of them.
Regarding what was stated, "of the words 'object of cognition' (prameya), 'knowable' (jñeya),' and so forth," he says "prameya" and so on:

In the case of the words "object of cognition," "knowable," and the like, there exists nothing that is to be excluded (apohya). For these are not employed by discerning people in isolation or without occasion.

To whom does it refer when it is stated that "there is no object of exclusion (apohya) for words such as 'knowable' (prameya)"? If this is said with reference to the word "knowable" alone, standing outside of a sentence and devoid of connection to any other word, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because a single word is meaningless precisely because it is never used in isolation. He demonstrates this by saying: "For it is not [used] alone, out of context. "Alone" means devoid of other words.
"At the improper time" (*akāṇḍe*) means without an introduction (*prastāva*).

For a word is employed by one who possesses discernment for the sake of benefiting the audience, not out of mere habit; nor would a benefit—characterized by the removal of doubt and error—be produced for the listener merely by the existence [of the word].

For instance, if the expositor were to produce a conviction free from doubt by removing the doubt and error that have arisen in the listener regarding some matter, only then would he have rendered a benefit to others.
Moreover, such assistance cannot be said to be possible by means of the [mantra] being employed alone.

Therefore, because the Veda assists in the removal of doubt and the like, as well as in the production of certainty, the employment of words is purposeful; thus he shows that this [Vedic] statement is employed for the sake of the sentence-meaning with the words beginning "But... (kintu): "But when there is the possibility of doubt or error on the part of someone regarding something, it is employed by the wise for the sake of removing those [doubts and errors]."
Because it produces cognitions free from doubt and error,
that very [speech] employed by him is experienced as fruitful by them.
Doubt (*āreka*) means uncertainty;
"of someone" refers to the listener,
and "regarding something" refers to the object.
"For the sake of their cessation" means for the sake of the cessation of those two: doubt and error.
"By that" refers to the term "the knowable" and so forth.
"By them" refers to those who possess discernment.
