Alternatively, it is said with reference to the very words such as "the knowable" that reside within the sentence; he demonstrates that this [objection] is unestablished:
"That which there..."—that which is there accepted by those of dull intellect as a ground for suspicion is precisely what is being rejected by him; otherwise, his utterance would be fruitless.
For why would he, being free from doubt on some point, ask a question;
or how could one of sound mind utter a word that does not produce a mental impression?

For in that case, by means of the words "object of cognition" (*prameya*) and so forth situated within the sentence, exactly that which is suspected by those of dull intellect and inert minds is excluded; therefore, it is unestablished that there is nothing to be excluded by the words "object of cognition" and so on.
"Otherwise" means:
if one were not to exclude what has been suspected by those of dull intellect.
It might be argued: "Indeed, nothing has been doubted by the listener. To this he says, "For something," and so forth.

If the listener were not in doubt regarding any object, why would he depend upon instruction from another? For one asks another for the sake of certainty; otherwise, one would be a madman. It might be further argued: "Even if there is indeed a ground for doubt on the part of the listener, nevertheless, that [doubt] is certainly not removed by that word. To this he says, "That which does not effect its refinement," and so forth.

The refinement (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the cessation of the listener’s ignorance and so forth—that refinement does not exist in that word; thus, it is "that which does not possess such a refinement" (*atatsaṃskāraka*).
The suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*.
"One who speaks thus" refers to the proponent.
The meaning is: "How could one whose intellect is sound be anything other than a madman?
This is because words are employed solely for the purpose of refining the understanding of the listener.
Regarding this, he states—beginning with "that which is to be cognized by visual cognition, etc."—what specific statement contains the point of doubt for the deluded mind that is here being refuted:
"That which is said to be 'form and so forth, cognizable by visual cognition and the rest,' is indeed something superimposed by someone; it is this that is negated."
"By that" refers to the statement: "form and so forth, which are to be cognized by visual consciousness and the others."
To the question "What is that which is superimposed?", he says: "Not by that alone which is dependent on the eye," and so forth.
Form, such as blue and so on, is not perceived solely by [a cognition] dependent on the eye;
rather, it is also [perceived] by a single, eternal consciousness dependent on the ear.

The notion superimposed by those of dull intellect— that even a permanent consciousness residing in the ear perceives forms such as blue— is refuted by the statement, "form is cognizable by visual consciousness.
The meaning is that form is indeed cognizable only by a consciousness supported by the eye, and not by a consciousness of the ear or other senses.
If it is a delusion that these [dharmas] are to be known as having forms such as momentariness,
then how could these dharmas be objects of knowledge for the cognition of an omniscient one?
"Are even non-entities to be known—those which do not produce cognition?
Such statements regarding the arising of delusions are called the "category of the knowable."
In this way, are all phenomena to be cognized by means of such forms as momentariness and so forth, or not? Or rather,
are they to be apprehended by the mind of an omniscient one?

Or rather, no. For if non-existence is characterized by the absence of all descriptions and does not even produce cognition, how can it be an object of knowledge? When such a doubt arises, this is said: all phenomena (*dharma*) are to be known in their form as momentary and so forth, and they are to be known by the cognition of an omniscient one; thus, non-existence is also an object of knowledge.
In this context, that which was superimposed upon phenomena—such as the form of being knowable through non-momentariness and so forth—is here negated.
To the question of how it can be turned back by mere words, he says "tādṛk" and so forth:
"Such knowability belongs to them because of the proof of their momentariness and other qualities;
for even in the absence of an [ultimately real] object of knowledge, they are established by way of this conventional nature."
"It is such" means that its nature as momentary and so forth is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, one might ask: how is the knowability (*jñeyatva*) of non-existence established? To this, he says "knowable," etc., [meaning] "by this very nature."

The meaning is that even non-entities possess the status of being objects of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) because they are established in some way by the intellect through the form of non-existence; otherwise, there would be no conventional discourse regarding them at all.

Now, it might be objected: in the context of the inquiry whether sounds are objects of cognition (*prameya*) by virtue of their impermanence or not, when the term "objects of cognition" is employed, even for a cognizer who is unaware of the specific context, a cognition of sounds and so forth arises in a floating or indeterminate form upon hearing the mere word "objects of cognition. If, therefore, the isolated word has no meaning at all, how can there be a comprehension of its meaning? To this, he says:
"The words 'object of cognition' (*prameya*), 'knowable' (*jñeya*), etc., [serve as] the cause for comprehension... [and so on].
Thus, having seen that which remains fixed within the statement even across different times;
The cognition that arises upon the apprehension of the isolated [word] with respect to various shifting meanings follows the authority of that [corresponding] sentence.
And that same [nature] exists indeed even in words such as "jar";
therefore, words like "jar" are equal to sounds such as "knowable."

This is the collective meaning here: there is no comprehension of meaning from the mere hearing of an isolated word; rather, for one whose mind is captivated by the similarity to a meaningful word encountered in sentences, there arises the conceit of comprehending meaning from the hearing of an isolated word.

For instance, in whichever sentences the hearer has previously perceived the word *prameya*, it is precisely regarding those objects that this cognition arises—unanchored in its referent and of a fluctuating nature.
And this is equally the case for words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth.

For instance, when the question is posed, "Shall I bring water with a jar or with my cupped hands?", if one uses the word "with a jar," a person who is unaware of the context will have an understanding that follows the preceding sentences, possessing an expectancy for as many meanings as the usage of "with a jar" has been observed in those sentences.

Therefore, just as words that speak of actual facts express specific objects, so too are words such as "object of cognition" (prameya) and the like; this is what [the author] demonstrates with the words beginning "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Regarding what was stated, "And in the conceptualization of the excluded object," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "In the conceptualization of the excluded object":

"In the conceptualization of the excluded object, it would be better to simply postulate a real entity; this [previous claim] is contradicted by the fact that there is necessarily an exclusion of others."
In that context, only that entity which is intended to be expressed is conceptualized;
therefore, there is an exclusion [of others], for not everything is intended to be expressed.
"An entity," and so forth.

For it is only an entity (*vastu*)—and not a non-entity—that we conceive as the meaning of a word by virtue of determinative conceptualization (*adhyavasāya*), specifically that which is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*). Therefore, when that [entity] is cognized, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of what is not intended to be expressed is indeed understood through implication (*sāmarthya*).
The determination of the meaning of words is not non-pervasive.

And it is precisely with regard to that which is a ground for doubt for one of dull intellect that the Teacher has said: "Having postulated something unknowable, inference [proceeds] regarding the knowable by means of its exclusion."
Regarding the passage beginning with "because of the negation of the form of cognition" (*jñānākāraniṣedhāt*), he says "the form of cognition," and so forth:
"But the negation of the form of cognition is not possible, because it is self-cognizable (*svavedyatva*).
For there exists a superimposing [cognition] that is without an external object (*nirālamba*) in many ways."
A certain inherent nature, restricted to each respective object, must necessarily be admitted as residing within cognition; and that very thing is its essential nature.

The term "aspect" (ākāra) has been used by us to mean a reflection, its appearance, a mental impression (ullekha), and a manifestation (pratibhāsa); the difference in terminology is of no consequence.
"It cannot be done"—the word "to do" (*kartum*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
How is it established that the form of cognition is self-cognizable? To this he says: "For it exists," and so forth.

In dreams and similar states, it is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*), as clear as it is for even a cowherd, that there exists a superimposing cognition which, even in the absence of an object, takes on the form of an apprehended object while lacking any external support.
Furthermore, it is not logical to assert that an object situated in another place or time is perceived by that [dream-cognition] in its own form, because that object lacks such a form at that time.
Nor is it logical for one thing to be perceived in the form of another, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, you must necessarily admit some specific quality residing within cognition itself that is produced by the object, by means of which cognition— despite being identical in its nature as pure awareness— is differentiated according to each respective object, such that there is an experience of blue alone and not of yellow. And once that is admitted, it follows by implication that cognition must indeed possess an aspect (*sākāra*),
because apart from the aspect, no other distinct intrinsic nature can be determined.

Therefore, since you have expressed that very same thing by the term "specific intrinsic nature" (svabhāvaviśeṣa), whereas we have used terms such as "aspect" (ākāra) or "mental impression" (ullekha), there is merely a dispute over names.

Regarding the phrase "of words such as 'thus' (*evam*)," and so forth, he says: "Of words such as 'thus,' there exists no 'not thus' (*naivam*)," and so on. [p.360] For words such as "thus," there is indeed no "not thus" and so forth.
"That which is to be excluded" is a clear definition of another mode [of cognition].

Thus, when another alternative—such as "it is not thus"—is superimposed, its exclusion by words such as "it is thus" and so forth is indeed determined with even greater clarity; therefore, there is no lack of pervasion in the established relationship between word and meaning.
Thus has the refutation stated by Kumārila been countered; now that which was stated by Uddyotakara is being countered.
Regarding that which was said: "What object is conceived as the excluded referent (*vyavacchedya*) of the word 'all'?"—to this [it is replied]:
"And in the case of that which is brought into linguistic usage," and so forth.

And since this [exclusion] exists even in the case of every word brought into common usage, its referent is that which is to be excluded; thus, "the exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is what is intended to be expressed.

Here too, just as with words such as "jñāna" and so on, the word "sarva" is never used in isolation; rather, it is always employed within a sentence. Therefore, that which is a point of doubt for one of dull intellect is precisely what must be excluded [by the qualification]. "Abhidhitsita" means intended to be expressed.
To the question, "What is this object intended to be expressed? he says: "All phenomena," and so forth.
"All phenomena are selfless," or "all persons have passed away"—in these cases, a totality is understood, while some particular part is excluded.
To the question "What is this part that is excluded?", he says: "Only some.
Only some external things, such as jars and so forth, are perceived as being devoid of self-nature; and thus the delusion regarding the movement of something [as having a real nature] is dispelled.
Regarding the objection beginning with "If it is argued that [the term] refers to one or more [parts], but not all," he replies with the verse beginning "And the negation of all parts...
"And the negation of all parts is certainly not intended in that case; this would result in the negation of its own meaning. Therefore, it is stated out of ignorance."

For if the negation of every single member [of the compound] were intended when the word "all" (sarva) is employed in a sentence brought into common usage, then the exclusion of its own meaning (svārthāpoha) would follow as a logical consequence. However, since only that which has been suspected by one of dull intellect is negated, how can the fault of subverting its own meaning arise? This same principle should be stated regarding words such as "and so forth" (ādi) as well.
Regarding what was said, "Of what nature is it, or is it non-existence? and so forth, he replies with the words "It is not existence," and so on:
"It is neither existence nor non-existence; it is characterized by neither difference nor identity.
Exclusion (*apoha*) is, in reality, neither dependent nor independent, and neither one nor many."
Why is it that existence does not occur? He says: "In that way, it does not exist," and so forth. It does not exist in reality (tattvena) in the manner in which it is determined;
therefore, it is neither existence nor non-existence, because it is determined as a real entity.

This [object] is not apprehended by the deluded as having an external form, nor does it exist in that way; therefore, because it lacks the nature of an external form, it is not a [real] entity (*bhāva*).
To the question, "Why then is it not a non-entity (*abhāva*)?", he says: "And it is not a non-entity, because it is apprehended as a real thing.
Since it is shown to have the appearance of an external form, one cannot say that it is absolutely a non-entity.
Now, as to why [the referent] does not possess characteristics such as difference or identity, he says: "Difference, non-difference, and so forth," etc.:
"All [concepts] such as difference and non-difference are established as residing in real entities;
yet the meaning of a word is devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). Therefore, these [concepts] are without a basis."

"Difference and non-difference," "distinction and non-distinction," and so forth—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), properties such as "being dependent" are included. For these are not properties inherent in real entities; how then could they find a footing in an exclusion (*apoha*) whose form is fashioned by the artifice of conceptual construction? As for what was said—"Since exclusion has the nature of an action, its object must be stated"—that is unproven, because the exclusion denoted by words consists of a mental reflection (*pratibimba*).
And because that reflection has the nature of an external object as it is apprehended through mental determination (*adhyavasita*), it is not a mere negation.

For this very reason, the two alternatives—"is it the object of a cow? or "is it the object of a non-cow?"—are untenable, since it is determined precisely as having the cow as its object by way of being a positive form (*vidhirūpa*).

Regarding what was said—"For by whom has 'non-cowness' been attributed to the cow, that it should thus be excluded?"—to that he replies with the verse beginning "And the exclusion of other objects," and so forth:
"For us, the word directly effects the exclusion of other objects;
but once its own meaning has been expressed, that [exclusion] is understood through implication."
That "it is not the self, it is another's self" has been established in detail;
therefore, this is stated here by one who is ignorant of the opponent's position.
For by whom has "non-cowness" been attached to the cow such that it must be excluded?
Thus, this is not excluded by the word through direct confrontation.

For if the word *eva* were to convey the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) by means of its primary sense (*pradhāna*), then this [objection] would hold; however, since it first of all produces a reflection of the object (*arthapratibimbaka*) as previously described, and the exclusion is understood through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*) once that [reflection] is grasped, this which has been stated is something trivial due to ignorance of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). This is the summary of the meaning. The remainder is easy to understand.
The conceptual analysis regarding exclusion (*vyatireka*) and so forth has already been refuted.
Regarding what was stated—namely, "Is this exclusion (*apoha*) the denotable object? and so on—he replies with the words "By which one... and so forth.
By which of these is its status as a denotable object being questioned?
What is the use of this for exclusion (apoha), or what is the use of [the example of] a jar and so forth?
In the investigation of whether the meaning of a word is exclusion (apoha) or a positive injunction (vidhi),
that which appears as "exclusion" is precisely what is thus cognized.
For this is the direct view: that the reflected image is indeed the meaning of the word.
And words such as "jar" and "tree" express that very same reflection;
because they produce it, they directly denote it, yet they exclude what is other than the object.
Therefore, there is no fault in the injunction, nor does any undesirable consequence follow;
as for the fault of the position that [the self] is inexpressible, it does not apply to us, since we do not accept that view.

In this regard, concerning the alternative that "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is the denotation [of a word], if this is raised with reference to the term "exclusion of others," then since it is accepted that this [exclusion] is denoted by that word precisely in a positive form (*vidhirūpa*), it is not logical to charge us with an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*). For instance, when the discussion is whether the meaning of a word is a positive entity or an exclusion of others, and it is stated that "the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others," there arises in the cognizer a cognition that determines the exclusion of others characterized as the aforementioned mental reflection (*pratibimba*).
However, by implication, the negation of a positive word-meaning follows.

Now, with respect to words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), even there, the exclusion (*apoha*) characterized as a reflection as previously described is produced directly by the words "jar" and so forth, and it is conveyed by them in a positive form; however, the understanding of the exclusion of others occurs through implication (*sāmarthya*). Thus, there is no undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*).
Nor is there the fault of lack of determination (*avyavasthā-doṣa*).

Since the exclusion of others is understood through implication, and since the position that [the exclusion] is not denotable (*avācya-pakṣa*) has been rejected precisely because it would be merely a restatement (*anuvācyatā*), there is no room for the faults arising from that position to arise. This he demonstrates with the words: "But the fault of the position that it is not denotable... (*avācyapakṣadoṣas tu...*)
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "oneness and permanence," he says "oneness," etc.:
Oneness, permanence, and so forth are merely conceptual constructs and not real;
therefore, making a joke about this indicates one who is a great scholar.

For if the description of oneness and so forth had been made from the perspective of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*), then it would indeed be a cause for laughter for you. However, since this was described by the Teacher as merely conceptual (*kālpnika*) in accordance with the perception of delusion (*bhrānti*), how could it possibly become a cause for laughter for a wise person? Rather, it is you alone who, failing to understand the intended meaning while offering criticism, become an object of extreme derision for the wise.
Therefore, regarding those very words [where] there is no connection with "na" (negation), as in the case of "ityādi," he says: "By the force of the restriction," and so forth.
By the force of the restriction, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is also understood;
otherwise, the restriction would be useless, since only its own nature would be understood.

It is not only where there is a connection with negation (*naṭ-yoga*) that the aspect of the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is understood; for even where there is no such connection with negation, it is indeed understood. This has been established by your own words when you made the restriction that "only its own nature (*svātman*) is understood.
Otherwise, the restriction would be utterly meaningless.
For it is most clearly determined that wherever only its own nature is understood, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is also understood by the force of that very restriction.
With the words "But for whom then," etc., the opponent points out precisely the lack of universal applicability (*avyāpitā*) in the establishment of the word-meaning as exclusion (*apoha*):

"For whom, then, even an external object is not admitted to exist otherwise [than as it appears], such as in the case of words like 'son of a barren woman'— by him, where is exclusion said to be expressed?"

For instance, in the case of a word such as "son of a barren woman," there exists no external object like a son upon which the exclusion (apoha) could be based through the differentiation from others; what, then, can be said to be the substratum for the exclusion that is its denotation? For an exclusion must necessarily have a real entity as its substratum, since it is not distinct from the thing itself which is differentiated from others.

He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "due to the absence of form" (rūpābhāvāt): "Because non-existent things lack form, words that denote universals and so forth are not even to be suspected [of denoting them]; they are established as indicators of mere appearance alone."

Since non-existent things such as the son of a barren woman lack any form or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), words referring to them cannot be suspected of denoting universals (*jāti*) and the like. For while one might suspect whether the referent (*abhidheya*) of words that function toward real entities (*vastu*) is some actual form or perhaps a reflection (*pratibimba*), since non-existence is defined precisely by its distinction from a real entity, how could there be any suspicion that words functioning toward it have a real entity as their object? Therefore, their lack of an object is perfectly clear; moreover, since for you [the Yogācāra] words produce nothing more than a reflection, this suspicion is simply out of place.

He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "artha" and so forth: "When a reflection appears— constructed solely from the latent impressions (vāsanā) arising from verbal discourse that is empty of external objects— that is what is expressed by words."
"By words" means by such words as "the son of a barren woman" and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding those words whose objects are real entities (*vastu*), he states the following— beginning with "tanmātra"— as a proof for establishing that they denote merely a mental reflection (*pratibimbaka*):
"These words, which directly illuminate that alone, are accompanied by doubt because they depend upon convention (*saṅketa*), just like the expression of an imagined object."

Those [words] that depend upon convention (*saṅketa*) illuminate merely the reflected images of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) produced solely by the latencies (*vāsanā*) deposited by empty talk devoid of objects—just as words such as "son of a barren woman," which denote imagined objects—and the words "pot" and so forth, which are the subject of dispute and are accompanied by doubt, also depend upon convention; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Having thus established his own position, he says "paropagata... and so forth, adducing a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to refute the opposing position:
"These sounds do not establish the existence of distinctions and so forth accepted by others; therefore, it should be understood that they are exactly like those [other cases]."

Particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the differentiation; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of genus (*jāti*) and so forth is intended. "Therefore" means because of its dependence upon linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).
"In that very same way" means:
like the expression of an imagined object.
Avoiding the charge of inconclusiveness regarding both reasons, he says: "The impossibility of convention," and so forth.
For the impossibility of convention regarding difference and the rest has already been established here previously;
and as for its fruitlessness, there is no doubt regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of those two reasons.

Because it is impossible to establish a convention [for it], and because it is not shared by anything else; for it has already been established—regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth—that a convention is impossible and that a convention would be futile.
Therefore, for those two reasons, there is no doubt regarding the exclusion [of the reason] from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
With the words beginning with "nanu," the opponent raises the charge of inconclusiveness regarding the first reason:
"But even on the view of apoha, how is the establishment of a convention possible?
And how can it be fruitful? For that [convention] is established for neither of the two [parties]."
For the cognition of the speaker and the listener is not mutually perceived;
nor is that [cognition] observed during the convention, yet it is examined during the actual usage.

For just as there is an impossibility and futility of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, the same applies to the position of exclusion (*apoha*). Consequently, since no convention has been established, it is also not logical that words should indicate that [exclusion] alone; thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
And how could there be efficacy? The word "is possible" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Of that" refers to the convention (*saṅketa*).
But how is it that a convention is impossible there? To this he says: "For that is established for two," where the word "for" (*hi*) indicates the reason.
Because that exclusion (*apoha*) consisting of a reflected image is not established as one for both the speaker and the listener—the two parties to the linguistic convention.
Why? He says: "For knowledge," and so forth.
Knowledge is indeed to be personally experienced by those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*).
For one person of limited vision cannot experience the cognition of another.
And in ultimate reality, the exclusion (*apoha*) characterized by the nature of a reflection is not distinct from cognition.
Consequently, since no single object that serves as the referent of a convention is established for both the speaker and the listener, where could the convention be made or apprehended?

For when a thing is unestablished, neither the speaker is able to establish a convention, nor is the listener able to grasp it, due to the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To explain: that reflection of the object which the listener apprehends as mounted upon his own cognition is not experienced by the speaker; and that which is experienced by the speaker is not experienced by the listener, because each experiences only their own respective appearance. Furthermore, demonstrating its lack of purpose, he says: "And not in convention," and so forth.
The reflected image that was experienced by the listener or the speaker at the time of the convention is not experienced at the time of linguistic usage,
because, due to its momentary nature, it has long since ceased to exist.
And that which is experienced at the time of linguistic usage was not seen at the time of the convention.
For at that time, it is something else entirely that is being experienced;
moreover, it is not logical for linguistic usage to apply to one thing based on a convention established for another, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
He provides a rebuttal with the words "of each its own," and so forth:
"Even though there is cognition of each respective appearance, that [error] persists;
because it is equal for both of them in the determination of an external object."

For even the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*) is not intended to be the denotable object (*vācyatā*) of words from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), such that one could raise the objection regarding the impossibility of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) therein. This is because this entire verbal transaction (*śābdo vyavahāraḥ*) is held to be erroneous (*bhrānta*) in accordance with its own internal appearance (*svapratibhāsa*), like the vision of two moons by two people suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). It arises merely as a conceptual determination (*arthāvasāyivikalpa*) from words due to the awakening of the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) for empty talk regarding objects.
That reflection (*pratibimbaka*) is said to be the denotable object of words because it is produced [by them], but not because it possesses the status of being a denotable object (*abhidheyatā*).

In this regard, although in ultimate reality each person—both speaker and listener—experiences only their own respective appearance, nevertheless, because the seed of error is identical for both, like that of two people with cataracts, the determination of an external object is exactly the same for both the speaker and the listener.
Nevertheless, the speaker has this conceit: "The very same object that I am conveying, he (the listener) understands.
The same should be applied to the listener as well.

If it is asked how this determination of a single object is mutually known by the speaker and the listener, [the answer is: even if it is not known in an ultimate sense, nevertheless, because the seed of error is identical, this conventional usage exists as a mere error according to one's own internal appearance—just like two people with ophthalmia; this has already been explained. Therefore, by virtue of the determination of a single object, the establishment of linguistic convention is indeed possible.
Regarding this, he states an example: "For just as one whose vision is impaired by cataracts speaks of two moons to those like himself, so too is all verbal usage considered to be."
"Equal to oneself" means for another person who is like oneself, that is, one who is afflicted with the same visual disorder (taimirika).
And he shows that the convention is not purposeless by stating "and its pervasiveness":
"And this pervasiveness of it is intended as a conceptual determination;
for these cognitions produced by words have a false appearance."

Furthermore, the fact that [the reflection] pervades the time of the convention and the time of its practical application is accepted by both the speaker and the listener only by virtue of their determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the reflected image of the object, not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). This is because, even at the time of practical application, the speaker and the listener harbor the conceit (*abhimāna*) that the two objects seen at earlier and later times are one and the same.
To the question, "Why is this not accepted in an ultimate sense? he says: "Because it appears falsely," and so forth.
Thus concludes the examination of words and their meanings.
In that regard, there are four types of divergent views held by others concerning the nature, result, object, and number of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In order to clearly demonstrate the definition of the means of valid cognition by refuting those views, and for the purpose of establishing the statement that "the two means of valid cognition are determined by their distinct characteristics," he says "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth: "Perception and inference [are the means of valid cognition] for the sake of establishing [their respective] adjuncts."
What has been stated by others is not established, for it possesses such characteristics.
"For the sake of establishing the limiting adjuncts" means for the sake of establishing the limiting adjuncts such as quality, substance, action, genus, inherence, and so forth.
"By others" refers to [the opponents].
By the Vaiśeṣikas and others;
"thus" refers to what is about to be said.

In this regard, there is a disagreement concerning the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*), such as the claim that perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by conceptual construction (*savikalpaka*) or having the nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*). To refute these [views], he states its definition: "Perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (*pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍham abhrāntam*).
Perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous;
conceptual construction is a cognition associated with verbal expression, consisting in the cause of linguistic convention (*klṛpti*), and not otherwise.

In this context, having restated that cognition is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), its status as perception (*pratyakṣatva*) is prescribed; for in every case of definition, it is the definiendum that is being prescribed.
Just as in the statement, "That which trembles is the *aśvattha* tree," the definiendum here is perception.
This is because it is the definition of "possessing the characteristic of being tall" that is under discussion here,
and not the definition of "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous," such that one could say that this [latter] is being enjoined.

Furthermore, since "knowledge" is obtained by implication through the negation of "conceptual construction"— just as when one says, "Let a cow without a calf be brought," the cow is understood through the negation of the calf— the word "knowledge" was not explicitly stated.
What, then, is the "conceptual construction" (kalpanā) intended here?
He states that perception is knowledge from which [such construction] has been removed, defining conceptual construction as "a cognition associated with verbal expression" (*abhilāpinī pratītiḥ*).

Now, is that [definition]—which consists in being the cause of conceptualization and so forth, and regarding which Śaṅkarasvāmin and others have stated detailed objections—to be accepted or not? To this he replies: "but not that which consists in being the cause of conceptualization and so forth."
The word "is apprehended" (*gṛhyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
By this, it is stated that the defects which have been asserted by the opponent on the basis of that [position] do not apply at all, precisely because that position is not accepted.

It should be understood that "postulation," "designation," and "being the cause thereof" pertain to universals (*jāti*) and so forth; for there can be no designation without the distinctions of universals and the like.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), one should include *vitarka* and *vicāra*, which are the causes of the grossness and subtlety of the mind associated with verbal expression, as well as [the cognition] through the conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper, and so forth.
"Designation" (*abhilāpa*) is the expressive word; it has a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*), and that [cognition] in which this [form] exists by way of appearance is described as such.

But from what source is such a cognition established? To this he says, "The connection of word and meaning," and so forth: "That [cognition] which, in the form of 'tree' and so on, is capable of connecting a word with its object, arises as if accompanied by verbal expression, even when words are not actually employed."
The connection is: "even when words are not employed in the form of 'tree' and so forth.
Alternatively, the connection with the preceding [phrase] is: "capable of joining word and meaning in the form of 'tree' and so forth.
By this, he demonstrates the establishment of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) through perception itself, because conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) is established in all living beings.
For it is shown that this [capacity] is indeed established as the cause for the performance of duties even from childhood, by means of the verse beginning with "atīta" and so forth:
"Because of the continuity of the latent impressions of the cultivation of the meanings of past names,
even one just born becomes skilled in the performance of duties through connection with that."

Past existence is past birth; therein, the cultivation of name and object (*nāmārthabhāvanā*) is the repeated practice of words and their referents. The latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), which is the capacity (*sāmarthya*) deposited by that [practice], has a continuity (*anvaya*) or persistence that exists even in an infant. Because of this, the infant indeed possesses a conceptual cognition (*pratīti*) accompanied by verbal expression.

Through the connection with such conceptualization, the infant becomes skillful and dexterous in its "course of action" (*itikartavyatā*), characterized by smiling, crying, sucking the breast, joy, and so forth.
Therefore, by means of this [skill] which is the effect, the aforementioned conceptualization is indeed inferred even in the case of an infant.
As it has been said:
"In this world, the procedure for action depends entirely upon words;
even a child understands it through the impressions (saṃskāra) previously deposited [in his mind]."
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, that [cognition] arises for them, presenting as if externally an object that exists internally within the measure [of time], distinguished by sounds in the form of coalescing syllables; through this, they subsequently become skilled in grasping linguistic conventions.

With the words beginning "cinta" (thought), he further states the establishment of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): "And that which is clearly experienced at the time of thinking, imagining, and so forth,
as if permeated by words, cannot be denied."

With the words "And of that" (*tasyāśca*) and so forth, he states its establishment even as being indicated by the effect known as verbal usage: "The status of word and object is erroneous due to conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*);
because of the impossibility of it being otherwise, this [status] would not be possible even as something similar if it were non-existent."
Since the real establishment of the relationship between word and object has been previously refuted and established as being erroneous,

if this conceptual construction were non-existent, then even such an establishment of word and object— even though it is erroneous— would not be possible; for it is established by virtue of that [conceptual] intention,
and because it has been demonstrated that other external things, such as specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, are unfit to be denotable objects.

But surely others do not describe conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) as merely a cognition associated with verbal expression; rather, they also describe it as that which is capable of being related to universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and so forth.
Why, then, is this [latter] not accepted? To this he says: "Universals and so forth," etc.:
"Others understand conceptual construction to be that which is capable of being joined with universals and the like."
Because [the self] has been excluded from being [identical with] birth and so forth, and because it is not perceived, that [connection] is not tenable.
"And because [it] is not perceived"— this connects with "of genus and so forth.
And this refutation has been stated while provisionally accepting the existence of genus and the rest.
With the words "of genus and so forth," he supports that very point regarding their invisibility:
"Because genus and so forth are not perceived, and because their connection does not appear,
how can a synthesis with an object be possible, as in the case of milk and water?"
"And like milk and water, etc.

means that just as it is impossible to effect a synthesis of milk, water, and so forth when they have become mixed because they do not appear distinctly, likewise, even though universals (jāti) and the rest exist, because they do not appear distinct from their substratum, it is impossible [to establish them] together with that substratum. This is the meaning.
If, then, conceptualization as the association with genus (*jāti*) and so forth is indeed not logical, how is it that the author of the definition stated:
"Conceptualization is the association with name, genus, and so forth"? He says: "For the sake of stating the objects to be abandoned and to be adopted, because of the mention of both... and so on.
This conceptualization (kalpanā), established as both "other" and "self," is declared to be twofold.

Among these, the conceptualization consisting of the association with genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which is established by others, is to be abandoned; the conceptualization consisting of the association with names (*nāman*), which is established by oneself, is to be accepted. Both types of conceptualization have been specified in order to demonstrate this. How is this understood? He says: "Because of the mention of two. Since there are names and genus and so forth—namely, name-genus-and-so-forth—their association; thus, two groups have been mentioned. Otherwise, it would have been stated simply as "association with name and so forth" or "association with genus and so forth."
It would have to be stated;
for if this were not an exhaustive enumeration, it would follow that the word "etcetera" (ādi) is redundant.

Now, an objection might be raised: "Since this is the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the subject at hand is indeed the demonstration of the absence of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) itself, not the demonstration of the absence of properties belonging to the object. Furthermore, the association of names, universals, and so forth with their possessors is a property residing in the object, not in the cognition; therefore, the author of the definition (*lakṣaṇakāra*) is stating something irrelevant. Anticipating this challenge, he says: "And this association of names and so forth...
This association of names and so forth has its immediate cause [in the preceding cognition].
Since it proceeds by way of implication, there is no mention of something irrelevant.
The immediate and uninterrupted cause that serves as its basis is a cognition permeated by verbal expression.
And because it arises in a form that synthesizes two entities, it is designated as "joining," even though no one at all joins anything, since all phenomena are devoid of activity.

Its projection occurs in two ways; that [connection] by which it arises is described as such. And because it conveys the meaning, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound even when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
Alternatively, it is because the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause.
And the purpose of this metaphorical attribution is to reveal the nature of that [cause] as producing an effect distinguished from other causes.

Alternatively, he shows that there is no fault by demonstrating that conceptualization is indicated as being precisely that which expresses; this is done by forming the compound "yojanā" (joining) in the sense of "that by which [things] are joined," namely the joining of name, genus, and so forth. Thus he says: "Name, genus, and so forth," etc.
"Or, that by which all these—name, genus, and so forth—are joined is [called] yojanā. Conceptualization is thus described as the cognition that is expressive.
With the words "Or rather" (*yadvā*) and so forth, he states another solution:

"Or rather, it is simply conceptual construction as established in our own system that has been set forth, because [the verse] is to be construed as: 'In every case, an object associated with a name is what is expressed.'"
If this is so, how is this passage from the Master’s *Vṛtti* to be interpreted? It is as follows:

"In the case of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), an object qualified by a name is expressed, such as ‘Ḍittha’; in the case of genus-words (*jātiśabda*), [an object] by its genus, such as ‘cow’; in the case of quality-words (*guṇaśabda*), by its quality, such as ‘white’; in the case of action-words (*kriyāśabda*), by its action, such as ‘cook’; and in the case of substance-words (*dravyaśabda*), by its substance, such as ‘staff-bearer’ or ‘horned one.
For by this passage, the fact that even an object associated with qualifiers such as genus and the like is being expressed is separately clarified; therefore, he says "in all cases," and so forth.
"Everywhere" means even in the case of words such as those denoting universals (*jāti*) and so forth.

What is meant is this: just as when arbitrary (*yadṛcchā*) words are employed, an object qualified by a name is expressed, so too in the case of words denoting universals and so forth—such as "cow" (*gauh*) and the like—an object qualified by a name is expressed; this is to be applied throughout the entire treatise.
How, then, should this other instrumental ending in the phrase "by genus, by quality, by action, or by substance" be construed? To this he says "by them," and so forth:
"By these [factors], the case-ending of the instrument (karaṇavibhakti) attains its fruitfulness;
the meaning established is that this [name] is [qualified] by genus and the rest."

An object qualified by a genus (*jāti*), acting as the instrument, is expressed as "cow" by means of its name; likewise [it is expressed] by means of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. Thus, through their connection with those [factors] such as the genus via the instrumental case-ending, they achieve their purposeful efficacy. If this is so, one might ask how the connection is to be understood in the sūtra: "the conjunction of name, genus, and so forth. He says: "of the name, with the genus and so forth," the word "conjunction" being the ellipsis to be supplied.
By the phrase "this very [conception]," he indicates that this conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is precisely what is obtained from the meaning of the compound.

The application of genus and so forth is "genus-application" (*jātyādiyojanā*); this application of genus and so forth to a name is what is meant by the compound "name-genus-application" (*nāmajātyādiyojanā*). This is the meaning established by the compound, so to speak.

Anticipating the objection that "if this were so, since there is an absence of grounds for application such as genus (*jāti*) in the case of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), the established rule would be non-pervasive," he says: "Because of the existence of a genus denoted by an arbitrary word, one should not consider this [rule] to be non-pervasive; however, its separate mention is due to conventional usage. *Yadṛcchāśabdavācyāyā jāteḥ sadbhāvato na ca / avyāptir asya mantavyā prasiddhes tu pṛthakśrutiḥ //*

This is what is meant: even those words such as "Dittha" and so forth, which are recognized as arbitrary names (*yadṛcchāśabda*), are unable—despite persisting from birth until the moment of death—to denote an object that is differentiated by a unique distinction at every single moment. Therefore, they adopt as their denotation a universal (*jāti*) inherent in the object, as delimited by the boundaries of its duration in time. Otherwise, if these words were established as having for their domain only those portions of the object distinguished by states such as childhood, how could they convey an object that is further qualified by distinctions such as old age?

Even for those who hold the view that the body is not momentary but rather persists over a period of time, it is established that in its various states, the substance is different at each stage due to the connection with parts that mature over time or due to the loss of parts.

Even when transformation is observed, that entity which is connected to a particular state is what is intended by the word; therefore, if it were to resort to another state, that very same entity would no longer be denoted by that word. Just as the word "milk," whose expressive power is determined to apply to milk, does not function for curd, so too [the word] would not function for another state even in the case of a body. Thus, a universal (*jāti*) must necessarily be admitted. Alternatively, even if the universal were not a real entity, the established rule [of linguistic usage] would still not be non-pervasive.

For indeed, those very same particulars, when their distinctions are not intended to be expressed, are taken as "universals" (sāmānya) and are everywhere designated by genus-words (jātiśabda). Thus, the author of the definition has specified that arbitrary words (yadṛcchāśabda) have a distinct characteristic from genus-words; he says this because of common usage (prasiddhi).

For in the world, words such as "cow" (go) and so forth are recognized as genus-words, whereas words such as "Citrāṅgada" and so forth are recognized as proper names (saṃjñāśabda); hence they are mentioned separately.
With the words beginning with "nanu," the opponent raises an objection:
"But surely, because it is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) that is denoted, a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) is merely a word of intention (*vivakṣāśabda*),
since it is dependent upon the speaker's intention."
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "It is true":
"It is true that this was stated by the knower of logic in accordance with worldly convention;
for only so much of this [term] has entered the path of linguistic usage."
"Indeed, it is of this much [extent]" means that it is fivefold, through the distinction of words for name, genus, quality, action, and substance.

[Objection: If indeed only the conceptual construction established by [the author’s] own system is intended, then for what purpose did the Teacher later describe a conceptual construction established separately by his own system with the passage: "But others say that a qualified object is expressed by words alone, which are devoid of [external] objects"? [Reply: He says: "But those universals and so forth...
These universals and so forth do not here exist as separate entities, as they do in the world; it was for the sake of this understanding that the passage beginning with "But others" was described.

This is what is meant: the author of the definition stated this for the purpose of establishing the point that universals (*jāti*) and so forth do not exist as ultimate realities distinct from individuals such as the brindled cow (*sāvaleyādi*), but rather they are conventional; it was not intended to present some other separate conceptualization.
"Others" refers to the Buddhists.
"By those devoid of [real] objects" means:
The meaning of the Master’s treatise is as follows: [it refers to] words that have as their object mere exclusion (apoha), independent of genus and so forth.

We have not merely accepted that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition associated with verbal expression; others must also necessarily accept it, for otherwise the world would be entirely incapable of linguistic convention. Demonstrating this, he says: "Even those who rely on conceptual construction as the association of universals (*jāti*) and so forth... "Even those who rely on conceptual construction as the association of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, by them too a cognition associated with verbal expression must necessarily be admitted."
Otherwise, because there would be no connection [between them], as in the case of two entities that are already established independently,
conceptual construction (kalpanā) could not be postulated at all, since it would be perceived as independent.
In this way, this entire universe would be capable of conventional usage;
therefore, it is held that this world of conventional usage is permeated by forms such as genus and so forth.
The association with universals and so forth is inseparable from the association with words;
and thus, the statement "it is called such" becomes fruitful.
Even regarding the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) accepted by others as the joining of genus, quality, action, and substance, conceptual construction is nothing other than the joining of a name.

For in that case, an object delimited by genus and so forth is apprehended as qualified by the name itself; otherwise, since there would be no joining—just like the apprehension of multiple objects independently—how could there be conceptual construction? Consequently, the entire world would be mute.
For this very reason, even while seeing a man joined with a staff, one does not join [the concepts] as "staff-bearer" until one recalls the specific name.

Precisely because all conceptual construction (yojanā) is pervaded by the application of words, the statement of the Teacher—namely, that "in cases such as 'cow' and so forth, an object qualified by a universal is expressed"—becomes meaningful.
Otherwise, if [the object were not already present], how could it be said to be "expressed" without a name?
For the act of denotation (abhidhāna) is a property of the word.
With the words "Therefore," and so forth, he concludes the establishment of conceptual construction (kalpanā):
"Therefore, since there is no dispute among the proponents established in all philosophical systems, this conceptual construction is to be proven by me without effort."
He states the intention of the author of the *lakṣaṇa*, who describes conceptual construction as having the nature of an established entity: "Having taken this into account," etc.
Having taken all this—the description of names, universals, and so forth—into account, he has here employed the inclusion of both his own and others' views in this manner.
They said to them, "Our difference from theirs is only this much," and immediately thereafter they uttered the sentence beginning with "But others... and so forth.

The statement regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, which occurs without the application of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, and without the application of names (*nāman*), was previously described in such passages as "it will come to be," and so on.
This refers to the description of names, genus, and so forth;
the word "he made" (*akarot*) is to be connected [to this].
The presentation of one's own and others' views is for the purpose of distinguishing between what is to be rejected and what is to be adopted.
If one asks, "How then is the *Nyāyamukha* treatise to be interpreted? he says: "In this way," and so forth.
In this manner, the *Nyāyamukha* treatise is to be explained by means of this direction [of interpretation].
Because of the connection with the word "cognition" (*jñāna*), it is "understanding" (*pratīti*) that is intended there.

In this regard, the *Nyāyamukha* states: "That cognition which, with respect to the form of an object and so forth, is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) by way of the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of non-difference between the qualifier and the designator, and which operates in relation to each sense faculty (*akṣa*), is perception (*pratyakṣa*). The "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) refers to the genus (*jāti*) and so on; the "designator" (*abhidhāyaka*) refers to the name. The "metaphorical attribution of non-difference" between these two occurs with respect to that which possesses the genus and so forth, and with respect to the bearer of the designation (*saṃjñin*). The mention of "metaphorical attribution of non-difference" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); even in cases where there is apprehension through distinction—such as "this has cowness" or "this is its name"—conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is indeed intended there as well.

But has it not been stated that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition that follows in succession? How then is the aforementioned conceptual construction obtained? To this he says: "Because of its connection with [the word] 'cognition' (*jñāna*).

This is what is meant: by demonstrating that cognition itself is perception (*pratyakṣa*) through its contrast with conceptual construction, it is shown that conceptual construction is a property of cognition.

Thus, the meaning is as follows: that cognition which is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of non-difference from names and so forth is perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, that cognition which is not thus non-conceptual is not perception because its nature consists of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). By implication, it is established that "conceptual construction" is a cognition associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpinī pratīti*), defined by its opposition to perception. In this way, the inclusion of both the higher and lower systems of thought has been demonstrated.
Alternatively, he shows that the Teacher has merely presented his own view by saying "Or rather" (*yadvā*) and so forth.
Or else: "The qualifier is the distinction (*bheda*) by which the word effects the exclusion of others;
and by this [qualifier], he effects the exclusion of universals (*jāti*) and the like."
"Differentiation" (bheda) means a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), that is, exclusion (vyāvṛtti).

"Its designator" refers to the designator of that [differentiation], and not of universals (jāti) and so forth; thus is the analysis of the compound "metaphorical designation of non-difference" (abhedopacāra).

Now, if conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is a cognition associated with verbal expression, then that [conceptualization] would be the subject (*dharmin*). But it is not the case that there is an implication of one subject within another subject, such that its negation could be made as a property (*dharma*) of that [other subject]; thus, your statement is incoherent. Likewise, if perception (*pratyakṣa*) is free from conceptualization, how can it be designated by the word "perception"?
Thinking that "the object free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍhārtha) is indeed an ineffable object, others such as Bharga and Bhāradvāja raise this objection.
Anticipating that all of this has already been refuted, [the author] says, "And thus it is of the nature of cognition," and so forth:
"And since conceptual construction is considered to be of the nature of cognition in this way..."
And the negation of identity is described as being [established] by perception.

Therefore, even though it is denotable by words such as "perception" (adhyakṣa) and so forth, its freedom from conceptual construction (kalpanāviraha) is not contradicted; for that [freedom from conceptual construction] does not consist in being denotable by words.
Otherwise, form, smell, and so forth would be non-conceptual;
therefore, this [position] has no foundation at all, as others of dull intellect have asserted.
If by the word "perception" perception itself is denoted,
how is it that it is understood as being "free from conceptual construction," and why would that be considered improper?
Regarding the phrase "the negation of identity":
by this passage, "that in which this conceptualization does not exist is perception," the author of the definition establishes the negation of identity.
The meaning is that it is not a cognition whose nature consists of such conceptual construction.
First of all, the objection that "the negation of what is to be superimposed" is untenable.

The second objection is likewise untenable, because it was not described as "an object free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) meaning an "unnameable object," but rather as "an object free from conceptualization" (avikalpaka).

Even though non-conceptual cognition is designated by means of words in accordance with conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), nevertheless, it does not become conceptual in nature, just like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

It might be argued: "Let the conceptual construction be as you have described; but how is it established that [perception] is free from conceptual construction? To this he says, "Perception," and so forth:
"Perception, free from conceptual construction, is experienced with extreme clarity."
Because even when the mind is attached elsewhere, there is still the perception of blue and so forth by the sense faculties.
By this, he demonstrates that the absence of conceptual construction is established through direct perception by means of self-awareness.
It might be argued that this very conceptual construction (vikalpa), while distracted by another object, apprehends the blue and so forth situated before one; to this he says "nāsāveva" and so on:
For that very conceptual construction does not apprehend that object, because it abandons the designation of the past and so forth, and because it attains the connection with its name.

For if that very conceptual construction were to apprehend that object, then it would apply the name of that very [object], such as "blue" and so forth, by abandoning the denotation of past objects and the like.
It has been stated that this is because one does not perceive the association of two expressions in a single [object], and because there is no abandonment of the denotation of the past and so forth.
"Its name" means the name of that which has become present; "the application of its name" means the joining of that name; "its attainment" means the reaching of it.
That is to say, it is a logical consequence (prasaṅga).

It might be thought: "In that case, another conceptualization (vikalpa) must then apprehend that object; why is this not understood? To this he says: "At that time, there is no other conceptualization associated with that name," and so forth. [The reason is: because the perceived [object] is not cognized [by that other conceptualization], and because two [conceptualizations] simultaneously are not admitted.

By this, he states that there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) and a contradiction with one's own tenet (*abhyupagamavirodha*) in the proposition of two simultaneous conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); "of the two" (*dvayoḥ*) is said [in reference to] the two conceptual constructions—this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
He concludes with the verse beginning "vikalpayet" and so forth: "Therefore, conceptual cognition is experienced as coexisting with [sensory] knowledge;
thus, it is clear that this sensory consciousness is non-conceptual."
The opponent might sometimes argue that "the coexistence with conceptual construction is unestablished"; therefore, anticipating this objection, he says "in succession," and so forth:
"If it is thought that cognitions arise only in succession..."
However, the conceit that [the cognition] occurs all at once is due to its rapid succession, like a whirling firebrand.
If [cognitions] arise sequentially, how is it that they are perceived simultaneously? To this he says: "But there is the conceit of simultaneous existence.
Like a fire-brand (*alāta*):

just as from the rapid whirling of a fire-brand there arises the perception of a single circle, so too, due to the rapid production of these cognitions, there is the conceit of their simultaneous existence.
Alternatively, by the word "firebrand" (alāta), the cognitions having that as their object are expressed through the metaphorical application of the object to the cognition;
the suffix -vatī is used here as before.
"No," he says, rejecting the prima facie position (*pūrvapak�s*).

"At that time, there exists no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) associated with the cultivation directed toward that [object], nor is there anything visible," so it was stated by the Master [Nāgārjuna].
He thinks as follows: it is not the proof of simultaneous existence that is under discussion here, but rather the absence of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in cognition.

And this [absence] is established by the non-perception of a conceptualization associated with the name of the object—even when the mind is directed elsewhere—at the time of experiencing an object present before one, provided that such a conceptualization has reached the conditions for perceptibility. Thus, no fault has been stated here.

For even if it were indeed perceived sequentially within cognition, it does not follow that the conceptualization itself is being perceived; therefore, there is no contradiction of the subject at hand. (1248)
And showing that even this conceit of simultaneous existence is not an error, he says "error," and so forth:
"Error, the conceit thereof, and its manifestation are continuous;
therefore, it is clear that there is indeed no simultaneity between the object and the cognition."
The word "error" (bhrānti) is to be connected with the subject under discussion, namely "not [so].
Regarding the phrase "conceit thereof" (tadabhimāna), the analysis of the compound is: "the conceit regarding that simultaneous occurrence" (tasya sakṛdbhāvasya abhimānaḥ).
The establishment of an error occurs by virtue of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), but here no such subverting cognition exists, by which it could be an error.
To explain why it does not exist, he says: "And that [cognition] is manifest and uninterrupted.
The word "that" refers to the awareness of an object present before one; it is experienced clearly at the same time as the mind is occupied with another uninterrupted object.
Since such a cognition of an object is precisely what is called perception, how can there be any error?
Showing that not only is simultaneous occurrence not at all a proof for establishing the status of illusion, but rather there is actually a refutation of it, he says "nartakī" and so forth:
"In states such as the viewing of a dancer, everything is perceived simultaneously;
even when there is an intervention by many [moments], that is an illusion due to the rapidity of its occurrence."

The cognitions of a creeper, a palm tree, and so forth, occur with such extreme rapidity that there is the conceit of their simultaneous existence; why, then, does this [same conceit] not also occur in this case?
Furthermore,
in a pure mental construction, no sequence could be determined;
for the rapid operation of all cognitions is brief, as they do not persist for long.
Therefore, in every object, there would be no perception of succession;
rather, there would be an appearance of simultaneous perception, just like the cognition of sound and other objects.
Even though each single cognition is separated by five other cognitions, in states such as watching a dancer, it appears as if uninterrupted.

For instance, at the very moment one beholds the dancer, one simultaneously hears the sound of music and so forth, tastes the flavor of camphor and the like, smells the fragrance of flowers placed in the nostrils, touches the sensation of the breeze from fans and cool breezes, and thinks of giving garments, ornaments, and so on.

Furthermore, if— due to the force of rapid production— an illusion of the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions arises even when there is a great interval between them, then in cases such as *latā*, *tāla*, *sara*, and *rasa*, because the auditions of the phonemes are extremely swift due to being separated by only a single intervening cognition, the appearance of the phonemes as occurring simultaneously would result. Consequently, when words such as *sara* and *rasa* are heard, there would be no distinction in their audition nor any distinction in the comprehension of their meanings.

Furthermore, when a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises in the form of reflecting on various objects of knowledge—which is not interrupted by heterogeneous sensory cognitions such as those of the eye—there is a rapid occurrence; thus, no determination of succession would be possible.

Moreover, since all cognitions are momentary and do not persist for long, there is a rapid occurrence of them all; consequently, the cognition of any object would not appear as successive, just like the cognition of sound and other [sensory] objects.
It is like the perception of sound and so forth during the state of watching a dancer.
Showing that the example "like a firebrand" is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), he says: "In the case of the firebrand as well," and so forth.
Even in the case of a firebrand, the illusion of a circle proceeds from a single [momentary] error;
it does not arise from the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) of successive visual perceptions, because it appears with perfect clarity.
For indeed, reconnection is performed by memory alone, and not by perception,
because an object that has passed away cannot be apprehended by seeing.
Furthermore, its object is not clearly manifest because it has perished;
therefore, it does not follow that this appearance of a wheel is clearly manifest.

For this is not a mental error that arises by sequentially joining together individual perceptions; rather, it is a single, simultaneous sensory error in the form of a wheel that arises through the power of a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because its appearance is vivid. Indeed, it is not logical for that which is bound to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) to have a vivid appearance.
For such a synthesis (*ghaṭanā*) is performed only by memory, not by sensory cognition, since the latter occurs by the power of the presence of an object and lacks the capacity to grasp a past thing.
Furthermore, the object of this memory is not clearly manifest; why? Because it has perished.
Therefore, since it would follow that [the cognition] lacks clarity, this is not a mental error (mānasī bhrāntiḥ).
What then? It is born of the sense faculties (indriyajā); thus, the example [you provided] is devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikala). //1254–1255//

Having thus established the absence of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he now establishes it through inference (*anumāna*), beginning with the words "And if," and so forth:
"And if that cause which establishes the nature of this entity does not exist, it is not established as such by the wise."
Just as a white horse, lacking a dewlap and other such features, does not exist in the nature of a cow,
so too there is no apprehension of an object qualified by qualifiers.
The basis for the existence of conceptual cognition is the presence of the universal;
otherwise, the spotted cow and other individuals would be over-extended as its counter-examples.
Nor is the reason unestablished, because [the existence of] genus and so forth is denied;
nor is there such a qualification, since [the object] is not apprehended as distinct [from its parts].

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That for which there exists no basis (*nimitta*) established for its specific nature is not so determined by discerning practitioners; for example, a white horse (*karka*), which lacks the collection of features such as a hump that serve as the basis for the designation "cow," is not determined as being a cow.

And there exists no basis for the apprehension of an object qualified by qualifiers—which would establish the existence of conceptualization (*savikalpaka*)—for perception, which arises by the power of its unique objects such as blue and so forth; thus, this is a non-apprehension of the cause (*karaṇānupalabdhi*).
By way of dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*), [the examples are] the brindled cow (*śābaleya*), the black cow (*bāhuleya*), and others.

The concise meaning is that the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) consists in the undesirable consequence that everything would be established in every way, and the consequence that the establisher would act without prior reflection (*aprekṣāpūrvakāritā*).
"Karka" means a white horse.
"Of the genus and so forth" (*jātyādeḥ*).
The word "of the particular" (*viśeṣasya*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Showing that even if universals (*jāti*) and so forth were indeed real entities, they would still not be unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "and because they are not perceived as distinct."

The phrase "from form and so forth, which are intended as the qualificanda" is to be supplied. [The opponent asks: "Even if there is indeed no discernment by way of distinction, why does it not still function as a qualifier? To this he replies: "And it is not the case that...
[meaning] it is not distinguished by way of difference.
Therefore, because there is no apprehension of an object qualified by a qualifier, this reason is not unestablished (asiddha).
It might be argued: "Let there be no qualifier such as 'genus' (jāti) and so forth; rather, the very nature of the word itself will be the qualifier. To this he says: "Even the name," and so on.
Even the name, which is the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the word, is certainly not the signifier.
For it has been refuted that the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) can be either the signified or the signifier.
Therefore, the relationship between the signified and the signifier is held to be merely superimposed; and perception apprehends the object as it is, without such superimposition.
Because [the cognition] exists when the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) exists, and because it is absent when that [characteristic] is absent;
and because it also varies when there is an intervention or the like.

There is no convention regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), nor even regarding the particular characteristic of the word, because neither of these persists at the time of linguistic usage.
Furthermore, there is no nature of the word other than the particular characteristic;
nor can an object that has not been subject to convention be connected with a word, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is conceptual construction possible without the application of words;
therefore, the relationship between the signified and the signifier is merely superimposed and not ultimate.
One might argue: "In that case, perception, by apprehending an object that is itself superimposed, would become conceptual. To this he says: "not superimposed," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "due to its absence":
the connection is that it is also [absent] due to the exclusion of that [particular].
That is to say, because of the absence of that particular (svalakṣaṇa), there is also an absence of that perception (pratyakṣa) through exclusion.
When asked, "When is there an absence of the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)? he says: "Due to intervention, etc. By the word "etc.," [he means] remoteness of place, time, and so forth.
With the words "incapable of convention" and so forth, he states yet another means of valid cognition:
"For the nature of blue and other [objects] does not partake of anything else and is incapable of conventional designation;
therefore, the awareness of them is not associated with verbal expression."
The essence (*ātman*) or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of blue and so forth is "incommunicable" (*aśakyasamaya*), meaning it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) for it.
To the question "How so?", he states the reason: "because it does not share [with others]" (*ananyabhāk*). That which "does not share" is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
This means that it does not present itself at the time of conventional usage;

because the convention exists for the sake of such usage, there is no linguistic convention [for it] here. Furthermore, this convention applies only to that which has become an object [of cognition], not to that which has not become an object; for as long as it has not arisen, [it cannot be so].

Perception takes as its object a nature consisting of blue and so forth; and having grasped a verbal expression once it has arisen, it might then apply that expression [to the object]. However, because of momentariness, at the time of the perception's arising and at the time of grasping the verbal expression, the perception no longer possesses the object as its object. Therefore, by what means and where could an application [of the term] occur? For this reason as well, the nature of blue and so forth is incapable of being associated with linguistic conventions (*samaya*). The word "of them" refers to blue and so forth.
"Not associated with verbal expression" means not permeated by linguistic designation (*abhilāpa*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: whatever has not grasped a convention (*samaya*) regarding an object cannot be conceptual (*savikalpaka*) with respect to that object; for example, visual consciousness is not conceptual with respect to odor. And since direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has not grasped a convention regarding its own nature, such as blue and so forth—this is the apprehension of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalambha*).
With the words "nanu" and so forth, he raises the objection that the first reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) according to the view of Sumati the Digambara:
"Granted, let it be that 'name' and so on are not the qualifying attributes of that [object];
nevertheless, the unestablished nature of the reason does not at all cease to apply, because—"
If there were no apprehension of an object in a form distinguished from other objects,
there would either be an apprehension of the mere object or no apprehension at all, as in the case of a jar [when not perceived].
If there is no apprehension of the form as delimited by the interior of the jar,
then there would either be the apprehension of the jar alone, or indeed the non-apprehension of the jar.
For he describes every entity as having a dual nature, consisting of both the universal (sāmānya) and the particular (viśeṣa). And the universal is of two kinds:
that which is delimited by a particular, such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth; and that which is undelimited, such as "existence" (sattā) or "being an entity" (vastutva) and so forth.
