In this regard, that which is undifferentiated and of a single form is the object of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), which consists of mere observation (*ālocanāmātra*); the other, however, is the object of conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*). This is its [the Buddhist] procedure. Kumārila, on the other hand, describes non-conceptual observational cognition as having the specific individuality (*vyakti-svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
But conceptual perception has a universal as its object.
Regarding this, Sumati, for the purpose of examining the perception consisting of mere observation (*ālocana*) as maintained by Kumārila and others, says:
"The proponent of that [view] should be asked this:"
Is that object standing before the sense-faculty apprehended in its own form, as distinguished by a property that does not occur in other objects? If he should say "no," [the opponent asks:]...

To this it is replied: If what is intended is the non-apprehension of an object in a form excluded from other objects—whereby, from the intended object, whatever is another object is excluded, and the form or nature residing therein is absent in that [other object]—then, if the non-apprehension of that object as qualified by such a form is asserted, there would either be the apprehension of that mere object; that is, there would be the apprehension of that very thing which is the mere object, being devoid of a nature that is impossible in other objects.
Or, if even that is not apprehended, then there would be only non-apprehension, a total lack of apprehension.
The example "as in the case of a jar" has been stated; he explains it with the following verse beginning with *ghaṭāntara* and so forth.

If that jar were not perceived by way of a form that does not exist in the jar taken as the limit of comparison, then there would either be the apprehension of the jar-in-general, meaning the apprehension of the jar-in-general as undistinguished by any particularity such as being made of silver, copper, or the like.

If even the apprehension of the jar-in-general does not occur, then there would be no apprehension of anything whatsoever, even of what is intended; thus, there would be a total non-apprehension of the jar.

Likewise, in this case as well, if there is no apprehension of the specific qualities (viśeṣa), it follows as a certainty that there would either be an apprehension of the mere object (arthamātra) or no apprehension at all.
Now, regarding the former position, it is said here:
"If it is thought that [the cognition] apprehends by means of an entity as excluded from other objects of apprehension,
then it would be conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*), like the cognition of a tree and so forth."

If sensory cognition is intended to be that which apprehends an object qualified by a nature that is impossible elsewhere, then it follows that it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because it apprehends an object qualified by some form, just like the cognition "this is a tree" and so forth.

It might be thought: "There is no such thing as a mere object (*artha-mātra*) which is perceived as qualified by its own nature; rather, that specific form which you and I consider to be a particular (*viśeṣa*) is what exists and is what is perceived. To this he says: "No particular exists that is untouched by the universal.
No particular exists that is untouched by the universal.
If it were grasped, it would not be perceived clearly because of its state of being a manifestation.

In this context, "mere" (mātra) refers to the universal (sāmānya), which is designated as "existence" (sattā). There exists no particular (viśeṣa) whatsoever that could be apprehended therein independently of that [universal]. You might think: "Even though that universal exists, it is not touched upon at the time of apprehension. To this he says: "And if it is unmanifest at the time of apprehension, it is not apprehended because of its imperceptible nature."

If, at the time of apprehension, that universal called "existence" (sattā) is not touched by sensory cognition and only the particular is grasped, then that particular being grasped would be devoid of existence—lacking the very nature called existence—and thus would become essence-less (niḥsvabhāva). Consequently, it could not be an object of sensory cognition, because it is without existence (vibhāvatvāt), meaning it is bereft of existence, like a flower in the sky.
To claim that cognition whose object is qualified is not conceptual construction is reckless;
for the state of being qualified is impossible without a connection to a qualifier.

Therefore, the conclusion is that for you who accept [this view] despite it being contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is a rash assertion to claim that there is a cognition of a qualified object and yet no conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Regarding this very point, he states the logical justification beginning with "not by means of a qualifier" (*na viśeṣaṇa*):
for one does not possess a staff without a connection to the staff; likewise, the sense is that even a qualified object is not tenable without a connection to a qualifier.
Therefore, that cognition which involves the apprehension of a connection with a qualifier is conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the cognition under dispute, which has a qualified object as its domain, is conceptual, because it has a qualified object as its domain, like the cognition "this is a cloth" and so forth.

He replies with the verse beginning "sajātīya" and so forth: "Cognition is held to have a qualified object because it grasps an object excluded from both similar and dissimilar things; it does not [arise] from a connection with qualifiers."

If, in this context, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is "because it has a qualified object due to its connection with a distinct qualifier," then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). For the Buddhist, there is no such thing as a "qualifier" at all;

by means of which, through the apprehension of its connection, cognition could have a qualified object. Rather, cognition is considered to have a qualified object because it apprehends the mere object itself as excluded from things of the same and different classes.
How then is there such a designation as "its distinctness" (*vaiśiṣṭyam asya*) or "this is its distinction," which implies a sense of difference? To this he says, "Difference," and so forth:
"Indeed, 'distinction' (*vaiśiṣṭya*) has been said to be difference (*bheda*), not the connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-saṅgati*).
Even when [an object] is expressed by the word 'distinct' (*bhinna*), it is not perceived as being permeated by that [qualifier]."

Difference (*bheda*) is the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from things of the same class and things of different classes. And this [exclusion] is not other than the excluded entity; for it is the entity itself that is so designated when there is a desire to know it as such alone, by means of the rejection of other differences.
This might be so, provided that the apprehension of an object distinct from things of the same and different classes occurs necessarily.
In that case, it follows that the apprehension is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because it functions with the form "this is distinct.

Otherwise, how could it have that as its object if it were functioning with a different form? For it is not logical that what functions with a different form should have that as its object, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even [the cognition] 'it is distinct,' etc."
How, then, is it designated as "different"? To this he says: "svabhāvāpara...
and so forth. When that [object] is apprehended as being distinct from all other entities without exception by its own nature, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises accordingly.

When all other entities distinct from its own nature have been excluded and apprehended, there subsequently arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines a difference, which follows the recollection of a verbal form and expresses "it is distinct" because of the manifestation of a unique aspect such as blue.

Now, if that [object] were not of the nature of verbal expression, or if its essential reality were not mixed with it, then even when it is apprehended by being conjoined with a name such as "distinct" or "non-distinct," it would not be truly grasped [as such].
Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is simply unestablished (*asiddha*).

Now, if the meaning of the reason "because it has a qualified object" is taken to mean that [the cognition] is qualified by virtue of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), rather than through a connection with a qualifier that is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), even then the reason is not necessarily conclusive (*anaikāntika*) in itself. Demonstrating this, he says "viśeṣaṇa... and so forth:
"The universal (*sāmānya*) is held by others to be unqualified by qualifiers."
Therefore, it is likewise equal even in that case [of the object] being apprehended by non-conceptual cognition.
For the universal (*sāmānya*) is of two forms: that which is delimited by a qualifier and that which is undelimited.
Among these, that which is undelimited is held to be graspable by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-vijñāna*).
This applies even to that [undelimited] universal.
Therefore, this quality of being graspable by conceptual cognition is equal [in both cases].
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because of the particular," and so forth.
For that universal is understood as distinguished by its particulars;
therefore, the cognition that apprehends it is necessarily conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
For that which is distinguished from this particular—that is, excluded from it—is perceived as the universal;
otherwise, it would not be a universal at all, because it would not be excluded from it.
Consequently, the cognition that grasps this universal as well—being excluded from the particular—would necessarily become conceptual (*savikalpaka*), since its object is something qualified.
And this does not occur according to your own view;
therefore, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) from the perspective of its own nature (*svataḥ*).

In this regard, it is said that Sumati himself, having anticipated the objection regarding the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason in a general sense, refutes it; he demonstrates that very point with the words beginning "nirviśeṣam" (without distinction), etc.:
"If a difference is apprehended without distinction, it is called a 'universal' (*sāmānya*).
Therefore, it is not logical for the universal to be qualified by that very particular (*viśeṣa*)."

There is no such thing as a universal (*sāmānya*) that possesses a nature distinct from particulars (*viśeṣa*), which, being apprehended as qualified by its own nature, could become the object of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*). Rather, it is the particulars themselves, when apprehended without their specific differences, that are called "universal. That is to say, they are designated by the word "universal" when they are perceived independently of their restricted individual natures. Consequently, how could there be any distinction of the universal from that particular, by virtue of which the cognition grasping it would be conceptual?
How, then, is there a non-confused determination of the universal and the particular? To this he says "vaiṣamya" and so forth:
"These [mental states], being known through their states of dissimilarity and similarity, indeed establish within themselves the status of the universal and the particular."

For these very distinctions, being perceived as either equal or unequal, sequentially undergo the status of being designations and designated objects as "universal" and "particular," thereby establishing the distinct domains for the linguistic usages of "universal" and "particular."
He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "This state of inequality and equality... etc.:
"If this state of inequality and equality is held to be differentiated, then the particularity of the universal remains exactly as it was before."
Now, if this state is indeed undivided and unmixed, how can there be a state of existence?
For there is no other possibility for existence than existing through mutual exclusion.
"Differentiated" (*pravibhakta*) means unmixed;
that is to say, the universal (*sāmānya*) is one thing and the particular (*viśeṣa*) is another.
The statement that "the universal is distinguished by the particular" is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Likewise, even for the particular, there is indeed distinctness from the universal;
for both are differentiated by way of their mutual exclusion of intrinsic natures.
This is what is meant by "abiding in an unmixed state."

It is unmixed. As stated by that same Sumati: "A particular (*viśeṣa*) is directly perceived only when it is permeated by the nature of universals (*sāmānya*) such as existence (*sattā*), and not otherwise; therefore, it is logical that the form of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) consists precisely in having a qualified object-sphere. Furthermore, since a universal can be directly perceived independently of everything else, its being the object of non-conceptual [perception] is not contradictory. This [particular], however, would not be stable if it were not unmixed.

If it is argued that neither a divided nor an undivided [entity] is accepted, he says "mutually," and so forth: because for things characterized by existing through mutual exclusion, the negation of one nature is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other; therefore, there is no third category.
Furthermore, demonstrating that the claim "differences are apprehended without distinction" is mutually contradictory, he says: "Apart from the nature of the particular," and so forth.
Apart from the nature of the particular, there is no other characteristic of difference. If their form is not touched upon, how can it be said that they are apprehended?
Furthermore, when that form and its touch are perceived as distinguished from other distinct entities,
it follows that the cognition regarding them must be conceptual.

For there is no particularity (*viśeṣa*) other than the particulars themselves. And if that particularity is not touched by a cognition that apprehends the universal (*sāmānya*), how could the particulars be apprehended by it? The point is that because they are not distinct from an unapprehended nature, they too would remain unapprehended.

Now, if it is held that they are apprehended, then, upon touching that form—which is to say, upon touching the form of the particulars—the particularity is also indeed apprehended, just like the apprehended nature itself, because it is not distinct from what is apprehended. Consequently, that cognition which is intended to have the universal as its object among these particulars would necessarily be conceptual (*vikalpaka*).

Furthermore, even if it were granted that the universal is not distinct from the particular because it is non-different from it, nevertheless, it is certainly distinct from such indefinable things as a rabbit's horn; thus, it would have to be graspable by conceptual cognition. But it is not so. Therefore, demonstrating that [the reason] is indeed inconclusive, he says: "And from the indefinable... and so forth.
"And the universal is perceived as distinct from the indefinable;
therefore, according to you, that too would be graspable by conceptual cognition."
If that which is qualified by it does not exist when it is absent, then is it now of the same nature as it?
If not, even so, why is its qualification by that [absence] not admitted?
It might be argued that because of the non-existence of a universal (*sāmānya*), there can be neither a particular (*viśeṣa*) nor a similarity (*sādṛśya*).

For it is conceived that non-existence (*abhāva*) is that which is nothing at all; and such a thing is neither distinguished from a universal nor equal to it, because that would entail its being an entity (*bhāvatva*).
To explain: if that void were distinguished from a universal, then it too would necessarily be a real entity.

For a non-entity cannot possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) termed "particularity" (viśeṣa), nor can it be described as "distinguished" (viśiṣṭa) without such an intrinsic nature termed "particularity.
Nor can it be [described] as "equal," because that would entail its being a real entity (vastu).
Indeed, a non-entity cannot have a form identical to anything else, nor is it logical for something to be "equal" without a common form, as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Therefore, taking emptiness as the limit of the universal, it is not logical for there to be either equality or distinction.
For instance, whatever becomes equal or superior by taking something as its limit, that very limit is seen to be both equal and unequal to it.
If that limit were not seen as equal or unequal to it, then the other thing which possesses the limit would likewise not be seen as equal or unequal.

Furthermore, there is no such thing as "non-existence" (abhāva) that is distinct from existence; rather, it is existence itself that is called "non-existence" when it does not become another form of existence. Therefore, how could this [non-existence] possess a specific distinction? Having taken up all of this which was stated by Sumati, [the author] says: "This very distinction of the entity is indeed of a nature other than that," and so forth.
For even though it is an entity, this distinction is indeed of a nature other than that.
And since the universal is not of the nature of non-existence, why is it not qualified by that [particular] for you?
Therefore, whatever cognition arises with respect to the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa),
all of it has as its object that which transcends the path of speech and is non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka).

For indeed, that which constitutes the distinction of a non-entity from the side of an entity is nothing other than the negation of its reality; it is simply the state of not having that nature, which is to say, a difference in definition.
And this is exactly the same for a universal as it is for a non-existent thing such as a rabbit’s horn.

For instance, non-existent things such as a rabbit’s horn are characterized by the absence of all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), whereas a universal (*sāmānya*) is not accepted as being thus; therefore, its distinction from that [non-existence] is perfectly clear.
Consequently, even if there were a distinction from non-existence, it would not follow that non-existence possesses the status of a real entity (*vastutva*); thus, this [objection] is trivial.
As for what was stated—that "non-existence is not something entirely different," and so forth—in that case, the meaning of what he himself had said was not analyzed.

For indeed, when it is stated that "an entity itself does not become another entity," a distinction of that [entity] from other entities is thereby expressed, because of the mention of its exclusion [from them]. This is merely the manifestation of confusion; so enough with this digression.
Therefore, with the words beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore), there is a summary of the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

By demonstrating the view of the followers of Kumārila (the Kaumārila) through the passage beginning with "For there is indeed indeterminate perception" (*asti hy ālocanājñānam*), he raises the objection that the reason (*hetu*) in the formal argument—"that for which there is no cause for the establishment of its form"—is unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*).
[Page 385] "If the initial indeterminate perception exists... (*asti hy ālocanājñānam ādyaṃ cet nirvikalpakam*).
It is like the cognition of infants, the mute, and others, arising from a pure object.
At that time, neither the particular nor the universal is perceived;
rather, it is the individual object itself, which serves as the substratum for both, that is determined.
Furthermore, that cognition by which an object is subsequently determined through its properties such as genus and so forth is also accepted as being of the nature of direct perception.

For instance, if "all perception" is made the subject (*pakṣa*), then in every case regarding the locus (*dharmin*) called perception, there is no apprehension of an object qualified by qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) when it is established as conceptual (*savikalpaka*); thus, this reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*), because apart from the initial non-conceptual awareness (*ālocanājñāna*), the apprehension of an object qualified by qualifiers such as universals (*sāmānya*) exists in other types of perception. Alternatively, if the opponent maintains that the reason is stated by taking the initial non-conceptual awareness itself as perception, then they consider the argument to be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
[The phrase] "resembling the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth" refers to this.
It is similar to the consciousness of an infant and similar to the consciousness of a mute and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), those who have fainted are included. The similarity consists merely in the absence of specific verbal expression.
Furthermore, the purity of the object arises from its being devoid of the two types of universals (*sāmānya*).
He clarifies this very point with the second verse, beginning with "not a particular" (*na viśeṣa*), and so forth.
Regarding the term "particular":
Intermediate generality (*avāntarasāmānya*) refers to "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth;
"generality" (*sāmānya*) refers to "great generality" (*mahāsāmānya*), such as "being an entity" (*vastutva*) and so forth.

"Being the substratum for those two"—by this, the pure object (*vastu*) is shown. Then, with the words "thereafter," and so forth, he makes manifest that very same non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*) as being unestablished in one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddhatā*). "Thereafter" means: [the passage beginning with] "thereafter."

After the apprehension of the pure object, that cognition by which the object is determined through qualifiers such as genus and so forth demonstrates the apprehension of an object qualified by its qualifiers.
By this, it is stated that [perception] possesses the quality of apprehending an object not previously apprehended, and that the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Even when there is conceptualization again and again, whatever realization may occur is accepted as being entirely direct perception, in accordance with its connection [to the object].
"Again and again" means in the third moment and thereafter. "As much as" means...
The phrase "to attain an object not yet attained" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "In accordance with its connection" means in accordance with the connection of that sense organ.

It might be argued: "If the object, endowed with all its properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, does not appear at the time of the initial operation of the senses, then it should likewise not appear at a later time, since there is no difference [in the conditions]. To this he says: "For those who have merely entered," and so forth.
For it is not the case that for those who have merely entered [a place], such as a inner chamber from the heat [outside], [the objects do not appear].
Furthermore, it is understood that objects do not appear [directly] to the sense faculties.
"From the heat" means from the luminous [nature].
It should be construed with "of those who have just entered."
"They are not perceived by the sense-faculties"— by this rhetorical question (kāku), he shows that, on the contrary, they are indeed perceived.
Having thus established the illustration, he says "yathā" and so forth, concluding with the application to the subject of the illustration:
"Just as, having first known [an object] by its own appearance alone,
they subsequently awaken to it in its true nature, so too [do they awaken] to the dharmas such as birth and the rest."

Just as one first perceives a mere appearance within the inner chamber and subsequently knows it specifically as "blue" and so forth, so too, having first known [the object] by way of its own essential nature (svarūpa), one will later possess direct perception (pratyakṣa) of its properties such as genus (jāti) and so on; thus, there is no fault.

If that is the case, then if there is a repeated realization following the initial sensory awareness (*ālocanājñāna*), and its validity is established by that sensory awareness, then suppose someone, having first perceived an object, subsequently closes their eyes and conceptualizes it according to properties such as its genus (*jāti*) and so forth; since there would be a new realization for him, that [conceptual cognition] would also have to be considered perception. To this, he says "yadi tu" and so on:
"But if, after perceiving [an object], someone were to close their eyes and conceptualize [it], that [cognition] would not be perception, because it does not follow from the [sensory] connection."
"Having perceived" means having known through the cognition of perception (*ālocanājñāna*).
"In the eyes" means... [the rest of the sentence is omitted in the source].
The connection is with the word "having closed [the eyes]. "Not following from a connection" means because it does not arise by way of a connection with the sense organs.

As it was stated by that very same Kumārila: "Thus, although [all cognition] is equally mere conceptualization, that in which there follows the fruit of a connection with the sense-faculties is perception; and this is well-known in the world even without such a definition."
He refutes this with the words beginning with "tad" (that):

"That is incorrect; if that cognition has proceeded toward the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then it does not contain verbal expression even when grasping universals (*jāti*) and so forth."
Thus, it has already been established previously that this particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is indeed inexpressible;
and the cognition that operates upon it is necessarily non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka).
In the phrase "even in the apprehension of universals (jāti) and so forth," the word "even" (api) is used in the sense of concession.

First of all, since universals and the like have already been refuted, they do not exist at all; therefore, how could there be validity in their apprehension? Granting, for the sake of argument, that they do exist, nevertheless, just like indeterminate perception (ālocanājñāna), cognitions occurring at a subsequent time would still be non-conceptual (avikalpa) because their objects are particularities (svalakṣaṇa), since it has been admitted that universals and the like are non-different from the particularity. This is the intended meaning.

The formal argument is as follows: whatever apprehends a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), such as sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*); and the cognition intended as subsequent direct perception (*uttarapratyakṣa*) apprehends a particular characteristic. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, this is a proof by reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*). Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it has already been established in the previous section on "Exclusion of Others" (*anyāpoha*) that this particular characteristic is indeed inexpressible.
Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
It might be argued that the reason is unestablished because [the cognition] has only the universal as its object; to this he says "jātimātra" and so forth:
"If there were a grasping of the universal alone, there would be absolute distinctness of the qualifier;
but this is not accepted by the opponents in the manner stated."
"The qualifier is absolutely distinct"— the remainder of the sentence being "from the qualified.
And this is not accepted by the opponents.
The absolute distinctness of the qualifier and the qualified— why is this not accepted? To this he says, "as has been stated," the remainder being "by that very [reason]."
To explain what that is, he says "yadi" and so forth:
For if the qualifier were absolutely distinct from the qualified,
then how could it produce in the qualified a cognition corresponding to itself?
Since even difference is admitted in a certain sense, he says "absolutely" (*ekāntataḥ*).
For instance, universals (*jāti*) and so forth are held by him to have a nature that is both different and non-different; they are neither absolutely different nor absolutely non-different.
And thus he said:
"And because there is a difference in cognition, it does not follow that color and the other [sensory objects] are one;
or rather, both unity and plurality are accepted due to the distinction between existence and color and so forth."
Thus it is said;
and furthermore:
"Indeed, the distinctness of birth and so forth from the manifest is not established at all."
Thus:
"otherness" means "distinctness."
"Corresponding to itself" means colored by the essential nature of the qualifier.
The point is that a qualifier is so called because it causes the qualified object to be apprehended as colored by the qualifier; otherwise, its status as a qualifier would be untenable.
As it has been said:
"That by which one is colored through one's own intellect is the qualifier of the qualified."

Now, it might be argued that because [the subsequent cognitions] have both the particular and the universal as their objects by virtue of having the particular and the universal as their respective domains, it is unproven that later cognitions have the mere particular as their object alone; to this, he says: "Of the particular and universal natures," and so forth: "It is not logical for a single cognition to be the knower of both the particular and universal natures; for if it were otherwise [i.e., if it were conceptual], there would be no difference between the preceding [cognition] and the others."
It is not logical for a single cognition to be the knower of both the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

For instance, that single cognition must be either conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). In the case of its being conceptual—that is, when it possesses conceptualization—it does not attain the perception (*vit*) of the aforementioned prior particular characteristic. "Otherwise" refers to the position of it being non-conceptual.
"Of the other" means of that which has a universal nature; there would be no cognition [of it].
[Page 388] Thus far, it has been established that if other cognitions have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, they would necessarily be non-conceptual (*avikalpa*).

Now, even granting that they are conceptual (*savikalpaka*), the author says "ekāntena" and so forth, demonstrating that their status as valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is not tenable because they apprehend what has already been apprehended:
"If [it is argued that] because there is absolutely no difference [between the universal and its instance], the universal and so forth are already grasped by the first [cognition],"...
Because it apprehends an object already known, the subsequent [cognition] is equal to a cognition based on memory.
For indeed, it is not accepted at all that universals and the like are absolutely different from the individual;
as it has been said:
"For the distinctness of the universal and so forth from the individual is certainly not established."

Thus, since the genus (*jāti*) and so forth are apprehended by the very first cognition of bare observation (*ālocanājñāna*), it follows that the subsequent determinate cognition (*niścayajñāna*) of the attributes such as genus is indeed not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because it apprehends an object already apprehended, like a mnemonic cognition (*smārttajñāna*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition apprehends what has already been apprehended is not a means of valid knowledge, just like memory; and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurring subsequent to perception is one that apprehends what has already been apprehended. This is an instance of the "perception of a property incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

In this regard, if the meaning of the reason is "grasped by way of the exclusion of the object of superimposition," then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). Alternatively, if the meaning of the reason is "because it is grasped in some way or other," then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to inference.
Demonstrating this, he says: "obscure," and so forth.
When there is an apprehension in the form of various indistinct universals, the object is not yet determined; rather, ascertainment occurs through successive stages.
Just as inference has as its object the exclusion of superimposition,
so too does certainty have as its object the exclusion of superimposition.

For it is thus: first, an object is apprehended by indeterminate sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*) in a vague form, not in a determinate form; however, subsequent determination is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its object is the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*), just like inference.

Just as when a subject (*dharmin*) such as sound has been grasped by perception, the determination of impermanence through [the reason] "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) becomes a valid means of knowledge, so too will this determination have the exclusion of superimposition as its object.
For you yourselves do not dispute that determination has the exclusion of superimposition as its object.
As it has been said:
"Because there exists a relationship of sublated and sublator between the mind of certainty and the mind of superimposition,
it is understood that the activity of this [certainty] occurs when superimposition is removed."
Thus it is said.
He replies with the words beginning "no," etc.:
"There is no validity [of inference] by virtue of its having the cutting off of superimposition as its object,
because that would entail that even memory is a valid means of cognition."

Because it prevents the superimposition that arises immediately after perception, inferential knowledge is accepted as a valid means of cognition; however, such [inferential knowledge] does not exist for you.
In cases such as "the cow is white" or "it moves," immediately following perception,
no superimposition (samāropa) is experienced in that cognition which could be what is being negated.

The validity of inference consists in the exclusion of an already arisen superimposition (*samāropa*), and not merely in the exclusion of the object of a superimposition; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even memory would possess validity. Furthermore, in the case of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "the cow is white and moving," which arises immediately after perception, there is no warding off of an arisen superimposition, because no superimposition has arisen in the interval. If it is asked how there is no arising [of a superimposition], he says: "the cow," and so forth.

For it is established by the non-perception of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility that conceptual construction does not arise as something non-conscious; thus, the non-arising of superimposition is proven.

Thus far, all this has been stated while provisionally accepting [the existence of] birth and so forth; now, demonstrating that birth and the rest do not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality—and therefore how perception could possess conceptualization by having them as its objects—he says "tattva" and so on:
Birth and the rest do not exist as identical, different, or both;
therefore, what conceptual cognition could ever attain the status of perception?
Because of the non-existence of a positive concomitance, because they do not appear as distinct [from one another],
and because the two realities exist through mutual exclusion, there is a difference between them.
For universals (*jāti*) and the like may, in some cases, be non-different from individuals, or different, or possess both natures by being both different and non-different.
First of all, the initial position is not tenable because of the absence of pervasion (*anvaya*); that is, due to the lack of concomitance.
For a form that follows through multiple entities is called a universal, and individuals do not thus interpenetrate one another such that they themselves could constitute the universal.

Alternatively, if through mutual penetration (*anvāveśa*) everything becomes a single form, it follows that the universal itself would be non-existent, because it [the universal] must have multiple substrata. Nor is the second position tenable; for despite their difference, they do not appear as distinct.
"Despite their difference" means despite the difference from the individual (*vyakti*).
And that which does not appear [to consciousness] cannot become an object of direct perception,
as it has been said:
"Individual instances do not follow after one another, and nothing else that follows after them appears."
And how could that which is non-different from cognition become a separate object?
Nor is the third position tenable, namely that [identity and difference] exist as distinct entities by way of mutual exclusion.
For when two things are defined by the characteristic of existing through mutual exclusion, the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other.
Alternatively, since otherness and identity are established through mutual exclusion— because the determination of one occurs through the exclusion of the nature of the other—
therefore, there is no connection with a third category.

But if perception is indeed non-conceptual, how can there be worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) by means of it? For instance, if one determines that "this is a means to pleasure" and "this is a cause of suffering," then one proceeds toward the attainment of the former and the avoidance of the latter.
Furthermore, it would follow that there could be no activity regarding inference and the object of inference;
for at the time of inference, the subject (*dharmin*) or the property (*dharma*) must necessarily be apprehended as already determined by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, that [object] cannot be apprehended as determined by perception, because perception is non-determinative in nature;
nor can it be apprehended by inference, due to the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā);
and since there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it follows that all worldly transactional activity would come to an end.

Therefore, to one who might object that this thesis of non-conceptuality is sublated by inference because it functions within the sphere of inferential and other conventional activities based on a logical mark (liṅga), he says "even though non-conceptual," and so forth:
"Even non-conceptual cognition possesses the power to produce conceptualization;
therefore, by means of that [conceptualization], it becomes a factor for all conventional activities without exception."
"By means of that" means that even non-conceptual [cognition], by way of conceptualization, becomes a constituent of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) as the cause of ascertainment (*niścaya*).

For instance, although perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), it arises determining an object such as fire— which is excluded from things of its own class and of other classes— by virtue of the arising of an appearance in its own form.

And because that [conceptual cognition] grasps an object established with a fixed form and conforms to the aspect of an object excluded from dissimilar classes, it manifests affirmation and negation regarding that very object, such as "this is fire" and "it is not a cluster of flowers and so forth. Since these two conceptual cognitions are indirectly connected to the real object, they are not accepted as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even though they are non-erroneous; for, despite the determination of identity between the perceived and the conceptualized, there is no apprehension of a previously unapprehended real nature of the object, since activity proceeds through that determination of identity.

For this very reason, because it is the cause of two conceptual alternatives, it also functions as the basis for indicating the absence of a third possibility. To explain: when something occurs in relation to a certain object, it determines that object because it appears as such; and since nothing other than that is perceived there, it excludes everything else. Furthermore, because all entities are established within a twofold division—as either the perceptible object itself or what is other than it—it indicates the non-existence of any other category.

If this is so, then since the subject (*dharmin*), such as sound, is already apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, the inferential conceptualization (*anumāna-vikalpa*) proceeding with respect to its impermanence and so forth would not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is not a fault.

Even when perception has arisen, only that aspect in which it produces a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) is said to be "grasped" as being fit for practical activity (*vyavahāra*). However, in a case where—due to the influence of a cause of error—the perception is unable to produce a determinate cognition because superimposition (*samāropa*) occurs, that object, being unfit for practical activity, is considered "as if ungrasped" despite having been grasped. In such a case, inference possesses validity as it proceeds to exclude the superimposition that has already occurred; this is not the case, however, for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising immediately after perception, because that lacks the exclusion of an occurring superimposition.

But what is the reason that, even when an experience arises regarding the nature of an object that is distinct from all others, a corresponding determinative recollection does not likewise occur? It is said: because it depends on other causes (kāraṇāntara). For a determination does not occur merely by the fact that something has been experienced; rather, that [determination] depends on other causes such as repetition, interest, or proficiency.
Just as, despite there being no difference between one who procreates and one who teaches, upon seeing his father approaching, one determines, "My father is coming," and not, "The teacher is coming."

In this regard, Bhāvivikta and others, refuting the status of [non-conceptual cognition] as a factor in conventional discourse even by way of the production of conceptualization, present the following proof, which he shows with the words "not non-conceptual," and so forth:
"A non-conceptual [cognition] is not capable [of producing] a conceptual one, because their objects are distinct;
and because it is non-conceptual, like the cognition of color-form and so forth, or like the eye and other [senses]."

Sensory consciousness is not the cause of conceptual mental consciousness, because their objects are distinct—just like the cognitions of form, touch, and so forth—and because it is non-conceptual—just like the eye and other sense organs.

Regarding the reason "because of the difference in objects," the two examples are "like the cognition of form and so forth"; regarding the reason "because of being non-conceptual," the example is "like the eye and so forth."
With the words "In this regard," etc., he states the refutation:
"In this case, there is no contradiction between these two [alternatives] with respect to conceptual construction;
nor is their object different, because they both determine that same object."
Both reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because no contradiction between the reason and the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) has been demonstrated.
"Of these two" refers to the two reasons.
Nor does the phrase "the object is distinct" indicate that, even though conceptual construction possesses an object, the reason "due to the difference of the object" is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Showing that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is without an object, and is therefore all the more unestablished even then, he says: "In reality, however," and so forth:
"In reality, conceptual construction proceeds without a basis."
There exists no object whatsoever that could be differentiated from it.
By the phrase "form, sound, and so forth," [the author] states that the example "like the cognitions of form and so forth" is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*):
"The cognitions of form, sound, and so forth certainly possess mutual causality;
therefore, this example which has been cited is one whose probandum is unestablished."
Because there exists causality among the cognitions of form, sound, and so forth, by way of their being mutual immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, by demonstrating the presence of this reason—namely, "due to the difference in objects"—in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), he states its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) with the verse beginning "fire, smoke, etc.
(agnidhūmādi): "Because of the causal relationship between the cognitions of fire, smoke, and so forth, a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is clearly observed in this case as well."
Regarding the phrase "in this case": the word "from" (*itaḥ*) indicates the reason, namely "due to the difference in objects.

Just as the cognition of a mark such as smoke is the cause for the cognition of that which possesses the mark—such as fire—even though there is a difference in their objects, so too will it be here; thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Having thus established that perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), he states the purpose of including the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) with the words beginning "hair-tufts" (*keśoṇḍraka*).

This inclusion of "non-erroneous" was made for the sake of excluding cognitions such as those of hair-tufts; for such [cognitions], because they are erroneous, are not accepted as valid cognition (*pramā*).
In this context, "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) should be understood as non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādita*), and not as having an aspect corresponding to the object as it exists in reality.

For otherwise, since the object is not established according to the Yogācāra position, the definition of perception intended by relying on both systems would suffer from the fault of being under-inclusive (*avyāpitā*).

Furthermore, non-contradictoriness consists in the capacity to bring about an object capable of the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), but it does not mean actual attainment, because obstacles and the like may occur.
If it is argued that, in this case, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" alone should suffice, and what is the use of including the term "free from conceptual construction," we say:
no;
for it would follow as an undesirable consequence that even inferential conceptualization would be perception.
"Some say that even that [cognition] is mental.

Some maintain that even that is mental; however, this is not so because it arises from the state of the sense-faculties, since its presence is observed when those [faculties] are present, and its modification is observed when they are modified.
And like the delusion of a snake and so forth, this [delusion] would cease even while the impairment of the sense organ has not disappeared, because it is a mental delusion and appears clearly.

Their intention is that it is not necessary to include the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) for that purpose. [Objection: Even if mental perception (*mānasa*) is admitted, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" must still be made; for this [definition] was not begun merely to provide a definition of sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*), but rather of mental perception as well, such as the cognition of yogins. In that case, even dream-cognition possesses non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatva*) because it appears clearly, yet it lacks non-erroneousness; therefore, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" is indeed appropriate in order to exclude that.
This is true;
however, since sensory error is also possible, this position of theirs is untenable. To demonstrate that [the cognition] is born of the senses, he says "this is not so," and so forth.
Because it occurs when the sense organs are present, this cognition of a mass of hair and the like is produced by the senses.
Furthermore, if it were a mental delusion, then it would cease solely due to the cause of that mental delusion, even though the impairment of the sense organ has not ceased;
the analogy here is like the delusion of a snake and so forth.
Moreover, there is another undesirable consequence: it would not result in a clear manifestation.
For that which is permeated by conceptual construction cannot have a clear manifestation of the object, since it functions solely through the delineation of a universal.

With the words "tadbhāva" and so forth, he anticipates the objection of an opponent: "The state of being produced by the existence of that [object] is unestablished in a direct sense and is inconclusive;
yet it is established in an indirect sense, because of its concomitance with that cognition of memory."

In the world, the fact that a change in the cause brings about a change in the effect is clearly observed even in cases where the effects arise through a succession of steps, as in the case of mules and the like.
"All mental delusions cease through investigation"—
this [rule] is subject to deviation by means of cognitions of generalities (sāmānya) regarding entities.
These [cognitions] do not, by their very nature, operate with respect to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity;
if it is argued that their cessation occurs in this way [due to the absence of such a characteristic], then the same applies to cases such as the two moons.
If it is argued that there is no cessation of existence [of the universal], then the same applies to the cognitions of universals;
nor is there [cessation] for the delusions regarding Īśvara and so forth among those who are intent upon their doctrines.
Even upon hearing millions of arguments, there is still a cessation [of inquiry];
on the contrary, those dull-witted people say again, "These are not valid arguments."

In this context, if the reason (*hetu*) is "being produced immediately upon the existence of that [object]," then the reason is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*). For it is not established for the opponent that error arises directly from the sense faculty, since that very [direct production] is what remains to be proven.

If, on the other hand, the reason is "being produced upon the existence of that" in a general sense, then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because such production exists even in the case of memory-cognition, which constitutes a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), since that too occurs through a mediated sequence (*pāramparya*). Furthermore, as for the property of "changing in accordance with its modification," that too is unestablished in the direct sense; and even if taken in a mediated sense, it remains strictly inconclusive.

Since, in the case of a mule born from a mare and a donkey, even though there is an intervention by stages such as the *kalala* and so forth, its being a transformation of the donkey is perceived later by way of its resemblance to the form of a donkey; therefore, direct production [of the effect from the cause] is not established by this.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that mental error is removed by investigation, there is also an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to cognitions of the general nature of entities (*bhāvasāmānyabuddhi*).

For even for you, who understand the non-existence of universals through reasoning, the conceptual construction (vikalpa) in the form of "existence" or "universal" does not cease regarding entities such as jars and the like.

Now, if you think that these cognitions of universals indeed do cease for one who investigates through reasoning, because they proceed by way of this mode [of apprehension]— namely, that they function through the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)— [we reply:]...
In that case, this too is not a valid response.
For even cognitions such as that of two moons, when analyzed through reasoning, do not operate with respect to a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); they cease precisely in this manner.
Yet, for all that, they do not thereby become mental [cognitions].
If it is argued that their existence does not cease, then that is the same for the cognitions of universals;
for even their own nature does not cease.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "being produced by the existence of that" and so forth:
"The state of being produced by the existence of that is not directly established for one whose mind is non-erroneous;
nor is an intervention established, for nothing is perceived in the interval."
Even one whose mind is unattached to objects perceives things such as a double moon;
therefore, because it is uninterrupted, there is no arising through a causal succession.
When it is possible to withdraw the cognitions of the generalities of entities,
cessation is indeed possible even for one who possesses the intellect of a Lord, according to his own will.
It is not unestablished, but rather it is indeed established; why?
Because there is no proof of an intervention by a non-erroneous cognition of a single moon, since that which is perceptible is not perceived in the interval.
He clarifies this very point with the words "for another purpose" and so forth.
It should be connected as: "the non-interruption of [the perception of] two moons and so on.
For this very reason, there is also no deviation in the principle that [an effect] undergoes change when its cause undergoes change.
For even that [cognition] is not obstructed in such a way that there would be a deviation [of the reason] by means of cases such as the *vegasara* (a type of horse).
Even for cognitions of general entities (*bhāvasāmānya*), when one effects their cessation at will, there is indeed a cessation;
however, since it is not possible to effect the cessation of cognitions such as those of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍraka*) by will, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).
If it is argued that even for sensory cognition, its cessation occurs by the power of volition when the eyes are closed at will, [we reply:
visual consciousness does not cease immediately upon the cessation of volition;
what then?

The closing of the eyes occurs by the power of volition, and once the eye has ceased [its operation], that visual cognition ceases; however, mental error ceases directly by the power of volition, so the two cases are not the same.

This is to be understood as follows: because even when the eye is directed, an object that one does not wish to see is nonetheless seen; therefore, volition does not have direct efficacy over the cognition of the eyes and other senses.
Others proclaim that cognitions such as that of a yellow conch-shell, even though they are erroneous,
possess the status of valid cognition because they do not fail to correspond with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
However, some of our own school do not accept the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*),

because even erroneous cognitions, such as the perception of a yellow conch shell and the like, are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*). For instance, such a cognition is not an inference (*anumāna*), since it does not arise from a logical mark (*aliṅgaja*).
And it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory.
For this very reason, the teacher Diṅnāga did not include the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) in his definition.

Since he designated pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) through such statements as "error is conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*), which is ignorance and inference," etc., the teacher’s intended definition was simply that [perception] is "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and "consistent with reality" (*saṃvādika*).
Regarding the phrase "sataimira" (with cataract), this word *timira* is a synonym for ignorance (*ajñāna*),
as in the expression "the destroyer of cataracts for the dull-witted. The meaning is that *taimira*— that which arises from *timira*— is deceptive.
He refutes this with the words beginning "That is not so" (tanna): "That which corresponds to the determined form does not exist;
even there, the attainment of causal efficiency [is required], otherwise an over-extension would follow."
Furthermore, since cognition in which hair and so forth appear possesses the quality of correspondence with reality,
it follows that its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)— due to factors such as light— is difficult to deny.
[395] Indeed, validity arises from two aspects: either non-contradiction with respect to the appearance (*yathāpratibhāsa*) or non-contradiction with respect to the determination (*yathādhyavasāya*).
In this case, there is no non-contradiction with respect to the appearance, because yellow appears and that which is as it appears is not attained.

Nor is there non-contradiction with respect to the determination, because it is precisely the yellow that is determined as being capable of a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), yet the attainment of such an action of that nature does not exist.
Nor can validity be established merely by non-contradiction with respect to an object that has not been ascertained, because this would lead to an over-extension;
for even in the case of a cognition of [illusory] hair and the like, there is the attainment of light and so forth, which were not actually ascertained.
Now, if you think that although the color (*varṇa*) as determined is not obtained, the shape (*saṃsthāna*) is indeed obtained, to this he says "not [the color]," and so forth:
"And a shape distinct from the color is not tenable;
nor is correspondence admitted for the color that is appearing."
This is easily understood.
With the words "If [one disregards] the form," and so forth, he states the cumulative argument:

"If validity is postulated while disregarding the form [of the cognition], because it does not contradict purposeful action, then the determination of the object must indeed have that [form as its] nature."
How could all that has been stated in such passages not be contradicted?
Therefore, the occurrence of correspondence arises from the ripening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as its cause.

For validity cannot be established merely by non-contradiction with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) while disregarding the mental aspect (*ākāra*), because that would entail the consequence that the objective aspect (*viṣayākāra*) lacks validity.
"In that form" means in the form of the appearance residing within cognition.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he shows that this contradicts the statement of the Teacher (Dignāga), namely: "For in whatever way the form of an object is presented—as white and so forth—in that very form is the object cognized.

However, it should be understood that the correspondence with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*) arises from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) solely through the maturation of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) from the previous experience of the object.

In the case of the cognition of a yellow conch, the cause for the maturation of the latent impression is the conch itself as white; it is through its predominance (*ādhipatya*) that such maturation occurs.
That non-contradiction whose origination is due to the ripening of latent predispositions (vāsanā) is so described.
He states "mental" and so forth to explain how pleasure and the like are directly perceived through sensation:
"The same reasoning that establishes the non-conceptual nature of mental and sensory cognitions is the proof for the non-conceptual nature of pleasure and the like."
Regarding the phrase "the principle" (*nyāya*):
it refers to the impossibility of establishing a convention (*aśakyasamayatva*) and so forth.

Although this principle has not been explicitly stated for mental cognition (*mānasa*), nevertheless, that same principle—the impossibility of establishing a convention—which applies to sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*), applies equally to it as well.

Alternatively, the cognition of a yogi here is mental, and that will be explained [later]. Since it is well-known from established doctrine (siddhānta), no definition of mental [cognition] has been provided here;
the sense is that its being uncontradicted by valid cognition (pramāṇa) has already been demonstrated by the Teacher himself, and thus it is not being demonstrated again.
With the words "non-cognizing," etc., he raises the objection of the Vaiśeṣika school:
"How indeed could those [atoms], which do not cognize even another [object], possess self-awareness?
If it is argued that these [atoms] become objects of cognition through a consciousness residing in the same substratum [as themselves]," [the response follows].
Not only are they not self-cognizing, but they are also non-apprehenders of external objects;
that is to say, they do not have the nature of cognition.
Their established tenet is that [external objects] are known by means of a cognition inherent (*samaveta*) within a single self (*ātman*).
He refutes [the objection] with the words beginning "nairantarya" (without interval): "Since the perception of external objects occurs without interval,
why is pleasure and so forth not experienced continuously at that time?"
If it is held that what is to be known is known by the mind alone and not by the [external] consciousness,
then its existence at that time is impossible, because its arising is described as being successive.

If it is argued that simultaneous birth alone is not accepted, but not simultaneous duration, we say no; for its duration is impossible due to the established proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
If it is argued that there is a simultaneous delusion due to rapid occurrence, that too has been refuted;
for there would be no clear manifestation in the domain of memory.
And if that error is conceived as having the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth, then it follows that the existence of pleasure and the rest is characterized by nothing other than that [error].
And when yogins perceive the pleasure and so forth of others through direct perception,
they too would become afflicted by it, because their experience would be identical.
For you, even in one's own case, the existence of suffering itself is not the experience;
rather, it is the cognition having that as its object, and such [cognition] exists in the mental continuum of another.
And this is the same in the case of inferring the suffering of others;
for that inference is described as having an object, not as being without an objective domain.

By this, he states that the proposition is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣaviruddhatā*). When pleasure and so forth are experienced simultaneously with the cognition that has an external object as its support, by which cognition could they be known as having a single common substratum? Not, first of all, by that very visual or other sensory cognition which has an external object as its support, because that has an external object as its support, and because pleasure and so forth are intended to be cognized only by a mental consciousness (*mānasa-cetas*) due to their being internally experienced.
Nor is there the possibility of a mental consciousness at that time, for cognitions arise only in succession.
Thus it is accepted.
Now, it might be argued that only the arising of cognitions is admitted to occur in succession, not their persistence;
but this is incorrect.
Since the momentariness of all living beings has been established,
even that illusion of simultaneity which arises through rapid succession has already been refuted.

Furthermore, a clear manifestation in the form of pleasure and pain would not be possible, because it is accepted that when pleasure and the like are objects of conceptual construction, they are cognized solely by the mental consciousness (*mānasa-cetas*).
And because that [conceptual cognition] is conceptual (*savikalpaka*),
it does not possess the appearance of a clearly manifest object (*spaṣṭārtha*);
for we accept as perception only that which is produced by sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) acting in conjunction with the immediately preceding object of its own domain.

Furthermore, if pleasure and the like were objects of apprehension (*grāhya*), they would appear as discrete entities, just like blue and other such objects. Yet, there is no perception of a form such as "pleasure" that is distinct from cognition. If it is argued that the apprehension of the form of pleasure and so forth as non-different from cognition is an illusion (*bhrānti*), [we reply:]...
In that case, the existence of pleasure and so forth as being of the nature of self-awareness is established,
because pleasure and so forth are characterized solely by the form of being pleasant and so on.
If that very nature is established for cognition, then pleasure and so forth are established as having cognition as their intrinsic nature.
However, since external objects are unestablished, error is likewise unestablished.
"Pleasant" (*śātā*) means agreeable; its opposite is "unpleasant" (*aśātā*); by the word "etcetera," equanimity (*upekṣā*) is included.

Furthermore, if it is not accepted that the very existence of pleasure and so forth—characterized by their arising within one's own continuum—is itself their experience, [then error cannot be established].
However, when the cognition of that object arises for yogins perceiving another's pleasure and so forth, their state would be identical to that of the person experiencing it.
One should not argue that the state is not identical because they belong to different mental continua (*saṃtāna*),
for it is not accepted that those [yogins] possess a continuity consisting of belonging to their own continuum.
What then? It is the arising of a cognition whose object is that [other mind].
And since that [arising] exists even for those who perceive the mental continuum of another, the same undesirable consequence follows.

Alternatively, if both are accepted as the cause of the experience of pleasure and so forth, then, given that they are experienced as residing within one's own continuum, the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of pleasure and so forth is established.
For in this way, the state of occurring within one's own continuum serves as the reason and as the differentiator from those occurring in the continua of others.

If [cognitions] were self-cognizing in nature, then for those such as the Mīmāṃsakas for whom yogis are not established, how could there be a reductio (*prasaṅga*) by means of them? To this he says "others," and so forth.
For unlike the Buddhists, for others inference does not, in the ultimate sense, have a non-existent object.
And consequently, in the case of inferring the suffering of another, the same would apply to the inferrer as well, provided there is an equal experience [of that suffering].
Pleasure and the like are perceived simply as pleasure, pain, and so forth, but they are not perceived as "cognition" itself;
therefore, they are not cognition, just like a jar or other such objects.
Śaṅkarasvāmin says: pleasure and the like do not have cognition as their intrinsic nature, because they are not designated as "cognition," just like a jar and so forth.
With the words "If it is so," etc., he states the refutation:
"If this is the case, even the cognition 'it is a convention' is not established for us; since that [cognition] exists in the mind, then at that time, non-cognition would also apply to that."

If the difference in intrinsic nature were to result from the difference in convention, then, since someone might establish the convention "this is non-knowledge" even with respect to knowledge, it would follow that because the designation "knowledge" does not exist in the mind at that time, non-knowledge would exist in reality even within knowledge itself.
It is evident that [the self] is of the nature of luminosity; if it were not so, it would follow that this would apply equally to pleasure, pain, and so forth—why then is all of this not [admitted]?

We shall explain the yogi’s cognition, which arises from the cultivation of the true nature of reality, is free from conceptual construction and error, and is perfected through stainless means of accomplishment.
Now, if it is argued that knowledge, being luminous by nature, is clearly experienced and therefore cannot be non-knowledge, then all of this would apply equally to pleasure and so forth as well.
Furthermore, the reason [adduced] is rendered inconclusive by this very point; thus, this argument amounts to nothing.
We shall explain this further.
In the *Sarvajñasiddhi*.
In order to refute misconceptions regarding the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), he says "the object," and so forth:

"The apprehension of the object is here intended as the result of valid cognition; alternatively, self-awareness (*svavitti*) is the result, while the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is either similarity of form (*sārūpya*) or even capability (*yogyatā*)."

When the external object is the object of cognition (*prameya*), the apprehension of the object is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), while similarity (*sārūpya*) is the means of valid cognition;
for even though self-cognition exists, it is because [the object] manifests according to its form.
However, when the nature of cognition itself is the object of cognition, self-cognition is the fruit, and capacity (*yogyatā*) is the means of valid cognition.

Based on its being perceived as possessing activity, that very capacity belongs to cognition alone, by virtue of which it cognizes itself and not jars and the like. Thus, cognition is characterized as self-illuminating precisely through its capacity acting as an instrument; therefore, capacity is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
As it has been said:
"In that case as well, because they do not possess the nature of both [subject and object], those [cognitions] are capable of the awareness of their own selves;
thus, that capacity is the means of knowledge (*māna*), the self is the object of knowledge (*meya*), and self-awareness is the fruit (*phala*)."
Thus [it is said].
With the words "cutting" (*chedana*) and so forth, he anticipates the objection of the followers of Kumārila:
"Just as when cutting is directed toward a *khadira* tree, no cut occurs in a *palāśa* tree, so too in the world, the axe is not one with the act of cutting. Thus [he asks].

[Page 399] Regarding one who asserts that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) are distinct, the Buddhist has stated: "If a distinction between the means of valid cognition and its result is admitted, then the means of valid cognition and its result would have different objects (*viṣaya*).
But this is not tenable;
for when an axe or similar tool is applied to a *paraśu* tree for the purpose of cutting, the cut does not occur in a *palāśa* tree."
Therefore, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) have the same object, they are non-different. Regarding this, Kumārila stated:
"But he who, desiring the identity of the object, would say that the means of valid cognition is the result..."
The distinction between the probandum and the probans is sublated by worldly convention; therefore, [your argument] is refuted.
Just as when cutting occurs, it happens in the *khadira* tree and not in the *palāśa*,
so too in the world there is no identity between the axe and the act of cutting.
Thus:
that by which something is cut is "cutting" (chedana).
He provides the answer with the words beginning with "no" (*na*):
"The establishment of the relationship between the probandum and the probans does not occur by virtue of being based on a fixed arrangement;
for that arrangement is indeed not tenable in a cognition that is devoid of forms."

The determination of the cognition of an object—such as that "the consciousness of blue does not belong to yellow"—has its basis solely in the conformity of the cognition to the object (*arthasārūpya*) and nothing else. Thus, the distinction between the means of proof and the probandum is established by way of their being the determiner and the determined, not by way of a relationship between producer and produced; for there exists no ultimately real relationship of agent, instrument, and so forth, because all phenomena are devoid of activity due to their momentariness. Indeed, knowledge, arising in the form of the object, appears as if it were determining the object and as if it possessed activity.
This very activity of bringing about the attainment of the object is what constitutes the function of cognition, and not merely its invariable concomitance [with the object].
For it is not the case that sprouts and the like do not arise in invariable concomitance with seeds and the like;
[if they did,] cognition alone would have to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, by means of this systematic determination (*vyavasthā*), it is demonstrated that cognition possessing an aspect (*sākāra*) alone is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not that which is aspectless (*nirākāra*);
and this determination is to be understood through the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) obtained subsequent to that [direct perception].
Therefore, with the words "imagined" and so forth, he states that there is no contradiction with worldly convention:
"Thus, an imagined distinction exists, as in the case of a bow and its like; however, this [distinction] based on the relationship of producer and produced is not accepted here."
"Like the bow and so forth": just as with the bow—

one says "he pierces with the bow," "he pierces by means of the bow," or "the arrow, having issued from the bow, pierces"— and thus various roles such as agency are attributed to the single bow without contradiction, so it is here as well.
And when a joint in wood or similar material is being split by the stroke of an axe, the stroke is said to enter [the gap]; therefore, unity is established there.

When the cutting of a tree or similar object by an axe is examined, it is found to consist precisely of the entry [of the axe] into the substance to be cut; and since that entry is a property residing in the very nature of the axe itself, it is in the ultimate sense identical with the act of cutting—thus, there is no contradiction.
With the words "But when the establishment [of the distinction] has occurred," and so forth, he shows this:
once the establishment has been achieved, one may indeed postulate it otherwise;
for the rule of formal arrangement is stated by way of the relationship between producer and produced.

Just as Kumārila established the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*) through the relationship of producer and produced by means of the passage beginning with "because it has the nature of being a result of determination," so too is our position likewise non-contradictory.
As the Master [Dignāga] stated: "In that case as well, the metaphorical application of the term 'perception' (*pratyakṣa*) to its causes, such as the eye and so forth, is not contradictory."

We say this much: at the outset, the arrangement of the probandum and the probans must necessarily be established by means of a formal distinction; for it is not reasonable to engage in activity with a fixed restriction according to the distinction of objects without first establishing a distinction between cognitions. And since the basis for establishing the distinction between cognitions is indeed similarity (*sārūpya*), it follows by implication that similarity is the most effective means of proof (*sādhakatama*). Furthermore, it is precisely from similarity that cognition becomes an instigator of action. And the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) belongs to that which instigates action; this is determined by one who desires to act, not out of mere whim.

As it has been said: "For every discerning person seeks both valid and invalid cognition for the sake of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, only that aspect by which a cognition functions as an instigator of activity must be demonstrated. Furthermore, when the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is established not through the relation of producer and produced, the instigating aspect—namely, the similarity of form (*sārūpya*)—is what is apprehended; otherwise, the establishment of the means of valid cognition by way of production would be entirely fruitless. For this very reason, the Master, considering that an establishment of the means of valid cognition through this [production] alone does not serve as a factor for engagement (*pravṛtti*), resorted to a figurative designation (*upacāra*).
Therefore, once that established order has arisen, let it be conceived as the relationship between producer and produced in another way;
even so, there is no fault at all.

With the words beginning "pariccheda" (ascertainment), he demonstrates that very establishment of the result according to the Kaumārila school: "For it is held that the immediately preceding [cognition], functioning as the result of ascertainment, is the cause with respect to the knowledge that is the means of valid cognition; however, the [subsequent] result is the supreme [result]."

If it is argued that its fruit is self-cognition, this is not tenable because of the negation [of external objects]; furthermore, if the means of cognition possesses the form of the object, the consequence follows that the means and the result would have different objects.
"Of that which has functioned" means of the eye and so forth that have been engaged.
"The supreme result" is characterized by the cognitions of rejection, acquisition, and indifference.
This was further stated by Kumārila himself: because self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is negated, its status as the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is untenable.
Moreover, if the objective aspect (*viṣayākāra*) constitutes the means of valid cognition, it follows that the means of valid cognition and its fruit would have different objects.
