For the objective aspect has the external object as its domain, whereas self-awareness has the nature of the cognition itself as its object.
Thus [it is said].
He replies with the words beginning "all" (*sarva*): "Because it would entail the consequence that everything is known, that [non-apprehension] cannot be negated;
nor is there a difference in meaning here, for self-awareness (*svavid*) is also considered to have an object."
Because it would follow that no perception of objects is established for one who does not perceive [the cognition] itself, self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) cannot be denied.
Nor is it logical to claim the consequence of having different objects, since self-awareness is also accepted as being a cognition of the object— by virtue of being its effect (*kāryatva*),
and not by virtue of being identical with it.
But self-awareness [occurs] because of its identity with that [object]; thus, there is no contradiction.
With the words beginning "svātirikta" (separate from itself), Śaṅkarasvāmī provides the proof:

"The means of knowledge produces an effect separate from itself because it is an instrument, like a knife and so forth; and if [the effect] were not separate, then another fruit would be considered useless."
By the logic already stated, there is no other fruit for the axe and so forth;
nor is their status as a "kāraka" established if it is intended merely in the sense of being a producer.
When there is the intention to express [the reason] as being a "prover" (sthāpaka), there is no contradiction whatsoever;
therefore, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika) because no contradiction has been demonstrated.
"The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) performs an action distinct from itself, because it is an instrument (*kāraka*), like an axe (*vāsī*) and so forth.
This [argument] has been refuted by the passage beginning with "futility" (*vaiphalyam*).
The word "hi" (*hi*) indicates the reason.

Furthermore, the example "like an axe" (*vāsyādivat*) is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because it has been established that [the axe] possesses oneness together with the act of cutting.

As for the reason "because of being a causal agent" (*kārakatvāt*), if one intends to mean the relationship between producer and produced, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), since [the subject] is intended precisely as a sustainer (*sthāpaka*).
Even if one intends the reason to mean "being a sustainer," it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because there is no contradiction [between the reason and the opposite of the probandum].
If one intends to speak of generality, [the reason] is simply inconclusive, because no contradiction has been demonstrated.

Now, one might object: "If cognition were to possess the form of the object, then the similarity to the object (*sārūpya*) would constitute its validity; however, it is not the case that cognition arises as having an identical form and identical nature with the apprehended object, because it belongs to a different category (*jātyantara*) from the apprehended object, just like taste and color. To this, he says "grāhya... and so forth: "If cognition does not indeed arise as having a form common to the apprehended object—because it belongs to a different category—just like taste, color, and so on, [then the objection stands]."
In the investigation of the grasped and the grasper, everything has been clearly described by us in accordance with logic, as well as this other point.
[Page 402] Since we, who follow the principles of the Vijñānavāda, accept this very point, nothing is lost for us.
For whatever indistinct refutation of the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) has been stated by you,
we shall now state a clear proof for the discernment of that object of apprehension.
Grasping at the object of apprehension is attachment; its discernment is its removal.
However, [the opponent] says that the means of proof is unclear, beginning with "sarva" and so forth:
"If there were similarity in every respect, cognition would become non-cognition;
if there were similarity in some respect, everything would be a cognizer of everything."
To the extent that there is exclusion from as many heterogeneous things as there are, to that same extent there is complete similarity in every respect;
however, through exclusion from only a few objects, there is partial similarity.
If that is so, how then was the validity [of cognition] stated to consist in its similarity to the object? To this he says "But...
and so forth: "But in the theory of the real existence of external objects, the possibility of similarity must certainly be admitted; it is for this purpose that it has been elucidated."
For in the view that cognition is a manifestation, even though the mind is distinct from the object of apprehension,
there may still be a figurative experience [of it] because the reflection possesses that same form.
But for one who maintains that consciousness is not the receptacle for the conformity to the object— which is what is desired by him—
for such a person, this mode of external perception does not exist at all.
"Sa" refers to the possibility of similarity or the aspect (ākāra).
"Nirbhāsa" is the conformity with the object; that which possesses this is "nirbhāsi" (that which appears).
"From the object of apprehension" means from the external object.
"Of the reflection" means...
"Of the form of cognition";
"because of having that nature" means because of its similarity to the object.
"Figurative" means metaphorical;
"cognition" [is used here in that sense].
The word "of the object" (*arthasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
"Vessel" (*bhājana*) means the substratum (*āśraya*).

As for the misconception regarding the object (*viṣaya-vipratipatti*), it has not been refuted separately because its refutation was already demonstrated by implication: since the universal (*sāmānya*) as a real entity (*vastu-bhūta*) has been rejected, and since perception is held to have a real thing as its object, there is no object other than the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus, it is shown by the force of the argument that there is no other object.

As for those who say that this definition of perception is indeed improper— arguing that a definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is formulated so that, by being characterized by that form, one might subsequently engage with it for the sake of others, and not out of mere whim— and that in the world there exists no capacity to induce engagement or withdrawal even in that which is characterized by "freedom from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and so forth—
that is incorrect.

For it is not possible to establish the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of things according to one's own whim, such that a definition (lakṣaṇa) could be formulated otherwise; rather, experts formulate definitions by restating the very nature of things as they exist, with the desire to communicate well-known specific characteristics.
For example, the solidity of earth.
Otherwise, it would be vitiated by the defect of impossibility (*asambhavitā*).
Furthermore, there exists no other defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) for perception (*pratyakṣa*) than being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and being non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
For it must necessarily be admitted that [perception] is non-erroneous, because it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And it is free from conceptual construction because its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in a direct manner; and since it has been established that the cognition of that [particular] is non-verbal because the particular cannot be the subject of a linguistic convention (*samaya*), the experts declare that this very definition is indeed consistent with logic.
Furthermore, it is not the case that for discerning people, activity and cessation do not occur on the basis of this definition.

For instance, having determined—according to the circumstances—that the cognition of a universal such as "the lifting of a jar," the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and likewise the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and so forth (which are postulated by others to be perception), are either conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or erroneous, they turn away from their insistence on the reality of the number and other properties postulated as the objects of those cognitions.
And having determined that the very thing which is to be designated—the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as blue—is the real entity (*vastu*), people engage with it.
And how even non-conceptual perception functions as a motivator for engagement has already been explained previously.
If this is so, then it would be appropriate to define the definition [of perception] as being merely "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), and not as "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*).

For indeed, that very form which is established prior to activity is what is fit to be set forth as the definition for those desiring to act, and not something unestablished, because such a thing is equivalent to non-existence.

Furthermore, there is no ascertainment of non-erroneousness prior to the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), for those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) are not able to know the truthfulness of a cognition without the apprehension of its effect; this is because, for them, the power of an object is always to be inferred from its effect.
Furthermore, since being "in accordance with reality" (yathārthatā) is characterized by the capacity to bring about the object as it has been shown,
there is no point in determining its conformity to reality at a later time, because one would not act again on that basis.
Therefore, this objection is not to be raised.

For indeed, since even cognitions such as that of a "tuft of hair" would otherwise result in being valid, the definition would suffer from the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*); therefore, it has been stated that the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) must necessarily be made.
Furthermore, as for the claim that limited vision (*arvāgdarśitva*) is the cause for the lack of certainty prior to purposeful action (*pravṛtti*), that too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For what necessary connection is there here that would prevent those of limited vision from ever ascertaining efficacy in any instance?
For if this were so, it would follow that nothing at all could be determined by them;
consequently, their lack of consciousness would be established.

However, even young animals—whose mental tendencies (*vāsanā*) regarding the knowledge of elements have been awakened through the power of habit—are clearly observed to avoid precipices and the like and to grasp at things such as the mother's breast, having already determined, even prior to acting, "This is a means to pleasure" and "This is a means to pain."

For indeed, even for those who cultivate what is unreal— those whose minds are overwhelmed by desire, grief, fear, and so forth— the capacity of repeated practice to produce a cognition with a vivid appearance is certainly observed, provided there is no reliance on the recollection of similarity and other such factors. However, where there is no such practice, their power is to be inferred solely from its effect, and not in all cases.
By this, the ascertainment of signs such as smoke is also explained.

For even in that case, since smoke and other such effects are by nature mutually and absolutely distinct in their own-being (*svabhāva*), and because the ascertainment of that distinction arises from causes such as repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), the ascertainment of the sign is possible; therefore, there is no rejection of inference. However, it must be stated how that very first engagement occurs, since it is only when that first engagement exists that repeated practice is established.
It is said [that it is so] because of doubt.
If it is asked, "How can perception, which is the cause of doubt, possess validity in that regard? [we reply:
How, then, can even that which is the cause of certainty possess validity?
If it is argued that [the cognition] causes activity because it produces a determination (*vyavasāya*) in one who desires the object,
this is equally true for the cause of doubt as well;
for even though in that case there is a determination contrary to the form of the object as it is being perceived, nevertheless, [it does not fail to produce activity].
In that manner, perception functions as an impeller, because there is no desire for what has already been thus determined;
nor does it function as a deterrent, because it impels the seeker by being the cause of the determination of the sought-after object as it is being cognized.

Otherwise, it would follow that a person seeking an object would neither engage with nor withdraw from it upon perceiving a cause for doubt; yet this is not the case. Rather, for those seekers who do not anticipate the arising of misfortune, the very fact of engaging out of desire possesses greater force.
In this respect, there is no distinction whatsoever between this [perception] and a perception that is a cause of certainty.

However, where there is exclusively either the cause for a determination of a form contrary to the object as it is perceived, or the non-production of any determination at all, it is logical to say that it lacks validity because it does not prompt the person seeking any object to act; this applies only there and not elsewhere—enough said.
Thus concludes the examination of the definition of direct perception.
Now he states the definition of inference (anumāna), beginning with "one's own and others'":
"Inference is held to be twofold by way of the division between one's own [purpose] and that of others;
inference for oneself is the perception of the object to be inferred from a mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics."
The statement of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics is further said to be for the sake of others;
an object that possesses only one, two, or two [other] characteristics is therefore considered a fallacious logical mark (liṅgābhāsa).

Inference is of two kinds, distinguished as that for one’s own sake (*svārtha*) and that for the sake of others (*parārtha*). Among these, that which is for one’s own sake should be understood as consisting of a cognition whose object is the inferable thing, arising from a mark (*liṅga*) characterized by the three features: its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), its existence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattva*), and its total exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛtti*). That which is for the sake of others, however, should be seen as consisting of the verbal statement that reveals the aforementioned mark possessing the three features.

Now, he asks why the definition of a fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*) has not been stated, and replies with the words beginning "each one," etc. [The examples are: "Sound is eternal because it is produced," "because it is corporeal," and "because it is non-cognizable. Each of these possesses only one form, because respectively only the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), its existence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), or its exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*) is present.

In that regard, an example of [the reason] having two out of the two forms is as follows: sound is impermanent because it is visible, because it is audible, and because it is incorporeal; these lack, respectively, presence in the subject (*pakṣasattva*), presence in the similar class (*sapakṣasattva*), and mere exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*).
As it has been said:
"Sound is eternal because it is produced, because it is corporeal, and because it is non-cognizable."
"It is impermanent because it is formless and inaudible, and because it is not visible to the eye."
Thus it is said.
With the words "otherwise," etc., he raises the objection of Pātrasvāmin:
"Surely, when there is 'inexplicability otherwise' (anyathānupapannatva), the status of being a valid reason is observed."
Since even that which possesses three parts does not exist [in such a case], those characterized by the three marks are impotent.
For he said: "The reason is precisely the state of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*), and not, moreover, that which possesses the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*).
For instance, when the state of being otherwise impossible is absent, even that which has the three parts—such as 'being his son' and so forth—is not seen to be a valid reason.
Therefore, those who say 'reasons possess the three characteristics' are impotent and unattached [to the truth]."
"Otherwise" means the impossibility [of the reason] without the probandum; that is to say, the existence of the reason only where the probandum exists.

With the words "otherwise," etc., he establishes the reason (*hetu*) as having the single characteristic of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*), by demonstrating its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in detail.
That which possesses the state of being otherwise impossible is accepted as the reason;
that object has a single characteristic, or it does not have four characteristics.
That which possesses the single characteristic of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*) is "one-characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
Only that is accepted as a logical reason (*hetu*) by both worldly people and investigators, and nothing else.

However, since the triad of properties—such as its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth—is implied by this very characteristic through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), it may also be considered "four-characteristic" (*caturlakṣaṇaka*).

Nor is it the case that [the logical reason] possesses four characteristics, because it is logically correct for it to have one, two, or even three characteristics in certain instances. For "inseparability from the probandum otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) is the single characteristic; thus, it is designated as "having one characteristic. Considering inseparability from the probandum together with its presence in similar instances (*sajātīyasiddhatā*) and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*), it is "two-characteristic. Having inseparability from the probandum, its occurrence in similar instances, and its exclusion from the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*), it is "three-characteristic. However, a reason is not intended to be "three-characteristic" merely by virtue of possessing the three properties of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth.
Because it is logically untenable for that [ignorance] to serve as a cause for right knowledge.

Alternatively, it is shown by the words "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth that the designation of a single characteristic is due to its predominance and its name, "the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), and not because of [the other three] such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), since those are subordinate and thus ineffective. He says:
"Just as in the world, one who has three sons is called 'one who has an only son' because that one son is a good son; let it be seen that it is the same here."

But is it not the case that, because of the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), only a reason possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) is logically a valid probans? To this he says "avinā... and so forth: "The relationship of inseparable connection is never found in reasons possessing the three characteristics;
it is observed only in those reasons which have 'impossibility otherwise' (*anyathānupapatti*) as their sole constituent."

Those whose single constituent part is "impossibility otherwise" (anyathā-asambhava) are called such; and those which are reasons (hetu) are "reasons having impossibility otherwise as their sole constituent part" (anyathā-asambhava-eka-aṅga-hetu).
[Page 406] The passage beginning with "otherwise" concludes the very point already stated:
"Only that which possesses the property of being otherwise impossible (anyathānupapannatva) is a valid reason (hetu).
Both types of examples may be present or they may not; for they are not the cause [of the cognition of the probandum]."

Where the condition of "being impossible otherwise" (anyathānupapannatva) is present, what is the use of the three [criteria]? Where the condition of "being impossible otherwise" is present, what is the use of the three?
"The two examples" refers to those characterized by similarity and dissimilarity. "Not the cause" means:
Because the understanding of the probandum [arises] from it;

immediately after the phrase "where there is the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapannatvam yatra*), the reading of the half-verse "not otherwise possible" (*nānyathānupapanna*) must be supplied.
Demonstrating the absence of an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) in the three-fold [reason], he says: "He is dark-skinned because he is his son, just as the others seen [to be] dark-skinned.
Thus, a reason possessing the three characteristics does not function for the sake of certain determination.
In that context, by the words "there, one," and so forth, he demonstrates the efficacy of a reason possessing only a single characteristic through an elaborate illustration:
"There, a reason with a single characteristic is devoid of the two types of examples:
'Existence and non-existence are essentially real, because they are somehow perceptible.'"
Existence and non-existence are in some sense of the nature of being, because they are in some sense apprehensible. In this case,
there exist no external examples of similarity or dissimilarity, whether consisting of formal application (*prayoga*) or of objective reality (*artha*),
because the entire aggregate of categories, which consists of existence and non-existence, has been made the subject (*pakṣa*).
And because there is no other [entity] apart from that,
and because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapatti*) and lacks negative concomitance (*avyatireka*), this [reason] has only a single characteristic.
"In some way" (*kathaṃcit*).
The meaning is "by some mode [of existence], such as being an object of knowledge" (*jñeyatva*).
Regarding the phrase "because it has existence as its nature," the term "in some way" (*kathañcit*) should also be connected here.
Therefore, this is the meaning: because they are perceived in some way, they possess an existent nature in some way.
Now he states examples of the reason possessing two characteristics:
"Because it is designated as the moon, the hare-marked one is not non-moon.
This is called another reason possessing two characteristics.
"This pain of mine is caused by a falling insect," so it is determined,
because its arising is obtained through contact with that falling insect.
The eye possesses a constant, superior power regarding its function of apprehending form,
because it is that which is being employed [in the act], or else because form is seen by means of it.
In some respect, the self, pots, and so forth, are non-existent in their nature,
because they are not perceived in any way whatsoever, like the horn of a donkey.
In some way, even things such as the self and the horns of a hare exist,
because they are perceived in some manner, just like the self, a jar, and so forth.
It is understood that someone belonging to you also resides there in that house,
because the word "your father" is heard here in this dwelling.
Furthermore, it is precisely through the principle of "inexplicability otherwise" (anyathānupapatti) that words, lamps,
and other such entities are seen to possess the capacity for making things known, even though they do not reside as properties within the subject (apakṣadharmatva).
Therefore, let for us the reason characterized by this single feature be the means of comprehension, owing to its primacy;
what is the use of other superfluous factors such as "being a property of the subject" (pakṣadharma) that have been postulated?

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is either "the moon is not non-moon" or "the moon is the moon"; the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is designated as 'moon' through its well-known conventional usage in the world" or "because it is pointed out as being the moon. By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), a clod of earth or similar objects serve as the example.

Furthermore, this other [inference] with two characteristics (*dvilakṣaṇa*) is stated: "This pain of mine is caused by a falling insect, because its arising is obtained through contact with a falling insect. The meaning is: that whose arising or production is obtained (*pratilabdha*) by the touch (*sparśa*) of a falling insect (*kīṭaka*), that is, a moth (*pataṅga*).
And here, in the compound, one should understand that there is an intention to express the general [quality] within the meaning of the external member; therefore, the suffix *ṭāp* does not occur.

The eye possesses the most efficient power (*sādhakatama-śakti*) for grasping existing form (*rūpa*), because, provided it is unimpaired, it is employed as an instrument by a person acting with foresight when there is a desire to see form and so forth, or because it is observed to effect the determination of form.
By contrast, the ear and other senses are different.
"Of that" refers to form (*rūpa*).
Here, since none of the three [types of] reasons are present, there is an absence of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), and thus [the argument] possesses only two forms.
[The inference is: The self, a jar, and so forth, are in some sense non-existent by nature, because they are in some sense unperceived, like the horn of a donkey.
In this case, a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) does not exist.

Every category consisting of entities, such as a jar and so forth, has been asserted in some way to have the nature of non-existence, and non-existence itself has been presented as the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Furthermore, there is no third category apart from existence and non-existence wherein the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhya-vyavaccheda*) could occur.
The exclusion of the probans would be indicated [as follows]:
"Horns of a donkey and the like possess some degree of existence, because they are perceived in some way, just like the self or a jar.
Here too, the absence of a dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) should be applied by means of the same reasoning as before.
"This house has your father as its occupant, because the voice of your father is heard within it.
In this case, since there is no example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), it possesses only two characteristics.

Likewise, the indicative nature (*jñāpakatva*) of words, lamps, and the like is observed—just like smoke and other logical marks—even in the absence of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). For words, lamps, and so forth, are not properties residing in objects such as jars; nevertheless, an object is cognized from the word and so on. Thus, it possesses two characteristics: the absence of counter-examples (*vipakṣābhāva*) and the impossibility of being otherwise (*anyathānupapannatva*).
The cause.

He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "That" (*tad*): "Is this definition of the reason understood in a general sense, or in relation to a subject (*dharmin*) whose specific qualities one wishes to know, or else in relation to the example (*nidarśana*)?"

In that regard, the reason’s state of being inseparable from the probandum (sādhya) would have to be either by way of generality, because of the inclusion of a specific locus (dharmin), or by way of a particularity. Even if it were by way of a particularity due to the inclusion of a specific locus, there are these possible positions: it would have to be either in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) whose particularity is sought to be known, or in the subject of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharmin). Such are the alternatives that may be conceived.

Regarding that, he states the fault in the first position with the words "sāmānyena" and so forth: "If, in this way, its existence in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) were to be revealed by means of a general [reason], it would not partake in the establishment of what is intended."

For it is not the case that visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*)—merely by virtue of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) with impermanence—is observed to be a prover of impermanence when sound is the subject (*dharmin*), provided it lacks the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*); thus, the first position is untenable.
"It does not partake in the intended proof" means that it would not achieve the intended proof regarding the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "For example.
Just as the non-deviation [of sound] from visibility is understood through its general absence, yet that [absence] is not a proof for its [existence] in sound.
If it is argued that its existence in the subject (dharmin) is being made known, then in that case,
that very same threefold nature (trirūpatā) is established even in your own view.
"And that" refers to visibility;
"of that" refers to destruction;
"proof" means that which makes [the object] known.
Now, if it is argued that the aforementioned fault shall not occur, and therefore the presence of that reason in the subject (sādhyadharmin) is accepted,
then in this case, that very threefold nature (*trirūpatva*) which is our definition of a reason has also come into existence within your own system.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Otherwise... and so forth.

Since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*) are understood through the principle of "otherwise being impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*), there arises a doubt regarding its presence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) because of its existence in that locus (*dharmī*).

Positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*); negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is absence from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); "resorting" (*saṃśrayaṇa*) means resorting (*saṃśraya*), that is to say, embracing.
By the phrase "by the teachers," he demonstrates that there is no contradiction with their view;
for even by the teachers, such a definition of the concise formulation was set forth:
"The reason is a property of the subject (grāhyadharma) which is pervaded by a part of that [subject]."

Regarding the term "property of the apprehended" (*grāhyadharma*): it means the property of the apprehended subject (*sādhyadharmin*), that is to say, the property of the thesis-locus (*pakṣadharma*).
Now, with the word "atha," he states the second position:

"If this characteristic of the reason is understood from a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as residing in the subject (dharmin) itself, then there is no non-establishment [of the reason]; however, the same does not hold for the probandum (sādhya)."
For if the probandum is not apprehended, there can be no certainty regarding the reason either;
therefore, the reason is useless, since the establishment of the probandum must come from something else.
Furthermore, there is the fault of mutual dependence regarding the ascertainment of the reason and the probandum;
for if either one of the two is unestablished, the other cannot be ascertained.

Now, the very definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) is that it possesses an inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) specifically within the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). As it has been said: "Others maintain that the status of being a reason belongs to that which is not seen apart from the probandum in the example; however, by me, [the reason] is held to be that which does not exist apart from the probandum in the subject. (NN)

And because of the Śābaras' reliance on presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) and the Bhikṣus' reliance on inference (anumāna), our inference is indeed different; it is held to be like Narasiṃha [a composite being].
"Subject" (*dharmiṇi*) means in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).
The meaning is: "of that which has the nature of being impossible in the subject of the thesis without this property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).

If that is so, then from the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which the reason is established as being inseparably connected with the property to be proven in the subject of the thesis, the property to be proven itself is also established; thus, the reason is redundant.

Now, if the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established, then the reason (*hetu*) is likewise certainly not established. This is because the definition of a reason is its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitā*) with the probandum in the subject of the inference (*sādhyadharmin*). Since that inseparable connection is not established when the probandum is unestablished, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because inseparable connection is necessarily contingent upon the establishment of both [the reason and the probandum]. If it is argued that the reason is established once the probandum is established through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what is the use of the reason at that point, since the probandum has already been established?
If the ascertainment of the probandum (sādhya) were to be made on the basis of the reason (hetu), there would be the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya).
To explain how this is so, he says "of the two," and so forth.

The establishment of the probandum is preceded by the establishment of the reason, because the reason exists for that purpose; and the establishment of the reason—characterized by its inseparable connection (avinābhāva) with the probandum—is preceded by the establishment of the probandum. Thus, mutual dependence is evident.
He states the third position with the words "even in the case of an illustration" (*nidarśane 'pi*).
Even if that [pervasion] were established in the illustration, there would be no cognition of the probandum regarding the subject (*dharmin*),
for its pervasion has not been ascertained through a universal application (*sarvopasaṃhārāt*).
"In the illustration" (nidarśane) means in the example-subject (dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi), which is distinct from the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin).
"In its establishment" (tat-siddhau) means in the establishment of the reason (hetu).

This is what is meant: if it is maintained that the invariable concomitance (avinābhāvitva) of the reason exists only elsewhere— in the example-locus (dṛṣṭāntadharmin)— and not through a universal application including the thesis-locus (sādhyadharmin), then how could the realization of the probandum (sādhya) arise from the reason within the thesis-locus?
And as to how this would not be the case, he says "nahi" and so forth.

With the words "Even he who... and so forth, [the author] now refutes the examples. As for this reason stated here—"because it is somehow perceived"—there is no doubtful object for it; thus, it is fruitless.

This reason which was stated—namely, "because it is somehow perceived"—is fruitless, because there is no object that is doubtful [of its existence]. That is to say, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*). For an object that is already established is not accepted as the subject for a logical reason.
What then? It is doubtful;
for it is said that a reason is stated when there is doubt.
Like a dissimilar instance, even if [the reason] were established, it would still not be a basis for the reason, because the probandum is already established.
Now, it might be argued that even here the scope of the reason remains doubtful; therefore, he says "of an entity," and so forth:
"For the identity of an entity with its nature is ascertained by everyone;
why then is its being the probandum stated in this manner?"
Since the fact that an entity has existence as its nature (*sadātmatva*) is already determined by everyone in some way (*kathañcit*), why do you state it thus:
"an entity has existence as its nature," or "it has that nature," or "the state of having existence as its nature"?
The term "of an entity" (bhāvasya) also includes that which is merely indicative (upalakṣaṇa).
Since its nature as an existent is certainly established in some way, such as through its status as an object of cognition (prameya), the logical reason (hetu) is redundant.
Now, since this point is unestablished for the Sāṃkhyas and others, he says "sarva... and so forth, in order to prove it:
"Even in the doctrine of the identity of all things, [the self] is manifested by some clear nature through the distinction of its modifications, essence, and so on."
Even those who rely on the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) as residing in all entities,
they too rely on such qualifiers as "in reality" (tattvataḥ) and so forth.
The Sāṅkhya doctrine of the identity of all entities is indeed revealed by those very Sāṅkhyas themselves as being of that nature through some essence or intrinsic character (*svabhāva*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "due to the distinction of the nature of transformation and so forth.
Here, "the nature of transformation" means having the character of transformation.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there are included the unconfounded primordial nature (*prakṛti*) whose essence consists of pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as the selves (*puruṣa*), which are distinct from one another and from primordial nature.
As for the phrase "even those," it refers to the Mādhyamikas;
they too have resorted to the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of all entities, but with the qualification "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*), and not in every respect.
And because [the Buddha] accepted that seeing, arising,
and so forth [exist] in reality— that is,
according to reason.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [the phrase] "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (paramārthataḥ) and so forth is included.
Furthermore, this must necessarily be accepted by all: that the nature of existence is determined in some way to have the character of being real.
It must be apprehended in some way, for otherwise it cannot be established;
if conventional usage were what is to be proven, a well-known example would exist.
If it were not intended in this way, then even this reason—"because it is somehow perceived"—would not be established.
Previously, the fault of the reason known as *siddhasādhyatā* (proving what is already established) was stated;
now, however, its lack of establishment (*asiddhatā*) has been stated.

Now, if a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is being established, then in that case where a legal proceeding was previously conducted, a well-known example (*nidarśana*) is possible; thus, it must possess exactly three characteristics (*trirūpa*). Otherwise, in the absence of an example, even that legal proceeding would not be established.
He states the refutation regarding the second application [of the reason] with the words beginning "candra" (moon),
etc.: "The state of being designated as a 'moon' also persists in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*),
whether it be in some young man or in camphor, silver, and so forth."
"Māṇavaka" refers to a person.

But surely, if a three-featured reason (*trirūpa-hetu*) is possible for establishing that [the hare-marked one] is the moon, then how is it that the Teacher stated there is an absence of inference for a person in the world who asserts that the hare-marked one is not the moon, when that person speaks to establish its moonhood? He said: "Even where there is an absence of inference due to the reason being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatva*), [the subject] is set aside by a contradictory meaning established by common linguistic usage (*śabda-prasiddha*), as in: 'The hare-marked one is not the moon, because it exists. Such a case is not a valid thesis (*pakṣa*)."
Anticipating this objection with the words "by this passage," he says: "In the proof of moonhood,
there would be the fallacy of the 'uniquely inconclusive' (asādhāraṇatā) reason,
provided that [the reason] is distinct from common consensus and relies upon the actual nature of the thing."
Regarding the phrase "based on the nature of the entity":
this refers to a proof that conforms to the existence or non-existence of a real entity;
it is in this context that "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇatā) is stated, but not with respect to a reason whose definition is based on common consensus.
Because it conforms to his own desire, there is indeed a positive concomitance (anvaya).
For this person, who is mistaken and denies all conventional consensus, cannot be made to understand that "moon-ness" resides in the moon by means of a definition based on common renown.
Nor is there any other logical mark (liṅga) functioning through the force of real entities (vastubala) by which moon-ness could be established in the hare-marked one.

Since the designation of "moon" and so forth depends solely upon mere intention and is therefore not an inherent property of the object, an inference has been stated against such a person that it lacks any corroborating example (*adṛṣṭāntaka*).
As it has been said: "The state of being the moon... [p.412]
"If he does not accept [the existence of] the moon, what cognition does he desire?"—
thus, with respect to him, that [reason] is considered "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) because there is no corroborating example (adṛṣṭānta).
Thus [ends the quote].
In some versions, the reading is *acandrasādhana*; in that case, it is to be connected with the word "thus" (*iti*).

When the proponent of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣavādin) has stated the reason "the hare-marked one is not the moon because it exists," and this reason for proving it is not the moon has been put forward, the Teacher has declared the cause for the absence of inference—which is the state of being over-exclusive (asādhāraṇatā)—for the respondent (uttarapakṣavādin) who proceeds against him to prove its moonhood. This was stated in the passage beginning with "even where there is an absence of inference due to over-exclusiveness," by relying on a logical mark (liṅga) that functions through the power of real entities (vastubalapravṛtta) rather than through conventional renown (prasiddhi).
Regarding the third reason as well, he says "falling," and so forth:
"No distinction is observed in the state of being made by a falling insect,
nor in that which has arisen through contact with a falling insect."
"No distinction is observed" refers to the reason and the proposition;
that is to say, the reason is merely a part of the meaning of the proposition.

For in this case, the fact that sensation has a specific insect as its cause is intended as the probandum; and since that very same point is stated by the reason using different words, there is no distinction between the reason and the proposition.

Now, if it is thought that the qualification "of that which is falling" is not employed, and instead the general reason is stated simply as "because its arising has been obtained," then [the reason] would not be a part of the meaning of the thesis; to this he says "patataḥ" and so forth:
"For the effect of 'this which is falling' must certainly be a qualification of the reason."
Otherwise, the charge of inconclusiveness (vyabhicāritva) would unavoidably follow.
The qualification must be applied so that there may be no deviation [from the rule] due to the sensation caused by being inside an insect.
However, if the conventional designation of "being an effect" is forgotten,
it may still be established as the probandum provided it possesses the three characteristics, based on a previously established instance.

Now, if the relationship of cause and effect is being established for something whose causal status has been forgotten, then in that case the reason would possess the three characteristics (trirūpa), because well-known instances of cause and effect, such as fire and smoke, exist as corroborative examples (dṛṣṭānta).

Regarding the passage beginning with "the eye and form," he says "of the eye" and so forth: first of all, the existence of the eye as a substratum (dharmin) is unestablished; and it is not proper to provide a proof for that, because it would entail the fallacy of proving what is already unestablished (asiddhi).
And the analysis is: "the proof of that is not tenable.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "non-establishment, etc.," the fallacies of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and contradiction (*virodha*) are included.
When existence (*sattā*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), every logical reason (*hetu*) fails to transcend these three defects.

For instance, if the property belongs to existence, there is the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*); if it belongs to both, there is the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); and if it belongs to non-existence, there is the fallacy of being contradictory (*viruddha*).
As it has been said [p. 413]:
"A property of an existent cannot be unestablished; that which relies on both [existence and non-existence] is inconclusive;
and a property or an existent that is contradictory—how can that existence be proven?"
Thus [it is said].

Now, if the capacity to produce visual consciousness is being proved with respect to the eye as the locus (*dharmin*), even then, since "capacity" (*śakti*) and "existence" (*sattā*) are synonyms, proving that [capacity] would result in proving existence itself.

Furthermore, even if it were distinct [from existence], because it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it would be unestablished; thus the reason (*hetu*) would suffer from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Thus, this [reason] "because of the apprehension of form" should also be regarded as unestablished (asiddha) due to its not being a property of the subject (apakṣadharmatva).

How, then, is the existence of the sense-faculties such as the eye established even for you? To this he says "But... and so forth: "But even when visible form and the other [objects] are present, visual cognition does not arise;
therefore, it is understood that at times the object alone is not the cause."
"At some time" means during the state when the eyes are closed.

For we do not establish [the existence of the cause] by directly perceiving the eye and so forth as "this"; rather, it is observed that cognition occurs in relation to certain forms and so on while experiencing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Thus, its dependence upon other causes and its impossibility based on those [forms] alone is what is being established. Therefore, that very cognition is the subject (*dharmin*), and there is no fault such as the unestablished nature of the reason (*asiddhi*).
That which is the other cause is conventionally designated as "the eye";
however, the conventional usage of distinction is based upon the established tenet (siddhānta).

It might be argued: "Let it be that, according to the principle stated, consciousness possesses the status of a subject (dharmin); nevertheless, the reason remains twofold. To this he says: "svahetu... [and so forth].
"The sprout and so forth, which arise determined by their own causes, also exist;
and thus, in that very example, the difference [between the two types of reasons] is extremely clear."
That whose arising is determined by its own cause— that is, bound to its cause— is described as such.
This means that things like sprouts, which have an origin dependent upon their own causes and are observed to occur only occasionally, are available as examples for such cases.
And the formal argument (*prayoga*) should be constructed as follows:

Those things which occur only occasionally (*kādācitka*) in the presence of something else do not arise from that alone, but are dependent upon other causes. For example, although earth and other factors are present, sprouts and the like exhibit positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) based on the presence or absence of the seed; likewise, although color-form (*rūpa*) and other factors are present, visual cognition occurs only occasionally in the states of the eyes being closed or open. This is an "apprehension of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*) in the case of negation.
In the case of affirmation, however, it is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "kathañcit" (in some way), he says: "In some way.
Furthermore, in establishing that jars and other things have a non-existent nature in some way, the futility of the reason and its lack of establishment are seen, just as before.
Here too, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the non-existence of jars and other such things has been established in some manner.

If, on the other hand, it is not established, then this reason—namely, "because they are not perceived"—is also not established; thus, the refutation should be stated as before, just as was said regarding the reason for proving that [the self] is eternal.
Regarding the statement that "because there is no counter-example (vipakṣa), there is no example based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta)," he says: "And there is," and so forth.
"And here too, there is a very clear illustration by way of dissimilarity:
for that very nature of theirs becomes the counter-example."
In any case, even when proving the existence of a self in those things that are actually selfless,
there is the establishment of what is already accepted, the non-establishment [of the reason], and likewise the attainment of a dissimilar instance.

When it is accepted that jars and other such things possess the nature of existence (*sadātmatva*) precisely in the form in which they are perceived, then that very nature would indeed serve as a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) for them;
for the reason— namely, "the state of not being perceived"— is absent from that nature.
In this way, the same arguments regarding the establishment of what is desired and so forth apply here in the usage of the term "kathañcana" as well.
"In selfless things" means in non-entities.

"Attainment of dissimilarity" (vaidharmyāpti) means that the attainment—namely, the pervasion (vyāpti)—of the dissimilarity characterized by the absence of the probandum through the absence of the probans;
"in the same way" refers to the possibility of such dissimilarity in the case of essential nature (svabhāva).

Regarding the passage beginning with "tvadīyetyādi," he says "pitṛśabdetyādi": Even when the connection of a house to a father is established through the hearing of the word "father" (*pitṛ*), the three-featured logical reason (*trilakṣaṇahetu*) is clearly present there.
In some cases, a voice previously perceived as connected to a specific object becomes unconnected [to it];
if that [object] was not previously experienced, the reason (hetu) is difficult to establish as being unproven (asiddha).
Regarding the phrase "of that," if there were no experience elsewhere in some other location of that which is connected to the father, the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*).
With the words beginning "in which" (*yasmin*), he demonstrates that very threefold nature (*trairūpya*):
"In which [place] it was previously perceived and not perceived. This refers to that place.
In that case, either positive concomitance (anvaya) or negative concomitance (vyatireka) is clearly observed.
A word, however, makes an object known in no way whatsoever as something external;
for there is no impossibility [of its referring to something else], and thus it is an indicator of something distinct [from the external].
And when that [intention] is to be communicated, the distinction is extremely clear;
for a word is not employed unless there is the manifestation of the speaker's intention.
A lamp, however, is not an indicator [of objects] such as blue by way of being a logical mark (liṅga);
rather, it is so called because it produces that which is capable of generating cognition.
When the indicator is of the nature of a logical mark (liṅga), one considers its presence in the subject (pakṣadharma) and so forth;
otherwise, why would this not be urged against the eyes and other sense organs?
Even by way of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*) is not a prover;
because it lacks the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), a one-characterized [reason] is therefore impotent.
For those [reasons] stated as having a single form, a dual form is also observed;
and for those stated as having a dual form, a triple form exists by virtue of their being properties of the subject (pakṣadharma).

If it is argued that [the object] is implied solely by the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), we say no; for in the case of sound and so forth, even though [impermanence] is desired, this [property of being visible] does not exist. Furthermore, in the case of visibility, that [impossibility otherwise] is absent.

The fact that a word is otherwise inexplicable in dependence upon an external object is unestablished; therefore, with respect to such an object, it lacks the character of a logical mark (*liṅga*), because its occurrence depends solely on [the speaker's] intention. Now, if it is said to depend on an object existing within the intellect, then it certainly possesses the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) just like smoke. For since a word is not employed when the desire to speak is absent, it is accepted as an indicator of the fire—due to being its effect—just like smoke, but not by way of being a denoter (*vācaka*).
A lamp, however, is not accepted as an indicator by way of a logical mark, unlike smoke.

What then? It is established as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) by way of producing a jar or the like that is capable of generating cognition, but not as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, it is entirely improper to consider such a thing—which has become a logical mark—as possessing the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth. Otherwise, one would have to urge that even the eyes and other sense organs possess the property of being features of the subject and so on.
The phrase "otherwise" and so forth is a summary of the subject matter under discussion.

Since the property of being visible (*akṣuṣatva*), although invariably concomitant with impermanence, does not prove that impermanence in sound, and since the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) must necessarily be relied upon in all cases, therefore, for those reasons stated as having only one characteristic, the possession of two characteristics is necessary; and for those stated as having two characteristics, the possession of three characteristics is necessary—precisely because of this requirement of *pakṣadharmatva*, reasons possessing only a single characteristic are indeed impotent (*klība*).

Nor should it be said that "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) exists even without the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), for you yourself have stated: "In the case of entities such as sound, even in the absence of being a feature of the subject, the capacity to indicate [the probandum] is observed solely through inexplicability otherwise.

Furthermore, since visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) is inexplicable otherwise than impermanence, yet it does not possess the status of a feature of the subject, there is indeed an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding what was said—that "he is dark-skinned because he is his son"—and that this [reason] does not lead to certainty even though it possesses the three characteristics, the author says here: "tatputratvādihetūnām...

etc. Because the reasons such as "being his son" have a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*), the presence of the three characteristics is not established, due to the lack of contradiction with dissimilar instances (*vijātīyāvirodhataḥ*).

And since there is no contradiction in the fact that his son will exist yet not be dark-skinned, this example lacks the three characteristics because its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful; thus, it is an unestablished (*asiddha*) example.
It might be argued: "There is indeed a contradiction;
for if the effect were to differ while the cause remains non-different, it would be causeless. To this he says, "Karma," and so forth:
"In every respect, due to the specific differences in the causes such as karma, food, and so on..."
For even in the case of his being that person's son, a change [in status] is indeed possible.

This [non-perception] is neither an essential nature, nor an effect, nor indeed the non-perception of a perceptible object; and for anything other than these, there is no non-deviation [from the object].

Since it is possible for there to be a change—such as being fair-skinned and so forth—due to specific actions like merit and the like, or due to differences in the conditions of food such as hot or cold, how could there be a contradiction? For the difference in causes is established.

Furthermore, the argument "because he is his son" is not an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) in the way that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is; for there is no other reality to "being produced" apart from impermanence. But if that is so, there is likewise no other essence to "being his son," since the designation "his son" applies to one who consists of the five aggregates of appropriation (*pañcopādānaskandha*) in relation to someone else, and not to [the property of] dark complexion. Nor is it an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
Because the relationship of cause and effect is not established;
nor is it non-perception, since its object is positive;
and because there is no contradiction, the absence of colors other than black is not established.

And there is no inferential mark (liṅga) distinct from this, because otherwise there would be an absence of a necessary connection (pratibandha). Nor can there be the capacity to indicate [the probandum] without a necessary connection, for that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Therefore, this is neither a logical reason (hetu), nor does it possess the three characteristics; how, then, could there be non-deviation (avyabhicāra)?
The non-perception of the perceptible is non-apprehension of that which has met the conditions for apprehension.
With the words "But surely... and so forth, he states the fault of the definition being too narrow:
"But surely non-deviation is observed in other cases as well, such as the blooming of night-lotuses and the rising of the ocean."
The rising of the moon is observed as the indicative mark (liṅga) of the presence of sunlight;
likewise, the existence of shadow is recognized in the regions beyond the light.
In the darkness, when a firebrand is seen, smoke is perceived from a distance;
likewise, the rising of the Kṛttikās leads to the conceptualization of the proximity of Rohiṇī.
Just as there is an inference of the blooming of night-lotuses and the swelling of the ocean from the rising of the moon;

by the inclusion of the term "and so forth," [there is the inference] of the blooming of day-lotuses from the rising of the sun, and the inference of shadow on the far side of mountains and such from the presence of sunlight; likewise, having seen from afar in the darkness a firebrand—a piece of wood half-burnt—there is the perception of smoke; similarly, from the rising of the Kṛttikā constellation, the proximity of the Rohiṇī constellation is perceived, because it is well known that the constellations rise in the very order they are recited, beginning with Aśvinī.
And since this entire [set of reasons] is not included within the three types of reasons, how can it be said that "there is no non-deviation for anything other than those"?
To this, he states the following reply, beginning with "tadatra" and so forth:
"In this case, such properties of the reason are considered to be inferred;
all those others, such as cognition and so on, have arisen at that same time."
The establishment of a cause from its effect occurs in this manner; otherwise, if such a relationship were impossible, there would be no way to understand anything at all.
For the reason that those [phenomena] such as awakening and the blooming of night-lotuses have arisen—that is, been produced—what are their characteristics?

They are simultaneous with them; that is, they are of the same time as the rising of the moon, the heat, and the torch. Such [phenomena] are considered to be inferred from the specific property of the cause, which is the nature of the cause itself.

This is what is meant: whatever cause produces the rising of the moon and so forth, which arise at the same time as the blooming of the night-lotuses (*kumuda*) and other phenomena, that very same cause functions as the auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) for the blooming of the night-lotuses and the like. Thus, those [causes] such as the rising of the moon, by inferring their own cause which has become thus, indirectly infer the objects—the blooming of the night-lotuses and so forth—which exist at the same time; they do not infer them directly. Therefore, this [type of inference] is included within the category of the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*) itself.

This must necessarily be understood: if, moreover, [signs] were to cause [an object] to be known solely through the absence of a connection, then they would cause anything whatsoever to be known, since there is no distinction in the state of being unconnected.
Therefore, even in this case, a connection must be stated;
and that [connection] exists precisely as characterized by the aforementioned nature of cause and effect.
If that is so, what is the obstacle to the rising of Rohiṇī when its rising has already been brought about? To this he says, "prabhañjana" and so forth:
"And a particular wind is the cause of the rising of Kṛttikā;
for that very same [wind], through its continuity, is the cause of the proximity of Rohiṇī."
And because the cognition of the causal property is that very cognition, it is considered to be the cognition of that;
this cognition exists independently, and there is no other [cognition] here besides it.
The wind is a disperser;
here too, because it depends on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is an inference of the property of the cause.
As it has been said:
The cognition of the existence of the intrinsic nature and so forth [of the effect] depends on a single causal complex;
this occurs through the inference of the properties of the cause, just as [the presence of] modifications in the fuel is inferred from smoke.
Thus it is said.

Now, one might object that the movement of the original object (bimba) from its reflection (pratibimba) is not included anywhere because the reflection is not a real entity; therefore, the definition is underinclusive. Anticipating this, he says: "And from the mark," and so forth.
And from the mark known as the reflection, an inference proceeds which is rightly directed toward its source; in that case, it is distinct from that which arises from a mark consisting of an effect.
With the words "simultaneously in one place" and so forth, he anticipates the objection of the opponent:
"Since two things cannot exist together in one place, there is no reflection of a real object;
therefore, how can its being an effect be logically justified if it were ultimately real?"
The reason for its being non-substantial is that two things cannot exist together in one place.

In whichever location the form of the mirror is seen, in that very same location the reflection is seen; yet, in a single location, there can be no coexistence of two forms because they possess resistance (*sapratighatvāt*). Therefore, the existence of two forms together in one place is impossible.
Consequently, this is an illusion.
Alternatively, it is because two things cannot exist together in one place.
Which two?
The reflection of the moon is seen on the surface of a mirror, just as water is seen in a well.
In one place there is a mirror surface, and in that very same place, internally, the reflection of the moon is seen like water in a well.
Furthermore, how is it that something arising in one location is perceived in another?
Therefore, there is no such thing as a reflection that exists as a real entity at all.
However, such is the power of its generality, and thus is that vision;
for the specific distinctions of the powers of phenomena are indeed inconceivable.
He refutes this with the verse beginning with "mūrta" and so forth:
"Even though this reflected image, being material, lacks substantial reality,
how could the consciousness appearing as that reflection be without substance?"
And in this context, that very [consciousness] is intended as the effect and the sign;
for, through its sovereignty over the objective image, it proceeds without any external support.
In this context, it is precisely such knowledge that is intended as the effect serving as the logical mark (liṅga), and not an external object known as a reflection.

How is it that the statement of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) is called "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*), when others have also proclaimed the statements of the thesis (*pakṣa*), conclusion (*nigamana*), and application (*upanaya*) to be inference for the sake of others?
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "The statement of the thesis," and so forth.
Even the statements of the thesis and the other members are described by others as being for the sake of others.
Because it does not constitute a member of the proof, the thesis is useless.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "asādhana" (not a means of proof).

"Siddhi" (establishment) is the means of proof (*sādhana*), which is to say, the comprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*); its "limb" (*aṅga*) is the cause thereof. The negation of that is "not being a limb of the means of proof" (*asādhana-aṅgabhūtatva*).
Therefore, the meaning is that because it is not a limb of the means of proof, it is useless and should not be employed.
If it were explained as "not being an instrument" and "not being a cause," it would constitute a part of the meaning of the proposition itself.
How is it not a member of the proof? He says: "Because of the lack of connection," and so forth.
Because there is no connection, it cannot directly establish the intended object;
nor is it appropriate [to do so] indirectly, because it does not indicate what is relevant.

If this [statement] is accepted as a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) because it possesses the status of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), due to its demonstrating the subject matter consisting of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*);
But surely there is a deviation here due to statements such as "permission granted," and that [statement] is fruitless where the object is already presented.
However, the property of indicating that which is unattached belongs to the probandum itself because it is precisely that which is being expressed.

What is meant is this: since there is no relationship between words and their objects, [the word] is not employed directly; nor is it employed indirectly, like the statement of a logical reason (*hetu*), because it does not indicate that which is attached.
As it has been said:
Therefore, they made the statement of the thesis (pakṣavacana) for the purpose of communicating one's intention;
since it merely brings about the arising of doubt, it is not a direct means of proof (sādhana).
"By the mere statement of the probandum itself, it is not even sufficient [to indicate the subject] through a traditional sequence.

Thus some think that, for the purpose of indicating the object of both the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*), the proposition (*pratijñā*) should be employed even though it is not a formal member (*anavayava*) [of the syllogism], just like the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) member.

Because of the statement, "Since the remaining two forms are seen, they are demonstrated by that," the example (dṛṣṭānta) is employed as a separate, non-componential element solely for the purpose of demonstrating the two forms distinct from the property of the subject (pakṣadharma). In response to those [who hold this view], he says "the example," and so forth.
The statement of permission is precisely "do this," [meaning] "prove that sound is impermanent.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), statements of command and entreaty are included.

Even for such a statement, there would be an instruction for the purpose of indicating its formal employment; for without these as well, the engagement in a proof could not possibly occur out of nowhere.

"It is fruitless" means that the object to be proven is understood even without it; for instance, when only this much is stated— "Whatever is produced is impermanent, and sound is produced"— the cognition "Sound is impermanent" arises even in the absence of the formal statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
If there is a formal determination of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and so forth, how can there be no employment of the thesis (*pakṣa*)?
For this reason, even the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) does not exist, since its basis is dependent upon that [thesis].

In that case, how is the formal distinction between the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and so forth established? For it is said that a "similar instance" is an object that is similar by virtue of the general property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), while the absence of that [property] is established as the "dissimilar instance" (*asapakṣa*).

For if there were no statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), then the three characteristics (*trairūpya*)—which depend upon it and are based upon its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—would not exist either; thus, everything would be incomplete and disordered.
He replies with the words beginning "no," etc.:
"In the statement of the proof, there is no conceptual differentiation such as 'similar instances' (sapakṣa) and so forth."
In the treatise, however, they are thus divided for the sake of conventional usage.

For instance, even a soldier or similar person who has not yet mastered the technical usage of terms such as "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) and so forth, when told merely that "where there is smoke, there is fire, and here there is smoke," understands the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and indeed realizes the presence of fire, even without the technical application of terms like *sapakṣa*. Therefore, at the time of the formal proof (*sādhana*), there is no systematic arrangement of *sapakṣa* and the rest.
To the question, "Where then does the usage of *sapakṣa* and so forth occur? he replies: "But in the treatise (*śāstra*)."

Alternatively, he demonstrates that even at the time of stating the proof (*sādhana*), the establishment of that [distinction] is not contradictory, by means of the passage beginning with "prakṛta" (the subject at hand): "Or rather, even that [establishment] is not contradictory if it relies upon the subject at hand; for the proponent states the proof for the opponent right at the outset."

Although there is no employment of the thesis (*pratijñā*) at the time of stating the proof (*sādhana*), nevertheless, that formal arrangement being made by relying upon the subject under discussion—the property-bearer to be proven—is not at all contradictory.

Nor should it be said that "at the time of the proof, the subject under discussion does not exist," because it is not the case that the proponent states the proof at an improper time or without occasion, even for an opponent who maintains that the thesis must be explicitly stated.

Granted that the subject (*dharmin*) whose specific property is to be known is the one under discussion, nevertheless, he explains how that formulation being made must be carried out by relying on the subject under discussion, with the words "jijñāsita" (to be known).
For, because it exists in that which has its specific property sought to be known, there is the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*).
The similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is so called because of its similarity to that [subject], and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) because of the absence of that [property] therein.
This is easily understood.

The definition of the *upanaya* (application) is: "The application is the subsumption [of the instance] under the subject of proof as being 'so' (*tathā*) or 'not so' (*na tathā*), depending on the example.

Regarding this, the venerable teacher Dignāga established that the statement of the *upanaya* is not a means of proof (*sādhana*), because it merely illuminates the meaning of the reason already stated, just like a second statement of the reason. To refute this reason, Bhāvivikta and others said: "Indeed, the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is not illuminated by the statement of the reason that follows immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*), because that [second statement] expresses only the cause [of the inference]."
"Sound is impermanent because it is produced. Now, as to whether that quality of being produced exists or does not exist in sound, its existence is understood through the application (*upanaya*).

Alternatively, the application serves for the purpose of reflection: previously, by the statement of the reason (*hetu*), "being produced" was indicated in sound in a general sense; therefore, because the inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with the probandum has been demonstrated in the example, the reflection of "being produced" in the specific case of sound is shown by the application, namely: "and so is sound produced."
Therefore, because it clarifies a specific distinction, there is no tautology.
To this, he says: "The proposition," and so forth.
Furthermore, since the reason has not been stated and the proposition itself has not been expressed,
the statement of the application (upanaya) cannot be made for the purpose of establishing its existence.
Since the mere existence [of the probans] was stated previously and its pervasion is revealed afterwards, the intended object is fully established; thus, the reflected image is useless.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of establishing existence," the remainder [of the sentence] is "of the reason, with respect to the subject.

This is the meaning here: since the employment of a formal proposition has been refuted by the aforementioned method, there is no such thing as stating a cause—such as "being produced" and so forth—immediately following it.

Consequently, the statement of the application (*upanaya*) preceded by the statement of the reason (*kāraṇa*) should not be made at all. If, on the other hand, the statement of the application is made for the purpose of establishing the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), then some other result of the statement of the reason must be specified.
To this, it might be argued that the very demonstration of its being a cause is that result.
That is not so.
What is the purpose of demonstrating [the reason] by that very [property of being a property of the subject], since it has already been shown that the probandum is established even otherwise?
Therefore, no result other than the demonstration of the property of being a property of the subject can be stated for the statement of the reason.

In that case, since the property of the reason residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) has already been established by that very statement of the reason at the outset, the application (*upanaya*) employed to establish it again clearly reveals itself as a mere tautology; how, then, could there be any lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) for the reason?

The reflection [of the reason] is also entirely useless; for, since the mere property of the subject (pakṣadharma) has already been stated by the statement of the reason, and its pervasion (vyāpti) by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) has been declared, the intended object is fully established. Thus, what is being said most clearly constitutes a redundancy; so how could there be any lack of proof (asiddhatā) regarding the reason here as well?
In this context, the definition of the conclusion (*nigamana*) is: "The restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the instruction of the reason (*hetu*).

In such cases as "therefore, [sound] is impermanent," the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) indicates the efficacy of the reason as established by the example; the subsequent restatement of the meaning of the proposition is the conclusion.
It is called a "conclusion" because by means of it the proposition, reason, example, and application are brought together (*nigamyante*), unified in a single purpose, and connected.

In this regard, there is not even the application of a formal proposition (*pratijñā*), much less a conclusion (*nigamana*) consisting of its restatement; therefore, the conclusion is not a member of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*). Concerning this, the venerable teacher Ācārya Diṅnāga stated that the conclusion is not a means of proof precisely because it is a mere repetition. To this, Uddyotakara and others reply: "There is no redundancy here, because the proposition is the statement of what is to be proven (*sādhya*), whereas the conclusion is the statement of what has been proven (*siddha*)."
Furthermore, there is no establishment [of the proof] without the conclusion (*nigamana*).

For, without it, even if the other members are stated, the doubt as to whether "sound is impermanent" does not cease. Therefore, the conclusion must be stated separately for the purpose of removing that doubt.
To this, he says: "The three-fold," and so forth.
Since the proof is established by the very power of the instruction on the three-fold reason, there is no suspicion of the contrary; therefore, the conclusion is redundant.

When "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), which has been shown to be invariably concomitant with "impermanence," is ascertained in the subject (*dharmin*) "sound," how can there be any suspicion of its opposite, "permanence"? For it is not reasonable for a person of sound mind to entertain a doubt about coldness regarding a fire whose nature is certain and surrounded by a mass of blazing flames. Nor does that suspicion cease merely through a statement of conclusion (*nigamana*) devoid of logical justification.

But Aviddhakarṇa says: "Since a single meaning is not established by scattered statements, the conclusion (nigamana) must be stated separately for the sake of establishing the connection. To this, he [the author] replies with the words "by means of connected [statements]."
A single meaning is established only by means of interconnected statements;
therefore, the conclusion need not be stated separately for the sake of establishing the connection.
