When the relationship between the reason and the probandum—characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from it (*tadutpatti*)—has been established, then by means of the objects [indicated], the statements regarding the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), being themselves related, convey a single object according to the intended purpose through their own force (*sāmarthyāt*).

Even though these statements are scattered, they are nevertheless related through the synthesis of a single object; therefore, a separate conclusion (*nigamana*) need not be stated for the sake of establishing that relationship.
Some indeed declare that inference is of two kinds,
distinguished by being "perceived through particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*) and "perceived through generalities" (*sāmānyaparidṛṣṭa*).
"Some" refers to Kumārila and others; for they describe inference as being of two kinds: that based on specific observation (viśeṣatodṛṣṭa) and that based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).
Regarding that, he asks what constitutes the "inference from the observation of particulars" (*viśeṣatodṛṣṭa*) and says:

"The relationship between which two very specific [particulars] has been perceived by direct perception, and with respect to which a cognition has been formed based on particulars such as cow-dung fuel and a particular location... etc.
When that very person, staying in that same place, goes [to the fire] at another time and perceives that fire again and again based on his previous cognition;
Its status as a means of valid cognition arises from the awakening to an object whose existence was previously doubted;
and this is what is called "perception of particulars" (viśeṣadṛṣṭa), as recorded by Vindhyavāsin.
However, when it must be stated that fire and smoke are distinct, in the case of inference based on generality (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), the sun is cited as a definitive example of "the goer" (*gantṛ*).

This is the meaning: previously, having perceived a particular fire and a particular smoke in a certain specific location by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), when one has subsequently gone far away and, upon seeing that same particular smoke again and again, infers that very same fire previously apprehended—this is inference through the observation of particulars (*tadviśeṣatodṛṣṭam anumānam*), because its object is a particularity previously grasped through direct perception.

Nor is it invalid on the grounds of apprehending what has already been apprehended, because there exists an additional [cognitive] function, namely the removal of doubt as to whether the fire remains or has ceased;
this is the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*).
Now, the meaning of the individual parts is stated: "the connection perceived through direct perception" (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasaṃbandha*).
What is the relationship [between perception and inference]?

To this it is replied by Śabarasvāmin that the definition of inference has been stated: "Inference is the cognition of one part [of an object] not present to the senses, based on the observation of one part of a known relationship.

That is of two kinds: that based on a relationship perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*) and that based on a relationship observed through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasambandha*).
Inference based on perceived connection (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*) is, for example, the cognition of the form of fire from seeing the form of smoke.
Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is, for example, the recollection of the sun’s motion after perceiving Devadatta’s arrival at another location preceded by his movement.
Regarding this, Kumārila, wishing to explain this inference based on perceived connection, says "pratyakṣa... and so forth.

"In perception" (pratyakṣe) means "inference [based on] that which has been seen as related through perception"—this is the connection. For in the preceding verse, it was the subject under discussion that "it is thus declared. The phrase "of which two" refers to these two.

Regarding those two specific instances of fire and smoke that have become the objects [of inference], a person has formed and produced the cognition that "these two, fire and smoke, originate from cow-dung fuel," and likewise has formed the mental conception of a specific location such as a mountain, thinking, "these two, fire and smoke, are situated in this specific location such as a mountain.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those two whose fuel is cow-dung are *gomayendhanau*"; "those two whose location is that [specific place] are *taddeśau*"; and thus, "those which are both *gomayendhana* and *taddeśa*" is the full analysis (*vigraha*).

Those two specific [qualities] are the starting point for all other specific fires, such as those found in forests of *sarja*, *sarala*, and *sallakī* trees; these include the fuel of cow-dung, the particularity of the location, and so forth.
The compound "matir" (cognition) is formed by the application of the rule for the locative case (*saptamī-yoga-vibhāga*).

When a cognizer has produced or generated such perceptual cognition, he subsequently perceives that very same fire through that very same mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke, while situated in that same place.
The connection is with the words "again and again.

In that case, the meaning is that the validity of that cognition—distinct from the previous cognition which was perceptual in nature—is its status as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Alternatively, the connection is that it cognizes that very same fire by means of the previous cognition as its cause.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that whose existence is being doubted" refers to something like, "Is the fire still there, or has it ceased? "That which is such" means that very object; thus, the analysis is "the cognition of that which is such. And this is what was stated by Vindhyavāsin: "Inference based on a relationship perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*) is inference based on the particular (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭam*). He states the inference based on the general (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*) with the words "fire, smoke," and so forth.

In this regard, the following objection arises: "When an inference is made based on the commonality of properties between one fire and another smoke, then there certainly exists an 'inference from what is observed in general' (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) regarding fire and smoke; why then did the author of the *Bhāṣya* set aside fire and smoke—which are proximate because they revolve within the mind—and instead cite the sun as the example for *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*? Anticipating this objection, Kumārila, explaining the intention of the *Bhāṣyakāra*, says: "Regarding another fire and another smoke... [etc.].

Regarding inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*), when fire and smoke were to be cited as examples, the author of the *Bhāṣya* instead provided the example of the sun. This was because the movement of the sun is never perceived at any time; thus, he did so intending to show that in the case of the sun's movement, only inference based on general observation is possible, and not inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣatodṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the sun alone is stated as the example in order to demonstrate a distinct domain of application, and it is not because there is an absence of inference based on general observation in the case of fire and smoke. //1443–1444//
With the words "In this regard," etc., he states the refutation:
"In this case, because the all-pervasive momentary destruction has been established,
there is no possibility for that very same previous inference [to function]."
If that oneness is imagined through the intention of expressing the unity of the continuum,
it has no stability whatsoever, nor does its substantiality possess any reality.
Regarding the term "pervasive" (*vyāpin*):
it refers to that which pervades all things, such as fire, smoke, and so forth.
If it is argued that there is unity because of the oneness of the continuum (*prabandha*) even though momentariness exists, he replies: "it is conceptualized" (*kalpitam*).
In that case, the unity [of the object] would be merely imagined and not ultimate; for from the perspective of ultimate reality, nothing whatsoever has any established existence.

Consequently, it would be untenable to say "by that very [cognition] situated in that same place. Furthermore, that which is imagined lacks the nature of a real entity; therefore, the statement "because of the cognition of an object whose existence is being doubted" would be incoherent.

Furthermore, it might be argued that the statement regarding "perception of particulars" (viśeṣato dṛṣṭa) was made by relying on a unity superimposed by conceptual construction (kalpanāsamāropita), and not on a real one. To this, he says "And not," and so forth:
"Nor do you admit that cognition is without an object;
and if its object were merely conceptualized, it would clearly be objectless."

It might be argued: "Even though the individual (vyakti) is perishable, the universal (jāti) remains imperishable; therefore, there will be a real unity, and it will not be the case that [the cognition] lacks an object. To this, he says "vyaktirūpa" and so forth: "Even upon the destruction of the form of the individual, the generic configuration (ākṛti) certainly persists for those two [the individual and the universal], provided that, because of the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga), that [configuration] also does not necessarily exist as a permanent entity."
For what reason have you stated this restrictive rule: "The relationship [of concomitance] has been perceived by direct perception only between two specific [individuals]"?

Having once perceived [the object] by means of inference, why is a subsequent inference regarding that very same object not accepted as a valid means of knowledge? For what distinction is there from the former?
If it is argued that this [subsequent cognition] is not a means of valid cognition because it apprehends an object already cognized—
just like a memory— then why is it not seen that the same applies equally to the former [cognition]?
If it is argued that there is a superiority [of inference] there because it removes doubt that has arisen in the interim,
why is this not equally true here as well?

Therefore, this perception of a generality, which dispels doubts as to whether something exists or does not exist, is itself free from further expectancy when it is recognized as "that very same thing."
"Form" (*ākṛti*) means "universal" (*jāti*). The word "if" (*yadi*) indicates an admission [of the opponent's position].

Since the opponent maintains that the universal and the individual are identical, how could the persistence of the universal be possible upon the destruction of the individual? Otherwise, because their conditions of acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) would be distinct, one would have to admit an absolute difference between the two. [The term] "existence" (*bhāva*)... [is used].
This is merely a concessionary argument (*abhyupagamavāda*).
Since the universal (*jāti*) has already been refuted in detail, how can it possibly exist? Even if it were to exist, even if it possessed existence (*sattva*), [it would still be untenable].
For that [perception] as well, momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) follows,
because momentary destruction has been established as being all-pervasive.

Furthermore, when one determines by means of inference that very same fire once again from that very same mark (liṅga), why then is that not described as "seen through particularity" (viśeṣato dṛṣṭa)?
If it is argued that the qualification "seen through direct perception" is intended because [the means of knowledge] apprehends an object already apprehended,
we say no.
That [removal of doubt] is equal even in the case of what is seen through direct perception.
If it is argued that there is an additional element in what is seen through direct perception— namely, the removal of doubt concerning the intervening state—
that additional element is equally present in what is seen through inference.

Therefore, in all cases, the inference regarding entities that perish moment by moment is only "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa), not what is called "inference based on specific observation" (viśeṣato-dṛṣṭa).
Some of evil vision, however, while expressing their own intention through these words, claim that inference is not a valid means of knowledge.
"Some" refers to the followers of Bṛhaspati and others. "By these" refers to [the following verses].

By such statements as "inference is not a valid means of knowledge," he points out a contradiction with his own words (*svavacanavirodha*). For, by speaking to another in order to communicate one's own intention—thinking that the speaker's intent is understood from the mark of speech—it is demonstrated that inference possesses validity; yet, by saying that it is not a valid means of knowledge, that very same thing is denied. Thus, there is a mutual contradiction.
And this refutation will be made explicit later on.
Because it is preceded by a logical mark possessing the three characteristics, inference for oneself is not tenable as a means of valid cognition;
for it is produced by that which destroys what is desired, just like false knowledge.

Even in the case of inference based on existence, the triple-characteristic (*trairūpya*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) does not exist as a cause of inferential cognition, just as the double-characteristic (*dvairūpya*) [of the probandum] does not; therefore, there is no inference.
Since contradiction with inference and the proof of contradictory [reasons] are possible in all cases, as well as the case of the non-deviantly contradictory (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

In this regard, the Cārvākas first establish [their position] as follows: inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is preceded by a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), just like false cognition.

Furthermore, [the argument] "the eyes and other organs are for the sake of another (*parārtha*), because they are composite (*saṅghātatva*), like the parts of a bed or a seat," is indeed intended to subvert [the opponent's] desired conclusion; for this [inference] is produced from a three-featured mark and is thus a false cognition.
Moreover, the possession of the three features is not the cause of inferential knowledge, because it exists even in cases that are not inference, just as the possession of two features does.
Moreover, in every proof, there is the possibility of contradiction by inference (*anumānavirodha*).

For example: "The property intended to be proven is not a qualification of the subject (*dharmin*), because it is a part of this [subject-object] aggregate, just like the essential nature of the subject.
By this [argument], all inference is rendered non-inferential.

Furthermore, in every inference that is formulated, there is the possibility of "contradictions regarding specific qualities" (*viśeṣaviruddha*). For example, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," someone might raise a contradiction regarding a specific quality:
"Just as this reason establishes impermanence, so too does it establish the absence of being a quality of space," and so forth.
Moreover, in every case, a "non-deviating contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) is possible.

For example, when it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," someone might state a non-deviant contradictory [reason]: "Sound is permanent because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*).
Such elaborations of examples are to be seen in the *Tattvaṭīkā*.
Likewise, Bhartṛhari said:
"Since the powers of things vary according to differences in state, place, and time,
the establishment of the nature of entities through inference is exceedingly difficult."
Even though its power is known, that power is obstructed with respect to this or that specific causal efficacy when it comes into contact with a particular substance.
Even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skilled inferents may be established in an entirely different way by those who are more proficient.
The potencies of entities differ according to differences in state, place, and time;

therefore, it is not possible to determine their existence through inference. Indeed, it cannot be established by inference that "Devadatta is incapable of carrying a load, because he is Devadatta, like Devadatta in his childhood state."
For in this case, there is a deviation [from the rule], since a difference in potency is possible due to a difference in state (*avasthā*).

Likewise, a difference in taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation (*rasa-vīrya-vipāka*) is observed among the *āmalakī*, *kharjūra*, and other fruits according to the difference in location; yet one cannot establish that "all *āmalakī* fruits are astringent," on the grounds that they are like the *āmalakī* currently being experienced.

Similarly, a difference such as coldness or heat is possible in the case of well-water and the like according to the difference in time; therefore, it is impossible to determine with certainty that "all waters are cold."
"Thus, etc.
The genitive case in "of states, places, and times" (*avasthā-deśa-kālānām*) is used in relation to the word "due to their difference" (*bhedāt*).
The genitive in "of entities" (*bhāvānām*) is used in relation to common usage (*prasiddhi*).

Likewise, the capacity for burning that belongs to fire—which is ascertained in respect to grass and the like—is obstructed when it encounters a mass of clouds; yet one cannot infer in that very case that "the mass of clouds is burned by fire because it is earthy, like grass.
Similarly, it is undesirable that an object established in one way by one person should be established in another way by another who is more proficient.
Inference for the sake of others, however, is not a means of valid cognition from the perspective of the speaker;
because it is a restatement, he does not himself apprehend the object through it.
Even with respect to the listener, this [teaching] is appropriate as being for his own benefit;
for what difference is there between a cognition rooted in hearing and one rooted in seeing?
Speech is not an inference for another with respect to the listener,
because it is a cause of cognition within the listener’s own mental continuum and because it is indicative [of the object].
Just as a sense faculty does not directly manifest that which is to be inferred,
so too [inference] is not that [direct manifestation], because it requires knowledge of the relationship of inseparable connection (avinābhāva).
Now, if it is argued that being for the sake of another (parārthatva) depends upon the exclusion of others (paravyāvṛtti),
that too is incorrect, because it would follow that even [a term] whose own referent is its object would be for the sake of another.
Another, however, says: inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) from the perspective of the speaker;

but from the perspective of the listener, it is indeed for one's own sake (*svārtha*). For what difference is there between one who understands that object through the door of sight and one who does so through the door of hearing?
Just as when the visual faculty is active, there is no designation of it as being "for the sake of another," so too, let there be no such designation when the auditory faculty is active.
"Vision" (darśana) refers to the visual faculty (cakṣurindriya),
based on the derivation that "it is by means of this that one sees.
"Consciousness" (saṃvit) [is as follows]:

Just as [the reason] applies to cognition, so too speech is not a *parārthānumāna* (inference for others) with respect to the listener, because it is either the cause of the cognition occurring in the listener's continuum or because it is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), like a sense faculty (*indriya*).
The two reasons are indicated by a copulative compound (*dvandva*): "being the cause of the cognition in the listener's continuum" and "being an indicator."
The phrase "just as in the case of the sense faculty" is an indication of an example.

This is another formal argument: speech is not an inference for others (parārthānumāna) with respect to the listener, because it does not directly reveal the object of inference, just like the knowledge of the relationship of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva). Therefore [it is not an inference for others].
Because it does not directly manifest the object of inference (*anumeya*).

Since it does not directly manifest the object of inference, therefore, with respect to the auditory organ, speech lacks validity, just like the cognition of the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). This is the meaning of the sentence.

"Inseparable connection" refers to the relation between the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*); the analysis of the compound is: "the cognition of that mark (*liṅga*) which has that very [relation] with the probandum as its connection."
Now, it might be argued that it is called "for the sake of another" (parārtha) with reference to the activity of another.

Even so, this is incorrect, because it would follow that even what is for one's own sake (svārtha) would be for the sake of another, since "otherness" (paratva) is relative, like the term "living abroad" (pārācāra).

He responds with the verse beginning "trirūpaliṅga" (the three-fold mark): "Is it not the case that having the three-fold mark as its antecedent is the definition of being concordant? And since validity has that as its definition, why is that [validity] denied by this [argument]?"

Regarding that, in the first application, he states the contradiction of the reason "because it is preceded by a mark possessing the three characteristics" with the words "characterized by correspondence. This is because correspondence is defined by this [reason]. Since the cognition produced from a mark possessing the three characteristics is indirectly connected to the real object, it is non-contradictory, just like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As it has been said:
"In this way, because the cognitions of the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) are indirectly connected to the real entity,
they are non-deceptive even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [entity]."
Thus [it is said]:
"and its characteristic" means the characteristic of non-contradiction.
As it has been said: "Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge.
For even in the case of perception, a proponent of valid cognition cannot point out any other basis for the establishment of its validity than non-contradiction.

And since that [non-contradiction] exists in what is produced by a three-featured logical mark (liṅga), why is its validity denied on the grounds of non-contradiction simply because it is preceded by a three-featured logical mark?

By this, the contradiction between the probandum and the probans is stated by implication. For instance, where there is the state of being preceded by a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), there is non-discrepancy; and where there is non-discrepancy, there is validity. Since validity and invalidity are characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthita*), a contradictory reason (*viruddho hetuḥ*) has been indicated through the force of the argument.

With the words "false cognition" (mithyājñāna) and so forth, he states that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*): "False cognition and [the cognition] common [to both sides] are said to be produced by that which subverts what is accepted, with respect to the opponent's position; this is not the case in reality."
For, in accordance with the actual state of things, that cognition is determined to be non-contradictory;
for this very reason, it is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding what is contrary to the proponent's intended [object].
Therefore, the reason is contradictory and the example lacks the property to be proven;
by this very same method, in the second [case], the reason is unestablished.

Since it establishes the opposite of what the proponent desires, that too is indeed a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, if invalidity were established for everything at all times in relation to another thing to be proven (*sādhya*), then the same consequence would apply even to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, it was called "false cognition" (*mithyājñāna*) only in relation to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), not according to the actual state of things.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *pūrva* refers to the position (*pakṣa*) of the first speaker; thus, *pūrvapakṣa* [means] the position of the former, and [the term refers to] dependence upon that.

For one who maintains that the eyes and other sense organs have as their sole purpose the production of a single result in which no excellence can be added, false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is said to occur from the perspective of that person's intention;
this is because the eyes and other organs are established as causes for multiple, impermanent cognitions and so forth.
Thus, there is a contradiction (*viruddhatā*).
Because the property of being preceded by a logical mark possessing the three characteristics (trirūpaliṅga) is absent in any invalid cognition whatsoever,
whereas it exists in that very valid cognition which is produced by that which subverts the desired [conclusion].
But surely, when one is attempting to prove a contradictory [thesis] against a Lokāyata, the example is not established at all?

The opponent does not accept that a cognition produced by something which thwarts what is desired is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); nor can an example be cited that is unestablished for either party. According to the principle that "only that which expresses what is certain for both sides constitutes proof or refutation," it is said: even if validity is not explicitly accepted here by the opponent through words, nevertheless, non-discrepancy (*asaṃvāditva*) is indeed accepted because it cannot be denied. For those who accept that [non-discrepancy], validity must also be admitted by him through the force of the facts, as that is the actual state of things. Thus, the contradiction is pointed out by the inherent power of the object itself, and not in accordance with the opponent's own assertions.
Alternatively, it is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it indicates a contradictory reason (*hetu*).

In this context, the contradictory reason is as follows: that which is non-discrepant (*avisaṃvādi*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); and knowledge produced by a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) is non-discrepant. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). It is not "unestablished" (*asiddha*), because that would entail the consequence of [all things] being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) and lacking causal efficacy; nor is it "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), because that would entail the consequence of direct perception itself being invalid.

Regarding the term *asādhyatā*: it is "unprovable" (*asādhya*) because there is nothing to be proven (*sādhya*) here; the state of being that is "unprovability" (*asādhyatā*), which is to say, the deficiency of a probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*).
Regarding the phrase "the second":
this refers to the passage beginning with "nor [is there] the three-fold form," and so forth.
"The reason's unestablished nature" means that the logical mark (*hetu*) is unestablished.
Because it does not exist anywhere in the absence of inference; "by this very [reason]" means by the principle beginning with "the mark possessing the three characteristics," and so forth.
Regarding the contradiction with inference and so forth, he states the rebuttal beginning with "that which is through identity" (*yattādātmya*), etc.:
"The proponents of logic declare that only that which is ascertained as being related through identity or causality is the means of proof for establishing [the probandum]."
In such a proof, there is no contradiction with inference or other such fallacies;
for that [proof] cannot possibly occur anywhere without its own internal reasons.
Furthermore, two mutually contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single entity;
therefore, there is no possibility of a "non-deviating contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
"Of such a kind" means that which is constrained by identity and causality.
"By way of its own nature and its cause" means: [by way of the essential nature and the cause].

Without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and without cause (*kāraṇa*), respectively, that mark (*liṅga*) would not exist, because it would follow that it is devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of a cause.

As for what was stated—that "the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) intended [to be proved] is not a qualifier of the locus (*dharmin*)"—if the property to be proven were not a qualifier of the locus, then the composite whole (*samudāya*) itself would not exist; consequently, the reason "because it is a part of that composite whole" would be unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, as for the claim that "in every inference there is the possibility of contradictions regarding particulars (*viśeṣaviruddha*)," that is incorrect.
Since a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is defined as one that proves the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*), and it is not the case that a specific property (*viśeṣa*) is intended to be proven;
furthermore, in the domain of inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta-anumāna*), a non-erroneous contradiction (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is impossible,
because it would entail the presence of two mutually contradictory properties in a single locus (*dharmin*).

Regarding that which was stated in the verse beginning with "of states, places, and times," he says "practiced" and so forth: "And for those whose characteristics have been practiced, when there is a correct ascertainment of the logical mark (liṅga), there occurs the operation of inference; otherwise, it is not called inference."
Since the potencies of entities differ due to variations in state, place, and time, the establishment of those entities through inference is therefore extremely difficult to achieve.
Even when an object has been inferred with great effort by skilled inferents, [it may still be subverted]. (TS 1476)
It cannot be established otherwise even by others who are more skilled;

for a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is well-ascertained is held to be the means of cognition, not one that is doubtful. Indeed, smoke that is suspected of being vapor or the like does not lead to the certain cognition of fire.
If it is asked, "How is the ascertainment of the logical mark itself achieved? [the answer follows].
[It arises] from repeated practice,
as is the case for those who know [the nature of] gems and the like.
For indeed, those who are familiar with the specific characteristics of each [object] distinguish smoke and so forth from vapor and the like precisely through such practice.
Moreover, those who act without having properly discriminated [the mark] certainly encounter fire;

therefore, since a well-discriminated logical mark (*liṅga*) does not deviate [from the object], the establishment of things distinguished by differences in state and so forth is not difficult to achieve. Furthermore, an object definitively ascertained through a well-discriminated logical mark cannot be made otherwise.

For it is not possible to effect a change in the nature of fire inferred from smoke that has been thoroughly ascertained, because it is impossible for a single entity to possess two contradictory intrinsic natures.

As for what was said—that Devadatta is incapable of carrying a load—and so forth, or that a mass of clouds is being burned by fire, that is not a valid logical mark (*liṅga*) at all, because it lacks the three required characteristics (*trairūpya*).
Indeed, the exclusion of a reason from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) cannot be established by mere non-perception.
As it has been said: "Invariable exclusion from the dissimilar class does not follow from mere non-perception.
What then? The necessity of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) follows from the restriction of the relations of identity (tādātmya) and causality (tadutpatti). As it has been said:

The restriction of inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva) arises either from the relation of cause and effect or from an essential nature that acts as a regulator; it is established by non-observation [of the contrary], not by observation.
Thus [it is said];
and in this case, there exists neither a relation of identity (*tādātmya*) nor a relation of origination (*tadutpatti*).
It might be argued: "How is it that a well-ascertained logical mark (*liṅga*) does not deviate? For there is no reasoning (*yukti*) for this. To this he says:
"For neither an essential nature (*svabhāva*) nor an effect (*kārya*) [exists] without an essential nature or a cause," and so forth.
For, since they would otherwise result in being devoid of a basis for their distinction, inference (*anumāna*) cannot exist without those two.

For there are only two kinds of logical mark (*liṅga*), namely: essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*). Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), moreover, is included within essential nature. And without a probandum (*liṅgin*) called either essential nature or cause, the occurrence of those two marks is impossible, by which—

There would be an inconsistency. Why is it not possible? He says: because it would result in both difference and causelessness (*bhedānimittatāprāpteḥ*). That is, the attainment of both difference and causelessness: for a self-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), difference results in the absence of self-nature; for an effect reason (*kāryahetu*), [difference] results in causelessness, which is to say, being without a cause. And no other logical mark (*liṅga*) is accepted apart from self-nature and effect, because otherwise there would be no necessary connection (*apratibandha*) and thus an impossibility of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
They lead them away;
it refers to their own nature and their activity;
this [term] ends in the dual number.

Regarding what was stated—that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is a means of valid cognition (*māna*)—he says "the statement of the three-featured mark" and so forth: "The fact that the statement of the three-featured mark is called 'inference for the sake of others' is because it indicates [the object] by being connected [to it]; this is from the perspective of the listener."
Thus, the status of being an inference is accepted here in a secondary and conventional sense;
because it indicates what is connected [to the object], there is no over-extension [of the definition].
If inference is not a valid means of knowledge, then your own contradiction is fruitless;
for no discourse whatsoever can convey the speaker's intention.

That which was stated regarding the speech being an inference for others (parārthānumāna) is said from the perspective of the listener; therefore, the fault arising from the absence [of inference] from the perspective of the speaker does not apply. Even from the perspective of the listener, it is called an "inference" either figuratively—because it indicates a three-featured mark (trirūpaliṅga) and is thus a cause of inference—or by convention, since the designation "inference" is applied specifically to that which indicates what is connected [to the object].

Consequently, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to the sense-organ (*indriya*) or to the cognition of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva-sambandha*), because these two lack the capacity to indicate what is connected [to the object].

For this very reason, this [verbal cognition] is distinguished from cognitions rooted in direct perception (*darśana*). To explain: through the cognition of perception, there is a direct apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*) such as smoke, but not through auditory cognition; for by that [auditory cognition], only the word itself is directly grasped. And the word is not a mark of an external object in the same way that smoke is, because a connection between the word—which is bound up with the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*)—and an external object is unestablished.

It is described as "for the sake of another" (parārtha) only insofar as it indicates that mark (liṅga), such as smoke, by virtue of convention, because it gives rise to a conceptual determination (adhyavasāyi-vikalpa) corresponding to it with respect to an external object.
However, when the intention to speak is what is to be understood, it is indeed "for one's own sake" (svārtha) from the perspective of the listener.
For instance, because it is an effect [of that intention], it is accepted as an indicator when there is the intention to speak of smoke.
Nor by way of being a designator, because from that [designation] no cognition arises; thus,
the utterance is fruitless.
This [position] is that inference is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For instance, there is no one to be persuaded who, upon hearing those words, understands the speaker's intention.
By this, he states the contradiction with his own words, and this has already been explained previously.

But Purandara says: "Inference that is well-known in the world is indeed accepted even by the Cārvākas; however, that which is called inference by someone who transgresses the worldly path is what is being refuted. Anticipating this objection and refuting it, he says "the worldly," and so forth.
If it is claimed that the worldly sign is accepted [as a means of knowledge], but not that which is conceptualized by others,
then surely even the world understands causes and so forth from effects and so forth.
In reality, however, that very point has been sufficiently stated even by the proponents of logic:
when something is accepted by worldly convention, what is it that you yourself have abandoned?
Regarding the phrase "nanu loko 'pi": the connection is that "the world also understands the defects of the reason" (*hetu*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "from the effect, etc. (*kāryādeḥ*), the inclusion of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is intended.
In this way, even in the phrase "the cause and so forth" (*hetvādīn*), there is only the inclusion of the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The plural number, however, is due to the distinction between individual instances.

That very mark (*liṅga*) which, being constrained by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), makes the worldly object understood—that alone has been called the "mark" by us. If that is admitted, what would be lost such that its status as inference (*anumāna*) should be denied?

Furthermore, it might be argued: "We do not accept any inference for ourselves at all; rather, the opponent accepts it as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, by accepting that [inference], my statement does not become fruitless or contradictory. To this, he replies with the words beginning "By that which is not a valid cognition" (*apramāṇena*): "And what does the opponent understand by means of this which is not a valid cognition?
And what kind of conviction could this be that is produced by something that is not a valid cognition?"

Furthermore, from what source has this certainty arisen that the other person accepts that as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For the acceptance by another is not perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), nor do you possess any other means of valid cognition by which such certainty could be established. Granting that such certainty might exist, even so, how does the other person come to understand it through that which is not a valid cognition and is merely accepted by the other? Indeed, this is no hardship at all.

Now, one might think: "Just as a sword is snatched from an enemy's hand and that very same enemy is struck down by it, so too, having seized that very thing which the opponent has accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the opponent is refuted. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Not produced by a means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇakṛta*). This is what is meant: if, out of delusion, the opponent has accepted something that is actually not a means of valid cognition as being a means of valid cognition, how can correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) be produced for the opponent by means of that which is not a means of valid cognition? For a means of valid cognition has as its fruit correct knowledge.
For it is not the case that any random cutting instrument taken up out of delusion under the thought "this is a sword" can cut another; thus, the example is not analogous.

Aviddhakarṇa says in the *Tattvaṭīkā*: "Now, why is the opponent made to understand by means of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for that which is established for both parties becomes the means of communication? This very [objection] is incorrect; because inference, being of the nature of speech, is not a means of valid cognition for the speaker, and yet the speaker makes the other understand by means of it, since the effort is for the purpose of making the other understand.
"There is no necessity for [the reason] to be established for both parties.
He anticipates this objection with the words "If inference," and so forth:
"If they were to consider inference as a means of valid cognition, it would not consist of verbal expression."
Because it illuminates [it], this [object] becomes exactly as that [cognition] is.

[433] Because it does not illuminate an object not previously known, that [cognition] is held to be non-valid; surely your own [position] is likewise [non-valid], since it merely indicates what is incapable [of producing a result].
"This" refers to the speaker;
"by that" refers to that which consists of speech.

With the words beginning with "unrecognized," he states the refutation: for it is not accepted that speech lacks authority because it indicates [the object] in dependence upon a speaker, but rather because it fails to illuminate an object that has not been recognized.
This [reason] certainly possesses the quality of indicating what is connected;
however, your inference does not indicate what is connected, so this is not the same.
Otherwise, it would indeed be established for both parties.
Therefore, it is logical that a means of valid cognition not deviating from that principle is appropriate for everyone, just like perception; this is the correct conclusion.
Thus ends the examination of inference.
Now, for the purpose of establishing the restriction to two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and for the purpose of addressing disagreements regarding their number,
he says "nanu" and so forth:
"But surely [there are more], because other means of valid cognition such as verbal testimony (śabda) are possible."
Why has the definition been specified for only these two means of valid cognition?

By this, he states the fault that the definition of valid cognition lacks pervasiveness, as well as the futility of the restriction "determined by two types of valid cognition" in the phrase *pramādvitayaniścitam*.
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said":

It is said that no means of valid cognition other than the two is tenable, because of the lack of application of the definition of a means of valid cognition; and even if such application were possible, it would be included herein.
"Because it is included herein" means within these two very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is what is meant: for anything other than the two means of valid cognition, the characteristic of being a means of valid cognition—namely, non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāditva*)—does not exist.
It is indeed so; and since it is included within this very [category], it is not stated as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In this regard, he demonstrates these two points: how other means of knowledge are invalid, or, if they are valid, how they are included within [the accepted ones].

Here, other means of knowledge—namely, verbal testimony (*śabda*), analogy (*upamāna*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), non-existence (*abhāva*), logical reasoning (*yukti*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), possibility (*sambhava*), tradition (*aitihya*), and intuition (*pratibhā*)—are accepted by others.
Regarding that, he speaks concerning verbal testimony (śabda), beginning with "From the knowledge of words," and so forth:
"Others have declared that verbal cognition (*śābda*) is the knowledge of an imperceptible object arising from the knowledge of words;
and that [cognition] arises from a sentence that is either authorless or uttered by a trustworthy person."
And this [self] is certainly not perceived, because its object is beyond the senses;
nor is it established as inference, because it lacks the defining characteristics thereof.
It is well-established that the subject (dharmin) as qualified by its property (dharma) is the logical mark (liṅga);
and there can be no inference so long as that [mark] does not have that [subject] as its object.
In this regard, Śabarasvāmin states the definition of verbal cognition (*śabda*): "Verbal [cognition] is the knowledge of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the knowledge of a word.

The cognition that arises with respect to an imperceptible object at a time subsequent to the apprehension of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called verbal, because it has come from the word.
And that is of two kinds.
[This cognition] is produced by words that are not of human origin and by the speech of a trustworthy person.
And this is distinct from direct perception because its object is beyond the senses;
nor is it inference because of the absence of the three characteristics [of the logical mark].

For it is held that the subject (dharmin) qualified by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is the object of inference (anumeya), neither the subject alone nor the property alone. And as long as the logical mark (liṅga) is not ascertained as having the subject as its object by virtue of being that subject's property, the operation of inference is not possible;
that is to say, as long as there is no ascertainment of the "property-of-the-subject" (pakṣadharmatva), there is no inference.
"Why does that very [cognition] not constitute the determination of the property's presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatva)? To this he says:

"And that which is here postulated as the subject (dharmin), that alone is its object of cognition (prameya). And there can be no determination of its being a property of that [subject] when the latter has not been determined."
And that subject (*dharmin*), such as a tree, which is postulated here in verbal cognition, is itself the object of knowledge (*prameya*), because it alone is what is to be established.

The meaning is that here the subject alone is the object of knowledge, not the subject as qualified by its properties. If that subject is not determined—that is, not ascertained—how can its status as a property (*dharmatva*) be ascertained?

If it has already been apprehended prior to [the cognition of] its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), what is the use of subsequently knowing it through the property-of-the-subject and so forth, by virtue of which it would constitute inference?

Furthermore, if that subject (dharmin) were already known prior to the ascertainment of its being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva), then the effort to ascertain its status as a property of the subject would be fruitless;
for every exertion is for the sake of cognizing the subject. If it has already been cognized, what is the use now of the effort to determine its status as a property of the subject and so forth?
This was stated while merely conceding the point for the sake of argument.
Furthermore, sound is not a property of a subject such as a tree, because it is perceived in the location of the speaker.

Thus, first, the absence of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) has been demonstrated. Now, demonstrating the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he says: "And there is no positive concomitance," and so forth.
"And there is no positive concomitance of the word with the object of cognition (*prameya*).
For the state of being a concomitant is perceived for all things through their functional activity."
"It is determined" means it is ascertained;
"by means of an operation."
"By way of real existence" means by way of being present;
this is what is meant: only that which exists can be a concomitant, not that which does not exist.
Demonstrating this very point, he says "yatra" and so forth:
"Wherever there is smoke, there is clearly a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the existence of fire;
but it is not certain in the same way that wherever there is a word, there is an object."
Since wherever there is smoke, fire is necessarily present, that fire is the concomitant of the smoke; however, the word does not have such a concomitance with its object.
Demonstrating how it does not exist, he says: "Not yet," etc.
First of all, that [sound] is not perceived in that place nor at that time.
If it were argued that this is because it is eternal and omnipresent, then that would apply equally to all sounds.
Because he has seen [the relationship] everywhere and because there is no apprehension of its absence,
it would follow that all words convey the entirety of all objects.
First of all, there is no existence of the object in that place occupied by the word;
for instance, the word "piṇḍakharjūra" (a type of date) is heard elsewhere, such as in Pāṭaliputra, yet that kind of date does not exist in that place.

Likewise, it is not the case that an object necessarily exists at the time of the word; for while words such as "Dilīpa" or "Mahāsammeta" are present [in the present], their objects may have been in the past or will be in the future. Thus, how can there be a concomitance (*anvaya*) of the word with its objects? Now, if it is thought: "Because words are eternal, they exist at all times; therefore, there is no difference in time between them and their objects. Nor is there a difference in place, because, being all-pervasive (*vyāpin*), they exist in all locations. Consequently, due to their eternity and omnipresence, there would be a concomitance of words."
In that case, since that eternal omnipresence (*nityavibhutva*) is equal in all words, it would follow that the denotation of specific objects by specific words is not possible.

What then? By whichever word [is used], there would be the denotation of every object whatsoever, because every word is observed everywhere—in every place and at every time—together with that [specific] object.
As for *vyatireka* (negative concomitance), it is the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*). Of that [concomitance]:
"Because there is no going" means because it is not perceived;
precisely because it is eternal and all-pervading.
Therefore, verbal cognition, like perception, would not be inference,
because it lacks the three characteristics [of a logical reason] and because it excludes such an object [as that which is to be inferred].
Having concluded with "therefore," he demonstrates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"That which is verbal is not inference" is the statement of the thesis (*sādhya-nirdeśa*). "By virtue of being devoid of the three characteristics [of a logical mark]" is the reason (*hetu*).
"Like perception" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"Because of the exclusion of such an object" is the justification of the reason (*hetu-samarthana*).

That is to say, because it is devoid of—that is, excluded from—such an object as the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*), which is the object of an inference arising from a mark (*liṅga*) such as smoke.

Granted that it is distinct from inference because it lacks the three characteristics [of a valid reason], how then can this verbal testimony possess validity? To this he says: "From the statement regarding the *agnihotra*," and so forth.
[p.436] Because the statement regarding the *agnihotra* and other such rites gives rise to unshakable knowledge.
Therefore, its status as a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) cannot be refuted either.
Because it is free from doubt and error, it is unshakable and immovable;

because there is no subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), it is a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of knowledge]. This is what is meant.
Thus Śabarasvāmin said: "And from this statement, 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice,' it is not understood with uncertainty whether heaven comes to be or does not come to be."

Furthermore, this [Vedic statement], being understood with certainty, cannot be false. For that cognition which, having arisen, subsequently perishes with the thought "this is not so," is a false cognition; but this [Vedic cognition] does not subvert itself in another place, at another time, or in another person. Therefore, it is non-false. As for worldly speech, if it comes from a trustworthy person and concerns an object of the senses, it is indeed non-false. However, if it comes from an untrustworthy person or concerns an object beyond the senses, it is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), as it originates from human intellect; for it is impossible for a mere human to know such things.

With the words beginning with "In that regard" (tatra), he states the defect of the definition—namely, its impossibility—with respect to this first definition of verbal cognition (*śābda*), namely: "And that [knowledge] arises from a sentence that has no author.
In that context, the possibility and the meaning of a sentence without an author are both untenable;
therefore, the first definition of verbal cognition is declared to be impossible.

For a sentence that is without an author is simply impossible, because pervasive momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has been established [by us], or else by the reasoning to be stated later. Even if its existence were possible, its capacity to convey meaning would not be possible; therefore, since it is impossible for this imperceptible object to be known from a statement lacking an author, the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is untenable.
Furthermore, he explains why there can be no statement that is without an agent by saying "capable," and so forth:
"Because the nature of being either capable or incapable always persists,
the cognition of that [nature] would either exist at that time or never exist at all."
In this regard, there are two alternatives: either a sentence that has no author must be capable of producing cognition, or it might at some time be incapable.
In the first case, because its nature as being capable persists, it follows that the resulting cognition would occur eternally.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: Whatever possesses unimpeded capacity for a given effect necessarily performs that effect, just as the final causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) does. Furthermore, a sentence that is not the work of a human author possesses unimpeded capacity for generating knowledge at all times; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Alternatively, whatever has its causes complete necessarily comes into being, just as a sprout with complete causes does. And the cognition arising from a non-human sentence has its causes complete; this is a reason based on essential nature.
Moreover, even in the second case, because that incapable nature would persist at all times, consciousness would never arise from it, just as a sprout does not arise when its causes are incomplete.

To the question, "How is it that [the teaching] does not fail to possess meaningfulness? he says: "Hatred, delusion, and so forth," and so on. Just as faults such as hatred and delusion are causes of falsity, so too are compassion, wisdom, and the like known to be causes of truth.
In the absence of a person who is their substratum, those two [the Veda and its meaning] cannot possibly exist either;
therefore, it follows that speech would be purposeless if it were not based on a person.
Meaningfulness occurs in two ways: either by having non-erroneous content or by having erroneous content, since there is no third category.
Furthermore, it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the causes of these two types of meaningful cognition are respectively its virtues and its defects.
For instance, just as a person overwhelmed by defects such as passion is seen to be a speaker of falsehood, so too one endowed with virtues such as compassion is seen to be a speaker of truth.

Furthermore, the person is the locus of those two qualities and defects, which are the causes of correctness and falsity; therefore, upon the cessation of the person, there is the cessation of qualities and defects, and upon the cessation of qualities and defects, there is also the non-existence of correctness and falsity.
In the absence of these, since no other mode is possible, it follows that a non-human (apauruṣeya) word would be purposeless, due to the absence of its cause.
For it is not logical for an effect to arise without a cause, as that would entail the consequence of its being causeless;
and consequently, there would be no restriction regarding place, time, substance, and so forth.
This should be understood as a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum).
Otherwise, if one were to establish [the Veda] independently [of human authorship], there would be a contradiction with what is observed.
For instance, the comprehension of meaning from such sentences as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice" is indeed perceived; and that which is observed cannot be denied.
Furthermore, since the lack of an author is not established for both parties, the reason (hetu) would be unestablished (asiddha).
In a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅgasādhana), however, both [reasons] are faultless.
For instance, if the Veda is accepted as being non-human (apauruṣeya), then its lack of purpose must be accepted;
because of the absence of a person, there is no cause for it having meaning.
Nor is it purposeless; therefore, by way of an incidental argument, it is demonstrated that [the Veda] must indeed be of human origin.

In order to support this very *prasaṅga*-proof, [the author], demonstrating the absence of contradiction with observed reality, says "artha... and so forth, preceded by a doubt: "If it is not [established] from the cognition of the meaning, then this [cognition] would arise from the explanation; for a person is seen to be independent when explaining a meaning according to his own desire."
If its capacity to illuminate the real object were inherent by its very nature,
then even one who has not learned the linguistic convention would have comprehension of the meaning from it.
A lamp is an illuminator by its very nature; it does not depend upon convention.
Furthermore, when there is another convention, understanding arises from that [lamp] with respect to a different object.
For even when a convention exists, a lamp does not illuminate smell, taste, and so forth;
nor is it possible for that capacity to be known.
"If not" (no cet) connects with "uselessness" (ānarthakyam). The implication is that, consequently, there would be a contradiction with observed reality regarding the thesis.

It would indeed be a contradiction of observed fact if the comprehension of meaning from the Veda itself were to arise without instruction; for the comprehension of meaning would occur from the side of the commentator by virtue of convention (*samaya*), and not from the Veda alone, independent of convention.
For instance, we observe that Mīmāṃsakas and others explain the meaning of the Veda according to their own will; and it is not logical that an inherent meaning should conform to human desire.

In this regard, it might be argued: "A person does not state a novel matter according to their own whim; rather, that which is inherently established is precisely what is revealed by the person. Therefore, there is indeed a contradiction with what is observed.

If that is so, then if this Veda possesses an inherent capacity to illuminate an existing reality, it would follow that even one who is ignorant of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) would obtain a cognition of the meaning from that Vedic sentence.
If it is argued that the Veda is the cause for the cognition of meaning only when dependent upon convention (*saṅketa*), and not by itself,
that is not so;
for lamps and the like, which are causes for the cognition of objects by their very nature, do not depend upon convention.

Otherwise, it would be the convention itself that possesses the capacity for the cognition of meaning through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and not an inherent relationship. Furthermore, even if the cognition of meaning were to occur with the aid of convention, there would still be a fault; thus he says "samaya... and so forth. A "different convention" (*samayāntara*) is a convention composed by the authors of *Niruktas* and others, as opposed to the convention composed by the Mīmāṃsakas.
If that [convention] were to exist, it would follow that the cognition of a different object from the one under discussion could not arise from that word;

for a lamp is not capable of illuminating things such as odors or tastes—which are not its objects of illumination—merely by virtue of convention. Even if there were indeed an application to a different object through the power of convention, he demonstrates that validity is still not established with the words "to be known" (*vijñātum*).

If a word were to function with reference to another object by the force of human intention, then, due to such confusion, that power to illuminate a real object could not be ascertained; how, then, could the comprehension of the intended object arise from it?
Alternatively, it is explained otherwise:
there are two positions regarding that innate power to illuminate a real object—whether it is restricted to a single meaning or restricted to multiple meanings.
Regarding that, he states the fault in the position that there is a restriction to a single object: "the existence of other conventions.
Regarding the second [position] as well, he says: "and that capacity cannot be known," because of the confusion [of capacities]; this is the intended meaning.
As it has been said:
"If words were restricted to a single meaning, there would be no comprehension of another meaning;
if they were connected to multiple meanings, there would be the possibility of contradictory manifestations."
Thus it is said.

Having thus demonstrated that the first definition of verbal cognition is impossible, and showing by way of conclusion that the reason "because it arises from unshakable knowledge" is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
Therefore, since the cognition of the object is untenable, how can there be its unshakability?
But that [word], being conventional and joined with the speech of a person, does not differ from the [actual] entity.
Those who know logic perceive no distinction whatsoever between these two; however, for those Vedic scholars who do not know the path of logic, this [distinction] remains unshakable.

When, the Veda being non-human in origin, the very comprehension of meaning as previously described is impossible according to that logic, then how could there be any stability for such comprehension? Furthermore, it was established earlier through the passage beginning with "This [comprehension] arises from interpretation," etc., that the comprehension of meaning which is observed to arise from Vedic sentences must be merely conventional (*sāṅketika*).
For this reason as well, it is logical that this [comprehension] is merely conventional.

Because the Vedic statement does not differ from that which has become human speech—that is, from that which has attained the status of human speech—it does not differ from human utterances; this is what is meant.
To the question "Why is this so? he says: "By those who know logic," and so forth.
"Of those two" means of the Vedic and the human [scriptures].
Since [both] can be produced by persons in every respect, there is no distinction whatsoever between the Vedic and the worldly.
He mocks them by saying, "Of those learned in the Vedas."

Regarding the second definition of verbal testimony as well—namely, "or that which is uttered by a trustworthy person"—he states the impossibility of this definition's flaw in the verse beginning with "āpta" (trustworthy).
Because a "trustworthy person" is not admitted [as a valid category], even the second definition is not tenable;
or, if such a definition of verbal testimony were accepted, that very person would remain undetermined.
Since the Mīmāṃsakas do not accept a person whose defects have been eliminated, they do not acknowledge an authoritative person (āpta) at all; therefore, how could there be validity for his word?
It is not possible;
it is not logical.

This means that [an author] is impossible. Even if such an authoritative person (*āpta*) were admitted, then, while the existence of such an authority is asserted, he is not determined by being specifically identified as "this is he"; thus, he is merely like something non-existent.
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determining the qualities or defects of such persons, because they are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).

Furthermore, since bodily and verbal behaviors are sometimes performed intentionally in a manner other [than what they signify], how can there be validity in such speech? For those who perceive only the words cannot determine them with certainty, lest there be confusion.
Generally, the conviction derived from someone's words is accepted as being based on that person's own experience;
for if that conviction is indeed the basis for the statement, then the statement serves the purpose of conveying what is beyond one's direct perception.
It is not otherwise, because of the absence of conditions; for even that which was previously without conditions [is so] due to the lack of conditions.
Indeed, there is no fixed rule that what is unerring in one instance must be so in all instances.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "That person whose speech is observed to produce conviction in the majority of cases, even though his faults have not been eliminated, is intended by us as a 'trustworthy person' (*pratyayita*), not one whose faults have been eliminated.
Therefore, it is the speech of that trustworthy person which is accepted; thus, in the definition of verbal testimony (*śābda*), the charge of impossibility (*asambhavitā*) does not apply.
This too is incorrect.

For it is not logical to conclude that because non-contradiction is observed in one instance, it must necessarily exist everywhere in that same way; for deviation is possible, otherwise the definition of non-deviation would be untenable.
Having thus specifically demonstrated the two-fold definition of verbal testimony (*śābda*), he states the general refutation beginning with "of words" (*vacasām*) and so forth:
"What connection could there be even for words toward external objects,
such that they might possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while making those [objects] known?"
Because of the perception by different sense organs and so forth, there is neither identity [between the object and the cognition] nor its arising [from it];
nor is it logical for anything else to possess non-deviation, because of deviation.

Indeed, there exists no connection between words and the objects denoted by them—neither characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) nor characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—by virtue of which these words expressing those objects might possess validity (*prāmāṇya*).
In this regard, first of all, there is no connection characterized by identity, due to reasons such as their being apprehended by different sense organs (*bhinnākṣagrahaṇa*).
Here, "apprehension by different sense organs" means apprehension by distinct sensory faculties.

For instance, sound is apprehended by the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*), whereas an object is apprehended by the visual faculty and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the distinctions of time, place, appearance, and causes are included. However, Kumārila says: "The argument that [an object] is distinct because it is apprehended by different sense faculties is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for instance, when many people see a single form (*rūpa*), then, due to its being apprehended by different sense faculties, a distinction in the form itself would follow."
Now, it might be argued that because there is no difference in the genus (*jāti*) of the visual faculty, [color] must indeed be apprehended by a single sense-faculty.

If that is the case, then even though existence (*sattā*) is apprehended by multiple sense-faculties, it possesses the property of being apprehended by a non-differentiated sense-faculty due to the non-difference in the genus of the faculties; thus, its unity is established.

Therefore, the determination of the difference or non-difference of entities is based on the difference or non-difference of cognitions, not on the difference or non-difference of the sense-faculties.
And it is said:
"Furthermore, that which is perceivable by multiple sense-faculties does not attain distinctness;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between [colors] such as blue, simply because they are perceived by different bodies [of sense-faculties]."

If it is argued that there is no difference [among the sense-faculties] because there is no difference in their genus (*jāti*), then that is the same as [the case of] being a sense-faculty (*indriyatva*).
Therefore, because the cognition is identical, existence (*sattā*) is not distinct on account of the difference among the sense-faculties.
Thus [it is said].
And this is incorrect, because even when difference is to be proven through a difference in cognition, the same [objection] applies.
For here too, one can say: "A difference in things follows from a difference in cognitions"; thus, this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For instance, when many people perceive a single form, there is indeed a difference in their cognitions because multiple visual consciousnesses arise;
yet at that time, there is no difference in the form itself.
If unity is postulated for the eye-consciousness based on the non-difference of its genus, then it would follow that color, taste, and so forth must also be one.
Even though there is a difference in the cognitions of those [objects], there is no difference in the class (*jāti*) of consciousness;
therefore, the statement that "the unity of color and so forth does not follow because of the difference in cognitions" would be contradicted.
Consequently, this is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*).

Now, even though there is a difference in specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), whatever kind of difference in characteristics exists, the conventional usage of "difference" and "non-difference" well-known in the world is based on whether they serve as causes for a single or multiple determinate cognitions (*pratyavamarśa*); it is such differences and non-differences of cognition that are adopted here. This applies equally to the sense faculty as well; so, enough of this digression.
[The phrase] "not arising from that" [is explained as follows].
Nor is there a relationship characterized by origination from that [the object], because of deviation;
for [the cognition] exists even in the absence of the object due to mere intention to speak.
Furthermore, nothing else devoid of such origination possesses non-deviation, as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Therefore, a word does not possess epistemic authority with respect to an object that is merely denotable.

If this is so, how is it that it was stated: "Verbal cognition is not a separate means of valid knowledge from inference; for it expresses its own object through the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), just like [the property of] being produced and so forth"?
Anticipating this objection, he says "from words," etc., demonstrating how its inclusion within inference is intended.
This intention to speak is inferred even from all utterances;
for that cause [of speech] is ascertained through perception and non-perception.
"From all [authoritative persons]" means even from those intended to be of human origin.
And that intention is understood from speech, because speech is its effect.
But not by way of being directly denoted.
For it has been ascertained through positive and negative concomitance within one's own mental continuum that the cause of words is that intention to speak (*vivakṣā*).
As for what was said—that "one speaks by means of the exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*)—therein "speaking" (*bhāṣaṇa*) means manifesting or making known.
And its commentary is as follows: "It indicates exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) by means of that which is connected to another object, just like 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth.

This must necessarily be understood; otherwise, the example "just like being produced" would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhanavikala*). For it is not possible for there to be a verbal expression (*bhāṣaṇa*) of "being produced" and the like, because that is a property of sound (*śabdadharmatva*).
Furthermore, because it is expressed through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the reason would be "uniquely inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇa*).
But surely, even regarding the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), it is not logical for a word to possess validity.
For instance, it does not have validity with respect to a particular intention, because of deviation;
since we observe that a person who is deluded may utter a sentence about one thing while intending something else.
Nor [is it established] with respect to the generality of the intention to speak, because that would be futile;
for the mere cognition of the intention to speak never serves as a factor in linguistic practice,
since it does not determine a specific object.

Anticipating this objection, [the author] states "of one who is deluded" (*bhrāntasya*) and so forth; he asserts the validity [of speech] with respect to a specific intention by saying "deluded or non-deluded" (*bhrāntābhrānta*) and so forth.

If, when one who is deluded intends one thing, another sentence is observed [to be uttered], then even such an intention does not proceed from that [sentence] because it is merely a general [intention].
The wise clearly determine the distinction between speech uttered by the deluded and that uttered by the undeluded, based on its nature and other such factors, without any further effort.
For one must necessarily admit a distinction between those things produced by the deluded and those produced by the undeluded; otherwise, a difference in causes would not be a differentiator.
And skilled persons certainly ascertain that distinction from the context and other such factors.
"Context" (*prakṛta*) means the subject matter under discussion.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), freedom from agitation, a serene countenance, and so forth are included.
To the question, "How is there indeed this distinctiveness of words? he says: "By the distinctiveness of the reasons.
This fault belongs to those who do not perceive the distinction among them by means of the distinctiveness of the reasons; however, for the logical mark (*liṅga*), there is no such fault.
Since smoke, whose nature is sometimes doubted,
might otherwise exist at a time when it is not being ascertained, it would not possess the status of a logical mark (liṅga) for fire even at that time.
This means "due to the difference in causes.
Therefore, an effect that has been well-discriminated does not deviate from its cause; thus, it indeed possesses validity with respect to the specific intention [of the speaker].
However, this fault belongs to those who do not discern the distinction among those words which serve as logical marks (*liṅga*), and not to the logical mark itself.
A logical mark (liṅga) is not accepted as a means of cognition by its mere existence; rather, it must be certain.
Therefore, this is a fault on the part of the cognizer.
For otherwise, since there would be no difference [between smoke and something else] when smoke is being doubted—such as whether it is vapor or the like—[the inference would fail].
Because it does not produce cognition (*agamakatvāt*), even that which is ascertained does not attain the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) when fire is the probandum.

Furthermore, when this entire verbal discourse is accepted as being purely erroneous—like the vision of two moons by two people with ophthalmia, occurring solely in accordance with one's own internal appearances—then how could there be the consequence of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) by pointing out a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding a particular intention (*vivakṣāviśeṣa*)? For in that case, ultimate validity (*pāramārthika-prāmāṇya*) is not admitted with respect to that particular intention.
And thus it has been said:
"Its status as inference is taught by taking its manifestation into the heart with respect to convention, but not with respect to reality."
Thus it is said.
Demonstrating the validity [of inference] even when the probandum is the mere intention to speak (*vivakṣā-sāmānya*), he says "teṣām" and so forth:
"Even for them, [inference] does not contradict the mere intention to speak,
because there is the certain existence of inference for the sake of establishing things such as being alive."

For all of these, whether employed by those who are mistaken or non-mistaken, there is no contradiction in their being inference with respect to the generality of the intention to speak (*vivakṣāsāmānya*), because of its absolute existence and its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). And:
"By the mere presence of that person, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*)..."
"The teachings issue forth at will even from walls and other such objects."
One should not suspect a deviation [from the rule] on account of this admission;
for even in that case, the initial intention alone is the cause,
since the activity of speech there proceeds solely by the force of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by previous vows.
