For instance, even when one who has thoroughly mastered a text is engaged in activities such as speaking or walking during the time of study and so forth, another conceptualization occurs;

yet this does not mean that prior volition (*pūrvasamīhā*) is not the cause of those actions. Otherwise, one might have to point out the fallibility of smoke as a mark for inferring fire and the like, simply because smoke is perceived in places such as a cowherd’s water-pot (*gopālaghaṭikā*).

Therefore, in every case, there is no possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) when the effect as a logical mark is considered in relation to its place, time, and other factors; thus, these [causal relations] are indeed invariably existent.
Nor is there futility, because activity undertaken for the sake of establishing [the existence of] living beings and so forth can indeed be fruitful;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), defects in the cause and other such factors are included.
Granted that the word is authoritative with respect to the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*);

nevertheless, what here is the subject (*dharmin*), what is the probandum (*sādhya*), and how is the relationship established, such that—by virtue of the presence of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*)—it would be included within inference and not constitute a separate means of valid cognition? To this he says: "With respect to the intention. And when the intention is the object to be understood, its possession of the three characteristics is perfectly clear.
For that [nature] is to be proven as residing in the subject (dharmin), which is the male, by means of the word "effect."
This person is perceived as desiring to speak about the meaning of the word "tree," because he is the user of the word "tree," just as I was in my previous states.

Where a speaker is perceived, the person is the subject (*dharmin*) and the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*); and in that case, the connection [between the word and the intention] is already established within one's own continuum. However, where no speaker is perceived, there the location (*pradeśa*) qualified by a person is the subject to be proven.
For even a location certainly possesses the quality of being a cause for sound.
Because one hears different kinds of sounds in mountain caves and similar places.
Therefore, in cases where others have rejected the three-fold character of the mark (*trairūpya*) and so forth regarding external objects,
we do not at all accept the validity of words in those instances.
But where this [triple nature] of theirs is intended, there it is clearly threefold;
however, when the intention to speak is what is to be proven, the possession of the three characteristics has been elucidated.
This being the case, verbal testimony would be a form of inference, like smoke and so forth,
because it possesses the three characteristics [of a valid reason] and because its object exists as such.

With the words "Therefore," and so forth, he states that the reason—"because it lacks the three characteristics"—is futile when the probandum is that sound is an inference in relation to external objects, since this would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

However, with the words "Where... and so forth, he states that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhatā*) in relation to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), because the three characteristics of sound have been demonstrated in relation to that intention.
Thus concludes the investigation into verbal testimony.
Concerning analogy (*upamāna*), he says "of what kind" and so forth:
"When a forest-dweller is asked by city-dwellers, 'Of what kind is a *gavaya*?', he speaks these words: 'As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*.'"
In this regard, its status as an analogy is well-known; however, in the Śabara [Bhāṣya], because it is not excluded from scripture (āgama), it is described in quite another way.
When one is asked, "What is a gavaya like?", the statement, "As is a cow, so is a gavaya," is well-known among the elder Naiyāyikas as being the nature of comparison (*upamāna*).

However, in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, Śabarasvāmin, considering that such a form of comparison is already included within verbal testimony (*śabda*) and thus it is not logical for it to be a separate means of knowledge, described a different kind of comparison:
"Comparison produces a cognition regarding an object not present [to the senses] based on similarity."
As [stated] by this passage: "Just as the sight of a gavaya [gives rise to] the recollection of a cow."
Desiring to explain this very point, he says: "Having seen a cow," and so forth.
When this person, having seen a cow in the forest, beholds a gavaya that possesses many common features [with the cow] and has a curved neck;
At that time, his cognition of the gavaya, which apprehends its mere form and is specifically conceptual,
is indeed perception itself.
"This animal has a form similar to a cow"— such [a cognition],
which arises when the operation of the sense faculties is present, is held to be the perception of the universal (jāti).

Having previously seen a cow and later gone to the forest, when one sees a *gavaya*, what kind of animal is it? It possesses many commonalities of parts—that is, it shares numerous similarities of its constituent parts—and has a rounded neck, being devoid of a dewlap (*sāsnā*). At that time, the initial non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perceptual awareness (*ālocanājñāna*) that arises, grasping merely the essential nature of the *gavaya*, is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, that which arises in the specific form of conceptualizing, "This animal is similar to a cow"—this too is certainly perception, because it arises through the operation of the sense organ (*akṣavyāpāra*).

It might be argued: "By the power of memory, a similarity that is actually non-existent arises through conceptualization, and not through the operation of the sense organs. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"In that case, even though that cognition arises after remembering the cow... and so forth.

"In that case, even though that cognition [of similarity] arises after remembering the cow, it would nonetheless fall within the range of the sense organs because of the presence [of the similarity] residing in the gavaya."
Although that cognition which apprehends similarity is preceded by memory, nevertheless, because it resides in the gavaya and is thus present, the similarity is within the range of the senses.
"Presence" (sannidhi) means being present (sannihitatva).
"Because it resides in the gavaya" is the reason for its presence.
Because the similarity resides in the gavaya, therefore its proximity [is established].
"But surely, since similarity resides in two things, how is its apprehension in one place, the gavaya, logical? To this he says: "For like a universal," and so forth.
"For similarity, like a universal, is fully present in each [of the two];
because it is perceived even when the correlative is not seen."
It is called "possessing a universal" (*sāmānyavat*) because it exists as something equal by virtue of the universal.

Although similarity resides in two things, nevertheless, since the state of possessing the universal is complete in each individual, it is indeed perceived even in one instance—such as a cow—even when the counter-correlate is not seen, because [the similarity] is present there.

It might be argued: "If similarity were a real entity (*vastu*), then it would be perceived; however, its status as a real entity is not established. To this he says, "Of similarity," and so forth: "And the reality of similarity cannot be denied;
it is the connection of many common parts with another class [of things]."

Similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the relationship characterized by the inherence (*samavāya*) of many common parts, such as the horns and so forth of cows and the like, within a single individual belonging to another genus, such as the *gavaya*.

Furthermore, a relationship is not absolutely distinct from its relata, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of cognitions such as "relationship" and so on.
The term "another genus" (*jātyantara*) is employed to indicate that there is no similarity where all common parts of the same genus are present.

Now, showing the essential nature of comparison (upamā), he says: "In that [state]... That cognition which operates within that very same state—namely, "This individual cow is equal to this animal"—is comparison.

The cognition that arises with the form "a cow is similar to this animal being perceived," having as its object a cow that is not present to the senses, is the means of valid cognition known as comparison (upamāna).
Showing its object of cognition (*prameya*), he says "therefore," and so forth:

"Therefore, that which is remembered, as qualified by similarity, would be the object of cognition of analogy (*upamāna*); or else, the similarity itself, as residing therein [in the remembered object], would be the object."

Since comparison (upamāna) possesses the characteristics as previously described, therefore that which is remembered—such as a cow—as qualified by its similarity to a gavaya and so forth, is the object of knowledge (prameya) for comparison;
or else, it is simply the similarity itself residing in the cow and so forth.

[Page 446] But surely similarity has been apprehended by perception, and the cow has already been made an object by memory; so what further additional object of knowledge (*prameya*) is there, through the comprehension of which analogy (*upamāna*) would possess the status of a valid means of cognition? To this he says: "By perception," etc.
When the similarity has been perceived through direct perception and the cow has been remembered,
comparison (upamāna) possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because that [cow] as qualified [by similarity] cannot be established by any other means.

Even though similarity is grasped by perception and the cow is made an object by memory, nevertheless, because the cow-individual as qualified by similarity is not established through either perception or memory,
comparison (*upamāna*) possesses authority regarding its cognition.
Regarding this very point, he states an illustration: "Even in the case of perception...
Just as even when the location is perceived and the fire is being remembered, inference does not lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because its object is specific.

Just as, even when the locus such as a location is perceived and fire is apprehended through memory, inference is not invalid—because its object is the location as qualified by fire—but is indeed valid; so too it is with comparison.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let it be a means of valid cognition; however, how is that comparison (upamāna) a distinct means of cognition from perception and the others? To this he says:
"Not so," for it is not possible for a cognition to be established as perception at that time, because it is devoid of the operation consisting in the contact between the sense organ and its object.
Furthermore, because the three characteristics [of a valid reason] are untenable, it cannot be an inference;
for the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the other [characteristics] are not possible here in any way whatsoever.
For similarity previously perceived is not grasped as a property (dharma);
and when it is being perceived in the gavaya, it does not serve as an inferential mark for cows.
To begin with, perception is not tenable because [the cognition] does not arise from the contact of a sense faculty with its object.
Nor is it inference, due to the absence of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*).

For in this case, one must postulate either similarity as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), or the gavaya and so forth which are actually perceived. And if that similarity were postulated as the inferential mark (*liṅga*), there would be two alternatives: it would have to be conceived as residing in the cow, or as residing in the gavaya.

In that regard, similarity residing in the object of cognition—the cow and so forth—cannot first be the logical mark (*liṅga*), because it has not been apprehended prior to the perception of the *gavaya*.
Nor is it logical for something unapprehended to function as a logical mark, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

One might then argue that the similarity residing in the *gavaya* will be the logical mark, since it is apprehended there; to this he replies: "And that which is being apprehended in the *gavaya* does not lead to the inference of cows, because it resides in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*), like the blackness of a crow [does not prove anything about a person]."

[Page 447] To the objection that, "after seeing a *gavaya*, this [similarity] will serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the cow because it has already been apprehended," he says: "The proposition" (*pratijñā*). Because it is a part of the meaning of the proposition itself, that which resides in the cow cannot be a logical mark; and since the *gavaya* lacks a necessary connection, it does not attain the status of being a logical mark for the cow.
Since similarity is the object of cognition (*prameya*), it is not logical for that very same thing to function as the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
To the objection that "the gavaya, then, will be the inferential mark," he replies: "The gavaya.
Even here, because of the difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇatva*), the gavaya cannot be the inferential mark.

"In that case, let there be no validity for analogy," [the opponent] says; to this, [the author] replies with "And it is not invalid," and so forth: "And that cognition is not invalid, because it reveals an object not previously known, since prior to seeing the gavaya, its similarity [to the cow] was not apprehended."
Since the cow qualified by similarity to a gavaya was not previously apprehended,
it is logical that this cognition possesses validity, as it brings to light the cow through the previously unknown attribute of similarity.
He refutes [this] with the words beginning "prameya" (the object of cognition):
"Since there is no real entity that is an object of cognition, its status as a means of valid cognition is not intended;
for if similarity were to exist, it would consist in the connection with many common parts."

Universals have already been refuted; how then could there be a multiplicity of them? And if their connection [with particulars] were the means of valid cognition, then that which establishes it must exist.
And the universal possesses both substantial reality and perceptibility,
because it is an object of cognition other than non-existence, just like a unique particular entity.

Because there is no object of cognition (prameya) [corresponding to it], just like a means of valid cognition distinct from the six [accepted] means of valid cognition, analogy (upamāna) is therefore not a means of valid cognition.

If it is argued that there exists an object of cognition consisting of similarity (sādṛśya), which is characterized by the connection with many common parts, and thus the reason [for its non-existence] is unestablished (asiddha)— that is not so.

Since universals have been refuted in the "Examination of Universals" (*Sāmānyaparīkṣā*), there is no plurality among them, nor is there any connection with them; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
This might be argued: "There certainly exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes universals; therefore, the reason is indeed unestablished."

In this regard, the proof is as follows: "The universal (*sāmānya*) is a real entity (*vastu*)," and "it is thus apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). These are the two propositions (*pratijñā*).
"Because it is a cognizable object other than non-existence" is the reason (*hetu*).
The meaning is: because its nature is that of a cognizable object other than the cognizable object that is non-existence (*abhāva*).
"Like a unique entity" is the illustration;
it is the definition of being a unique entity.
With the words beginning "abhāva," he states the refutation: for those who maintain that the object [of inference] is a universal (sāmānya) included within the category of non-existence,
there is a lack of proof regarding the first probandum, and furthermore, [the reason] would be a part of the meaning of the thesis itself.

In the phrase "sāmānyārtha" (the object that is a universal), the word *artha* refers to the object of cognition (*prameya*). Since for Buddhists—who maintain that universals lack intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*)—there is no existence of a universal distinct [from particulars], the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in both propositions.

Furthermore, in the first thesis, where the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is characterized as a real entity (*vastu*), the reason suffers from the fallacy of being a part of the very meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśabhāva*).

For indeed, a thing is nothing other than the negation of non-existence, since the definition of existence is the exclusion of non-existence; thus, that very same [thing] is presented under a different name as the reason.
And since that is also the probandum, there is the fallacy of the reason being a mere part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).
Furthermore, analogy is not a means of valid cognition because its nature is that of memory, just like any other memory.
Demonstrating that its nature is indeed memory, he says "In this way," and so forth:
"But in that case, [the cognition] is properly connected with the parts of the cow's form..."
Certain parts of the gavaya are the causes for the cognition of similarity.
In that case, when the gavaya is seen, there arises in him a memory of those parts of the cow's form which have been seen many times before.
For this very reason, when a gavaya is seen, our cognition does not occur [as "this is a cow"] by way of its similarity to a horse and so forth; otherwise, what would be the difference?

By their very nature, even in the absence of a real entity called "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), certain parts of the *gavaya* serve as the causes for conceptual cognitions that involve a common reflective judgment (*tulyapratyavamarśa*) alongside the parts belonging to the cow. There is no distinct entity named "similarity" other than those parts which are the causes of the common reflective judgment, because no such separate entity appears in the cognition. Therefore, upon seeing a *gavaya*, there arises in regard to the parts belonging to the cow a cognition in the form of a memory—produced by the force of repeated observation—but it does not grasp an entity called "similarity."

Otherwise, since a connection with many common parts exists even in the case of horses and the like, why would a cognition not arise there as well upon seeing a gavaya, just as it does regarding a cow?
For there is no distinction here, as similarity is present in both cases.
"Otherwise" means: [if this were not the case].
If they were not seen repeatedly, this fault would arise;
however, in the case of memory, this fault does not apply, because memory occurs only with respect to that which has been previously seen repeatedly.
Furthermore, this is due to the specific, restricted capacities of the causes that awaken memory.
It might be argued: "Let it be that this is memory; nevertheless, why is memory itself not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa)? To this he says, beginning with "vijñāta":
"Because it reveals an object already known, this [memory] is therefore not a valid means of knowledge.
How, then, could there even be the status of a separate means of knowledge for it?"
"This" refers to memory.
Having conceded that similarity is a real entity, he states the invalidity of comparison (*upamāna*) according to the opponent's own view with the words "Or let it be," and so forth:
"Or let similarity be a real entity; however, like a universal (*sāmānya*), it resides in the cow."
Even when the counter-positive is not perceived, that which is actually seen standing before one [is apprehended].
And thus, its nature as a form of recollection does not cease in any way;
for similarity within the cow-nature is cognized by its mere existence.
However, the similarity with the gavaya is not thus ascertained;
rather, it is through comparison that one cognizes its dissimilarity from what was previously remembered.

Granted that similarity is a real entity and, like a universal (*sāmānya*), is fully present in its entirety [in each individual]; nevertheless, when a cow standing before one is apprehended by perception prior to seeing a *gavaya*, that similarity—which is non-different from the cow—is already apprehended as being present before one, just like the very nature of the cow itself.
Otherwise, its non-difference would not be established.
Consequently, because it is the apprehension of what has already been apprehended and thus possesses the nature of memory (*smṛti*), it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It might further be argued that although similarity was previously apprehended in its mere existence, it was not apprehended in this specific form—namely, "this is the similarity of the cow with the gavaya";
however, analogy (upamāna) cognizes it in this very form, and therefore its character as a form of memory is unestablished.
Regarding this, he says "yadi nāma" and so forth:
"Even if it was not previously grasped by that very name,
it was nonetheless grasped by its own nature, which is what constitutes its essence."
Even if the cow-substance, as qualified by the name "similarity to a gavaya," was not apprehended prior to the sight of the gavaya, its own essential nature (svarūpa) was indeed apprehended;
that is to say, its intrinsic essence was apprehended.
To the question "What is that essential nature?", he says: "That which is designated as its self."
That which is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that lump of clay is designated as its "self" (*ātman*);
by means of that essential nature, characterized as its own inherent being (*svabhāva*), it is grasped—this is the meaning.
If it is indeed apprehended, what follows? To this he says: "Neither name nor form," and so forth.
If there were no apprehension of that which is neither name nor form among entities, then even for those who have fully realized the true nature of the self, there would be a state of non-cognition.

Indeed, the name is not the very nature (svarūpa) of things, such that if that name were not previously apprehended, there would be no apprehension of the object even when it has been grasped; and especially for one who maintains that perception is determinate in nature, it is not proper to say that [the object] was "not apprehended."
And if the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were established by this much alone,
there would be no limit to the number of means of valid cognition, since they could also be means of valid cognition in other ways.

Furthermore, if another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to be postulated on the mere basis of a slight similarity such as the cognition "this is similar to that," it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

[For it has been said: "Perception, inference, verbal testimony along with comparison, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and non-existence (*abhāva*)—these six are the means of establishing what is to be proven."
Thus, there would be a limitation to the number of means of valid cognition.
Demonstrating that very same over-extension, he says "tarupaṅktyādi" and so forth:
"Upon seeing a row of trees and the like, from the sight of a single tree and the cognition of a second tree, there arises the determination: 'This is that [first one].'"
If it is argued that [recognition] is not a separate means of valid cognition because it does not depend on similarity and so forth,
and because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, then the same [objection] applies to analogical cognition as well.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of rows of ants and the like is intended.
At the time of perceiving a row of trees and so forth, the determination "this is the first tree" does not arise from the perception of the first tree alone.
However, when the second tree is apprehended, the determination that arises regarding the first tree—"this is the first tree"—would have to be a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Why?
Because it does not depend on similarity and so forth.
Since it does not depend on similarity, this is not an analogy (*upamāna*).
It is not perception because it does not depend on the operation of the senses;
it is not inference because it does not depend on a logical mark (liṅga);
and it is not verbal testimony because it is independent of words.
It is not presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because it does not depend on a perceived or heard object that would otherwise be inexplicable.
It is not non-existence (*abhāva*), because it depends on the cessation of both means of knowledge and their objects.
Likewise: "This was before this; this is after; this is long, this is short, this is large."
It must be stated that in such cognitions as these, the consequence follows that they would be considered valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that this is not a distinct means of knowledge because it is a memory (*smṛti*) and thus apprehends what has already been apprehended, [we reply:]...
The same applies to analogies (*upamā*) as well:
they consist of apprehending what has already been apprehended.
The plural form in "in analogies" (*upamāsu*) is used because there is a plurality of individual instances.
And when a gavaya is perceived, there arises a cognition of its dissimilarity to a horse and so forth; why is that not another type of valid cognition?
If it is argued that [the cognition] is not included within non-existence, it is not so, because it relies upon existence;
or, in the case of mutual non-existence, it is the same regarding cognitions of similarity.

Furthermore, just as the cognition of similarity in a cow based on the sight of a gavaya is established as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why should the cognition of dissimilarity in a horse and so forth based on the sight of a gavaya not also be established as a distinct means of valid cognition?
If it is argued that it is not a distinct means of valid cognition because it is included within the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva*),
this is not tenable.
Why?
Because it has existence as its objective support;
for non-existence has non-existence as its object.
It might be argued:
"Dissimilarity (vaisādṛśya) is indeed the absence of similarity; therefore, it is certainly included within non-existence. To this he says, "If there were mutual non-existence," and so forth.

If, while mutual non-existence exists, a non-existent object of cognition (*prameya*) is established, then such an object of cognition is equal—that is, identical—to those cases of similar cognition which are intended as analogies (*upamāna*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "Of similarity," and so forth.
For just as the distinction of similarity is cognized there, so too is the distinction of all common parts understood.

Just as in that case of the cognition of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-jñāna*), the distinction from similarity is perceived, so too in the cognition of similarity (*sādharmya-jñāna*), the absence of all commonalities of parts is understood; thus, there would be an inclusion within non-existence (*abhāva*), just like the cognition of dissimilarity.
Regarding this very point, he states the proof, beginning with "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*):
"If [an object] is apprehended through the connection with many commonalities of parts (*avayavasāmānya*),
then it would follow that its true nature (*tattva*) consists in the connection with the commonalities of all its parts."
"By which" is an instruction regarding the cause;

that is to say, "by which," meaning "because," in the cognition of similarity (*sādharmya*), the connection with the generalities of many parts is apprehended, but not the connection with the generalities of all parts; therefore, even here, there is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Otherwise, if there were a connection with the commonality of all parts,
then it would follow as a logical consequence that the essence of "cowness" belongs to the *gavaya*.

Some maintain that comparison (*upamā*) is the cognition of the connection between a name and its referent, occurring upon the perception of an object with a similar nature to one previously heard from a statement concerning a particular place.
"By some" refers to the Naiyāyikas. They state the definition of analogy (*upamāna*) as follows: "Analogy is the means of establishing what is to be established through well-known similarity."

That which has a well-known similarity, or whose similarity with something well-known exists, is the *gavaya* characterized by "well-known similarity" (*prasiddhasādharmya*). Based on that, the means of establishing—the proof—of the object to be established, namely the relationship between a name and the thing named, is *upamāna*.

For this very meaning has been stated by others in a different manner: "Upamāna is the comprehension of the connection with a designation [arising] from the cognition of similarity, depending upon the recollection of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by authoritative testimony (*āgama*)."

The statement "the gavaya is like a cow" is the traditional instruction (*āgama*). The quality (*guṇa*) called a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) which is deposited by that [instruction] gives rise, through the sight of a gavaya in the forest, to the recollection of the meaning of that traditional instruction; the cognition of similarity which depends upon that [recollection] is what has been described as such.
"Designation" (*samākhyā*) means a name, that is to say, a word (*śabda*).
Therefore, the apprehension of the relationship between that [similarity] and the object is analogy; thus, the meaning is exactly the same.

Regarding that, he states the refutation with the words "tatrāpi" and so forth: "In that case as well, the unconfused comprehension of the connection between the name and its referent would occur only at the very moment of hearing that extended application statement."
Likewise, because it apprehends an object already grasped, analogy lacks the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
just like memory, due to its lack of an instrumental function.

In that case, since the cognition of the relationship between the name and the object has already arisen at the time of hearing the extended application statement (*atideśavākya*), the subsequent cognition—because it apprehends what has already been apprehended—is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like memory. One might argue: "Even if it apprehends what has already been apprehended, it will still possess validity; what contradiction is there here? To this he says: "Because of the lack of the sense of being an instrument" (*karaṇārthaviyogataḥ*).
The sense of being an instrument is the state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*), [a status] which exists through its operation upon an action that has not yet been accomplished.

It might be argued: "Previously, the comprehension of the connection with the name had not occurred at all; therefore, because it would be grasping what has already been grasped, the reason is unestablished. To this he says:
"Now, even if that [comprehension] has not arisen, one nevertheless understands:
'This is that for which the name was heard by me'—how could that be then?"
If the comprehension of the connection with the name had not previously arisen, then this cognition in the form "This is that gavaya whose name was heard by me before" would not have occurred.
He states the proof for this very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*):
"For instance, when one perceives a gavaya without having heard its name,
no one is able to know that 'this is the name heard by him.'"
But Aviddhakarṇa says that one understands [the object] in a general way through scripture, whereas the understanding of its specific details comes from analogy (*upamāna*).
Therefore, he anticipates that view with the words "if analogy has been employed.
That is, if analogy has been employed when there is a grasping of similarity...
One understands the relationship by means of its having a specific object.
He for whom the simile and the sentence of extension have been employed is described as such.
He explains the meaning of this very point with the second verse, beginning with "For from scripture" (āgamāddhi):
"For he knows that relation through scripture as having a universal for its object;
but he cognizes it as having a particular for its object by relying on analogy."
The specific object is the gavaya.
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (surely):
"Surely, elsewhere [it is held] that there is no cognition of a relation through a name;
for the cognition of that [name] in another object would lead to an over-extension."
The word "no" (na) is connected with the word "is appropriate" (yujyate).

For when a connection with a name has been understood in one context, it is not logical for that same name to be understood as referring to a different object, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Demonstrating that very same over-extension, he says: "For indeed,
when someone has grasped the name 'Citrāṅgada,' they do not later recognize that same word as referring to one who wears a beautiful crown."
Therefore, previously, when this was known by the intellect as an external object within that conceptual reflection— which is designated by the name "universal"— it was so perceived.

Even when perceiving a gavaya, one understands it as being in that very place; one who does not discern the distinction between the perceived object and its mental construction conceives of it as being external.

*Aṅgada* is an ornament called a bracelet; one who possesses such a variegated *aṅgada* is thus described. For when someone is told, "Devadatta is Citrāṅgada," that person does not, at a later time, apply the word *Citrāṅgada* to Yajñadatta, who wears a crown.
A *kirīṭa* is a crown; one who possesses that beautiful crown is thus described.
Therefore, let there be no over-extension [of the term].

In whatever object a name is apprehended by a cognition that—though superimposing conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—determines it as an external object, that name is understood to apply to that very [conceptualized] thing even when a *gavaya* is perceived, and not to the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) called "gavaya."
And that very conceptual reflection is conventionally designated as the "universal";
it is imagined,
because it has been refuted.
If that is so, how then does the conceit of an external particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) arise? To this, he says "the visible," and so forth.

Now, [the author] asks: "What contradiction is there in the application of words and so forth to the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)? and says: "In this way," and so on. And it should be understood that conceptual constructions (vikalpa) and verbal expressions (dhvani), which have the particular characteristic as their object, have also been refuted in detail.

Since, in the "Examination of Words and Objects," it was refuted in detail that words and conceptual constructions have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, therefore the referent of a word is nothing other than that which is superimposed by conceptual construction.
Even though those [objects] fall within their range, it is indeed inference alone that occurs;
and its being produced from a three-featured logical mark (trirūpaliṅga) is understood in this very way.
For that which is similar to a cow is indeed the object of the word "gavaya," just like the gavaya present in the intellect at the time of grasping the convention.
Or, let it be granted that those conceptual words have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object;
even so, because it is included within inference itself, analogy (*upamāna*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Anticipating the objection—"How can this be included within inference without being produced by a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*)?"—the author states "trirūpa... and so forth, in order to demonstrate that it is indeed produced by a mark possessing the three characteristics.

The reason (*hetu*) is "being similar to a cow"; the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is "being within the range of the word 'gavaya'"; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the mentally present *gavaya* appearing in conceptual cognition at the time of grasping the linguistic convention;
and the subject (*dharmin*) is the *gavaya* currently being perceived.
It might be argued: "At the time of establishing the convention, 'the gavaya is like a cow,' the gavaya has not yet been established in the mind;
therefore, the example is unestablished. To this, he says: "Even though it is present in the mind," and so forth. [The verse continues:
"Even if it were present in the mind, if it were not [present] at that stage..."
In what respect is this convention established, and in what way is it similar to a cow?
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that it is not only [the object] that is not within the range of the eye.

If nothing conforming to the similarity with a cow were to appear in the cognition, then on what basis would this convention—"this is similar to a cow"—be established? Yet, the convention is indeed established; therefore, one must admit that some form conforming to the similarity with a cow, residing in the cognition, appears at the time of the convention.

Thus, having first accepted the relation between word and object as the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for analogy (*upamāna*), it has been demonstrated that this [analogy] lacks validity because it apprehends what is already apprehended and because it is included within inference (*anumāna*). Now, there is no further relation distinct from the related entities themselves, and those two related entities have not been apprehended by any other means of knowledge. For instance, at the time of the convention, the word was apprehended by auditory cognition, and subsequently, the *gavaya* standing before one was apprehended by the eye; so what further object of knowledge remains, by virtue of which analogy might possess validity?
Establishing this, he says: "There is no relation," and so forth.
It has already been proven that there is no relation existing apart from the related entities;
furthermore, at the time of the convention, the word was already grasped by the auditory consciousness.
This animal standing before one is seen by the eye;
however, the synthesis of two things known separately is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*).
Because it involves the apprehension of a connection— just as in the case of [the perception of] fragrance and sweetness—
the cognition of the application of that name does not transcend the nature of memory.
By this, he states that [comparison] is not a valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇya*) because it apprehends what has already been apprehended;
this was established in the "Examination of the Category of Quality" (*Guṇapadārthaparīkṣā*).

It might be argued: "Even if the two related entities are apprehended separately by the cognitions of the auditory organ and so forth, their connection (*ghaṭanā*) is performed by comparison; therefore, comparison would possess validity through that connection. To this, he says "separately," and so on.
"Like 'fragrant,' 'sweet,' and so forth":
here the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the locative (*sapramyarthe*).

The meaning is that just as in cases such as "that which is being experienced by the Buddha is sweet" or "it is fragrant," the cognition whose nature consists in the apprehension of a connection with an object is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too this [cognition] ought not to be one either.

Therefore, the cognition of the connection with a name—that is, the knowledge of the relation between a name and its referent—does not transcend the nature of memory, according to the principle already stated.

It might be argued: "The connection with a name is not established anywhere by way of similarity; rather, it is observed to be made directly by pointing out the named object itself, as in 'this is a cow,' and not when the object is beyond the senses. To this, he says "ananta... and so forth: "And cognitions of the application of names, produced through infinite means, arise even without depending on similarity, as in the case of kings and others."
"Samākhyā-yoga-saṃvidah" means cognitions of the connection with designations; "in Narapā and others" refers to [the case of] Narapā and so forth.
Among kings and others.
To demonstrate that very state of being produced by the final means, he states the example beginning with "sitātapatra": "The lord of men, whose feet are shielded from the sun by a white parasol,
stands in their midst"— this is declared according to the specific instruction.

When that [object] is seen at a later time, the cognition that "this has that name" would then have to be considered a different means of valid cognition (pramā), because it does not depend upon similarity or other such factors.
For example, suppose someone says to another, "Go on this business to see the lord of men as he goes along with many men mounted on elephants, horses, and so forth.
He replies, "Which among them is the lord of men?
He says, "The one among them under whose white umbrella the rays of the sun—the feet of the sun—are concealed, he is the lord of men."

Having received that instruction and gone there, upon seeing the king distinguished by the aforementioned characteristics, the cognition that arises—"This is he who was named Narādhipati"—would also, according to your view, result in yet another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Why? Because:
Because it does not depend on similarity and so forth;
by this, he demonstrates that it is not included within the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Aviddhakarṇa, however, maintains that there are only two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and that there is no object of cognition (prameya) other than the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa). To refute this, [the author] provides the following proof: "Perception (pratyakṣa) is accompanied by another means of valid cognition distinct from inference (anumāna), because it is a means of valid cognition, just like inference.

Or alternatively: "Inference is accompanied by another means of valid cognition distinct from perception, because it is a means of valid cognition, just like perception. Likewise: "The particular characteristic is accompanied by another object of cognition distinct from the universal characteristic, because it is an object of cognition, just like the universal characteristic."

Or else: the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) is accompanied by another object of cognition distinct from the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), because it is an object of cognition, just like the particular characteristic.
This very point he expresses with the word "anya" (other).
Another [proponent] establishes the existence of another means of valid cognition through the power of inference:
that perception is conjoined with another means of valid cognition distinct from inference.
Because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) like inference, inference is likewise [dependent on a logical mark].
This reason is not at all unconnected [to the probandum], because it reveals a sublation (*bādhā*).
In this very way, your position would contradict the fourfold nature of the means of valid cognition; whatever response you have to that [objection] will be the same here as well.
"Associated" (*saṅgata*) means "connected," that is to say, "accompanied by a second.
This is an elliptical expression; it should be understood as including the proof of other objects of cognition as well.

Since no subverting argument against the presence of the reason in the counter-example of the probandum has been presented, the necessary connection between the probandum and the probans has not been demonstrated; therefore, all these reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because their exclusion from the counter-example is doubtful.

Furthermore, the fixed number of four means of valid cognition—namely perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony—would be contradicted, because by this very same method other means of valid cognition would exist.

For instance, it could be argued as follows: "Perception is accompanied by another means of valid cognition distinct from inference, comparison, and verbal testimony, because it is a means of valid cognition, just like inference.

Moreover, the threefold nature of the objects of cognition (prameya) that is asserted—namely, the universal, the particular, and that which possesses both universal and particular characteristics—[would likewise be undermined].

That too would be contradicted, because it is possible to establish other objects of cognition in that very same manner; whatever response you have in this matter will also be ours, so enough of this prolixity.
Thus concludes the investigation of analogy.

With reference to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), he says: "When an object known through the six means of valid cognition cannot be otherwise [accounted for], and it leads one to postulate another unseen [fact], that is cited as presumptive testimony."

Arthāpatti is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which consists of a conceptual construction regarding an imperceptible object, such that an object determined by the six means of knowledge—namely perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, presumption (*arthāpatti*), and non-existence (*abhāva*)—in a certain place, time, and so forth, would otherwise be inexplicable; that is, the thought: "If such an object did not exist, this [observed fact] would not be possible. This was illustrated by Śabarasvāmin as follows: "The postulation of an unperceived [object] when a perceived or heard object is otherwise inexplicable."
For example, when Devadatta is alive, the postulation of his being outside based on not seeing him in the house.
"Seen" (dṛṣṭa) means apprehended by the five means of knowledge other than verbal testimony; "heard" (śruta) means understood through the means of verbal testimony.

In this regard, he states the examples for presumption (*arthāpatti*) preceded by the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in their respective order, beginning with "therein" (*tatra*), etc.: "Therein, from burning known through perception, there is the power to burn."
From the inferred movement of fire [in smoke], there is the possession of that power in the sun.

The potencies of all entities are established through the presumption based on their effects; and these potencies, being unprecedented, are understood even without the apprehension of a [prior] relationship.

Among these, presumption based on perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikārthāpatti*) is, for example, the postulation of the burning power of fire after having experienced the act of burning through perception.

Presumption based on inference (*anumānapūrvikā*) is, for example, the postulation of the sun’s possession of the capacity for motion following its inferred movement due to its arrival at another location. Furthermore, the capacities of all entities are always established by means of presumption based on the necessity of their effects.
This presumption (*arthāpatti*) is sometimes preceded by perception alone, as when the capacity of a cause is understood after perceiving its effect through direct perception.
However, when the capacity of a cause is understood after apprehending the effect through inference or other means, then the presumption of the effect is preceded by inference and so forth.
Those [presumptions] for which the means of proof is the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of the effect are described as such.
Nor can it be said that the causal capacity has already been apprehended previously, because those capacities are always understood as being new.
Therefore, since there is no apprehension of an object already apprehended, its status as a valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇya) is indeed established.

In this regard, one might argue that capacities (śaktayaḥ) are inferable through the mark of their effect (kāryaliṅga) and are not accessible through the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); to this he replies: "except for the apprehension of a relation" (sambandhagrahaṇādṛte).
Since they are understood without the apprehension of a relation, they are therefore not inferable.
Demonstrating that very absence of the apprehension of a relation, he says: "And not...

[na ca]. "Neither is a prior relation of these [words] with their effects apprehended, nor is another [relation] apprehended now, by virtue of which there might be here the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharma) and the positive concomitance (anvaya)."

Furthermore, the relationship between these potencies and their effects has not been apprehended prior to the time of inference, as is the case with fire and smoke in a kitchen or similar place, because those potencies are beyond the reach of the senses.
By this, the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is stated;
nor is the relationship apprehended now at the time of inference, precisely because they are beyond the reach of the senses.
By this, the absence of the property in the subject (pakṣadharmābhāva) is stated;
for it is illogical that the effect should be a property of the potencies residing in the cause.

Or, if one takes the position that the auditory faculty and so forth are [the subject], whatever reason is employed will all result in being "unestablished in its locus" (āśrayāsiddha), because the property-bearer (dharmin) is unestablished.

Furthermore, when the powers residing in the auditory organ and so forth are made the subject of the inference, then whatever reason (hetu) is employed to establish those powers within the subject of the auditory power and so on, every such reason would be unestablished in its substratum (āśrayāsiddha), because the powers that serve as the substrata are themselves unestablished. Therefore, all powers established through the presumption based on the effect (kāryārthāpatti) are not inferable.
Upon hearing such statements as, "Fat, he does not eat during the day," the resulting cognition of his eating at night is called presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*).

In that regard, presumption based on verbal testimony (*śābdapramāṇapūrvikārthāpatti*) is, for example, the postulation of such a meaning as "he eats at night" upon hearing a statement such as, "Devadatta is fat, has not taken any elixirs, and does not eat during the day."
It might be thought that the meaning "he eats at night" is understood from this very sentence, "Devadatta is fat and does not eat during the day"; therefore, [the author] says:

"Nor is the referent of words such as 'night' [understood]. Neither the referent of words such as 'night' nor the connection between the referents of words such as 'day' is apprehended in the sentence concerning the daytime.
There is no distinction by which that sentence could be the means of conveying it;
furthermore, because it is occupied with another meaning, there can be no postulation of a second meaning.
Therefore, this [meaning] is understood through another sentence present in the mind;
thus, even though it has not yet arrived, that sentence is apprehended.
The means of valid cognition for that [Veda] must be stated among perception and the others;
however, perception is certainly not accepted in the case of a sentence that has not been uttered.
This is not inference, for it is never [established] together with an example;
yet, if the status of being a logical mark (liṅga) is admitted even when a relationship has not been perceived.
By the mere utterance of that [word], the comprehension of the entire sentence occurs;
because it is devoid of [external] relations, it is not distinguished from anything else.
For the meaning of a sentence is of two kinds: namely, conjunction (*saṃsarga*) and exclusion (*bheda*).
Among these, conjunction is the non-differentiation of word-meanings from one another, like milk and water;
and exclusion is their existence in a relationship of that which is excluded and that by which it is excluded.
Alternatively, *saṃsarga* (relation) is the fixed connection between the means and the end to be accomplished,
while *bheda* (distinction) is the exclusion of heterogeneous things;
this twofold meaning of a sentence is not possible [in the case of an eternal Vedic injunction].
For instance, the meaning of words such as "day" (divā) is not the meaning of "eating at night" (rātribhojana) in the form of a connection (*saṃsarga*), because they are absolutely distinct;
nor is it in the form of a distinction (*bheda*), because the words "day" and so forth do not function by way of excluding non-night.
Now, suppose it is thought that "he eats at night" is another, second meaning of the very sentence concerning daytime; to this he says, "having another purpose.

Since [the sentence] is exhausted by the mere prohibition of eating during the day and so forth, it is not capable of simultaneously establishing another matter, namely eating at night and so forth; thus, there is no basis for postulating a second meaning.
Therefore, "he eats at night" is the meaning of a different sentence altogether.
"By the Buddhists" indicates that it is not based on verbal testimony;
"even though it is not derived from scripture" means even though it is not based on verbal testimony.
Since the absence of verbal nature has been established by the aforementioned reasoning,

one must state the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends that sentence which is understood as "he eats at night. That means of valid cognition would have to be one of the [six], such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.
And yet it does not so occur;
therefore, the point is that this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, while refuting its being any one of the [standard] types such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, he says "nanu" and so on.
In that case, it is not logical for the unuttered sentence regarding eating at night to be considered perception, because it is not being heard.
Nor can it be considered inference, due to the absence of a [logical] connection.
For this sentence concerning eating at night has never been observed in conjunction with that sentence concerning the daytime [meal], such that a connection could exist between them.
Nor is there any other indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Furthermore, one might argue that even if the relationship [between the mark and the object] is not perceived, it will still function as an indicative mark; to this, he says "yadi" (if).

For if something whose relationship is unestablished could function as an indicative mark, then from the utterance of the sentence concerning the day, there would follow the comprehension of all possible sentences, and not just the sentence concerning eating at night.
Why?
Because, being devoid of a [logical] connection, the sentence regarding eating at night does not differ from any other sentence;
that is to say, due to the absence of a connection, every sentence is equally indistinguishable.

He states [the type of inference] preceded by analogy (*upamāna*) with the words "gavaya," etc.: "The capacity to be apprehended by that cognition which is a cow as analogized to a *gavaya* is cognized through the power produced by the force of analogy."

That capacity of the individual cow, which has been compared by means of a gavaya, to be grasped through the cognition of comparison—that capacity which arises by the force of comparison—is measured by presumption (*arthāpatti*).
He states the [inference] preceded by presumption (*arthāpatti*) in the passage beginning with "abhidhā" and so forth:

"The denotative function (*abhidhā*) cannot be established otherwise; having understood the expressive capacity [of words] through presumption alone—since there is no other way to account for it—" [one proceeds].
The certainty that sound is eternal is established by yet another *arthāpatti* (presumption):
for that which is non-eternal cannot maintain continuity through convention and linguistic usage.
Designation (*abhidhāna*) is the act of denoting; that is to say, the communication of meaning.

This would not be established for a word otherwise, without its expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*). Having understood—that is, having realized—this capacity to convey meaning, and because there is no other recourse for that non-expressive power except for the eternity of the word, the certainty of the word's eternity is established once again by means of another *arthāpatti* (presumption).
Furthermore, he explains how expression cannot be established without permanence by saying "for that which is impermanent," and so forth.
For instance, if what was perceived at the time of the convention were not to persist at the time of usage,
then the making of the convention would be entirely purposeless.
Because that [word] exists for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
and because at the time of such usage, the relationship between the word that persists and its [corresponding object] has not been previously grasped;
or else, because there is no other way to account for it.

Because there is no cognition of that word existing at the time of conventional usage as being anything other than the word perceived at the time of the convention—due to the determination of its non-difference—he asks, "How is there a determination of non-difference? and replies with the words beginning, "For it is impermanent," and so forth.

He states the presumption based on non-existence (*abhāvapūrvikārthāpatti*) with the words "pramāṇa" and so forth: "That which is described here as the establishment of Caitra’s existence outside the house, qualified by the absence of Caitra determined through the non-operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*)."
One should cite that other presumption (arthāpatti) which arises from non-existence;
for this too is distinct from inference because it lacks the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and other such factors.

When the object of cognition is either an external region distinguished by a particular thing, or that particular thing distinguished by a region, how can the absence of apprehension [of it] be a property of the subject (pakṣadharma)?
In this case, the absence from the house while alive is postulated as the property of the subject (pakṣadharma);
and the cognition of that [absence] does not arise without the cognition of his being outside.

But that absence from the house which is devoid of [the qualification of] being present [therein] is not a prover [of external existence], because it is observed even in the case of those who are dead, since their movement is outside.

When the absence of Caitra is determined—that is, ascertained—through the non-existence (nivṛtti) of means of valid cognition such as perception, one has a house qualified by that absence; from this [knowledge], namely "Caitra is not here in the house," while Caitra is alive, there arises the establishment of his being outside, in the form of the certainty "Caitra exists outside. This is what was described by Śabarasvāmin in this commentary (*bhāṣya*), and it is cited as an illustration to indicate other types of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). For example, when Devadatta is alive, the postulation of his being outside—which is unperceived—is based on his non-perception within the house.
This is an example of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) preceded by non-existence (*abhāva*).
Since logicians generally maintain that this [form of *arthāpatti*] is a type of inference (*anumāna*), the author states "the subject (*pakṣa*)" and so forth in order to refute that view.

Because its factors—such as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so on—are not constituent parts nor causes of it, it is therefore distinct from inference, just like perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For instance, there are two kinds of objects of cognition (*prameya*): either an object such as Caitra qualified by an external location, or an external location qualified by Caitra. Since both of these types of objects exist, how could the absence of an object such as Caitra from the house—being *vyadhikaraṇa* (residing in a different locus)—be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)?
The intention is that it could not be so at all.
Furthermore, if the absence from the house were conceived as a property of the subject, it would [only apply] in the case of a living Devadatta.
There are two positions: that the absence from the house is what is being conceptualized, or that it is [conceptualized] in a general sense.
Regarding these, he states the fault in the first position with the words "of one who is living," and so forth, and with the phrase "the cognition of that."
The cognition or certainty regarding that living Devadatta does not arise without having apprehended his existence outside [the house].
By this, he states that the reason is either unestablished (*asiddha*) or, if it were established, would constitute proving what is already established (*siddhasādhya*).

Furthermore, showing that even in the second case the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—because the absence from the house is observed even in the case of those such as Devadatta who are dead—he says: "But the absence from the house... [gehābhāvastu...].
"Being present" means the state of being alive.
Thus, there are six types of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Among these, by four [types] capacity (*śakti*) is the object of cognition; by one, the eternity of sound; and by another, an external substance.
With the words "In that regard," etc., he states the refutation: first of all, the definition here is untenable.
For instance: since a perceived object such as something seen or heard cannot be accounted for without that unseen [force], there is the postulation of the unseen.
In this regard, it is examined:
has a relationship between that unseen [force] and some perceived or heard object ever been observed, or not?
If, however, it has been perceived, there follows the consequence that it is an inference, because it is based on the means of perceiving a relation.

If, on the other hand, it is not established [as perceived], then in that case the non-burning nature of fire would also have to be postulated, since there is no distinction in its having an unperceived relation.
If it is thought that the non-burning nature is not postulated because fire has not been perceived as being accompanied by non-burning, [we reply:]...
In that case, even the property of being a burner (*dāhakatva*) need not be postulated, since it too has never been observed in connection with [the smoke] anywhere.
Therefore, once a relationship is established, it is logical to postulate a second related term upon seeing one related term that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*).
And if it were conceived in this way, since it would have the perception of a relation as its means, it would be included within inference itself.
Furthermore, the examples provided are also inappropriate.

Regarding the claim that "the capacity of an object already established through perception and other means is cognized by means of the four types of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)," he states a general refutation of this with the words beginning "tatra śaktātirekeṇa" (in that case, apart from the capacity...).

In that case, there is no such thing as "potency" (śakti) over and above the potent object itself which could be understood through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); for the potent object is indeed directly perceived.

Since power is not in reality anything other than the entity itself, and that potent object is indeed perceived through direct perception, [the inference] is not a valid means of knowledge because it apprehends what has already been apprehended.
The mention of "direct perception" (*adhyakṣa*) is merely illustrative.
With the words "of burning and so forth," etc., he states a specific refutation of the example of presumption based on perception:
"But as for the cause of burning and so forth, which is observed to be fire and the like—
what other power could there be than that [cause], such that it is free from doubt and error?"

But if the effects were distinct [from the cause], since it would be that [cause] alone which is employed [in their production], the entity would be a non-agent; for if there is employment [of the cause], it is not differentiated [from its own prior state].
For the nature capable of causal efficiency is the defining characteristic of power;
and thus this entity, being of such a nature, is determined through direct perception.
"Without doubt and without error" is an adverbial modifier of the action.

Now, if a distinct power (*śakti*) is admitted, then since it is the power alone that is operative toward the effects, the entity itself would result in being a non-agent; consequently, the consequence of its being a non-entity follows, because the definition of an entity is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

Now, if it is argued that utility must be admitted so as to avoid the consequence of [the entity] being a non-entity, then, when that utility is admitted, that power is not distinct—that is, separate.
Why?
Because whatever nature (svabhāva) is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), that alone is power; there is no other definition of power apart from this.

As for the designation "the power of an entity," which appears as if it were a distinct entity, that is simply the entity itself being spoken of in such a way when there is a desire to know only that [power], by excluding other differences.

It might be argued that the definition of capacity (*śakti*) is not the performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*); what then? It is something else entirely. To this he says "anyā" and so forth:
There is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for establishing a different definition;
even if it were known, it would serve no purpose, because the [desired] effect is accomplished through its form alone.

There is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for the establishment of another characteristic of power, by which such a means could distinguish this power from non-existence, which is characterized by the absence of all capacity.
Nor is there any purpose served for those seeking causal efficacy by knowing such a thing as that;
for the accomplishment of causal efficacy arises from the very nature of an entity that is useful by virtue of its own form.
As it has been said: "What is the use of investigations regarding that which is capable of purposeful action?
What is the point for a lustful woman to examine whether a eunuch is handsome or ugly?"
If another definition of capacity is understood through presumptive testimony based on an effect,
this cannot be so, for it exists in reality because the effect could not otherwise exist.

It might be argued: "There is indeed another definition of power (*śakti*), namely that its nature is that which is to be inferred because an effect would otherwise be impossible; thus, being inferable from an effect is the definition of power. This is not a valid definition of power.
Why?
Because the effect occurs otherwise;
that is, because the effect is established even without a distinct power (śakti).
To the question "How so?", he says: "For this indeed exists as a real entity (bhāva)."

Since this effect arises—that is, comes into being—from a certain entity or thing, the existence of the effect is possible even otherwise; so what is the use of postulating a separate, distinct power?
For fire, when perceived as distinct from water and other such things, is capable of burning and so forth; what need then is there for any other capacity?
Clarifying this very point, he says "water and so forth," etc.
If that power were not absolutely distinct, it too would possess a dual nature;
yet it could not exist because of contradiction, since it is also non-different from direct perception.

It might be argued: "This fault would indeed occur if we were to admit that power is absolutely distinct from the entity; however, what then? We hold that it is of a dual nature, being both distinct and non-distinct. But this too is not tenable.
Why is this so? He says: because of contradiction.

If [the two] are distinct, how could they be non-distinct at that very same time? Or, if they are non-distinct, how could they be distinct? It is a contradiction for two properties whose definitions consist in mutual exclusion to be perceived simultaneously in a single substratum.
Indeed, it has already been explained that otherness consists precisely in this: that one thing does not have the nature of the other, just as one self does not have the nature of another.

Granted that the power may possess a dual nature; nevertheless, that power which consists of both aspects is indeed perceptible, because even the distinctness of the power from the entity is observed—it is not exclusively non-distinct such that it would remain imperceptible.
Consequently, the claim that the power is eternally inferable solely through its effects would be contradicted.
And since its status as perception is established, the exclusion of its being an object of inference serves no purpose,
because an inference will not be sought regarding this subject.

Moreover, as for this exclusion of the capacity (*śakti*) from being an object of inference—stated in such passages as "the capacities of all entities are established through the presumption based on their effects"—it does not cause us any harm.
Why?
Because we do not accept inference with respect to this object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since inference consists in the cognition of objects that are beyond the senses (*parokṣa*).
By this, he states that what is to be proven is already established.

Regarding what was stated, "In the case of the capacity of the auditory organ and so forth," he says here: "But those entities such as the auditory organ which are not within the range of perception— their very existence, characterized as a capacity, is understood through an inferential mark."

But was it not previously established that existence itself is indeed what is being proven? How then can it be said that "existence is cognized"? To this he replies with the words beginning "kāraṇāntara-":
"For that cognition of sound and so forth depends upon other causes;
even when [the object] exists, it does not occur because of the absence of those other causes, just like a sprout and the like."

Existence is not established directly; rather, what is established is that the subject—the cognition of hearing and so forth—depends upon other causes. This is because, even when other causes of that [cognition], such as mental attention (*manaskāra*) and the like, are present, the cognition of hearing and so forth may still be absent.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever occurs only occasionally despite the presence of a certain thing depends upon other causes, just as a sprout occurs only occasionally despite the presence of earth and so forth.
Since the cognition of hearing occurs only occasionally despite the presence of mental attention and the rest, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

When it has been established that [the ear] depends on other causes, it is said that existence is understood in this manner—that those other causes are well-known as the ear and so forth—and not by way of direct perception; thus, there is no fault.

Regarding what was stated—"from the movement of the sun as inferred"—he says here, beginning with "upādāna": "And when the birth occurs continuously in a location not identical to that of its material cause... [p.464]
Just as in the case of a flame and the like, [the sun's] movement is perceived through its extension across different locations.
Because it is a specific quality of a stable entity, this [attainment] does not result in anything else;
its reaching another location is a distinct capacity, which has already been refuted.
By this, he states its inclusion within inference (*anumāna*).

For it is as follows: whatever is observed to reach another location necessarily arises by abandoning the location of its own material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), just like a flame or similar things reaching another location; and the sun likewise reaches another location—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).

Nor is this inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because for an entity that is stable and uniform in nature, such reaching of another location is not possible, since it would entail not abandoning its nature as restricted to its previous location.
Or, even in the case of abandonment, there is simply the production of something unprecedented;
this itself is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

It might be argued: "This presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) was cited with respect to the capacity (*śakti*) being established, not with respect to its production; so how can the inclusion of this *arthāpatti* within inference (*anumāna*) be asserted? To this he says: "But capacity has been refuted elsewhere."
Regarding the example of presumptive testimony based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), such as "Fat Devadatta," he says: "Fat," and so forth.
There is no certainty regarding the meaning "He is fat and does not eat during the day," because a person might speak otherwise due to the influence of hatred, delusion, and the like.
By this, he states that the fact of being preceded by verbal testimony (*śābdapramāṇa*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
It might be argued: "The implication of another sentence is not made by depending on the comprehension of the meaning from the first sentence;
rather, it is done by the first sentence alone. And that [meaning] is indeed established through direct perception. To this, he says: "without depending on the comprehension of the meaning."

If, moreover, another sentence with its own meaning were to be implied by [the first] without regard for the intended sense [of the former], then that would constitute an implication (ākṣepa) of one statement by another.

A sentence that does not depend on the comprehension of meaning is one that is independent of the comprehension of meaning (*arthagatyanapekṣa*). If, by means of such a mere sentence alone, another meaningful sentence were implied, then there would be an over-extension (*ākṣepa*); for the implication of yet another sentence would follow from the sentence regarding eating at night, because there is no distinction between them insofar as they lack a [necessary] connection. Now, if it is argued that the sentence implies the meaning because of its logical connection to the fact (*vastu*), then that fault remains when there is dependence on the comprehension of meaning.
With the words "Now, etc.," he raises an objection regarding the opponent's intention: "Now,
if it is held that the comprehension of the object occurs there by way of an apprehension,
or if it occurs through another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), let it be so."

Now, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), one might argue—following the principle that one must rely on the actual state of affairs—that the understanding of the meaning is intended here in the form of another person’s assent, because that other speaker has been accepted as trustworthy (*āpta*).
Or else, the knowledge [of the fact] "Devadatta is fat and does not eat during the day" may arise from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception (*pratyakṣa*).
To this, he replies with the words "Let it be," and so forth.
Let there be the comprehension of the matter of eating at night from that [fatness] qualified by the absence of eating during the day;

however, since another sentence present in the mind would not function as a communicator under such circumstances, it would be included within inference itself and not constitute a separate means of knowledge—this is the intended meaning.

Showing that very inclusion, he says "kṣapā" and so forth: A man associated with eating at night is understood to be desired [as the subject], because of his fatness despite the absence of eating during the day, like someone other than him.
The intended, specific person under discussion is one characterized by eating at night.
The reason (*hetu*) is "because of being fat despite the absence of any deficiency in eating.
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like other persons [who do not eat at night]."
And this is a reason based on an effect.
To the question, "How is the relationship of cause and effect established in this case? he says: "When there is food," and so forth.
When food is present, corpulence [occurs]; this is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Therefore, by virtue of that connection, there is the cognition of one thing from another thing in reality.

Since the causal relationship between fatness and eating is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just as that between fire and smoke, it is therefore logical to infer the actual fact of eating from the fact of fatness, because of their connection as cause and effect.
However, it is not logical for one sentence to be understood from another sentence that lacks a necessary connection, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
To demonstrate that very same over-extension, he says "sarvasambandha... and so forth:
"For how could a sentence devoid of all relations be understood?
Otherwise, everything would be understood from a single sentence."
How could a statement devoid of, or lacking, every kind of relationship—characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—be understood? It could not be understood at all.

For otherwise, even that which is devoid of every relationship would be understood; consequently, from any single object whatsoever, such as a jar, everything, including jars and so forth, would be understood.
But this is not the case; therefore, it must be admitted that comprehension arises from a necessary connection.
The phrase "for thus" (tathāhi) serves to support this very over-extension (atiprasaṅga): for if there were no relation, or if it existed but were not determined,
this sentence being understood would result in being invalid (apramāṇaka).
