The accepted position is that there must be a relation.
First of all, at any given time, there is simply no relation between one sentence and another sentence; even if a relation exists, if it is not ascertained, it is as good as non-existent.

Consequently, when a meaning is cognized while the relation remains unascertained, that cognition would lack a valid basis (*apramāṇaka*). It would be a cognition without foundation. And if cognition were without foundation, the absurd consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) that everything could be cognized from everything would be unavoidable.
With the words "of that which is connected," etc., he anticipates the opponent's opportunity for objection:
"If it is not by royal decree that the validity of what is connected is established,
then how could the validity of perception exist without a connection?"

Regarding this, the opponent says: "If you claim that what is related possesses validity, then this is merely a royal decree; surely there must be some reasoning here. For instance, if 'the validity of what is related' were not a royal decree, then how could one explain the validity of perception without association—that is, without a relation?"
To this, he states the following reply, beginning with "nanu":
"If [an object] were understood despite being unrelated, why would there not be comprehension of anything else as well?
For no distinction whatsoever is observed in the state of being devoid of a relation."

The status of being a means of valid cognition is established even in the case of perception solely on account of its connection [with the object]; for validity consists in correspondence, and that arises from the fact that [the cognition] acquires its own nature through the object.
Now, if something unrelated were understood, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because there would be no distinction; you have offered no answer to this.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that how can perception possess validity without a relation—that too is entirely inconsistent.
For indeed, no one accepts the validity of perception without a relation.

What then? Validity is established through connection alone, even in the case of perception—that is, in direct sensory apprehension. He states the justification for this in the passage beginning with "for correspondence" (*saṃvādo hi*). Correspondence is the capacity to reach the object; it is validity.
Furthermore, how could that correspondence be necessarily established for perception unless its own existence were derived from that object?
To address the question, "What fault is there otherwise? he says: "Because it is not caused by that.
It is not logical for there to be correspondence with that [object] when it is not caused by that, or when it is causeless;
otherwise, there would necessarily be correspondence with all things.

That which has that object as its cause is "taddhetu"; that which does not have that as its cause is "ataddhetu," meaning it has another cause. Therefore, from a perception that is *ataddhetu*—that is, from one that lacks that [specific] cause, or from one that is causeless due to the absence of all causes—that correspondence with the object, namely correspondence with reality (*arthasaṃvāda*), would not occur with necessity.
What then? The same undesirable consequence applies here as well: that there would have to be a correspondence with all objects in their entirety.

Alternatively, the positive statement (anvayavākya), "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," while inferring its own specific cause—the intention to speak—by means of the inference of a property of the cause (*hetudharma*), implies by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) the negative statement, "He eats at night," just as smoke implies a transformation of fuel. It does not, however, do so directly. Demonstrating this, he says, "The second," and so forth.
Alternatively, the intention [of the speaker] appearing as a second sentence is inferred;
by this same means, it is held that the understanding of the negative concomitance (vyatireka) arises from the affirmative sentence (anvaya).
"By this" means by the inference of a property based on a reason (*hetudharmānumāna*), and not directly.
For from the statement of positive concomitance (*anvayavākya*), such an intention (*vivakṣā*) is understood, in which the statement of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavākya*) also appears.

Otherwise, if eating at night were not included within the intended meaning, and if the desire were merely to establish the simple negation of eating, then one would have simply said, "Devadatta does not eat."
"But not by day, for he is fat"— this is the understanding of the negative concomitance (vyatireka); that is,
the understanding of the sentence expressing negative concomitance.

Regarding the statement "the cow which is compared to a gavaya," [the author] says: "Of comparison" (*upamāyāḥ*). Once the validity of comparison as a means of knowledge has been refuted in detail, the validity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arising from it is likewise precluded.

"Let it be granted that analogy (*upamāna*) possesses validity; nevertheless, since presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) preceded by analogy merely apprehends what has already been apprehended, its separate validity is not tenable, because there is no distinct object of cognition (*prameya*) characterized as a 'capacity' (*śakti*). Demonstrating this, he says "upamāna... and so forth:
"The cow is held to be the objective support (*ālambana*) of the means of knowledge that is analogy.
And an objective support is considered to be produced by its own existence alone, [and thus] the generator of its own cognition."

Therefore, what need is there for another power here, which would have to depend on an inference? The status of presumption (*arthāpatti*) as a means of valid cognition is based upon analogy (*upamāna*).
"Yadgatyartham" means for the purpose of understanding the capacity;
the rest is easily understood.
Regarding the passage beginning with "abhidhānānyathā," he states that the example for the presumption based on presumption is inconclusive, starting with "ananyatva":
"Even in the absence of non-difference, the communication of meaning by words is not contradicted,
just as [meaning is conveyed] through causes such as the movement of the hand."

For just as the communication of meaning by impermanent things such as the shaking of hands or the winking of eyes is not contradictory, so too it is not at all contradictory for words even in the absence of non-difference; thus, this example is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
In this context, "otherness" (*anyatva*) is impermanence (*anityatva*), and "non-otherness" (*ananyatva*) is permanence (*nityatva*). This is the sense.

But was it not said that "the impermanent does not participate in the continuity of conventional usage through linguistic convention"? To this, he replies with the words beginning "tulya" (equal): "Just as movement [is possible] because it is the cause of a uniform reflective awareness, so too the capacity of words to convey meaning is not contradicted."

Although there is no continuity (*anvaya*) among particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) because they are momentary, nevertheless, some particular characteristics, by their very nature, become causes—either directly or through a lineage—for an erroneous synthetic cognition (*pratyavamarśajñāna*) that has a non-differentiated form; being grasped as a unity, they become signifiers (*pratyāyaka*) by virtue of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*). For example, "non-trembling" [is] a signifier; this is the remainder of the sentence.

In order to point out that the example of "trembling" is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), the opponent says: "Indeed, those actions which are observed to reside in perceptible substances— their eternity is accepted just like that of [the color] *varṇa*, on account of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)."

Just as the permanence of phonemes is accepted by us on the basis of recognition, so too is it for actions such as those of the hand; thus, the example is not devoid of the probandum—namely, impermanence—and there is indeed no deviation [in the reason].

If this is so, and these actions of the hands and so forth are eternal, why is their perception not constant? To this he says: "Due to the absence of a manifestor, there is a continuous non-perception of them."
That which is the producer for you is itself considered to be the manifester.
"Of these" means of the activities;
"the state of being continuously unperceivable."

The opponent's intention is that the rebuttal is the same for both sides: just as for you there is no eternal perception due to the absence of a producer, so for us there is none due to the absence of a manifester.
He replies with the words "Not so," and so forth:
"It is not so; for if its capacity were unimpeded, that cognition would exist continuously. But upon its separation from that [capacity], it would never exist at all."
Consequently, it is their manifestors that come together, not their causes;
as for recognition regarding permanence, it has already been refuted previously.

In this regard, there are two possible alternatives concerning those actions which are intended to be manifested: they must either be inherently capable of producing cognition or not. If they possess such capacity, then cognition arising from them would occur eternally, because that capable nature, being permanent, could not be obstructed by anything.
Because it is impossible to obstruct [the cause] without imparting some excellence (atiśaya) to that which cannot have excellence added to it.

Now, if there is incapacity, then upon the separation from that [cause], there would be a separation from capacity; consequently, the cognition resulting from that [cause] would never arise—so what is the efficacy of the manifestor?
Therefore, for those actions which are held to be eternal, causes conceived as their manifestors cannot be logically consistent in any way.

However, in the case of non-eternal things, it is logical that there is the production of a new nature from a manifestor; thus, manifestors are appropriate with respect to them. Regarding what was said—"Their eternity is accepted just like that of phonemes on account of recognition"—he replies: "Recognition."
When permanence is to be proven, recognition is put forward as the reason; however, that has already been refuted previously in the examination of the stability of entities.

Regarding what was stated—"from that which is qualified by the absence of Caitra as determined by the non-existence of means of valid cognition"—he says "in the house," and so forth: "But the existence of Caitra outside [the house] is not logically established merely from his absence in the house; for this is otherwise possible due to the suspicion of his death."

If the absence from home of one who is alive is intended to establish his existence outside by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), this is not at all the case, because even there there is no certainty.
For one who does not see Caitra in his house, limited perception is indeed not a means of valid knowledge;
yet, some connection with his being alive still persists for him.
"Otherwise also":
the absence of Caitra in the house is possible even without his being outside;
by this, he states the inconclusiveness [of the reason].

Now, it might be argued that in this illustration of presumption (*arthāpatti*), it is not mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*) that is stated as the reason for Devadatta’s absence from home while he is alive, but rather his specific absence from home while being alive.
This is not correct.
Why?
In that case as well, because Devadatta’s life is subject to doubt, the reason would suffer from the fallacy of being "doubtfully unestablished" (saṃdigdhāsiddhatā).
He states the cause for this uncertainty with the word "in the house":
for one who perceives only what is near at hand, there is indeed doubt, since there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to ascertain Caitra’s being alive.

It might further be argued: "Even if the means of valid cognition consisting of perception does not exist for one of limited vision regarding Caitra’s being alive, inference and the like certainly do exist. To this he says "atha" and so forth: "If his state of being alive is ascertained by means of words and the like, and his absence is ascertained due to his non-existence in the house, then [the non-apprehension] possesses the status of a means of valid cognition."
Regarding the phrase "by means of sound, etc.":
either the sound uttered by him is heard, or at that time, a witness who is hidden behind a wall or similar obstruction says, "Caitra is practicing austerities; he is alive.

And because of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāva*), which takes the form of the cessation of perception and the other [means of knowledge], when there is the ascertainment of Caitra's absence in his own house, the absence of Caitra qualified by his being alive is established. Thus, the validity of this presumption (*arthāpatti*) arising from non-existence would indeed be established.

He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "tadāpi" (even then): "Even then, the fact that [the person] is not connected to the house is ascertained through the perception or non-perception of his sight; therefore, his existence outside is determined precisely by the inferential mark (*liṅga*)."
For he who is not connected with the house necessarily exists outside,
just as a man seen standing in the courtyard of a house is [inferred] by those standing at the door.
Even an adversary here is included within the category of "existent";
therefore, this [form of] presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) does not differ from inference (anumāna).
By this, he states its inclusion within inference (*anumāna*).

For instance, Caitra is the subject (*dharmin*) here; his being outside is the property to be proven (*sādhya*); the reason (*hetu*) is his non-perception at home despite being alive, which functions as the effect (*kārya*);
and a person standing in the courtyard of the house serves as the example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
But "inside the house" is the example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
"Sadanam" means the house.
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is ascertained precisely by means of these two examples.
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*);

for, first of all, his absence from the house is ascertained through the non-perception of a perceptible object (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), while his being alive is established by the opponent's own admission.
However, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the reason remains doubtful.
There is indeed no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the certainty of [the person's] being alive.
But was it not said that there is sound and so forth?

If that is the case, then since the state of being alive is ascertained from that very same means of valid cognition—namely, sound and so forth—the existence outside [the house] is already established; what, then, is the purpose of postulation (*arthāpatti*)?
Therefore, by accepting the opponent's own admission,
it has been demonstrated that presumption (arthāpatti) is included within inference (anumāna), having accepted its logical reason as established.
Thus ends the examination of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
With reference to non-existence (*abhāva*), he says "pramāṇa" and so forth: "Where the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not arise with respect to the nature of an object,
there the status of non-existence as a means of valid cognition exists for the purpose of awakening one to the existence of that object."

In this regard, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that existence and non-existence—the two characteristics of being and non-being—constitute the substantiality of things, and that every category of object possesses a dual nature consisting of both existent and non-existent aspects.

Since an entity is thus established as having a dual nature composed of both existent and non-existent aspects, there is a portion of the entity’s form known as the "non-existent aspect" in which the five means of valid cognition, up to and including *arthāpatti*, do not arise.
For what purpose?
For the purpose of awakening to the existence of a thing— that is, for the purpose of awakening to the existent aspect of a thing—
there is the status of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the object of cognition (*prameya*) which consists of the aspect of non-existence.
By this, only its object has been indicated, but not its own essential nature.

To the question, "What then is its nature? he says: "The non-arising of perception and so forth," and so on. The absence of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva) is held to be either the non-modification (apariṇāma) of the self or a cognition of another object.

The non-arising of the means of valid cognition, beginning with perception and ending with presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), is accepted as the "absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*).
This term *pramāṇābhāva* is either a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound or a *karmadhāraya*.
In some readings, it is given as *pramāṇe 'bhāvaḥ*.
In this context, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), and the singular number denotes the class (*jātāvekavacana*).
The meaning is that among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), non-existence (*abhāva*) is a means of valid cognition.
As Śabarasvāmin has stated: "Non-existence, too, is the absence of a means of valid cognition [regarding] an object not in contact [with the senses], in the sense that [the object] does not exist."
Now, as to what this "non-arising" (anutpatti) is, he says: "It is either the non-modification of the self, or consciousness [of] another object.

This non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge refers to the substance of the self (*ātman*) in its state of equilibrium, which has not been modified into the form of cognition of objects such as a jar that are intended to be negated; or it refers to the cognition of a floor-surface devoid of a jar and so forth.
But surely, "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is said to be the absence of a real entity?

How, then, can this [non-existence] be a real entity? For one might suspect that a real entity cannot be an absence. Anticipating this, he states "due to the absence of valid cognition" (*pramābhāvāt*) while establishing that non-existence is indeed a real entity: "And it is through the absence of valid cognition that the non-existence of entities is apprehended;
and this [non-existence] is divided fourfold according to the distinctions of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth."

If non-existence (*abhāva*) were not a real entity (*vastu*), then, because it would be devoid of all causal capacity (*sāmarthya*), there could be no cognition of non-existence; furthermore, the fourfold division of non-existence—into antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth—would not exist. But this is not the case. Therefore, the reality of non-existence follows from the fact that the cognition of non-existence would otherwise be inexplicable, and from the fact that the worldly linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) based on its fourfold division would otherwise be inexplicable. Some maintain that these two [arguments] constitute the means of valid cognition known as presumption (*arthāpatti*). Others, however, describe the statement "and it is divided fourfold" as being an inference (*anumāna*).
And they establish this through the following formal argument: non-existence is a real entity because it is differentiated, like a jar or similar objects.
Furthermore, demonstrating how this [non-existence] is divided fourfold, he says: "In milk, curd... and so forth.
That which does not exist in milk, such as curd, is conceived as antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
The non-existence of milk in the curd is characterized as non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).
That which is the absence of a horse and so forth in a cow is called mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva).
It does not possess the form of another; therefore, its non-existence is by way of its own nature.
The parts of the head that are sunken and devoid of growth or hardness are held to be an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) in the form of a rabbit's horn and the like.

Furthermore, this conventional discourse based on the distinction between causes and so forth would not exist if non-existence did not occur through its various divisions, such as prior non-existence and the rest.
When it is perceived in the world that the effect characterized as curd or a jar does not exist in its cause, such as milk or clay, this is called prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
If prior non-existence did not exist, the effect such as curd would indeed already exist in the milk and so forth.
Similarly, the absence of what is called "milk" in the curd is called posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).
Otherwise, milk would indeed exist in yogurt.
The absence of one thing, such as a cow, in another thing, such as a horse, is called mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Since that cow and so forth do not possess the nature of another, namely the essence of a horse and so forth, therefore the mutual non-existence of those two is spoken of.
Otherwise, horses and the like would indeed exist in cows and so forth, if mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) did not exist.

The parts of a rabbit's head that are devoid of concavity, growth, and hardness, and which are absolutely non-existent in the form of horns and such, are called absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Although in this case, according to the actual state of things, it is a case of mutual non-existence, it is nevertheless described as absolute non-existence in accordance with worldly convention.

For in the world, the conventional usage of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) generally occurs through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in "This is a cow, not a horse," but not in the form "This horn does not belong to a rabbit.
If absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) did not exist, the horn would indeed exist on the rabbit.
And thus Kumārila said:
"Milk would indeed become curd, and curd milk; a cloth in a jar;
a horn on a hare; and consciousness in earth and the other elements, and form in the self."
In water, there are smell and taste; in air, those two along with form;
and in space, those together with touch—if these [elements] were not the means of valid cognition for this [world].
Thus:
therein, consciousness is the self;
form is solidity.
"With form, those two together": those two, odor and taste, would exist in the wind accompanied by form.
"Those [are] with tangibility": thus [it is said].
Those forms, tastes, and smells, together with tangibles, would exist in the void, in space.

Furthermore, there would be no worldly convention based on the distinction between causes and so forth if non-existence did not possess distinctions such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest.
Just as one who desires curd takes up milk, but one who desires milk does not take up curd; likewise, one who desires a cow does not take up a horse, nor does one who desires a horse take up a cow.
Thus, conventional usage proceeds through such distinctions as cause and so forth.

Now, it might be argued: "Even if this [entity] has undergone a fourfold division, it must nonetheless exist as a real entity (vastu). Why so? To this he says: "And these divisions could not belong to a non-entity," and so forth.
These divisions would not belong to a non-entity; therefore, its status as a real entity [is established].
That which is the absence of effects and so forth is itself the existence [of the cause] by way of the cause and so forth.
For a distinction is not possible for that which is non-existent, because such a distinction has existence as its basis.
Therefore, non-existence is a real entity (*vastu*).
To the question, "In what sense, then, is this a real entity? he says: "Of effects and so forth."

The very existence of the cause, such as milk, is the non-existence of the effect, such as curd; and the very existence of the effect, such as curd, is the non-existence of the cause, such as milk—this is what constitutes the reality of non-existence.
Furthermore, establishing its status as a real entity by means of inference, he says "Or else," and so forth:

"Or else, since it is itself the object of the cognitions of inclusion and exclusion, it should therefore be understood as a real entity, like a cow and the like; and it should be known [as such] because it is an object of cognition."

The thesis is that non-existence is a real entity (vastu); the two reasons are "because it is apprehended by a cognition of both inclusion and exclusion" and "because it is an object of knowledge" (prameyatva); the example is "like a cow and so forth."
In this regard, the inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttibuddhi*) is the uniform conceptualization (*pratyaya*) that "non-existence is non-existence" across all four types.

The exclusive cognition (*vyāvṛttibuddhi*) is the conceptualization characterized by distinctions such as "this is prior non-existence, not non-existence through destruction. Regarding these, Kumārila has described three kinds of non-existence.

The first [type of non-apprehension] is the non-modification of the self; the second is the cognition of a specific other object, based on the statement: "It is either the non-modification of the self or the cognition of another thing"; the third consists merely in the cessation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-nivṛtti-mātra*). An inference is that cognition which is produced by [the three-featured middle term]. And because of the statement: "And for that which is of the nature of non-arising, there is never dependence upon a cause. Regarding this third type, non-existence (*abhāva*), having raised an objection, he says in order to refute it: "If it is non-existence, how can it be a means of valid cognition? (*mānaṃ katham abhāvaś cet*)?
If non-existence is [the object of] cognition, how can there be a means of cognition (māna)? And what kind of object of cognition (prameya) would there be here?
For just as the object of cognition is indeed non-existence, so too should the means of cognition be accepted as such.
Now it is asked: "How is non-existence, characterized by the non-arising of perception, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
To this it is replied: "And what is the object of cognition (*prameya*) in this case? If it is argued that the object of cognition has the nature of non-existence,"
If that is so, then let it be accepted that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is exactly as the object of cognition (prameya) truly is.
Why, then, is it asked, "How can non-existence be a means of valid cognition? For it is not logical that a mere definition should be the means of valid cognition.
"Let it be that non-existence (abhāva) is a means of valid cognition; however, how is it distinct from perception and the other [means of knowledge]?

To this he says "abhāva... and so forth: "It is distinguished from perception and the rest because it is denoted by the word 'non-existence. For the non-existence of the means of knowledge is like the non-existence of the objects of knowledge."

Alternatively, non-existence is measured by a means of valid cognition corresponding to its own nature, because it is an object of cognition, just like existence; therefore, it is distinct from that which consists of existence.

The non-existence of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as perception and the rest, is itself a means of valid cognition distinct from perception and so forth, because it is denoted by the term "non-existence," just like the non-existence of an object of cognition (prameya). Alternatively, the subject (dharmin) is the object of cognition called "non-existence"; its state of being an object of cognition through a corresponding means of valid cognition is the property to be proven (sādhya); "because it is an object of cognition" is the reason (hetu); and the object of cognition called "existence" is the example (dṛṣṭānta). And that corresponding means of valid cognition is established as being other than the positive nature of perception and the rest.
He responds with the verse beginning "tadatra" and so forth: "In this regard, the transformation of an eternally existent entity has been refuted;
its existence as something occasional, being the opposite of that [eternity], is not tenable."
By this, he states the impossibility of the first definition of non-existence, namely "the non-modification of the self.
For, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), "non-modification" is intended as a characteristic that is the opposite of modification and is occasional (*kādācitka*).
Otherwise, if it were not intended to be occasional by way of exclusion, then there would always be the cognition of the existence of the entity.

Furthermore, that aforementioned non-transformation is not possible for the self (*ātman*), because transformation has already been refuted for an eternally existent entity (*nityasattva*). Therefore, how could there be a recourse to its opposite, non-transformation, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? In this context, "eternally existent" (*nityasattva*) means that which is both eternal and an existent entity (*sattva*).
Alternatively, it is so called because its existence (sattva) or being (sattā) is eternal; that is to say, it is "eternal. [The phrase] "the existence of its opposite" refers to this.
The opposite of that transformation is non-transformation; it is not logical for that [non-transformation] to be occasional.
Rather, it should exist at all times, because the Self is one and eternally of a single nature.
Now, if it is thought that non-transformation (*apariṇāma*) does not consist of a thing that is the opposite of transformation,
but rather consists merely of the negation of transformation,
and therefore its characteristic is not impossible— regarding this, he says: "The negation of that," and so forth.
If what is intended here is merely its negation,
then its status as a real entity would always be understood, since that negation does not exclude it.
The negation or rejection of that transformation is itself "mere-that" (tanmātra); that which has this as its very self or nature is called "non-transformative.
Because this non-transformative state—which is of the nature of negation—is eternal and of a single form, there is an absence of transformation in the self.
Having conceded the point by saying "let it be so," he states the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpitā*) as a defect of the definition:

"Or let there be no transformation for this [consciousness]; nevertheless, there is still inconstancy (*vyabhicāritā*), because even when that [transformation] exists during states such as sleep or fainting, the object may still be present."
If it is argued that this [consciousness] is perceived in the form of the cognition of a jar and so forth because, when other conditions are present, something distinct from them is seen;
[475] At that time, what distinction was stated regarding this second position from which these two positions were indicated by you through an alternative formulation?
"Vyabhicāritā" means over-extension (ativyāpitā).
By the word "etc. in "fainting etc.," states such as being obstructed or having one's back turned are included.
"Even in its absence" means even when the substance of the self exists in a state not transformed into the form of cognitions such as that of a jar.

When there exists another cognition distinct from the causal condition consisting of the objective support (the jar), the very cognition of a location devoid of the jar and so forth is accepted as "non-transformation."
Because it has not undergone transformation into the form of cognitions such as that of a jar;
"of that" refers to the self;
"this" refers to [the cognition].
[It would be] non-transformation.
This being the case, no distinction would have been stated between this [position] and the second alternative, namely that consciousness [arises] from another object;
consequently, the presentation of two alternatives would be purposeless.
With the words "in another object" and so forth, he states the fallacy of deviation regarding the second definition of non-existence:
"If the non-existence of everything were understood when another object is known and [that cognition] occurs,
then even the non-existence of something unobservable would be apprehended by relying on that second definition of non-existence."
"Even of that which is invisible" means of that which is remote in terms of place, time, or intrinsic nature. "The absence of a second" means...
Or consciousness [is established] upon another object; in this regard—

If it is argued that the non-existence of an object possessing a form identical [to the one perceived] is cognized when other causes for its perception are present, provided that there is no cognition of anything else distinct from it;
Furthermore, it might be argued that what is intended to be proven is not the non-existence of every unperceived thing; rather, it is this:
"that which possesses a form equal to its capacity for perception would be perceived by him [the observer], like a spot of ground devoid of a jar or similar objects.
That is to say, it refers to something that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*).
"In the cognition of another thing as distinct from that" refers to the cognition of a location as distinct from a jar or similar objects.
He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "śakya":
"The non-existence of a perception itself is established when there is the appearance of an object that is capable of being seen;
this being the case, it can be so designated for others as well, and is not inconsistent."
How can a cognition that has arisen with respect to one object be known?
If it is held that cognition is not perceived and is known only through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), [then how can this be so]?
Since that [presumption] as well consists essentially of cognition, from where would its own status come?
If it were explained by another presumption, an infinite regress would result.

If the non-existence of a means of valid cognition and likewise the non-existence of an object of cognition were themselves entities, then since they would be included within perception, how could they not be [perceived]?

"Of that which is capable of being seen" refers to an object that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). "That which has the appearance (*ābhā*) or form (*ākāra*) of such an object" means it possesses the appearance of an object capable of being seen; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both the appearance of a perceptible object and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Not of others" refers to inference (*anumāna*) and the other means of knowledge.

Since for them the object is exclusively a hidden (parokṣa) thing, and there is no cessation of that which is hidden— distant in terms of place, time, or intrinsic nature— upon their cessation; therefore,
their cessation is fallible.
Consequently, in the phrase "the non-arising of perception and so forth," the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi) would be purposeless.

Furthermore, it must necessarily be admitted that if the cognition of an object other than that [negated thing] were determinate (*niścita*), it would thereby establish the absence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

Otherwise, if the establishment of absence from that [other cognition] occurred merely by its existence (*sattāmātra*), it would follow that the absence of everything could be established for every person from even a single cognition arising in one individual.

In that regard, how could that very cognition which has arisen with respect to an object other than that [perceived one] be known by the Mīmāṃsaka who maintains that cognition is imperceptible? It could not be known at all.
If it is argued that it is known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), [the response follows].
The connection with the subject at hand is "it is known.
As it has been stated: "Since cognition is not established when the object is unknown, that cognition is inferred from the mark (liṅga) which is the knowledge of the object.
For in this context, the statement of the mark expresses the impossibility of [the effect] occurring otherwise.
The meaning is: "from the knowledge of an object that is otherwise inexplicable" (*anyathānupapanna*).
That is to say, it is inferred, which is to say, it is cognized.
If this is so, then since that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is also of the nature of a cognition, it must be stated: from what does its own apprehension arise?
If it is argued that this refers to another presumption (*arthāpatti*), then in that case there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, if the reality (*vastutva*) of non-existence is admitted, then just as the absence of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*) is a real entity, so too is the absence of an object of knowledge (*prameyābhāva*). Consequently, since non-existence is a real entity, why is it not admitted to be simply perceptible (*pratyakṣa*)? For if it were, one would not need to postulate another distinct means of knowledge called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) for its apprehension.
With the words "of the effect and so forth," he establishes that [non-existence] is indeed included within perception:
"For the non-existence of the effect and so forth is indeed the existence of the cause and so forth;
and that, having a nature distinct from others, is apprehended by perception itself."

And so it has been said: "The non-existence of effects and the like is indeed the existence of causes and the like. Furthermore, that existence of causes and the like—which is a self-nature distinct from others and whose essence is distinct from effects and the like—is simply perceptible (*pratyakṣa*). What other object of cognition (*prameya*) could there be for non-existence such that it would require a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That which has no object of cognition distinct from another is not a separate means of valid cognition with respect to that [other], just as a seventh means of valid cognition [does not exist]. And there is no object of cognition for non-existence that is distinct from the perceptible object of cognition; this is a non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
In this regard, another [opponent], raising the objection that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), says "svarūpa" and so forth:
"In an entity which is eternally of the nature of both existence and non-existence by way of its own form and the form of others, some aspect is cognized by some people at some time."
And when the aspect of existence is apprehended through the operation of perception and the other means of knowledge,
then the operation of non-arising functions toward the aspect of non-existence that one wishes to apprehend.

There would be an absence of objects of cognition (*prameya*) if an entity were of a single nature alone; however, since an entity consists of both natures—being existent and non-existent respectively by way of its own form (*svarūpa*) and the form of others (*pararūpa*)—and that entity being thus dual-natured, some aspect of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is known by certain means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but not everything is known by all [means].
This very point is shown by the passage beginning with "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

When the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) is apprehended, then the operation belongs to the five means of knowledge beginning with perception, and not to non-existence (*abhāva*). When the negative aspect (*abhāvāṃśa*) is intended to be apprehended, the operation of those [five]—perception and the rest—is their non-arising; that is to say, non-existence [is established] through the non-arising of perception and the others.

The reason would be unestablished if a single entity possessed a dual nature; however, since it is contradictory for a single entity to have a dual nature, [the author], demonstrating this, says: "The very intrinsic nature," and so forth.
"Indeed, the very intrinsic nature of things is held to be excluded [from others];
and this [nature] exists as that very essence, while it is perceived through this [other] essence."

A thing is not excluded from another thing by means of the form of the other; rather, it is by its own form. Therefore, it is the very own-form, the very intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of things, that is perceived as excluded from other things, because they abide in their own respective natures.
By that very nature through which it is excluded [from others], that object is indeed existent and not non-existent;
and since this object is perceived directly by means of this self-nature excluded from others, there is no perception of a second form.
Thus, the proposition that [reality] possesses a dual nature has first been shown to contradict direct perception; now, demonstrating that it contradicts inference, he says: "Arthakriyā...
That which is capable of causal efficiency is called "existent," while that which is otherwise is called "non-existent.
It is not logical for these two to coexist in one place, because they are contradictory.
If it is capable regarding its own probandum but incapable regarding another,
then indeed this duality of nature cannot exist within a single entity.
If it is maintained that one thing is indeed incapable [of producing] another, then two distinct entities are obtained; therefore, there is no duality of form for a single entity.

That which performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*) is existent, just like the form that is accepted as being existent; and the form that is accepted as being non-existent does not perform a purposeful action. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, two things that are mutually contradictory cannot be perceived simultaneously in a single entity, just as in the case of shade and sunlight, or cold and heat. Since the forms of existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, this is a "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
With the words "In its own probandum," etc., the opponent raises the objection that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For indeed, that very same single entity is capable of performing the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by itself, yet it is incapable of performing the causal efficiency to be accomplished by another; therefore, the reason characterized by the performance of causal efficiency is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For the performance of causal efficiency by an entity is not established with respect to a causal efficiency to be accomplished by another.
Nor is there a mutual contradiction between the forms of existence and non-existence, because of the difference in perspective (*apekṣābheda*).
For indeed, it is with reference to its own specific effect that something is called "non-existent"; otherwise, there would be a mutual contradiction.
To this, he states the resolution: "But surely that very same [thing].
That very nature of the entity which is capable regarding its own effect is the same that is incapable regarding another's effect; it is not anything else.
For an entity does not become different merely because of a difference in its relations,
since it is partless;
that is what is meant by "that" (tad).
Therefore, it is directed toward that object;
consequently, there is no possession of two forms in a single thing.
Now, [the author] says "it is indeed another" to show that the form which is incapable of performing a different purposeful action is simply another, and not that very same form.

In that case, then, you have merely established two distinct entities: that which is capable of causal efficiency is one thing, and that which is incapable is the second; you have not, however, demonstrated that a single entity possesses both natures.

Regarding the third characteristic of non-existence, which consists merely in the cessation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he states the refutation with the words "of non-existence," and so forth:
"If the reality of non-existence has already been accepted previously,
for what purpose is its formlessness (nīrūpatā) described again?"
"It was previously accepted" refers to the statement that it is either the non-transformation of the self or consciousness, or another entity. Furthermore, its "formlessness" [is as follows]:...

The intended meaning of the forthcoming argument is that, because of the statement "error should also be regarded in this same way," and because a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is characterized by the apprehension of an object, it is not logical for that which is formless (nīrūpa) to possess the status of a means of valid cognition.
Showing this very intention, he says: "Of that which is formless," and so forth.

For it is not logical that a formless thing should possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) upon the loss of its cognitive form; for that [status] is characterized by the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*).
This is the proof of validity:

that which does not have the nature of the apprehension of an object of cognition is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as a jar or the like; and non-existence (*abhāva*) is devoid of the apprehension of an object of cognition. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

It might be argued: "The eye and other [senses] are not of the nature of the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya-adhigati-rūpa*), yet they are called 'means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇa*) because they are the causes of the apprehension of the object of cognition; likewise, non-existence (*abhāva*) [is a cause]. Thus, the reason [you provide] is inconclusive. To this he says, "Because it is the cause of that," and so forth: "If it is called a 'means of valid cognition' because it is the cause of that [apprehension], like the eye and so on, then for that which is formless (*nīrūpa*), the possibility of being a cause never exists."
And how can that non-existence be cognized as distinct from the very nature of cognition?
If it is argued that it is known precisely through the absence of a means of valid cognition directed toward it, then there would be an infinite regress.

If non-existence were to be understood from the absence of a means of valid cognition due to the absence of an object, and from the absence of an object due to the absence of a means of valid cognition, there would be a mutual dependence.
Therefore, that which is the vision of one is said to be the very same as the vision of another;
and that [vision] is established independently because it is non-inert by its own nature.

Nor is it appropriate to assume [the existence of an object] through metaphorical designation on the grounds that it is the cause of valid cognition; for since that which is formless is characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity, the possibility of its being a cause is not tenable.
Or, if such a possibility were admitted, it would entail the loss of its formlessness.
Furthermore, because there would be no distinction [between states], it would follow that consciousness could never cease as long as that [formless entity] exists.

Furthermore, it has been stated previously that it is not logical for that which is unestablished to possess the capacity to indicate [an object], as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, it must be explained how that non-existence (*tasya abhāvasya*) is established. It cannot be established by itself, because that would entail the undesirable consequence that even the absence of an object of cognition (*prameyābhāva*) would be established by itself. Consequently, the conceptualization of non-existence would be useless, since its purpose is the establishment of the absence of an object of cognition; and that absence of an object of cognition, like the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*), would be established by itself.

Nor is its establishment through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), because since this [external object] is distinct from the nature of cognition, how could it be apprehended by self-awareness? For that [self-awareness] perceives only the essence of cognition itself. If, on the other hand, its establishment is due to another [means], namely the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that object, then how is the establishment of that very absence of a means of valid cognition itself achieved?
If that [non-apprehension] were also established through something else, there would be an infinite regress.
As it has been said:
"Otherwise, the non-existence of an object is understood through non-apprehension."
"The non-existence of apprehension would have to be established by something else, leading to an infinite regress."
Thus [it is said].
Now, lest there be an infinite regress due to the absence of an object of cognition (*prameya*), its establishment is accepted;
however, this being the case, a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*) results.

For in this way, because the object of cognition (*prameya*) does not exist, the non-existence of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established; and when that [means] is established, the non-existence of the object is established. Thus, the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) enters here most clearly. This is like the case where the eye-stylus comes out while the molasses is being inserted.
Therefore, the non-perception of one thing is simply the perception of another; thus, what is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is not a separate means of valid cognition.

[This follows] from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It might be argued: "How is that single apprehension established? For there too, the same objection applies as in the case of non-existence. To this he says: "And that," and so forth. And that perception of a single [object] is established by itself independently, not through anything else; thus, there is no consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Why?
Because by its very nature and essence, it is non-inert, having the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*).
Nor does there follow the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [the status of] consciousness to other things merely by virtue of their existence, because others do not possess that nature.
Now, as to why there is such hostility toward the establishment of cognition through another [means], he says "of cognition," and so forth:
The establishment of cognition from something other than itself— whether from a logical mark (*liṅga*), from another cognition,
or from the impossibility otherwise— is in no way possible.
If each of the three investigations were possible, there would be for you many unstable and proliferating regressions in this case.
Therefore, because only one [object] among those of equal capacity is perceived,
the capacity for the determination of non-existence is understood to belong to the others.
When there is the cognition of any single thing, how can the sky be understood as devoid of the moon, and how can the absence of all sounds be determined in some place?

Some maintain that cognition (*buddhi*) is to be inferred from its mark (*liṅga*); and that mark is either the knowledge of the object, or the action-form, or the sense-object, or the manifest object, and so forth.

Some maintain that cognition is perceived by another cognition, and not as having the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvid*), because there is a contradiction between being an agent and being an object with respect to itself. Others [infer it] through the impossibility of the known object otherwise; for the object is not established if cognition does not exist, since the object is inherently insentient (*jaḍa*) by nature.
Therefore, three positions have been stated.

Regarding the successive questioning of each of those three—namely, the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth—as to how that very mark and the rest are established, if such [establishment] were possible, many infinite regressions (*anavasthiti*) would ensue.

For instance, since that triad of the mark and so forth is unestablished if cognition is unestablished, its establishment must be sought through something else; and if yet another mark and so forth are resorted to therein, an infinite regress results from the questioning at every stage.

Therefore, from the perception of one thing, the non-existence of others is understood; when a negation is to be made regarding a particular place and time, the negation must apply only to those things that possess an identical nature of perceptibility,
because it is impossible to negate other things there.
However, when identity is negated, the negation of everything must necessarily follow, because everything is established as being "other than that," on the grounds that "it is not of that nature,
but of another nature."

Now, when one determines the absence of the moon in the sky, at that time there is no perception of anything else there, such that it could be said that "the proof of the absence of another follows from the perception of one. For there is nothing called "space" (*ākāśa*) that exists in an ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), which could be seen as devoid of the moon.

Furthermore, even that entity imagined by others to be real is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). And as for the certainty of the absence of sound in a certain location, from the perception of what does that arise?
It cannot be said to be from the perception of the ground (*bhūbhāga*), because the ground and sound do not share a common state of perceptibility (*tulyayogyāvasthatva*).

For instance, a portion of the earth is visible, whereas sound is audible; yet, it is accepted that between two things in an equal state of perceptibility, their difference is mutual, according to the statement: "The difference between two things associated with a single cognition is not mutual.

Nor should it be said that [the self exists] because time is perceived; for there is no time distinct from external objects whose perception could occur, and even that part of time which is accepted by others is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "prakāśa" (light): "The perceiver considers that very mass of light and darkness to be space, because there is neither existence nor perception of anything else."

Even the absence of all other sounds is understood from the non-perception of their effects; and that [non-perception] is established for others through the self-cognition of their respective cognitions.
Regarding the phrase "of the mass":
it is to be connected with "in consciousness.
For the perceiver perceives that very mass of light and darkness as "space," and nothing else.
For instance, one perceives it during the day or at night as "this is the color of an indranīla gem" or "this resembles a mass of clouds.
Yet, for the imagined space (*ākāśa*), there is no color, shape, or the like;
therefore, [the perception] must be of something other than that.
Because space, as postulated by others, does not exist apart from masses of light and darkness;
and even if it did exist, it would be beyond the reach of the senses.
Furthermore, the absence of all sound is understood through the non-perception of its effect, namely auditory cognition.

And that non-apprehension is established through the perception of other cognitions, such as those of the eye and so forth; thus, even in this case, there certainly exists a single apprehension characterized by the perception of another cognition. Now, it may be argued that the existence of a cause is not necessarily pervaded by the existence of its effect, such that the cessation of that effect would entail the cessation of the cause as well, since causes do not invariably produce their effects.
We do not say that every existence of a cause is pervaded by the existence of its effect;
rather, it is only that specific [existence] characterized by unimpeded capacity that is negated here, not every [existence].
For instance, even where the non-existence of a jar is established through the perception of a bare location, that too is simply the non-perception of the effect known as the perception of the jar.

Since it is only the absence of a jar that meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) which is being proven, and not the absence of every [jar], what, then, is "meeting the conditions for perception"?
It is precisely that whose capacity is unimpeded.

Since the specific nature characterized by perceptibility has been described such that whatever is a [perceptible] nature is necessarily perceived, otherwise even here the existence of a jar would not be pervaded by the perception of the jar; and consequently, when the pervader is absent, the non-pervaded would not be absent, and thus the absence of the jar would not be established.
Therefore, every non-perception of a nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is a cause for the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāra*).
From the perspective of ultimate reality, it should be understood as simply the non-perception of an effect.

With the words "In this way" (*ittham*) and so forth, he states that the reason— "because it is denotable by the word 'non-existence' (*abhāvaśabdavācyatvāt*)"— is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). And thus, since its nature as a real entity (*vasturūpatva*) is established, its being denotable by the word "non-existence" remains uncontradicted even when [non-existence] is included within [the category of existence].
"Thus" means:

by [the statement] beginning with "that which is the view of one is said to be the view of another," [it is shown that] even if [the views] are included within one another, they remain uncontradicted.
The meaning is that even though non-existence is included within perception, its being denotable by the word "non-existence" is not contradictory.
By this, he states that the reason is not excluded from the counter-example (vipakṣa).

Or, if it is argued that "non-existence is measured by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) corresponding to itself," in this case, the point is already established; for such a correspondence indeed exists.
"Such is its conformity":

non-apprehension characterized by the non-perception of another [object] is non-existence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, some raise this objection: "Indeed, a cognition whose object is the mere absence of a thing has no inclusion within perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of valid cognition], because it has the mere absence of a thing as its object, whereas perception has only a positive thing (*vastu*) as its domain."

Nor is this [cognition] invalid, because it is non-contradictory; for you who maintain that things undergo destruction without any persistence (niranvaya-vināśa) do not deny the absence of the thing itself.
This too has been refuted by the following:
for that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not take as its object a mere non-existence devoid of the specific qualifications of place, time, and so forth.
What then? [It is] precisely with a qualification, in the form "there is no jar, etc., in a certain place, etc.

And this occurs solely through the power of perceiving the bare place, etc.; thus, it does not possess a separate status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because one conceptualizes the bare place, etc., exactly as it was already grasped by perception.

Or, even if there were a perception of an absence devoid of qualifications, it would not be logical for the cognition grasping it to be a means of valid cognition, because its object is not a real entity (*avastu*).
Furthermore, since the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by those seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is based upon real entities (*vastu*), this [objection] is trivial.
Thus concludes the investigation into non-existence.
With reference to reasoning (*yukti*) and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), he says "when this exists," and so forth:
"When this exists, that necessarily comes to be; when it does not exist, that does not come to be.
Therefore, from this, that necessarily arises. This is what is called reasoning.
The sage Caraka says that this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
for it is not inference, since no corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta) can be found here.
When an object is known through a certain perception, the non-existence of that object is understood from the absence of that perception; this is considered "non-apprehension."
This [scriptural testimony] is also a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it does not depend on examples and the like;
for even the non-existence of something in an example is established by this very [means].

The realization that something is an effect because it exists only when that [cause] exists is this logical reasoning (*yukti*). And since this involves conceptual construction (*savikalpaka*), it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); nor is it inference (*anumāna*), because there is no corroborating example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For even an example would itself require the realization of its being an effect of that [cause] based on its existing only when that exists; for that too another example would have to be sought, and for that yet another—thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, the physician Caraka says that this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Likewise, the cognition of non-existence through the cessation of apprehension is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
If this too were a distinct means of valid cognition, its logical justification would have to be sought in the same manner as that of reasoning (*yukti*).
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "kārya" (effect), etc.:
"The cognition of the absence of the relation between cause and effect is not constrained."
Therefore, in this case, there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans, because [of the following].

"Cause-and-effect relation" (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and "non-existence" (*abhāva*); thus, "the cognition of cause-and-effect relation and non-existence" is a compound formed by analyzing [the terms]. In this context, the connection is respectively: the cognition of the state of being cause and effect is through reasoning (*yukti*), and the cognition of non-existence is through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
Regarding the phrase "in this":
even in these two means of valid cognition—reasoning and non-perception—there is no difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).
To the question "How so?", he says:
"The state of being cause and effect is nothing other than the occurrence [of the effect] when that [cause] exists;
apart from the perception of the visible and the non-perception [of the invisible], no other non-existence is cognized."

To begin with, there is no distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). For instance, the probans is the fact of "occurring when that occurs" (*tadbhāvabhāvitā*), while the probandum is the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*); yet no distinction between these two is perceived, because they are synonyms, like the words *taru* and *pādapa*.

Furthermore, even in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), there is no distinction; for if what is intended is merely the cessation of perception, then since that is unestablished, the same faults as before—such as infinite regress—must be stated.
If, on the other hand, non-perception is simply the perception of something else, then it is included within the very category of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).

And by this [reasoning], non-existence is not being proven, because that [non-existence] is established by perception itself; for this very reason, he says: "leaving aside the non-perception of the perceptible," and so forth.
Now, if it is thought that the absence of cause and effect is not being proved with respect to the navel, but rather their conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
then he says:
"In the proof of the capacity for the conventional usage of their existence," and so forth.
The object understood at the time of convention exists; this is the illustration.

The existence of those two—the cause and the absence of the fruit—is "their existence" (*tadbhāva*); the conventional usage regarding that is "the conventional usage of their existence" (*tadbhāvavyavahāra*).

The fitness for that [usage], characterized by the operation of cognition and verbal designation, is what is being established. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things whose nature is invariably perceived immediately after the operation of something else are fit for the conventional usage of being its effect. For example, jars and the like, which were experienced at the time of convention, have a nature perceived immediately after the operation of a potter and so forth. And likewise, sounds have a nature invariably perceived immediately after the operation of the palate and other [articulatory organs]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Likewise, when the conventional usage regarding non-perception is to be proven, the formal argument is as follows: those things which are intended to have reached the conditions for perception, yet are not perceived in certain locations, are fit for the conventional usage of their absence—just as, for example, the heads of rabbits and the like are fit for the conventional usage of the absence of horns. And there is a non-perception of the categories such as "universals" (sāmānya) as accepted by others, even though they are intended to be perceived and are held to reside in spotted cows and other such individuals; this is thus a non-perception of the essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi).

Because there is the perception of brindled cows and the like as distinct from that [universal], the reason is neither unestablished (*asiddha*) nor inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti*) will be refuted later and the conventional usage of non-existence is based solely on this much. Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Thus concludes the investigation of reasoning and non-apprehension.
In this context, "possibility" (sambhava) refers by implication to the aggregate;
upon the cognition of the possibility, there is the cognition of the constituents of that aggregate.
Just as when the existence of a thousand is known, the existence of hundreds and so forth is cognized.
And this, it is said, is not an inference because of the absence of an example.
Regarding this, he states the refutation beginning with "samudāya" (the aggregate) and so forth:
the members of the aggregate are the causes for the establishment of the aggregate.
The cognition of the possibility of a hundred and so forth arises from a thousand, being produced by the mark of the effect.

Since there is no aggregate distinct from its constituent members, the constituents themselves are the cause for the establishment of the aggregate; therefore, the cognition that a hundred or other numbers arise from a thousand is produced solely by the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅga*).
Thus concludes the investigation into possibility.

Others, however, maintain that tradition (*aitihya*) and so forth are additional means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Among these, *aitihya* is a succession of rumors whose speaker is unspecified, such as: "A yakṣa dwells in this banyan tree.
*Pratibhā* (intuition) is knowledge that arises suddenly, regardless of place or time, which indicates the existence or non-existence of something.

Just as it happens for a young girl [who thinks], "Today my brother will come," and that indeed turns out exactly so, it is considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To this, he states the refutation, beginning with "aitihya" and so forth.
Tradition, intuition, and the like are for the most part subject to deviation;
it is not at all tenable that such things possess the status of valid cognition, as this would lead to over-extension.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth are included,
because these too have been accepted as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by certain others.
[The phrase] "due to over-extension" (*atiprasaṅgataḥ*) means:
Since even that which occurs at the end of a dream is sometimes seen to be true, it would follow that it constitutes a separate means of valid cognition.
This concludes the investigation into tradition and other such means of knowledge.

Having thus refuted other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in detail, he says "Or rather" (*athavā*) and so forth, in order to refute them in brief: "Or rather, this effort is exerted in vain, because objects are established as being of only two kinds: perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) and imperceptible (*parokṣa*)."
For an object is indeed of two kinds: perceptible and imperceptible.
But is there not also another [category], namely that which is both perceptible and imperceptible—neither perceptible nor imperceptible? To this he says "both," etc.:
"Indeed, that other [entity] consisting of both or neither is not tenable;
for in a single cognition of a single thing, action and non-action are contradictory."
For an object that directly produces knowledge is called "perceptible" (pratyakṣa),
while that which is the opposite of what has been described is considered "non-perceptible" (parokṣa) by the learned.
First of all, this [cognition]—whether verbal testimony, analogy, or the like—does not have the primary object as its domain;
for it would either be included within perception or be as futile as memory.
Even if all [cognitions] have as their object that which is beyond the senses, how could it be an object?
For if this were not directly perceived, it would not be an object, just like a perceptible thing that is not perceived.
Even if there is a cognition based on another [cognition], what is its status? Is it connected [to its object] or otherwise? And is it not an appearance of difference, or is it not so?
If that [cognition] were to arise from something unrelated, an absence of restriction would follow;
nor is pervasion (vyāpti) tenable if there were only the appearance of difference.
Inference is clearly defined as a cognition whose object is beyond the senses, which rests upon a related entity, and which does not apprehend the specific differences within that object.

For it is not logical that a single entity should possess a convergence of multiple mutually contradictory properties, because that would entail the loss of its unity. To explain: an object is called "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) when it is the direct cause of a specific cognition that, without mediation by a mark (*liṅga*) or other factors, determines the object exactly as it was apprehended.
On this basis, it is established that cognitions such as "sound is momentary" have objects that are not perceptible.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity to simultaneously perform and not perform an action toward the same thing, whereby it could possess the dual nature of being both perceptible and non-perceptible based on whether or not it generates a cognition.
Nor is it logical for an object to possess a nature that is neither [one nor many], because the negation of one nature in a thing is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of another nature.

However, there is no contradiction in multiple things performing an action in a single place—as, for example, color and taste [acting] upon visual consciousness—or in a single thing performing an action in multiple places—as, for example, color [acting] upon both visual and auditory consciousness. For this reason, he stated "of one, in one" (*ekasyaikatra*).
Therefore, the object is indeed of two kinds.

In this regard, there are two possible positions concerning the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda*) and the other means of knowledge: it must apply either to an object that is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) or to one that is beyond perception (*parokṣa*).

First, it cannot apply to a perceptible object; why? Because, since verbal testimony and the rest have objects that are not distinct from what is already included within perception, they would be redundant. Alternatively, if it is argued that after an object has been apprehended by perception, these [other means] effect its apprehension again at a later time, then he says: "Or [there is] futility."
For if it were apprehended [by another cognition], there would follow the consequence of its being invalid, like that which is not apprehended or is not remembered.

Even in the second alternative, if that remote object becomes the object [of the cognition], it must either be directly [perceived] or indirectly through another locus. In that regard, it cannot be direct, because that would entail its being non-remote (immediate), like an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Precisely for this reason it is called "remote" (*parokṣa*): because it does not produce cognition directly. If it were to produce cognition directly, how could it be said to be "remote"? This must be explained.

Regarding the comprehension of an imperceptible object even by means of another [perceptible] support, four possible positions arise: it must be either from that which is related or from that which is unrelated, and it must be either an appearance of difference or an appearance of non-difference.
An example of an appearance of difference is the cognition of a specific fire—such as one produced from grass or leaves—from the universal "smoke."

If [the cognition] were an appearance of non-difference, such as that which determines fire alone as excluded from heterogeneous things based on smoke, then because there would be no connection [between the reason and the object], there would be a lack of restriction in comprehension; for everything could be understood from anything whatsoever.

If, on the other hand, it were an appearance of difference, then the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the probandum would not be established, because a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with a particular [instance] is impossible.
Consequently, it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

"Not grasping that distinction" means [a cognition] that is devoid of the appearance of difference and which determines (*adhyavasāyinī*) merely the object as excluded from those of a different class (*vijātīyaparāvṛtta*).
Just as from smoke there is the cognition of fire alone,
if [the cognition] were of such a nature, it would clearly be inference, because it has the perception of a relation as its means, like the cognition of fire from smoke.
Thus concludes the examination of other means of valid cognition.
In order to support the statement that "[it] is not mixed with even the slightest part of another nature," [the author] says "nanu" and so forth, beginning with an objection:
"But surely an object consists of multiple natures, like a variegated gem;
if that is the case, what contradiction could there be for [qualities such as] existence and the rest by their very nature?"
As it has been said:
"That which is capable of causal efficiency is called 'existent,' and anything other than that is called 'non-existent.
A coexistence of these two in a single locus is not tenable, because of their mutual contradiction."
Thus it is said.
In this regard, the shameless ones (ahrīka) and others raise this objection:
every entity indeed possesses a manifold nature by virtue of consisting of both the universal (sāmānya) and the particular (viśeṣa), just like a variegated appearance.
[The opponent objects: "Since there is a jewel, how can there be a contradiction between existence (*sat*) and the other qualities, such that it is said: 'There is no co-inherence in one place'?
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), activity, non-activity, unity, and others are included.

Although this objection has already been refuted by the passage beginning with "But surely that very [thing]," it is stated again here either for the sake of a detailed exposition or to present another line of argument.
In that regard, in order to prove that [the object] consists of both the universal and the particular, the shameless one (Ahrīka) states two syllogisms in sequence:
"An entity is not distinct from a sky-flower because it is not equal to other entities;
if it were devoid of inequality, its difference from them would not be established."

Regarding any intended object such as a jar: if that jar or other entity were not distinct from another entity such as a cloth—that is, if it were not excluded from it—then it would have no distinction from a sky-flower, because it would be excluded from all other entities whatsoever; and for something excluded from all other entities, no other possibility exists except that of being a sky-flower.

Therefore, by one who accepts that this entity is not equal to a sky-flower, it must be admitted that its being a real entity (*vastutva*) consists in a generality (*sāmānya*) that is equal to other existing things; thus, its nature as a generality is established.

If it is asked, "How then is its nature as a particular (*viśeṣātmatva*) established?", it is said in response: "If it were devoid of inequality [with them], it could not be proven to be distinct from them. That is to say, if that very entity, such as a jar, were devoid of that inequality which it possesses with respect to another entity, such as a cloth—meaning, if it were not unequal to that jar and so forth—it would not be distinct from them.
In that case, this jar and this cloth—such as a jar being distinct from a cloth and so forth—would not be established as different, just like its own essential nature; yet they are indeed distinct.
Therefore, the fact that [substance] consists of particularity is also established.
With the words "In every way" and so forth, he extensively establishes the meaning of these two very arguments:
"For if, in every way, the incomparability of this entity with another entity is intended,
its status as an entity would necessarily be lost."
For when an entity has ceased to exist, what other possible state could be conceived for it, except non-existence? It is perceived as nothing else, like a lotus in the path of the stars.
Therefore, by one who desires that this entity not be equal to a sky-flower, its "entityness" (vastutva) must be accepted as a universal (sāmānya); that is its commonality.
Otherwise, he states another argument to prove that [the cognition] has a universal nature, beginning with "For otherwise, that cognition... [etc.]:
