"For otherwise, that cognition would not occur restrictedly to things such as crows' beaks;
rather, why is it that this [cognition] occurs restrictedly only to certain entities?"
If it is argued that this restriction arises from similarity, then for us that very thing is the universal;
thus, the capacity inherent in the nature [of things] has been described by this very [point].
Therefore, absolute difference does not at all apply to anything;
for every thing is differentiated from others by way of its own objective form.

Regarding the term "otherwise": if an entity were not similar to other entities, then one must state the reason why the non-different cognition "this is an entity, that is an entity" occurs only with respect to jars and the like, and not with respect to things such as a crow's teeth. If you say that similarity (*sārūpya*) is the cause, then it is established that this very thing is the universal (*sāmānya*), because similarity is a synonym for universal.

If you say that there is a persisting capacity (*anuyāyinī śakti*) only in jars and the like, but not in things such as a crow's teeth, and therefore the capacity inherent in their own nature (*svabhāva*) is the cause; [we reply: ...
It has been described and explained by Sāyaṇa with the very same reasoning;
that is to say, the response here is the same as in the case of the similarity [of the universal],
because it would follow that the universal itself would possess the nature of a universal.
Therefore, it is established that all things, such as pots and the like, are mutually non-different in their nature as real entities.
To establish the distinction, he says "that which has been made a limit," and so forth:
"If that object were devoid of dissimilarity from the objects taken as limits, then it would not be distinct from them; there would be non-difference, just like its own nature."
Indeed, dissimilarity is defined as being distinct from their own nature;
yet to say that dissimilarity is not distinct [from them] is mutually contradictory.
Therefore, by one who accepts that objects are distinct in some respect, their dissimilarity must also be accepted; for from this [distinction] follows their nature as particulars.
Regarding the phrase "from those taken as limits":

if the jar and so forth were devoid of dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) from other objects such as cloth and the like, then, due to non-difference, that jar and so forth would not be distinct from those cloths and the like; for there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-distinction, just as it is with its own essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*).
To explain: that very essential nature of the jar and so forth which is distinct from those cloths and the like is indeed what is called dissimilarity, and nothing else.

Furthermore, even though there is dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) among cloth and other such things, there is no difference (*bheda*) between them and pots and the like; thus, your own statement is self-contradictory, because "difference" and "dissimilarity" are synonyms.

Having thus established that [the object] consists of both the universal and the particular, he says—demonstrating that these two, the universal and the particular, serve as the basis for linguistic usage without confusion: "This entity is indeed of a single nature.
This entity, though of a single nature, is held to have multiple forms;
and these [forms] exist as being grasped by cognitions of inclusion and exclusion.
These first [categories] are proclaimed as "universals" (sāmānya) because they are inclusive;
however, the others are designated as "particulars" (viśeṣa) because they are exclusive.

[489] This is the ultimate truth in this matter: like a variegated gem (*mecakaratna*), a single entity possesses multiple forms (*ākāra*). Among those forms, some are apprehended by inclusive cognitions (*anuvṛttibuddhi*), while others are apprehended by exclusive cognitions (*vyāvṛttibuddhi*). In that regard, those apprehended by inclusive cognitions are designated as "universals" (*sāmānya*) because they are inclusive; however, those others which are apprehended by exclusive cognitions are conceived as "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) because they are exclusive. Therein, an inclusive cognition has a non-differentiated form such as "it is an entity, it is an entity," whereas an exclusive cognition has a differentiated form such as "this is a jar, not a cloth."

To this, he provides the following rebuttal, beginning with "If they were mutually identical in nature," and so forth: "If the universal and the particular were mutually identical in nature, there would be a confusion [of the two] in reality; thus, this dual nature is not logically tenable."
Even if these two lack mutual intrinsic nature, their distinctness follows as a consequence; yet even in such a state, a dual form is not logically possible.
In this regard, there are two positions: is that which is the universal (sāmānya) itself the particular (viśeṣa), or rather, is the universal one thing and the particular another?
Regarding these, in the first position, if the universal and the particular were mutually identical in nature, there would be confusion (saṅkara).

Consequently, because there would be no distinction such as "this is the universal" and "this is the particular," it would not be logically possible for a single entity to possess a dual nature in ultimate reality.

Now, if the second position is adopted on the grounds that there must be no confusion [between the two], then even if their mutual non-identity is accepted, a plurality—that is, a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—would result for the universal and the particular. For this lack of confusion between the two would only occur if there were a plurality between them; and if such plurality exists, then merely two distinct entities have arisen, and thus it is not logical for a single entity to possess a dual nature.

Now, it might be argued: "Even if there is indeed a mutual distinction between the universal and the particular in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nevertheless, the entity consisting of both the universal and the particular is nonetheless non-different.
But this is mutually contradictory.

For instance, if the non-difference of the universal and the particular from a single entity is admitted, how could a mutual distinction between their intrinsic natures be established? Because, if they are non-different from one [entity], it follows that they themselves must be non-different, just like the intrinsic nature of that single entity.

Furthermore, if the mutual distinction of the natures of the universal and the particular is admitted, a single entity that is non-different from them cannot be established; for, being non-different from those two, that which is intended to be one would result in duality, just like the nature of the universal and the particular themselves.
Therefore, the claim that "one [entity] consists of both" is mutually contradictory.
With the words "Even though," etc., he raises the objection of Sumati:

"Even though there is a single nature, a distinction of properties is established here; and there is no contradiction in the existence of distinctions, just as in the case of the potencies of causal factors."
Furthermore,
it is not untenable that even when the universal and the particular are of one essence,
a distinction is observed that conforms to worldly practice.

Indeed, at the outset of the objection, he [the author] states the rebuttal: "If one does not admit that the universal and the particular are devoid of each other's intrinsic nature, then they would result in being conflated.
This is not a fault;
for even though there is conflation due to their having a single intrinsic nature, a distinction between their properties (dharma-bheda) is established, just as in the case of causal potencies."

For instance, the causal potencies are perceived as having distinct natures due to the differentiation of effects— such as "the cloud flashes" and "it flashes from the cloud"— even though they remain inseparable from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the substance,
despite their state of being intermingled. If this were not accepted, contradiction with both worldly experience and the treatises would necessarily follow.
Moreover, there is indeed nothing that is logically untenable regarding what is perceived.

For instance, even though the universal and the particular are of the same nature as a single entity, their non-confusion is observed despite their difference; this very fact constitutes the following of worldly practice (*lokayātrā*).
"Worldly practice through difference" means *bhedalokayātrā*; that by which such practice is followed through a state of identity is what has been described in that way.

The formal argument is as follows: the linguistic usage of difference regarding a single entity is based upon a difference in its properties, as in the case of the potencies of an agent; and this linguistic usage of difference regarding a single entity—characterized by both the universal and the particular—is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely):
"But surely, if there is a single nature, a distinction between properties is not established;
for it is an unconstructed distinction that is designated as 'manifoldness'."
By this, he states that the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because it proves the opposite of what is intended.

For the proponent intends to prove a distinction between phenomena (*dharma-bheda*) in an ultimate sense; yet such an unconstructed distinction between phenomena is not established, because the unity of the entity is admitted, and because distinction is incompatible with that single entity. Since "distinction" denotes plurality (*nānātva*), how could that which is plural be one?

Showing that in the example there is not only a lack of the probandum (*sādhya*), but rather that the reason (*hetu*) is pervaded by the opposite of the probandum, he says "the state of being manifold," and so forth:
"And the manifold nature of the potencies is constructed merely by the speaker's intention."
For if they consist of a single reality, then even here, difference is not logically tenable.

It might be argued: "Even if 'difference' (bheda) is defined as manifoldness (nānātva), how could that very manifoldness of a single entity be real and yet contradictory, such that proving its opposite would constitute a contradiction? To this, he says "one" (eka) and so forth:
"That indeed is called 'one' which is proclaimed to be 'that very same thing'."
But that which is manifold in nature is not truly that [single entity] again.
The state of being that and the state of not being that are mutually contradictory;
this [pair] cannot be conceived in any way within a single entity.

That which is prescribed as "this is that" in its true nature is said to be one, as in the case of consciousness and the person (*puruṣa*). When the true nature of an existing entity is denied, there is multiplicity, as in the case of the elements and consciousness.

Consequently, since affirmation and negation cannot coexist in a single locus, there is a mutual contradiction between unity and multiplicity—which are characterized by the presence or absence of that [nature]. Thus, the distinction of properties in a single entity is merely conceptualized.
To explain how there is a contradiction between the existence of that [one] and the non-existence of that [other], he says "vidhāna" and so forth:
"For affirmation and negation are mutually contradictory;
they cannot be established by anyone with a sound mind in a single locus."

It might be argued: what is the basis for the conceptualization of a distinction between properties (*dharma*), and there must necessarily be a distinct basis for this, otherwise there would be a confusion of entities;
and therefore, that distinct basis itself is the ultimate distinction between properties for us. To this, he says "of the same class" (*sajātīya*) and so forth.
An object is excluded from many things both similar and dissimilar;
however, its differentiation into distinct properties is spoken of by virtue of its exclusion from this or that [particular thing].
Therefore, it is logical that even a single entity possesses an imagined nature of infinite forms;
however, for a real entity, even a dual nature is not consistent.

The compound *sajātīyavijātīyam* is a *karmadhāraya* meaning "homogeneous and heterogeneous," and the analysis of the phrase is "that thing which is excluded from those. Of that single entity, the exclusion (*parāvṛtti*) from each respective homogeneous and heterogeneous [thing] is the basis for the establishment of distinct properties (*dharmabheda*). Therefore, since even a conceptual multiplicity is possible, a real dual nature (*dvairūpya*) in a single [entity] is not tenable.

By the word "api" (also/even), he indicates that if the probandum were merely the fact of being preceded by a difference in properties in a general sense, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

It might be argued that there is an inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to cases such as Narasiṃha; for indeed, Narasiṃha and others, though possessing a single nature, are observed to be non-contradictory with a dual form in a real sense. To this he says: "Narasiṃha and others.
"For those such as Narasiṃha who are described as having a dual form—even for them, a dual form existing in reality does not exist at all."
For that [cognition] has as its nature an aggregation of many atoms and does not possess a single form;
indeed, that which is variegated is not one, like a collection of jewels of various kinds.
If there were identity, there would be no appearance of diverse forms because of the lack of duality;
nor would there be non-obstruction when even a space the size of a fly’s foot is covered.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the *mecaka* gem and others is intended.
As for the phrase "he indeed":
it refers to Narasiṃha.

*Sandoha* means a collection (*samūha*). One who possesses form (*rūpa*) is "possessed of form" (*rūpavān*). Thus, the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "one who is possessed of form by means of one [form]."

By this, he states that the example is unestablished for the opponent; for a Buddhist, Narasiṃha is not established as a single composite entity, because he is a collection of many atoms. Regarding that, he states the proof for the refutation of his unity: "Whatever is variegated is not one, just like a collection of jewels of various kinds; and Narasiṃha is variegated. This is either the perception of a contradictory nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalambha*) or the perception of something contradictory to a pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalambha*). If there were oneness, the appearance of various forms—which is caused by a dual nature—would be untenable; this serves as the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*), because the determination of difference is based upon a difference in manifestation.

Furthermore, the undesirable consequence that the obscuration of one part would entail the obscuration of the whole serves as a subverting proof; for it is not logical for a single thing to simultaneously possess the contradictory properties of being obscured and being unobscured.
If Narasiṃha is merely a collection of multiple atoms, how then can there be a cognition that determines a single object as possessing two forms? To this he says, "Nṛsiṃha," and so forth:
"Those atoms are the causes of the recognition that runs through the parts of Nṛsiṃha, because they produce a specific cognition by their very nature."
In this very same manner, variegated jewels and other such things are explained;
for multiplicity is indeed contradicted by unity.

That recognition which is interwoven with and made manifest by those parts belonging to the two *nṛsiṃhas* (the man-lion) is what is thus described. When such a recognition has those very atoms as its causes by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*), then what is the use of further postulating a "whole" (*avayavin*)?
If it is asked, "From where does such a nature belong to them?", he says: "Because of the arising from a specific cognition," that is, because of their production from a specific cause.
In this context, the "specific cognition" refers to the karma conducive to a particular movement and the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth, produced from its own kind.
By this very analysis of Narasiṃha, the "black jewel" (mecakarata) and others have been explained; thus, no separate refutation of them need be stated.
Regarding what was stated—"And every thing is distinct in its own form, yet not mutually [distinct]"—he says here:
"The nature of a thing is defined as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamarthatva*).
If that [capacity] were pervasive, then everything would perform every effect."
A single thing is a producer of an effect because it possesses efficacy;
and since that [efficacy] is no different in the other [cause], how could it not be a producer?
If it is maintained that the very substance of blue and so forth is what persists, then it follows that white,
yellow, and the rest would also perform the function accomplished by blue.
From that, only one has arisen, devoid of a second self;
therefore, for us, the entire universe is neither one nor many, yet it exists in manifold forms.
If that very [entity] were not a real thing, like the "existence" (sattva) in the system of Kaṇāda,
then for you there could be no single entity possessing multiple forms, because of its divided nature.
Furthermore, the association with contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of the difference between entities;
otherwise, even if one desires it to be so in some way, there would be no difference between blue and yellow.
Since change occurs through following [a sequence], and that [change] exists in both the universal and the particular,
how can it be said that there is no clear distinction between the two?

That form which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) is called "reality" (*vastutva*), and nothing else. If that [form] were to follow through everything, it would follow that everything performs every causal function; for all things are held to be producers by means of that very form, and since that form is indistinguishable everywhere, anything whatsoever could arise from anything whatsoever. Furthermore, is this blue, yellow, and so forth itself reality, or is it something else?

If that [entity] were identical to those [qualities], then because it would follow after them, even white, yellow, and so forth would result in performing the causal function of dyeing cloth with blue and the like.
Furthermore, since there would be no second nature, the entire world would be a single class of entity; thus, the meaning of the thesis—that "the one has many forms"—would be lost.
Alternatively, if substantiality (*vastutva*) were something other than blue and the rest, like the "existence" (*sattva*) postulated by Kaṇāda.
Just as for Kaṇāda, the eater of grains, it is accepted that "substantiality" (*vastutva*) is a distinct entity called "existence" (*sattā*);
even so, it is all the more illogical for one thing to be many, because they would be absolutely separate.

Furthermore, those two things which are associated with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsargin*) are distinct, just like cold and heat; and such association with contradictory properties exists between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), due to their being pervasive and otherwise, respectively—this is clear.
Such is the distinction between the two:
alteration is the state of not being concomitant.

And if difference were not admitted even when there is a connection with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*), then that difference which is accepted in some way as a non-distinct form between blue and yellow would not exist, because Kumārila has described the difference of blue and so forth by stating: "On account of the difference in cognition, the unity of color and the rest does not follow."
With the words "Just as," etc., he again demonstrates the inconclusiveness [of the reason] according to the view of the Kaumārila:
"Just as in the case of a variegated color, there is a restriction of the color as desired,
so too, because an entity is manifold, there is the determination of both difference and non-difference."
But when a variegated object is apprehended simultaneously,
then all distinctions such as difference and non-difference completely dissolve.
The term *kalmāṣavarṇa* means a variegated color.

Just as one may, according to one's wish, determine and ascertain the color of that [variegation] by specifying it as "blue," "yellow," "red," and so forth, in the same way, regarding a manifold object (*citra*)—which consists of multiple forms, possesses the nature of existence and non-existence through its own and other forms, and has a dual nature consisting of both universal and particular forms—one determines its difference or non-difference according to one's will.

When one desires to ascertain difference, then one ascertains it; but when one apprehends, all at once, an object consisting of both the universal and the particular, then the objection regarding difference, non-difference, and so forth, dissolves. The meaning is that it does not arise, because the variegated object is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

In this regard, there is the following objection concerning identity and difference: since the universal is non-different from distinct individual objects such as horses and so forth, it follows that the universal itself must possess a diversity of forms, just like the individuals. Alternatively, because the individuals are non-different from the universal, the lack of distinction among the individuals follows, just as there is none in the universal. Likewise, how could difference and non-difference coexist simultaneously between the universal and the particular? By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one should understand other mutually contradictory pairs such as unity and plurality, as well as statements such as "that very thing is the universal and that very thing is the particular."

Anticipating the objection that, if this were so, there would be a perception of the variegated [object] everywhere and not through either succession or simultaneity, he says "of the object" and so forth:
"The form of an object possessing multiple forms is intended according to the speaker's desire;
there is no other way for words [to function] than through simultaneous or successive operation."
Whether simultaneously or sequentially, whatever form—be it universal, particular, or otherwise—is established for this [entity], that is due to the force of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
When one intends to express its forms as both existent and non-existent, or as universal and particular, simultaneously, then its form is established accordingly.
Alternatively, when one intends to express it sequentially—as existent, as non-existent, or as universal and particular—then that [respective] form is established for it.
For its entire nature is designated by means of both succession and non-succession, just as a treasury of various jewels is [designated] by emeralds, rubies, and so forth.
To the question, "Why is it not indicated by another mode apart from succession and non-succession? he says: "There is no other method of verbal expression.
This should be understood in connection with the phrase "by simultaneous and successive occurrences."
*Vidhiḥ* means a method or manner.
He responds with the words "Not so," and so forth:
"It is not so; for unity has just been refuted regarding variegation.
Variegation, which consists of multiple forms, cannot coexist with unity."
For as many aspects as there are that are real within that entity, so many entities have arisen; thus, the non-existence of oneness is established.

The statement that "the manifold is one" is mutually contradictory; this has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "that which is manifold is not one," and so forth. For "manifold" denotes multiplicity, and between oneness and multiplicity there exists a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion.
Therefore, multiple real forms cannot exist within a single entity. Even if they were to exist, it would still not be established that one thing is manifold;
for in that case, there would simply have arisen as many other distinct entities as there are forms.
If it were established as being ultimately real,
then one thing could not possess multiplicity, because of their mutual contradiction.
Regarding what was said—that for a thing that has ceased to exist, what other possible state could there be—he replies with the verse beginning "From one [thing]," and so forth:
If [the non-existent] were different from a single entity, it would be devoid of identity with it;
yet it is not like a sky-flower, for even that [non-existent] is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
For if the exclusion from "mere entity" (*vastumātra*) were used as the reason to prove that [the pot] is no different from a sky-flower, then the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*).
Indeed, the exclusion of a pot from "mere entity" is not established;
rather, it is [its exclusion] from other specific entities, setting aside its own intrinsic nature (*svasvabhāva*).
Now, if exclusion from a particular entity is adduced as the reason [for the lack of intrinsic nature], then that reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For instance, an entity such as a pot, being excluded from one particular entity such as another pot, would be established as lacking identity with that other, yet it would not be entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), because even that [latter] entity possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
With the words "capable," etc., he supports this very point of inconclusiveness:
"The form of that which is capable does not reside in one thing while existing in other things;
for it has been described [that there is] a difference due to the diversity of the perception of the effect and its manifestation."
However, the state of not having that entity as its nature is consistent with its non-connection with it;
it is not a lack of distinction or a state of non-existence, because the defining characteristic of an entity is present.

For if the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*), characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), were indeed pervasive (*anuyāyin*), then that which is excluded from it would lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), because a real entity is defined by the capacity for causal efficiency. However, as was stated previously, the form of one thing—such as blue—which is incapable [of performing the functions] of others, such as white, does not subsist in them; this was established by the passage beginning, "If the very nature of blue and so forth is accepted as the pervasive reality," and so on.
Why?
Because of the difference in effects and because of the difference in their appearance in perception.
Apprehension is cognition; its manifestation is its aspect (*ākāra*).
By the word "etcetera," arising, abiding, cessation, and so forth are included.

Therefore, by the reason of its non-contact with those [characteristics], it is appropriate to establish that it does not have the nature of that object; it is not appropriate to establish its lack of reality as something undifferentiated and without qualification.
Why?
Because even there, the characteristic of existence—which is the capacity for causal efficiency—is present.
Now, if there were absolute difference, how could there be a recurring cognition of "this is a real entity" with respect to various things?
And how could the difference of a real entity from a sky-flower be established if there were no similarity? To this, he says: "That too," and so forth.
If one conceives that even that [exclusion] is a real entity because it is capable of causal efficiency,
then its similarity— consisting in the exclusion of what is incapable— is likewise a conceptual construction.
Therefore, even though there is absolute difference, a conceptual similarity exists;
an entity is similar to other entities, yet it is distinguished from a sky-flower by virtue of that [existence].
Regarding the phrase “exclusion from the incapable” (*asamarthaparāvṛtti*):

the “incapable” refers to things such as the son of a barren woman; exclusion from them means not having their nature. And because a conceptual similarity exists [between real things], it was said: “A thing is not equal to another thing.”
Thus, that [reason] is unestablished.

With the words "nanu" and so forth, [the author] anticipates the objection of Sumati: "Now, if that very nature by which an entity is distinguished from similar and dissimilar entities were also the same by which it is similar to those of its own class..."
If it were cognized as being identical even with those of a different class, then,
because its nature would be undifferentiated, it would not be cognized in that way.
Therefore, although it is not identical to its own kind, that by which this [entity] exists, and that with which it is similar—
there is a difference between those two natures.

He says: If that entity were similar to its own kind by means of that very nature through which it is excluded from both its own kind and other kinds, then it would be perceived as identical even with those of other kinds, because that nature is not distinct [from them].
Yet, it is not so perceived.

Therefore, one must acknowledge a distinction between those two natures: that nature by which [an entity] is not identical with its own class (*sajātīya*), and that nature by which it is similar to it. [Objection:
If it is of the same class, how can it be non-identical with it? And if it is non-identical with it, how can it be of the same class? This is mutually contradictory. [Response: This is not a fault.

Since everything whatsoever is accepted by the opponent as consisting of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), therefore, by way of the universal such as "being an entity" (*vastutva*), everything is said to be "homogeneous" (*sajātīya*); yet, by way of its particular form, that very same thing is accepted as "heterogeneous" (*vijātīya*). Thus, with respect to that [particular], it is again designated as "non-similar" (*asamāna*); hence there is no fault. Regarding the phrase "of the similar and other entity" (*samānāparavastunaḥ*):
that which is both "similar" (*samāna*) and "other" (*apara*) is the "similar-and-other entity" (*samānāparavastu*).
The word "aparam" means "dissimilar"; the remainder is not analyzed because it is easy to understand.
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "by that very [nature]," etc.:
"It is understood that this [object] is identical by virtue of that very intrinsic nature,
because it serves as the cause for a single unifying cognition through its exclusion from others."
It is said to be "identical" by virtue of that very same nature, because it is the cause of a single reflective cognition (*ekapratyavamarśapratyaya*).
What is meant is this: those things which do not function as causes for a single reflective cognition are designated as "dissimilar," whereas those which do so function are designated as "similar."

Now, raising the objection— "Why do not all things become causes for that very same unitary reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*), since their difference (*bheda*) is no different?"— he says "only some," and so forth:
"For only certain things are the causes of a single reflective awareness,
because of a restriction based on their specific capacity (*samartharūpaniyama*), even though they are distinct, just like sense organs, nectar, and so forth."
Intrinsic natures do not admit of questioning, such as "Why does fire burn or is hot, and not water?

However, it is appropriate to ask, "From what does this nature of his arise? For if it were causeless, being independent, it could not be restricted to a specific thing, which would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Therefore, one must say that it arises from its own cause; and if one asks "From what does that [cause] arise?", there is a beginningless succession of causes.
"Akṣa" refers to the sense organ;
"amṛta" refers to *guḍūcī*;
the word "ādi" (and so forth) is connected with each [term].

Just as the power to pacify fever and other ailments belongs only to *guḍūcī* and similar substances and not to others, and the power to produce specific cognitions belongs to the sense organs, objects, light, and mental attention (*manas*) and so forth, so too there is a restriction of capacity for certain things alone even regarding a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*). Alternatively, the word "tree" (*akṣa*) may denote the *vibhītaka* tree; in this case, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is connected with the entire group.
Now, with the words "nanu nīlādi" and so forth, he raises the objection that the example is unestablished: "But how can the eye,
if it is held to consist only of parts whose nature is excluded from blue and so forth, produce the cognition of blue and so forth?"

Just as the ear is not the producer of that [cognition] because it is distinct from the blue and so forth which produce the cognition of blue and so forth, let the eye also be accepted as being likewise.
For what other "producer" (janaka) could there be apart from that which is the producer?
Therefore, it is certain that there is also a positive concomitance (anvaya) among entities.

If it is maintained that the eye consists exclusively of the aspect of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from blue and so forth, and not of the aspect of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*), then the eye would not be the producer of the cognition of blue and so forth, because it would be turned away from the nature of producing that [cognition]. For whatever is turned away from the nature of producing something does not produce it; just as the ear, being excluded from blue and so forth which produce the cognition of blue and so forth, is not the producer of that cognition of blue and so forth.

Furthermore, the eye would be excluded from being the producer of the cognition of blue and so forth, which leads to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving something contrary to the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi).
But such is not the case; therefore, the opposite must be true.
For whatever is the producer of something is not deviated from the nature of being its producer;
just as blue, which produces the cognition of blue, is not deviated from its own nature.
And since the eye is the producer of the cognition of blue, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
In this way, blue and the other [colors] should also be stated as being the subject (pakṣa).

Therefore, by means of the reversal of the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga-viparyaya), he states the non-establishment of the example, [concluding that] there is indeed a commonality (anvaya) among entities.

Furthermore, one might argue that the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅgasādhana) is inconclusive because [the object] could both be excluded from that [other object] and yet be its producer; to this he says "otherwise," and so forth:

"Otherwise, since there would be no distinction, why is it not accepted that even hearing and the rest are producers of that [cognition], just as the eye is [a producer] with respect to the distinctions among color-forms and so on?"

The undesirable consequence that the ear and other sense organs would also produce cognitions of blue and so forth serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary position, because they are indistinguishable in their difference [from the eye].
For the eye possesses a certain difference from blue and the rest, and by virtue of that same difference, the ear and other organs are identical to the eye and the rest;
that is to say, just as the eye is excluded from blue and the rest, so too is the ear.
He responds with the verse beginning "Exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), etc.: "The exclusion of the eye and other [senses] as being producers is not established, because,
without distinction, their very self (*ātman*) is also considered to be a producer."
The exclusion of entities from their own intrinsic nature is not tenable;
for if there were a turning away from intrinsic nature, it would follow that they are devoid of intrinsic nature.
If their exclusion from other producers is described, then that which consists in not having the nature of those other producers must be stated; and that is exactly what we accept.
For its producer is not described as having that [nature] by its very own essence;
rather, all those [factors] are fixed therein, having arisen from their own respective causes.
But if these [causes] produce a single effect because they follow after a single self-nature,
then since that self-nature exists even in one [cause], what is the use of other auxiliary causes?
If some [causes] are not producers due to a deficiency in certain specific qualities, then surely they are incapable because of their difference;
or if there is no difference, how could they be deficient?
Just as, despite their distinctness, not everything is the cause of everything,
so too would there be a restriction based on the fact that diversity itself is without distinction.
Even when there is difference, a certain thing may be a producer due to the restriction of its own nature;
but if there were identity, how could one and the same thing be both the producer and the non-producer of another?
If it is argued that there is also differentiation here, let it be so; but is that [differentiation] of that very entity itself?
For differentiation is not something other than its continuity; indeed, differentiation is not a causal factor.
That alone is the real entity which is capable of causal efficiency;

and that which does not persist [through change] does not produce an effect, while that which persists is not born [as a new thing]. Furthermore, it is with reference to that very nature (ātman) that a person engages in action.
Difference and non-difference, which are merely conceptualized, exist only as residing therein.
Otherwise, there would indeed be difference by way of the self-nature and similarity by way of exclusion;
however, no real entity persists [as a universal], because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of [indiscriminate] activity and so forth.
If it is described as a reason that there is merely an exclusion from the nature of producing that [cognition] without distinction,
then the reason is not established;
for it is not established that the eyes and so forth are excluded without distinction from the nature of producing cognitions of blue and so on.
For even that which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those [causes], such as the eye and so forth, is accepted as being productive.

What restriction is there here that the effect must be produced by that [nature] alone and not by another? We see no contradiction in the fact that another might produce it, and that this [nature] might also do so.

However, if there were an undifferentiated exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), then it would follow that it could arise even from its own intrinsic nature; and from that, the consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) would ensue.
Therefore, it is not logical for there to be an exclusion of entities from their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Now, if the exclusion of the eye and so forth from something else—either from their own intrinsic nature or from another producer—is what is intended as the reason (*hetu*), then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For in that case, while something might be excluded from another nature and thus not possess that other nature, it would not follow that it is not a producer of that [effect].

Since everything is a producer only by its own nature and not by the nature of another, and since that [entity] is accepted as a producer by virtue of its own specific essence from which it does not deviate, how could it be a non-producer? Thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If, however, "not having that nature" is established through a process of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*), then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the mutual distinction between the natures of entities is accepted. This refers to "the state of not having the form of producing that."

That which is both "that" and "progenitor" is the progenitor of that, namely form and so forth (*rūpādi*). Its "form" is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). That which lacks this is "that which has a non-progenitor-form. The state of being that is its "reality" (*tattva*). This means, in short, its being devoid of the progenitor-form of that other [thing]. Alternatively, one may form a *karmadhāraya* compound by taking "that" and "progenitor" together as "that-progenitor," and then taking "that-progenitor" and "form" together; having thus formed the *karmadhāraya*, a *bahuvrīhi* should be constructed with the negative particle *nañ*.
Alternatively, the *bahuvrīhi* compound consists of three words.

Now, one might raise the objection: "When a particular effect is to be produced, from where does that very nature of those [causes], such as the eye and so forth—which is mutually distinct—originate, by virtue of which they would be restricted to that specific effect? Anticipating this, he says, "restricted. As for what was stated—that because there is no distinction in their difference, why is it not desired that hearing and the other [senses] also be producers?—that has been refuted by this.

Therefore, due to the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even though there is a distinction [between causes], it is not at all contradictory that only some [of them] are productive and others are not.

However, if on the other hand, the eye and so forth were productive despite being distinct because they are followed by a single intrinsic nature, then that single productive nature would exist in each individual cause; consequently, the effect would arise from that single [nature] alone.
And thus, there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the uselessness of the remaining auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*).

Now, if it is argued that an effect does not arise from a single cause due to the absence of other specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), [we reply: those specific qualities which are held to be absent are incapable [of producing the effect]. Why? Because they are distinct—meaning they are different from the nature (*svabhāva*) that is considered capable and which persists [through the causes]. Furthermore, it is not logical that the non-production of an effect should result from the absence of something that is incapable; for if that were so, it would follow that nothing at all could ever be produced. Alternatively, it might be argued: "We do not maintain that there is an absolute difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*); therefore, the reason 'because of difference' (*bhedāt*) is unestablished (*asiddha*. To this he says: "Or, if there is no difference, how can they be absent? (i.e., if the specific qualities are not different from the universal, their absence would imply the absence of the universal itself).

If it is accepted that there is no difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particulars (*viśeṣa*), then one must not say that "one [particular] is not a producer because of the deficiency of other particulars.
Therefore, while that universal remains intact and unimpaired, the deficiency of the particulars—which are non-different from it—is also unestablished.
For it is not logical that something which does not share the same acquisition and preservation (*ekayogakṣema*) as another should be of the same nature as it.
Moreover, this same undesirable consequence applies to you as well; since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is indistinguishable, why would everything not produce everything?
Just as, according to you, despite the lack of distinction in positive concomitance, everything does not become the producer of everything, so it is for us as well—thus, this objection is trivial.

Furthermore, even though there is no difference in their being distinct entities, the fact that one produces [an effect] while another does not must arise solely from the specific restriction of the nature of the producer—on the grounds that the nature which belongs to one does not belong to the other. This being so, nothing at all is contradictory.

However, when a single, continuous, unitary self is held to be the producer, then how could both affirmation and negation—namely, being a producer and not being a producer with respect to a single effect—be logically applicable to a single substratum?
For these two are not contradictory if they have different loci; it is for this reason that he says "of one" (*ekasya*).

Furthermore, it might be argued: "We do not maintain that there is exclusively identity (anvaya), such that there would be a contradiction of one thing being both a producer and a non-producer in the same locus.
What then?
There is also difference (bheda) here."
Therefore, its non-productivity is not contradictory.
Let there be a difference; however, it must be stated whether that difference is intended to belong to that very same persisting entity which has a productive nature, or rather to something else.

It cannot belong to that very same entity, for it is not logical for a thing to turn away from its own nature, as that would entail the consequence of it being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).

Nor does it belong to another; for if there were a difference [between them], it would be illogical for that very nature which is the producer to be non-producing when undifferentiated, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Or, even if there were a difference of that [nature] from its own self-nature, the contradiction between being a producer and being a non-producer for a single entity would still not be resolved.
For, due to that very difference, that same single entity would become a non-producer.
Is it not the case that there is no other "continuity" (*anvaya*)?
Rather, it is that very thing which is the continuity. Consequently, the contradiction regarding the same thing being both a producer and a non-producer remains exactly as it was.
For that which "continues" (*anveti*)—the continuity—is said to be the very nature (*svabhāva*) that is the producer.
The word "nanu" serves to draw [the listener] into the discussion.

Furthermore, since the accomplishment of an effect arises from particulars alone through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), only those [particulars] possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), not the universal (*sāmānya*); for the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*) is defined by its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, whether the universal is different or non-different from the particular is of no concern to one who seeks causal efficiency; for those seeking causal efficiency deliberate upon difference and non-difference only with respect to that very nature which is fit for causal efficiency and toward which they act with that aim, not out of mere habit.

Otherwise, if difference and non-difference were not accepted as being conceptual constructs, then for that [entity] which is capable of causal efficiency, its difference from its own nature (ātman) would indeed exist ultimately; and by means of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which conforms to the appearance in conceptual cognition, there exists indeed a determination of its state as a universal, established through convention.

Since the investigation into difference and generality is concluded merely for one who seeks causal efficiency, what is the use of investigating the difference or non-difference of a universal that does not perform any causal function?
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let the universal be the very thing itself; what is the use of a postulated exclusion (vyāvṛtti)? To this he says "vastu" and so forth.

If a jar or the like were to follow along with the form of a cloth or the like, then one seeking to fetch honey, water, and so on, would also act toward the cloth and such things; thus there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of such activity and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the undesirable consequence of [the jar] having the same arising and cessation, and so on, is implied.

Now, if this is also accepted by others, just as it is by the followers of the Sugata— that from whatever [exclusion] an object is not excluded, conceptual distinctions based on that [exclusion] are postulated as apprehending its specific features— then, regarding this, he says "of that which is fashioned by conceptual construction," and so forth:
"In the description of a mere variety fashioned by conceptual construction,
what excellence indeed has been proclaimed by the Brahmins, the Nirgranthas, and the Kāpilas?"
"Of variety" means of differentiation.
With the words "by the breaking of the *vardhamānaka*," etc., he raises the objection of Kumārila's view:
"When a *rucaka* (necklace) is made by the breaking of a *vardhamānaka* (a golden vessel),
then there is sorrow for one who desired the former, and joy for one who desires the latter."
But for one who seeks gold, there is neutrality; therefore, the object consists of three natures.
In the absence of arising, persistence, and destruction, the three cognitions would not exist.
For he has said: because they possess the nature of arising, abiding, and perishing, every entity indeed consists of three aspects.

This is because even from a single object, a triad of effects such as pleasure and so forth is observed. To illustrate: when a *vardhamānaka* (a type of golden vessel) is broken and fashioned into a *rucaka* (a necklace), then for one desiring the *vardhamānaka*, sorrow arises; for one desiring the *rucaka*, joy arises; but for one desiring the gold itself, there is equanimity. And if the entity were of only a single form, then the cognition would be of only a single aspect, not of three kinds.
The *vardhamānaka* and *rucaka* are specific types of vessels.

This might be the case: even if it is established that an entity consists of three natures, from what [source] does it follow that it consists of three natures in the form of destruction and so forth? To this he says: "Not without destruction," and so on.
Without destruction there is no sorrow; without arising there is no happiness;
without stability there is no equanimity. Therefore, there is the permanence of the universal.
Therefore, there is the permanence of the universal.

Since neutrality is not [established] by means of subsistence and so forth, but rather because neutrality is invariably concomitant with subsistence, the permanence of the universal—namely, the quality of being of the same class—is thereby cognized.
He refutes this with the words "This, moreover," and so forth:
"This too is not tenable for us, because [the three] lack a common substratum;
for arising, subsistence, and destruction do not have a single object as their substratum."
Because mutually contradictory things would result in being simultaneous,
all of this is free from confusion only if momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgitva) exists.
How could sorrow arise for anyone upon the destruction of a growing object made of gold, if there were no continuity [of that very substance]?
In every way, joy arises at the birth of the earring, which is of the very same nature as its prior form; however, there is no persistence of anything whatsoever.
"Because they have no common substratum"—this is the summary statement (*grahaṇakavākya*).
Its explanation begins with "arising, duration," and so forth.

For if even a single entity were tri-natured by way of having arising and so forth as its intrinsic nature, then arising, duration, and destruction—which are mutually contradictory—would follow as occurring simultaneously; and the simultaneous existence of contradictories in one place is not logical, for otherwise there would be no contradiction at all.

If it is asked, "How then is the arising of the three cognitions logically possible?", [the author] says "But this... to show that one should listen to how it is logical. A "vardhamānaka-thing" is a thing whose nature is a *vardhamānaka* (a type of golden vessel). What is its qualification? It is "of the nature of gold" (*kaladhautātmā*); the analysis of the compound is: that which has gold (*kaladhauta*)—meaning gold—as its very essence or intrinsic nature (*ātman*). When that [vessel] undergoes destruction by its own inherent force (*svarasena*), sorrow arises in someone who desires it.

But when there is the birth—that is, the production—of a previously non-existent entity called a *rucaka* (necklace), which is essentially gold, pleasure arises for someone who has identified it as a *rucaka*.
However, there is no persistence of anything that is essentially gold, because production and destruction are without continuity (*niranvaya*).
If this is so, then how does the notion of neutrality arise? To this he says, "When gold," and so forth:
"When a person of deluded intellect perceives two entities consisting of gold, he then imagines stability because of their identical subsequent state."
If gold were of a fixed nature, then that nature—such as its brilliance and so forth—would be perceived in its prior, subsequent, and other states; otherwise, there would be a plurality of natures.

When a person of deluded intellect perceives, in succession, two states consisting of gold—namely, those called *vardhamāna* and *rucaka*—even though he perceives the distinction between their natures, he is deceived by the production of successive similar entities. Because he is unable to discern [the difference], he is thus deceived by the appearance of another similar entity as a cause for error, and consequently, he believes in the stability of the gold throughout both states.
Regarding the phrase "by the appearance of another similar entity" (*samānāparabhāvena*):

the "appearance of another similar entity" (*samānāparabhāva*) refers to the arising (*utpāda*) of another entity that is similar by virtue of the common property (*sādharmya*) of being merely the exclusion of what is not gold (*ahemavyāvṛtti*).

But how is it determined that one is deceived by the appearance of similar subsequent states and thus imagines stability, rather than [thinking] that the thing itself actually exists in that way? To this he says, "Of gold," and so forth.

If gold were stable, then even the *rucaka* (necklace) and other forms, which are not distinct from it, would be perceived during the states of the *vardhamāna* (earring), since they have reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).

Otherwise, if the bracelet (*rucaka*) were not perceived during its state as a bowl (*vardhamāna*), and the bowl were not perceived during its state as a bracelet—despite both having met the conditions for perception—then there would be a mutual difference between the two. Furthermore, because gold is non-different from those two, it would follow that gold itself must be different [from its own nature], just like their individual natures. Having considered this, he says: "Otherwise, there would be multiplicity.
As for the proof of difference stated previously, beginning with "from the objects taken as limits," the refutation is stated that this merely proves what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Thus concludes the examination of the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda).
In order to support the statement that "there is no transition," he says "gold" and so forth:
"If one considers stability based on the similarity of the persistence of gold, then even the Buddhists must accept some entity that possesses distinct states."
Regarding the statement "but there is no persistence of anything," this objection is raised:

"How can it be said that there is no persistence of anything, when even certain Buddhists, such as Dharmatrāta and others, maintain that an entity persists through the three times due to a difference in its states, by analogy with the persistence of gold [through various ornaments]?"
He demonstrates this very point with the second verse:
"Just as gold does not abandon its essential nature even when there is a difference in its states,
so too this entity does not relinquish its substantiality throughout the [three] time-periods."
Otherwise, knowledge of the past and the unborn would have a different object;
and how could the Protector have taught that consciousness is based upon two [conditions]?
And since karma that has passed away is devoid of substantiality, how can it be held to yield a fruit?
Furthermore, how is it that the knowledge of the past and the future is differentiated for yogins?
Therefore, past and future [dharmas] do not have substance or exclusion as their objects,
because they possess the nature of being included within the time-periods (*adhvan*), just like present [dharmas], due to their existence and so forth.

In this regard, the Venerable Dharmatrāta is one who asserts the alteration of state (*bhāvānyathāvādī*). He reportedly says that for a dharma moving through the time periods, there is only an alteration of its state, but not an alteration of its substance (*dravya*).

Just as gold, which is the cause for the designations "bracelet," "armlet," or "earring," undergoes an alteration of its qualities but not of the gold itself, so too a dharma undergoes an alteration from its future state and so forth.

For indeed, a dharma attains the state of the present by relinquishing its future state, and it attains the state of the past by relinquishing its present state; however, there is no alteration of its substance (*dravya*), because the substance remains constant in all states.
Otherwise, it would follow that what is future is one thing, what is present is another, and what is past is yet another.
What, then, is this "state" (*bhāva*) intended by him?
There is a specific quality by which the application of designations and cognitions such as "past" and so forth occurs.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka is one who speaks erroneously regarding the characteristics;
he, it is said, asserts the following:

When a dharma exists in the time-periods (*adhvan*), if it is past, it is endowed with the characteristic of the past, yet it is not dissociated from the characteristics of the future and the present. Just as a man who is attached to one woman is not thereby unattached to the others, so too should the future and present [characteristics] be understood.
This differs from the previous [view] because its conventional usage depends upon the attainment of the activity (*vṛtti*) of the characteristics such as the past.
The Venerable Vasumitra is the proponent of the theory that there is a difference in state (*avasthānyathātva*).

He [Vasumitra] indeed says: "A dharma, as it moves through the time-periods (*adhvan*), is designated as one thing or another by virtue of its changing state (*avasthāntara*), but not by virtue of its substance (*dravya*), because the substance remains undifferentiated throughout all three times.

Just as a clay ball, when placed in the 'ones' column is called 'one,' in the 'hundreds' column 'one hundred,' and in the 'thousands' column 'one thousand,' so too an entity (*bhāva*) situated in its activity (*kāritra*) is 'present'; having fallen away from that, it is 'past'; and not yet having attained it, it is 'future.'"

Its conventional usage depends upon its state, as in the case of a clay ball; for there is no change in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but rather, through connection with a particular position, another designation arises that indicates a different number.

Buddhadeva is one who holds the view of "alteration" (*anyathānyathika*); he indeed says that a dharma, while existing in the time-periods (*adhvan*), is called by various names in relation to what precedes and follows.

Just as a single woman is called both "mother" and "daughter," this conventional usage depends upon what precedes and follows. That which has only the prior and no subsequent is the future; that which has both the prior and the subsequent is the present; and that which has only the subsequent and no prior is the past. These four are all proponents of existence (*sarvāstivādins*), designated respectively as those who maintain change in essence (*bhāvānyathātva*), change in characteristic (*lakṣaṇānyathātva*), change in state (*avasthānyathātva*), and change in relativity (*anyathānyathika*). Among them, the first does not differ from the Sāṃkhya doctrine because it maintains the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*).
Whatever refutation applies to that [theory] should be understood to apply to this one as well.
For instance, transformation would have to occur either without abandoning its prior intrinsic nature or by abandoning it.
If it occurs without abandoning it, then there follows the undesirable consequence of the confusion of the time-periods (*adhvan*).
If, on the other hand, it is by way of abandonment, then there is a contradiction with its eternal existence.

This same confusion applies to the second proponent as well, because everything would then possess all characteristics due to the universal conjunction of characteristics. However, a person is said to be "attached" through the manifestation (*samudācāra*) of passion, which is a distinct entity from the person, and "detached" merely through possession (*samanvāgama*). But for a dharma, there is no such thing as the manifestation of a characteristic or possession of a characteristic that is characterized by "acquisition" (*prāpti*), because that would entail the consequence of the characteristic being something other [than the dharma], just like acquisition itself. Thus, there is no similarity between the example and the subject of the illustration; otherwise, three time-periods would result within each single time-period.
For instance, in the past time, the preceding and succeeding moments are the past and the future, while the middle moment is the present;
this direction of refutation against them is clear.
Starting from the third [moment] itself, the examination of the three times is undertaken once more.
However, by means of the gold analogy, only a preliminary presentation of the established doctrine (siddhānta) has been made; it is not Dharmatrāta’s view alone that is intended.

And so he will say: "This distinction of the time-periods (adhvan) is merely conceptualized on the basis of activity (kāritra). Furthermore, for Dharmatrāta, the determination of the time-periods is not by means of activity; what then?
[This is] Vasumitra’s [view].

In that regard, if the past and the future did not exist, then the cognition regarding Mahāsammata who "was" and Śaṅkha the Cakravartin who "will be"—that is, regarding those things that have passed away and those not yet born—would be entirely without an object.
And consequently, there would be no cognition at all due to the absence of an object; such is the meaning.

For consciousness consists of the representation of each respective object; and if there were no object of knowledge (*jñeya*), there would be nothing for it to know, and thus it would simply not be consciousness.
Furthermore, the Blessed One stated that "consciousness arises in dependence upon a duality," specifying: "What is the duality? It is the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental objects (*dharma*).
If the past and future did not exist, then consciousness having them as its objective support would not arise in dependence upon a duality, which would contradict the scripture (*āgama*).
Furthermore, past karma would not yield its fruit if it were *niḥsattva*, meaning devoid of existence, because at the time the fruit arises, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) would be absent.
Moreover, that which is non-existent lacks the capacity to produce an effect, since the definition of non-existence is the absence of all causal efficacy.

Furthermore, there would be no distinct cognition for yogins regarding objects such as the past and so forth, categorized as "Māndhātṛ was," "Brahmadatta [was]," "Śaṅkha will be a universal monarch (*cakravartin*)," or "Maitreya will be a Tathāgata."
For there is no differentiation of non-existent things.

Therefore, past and future entities such as Śrī, Harṣa, and so forth, are not of the nature of a negation of substance, because they are taught as being included within the temporal periods (*adhvan*) as form and so on, just like the present.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, if past form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not be indifferent toward past form."

"For since past form exists, therefore the learned noble disciple is without regard for past form," and so forth; likewise, "whatever form there is—past, future, and so on—all that, being condensed together, receives the designation 'form-aggregate' (*rūpaskandha*)," and so on.
Those things, such as form and the rest, which are subsumed by way of time-period (*adhvan*) are called "subsumed by time-period.
By the word "and the rest" (*ādi*), feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates are included.
Their state is "the nature of form and so forth.
Here too, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is understood that they are taught as suffering, origin, impermanence, non-self, and so on.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Since [the dharma] exists eternally like space, how then is there a distinction between the past and so forth?
To this he says, "And it is not thus," and so on:
"And it should not be thought here: 'From what, then, does this distinction of time-periods (adhvan) arise?'"
This distinction of the time-periods (adhvan) is conceptualized by means of their functional activity (kāritra).
That which is engaged in its activity is called "present";
that which has fallen away from its activity is "past," while that which has not yet attained it is "future."
The activity (*kāritra*) of phenomena consists in projecting their fruit, but it does not produce it;
nor is there projection by past [phenomena], and therefore activity is not possible for them.

Since that which has attained its activity is called "present," that whose activity has ceased is "past," and that which has not yet attained its activity is "future," the time-periods (*adhvan*) are thus established by means of activity (*kāritra*).

What, then, is intended here by "activity"? If it is an operation characterized by seeing and so forth—such as the seeing and so on of the five [faculties] beginning with the eye, whereby the eye sees, the ear hears, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, and so on; and likewise, consciousness also possesses the quality of being a cognizer, since it "cognizes," and thus forms the objective domain of the faculties for visible forms and the rest.

This being the case, since the visual faculty (*cakṣus*) that is present and of the same kind (*tat-sabhāga*) lacks functional activity (*kāritra*) during states such as sleep, it would not possess the status of being "present.

Alternatively, if functional activity is defined by the characteristics of giving and receiving a fruit—just as the factors co-arising with the eye, such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth, constitute the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*); and the visual faculty produced immediately thereafter constitutes the fruit of human effort, the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*), and the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*)—then the eye is called "present" because it gives this fruit through its state of being a cause by way of producing [them], and receives [it] by way of maintaining its causal status.
If that is the case, then it would follow that even past causes—namely, the homogeneous, pervasive, and ripening causes—are present, because they are admitted to be giving their results.
Alternatively, if it is maintained that the activity (*kāritra*) consists exclusively of the characteristics of both giving and grasping a result, [then the same fault follows].

In this way, there would be the undesirable consequence that the past [dharmas], by virtue of being homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*) and so forth, would possess half the status of the present. Fearing this fault, the Master Saṃghabhadra says: "The activity (*kāritra*) of dharmas is said to be the capacity to project a fruit (*phalākṣepa-śakti*), but not the actual production of a fruit. There is no projection of a fruit for past homogeneous causes and the like, because the projection has already been completed during their state as present. Nor is it logical for that which has already been projected to be projected again, as that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, since activity is impossible for past [dharmas], there is no confusion of their defining characteristics."
He replies with the words beginning "By them":
"They must accept that this activity is either different from the dharma or of the very same nature as it;
for there is no other real possibility."
If they are distinct, then let it be understood that present things lack intrinsic nature (asvabhāvatā) prior to or after [the activity],
just as the causal state, conditioned nature, and so forth, are absent from the activity itself.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of permanence due to the constant persistence of its own nature;
for there exists no characteristic of permanence apart from this [nature].

They must accept that this activity is either different from or non-different from the dharma, because difference and non-difference are characterized by mutual exclusion; for the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other. There is no other possibility for a real entity.
In that case, if it were something else, then present things would result in being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in their prior and subsequent states,
because they possess causality and conditionedness— just like a cause possessing its activity.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [properties such as] substantiality (*vastutva*) and so forth are included.

Otherwise, if there were no lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) both before and after [an entity], then it would follow that all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are permanent, because intrinsic nature is established at all times. Furthermore, there is no definition of permanence other than eternal existence, as it has been said: "The wise call that permanent which is an intrinsic nature that does not perish."

It might be argued: "Granted that eternity is a capacity, but how is there a contradiction between the reason—such as being a cause or being conditioned—and the opposite of the probandum? To this he says, "Of the eternal," and so forth:
"The causality of an eternal entity has already been [refuted] due to the contradiction with succession and simultaneity."
For it is clearly denied that the state of being conditioned can have a locus in what is eternal.
Furthermore, if one describes *kāritra* (activity) as being distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth,
an unavoidable contradiction with one's own established tenets (*svasiddhānta*) results.
Regarding the word "previously":
this refers to the examination of the permanence of entities.
Since it is accepted that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are impermanent, it is clearly understood that the state of being conditioned cannot possibly exist in what is permanent.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with established doctrine in describing *kāritra* (activity) as something distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*) and the sense-bases (*āyatana*). For it has been stated by the Blessed One: "O Brahmin, 'everything' refers to all things, namely the five aggregates, the twelve sense-bases, and the eighteen elements."
Even if activity were non-different from the dharma, because it would not be distinct from it,
it would follow that it exists at all times, just like the essential nature of the dharma itself.
Consequently, this division of the paths is not conceived by virtue of that [unconditioned];
for there is no falling away from it, nor attainment, nor non-attainment, in terms of such divisions.

[508] Now, if it is admitted that the activity (*kāritra*) is non-different [from the dharma], then, because it is not distinct from it—just like the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the dharma—it too would follow as being present at all times. Consequently, this distinction of the time-periods (*adhvan*) based on activity—whereby the past is that which has fallen away from activity, the present is that which has attained it, and the future is that which has not yet attained it—would not exist. For if there were a distinction of this activity through attainment and non-attainment, then this distinction of the time-periods would be possible; however, those [states] do not occur as distinct, because for that which is eternally established in a single form, there is no distinction.
Alternatively, because it is not distinct from its activity, the dharma would be like the activity itself:
it would possess only a middle that is delimited by what precedes and follows it.

Furthermore, because it is not distinct from its activity (*kāritra*), the dharma itself would also possess an existence that is empty at its prior and posterior limits, just like the activity. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which is cut off at the prior and posterior [ends]" means "empty at its prior and posterior limits," and "all that" refers to "only the middle. That which possesses this [existence] is called "possessing that" (*tadvān*).
With the words "activity" (*kāritra*) and so forth, he mocks [the opponent] by pointing out their acceptance of mutually contradictory positions:
"Activity does not exist at all times, yet the phenomenon (*dharma*) is described as existing always;
and activity is not other than the phenomenon—this is clearly the work of the gods! (*devaviceṣṭitam*).
If, even in that case, the persistence of the entity depends upon another activity,
then surely this same objection applies everywhere.
If that were so, it would follow that phenomena such as form do not exist at all times, because they are not distinct from their activity; thus he says, "And the phenomenon always exists.
Even so, it would follow that the activity is something other than the phenomenon; therefore he says, "And the activity is not other than the phenomenon."

The gods, such as Īśvara and others, act out of their own autonomy without considering what is logical or illogical; thus, just as their activity proceeds independently of reason, so too does this [case].

Furthermore, if the future status of an activity is asserted to exist even in the absence of that activity itself, then one must not say that "the time periods are established by means of activity," because that would involve a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Just as the future status of an activity is established in dependence upon its own essential existence (*svarūpasattā*), so too...

Since entities themselves will possess states such as "future" and so forth, what is the use of postulating a "function" (*kāritra*)? Alternatively, if a function is further admitted for the function itself in order to avoid the fault of deviation, then the same inquiry regarding its distinction [from the entity] and so on applies there as well,
resulting in the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

As for what was said— that even if there is no difference [between the activity and its substratum], the activity would follow as being present at all times because it is indistinguishable from the nature of the dharma—
the Venerable Sahantabhadra says in response:
"It is observed that [activity] can exist even when distinct from the essential nature, just like the quality of resistance (*sapratighatva*)."
If there were a distinction, this would not at all assist what is under discussion.
For no property such as resistance and so forth is considered to be occasional for a persisting entity;
rather, it is because the entity itself arises in that manner at certain times.

A qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaka-dharma*) is observed even when it is distinct from the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), such as the quality of resistance (*sapratighatva*) and so forth belonging to earth and the other elements. For although these [elements] are not distinguished by being "entities" (*padārtha*), they are nevertheless perceived as qualified by attributes distinct from their intrinsic nature—such as being resistant or non-resistant, visible or invisible; in the same way, it is argued that [the entity] is also qualified by its activity (*kāritra*). This, however, does not assist with the matter at hand.

For this is the point at issue here: if it is admitted that the activity (*kāritra*) is non-different from the entity (*padārtha*), then because there would be no distinction in the activity—which constitutes the very self of that single entity—this differentiation of the time-periods (*adhvan*) based upon it would not be possible.

However, earth and the other elements are distinct from one another due to their association with mutually different characteristics; thus, it is logical that some are resistant (*sapratigha*) while others are indeed non-resistant (*apratigha*), such as feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest.

It is not the case that those very things which are non-obstructive are themselves obstructive; for there exists no single, persisting essence among earth and the other elements such that the property of being obstructive could be merely occasional.

What then? There is the arising of an impartite entity as it is differentiated from its own and other classes; therefore, it is not logical for a property non-different from its own nature to be the differentiator of a single thing.

Regarding the question, "How can there be a designation such as 'the resistance of form' (*rūpasya sapratighatvam*) as if it were distinct [from the thing itself]?"—if a property not distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*) were not a differentiator—he says: "anākṣiptetyādi" (beginning with *anākṣipta*).
"The entity itself is spoken of in that way [as having resistance], without implying any other distinction;
and by the word 'of that form' (*tadrūpasya*), the mental impression (*vāsanā*) is also [indicated]."
"Not by way of excluding other distinctions" means by way of rejecting other specific differences.
"Is spoken of in such a manner" refers to this.
"As if it were a negative concomitance (vyatireka). "That" refers to the state of being possessed of resistance (sapratighatva).
"By means of sound" refers to the resistance (*pratighatva*) of form;
here he provides an example: "and even the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the mind.
