The compound particle *apica* should be understood as having the sense of "just as" (*iva*).

Furthermore, he himself says: "Activity (*kāritra*) is not other than the phenomenon (*dharma*), because its own-being (*svabhāva*) is not perceived apart from it; nor is it merely the phenomenon itself, because even when the own-being exists, [activity] is sometimes absent.
Yet it is not that there is no distinction, because activity is previously non-existent, like a continuum (*santāna*).

Just as the uninterrupted arising of phenomena is called a 'continuum,' and this is not distinct from the phenomena because it is apprehended as inseparable from them, nor is it merely the phenomena themselves because that would entail even a single moment being a continuum, nor is it non-existent because its effects exist."
And it is said: "The effect of a continuum is intended, yet no such continuum exists at all;

in the same way, understand through reasoning that the establishment of the time-periods (*adhvan*) occurs by means of functional activity (*kāritra*). To this, he replies with the verse beginning "identity or otherness," and so forth.
Now, it is described as being inexpressible in terms of either identity or difference;
in that case, surely its causal activity would be merely conventional, like a continuum (saṃtāna) and so forth.

And therefore, because it is merely imagined, that [conceptual object] is not of use anywhere in an effect; for only a real entity (*vastu*), like a continuum (*santati*), is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
And since this presence of it is not real,
that [threefold] establishment of the time-periods (adhvan) as ultimately real is not tenable— just like [the reality of] a continuum (saṃtāna) and so forth.
//1809// "Like a continuum and so forth."

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of a collection (samūha) and so forth is intended. Just as the continuum (santāna) is devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva)—because it cannot be described as being either identical to or different from its constituent members (santānin), like a person (pudgala)—so too would activity (kāritra) be devoid of intrinsic nature. For if intrinsic nature existed, identity or difference would necessarily follow; and consequently, that activity, being merely conceptualized (kalpitatvāt), would not be functional toward any effect, just as a continuum is not.
Indeed, there is no functional utility for a conceptualized continuum toward any effect, because it lacks intrinsic nature.

Because the arising of an effect is necessarily tied to its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), it is the real entity (*vastu*) alone— possessing the nature of a continuum (*santānin*) and capable of causal efficiency— that exists; the continuum (*santāna*) is not a conceptual construction.

Furthermore, since activity (*kāritra*) exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), it has no real presence—whether prior to, simultaneous with, or subsequent to [the entity]—from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, the establishment of the three time periods (*adhvatraya*) based upon that [activity] would likewise be merely imagined (*kalpita*) and not ontologically real (*bhāvika*).

Even so, it might be argued: "Let activity (*kāritra*) be a conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*); let the establishment of the time-periods (*adhvavyavasthāna*) based upon it also be a conceptual existence. And what fault is there in that? To this he replies: "That which is called activity... "The capacity to project a fruit (*phalākṣepaśakti*), which is designated as 'activity' and falls within the range of verbal expression—since only a capacity is a real entity (*vastu*), how can that [activity] be a conceptual existence?"
If this very form is held to be that which performs functions such as burning and cooking,
why is it not admitted to exist in its past and future states as well?
If that very same thing is indeed a single self, how can there be for it both non-action and action, as well as the cessation of action?
How indeed can these mutually contradictory modes be applicable to a single, undifferentiated reality?

If it is argued that this entity is not without distinction because, upon the abandonment of one state, another state is assumed, [we reply: it is still conceived as being neither existent nor non-existent.
Are the states indeed distinct from the entity because they do not attain the status of being its agent?
For it is precisely through the existence of those very states that the existence of the effect is perceived.
For you have described the capacity to project a fruit as the "activity" (*kāritra*) of dharmas.
And how could that capacity to project a fruit be a conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*)?
The meaning is that it could not be so at all.
Consequently, the implication is that the establishment of the temporal periods (adhvan) based on that [efficacy] must be accepted as truly real.

Furthermore, regarding this form of fire and so forth which is perceived as performing purposeful actions such as burning and cooking—is that very same thing in its past and future states, or is it something else?
If it is that very same thing, how can mutually contradictory properties such as non-efficacy and so forth be compatible within this single, undifferentiated entity consisting of form and the rest?
By means of which there would be the sequential establishment of the future, present, and past.
For if there were unity even when contradictory properties are superimposed, then the distinction between different things would be destroyed;
and consequently, the entire world would be nothing but one.
And if they were identical, there would follow the consequence that they arise simultaneously and so forth.

Now, if it is conceived that the entity is not undifferentiated throughout the time-periods (*adhvan*) because it is differentiated by the distinction between abandoning and assuming states, even so, it must be stated whether those states are different from the entity or non-different.
The opponent says: "No."
The connection is that "they are distinguished from existence.
Why?
Because of the consequence that existence would be a non-agent, which entails the predicament of its being devoid of agency.
For it is through positive and negative concomitance that the capacity of those very states toward the effect is established.
Regarding this, he states the refutation beginning with "abhedam" and so forth:
"How can they accept the non-difference of a thing across the time-periods (adhvan),
when those [states] arise after not having existed and perish while being of that very nature?"
And in the middle state, it is an agent by its very own nature;
and that same nature belongs to it even in the other two states.
In that case, how could there be for him the notions of "action" and "cessation of action"?
Furthermore, if his agency were by means of another's form, he would again incur the state of non-agency.
If fire and the like in their past and future states were considered something other [than their present state],
then this fault of confusion and so forth would have no basis in this position.

Thus, it is now produced as something capable of causal efficiency precisely by not having existed before, and it does not persist after having come into being; therefore, its nature of lacking continuity is established.
How can they accept or admit that the states (avasthās) are non-different from the entity (vastu)? They certainly cannot,
because the states come into being after not having existed and perish after having existed.
And yet, the entity is not accepted as being such [i.e., momentary], because its existence at all times is admitted.
Therefore, how could those [states]—which come into being after not having existed and which perish—be logically identical with that [entity]?
Certainly not.
Because their acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are distinct.

For otherwise, since they would be identical with that [entity], it would follow that these states also exist eternally, just like the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing; or else, because they are not separate from the entity, it would follow that the entity itself is non-existent prior to its arising and so forth, just like the specific forms of the states themselves.

Granted that there may be a conceptualization of distinct states, even so, the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) has not been avoided. To explain: in the intermediate state, does the entity act by its own nature (*svarūpa*) or by the nature of another? If it acts by its own nature, then since that very same nature exists in both other states—the past and the future—how could there be the loss of action and non-action for this agent-nature?
If, on the other hand, it acts by the nature of another, then its status as a non-agent would follow once again, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it is a non-entity.
Thus, first of all, it is not logical that the very same entity, such as fire, exists in both past and future states.

Now, suppose it is something else; in this case, the fault of the confusion of mutually contradictory properties—such as activity and non-activity—would not occur in a single locus, because the entities would be distinct.

However, since that entity such as fire which is capable of producing effects like burning and cooking arises after having not existed and perishes after having existed, there would be a contradiction with the admission of its eternal existence, due to the absence of any underlying continuity (*anvaya*).

It might be argued: "Even if a thing, having not previously been capable of performing a function, arises, and having arisen, passes away, nevertheless, in its past and future states, the entity exists indeed as something incapable of performing a function; therefore, there is no contradiction with the acceptance of its eternal existence. To this, he says: "That very same [entity]."
That alone is a real entity which is capable of causal efficiency;
and that [efficiency] does not exist in those two [non-entities]. Since it does not exist in them, the production of an effect from them is impossible.
"That very [thing]" refers to that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*).
"Of those two" refers to the past and future states.
"That which exists" refers to that which is unfit for causal activity (*akāryayogya*).

Furthermore, it might be argued: "The capacity for an effect is indeed admitted in the case of past factors such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*); therefore, the claim that 'no effect can arise from that' is unproven. To this he says: "And the past... "And this past entity, because it comes into being after not having existed, clearly becomes present, just like any other [present thing], and also by virtue of its occasional occurrence."
If there were no cause, existence or non-existence would be constant, as it would not depend on anything else;
therefore, an object whose existence is determined by a cause is called "present."

Others maintain that conditioned phenomena such as form possess the nature of being conditioned due to their association with birth, duration, and so forth, and that they differ from things like cessation through deliberation.

In that regard, what specific distinction does "birth" produce such that it is said to be its producer? For that [entity], which is other than the unborn due to its own nature, there is nothing further [to be produced].
[Page 513] Furthermore, an excellence that is non-different from that [entity] cannot be produced,
because it exists even prior to its completion, just as it does at the time subsequent to its completion.
There is no other excellence [in the effect], because it would be distinct [from the cause] and thus unconnected;
furthermore, there would be the consequence of the non-existence of the effect, since it is non-existent prior [to its production].
Whether there be change, persistence, or destruction, the same faults regarding the alternatives of identity and difference necessarily follow concerning aging and the rest.
"Like anything else" means like the present time, which is not a subject of dispute.
"And also because of its occasional occurrence" means...

The connection is that "the present [entity] is established like any other. Nor is this reason devoid of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*); for indeed, whatever object is produced by causes and conditions is called "present," and whatever is occasional is necessarily caused by causes and conditions. This is because for that which is causeless, there are only two possibilities: namely, eternal existence or eternal non-existence, since it does not depend on anything else. Therefore, whatever is occasional necessarily has its existence produced by causes and conditions; and whatever has its existence produced by causes and conditions...

Thus, it is established that [the dharma] must necessarily exist as present; there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between being present and being occasional. Furthermore, if the past and future existed substantially (*dravyataḥ*), it would follow that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are eternal.

Consequently, it would follow that there is no distinction between form and the other [conditioned phenomena] on the one hand, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*) and the like on the other.

Now, if it is the view of others that form and the rest possess the nature of the conditioned because they are associated with the characteristics of the conditioned, whereas space and the like do not—and that for this reason form and the rest differ from analytical cessation and so forth—that is incorrect. For these four are the characteristics of the conditioned: birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
In this regard, it is accepted that their functions are such that birth produces, duration stabilizes, decay causes aging, and impermanence destroys.

Now, regarding birth: what specific quality does it produce such that it is called the "producer" of form and so forth? Does it produce a quality from that form and so forth which is distinct and separate, or one that is non-distinct and not separate? These are the two positions.

In that regard, it cannot first be non-distinct [from the universal], because this particular (viśeṣa), being already accomplished even prior to the operation of the universal, is incapable of being produced, just as it is after its accomplishment;
for the production of what is already accomplished is not possible, as it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress.
Nor can there be a distinct excellence (atiśaya), for the same reason as after its accomplishment.
For it is not logical for an already established entity to undergo an action, as that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.
Nor is a distinct excellence (*atiśaya*) produced; for if it were distinct, the relationship between this [entity] such as form and this excellence would be unestablished.
To explain: the relationship cannot be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), because their distinctness has been admitted.

Alternatively, if it were not accepted, the previously mentioned fault would follow. Nor can the relationship be characterized by origination from that [cause], because origination belongs to the universal (*jāti*) itself.
Furthermore, there is no other relationship, since [relationships] such as that of container and contained are included within origination from that.

Now, if its production is admitted, then since the particularity (viśeṣa) arises from that alone, it would follow that it is produced eternally; what, then, would the universal (jāti) do? If it is argued that [the cause] produces it by depending on the universal, this is not so, for dependence upon a universal that provides no assistance is illogical due to the consequence of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Or, if there is assistance, then in considering whether that assistance is identical to or different from the entity—just as in the case of a specific excellence (atiśaya)—there follows the consequence of an infinite regress.
Therefore, if there were a difference [between the entity and its qualities], a relationship would not be established.
Furthermore, since that excellence (*atiśaya*) would have existed previously, one would be forced to accept the doctrine of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*).

Thus, when aging effects alteration (*anyathātva*), stability effects persistence, and impermanence effects destruction—if one considers these [qualities] such as alteration in terms of the dilemma of whether they are different or non-different from the entity, whatever faults [were stated] regarding "birth" (*jāti*) must also be stated regarding aging and the others.
These [factors], such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, initiate their own respective effects by way of a restriction of capacity; and that nature of theirs exists both before and after.
And since its nature is capable [of action], why does it not then initiate its own corresponding activity? If that activity were to begin, there would be an infinite number of time-periods.

Furthermore, as for the fact that birth and the other [phases] initiate their own effects, this is accepted because of the restriction of their capacity-inherent nature; and since that capacity-inherent nature exists in them at all times, it follows that they would always initiate their own effects.
Nor can there be a deficiency of causes and conditions, because those too are eternally present.

Furthermore, because birth and other factors perform their own functions, such as production, in both past and future states, it would follow that there is an infinite number of time-paths (adhvan) within a single time-path.

Furthermore, are entities such as the past and so forth momentary or not? If the former, then for those two [past and future], that same state of having immeasurable time-periods (adhvan) would again follow.
That moment which arises is the present;
that which, having arisen, has perished is the past; and that which is yet to be is the future.
Furthermore, there are two positions: that past and future [phenomena] are either momentary or not momentary.
In that regard, if the first position holds—that they are momentary—then the very same infinite number of time-periods (adhvan) results;
he demonstrates this by the phrase "that which is a moment."
Moreover, if those [conditioned phenomena] were non-momentary, your established doctrine would be contradicted;
for in your own tenet, it is proclaimed that all conditioned phenomena are momentary.

Now, if the position is that they are non-momentary, this being the case, there is a contradiction with the established doctrine (*kṛtānta*); for "established doctrine" refers to the final tenet (*siddhānta*). Thus, the tenet is that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary.

Even if there were a contradiction by reasoning, if [things] were real, they would necessarily be subject to momentary destruction, just like present things; for the necessary connection in this case has already been established.
Furthermore, the thesis is not only in contradiction with established doctrine (siddhānta), but it is also in contradiction with authoritative testimony (āgama).
For instance, according to the rule: "Whatever exists is momentary, just like the present; and since the past and future exist, they too must necessarily be subject to momentary destruction.

Moreover, as previously established in the section on momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga), the logical connection (pratibandha) of this reason has been proven; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva).

For indeed, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is the definition of existence; and since causal efficiency is incompatible with a non-momentary entity—given that it cannot occur either successively or simultaneously—the cessation of causal efficiency entails the cessation of existence, which is its defining characteristic. Thus, existence is excluded from the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*).
These past and future [entities] would either be capable of causal efficiency,
or, if they possess the reality of such capacity, they would be present, just like anything other than them.
But if they were non-existent, then, being devoid of all causal capacity,
they would follow as being either destroyed or unborn, like a lotus in the sky.
Furthermore, all uncreated things such as space are subject to the same logical inquiry;
since they do not establish the absence of inconclusiveness, they too cannot be the basis [for the argument].
The capacity for restricted purposeful action in entities arises from conditions;
if they were causeless, everything would be applicable everywhere at once.
The characteristic of a present entity is nothing other than its birth from a causal complex that produces a capacity for a determinate purposeful action. And there is no other [characteristic].
And since that [nature] exists for you as an undivided whole belonging to both the past and the future,
why does the status of being present not follow for these [entities]?
Furthermore, there are two possible positions regarding these past and future [entities]: they must either be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) or not capable.
If they are capable, then by virtue of the existence of that capability, they would follow as being present, just like the present which is beyond dispute.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*) is present, just like the present things that are not subject to dispute; and past things and so forth are capable of causal efficiency. This is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) based on a reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Nor is this inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because if presentness were excluded, it would follow that destroyed and unborn things would be devoid of all capacity, like a sky-lotus.

The formal argument is as follows: those things which do not exist in the present are not capable of anything whatsoever, just like a sky-lotus; and past entities and so forth do not exist in the present. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Nor is there an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) factors—space, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyānirodha*)—because these too are included within the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*).
Therefore, there is no basis for the assumption that [the reason] is inconclusive.

For it must be admitted that this capacity of entities for specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) arises from conditions; otherwise, if it were causeless, then in the absence of a determining cause, entities would not possess specific capacities. Consequently, everything would be applicable toward every effect.
Therefore, since it is not logical for there to be a restriction of capacity in unproduced things such as space, there is no basis for the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) based on them.

Nor is there the possibility of the first reason having a doubtful presence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because that which is produced by causes and conditions—the capacity for a restricted purposeful action—is precisely the definition of the present. And since this definition of being present exists in its entirety even in past and future things, why would the consequence of their being "present" not follow, given the absence of any other distinguishing factor?
Therefore, this effort toward union with heaven or liberation is fruitless;
for no fruit achievable through exertion is perceived here.

Furthermore, for one who holds that the past and the future exist as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*), their fruit also exists eternally; thus, effort aimed at attaining heaven or liberation would be fruitless, because there would be no fruit whatsoever to be accomplished through exertion. What efficacy, then, could there be in effort characterized by vows, observances, and the like?
If it is argued that its efficacy lies in production (*utpādane*), [we reply:]...
In that case, it is established that production is "coming into being after having not existed.
But if that [production] also exists [already], then what now has efficacy, and where?
If you say, "The efficacy is in making [the thing] present," [we reply:]...
What is this so-called "making present"?
If it means being drawn from another location,
then it follows that the entity must be eternal, because it would exist at all times.

Since formless entities such as sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest are devoid of activity, how could there be an "attracting" (*ākarṣaṇa*) of them? Furthermore, it is established that this attracting occurs by way of something coming into being after not having existed before.

Heaven (*svarga*) refers to the summit of Mount Sumeru and so forth; liberation (*apavarga*) is *mokṣa*; the attainment of these two is their conjunction (*saṃsarga*), for which effort, vows, observances, and the like are required.
Now, if their capacity for causal efficiency is not admitted,
then for this very reason they are non-existent, like a flower in the sky.
Now, if the second position is adopted— that they are incapable of causal efficiency—
then, in that case, precisely because they are devoid of causal efficiency, they would follow as being non-existent, like a sky-flower;
for non-existence is characterized by the absence of all capacity.

Having thus stated the means of valid cognition that establishes the non-existence of past and future [entities], he says "The reasons," etc., in order to refute the means of valid cognition that establishes their existence: "But reasons, which are properties of an entity, do not share in the proof of what is unestablished; or else, because of the establishment of presentness, they are contradictory due to the sublation of the locus."

For the previously stated reasons, such as "because they are subsumed within the time-periods," are unestablished with respect to their locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because the subjects (*dharmin*), such as the past and so forth, are themselves unestablished.
As it has been said: "A property of an existent does not exist when [the subject] is unestablished.

Even if they were established, since the existence of the present is already established, these reasons would be contradictory (*viruddha*), as they prove the opposite of the essential nature of the property (*dharmasvarūpa*).

How then is the inclusion within the time-periods of past and future form and so forth explained? For a rabbit’s horn, being absolutely non-existent, is not established as either past or future. To this he says: "Having been," and so forth. Form which, having come into being, has ceased, is declared to be "past.
That which is yet to be when the completeness of conditions exists is "future."
It has been established that, if [the object] were existent, it would follow that it exists [at that time];
for the mere state of being present is the definition of the present.
This is easy to understand.
If so, how then was the existence of form, sensation, and so forth taught? To this he says: "Dependent upon a duality.
That which was stated by the Seer of Reality—that consciousness arises dependent upon a duality—is a teaching intended with reference to the mind together with its objects.

For consciousness is of two kinds: that which has an object and that which lacks an object; it was with reference to that which has an object that the Blessed One taught the doctrine of consciousness having a twofold support.
Now, as to how it is determined that even cognition exists without an objective support (*anālambana*), he says: "Of the cognitions of an eternal God and so forth," and so on.
For there is no objective support whatsoever for the cognitions of an eternal God and the like, because those [objects]—such as words, names, and other dharmas—are devoid of those forms.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), imagined entities such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and time (*kāla*) are included.
Furthermore, one should not think that these cognitions have sound and so forth as their objective supports; thus he says "sound, name, etc.

The "form" (*ākāra*) of that [object], such as Īśvara and so on, consists of its eternality, its being the cause of all things, and so forth—whatever is determined by that cognition. The "separation" from that form belongs to the sound or the name, which is a specific type of dissociated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the cause (nimitta) and so forth, which are accepted by others as having the nature of a reflection of the object (arthapratibimbaka) and the like.
If, then, consciousness exists even without an object, how is it designated as "knowledge" (*jñāna*)?
For it is proclaimed that "it is called consciousness because it cognizes" (*vijānātīti vijñānam*); and if there is no object to be known, what would constitute consciousness?
To this he replies: "merely by way of following after awakening" (*bodhānugatimātreṇa*).
It is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) merely by virtue of its following after awakening; and that [awakening] is conceived as its non-insentient nature due to its luminosity.
If it is argued that even the following of awakening is not possible without awakening itself, he says: "And that.
That is the following of awakening;
[it belongs] to this consciousness.

What is being said? That which is its non-inert nature is designated as "the nature of consciousness" because, due to the absence of any other object to be illuminated and the lack of any other illumination, it has the nature of light—like light existing in the sky.
To the question of how an action that has passed away can yield a fruit, he says: "The ripening cause," and so forth.
It is not accepted that a past [action] yields a fruit;
rather, the fruit is held to arise from the continuum of consciousness which has been perfumed by it.
It has been perfumed through a succession [of moments] such that it is capable of producing a fruit; it has been generated.

If this is so, how did the Blessed One say: "There is that karma which has been exhausted, ceased, and transformed"? It was with reference to that very same latent impression (*vāsanā*) within the continuum of consciousness (*cetaḥ-santati*) that he declared "there is karma"; it was stated figuratively (*bhaktyā*), just as one might speak of the non-destruction of the root.
The word "by devotion" (bhaktyā) means figuratively (upacāreṇa).

Just as when a continuous stream of fruits such as gold produced from a primary substance has come into being, even though the primary substance itself has perished, it is said that the primary substance has not perished; so too is it with karma.

To the question, "What is the purpose of teaching by way of figurative designation? he says: "For the destruction of the view of annihilation. Thus has it been revealed by the Teacher; otherwise, how could the teaching in the *Śūnyatā-sūtra* be interpreted?

If it were said that "past karma does not exist," then disciples would conclude that even the capacity to produce a fruit—which was deposited by past karma through a continuous succession—is non-existent; thus they would fall into the view of nihilism. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Karma exists.
Otherwise, if the past existed in its own right, how could the teaching in the *Paramārtha-śūnyatā-sūtra* be interpreted?

The eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation. For the eye, having not existed, comes to be, and having existed, it passes away. If it is argued that "it comes to be after not having existed" refers to the present time, this is not so;
for the time-period is not a different entity from the phenomenon itself, since those very phenomena are said to exist in such a state within the time-periods.
Now, if it comes to exist after having been non-existent in its own nature, then it is established that the future eye does not exist.

Furthermore, if conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were eternally present, there would be an absence of cause and effect, and consequently an absence of the truths of suffering and its origin. Due to that absence, the truths of cessation and the path would also be absent. Thus, because of the non-existence of the four noble truths, thorough knowledge, abandonment, realization, and cultivation would not be tenable. And due to their absence, there would be no persons established in the fruits or those entering toward them; therefore, the entire teaching (*pravacana*) would be nullified. Hence, the conceptualization of a collection of entities such as the past and so forth is not sound.

To the question of how the knowledge of the past and future is distinguished for yogins, he says: "By way of succession," and so forth. Yogins know that form of the present which has entered into a state of causality, whether by way of succession or directly.

And subsequently, they follow [the object] by means of pure mundane cognitions whose nature is accompanied by conceptual construction, even though these [cognitions] do not have reality as their actual object.
Based upon that actual and future subsistence of cause and effect,
the teachings concerning the past and the future proceed.
The teachings of the Tathāgata proceed entirely without effort, arising from a continuum of gnosis that is free from the entire web of conceptual construction.
With respect to past objects, it has attained the state of being an effect; with respect to future [objects], it has the state of being a cause.
"By those whose nature follows conceptual construction" means by those possessing conceptual construction (*savikalpa*).
"In reality, by means of non-objects" means that because cognitions accompanied by verbal expressions do not take the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object.
"That" refers to this reason.
The teachings concerning the past and so forth proceed for yogins who are not yet purified, based upon the actual and potential continuity of cause and effect.
However, for the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, even pure mundane knowledge does not exist, because he is eternally in meditative equipoise due to the abandonment of all ignorance,
and because conceptual construction has ignorance as its very nature.
As it has been said:
"This conceptual construction itself has come to possess the nature of ignorance,
because it proceeds by superimposing its own form upon an external object."
Thus, by the power of the equipment of merit and wisdom from his previous vows, the teachings of him—whose physical form is like a wish-fulfilling gem—proceed spontaneously and without effort.
Thus concludes the examination of the three times.
In order to support the statement that "it is without beginning or end," he says "If... and so forth, preceded by an objection:
"If no persisting entity whatsoever exists here, then there would be no other world, because of the non-existence of one who goes to the other world."
"Something" refers to the self (*ātman*) and so forth.

Among these, because the self has already been refuted previously, it lacks persistence precisely due to its non-existence; and as for consciousness and the other aggregates, because they are momentary and because continuity (*anvaya*) has been refuted in the examination of the three times, there is no continuity.
But [the opponent might argue] that the body and so forth will be the ones who go to the next world; to this he says "deha" and so on:
"When the body, intellect, sense-faculties, and so forth perish at every moment, it is not logical for them to belong to the next world, nor is any other [entity] admitted."
Therefore, just as fermented acids, wine, and so forth arise from specific elements,
so too does cognition either arise or is manifested from those very same elements.
By the word "etcetera," feeling, perception, and mental formations are included;
nor is anything else admitted, namely,
a self.
This is understood as merely conforming to the position of the Lokāyata.
For its aphorism is as follows: "Because there is no one who goes to another world, there is no other world.
Likewise: "Earth, water, fire, and air—these are the four principles; from them arises consciousness."
Regarding this, some commentators explain that consciousness arises from them, while others say it is manifested; therefore, he states the two positions: "It is born, or else it is manifested.
"Sourness" refers to acidity.
"Surely," etc.
The power to produce intoxication;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the capacity to produce fainting and so forth is included.

Now, is it not well known that consciousness arises in dependence upon the eyes and so forth, as well as their objects such as visible forms? Why then is it said that consciousness arises from those [elements] alone? To this he replies: "A particular configuration.
And it is in a particular configuration of earth and the other elements that this designation—'body,' 'sense-faculties,' and so on—is applied; for no reality other than this exists.
And thus their Sūtra states: "The designation 'object' and 'faculty' applies to that collection.
For there are no faculties and so forth apart from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); they are merely designated as such because of a particular configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) of them.
Nor is that which is called "configuration" something other than the things configured.
Moreover, this set of four great elements is established by direct perception.
Apart from these, there is no other reality established by direct perception.
Nor is there any means of valid cognition other than direct perception by which another [reality], such as the next world and so forth, could be established.
There is no relationship of cause and effect between the two cognitions under dispute,
because they reside in different bodies, just like the cognitions of a cow and a horse.
Nor are cognitions held to be produced by the consciousness of the intended object,
because they possess the nature of cognition, just like cognitions connected with another continuum.

Furthermore, if there were an absence of causal relation between the mind residing in the past body and the mind of the first birth, as well as between the mind at death and the subsequent mind, then one might postulate a future world on the grounds that the continuity of consciousness would not have ceased. However, such is not the case; for there is no relationship of cause and effect between those two minds under dispute—the first and the last—because they reside in different bodies, just like the cognitions residing in a cow and a horse.

Alternatively, the cognitions of birth are the subjects (*dharmin*); the probandum (*sādhya*) is the negation of their being produced by the final consciousness residing in a past body; "because they are cognitions" (*jñānatvāt*) is the general reason (*hetu*); and the cognitions belonging to other continua (*saṃtāna*) serve as the examples (*nidarśana*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: if something is a cognition, it is not produced by that intended final cognition residing in a past body, because it is a cognition, just like a cognition belonging to another continuum.

Furthermore, these cognitions existing within the intended body are of the nature of knowledge; thus, there is the perception of a property pervaded by its opposite (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), because the state of being knowledge (*jñānatva*) is pervaded by that which is opposed to being produced by the cognition of the intended [body].
Thus, the negation of a past birth has been established.
Now, for the sake of negating a future birth, he says "of one with attachment," and so forth:
"A mind that dies with attachment does not effect a connection with another mind."
Just as for one whose afflictions have been removed through the state of the knowledge of death.

The death-consciousness of one who possesses attachment does not link to another consciousness, because it is a death-consciousness, just like the final consciousness of an Arhat; this is an "observation of the contradictory of the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi).
As for the case of one whose defilements have been eliminated, it is as follows:
[their] death-knowledge.
From where, then, does the arising of the mind occur? To this he says: "From the body alone," and so forth.
"Therefore, it is logical that knowledge arises from the body itself when it is presided over by the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the downward breath (apāna); this has been declared by Kambalāśvatara."
And thus the Sūtra says: "From the body alone," as stated by Kambalāśvatara.

But surely, even when the body has not yet been formed—in states such as the *kalala* and so forth—consciousness certainly exists, albeit in a state of fainting; and since that is established as being produced by a preceding moment of differentiated consciousness, how can there be the restriction that [it arises] "from the body alone"? To this he says: "In the *kalala* and so forth," etc.
The claim that consciousness exists in the *kalala* and other such stages is reckless.
For, because the sense faculties have not yet arisen, no object is perceived therein.
Furthermore, no form of cognition other than the comprehension of an object is logically possible;
therefore, its existence even during states such as fainting is not tenable.
Nor does that [consciousness] persist at that time in the form of a potentiality (śakti),
for since potentialities lack a substratum, their persistence cannot be conceived.
If the self, which is the substratum of cognition, does not exist, then the body alone must be its support;
and when the body finally ceases to exist, what would be the support for the functioning of cognition?

The sense faculty and its object are indeed the causes for the arising of consciousness, because knowledge consists in the apprehension of an object; and since the sense faculty and the object are absent during the embryonic stage (kalala) and so forth, how could that effect—consciousness—exist? Thus, by the non-perception of its cause, the absence of consciousness in states such as fainting is established; this is the general meaning. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to postulate that consciousness exists at that time in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), because there is no substratum for knowledge (*jñānāśraya*)—neither the self (*ātman*) as imagined by the Naiyāyikas and others, nor a continuum of consciousness (*vijñānaprabandha*)—at that time.
Furthermore, it is not logical for power to be without a substratum;
therefore, by implication, the body itself is the substratum at that time.

This is because any other [substratum], such as a self that is the support of cognition, does not exist then—whether it be the entity that is the support of cognition, namely the continuum of consciousness, or a self.

Furthermore, at the end, in the state of death, when the body—the substratum—ceases to exist, how could consciousness remain without a substratum? Thus, the non-existence of future births is established.
If another body is perceived as having taken refuge in a different body produced immediately after that [previous one],
how is it understood that [the self] exists?
And how could that consciousness, which has proceeded from a different body— like the minds of elephants, horses, and so forth— be connected to a single continuum?
Therefore, one must accept some person who is the substratum of cognition, beginningless and endless, and subject to transmigration; otherwise, there is total nihilism.
Now, it might be argued that mental activity will occur by depending on the body belonging to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which arises immediately after death; but this is incorrect.
For no other [entity] is observed to arise immediately after death, and it is not logical to ascertain the existence of something that has not been observed.
Because that [intermediate state] would be the object of the conventional usage of "non-existent.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a consciousness belonging to one continuum (*ekasantāna*) to take recourse in another body, because this would entail the loss of its connection to that single continuum—just like the minds of an elephant and a horse.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever consciousness functions in different bodies is not connected to a single continuum, just like the minds of an elephant and a horse; and the minds of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the death-existence (*maraṇabhava*) function in different bodies. Thus, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving something incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalambha*).
But this is not the case; therefore, there is a reversal [of the reason].

Whatever is connected to a single continuum does not function in a different body, just as the mind of an elephant does not depend upon the body of a horse. And since the mind of a living being is connected to a single continuum, this is an "observation of the pervasion by the contradictory" (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
This is because being connected to a single continuum is pervaded by functioning in a non-different body, which is the opposite of functioning in a different body.
"Single," and so forth, is the conclusion.
"Beginning" (ādi) means origination; "end" (nidhana) means destruction. That which has neither beginning nor end is "without beginning or end" (anādinidhana). "Nara" refers to the self (ātman).
Alternatively, by the phrase "nor is there anything beyond," this sutra indicates that because there is no one who goes to the next world, there is no next world.

He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "tadatra" and so forth: "In this regard, there is no other 'next world' whatsoever than the continuum of the appropriation, that which is appropriated, and the elements, such as consciousness."
A certain state characterized by fixed limits is proclaimed;
and of that [state], which is beginningless and endless, there is the designation of "subsequent," "prior," and "here."
Just as those who are attached to the pleasure of what is merely seen imagine the next world to be in another place or the like, so too is it described by us here.
If, however, the next world is denied as being distinct from that [present body],
then the proof is futile, because there is no dispute regarding its non-existence.
Since a continuum is not a real entity, there is no possibility of it undergoing different states;
how then could the world or another [being] established within it be real?

Indeed, the moments are not what is expressed by the word "continuum," for they are the members of the continuum; rather, they are presented collectively as a "continuum" for the sake of brevity, just like a forest or similar entities.

In this regard, what is this so-called "other world" (paraloka) that you seek to negate? Is it something other than the four aggregates beginning with consciousness—which stand in a causal relationship as material cause and its effect—or is it those very same [aggregates]? The first position is not tenable, because such a thing is not admitted.
For there exists no "other world" here other than the continuum of consciousness and the rest, which consists of material cause and its effect, such that it could be admitted.

Rather, it is only a certain limitation consisting of a boundary such as a period of a hundred years or more of that beginningless and endless continuum of cognition and so forth that is established as "the next world" or "this world" or "the previous [world].
Just as you, out of attachment to the pleasure of what is merely perceived, imagine a certain extent of the sensory domain—such as another place—to be "the next world" and so on;
as it has been said: "A person is only as much as is within the range of the senses; furthermore, another place, another time, or another state is called 'the next world'."

If, however, a negation is made of a "next world" that is distinct from the continuum of consciousness and so forth existing in the relationship of cause and effect, then the proof is futile because it establishes what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*), since such a [substantially separate] next world is not admitted.

But surely, since the continuum (*saṃtati*) is not a real entity (*avastu*), any specific state (*avasthāviśeṣa*) established within it must also be non-real; consequently, this "next world" established within that specific state of the continuum would also not be ultimate (*apāramārthika*).
This is not a fault.

By the term "continuum" (*santati*), the very moments (*kṣaṇa*) which are the actual entities (*vastu*)—the members of the continuum—are revealed collectively and simultaneously for the sake of linguistic convenience, just as the *dhava* trees and others are denoted by the word "forest. [Objection:

How then was it previously stated in the discussion beginning with "like the activity of a continuum" that the continuum is not a real entity? [Response: He says, "Because it is conceived as a unity," and so forth:
"It is considered to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) because it is conceived as a unity."
They cannot be described as being either identical to or different from [the self], like a row of lotuses in the sky.
And how could that [mind], which is beginningless and endless, ever attain accomplishment,
if this mind were considered to be without cause by virtue of its being primordial?
Whether it arises from an eternal cause, or is eternal and exists by itself,
or is produced solely from the elements, or else is born from mere cognition;
It is not logical that the initial consciousness at conception and so forth should be without a cause;
for if it were so, its existence as something occasional would be impossible in every respect.
Nor was it created by eternal entities such as mind, time, space, God, or the self;
for precisely because of that, it would follow that it must exist eternally, yet those [entities] do not exist.
To claim that consciousness is a single entity with a permanent nature is a rash assertion,
for the distinctness of mental states such as those perceiving forms, sounds, and so forth, is clearly perceived.
Its manifestation does not arise from the elements such as earth, fire, water, and so forth;
nor is it the manifestation of all minds simultaneously, because that would entail the absurd consequence of universal simultaneity.
For that [entity], namely the four great elements, is held by others to be of a stable nature;
moreover, the dependence upon auxiliary causes in regard to a stable entity has already been refuted.

As for that continuum which is conceived as a unity, it is considered to be a non-entity because it cannot be described as being either identical to or different from [its constituent moments], like a row of lotuses in the sky; we do not establish the existence of the next world based on a particular state of that [continuum]. If, however, the negation of this very continuum of consciousness and so forth—designated as the "next world"—is what is intended, then the negation of the next world cannot be accomplished by means of negating its essential nature, because what is perceived cannot be denied.
What then?
It is by way of negating the properties of having no beginning and no end.
And how is it that this very [continuity], which is without beginning or end, is not established?

If that first mind of birth is considered to be without a cause, or produced from causes such as an eternal consciousness or a Lord (Īśvara), or if it is itself eternal, or produced from the mere elements (bhūta-mātra), or caused by a cognition existing in another continuum—these are the five positions. For if the preceding mind were caused by each successive prior cognition within its own continuum, then the beginninglessness of the mental continuum would be established; it could not be otherwise. It is with this intention that these positions are presented.
In this regard, the first position is not tenable because it entails the consequence of eternal existence and so forth.
For entities become occasional precisely through dependence; and that which is causeless does not depend on anything at all—so why would it ever cease?
Nor is the second position tenable for the very same reason, as it likewise entails the consequence of eternal existence.

For the non-existence of effects is due to the deficiency of their causes; therefore, it must be explained why that which possesses its causes in their entirety should not come into being. Nor is the third position tenable; why? Because of the absence of that [cause], there is always an absence of existence.
With the words "one" (*ekam*) and so forth, he demonstrates that very absence [of the self].
By this, he states the contradiction of the proposition with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). With the words "the earth" (*kṣoṇī*) and so forth, he refutes the fourth position.
*Kṣoṇī* means the earth (*pṛthivī*).
The same fault applies here as in the position that [the world] arises from causes such as an eternal God; for the four great elements are asserted by others to be eternal.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that production from an eternal [cause] occurs through a sequence dependent upon auxiliary causes, because it has already been thoroughly demonstrated that an eternal [entity] does not depend on an auxiliary cause that provides no benefit.
[Objection: Perhaps this very [world] is also described by others as being momentary.
How is it that, when those very [entities] exist, your own accepted position is not contradicted?
Granted that this [position] may be refuted; nevertheless, it is accepted as being logical:
that all things are determined by every means of reasoning to be momentary.

Now, the intention [of the author] is this: even if those other Cārvākas, out of fear of the aforementioned faults, were to accept that these four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are momentary, there would still be a fault.

For, in the first place, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the opponent by which the causal relationship between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the body could be established, such that their conventional usage might be proven.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Wherever there exists some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the existence of something for another person, by which that person’s conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding it must be performed by a discerning individual—just as, for example, there is no conventional usage of "cold" with respect to fire;

and there is no such means of valid cognition for establishing a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the intellect and the body. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Nor is the reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*); for the causal relationship is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), and that is determined only through specific positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), not merely by observation and non-observation.

In that context, when one must determine the effect through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), one must rely on the following: that upon the perception of certain [factors], something previously unperceived—which had met the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*)—is now perceived.

Otherwise, if one were not to require that it was previously unperceived while meeting the conditions for perceptibility, then it would be possible to suspect either that the effect already existed there previously or that it had moved from another location;
by which means the causality of walls and other such things situated beforehand would not be negated.
However, when non-perception of that which has met the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is demonstrated, that [doubt] is refuted,
because in that case there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of it.
Thus, first of all, the determination of the effect is established through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Even when determining an effect through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), one must rely on the principle that "when all other capable causes of that [effect] are present, it does not occur in the absence of this one alone. Otherwise, if one merely demonstrates that "it does not occur in its absence," its capacity would remain doubtful, because another capable cause might also be absent. Consequently, one could even suspect: "There is indeed something else capable there; it is withdrawn due to the absence of that [other thing], and as for the fact that its withdrawal is observed upon the withdrawal of this [present cause], that is merely a coincidental concurrence."
Just as the *piṇḍakhajūra* fruit, which grows in a region where maternal marriage is customary, does not exist in other regions where maternal marriage is absent;
therefore, the qualification "when [other causes] are capable" must be added.
For in this way, its status as the sole cause is determined, since the effect follows only the absence of that [specific cause].
For the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of that which provides no assistance is not followed by anything else, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Thus, the causal relationship is understood without doubt through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and not otherwise.
Yet, such a positive or negative concomitance is not established for body and mind.

For instance, it is not possible to establish a certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between one's own body and the cognition [of it], because at the time of conception and so forth, prior to the arising of consciousness, there is no perception of the body alone; indeed, there is no perception without consciousness.
Furthermore, since consciousness is likewise unperceived in another's body, there is no apprehension of a temporal sequence [between them].
Therefore, there is no certainty of positive concomitance.
Nor is there a certainty regarding negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

For even in that case, it is not possible to know the absence of one's own cognition through the absence of one's own body, because [the self] is entirely non-existent [as a separate entity]. Nor can the absence of a cognition related to another's body be ascertained through the absence of that other person's body.

Because that cognition, by virtue of meeting the conditions for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*), remains subject to doubt as to whether it is distinct from the body even when the body has ceased to exist;
for this very reason, there is no certainty regarding its distinction from the body even in the case of a wall or similar object where the body is absent,
since there too one doubts whether it exists, given that it meets the conditions for non-apprehension.

Furthermore, it is not logical to determine non-existence merely from the observation of the absence of effects such as movement; for causes do not necessarily possess their effects. Moreover, since the specific cause for assuming a particular body—characterized by craving and misconception—is absent there, one must entertain doubt: is the absence of cognition in that wall or such place due to the lack of its own cause, or rather due to its being distinct from a body?
Therefore, the reason [adduced] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Nor is [the reason] contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and the consequence of losing the status of a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*).
If you ask, "What then is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the claim that the body is not the cause of your intellect?"—we reply: such a proof certainly exists.

And thus, regarding the fact that the body is not the cause of mental cognition, he will present the proof beginning with "mental cognition is independent" (*svatantrā mānasī buddhiḥ*). Since the body is not its support—because that very [cognition] exercises sovereignty over the reconnection with another body—the establishment of the next world follows.

Furthermore, let us consider whether the body is the cause of mental cognition (*manomati*). Is it a single composite whole (*avayavin*), or is it multiple, consisting of an aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*)? Is it endowed with sense faculties (*sendriya*) or devoid of them (*anindriya*)? And is it the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) or the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*)? Thus it is analyzed. In this regard, first of all, a single composite whole is not tenable, because such a thing has already been refuted previously and because it would entail the loss of the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Indeed, it is not logical for a single entity to possess a fourfold nature, as that would result in the abolition of the conventional usage of "the many."
Nor should it be accepted as being composed of an accumulation of multiple atoms.
Furthermore, those atoms would have to be either causes individually or collectively.
They cannot be individually, because that would entail the consequence that a distinct conceptualization arises for each atom, just as a sprout arises from each individual seed.

Nor do they [arise] from the collection [of all causes], because even if a single member such as the nose were missing, it would follow that mental consciousness would not arise—just as a sprout does not arise when any one of the factors such as earth is absent.

For an effect that is dependent upon a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does not occur in the absence of any one of its members, as that would entail the loss of its very nature as being dependent on that complex. Alternatively, perhaps every [factor] is a cause of consciousness according to its proximity.
In that case, there ought to be a distinction between the two [mental cognitions] produced by a body with deficient limbs and one with non-deficient limbs, because of the difference in their causes;
otherwise, the difference in the effect would be without a cause.
Furthermore, when a person who previously possessed non-deficient limbs subsequently develops deficient limbs, there is no distinction whatsoever in the mental cognition (*manomati*).
For the refinement resulting from learning and so forth continues at that time as well, remaining entirely unimpaired.
Furthermore, the mental cognition residing in the bodies of elephants and the like would result in being superior, whereas human intellect would not;
those who take birth following a body of childhood would possess dull intellects, while those with large bodies would possess sharp intellects.
Because it is observed that the decrease and increase of an effect correspond to the decrease and increase of its cause;
for it is not logical that something should be the effect of another when a change in the latter does not produce a change in the former, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, it would follow that the differentiation of effects is without a cause.
Nor is the position that it arises from the sense faculties together tenable.
For in that case, would mental cognition arise from each sense faculty individually or from them all collectively?
It cannot be from each individually, because even when one particular sense faculty is impaired, mental cognition remains unimpaired.
For instance, even when the sense organs and their functions are impaired by diseases such as numbness, the mental cognition experiences its own existence as unaltered, singular, and complete.

Furthermore, it is not logical for something to be the effect of another if it does not undergo modification when that other thing is modified, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Moreover, like visual and other sensory cognitions, it would follow that [mental cognition] would grasp only specific objects, be non-conceptual, and have a mode of operation dependent on the presence of an object, since its cause is not distinct [from those].
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of multiple conceptual constructions arising simultaneously.
Nor is the position that [the object] arises from all [the senses] tenable, because it would follow that [the cognition] would be absent even when a single sense organ is missing,
just as a sprout or the like ceases to exist when a single auxiliary cause is removed.
Nor is the position that it is "not possessing sense-faculties" tenable, because it would follow that even a hand and so forth severed from the body could be the cause [of cognition].
If a specific [condition] were the cause, then it must be accepted as being precisely that which possesses sense-faculties;
for nothing other than that which possesses sense-faculties can be shown to be "specific."

Nor is the position that it is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) tenable. For instance, that specific cause is established as the material cause which, by constantly presenting its own existence, assists that nature which follows all the particularities found in the effect; and without the production of a modification in that [cause], the effect would be incapable of modification. For example, each preceding collection of clay is the material cause of each succeeding collection of effects designated as "pot."
For this very reason, whoever wishes to transform something transforms it only by transforming its material cause (*upādāna*), and not otherwise.
For when the preceding material cause possesses unimpeded capacity, no one can effect an obstruction to the arising of the subsequent effect.

Just as, in the case of a subsequent effect such as a jar that is about to arise, it is impossible to bring about a transformation without first allowing the preceding clay-substance to produce its own capable moment; [otherwise], the production of the transformation could not be accomplished.

In every case of producing a transformation, this is precisely the sequence: namely, the production of a moment that takes up a different capacity. Otherwise, nothing could directly produce a contradiction.

For if it were possible, there would be a direct production of a transformation in the effect itself—just as one produces a transformation in the cause—rather than exclusively by way of producing a transformation in the material cause (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the fact that a lamp is the subject of the production of a modification in its light situated in another location by means of an intervening obstruction, the lamp is not the direct material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of that light.
What then? It is each preceding moment of light, because it produces a modification characterized by the arising of a subsequent moment of light that is incapable [of further propagation].
Light is obstructed by a screen.
Furthermore, when one thing is modified with reference to another specific object, it is not the production of that [other] object; for example, a cow being modified with reference to a gavaya.

And yet, without modifying the body, the mental cognition undergoes a modification characterized by dejection and so forth through the performance of undesirable actions and the like. This is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

But surely, when there is a disorder of the body such as the back due to the improper digestion of food and so forth, a transformation of the mental consciousness characterized by passion and the like is indeed observed.
Even if it is observed, what of it?
For the reason [of the argument] is not rendered unestablished by this much alone.
For it is intended here merely this: that when something, despite being unchanging, can undergo transformation through another, that [other] is not its material cause (*upādāna*).

And since it is possible for the intellect to undergo transformation at certain times—even without the body undergoing transformation—due to the performance of undesirable actions and so forth, how can the reason be considered unestablished (*asiddha*)?
Nor does such occasional conformity to its transformations establish that [the body] is its material cause.
This is incorrect because it leads to an over-extension of the principle.
For in that case, even the object itself would become a material cause (*upādāna*).

To illustrate: by the power of seeing a loathsome object such as the blood of a tiger, a mental transformation characterized by delusion and so forth certainly arises in someone of a timid mind; yet, despite this, that mental cognition does not thereby become dependent upon that object.

Furthermore, since we observe physical changes when the mind is afflicted by discursive thoughts such as desire or grief, it would follow [absurdly] that the body is also the material cause (*upādāna*) of those mental states. However, it is logical that only that which invariably and directly conforms to the transformation of another is the material cause of that other.
Now, a transformation characterized by passion and so forth does not invariably arise from the nourishment of the body;
for in some cases, even in a person with a well-nourished body, such states do not occur if they possess analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyāna*).

Likewise, even in the case of a person whose body is utterly wasted away and who is full of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), or in the case of some animal whose physical dimensions have diminished, one observes an extreme degree of passion and so forth;
yet it is not logical that something which occurs despite the absence of another thing should be the effect of that other thing, for this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor does passion and so forth arise directly from the body, because it is mediated by improper mental attention and other such factors.

For instance, when there is nourishment of the body, there occurs within it the experience of pleasure and so forth produced by objects characterized as being fit for internal activity. In that state, for one who possesses a non-material body, whose mind is pervaded by misconceptions such as permanence regarding that pleasure and its means, there arises the conceptual construction of "this is beneficial to me" or "this is harmful," consisting of the idea of self-benefit, retaliation, and so on. From that, there arise satisfaction, dejection, and the like; and from those, there is the production of determinations (*adhyavasāya*) toward objects such as pleasure. This is indeed established through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Since passion and the like are observed only when mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and so forth arise, and are not observed even when nourishment and the like are present if those [mental states] do not arise,
it follows that nourishment and the like do not directly cause modifications in the mental consciousness.
For this very reason, because it does not provide direct assistance, it is established that the body is not even a contributory cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) for it.

Since it is well-established that earth and other factors act as cooperative conditions for sprouts and the like through direct assistance, otherwise there would be an over-extension [of the principle].

Therefore, passion and the rest proceed solely from the awakening of preceding seeds of their own kind. However, for some who lack the practice of analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyāna*), the nourishment of the body, youth, time, and so forth, become causes for the awakening of those latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Or, let it be granted that the body is sometimes a direct benefactor to the mental cognition proceeding from its own material cause;
even so, its cessation is not established upon the cessation of the body.
Just as there is no cessation of jars and the like even when fire ceases, because they proceed from their own material causes, there is no undesirable consequence here.
Nor is the reason inconclusive, for that would lead to over-extension;
nor is it contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Therefore, the body is not the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
Nor is it a cooperative cause; thus, it is established that mental cognition arises solely from preceding cognitions.

It might be argued: "Those two which are subject to a rule of coexistence stand in the relation of material cause and effect (*upādāna-upādeya*), like a lamp and its light. And there is a rule of coexistence between the body and mental consciousness; therefore, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*)."
Therefore, this reason is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*),
because it is admitted that mental cognition (*manomatih*) exists even without a body in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Nor does it establish what is desired, because it would entail the consequence that mental cognition is also a material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the body.
And there is inconclusiveness [of the reason],
because coexistence is possible even due to a difference in causes,
as in the case of fire and the fluidity of copper.

For instance, copper, acting in conjunction with fire, initiates fluidity, but not by itself; likewise here too, the material cause of the body, such as the *kalala* stage, acting in conjunction with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), initiates a subsequent body. Therefore, their coexistence is not due to a relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*); thus, [the reason] is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, one might argue: "Even though at later times mental cognition arises from each preceding cognition, nevertheless, that which occurs at the very first moment has the body as its material cause; therefore, the proof of beginninglessness [of consciousness] is not established. This is incorrect.
For it has already been demonstrated that there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever that establishes this conceptual construction.
If it is argued that there is likewise no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), we say no; for such subverting evidence certainly exists.

For instance, if mental cognition, having arisen once from the body, were subsequently to arise from its own kind, then at all subsequent times it would arise only from preceding mental cognitions and not from heterogeneous cognitions such as those of the eye and so forth; for smoke, having once arisen from fire, does not subsequently arise from another heterogeneous source.
Furthermore, mental cognition is not experienced at later times as arising solely from mental cognitions;
rather, it is produced by indeterminate immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, that which is perceived as arising first from a particular cause cannot possibly arise from something other than that, for that would entail the consequence of being causeless (*ahetukatva*).
Moreover, mental cognition (*manodhī*) is experienced as arising immediately after a specific visual or other sensory consciousness;
therefore, it is established that it does not arise solely from an indeterminate consciousness.

Furthermore, if the body were the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of mental cognition only at the very first moment and not at subsequent times, then why would it not proceed independently of the body? For it is not reasonable that it should have any dependence on a body that provides no assistance. If it is argued: "Even for one who holds that cognition is preceded by another cognition, why does it not proceed in isolation?"—the answer is: No.
It indeed proceeds,
as in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Since that [desire] which possesses longing for what is appropriate proceeds with regard to that [object], there is no fault at all.

Furthermore, if it is subsequently admitted that the body also serves as a supportive condition (*upakārin*), then there would follow the undesirable consequence of the production of a manifold stream of consciousnesses.
This is because the body, which has become the material cause (*upādāna*) of subsequent cognitions, remains present as a producer of them in its unimpaired state.

For instance, whatever cognition arises from the body, each of those would produce a further, distinct cognition; thus, for a single living being, immeasurable streams of consciousness would be produced at every moment.
And there is no such experience [of this].

Nevertheless, it might be argued: "It is not intended that the body exerts a separate influence as a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) at a later time; rather, the body is an auxiliary (*upakārin*) because it acts as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*) for the production of successive effects by the mental consciousness (*manodhī*), which proceeds from its own material cause in a continuous stream. Therefore, that [consciousness] does not proceed independently of the body."
This too is false;
for that which is well-known as the producer of something in a certain manner does not produce it otherwise when producing it, because there is no distinction [in its causal capacity].
Thus, light and so forth possess the status of being producers by way of being the objective support (*ālambana*) for visual consciousness when the eye is unimpaired.
Having been experienced, it does not again become the producer of that [cognition] in any other way; as it has been said:
"Indeed, production is not something other than being an object of apprehension; such is the characteristic of being an object."
For otherwise, form and the other [sensory objects] could not directly assist the Buddha.
As stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*:

otherwise, there would be no determination of the difference or non-difference in the nature of an effect as produced by its cause, because it would not conform to the assistance [received] from that [cause].
Consequently, it would follow that [consciousness] is causeless;
moreover, you have not apprehended any other form of material causality (*upādānatva*) for the body at the initial moment than its being a direct producer (*sākṣājjanakatva*) of consciousness.
What then?
It is precisely the state of being a direct benefactor;
and since that exists even at a later time, why should it not be the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*)?
Or, if it were something else, then let there be no [material cause] even previously, because there is no difference [in the conditions] as there is afterwards.

Nor can it be argued that even at a later time, the body itself—acting as a cooperative cause for the preceding consciousness—will serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the subsequent cognition; for the status of the body as a material cause has already been refuted in detail previously.
