Furthermore, this would entail the undesirable consequence that even the cognition of the first birth must be preceded by another cognition.
For this very reason, this refutation by the Master applies all the more strongly even to the position that the elements (*bhūta*) are impermanent.
As it has been said: "If cognition, once arisen from the body, were restricted by its own kind, or if it were [restricted] by something else, then why would there be a cessation of the capable body?
Therefore, the beginninglessness of mental cognition is established;
or rather, all cognition whatsoever is established as being without beginning without distinction."
For instance, as for this initial cognition, it must be either a sensory cognition (*akṣabuddhi*) or a mental cognition (*manobuddhi*).

It cannot be the first position, because in those who are asleep, unconscious, or whose minds are otherwise engaged, sensory cognition does not arise despite the presence of the sense organs, due to the absence of a corresponding mental attention (*anuguṇamanaskāra*).
Therefore, the sense organ alone is not the cause of sensory cognition.
Rather, it is determined that [the arising] is dependent upon a specific mental attention (*manaskāra*),
because the relationship of cause and effect is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, that which is ascertained to arise first from a certain [cause] cannot arise first from something other than that, for that would entail the consequence of being causeless (*ahetukatva*).
Like smoke without fire,
visual cognition, when arising first of all, arises only in dependence upon a corresponding mental attention (*manaskāra*).
Therefore, it is established that the sense faculty alone is never its cause.
Otherwise, the undesirable consequence of [cognition] being causeless would serve as a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
Nor is the position that it is mental cognition (*manobuddhi*) tenable;
for [mental cognition] does not function independently with respect to an object not perceived by the sense organs, because that would entail the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth.
Or rather, it must be stated whether that [cognition] which arises is conceptual (*savikalpika*) or non-conceptual (*avikalpika*).
In this regard, the first position is not tenable;

for a conceptual cognition, when it arises, always proceeds as permeated by the form of expressive words, because it is constantly experienced as having the nature of internal discourse (*antarjalpa*).

Furthermore, this assumption that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) takes on the form of the expressive word must arise either through the force of grasping a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), or because the nature of the word—which is essentially expressive—possesses the character of being a property of the cognition itself (and thus grasps the word-meaning just as it grasps the awareness-form), or due to some other conceptualization.
Among these, the first position—that it arises from grasping a convention—is not tenable, because the convention was not previously grasped.
Nor is the second position tenable.

For the nature of sound is twofold: that which consists of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and that which consists of the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Now, as for that which consists of the particular characteristic, because it is not expressive and has the form of a direct experience, it does not constitute the conceptual nature (*savikalpakatva*) of cognition; nor is it a property inherent to the cognition itself, because it appears as an external form like blue and so forth. Otherwise, even blue and other such objects would have to be properties of cognition, as there would be no distinction between them.
Consequently, the entire universe would be nothing but consciousness alone, and not a transformation of the primary elements (*bhūta*).

Now, one might object: "In the view that cognition possesses an aspect (*sākāra-jñāna*), the mode of appearance such as blue is a property inherent to the cognition itself, yet it manifests as an external form; so why is it said that because it manifests as an external form, it is not a property of the cognition's own nature?
This is true.
However, because cognition appears in such a way due to being colored by an external object,
it is established that this [appearance] belongs to the external object and not to the cognition itself;
for its own nature resides precisely in that [external object].
In the case of cognition, however, because it is produced by the imposition of an object, it is adventitious.
Therefore, the essence of the word (*śabdātmā*)—in its form as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—is neither the signifier, nor is it a property of the essence of cognition.
Even if that which has the form of a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is the signifier, nevertheless, it is not a property of the essence of cognition.

Because that [universal] is applied to the external particular sound (*paraśabdasvalakṣaṇa*) which is apprehended by the auditory organ, it is not applied to the cognition itself. For a universal residing in one thing cannot be applied to another; otherwise, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of applying it to everything.
For in that case, "cowness" (*gotva*) would also have to be applied to horses and so forth.

Furthermore, when the substratum (*dharmin*)—which is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word—is not apprehended, its property (*dharma*), which consists of the expressive [word-form], cannot be applied to it;
for properties, being dependent upon the substratum, are not apprehended independently.
Nor can the substratum, whose nature is the specific characteristic, be apprehended by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
This is because that [conceptual cognition] has the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

Therefore, it is established that conceptual constructions arise from the awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of beginningless particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Nor is the position tenable that [conceptual cognition arises] from the apprehension of the meaning of words; for words do not exist in the object, nor are they identical with it, since otherwise even one who has not learned the linguistic convention would necessarily have a cognition [of the object through words].
Furthermore, it would follow that there would be no restriction regarding objects according to one's desire.
Moreover, even though an object does not differ in its nature as impermanent and so forth, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not simultaneously construct all its aspects;
for conceptual construction arises only by grasping a single, specific aspect through the exclusion of other aspects.
Therefore, the cause must be stated by means of a conceptualization of a single form;
and it cannot be stated as anything other than habitual practice, as is the case with conceptualizations such as [the perception of] a corpse and so forth.
Consequently, since conceptual cognition functions by the force of prior habitual practice, it is established that conceptual cognition is beginningless.
If, on the other hand, the position is that [the cognition] is non-conceptual, then a conceptual cognition would never arise at all.
If it is argued that it arises at a later time by virtue of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) according to the previously stated principle, we say no;
for it is impossible for one who abides in non-conceptual knowledge to perform the act of establishing a convention.
For indeed, as long as neither the generality of the word nor the generality of the object appears in the intellect, a convention cannot be established.
Furthermore, a generality does not appear in conceptual cognition;
and that which does appear—the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—is neither the locus of nor the object for the establishment of a convention.
Because that [convention] exists for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*),

and because it is impossible for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) perceived at the time of the convention to exist at the time of usage, one must necessarily admit that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) exists prior to the making of the convention regarding the particular characteristic.
And since that [conceptual construction] is not established without repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), its beginninglessness (*anāditā*) is proven.

Furthermore, if it is not accepted that the cognition occurring at the first birth arises from the continuity of latent impressions (vāsanā) instilled by practice in previous lives, then how could a newborn infant— even one belonging to the animal realm— possess the discernment (*vyavasāya*) that "this is a means to pleasure" or "this is a means to pain," by virtue of which it seeks the breast and other such things that are means to pleasure? And why is it that, failing to obtain them, it begins to cry, yet upon obtaining them, its crying suddenly ceases and it engages in activities such as feeding?
For he has never experienced that the breast and so forth are the cause for allaying the pain of hunger and the like,
nor has he experienced that falling from a precipice and so forth are causes of injury;

yet even a newborn infant of a monkey or other species, fearing death due to the suffering arising from falling down a precipice, clings tightly to its mother's bosom and avoids places such as precipices.

For it is not the case that things whose fruits are the means to unexperienced desirable or undesirable ends are invariably sought to be abandoned or acquired, as this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
The analogy of iron being drawn toward a magnet is also untenable; for it is not without a cause, as that would entail its existence at all times and so forth.

Or, if it does have a cause, then just as the magnet is pointed out as its cause—established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)—so too must a cause be postulated for this performance of abandonment and acquisition.
And this [mental activity] cannot be pointed out as being anything other than the result of habituation (*abhyāsa*).

Therefore, the conventional behavior (*vyavahāra*) of fools—characterized by the grasping of the desirable and the rejection of the undesirable—is produced solely by prior habituation; thus, it is established that the intellect (*buddhi*) is beginningless. This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, he will state the common refutation starting with "and [the intellect] is independent and mental" and "moreover, in the case of suckling at the breast," etc.; so, enough of this prolixity.

Furthermore, for those Cārvākas who accept momentariness, their own admission—their own established tenet—is contradicted; namely, the admission that the primary elements (*bhūta*) are eternal is contradicted. [If you say:
"If, out of devotion to logic, you have no regard even for your own position..."
Let this supreme principle be accepted: that the elements themselves do not exist.

If, on the other hand, momentariness is accepted because it is supported by reasoning, then the system of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) should be accepted as superior; for in that case as well, the support of reasoning—the ground for acceptance—is equal.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Neither do they have the nature of a composite whole, nor is their being of the form of atoms logical;
because atoms are impossible—this will be explained [later]."
"Of these" refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
"Will be explained" means immediately following this, in the examination of external objects (*bahirarthaparīkṣā*).

If the elements do not exist at all, how then do they appear? To this he says: "Having no nature external to reality," and so forth: "Having no nature external to reality, they appear within consciousness due to the maturation of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), as in dreams and the like, and not from anything else."
"Other than that" means external to consciousness; that is to say, outside of it.

How, then, are worldly and scriptural conventions such as "earth" and so forth established? To this he says: "Relying solely upon the appearance of consciousness," and so on. This fourfold great element is not real; it is merely conceptualized by relying upon the manifestation of consciousness alone, like a dream or an illusion.

If the primary elements do not exist, then what is the cause of cognition? To this he says: "Of that other," and so forth. In the absence of those [elements], it is not logical for anything else to be the cause; rather, a preceding cognition appearing as an element would produce the subsequent one.
"Of that other" means:
of the four great elements other than that consciousness.

Thus, it has been established that the initial consciousness does not arise solely from the elements (*bhūta*). Now, in order to refute the position that it is produced solely from a derivative consciousness (*janyavijñāna*), he says "santānāntara...
and so forth: "If the consciousness of another continuum is held to be its cause, then is that [consciousness] its material cause (*upādāna*) or its auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*)?"
If it is held that the substratum is the desired [basis] for the continuity of the son's cognition,
then there would have to be a persistence of the specific impressions from learning and so forth belonging to the parents.
Furthermore,
the relationship between the substratum and that which is derived from it is established and ascertained through positive and negative concomitance within one's own continuum.
If one postulates that [the cognition] arises from the power of its own material cause (upādāna) while having [another mind] as a cooperative condition (sahakārin),
there would be no contradiction whatsoever regarding the mind belonging to another continuum (santānāntara).

That mind belonging to another continuum, such as that of a mother or father, would have to be either the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) or the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). It cannot first be the material cause, because it would follow that even in the continuum of the son's cognition, the specific impressions (*saṃskāra*) derived from what was heard by the mother and father and so forth would not arise—just as [the impressions] of the parents themselves do not persist in their own subsequent cognitions. For it is established as the nature of the material cause and its effect that in subsequent moments there is a following after the impressions of the preceding moment.
Because [the relationship] is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance within one's own continuum.

Now, if it is thought: "Just as when one lamp produces another lamp, the subsequent lamp does not arise as qualified by the characteristics of grossness and so forth belonging to the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding lamp; rather, there is the production of a mere lamp devoid of such refinement. However, the distinction of that other lamp arises from other factors such as its own wick and fuel—just as the cognition of a quality arises from the possessor of that quality."
That is not so; because even in its own substrate, the conditioning of a lamp and the like establishes a continuum,
owing to its instability.
For instance, when fuel is added, the true nature of that very lamp is observed;
however, the cultivation of learning and so forth is not unstable in this way, because it persists for a long time.
Therefore, it is not logical that there could be the occurrence of mere cognition devoid of cultivation, as in the case of a lamp or similar things.

Furthermore, in the case of a lamp and such, the distinction and non-distinction are merely conceptualized based on the production of a greater or smaller accumulation of atoms; however, there is no distinction or non-distinction therein regarding the characteristic of a single entity.

In this case, however, within the very same characteristic of a single entity, there is a distinction due to the cultivation of hearing and so forth as it exists in the mother’s cognition, while there is non-distinction as it exists in the son’s cognition—so who is to be instructed by whom? Moreover, this undesirable consequence is stated regarding the status of being a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*); yet one lamp is not the material cause of another lamp because they belong to different continua (*saṃtāna*). Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
Furthermore, for those moisture-born beings for whom there is no mother at all, how could their cognition arise from another consciousness? Enough of this digression.
Now, if the position is that [the previous cognition] is a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Therefore, he provides the proof for the fact that [consciousness] has no beginning:
"Therefore, the initial consciousness therein arises from the power of its own material cause,
because it is a consciousness and so forth, like the present mind."

The formal argument is as follows: Whatever entity has the four aggregates of consciousness, sensation, and mental formations as its nature arises from the power of its own material cause, because it possesses the nature of consciousness and so forth—just like those same four aggregates in states such as youth. And the complex of the mind and so forth at the first moment of birth has the nature of consciousness and so forth; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
In this context, the mention of "initial consciousness" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); sensation and the other aggregates must also be understood to be included.
He states the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) in the verse beginning with "anyahetu" and so forth:
"When the absence of a cause is established by the rejection of any other cause,
it follows that this [characteristic] of a fixed property would not belong to it otherwise."

Since other [entities] such as the eternal mind, time, space, and the Lord (Īśvara) have already been refuted, and since its own material cause is not admitted, it would follow that [consciousness] is without a cause; consequently, this determined property characterized by being consciousness and so forth would not exist.
For there can be no specific determination of an accidental intrinsic nature, as there would be no regulating factor.

Therefore, the impossibility of the occurrence of determinate cognitions and other such phenomena, as well as the impossibility of their occasional nature, constitute the subverting evidence against the absence of a cause.

Having thus established past birth, he says "maraṇa... and so forth, providing the proof to establish future birth as well: "The consciousness at the moment of death is capable of giving rise to its own effect, because it belongs to one possessed of passion and attachment, just like previous consciousness."

Whatever mind is accompanied by passion (*sarāga*) is capable of giving rise to another subsequent mind that takes it as its own material cause (*svopādeya*), because it is characterized by passion, like a mind in a previous state; and the mind at the moment of death is indeed accompanied by passion. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*); for whatever mind is devoid of the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*), which is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to enjoyments and the like, is necessarily accompanied by passion, because it is devoid of the antidote, like a mind engaged in sexual enjoyment.

Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since the arising of a subsequent mind is caused by this much alone; thus, the impossibility of the complete cause [producing anything else] serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
He demonstrates this very point with the words "in whatever form," and so forth:
"In whatever form consciousness produces a certain determination,
why does it not remain an agent, maintaining that same undivided form both before and after?"
"Bearing that" means its own form, that is to say, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
With the words "In the opponent's position" and so forth, he raises the objection that both examples lack the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*) in both syllogisms:
"And in the opponent's position, the established rule is that such cognition arises from the body alone;
how then can those two examples be established as being endowed with the property to be proven?"
But has not the causality of the body already been refuted?
Because the mind is attained simultaneously [with the body], there is no additional [cause] beyond it.
Since it is determined that consciousness of memory, attachment, and so forth is cultivated through mental application, wholesome states, and the like, it is impossible to deny its existence.
The decrease and increase of cognitions are observed to depend on their preceding states,
resulting from the specific decrease or increase in the practice of learning, arts, and so forth.
But when attention (*manaskāra*) is deficient, because there is no apprehension of another object to be known,
it cannot be said that cognition functions as the cause of cognition.
The reason "because they exist in different bodies" is unestablished;
for what kind of activity could there be for the formless mind, which does not fall [into a body]?
For instance, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) consists in arising from its own material cause (*svopādāna*) and being capable of producing its own effect (*svopādeya*).

For one who holds the view that consciousness arises eternally from the body alone, no example (*dṛṣṭānta*) endowed with the aforementioned property to be proven is established anywhere. Therefore, how can there be the presentation of these two examples—“like the present mind” and “like previous cognition”?
This is not a fault.

The causality of the body has already been refuted by the statement, "lest there be the consequence of simultaneity of cognitions," because there is no additional auxiliary cause to be depended upon, and dependence is impossible for that which is eternal.
As for the position of impermanence, however, the previously mentioned and the current objections apply.

Nor is it logical for something established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to become unestablished merely by virtue of [the opponent's] non-acceptance, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
and if that were so, nothing whatsoever would be a proof for anyone.
As it has been said: "Not everything is a refutation simply because it is undesired."
Furthermore, when a memory arises immediately following an intentional thought (*ābhoga-citta*) and is well-ascertained, then passion (*rāga*) arises from a thought of beauty and so forth.

For instance, passion arises in those possessed by passion who contemplate the beautiful—thinking, "She is lovely," "She is young," "She has a slender waist," "She has a beautiful face," and so on. Likewise, hatred arises in one who contemplates an equal [person] as having done harm, or thinking, "He is doing harm, or he will do harm," and so on; since this arising hatred is certain, how can it be denied, especially by one who asserts that perception alone is the source of knowledge?

Likewise, it is observed that through the increase or decrease of specific prior practices such as learning and craftsmanship, there is a corresponding increase or decrease in subsequent cognitions; similarly, it is observed that due to distraction toward another object, there is a failure to grasp a different object because of a deficiency in mental attention (*manaskāra*). Therefore, the fact that cognition is the cause of cognition is beyond dispute, as it is consistent with reason;
however, this is not the case for the primary elements (*bhūta*), because that would contradict reason.
It is precisely for this reason that the status of cognition as the cause of cognition is being established.

Regarding the first instance in the passage beginning with "the relation of cause and effect," the reason "because of residing in different bodies" is unestablished (*asiddha*). For if "residing" is intended to mean a relationship characterized by that between a support and what is supported, then this is clearly unestablished for the mind within bodies, since the mind—possessing the property of not falling—is not subject to falling even though a causal relationship exists; this is because the mind, being formless (*amūrta*), lacks the property of falling. Furthermore, a support is not logical for that which has the property of not falling, as it would be ineffective (*akiñcitkaratva*).
If that is so, what does the support do for water and the like? To this he says: "It would be," and so forth.
It would be the support of water and the like by virtue of preventing their falling.
And for those mental states that have no destination, what is the use of supports?
If it is postulated here that "subsistence" consists in identity (*tādātmya*), that too is incorrect; for according to your [view], it is not logical for cognition to have the body as its nature.

An entity that possesses form by its very nature, arising by abandoning the location of its own material cause (*upādāna*), has its substratum (*ādhāra*) established through the obstruction of its movement, because that substratum is the cause of its production at the location of the material cause.

However, it is not possible to establish such a substratum for an entity that is formless. Furthermore, if "subsistence" (*vṛtti*) is intended to be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), that too is not established.
It is not reasonable for you, who are attached to external objects, to say that consciousness has the body as its nature;
however, for me, the proponent of consciousness-only, it is reasonable because the body has the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its intrinsic nature—this is the intended meaning.
To the question "Why is this not logical?", he says "In the case of identity," and so forth:
For if there were identity, then just as the body is clearly perceived by others,
why is the mind characterized by passion, hatred, and so on, not likewise perceived?
The mind is known only by itself, whereas the body is known by both oneself and others;
those two, being thus distinct, are like a dancer and the base of his belly.
For if the body were perceived by others, it would follow that passion and the like are also perceived, because they are non-different from it.
Nor is there an inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to the power of a seer (*vipraśakti*), because that power is not perceptible at that time.
However, consciousness is not imperceptible, for if it were, it would follow that even the self could not perceive it.

Furthermore, whatever two things are respectively determined as both [aspects] and determined as one [aspect] are distinct, just as the experience of the stomach's base and the actor, or as the body and consciousness which are respectively determined as both and determined as one; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
"By itself" means by its own self.
But from the perspective of non-dual knowledge (*advayajñāna*), this reason is not established;
for [consciousness] experiences its own respective manifestation, just as in the case of ophthalmia and similar conditions.
Since the body of consciousness is observed to perish immediately after its arising in an uninterrupted succession, why is its momentariness not accepted if it possesses such a nature?
If this were so, the refutation of the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*) being carried out by this very reason would be unavoidable; therefore, he says: "This reason is not established.
This means that the fault of the reason is its lack of establishment (*asiddhatā*).

For instance, the fact of being ascertained by both parties is not established for the proponent of consciousness-only, because [for him] there is always only the experience of one's own internal appearance.
It is like the vision of two moons by two people suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*).
Furthermore, at the time of cognizing an object of a different character, the mind is clearly observed to perish immediately after its continuous arising.
Consequently, if the body were admitted to possess that same nature, it would follow that it is momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

Thus, first of all, occurrence characterized by identity is not established. Now, if it is occurrence characterized by origination from that, would that origination from that occur by way of a support, as in the case of visual consciousness and its supports such as the eye;
or by way of non-deviation from that, as in the case of smoke which does not deviate from fire?
In this regard, both types of occurrence are unestablished.
For instance, mental cognition (*manodhī*) does not depend on the body in the same way that sensory cognition does, because it is not invariably and directly affected by the body’s transformations.
Nor is it necessarily concomitant with it, since its existence is admitted even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) where there is no body.

Nevertheless, even while granting the premise for the sake of argument, [the author] states that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), saying: "because it arises based upon that, or because of its non-deviation from that."
If it is claimed that [the word] functions there because it arises based on that [object], or because of its non-deviation from it,
even so, there would still be deviation.
Even cognition in its prior state, though perishing moment by moment,
certainly effects a continuous reconnection as it functions within the body.
If there is no distinction there because of being a single continuum,
then let there be no distinction elsewhere either, due to being a single continuum.

For indeed, since there is no contradiction between the linking of a subsequent consciousness and the occurrence of consciousness within the body, just as the consciousness existing in the state prior to the moment of death links [to the next life] even though it occurs in a different body—because the body is momentary—the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

If, on the other hand, it is imagined that consciousness occurs in a non-different body because the body is non-different due to being a single continuum (*ekasantāna*), then the same applies to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body as well.
For instance, this body in the next world is merely a specific state within the continuum of the body characterized by the five sense bases, just like the different states of childhood and old age.

Furthermore, regarding the second syllogism, because no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been presented against the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*) for the reason "because it is cognition," its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) is quite evident; thus, it was not explicitly mentioned.
Regarding the third application, beginning with "the knowledge of death accompanied by passion," he says "of one whose outflows are exhausted," and so forth:
"How is it considered that the consciousness of one whose outflows are exhausted is without rebirth?
If you say it is because of the tenets of others, no, because their authority is not accepted."
That for which there is no connection with another mind is "non-connection.
By this, he states that the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is unestablished for one of the two parties in the example.
For instance, how could it be established for a Cārvāka that the death-mind of Arhats does not connect with another mind?

Now, it might be argued: "In the Buddhist doctrine of others, it is recited: 'Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; I know no further existence beyond this. Therefore, non-reconnection [to rebirth] is established.

This is incorrect, because the Lokāyata does not accept the authority of another's doctrine. How could he reach a certainty based on that which is accepted as authoritative by another? For if he did, it would follow that he must also reach a certainty regarding the next world.

If that [object] is understood from some other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), then why was that very thing not stated as the proof? Why was something non-informative, which merely indicates dullness, put forward? For it is not the case that something else is not a proof for it, such that it would not be mentioned.

Even by resorting to their own tenets, [the author], demonstrating that for certain Buddhists the example is not established as being endowed with the property to be proven, says: "And those here who are wise," and so forth:
"And those here who are wise proclaim the Jinas to be those whose nirvana is non-abiding, and [proclaim] the finality of that vehicle, as well as of the two vehicles."
For you, even when relying on the tenets accepted by the opponent, the example would be unestablished with respect to those [reasons] and would not be endowed with the property to be proven.
"In this world" refers to the teaching of the Sugata;
"the wise ones" refers to the Mahāyānists;
"some" refers to the Mādhyamikas.
For they say that the non-abiding of the Buddhas is nirvāṇa,
because of their non-abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
and they say that the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas culminate in the single vehicle of the Buddha.
Because of the statement: "This knowledge is indeed one, namely, the Mahāyāna."
Having thus stated the fault of the example, he states the fault of the probans as being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*), saying:
"And because no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) has been stated, there is a doubtful exclusion (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*);
due to the possibility of the existence of heterogeneous instances (*vijātīya*), there is deviation (*vyabhicāritā*)."
"Because no subverting [reason] has been stated" is the reason for the fallacy of doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*).
"That which is suspected," and so forth, however, refers to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāritā*).
The existence in what is of a different class is "existence in the heterogeneous" (*vijātīyasadbhāva*).
Of what? It is understood that this refers to "for what reason.
And the analysis of the compound is: "this suspected existence of a heterogeneous entity."
Nor is the consequence of [the absurdity of] death a subverting proof, because from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), there is no such thing as a "self" or the like that dies;

rather, it is merely when a dissimilar continuum arises that, due to the cessation of a particular state designated by a specific class-name, such conventional usage occurs in both the world and the treatises.
Regarding the statement that it is reckless to claim that consciousness exists during the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*, he says "In the *kalala* and so forth," etc.:
It is not reckless to say that consciousness exists in the *kalala* and so forth;
for even though the sense faculties have not yet developed, why should cognition not exist there?

The claim that "all consciousness arises from the power of the sense faculties and their objects" is perceived as a rash assertion, because that [consciousness] occurs otherwise in dreams and similar states.
Its form is also determined as distinct from the apprehension of the object;
therefore, its existence is established even in states such as fainting.

If all cognition were known solely by the power of the sense-faculties and their objects, that would be a rash assertion; for in states such as dreaming, mental consciousness (manovijñāna) manifesting blue and other colors is experienced even when the eye and other sense-faculties are absent and even without an object such as a visible form. Nor can it be said that the body-faculty (kāyendriya) is its support at that time, because it manifests as blue and so forth, whereas the consciousness of the body has tangible objects as its domain.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that all consciousness consists of the apprehension of an object;
thus, the existence of consciousness even during states such as fainting is not contradicted.

Furthermore, it might be argued that while the subsistence of consciousness in the form of a potentiality is not contradictory, its subsistence in its own essential nature is contradictory; to this he says, "Nor even...
Nor does the intellect subsist in such a way even in the form of a potentiality;
for at that time, the subsistence of cognitions is held to be in their very own essential nature.
And as for your claim that the mind does not exist in states such as sleep or fainting—whence is this certainty?
If you say it is because of the absence of sensation, then from where has that [absence] been established?
If such a certainty regarding them arises for you as "I do not know the mind," then, that being the case, the existence of the mind is established.
It might be thought: "If consciousness exists during these states [of deep sleep, etc.], why would there be no memory of them upon waking, which would have their form?"
Therefore, that [memory] would not occur at all because of the impossibility of proficiency and so forth;
it would not proceed, like the mind of a newborn infant.
For if there were some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that ascertained that the mind does not exist during states such as sleep or fainting, then there would be a contradiction.
If it is argued that the non-perception of self-awareness (*svavedanānupalambha*) is the ascertainment-proving means of valid cognition, we say no;
for from what is the non-perception of self-awareness established?
For in that state, there is no certainty regarding the absence of consciousness.
Moreover, if you maintain that in those states of fainting the certainty "I do not perceive the mind" arises, then by that very certainty so produced, the presence of a mind is established.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "If the mind were present during states such as sleep, why would there be no recollection for a person who has awakened?"
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of one who is free from fainting and one who is free from intoxication is intended.
Thus, this non-remembrance (*asmaraṇa*) is not a valid reason for establishing the non-existence of what was experienced.

For if remembrance occurred solely on the basis that something was experienced, then [non-remembrance] would indeed [prove non-existence]; however, even when there has been experience, remembrance does not occur due to deficiencies such as lack of acuity, lack of practice, or lack of interest.

"Just as in the case of the mind that has experienced states such as being newly born [and so forth], even though it exists, what is your proof [of its existence] if there is doubt even when recollection does not occur? Challenging [the opponent] in this way, he says "If this is so," and so on:
"If this is so, how is its existence determined in these [states]?"
This is understood from the very reason previously described.
If the mind is not admitted to exist in states such as dreaming or fainting,
then there would either be death at those times, or else there would be an absence of death upon their arising again.
Mental cognition is independent because it does not depend on the eyes and other sense organs;
it functions solely by the power of its own material cause, as in dreams and similar states.
"Of this" refers to consciousness.
"In these" refers to states such as sleep and so forth.

In that regard, the previously described reason is as follows: the initial consciousness of a person who has awakened arises from the power of its own material cause (upādāna), because it is a consciousness, just like the recollective and other types of consciousness that occur immediately after an act of attention.
Nor is this reason inconclusive, because the necessary connection has already been established by previously refuting other causes.
Furthermore, if the mind were not present during states such as sleep, then death itself would occur.

Alternatively, if it is maintained that consciousness arises again in such a body where consciousness has been completely and rootlessly departed, then, if its arising therein is admitted, the absence of death would follow, because it would entail the absurd consequence that even a dead person’s consciousness could arise again, just like one who has awakened from sleep.
Because the mental consciousness (*manobuddhi*) alone possesses the capacity for linking to another birth;
thus it has been said: "The cutting off, the linking, detachment, falling away, and the attainment [of the fruits] are accepted as occurring in the mental consciousness alone."
Therefore, demonstrating that mental cognition (*manobuddhi*) relies solely upon its preceding cognition, he says "independent" (*svatantra*), and so forth.

Independence is the reason for not requiring [other causes]. This mental cognition always arises from its own material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) alone, because it does not depend on other causes such as the eye, which are distinct from its own material cause, just as in the state of dreaming. (1928)
By the phrase "for thus" (tathāhi), he dispels the unestablished nature of the reason:
for indeed, conceptual constructions do not depend upon the sense faculties and their objects,
because they occur even in the absence of those operations, as in the case of [mental images of] sky-lotuses and the like.
"Even in the absence of their activity" means even when there is no activity of those two, namely the sense faculty and the object.
For it is not logical that something should be the cause of another if the latter exists even in the absence of the former's activity, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It might be argued: "Let it be that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a sky-lotus and the like is independent of sense-faculties and objects, since it occurs even in their absence.

But as for the conceptual construction 'this is blue' which arises when the eye is directed toward an object present before one, such as something blue—how can that be independent of sense-faculties and objects, so that the reason [of the argument] would not be unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*)? To this, he says: "Of those two," and so forth.
Even when those two exist, whatever conceptual construction of the past and so forth arises is determined to be exactly the same [as an illusion], due to its coloring by an unreal object.
Because it appears as the word and the object, the form of the real entity does not appear in conceptual constructions;
indeed, all of this has been established in detail.
"Of those two" refers to the sense-faculty and the object.

"Having an unreal object" means that this conceptualization of an imagined object and so forth has an appearance (*nirbhāsa*)—an unreal coloring (*uparāga*)—which is empty; such is the conceptualization of space and so forth, which has an unreal object.
The meaning is that this [conceptualization of the self] is also devoid of an object, being equal to that.

How so? For every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it functions through the verbalization of words, manifests the object of a word (*śabdārtha*). And where the object of a word manifests, the nature of the real thing (*vasturūpa*) does not manifest there, because a word does not function with respect to the nature of the real thing, since the word has not been conventionally established (*asaṅketita*) for that [real thing]. This has been demonstrated in detail in the *Śabdārthaparīkṣā*.

Since the reason exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory (*viruddha*); nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because if it were not produced from its own material cause (*svopādāna*), it would follow that it is causeless (*ahetuka*). //1932–//

If it is argued that [mental cognition] is not without a cause because it is dependent upon the body, having raised this doubt, he says "in states such as torpor" and so forth: "In states such as torpor, even when there is a physical transformation, there is no change in mental cognition; therefore, it is not dependent upon that [body]."

For even when there is a physical alteration due to afflictions such as numbness (prasuptikā), the mental cognition remains unaltered; thus, this mental cognition is not dependent upon the body. That which is not directly modified by the modification of something else is not dependent upon that thing—just as a horse, which is not modified by the modification of a cow, is not dependent on it. Furthermore, the mental intellect (manobuddhi) is not directly modified by the modification of the body during the state of numbness; this is the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi).
With the words "even very slight," etc., he demonstrates that being dependent upon that [organ] is pervaded by being subject to modification through the modification of that [organ].
For even when there is a very slight modification of the eye or other organs, such as the presence of cataracts (timira),
the cognition dependent on the eye and so forth arises indeed as modified.
Even upon the destruction of that body, the mental wisdom, having that [body] as its support,
continues by the power of its own material cause alone, without contradiction.
And since that pervader is absent here, it is established that cognition is not dependent on the body.
Therefore, even upon the cessation of the body, it will not cease; thus there is no contradiction.
For when something is not dependent upon another, its cessation does not necessarily entail the cessation of the former.
For example, upon the cessation of a cow, there is no necessary cessation of the *gavaya* (wild ox).
Furthermore, the body is not the substratum (*āśraya*) of mental cognition; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Regarding what was stated in the two verses beginning with "In another body produced immediately after death," he says "Even alone," and so forth.
Since even the mental consciousness alone is thus non-contradictory,
we are not constrained by this to prove the existence of another body.
And this [non-perception] cannot be denied, because it persists even when there is no perception;
it would be like the non-perception of clear or slight smoke by one with weak vision.

This is the intended meaning here: the afterlife is what one wishes to establish in this context, and how is that established? It would be established if consciousness (*buddhi*) were proven to be beginningless and endless;
for it is a specific state of this very consciousness that is designated as the "afterlife.
It does not depend on the body, because the afterlife is accepted even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where there is an absence of a body.

If that continuum of consciousness is established as being without beginning or end, then our "other world" (paraloka) is established; thus, we make no effort to prove the existence of another body, as it would be fruitless.
Furthermore, its negation cannot be effected merely by its non-perception.

For indeed, such non-perception might occur for you—a person with dull vision—due to a deficiency in cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, even though that body exists within a particular class of beings. We say this is like the non-perception of thin smoke; therefore, negation is not established by mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
For it is described that the subsequent existence (*uttarābhava*) is visible to those of the same class, to those with pure divine eyes, and to others;
for this very reason, there is no rejection of the "transporting body" (*ativāhika-śarīra*) postulated by the Sāṃkhyas.

Furthermore, even the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*) would not be perceived due to the distance of location, because of its arising in a very distant place or because of the distance of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*), like the bodies of piśācas and the like.
Even when there is no spatial distance, it is impossible for one with limited vision to ascertain that "this very living being has become the nature of a moth" and so forth;

this is because its body has been transformed through the application of medicine possessing inconceivable power. [Verse 1937] If so, how can cognitions that depend on different substrates be said to be connected within a single continuum? To this he says: "even though they depend on different bodies."
Even though it resides in different bodies, because it conforms to their specific characteristics,
the prior cognition is connected to a single continuum, like a continuous stream.
Moreover,
even those born just at the moment of birth engage in the desire for suckling at the breast and experience aversion toward injury.
And this [self] is inferred from effects such as weeping, suckling at the breast,
and so forth; yet all that is of the nature of conceptual construction, and it is like a mere attachment to a name.
"By way of conforming to its specific qualities": the cognitions of this life conform to those specific qualities of the cognition existing in a previous birth.
And so it has been said: "Through the practice of yoga, auspicious and inauspicious actions become habitual for persons."

"That which they perform effortlessly, even without instruction, as if in a dream during another birth"—regarding this, that which was stated by the Cārvāka, namely: "Because the body of this world and the body of the next world are distinct, the two consciousnesses belonging to them do not constitute a single continuum," and so forth; [and] "The first consciousness at the beginning of the womb does not belong to the same continuum as the one under dispute, because its body is distinct, like the consciousness of a buffalo or a boar. [Response: This is not so. Just as a person who has mastered a craft remembers it effortlessly upon being born again, so too does one who has practiced yoga remember it. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that one who has practiced in a previous life performs such actions effortlessly in this life, just as one who has practiced in this life performs them effortlessly in the next. Therefore, the claim that "because the bodies are distinct, the consciousnesses are not of a single continuum" is refuted by the example of those who have attained mastery through practice. Moreover, the argument that "the first consciousness in the womb does not belong to the same continuum because the body is distinct" is inconclusive, for it fails to account for the continuity of consciousness across different births. Thus, the existence of a single continuum is established.
By this, that [objection] is refuted.
Moreover, the next world is established for the following reason as well:

whatever conceptual construction there is, it is preceded by the practice of auditory experience of words, because it is a conceptual construction, just like a conceptual construction occurring in states such as youth.
This conceptualization belongs to those just born, such as the desire for suckling at the breast; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Nor is the reason unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because that [desire] is established by the observed effect of suckling the breast and so forth in those who are just born.
The subject (*dharmin*) is established;
for it is not logical that crying, suckling at the breast, and so forth could occur in one who does not conceptualize [the object] in the form of attachment, aversion, and the like.
Nor is it unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*); he demonstrates this by stating, "And all that consists of conceptualization."
That [desire], such as the longing to suckle at the breast,
is entirely of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), having conceptualization as its essence,
because it is experienced in the form of yearning and so forth.
Showing that it is also not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "And that indeed is accompanied by a name.
"That" refers to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Since every conceptual construction proceeds by means of the verbal expression of a word, it is necessarily accompanied by a name.

Furthermore, we have already demonstrated in detail that this association with names is not possible for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) without the prior habituation to linguistic convention (*saṅketa*). Now, it might be argued: "Granted that the association with names is preceded by habituation, even so, this does not establish what is desired [by the opponent]. On the contrary, it establishes the opposite—namely, that it is preceded solely by worldly habituation. To this, he says: "Not name and form," and so forth.
Name-and-form has not been practiced in this life;
therefore, in the absence of another existence for them, its total cessation would follow as a logical consequence.
This is what is meant:
the practice of those just born in this world is sublated by the cognition of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And it is not logical for a reason (*hetu*) to be contradictory when its subject matter (*pratijñārtha*) is being sublated, according to the principle that "there is no contradiction when there is no sublation."
Regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*):
the form of the name— the expressive nature which, though it is a mental construct, is superimposed upon external objects—
and [the form] of those [objects].
Regarding "of those that have just arisen":
"their cessation" means the cessation of those [mental factors] such as longing and so forth; that is "their cessation."
With the words "tannāma" and so forth, he concludes the meaning of the aforementioned proof:
"This [cognition] arises through the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the repeated practice of familiarity with those names;
because it has the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is now like a conceptual construction."
The word "tat" means "tasmāt" (therefore).
With the words beginning with "yannāma," he demonstrates the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*):
"That conceptual construction which arises for them, born from the ripening of the latencies of repeated practice and familiarity, is established as another existence."

The term *nāma* refers to a word; its *saṃstava* means familiarity or experience—that is to say, its repeated occurrence. The compound *yannāmasambhavābhyāsa* (the habituation to the arising of which name) is formed by splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*) to allow for the locative case (*saptamī*). The latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by that [habituation] undergoes maturation (*paripāka*), which is the acquisition of functional activity (*vṛttilābha*) toward the production of an effect corresponding to itself; "born from that" (*tato jātaḥ*) is the etymological sequence.
"Of them" means "of those who have just been born."

With the words "nāmābhyāsa" and so forth, he raises an objection from the perspective of an opponent using a *prasaṅga* argument: "If their [cognition] proceeds solely through the power of the repeated practice of names,
then why do they not possess clear speech or memory like that of eloquent orators?"
If the activity of conceptual thought proceeds from the habituation of prior conventions, then it would follow that even an infant would have the recollection of prior conventions;
for it is not logical that the persistence of habituation occurs without recollection.
Furthermore, it would follow that there would be the occurrence of clear speech, as in the case of eloquent speakers.
Consequently, the establishment of linguistic conventions would be rendered purposeless;
yet this is not the case.
Therefore, due to the absence of recollection and the non-occurrence of distinct speech, [the cognition] must be preceded by prior practice.

By the phrase "it is contradictory," he states a fault in the thesis by means of the reversal of the reductio (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*), specifically through the negation of the essential nature of the property (*dharma-svarūpa*).
By the words "more powerful" (*paṭīyasa*) and so forth, he states that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) even in the reversal of the reductio (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*):
"Because they are disturbed by ripening due to a more powerful impairment,
this activity of theirs would not occur, as in the states of *sannipāta* [disorder]."

For prior habituation is not always pervaded by recollection and so forth, such that it would cause recollection and the like to arise; nor would it cease upon their cessation. To the extent that there is a persistence of prior habituation, yet no recollection occurs—as, for example, in the state of *sannipāta* (a critical illness).

Likewise, even in a dream, there would be a continuation of previous habituation, yet there would be no recollection. The mention of "sannipāta" (a derangement of the humors) is an illustration; [the same applies to] "one who falls [into such a state]."
"Due to dwelling in the womb" and "due to the agitation of ripening" mean that there is an agitation of the ripening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
There is no occurrence [of memory] in the form of distinctions such as specific place, time, and intrinsic nature as they were experienced.

In this regard, that which was stated by the Cārvāka— that the recollection of past births is unproven because everyone who has come from the same village remembers [only their recent past]— is refuted.
By this, it is refuted;
for even when all have come from a single village, they do not remember [the same thing],
because among them there are some of dull intellect who indeed become forgetful.
"Of these" refers to the words.

With the words "even the slightest" and so forth, he states that the reason [in the opponent's argument] suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished (asiddha) with respect to a portion of the subject, by means of a counter-reductio (prasaṅgaviparyaya):
"But for those great-souled ones, even the slightest injury does not occur;
their words are heard clearly, and that tradition (smṛti) is manifest."
"Of the great-souled ones" means of those possessing merit.
Furthermore, he states another argument for establishing the existence of the next world, beginning with "And these [qualities] such as attachment and aversion":
"And these [qualities] such as attachment and aversion, being intense through the practice of habituation,
are determined to exist by means of positive and negative concomitance."
Those who appear for the first time here are devoid of prior practice;
what could be the cause of their birth if there were no other existence?
For their arising does not occur simply through the proximity of an object;
because even when that [object] is present, they do not arise if analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyāna) exists.
And because their predominance is observed upon the cessation of analytical discernment,
and because their perversion increases even with respect to objects that have perished or not yet arisen.
Attachment and other such passions arise by superimposing qualities such as beauty, ownership, and permanence upon women and other objects; yet the objects themselves do not possess those forms.
Even those [mental states] belonging to this world proceed without an external object, solely through the power of similar habitual practice,
because they are characterized by passion and so forth, just like those that follow.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the proficiency regarding passion, hatred, envy, intoxication, pride, and so forth, as well as wisdom, compassion, loving-kindness, and so on, is preceded by practice; for instance, it is observed in this very life that the proficiency of a person—whether acute or dull—in the aforementioned qualities occurs by virtue of practice.

Furthermore, there exists in some person, even in this life, such proficiency regarding various [qualities] in the body and so forth, despite the absence of any visible practice in this world; thus, this is a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*).
Since the causal relationship has been ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
For this very reason, he says: "They are ascertained by means of positive and negative concomitance.
If it is argued that the reason is contradictory because it proves that they are preceded by practice in another life, we say no;
for it is incorrect to prove that they are preceded by practice in another life on the grounds that those first-arisen, intense passions and so forth are devoid of practice in this life.
Nor is it logical for [these qualities] to be causeless, because that would entail their being eternal or existing from the very beginning.
Therefore, if there were no other life, what would be the cause for the production—the arising—of those intense passions and so forth?
Consequently, it is established that practice in a previous life is indeed the cause, and thus the existence of another world is proven.

The object of perception (*ālambana*) is not the cause [of passion and so forth], because even when an object is present, passion and the like do not arise at times when there is the presence of analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) such as the contemplation of the foul (*aśubha*). Discernment is the wisdom that takes the foul and so forth as its object and serves as the antidote to passion and the like.
Since it is observed that passion and the like arise even in the absence of an object, it is not logical that their existence depends upon the power of the object.

For instance, even with respect to objects that are past or future, when a person’s misconceptions regarding increased pleasure and so forth have intensified through the power of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*), those afflictions such as attachment are seen to become powerful once analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) has ceased.

Indeed, it is not logical for something to be the cause of another when the presence or absence of the latter does not correspond to the presence or absence of the former, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For this reason as well, the arising of the afflictions and so forth does not occur by virtue of the objective support (*ālambana*).

For if they were to proceed exactly according to their object, then they would proceed under the influence of that object, as is the case with the cognition of blue and so forth; however, they do not proceed in this way.
Rather, they proceed toward women and the like by superimposing aspects such as "mine," permanence, and pleasure, even though these have never been experienced.
Furthermore, objects do not possess forms such as beauty;
nor is it logical that something which is devoid of a particular form can be the objective support (ālambana) for that [cognition], because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Therefore, since they have superimposed objects as their domain, passion and the other afflictions are without an objective support.

And thus it is established that even those [afflictions] such as attachment which are primary—that is, those first arising in this very life—proceed by virtue of the repeated practice of their own kind.
If, then, objects are not the cause, why is it that attachment and the like are observed to arise when an object presents itself?
To this he says: "When an object presents itself," and so forth.
But when objects present themselves, there arise the experiences of pleasure, pain, and so forth;
therefore, these are born from the ripening of homogeneous latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Afflictions such as attachment and aversion belong to those who hate analytical discernment and who,
according to their strength, are subject to improper mental formations.
Objects themselves are not directly the causes of attachment, aversion, and so forth;
for if that were the case, there would be only a single affliction in all [beings], just as there is a single cognition of them.
For this is the sequence: when an object presents itself, pleasure born of the sense-faculties arises.

From that pleasure, provided there is no lack of analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyāna*), for those who abide in a state of mental attention characterized by the misconceptions of "I" and so forth, the ripening of the latencies (*vāsanā*) previously deposited by passion and other afflictions occurs; from that, the afflictions such as passion arise. Thus, objects are not the direct cause. One might argue: "This is merely a description of your own tenet, and there is no reasoning here. To this he says: "One," and so forth.
"Single" means having a single form;
"therein" refers to the object;
"of that" refers to the object.
"Like awakening" means like the aspect that apprehends blue and so forth;
and no affliction arises there with a single [afflicted] aspect.
For instance, with respect to a single female form, one observes the occurrence of various mental states: passion in some, hatred in another, and envy in yet another.

It might be argued that the initial passion and so forth in this life do not arise from previous habituation; rather, they arise from observing the sexual conduct of others or from the instruction of others. To this, [the author] replies: "By the perception of the activity of others," and so on.
Nor is their activity [established] through the perception of other activities or through hearing from others,
because such activity is observed to be subject to deviation.
The livelihood of others means, in short, their conduct.
With the words "adṛṣṭa" and so forth, he demonstrates that very same inconclusiveness:
"Boars, deer, and the like, who have neither seen nor heard of such occurrences,
nevertheless undergo transformation upon contact with those of their own kind."
"Vṛttānta" refers to the practice of sexual intercourse and so forth.
"Sabhāgā" means a similar or corresponding state of existence (*gati*), such as that of female pigs and others; they are so designated because of that.
"Contact" (*samparka*) with them means being in close proximity (*samavadhāna*).
"Corruption" means perversion;
that is to say, the practice of sexual intercourse.
The qualities unaccustomed to cyclic existence— such as wisdom, ethical discipline, compassion, and so forth—
proceed by their own inherent nature, and not like pride and the other afflictions.
This must necessarily be understood: that the spontaneous occurrence of passion and the like arises solely through the power of habituation.
For instance, those qualities such as wisdom and ethical discipline, which are unaccustomed to cyclic existence and have not been practiced within it, do not function spontaneously or without effort;
this is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), like intoxication and so forth.
"Intoxication" (*mada*) means arrogance (*darpa*).
Otherwise, like intoxication and the rest, even wisdom and the other [faculties] would function by their own natural impulse.
Some say that passion arises from phlegm (*śleṣman*), hatred from bile (*pitta*), and delusion from wind (*vāta*).
To this, he replies with the verse beginning "balāsādī" and so forth: "And their arising does not occur through the influence of phlegm and the other humors."
As before, because deviation is perceived in every respect.
Therefore, since these [qualities] which occur at the beginning of life are preceded by practice,
that very other existence is established; thus, the doctrine of non-existence is refuted.
In this context, *balāsa* refers to phlegm (*śleṣman*).

The phrase "as before" means as was stated regarding the deviation [of the reason] with respect to objects, beginning with: "Because even when there is the presence of analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyāna*), that [result] does not arise," and so forth.
Furthermore, the increase or decrease of passion and the other afflictions does not occur through the increase or decrease of phlegm and the other humors.
Nor is it logical for something to be the effect of another when its variation does not entail the variation of that other, for this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Likewise, intense hatred is observed even in one with a phlegmatic constitution, yet intense passion is not; conversely, one of a bilious nature is observed to have intense passion, yet intense hatred and so forth are not—thus a confusion of causes is seen.
Furthermore, it is not logical for something to be the cause of another if the latter exists even in the absence of the former.

Since one observes that a person who is lustful in a certain state may also be hateful in that same state, passion and the like are not properties of phlegm and so forth, because of this deviation as well.
Therefore, [the author] concludes with "tasmāt" (therefore).

Regarding the phrase "those preceded by practice" (*yadabhyāsapūrvakā*): the analysis of the compound is as follows—*yadabhyāsaḥ* means "practice in something," and those for whom that is the preceding cause (*pūrvakaṃ kāraṇaṃ*) are *yadabhyāsapūrvakāḥ*.
With the words beginning with "here" (*ihatya*), [the author] anticipates an objection from an opponent.
If it is to be proven that [the Veda] is preceded by study in this life, there is sublation by what is perceived and what is accepted;
if it is to be proven that it has causes belonging to another existence, the illustrative example (nidarśana) is devoid of the property to be proven (sādhya-śūnya).
But if the probandum is stated without qualification, this reason is contradictory,
because it likewise excludes the cause consisting in the practice of another birth.

In this regard, the following objection arises: Is the probandum (sādhya) that passion and so forth occurring for the first time in this life are preceded by practice in this very life; or that they are preceded by practice in a future life; or, without distinction, merely that they are preceded by practice? If that [merely being preceded by practice] were established, then by implication, the intended [specific] fact—that they are preceded by practice in a future life—would be established. Thus, all three positions would be established. Regarding these three positions: in the first case, there is subversion of both what is observed and what is accepted. For it is not observed that passion and so forth occurring for the first time here are preceded by practice in this life, nor is this accepted by the proponent of the other world (the afterlife). Thus, there is subversion of both the observed and the accepted.

In the second position as well, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), for there exists no instance anywhere of a Lokāyata [teacher] who is endowed with the prior practice of a future life. In the third position too, the logical reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because, just like the example itself, it proves the absence of that which is intended—the state of being preceded by practice in another birth.
He offers a rebuttal with the verse beginning "In a general sense... (*sāmānyenaiva*).
The probandum is indeed established in a general sense, and there is no contradiction in the reason;
for this [reason] has no contradiction with that [probandum] by which it would exclude it.
In this context, it is precisely the third position that is intended; nor is there any contradiction in the reason (*hetu*). Why?

Because there is no contradiction anywhere between this state of possessing passion and so forth (*rāgāditva*) on the one hand and its being preceded by practice in another existence on the other, such that the latter would exclude the former’s being preceded by practice in a future life (*pāralaukika*).
Furthermore, this distinction between "this world" and "the next world" is merely a conventional designation based on a difference in states,
just like the distinctions between childhood, youth, and so forth. However, since beginninglessness is established by this very method, one should not become attached to this [distinction].
"This is like an opponent" — this [is the meaning].
Thus concludes the examination of the Lokāyata.
Chapter: Examination of External Objects (*Bahirarthaparīkṣā*).

Regarding the phrase "resembling a reflection," the Proponent of Cognition (*Vijñānavādin*) now introduces this [argument] in order to establish the specific qualification of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

In this regard, the view of the Buddhist Vijñānavādins is as follows: this triple world is nothing but representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), and that consciousness is infinite and impure for those who have not realized reality due to the distinctions between the mental continua of individual beings, yet it is pure for those who have abandoned all defilements. Furthermore, it arises in every moment as something ever-changing for all living beings, and is not a single, unchanging entity as held by the followers of the Upaniṣads and others.

In this context, "representation-only" is intended through these two aspects: because when there is an absence of an external object of apprehension (*grāhya*)—such as the nature of earth and so forth—there is also an absence of the state of being an apprehender (*grāhaka*).
Or, even if another continuum exists, [consciousness is devoid of the characteristics of grasped and grasper].
Regarding this, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: whatever is cognition is devoid of the duality of grasped and grasper, because its cause is the very nature of being cognition.
Furthermore, one should not consider this reason (hetu) to be non-pervasive (avyāpti).

For instance, there exists no external object such as earth and so forth that can be its [the cognition's] apprehended object, because such an object is devoid of a nature that is either unitary or manifold.

The formal argument is as follows: whatever does not possess a nature that is either unitary or manifold cannot be apprehended as an existent by a discerning person, just like a lotus in the sky; and the earth and other elements postulated by opponents are likewise devoid of a unitary or manifold nature. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Since existence is pervaded by both unity and plurality due to the absence of a third category, the impossibility of a relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the opposite case; thus, the immediately preceding reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Here, pointing out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of this reason, and demonstrating the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge for this proposition—namely, that "this supreme principle must be accepted [in which] even the primary elements (*bhūta*) do not exist"—the opponent says "If, apart from cognition... and so forth, in order to demonstrate the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the first reason: "If the fourfold set of elements does not exist apart from cognition, then why is it that this appears so clearly and distinctly?"
If you accept the non-existence of that very thing even when it appears in such a way,
what proof could you have for the existence of the mind itself?

By the word "separated" (*vicchinna*), he demonstrates the establishment of the object of cognition as distinct from the cognition itself; by the word "clearly" (*vispaṣṭa*), however, he indicates its status as direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*).
Strengthening this very point as a corollary, he says, beginning with "of that which is thus," etc.
(vv. 1965–), and he provides the rebuttal beginning with "while appearing," etc. (v. 1966).
What is the nature of this external object that appears? Does it manifest with the intrinsic nature of atoms, or rather with the characteristics of a composite whole?
First of all, the form of atoms is not perceived,
because there is no perception of a cognition that appears as a single, partless, and manifold entity.
For atoms would appear as devoid of any distinction of parts; otherwise, they could not be objects of direct perception, because they do not impart their own form [to the cognition].

In this regard, an object established by direct perception, if it were external, would have to be one of the following options: either multiple atoms (paramāṇu) that are not distinct [from one another], or a single composite whole (avayavin) composed of them, or a gross object that is not so composed. Among these, the first option is not tenable, because no cognition is ever perceived that apprehends multiple partless atoms as having material form;
rather, cognition is always experienced as having only a gross form.
The reading "pratyaye teṣām aprativedanāt" is an uncompounded [compound] ending in the locative case.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not appear with its own form in a cognition intended to be perceptual is not to be grasped as being perceptual, just like a lotus in the sky; and the atom—which is multiple and corporeal—does not appear in a cognition intended to be perceptual that apprehends a gross form. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), because perception is pervaded by the appearance of the form of [its] self.
Establishing that very pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says "devoid of... and so forth (verse 1967).

Now, it might be argued that because of the established doctrine that [atoms] arise and perish only in an aggregated state, there is no appearance of individual atoms; as the Venerable Śubhagupta has stated:
"Individual atoms have no possibility of existing independently."
For this reason as well, atoms do not appear individually.
Thus, showing that this is the answer, he says: "Even by way of association. Even when produced through association, they appear in their own intrinsic nature alone.
If those [states] do not abandon their partless nature, they do not belong to them in those conditions.
If form possesses a limit of diminution,
how indeed could it not be material, like sensation and the other aggregates?

"In those ten states" means in the states of conjunction. Furthermore, he points out the contradiction with his own statement in the proposition by saying "having undergone diminution," etc., implying that if atoms were partless, they could not then be admitted to be corporeal.
That form or intrinsic nature (svabhāva) by which the limit of diminution is attained is what has been so described.
