This is what is meant: if things do not possess a nature that diminishes through the division of diminishing parts—that is to say, if they are partless—then they cannot be established as having material form (*mūrta*), like sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, because there would be no distinction [between them].
With the words "tulyetādinā" (by [the verse] beginning with *tulya*), he anticipates the rebuttal of the Venerable Śubhagupta:
"Just as there is the delusion of permanence due to the arising of similar subsequent moments,
so too there is the delusion of grossness when there is the apprehension of an uninterrupted stream of homogeneous [moments]."

For he says: just as for one who is deceived by the production of successive similar moments, there arises the delusion of permanence regarding sound and so forth even though they are perceived directly, so too, when atoms situated in contiguous locations are grasped simultaneously as belonging to the same class, there occurs a mental delusion that they are "gross.
Consequently, the reason—"because there is no cognition of multiple partless forms"—is unestablished (*asiddha*).
He states the refutation with the words "by the power of its own operation," etc.:
"If perception were to produce [its result] solely by the power of its own operation,
how could the objects of reflective cognition (parāmarśa-vijñāna) be within the range of perception for you?"
If entities are determined by valid cognition to be momentary,
how can atoms be understood as being yellow, white, and so forth?

If it is argued that the form consisting of an accumulation of subtle atoms is the first object of visual perception because of its grossness— just like mountains and so forth— and that this inference applies here as well;
For grossness is indeed a property of an object, and it is not established in either of the two subjects [the whole or the atoms];
for there is no gross composite whole, nor are the atoms of such a nature.
Furthermore, although its form is presented as existing through the extension of space,
there remains doubt because it appears as a form manifested by a deluded consciousness.
If that [cognition] is not so because of its falsity, then since no distinction has been established,
what excellence does it possess if it merely accords with the result?
Even when there is a correspondence with a cognition that manifests an object, it is indeed said:
"Because of the restriction of causal capacity, that [correspondence] could otherwise be possible."
By the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), he shows that [perception] is independent of the operation of logical marks (*liṅga*) or scripture (*āgama*).

For indeed, although perception arises without distinction [toward all objects], it is only in respect to that aspect where it produces a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the apprehended form that it is accepted as "perception" by virtue of its fitness for conventional usage (*vyavahārayogyatā*); however, in respect to that where it does not produce such awareness, even though it has been apprehended, it is as if unapprehended.
Consequently, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

For in the statement "because of the non-apprehension of the cognition," the intended meaning is that [the object] does not appear in the cognition—which is claimed to be perceptual—serving as the cause for its subsequent conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*).
Furthermore, as for what was said—that this notion of "gross" is a mental error—that too is incorrect;
for the designation of something as an error can only occur when it has been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Just as the apprehension of permanence is established as an error because momentariness has been proven by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), atoms are not likewise established by valid cognition, since they themselves are currently under investigation. Furthermore, this illusion of grossness is not mental, because it appears with clarity.
Furthermore, for that which is bound up with conceptual construction, a clear form is not tenable, because the form of a universal is indistinct;
nor is conceptual construction tenable without the form of a universal. This might be argued:

Just like impermanence and other such properties, atoms are indeed established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance: whatever is gross is composed of an accumulation of subtle [parts], just as mountains and the like; and the first visually perceptible substance consisting of parts is gross. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
The inclusion of the term "visually perceptible" is for the purpose of excluding non-visually perceptible things, such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.

In that regard, if the reason "because of grossness" is stated by relying on a grossness that is ultimately real and a property of the thing itself, then since grossness is not established for the proponent in either of the two subjects—the subject of the thesis or the subject of the example—the reason is unestablished and the example is devoid of the probans.

Now, if that form which appears through the extension over space—which is delightful when not investigated and well-known even to cowherds—is called "gross" because of its grossness, then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since such an appearing form exists even in erroneous cognitions like dreams, despite the absence of an accumulation of atoms.

If, however, the qualification "provided it is non-erroneous" is added, then for the Vijñānavādin, there is no distinction or difference whatsoever between the form of a cognition from healthy eyes and the like, and the form of a cognition such as a dream.
First of all, since non-erroneousness is not established anywhere, even the qualification [of the definition] remains unestablished.

It might be argued that there is indeed a distinction between the cognition of one with healthy eyes and so forth and the cognition of a dream, by virtue of the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
In that case, what is this so-called "correspondence with purposeful action"?

If [the opponent claims] that the attainment of an external object is [the correspondence], that is not established, because the very establishment of the external object is what is currently under discussion as the probandum (*sādhya*). If, on the other hand, "correspondence with purposeful action" (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*) is simply the cognition appearing as the desired purposeful action, then this [correspondence] can occur otherwise even without being based on an external object; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
To the question, "How can it be conceived otherwise? he says: "Because of the restriction of capacity (*sāmarthya-niyama*) due to the cause."
Because of the restriction of the specific capacity of the cause, namely the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
For only a certain immediately preceding condition is capable of producing a certain consciousness, not every [condition] every [consciousness].
Just as you [hold] regarding external objects, the restriction is established for that very reason.
With the verse beginning "tulyam" (equal), he demonstrates the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason "because of non-perception" according to the view of Sumati the Digambara:
"When a form that is equal is perceived, and that which is unequal is not perceived at all—
if atoms possess a dual nature, then why is this not logically possible?"
Because every entity consists of the nature of both the universal and the particular,
and because its own form is both similar and dissimilar, atoms are traditionally held to possess two forms.
In that case, whatever form is common [to many atoms] is the object of sensory cognition;
therefore, it follows that cognition has a single form only with respect to atoms themselves.
"However, some of poor intellect imagine in a confused manner that the form which is held to be the yogi’s direct perception is something unequal [to ordinary perception]."
For he says this: because all entities possess the nature of both the universal and the particular, atoms have two forms, namely, a similar and a dissimilar form.
Among these, that form which is common is apprehended by the sense organs, not that which is uncommon.
Consequently, a cognition of a single form with respect to atoms is not contradictory; thus, atoms are established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Thus:
"confused" means "without a fixed basis."
Because there is an absence of even a single definitively determined form.
But has it not already been stated that a thing possesses two forms, which is to say its form is determined? True, it was stated; however, showing that what was stated is untenable, he says:
"How indeed can two forms be logical for a single thing? In that case, two distinct things would result, by virtue of having mutually different forms."
But if they were of the nature of one another, that duality would be contradicted;
furthermore, the specific distinction [between them] would be perceived by the sense organs such as the eye.
For in this way, because the entity would be different from the two forms, it would follow that there are indeed two distinct entities;
since there would be only two distinct forms existing separately from one another, it cannot be said that a single entity possesses two forms.

Alternatively, since the two forms are not distinct from the single entity, the two forms would have a mutual identity just like the nature of the single entity itself; how then could one thing be dual-natured?
Furthermore, because the particular form is not distinct from the universal form, it would follow that the particular form must be perceived [by the senses].

Consequently, this unconfused distinction—which is intended such that the common form is the object of sensory cognition while the uncommon form is the object of yogic perception—would not be established.

Furthermore, not only is the claim that "one thing has two forms" mutually contradictory, but this is even more contradictory: namely, that it shows one thing to consist of two mutually opposed forms. As for the passage beginning with "paraspara...
"How could that which consists of two mutually opposed natures be a single form?"
For instance, since similar and dissimilar forms are characterized by their existence through mutual exclusion, how could that [single object] be of the nature of both?
With the words "And because of cognition," etc., he raises the objection of Kumārila’s view:
"Furthermore, contradictory things cannot possibly exist even in a single [locus], because they are cognized."
If that which has a single form were not one, it would not be the word of Īśvara;
for it must be accepted exactly as it is perceived.
For he said: "It is not the case that mutually contradictory forms cannot exist within a single object.
Why?
Because of consciousness (*saṃvitti*)."

For it is not a command of kings that a single entity must exist in only one form; rather, whatever is perceived in a certain way must be accepted as being exactly so, because the determination of an entity is based upon cognition.
And cognition is observed to occur in both singular and plural forms, due to distinctions such as existence, color, and so forth.
Therefore, it is established in that very manner.
He refutes this with the words beginning "That is not so" (*tanna*):
"Because there is cognition even of what is non-existent, as in the case of the form of a yellow conch-shell and the like;
moreover, since there is no other characteristic of difference than the association with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṅga*)."
This being the case, no cognition whatsoever would be erroneous, and there would follow the undesirable consequence of the abolition of all conventional usage based on differentiation.
Alternatively, if some [cognition] were to be considered erroneous because it is sublated, [then...]

In that case, how could the cognition of many [atoms] in a single [moment] not be sublated, and thus be non-erroneous? Thus, first of all, since atoms are established neither by perception nor by inference, there is no contradiction with perception regarding the thesis that denies external objects,
nor is the reason unestablished.
Now, another [opponent], pointing out that the reason "because of being devoid of a nature that is either one or many" is of doubtful unestablished status (sandigdhāsiddha), says: "Mābhūd," etc.

"Let there be no establishment of atoms by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); let there be doubt [regarding them]. But how could those who are discerning (prekṣāvat) have a certainty of their non-existence?"

He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "conjoined" (saṃyuktam): "The form of an atom situated in the middle [of a cluster] is conjoined, located at a distance, and arranged without interval, facing a single atom."
If that very same atom is conceived as facing toward another atom, then,
this being the case, the accumulation of mountains and the like would not be possible.
If it is maintained that the form facing another atom is different [from the form facing other atoms],
how indeed could there be a single atom under such circumstances?

The formal argument is as follows: whatever is devoid of a nature that is either one or many is fit for the conventional designation of "non-existent," just like a lotus in the sky; and the atoms postulated by the opponent are devoid of a nature that is either one or many. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Nor should it be thought that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*);
for, first of all, the unity of atoms is unestablished, because in those forms accumulated as mountains and so forth, there exists a differentiation of spatial parts (*digbhāgabheda*).

By demonstrating that the differentiation of spatial directions for those very atoms is necessitated by the otherwise inexplicable accumulation of cavities and so forth, he first states the negation of their unity, beginning with the words "joined," "situated in a distant place," and so on.

Regarding this, some say that atoms join one another; others say they are always separated by intervals and do not touch; while still others say that when there is no interval, the term "touched" is used metaphorically. Now, in all three of these positions, if the atom situated in the middle and surrounded by many others were not to possess a differentiation of spatial directions, [the following would occur].
In that case, there would be no accumulation of the collection of mind and mental factors, because they are partless.

For instance, if the central atom were facing another atom with the very same form by which it faces one atom, then all the surrounding atoms would occupy the same location; consequently, no accumulation could occur.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which has a nature facing a single-form atom must occupy the same location, just like the atom situated in its eastern direction, or like the eastern mansion facing a single mansion; and all the atoms standing in a surrounding circle have a nature facing a single-form atom.
This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Therefore, there could be no accumulation (*pracaya*).
If, on the other hand, it faces [another atom] by means of a different form, then because a distinction of spatial directions exists, it would not possess unity, just like a jar or similar objects.

But the venerable Śubhagupta says: "Just as a single universal, which is of a single nature, is not conceived as truly real despite its exclusion from non-existent things such as non-substances, so too here, although atoms exist in many locations, their multiplicity is conceived, but not in an ultimate sense.
For there is no such thing as a category called 'direction' imagined by Kaṇāda and others; since that [direction] has a single nature, the cognition of 'east' and so forth could not be manifold."

If it were argued that only atoms (*aṇu*) situated in a sequence are what is denoted by the word "direction," and therefore, because they possess a distinction of spatial parts (*digbhāga*), the statement [of the opponent] would merely refer to being surrounded by many [others], and not to having constituent parts (*sāvayavatva*), this is incorrect.

For, since atoms—like the mind (*citta*)—are partless in the ultimate sense, they have no upper or lower portions; thus, there could be no surrounding by many [others] at all, just as in the case of the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*).

Furthermore, since the surrounding atoms do not exist in an ultimate sense, how could there be a state of being situated in the midst of many by way of them, through which a spatial multiplicity might be imagined?

If, even in the absence of an ultimate distinction between upper and lower parts, there were still a surrounding by many [atoms], then this would also apply to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Consequently, like the atoms, the mind and its associates would also possess spatial location.
If not, then this would apply even to atoms;

consequently, there would be no accumulation, just as in the case of the mind and so forth—this is the certainty. It might be argued: "Just as there is a temporal contiguity for the present moment of consciousness (cittakṣaṇa) with respect to past and future moments of consciousness, yet the present moment of consciousness possesses parts like a *kalā* or a *muhūrta*, so too, even though atoms are surrounded by many others, they will not possess spatial divisibility."
This is incorrect.
For the characteristic of a present moment of mind does not, in the ultimate sense, possess continuity with the preceding and succeeding moments, because those two do not exist at that time.

Nor is it logical for there to be a real sequence of priority and posteriority with something non-existent; rather, the existence of the preceding and succeeding moments is merely conceptualized through the medium of the claim that there is no causal relationship between simultaneous things, and is thus constructed, like the existence [of a thing] before and after its destruction.
Furthermore, spatial priority and posteriority cannot be imagined for atoms in this way, because it would entail the impossibility of their aggregation.
Moreover, it is not logical that entities should be without cause, as that would entail their eternal existence and so forth.
Even by one who maintains that entities are merely conventional, the causality of all entities must necessarily be admitted.

And if there were causality, it would first of all not be logical for cause and effect to exist simultaneously; nor could it occur prior to the arising of the effect, because the cause would lack efficacy due to its non-existence at that time;
nor could it occur later, because once the effect has already arisen, the cause would have no further utility.
Therefore, the prior existence of all causes must necessarily be accepted.
As it has been said:
"Because that which is non-existent lacks causal capacity beforehand, and because it would be useless afterwards..."
All causes must exist prior [to their effect]; therefore, an object does not exist simultaneously with its own cognition.

Thus, even though all entities are partless according to reason, there would exist a sequence of priority and posteriority caused by time, just as there is a sequence caused by space when there is divisibility; and it has been stated that this would apply to the mind and mental factors as well, since there is no distinction [in their lack of parts].
If it is argued that there is a distinction caused by corporeality, we say no.

That very [reason] is unestablished if there is no possession of parts (*sāvayavatva*). It would merely be a restatement of the same point through a synonym, and not a distinct qualification; therefore, this is trivial.

Consequently, since a temporal priority and posteriority produced by time is logically established for all entities, that further additional spatial priority and posteriority belonging to some [entity] is not possible without the possession of parts; thus, what was said is correct.
For that which possesses a distinction of spatial directions, unity is not tenable; enough of this elaboration.

On this point, some say: "In that case, let atoms be merely minute spatial points (*pradeśa*). Even if one further conceives of parts within them, those very points will again possess the nature of atoms. If this leads to an infinite regress, it cannot be used to establish that atoms have only a conceptual existence (*prajñaptisattva*) by means of the consequence of having parts. Furthermore, even if they do have a conceptual existence, one must necessarily admit a basis for that conception; that which serves as the basis for its conception will itself be the atom."
Now, even if the non-existence of atoms is being proven in this way, the reason (*hetu*) "because of the distinction of spatial directions" (*digbhāgabhedāt*) remains unestablished (*asiddha*).
For things that are absolutely non-existent, such as the horns of a donkey, do not possess distinctions of spatial directions such as east and so forth.
Nor is this a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum), because the opponent does not accept the existence of distinctions of spatial directions.
Regarding this, he states the rebuttal beginning with "apeta" and so forth:
"And that atom which is asserted by others to be devoid of any division of parts..."
It is precisely regarding that [subject] that this reflection was made; therefore, there is no possibility of an undesirable consequence arising from it.
When they accept that parts possess the nature of atoms,
then a fall from their own thesis necessarily follows for them.
And here, because it is a proof by way of a reductio (*prasaṅgasādhana*), there is no fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*);
for unity is indeed negated on the strength of the "connection" (*yoga*) and other properties accepted by the opponent.
Thus, in all these positions, it is not logical for that [self] to be a single entity;
and because a single [entity] is not established, its having a manifold nature is also impossible.
Therefore, for the wise, the atom is incapable of being determined as existing,
because it is empty of both a unitary and a manifold nature, like a sky-lotus.
For the proponent of atoms must necessarily admit that some entity exists with a fully established form as an atom;
otherwise, due to infinite regress and the lack of a determined form, the very non-existence of the object would be established by his own logic,
and he would thus have accomplished the very point desired by his opponent.

Therefore, when an investigation is conducted regarding that very thing which has been established by you as being minute (*aṇu*)—provided it does not rely on the conceptualization of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—how could there be an infinite regress? Only if, through an infinite regress, a contradiction with your own accepted position were created;
however, nothing undesirable has been brought about for the opponent.
Since the opponent's desired conclusion is established by this much alone, this is indeed a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum).
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*).

For the opponent has indeed accepted that atoms possess conjunction (*saṃyuktatva*), contiguity (*nairantarya*), and being surrounded by many [atoms] with intervals; otherwise, how could there be cognition? Consequently, even if the distinction of spatial parts (*digbhāgabhedo*) is not explicitly admitted in words, it nonetheless follows by the very force of accepting properties such as conjunction;

for, as it has been said, if there were no distinction between upper, lower, and other parts, the three positions regarding conjunction and so forth would be untenable, just as in the case of the mind (*citta*) and its concomitants.
As for what was said—that since the designation of an atom must necessarily admit a substratum (*upādāna*), that which is the substratum will itself be the atom—this is indeed [addressed] here:

the maturation of the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) deposited by hearing and reflecting upon false treatises is the basis for the delusion of atoms, namely the cognition appearing as dust motes in a window-lattice and so forth.

For it is not logical that the very thing designated should be its own cause, because that would entail the consequence of it being a non-designated entity (*aprajñaptisat*); otherwise, in the designation of a self (*ātman*), the self itself would be the cause and not the aggregates (*skandha*).
Consequently, there would also be no negation of the self [as being] like an atom.
Thus, in the first place, the oneness of atoms is unestablished;
because that [oneness] is of the nature of doubt, the reason used for establishing the conventional usage of the non-existence of atoms is not unestablished.

Having thus established that the external object is devoid of a manifold nature, he now says "And because of the impossibility of an atom," etc., in order to establish that it is also devoid of a unitary nature:
"Since a composite whole does not exist because of the impossibility of an atom,
for it is held by others to be composed of atoms."

Even for those who maintain that a gross object is not composed of atoms, that object—like an atom—is not logically one, because it is divided according to its spatial directions; for if it were one, the consequence would follow that when the hand or another part moves, the whole must move.
Since this point is clear and has been threshed out many times, it is not improper to omit a separate refutation of it here.

Thus, in establishing the non-transactional status of external objects through the formal argument beginning with "that which possesses neither a unitary nor a manifold nature," the reason is not unestablished; consequently, the non-existence of external things such as earth—which are the objects of apprehension—is established. Since that [external object] is unestablished, the status of being an apprehender, which is conceptually constructed in dependence upon it, does not exist for cognition either; thus, the state of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā) is established.

Thus, having established the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) because of the impossibility [of external objects], he now says "without appearance," and so forth, establishing it by means of the absence of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper:
"Cognition does not cognize an external object in any way— whether as being without appearance, with appearance, or even with the appearance of something else."

It is not logical for the external object to be apprehended by a cognition that is formless, nor by one that possesses a form, nor by one that has a form other than the form of the object; furthermore, there is no other mode possible. Therefore, it is established that cognition is always self-cognizing (*ātmasaṃvedana*), even when an external continuum exists; thus, the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is proven.
Some, however, maintain that a cognition with one form can cognize an object with another form, as it is said that even a cognition having a yellow form may grasp a white conch.
As Kumārila stated:
In all cases, the external object of perception consists of a difference in place and time,
whether in a single birth or in different births, and always even at another time.
Thus, for this reason, a third alternative has been raised.
Now, one might ask: "Why do these conceptual constructions, such as non-manifestation and so forth, not also apply to self-awareness? To this he says, "Consciousness," and so on:
"Consciousness arises as something distinct from insentient forms;
this very non-insentience is its self-awareness."
For self-cognition is not intended here in the sense of being an apprehending subject;
rather, it is because [consciousness] itself, by its very nature, has the character of luminosity, like light existing in the expanse of the sky.

Now, as to why it is not accepted [as being established] by way of the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender, he says: "By way of the relationship between action and agent," and so forth: "But its self-cognition does not occur by way of the relationship between action and agent, because for that which is single and partless, a threefold nature is untenable."
Therefore, since this [consciousness] has the nature of awareness, its self-cognition is indeed logical;
but how can there be a cognition of another, namely an object-form, by means of it?
The three-fold nature [of cognition] exists through the distinction between the object of knowledge, the knower, and the awareness thereof.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even for external objects, there will be cognition without the relation of apprehended and apprehender, just as there is self-cognition; to this he says, "For its form is not [that] of another," and so forth:
"For its form is not that of another, by virtue of which [it could be said that] when that [other] is cognized, [the object] is [also] cognized;
because, from the perspective of ultimate reality, entities are distinct from the cognizable."

Even if a single form such as "existence" is conceptually constructed among entities by way of the exclusion of "non-existence" and so forth, nevertheless, for the purpose of demonstrating that [form], he says "in ultimate reality" (paramārthataḥ), meaning that from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no unity at all because of their difference.

It might be argued: "Even if the external object is indeed distinct from cognition, it will nevertheless be cognizable, just like cognition itself. To this, he replies with the verse beginning "by virtue of having the nature of awareness" (*bodharūpatayā*), etc.:
"For it is logical that cognition is cognizable because it arises in a form that is distinct [from the object];
but the object does not arise as awareness—so how can it be cognized? (2004)

Having thus established self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), he now states the following— beginning with "nirbhāsi" and so forth— in order to demonstrate how it is untenable for an external object to be known by a cognition that lacks its form:

"But on the view that cognition possesses an appearance (*nirbhāsi-jñāna-pakṣa*), even though there is a difference between the two in reality, there may still be a figurative (*bhākta*) awareness [of the object], because the reflection has that same nature."
But for one who maintains that cognition is not colored by the form of the object,
even this mode of external perception does not exist at all.
"Of the reflection" means of the form of cognition;
"because of that nature" means because of its similarity;
"figurative" means non-primary.
This [other] one as well is not primary; it is merely a conceptual construction based on its resemblance [to the primary].

Now, it might be argued as follows: "Just as a sword cuts an elephant and the like, or as fire burns what is to be burned, and yet these [instruments], such as the sword, do not possess the form of the elephant and so forth; in the same way, cognition will determine its object even without assuming the form of that object. This is the doubt raised by the words "it might be thought" (*syān matir*), etc.: "It might be thought that just as swords, flames, and the like, perform cutting, burning, and so forth with respect to elephants, things to be burned, and the rest, even though they do not possess the nature of those [objects]. (Verse 325)
The genitive case in "dantidāhyādeḥ" (of the elephant, the combustible object, etc. is used in relation to "chedadāhādi" (cutting, burning, etc.).
"Adaḥ" refers to this very knowledge.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), such things as lamps and so forth are included, which serve as illuminators of blue and other colors, and so on.
He provides the answer with the words "tadidam" and so forth:
[p.561] "This is inconsistent because those things which are established as existing in such a way are the causes for their arising in that manner; cognition, however, is not a producer in that way."

For swords and the like are well known as "burners" (dāhakas) and so forth only because they are actually the producers of elephants and the like; for instance, when struck by the edge of a sword or similar weapon, elephants have their joints severed, and likewise, through contact with fire, fuel takes on the form of charcoal and so forth. Similarly, jars and other objects also become capable of generating cognition by virtue of light; however, no such benefit is conferred upon the object by the cognition. Rather, it is by the object itself that the consciousness is clearly produced. Thus, how could that [cognition], which effects nothing at all, be the knower of it?

Nor is it reasonable to assume that for consciousness, the very fact of being an effect constitutes its capacity to cognize that [object], lest it should also follow that it possesses the capacity to cognize the eye and so forth.

But the Venerable Śubhagupta says: "Even though consciousness does not assume the form of the object, it apprehends the object because its nature is that of discernment (*pariccheda*). Therefore, one should not raise the doubt: 'How does it discern? Like what does it discern? And he says: "If that [consciousness] has the characteristic of discernment, how is it the grasper of that [object]?"
Therefore, there is no suspicion regarding consciousness, nor even the question of what it might be like.
Thus it is said;
regarding this, he says "that nature of discernment," and so forth: "That nature of discernment is established for consciousness."
If a determination in the form of cognition were possible for that which is to be grasped, [then it would be an object].
Otherwise, it would have to be clearly stated that cognition is of the nature of discernment; yet, in this way, the experience of the object has not been specified.
For all this would be possible only if it were established that [cognition] consists in the determination of an object distinct [from itself]; however, that very point is not established for us.
To explain: cognition does not determine [an object] by its mere existence, because that would entail the consequence of determining everything.
Nor does it do so by way of being its effect, because that would lead to the absurdity of the eyes and other [senses] also being determined [by that cognition].

Furthermore, the theory of cognition possessing a form (sākāratā) is not accepted [by us], such that by virtue of having that same form, the cognition would be non-distinct from the object and thus its cognizer. Therefore, if the determination of the apprehended object were to be of the nature of cognition itself, then cognition would possess the nature of determining the object.
Otherwise, how could it be clearly stated that cognition has the nature of determining the object?

Therefore, because there is a determination of the object and yet a distinction [from it], the very nature of cognition has arisen; thus, the state of "representation-only" (vijñaptimātratā) is established.

It might be argued: "There must be some specific quality belonging to this [cognition] by which it determines the object alone, and not [the object as something external]. If you say there is no such quality, [we reply:
although it is impossible to point out every unique entity, it is nevertheless described through conventional designation (udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtti).
Otherwise, one would not even be able to state a distinction between form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects].
Furthermore, it would not be clearly and unambiguously indicated that cognition is the awareness of an object by means of a form that is not thus determined.
Therefore, this claim—that entities are well-established when their existence is established by means of an undetermined form—is trivial.
It might be argued: "In the absence of an object to be delimited, whose would this delimitation be? To this he says: "Whose is that delimitation? and so forth.
"Whose is that delimitation?"—this question does not deserve to be raised;
for that delimitation is its very nature, just as [the nature] of pleasure and so forth is their continuity and so on.
For the self itself is what is called the "ascertainment" (pariccheda) of that [object], by virtue of its nature as luminosity.

Just as with pleasure and so forth, there is the expression "the continuity of pleasure"; for that [continuity] does not become something other than the pleasure merely because of the use of a distinct designation such as "of pleasure.

Therefore, although there is a designation that appears as if it were distinct—such as "the ascertainment of blue" or "of yellow"—nevertheless, it is simply the intrinsic nature [of consciousness] that is so described, because it manifests in the form of blue and so on, since cognition has the nature of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana).

Now, what is this meaning of "self-cognition" (svasaṃvit) by the force of which it is so described? To this he says: "Its own nature," and so forth. "It does not depend on anything else for the cognition of its own nature; nor is this [nature] unknown—this is the meaning of self-cognition."
With the words "engaged," etc., Kumārila raises an objection regarding the point that cognition does not depend on anything else for the awareness of its own nature:
"For when engaged in the cognition of an object, cognition does not reach [i.e., cognize] itself;
therefore, even though it is illuminating, it awaits something else for its own apprehension."

For he says: although cognition is of the nature of illumination, it nevertheless requires another for its own manifestation; it does not, however, reach or apprehend itself, because it is occupied solely with the illumination of the object. Indeed, it is not logical for that which is occupied with one thing to simultaneously operate upon another without abandoning the former.
Anticipating the objection that a lamp might constitute a counter-example [to the definition of consciousness], he states an alternative position, beginning with "of such a kind" (*īdṛśam*):
"Or, its nature as illumination consists in being of the essence of the experience of an object;
since it lacks the experience of itself, it is not an illuminator of itself."
[Objection: But if it lacks the nature of self-illumination, how can its status as an illuminator of external objects be established? To this, he says "sati" and so forth:
"And just as the status of being an illuminator is observed in the case of the eyes and other [senses] with respect to form and so on when they exist, so too will it be in this case."
Just as the status of the eye and other faculties as illuminators of objects such as form is established even though they lack self-illumination, so too will it be in this case regarding cognition.
It might be asked: "Why does [cognition] abandon its own internal nature, which is more proximate, and manifest only the external? To this, he says: "The quality of being a manifestor," and so forth.
The quality of being a manifestor applies to the external object, but not to itself, because of a lack of capacity.
Furthermore, the capacity of all entities is not subject to such questioning.
To the question, "Why is there no power for self-illumination?", he says: "And the power of all entities," and so forth.
As it is said: "Fire burns, but space does not; who can be questioned about this?"
With the words "But surely," and so forth, he provides an objection:
"Surely, the cognition of an object is designated as nothing other than knowledge itself. Since that [cognition] is the very nature of [knowledge], what other operation could there be?"
As for what was said—that [cognition] is "engaged" (*vyāpṛta*) in the apprehension of an object—that is inconsistent. For the apprehension of an object is not something other than cognition.
To explain: "apprehension," "perception," "comprehension of an object," and "representation"—these synonyms denote nothing but cognition itself.

And when that apprehension of the object is of the very nature of that [cognition], being of the same essence as cognition, what other operation (*vyāpāra*) could there be belonging to cognition—distinct from its own self—which consists in the awareness of the object, such that one could say it is "engaged" in the apprehension of the object?
Moreover, it is not logical that activity should reside in the self alone.

It might be argued: "How is it established that the cognition of an object has the nature of knowledge itself, such that 'knowledge' (jñāna) and 'cognition of the object' (arthasaṃvitti) are synonyms? To this he says: "The experience of the object is its form," and so forth.

If the experience of the object were its form, and if that [form] consisted of knowledge, then it would be logical for knowledge to have the nature of the experience of the object; however, that is not the case.
Because it would follow that the object already present must be abandoned,
the cognition of the object is not established for that [consciousness], even though it possesses by its own nature the essence of experience.
The experience of an object must necessarily be admitted as its form, that is, its intrinsic nature;
otherwise, how could cognition operate upon it?
For it is not logical for anything to exercise an operation toward such things as a rabbit's horn when they do not exist.

Furthermore, if that nature which consists of the experience of the object were non-different from cognition, then that which was stated—that cognition possesses the nature of experiencing the object, or that its luminosity (*prakāśatva*) is of such a kind as to consist of the experience of the object—would be tenable.
One might think that the opponent, when pressed, would eventually admit that cognition is non-different from the experience of the object; therefore, [the author] says: "And that does not exist.
That is to say, the experience's non-difference from cognition does not exist.
The meaning accepted—that is, the position characterized by the absence of self-cognition for cognition—would entail its abandonment.
This is because, if one accepts that cognition is not distinct from the experience of the object, it would follow that cognition possesses self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).
It might be argued: "It is not intended that cognition is an illuminator by virtue of having the nature of experiencing the object; what then?"
He says, "But of that, by itself," and so forth, meaning precisely because [cognition] consists solely of the nature of experience (*anubhava*). Regarding that cognition:

even if only the nature of experience were produced and not the nature of experiencing an object, then the cognition of an object could not be established through distinctions such as, "This is the awareness of blue, not of yellow."

To the question "Why would it not be established?", he says: "For there, etc. For in that case, there exists for the other [the opponent] no basis of proximity such as the reflection of the object, as there is in the position of consciousness with forms (sākāravijñānapakṣa).
"Of another" refers to the proponent of non-aspectual cognition (*anākārajñānavādin*), who holds this view:
that the external object possesses aspects (*sākāra*) while the cognition is aspectless (*nirākāra*).
Regarding the claim that its luminosity consists in the experience of objects, he says "by nature," and so forth:
"If, by its very nature, it is insentient in form, it has no self-experience;
then, due to the absence of awareness of cognition itself, there would be no experience of external objects."

If consciousness does not cognize itself because it is insentient in nature, then, since it would not be perceptible by itself, the experience of objects would likewise not be admitted as being perceptible.

It might be argued: "Even if cognition (*jñāna*) were not perceived, why should the experience of the object (*arthānubhava*) also be unperceived? For it does not follow that because color (*rūpa*) is unperceived, sound (*śabda*) must also be unperceived. To this, he says: "The so-called experience of the object," and so forth.
The so-called experience of the object is designated as nothing other than cognition itself.
If its nature is that of non-establishment, what else could its establishment be?
For we do not determine any other form of cognition apart from the experience of the object.

Not determining it [as such], yet employing our own words—which express a certainty regarding what is actually another [nature]—we would deceive ourselves and others. Since the form of that cognition is unestablished, what other established nature could there be for that experience of the object? None at all.

Furthermore, it might be argued that its establishment will occur through another cognition; to this he says "by another cognition," and so forth: If that object is experienced by another cognition while its own experience is occurring, when indeed would it be established, given that its establishment has not yet been achieved?
If [the cognition] is unestablished in the arising of the knowledge of that [object], yet established in the self-awareness [of the subject],
while being established in the awareness of others— this is indeed a well-spoken statement!

Because knowledge is unestablished, it is not tenable to say that the manifest is "manifest" when its manifestation is itself unestablished. For instance, even at the time of the object's own experience, there is no establishment of the object, because the experience—whose very nature is the manifestation of that object—is itself unestablished at that time. It must therefore be stated: when will its establishment occur?
If it is argued that its establishment will occur at the time of the arising of the cognition of that cognition— that is, at the time when the cognition of the cognition of the object arises—
this is a most excellent statement!
For how indeed can that which is not established at the time of its own experience be established at the time of another's experience?

"Let [the second cognition] indeed be established provided that there is no infinite regress; however, that [regress] is difficult to avoid," showing this, he says: "If there is an experience of that [second cognition] as well... and so forth. If that [second cognition] is not established through experience, then the first one is also unestablished.
In that case, if another consciousness were to arise, an infinite regress would result.
"Of that" refers to the second [cognition], the cognition of the cognition of the object;
"of the first" refers to the experience of the object.
"Non-establishment" means that there is no establishment of this [second cognition]; it is unestablished (*asiddha*), and its state is non-establishment (*asiddhatā*).

Furthermore, if it is admitted that there is an experience by means of another cognition, then a memory certainly arises regarding that other cognition as well, in the form "the cognition of my cognition has arisen. For that too, an experience by yet another must be asserted; for a memory is not possible regarding what has not been experienced. Consequently, one must state who—engaged in no other task—is producing these chains of cognitions.
It cannot be the object, because its scope is limited to the primary cognition.
Nor can it be the sense organ or light, since their utility is restricted solely to the visual cognition.
Nor can it be without a cause, for that would lead to the consequence of its existence at all times.
If it is argued that the preceding cognition itself produces each subsequent cognition, he says "in another object" and so forth:
"In that case, there would be no transition to another object, yet such a transition is observed."
In the transition to another range of objects, that which is final [is known] both from itself and from another.
It would not be established; and if that is unestablished, all [other things] would likewise be unestablished.
Consequently, the entire world would be plunged into blindness.
If the final [cognition] is established by itself, then the same must certainly hold for the others as well;
because they possess the nature of cognition, otherwise they would not have the nature of cognition, like a jar or other such objects.

For in this way, the transition to another object would not be possible; for each preceding cognition is established as the object of each succeeding cognition and is proximate to it by virtue of being its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). How, then, could one abandon such an internal factor and grasp an external object? Nor is the object capable of obstructing that [succession], even though it is present, because it is an external factor. If, on the other hand, it were to obstruct it despite being external, then no one would ever experience a cognition at all.
For there is no state whatsoever in which an object is not present;
otherwise, even memory would be severed due to the absence of prior experience.

Furthermore, regarding those conceptual constructions concerning the past that arise without the presence of an object, because there would be no cause for their transition [to another object], they would persist in a succession of concepts until the end of *saṃsāra*, and thus no one would ever engage in reflection upon objects.
Granted that the transition to another object may indeed be untenable;
nevertheless, it must be stated by what that other cognition would be experienced.
Now, if it should be argued that the subsequent cognition itself, while grasping another object, grasps both the preceding cognition and the object—this is incorrect.

For instance, when a cognition apprehending form occurs immediately after a cognition of sound, then because the cognition of sound appears in that cognition apprehending form, it follows that the word itself—which has become established therein—would also appear. Even for one who maintains that cognition is formless (*nirākāra*), it is not logical for there to be an apprehension of the grasper of that [word] without the apprehension of the word; for it is not tenable to apprehend the possessor of a staff (*daṇḍin*) without apprehending the staff. Thus, in the visual cognition apprehending form, there would also be an appearance of the word.

Likewise, even in the case of a conceptual cognition (*cintājñāna*) whose object is the letter *a* and so forth, according to the aforementioned principle, there would be two verbal expressions (*abhilāpa*) in a single [cognition] in the manner already described.

For instance, when one reflects upon the letter *a* immediately after reflecting upon the letter *i*, then that conceptual cognition of the letter *a* also reflects upon the apprehension of the letter *i*; consequently, the verbal expression of the letter *i*, which is mounted upon its own cognition, would appear within the cognition that expresses the letter *a*.
Furthermore, every object whatsoever would appear twice, because it would manifest at the time of its own cognition.
It is incorrect to say that such an appearance does not exist, because [otherwise] there would be no apprehension of the two by means of cognition.

Furthermore, one might argue: "Let the final cognition remain unexperienced and unremembered; what fault would there be? To this he replies: "the transition to another object-domain. Since self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is not admitted, there is no establishment [of cognition] through itself; nor is there establishment through another, due to the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If that final [cognition] is unestablished, the preceding one is also unestablished, because its perceiver is not directly perceived (*apratyakṣopalambhaka*). Consequently, the object too is unestablished, and thus nothing whatsoever would ever be perceived.
Consequently, the entire world would fall into blindness.

Now, if—out of fear of the aforementioned defects regarding that final [cognition]—its establishment is admitted to be self-evident through its own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), then, for the same reason, since all cognitions are indistinguishable in their nature as cognition, it follows that self-awareness [is likewise established].

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is a cognition does not depend on the operation of anything else for its own awareness, because it is a cognition, like the final cognition; and the cognition under dispute is indeed a cognition. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Otherwise, that which is not established by itself would, like a jar or other such objects, be of an insentient nature and thus lose its very status as cognition; this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
He states "producing consciousness," etc., to show how a fixed distinction is observed even when there is the quality of being an illuminator:
"The eye, while producing consciousness regarding form, is its illuminator;
yet because [consciousness] possesses the nature of awareness, there is no comparison between it and that [eye] by means of knowledge."
The eye, in producing a consciousness whose object is form, is said to be the illuminator of form;
however, consciousness does nothing at all to the form, because it is simply the cognizer of that which lacks form.
And it is not logical for something to be an illuminator without performing any action, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Therefore:
analogy (upamā) is similarity (sādṛśya).

With the verse beginning "That which is cognition," etc., he provides a proof for the proponent of formless cognition (*nirākārajñānavādin*) in order to establish the non-difference between the forms such as blue and their corresponding cognitions:
"Whatever is necessarily the cognition of something must be non-distinct from that [object], or it does not differ from it."
Just as the self-nature of the cognition of blue, or like a second moon,
this is the experience of the cognition of blue because it is the experience of the form of blue.

That which is the cognition of something is itself the cognition of that very thing, necessarily and not otherwise; therefore, [the second "that" (tat)] denoted by the second *yat* is made entirely non-different from that which is denoted by the first *yat*.
Alternatively, non-difference is to be proven by way of contraposition.
This is what is meant:
whatever is experienced as not separate from something else is non-different from it, just as the cognition of blue is non-different from its own nature.

Or, for example, just as a second moon appearing in the manifestation of the cognition of one with ophthalmia [is not real], so too is this "cognition of blue" [not real]. This is the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*). Here, the subject (*dharmin*) consists of both the form of blue and its cognition.
The property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is the non-difference of those two;
the reason (*hetu*) is the necessity of simultaneous apprehension as previously stated.
It is precisely such a meaning of the reason that is intended in the Master’s formulation beginning with "because of the necessity of simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*).

Regarding this, the Venerable Śubhagupta says: "This reason is contradictory, because in common usage the word 'together' (saha) never occurs without another [thing]. Therefore, if there is simultaneous cognition (sahavedana), this reason is contradictory."
Thus [it is said]. This is incorrect;
for that whose existence is restricted solely to the counter-example (vipakṣa) is a contradictory reason (viruddha-hetu).
Nor is it [the case that this concomitance] exists only in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), because it also exists in the similar instance (sapakṣa).
For instance, in the world there is the conceit of perceiving two moons simultaneously, yet in ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ) there is no difference between them;
nevertheless, because of the simultaneous perception of the two moons, people say "together."

In this case as well, although the aspect (*ākāra*) is not distinct from cognition, it appears as if external; thus, by treating it as a second [entity], the word "together" (*saha*) is employed based on an imagined distinction.

Indeed, not all verbal usage conforms to the actual state of things, such that the mere use of the word "together" would imply a difference in the logical mark (*liṅga*) bound to the real object, which would render the reason contradictory (*viruddha*).

Furthermore, he himself said: "If the word 'together' means 'identical in meaning,' then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*); for instance, in the spectacles of actors, the moon, or wrestlers, there is no apprehension of blue and so forth by a single [perceiver] alone."
Nor is there apprehension by a single [cognition] of both the blue object and its apprehension;
for even when the blue object is apprehended, the apprehensions of that [object] belonging to other mental continua are not apprehended.
And since all moments of consciousness of living beings are determined by the Omniscient One, how could it be established that there is apprehension by a single [cognition] alone?
Furthermore, the restriction that there is only a single apprehension is established only when the apprehension of another object is negated;
however, the negation of the apprehension of another object is impossible, because affirmation and negation are inapplicable to that which is remote by its very nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*).

If, on the other hand, the word "together" (*saha*) intends to express simultaneity in time, then the reason is in every way inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the Buddha’s cognizable mind and the mind and mental factors [which are simultaneous with them].

It is argued that just as, for instance, in the case of the Buddha, the Blessed One, there is indeed a distinction between the mind of another continuum that is to be known and the Buddha’s own knowledge—even though they are necessarily perceived together—likewise, even if mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta*) are perceived together, they are not one and the same; therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This entire argument is incorrect, for the meaning intended here by "perceived together" (*ekopalambha*) is not "perception by one and the same [subject]."
What then? It is that the apprehension of cognition and the object of cognition is one and the same, not distinct.
For the very apprehension of cognition is the apprehension of the object, and the very apprehension of the object is the apprehension of cognition; this is the point.

Furthermore, in performances such as those of actors, dancers, or wrestlers, there is no apprehension of cognition that does not entail the apprehension of an object, nor any apprehension of an object that does not entail the apprehension of cognition. How, then, can [the reason] be unestablished (*asiddha*)?
Nor is there the fault of being "doubtfully unestablished" (*saṃdigdhāsiddhatā*).

For indeed, even by the opponent who maintains the existence of external objects, it is admitted that whatever constitutes the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of the cognition is itself the [cognition] of the object.

By this, the objection regarding the fault of being unestablished—which was raised by analyzing "single apprehension" (*ekopalambha*) as "the apprehension of one thing alone"—should be seen as refuted precisely because that [opponent's] position is not accepted.

Furthermore, the moments of consciousness existing in the mental continua of others are not determined by the mind of the Blessed Buddha, because that Blessed One, through the removal of all obscurations, is free from the stain of subject and object.
As it has been said: "For him there is no object to be grasped, nor is there grasping by him; he is empty even of being graspable by another cognition."
However, the unimpaired performance [of his activity] occurs through mere sovereignty.
As it will be stated: "The welfare of others proceeds constantly and without effort, being established by former vows; because he accomplishes all aims, he is accepted as omniscient.
Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

Now, one might object: "Did not the Master Dharmakīrti, by presenting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the passage, 'If it is argued that the object is perceived first because it is the cause of cognition, and the awareness [of it] afterwards,' show here that the word *saha* (together) has the meaning of 'simultaneity' and not the meaning of 'non-difference'? For when simultaneity is intended, it is appropriate for the opponent to point out a difference in time, but not when there is non-difference. This is not so.

Since a difference in time is necessarily pervaded by a difference in substance, the demonstration of a difference in time is all the more appropriate for establishing multiplicity in perception, because the pervaded does not deviate from the pervader.

Nor is the reason inconclusive due to the mind cognizable by a Buddha; for in that case, there is no restriction to a single perception, since that mind is experienced individually by each [of those Buddhas].
For this very reason, the investigation into the reversal of the mind applies to them as well, because each experiences only its own self.

Alternatively, let it be that there is a cognition of another's mind by the Blessed One’s mind; even so, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā), because [the possibility of such cognition] has been necessarily excluded.

For that [possibility] has been necessarily excluded in cases where a mutual difference in perception is even possible; however, it is not the case that there is a difference in the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of perceptions through a distinction in their temporal continuum.
Therefore, this is the meaning: that for which there is apprehension is only the apprehension of that [object] itself, and not anything else.
Furthermore, the apprehension of the Blessed One’s cognition is not exclusively the apprehension of a mind belonging to another continuum;

nor is the apprehension of a mind belonging to another continuum exclusively the apprehension of the Blessed One’s cognition, for there is also something else, since one's own mind is also experienced as distinct.
For this very reason, there is no deviation [of the reason] with respect to color-form (rūpa) and light;

for light is perceived even by itself, and color-form is also perceived by certain specific living beings even when devoid of light. Therefore, since its presence in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is impossible, the logical reason (hetu) is not inconclusive (anaikāntika).
It might be argued: "Even if existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not certain, it is at least doubtful.
Consequently, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its exclusion from the counter-example is itself doubtful.

For instance, since the relationship between object and subject is fixed, the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) is possible even otherwise; because the very nature of cognition is that of a grasper, since it has the property of grasping an object, and the nature of that object is likewise that of being grasped by it; and because these two depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*), they necessarily exist together."

For it is thus: from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), only a cognition whose nature is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object such as blue is produced, not one whose nature is the determination of the eye and so forth;
and furthermore, it is the blue and so forth that are produced in the form being determined by that cognition, not the eye and so forth.
And it has been said:
"There is no grasper other than cognition, apart from the visual objects;
therefore, their simultaneous awareness occurs, not because of the non-difference between the blue object and its cognition."
"The very same causal complex that produces cognition characterized by the object would also produce the illumination [of consciousness] itself,
just as it does the form of the world, whereby there would be simultaneous perception."
Thus [it was said].
To this, he replies with the words "not of the nature of cognition," and so forth:
"If the supreme self is not of the nature of cognition, how [could it be] in the experience of the cognition of blue?"
If there were no identity between those two, then there would be no cognition of the blue form.

For it is not logical that there should be a rule of simultaneous apprehension for a distinct entity without a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is there any such connection here for the cognition of a distinct object.
To explain: if a connection were to exist, it would have to be either identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
First of all, identity (*tādātmya*) is not what the opponent intends here, because that very [identity] is the probandum (*sādhya*).
Nor is it simultaneous perception due to origination from that (*tadutpatti*), because there is no relationship of cause and effect between two things that exist simultaneously,
and because it would follow that the eyes and other [faculties] would also be perceived.

Nor can it be said that the relationship of object and subject exists merely through simultaneity due to the power of a prior causal complex (*sāmagrī*), for this would entail the absurd consequence that the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*)—as well as the eye and other sense organs—are mutually related as object and subject.

Nor is it reasonable to argue that there is no such over-extension because the causal complex produces them in the form of specific objects and subjects; for the very nature of object and subject is what is currently under investigation and is thus unestablished.

Indeed, a relationship of object and subject is logical only once a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established; yet it is precisely that connection which is being examined in the determination of the status of object and subject.

Furthermore, there is no other causal connection (*pratibandha*) apart from identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) by which the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) could be established. Nor is it logical that the relationship of object and subject arises through identity or causality; this has already been examined. Therefore, since there is no simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*) of a distinct entity in any way, how can the reason be said to have a "doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar class" (*saṃdigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika*)?
He states a second proof for the sake of establishing that [cognition] possesses an aspect, beginning with "This cognition," and so forth:
"All this is cognition, and it does not have an external object as its domain;
and cognition [of blue], like the self-cognition of its own nature."

Whatever is a cognition, that does not have an object distinct from its own knowledge, just like self-cognition; and this [cognition] of the form of blue and so forth is a cognition—this is the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (viruddhavyāptopalabdhi).
For cognition is pervaded by having no object other than itself, which is the opposite of having an external object as its domain.

Establishing that very pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "Primarily it does not grasp the object," and so forth. "Primarily it does not grasp the object because it is established in its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because it is devoid of the coloring (*uparāga*) of the object's form; nor [does it grasp it] figuratively."
This is the proof directed against those who maintain that some form of cognition exists which resembles pure crystal and is unmarked by the forms of objects.

Because all phenomena are devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*), in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) there is no grasping of anything by anything; rather, consciousness, appearing in such a way through its nature as luminosity (*prakāśarūpatā*), is said to be the grasper of itself.

Furthermore, it is not logical for cognition to be the primary grasper of an object, because all entities are established within their own respective intrinsic natures (*svasvabhāva*); for that which is the nature of one thing is not also the nature of another.

It might be argued: "Indeed, the self-awareness of cognition is not intended to be exactly like that of an object. Rather, the 'cognizedness' of an object consists simply in its being the producer of a cognition that bears its own image. Consequently, if primary awareness were adduced as the reason [for the existence of the object], then the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*). Even if, on the other hand, it is based merely on the commonality of being denotable by the word 'awareness' in some sense, even so, the desired conclusion is not established from such a [reason]. For the possession of horns is not established for a *gavaya* and the like simply because of the similarity of the word 'cow' (*go*)."

Now, if—on the basis of the blue and other forms established within cognition as the subjects (*dharmin*)—both types of reasons are intended in the position of *sākāra*-jñāna, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
As it has been said:
"In the position of *sākāra*-jñāna, that which appears [within cognition] is the object of awareness."
And if its non-difference were what was to be established, it would result in proving what is already proven.

Anticipating this entire objection from the Venerable Śubhagupta, [the author] says: "By means of the coloring of the object's form," and so forth. "The coloring of the object's form" (*arthākāroparāga*) refers to that which is both the form of the object—meaning similar to the object—and the coloring, which is to say, the manifestation.

This [statement], being a twofold proof directed against the proponent of formless cognition (*nirākāravādin*), does not involve proving what is already established, nor is there a perception of anything else through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because the basis for such a designation is absent.

[571] Thus far, it has been established that cognition without an appearance does not cognize an external object. Now, establishing the second position—that it is with an appearance—he says: "Let it be then," and so forth.
"Let it be then that cognition, possessing similarity [to its object], is the cognizer of the external."
Since that too is entirely untenable, the status of being an experiencer is not logical.
For a real form is not tenable, because the determination of an object would have to depend upon it;
nor could an object be cognized by means of a false form, since such a form exists even in erroneous cognition.
If it is asked how there can be falsity for those [cognitions] possessing aspects (*sākāra*), he says "from cognition," and so forth:
"Because they are not distinct from cognition, there would be no multiplicity of aspects;
and consequently, by the force of that [unity], the establishment of the awareness of objects does not exist."
Since it is not distinct from its aspects, there would either be multiplicity in the cognition;
otherwise, how could the unity of these two be conceived?

In the perception of a variegated carpet, because the forms are not distinct from a single cognition, they cannot possess multiplicity, just like the nature of the cognition itself. Likewise, because the cognition is not distinct from the forms, it too would result in being manifold.

However, those who maintain that even cognitions of the same kind arise simultaneously in variegated carpets and the like as many as the number of forms—just like heterogeneous cognitions of form, sound, and so forth—[are the ones being addressed].
Furthermore, in that case, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Just as many forms such as blue and so forth are perceived in a multicolored carpet, so too, even in a single form such as white, there are many forms consisting of its near, middle, and far parts; thus, the cognition regarding that [white object] would also consist of multiple natures, and consequently, it would follow that it is not unitary in nature.
If you say, "This is indeed accepted," then it must now be stated: what is this single cognition?
If you say it is that which has partless atoms as its object, [we reply:]...
This is contrary to experience;
for nowhere is a partless atom-like form observed appearing in cognition,
nor is it logical that immaterial things should have a spatial arrangement characterized by priority and posteriority.
By what means could the postulation of multiple cognitions be valid for the sake of establishing its reality?

If the appearance of spatial extension were unreal, how could the forms (ākāras) be real? For no form of the cognition of blue or other colors is perceived apart from the appearance of blue and so forth situated in spatial extension.
Therefore, the postulation of multiple cognitions is indeed futile.

He states another refutation with the words "sarvātmanā" and so forth: "If there were identity in every respect, then knowledge would possess the nature of non-knowledge and the like; if there were similarity in some part, then everything would be a cognizer of everything."
Ignorance is the state of being insentient.
By the word "etcetera," [qualities such as] the absence of attachment, the absence of aversion, and so forth are included.
Relying on this third alternative position—that there is an appearance of something else—he says, "even having another form," and so forth:
"How can even a cognition that has another form be the cognizer of something else?
Everything would then be cognizable by everything, and the cause would not be the restrictor."

Furthermore, it might be argued that "whatever cognition is produced by a particular [cause], that [cognition] alone would be its perceiver; therefore, not everything will be perceivable by everyone. To this, he says: "And the cause is not the restrictor," because it would follow that even the eyes and other sense organs would be objects of perception—this is the intended meaning.
With the words "Just as," etc., he anticipates the rebuttal of the Venerable Śubhagupta:
"Just as, according to you, cognition is in reality formless (*nirākāra*) and yet perceives unreal forms,
so too would it perceive everything that is real."

For he said: "Just as for you Vijñānavādins, consciousness is held to be ultimately formless—according to the statement that 'cognition is like the purity of the elements, gold, or space'—and yet it perceives that form; so too is the external object."
To this, he says: "It is unique," and so forth.
This very nature of cognition belongs exclusively to the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*); therefore, for others, that [cognition] is not primary in any way whatsoever.
Based on their dependence upon a single causal complex, as well as the relationship of cause and effect and so forth,
the perception of an existing entity may indeed be called figurative.
But for an entity that is formless, there can be no dependence upon a single causal complex;
nor is there anything else [to serve as its object], and thus it has not even a figurative cognition of itself.
For that which is unreal cannot have primary awareness (*mukhyasaṃvedana*).

To explain: that very nature of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) which is luminous by essence, unique, the locus of the "I"-conception (*ahaṅkāra*), and which manifests in the form of pleasure and so forth—that alone is their primary awareness.
Therefore, it is not logical for other unreal forms, distinct from the nature of cognition, to have that as their primary awareness.
This is precisely because those [entities] do not exist;
nor is it figurative, because there is an absence of any basis for metaphorical application (*upacāra*).

For instance, dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*) constitutes the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), similarity (*sārūpya*) would be included as the grounds for such metaphorical application.
And all this does not exist for that which is non-existent;
nor is there any other basis for metaphorical designation.
It is simply that, through the power of ignorance, a deluded cognition arises which, though having no object, displays the appearance of what is non-existent.

If it is argued that "that very error will then be the basis for the metaphorical designation even when there is no cognition of a non-existent aspect," he says in response: "Or rather," and so forth.
Or rather, it is designated as "it cognizes an unreal aspect."
For one does not know it as reality through delusion, since that [delusion] is devoid of an object.
If you also claim that consciousness is the cognizer of such [an object] due to error, then it is evident that your [consciousness] is devoid of an object.
The word "that" refers to the cognition described as having non-existent forms as its object;
for, in ultimate reality, there exists no cognizable thing with a non-existent form, because if it were admitted to be cognizable by way of affirmation, it would follow that it must be existent.
Furthermore, he himself said:
"That [cognition] is both with form and without form, simultaneous yet produced from what is not simultaneous";
why, then, does reflection not proceed even regarding cognition that is Buddhist?
Thus:

just as the consideration is made that it is not logical for an object to be apprehended by a cognition possessing a form (sākāra) and so forth, why is such a consideration not likewise made regarding the apprehension of an object by the knowledge of the Blessed One? To this he says "sākāram" and so on:
"Whether possessing a form or being formless, [cognition] is not logically the perceiver of anything else."
Thus, even regarding Buddhist consciousness, such reflection does not proceed.
For the Blessed One’s gnosis is not held to be a grasper of that [object], such that one would need to engage in this kind of analysis here;
rather, because he is free from all obscurations, it is accepted that the conceptual construction of grasped and grasper does not exist for him.

Now, one might object: "Even if there is no external object to be grasped, nevertheless, another mind certainly exists within a different continuum; why then should that not be the object of the Blessed One’s cognition? To this, he says: "In the perception of another's passion and so forth...
