"In the perception of another's passion and so forth, because of the arising of a similarity [to it], the existence of obscuration follows according to the view of those who maintain direct apprehension (*aupalambhika*)."

For the experience of passion and so forth existing in another continuum can only be justified by way of similarity (*sārūpya*) and not otherwise, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Consequently, if there were similarity in every respect, then even the Blessed One’s cognition would be impassioned;
this being the case, the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) would remain unabandoned, which results in the presence of an obstruction.

They are called "those who hold to apprehension" (*aupalambhika*) because they persist through apprehension; this refers to their view or doctrine. Alternatively, the meaning is: when the Blessed One’s vision—his cognition—is accepted as being characterized by apprehension (*aupalambhika*).

Even if there were partial conformity (*sārūpya*), nevertheless, because the two forms have not been abandoned, the existence of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) follows, since it is stained by the form of the apprehended object. For it is illogical for a single [cognition] to possess two real forms; therefore, it must necessarily be established as being erroneous.
Furthermore, because the seed of delusion—which is not a fault and is minimal—has not been abandoned, the Blessed One would remain one whose obscurations have not been eliminated.
If he knows nothing at all, how then could he be omniscient? To this he says: "Like the wish-fulfilling tree," and so forth.
Like the wish-fulfilling tree, the Sage is not moved by the winds of any conceptual constructions.
Even when unmoving, it indeed brings about the fulfillment of the aims of the world.
Therefore, they say that even though he is not seen, the Jina is omniscient in every respect,
because the performance of all the tasks of an omniscient one occurs effortlessly and without remainder.
Regarding the term "non-perception" (*adarśana*): he is called "non-perceiving" because he has no perception or apprehension [of objects].

Because, through the power of his previous vows, he spontaneously accomplishes the welfare of the entire world according to their capacities—like a wish-fulfilling gem—they call him "omniscient," not by virtue of the power of apprehension.
Because it is impossible to perceive any other intrinsic nature in any way whatsoever.
Having thus stated the means of valid cognition that negates external objects, [the author] says "dhiyaḥ" and so forth, in order to address the proof for them as formulated by others:
"If the cognition possesses a form such as white and so on, how can that [external object] be its experience?
If the cognition possesses a form such as white and so on, what is the means of valid cognition for the external object?"
For the establishment of external objects must occur either through perception or through inference, since any other existing means of valid cognition is included within these two.

In that regard, it cannot first be established through perception; for the apprehension of an object by a cognition regarded as perceptual would have to occur either by means of a formless cognition or by means of one with a form.
It cannot be by means of a formless cognition, because there would be no basis for the necessary proximity [between the cognition and the object].

If cognition were to possess forms such as black and so forth, then because only a single form—such as blue—residing within the cognition is perceived, the external object would necessarily be indirect (*parokṣa*) and not perceptual (*pratyakṣa*).
For two blues are never experienced: one as a reflection in the cognition and another as its projector. Thus, in this way, [the existence of an external object] is not established through perception.

If it is argued that its establishment must therefore be through inference (*anumāna*), on this point the Venerable Śubhagupta offers the following proof: "Whatever is a form of cognition (*jñānākāra*), provided it is reliable (*saṃvāditva*), is produced by another object of that same kind; for example, the apprehending form [of a cognition]. And this form of cognition—the specific appearance of blue and so forth for one whose sense faculties are unimpaired—is reliable. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
This very point is raised as a doubt in the passage beginning with "nīlādi" (blue, etc.):
The appearance of blue and so forth is established as being of the nature of cognition because it is reliable;
its birth from a cause of a similar kind is like that of [other] cognitions.
Regarding the phrase "by way of correspondence" (*saṃvāditvena*):
this is an instrumental case used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*).
By means of that nature of the form of cognition which is characterized by correspondence—and acting as the cause—the birth of the form of cognition from a source of a similar kind is established.
The meaning is: "like cognition," that is, like the form of the apprehending subject.
With the words beginning "bāhyārtha," he states the refutation: "If that which is the attainment of an external object, or its capacity for such attainment,
is intended by 'conformity' (saṃvāditva), then that is unestablished for one who denies the existence of external objects."
If causal efficacy is intended as the criterion for being a cause in a cognition,
then even in the case of a cognition that lacks a real objective basis, such correspondence can still be established.

In this regard, if "conformity" (saṃvāditva)—meaning either the attainment of an external object or the capacity of that means of valid cognition—is intended as a qualification of the reason (*hetu*), then it is unestablished for the proponent of Cognition-Only (*vijñaptimātravādin*) who denies external objects; thus, the reason is "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*). Alternatively, if "conformity" is held to mean being the cause of a cognition that manifests the desired purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then, because no subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) has been shown against the contrary case, the exclusion from the dissimilar instances is doubtful; thus, the reason is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), since even a cognition devoid of an objective basis (*nirālamba*) is not incompatible with such conformity.
To establish precisely this lack of contradiction,
he says: "Just as the capacity of external water and so forth is held to be restricted,
so too in cognitions these [restrictions] exist, because they are not distinct from consciousness."
Even though this [object] is common to both [perception and inference], it is clear through the appearance of inference;
for the form of fire and so forth is not clearly manifest in that [inference].

Furthermore, even though the appearance of inferential cognition lacks an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*), it possesses correspondence (*saṃvāditva*). Thus, because the existence of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is certain, the reason—such as "being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatva*)—is clearly an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) that is over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*). It might be argued that the lack of an objective basis for inferential conceptualization is unestablished (*asiddha*); to this he says: "Clearly [the cognition] of fire, etc. and so forth. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is devoid of the form of a thing does not have that thing as its object, just as a cognition of color (*rūpa-jñāna*) does not have sound as its object; and inference, as a means of valid cognition, is devoid of external form. This is the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).

Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*). For instance, that distinct form which belongs to fire and the like is not identical to the form of inferential cognition, because the latter is indistinct. Otherwise, just as the established form—distinguished by its specific nature such as being produced from grass or leaves—appears in perceptual cognition, it would likewise appear in inferential cognition. However, in inference, external objects and the like do not appear by abandoning their established forms; rather, they appear only in the form of a general characteristic (*sāmānyarūpa*) that conforms to the indicator (*gamaka*).
Furthermore, it has already been established that it is not logical for a single entity to possess two mutually contradictory aspects consisting of both the universal and the particular.
Nor is the reason contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
With the words "from the reasons such as being an object of cognition" (*prameyatvādihetubhyaḥ*), he raises the objections of Uddyotakara;
from the reasons such as being an object of cognition, [it follows that] there is a mind belonging to another continuum.
If [the object] appears as spatially distinct from the internal experience, [then it is external].

He said: That which appears as spatially distinct, such as blue and so forth, is distinct from internal experience because it is an object of cognition (*prameya*), because it is impermanent (*anitya*), because it is an effect (*kārya*), because it is a cognition (*pratyaya*), and because it possesses a cause (*hetumat*), just like the mind of another continuum (*santānāntara*).
Even here, there is no deviation in the nature of this consciousness;
for it is [non-deviant] despite being observed by those with unsteady eyes through such things as double moons.
"In this case as well" means in all the reasons;
"erroneousness" means being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*).

Even in internal experience, because properties such as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) exist, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) due to things like the double moon appearing in the cognition of one with cataracts and the like.

Indeed, the "being an object of cognition" of the double moon and so forth should be understood as their being the objects of a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpakajñāna*) that apprehends them as "double moon" and so on;
for, with respect to the cognition in which they appear, there is no apprehension of those [external] objects.
As it has been said: "That which is the realization of the object through [the removal of] hair and so forth is liberation."
With the words "Otherwise," etc., he raises the objection regarding the lack of proof for the object of deviation according to the view of Kumārila:
"If it is argued here that the external object itself is what is cognized,
then surely this appearing form is not of the nature of that object."
And because it appears in this manner, it is cognized by consciousness;
however, the intrinsic nature of an external object does not appear there in such a way.
How indeed can that which is not appearing be an object of cognition? Furthermore, to claim that one cognizes it in another way is mutually contradictory.
For this very reason, it is impossible to prove that cognitions are self-cognizable,
because we observe that there is an awareness of the manifestation as being identical with the self.
Therefore, this deluded cognition does not conceptualize an object at all;
rather, it conceives of what is otherwise as being so, and thereby perceives itself [as such].

For he (the opponent) says: "In this case, in the cognition of a yellow double moon and so forth, it is precisely the external object, such as a conch-shell, which is presented as the locus of error that is apprehended in the form of yellow and so on;
therefore, the error is not established.
To this, [the author] replies with the words "ākāra" and so forth.
This is the summary of the meaning here: it is logical that whatever form appears in a cognition is precisely what is cognized by it; otherwise, every cognition would have everything as its object.
Being manifest is pervaded by being cognizable.

Now, in a cognition having a yellow form, a white form does not appear, because the [white form], which is intended to be seen, is not perceived. Thus, when the pervader—manifestness—is absent, the pervaded—cognizability—is also absent.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever form does not appear in a cognition is not cognized by it, just as color does not appear in the cognition of sound; and when a yellow form is known, the white form of a conch shell does not appear. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

By the phrase "and [the cognition] knows that," he points out a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*); for this very reason, through a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), he establishes self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).
By this, that which is asserted by the followers of Jaimini—that "our cognition is imperceptible and formless"—is refuted.

The conclusion is expressed by the words "Therefore" and so forth. The connection is as follows: while it is indeed conceptualizing, it does not conceptualize an object as being otherwise than it actually is. And by this, he refutes what was stated by Kumārila.
With the words "Now," and so forth, [the author] states the very chain of arguments of Kumārila:
"Now, that which is the apprehender of color is distinct from that which is apprehended by it,
because it is not cognized when that [object] is cognized, just like the apprehender of taste and so forth."
For when that [object] is being reflected upon as distinct from its grasper,
it is necessarily not so reflected upon, just like the grasper of taste and the like.
The two must be established as mutually distinct, like taste and other [sensory qualities], or else,
due to the lack of cognition of their identity, they would be like the cognitions of different mental continua.
Cognition does not apprehend its own part, because it is a cognition, just like its own causal capacity;
furthermore, there is a refutation of its being an object of apprehension, for latent impressions are devoid of both [subject and object].
Caitra’s cognition, being a cognition, cannot be the cognizer of the apprehended portion of a cognition arising from that [same source],
just as it is not the cognizer of a cognition arising in another body.

This cognition which apprehends form is distinct from that form which it apprehends, because while that form is being cognized, this [cognition] is not cognized, just like the apprehender of taste and so forth.

Alternatively, the apprehended object, such as form, is distinct from its own apprehender, since it is not perceived by one who perceives that apprehender, just like the apprehender of taste and so forth.
Or else, the dyad consisting of the form and its apprehender are mutually distinct, because when one is perceived, the other is not perceived, just as in the case of taste and form.
Alternatively, [it does not perceive itself] because it is not known as a unity, like the mind of another continuum;
or else, cognition does not grasp its own part because it has arisen from cognition,
and the power of cognition is what is called "latency" (*vāsanā*).
In this same manner, the negation of the cognizability of cognition must also be established, as follows: "A portion of cognition is not cognizable by cognition, because it has arisen from cognition.

To the question, "How is the example, which possesses the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), established in these two preceding applications? he says: "For the latent impression (vāsanā) is devoid of the dyad.
By the dyad, that is, by the state of being the grasped and the grasper.

Alternatively, there is another formal argument: this [subject’s] cognition does not apprehend that portion of the cognition produced from Caitra’s cognition, because it is a cognition, just like the cognition arising in the bodies of others, such as Maitra, with respect to that portion of the cognition produced from Caitra’s cognition.
He states the refutation with the words "because of non-distinct perception" and so forth:
because of the non-distinct perception previously established here,
there is no proof [of the opponent's position] regarding the range of arguments ending with the lack of recognition of a single form.
Regarding the phrase "because they are not perceived separately":
since blue and the cognition thereof are necessarily perceived together,

and because it is established— through the proof of self-awareness— that for one whose perception is not directly perceived, the seeing of an object cannot be established, the reasons [adduced by the opponent], up to and including the lack of knowledge of identity due to the non-difference between blue and its cognition, are therefore unproven.
With the words "sabāhir" and so forth, the opponent sets forth his proof: "Indeed,
it is stated by the phrase 'connected with an external location' that the cognition of the form of the apprehended object occurs without the experience of an apprehending subject."

By this passage—"The external object possesses a form; it is perceived directly as connected with an external location"—the commentator Śabara has demonstrated that the cognition of the apprehended object occurs even without the experience of the apprehending subject.
Consequently, the principle "because there is no cognition of [the subject] within the cognition [of the object]" is established.
To the question, "How are the second and subsequent reasons established? he says: "I do not remember," and so forth:
"And I do not remember that any object was apprehended by me at that time;
[rather,] they remember the arising of the apprehender as devoid of the form of the apprehended."
Therefore, if there were non-difference [between the object and the cognition], there would be recollection even of the apprehended object;
however, it is only when there is the existence of the recollection of the apprehending subject that this [object] is grasped therein.
Thus, through positive and negative concomitance, the distinctness of these two is established;
and in this way, these reasons are also well-established in the subject of the thesis.

Even when there is recollection of the apprehended object (*grāhya*), a recollection of the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) is observed. If, moreover, the apprehended were absolutely non-different from that apprehending subject, then there would also be a recollection of the apprehended, just as there is of the apprehender; yet such is not the case. Therefore, because they possess distinct fates (*yogakṣema*), the apprehended and the apprehender are different. It might be argued: "A recollection of the apprehended indeed occurs. To this he says: "In the presence of the recollection of the apprehender," and so forth.
"Therein" means at the time when the recollection of the apprehender exists.

The particle *eva*—meaning "only"—is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*) to indicate that it is precisely this apprehender (*grāhaka*) that is apprehended, and not the apprehended object (*grāhya*).
This is because of the presence and absence of the recollection of the apprehended and the apprehender respectively.
For instance, even when there is the presence of the recollection of the apprehender, there is an absence of the memory of the apprehended.
He refutes [this] with the words beginning "of one for whom apprehension is unestablished": "For one for whom apprehension is unestablished, the cognition of an object is not established;
therefore, there is no awareness of the apprehended object apart from the experience of the apprehender."
He states that the claim "this connection with an external object is perceived through direct perception" is inconclusive, beginning with the words "avasthā" and so forth:
"Just as yellow and other colors are seen by those with diseased eyes, so too is [the object] perceived;
yet, while it is cognizable as distinct from the apprehending portion, another [external object] is not so."
The word *niṣkṛṣṭam* (extracted) marks the pause here.

The word *tathā* (likewise) means that just as yellow and so forth—which are considered real—are clearly perceived as connected with external space, so too [the object] perceived by one whose eyes are afflicted by jaundice (*kāmalā*) and the like should be observed in the same way.
If it is indeed so observed, what follows? He says: "And it is not [perceived] as distinct from the apprehending portion" (*grāhakāṃśāc ca saṃvedyaṃ na*); this marks the pause.
Regarding the phrase "from the aspect of the grasper" (grāhakāṃśāt),
the word "extracted" (niṣkṛṣṭam) is to be supplied.
The ellipsis is to be completed as "it does not become an object of cognition" (saṃvedyaṃ na).

Therefore, this is the meaning: that yellow and so forth, perceived by those with ophthalmia and the like, cannot be separately cognized as extracted from the aspect of the apprehender; yet it is nevertheless perceived as connected with external space. Consequently, this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Likewise, "the other"—that is, even that which is regarded as real, such as yellow and so forth—is similar in both cases by virtue of this mere appearance of being distinct and clear. Thus he establishes the similarity between the two.
"I do not remember anyone [in particular]," he said; thus [the author] states "unperceived" and so forth.
That memory concerns an external form whose specific details were not perceived.
However, it does not concern a form distinguished from everything else, because repetition and the other necessary conditions for such a memory are impossible in that case.
By this, he states that when there is recollection of the apprehender (*grāhaka*), the non-recollection of the apprehended (*grāhya*) is unestablished.
This might be argued: if that recollection pertains to the apprehended, why is it such that its specific features (*viśeṣa*) are not characterized?
For, just as that apprehended object is distinct from everything—both homogeneous and heterogeneous—it should be recollected in exactly that same way.

For in this way alone could that [conceptual cognition] have that [particular] as its object; otherwise, how could it—failing to grasp its distinction from others—have that as its object? For this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus he says "from all," and so forth.
This is what is meant:
conceptual cognition does not possess the capacity to grasp an object exactly as it exists, because its domain consists of non-entities (*avastu*).

Merely by the force of experiencing such objects as they are, wherever there exist causes for determination such as desire and so forth, the mnemonic cognition (*smārta-pratyaya*) which determines that [object's] form is entirely without an object (*nirviṣaya*).

In ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), because it proceeds by determining what is not an object to be an object within its own appearance, every [cognition] arises as nothing but an error (*bhrānta*).
However, the establishment of its object occurs through the power of that determination, not in ultimate reality.

Furthermore, the determination of the apprehended object does not exist even in the case of memory; it is merely that, due to the absence of causes such as the proficiency of prior practice and the degree of proximity, its specific features remain unperceived, whereby it is distinguished from other instances of recollection.
It might be asked: "How is it determined that there is a determination of the apprehended object (*grāhyādhyavasāya*) here in memory? To this he says, "Apprehended," and so forth:
"Only when [the object] has been apprehended does such recollection occur, and not otherwise;
nor is recollection experienced as being like a pure crystal."

The inconclusiveness of the reason is evident even in the case of the latter two [examples] due to cognitions such as that of a conch-shell appearing yellow; this same direction applies to other proofs as well.

For if that memory did not determine even the object of apprehension when its specific qualities are unobserved, then one would not proceed even toward a reflective awareness of the object in a general form, such as "something was apprehended. Nor is the subject remembered alone, with a form unstained by the forms of the objects of apprehension and resembling a pure crystal, such that it could be said: "They remember the arising of the subject as devoid of the form of the object."

Therefore, the non-remembrance of that [object] at the time of its remembrance [of the cognition] is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, regarding these two latter reasons—"because it arises from a cognition" and "because it is a cognition"—the cognition of a yellow conch and the like, although arisen from a cognition, is a cognizer of its apprehended object (the yellow color, etc.); thus, other [cognitions] are likewise [cognizers of objects]. Consequently, these two reasons are inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).

Moreover, it has been established that the cognition of a yellow conch and the like is without an external objective support (*nirālambana*); for this very reason, since there is an awareness of the form of yellow and so forth residing within oneself, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is established—this too has been demonstrated.

"This is the direction" means that this is the general line of refutation to be applied elsewhere as well, when an opponent has put forward an argument to establish external objects. As it was said by the opponent: "How is non-duality intended to be proven? Is it because of the non-existence of the appearing forms such as blue and so forth, and of the nature of cognition which is established through experience? How can this [position] be maintained? For if that were the case, it would result in the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of everything."

To this it must be said: there is not a total non-existence [of all things], because external objects such as earth and so forth, which are distinct from [the cognition] itself, do exist by way of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). However, since another mental continuum (*santānāntara*) does not exist in the form of an object of apprehension, cognition is empty of the aspect of the apprehended (*grāhyākāra*) in relation to that [other continuum]. Furthermore, the agency of cognition—which is conceptually constructed in dependence on that [apprehended object] by virtue of the definition "that which cognizes is cognition"—is absent; thus, [cognition] is empty of the aspect of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*). This is not, however, because there is a total non-existence of the specific characteristic of cognition itself in every respect. And so it has been said:
Whatever cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth appears as if external,
there is no truly real object of knowledge existing externally in reality.
And that nature as agent which is attributed to consciousness in dependence upon that [object] is not real; therefore, it is not perceived even in non-dual consciousness.
Thus, by doing so, this reading of the Prajñāpāramitā also becomes well-explained: "Consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness, by virtue of the emptiness of characteristics."

Thus, having established the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the probandum in the fundamental syllogism beginning with "if there were ignorance," he concludes with the passage beginning "the subject of dispute" (*vivādāspadam*).

The mind, which has entered the field of dispute, is non-dual because of its nature as consciousness (*vijñānatva*); therefore, it is devoid of both the state of being an object of cognition and that of being an agent, just like a reflection.

By this specific qualification of the subject of the dispute (*vivādāspada*), he says the following: here, the specific instance (*viśeṣa*) of consciousness with healthy eyes and so forth is the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*), not every [consciousness]; however, "because it is consciousness" (*vijñānatvāt*) is the reason (*hetu*). Therefore, the reason does not suffer from the fallacy of being a mere part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).
The qualification "non-dual" (*advaya*) is used because of the absence of the state of being both object and agent (*vedyakartṛtva*).
The meaning is that "non-dual" is intended by way of the lack of the duality of object and agent, but not because of total non-existence.
Regarding the phrase "like a reflection" (*pratibimbavat*):

because the object is metaphorically attributed to the subject (*viṣayiṇi*), the cognition of the reflection is expressed by the word "reflection. Alternatively, the suffix *-vati* should be understood as following a locative case ending; thus, by implication, it is the cognition itself that is obtained as the locus (*ādheyatayā*).
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is the very nature (*svabhāva*)—not the state of being a knower—that is thus indicated by the exclusion of other distinctions;
nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
With the words "But surely," and so forth, [the author] points out that the other example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
For surely, even in the case of a reflection, cognition is held to have an objective support (*sālambana*),
because one perceives one's own face and so on in that manner when the visual rays are turned back.

Because the rays of the eyes, being reflected by the surface of a mirror or similar object, turn back and come into contact with one's own face and so forth, they consequently become the cause for the perception of the face and such in that manner.
Therefore, it is one's own face and so on that is seen in the form of being inside the mirror and so forth.
Consequently, it is not established that the cognition of a reflection is devoid of the duality of the apprehended and the apprehender.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "not by way of facing [it]," and so forth:
"It is not seen as facing [it], for one's own face and the like are not perceived in that manner;
moreover, because of the perception of differences in size, location, and so on, it is like any other external object."

"There is no such perception of one's own face and so forth" means that there is no such seeing of one's own face and so forth because it is not perceived directly [as it truly is], and because it is seen with differences in location, size, color, and so on; this is the connection [of the sentence]. "Like other objects" [is the meaning of the compound].

It is like the objects such as sound and so forth. What is meant is this: that cognition which perceives the face and other such things would have to grasp them exactly as they are situated; for it is not logical that a cognition having one form should have something else as its object, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). For instance, one standing facing south and looking into the surface of a mirror sees one's own face facing north.

Likewise, even though one's own face is large, a small reflection of it is perceived on the surface of a very small mirror; furthermore, that reflection appears as if connected to the mirror's surface and as if having entered deep below it, yet the mirror's surface is not so thick, nor is the face or other features actually connected to it. Similarly, in a lake of clear water, the reflections of trees and mountains standing on the bank are perceived with their branches and peaks turned downwards, yet they do not exist in such a state.
Therefore, the cognition of a reflection is not a grasper of one's own face and so forth, because it appears as something distinct from that [face], just like the cognition of a word.
The Venerable Śubhagupta, however, said:
"When consciousness-only is to be established, whatever proof such as 'being cognition' is adduced,
all of it is called *śeṣavat* (analogical) because it does not exclude heterogeneous instances."
To this he replies with the words "the nature of consciousness" and so forth:
"The nature of consciousness is luminosity, and that has no basis in the apprehended object;
because [luminosity] is incompatible with the absence of manifestation and the like, its pervasion [of consciousness] is thereby ascertained."

In the immediately preceding cognition, which possesses the capacity [for apprehension], we do not accept that the status of being an object resides in the apprehended aspect (grāhyāṃśa) as something ultimately real; by this, [the cognition] is established as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
The proof of representation-only has been clarified by the wise;
we have followed its direction in this determination of the ultimate truth.

For the pervasion has already been established by the statement beginning with "firstly, [the cognition] is without appearance" and "with appearance," and thus the reason is not inconclusive. It was stated by the venerable teacher Dignāga for the purpose of defining the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
"That which is an internal form of the object of knowledge appears as if it were external."
That object [is established] because it consists of the nature of cognition and also because it is the condition for that [cognition].

Thus, by this [statement], the determination of the object within the apprehended portion has been established. Furthermore, it was said: "Alternatively, because it deposits a capacity, even that appearance of the object produces a capacity residing in consciousness for the sake of generating an effect corresponding to itself; thus there is no contradiction."

By this, its causality is established, because that appearance bestows a power which serves as the cause for the production of an effect corresponding to itself in the immediately subsequent cognition.
On this point, a refutation was stated by that same Venerable One:
"Even if the objective aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*) were the instrument (*karaṇa*) of sensory consciousness..."
Because it does not appear as that [object], the object is not its [direct] domain in the same way as the sense organ is.
By such [words] as these.
Here [the author] says "in the capacity," etc.
In the phrase "in the capacity" (*śaktau*) and "in the immediately following cognition" (*anantare jñāne*), the two locative cases are in different grammatical coordination (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "knowledge in the immediate [condition]":

the power residing in the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), which is called the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and is capable of producing the cognition of such-and-such an object-appearance, is not accepted as being ultimately real.

Since it has been demonstrated in detail by the Master that it is not tenable for something distinct from atoms and so forth to serve as an objective support (*ālambana*), [the opponent might object]: "If the objective support is denied in every respect, there would be a contradiction with direct experience (*pratītibādhā*); furthermore, since the Sūtra states that there are four conditions—namely, the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), the immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), and the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*)—there would also be a contradiction with what is accepted (*abhyupetabādhā*). To demonstrate the absence of such contradictions, [the Master] explains how the objective condition intended in the Sūtra and in the world is established conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), and not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*).
But from the perspective of ultimate truth, all conditions whatsoever are indeed without objective support.
Thus concludes the examination of external objects.
In order to support the statement that "he is unattached to independent scripture," he says "others," and so forth:
"Others here, however, whose intellects are stained by ignorance, have declared:
'This [scripture] is not tenable as being mind-only, because it is contradicted by [other] scriptures.'"
"Others" refers to the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas).
They say this: "Injunction alone (*codanā*) is the basis for the determination of dharma, adharma, and so forth; it stands as a light for all living beings, like a common eye.
Therefore, that alone must necessarily be resorted to as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by discerning persons seeking dharma, and nothing else, such as the words composed by human beings."
For instance, the speech of a person whose mind is overwhelmed by passion and other afflictions as well as ignorance is not capable of making known an object beyond the senses without error.
Therefore, dharma and so forth are not to be apprehended through such speech.
Nor are they to be apprehended through the direct perception of one with limited vision, because, being beyond the senses, they are absolutely imperceptible.
For it is thus: *dharma* and *adharma* are characterized by the capacity to accomplish desirable and undesirable ends, respectively.
As stated in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*: "That alone which brings about the highest good (*śreyas*) is expressed by the word *dharma*.
How is this understood? When someone performs a sacrifice, people describe him as 'righteous' (*dhārmika*)."
And whoever is the agent of something is designated by that [action], as in "cook" or "reaper.
Therefore, that which unites a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is what is expressed by the word *dharma*.
By this, it is established that *dharma* is the capacity of substances and so forth to accomplish a desired object.
For instance, by the word *yāga* (sacrifice), substances, qualities, and actions—which are specific means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*)—are denoted;
and it has been shown that the application of the term *dharma* occurs with respect to these.

Although those substances and so forth are perceptible in their own nature (*svarūpa*), they are not perceptible as being means to the highest good; and it is in that capacity—that is, as being means to the highest good—that they are intended to be *dharma*, not merely in their own nature.
As it has been said:

"For the welfare of man is indeed human pleasure; that is to be accomplished by means of substances, qualities, and actions characterized by Vedic injunctions (codanā). Therefore, dharma-ness resides in these alone."
Although these are perceptible by the senses, they do not have that [sensory] nature as their intrinsic property;
for their status as the means to the highest good is always understood from the Veda.
"And because it possesses that nature, it is a dharma; therefore, it is not within the range of the sense faculties.
Regarding the phrase "and because it possesses that nature":
In the sense of being the means for achieving the highest good (*śreyas*).
Therefore, it is established that *dharma* is fitness (*yogyatā*).
By contrast with *dharma*, it is clearly understood through implication that *adharma* is likewise fitness for achieving undesirable ends.

Furthermore, one whose vision is limited cannot perceive capacity directly, because it is always to be inferred from its effects. As it has been said: "The capacities of all things are established through the presumption based on their effects."
Otherwise, indeed, the very status of being a person of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) would be lost.
Nor is the perception of a yogi [valid] regarding objects beyond the senses, because it is a form of perception, just like other forms of perception.

Furthermore, inference is not suitable for the comprehension of *dharma* and *adharma*, because an object is determined by inference only when its relationship [with the logical mark] has already been perceived.

Furthermore, because *dharma* is not an existing entity (*atathābhūtatvāt*), analogy (*upamāna*) is also incapable of making *dharma* known; for analogy produces a cognition regarding something not present by means of similarity, as in the case of seeing a *gavaya* which brings about the recollection of a cow; yet, no object similar to *dharma* is possible or perceived.

Nor can there be an inference based on similarity from which its [the Veda's] existence might be conceived; nor is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) capable of bringing about the cognition of dharma and adharma.
For presumptive testimony consists in the postulation of an unseen object when a seen or heard object would otherwise be inexplicable.
Furthermore, no object whatsoever is impossible without *dharma*, such that it would necessitate its postulation.

Even non-existence (*abhāva*), as the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*), is capable of establishing the fact that "it does not exist," but not in the sense of a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

Therefore, if the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) were unable to rescue *dharma* and *adharma* from the jaws of non-existence, they would be swallowed by it; thus, objects such as *dharma* are characterized by injunction, not by the senses and other such means.

For an injunction (*codanā*) is capable of making known objects of such a nature as the past, the present, the future, the subtle, the concealed, and the remote; no other sense organ whatsoever is so capable.
Therefore, an injunction must necessarily be accepted as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And they say that an "injunction" is a sentence that impels one toward action or restrains one from it.
Likewise, "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma" is an instigating [injunction], while "one should not harm living beings" is a prohibitive one.
And as for the means of establishing the authority of that [prohibition], your proposition— that "one should sacrifice" consists of the three realms— is not tenable.
Why? Because of sublation by scripture (*śruti*). That is, because of sublation by the Veda, since [the Veda] reveals the Agnihotra and other rites as being distinct from the mind.
Furthermore, because it exists independently of the mind itself,
the claim that [the world] is "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) is merely an illustration;
likewise, the propositions of momentariness, selflessness, omniscience, dispassion, and so forth, are indeed contradicted as well.
Because it persists by elucidating a meaning that is contrary to that [position].
It might be argued: "All this would be sublated if its validity were established. To this he says: "For that is the authority," and so forth.
For that [Veda] is established as the authority for all, because it is not composed by a human being;
whereas human utterances undergo falsity.
Valid cognition is non-erroneous knowledge; because it is the cause of that [knowledge], the [Veda] is also called valid cognition.
To the question "How so?", he says: "By virtue of not being composed by a person," meaning because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
By this, he establishes that [the Veda] is the cause of non-erroneous knowledge through the absence of the collection of defects such as passion, which are the causes of falsity.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is free from contact with defects that are causes of falsity is a cause of non-erroneous knowledge, just as the eye is when it is not afflicted by defects such as cataracts; and the Veda is free from contact with defects such as passion—which are causes of falsity—because it is authorless (*apauruṣeya*). This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
To ward off the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) by means of a counter-example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), he says: "falsity" (*vaitathyam*).

For by this absence of the probans, he demonstrates the pervasion (vyāpti) of the absence of the probandum. To explain: defects are the causes of falsity; wherever they are present, there alone they bring about their own effect, falsity, and not elsewhere, because an effect cannot exist without its cause.
Alternatively, if it were possible [for them to exist without a cause], it would follow that they are causeless (*ahetukatva*).

Nor is it logical for something to be the effect of another if it arises without that [cause], because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, since the causal relationship between falsity (*mithyātva*) and defects (*doṣa*) is untenable, the consequence of being causeless applies to falsity. This serves as a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary position; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: for whatever is not present where a certain cause is absent, that thing does not arise there—just as smoke, whose cause is non-existent, does not arise.
And since the collection of defects such as falsity, cause, and delusion does not exist in the Śruti, there is a non-perception of the cause [for error].
Demonstrating that [the reason] is not unestablished (asiddha), he says: "The faults exist," and so forth:
"Indeed, it is suspected whether faults exist or do not exist in the case of what is spoken by a person;
but since there is no author for the Veda, for us there is no suspicion of faults whatsoever."

For defects (doṣa) reside in the person, as they are its properties; how then could they exist without their own substratum? Or, if they were to exist [without it], it would follow that they are non-dependent. For this is the nature of that which is dependent: namely, its conformity to its substratum.
And the person, who is the substratum of the defects, is the agent; since he has ceased [from activity] upon hearing the Veda, whence can there be any suspicion of defects?
Those that have perished [are lost]; by this, even the fallacy of being unestablished due to doubt is [refuted].

It might be argued: "How is the non-existence of an agent who is the locus of faults established? To this, he demonstrates that non-existence through the cessation of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that would apprehend such an agent, beginning with the words "The agent, first of all," and so on:
"The agent is not perceived; yet it is claimed that he existed at some time or other.
[This claim] is based on ignorance, for its connection has never been perceived before."
Even though it is devoid of inference, it is postulated that "it exists"; yet scripture (āgama) also does not establish it, for there is no such thing as a created or uncreated [scripture].
Since it is not itself an authoritative means of knowledge, that which is produced by it cannot make [the object] known;
for even the truth of the words of Manu and others is indeed established by that [Veda].
But how could one who is unrelated [to the Veda] and hostile to it be a speaker of truth?
Therefore, for us, there is no tradition regarding an author of the Veda other than [the Veda itself].
If someone resembling the author of the Vedas were seen at present,
then by means of that analogy, there would also be an analogy for the [Vedic] author.
If nothing whatsoever could be established as authoritative without an author of the Veda,
then an author of the Veda would certainly be known through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
Is it not the case that there is nothing in the Veda which cannot be established without that [author],
whereas when he exists, much— such as its authority— is not established?
Because it is inaccessible to the five [means of knowledge], it is understood through non-existence alone;
therefore, its existence is difficult to establish, since it is sublated by the absence of any means of valid cognition.

First of all, an author of the Veda is not established through perception; for it cannot be pointed out by specifying "this is he," because he is not perceived at present. One might instead postulate that "there was an author," but since such a person is unperceived, the implication is that it is claimed he existed at some time without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is he established through inference; thus he says, "one who has never been seen before," and so forth.

The relationship characterized as that between the produced and the producer, which is now asserted by those who revile the Veda with respect to an unseen author, is caused by ignorance, because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes it known.
For no one is able to apprehend a relationship between smoke and an unseen fire.
Therefore, that author is postulated even though he is devoid of inferential support.
Because of the word "api" (also), it is not only lacking in direct perception;
he states the cessation of verbal authority (*śābdapramāṇa*) with the words "āgamo 'pi" and so forth.
Since there is no uncreated [scripture] apart from the Veda, it cannot first be uncreated.

Nor is it something created, because that [created scripture] would itself lack authority. To explain: if it were created, the scripture would either have as its author a person such as Manu who is connected to the Veda, or it would have been composed by someone such as a sage whose goal is not connected to that [Veda]. With reference to the first position, he says: "of the words of Manu and others," and so forth.
"Produced by that alone" means produced by the Veda alone;
by this, he states the absence of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*).
Regarding the second position, he states the fault with the words "but [the Smṛti] is unrelated," meaning it is unrelated to the Veda because it lacks authority therein;
[he further states it is] "composed by another."

The scripture concerning the author of the Veda has an unrelated person as its author; it is a source that purports to establish an author of the Veda. By stating "one who resembles the author of the Veda," and so forth, he asserts the non-existence of such a comparison.

He states the non-existence [of the Veda] through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), saying "not respected by the author of the Veda. Regarding the term "cognized" (*pramita*): it means determined by the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"By that" means by the agent;
"something" [is what is meant].
That which has been cognized;
[the locative] "in this" refers to the agent.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "validity and so forth," the establishment of dharma and other categories is intended.
Regarding the phrase "by non-existence alone":
it is understood that [something] does not exist precisely by means of the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva*).
Because that [object] is the domain of negation;
or rather, it means that it is understood as "it does not exist" by way of its nature as non-existence,
due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Because of the sublation by the absence of means of valid cognition" (pramāṇābhāvabādhanāt):
the absence of means of valid cognition is their cessation;
that is to say, the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa).
Because it is contradicted by that [reasoning], it is established that there is no author of the Veda. //2088//

It might be argued: "If the authority of the Veda is established by first proving its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) in this way, then alas, the authority of the Veda is rendered extrinsic (*parataḥ*). For indeed, the authority of the Veda is not cognized as long as its non-human origin has not been proved. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The non-human origin of the Veda is intended for the purpose of removing non-authority; yet even that [non-human origin], because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), cannot be established by means of proofs (*sādhana*)."

By this he means the following: we do not establish validity (*prāmāṇya*) in a positive form as something unestablished. Rather, what is done is the removal of that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) which has been attributed by the opponent. Once the exception (*apavāda*) is refuted, the general rule (*utsarga*) remains established by itself, unobstructed. Nor is authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) being established, for if it were, it would follow by implication through the means of its proof that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
Rather, because it is a non-entity (avastu) characterized merely by the absence of human authorship (apauruṣeyatā), [it cannot be a cause].
If it is not established [by proof], how then is it established by itself? To this he says: "That which," and so forth.
Whatever argument a logician might state as a proof for its being of human origin, by the refutation of that, the Veda's lack of human authorship is established.

Now, one might object: "Even if the opposing position has been refuted, how can the establishment of one's own position occur for one who does not prove it through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such that the proponents of the Veda would have their purpose fulfilled? To this he says: "For those two positions which are real entities," and so forth. "For when two positions are real entities, like [the doctrines of] Primordial Matter (pradhāna) and atoms (paramāṇu), the non-establishment of either one does not by itself establish the other."
He explains the phrase "like the Pradhāna and the atoms" with the words beginning "of the state of having the Pradhāna as the cause.
Even though the proof for the state of having the Pradhāna as the cause has been refuted,
the thesis— that the world is produced by atoms— is established by means of another reason.

Although the Vaiśeṣika has refuted the proof for the world having the *pradhāna* as its cause as proposed by the Sāṅkhya, nevertheless, the world must still be proven to be produced from atoms by means of another reason; it will be the same here as well.
Regarding this,
it is said: "The means of proof that is stated for the purpose of establishing the position of existence—
when that has been correctly refuted, non-existence itself is established."
Having refuted that which is asserted by others as a proof regarding the two limits— the prior and the posterior— the proponents of the Veda have accomplished their purpose.

The position of existence (*bhāvapakṣa*) is the state of being produced by a person (*pauruṣeyatā*); its cessation is the position of non-existence (*abhāvapakṣa*). Since these two are defined by mutual exclusion, the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other; thus, non-existence is established by itself—this is the meaning. For instance, when Buddhists put forward a proof to establish the two extremes of the Veda—the initial and final limits characterized by origination and destruction—the proponents of the Veda achieve their goal simply by refuting that proof. Through this, the desired conclusion is established: that the Veda is not produced by a person, which is characterized by the absence of those two extremes. Thus, they have accomplished their purpose.

[Objection: Even if that proof [of the Veda's non-eternality] has been refuted, the eternality of the Veda, which consists in its being of the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), must still be established through a different effort. Therefore, how could those who know the Veda be considered to have accomplished their purpose without establishing its eternality? To this he says: "Eternality is the nature of the thing," and so forth. Even for those who do not establish that eternality which is the nature of the thing, its establishment occurs of its own accord once the two types of prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) have been destroyed.
The two opposing positions constitute the proof for the two extremes of the beginning and the end.
He demonstrates how the eternity [of the Veda] is established by itself once the two preceding positions have been refuted, in the passage beginning with "The former limit of the Veda," and so forth:
"The former limit of the Veda is characterized by being of human origin;
the latter is of the nature of destruction. Indeed, the absence of these two is eternity."

It has been stated that because permanence is characterized by the exclusion of both the prior and posterior limits, and because between two things characterized by mutual exclusion, the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the existence of the other.

If this is so, and if its non-existence constitutes eternity, then it follows that eternity would not be a property of the thing itself; to this he says: "That which is not produced at first. That Veda which is not produced at first and never subsequently perishes—let that very [non-perishing] be understood as its eternity, if that is what you maintain.
For permanence is intended here by way of non-origination and non-destruction;
and since these two consist in the nature of non-existence, they do not depend upon their own means of proof.

By this, he demonstrates that for the Veda, which is an existing entity (*vastubhūta*), this property resides in its very nature. Anticipating the opponent’s opportunity to object—namely, that if it is thus an existing entity, then its eternality must be something to be proven—he states "it is to be known" (*jñeya*) and so forth.
"To be known" means it is to be cognized by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is to say, it is something to be established (*sādhya*).
"And those two" refers to non-producedness and non-destruction.
"Its own proof" (svasādhana) means the proof of its own intrinsic nature.

The point is that even for non-existence (*abhāva*), there is no contradiction with its being a real entity (*vastu*); thus, even though eternity (*nityatva*) is characterized by being uncreated and indestructible, it does not follow that it is a non-entity.

Thus, first of all, since the absence of an author in the Veda is established by the exclusion of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the reason—"because it is free from the contact with defects that cause falsity"—is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*); nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is absent in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Thus, the authority of the Veda is established.
Now, he begins a detailed refutation of the two arguments put forward by opponents to prove the non-authority of the Veda.

In this regard, these are the two means of proof: that which is perceptible by the senses and that which follows immediately upon effort are impermanent, just like a jar; and sound is likewise. Thus, when the impermanence of sound is established through the general nature of a reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the impermanence of the Veda is also established; consequently, by implication, its falsity will be proven—just like the words of a human being—this is the intention of the opponent, such as the Buddhist. Here, he demonstrates in detail the sublation of the thesis (*pratijñābādhā*) by means of verbal testimony (*śabda*) and other pramāṇas.
First, he states the sublation by verbal testimony, beginning with the words "the meaning of the Vedic sentence," etc.
For one who asserts, by means of inference, that the meaning of the Vedic statements is false,
his position is overturned by the power of Vedic knowledge.
That which has come from the Veda is "Vaidika," such as [the statement] "Heaven results from the Agnihotra" and so forth.
By its power, the opposing position is set aside, because it is being sublated by it.

As it has been said: "And this [Vedic injunction] does not produce a doubtful cognition as to whether it exists or does not exist; nor does there arise, at another time, in another person, in another place, or in another state, a further uncontradicted cognition that 'this is false.'"

Even that inferential cognition which arises—thinking that because a misconception regarding another object has been seen, a misconception here too is established—is sublated when it is contradicted by this direct perception.
But surely, how can there be the sublation of one by the other when they are of equal strength?
Or, if there is sublation even when they are of equal strength, why would it not then also be sublated by inference? To this he says: "And that is like perception.
Because it is equal to perception, the Vedic [word] is more powerful.
It cannot be sublated by inference in any way whatsoever.

If that is so, how then is inference sublated by it? To this he says "pratyakṣa" and so forth: Since the treatise itself is established as being included within the category of direct perception (pratyakṣa), it is more powerful; thus, it is the sublater of inference.
As it has been said: "The cognition based on the words of the Veda is indeed perception; and inference that contradicts perception does not constitute a valid means of knowledge."
How is it that scripture (*āgama*) is stronger than inference (*anumāna*), such that it is equal to perception (*pratyakṣa*)? To this he says:

"Because it is independent of an example. Because it is independent of an example and because it is free from defects, scripture possesses a lightness (*lāghava*) in its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that inference does not possess.

Therefore, when there may be doubt regarding a matter based on both scripture and inference, a definitive conclusion must be reached by means of scripture alone, because scripture possesses greater authority.
Regarding the phrase "in being a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatve*): it is a locative case indicating the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), expressing consideration for parsimony (*lāghava*).
Such [parsimony] does not belong to inference.
This is because it depends upon examples and because defects exist;
as for the defect, it is due to its being sublated by Vedic knowledge which is equivalent to perception.

[Page 590] Now, one might object: "Only that which is established for both parties can constitute a refutation; however, for a Buddhist, scripture (*āgama*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because of the definitive restriction that there are only two such means of knowledge. Therefore, how can a refutation be effected against a Buddhist by means of the invalidity of scripture, which is unestablished for him? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For me, it is not a means of knowledge," and so forth:
"Even though the Veda makes known its meaning, it cannot be declared by a speaker who speaks falsely out of mere malice, on the grounds that 'for me, it is not a means of knowledge.'"
Nor would there be invalidity due to hatred or lack of consensus;
nor is validity established through pleasure or approval.
Moreover, even those who hate the Veda do not utter anything that constitutes a reason for its lack of authority; if they did, they would not be speakers of truth.
How can those who remain at a distance perceive the cause of falsehood, when it is unknown even to those constantly devoted to the activities of memorizing, studying, and explaining [the scriptures]?
For those who are engaged in a particular matter and whose purpose is bound up with it are authorized to know the merits and defects pertaining thereto.
But as for those wicked haters of Brahman who have been cast far outside the Veda—
how can they speak shamelessly of the merits and defects of the Veda?

He thinks as follows: "The establishment or non-establishment of a thing does not occur through mere desire, such that the authority of scripture (*āgama*) would not be established by mere assertion alone. Rather, that which is established by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established for both parties. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the conviction arising from sentences such as those concerning the *agnihotra* is more firmly grounded; how then can it be said to be non-authoritative?
This [objection] of yours is merely words, devoid of reasoning—this is the summary of the meaning. [The phrase] 'because of being unaccepted'..."
"World-approval" means being authorized by the world;
"those standing at a distance" refers to the Śākyas and others [who stand] apart from the Veda.
Because they are excluded from activities such as the maintenance (*dhāraṇā*) of that [Veda].

Regarding the phrase "those for whom the purpose is bound to it": therein, in the Veda, "bound" means stated; "purpose" refers to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) characterized by sacrifice and the like, which belongs to those [Smṛtis].
"Brahmādviṣaḥ" means those who hate the Vedas; or else, "brahman" refers to the knowledge produced from them. //2111 //2112 //2113 //

Alternatively, even if there were no contradiction by scripture, the meaning of the proposition is nonetheless faulty because it is contradicted by means of valid cognition such as direct perception; demonstrating this, he says "Furthermore," and so forth:
"Moreover, the eternality of sound and its omnipresence are established by auditory recognition; who could determine the opposite?"
By this, he states the sublation by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For indeed, because it is recognized through direct perception as "this is that very same thing" at all times, its permanence is established by the direct perception known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Furthermore, because it is recognized in every location, its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is also established. Who, then, would determine the opposite of permanence and omnipresence? No one at all.
The opposite of permanence and omnipresence is impermanence and non-omnipresence.
Therefore, he concludes:
"Thus, the oneness [of the self] at all times and in all places is established by direct perception and recognition; that [oneness] is the sublater of this [position]."
"At all times" means in the past, future, and present.
"Of this" refers to the misconception.
With the words "of the flame, etc.," he raises the objection that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is fallacious; [the objection being:

"If it is argued that there is recognition even though the flame and so forth are momentary, we say no. For in that case, what is recognized by us is the universal (*sāmānya*), which is indeed eternal."
But in whatever aspect there may be a cognition of difference due to some limiting condition (upādhi),
in that case there is no recognition, as it has been determined by the cognition of difference.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of hair, nails, grass, and so forth that have grown back after being cut, as well as waterfalls and the like; for even in those cases, there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), such as: "These are those very same hairs," "Those are those very same blades of grass," "That is the same stream of the waterfall," and "That is the same water of the river.
This is not so;
for in those instances, it is the universal (*sāmānya*)—such as "fire-ness" (*tejastva*) and so forth—that is recognized.
And since that [object] is indeed accepted as eternal, how can there be any deviation?
As for the individual form (*vyaktirūpa*) which is impermanent, that is not recognized at all through recognition; so how could there be any deviation?
Regarding the phrase "in whichever part":
"At first, it is weak" means by some limiting condition (*upādhi*),
such as its weakness or its upward movement and so forth.
To the question "How is this understood?", he says: "ascertained by a cognition of difference.
The meaning is that this is understood through a cognition of distinction.
He states the sublation by means of inferences in the verse beginning with "deśakālādi" and so forth:
"The cognitions of the individual instances of the word 'cow', though differentiated by place, time, and so on,
are either all identical in their object, or else they do not have various objects as their domain."
Because it arises as "cow," like a presently arisen cognition;
for by the cognition of the word "cow" yesterday, this very word "cow" was manifested.

Just as this [subsequent cognition] cognizes that [object], being produced by the same cause as the first [cognition] which arose with the word "cow" as its object, so too does it [cognize it] like the preceding cognition.
Or both [the universal and its cognition] may have a single object, like a single cognition;
or all cognitions of "cowness," though divided by place, time, and so forth, may [have a single object].
The cognitions produced by each utterance of the word "cow" must have that same word as their cause, because they are cognitions of "cow," just like a single cognition [of a cow];
or else, the word "cow" uttered yesterday exists even today.
"Because it is cognizable by the cognition of the word 'cow', like a sound uttered today;
for the word 'cow' being heard today was indeed heard by me yesterday."

For this very reason stated previously, a word— whether it be the sound uttered at that moment or the expressive linguistic unit— is stable and persists for a long duration, like a sound that has been articulated yesterday.
Because it functions as a cognition of an object of knowledge that depends upon the experience of a relation,
that which is such is observed to be stable, like the aspect of the generality of smoke.
But that which is unstable is not a communicator dependent upon the knowledge of a relationship,
because its cause is immediate, like the light of a lamp or a flash of lightning.
Therefore, the position that sound is impermanent is contradicted by all these firm and established inferences; consequently, it is established that sounds are eternal.

The cognitions regarding the individual instances of the word "cow" (go-śabda), which are distinguished by the appearance of various differences such as place, time, fast, medium, or slow [articulation], have a single object as their domain; they do not have multiple objects as their domain, because they arise by apprehending the form "cow," just like a cognition of a cow produced at the present moment.
Alternatively, whatever cognition has the word "cow" as its object, that has the word "cow" as its object today, because it has the word "cow" as its object.

It is like the cognition of the word "cow" produced today. The cognition of the word "cow" from yesterday has the word "cow" as its object; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Alternatively, the subject (*dharmin*) is the cognition of the word "cow" from yesterday; the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is that it has the word "cow" from yesterday as its object; the reason (*hetu*) is "because it has the word 'cow' as its object"; and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the cognition of the word "cow" from yesterday.
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "this" (iyam) and so forth:
"this" refers to the present [cognition];
"that" refers to the word "cow" perceived through the cognition of the word "cow" from yesterday.
"Because of that cause" means because they have the word "cow" as their object.
Alternatively, both the past and present cognitions have a single object, because they have the word "cow" as their object, just like a single cognition of the word "cow."
And by the word "both," he demonstrates this very point:
the reason is not explicitly stated because it is easily understood from the context.

Alternatively, all cognitions of "cowness," though differentiated by distinctions of place and so forth, are produced by the single word "cow," because they are cognitions of "cow-ness," just like the cognition of a single cow.

Previously, the cognitions having the word "cow" as their object were the subject (*dharmin*), and having a single object was the property to be proven (*sādhya*); now, however, the cognitions having the universal "cowness" (*gotvajāti*) as their object are the subject, and being produced by the same word "cow" is the property to be proven—this is the distinction.
"Hyastanoccāraṇaḥ" means that its utterance occurred yesterday;
this is the indication of the subject (*dharmin*).
Even today, its continued existence is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); the rest is easily understood.
"The word 'cow' being heard today" is the indication of the subject (*dharmin*);
for that [word], its being heard even yesterday is the property to be proven.
"From what was previously stated" means because it is cognizable through the cognition of the word "cow.
Alternatively, "whatever expressive word there may be" is the statement of the subject (*dharmin*).
Its property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is the state of occurring over a long period of time.
The reason (*hetu*) is "because it functions as the cognition of an object of knowledge dependent upon the experience of a relation.

It is so described because it is both that which depends upon the experience of a relation (*sambandhānubhavāpekṣa*) and the functioning of the cognition of an object of knowledge (*jñeyajñānapravartana*).

Therefore, it should be understood that "stable" is the qualifier of that which is stable; by the phrase "existing for a long time," he indicates that what is intended is stability in terms of time, and not stability in terms of space as in the case of a mountain or similar objects—this is shown by the qualifier. "Like that which possesses the general nature of smoke" is the illustrative example.

Because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) lacks continuity, it cannot function as a logical mark (*liṅga*); thus, only the universal aspect (*sāmānyabhāga*) serves as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The phrase "because it is unstable," and so forth, expresses the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
The phrase "because it is a cause existing at that very time" [explains the reason].

That which has for its cause a connection that is "pertaining to that time"—meaning existing at that specific moment and persisting through the period of linguistic usage—is described as such; the state of being that is its "nature" (*tattva*). //2121//
But surely, by this same line of reasoning, one could also assert the unity of jars and other such things.
For instance: "All cognitions of individual jars, though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, have a single object;
they do not have multiple objects as their domain, because they arise with the thought 'jar,' just like the cognition of a jar arising at the present moment," and so on.
Furthermore, oneness is neither desired nor observed in the case of jars and the like;
therefore, suspecting that all these reasons are fallacious (vyabhicārin), he says "ghaṭādeḥ" and so forth:
"If oneness were to result for jars and the like, then [the argument] regarding the genus would be a proof of what is already established (siddhasādhana)."
If one were to bring about the attainment of oneness among individuals by this method, [it would be as follows].

Likewise, it must be stated that [the opponent's position] contradicts what is perceived, since the distinction between individual instances is well-ascertained by means of perception and other valid cognitions, for which verbal testimony is the authority.

If, by means of a universal (*jāti*)—that is, by way of its universal form—the oneness of jars and so forth is established through a *prasaṅga* [reductio], then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
As it has been said: "For its part called the universal is considered eternal, while the other [part] is perishable.
Alternatively, if the oneness of individual forms (*vyakti*) is established through a *prasaṅga*, even then there is no deviation [from the rule].
Because this proposition is sublated by perception and other means of valid cognition;
for all reasons (*hetu*) intended here are understood to be qualified by the condition that their object be unsublated.
Therefore, the intention [of the author] is: "How, then, could there be any deviation (*vyabhicāra*)?"
"Contradiction with what is perceived" (*dṛṣṭaviruddhatva*); the word "of the proposition" (*pratijñāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The remainder is easy to understand. //2131//

Furthermore, he states the sublation of the thesis that sound is impermanent by means of inference (*anumāna*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). In this regard, the inference is as follows: "Those two whose relation is non-artificial are themselves non-artificial, just like space and an atom; and the relation of sound with its object—designated as a 'universal' (*jāti*)—characterized by the state of signifier and signified, is non-artificial. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
To avoid the charge of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*), he says: "And if the relation were artificial," and so forth.
"And if the relation were artificial, it would follow from the abandonment of its application."
Because it would reside in only a single individual instance, it could not be universal.
Because of the confusion [of properties] such as being an earthly substance, being a real entity, and having a tail,
there could be no determination of "cowness" without a multiplicity of applications [of the term].
Therefore, the word is uncreated and never perishes,
because of its eternal connection with the eternal [meaning], like space and atoms.
And in this context, the phrase "if the relation were artificial" (*kṛtrimatve ca sambandhasya*) is to be supplied.

If the relation were artificial, then because it would terminate with its employment—that is, upon the destruction of the word's usage—the word itself would also be destroyed. Consequently, it would not be universal, meaning it would not persist through all usages. Why? Because it would reside in only a single individual instance (*tadekavyaktiniṣṭhatvāt*), specifically residing in only one individual cow.

In this context, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is as follows: when a universal (*sāmānya*) resides in many individual cows, even in the case of a single individual cow present before one's eyes, the cognition of "cowness" (*gotva*) alone as extracted from the word "cow" would be impossible without a word. To explain how this is so, he says "earthen," etc. This presumptive testimony is preceded by verbal authority (*śābdapramāṇa*).

Therefore, he concludes the inference that "sound is non-artificial" with the words "by means of the eternal," referring to the object designated by the term *jāti*. This is because of its connection [to that object] eternally, at all times.
Just as [the conjunction] of atoms with eternal space. //2133-2135//

Avoiding the charge of inconclusiveness regarding presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), he says: "And the word 'cow', when heard once, having as its object multiple universals present before it, does not attain the status of denoting its own specific meaning in isolation."
By means of numerous auditory perceptions, this [cognition] excludes such qualities as being a living being and so forth,
as well as the movement toward white objects and the like, and the possession of a dewlap, a tail, and so on.
Having first apprehended individual instances such as the brindled cow or the hornless cow according to their respective causes,
one eventually arrives at the understanding that [the word] denotes the abstract universal "cowness" (gotva).
