As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "But indeed, when the word is eternal, having been uttered many times and previously heard in connection with various individual cows, it makes known that it denotes the universal (ākṛti) through positive and negative concomitance; therefore, it is also eternal.
[The phrase] "individuals have their own respective causes" means that they are distinguished by their own respective differences.
For their distinctness is the basis for the cognition of difference.
Therefore, those whose own distinctness is the basis for the cognition of difference are "those based on themselves" (*svanibandhanāḥ*).
This is to be connected with the word "avoiding" (*varjayan*). //2136–2137//
It might be argued: "Even if it is indeed perceived after a long time, how is it established that the word exists at all times? To this he says: "For that duration," and so forth.
"If this [word] were to remain stable for that duration, who would destroy it later?
Its perishability cannot be further imagined by any other cause."
Just as jars and other objects are understood to perish through being cut by weapons or through decay, there is no such cause for sound.
"For that duration" means for the duration of the time required to convey its own specific meaning.

Now, one might object: "Just as jars and other things, though stable for that duration, undergo destruction later due to hammers and the like, so too will it happen for sound. To this he says, "It is possible for this," and so forth. "Furthermore" (bhūyaḥ).
Furthermore:

just as jars and the like undergo destruction through being cut by weapons and so forth, or through decay, no such cause exists for sound. Why? Because [sound] is formless (*amūrta*), whereas jars and the like possess form (*mūrta*). This is the intended meaning. //2139//

As it has been said: "If the oneness of jars and the like is [the object of the argument], then since oneness is accepted for the genus, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, however, one intends to establish the oneness of individual instances by this same method..."
In that case, it must be stated that [the position] contradicts what is perceived by all means of valid cognition.

Thus, here too, the same applies: if the identity of *ga* and other [phonemes] is asserted, then since the universal (*jāti*) is accepted [by us], it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). All this must be stated. For instance, just as there are many individual instances of cows and so forth due to differences in place, time, and speaker, so too there are many individual instances of the phoneme *ga* and others; and just as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth reside in those [individuals], so too the universal "ga-ness" (*gatva*) and so forth is accepted. Anticipating the objection that "all this is the same," he says: "Of place, time, and speakers," and so on.
Furthermore, although there is a difference in place, time, and speaker, the phoneme such as *ga* is not differentiated, since the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of it therein is perfectly clear.

The intention is that the identity of individuals is established through perception known as recognition; for inference does not become a valid means of knowledge when it contradicts perception, since perception is the eldest among all means of knowledge.

[Objection: Surely the distinction between individual instances is established by the difference in perception—such as fast, medium, or slow; so why is it said that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is perfectly clear? [The author] replies: "For even when there is a difference of fast and so forth...

For even when there is a difference of fast and so forth, another distinct cow-instance (*gavyakti*), separated from other cow-instances, is not perceived as being fully accomplished (*niṣpanna*). It is not clearly perceived as a completed entity.
"Accomplished" means unconstructed;
"severed" means cut off.

"Different" means that the manifestation as *ga* (the sound *ga*) is distinct [from other manifestations]. The point is that because it is unified by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is no other manifestation as *ga*.

[Page 596] But surely, it is only the universal (*jāti*) such as "g-ness" (*gatva*) that is recognized through re-cognition, not the individual instance (*vyakti*); so how can there be re-cognition of the individual? To this he says, "The letter *ga*, etc.

The letter *ga* does not exist as a substratum for a completely abstracted "g-ness," because it cannot be determined by a cognition other than that of the letter *ga*, just like the "g-ness" postulated by others.
"Because it cannot be defined by a cognition other than that of the letter *ga*":
*gānya* means "other than *ga*"; *buddhiḥ* refers to the cognition thereof; because it cannot be defined by that, i.e., because it is not apprehended.
It is like the *gatva* (the universal "ga-ness") postulated by others.
Because it is the established tenet of others that universals are devoid of further universals.
"And because it is a phoneme, this too is to be proven": And because this [phoneme] is a phoneme, just like the letter *kha* and so forth,
and because no absence [of the property to be proven] is observed, nothing seen here can exclude [the probandum].

The ellipsis is "the negation of being *g*-ness. In this regard, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is a phoneme (*varṇa*) is not the substratum of an absolutely distinct *g*-ness (*gatva*), just like the phoneme *kha* and others; and this *ga* is a phoneme. This is an apprehension of a pervading property that is contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
For indeed, being a phoneme is pervaded by that which is contradictory to being the substratum of *g*-ness.
And he says "of the exclusion," etc., because there is no contradiction with what is perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) in this thesis.
"Exclusion" (*vyatireka*) means difference;
"perceived" (*dṛṣṭa*) means direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It might be argued that for a Buddhist, this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For indeed, the cognition of oneness is held to be based solely on the exclusion of others (*anyāpohana*), and not on a distinct property of "going" (*gati*). Therefore, even if a distinct "going" is refuted, the oneness of the phoneme is not established by virtue of the cognition of oneness, because that [cognition] is based on the exclusion of others. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But the nature of the phoneme, established for both parties, such as its eternity and so forth, should be accepted as it is admitted for the imagined [phoneme]. [The verse: But the nature of the phoneme, established for both parties, such as its eternity and so forth, should be accepted as it is admitted for the [imagined] phoneme. Just as it is accepted for the conceptualized [phoneme], so too should it be accepted for the [phoneme] that is already established.
Due to that oneness of the phoneme, a single cognition arises;
the existence of distinct cognitions occurs because of the difference in the manifesting agents.

Why, abandoning the nature of the phoneme (*varṇa*) which is established for both [parties], are properties such as eternality, manifoldness, and pervasiveness attributed only to the imagined *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), based on the statement that "the properties of a genus (*jāti*) are established"?
It is logical to postulate only that which is established for both; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating something unperceived.
Therefore, it is precisely because of the unity of the phoneme that a single cognition of recognition arises.
If this is so, one might ask how the specific cognitions of fast, medium, slow, and so forth could arise; to this he says "the cognitions of specific qualities," etc.
The manifestors are the conjunctions and disjunctions of the air.

[Objection: But since air is not an object of the auditory organ, its conjunctions and disjunctions are likewise not objects of the auditory organ. Therefore, how can there be a perception of the manifested (vyaṅgya) when the manifestor (vyañjaka) is not perceived? For it is not reasonable that a jar or the like, which is manifested by light, could be perceived when that light is not perceived. Thinking thus, the opponent raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), etc.:
"But surely for one for whom both [the air and its conjunctions/disjunctions] are objects of the auditory organ, there would be two cognitions."
But since you [maintain that] the entity is beyond the senses, how can there be a cognition of its specific qualities through the sounds?
Regarding the phrase "of whom":

for one such as a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), whose manifestor is sound (*dhvani*) consisting of resonance and not consisting of the conjunctions and disjunctions of air, both the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) are perceptible by the ear; thus, there arises a twofold cognition—a single cognition and a cognition of particulars.

But for you, the Mīmāṃsaka, how could there be a cognition of particulars through *nādas* (sounds) consisting of the conjunctions and disjunctions of air? Why? Because they are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriyatvāt*).
The word "of sounds" (nādānām) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
He provides a rebuttal with the verse beginning "nādena" and so forth:
"When a sound is perceived by the auditory organ as refined by the resonance (nāda), some maintain that its cognition occurs through the association with that [resonance]."
"By means of its proximity" means by means of the proximity of the sound;
that is, of that resonance (nāda).
"Cognition" means apprehension.

Some maintain that although the mere sound (*nāda*) is not perceived by the ear, nevertheless, there is indeed the perception of it when it is conjoined with the word (*śabda*); such is their view, for they hold that two distinct cognitions must necessarily arise.
With the words "or not at all," he also establishes two types of cognition even in the case of non-apprehension:
"Or rather, when they are apprehended, there is a cognition of the word [as a whole] by virtue of them;
and because it conforms to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), one perceives [qualities such as] magnitude and so forth."
"Of them" means of the sounds,
which consist of the conjunctions and disjunctions of air.

He says, "But the cognition of the word [arises] by virtue of that," in response to the question: "How could there be a cognition of the manifested (vyaṅgya) when its manifestor (vyañjaka) has not been grasped?
[This means] "by virtue of the sounds" (nāda);
that is to say, merely by their existence.

Granted that there is the apprehension of the mere essential nature [of sound], but how does the apprehension of specific qualities such as magnitude occur? To this he says: "Because it conforms to the latent impressions" (*saṃskārānukṛteḥ*), and so forth.
When a great latent impression is produced in the auditory organ by great sounds, then magnitude is perceived in the sound; when, however, it is small, then smallness is perceived.
In this way, the distinction of degrees—such as more or less—is also to be understood through conformity to the latent impressions.

But surely, according to your view, this magnitude and so forth that is perceived resides only in the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and not in the manifested (*vyaṅgya*); and since that [magnitude] is unperceived due to the non-perception of the manifestor, how could one superimpose upon the word magnitude and so forth residing in the manifestor without having first perceived them?
For there can be no superimposition of water and the like—which have not been made an object of cognition—upon a mirage; to this he replies with the verse beginning "sweet as bitter," etc.
Just as those with deranged minds, due to a disorder of bile, perceive sweetness as bitter and white as yellow, so do they apprehend the object.
Just as those running with great speed or those traveling by boat perceive mountains and other objects as moving due to their own motion, even though those objects are actually stationary.
Those whose eyes are smeared with the fat of a frog perceive bamboo as snakes;
likewise, due to the smallness or largeness of the individual instances, they perceive the universal that resides within them in the same way.
Just as these [senses] perceive their objects without grasping at signs (nimitta),
so too will there be an error regarding the manifested (vyaṅgya) without one having understood that which resides in the manifestor (vyañjaka).
Just as, due to a disorder of bile (*pitta-doṣa*), people perceive objects such as sweet things in the form of bitter ones without even grasping the true nature of the bile;
or just as those whose vision is affected by the rapid movement of a boat or by spinning perceive mountains and other objects as moving or spinning;
and just as those whose eyes are smeared with the fat of a frog see bamboo poles in the form of snakes.

And just as people perceive the universal residing in its instances—as having smallness or greatness based on the smallness or greatness of those instances—so too they perceive the great universal called "Being" (sattā) as large, while [universals] such as "cowness" (gotva) are perceived as small.
Otherwise, since everything would be identical due to the eternal and all-pervasive nature [of universals], by what could the smallness or greatness of a universal be determined?

Therefore, just as these [tastes] such as sweet and so forth are perceived in the form of bitter and so forth without the perception of the cause—namely bile and so forth—in the same way, there will be an illusion of magnitude and so forth regarding sound without having grasped the magnitude and so forth residing in the manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
Regarding the word "without having understood" (*abuddhvā*), there is a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) in relation to the action of erring; otherwise, the suffix *-tvā* would not be applicable.

Now, how is it understood that this cognition of shortness, greatness, and so forth regarding sound is due to external conditions (*paropādhika*), and not because of the actual existence of distinctions such as greatness within the sound itself? To this he says: "The distinction of shortness and so forth by its own nature," and so on.
"But a distinction of shortness and so forth by its own nature contradicts [its] eternality and other [qualities]. How can that which exists at all times be itself measured in morae (*mātrika*)?"
Therefore, its pronunciation should be understood as lasting for one mora, or two morae, or three morae; the phoneme itself is not inherently of one mora.
By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of distinctions such as long, protracted, acute, grave, circumflex, and the six musical notes (ṣaḍja) and so forth.
The phrase "it contradicts eternality and so on" means that eternality is established through recognition (pratyabhijñā). This is the intended sense.

With the words "nanu" and so forth, he raises an objection regarding the non-establishment of manifestation according to the view of the opponent: "Indeed, the manifestation of the word-sound by means of articulated sounds (nāda) is not tenable;
for that [manifestation] would have to occur either through the refinement of the sound, or of the sense organ, or of both."
Therefore, if the word-sound were being refined, it would be perceived by everyone;
for there can be no refinement in a single location of that which is partless and all-pervading.

This manifestation of sound must occur either through the refinement of the sound by means of the conjunctions and disjunctions of air, or through the refinement of the sense organ, or through the refinement of both the sound and the sense organ. In that regard, if the sound were refined, then having been refined in one place such as Pāṭaliputra, it would be perceived by those situated in all places simultaneously, because it is omnipresent.
Furthermore, if it were argued that only one part of it is refined and not the whole, he says: "of that which is partless."
For sound is indeed partless because it is incorporeal; even if it were all-pervading, how could there be a refinement of that which is partless by means of a single part?

Furthermore, it might be argued that even for that which is partless, there will be a differentiated refinement (saṃskāra) due to the difference in its substrates; to this he says, "nor also" (nacāpi):
nor indeed would there be a restriction of the refinement by means of a difference in the substrate, because sound is without a substrate, just like space, the self, and so forth.
But surely, sound is without a substratum, like space, the self, and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, since sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), and qualities depend upon a substratum possessing those qualities, space must be the support of sound. To this he says: "Now, even if space were the support," and so forth.
"Even if space were the support there, since it is partless, there could be no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a specific location, because sound is perceived as being present in its entirety."

Since that space (*ākāśa*) is also partless, there can be no differentiation of its refinement (*saṃskāra*) based on a difference in supporting locations. Now, one might object: "Even if space is partless, nevertheless, due to the difference in what it is conjoined with—just like the space within a jar and so forth—the space delimited by the extent of the ear-cavity will be differentiated. To this he replies: "Because sound is perceived as a whole (*kṛtsnaśabdagateḥ*). The connection [of the phrase] is: "there would not be a refinement of a specific location (*pradeśasaṃskāra*)."
For a word is indeed perceived as an indivisible whole, and that perception would not occur if only a single part of space were refined.
Concluding this very point, he says "nahi" and so forth: "Indeed,
it is not possible for that which is established as pervading the entirety of space to be perceived in its totality when it has been refined by only a single part."
For sound, which exists pervading space, cannot be perceived in its entirety when it is modified by only one part of that [space].
He states the refutation regarding the position that the sense organ is a refinement (*saṃskāra*), beginning with "In the position that the ear is space (*ākāśa*)," and so forth:
"And in the position that the ear is space, because of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*), there would be an equal reach;
consequently, the cognition of sounds here would follow even when they are at a distance."
In this way, the auditory organ would be one and the same for all living beings;
therefore, at the time of a single hearing, they would all hear together.

For those who hold the position that the auditory organ is space (*kha*), since space is a single entity and all-pervading, its contact with all sounds would be equal; consequently, it follows that even a sound located at a distance would be perceived.
Furthermore, the auditory organ of all living beings would be one and the same.
Thus, when one person hears, everyone else would hear at that very moment, because the auditory organ is non-different [in all cases].
And it must be stated that if there were hearing by only one, there would be the fault of everyone not hearing.

It might be argued as follows: "The auditory organ (*śrotra*) is space delimited by the ear-canal (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), which is conditioned by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). Therefore, since the auditory organ is established in that portion of space occupied by the ear-canal, these two defects—that the auditory organ would have equal reach due to its omnipresence (*vibhutva*), and that there would be a single auditory organ for all living beings—are groundless.
To this, he replies: "Because it is partless" (*tasyānavayavatvāt*).
And because it is partless, it is not conditioned by merit and demerit.
The region of space would constitute the ear for the sake of establishing the two-fold arrangement.

For that which is partless does not, in the ultimate sense, possess spatial divisions, by means of which some particular region of space could become the auditory organ (*śrotra*). There are two established positions: the establishment of the inequality of [the range of] contact, and the establishment of the multiplicity of auditory organs.
Alternatively, there are two distinct conditions regarding the apprehension and non-apprehension of sound.
Furthermore, the auditory faculty, once refined, would perceive all sounds;
for the eye opened toward a jar does not fail to perceive a cloth.
This very same [objection] must also apply to the recollection of an object,
because the latent impression (saṃskāra) exists in the same location [as the object] without distinction.
Furthermore, the auditory organ, once refined, would cause all sounds to be perceived— that is, grasped— at one and the same time;
for it is common to all sounds,
and because those sounds are omnipresent, they occupy the same suitable location without distinction.

It might be argued that for the sake of comprehension alone, the speaker prepares the listener’s auditory faculty so that it perceives only that specific sound and no other; to this, he replies with the words "of the jar," and so forth.
For it is not the case that [the other sounds] are not perceived; rather, they are indeed perceived, because the suitability of the location is equal—this is the intended meaning.
To the question, "How then is there the perception of all sounds? he replies: "Because the embellishment occurs in the same location, there is no distinction."

For all sounds, by virtue of their omnipresence, reside in the same location as space; consequently, their refinement (*saṃskāra*) is likewise without distinction, which entails the undesirable consequence that all [sounds] would be perceived. In some readings, it says: "for the refinement is without distinction" (*saṃskāro hyaviśeṣataḥ*); here, the word *hi* indicates a reason.
"Without distinction" (*aviśeṣataḥ*).
The suffix *tasi* is applied to the word ending in the third case by virtue of its inclusion in the group beginning with *ādi*.

Consequently, the meaning is as follows: since the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words has been performed without distinction, and because they reside in the same location, it follows that there would be the apprehension of all words.

It might be argued: "Even if the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is without distinction, nevertheless, only that sound which is intended to be grasped by the listener is perceived, and no other. To this, he replies with the verse beginning *sthiravāyu* and so forth: "And its refinement would occur through the approach of a steady wind; for it is observed that when an obstruction is removed, there is the perception of that [sound] in its own location."
For wind is of two kinds: stable and unstable. Of these, that which is stable remains covering the sound like the dense darkness of night.
And conjunctions and disjunctions are produced in it by the wind arising from the effort of the speaker.

By those conjunctions and disjunctions, the removal of that stable wind is effected; and this alone is the embellishment (*saṃskāra*) of the sound, and nothing else such as the nourishment of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because, being eternal, it is of a single uniform nature.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says "It is seen," and so forth.
"It is seen" refers to both worldly experience and the treatises.
Just as, when darkness has departed, there is indeed the perception of a jar or the like situated in front, even if it is undesired, because it is located in a suitable place.

As for what was said—"In that case, the word would be perceived by everyone if it were being refined"—there is no fault therein, because even a single word may be unrefined with respect to one person and refined with respect to another.
For example, a single woman is both a mother and a daughter due to a difference in relation; thus he speaks of "the states of being refined and unrefined.
These states of being refined and unrefined are not established by the oneness of the word.
And if they were admitted to exist in a single state, they would either all be perceived or none at all.

If the sound were a single entity, its two states—being refined (*saṃskṛta*) and being unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*)—could not exist simultaneously, because the state is not distinct from the substratum of the state; thus, like the nature of the substratum itself, the two states would necessarily become one. As for the case where a single woman is called both "mother" and "daughter," there the distinction is merely verbal, not real.
In this case, however, it is not merely the designation that differs, because the sound remains present without distinction in its capacity to be perceived by all persons.
Consequently, there would be neither perception nor non-perception [of it].
For it is not logical that a thing should lose its nature—which is determined by its causal efficiency—merely through a change in designation.

If it is argued that its nature is indeed such as to be apprehended by specific individuals alone, and therefore its apprehension and non-apprehension are not contradictory due to differences in human capacity, we say no;
for if an object has not been apprehended by a person at one time, it would never be apprehended by that person at all.
But this is not the case.

Therefore, lest there be a loss of its unity, one must accept that sound possesses only a single state, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "If only one state is accepted," and so forth.
[On p. 602, he states the fault in the view that both are embellished: "The faults stated for each individually would apply to the embellishment of both as well;
therefore, in no way is a manifesting agent (vyañjaka) tenable with respect to sound."
The defects that were stated regarding the refinement of the word individually and the refinement of the sense organ individually would also apply if both were refined;
therefore, he concludes with the word "ataḥ" (therefore).
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "uttaram" (the answer): "The answer has been described by the author of the Bhāṣya as arising from the refinement of the auditory organ;
and the difference in hearing, resulting from the difference in that [refinement], is established for each individual listener."

Regarding the phrase "by the author of the Bhāṣya": as it has been stated—"Even for one who holds that [sounds] manifest [the word], this fault does not apply; for the conjunctions and disjunctions do not assist the ear-cavity situated at a distance, and therefore they are not perceived by that auditory organ which is located at a distance.
The phrase "due to its division" means due to the division of the ear-cavity and the auditory organ.
A difference in scripture is a difference in cognition.
But how can there be the manifestation of one thing through the refinement of another? To this he says: "Just as in the case of a jar," and so forth.

Just as a lamp or similar object is held to be the manifester of a jar and the like, so too sound would be [the manifester] precisely through the assistance of the eye when the auditory faculty has been refined.

For just as a lamp or similar object, by assisting the eye, becomes the manifestor of a jar or other thing, so too sound, through the refinement of the ear—that is, by means of the ear's refinement—will be the manifestor of the word-sound.

Now, it might be asked: "In what manner is the embellishment (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ produced by the sound, since [the organ] is already established? To this he says: "And there is no objection here. There is no objection here as to in what form the embellishment occurs; for since the same applies even to the case of production, the capacity (*śakti*) in that case too is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriyā*).
The remainder of the argument is that the objection is equally applicable even to the case of production (*utpatti*).

For even if sound were produced from causes, the objection would be identical; there too it could certainly be asked: "In what form is the sound produced by the cause—whether by means of sound-waves consisting of conjunctions and disjunctions of air, or by some other cause?"—since the capacity (*śakti*) in that case as well is beyond the reach of the senses.

In that case as well, when the production of sounds is being carried out, just as the productive power of the causes of sound is beyond the senses, so too is it in the case of manifestation; thus the objection is equal.
To the question, "If power (*śakti*) is beyond the senses, how is it to be inferred?", he says: "Eternal," and so forth.
Since power is eternally to be inferred from its effects, why is it being questioned?
In that case, the only proof perceived is the mere fact of its occurring when that [other thing] exists.

Whether it be the power of production or the power of conditioning, in every respect, whatever power there may be, it is always to be inferred from its effect. Therefore, it does not deserve further questioning. To the question, "What is that effect by which it is known?", he says: "tadbhāva... and so forth.

When that exists—that is, when the manifestation of the sound-phonemes (dhvani) exists—the fact that the apprehension of the word is brought about by them is precisely the proof for the capacity to manifest the word therein.
That is to say, the capacity is inferred from its effect, which is the apprehension of the word.
By the inclusion of the term "only" (mātra), the view that [the capacity] arises [de novo] is excluded.
He concludes with the word "ataḥ" (therefore): "Therefore,
by means of this very power which is beyond the senses,
these causes of manifestation manifest while bestowing a power upon the sense-organ that is itself beyond the senses."
Therefore, these sounds manifest as the causes of manifestation, producing through their supersensory power a supersensory capacity in the auditory organ;
the phrase "of words" is to be understood here.
Now, he says "of those who," etc., to address the question: why are sounds not understood as being merely the causes of production?

For those [who hold] that this sound is perceived by the ear when it has been produced without reaching it, for them, because non-arrival is equal [in all cases], [the sound would be heard] even from distant or obstructed locations and so forth.
In that case, the perception and non-perception of objects situated far and near would be identical;
there would be no sequence [of cognition], nor would there be the possibility of degrees such as intense or faint.
According to those Buddhists for whom sound is apprehended by the ear as being "unreached and arisen" (*aprāptajāta*)—
that is, it is both not reached [by the sense organ] and yet has arisen—

[it is held that] the eye, ear, and mind have objects that are not reached, because of the established tenet that sound has as its cause the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), whether they are appropriated (*upātta*) or non-appropriated (*anupātta*).

According to their view, since sounds situated at a distance, behind a barrier, or nearby are equally unattained by the auditory organ (*śrotra*), there would be an equality in both perception and non-perception for persons standing far away and those standing nearby; that is, the manner of perception for one nearby would be exactly the same as for one far away, because there is no distinction [in the lack of contact].
Furthermore, there would be no sequential perception, such that those nearby perceive first and those far away perceive later.
Nor would there be a difference in the hearing of intensity, such as loudness or subtlety—that is, what is heard loudly by those nearby would be heard faintly by those far away.
In this way, the distinction of degrees—greater or lesser—should also be applied.

Now, one might ask: "Why does this undesirable consequence not apply even to that Mīmāṃsaka for whom the sound, having been produced, is perceived by the auditory organ? To demonstrate the distinction [between his view and ours], he begins with the words "Therefore," and so forth: "Therefore, let this conceptual construction be examined even from the perspective of a Vedic scholar:
'The air within the body, struck by effort, is produced'—of this there is no doubt."
It conforms to the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other articulators;
and because it possesses momentum (*vega*), it necessarily persists for as long as that momentum lasts.
Due to its movement, conjunctions and disjunctions necessarily arise between it and the parts of the self, as well as with the still air.
Having reached the space of the ear, it imparts its capacity to the sense of hearing;
and because the cognition of sound occurs when that [capacity] exists, an imperceptible impression (*saṃskāra*) is postulated.
Like the capacity for origination, that [capacity] too is not anything additional for us;
likewise, its particularity would also arise from the apprehension of a particular.
The mention of the *śrotriya* is intended to demonstrate that he is not a mere logician;
by this, he expresses the excellence of his own position through an indirect statement.
To the question "What is that conceptualization? he replies with the words "struck by effort," and so forth.

Effort (*prayatna*) is the operation of the articulatory organs (*karaṇa*), such as the palate. Driven and impelled by that effort, the abdominal air (*vāyu*) rises from the region of the navel, expands in the chest, turns at the throat, strikes the head, and moving through the mouth, it exits.
This very process is shown by the passage beginning with "it" (*sa*).
That air, as it goes out, experiences conjunctions (*saṃyoga*) and disjunctions (*vibhāga*) with the palate and other organs.
And as he goes, he does not go as far as space;
rather, he goes only as far as his momentum—that is, he goes exactly in accordance with whatever speed he possesses.
Why? Because he possesses momentum.
And as that air moves, conjunctions and disjunctions arise between its own constituent parts and the still, stable air.
That [air] necessarily reaches the cavity of the ear and bestows power upon the auditory organ.
Since sound is perceived when those conjunctions and disjunctions of air exist, an imperceptible refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ is postulated.

Just as you accept that the production of one sound by other sounds or by various physical properties is observed—even if it is not directly perceived—so too is the case with *saṃskāra* (the latent impression).

As stated in the Bhāṣya: "The parts [of air] impelled by a blow, striking against other stationary objects and producing conjunctions and disjunctions in all directions, continue to exist as long as their momentum lasts. And because air is imperceptible, these conjunctions and disjunctions are not perceived.
It is only while they have not ceased that the sound is perceived, not when they have ceased."

If this is so, then no distinction has been stated between the position that [the sound] is produced (*utpatti-pakṣa*) and the position that it is manifested (*saṃskāra-pakṣa*). To this he says, "In the very same way," and so forth.
That distinction—the distinction in the manifestation—is established from the distinction in the apprehension of the sound.

Therefore, for those standing at a distance or nearby, the apprehension and non-apprehension are not the same, because the manifestation differs according to the difference in persons. //2176 //2177 //

To the question, "How is it that sound is not perceived when there is an obstruction such as a wall? he says: "Obstruction by a wall, etc. and so forth. An obstruction by a wall and the like is indeed possible for the wind (mātariśvan);
by that [obstruction], there is also an impact upon the location of the ear, and thus [the sound] possesses an intense manifestation.

And because that [wind] functions in a sequential manner, it serves as the cause for the intensity or mildness of the sequence of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), as well as for the perfection of its perishability and velocity.

Although sound is not subject to resistance (*pratighāti*), nevertheless, because both the wind (*mātariśvan*) and the wall are corporeal (*mūrta*) and possess the quality of resistance, the sound does not reach the location of the ear; thus, no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ occurs, and consequently, there is no hearing of what is obstructed. For those who maintain that perception occurs without [the object] reaching [the sense organ], this very fault applies. To the question, "In that case, how is there a distinction in the intensity and the degree of audibility?", he says: "There is also an impact upon the location of the auditory organ."
The word "is appropriate" (*yujyate*), which is the subject under discussion, is to be applied everywhere. Regarding the phrase "the perfections of perishability and velocity":
the connection is made by changing the case endings, such that it means "the perfection of perishability and the perfection of velocity are appropriate."
Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "those perfections of velocity are perishable.
Or else, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that wind which possesses perishable perfections of velocity.
And from that, the connection is: "therefore, it is logical that [the wind] has the state of being the cause for the intensity or mildness of the sequence of formative forces (*saṃskāra*)."
The sequence of formations is logical because that wind functions sequentially;
its intensity is logical because it is endowed with the perfection of velocity; and its mildness is also logical because of its perishability.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), distinctions such as "more" and "most" (taratama) and so forth are to be applied.

[Objection: But surely, regarding the position that space is the auditory organ (*śrotra*), many defects in the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotrasaṃskāra*) were previously stated, beginning with "because of its non-omnipresence, there would be an equality of contact," and so forth; so how is it that the Commentator later describes the answer as being due to the refinement of the auditory organ? [Response: To this he says, "The auditory organ is not necessarily space," and so on.
We do not necessarily accept that the auditory organ is space, nor is space partless, because that has been refuted by the Jains and the Sāṃkhyas.

Therefore, the auditory organ— which is either a specific portion of space or some other distinct entity— is established in each individual person, as it is known through the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) of its effects.
Therefore, it has been stated that the defects inherent in that position do not apply simply because he does not accept it;
nor is space without parts—
this is the connection [of the sentence].
Why? Because of the refutation of the Jain and Sāṅkhya positions; for the Jains (Ārhata) and the Sāṅkhyas have denied that space (*vyoman*) is partless.

Indeed, the Mīmāṃsakas do not refrain from employing what is well-established in the systems of others. For whatever is established through reasoning is accepted by them; otherwise, their very status as Mīmāṃsakas would be lost.
Consequently, there is no fault, because one accepts the ear as being of the nature of space (*ākāśa*), as established by the Jainas and Sāṅkhyas;
or else, it is "another entity," namely that which is designated as the *karṇaśaṣkulī* (the ear-cavity).
"Accessible through presumptive testimony regarding an effect" means accessible through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the perception of the word.

Alternatively, demonstrating that there is no fault even in the position that the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is partless space (*anavayavākāśa*), he says: "Even though [space] is all-pervading and one," and so forth.
[p.606] Even though it is all-pervading and one, nevertheless, there is the refinement (*saṃskṛti*) by means of the sound (*dhvani*).
But that person upon whom it is focused perceives the sound.

Although the auditory organ is both all-pervading and unitary— this being the ellipsis for "the ear"— nevertheless, that person alone in whose physical locus, namely the ear-cavity, the refinement by means of the sounds occurs perceives the sound, and no other does.
By this, it is stated that the embellishment (saṃskāra) belongs only to the locus (adhiṣṭhāna) and not to the auditory organ itself.
The intention is that since that locus differs for each person, the aforementioned logical fault does not follow.
He demonstrates that there is no fault even if the auditory organ itself is refined by saying, "But even if...
But even if the refinement belongs to the sense organ, it would occur only in the location of its physical basis;
therefore, the ear would not hear sound if the concha were not refined.
The physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the ear-cavity;
it is through the refinement of that [basis] that the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is refined, not the faculty in isolation.

Therefore, because its basis has not been refined, the ear does not hear for those who are situated at a great distance, or for those whose minds are elsewhere, or for the seven types of unconscious beings, or for those in a state of fainting.
That whose ear-cavity is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is described as such;
the suffix *-tasi* is used here in the sense of the locative case, meaning "in the location of the physical basis" (*adhiṣṭhānadeśataḥ*).

Now, if sounds either refine the substratum, the location thereof, or the sense organ, why is it that those sounds whose existence is perceived only in certain places do not act as refiners of the sense organs and substrata of all classes of living beings? To this he says: "Because they have not reached the region of the ear," and so forth.
Because the sound has not reached the region of the ear, there is no refinement of the auditory organ;
therefore, the restriction regarding refinement is established by way of the difference in the substratum.

Even if the sounds (nāda) produce an impression on the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) or an impression on the sense organ located in that place, nevertheless, they produce an impression only when they have reached the object that is the locus of the impression, not when they have not reached it; therefore, there is no impression upon the substrata and so forth of all persons. The mention of the "ear" (śrotra) is merely illustrative.
The refinement of the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna-saṃskāra*) also certainly does not occur.
In some versions, there is the reading "or because it has not reached the region of the ear.
In that case, the previous refutation was stated by relying on the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra-saṃskāra*) through the medium of the refinement of the locus.

Now, even if there were no refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra*) by means of the refinement of its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there would still be no fault; for only those air-currents that have reached the base of the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) are capable of refining the auditory organ, not those that have not reached it. Therefore, another alternative view has been stated.
"Therefore" (*ataḥ*) is the conclusion.
With the words "nanu" and so forth, he anticipates the objection raised by the opponent against all three positions just mentioned:
"Surely, for one who maintains that there is a single sense-faculty, the sense-organ, having received its refinement upon a single substratum, would become the cognizer in all bodies."

For one who maintains that the auditory faculty is a single entity, it would follow that even the deaf and others would possess the capacity for hearing; because the auditory faculty is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and thus identical across all bodies due to its conditioning in one place, it cannot be joined with two mutually contradictory properties—the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Consequently, the established distinction between states such as deafness would not exist.
He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "puṃsām" (of men):
"The production of cognition is held to occur in specific regions of the bodies of men;
therefore, because of its spatial separation from the primary [cause], the refinement of the auditory organ is deficient."
Although the selves of persons are omnipresent, the Mīmāṃsakas and others maintain that the arising of cognition occurs only within bodies that are grasped by merit and demerit.

Therefore, because the primary element (pradhāna) and the body occupy different locations—that is, they are spatially distinct—the refinement of the ear, even though it is likewise omnipresent, is ineffective; thus, there is no occasion for the aforementioned fault.
In some places, the reading here is "sā saṃskṛtiḥ"; in that case, the connection is "that refinement belongs to the auditory organ."

But surely, since the self is omnipresent, the consequence that sound would be perceived everywhere remains unavoidable; to this he says: "Even though it is partless... "Even though our self is partless and perceives [sound] in its entirety, the statement that it perceives it only within the body is not faulty."
And by this very same reason, the condition of deafness and so forth is established;
that very [body] is not to be enjoyed by another because it is governed by dharma and adharma.
Just as one who has been installed as a lord in that place does not receive the enjoyment [of the office] while still remaining there, so too a deaf person does not hear when others are listening.
This is what is intended:

even if this is so, nevertheless, because the soul's apprehension of sound is restricted solely to that portion of the body which has been brought under control by the *dharmas* and other factors, there is no fault.

If it is asked, "How can there be a distinction between the apprehension and non-apprehension, or the refinement and non-refinement, of the ear—which is an indivisible part of the undivided soul?"—the answer is: no.

"Just as space, though partless, appears divided into 'the space within a jar' and 'the space within a pot' due to the difference in the objects with which it comes into contact, so too will it be here.

For this very reason, he shows that although the auditory organ is all-pervading and partless, its conditions such as deafness are established due to the difference in the objects with which it is in contact" (referring to "deafness and so forth").
Regarding the phrase "by this":
it means by the reason of the difference among those possessing conjunction (*saṃyogin*).
If it is granted that those possessing conjunction are indeed distinct, one might ask: why is it that only a certain person becomes deaf? To this he says: "that very [sound] is unenjoyable."
That very same auditory organ does not become an object of enjoyment for another person; why?
Because it is not brought under control by that other person's merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma).
Clarifying this very point through an illustration, he says: "Just as there," and so forth.

Just as someone who is the owner of a village or the like, while still residing and being present in that very village, might be deposed from his ownership by the king and consequently no longer receives the enjoyment of that same village; in the same way, a deaf person does not hear, even though another person elsewhere is hearing. //2190 //2191 //2192 //

But surely, since the triad of the auditory organ, sound, and space are all partless and omnipresent, they cannot exist in specific locations. Therefore, how can the distinction between perception and non-perception—determined by their existence in a single location—be established? To this he says: "Of the auditory organ, sound, and their substrata," and so forth. Indeed, these [three] themselves have no parts.
Nor does it involve subsisting in only one part; even so, this is not defective.

The ear, sound, and the substratum of sound—which is space—are the "ear, sound, and their substrata. It is not that these are themselves [the whole], but rather they exist as metaphorical designations due to the distinction of their conjuncts; thus, regarding the word "themselves," he says: "Nevertheless, this..."
The occurrence in a specific location, the necessity of being perceived, and so forth.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Of the manifestors," and so forth.
For the manifesting winds possess distinct locations for their constituent parts and a distinction in their genus; by that very fact, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is established as distinct.
Those whose locations for the constituent parts are distinct, being designated as the bases such as the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), are described in that way.
The state of having such distinct locations for the constituent parts is "distinctness of location" (*bhinnāvayavadeśatā*);
and there is also "difference of genus" (*jātibheda*).
Because of the difference in the causal complex, such as the difference in the nature of the substratum and so forth.

Now, was it not already stated that "the auditory organ, once refined, would perceive all sounds"? To this, he provides the answer beginning with "impelled for another purpose," etc.: "Just as wind impelled for one purpose does not produce another, so too that which is capable of refining one phoneme will not produce another."
"For the sake of another" means for the sake of producing another phoneme;
"capable of conditioning another phoneme."
The impression (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory faculty which has the purpose of perceiving another phoneme is expressed by the term "the impression of another phoneme";
it is not, however, the impression of the phoneme itself, because the impression of the auditory faculty is the subject under discussion.
[The phrase] "it will not produce another" [is used].
The meaning is that it will not embellish another phoneme by means of the embellishment of the auditory organ.
Alternatively, he says "by others," etc., to explain why this restriction applies specifically to the winds:
"Just as one phoneme is not produced by other conjunctions of the palate and so forth,
likewise, the projection of another sound does not occur through those [conjunctions] that produce a different sound."
The intention is that the manifesting breaths, which are the sounds (*dhvani*), are distinct due to the differences in the conjunction of the palate and other articulatory organs.
The phrase "the phoneme is not other" implies the ellipsis "is produced."
The "projection" (*kṣepa*) of other sounds means their impulsion.
There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the phrase "by means of the contacts of the palate and so forth that carry over to other sounds."
Therefore, he concludes:
"Therefore, since both production and manifestation are established through the presumption of an effect,
there would be an equal difference in capacity in all cases, whether regarding effort or the desire to speak."
The term *utpattyabhivyaktyoḥ* ends in the locative case.
Regarding both the production (*utpatti*) and the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of sound, the difference in capacity of effort (*prayatna*) and the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) is the same.
Why? Because it is understood through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the effect (*kāryānyathānupapatti*).
That is to say, because in both cases presumptive testimony based on the effect (kāryārthāpatti) is operative.

Thus far, it has been argued that there is no fault in the manifestation of sound through the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ—whether one accepts the auditory organ as being of the nature of space (*ākāśa*), as color-and-form (*varṇa*), or as the ear-cavity (*śaṣkulī*), according to their respective systems or common worldly understanding.

Now, however, relying on the auditory organ characterized as the quarters of space (*dik*) as established in the Veda, the author says "Or rather," etc., demonstrating that there is no fault in the manifestation of sound due to the specific refinements of that [organ]:
"Or rather, following the Veda, one should form the conviction that the quarters of space constitute the auditory organ."
For it is stated in the Veda that the sense of hearing is by no means composed of space and the other elements.
For it is said that "the quarters are the ear" during the periods of dissolution;
and that statement regarding [the senses] returning to their primordial nature is like the case of the eye and the other organs.
Regarding the phrase "the conviction that the quarters are the ear":
the meaning is that one must arrive at the certainty that the quarters themselves are the ear.
To the question "How so?", he says: "not consisting of space."
If this is so, and it is not even stated in the Veda that "the ear is the quarters," how then is this understood? To this he says: "The quarters are the ear," and so forth.

"Dissolutions" (layāḥ) mean mergings into their respective primordial natures (prakṛtiṣu), which are their inherent conditions (svabhāveṣu). At the time of destruction, the eyes and other senses of living beings dissolve into their own respective primordial natures.
And regarding that dissolution, it is said in the Veda with reference to the bound soul (paśu): "May his eye go to the sun, his hearing to the quarters.
Here too, the connection is with "may [it] cause to go";
thus, "gamayatāt."
The meaning is that whatever has come from a certain source should go back there.
Therefore, although it is not explicitly stated in the Veda that "the ear is the quarters," nevertheless,
by the force of the statement, "May he lead the ear to the quarters," this is indeed effectively stated.
To the question "How so?", he says "And that," and so forth.
That statement, "the ear goes to the directions," is intended to demonstrate that the ear returns to its primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The meaning is: let the ear, as the agent, go to the directions which constitute its primordial nature.
To the question "In what way?", he says: "Like the eye and so forth."
He explains this very point with the words "sūryam asya" and so forth:
"May his eye lead him to the sun, as has been stated."
The consciousness whose nature is fire is likewise the ear, which has space as its essence.

Just as by the statement "May his eye go to the sun," the knowledge of fire as its material cause (*tejaḥprakṛti*) is expressed—where "of the eye" is to be supplied as an ellipsis—in the same way, by the statement "The ear is the quarters," the ear is said to have the quarters as its nature; such is the connection of the words to be made.
The meaning is that "the knowledge of fire as its material cause" refers to having fire as its constituent essence (*tejomayatva*).
Now, as to what kind of direction that is, he says "Direction," and so forth:
Direction is one and all-pervading, established as far as space extends;
it is delimited by the cavity of the ear, like the auditory faculty which is a portion of space.
This is an elaboration of [the fact that] space is omnipresent, [expressed by the statement] "it is established as far as the sky extends.
If this were so, the distinction between the deaf and others would not be possible because direction is one; to this he says, "in the ear-cavity," and so forth.
Space is not the auditory organ in its entirety; rather, what is it?
It is delimited by the boundaries of the ear-cavity.

[Objection: But since it is partless, how can a division of parts be obtained for it? [Reply: He says, "as much as": whatever reasoning there may be for the assumption that space possesses motion, that same [reasoning] applies equally to its division according to directions; however, it is distinguished by scripture.
"Just as there is an assumption of parts for space due to the difference in its conjuncts, so too will it be for the directions.
To the question, "What then is the distinction of this [position] from the position that the ear is space?", he says: "From scripture (āgama)."
Therefore, by way of this conclusion, [the author] indicates the established status of the deaf and others:
"Therefore, that portion of the substance of space which is governed by merit and demerit,
and which is delimited by the cavity of the ear— that is the auditory organ (śrotra), and it is what is refined."
Demonstrating that there is no fault even in the view that the embellishment belongs to the object, he says: "Even in the case of the object's embellishment... [The verse continues:
"Even when the object is embellished by that [sound], only one [person] has it embellished;
and because of the difference in capacity among men, it is not perceived by all."
As for what was said—"In that case, the word would be perceived by everyone if it were being refined"—there is no fault therein.

Why? Because of the difference in the capacities of men; due to the proximity or non-proximity of the wind that refines the auditory organ, the refinement of the auditory organ differs, and thus there is a difference in capacity.

But surely, since sound is eternal and omnipresent, and thus indistinguishable with respect to all persons, how can there be both its apprehension and non-apprehension? To this he says, "Just as," and so forth:
"Just as this [sound], even while being produced, is not perceived by everyone..."
Although it exists for all [beings] through the distinctions of direction, place, and so forth, it...
In the same way, a sound whose refinement is produced by sounds situated nearby is heard by those very [hearers] who are near, but by no means by those situated at a distance.

Now, how is it determined that the refinement (saṃskāra) of the object arises from the winds and not from the object itself? To this he says: "Because the production of sound has been refuted" and so forth; because [the production of sound] is otherwise impossible.
The production of a specific refinement is determined from the sounds.
Since the omnipresence and unity of sound are established through recognition (pratyabhijñā), there is no production of sound.
Therefore, it is understood by implication that the production of a refinement (saṃskāra) arises from the articulated sounds (dhvani), but not the production of the sound itself.
But surely, as in the case of the seed and the sprout, the fact that words are the effects of sound is established by their occurring only when that [sound] exists (*tadbhāvabhāvitayā*).

For just as the sprout and so forth are known to be the effects of the seed and so forth because they are perceived only when the seed and so forth exist, likewise, since words are perceived only when sound exists, why should they not be its effects? For the conventional usage of "effect" is based solely on this much. To this, he says: "by their occurring only when that exists," and so forth.
And here, the state of being manifested by that [object] is what makes known the existence of the capacity;
this is accepted just like the capacity of the auditory organ, for the cognition is indeed withdrawn there.

For just as there is the perception of sound when the auditory organ exists, yet one does not infer from that—that the existence [of sound] follows from the existence [of the organ]—that the auditory organ possesses a power of producing sound; rather, it is a power of apprehending it. So too here, the fact that [the cognition] occurs when those [sounds] exist would merely indicate the presence of a general capacity for the sounds, but not a capacity for producing them. That is to say, its connection is with capacity in general, and not with a specific capacity. Therefore, it is established that this [reason] is inconclusive (vyabhicārin) when a specific capacity is the property to be proven (sādhya).
"How, then, is the specific nature of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) understood? To this he says: "For the cognition is withdrawn there.

Since permanence has been established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the author of the Bhāṣya has withdrawn the cognition to that specific latent impression by way of *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility otherwise); the meaning is that the power of the latent impression is not inferred merely from the fact that [the cognition] occurs when that [impression] exists.

Regarding what was said concerning the position that both [the speaker and the hearer] perform the refinement—that the faults stated for each individually would apply when both are refined—the author here replies: "But in the case of the position of dual refinement, those two faults are indeed in vain; for since [the word] is not perceived by anyone due to the deficiency of either one [of the two], those two faults are futile.
In the case of the position of dual refinement, those two faults are indeed in vain.
For because of the deficiency of either one, the word is not understood by anyone at all.
The two faults that were previously stated regarding both positions are indeed futile and meaningless.
To explain how this is so, he says "by which," and so forth.
"By which" means:
Because,
due to the deficiency of either the refinement of the auditory faculty or the refinement of the object,
the sound is not perceived.

For instance, even when there is refinement of the sound (*śabda-saṃskāra*), a deaf person does not perceive the sound due to the deficiency in the refinement of the auditory faculty (*śrotra-saṃskāra*). Likewise, for one who is not deaf, there is non-perception of the sound if it has not been manifested.
In some versions, the reading is: "The statement regarding these two faults is false."
And that is easily understood.
Now, if sound is omnipresent, how is it that its multiplicity is perceived through spatial division, as in the case of a jar or similar objects?
Since it exists everywhere, it would logically be perceived everywhere in an undivided form.
Furthermore, for something that is omnipresent, distinctions such as being distant or near are not tenable.
Nor can it come from any particular place, because it is present everywhere.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is eternal to possess distinctions of intrinsic nature such as long, short, slow, or faster;
nor is a distinction of time logical [for it].

Therefore, because it is perceived as distinct according to differences in place, time, and intrinsic nature—just like a jar and other objects—it is established that sound is both distinct and impermanent. How then can it be said: "Since the production of sound has been refuted, its [perception] is otherwise inexplicable; thus, the arising of a specific refinement from articulated sounds is determined"?
Thus it is said.
To this, he says: "In water and so forth," and so on.
Just as the single sun is perceived as having many forms in water and other media simultaneously, and yet there is no actual division in it, so too should sound be understood.
By this distinction of place, he states that the property of being perceived is inconclusive.

[Objection: "But surely, in the case of the sun, there exists a distinction in its substrates such as water and so forth, which causes the delusion of its multiplicity; however, here [in the case of sound], no cause for error is found. Since the reason (hetu) with its qualification was intended to mean 'when no cause for error exists,' how can the reason be subject to deviation (vyabhicāritā)? [Reply: He says: "Because it is dependent upon the manifesting sounds (dhvani).
Because it is dependent upon the manifesting sounds, it is perceived in that specific location.
And the capacity of sounds does not extend to pervade the entire sky without interruption.
Because it has been interrupted in form, that [word] is not perceived everywhere;
rather, in that case, the perception follows the sounds, since those sounds occupy different locations.
Because their internal spaces are not filled, a separation is perceived;
and because they occupy only a small portion [of space], there arises the notion that sound itself is non-omnipresent.
Because they possess motion and velocity, from whichever direction those [air currents] come,
the hearer perceives the sound as coming from that very direction.
In this case as well, it is the same: the difference between the manifesting sounds (*vyañjaka-dhvani*) exists as a cause for error.
This is because [the perception] is dependent upon the manifesting sounds;
the words "of the apprehension of the word" (*śabda-grahaṇasya*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
"In that place" means the place of the sound (*dhvani*). "That" refers to the word (*śabda*).
Explaining how the manifesting sound (*vyañjaka-dhvani*) becomes the cause of the illusion of being interrupted and so forth with respect to the word, he says "And not," and so on.
The word "asau" (this) refers to sound; "of the sound" is the ellipsis for "śrutiḥ" (hearing);
"therein" means in the location of space.
The phrase "the state of having the internal space filled by sounds" is to be understood [as the object of expectation].
And "of them" means "of the sounds."
They are called "sounds" (dhvanis) because they proceed from that [source]. //2211 //2212 //2213 //2214 //
But is it not the case that even for the sun, which is a single entity, its perception through spatial separation is unestablished?
For indeed, by means of the eye, distinct and separate reflections of the sun and so forth are discerned in each individual vessel;
but the sun itself is not.

Anticipating the objection of an opponent who thinks, "But for you, who do not accept the reflection as a distinct entity, we see no cause whatsoever for its perception when the original object is not perceived," he says "He said," and so forth:
"For what reason are the reflections, though distinct, perceived simultaneously and individually in each separate vessel by that [perceiver]?"
The opponent says:
"Simultaneously," that is,
by way of simultaneity (*yaugapadyena*).
To this, he states the following reply: "In this regard we say," and so forth.
Here we say that when, by the solar light shimmering in the water, the visual light is turned back in the opposite direction;
The sun assumes its own form in manifold ways according to the various vessels; since its form is thus divided, how can there be any multiplicity in its essence?

The visual light, having been turned back and drawn toward [the eye] by the solar light—which resides in the region of water and possesses the nature of flowing—is made to grasp the Sun, the Āditya, exactly where it is situated.
Just as the vessel [holds the reflection], so far as the vessel extends;
therefore, although it appears as a distinct form, how could there be any multiplicity for it? Certainly not, because the activity of the eye is one—this is the intended meaning.
Showing that even though it is not actually divided, it is perceived as if divided solely by virtue of the activity of the eye, he says "slightly," and so forth:
"Just as when the eye is slightly pressed with a finger,
even a single object is perceived as distinct due to the differentiation of the eye's activity, so it is for us."
Slightly, even a little:
when the eye is closed or pressed with a finger, even a single object appears as distinct and manifold. Why? Because of the diversity of the visual faculty's functioning (*cakṣur-vṛtti*).
In exactly the same way, not even a single distinct sound will be apprehended by us; thus, there is no fault.
"But others," etc.
However, others who seek the arising of a reflection raise this objection:
"If that very [object] were perceived, why is it not seen above?"
How could there be a perception of a reflection from below in wells and the like?
And how could one who is facing east, while looking at a mirror, become one who faces west?

Thinking that the argument previously stated—that "just as even the single sun is seen as having a manifold nature in water and other media"—is subject to the fallacy of an inconclusive reason (*hetv-avyabhicāra*), those who maintain that the reflection is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) raise this objection:
"If it is the very same sun that is being seen and not a reflection, then why is it not seen above?
For its perception would indeed be such [as you claim] only if it were grasping the actual form situated in its own location."
It cannot be otherwise;
for if it were otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle.
Furthermore, how could the sun and other distant objects be perceived when they are situated far below in wells and the like?
If a reflection were not produced there,
for the sun and so forth are not actually situated there in that manner;
moreover, how could one who is facing east while looking into a mirror become facing west?
For at that time, his face was not seen turned toward his back.
With the verse beginning "apsūrya" (the sun in the water), he prescribes [the following]:
For those who see the sun in the water, the eye constantly functions in two ways;
one part goes upward and the other downward. Among these, that which is illuminated by the upward rays [perceives the sun].
Because it does not abide directly upon its substratum, the Self does not reach the sun;
though it is situated beyond the further shore, it perceives it through a downward-turned function.
Because it is one with that [sun], one perceives its upward movement as if it were downward;
for that reason, the sun is perceived as being directly below, even though there is an intervening space.
He thinks as follows: if the sense-organ, having gone outside, were to perceive the sun, then it would follow that one would see it only when situated above and not below.
However, that sense-organ is held to be the perceiver only within the body, which is governed by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and not when situated above.
As it has been said: "If the sense-organ, having gone outside, were to perceive the object right there [in the external world]..."
"Therefore, this would indeed be so; [it is] the awakener of reality within the body. Such is the sequence:
for those who see both the water and the sun in a vessel of water, the single eye of those beholding the solar reflection in the water functions in two parts, one upward and one downward.

Therein, the Self, as the Puruṣa, does not perceive the sun manifested by the upward part. Why? Because the locus is not straight; that is, because the locus of the visual organ is not then situated in a straight line [with the object].
However, by means of a serial transmission of solar radiance, the sun is perceived through its downward function, which serves as the instrumental cause.

For indeed, it is said that the solar radiance imparts itself to the luminous body, the luminous body to the function, and the function to the eye, and the eye to the self; this is the serial transmission from the luminous sun. Thus, one regards the sun—which is actually above and possesses an upward function—as if it were below, as if situated beneath.
What is the self?
It is not something other than the sun situated below; why? Because of its oneness—that is, because that sun is non-different [from it].
Others say it is the eye.

Therefore, precisely because the visual organ functions without being obstructed, the sun is seen below with an intervening space in wells and the like, as well as [reflected] in water and so forth due to the differences in the vessels;
otherwise, how could there be a perception of it without distinction? //2221//
Regarding what was stated previously—"one looking at a mirror facing east," and so forth—it is said there:
"In this way," and so on.
In this manner, by means of the eastward-turned function, that which is presented by the westward-turned function [is perceived].
Perceiving the face through delusion, one understands it to be the inner self.

It is said that first the visual rays go out from the face toward the location of the mirror and so forth; this is called the forward movement (*prāṅ-vṛtti*). When those rays strike the mirror or similar surface and return, they reach one's own face exactly as it is situated; this is the backward movement (*pratyag-vṛtti*).

In this regard, the forward-directed activity (prāṅnatā vṛtti) presents its own face to the inward-directed activity; and that inward-directed activity [presents it] to the Self. Consequently, the Self—due to delusion—thinks, "I shall go toward my own face," which is actually presented by the inward-directed activity as being turned away from itself.
The point is that the very diversity of the visual activity is the seed of this delusion.
Having accepted the arising of a reflection as a solution, he says: "And even if it exists in multiple locations," and so forth.
Even though the reflection exists in multiple locations, because it is apprehended by a single cognition, its plurality does not exist at all.
Even though the reflection is a distinct entity, there is no plurality among those reflections;
why? Because they are apprehended by a single cognition, being accessible to a common cognition.
Likewise, since sound too is accessible to a single cognition, its unity is established.
But surely, how could there not be a plurality for that which is perceived as being in different locations?

Surely, since its distinctness is established by the fact of being perceived in different locations, how can that be sublated by a single cognition? To this he says "by difference of location," and so forth:
"This distinctness due to difference of location is inferential."
But since that very [object] is directly perceived, the cognition [of it] serves as a sublater.
"An obstructer" (bādhaka):
the sense is that perception is the eldest among all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Demonstrating that the state of being perceived is inconstant due to differences in place and time, and thus constitutes a lack of validity, he says "paryāyeṇa" and so forth:
"Just as a single [object], though moving through different places in succession... [p. 616]
Just as Devadatta does not split, so too sound does not split.
Likewise, it should be understood that the word "not different" refers to [difference] in terms of place and time.
Thus, by way of deviation in space, the deviation of both has been stated.
Now, by way of deviation due to the difference in time, he states the deviation of both perceptions—those occurring at different places and times—with the words "jñātaikatva" and so forth:
"Just as one thing, whose unity is known, when being seen again and again..."
Sound is not [differentiated] by a difference in time, nor likewise by a difference in location.
He whose cognition is oneness through recognition and so forth is "thus" (tathā).
The phrase "not by way of place" is an illustration; likewise, he is not different even by way of time.
Because there is no contradiction, the demonstration of deviation in other cases is made by means of the deviation in the single instance.

With the words "paryāyāt" and so forth, he raises the objection that the example is dissimilar: "If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of succession, let it be seen that this is also due to omnipresence;
for whatever property is established by observation is accepted as belonging to all."

For instance, in the case of Devadatta, even though he is perceived at different places and times, there is no difference [in his identity]; in that case, there exists a cause for non-contradiction in the form of "paryāya" (successive occurrence). But in the case of sound, there is nothing of the sort; therefore, there is a disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration.
To this, he states the cause for non-contradiction here as well: "Let it be seen also because of its pervasiveness.
The connection is with the word "non-contradiction" (*avirodha*).
By the word "also" (*api*), he indicates both this point—that "the intervals between sounds are not filled"—and that which was stated previously.
To the question, "Why is pervasiveness accepted? he replies: "For the sake of establishing what is observed" (*dṛṣṭasiddhyai hi*).

That property which is appropriate for the purpose of establishing the perception of a single sound across different directions and locations is accepted precisely because it cannot be explained otherwise (*anyathānupapattyā*).

And here, since the apprehension of sound at all times and in all places would not be established without its being eternal and omnipresent, its eternity and omnipresence are established through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti).

Demonstrating that even the state of being perceived through a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāritā*), he says: "Just as in a large dug-out pit of earth there is a cognition of vastness in the sky,
and in a small one a cognition of smallness, so too is the cognition regarding that which is absolutely unproduced."
Therefore, in this very context, there is a confusion of thought regarding the application of the term "extrinsic adjunct" (paropādhi);
moreover, grossness and subtlety are not perceived as residing within the word itself.
The conception of intensity or dullness in cognition is a conceptualization of magnitude or smallness;
and that [conception] indeed becomes sharp when [an object] is illuminated by a great light.
When manifested feebly, [the cognition] is always feeble even with respect to a jar and the like;
thus it is established that all such properties as length and so forth are attributes of the sound.
The intended meaning here is as follows: if the distinctions such as intensity and dullness residing in the sound are adduced as the reason (*hetu*), then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For how could one who maintains that sound is eternal assert that it possesses intrinsic distinctions (*svabhāvabheda*) based on external conditions?

Alternatively, if the cognition of those objects characterized by intensity, dullness, and so forth is stated as the reason—since that cognition is not possible without a distinction in the intrinsic nature [of the object]—then the reason remains unestablished.
In that case, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For just as when a large pit is dug in the earth, a cognition of "largeness" and so forth arises with respect to the sky (*vyoma*) or space (*ākāśa*) which rests therein—even though largeness and such qualities do not exist in space by its own nature—likewise, even in the case of sound, which is absolutely uncreated (*atyantākṛtrima*), this difference in cognition will arise due to the difference in the manifesting sounds (*vyañjaka-dhvani-bheda*), even without any such difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*).
He states this very point in the passage beginning with "Therefore, in this case, thus... and so forth.

If it is asked, "How is it known that this [intensity] is due to external conditions (*paropādhi*) and not inherent in the sound itself? he says, "And not... and so forth.
