By this he means the following: one is deluded by superimposing the intensity and dullness—which actually belong only to the cognition—onto the sound; however, there is no possibility of grossness and so forth existing in the sound inherently, because its oneness is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Furthermore, if it were argued, "If there were no such difference in the nature of the object, from where would the difference in cognition arise? he says, "And that [cognition] is sharp," and so forth.

For just as in the case of a jar and so forth, even though there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), a distinction will arise from a distinction in manifestation; thus, there is no fault in [the case of cognition] where there is no inherent difference in intrinsic nature. //2230–2231//
Furthermore, demonstrating that the proposition of the impermanence of sound is contradicted by the fact that the expressive capacity of sound would otherwise be inexplicable, he says:
"And a word whose connection with its object has not been perceived cannot be expressive;
for if it were so, even every entirely new [word] would convey its own meaning."

This presumption (*arthāpatti*) is preceded by another presumption; for the expressive capacity of a word is established through the fact that verbal cognition would otherwise be inexplicable. That capacity, moreover, is itself inexplicable without the eternity of the word. Thus, this is a presumption preceded by a presumption. He explains this very point in detail: "A word does not become expressive by its mere existence as long as its relationship [with its meaning] has not been grasped.
If it were so... [he says].

If even that which has no perceived relationship [with its object] were to be expressive, then even a word such as "cow" (*go*), previously unheard and never before encountered by inhabitants of the Coconut Island (*nālikeradvīpa*), would manifest its own meaning.

[618] But surely, since there is no dispute on this point among anyone, the argument proves what is already established; for no one accepts that a word whose connection [to its object] is unknown can be expressive.

How then is it established by this [argument] that it has a known connection, given that it is eternal? To this he says: "The observation of the connection," and so forth. And the observation of its connection is not possible for something that is non-eternal.
If the establishment of the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning] is required, then its persistence over a period of time is certain.
Having placed the word and its meaning before one, their relationship is established, and once established, it would be known at a later time;
however, because a word perishes as soon as it is uttered, this is untenable.
Thus he says: "It is not possible for that which is impermanent."
If it were to remain for that long, then alas, its continued existence at other times as well would be unavoidable, since there is no contradiction;
as it has been said: "Who could destroy this thing after it has remained stable for that duration?"

Furthermore, it might be argued that [the word] would persist until the time of the connection [with its meaning] and subsequently perish of its own accord; to this he says "in another," and so forth:
When the connection has been known in one case, another [word] cannot be the communicator [of that meaning].
For when the connection has been known in the word "cow" (go), the word "horse" (aśva) is not the denoter.
"In another [time]" means at the time when the convention occurs.
The remainder is easily understood.
With the word "Now" (atha), he anticipates the opponent's objection:

"But suppose there is some other [cause] which, by its very nature, is the awakener; since there would be no restrictive basis for that, how could there be a certain determination as to what that [nature] is?"
Now, as for the argument that "another [word] also [could be expressive]"—

if it is claimed that a word existing at the time of usage would be expressive by its very nature, just like a word existing at the time of the convention, that is incorrect; because, in the absence of a basis, there can be no certainty that this particular word is the expressive signifier of this particular object.

But surely, how can it be said that there is no certainty? For since that from which the cognition of an object arises is clearly ascertained to be the indicator of the object by its very nature—thus he says "yataḥ" and so forth: "Since the conventional usage is established merely by the fact that 'from this [cause] there is a cognition,' this might indeed be so for the listeners, but it is not tenable for the speakers."
It is true that for listeners (*śrotr̥̄ṇām*), this certainty may arise—that "this [word] is the communicator of this meaning"—because for them, the cognition of the object arises from it.

For speakers (*prayokt̥̄ṇām*), however, this is difficult to obtain; for they do not themselves comprehend the object from that word, but rather employ the word solely for the purpose of communicating to another.
How, then, can a definitive conclusion be reached by those who speak?
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "without knowing," and so forth:
"How could that person intend to speak the word at the very outset without having known it? If he knows it, then it must necessarily have been apprehended by him previously."

Thus, this fault applies to the position of ignorance; however, even in the position of knowledge, since it must necessarily have been known previously, its permanence follows by force of logic. Demonstrating this, he says: "If [the self] knows," and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Just as light from a lamp or similar source illuminates an object even though it is newly produced, so too will a word convey its meaning. To this he replies: "Because light is subordinate to perception... "Light is an illuminator despite its novelty, because it is subordinate to perception; but a word is not expressive even at a distance, because its similarity [to the object] is not perceived."
Being subsidiary to perception (*pratyakṣaśeṣatvam*) means being a constituent part (*aṅgabhāva*) of perception.

By means of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of its object or the refinement of the sense faculty, it becomes a manifestor even though it is new, as it attains the status of a constituent part within perceptual cognition.
Since sound directly conveys objects that transcend the senses, it is not a constituent part of perception; therefore, there is a difference [between the two].
Alternatively, that which is an auxiliary factor of perception reveals its object even without depending on the thorough knowledge of a relationship,
just as the eye and light are auxiliary factors of perception;
therefore, it reveals even something previously unknown.
But there is a disparity [between perception and verbal testimony], because sound, having as its object that which is beyond the senses, is not an auxiliary factor of perception.
Now, one might argue that even a new word will be expressive by following its similarity to a previous one; to this he says, "because similarity is not perceived," and so forth.
For it is not logical that expressiveness occurs through the medium of similarity when that similarity is unperceived, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, let alone the cognition of similarity; demonstrating that similarity itself is impossible, he says:
"And on the basis of the similarity of which single [object] could another be conceived as its designator, when the previous [objects] are equal in their lack of perceived connection?"
If it is argued that [the object] was previously seen as possessing its meaning, how could it have such a brief duration?
For that which is not perceived two or three times is not recognized as possessing its meaning.

For if one expressive word were established as such, another might be postulated as being likewise on account of its similarity to it; however, that is not possible, because all words are perceived as being connected with their meanings.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "That word which was observed previously at the time of the convention is indeed meaningful, while the others will possess similarity [to it]. To this he replies: "From where could it have such duration? For how could that previously observed word persist for such a length of time, given that it perishes as soon as it is uttered?
If it is argued, "Even if [a word] perishes as soon as it is uttered, why should it not still possess meaning? he replies with the words "twice or thrice," and so forth.
For the knowledge of the relationship between a word and its meaning arises from repeated observation.

Now, if it is argued that it is precisely that word which becomes meaningful when other words of the same class are not apprehended, that is incorrect; thus he says: "For those who have not perceived other words," and so forth.
"At that time, for those who have not perceived other words, it is meaningless;
yet for those who hear other words, it would be meaningful—this is a marvel!"

For those cognizers to whom another word is not yet known, that [word] does not convey the meaning at the time of hearing, because at that time there is an absence of similarity based on a perceived difference.
Yet, for those very same cognizers once they have come to know other words, that very same [word] conveys the meaning; this is extraordinary.
For how indeed could action and non-action, which are mutually contradictory, belong to one and the same [person]?
"Those for whom there is another hearing" means those perceivers whose hearing has as its object other words of the same class.

Having thus established the permanence of the word through the impossibility of its denotative function otherwise, he now says "First, the word... and so forth, establishing it through the impossibility of the creation of the relationship [between word and meaning] otherwise: "First, the creation of the relationship is not possible without having uttered the word; nor is there any use for a relationship with that which has perished as soon as it is uttered."
Because it is lost due to that lack of connection, the former [word] is indeed meaningless;
how could the latter be understood as meaningful when its connection has not been established?

First there is the utterance, then the establishment of the relationship [between word and meaning], and then linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). How could such a sequential process of usage occur for that which is non-sequential and perishes as soon as it is uttered? Not only is it impossible to establish a relationship with what has already perished, but there is no purpose in doing so either, because it does not persist until the time of usage, and because the convention (*saṅketa*) exists solely for the sake of usage.
He concludes with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
That which lacks a connection is "unconnected. Because it has perished from its true nature, the word existing at the time of the convention is first of all meaningless.
To the objection that the word existing at the time of practical usage will then be meaningful, he replies with the words "The latter," and so forth.

If, then, the sequential utterance and so forth of that which is non-sequential are untenable, let them occur simultaneously; to this he says, "The utterance of words," and so on: "Who could ever perform at once anywhere the actions pertaining to the utterance of words, the establishment of their relations, and conventional usage, since they are by nature sequential?"
The utterance of a word, the establishment of its relationship [with its meaning], and worldly usage—these three actions are by their very nature successive; they cannot be performed simultaneously.
And if simultaneity were absent, the establishment of the relationship would be impossible.
If one were to wait for this succession, it would have to be admitted that the word persists for a period of time.
"Of those divided by place, time, and so forth" is the conclusion.
Because for persons divided by place, time, and so forth, another word is not heard,
even a single word with an artificial connection is not established beforehand.
Even when explaining the relationship [between words and objects], this same rebuttal would apply:
for it is impossible to provide a description of things that have perished, those that are non-existent, or those that are present [only momentarily].
By the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of stages such as infancy, childhood, and so forth is intended.
Regarding the term "previously" (pūrvam), it should be connected with the phrase "because of hearing another word" (śabdāntaraśruteḥ).
"Perished," and so forth:
"perished" means past; "non-existent" means future. Since neither of these two exists, it is impossible for them to have what is called a relationship.
Even the present [word], while being uttered, perishes immediately after; how then could it endure for such a duration of time?
He demonstrates this very point with the words "meaningful," and so forth:
"Let it be stated which word is meaningful for both the listener and the speaker;
for when a word has been heard previously, that [same] word cannot be uttered [anew]."
First of all, he does not utter a word that possesses meaning; rather, he would speak what is similar [to it].
However, a word that is similar to one possessing meaning cannot logically apply to the hearer in that context.
Because there is no apprehension of it as possessing meaning, it does not itself possess meaning;
this same consequence follows when the speaker becomes a listener.
For a speaker is not able to communicate to a listener what was previously heard, because that [previous cognition] has already ceased. Furthermore,
even that which he attempts to demonstrate, he would be unable to demonstrate as possessing meaning,
because its connection [with words] had not been established previously.
It might be thought that one could say something "similar" to this;
however, even that is not possible, as he says: "not similar to that which possesses meaning," and so forth.
For no similarity with anything whatsoever is intended here; rather, [the similarity is intended] with that which possesses meaning, and that is untenable.

For if some word were perceived by the listener as possessing meaning, then its similarity [to another] would be possible; however, since at the time of the initial convention there was no apprehension of it as possessing meaning, this is not tenable.
To the objection that "the one being uttered now will then be meaningful," he says: "And not that," and so forth.
And that which is being uttered is not meaningful, because—as has been stated—it lacks a previously established relationship [with its meaning].

By the words "of the speaker," etc., he demonstrates that when the speaker himself becomes a listener in turn, then for him too this entire collection of faults arises—namely, that "he does not utter a word possessing a [real] meaning," and so forth.
Thus, by this, it is stated that for all speakers whatsoever, no word at all is possible that possesses a [real] meaning. //2249 //2250 //2251 //
Therefore, he concludes with the word "tasmāt" (therefore):
"Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning must be accepted as being indeed eternal;
it is not logical for it to be conventional, because that is impossible in every respect."
With the words "svataḥ" (by itself) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's prima facie argument:
"The expressive power of the signified and the signifier does not exist inherently between them;
if it is argued that human cognition arises from convention, like the winking of an eye."

The expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*) of the signifier and the expressed power (*vācya-śakti*) of the signified do not exist inherently (*svābhāvikī*) between them respectively. If so, how does cognition arise from a word? To this he says: "Cognition [arises] from convention" (*samayāt*), and so forth. That whose causal status with respect to something depends upon a convention is not inherent to it, as in the case of a wink regarding comprehension; and since the causal status of a word with respect to comprehension depends upon convention, there is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).
And by this, he refutes in detail the objection raised against the proposition of impermanence.

He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "samaya" and so forth: "Is the convention (samaya) established for each individual person, or for each utterance, or was it created once at the beginning of the world by some single being?"
Furthermore, the relationship would have to be either distinct for each [individual] or it would be one;
if it were one, it could not be produced, and if it were distinct, there would be a cognition of difference.

"This is its name"—this convention (*saṃketa*) might be established for the sake of comprehension either with respect to each individual person, or it might be established at the beginning of the world, at the time of the world's creation, by some creator such as Īśvara, all at once and effortlessly; thus there are three alternatives. Or, it may be [established] for each [person].

Furthermore, regarding the relationship between word and meaning, if it were being established, one would have to consider two possibilities: either it would differ for every sentient being, or it would be one and the same.
On the view that it is one, because it would follow [through] the differences of genus, place, and time, it could not be something produced;
the implication is that it would necessarily be eternal.

If, on the other hand, [the word] possessed a distinct nature for each individual being, then a cognition of difference would necessarily arise for each being, because the difference in cognitions is based upon the difference in the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). However, even when words such as "cow" are employed a hundred times, no cognition of difference arises for those engaged in linguistic usage, since their usage proceeds solely through the determination of non-difference.

Furthermore, if the relation were distinct for each individual being, then there would necessarily be a cognition of difference; consequently, the cessation of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) would follow. Demonstrating this, he says: "Because of the difference between the cognitions of the speaker and the hearer...
[p.623] ...And because of the difference between the cognitions of the speaker and the hearer, linguistic convention is impaired.
For the relationship [of the word] is one thing for the speaker in his own mind, while it is another for the listener.
Regarding the phrase "due to difference" (*bhedāt*):
the word "of the object" (*viṣayasya*) is to be supplied.

By this, the meaning becomes as follows: because there is a difference between the objects that are the contents of the cognitions of the speaker and the listener, linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) could not occur through the determination of a single object.
To the question "How so?", he says: "For [the object] is other than the speaker."

Regarding what was said—that the convention (*samaya*) pertains either to each individual person—the author states the refutation: "To whom could the speaker resort in order to establish the relationship for both the hearer and himself? and so forth.
To whom could the speaker resort in order to establish the relationship for both the hearer and himself?
For that which has already been seen by him does not produce it for the listener.

Even that which produces something new does not establish [the existence of a universal], if you argue that this is the same in the case of a jar and so forth; [we reply] no, because the universal is well-established.
Although an individual whose capacity is already known cannot be produced,
that which is produced has not yet had its capacity for the effect ascertained.
Nevertheless, the capacity for pronunciation and so forth is established by way of the form (ākṛti);
that [capacity] has no beginning, whereas the relationship [between word and meaning] is therefore something that has a beginning.
If its universal is also admitted to be eternal, even so our own position is established; however, the possibility of two forms [of the universal] does not arise.
For the relation is indeed nothing but power (śakti), and no difference in this [power] is perceived;
since it is to be inferred from its effects, it conforms to their differences.
And the postulation of the existence of a power is based on the impossibility of [the effect] occurring otherwise;
however, when the purpose is accomplished by one alone, the postulation of many is not desired.
It does not produce that [cognition] for the hearer because it has perished; thus,
it is not a demonstrator of what has been seen.
Because it has not been previously seen;
[the phrase] "even in the case of a jar and so forth" raises a doubt regarding the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the refutation by pointing out an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

The same logical consequence applies even to things such as a jar; for instance, that jar which is seen to be capable of causal efficiency cannot be produced, because it has already been completed and then perished.
And that which is being produced now is not seen to be capable of causal efficiency, because it is not yet completed.
To this, the author replies: "Not so, because [the capacity] is established through its general nature (*sāmānya*)."
"No" is the rejection of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
Why?
Because the existence of the universal (sāmānya) has been established.
The meaning is that this is established by implication through its distance [from the subject].
Clarifying this very point, he says "yadyapi" and so forth:
although an individual jar whose capacity for fetching water and such has been observed cannot be produced, because it would have already perished once it was completed.
Even if the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) has not been ascertained in a particular instance that is currently present,
nevertheless, the capacity for causal efficiency is established in every individual instance precisely by means of its generic form (*ākṛti*).
To explain how this is so, he says "tasyāḥ" and so forth.
"Of that" refers to the generic form (*ākṛti*).
In some places, the reading is "nor has it a beginning" (*na ca tasyādimattā*);
this is its meaning: nor does that capacity for fetching water and so forth have a beginning, because the generic form is eternal.
And because that [universal] is absolutely non-different from its substratum, as it has been said: "The distinctness of genus and so forth from the individual is not at all established.
If it is argued that the relation, too, may be beginningless by way of the form (ākṛti), he says "But the relation... and so on, to show that this is incorrect.

Furthermore, even if you were to accept that the relationship between word and meaning possesses an eternal universal (*sāmānya*), our position—that what is called "eternal" is not a real entity—would still be established.
If it is argued that the word itself is not established in this context, he says: "(... but the occurrence of two forms is not possible.
The two forms are the relationship and its universal.
Only a single form is possible, but not a universal, because that [universal] must reside in multiple individuals, whereas the relation is unitary.
To the question, "How is the relation unitary?", he says: "For it is indeed power," and so forth.
For there is no relation distinct from the capacities themselves.
If that is indeed the case, what follows? To this he says: "And difference," etc.
Difference is not oneness.

Regarding the question "Why is she not seen?", he states the reason with the words "For she... and so forth. For she is always to be inferred from her effects, as it has been said: "The powers of all entities are established through the presumption based on their effects."
Consequently, it conforms to and follows after a difference in effects (*kāryabheda*) in order to indicate a difference residing in itself;
the meaning is that without the observation of a difference in effects, it is impossible to know a difference in capacities (*śaktibheda*).
And in this case, no difference in effects exists.
For its effect is indeed cognition; and that cognition must have either the word as its object or the meaning as its object.

First, there is no distinction in the case of the former, because the word is always recognized as being the same. Nor is there a distinction in the case of the cognition having the meaning as its object, for even when the word "cow" and others are uttered a hundred times, no different kind of cognition arises.
He states the [opponent’s] accumulation [of arguments] with the words "otherwise," and so forth.
For it is by the impossibility of the cognition of meaning that the power between the signified and the signifier is postulated.
And since the intended object is established by a single power alone, the postulation of multiple powers is purposeless.

Nor can a difference in powers be inferred on the grounds of "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti), because that [reason] is effective only with respect to the mere existence of a power. //2257//56//
For this reason as well, it is illogical for the relation to be produced; therefore, demonstrating that the relation is indeed eternal, he says:
"And at the time of explaining the relation," and so forth. "When a word such as 'cow' is uttered, some understand it for the sake of the cognition of the relation, while others do not."
In that regard, if the connection did not exist, no one would ascertain any object;
if it did exist, there would be universal cognition, because nothing would remain ungrasped by anyone.

For instance, when it is said, "This cow must not be touched with the foot," some persons, having ascertained the relationship between the signifier and the signified, understand the meaning precisely by means of that relationship;
others, however, whose knowledge of the relationship is lacking, perceive only the phonetic form itself and not the meaning.
In that case, if the relationship were not a real entity (*vastubhūta*), then no person at all—even one who is proficient in linguistic usage—would ever ascertain the meaning.
For existence and non-existence, being mutually contradictory, are not possible for a single thing;
therefore, the relationship is indeed eternally established.

Anticipating the objection—"If the relationship is eternally established, why is there no comprehension of meaning for everyone at all times?"—the author provides a detailed rebuttal, beginning with the words "existence" (*astitva*).
"No" serves to avert this undesirable consequence;
why? Because it is not apprehended by anyone.
Even if it has indeed not been apprehended, why would it not produce its own effect?
For seeds and the like do not abandon their own function simply because they are situated within a hole in the ground or a chasm; thus he says, "Because it is a signifier," and so forth.
For a relation, being a signifier, depends upon the cognition of its own nature.
Therefore, although it exists, that illuminator is not apprehended.
For the property of an indicator is one thing, while that of a producer is another; since a word is an indicator of an object like smoke, but not a producer of it like a seed, there is no fault.
But surely, existence and non-existence are untenable for a single thing because they are mutually contradictory; likewise, apprehension and non-apprehension [would be contradictory].
If there is no contradiction between these two, then what is this hostility toward existence and non-existence? To this he says: "Of an existing object," and so forth.
It is observed that an existing object is sometimes not apprehended.
But the existence of that which is absolutely non-existent is not established in any way whatsoever.

Existence and non-existence, being contradictory, cannot both belong to a single entity; nor is the contradiction between "being known" and "not being known" the same as that between existence and non-existence.
For knowledge has the person as its locus; thus, it is not contradicted by the differences [between persons].
Furthermore, the knowledge residing in another person is not excluded by that [knowledge].

For the superimposition of mutually contradictory properties upon a single substratum (*dharmin*) is a contradiction, but not so upon different substrata. Since apprehension and non-apprehension have as their locus different substrata depending on the difference of persons, they are not contradictory; however, existence and non-existence are not [non-contradictory], because it is accepted that those two must have a single substratum. This is the summary of the meaning. //2267//

But surely, even in the case of the two positions regarding apprehension and non-apprehension, by implication, existence and non-existence—which are mutually contradictory—would likewise necessarily occur in a single substratum. For apprehension and non-apprehension are pervaded by the existence and non-existence of the object-entity, since the former are dependent upon the latter. Otherwise, one would have to state the reason why, between two persons in equal proximity and possessing equal sensory capacity, only one sees while the other does not. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The blind and the non-blind," and so forth.
A white object situated near the blind is not perceived by the blind, yet it is perceived by others; therefore, its existence or non-existence does not depend upon them.

For just as when a form is situated near both a blind person and one with unimpaired vision, only the latter perceives it and not the former, yet its existence or non-existence as a white form does not depend upon them; so it is with respect to the relation as well.
To dispel the expectation as to what the reason for this is, he states the justification beginning with "śaktyaśaktyoḥ" and so forth:
"But because of the difference between the capacities and incapacities of men, there is no contradiction in that case;
for indeed, there is no other cause here for the perception [of the object] than its connection [with the sense organ]."

This explains that the existence of the object (*arthasattā*) alone is not the cause of its apprehension; rather, it is the capacity residing in the person (*puruṣagata-śakti*). Therefore, even when an object exists, its non-apprehension by a certain person due to a lack of capacity is not contradictory; thus, non-apprehension is not pervaded by the existence of the object. If this is so, then even in the absence of a [real] relation, the apprehension and non-apprehension of an object will occur for persons due to the distinction between their capacity and incapacity, and everything remains the same. To this, [the author replies] with "for there is no other," etc. The sense is that the cognition of an object is preceded by the apprehension of the relation.
The word "other" is connected with the reason; [the phrase] "of perception" refers to the cognition of the meaning of a word.
The sixth case ending in the word *hetuḥ* expresses this dependence;
the fifth case ending in *sambandhāt* expresses dependence on something else;
and *atra* refers to the linguistic usage of words and their meanings.

Others, however, explain that there is no contradiction therein because of the difference between the capacities and incapacities of men; they interpret the phrase "due to the connection" (*sambandhāt*) as meaning "due to the capacity of the person" (*puruṣa-śakteḥ*),
and "herein" (*atra*) as referring to the white [substance].
Concluding the application of the example, he says "In this very way," and so forth:
"In this very same way, the perception of conventional usage is equal to the sense faculties;
those who possess it understand the object from that [perception], while others do not, like the blind."
That from which conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) proceeds is "conventional usage," namely, the relationship between word and object.
The apprehension (*upalambhana*) of that is its thorough knowledge;
this is equal to [the function of] the sense faculties.
For it is thus:
those who possess the sense faculty perceive the object; however, those who do not possess it do not perceive the object even when the object is present.
Thus, it is said that those who possess the thorough knowledge of the relationship understand the meaning from the word;
however, for those who do not possess it, they do not perceive it even though the relationship exists—everything else being the same.
It must be stated by whom this relationship was first communicated to its initial creator. If you say it was by himself, that is not so, because the same consequence would apply to others as well.
If you say it was from another, and for that one also from yet another, then, since there is thus no beginning, it is shown by the words "of all," etc., that it is not created by anyone:
"Because for all those who are ignorant [of its origin], it is established through a continuous succession of predecessors."
Since the relationship is established as such, no beginning of the relationship or the like exists.
The relationship between word and meaning is preceded by the linguistic usage of elders, because it is a relationship, like any other relationship existing at present;
and that which is the subject of dispute is indeed a relationship—this is an argument based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Thus, it has first been established that a convention is not possible for each individual person; now, refuting the claim that it occurs with every utterance, he says "pratyuccāraṇa" and so forth:
"The production [of a convention] at every utterance is not tenable from the standpoint of worldly practice;
moreover, there is no such activity at the beginning of creation, for such a time is not admitted."
For it is maintained that the entire world has never been otherwise than it is now;
even so-called "great dissolution" is not known to exist in an ultimate sense.
Night is indeed called dissolution (pralaya) because all activities are absorbed therein;
and day is designated as creation (sṛṣṭi) because it brings forth all movements.
Dissolution may take the form of the destruction of a region or the destruction of a lineage;
however, we have no authoritative means of knowledge regarding a dissolution that consists in the total annihilation of everything.

"From the perspective of conventional usage" means from the occurrence of linguistic convention; for otherwise, since no prior connection [between word and object] would have been established, the occurrence of linguistic convention would not be possible— this is the sense.
Regarding what was stated—that [the world] exists both now and at the beginning of the universe—he provides the rebuttal with the words "at the beginning of creation" (*sargādau*).
"Of such a kind" (*tādṛk*) means devoid of the relationship between word and object, consisting of the cycle of creation and transmigration.
"Not of such a kind" (*anīdṛśam*) means...
[The world] consists of the total cessation [of existence], because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for its existence.
If so, how is the conventional usage of terms such as "dissolution" (pralaya) established in the world? To this he says: "There is no great dissolution," and so forth.
"It is known" means by the world;
"ultimate" means pertaining to the ultimate truth.
The intention is that the imagined nature (parikalpita), which consists of the total annihilation [of things], is not to be rejected.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "or night," and so forth.
Then, he asks why the ultimate nature (pāramārthika) is not accepted, and answers with the words "but at the time of dissolution," and so forth. //2274//

Granted that there may be an ultimate dissolution (*pralaya*), nevertheless, since at that time there would be no creator such as Īśvara or anyone else who possesses unimpaired impressions (*saṃskāra*) of memory and wisdom, it is not logical for there to be a cause for the [re-establishment of] the relationship [between word and meaning]. Demonstrating this, he says:

"And there is no one with unimpaired memory," and so forth: "And there is no one with unimpaired memory, such as Īśvara or another, who is stable and capable of performing creation and dissolution, and who could establish the relationship."
"It is not tenable" because that has been refuted in detail.
With the words beginning with "nanu," he anticipates the opponent's objection:
"But surely, because the sequence is impermanent, the expressive word would be impermanent;
for it is the word that is accepted as the expressive unit, and the cognition of it depends upon the sequence."

For it is the sequential arrangement (*ānupūrvī*) that is intended as the word (*pada*), not the *sphoṭa*; and since that sequence is dependent upon human will, it is impermanent. Consequently, the letters (*varṇa*) themselves would also result in being impermanent, because the sequence is not something distinct from the letters.
To explain how this is so, he says "the word," and so forth.

For it is held that the word, consisting of phonemes, alone is the signifier; since the cognition of a word is produced by the sequence of phonemes and not by a *sphoṭa*, and that sequence is of human origin.
He explains this very point with the verse beginning "Because the phonemes are omnipresent":
"Because the phonemes are omnipresent, they do not possess a sequential occurrence by their own nature;
since sequence is an effect of impermanent sounds, it is therefore perishable."
And its dependence on a person would arise from the power of his intention to speak;
consequently, the eternality of phonemes [claimed] by you would be rendered fruitless.

For you Mīmāṃsakas, because the phonemes (*varṇa*) are omnipresent, there is no sequence produced by space; nor is there one produced by time, because they are eternal. Therefore, the sequence is produced by the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*).
And since those [sounds] are impermanent, that which is produced by them is also impermanent—this is the intended meaning.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: whatever is produced by something impermanent is itself impermanent, like a jar or other such things; and the sequence of phonemes is produced by something impermanent. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Whatever arises by virtue of a person's lack of intention to speak should be treated as being of human origin by a discerning person, such as the movement of the hands or the winking of the eyes; and since the sequence of phonemes arises by virtue of a person's will, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Furthermore, it might be argued that even without a sequence, the phonemes themselves, as delimited by the auditory organ, will be the conveyors of meaning; to this, he says "na ca" and so forth:
"And phonemes, not recognized through a sequence, are not conveyors [of meaning].
Thus, the status of being a word belongs only to those situated in a sequence; therefore, this consequence follows."
However, for those for whom the word (*pada*) is something distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*) and devoid of sequential order,
it is only for them that this postulation of the eternity of the word is meaningful.
For it is not observed that phonemes alone, without a sequence, are the cause for the comprehension of meaning; therefore, a sequence must necessarily be admitted for them.
This being the case, it follows for you Mīmāṃsakas that the word-status and the expressive capacity belong to the sequence itself, and not to the phonemes in isolation.
Furthermore, because that sequence is impermanent, the expressive entity would also be impermanent.
Consequently, the postulation of the eternity of sound is futile;

for it is the expressive sound that you intend to prove as eternal, and not any other. Therefore, your proof of the eternity of isolated phonemes is irrelevant to the matter at hand, because such phonemes lack the capacity to express meaning.
Furthermore, that which expresses meaning in the form of a sequence is not accepted as eternal; thus, every such effort is entirely fruitless.

However, for those grammarians who maintain that the expressive unit is a partless word called *sphoṭa*, distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), this postulation of the eternity of sound is meaningful, because that entity known as *sphoṭa* is eternal.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Not yet," and so forth.
First of all, the status of being a word does not follow for that which possesses a sequential order;
for this [sequential order] is not observed to be an illuminator when it is supported by a separate entity.
The meaning is as follows: "Successive nature" (anupūrvasvabhāva) is "succession" (ānupūrvam); it does not follow that this mere succession possesses denotative power for us, because it is fallible.
Demonstrating this very point, he says "nahi" and so forth. [He explains:
"having another entity as its substratum."
The support for jewels, pearls, and so forth.
Nor is it accepted that the expressive [word] consists solely of the substratum and the measure of the phonemes; how so? He says: "This is merely a property.
This is held to be merely a property of them, not a separate entity.
In this way, the phonemes themselves, as they are being perceived, would be the conveyors of meaning.
"It is not a separate entity" means that it is intended [to function] as an independent designator;
otherwise, there would be an ultimate distinction between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin).
And that [word] is not desired [as the object];
rather, what is it? It says "in this way," etc., meaning "in this manner" by means of a specific sequence.

This is what is meant: it is not the sequence alone that is expressive, nor the substratum of the phonemes, nor the phonemes alone; rather, it is the phonemes themselves, as qualified by the sequence, that are expressive.

Therefore, the sequence does not possess primacy with respect to expressiveness, because it is perceived as a subordinate quality (guṇībhūta) insofar as it is perceived as possessing those [phonemes]. Rather, it is shown that the primacy belongs to the phonemes, since they are perceived as the substrata (dharmin).

Regarding the two reasons stated—that [the word] is an effect belonging to a temporal sequence (*anityadhvanikāryatva*)—he declares their unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) with the words "And not of the sequence," and so forth:
"Nor is there the state of being an effect in the case of the sequence, because it is adopted from what was previously established;
for no speaker adopts a sequence independently."
Just as he intends to speak it exactly as it was spoken by others, so too do others; therefore, his connection [to the tradition] is beginningless.
"Because of the adoption of what is already established" means because one adopts a sequence that is already fixed. He clarifies this very point with the words "The speaker does not," and so forth.
For sequence, like relation itself, is indeed beginningless.
He concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tena*) and so forth: "Therefore, this permanence may exist through conventional usage even in the absence of immutability;
however, we must strive to refute the independence of persons regarding [the sequence of] actions."

By employing the genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) in connection with the gerundive suffix *kṛtya* in the word "na," that fault which was prescribed—the prohibition of independence regarding the sequence—is not incurred.

Therefore, even though this sequence lacks [ontological] permanence like that of mountains and so forth, its eternality is to be understood solely from the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), despite its being immutable (*kūṭasthatva*).

Thus, by this, the eternality of the sequence is stated as being one of conventional usage (*vyavahāranityatā*), and not an immutable, absolute eternality (*kūṭasthanityatā*) such as that of mountains and the like.

If this is so, why is it not accepted that for phonemes (*varṇa*) as well, it is precisely the sequence that possesses conventional permanence? To this he says: "Of the phonemes also... [The full verse is: "But for the phonemes also, it will not be established in this way even if they are not eternal; for while the phonemes are eternal, the arising of the sequence results from usage."
The construction of jars and other objects exists within eternal atoms;
for in their absence, such construction would be rootless and could not be apprehended.

For even if phonemes possess non-eternal permanence (*akauṭasthya-nityatva*) due to their sequential nature, the linguistic practice of comprehending meaning is established through the permanence of that practice itself.
To the question "How is it not established?", he says: "In the case of eternal [phonemes]," and so forth.

For if phonemes were eternal by virtue of being immutable (*kūṭastha-nityatā*), then, given the possibility of linguistic practice through a succession of persons, there would be the arising of sequence—that is, the acquisition of the sequence's own-being—just as the construction of jars and other objects originates from atoms.
In some places, the reading is "kramādayaḥ" (sequence, etc.).
There, by the word "etc.," connection, recognition, and so forth are included.

Now, he asks: why is it that a composition is not possible even for both [types of entities]—phonemes and atoms—without their being eternal? To this, he says: "tadabhāve" (in the absence of that), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the absence of that":
it refers to the absence of the state of being eternally immutable (*kūṭastha-nitya*) in both phonemes (*varṇa*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Now, one might object: just as there are atoms that initiate the production of jars and other objects, there are also subtle parts of phonemes; as they say: "Of phonemes too, there are parts that are quarters of a phoneme."
How then can the immutability and eternity of the phonemes (varṇas) be described?
This is not a fault;
for it has been established by the refutation of the sphoṭa that there are no constituent parts of phonemes.

Furthermore, if phonemes were not eternal by virtue of being immutable and permanent, then the intention—"I am uttering words already uttered by another"—would not occur in any speakers; yet such an intention does indeed exist. Therefore, demonstrating that this intention is not tenable without the eternity of phonemes, he says: "If there were such an intention as 'I speak what has been spoken by another,' etc.
"If there were such an intention as 'I speak what has been spoken by another,' it would certainly [be impossible]."
And thus, the consequence of eternality would follow; nor do you possess any other defining characteristic.

Now, one might object: "If the sequence of the phonemes *ga* and so forth is not ultimately eternal, nor are the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), nor the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs that impel them; and if one cannot produce those very things that impel the sounds, and as for those new ones one does produce, they have not been observed to be the impellers—then how can phonemes, manifested in a sequence, become the cause for the cognition of distinct meanings? Anticipating all this and providing a rebuttal, he says: "Just as by means of a universal (*jāti*), etc.
"Just as the characterization of worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding jars and other objects occurs by means of a universal (*jāti*)."
In the same way, [the existence of] sequence and so forth will be established by means of the universal (jāti).

Just as, despite the impermanence of things such as a jar, linguistic usage is established by relying on its genus (*jāti*), so too will it be established for sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) and the like, even though they are impermanent.
To explain how this serves as an illustration for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), he says: "The universals (*jāti*) of the palate and so forth," and so on.
First of all, the universals of the palate and other [articulatory organs] are established in all persons;
the speaker, having characterized those sounds by means of them, emits them.
And their distinct types are the causes for the manifestation of sounds;
they operate as long as the phonemes last, or rather, the individual manifestations are associated with them.
For instance, the universals (*jāti*) of the palate and other articulatory places are established in all persons because they inhere in the palates and so forth that inhere in all persons.

And the speaker, having perceived and determined the palates and other places by means of those very universals of the palate and so forth, subsequently emits and impels the winds that manifest the sounds;
for according to the logical principle, "there can be no cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) being apprehended."

Although these sounds (dhvanis) are impermanent, nevertheless, just like the universals (jāti) such as "cow" or "horse," there exist as many universals as there are phonemes (varṇas). These very universals, acting in conjunction with the individual instances (vyaktis), become the causes for the manifestation of the word-sounds.

Alternatively, there is another position: it is the individual instances of the sounds themselves that, acting in conjunction with the universals, proceed toward the manifestation [of the phonemes] in accordance with the phonemes.

Now, one might object: although there are distinct universals (*jāti*) of phonemes (*dhvani*), even so, those phonemes—though characterized by their respective universals—are not capable of producing the sequence of letter-manifestation without a [temporal] sequence themselves. For indeed, even though they are differentiated by the difference of their universals, they possess no inherent sequence of their own, because they are partless (*niravayava*). Therefore, how can the determination of a sequence among letters be produced by the sequence of the manifestors? Anticipating this doubt, he says "tatra" and so forth.

In that regard, the sequential order of the sounds would be preceded by the sequence of conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other articulators; furthermore, both [the sounds and their universals] are eternal by virtue of their respective universals (*jāti*).

Although the sequence of phonemes (*dhvani*) does not exist inherently, nevertheless, it is precisely the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other articulators that bring about their sequence.

Furthermore, both the sequence of the conjunctions of the palate and so forth, and the sequence of the phonemes themselves, possess eternity by way of the universals (*jāti*) inherent in their respective substrates; thus, everything is free from confusion.

But how can the permanence of a sequence—which is itself impermanent—be characterized by its genus (*jāti*), such that, being thus characterized, it may become a factor in linguistic convention? To this he says: "Just as," and so forth.
Just as the parts of [actions] such as revolving are characterized by their genus and so on...
In this way, there would be a sequential continuity involving the palate and other articulators, as well as the sounds and phonemes.

Just as the sequential occurrence of specific actions such as the movement of bees—and by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of ants and so forth—is characterized by their respective classes (jāti) and serves as a basis for linguistic usage;
here, by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of the classes of ants and so forth is intended.

In the same way, the sequential occurrence of the palate and other articulators as they bear upon sounds and phonemes is characterized by the classes of the palate and so forth, and thus becomes available for linguistic usage. This is the connection [of the sentence].
Regarding the phrase "that which possesses the parts of the palate, sounds, and phonemes":
the compound is analyzed as *tālvādayaś ca dhvanayaś ca varṇāś ca* (the palates and so forth, and the sounds, and the phonemes); that which partakes (*bhajate*) these is thus described.

By this, it is stated that the sequence of the conjunction of the palate and so forth, characterized by its own genus (*svajāti*), is the cause for the exclusion of [mere] sound (*dhvani*); and the sequence of sounds, likewise preceded by the sequence of the conjunction and disjunction of the palate and so forth and characterized by its own genus, is the basis for the sequence of the manifestation of phonemes; and that too is the basis for the cognition of meaning. This is what is meant.
In some places, the reading is "bhāgāḥ" (parts). In that case, the connection is as follows:

just as the parts or portions of actions such as revolving, which possess a sequence and are characterized by their genus or by some other property, become the causes for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).

Likewise, some read: "The sequential recurrence residing in the palate and other [articulatory organs] is a factor in linguistic usage; thus there would be a recollection of the sequence. In that context, by such a connection, just as the parts of [the yogic acts of] whirling, exhaling, and so forth, which are characterized by genus and the like, are recollected.

In this way, there will be a sequential recollection of the palate and so forth, which possess the sounds and phonemes, which have the palate and so forth as their objects, and which are characterized by the universals (jāti) of the palate and so forth.

Alternatively, showing that the sequential order of sounds is not produced by the sequence of conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other articulators, but rather is inherent (*svata eva*) because they possess parts, he says: "Of the individuals (*vyaktīnām*).
Or rather, it is precisely because of the subtlety of the individuals that the properties of the genus (*jāti*) are determined;
and by virtue of that, even though phonemes (*varṇa*) are all-pervading (*vyāpin*), their sequential apprehension occurs.
Regarding sounds:
for those parts of them which are initiatory and sequential are subtle, and by means of them the accomplishment of linguistic usage is not achieved.
Therefore, among those [parts], properties such as eternality, which have the nature of universals (*jāti*) and serve as the causes for the manifestation of specific sounds, are investigated.
That is to say, they are determined.
What, then, would be established by this? He says: "By virtue of that," and so forth.
For even though the phonemes are all-pervading, they appear as if they possess a sequence due to the influence of the sequential sounds (dhvani).
With the words "In this way" and so forth, he concludes the subject at hand:
"In this way, all the qualities of sound, being established as eternal, would—
by following along with the phonemes— be the means for the comprehension of different meanings."
The qualities of sound— such as its sequence, intensity, dullness, and spatial location—
are established as eternal by way of the universal (jāti).
Following after, pursuing.

Thus, even if it is true that, because letters are eternal and all-pervading, sequences and so forth cannot exist in them by their own nature, nevertheless, it has been demonstrated in detail that these [properties], though residing in the manifesters, serve as the means for the comprehension of meaning in relation to the letters.

Now, showing an alternative position—that these divisions, which consist of time and are conditioned by the sounds (dhvani), are apprehended in the letters and serve as the means for comprehension—he says "sequence" and so forth:
"The sequence of letters, as well as those which are short, long, and protracted..."
Those divisions of time are known to have sound as their limiting adjuncts.
Those divisions of time for which sounds—meaning manifesting winds that serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) acting as qualifiers—are present, are so described.
But surely, for those who maintain the existence of time, it is accepted that time is one, all-pervading, and eternal,
as it has been said: "Apart from its activity, [time is the cause] of those things that possess dimension and action."
Some declare time to be an eternal, unitary, and all-pervading substance.
Thus, to the question of how its division is tenable, he says: "And time is one," and so forth.
Time is one, all-pervading, and eternal; yet it is perceived as divided.
Like a phoneme, it is manifested by something in a particular place among all entities.
Its status as a factor in the communication [of meaning] occurs when it is manifested through the phonemes;
however, because it exists elsewhere as well, its own essential nature is eternal.

The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even though divided" (*pravibhakto 'pi*) is to be connected with the ideas that [time] is "unitary," "eternal," and "all-pervading," because its position in the sequence has been shifted.
How is it divided? He says: "as in the case of phonemes, in all things.

This is what is meant: just as a single, eternal phoneme such as *ga*—when manifested by a particular sound (*dhvani*) in a certain location—is perceived as divided according to distinctions of place and so forth, so too is time.

Although this [Sphoṭa] pervades all objects, nevertheless, when it is manifested by some particular action in a certain object, it is perceived as divided; but when it is manifested in the phonemes (varṇas), it becomes the means for the cognition of meaning.
If it is then asked how its eternal omnipresence is understood when it is divided, he says: "In other cases as well," and so forth.
Because it exists in other things as well, such as creepers and young shoots—just like existence (sattā)—its eternity and omnipresence are established.
The mention of "permanence" is an illustrative indication.
Therefore, there exists no such perishable property of a word;
thus, for those who maintain the eternity of phonemes, the word is established as eternal.
The conclusion regarding the establishment of one's own position is stated with the words "Therefore" and so forth.
"Something of such a kind" refers to that which has the nature of succession and the like.
If, then, sequence is a property of time or a property of the manifesting sound (*dhvani*), and not ultimately a property of the phoneme (*varṇa*), how can it serve as a factor for communication?
For a property of one thing does not belong to another. To this he says, "Even a property of another," and so forth:
"Even a property of another serves as a factor [for cognition], like the speed of a horse and the like."
And because of permanence, all [entities] have presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as their means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It has been stated [in the verse] beginning with "those who have boarded a boat and are traveling," for the mention of those "boarded on a boat" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all those who have boarded any vehicle.

"Like the speed of a horse, etc. means that just as the speed residing in a horse or similar animal becomes a factor for men mounted upon it to reach another location, and for the perception of movement in trees and so forth, so too the sequence residing in the sound (dhvani) is a factor for the syllable (varṇa) in conveying its meaning.

Having thus established in detail that the thesis of the non-eternality of words is sublated by the means of valid cognition known as presumption (arthāpatti), he says "In the case of eternality," etc., while concluding.
Therefore, the conclusion "tasmāt" (therefore) should be understood here as applying to all [factors]. Regarding the phrase "of all":

it is not only the permanence of the phoneme (*varṇa*) that is established through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of meaning; rather, what is it?—the permanence of the palate and other articulators, as well as of the sounds (*dhvani*).

As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "For if the word perished as soon as it was uttered, one [sound] would not be able to convey the meaning to another; therefore, it would not be uttered for the sake of ultimate purpose.
But if it does not perish, then because it is perceived many times, the comprehension of the meaning is logical."
Demonstrating that the thesis is also sublated by one’s own words, by what is accepted, by scripture, and by common cognition, he says:
"Contradiction with one's own statements, etc. In the proof of the impermanence of sound, every thesis is uttered for the sake of communicating the object to be proven.
And it has been established that this [scripture] does not speak its own meaning while being impermanent;
therefore, because it conveys the understanding of the meaning through its permanence, there is no sublation by the word itself.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the contradiction with what has been accepted (*abhyupeta*) and so forth is included. It has been established by such statements as:
"A word whose connection to its object is not perceived cannot be expressive," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "because it is established through the cognition of the meaning": from the cognition of the meaning (*arthapratyaya*), that is, from the comprehension of the meaning (*arthapratīti*), it is "established" (*āpanna*), meaning proven. Thus, "established through the cognition of the meaning" (*arthapratyayāpanna*) means:
because its permanence is established by the fact that it could not otherwise be accounted for (*anyathānupapatti*) given the comprehension of the meaning. This is the sense.
He states the contradiction with what has been accepted: "By asserting the capacity to denote an object and then proving it,
a person contradicts perishability by means of what was previously accepted."
Even by means of scripture (*āgama*), which relies on the capacities for understanding meaning specific to each treatise,
the non-momentariness of all proponents is not invalidated.

[The author] states the contradiction with scripture (*āgamabādhā*) with the words "by the capacities for the comprehension of meaning," and so forth. The supplement is: "because of the subversion of the meaning of the thesis by those [capacities] which belong to words for the comprehension of meaning."
He states the contradiction by means of common experience with the words "sarvaloka" and so forth:
"And there is a contradiction by what is well-known to all the world, according to the direction previously stated;
there is also a conflict with inference by the very same reason mentioned before."
Because auditory recognition leads to the determination of the non-difference of sound,
the contradiction with direct perception has already been established previously.
The direction previously mentioned is that stated in the immediately preceding verse.
However, it should be read as follows:
"By means of the capacities for the comprehension of meaning, which are determined by the whole world..."
By worldly consensus, the perishability [of all things] is established for all proponents of philosophical views.
Thus,
reminding [the opponent] of the previously stated contradiction with inference and so forth, he says: "There is also a contradiction with inference," and so on.
The previously mentioned reason is of various kinds:
"The cognitions of individual instances of the word 'cow', though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, must all have the same object; otherwise, they would not have a single object."
By [the argument] beginning with "Because it arises as 'cow,' like a presently arisen cognition," etc.,
[it is shown that] it has already been [established].
Furthermore, since the eternity and omnipresence of sound are established by auditory recognition,
who could possibly determine its opposite?
By this [verse], v.2117.
Desiring to set forth certain remaining faults of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) and faults of the reason (*hetudoṣa*), he says "And it must be stated," and so forth:

"And it must be stated what kind of sound this is that is being proved to be perishable— is it composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), or is it material (*paudgala*), or is it a quality of space (*ākāśa*)?"
Alternatively, [the word] is distinct from the phonemes; it consists of *nāda* and has the nature of air, being non-expressive.
The *sphoṭa*, which consists of words and sentences, [is that which brings about] the exclusion of others through similarity.
Let these [entities] be impermanent; we do not maintain their permanence.
[If you argue otherwise,] there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualification and the fallacy of a reason whose locus is unestablished.
He states the conceptual distinctions regarding sound according to the differences in philosophical tenets:

therein, sound is held by the Sāṃkhyas to be composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), because its nature consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; it is held by the Digambaras to be composed of atoms (*paudgala*).
Individuals (pudgalas) are called atoms (paramāṇus); this [body] belongs to them, meaning it has their nature.
The followers of Kaṇāda maintain that sound is a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇa*).
According to common worldly usage, it is held to be of the nature of *nāda* (articulate sound) and distinct from phonemes (*varṇa*).
As it is stated in the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya*: "Alternatively, in common usage, 'sound' (*dhvani*) refers to that which conveys each individual object."

The form of the wind (*vāyu*) is inexpressible according to the grammarians of phonetics (*śikṣākāra*), as they say: "The wind attains the state of sound. Furthermore, that which consists of the word-sphoṭa (*padasphoṭa*) and that which consists of the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*) are accepted by the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).
As it has been said:
"In the intellect, whose seed has been sown by the preceding sounds and which has reached maturity through repeated practice, the word is apprehended together with the final sound."
Thus:
Vindhyavāsī maintains that "conformity" (sārūpya) means similarity (sādṛśya).
The Buddhists, however, maintain that what is intended as the expressive [function] is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), which is the negation of what is other.

In that regard, if the impermanence of things such as those desired by the Sāṅkhyas and others is being proven in this way, then there is the fallacy of the thesis known as *siddhasādhyatā* (proving what is already established).

By the phrase "it is indicated by its very own nature," that which is already established in form is excluded; therefore, if one were to prove something already established in form, there would be the fallacy of the thesis known as *siddhasādhyatā*.
This is because [the phrase] "it is indicated by its very own nature" has already ruled out that which is established in form.
Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsakas do not intend to prove the eternity of such a sound.

Moreover, with respect to us [the Buddhists], there is the fallacy of the subject having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣatva*), because the specific nature of the subject—sound as consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and so forth—is unestablished;
and there is also the fallacy of the reason (*hetu*) having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).
Because such a subject (dharmin) is unestablished. //2310//
Now, as for the word "atha":
if this position favored by us were [your own], then these two would belong to you yourself;
or else, if it were said that they are merely words, then in that case, "word-ness" (śabdatva) would be the entity.
And that [universal] is impermanent for all; thus it contradicts what is accepted as eternal.
Whatever universal is imagined here by anyone is held to be eternal.

Now, if this position were held by us Mīmāṃsakas—that the phonemes themselves, such as *ga* and so forth, are the word and that there is no distinct entity [apart from them]—then for the Buddhist and others, two faults would follow: the fault of the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*) known as "having an unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣatva*), and the fault of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) known as "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhatā*). If, on the other hand, it were said to be "mere sound" (*śabdamātra*), the remainder of the sense being that it is intended as the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*).
And consequently, for you, the universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) would result in being impermanent—the word "would follow" (*prāpnoti*) being supplied here.
For, when all particularities have been abandoned by the word "mere" (*mātra*), what else could remain as "mere sound" apart from the universal?
Therefore, by implication, you yourselves would have proposed that "sound-ness" itself is impermanent.
If it is argued, "Let it be so," [the author] says "no," beginning with the words, "And that is desired by all as eternal," and so forth.

For even by the Buddhists who propound the theory of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others), it has been stated: "Because the properties of a genus are established. By this, the fault of contradicting one's own accepted tenets (*abhyupetabādhā*) is stated.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "whatever here," and so forth.

Whatever universal (*sāmānya*) has been established by anyone according to their own philosophical system, all of that is held to be eternal by all proponents [of such systems]. Otherwise, because of its arising as one thing after another just like an individual (*vyakti*), it would fall under the category of individuals; consequently, its very nature as a universal would be lost.

[637] Having thus first pointed out the defect of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) by means of an alternative regarding the property-bearer (*sādhyadharmin*), he now says "And impermanence," etc., wishing to point it out by means of an alternative regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*):
"If impermanence is said to be absolute perishability,
then for us [Buddhists], the thesis would have an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*)."
If it is somehow desired that there be a designation of impermanence,
then that [impermanence] is held to consist in manifestation, because it is distinct from the state of non-manifestation.

If that which is intended as the probandum—impermanence characterized by absolute, traceless destruction—is accepted, then for us Mīmāṃsakas, there is the fallacy of the subject (*pakṣadoṣa*) consisting of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*).
For, just as for the Sāṃkhyas, the qualification of "traceless destruction" is unestablished for the Mīmāṃsakas;
this is because even when jars and other such things disappear, they persist in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*).
For even in the case of a lamp and the like, it is held that the light particles move very rapidly to another location.
Now, if you intend to establish the designation "impermanent" in some way or other, then there is the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For even in the case of eternal things, the designation "impermanent" is indeed accepted based on the states of manifestation and non-manifestation.

Thus, first of all, this proposition that "sound is impermanent" has been refuted in detail. Now, pointing out the fault in the reason "because it is perceptible by the senses," he says: "And when the reason is conceived as being merely perceptible by the senses, a deviation [from the probandum] is now perceived through the example of 'universal' (jāti) which has already been established."

If the reason—“being merely perceptible by the senses” and so forth—is devoid of such qualifications as “while being an effect,” then that unqualified reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its generality (*jāti*), because it has already been established previously;
for its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not proven.

It might be argued: "Even if the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established because the opponent accepts the universal (*jāti*), nevertheless, since the Buddhist and others—the proponent themselves—do not accept the universal, [the reason] is indeed established; so how can it be inconclusive? To this he says: "Unestablished," and so forth:

"Just as when the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is unestablished for the opponent, the reason is not obtained, so too it is with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)."

According to the principle that "only that which expresses what is certain in both respects constitutes either a proof or a refutation," just as a reason (*hetu*) becomes defective when either [of its two requirements]—the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)—is unestablished, so too it is indeed defective when either of the two, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), is unestablished.
The connection is made by changing the grammatical number in the phrase "when positive and negative concomitances are unestablished" (*anvayavyatirekayor asiddhayoḥ*).

If only that which is established for both parties is a valid proof or refutation, then how is it that you have alleged a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) against the Buddhist on the grounds of the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) nature of the "pseudo-reason" (*jāti*)? To this he replies with the verse beginning *tatra*: "Even if that pseudo-reason were unestablished for the proponent of the proof, it would nonetheless remain a non-reason so long as it has not been refuted."
Although for a proponent of proof such as a Buddhist, "being born" is established as a property of the counter-example (vipakṣa), nevertheless, doubt does not cease;
for that [doubt] cannot be refuted. Thus, the sense is that there is a "doubtful exclusion from the counter-example" (saṃdigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika).

Furthermore, he states another refutation of the probandum and the probans through a different alternative: "And [the inquiry] regarding being an effect, being perceptible by the senses, and so forth...
In the case of being an effect, being perceptible by the senses, and so forth, there is an investigation as to what the entity is;
and this is clear regarding whether it is non-different from the individuals, or whether there is difference, or both difference and non-difference.

In that regard, the [fallacies of] being unshared (*asādhāraṇa*), unestablished (*asiddha*), lacking the probandum (*sādhyahīna*), and lacking a similar instance (*sapakṣatā*) should be stated according to the specific options, with reference to the first [alternative].
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), impermanence (*anityatva*) is included.

In that regard, an investigation must be made as to what the nature of [the property] such as perceptibility (*aindriyakatva*) is: is it non-different from the individuals (*vyakti*), or is it distinct? Likewise, if the position of distinction is taken, an inquiry must be made regarding those differences: is that which is distinct from them variously different, or is it one and the same? In that case, if the position of non-distinction is held, the reason (*hetu*) of perceptibility would be "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), because it is non-different from the individual; like its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it would lack any following after (*anugama*) other individuals.

Even in the case of the position of difference (*vyatireka*), since the Mīmāṃsaka does not accept difference, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is unproven whether [the universal] is distinct or non-distinct with respect to each individual (*prativyakty*).
For this very reason, the fault regarding the position of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*) has not been stated;
for that [fault] would only have scope once difference were established.
Even in the case where impermanence is treated as a distinct entity (*vyatireka-pakṣa*), the concordant instance (*sapakṣa*) lacks the property to be proven;
that is to say, the example is deficient in the probandum.

Even in the case where it is not treated as distinct (*avyatireka-pakṣa*), the example likewise lacks the property to be proven, because one individual instance does not follow into or coalesce with another individual instance.
Now, he states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason "because of being immediately following effort" with the words beginning "immediately following effort":
"Knowledge immediately following effort is the proof for [things] being produced and impermanent;
yet even there, there is inconclusiveness because of [the existence of things] distinct from the momentary."
With the three— cessation through deliberation, cessation not through deliberation, and space—
the cognition of cessation through deliberation occurs indeed upon destruction preceded by intelligence.
Their cessation occurs without prior cognition, through non-analytical means;
and both of these are held to be unconditioned because they are indestructible and so forth.
For "being perceived immediately after an effort" is what is meant by "arising immediately after an effort.
And because this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) even with respect to the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), it does not prove that produced things are impermanent.

To explain: Buddhists maintain that there are three kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entities—cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyānirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*)—which are non-momentary, eternal, and distinct from momentary things.
Showing that this reason applies there as well, he says "preceded by intelligence," and so forth.

That destruction of jars and the like which is preceded by intelligence is *pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation), whereas that which is not preceded by intelligence is *apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation); such, indeed, is the Buddhist system.
"Of them" refers to jars and the like.
"And those two" refers to cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"Even though they are unconditioned" (*akṛtaka*); by the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that they are also eternal (*nitya*). //2322//
Just as these two possess the qualities of being uncreated and eternal,
and just as their occurrence within that [proposed] reason is established, he says "They say," and so forth, demonstrating it according to the opponent's own view:
"For they say that destruction is established by its own nature and is without cause."
For indeed, from wood through connection with fire, there arises a continuous series of embers.
Intrinsic destruction, however, is established in mere birth;
it is subtle and unperceived due to its occurrence within a continuous stream of similar moments.
