When a cause of a different character falls upon a similar continuum,
then the gross [entity] is manifested by an effect of a different character.
Since a dissimilar continuum arises from that cause,
destruction— though not produced by that very [cause]— is clearly manifested by it.

"Those" refers to the Buddhists. Now, one might object: "Wood is destroyed by fire, and a jar by a staff; thus, causes of destruction are observed. How, then, can there be causelessness? To this he replies with the words "For it happens," and so forth. For fire and the like are determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be the causes of other entities, such as charcoal and the like, but not of destruction itself.
Because that [destruction] is established by its very nature (*nisargasiddhatvāt*).
If, then, destruction is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), why is it not perceived even before the impact of fire and so forth? To this he says "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) and so on:
for the dull-witted, deceived by the arising of a similar [moment], do not perceive the subtle destruction.
However, because a similar continuum arises, they imagine [the object] to be undestroyed.
A dissimilar cause, such as a hammer and so forth,
produces a dissimilar effect, such as potsherds and so forth.
In this state, indeed, the grossness of destruction becomes manifest.
The conclusion is made with the words "by that," and so forth;
[this refers to] a dissimilar continuum.
"Distinct from the cause"— this is a grammatical coreferential construction (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) meaning "because of which cause.
"By that very same" means by that very cause.
"From which" refers to that which has been previously specified;
its connection with the subsequent term "is manifested" is to be understood.
Demonstrating that the reason (hetu) occurs in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), he says "sa mudgara... and so forth: "That [sound] follows immediately after an effort such as the stroke of a hammer;
because it is seen to be unproduced, the reason would be fallacious."
Regarding the word "that":

both kinds of cessation are called "immediately following the effort of striking with a hammer and so forth" because they are known immediately after the effort of striking with a hammer and so forth.
It was stated [above] that "by three [reasons].
Having demonstrated the deviation [of the argument] with respect to two of them, he says "even space," etc., demonstrating deviation even with respect to the third, space:
"Even space, though eternal, when it is covered by earth and water..."
It is manifested through the exclusion of that [other], by means of its own sound, cutting, and so forth.
When knowledge is observed even in that case immediately following an effort,
then the reason stated there— namely, "because it is observed"— is inconclusive.
"By its removal" means by the taking away of that earth and so forth, which serves as the instrument for digging and the like;
"therein" refers to the word.
Perception is knowledge that arises immediately after an effort.

Having thus stated the defects of the reason (*hetu*), and desiring to state the defects of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he says "sapakṣo 'pi" and so forth: "In this case, even the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is problematic; there is a deficiency regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the literal sense of the word.
Even in the position that it is characterized by an individual (*vyakti*), there is the conceptualization of whether it is other than or non-other than the universal (*jāti*)."
If there is difference, the locus (dharmin) is not established; nor is it established for others if there is non-difference.
Even though there is no distinction [between the two], that entity is neither impermanent nor permanent for me.
For its portion called "birth" is considered eternal, while the other is perishable;
indeed, it has been previously established that a single entity possesses a variegated form.
The example (dṛṣṭānta) is the similar instance (sapakṣa).
Is that intended in its literal sense (śrutyartha), or rather as an individual manifestation (vyakti)?
If it is the literal sense, then there is the fault of the example being devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikalatā).
For instance, "śruti" means sound;
its "artha" is the denoted object.

That, moreover, is a universal such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and so forth, and since that is accepted as eternal by all disputants, there is no concomitance of the property to be proven—impermanence—with respect to it.
In some places, the reading is *jātyartha*;
in that case, a *karmadhāraya* compound should be formed. The meaning remains exactly the same.

Now, as for the second alternative, even then one must consider whether that individual, which is intended to serve as the example, is different from the universal or non-different from it. If it is different,
then the subject of the example is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the Mīmāṃsaka.

For the Mīmāṃsaka does not, like the Vaiśeṣika and others, maintain that the universal (jāti) is absolutely distinct from the individual (vyakti), as it has been said: "But the existence of the universal and so forth as something other than the individual is certainly not established. If, on the other hand, the position taken is that they are non-different, then for opponents such as the Buddhists, the property of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharma) remains unestablished.
For others do not consider the universal (*jāti*) to be non-different from the individual (*vyakti*).

Now, if the pot is adduced as an example while setting aside the dilemma of difference and non-difference, even then, he says "even though there is no distinction," and so forth, demonstrating that for us the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*);
"that" refers to the entity that is the pot.
To the question "How so?", he says: "The part," and so forth.
For of this substantial entity that is a jar, the portion designated as the universal (*jāti*) is eternal;
the other portion, however, designated as the individual (*vyakti*), is perishable and subject to destruction.
It might be asked: "How is it logical for a single thing to possess two mutually contradictory natures? To this, he says: "Having a variegated form," and so forth. //2332 //2333 //
Desiring again to state the faults of the example by way of an analysis of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), he says "impermanence," and so forth:

"Impermanence is thus analyzed: if [it means] destruction, there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyahīnatā*) for me; but if it means something else, there is [a deficiency] for you. This is the direction for stating the refutation."

If that impermanence, characterized by destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśa*), is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*), then for me, the Mīmāṃsaka, the example lacks the probandum. For we do not accept the absolute annihilation of entities, because they persist in the form of potentiality (*śakti*).
Although "destruction" (*nāśa*) is a general term, nevertheless, by virtue of the context, its application is understood to refer to a specific object consisting of destruction without residue.

Otherwise, how could the consequence of the example being deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*) be appropriate? One might object: "But has not impermanence already been analyzed through the passage beginning with 'If impermanence were said to be absolute destruction' and so forth? Why then is it analyzed yet again?
True; however, that was for the purpose of exposing a fault in the thesis (*pakṣa*), whereas now it is for the sake of the example—this is the distinction.

Now, if it is not the impermanence characterized by destruction without residue that is intended, but rather another [kind] characterized by manifestation and disappearance, he says "in the other" (*anyasyām*).
This is to be connected with "impermanence" (*anityatāyām*). The word "of yours" (*bhavatām*) [is used].
It should be construed as "deficiency of the probandum" (*sādhyahīnatā*).
In that context as well, the word "of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntasya*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
For destruction with a causal continuity (*sānvaya-vināśa*) is not accepted by you Buddhists, as it is by the Sāṃkhyas.

Therefore, according to your position, the example would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); thus has this method for refuting the proof of the non-eternality of sound been explained to the wise, and other matters should also be investigated and formulated by the learned themselves.
With the words beginning "padārtha," he anticipates the objection of the opponent:
"Even if the eternality of the word-meanings and the relationship between words has been established,
the status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) with respect to the sentence-meaning is not at all proven here."
For, according to convention, the understanding of men arises like the technical terms *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and so forth; thus,
even though an object is devoid of a [corresponding] cause, it has been conceptually constructed by the ritualists (*yājñika*).
Moreover, because it is a compilation like other narratives, it is of human origin;
and since there is no such thing as an authoritative person, the Vedas lack the status of valid cognition.
For the meaning of a sentence consists in the injunction or prohibition of a specific action as delimited by a particular means;
it is in that alone that the authority of the *codanā* resides, not in the individual word-meanings.

Consequently, when the authority of the Veda is to be established, the demonstration of the eternity of all three—the words, their meanings, and their relationship—is irrelevant to the subject at hand.

Furthermore, whatever apprehension of the meaning of a sentence occurs, it arises from convention (*saṃketa*), just as the cognition of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and so forth arises from sentences such as "āT-guṇaḥ. And since the apprehension of the meaning of a sentence originates from an injunctive statement (*codanāvākya*), this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). He demonstrates this very point with the words "from convention" (*samayāt*) and so forth, [concluding] with "like *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and so forth."
The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the locative case.
He provides the justification for this very point with the words "even without cause," and so forth.

It is conceivable that even though [the act] is without cause—that is, without a [valid] basis—the performers of sacrifices (*yājñika*) might, by means of their own unrestrained imagination, offer the *agnihotra* solely for the sake of a livelihood, having fabricated the meaning of Vedic passages such as "one who desires heaven should sacrifice."

Furthermore, whatever is a composite form is of human origin, such as stories like dramas or narratives; and the Veda is a collection of words—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Consequently, because it is of human origin, the Veda would lack authority, like the speech of a man in the street.

If it is argued that it will nonetheless be authoritative despite being of human origin because it was composed by a reliable person (*āpta*), the author replies with the verse beginning "And there is no reliable person," etc. (2336).

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "sambandha" and so forth: "The eternity of the sentence must be asserted on the grounds of the same logic used for the non-creation of the relationship [between word and meaning]; it might even be possible in the case of *vṛddhi* and so forth, because they consist of the usage of observed objects."

The understanding [of the Veda] is based on convention; however, this is not tenable because by whom has the relationship between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth—which is indeed beyond the senses—been perceived?

The same logic that was stated regarding the non-establishment of the relationship between words and their meanings—namely, "What relationship could a speaker convey to a listener and an author? and so forth—must also be asserted for the eternality of Vedic sentences.

Regarding the claim that "human understanding [of Vedic terms] arises from convention (*samaya*), just like [the application of] *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and so on," he points out its lack of necessity by stating "because it concerns empirical usage" and so forth.

Since the usage of *guṇa* and so on occurs when objects such as *adeṅ* are perceived, comprehension in those cases can indeed be assumed to arise from convention; however, this is not the case with the Vedas, because since heaven and the like are beyond the senses, it is impossible to establish a convention for them.
If this were so, it would follow that it is purposeless; to this he says:
"And there is no purposelessness for it," because the cognition of that object arises from it.
Such a counter-argument must be stated regarding the state of being a composite.
All study of the Veda must be preceded by study under a teacher,
because it is designated as "Vedic study," just like one's current study.
The word "tasya" (of that) refers to the Veda.
Regarding the proof [stated] as "because of being a composite," he says "saṅghātatvasya" and so forth, demonstrating that this very reason is inconclusive by means of a counter-argument.
But surely, one could say the same regarding the study of the *Bhārata*: "Whatever is the study of the *Bhārata*, all of that is preceded by study under a teacher, just like the present-day [study].
And yet, it cannot be established in this way.
Therefore, suspecting that the counter-argument (*pratisādhana*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for that reason as well, he says: "Even in the case of the *Bhārata*," and so forth.
The same would apply even in the case of the *bhārata*, but it is sublated by the memory of its author;
whereas in the Veda, there is no such memory, even that which is based on explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

The same consequence would apply to the *bhārata* as well; however, since an author is remembered as being pervaded [by the work] there, the subject of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) is sublated by that memory of an author, and thus no such consequence arises.
But in the case of the Veda, there is no such memory—of an author, it should be understood.

But surely, even in the Veda, an author is indeed remembered; for instance: "Agni and Āva created the Sāmans, the Sāmaga on Mount Kapotaka, and the Atharvans and Āṅgirasas [created the Atharvans]. To this, he says: "And that which is based on an explanatory passage (arthavāda). Even that memory of an author found in the Veda is based on an explanatory passage—an *arthavāda* being a statement whose primary purpose is not the literal meaning, but praise or censure—and that which has such a passage as its basis is described as "based on an explanatory passage."
Nevertheless, in the phrase "they made," the verb *karoti* does not have the sense of performing an action;
rather, it has the sense of remembering.
The meaning is: "they made" means "they remembered."
To explain how this point is established, he says: "The past and the future," and so forth.
The past and future times are devoid of a knower, because they are time, just as the present time is observed in the world.
It should be understood that Brahmā and the others are not the creators of the Vedas,
because they possess the quality of being persons and so forth, just like the men under discussion here.
The two means of valid cognition are easy to understand.

Then, having concluded the entire subject matter under discussion with the words "tataśca" and so forth, he establishes it through formal proof: "Therefore, let it be clearly understood that the Vedic word is non-false regarding its own meaning, because it does not depend upon a speaker, just like the cognition of a word-meaning [arising from] a word."
The cognition produced by that is correct, namely this cognition arising from an eternal sentence; it is like the cognition produced from that which has the nature of the sentence as its object.
The validity of the cognition produced by an injunctive statement is established in the same way as that of the cognition arising from the words of a trustworthy person.
For this means of knowledge arises from the speech of a trustworthy person who has not acted otherwise;
thus, there is no contradiction in it even when there are differences in time, state, and so forth.
And since the Veda is established as a valid means of knowledge, the beginningless succession of disciples and teachers— even when postulated— serves to ensure its faultlessness.

If a statement produces knowledge regarding its object without depending on a speaker who acts as its author, it is not false in that regard—just as a word [produces knowledge] regarding its referent. Since the Vedic sentence produces cognition regarding its own meaning without depending on a person acting as its author, this is an "observation of the contradictory of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). For falsity is pervaded by the quality of producing cognition that depends upon a person acting as its author; and its opposite is the independence from a speaker regarding its own meaning.
Regarding the phrase "like the cognition of words":
this is intended primarily to demonstrate that words are the cause of non-contradictory cognitions;
it is not, however, intended for the cognition of words to serve as an illustrative example.
What then? It is the words themselves.

For in this case, the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) consists of the sounds; and since its property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is non-falsity by virtue of being the cause for the arising of non-discrepant cognition, it is logical that the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) should be of exactly that same nature.
Otherwise, the example would be deficient in the property to be proven.

Furthermore, there is another formal argument: that cognition produced by an eternal sentence is correct because it corresponds to reality, just like [the cognition] whose object is the nature of the sentence itself; and the certainty regarding the attainment of heaven and so forth from the *agnihotra* and other rites is produced by an eternal sentence. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Since eternality has been established in detail previously, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
The passage beginning with "codanā" has already been explained above.

Likewise, there are two further applications: that cognition which is produced by a statement not composed by a human author and which is free from contradiction regarding differences of place, time, person, and state is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like the cognition produced by the statement of a reliable person (*āpta*); and this cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is likewise [free from contradiction]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). There is no lack of proof for the first reason, because the fact that [the Veda] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) has been established in detail.
Nor is it the case for the second [alternative].
As it has been said: "From the statement 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice,' it is not understood in a doubtful manner—[namely], that 'it may or may not happen for everyone.
And that which is understood without doubt cannot be false."

"For that which, having arisen, perishes with the thought 'this is not so,' is a false cognition; yet this [Veda] does not undergo subversion at another time, in another state, or in another person; therefore, it is non-erroneous.

Consequently, it is established that the Veda—like light—is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by its very nature, serving as the cause for the determination of dharma and other matters common to all the world.
And thus, it remains settled that the doctrine of "mind-only" (*cittamātratā*) and so forth, as described by the Buddhists and others, is untenable. //2346//

[Page 645] Now, one might object: "If the Veda is self-evidently authoritative (*pramāṇa*), like light, and is common to all people, why is it that certain individuals such as the Buddhists disagree with it?
For it is not logical that it should lack authority for them. Anticipating this doubt, he says "Therefore," and so forth: "Therefore, since the Veda is like light—the eye for all the world—"
It is said that for others, there is indeed a repulsion born of unrighteousness, like that of an owl.

Just as, for instance, when the sun—with its mass of exceedingly sharp rays—has dispelled the entire spread of darkness and shines everywhere before the eyes common to all people, yet for those such as owls whose eyes are extremely deficient in perception due to the obstruction of their own karma, visible form does not enter the path of their vision; so too, the Śākyas and others, whose eyes of intellect are struck by the darkness of unrighteousness, encounter only resistance even though the Veda stands as the sole eye for the entire world.
The word "kila" indicates a lack of approval [with the author's view].
He clarifies that very point with the words "all this," and so forth:
"All this is merely the manifestation of false pride on the part of the twice-born;
it has occurred by chance like the letters carved by a woodworm, for not a single well-spoken word belongs to them."
"Like the mark made by a woodworm" means even by way of the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (the accidental coincidence).

In this regard, concerning what was stated—that that which is free from the contact with defects that cause falsity is a means for producing non-erroneous knowledge, and so forth—the author, while for the sake of argument accepting the establishment of the reason (*hetu*), points out its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) by saying: "Even when the agent is absent," and so on.
For even if the agent were non-existent, this [scripture] would certainly not attain the status of having true meaning.
Due to the deficiency of those causes and qualities, even in the absence of defects, it is like something with a false meaning.
This refers to the Vedic scripture.

Just as one possessed of passion and other such defects is seen to be a speaker of falsehood, so through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), defects are determined to be the causes of falsity in speech; likewise, since one endowed with qualities such as compassion is seen to be truthful, qualities such as compassion are determined to be the causes of truthfulness.
Consequently, by the cessation of the cause, truthfulness would also cease, just like falsity.
Even if the lack of human authorship were established, truthfulness would not be proven; therefore, the reason is inconclusive.
Now, as to how the cessation of qualities is ascertained, he says: "The qualities exist," and so forth.
Regarding human compositions, it is suspected whether qualities exist or do not exist;
therefore, [in the case of the Veda] the suspicion of qualities does not even arise for us, since [otherwise] futility would result.
He shows that the very same reason you have stated for the absence of defects applies equally to the absence of the qualities that are the cause of truthfulness.
Having concluded with the words "Therefore," etc., he demonstrates the consequence of the non-existence of both truth and falsity through the non-perception of their causes:
"Therefore, because there is no recourse to the causes of truth and falsity—
namely, wisdom and its opposite, compassion and its opposite— that duality does not exist."
In this context, the connection is respectively as follows: wisdom and the like are the causes of truthfulness, while lack of compassion and the like are the causes of falsity.
"The two" refers to truthfulness and falsity.
He demonstrates what follows from the non-existence of duality with the words "pointlessness," and so forth:
"Therefore, pointlessness results, like the sentence 'six cakes' and the like;
yet if meanings connected with action and factors of action are indeed perceived."
This understanding of yours might arise from the narrative of a person, like the story of Urvaśī and others,
even though the work itself lacks that purpose, due to its inherent nature.
It would follow that the Veda is as meaningless as the speech of a madman, such as "six cakes, ten pomegranates," and so forth.
Now, for the Buddhist who seeks to prove the meaninglessness of the Veda, his proposition would be contradicted by what is perceived;
for from the statement, "From the Agnihotra sacrifice, heaven arises," the comprehension of its meaning is directly experienced.
Anticipating the objection as to how that [Veda] could be excluded, he [the author] wards off the opponent’s opportunity for speech with the words beginning with "eṣā" (this).

He thinks as follows: if the meaninglessness of the Veda were established independently, then there would indeed be a contradiction of the thesis; however, this is merely an application of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum). And in that case, there is no possibility of contradicting the thesis by means of the *prasaṅga*, because the very thing being proposed in that context does not exist.

Merely by means of the exclusion of the pervading property (*vyāpakadharmanivṛtti*), even for one who does not accept the exclusion of the pervaded (*vyāpyanivṛtti*) in another case, a contradiction in speech (*vacanavyāghāta*) is demonstrated through the consequence of an undesired outcome (*aniṣṭāpatti*).
Nor is there subversion by perception (*dṛṣṭabādhā*).
For this cognition might arise from even a meaningless Veda due to the influence of human interpretation.

Just as when a certain person, being ignorant, explains a Vedic sentence such as "Heaven results from the Agnihotra" by saying that the life stories of Bharata, Urvashi, and others are being narrated therein, he nevertheless subsequently attains a cognition of that meaning from that very sentence;
yet that [sentence] is not meaningful in that sense.
In the same way, this cognition of meaning might arise even from the Veda which is inherently meaningless; how, then, can there be a subversion of the proposition by perception?

Furthermore, even if it were granted that only the fault which is the cause of falsity is eliminated and not the excellence [of the means], nevertheless, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason remains unavoidable; demonstrating this, he says: "Even in the absence of faults," and so forth. "Even in the absence of faults, truthfulness is not established because of the existence of something else. There exists yet another category called 'uselessness' (*ānarthakya*); therefore, there is a third group. [This means: Even when faults are absent, truthfulness is not proven, because there is the presence of other factors. Since there is also a further distinct category known as "uselessness," there is a third group [of possibilities]. Thus, the reason remains inconclusive.
For if there were no third category of words apart from truth and falsity, then in the absence of one category, the existence of the second would be necessarily entailed.

However, since there is also a third category—meaninglessness—then the determination of truth does not follow from the exclusion of falsity, because the other third category, meaninglessness, has not been excluded.
Alternatively, the Veda—or the Person—exists inherently capable of producing the cognition of true objects;
therefore, this [Veda or Person] is considered to be a true object, being free from desire.
If this were so, then cognition would always occur without interruption,
because its cause is eternally present, just as it is at the moment in question.
Or else, at the time of a single cognition, everything produced by it would exist [simultaneously],
since that which is capable through its causality is precisely what is intended by the term "cognition."

It might be argued as follows: if the truthfulness of the Veda were admitted to be caused by qualities such as compassion, then—since those qualities reside in a person and would cease upon the cessation of that person—truthfulness, like falsity, would also cease. However, because the Veda possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), its capacity to cause knowledge of true objects belongs to its very nature and is not produced by qualities; therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is not inconclusive, nor does it entail the consequence of the Veda being purposeless. Anticipating this response from the opponent and refuting it, he says: "If it were so," and so forth.
The intention is that just as this Veda possesses meaningfulness by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*), so too its falsity is possible; thus, the reason [adduced] is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This he will state later.

Furthermore, if [the Veda] were by nature a cause of knowledge, then knowledge arising from it would necessarily occur at all times and simultaneously, because its causes would be unimpaired; how then could there not be the consequence of its meaninglessness?

The formal argument is as follows: whenever something has its complete cause, it necessarily exists at that time; for example, the cognition produced by the *agnihotra* and other Vedic injunctions exists at the intended moment. And the cognition of the Omniscient One, which has the Vedic sentences as its cause, possesses its complete cause in every state. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

And regarding the position that [all cognitions] arise simultaneously, he states another fault with the words "tataḥ param" and so forth: "Because its capacity to produce cognition is subsequently exhausted, this Veda would not be eternal; or, if the capacity remains, cognition would arise again."

For instance, if the Veda were to produce all cognitions simultaneously and subsequently lose its capacity to produce further cognitions, then, due to the exhaustion of that capacity which is identical with its own nature, it would follow that it is subject to decay.

On the other hand, if it does not lose that capacity, then there would be the undesirable consequence of cognitions being produced again at a later time; thus, in no way can an eternal entity possess the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
[Page 648] With the words "But even if," etc., he raises the doubt that the reason— "that which has its causes unimpaired"— is unestablished (*asiddha*):
"Even if it depends on auxiliary factors such as explanations and the like,
and because those [auxiliaries] exist sequentially, that cognition is held to be sequential."
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "exegesis, etc.," the inclusion of convention (*saṅketa*) and so forth is intended.
And "of these" refers to exegesis and the rest.
He refutes this with the words "not so," and so forth:
"It is not so; for what kind of dependence could there be for that which is already capable?
If it becomes capable through connection with that [auxiliary], then what end is there to its eternality in your view?"
For one who is incapable would depend upon another, out of a desire to produce a nature that is capable;
but for that which is already capable, there is no deficiency in its nature—so what kind of dependence could it have?
If you instead maintain that what was previously incapable becomes subsequently capable through association with auxiliary causes, then you must abandon all hope for the eternity of the Veda.
To the question "How so?", he says: "If that which was previously incapable is made capable by them once again,
then this [knowledge] would necessarily be of human origin, for it is a factor of cognition based upon men."

The intended meaning is that [the capacity] is non-different [from the Veda]. However, if there were a difference, the relationship would be unestablished, and it would follow that the Veda is not a causal agent; for one must say that the effect arises from the capacity alone.
Thus, it is said to be "an auxiliary to knowledge."

The Veda that serves as an auxiliary to knowledge is born from a human source; the very nature of the Veda is also born from a human source, since it is not distinct from the Veda, and thus it too is indeed born.

Furthermore, showing that not only does the consequence of impermanence follow from dependence on another, but that the postulation of its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*) would also become pointless, he says "nahi" and so forth: "For this Veda, even if it were to remain [eternally], does not produce knowledge for us until it has been illuminated by persons who act as lamps."
Therefore, one should not postulate that its lack of human authorship is the cause of its knowledge of reality; for this knowledge proceeds from the explanations of men.
Even if this authorlessness of the Veda were true, it would nevertheless be purposeless;
for the desired fruit of this [authorlessness] is knowledge, and that depends upon persons.

If its authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatā*) is postulated for the sake of knowledge that accords with reality, then even that postulation is incapable of producing such knowledge independently of a person; thus, that postulation is futile.
Let it be that persons alone, being authoritative (*pramāṇabhūta*), are the composers who serve as the cause for knowledge that accords with reality.
What now is the use of this "authorlessness" (apauruṣeyatva), which merely stands by as something already established?

Now, if it is argued that the Veda must be accepted as always capable [of producing knowledge]—lest there be the consequence of its impermanence and the assumption of its being non-human (apauruṣeya) be rendered futile—then he shows that the same fault as before follows, with the words "If it is capable," and so on:
"If this [Veda] is always capable, why does it depend on anything else?
For if the cause is solely its own capacity, then for you, knowledge would necessarily arise from it."
It might be argued that even if there is dependence on persons, the quality of being non-human (apauruṣeya) is not rendered futile;
for it is only an already existing object that is revealed by persons, not something new created.
For if they were to create something new, their independence would have to be admitted.
And therefore, being overwhelmed by passion and other afflictions, who could restrain them as they compose a scripture with perverted meanings?
Showing that this same collection of defects applies equally even when an explanation is made by persons, he says "Independent," and so forth:
"In this world, independent persons [compose] an explanation of the Veda according to their own whims."
Those who act thus cannot be obstructed by anyone at all.
Therefore, it is suspected that these [opponents], being corrupted by defects such as delusion and pride,
might even provide a distorted interpretation of the scripture.
Moreover, no human being is accepted [by you] as an independent knower of the meaning of the Veda—that which consists of supersensible objects—who could then explain that Vedic meaning.

For his capacity to perceive supersensible objects is said to result from his thorough knowledge of the Vedic meaning, not independently; yet his thorough knowledge of the Vedic meaning cannot exist without his capacity to perceive supersensible objects. Thus, it clearly and most certainly follows that there is a circular dependency. Demonstrating this, he says: "Nor is there even a single human being among them who is perceived as a seer of the supersensible," and so forth.
For knowledge of the relationship between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth, is certainly not without an injunction.
Because for you there is no direct seer of supersensuous objects;
for he alone sees who sees through the eternal word.
Knowledge that has no prompting (codanā) is "non-prompted" (acodana); that is to say, it is independent of prompting. He states the reason for this with the words "because."
To the question "How even this [is so]," he says: "By means of speech," and so forth.
As it has been said: "Therefore, there exists no direct seer of supersensible objects;
rather, he who sees by means of eternal speech, he truly sees."
It might be argued that the Veda itself, without depending on human activity, will communicate its own meaning to this person;
therefore, the charge of mutual dependence does not arise. To this, he says "The Veda," and so forth:
"The Veda does not always speak its meaning to a person independently, being devoid of intention."
But it depends upon an explanation by a person that is like a blind man's staff.

For the Veda does not itself communicate its own meaning to one who has never heard it before and who is ignorant of the convention; what then does it do? To this he says: "like a staff held by the blind," and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: that which is similar to a staff (*yaṣṭi*) grasped or taken up by the blind.
To the question, "What is the fault in its being dependent? he says:
"Being drawn by that [desire], it might even fall onto a wrong path;
therefore, it is not logical for the Veda to be like light or to serve as an eye."
"Sa" refers to the Veda;
"tayā" refers to a male commentary;
[the phrase] "he might fall even into a wrong path" [is used].
Because it reveals a contrary meaning,
that which was stated— "Therefore, one must never disagree with the Veda, which, like light, is the sole eye for all the world"—
is untenable.
With the words "of that which is independent," etc., he concludes the subject at hand:
"And if it were to produce cognition while being independent,
its validity would clearly not even be possible, because of its dependence on a person."
For it has been established that it is not logical for that which possesses the capacity [to produce knowledge] to do so in dependence upon a person.

Let it be granted, for the sake of argument, that even a capable [means of knowledge] produces knowledge in dependence upon a person; nevertheless, even if it produces knowledge in dependence upon a person, its validity (*prāmāṇya*) cannot clearly be possible—this is the construction of the words.
The particle *api* is displaced in order; it should be understood immediately after the phrase "even while producing knowledge."
Clarifying the meaning of this very point, he says:
"Because it is the cause of cognition in accordance with reality, its status as a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is indeed established;
however, if it were dependent upon human interpretation, the conception of it as a means of knowledge would not be sound."
The conceptualization of pride is not virtuous;
for it has already been established that because one is dragged by it, one may even fall onto a wrong path.

And therefore, as it has been said: "When the Veda is established as a valid means of knowledge, the beginningless succession of disciples and teachers, even if postulated, serves to ensure its faultlessness."

Showing that this is incorrect, he says "ittham" and so forth: "In this way, since the Veda is not established as a means of valid cognition, even if an beginningless succession of pupils and teachers is postulated, it does not serve to avoid the fault."
In the word "asthita," one should understand that there is an elision of the vowel *a*.

To the question "Why is this not tenable?", he says: "Because even one among them... Since not even a single person among them is considered to possess supersensuous vision, and since this [tradition] is imagined as being beginningless, it is therefore a succession of the blind.
If indeed this has become a succession of the blind, what of it? To this he says: "By the blind, the blind," and so forth:
"The blind man led by the blind does not surely find the correct path;
likewise, the conception of beginningless [ignorance] for this [tradition] is fruitless."

As it is stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya: "In matters of this kind, the word of a human being does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge, just as the word of the blind does not regarding specific forms."

Having thus accepted the beginninglessness [of the Veda] as established through the succession of disciples, the author states the fault [in that position]; yet, demonstrating that even this is not established, he says "from another" and so forth:
"Even Manu, Vyāsa, and others are knowers of the truth of the Veda from another source;
there is no proof for the claim that this [Veda] was composed by them alone."
"It is not valid cognition," because it is absolutely beyond the reach of the senses.

It might be argued as follows: "Validity is not desired on the basis of being non-human (apauruṣeya) because it is the cause of non-erroneous knowledge; rather, it arises from the eternal relationship between word and meaning alone, which possesses a true object. And that [true object] occurs only when there is non-human authorship. To this we reply: even in that case, the reason is indeed inconclusive (anaikāntika). For what is the reason for this restriction—that that which is non-human must necessarily possess a true object?
Granted that this may be so, he says the following to show that there is nevertheless a fault:
"Let it be that validity arises merely from a real object and an eternal connection;
however, no one can ever determine that supersensible conjunction."

Since those objects are beyond the senses, yoga residing in them is also beyond the senses; and all these men are always, by their very nature, incapable of perceiving what is not within the range of the senses.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has truth as its object and is an eternal relation.
For the eternal relation is indeed postulated; if it were not the cause for the cognition of the object, then that postulation would be useless.
And it has no other nature besides being the generator of the cognition of the object.
For this alone is the function of a relation: the production of the cognition of an object. How could that which does not perform this function be a relation?

Nor is this [relation] a cause for the cognition of an object by its mere existence; rather, it is so when it is known. Otherwise, there would be cognition from it even for one who has not grasped the convention. Furthermore, it cannot be known by anyone, because since the related objects such as heaven (*svarga*) are beyond the senses, the relation itself is also beyond the senses.
If it is argued that those who perceive supersensuous objects will know it, he says: "for those who do not see what is beyond the senses," and so forth.
As it has been said:
"Therefore, there exists no direct perceiver of supersensuous objects;
he who perceives through the eternal Word, he truly sees."
Thus, those who do not perceive with their own eyes are those who do not see objects beyond the reach of the senses.
If it is argued that the Veda itself will declare this, he replies with the words "this is mine," and so forth:
"That Veda does not say, 'This is my connection with the meaning';
rather, a connection with the meaning devised by humans is no different from [the claims of] human authors."

For these venerable Brahmins do not say, "Let this object of mine be accepted by you"; rather, with his compassion greatly increased, his mind solely inclined toward the city [of the heart], and being devoted to the welfare of others, the Person of the Veda (Vedapuruṣa), like a generous donor, himself bestows his own wealth upon the Brahmins. [The opponent objects: "In that case, they will simply imagine it for themselves. To this he replies with the words beginning "naraklṛpta" (fashioned by hell).
He demonstrates that very non-difference with the words "tadyathā" and so forth:
"Just as it is suspected that there may be error in that which is of human origin,
why should that same suspicion not also apply to that which is merely imagined by men?"

Thinking, "I might understand the meaning as being confused," the person who is the cause of confusion [thinks this]. Just as words employed by people themselves become confused when they are thrown into disorder, so too do the meanings devised by them; what difference is there in this case?
*Sā* refers to the state of being contrary (*viparītatā*). *Śaṅkyā* means that which is to be suspected (*śaṅkanīyā*).

Previously, it was established that since the Veda lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*), the postulation of a succession of pupils and teachers is futile; now, [the author] demonstrates that even if its authority were granted by way of an eternal relationship, the postulation of a succession of pupils and teachers is nonetheless useless in either case, beginning with the words "Even if the means of knowledge...": "Even if the Veda were established as a means of valid knowledge, this beginningless succession of pupils and teachers, though postulated, has become a lineage of the blind."

Regarding what was stated— "Could that not indeed be a doubt even concerning what is imagined by men?"— the opponent here demonstrates the impossibility of such doubt with the words beginning "nanu" [p.653]:
"Surely, a cognition regarding heaven and so forth arises free from suspicion and the like."
Like the statements regarding the Agnihotra and other rites, and like unshakable perceptual cognitions.
If one were to perform that [action] without relying on it, how could the Veda possess the status of a valid authority?
For no one understands a doubtful meaning from such a statement.
*Āreka* means doubt. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), error (*viparyāsa*) is included.
As it is stated in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*: "And from this statement, 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice,' one does not understand with doubt whether heaven exists or does not exist."
And this [cognition], being understood as definitively determined, cannot be false.
For that which, having arisen, subsequently perishes is a false cognition;
however, this [cognition] does not undergo subversion at another place or at another time.
"Therefore, it is not false.
For otherwise, why would your mind—not even as you experience a mass of fire whose interior is blocked by a spreading multitude of clearly visible sparks—not be tossed about on the swing of doubt?
And consequently, not even a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would belong to you; such is the intention of the opponent.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition is free from doubt and error is an object of the epistemic practice (*pramāṇa-vyavahāra*) of discerning persons, just like the cognition that causes the determination of fire for one whose mind is not deluded and who seeks its effects, such as burning or cooking; and the cognition arising from sentences such as "the Agnihotra [is to be performed]" is likewise free from doubt and error. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*). The phrase "it would not take hold" is to be connected with the word "validity" (*pramāṇatām*).
Forming the thought, "I shall do that."
He replies with the words "Not so," and so forth:
"It is not so, because doubt arises [regarding them], just as it does regarding contradictory or irrelevant statements;
for discerning people do not perceive any difference whatsoever among these."
For certainty regarding existence or non-existence is not possible with respect to that which transcends the senses.
If it is argued that certainty arises from the Vedic sentence, why should it not arise from other [sources] as well?

If the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is that a cognition free from doubt and other such defects arises for discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*) from the Vedic sentence, then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). For instance, just as there is doubt for discerning persons regarding the statement "heaven does not arise from the *agnihotra*," so too is doubt exactly the same regarding the statement "heaven arises from the *agnihotra*. This is because, in matters beyond the senses (*atīndriya-artha*), there is no cause for determining existence or non-existence, and because the correspondence with reality (*arthasaṃvāda*) is not perceived in either case.
[The phrase] "like a contrary or another [non-Vedic] sentence" [is used].
The suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the seventh case.
Now, it might be argued: "If certainty arises from the Vedic sentence itself, why then seek another cause? To this, he says "anyādṛk" and so forth.
[This refers to] a certainty that determines a meaning contrary to the meaning of the Veda.
"From another" means:
why does it not arise from human [authorship]? It certainly does.
Consequently, that too would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because at that time there is no difference between the two, as no sublation is perceived in either case.

If it is argued that an unshakable conviction arises for discerning Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), and therefore the reason is not "unestablished" (*asiddha*), [the author] shows that even if it were so established, its "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntikatā*) remains unavoidable by stating "of Vedic scholars," and so forth:
"But this unshakable cognition arises for Vedic scholars whose minds are overwhelmed by faith; for others, it is the same as that which arises from other [causes]."

For instance, among the followers of the Sugata and others, an unshakable conviction arises that the occurrence of suffering in the miserable realms results from sacrifice accompanied by the killing of living beings.
And no sublation of this cognition is observed at present;
if it is suspected in some case or at some time, that suspicion is equally applicable to the Vedic statement as well.
"Unshakable" refers to the intellect.
"Of others" refers to the Buddhists and so forth.
"From another" refers to the statement that the production of suffering through misfortune arises from sacrifice, which is based on the killing of living beings.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "for thus," and so forth;
it is easily understood.

Furthermore, he demonstrates the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the Veda’s lack of human authorship with the verse beginning "narecchā" and so forth: "If the Veda were to reveal its own meaning by itself, independently of conventions dependent upon human will, then it would be appropriate for it to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
For even when its own object is being misrepresented otherwise by those whose intellects are overwhelmed by defects such as delusion and pride, it does not abandon that object.
Because it swiftly produces a cognition directed toward that very object,
and not because it illuminates some other purpose desired by persons.
If it depends upon human intention, it does not differ from that which is of human origin;
for its manifestation would then be dependent on that [intention], and thus it could even be erroneous.

Because desire is independent, the Veda—which depends on conventions subject to that [desire]—would not reveal its own intended meaning, as there would be no restriction [on what it reveals]. However, when the Veda conveys its meaning independently of that [desire], it is then fit to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it generates the comprehension of its own meaning more swiftly by disregarding human interpretation; for otherwise, even when being interpreted differently, it would not abandon the revelation of its own meaning by its very nature, just like the eye and other sense organs. This is the collective sense.
"Being proclaimed" (*ākhyāyamāna*) means "being interpreted" (*vyākhyāyamāna*).
"Aram" means "swiftly."
"Jhagitīti" means "instantly";
that human desire is indeed inverted.

[655] Let it be granted that there is an intrinsic connection with the object due to the Veda’s being non-human in origin; nevertheless, even so, the desired conclusion is not established. To demonstrate this very inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), he says "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth: "Moreover, just as the truthfulness of the non-human [Veda] is accepted as natural, why is its falsity not likewise suspected?"
For its truthfulness indeed arises from its being the cause of the cognition of a true object;
likewise, its falsity is also suspected to be intrinsic, based on its being the cause of the cognition of a false object.
"Prākṛta" means that which exists in the primordial nature (prakṛti); the sense is "natural."

Showing that the very fact of being composed by an authoritative person (*pramāṇabhūtapuruṣa*) should be accepted as the cause of the Veda’s validity, rather than its "uncreatedness" (*akṛtakatva*), which indicates mere dullness, he says "Furthermore," and so on: "Furthermore, if you are indeed insistent upon the validity of the Veda, then let effort be directed toward [establishing] its having a faultless author and the like."
For this [scripture], composed by a faultless author and illuminated by faultless commentators,
shines forth in this world as a means for attaining knowledge of the true nature of reality.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "because of being composed by a faultless author, etc.," the status of being an expounder (*vyākhyātṛtva*) is included.

Now, [the author] asks: "How can the authority of that which has been explained by those free from faults be established? To this he says: "Of those endowed with wisdom, compassion, and so forth," and so on. For indeed, the well-ascertained true words of even human beings, when they are endowed with wisdom, compassion, and so forth, are causes for knowledge in accordance with reality.
As Śabarasvāmin has stated: "But as for that which is worldly speech, if it comes from a trustworthy person or concerns an object of the senses, it is indeed non-false.
Thus, "possessing true speech" means they are excellent.
Furthermore, demonstrating that the quality of being non-human-made (*apauruṣeyatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "Merely because it was not made by a human," and so forth:
"Even though it was not made by a human, it does not necessarily produce knowledge of things as they truly are;
for it is observed that forest fires and the like serve as causes even for false cognition."

For it is not only due to the imposition of human defects that there is an error of cognition regarding objects; for even forest fires and the like, which are devoid of such [human] defects, produce false cognitions regarding blue lotuses and other things.
"Forest fire" (dāva-vahni) refers to a fire located in the woods.
Furthermore, that which arises spontaneously from the friction of bamboos and the like should be understood here as the subject of this deviation.

The meaning is that since the production [of fire] by means of rubbing sticks and so forth is performed by persons, it is impossible for it to be non-human (apauruṣeya); therefore, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) from the reason.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of mirages and the like is intended.
He demonstrates that very fact of being the cause of false cognition with the verse beginning "raktaṃ" and so forth:
"For a blue lotus is indeed perceived as red when there is the light of fire.
If it is argued that fire and the like are not a valid reason because they are produced, that is not tenable."
Now, one might think: "It is not merely 'non-human authorship' (*apauruṣeyatva*) alone that we have described as the reason;
rather, it is qualified by the condition 'being uncreated' (*akṛtakatve sati*).

Alternatively, the mention of 'human authorship' is intended to indicate 'being created,' so there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of a fire caused by lightning, which is created. Anticipating this response from the opponent, [the author] says "of fire and so forth," etc.
Its cause is the cause of false cognition.
He refutes [the objection] with the words beginning "What is the artificiality of objects? etc.:
"What is this artificiality of objects that serves as the basis for false cognition?
For if it were so, smoke would not be a correct indicator of fire."

A qualification is that which excludes the reason from its opposite; otherwise, if certainty could be obtained for a reason through any arbitrary qualification whatsoever, then there would be no uncertain reason at all, since a qualification can always be easily applied everywhere by virtue of one's own desire. Furthermore, the qualification "being uncreated" does not exclude the Veda’s status as a cause of false cognition. For if being created were established as a cause of false cognition, then that [status of being created], upon being excluded, would also exclude that [false cognition].
Perhaps another might say, "It is already established. To this, he replies with the words "For in this way," and so forth.
If being produced were the basis for false cognition, then it would follow that non-producedness is the cause of right cognition.

This is because it is impossible for two mutually contradictory states, such as right and false cognition, to have a single cause; for it is not logical that fire, which has heat as its cause, should also have cold as its cause.
And therefore, because it is produced, we say that it could not be the cause for the cognition of fire as it truly is.
Furthermore, it might be argued that it is not determined in this way that "being produced" is the cause of false cognition alone and not of anything else;
rather, since "being produced" is the sole basis for false cognition and nothing else, the existence of any other cause for it is being negated.
However, this is not a negation of the fact that correct cognition has "being produced" as its cause.
Nor is it maintained that every produced thing (*kṛtaka*) without distinction is a cause of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*),
such that— due to their mutual contradiction— the capacity of correct and false cognitions would imply that the opposite of the "produced" must be the cause of correct cognition.

Rather, because the "produced" is manifold, only some things are causes of false cognition, such as jaundice (*kāmalā*) and the like, while others are causes of correct cognition, such as the unimpaired collection of sense faculties and so forth.

Otherwise, since some produced thing such as snow is observed to be a cause for cold touch, one would have to postulate by implication that an unproduced thing is the cause for hot touch, which is the opposite of cold;
yet this is not the case.

Therefore, since the production of smoke is not denied to be a cause for right cognition, smoke indeed remains the basis for right cognition. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And thus, even that which is non-human," and so forth.
And thus, even if it were non-human in origin, the Veda would not at all be established as the basis for right knowledge; therefore, this postulation of its [origin] is entirely in vain.

For if the state of being produced were the basis for both correctness and falsity, then that [state of being produced], upon ceasing, would cause both false and correct cognition to cease; consequently, the Veda’s status as a cause of correct cognition would not be established by its unproduced nature, since that [unproduced nature] would not be the basis for it. And thus, the qualification would be useless, and the reason would remain inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Alternatively, it might be argued that by the phrase "by virtue of not being created by a person," the aforementioned reason—possessing both positive and negative concomitance—is not indicated; rather, this is simply a formulation based on negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone.

For just as falsity—the opposite of the probandum—is pervaded by "being produced," which is the opposite of the reason (since falsity is observed only in human compositions), therefore, wherever "not being produced"—which is incompatible with the pervader of falsity—is present, there, through that incompatibility, the pervader of falsity (i.e., being produced) is excluded; and by the force of this, the exclusion of the pervaded (falsity) is also established. Thus, the conclusion that "what is not produced has a true object" follows by implication even without a positive concomitance (anvaya); hence, the demonstration of anvaya is redundant.
True, this is so.
If the relationship of pervader and pervaded between the contrapositives were established, it would be so;
however, it is not established.

For instance, if there were a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the reason in the counter-example of the probandum, then there would be a pervasion between the two counter-examples; but that does not exist.
Nor is the non-existence [of something] established by mere non-perception, because that would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).
It might be argued: "Since falsity is observed in what is produced (*kṛtaka*), which is the opposite of the unproduced (*akṛtaka*), its absence in the unproduced is established by implication.
This is incorrect.

For it is not possible to determine the absence [of a property] in one place by means of its observation elsewhere; for even in a single case, there is the observation of a contradictory pervader (*viruddhavyāpaka*). To illustrate: a single impermanence is seen to pervade two contradictory properties—those produced immediately after effort and those not so produced. It does not follow that because impermanence is observed in what is produced immediately after effort, it must therefore be absent in what is not produced immediately after effort.

Furthermore, if falsity were established merely by the fact that it is observed there [in the case of human speech], then since unreality is also observed in some human compositions due to their being produced (*kṛtakatva*), that [unreality] too would be pervaded by it. Consequently, upon the cessation of being produced, just as falsity ceases, unreality would also cease; thus, truthfulness would not be established on the basis of being non-human (*apauruṣeya*). Enough of this.

Thus, having at length demonstrated the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the reason— namely, "being free from the defects of causes for falsity"— whether this refers to its being unauthored (*narākṛtatva*), or to its being uncreated (*akṛtaka*) as implied by that, or to its being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*) as directly expressed by its own word, [the author], desiring to demonstrate its lack of established validity (*prasiddhatā*), concludes by saying "And therefore," and so forth: "And therefore, the proof of authorlessness, manifestation, and permanence,
as well as the connection between eternal words and their objects, has been described in vain."
Even though that [defect] exists, its status as a cause for knowledge of reality is not accepted; this has been explained in detail immediately following.
Therefore, we do not hold it in high regard when he refutes this very point;
for who would take the trouble to refute that which is irrelevant to the matter at hand?

The compound *apauruṣeyatvavyaktinityatvasādhanam* means "the proof of authorlessness, manifestation, and eternity. A *sādhana* is that by which something is proven; it is the logical reason (*hetu*).
And that has been previously stated to be of various kinds.
"In that" refers to [the qualities] such as being authorless (*apauruṣeya*).
"Of this" refers to the Veda.
"It is accepted" means it is established. "In detail" means extensively.
"This refutation" refers to the critique of [the Veda's] lack of human authorship and so forth.
Since it has already been established that even if that [reason] were present, the desired object would not be proven, any attempt to refute it would be irrelevant to the subject at hand.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "yathārtha" and so forth:
"For here, the subject under discussion is that the Veda is the cause of knowledge corresponding to reality;
and it has been established that even if [the Veda] were not composed by a person, this [status] would not be proven."
Regarding the phrase "it is mere vainglory" (*āhopuruṣikā*): here, "vainglory" refers to whatever is stated in brief;
for by means of this, those of subtle intelligence perceive the various destinies as they disperse.
"One who has the conceit [thinking] 'Oh, what a man I am! is an *ahopuruṣa*; the state of being such is *āhopuruṣikā*.
The suffix *-vuñ* is applied because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group;
it denotes nothing other than conceit (*abhimāna*)."
Intellect itself is "vision" (dṛk) due to their common characteristic; those who possess such subtle intellectual vision are described as such.
Regarding what was stated, "Because he is inaccessible to the five [means of knowledge]," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "Of the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇānām*).
Even by the cessation of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) does not cease to exist,
because they do not possess the status of being a pervading cause (*vyāpaka-hetu*) in that regard.
By this, he demonstrates the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the primary reason (*mūlahetu*).
For it is either an essential nature (*svabhāva*) or a cause (*kāraṇa*), acting as a pervader (*vyāpaka*), that, when excluded, excludes the pervaded (*vyāpya*) or the effect (*kārya*),
because those two are necessarily bound to it through identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from it (*tadutpatti*), respectively.
Even in their absence, it is impossible for your [proposition] to be pervaded by the effect;

for those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot possibly function as pervasive causes with respect to every object. To explain: because an object remote in space, time, or nature can exist even without a means of valid cognition, there is no pervasion by it; nor is the means of valid cognition the cause for that very reason, since the means of valid cognition itself is the effect of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Furthermore, an effect, when ceasing, does not cause the mere cause to cease, because deviation is observed.
Nor is it logical for that which is neither a cause nor a pervader to be a negator, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, it is established that the absence of the mere means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is deviant with respect to the absence of the mere object of valid cognition (*prameya*), which is the probandum.
Making manifest that very same inconclusiveness by demonstrating its possibility in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), he says: "By five," and so forth.
Even though it is not accessible through the five [means of knowledge], it is not understood solely through non-existence;
the author of the Veda [is not understood thus], like stories and the like whose authors are unknown.
The word "tat" means "therefore.
The phrase "even though unapproachable by the five" is connected with the distant term "the agent of the Veda. Those narratives and the like whose agents are unknown are described as such.
First, a *karmadhāraya* compound is formed with words such as "ākhyāyikā" (narrative) and so forth; from that [compound], ending in the sixth case, the suffix *vati* is then to be applied.
With the words "But even if," etc., he raises the objection that the reason is unestablished with respect to the domain of deviation:
"Even if their author were to be inferred on the basis of their meaningfulness or on the basis of their being the meaning of case-endings, why could the same not be the case for the Veda as well?"
"Of these" refers to narratives (*ākhyāyikā*) and so forth.
"Why not likewise for the Veda? means:
why is an author not inferred for the Veda as well, by means of its being meaningful and having distinct meanings, since there is no difference [between it and those works]?
And consequently, the absence of a means of valid cognition is unestablished.
Furthermore, there are two positions: [the reason] is either the cessation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for all sentient beings, or the cessation of one's own means of valid cognition.
Showing that in the first position the reason is "unproven due to doubt" (*sandigdhasiddhatā*), and in the second it is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntikatā*), he says "sarvasattva... and so forth:
"But being unapproachable by all sentient beings is sometimes doubtful."
For it is even suspected that someone might know [the truth] through some kind of pride.
By means of which all living beings situated within the three worlds are clearly capable of ascertaining this [Self] with their entire being, without any limitation.
But the fact that [the object] is not perceived by oneself is inconclusive;
for, according to you, the absence of that [object] is not ascertained by the mental constructs of other persons.
The phrase "this [is so]" means that no creator of the god is known by all sentient beings;

thus, with the words "for instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth, he establishes precisely the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāritā*) through the volitions of students and others belonging to other persons.

Regarding what was stated—that the creator is not perceived—he says "And the students... etc., in order to demonstrate that this [claim] is unproven: "And the students of the Vedas are considered by direct perception to be their creators; for it is not logical that they are merely manifestors, since the manifestation of eternal things is impossible."
If it is accepted that no creator whatsoever has been seen, then because the students have indeed been seen, the reason is clearly unestablished (*asiddha*). Alternatively,
if it is intended that an original creator has not been seen, even then the reason is unestablished due to doubt (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*),
because it is possible that he was seen by someone at some time.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the students are not the authors [of the Veda], but rather its manifesters; to this he says "for not," and so forth.
"They" refers to the students.
And how the manifestation of eternal things is impossible, he will demonstrate later.
If it is asked, "How can there be a manifestor even for impermanent things such as a jar?"—
it is true;
even in that case, no manifestor is possible.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is it that lamps and the like are perceived as manifestors?
[The answer is: No;
for in that case, the lamp and so forth are indeed producers, since they produce a jar that is capable of generating consciousness.
In the world, something is recognized as a "manifestor" (vyañjaka) for the purpose of making known a specific generative nature;
however, no such manifestor is possible for the Veda, because its nature is unmanifest, unproduced, and devoid of prior or posterior states.
Granted that there may be a manifestor of the eternal; nevertheless, showing that such a manifestor does not differ from a producer, he says: "Upalabhya... and so forth.
For those things whose nature is to be perceived, their manifestation occurs when that [manifesting] operation is present.
If they were already existent even prior to that, their perception would necessarily follow at that time as well.
For it is not logical that a manifestor (vyañjaka) should be something that effects nothing, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
If it effects something, then its very nature must be admitted to be that of a producer (janaka),
since the production of a produced particularity is characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature (svabhāvāntara).
"Of those whose nature is perceptible" refers to the Vedas.
Now, it might be argued: "The Vedas existed even previously with a perceptible nature; so how can their existence [at present] be due to that activity? To this he says, "of them," and so forth.
"Of them" means of the Vedas whose nature is perceptible.
He establishes this through the argument beginning with "tatkārya" (its effect):
"The Veda is determined to be capable of the conventional usage of its effects and so forth,
because it exists when that [Vedic agent] is active, just as a sprout and the like [arise] from a seed and the like."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever comes into existence when there is the operation of something X is fit for the conventional designation (*vyavahāra*) and so forth as the effect of that X; for example, a sprout and the like, which come into existence when there is the operation of a seed and the like, are the effects thereof. Since the Veda possesses an observable nature when there is the operation of a reciter, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). "Conventional designation" (*vyavahāra*) refers to the performance characterized by rejection and acquisition;
by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), knowledge and verbal expression are included.
The reason is not unestablished, because it would follow that [the effect] would have been perceived even prior [to its production];
nor is it inconclusive, because there is no other cause for the conventional usage of the term "effect."

[Page 661] It is correct [to say] that "the relationship [between word and meaning] was not previously perceived," and so forth; regarding this, he says "because of the nature of the sequence of phonemes," and so on: "Because they consist of a sequence of phonemes, like dramas, narratives, and the like, one understands through inference that the Vedas are of human origin."

The formal argument is as follows: whatever has the nature of a sequence of phonemes (vyañjana) is of human origin, such as plays, narratives, and the like; and the Veda has the nature of a sequence of phonemes. This is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
The reason is not unestablished (asiddha), because phonemes manifest only in a sequential order.

Showing that it is also not inconclusive (anaikāntika), he says "otherwise" and so forth: Otherwise, the nature of succession would not exist due to [the object's] permanence and its pervasive nature; nor is there a sequence of manifestation, because manifestation is incompatible with permanence.
"Otherwise" means that if it were not of human origin, but rather its eternality and omnipresence were described, then there would be no sequence.
For instance, a sequence produced by time—such as that of a seed, sprout, and creeper—is not tenable here, because all [phonemes], being eternal, exist simultaneously.
Nor is a sequence produced by space—like a row of ants—possible, because all [phonemes], being omnipresent, occupy the same location in space, namely the sky.
Nor is it produced by manifestation, because manifestation is impossible for that which is eternal, since no excellence can be imparted to it.

Regarding what was stated—that even scripture (*āgama*) does not establish that [the self exists] because "that which is produced and that which is unproduced exists," and so forth—the author replies with the verse beginning "of scripture" (*āgamasya*), etc.: "The validity of scripture, of analogy (*upamāna*), and of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has already been refuted; therefore, their introduction here is not appropriate."

"Prohibited" refers to [the discussion] in the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Of these" refers to scripture (*āgama*), comparison (*upamāna*), and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Regarding what was stated, "for the purpose of removing invalidity," and so forth, he says here:
"invalidity," and so forth:
"The authorlessness of the Veda is for the purpose of removing invalidity."
Furthermore, that [non-existence], being a real entity, must indeed be established by means of proofs.
To the question, "How can that [validity] be a real entity (vastu)? he says, "Because of scripture," and so forth.
This independence of scripture is desired because it does not depend upon human activity;
and that [validity] is either a property residing in the real entity or a nature of the entity itself of such a kind.

By the term "authorlessness" (*apauruṣeyatā*), the independence of the Veda is expressed; for it is employed with the connection that "the Veda is a means of valid cognition precisely because it is independent of human activity. Otherwise, what excellence would be established merely by demonstrating the absence of human authorship?
And that quality of being non-human (apauruṣeyatā) is a property of the thing (vastudharma) for those who hold that the distinction between property and property-bearer is ultimate.

However, in reality, it is the very nature of the thing itself that is spoken of in that way when there is a desire to exclude other distinctions; thus he shows this by saying "or the essence of the thing.
"Of such a kind" means independent (svatantra).
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "for the sake of establishing the position of existence," he says "the position of existence," and so forth:
"And whatever proof is stated for the sake of establishing the position of existence—
even when that [proof] has been refuted, non-existence does not establish itself."
Even when [a reason] exists as a means of proving that state, there would be no certainty of that state;
however, from the mere exclusion of that state, there is no certainty [of its absence].
Even when means of valid cognition have ceased, since the non-existence of objects is not established,
it follows that for both [parties], there is no proof of the thesis that "it does not exist."

For when the means of proof (*sādhana*) employed for the sake of ascertaining a given object is refuted, there would merely be the absence of ascertainment regarding that object; however, this does not imply the non-existence of the object itself, since it has been established that even when the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is absent, the object of cognition (*prameya*) is not necessarily absent—this being due to the distinction between being a cause (*hetu*) and being a pervader (*vyāpaka*). Thus [it is said]: "It exists."
When [this] is thrown out,
it is only appropriate to say that for both positions there is no establishment;
the word "iti" is to be supplied.
And that [phrase] "it does not exist" is to be understood as following immediately after this.
Strengthening this very point by means of an illustration, he says: "Not because of formlessness.

Even when it is stated, "Not because of formlessness, as in the case of sound [which is not eternal], due to deviation in the case of pleasure and so forth," the perishability of sound is not established.

For example, when a proponent of eternalism (nityavādin), desiring to establish that sound possesses an ontologically real eternity, employs the formal argument: "Sound is eternal because it is formless, like space," and the opponent refutes this proof of an ontologically real eternity by stating: "It is not logical that sound is eternal because of its formlessness, since [the reason] is inconclusive due to cases such as pleasure (sukha) and so forth"—even though the proof of an ontologically real eternity has been rejected, the impermanence of sound is nonetheless not established. This case is exactly like that; such is the remainder of the sense.
The word "yathā" (as/for example) is displaced in order;
it should be understood as occurring immediately after the phrase "ukte 'pi" (even though it has been stated).
