Immediately after the word "sound" (śabda), the phrase "it is established as eternal" (nityaḥ siddhyati) must be supplied;
or else, it should be understood as an elliptical usage (ekadeśaprayoga), like the word "Bhīma" and others.
As for what was said regarding "the former and the latter" and so forth— that is,
"that which was stated by others as a proof concerning the two extremes of the former and the latter"—
even in the refutation of that, these proponents of the Veda have not achieved their purpose.
"Tad" means "therefore.
"Having failed to achieve their purpose" refers to the non-establishment of their own position.

Regarding what was stated— that "eternality is indeed intended [to be established] by way of being uncreated and being indestructible," and so forth— he replies with the words beginning "akṛtatvāt" (by way of being uncreated):
"If eternality is intended [to be established] by way of being uncreated and being indestructible..."
Since they consist merely of negation, that [non-existence] is the same even in the case of the indefinable (nirupākhya).
Therefore, like the king of the sky, eternity does not exist in reality;
just as that is so, its authority in the Veda likewise cannot be established.

In this regard, there are two possible conceptualizations: is eternity intended by way of non-production and non-destruction in the form of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or rather in the form of relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*)?

Regarding the first position, because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to examples such as a sky-lotus, the eternity of the Veda as a real entity is not established. For instance, although the production and destruction of a sky-lotus are denied, its eternity as a real entity is likewise not established.
Likewise, since this is also the case with the Veda, the reason [adduced] is inconclusive;
consequently, its authority would not exist at all, just like a flower in the sky.
Showing that [the reason] is also unestablished (*asiddha*), he says "because of being produced," and so forth:
"The negation of being produced and being perishable is not established either;
since it has been stated that [these] exist in the proof, that permanence is not established."
When it is objected that [the reason] is non-existent (*asat*), [the response is] "therefore" (*tat*);
that is, for that reason (*tasmāt*).
Now, if the second position is held, then it should not be said that "those two, being of the nature of non-existence, do not depend upon their own means of proof.
He demonstrates this with the words "paryudāsātmakābhyām" and so forth:
"If permanence is intended by means of those two which are of the nature of exclusion (paryudāsa)..."
Because they consist of that very nature, those two would depend upon their own means of accomplishment.

For those who do not establish that permanence is the very nature of the entity, that [permanence] does not exist of its own accord; rather, its establishment occurs once the two opposing positions have been refuted.
This is easily understood.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "he who asserts the falsity of the meaning of Vedic sentences by means of inference," he replies with the verse beginning "viniścita-trirūpam" (the well-ascertained three-fold [reason]).
And that means of proof which has been set forth as having its three-fold character well-ascertained—
Even by your father, that [objection] could never be refuted.

Regarding the phrase "it has been explained": in the *Anumānaparīkṣā*, it was stated that [inference] arises from the marks (*liṅga*) of essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*).
That cannot be refuted, because it is necessarily connected to real entities (*vastu*).

Furthermore, the alteration of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a real entity cannot be effected by anything, because such alteration is characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature.
Nor does anything at all happen to that entity when a different intrinsic nature is produced, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, whatever entity is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no sublation of it by anything whatsoever.

For otherwise, if that which possesses the characteristics of a valid means of knowledge were subject to sublation, its very definition would be undermined; consequently, due to a lack of confidence in all cases, it would not be a valid means of knowledge anywhere.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "for he does not perish," and so forth:
"For that Person who is declared in the Veda as 'he does not perish'—
the sublation of him by means of inference is clearly established in the teaching of selflessness."
Other [reasons] such as "being of a certain birth" and so forth have also been stated; they are sublated therein, and what has been established there is proven.
Furthermore, that inference, whose necessary connection has been made known, is the prior sublater.

Thus it is said in the Veda: having introduced [the subject] with "This very one is the Self," they declare, "He is indestructible, for he is not destroyed. Furthermore, it is said: "Verily, this Self, O Maitreyī, is indestructible and of an imperishable nature. "Indestructible" (aśīrya) means that he is not destroyed; the meaning is that he is eternal.
"Are" is a term of address.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "jāti etcetera," there is the inclusion of qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), actions (*karman*), and so forth.
Furthermore, the manner in which that *jāti* and the rest are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been established in the "Examination of the Six Categories" (*Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*).
And that inference which subverts the self is also one whose necessary connection has been made known in the section on selflessness.

Now, one might object: "If that [Vedic injunction] is being established as authoritative in the Veda, how can it be sublated here by inference? Or, if even an authoritative means of knowledge were to be sublated, why would inference not likewise be sublated by it? Anticipating this doubt, he says "tasyāḥ" and so forth:
"What fool would think there could be a sublation of that [inference], which is firmly bound to the actual state of things?"
Either by means of a mere, empty sound, or by means of the cognition that arises from it.
"Of that" refers to inference (*anumā*).

Since verbal cognition is based solely on the speaker's intention, it has no necessary connection to the object of knowledge (*prameya*) as a real entity; therefore, it is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to that [object].

Inference, however, arises by the force of a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is connected through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), and thus it is connected to that real entity. Therefore, inference alone is the valid means of cognition, and for this reason, it is the sublater.
"By that which is to come" means by that which is to come in the form of sound.

He demonstrates that if even a word that is unconnected to a real object were to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by stating: "even from a human statement" (*puṃvākyād api*).
That cognition which proceeds even from a human statement regarding a supersensible (*atīndriya*) object—
Why do you not accept that this [inference] is also equivalent to direct perception?

Why would the sentence "Heaven does not result from the Agnihotra" not also possess authority? For there is no distinction between the two cases, as both are equally unimpeded [in their status as statements].
Showing that very lack of distinction, he says "dṛṣṭānta" and so forth:
"Because it is independent of an example, there is an absence of defects due to its non-observation;
yet, if an invalidation of that [non-observation] is suspected because it rests upon a human being..."
If this were so, this doubt would not cease even regarding the Veda;
for its status as a cause of false cognition would be inherent in it from the outset.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even if no fault is perceived at that time, it is still possible [for a fault] because [the Veda] has a person as its basis; this is equally true for the Veda as well, for just as its natural quality of having true meaning might be suspected, so too its having false meaning might be suspected—there is no distinction whatsoever.

Regarding what was stated, "My [word] is not authoritative," and so forth—he demonstrates that this very point can indeed be asserted even in the case of a human-authored statement such as "Heaven does not result from the *agnihotra* sacrifice," by saying "My [word] is not authoritative," and so on:
"Even though the word 'my [word] is not authoritative' makes its meaning understood, it cannot be spoken by a person out of mere malice; it cannot be spoken by one who is honest."

The meaning of the sentence is this: even if this human word, "Heaven does not result from the Agnihotra," makes its object known, one cannot say, "This is not a means of valid cognition for me, the Mīmāṃsaka," merely out of malice toward what is correct.
By this, he states that both non-human (apauruṣeya) and human (pauruṣeya) words are equally the basis for cognition regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses.
Consequently, since they are equal in being the basis for cognition, to claim that validity belongs only to the non-human and not to the other is devoid of reason.
Nor can it be argued that because defects reside in persons, falsity is suspected only in those [texts] dependent on persons and not in those that are authorless (apauruṣeya);
for even in the case of authorless texts, the possibility of their being causes for the cognition of false objects is conceivable.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "Thus, regarding supersensible objects": "Thus, regarding all supersensible objects, every word possesses equal strength and weakness;
for what reason here do you hold this partiality toward only one?"
"Every" refers to that which is of human origin;
"in one and the same place" refers to that which is not of human origin.
Regarding what was stated, "even for one who hates [the Veda]," and so forth, he says there: "The reasoning just mentioned," and so forth.
The reasoning just mentioned is the cause for the lack of authority of the Vedas.
The wise speak thus; therefore, they may be considered speakers of truth.
"Regarding the phrase 'as just stated':
because sound functions solely according to [the speaker's] will, there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the actual object, and so forth.
Regarding the term 'the wise' (*prājñāḥ*):"

The followers of Sugata [the Buddhists] maintain that, as stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "In the case of the Vedic word, there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as the means of conviction, and inference does not become a valid means of knowledge when it contradicts direct perception. Furthermore, regarding what was said—that "the injunction (*codanā*) alone is capable of making known such matters as the past, the present, the future, the subtle, the hidden, and the remote, and no other sense organ can do so"—all of this is refuted by this very [argument], because all of this is equally applicable even to human speech.
Regarding what was stated concerning "retention, study, and exposition," and so forth, he says: "By those whose intellects have been rendered dull by Vedic meditation born of false attachment,
it is no wonder at all that the cause of falsity remains unknown."
For no fault whatsoever is observed among the Persians and other such deceivers who are always intent upon that practice, such as the marriage of a mother and so forth.

The compound is formed by first combining *mithyānurāgeṇa saṃjātam* and *tadvedākhyānam*, and then forming a third-case (instrumental) tatpuruṣa compound with that result; thus, they have been rendered dull-witted by that [combination].
Furthermore, *ādhyānam* means reflection in successive order;
for through false attachment, one fails to perceive even existing defects.
Just as among the Persians and others there is the practice of marrying one's mother and so forth, this is not at all surprising.

Regarding what was stated, namely "Furthermore, as for the eternity of sound," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "pratyakṣa" and so on: "But perceptual recognition has already been refuted;
and because it is erroneous and conceptual, there is no certainty regarding eternity from it."

For the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is "free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). Now, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not free from conceptual construction, because it proceeds by delineating the form of a word in the thought "this is that very same [thing].

Nor is it non-erroneous, because it synthesizes the identity between what was previously seen and what is presently occurring. Furthermore, it is not the case that exactly what was previously seen is seen later, because a sequential cognition cannot arise from that which is non-sequential.
For an effect must possess the nature of coming into being from something; if its cause is present in its entirety at a time when the effect does not occur, why would the effects be delayed?
Furthermore, since that which is eternal cannot be assisted, no dependence upon anything else is possible.
Therefore, the cognitions arising from it would necessarily occur simultaneously.

The formal argument is as follows: whenever something has its complete causal complex, it necessarily occurs at that time; for example, visual cognition when the entire collection of causes such as the eye is present. Furthermore, in every state, the cognitions produced by words such as "cow" possess their complete causal complex. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Therefore, because it is erroneous and conceptual, recognition is not established as being perceptual; this was already demonstrated previously in the examination of the permanence of entities.
Nor is recognition established everywhere by way of its own nature; demonstrating this, he says "vyāvartamāna... and so forth:
"Furthermore, the cognition regarding sound is for the most part of an excluding nature, because one observes:
'This was uttered by a parrot,' and 'This [was uttered] by a maina.'"
If you claim that this [difference] is due to the difference in manifesters, we shall set forth the refutation of manifestation;
moreover, by this very logic of yours, all this would become one.
Consequently, there would be neither any manifestor nor anything manifested;
for when a single thing is undivided, the conceptualization of distinction is contradicted.
These words are of human origin, and these others are not made by anyone;
even this established distinction of yours would not exist if it were dependent upon recognition.

For when sounds are uttered by parrots, mainas, and the like, there arises a cognition that turns away from its object due to the determination of mutually distinct objects—thinking, "this was uttered by the maina" and "this by the parrot. Thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not established in all cases.

If it should be argued that this mutually exclusive cognition regarding the utterances of the parrot and others arises because of a difference in the manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*), this too is untenable, because the existence of a manifesting agent will be refuted later.
He states this very point in the verse beginning with *so 'yam* (that is this...).
"This is that" is the cognition whose form is one of exclusion (*vyāvartamāna*).

Furthermore, if even the established difference between words were determined as being produced by the manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*) and not inherent (*svataḥ*), then there would be a lack of confidence in all cases; thus, bringing forward this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says "And for this very reason," and so forth.
"Everything" means the universe.
If it is argued, "Let it be so," [the author] replies with "Therefore, not," and so forth.
There would be no conventional usage based on distinction—such as "this is the manifestor" and "this is the manifested"—because there is no difference [between them].

Likewise, for you who rely upon recognition as the basis for your position, there could be no established distinction between these [Vedic texts] being of human origin and those such as "śaṃ no devīḥ" being of non-human origin, because there is no difference [between them].
With the words "Some [say]... and so forth, the opponent demonstrates the distinction between Vedic and worldly [words].

Some maintain that certain [Vedic words] possess only a fixed sequence; because they are established through a sequence of manifestors, they are accepted as non-human (apauruṣeya) and are endowed with a restricted order.

Because the fixed arrangement of the sequence of manifestors is constant, certain [mantras], such as *śanno devīḥ* and others, are perceived as having a strictly fixed order; therefore, it is established that those which possess a fixed sequence are non-human (apauruṣeya), while by implication, those contrary to them are human (pauruṣeya).
He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "nanv ayam" and so forth:
"But surely this quality of being produced by a person consists in the sequence of the manifesting [articulations] such as the palate;
therefore, its reversal might possibly occur at some time."

The state of having a fixed sequence is unestablished. For it is accepted [by you] that this [sequence] is due to the restriction of the sequence of the manifestors; yet that sequence of the manifestors, such as the palate and so forth, is not fixed because its occurrence depends upon human will, since human will possesses autonomy.
As it has been said: "Where there is autonomy of will, what indeed can be called a restriction?"

Furthermore, since there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish that this very sequence for [the mantra] beginning with "śaṃ no devīḥ" has existed at all times and will continue to exist, it is possible that the sequence might sometimes be otherwise.
Regarding what was stated—that there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) even though flames and the like are momentary—the author replies with the verse beginning "tejastvādi" and so forth.
The universal (*sāmānya*) such as "fire-ness" (*tejastva*) has already been refuted in detail;
therefore, for us, that which is to be recognized cannot be an eternal universal.

Showing that all of this can be postulated even regarding the [transient] phonemes (*varṇa*), he says "in the phonemes" and so forth: "This recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is possible even with respect to perishing phonemes, whether by considering the universal (*sāmānya*) as the object of recognition, or by [considering it] specifically with regard to those [phonemes]."
However, in whatever aspect— such as rapidity, slowness, and so forth— a cognition of difference arises, there can be no recognition; for that [aspect] is a particular (sāmānya).
It has the characteristic of being excluded from others.
Regarding the statement that "the cognitions of the individual instances of the word 'cow' are differentiated by place, time, and so forth," he says "the oneness of the word," etc.:
"But when reasons are employed for the purpose of establishing the oneness of the word,
the necessary connection is not established because [those reasons] do not contradict anything of a different class."

Regarding those applications of inference stated for the purpose of establishing the oneness of sound, because no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been shown against the opposite of the reason (*hetu*) once it is established, they are in every respect inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding the statement, "Whatever is such as this is seen to be stable, like the portion that is smoke-in-general," [the author], demonstrating that this example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), says "dhūmasāmānya... and so forth.
Even the portion that is smoke-in-general is certainly not...
[omitted] ...it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Only a real entity (vastu) that is excluded from what is heterogeneous is called a universal (sāmānya) and a logical mark (liṅga), and nothing else; and since that is necessarily impermanent, the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikalatā).

Regarding what was stated—that [the fault] would apply to the oneness of a jar and so forth—he shows that this rebuttal is equally applicable to phonemes by saying "of *ga* and so forth," etc.: "If the oneness of *ga* and so forth were also established, then the proof of what is already accepted for the universal (*jāti*) would be redundant;
for the exclusion of what is not of that nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*) is indeed non-different and merely conceptual."
If there were a merging of individuals into oneness, there would be inconclusiveness;
for in each individual application [of the word], the distinction between phonemes is determined by the auditory organs and so forth.

If, by means of an elaborate argument beginning with "divided by place, time, and so forth," the unity of a universal characterized as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is sought to be proven, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); for in all cases, a universal characterized by the exclusion of what is not that [form] is accepted as one by virtue of its determination through a single cognition.

If, on the other hand, the unity of individual particulars (*vyakti-svalakṣaṇa*) is sought to be proven, then because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is sublated by perception and inference, the reasons (*hetu*) are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This is what is meant by "by the senses and so forth."
*Akṣa* means the sense faculty (*indriya*); that which arises therein is *ākṣa*, meaning "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), inference (*anumāna*) is included.
The plural number is used with reference to the distinction between individual instances.
To the question, "How is difference apprehended through direct perception? he says:

"That distinction between the agreeable, the disagreeable, and so forth, which has come within the range of direct perception—the difference is established because cognitions occur successively, as in the case of a young girl."

For cognitions of the individual instances of the word "cow," though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, do not have a single object, because they appear as distinct, just like the cognitions of taste, color, and the like.
For the manifestation of the distinctions of *ṣaḍja* and so forth is ascertained by direct perception;
nor will it be stated that this [distinction] is due to the manifesting agents.
"Favorable" means agreeable;
the opposite of this is "the reverse.
He also states the sublation [of the opponent's view] by means of inference, beginning with the words "of cognitions," and so forth.
The meaning of this will be clarified by the passage beginning with "those of yesterday and today" and so forth.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognitions appear as distinct do not all have a single object, just like cognitions whose objects are taste, color, and so on; and the cognitions of individual instances of the word "cow," which are distinguished by place, time, and other factors, appear as distinct. This is an apprehension of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). To ward off the charge that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says "ṣaḍja-etc. and so forth.
Establishing the meaning of the statement that "the difference [of cognitions] is proven because cognitions occur sequentially, as in the case of a young girl," he says "hyastanā" and so forth:
"All these cognitions of the word 'cow' belonging to yesterday and today..."
They do not have a single object, because they arise sequentially, like the cognitions of color, smell, and so forth.

The formal argument is as follows: those cognitions that occur sequentially do not have a single object, just like the sequential cognitions of taste, color, and so forth; and these cognitions of the word "cow" from yesterday and today occur sequentially. This is an observation of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
With the words "otherwise," etc., he refutes the inconclusiveness of both reasons:
otherwise, all cognitions would have a single object,
and there would be a contradiction regarding their sequential occurrence despite the presence of a capable cause.
Regarding the phrase "of all cognitions":
this refers to cognitions of taste, form, and so forth.

It constitutes a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the reason "because they appear as distinct," which [otherwise] would entail the consequence that these cognitions have mutually non-distinct objects.
And "contradictory to sequential existence" refers to the [reason] "because of arising in succession."
Regarding what was stated, "And if [the relationship] were artificial," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "By nature alone" (*prakṛtyaiva*):
"By nature alone, even though there is a distinction among entities, there is a restriction of their capacities for the sake of a single conceptual synthesis; this has been established previously."
...and because of the act of synthesis (pratyavamarśa), [distinctions such as] the oneness of the word and so forth do not exist either;
the world considers the multiplicity of usage to belong to a single word.
The relation is established because it resides in multiple individuals;
therefore, it is universal, for it has attained oneness despite [residing in] distinct individuals.
This is easily understood.

Now, as to why it is called "the world" (loka), he says: "In reality," and so forth. In reality, however, no connection exists between a word and its object, because of their difference and because [the word] does not arise [from the object]; therefore, it is superimposed by those who are deluded.
For this has already been explained in detail previously:
the entire established status of words and their meanings is subverted because pervasion is impossible.

By the phrase "because of difference," [the author] negates the relation characterized by identity (*tādātmya*). By the phrase "because of non-origination from that," he negates the relation characterized by origination (*tadutpatti*).

There is no relation other than these two; furthermore, without such a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), a restriction on a word’s capacity to convey meaning would not be logical, as it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, it was already established in the previous discussion on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) that the relationship between word and object is superimposed.

Therefore, in the formulation beginning with "sound is non-artificial," one who points out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) of both the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) says: "The eternity of cowness (*gotva*) has been refuted, and the relation (*sambandha*) is also merely conceptualized; atoms, space (*ākāśa*), and so forth have also been rejected; therefore, that [cowness] does not serve as the reason or the example."

By the phrase "the eternality of *gotva* has been discarded," he states that eternality is unestablished (*asiddha*). By the phrase "the relation is also merely conceptual," he [indicates] that [the reason] "because of a relation" is likewise unestablished. By the phrase "even atoms, space, and so forth have been rejected," he states that the claim "like the dimension of space or an atom" is unestablished; thus, it is "discarded. This has been refuted in the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*.
"Neti" is a negation;
"tat" means "therefore."
Regarding the passage beginning with "possessing multiple capacities in the presence [of the object]," he says "extracted," and so forth:
"Let it be established after a long time that [the word] denotes the extracted universal *gotva*,
because it is determined by those who are deluded as having a single form."

To the question, "How is its erroneous nature established? he says: "Because of its momentariness in reality," and so forth. Since it is momentary by its very nature, it does not remain stable even for that duration; why then is its continued existence desired even later?
Regarding the statement that "there is cutting by means of axes and so forth," he says "even in the case of a jar" and so on:
"Even in the case of a jar and the like, there is no cause whatsoever for its destruction;
since this has been established, how could it apply to sound?"
Thus, this too has been indicated in the *Sthirabhāvaparīkṣā* (Examination of Enduring Entities) by means of establishing that destruction is causeless.

Since there is no cause of destruction even in the case of a jar or similar objects, how could one exist in the case of sound? The term "cause of destruction" is to be connected with the distant word [“there is not”].
By this, it is stated that the probandum is already established [for the opponent] and that the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "of place, time, and the agent," he says "viplava" (confusion) and so forth:
"The confusion of recognition has been established previously;
the property [of the object] differs due to the difference in place, time, and the agent."
Indeed, through direct perception, another distinct and clear manifestation of the cow is cognized by way of its various divisions, such as the notes ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, pañcama, and so forth.
Nor is this establishment of difference justified by a difference in manifestors;
for it will be stated later that manifestation does not exist in eternal things.
This is easy to understand.

Regarding the application [of the argument] beginning with "the letter *ga* is eternal," he states the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in the passage beginning with "and distinct from the letter *ga*":
"And a universal called *gatva*, distinct from the letter *ga*, is asserted to be real; since it is not [so] in the actual usage, the fault of proving what is already established is unavoidable."
"It is desired" connects with "no," which is to be stated hereafter.
Otherwise, even for that which consists of the exclusion of others (*anyathāpoha*), there would be no common substratum for the property of "cow-ness" (*gotva*).
If you argue that it is indeed so, we say no, because this would result in the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).

Since there is no color distinct from the form of the letter *ga*, of what subject could "the state of not being determinable by a cognition other than that of *ga*" be a property? For a property must belong to a subject.

Now, it might be argued: "Even though it consists of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), it does not have *ga*-ness as its substratum; this is what is being proven by this method, so there is no proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). [The author] rejects this prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by stating: "For you do not maintain that the letter *ga* and so forth are not the locus of the exclusion of others.
For if it were proven in this way, the reason (*hetu*) would result in being unestablished (*asiddha*). To explain:
the so-called "exclusion of others" is not something distinct from the object itself as excluded from others. What then? It is simply the object itself.

That very form of the individual manifestation as the letter *ga*, which is the exclusion of heterogeneous things, is expressed by such synonyms as "the exclusion of other differences," "the rejection of other distinctions," "exclusion of others," and "other-exclusion" (*anyāpoha*), when there is a desire to know that alone.

However, if its existence as the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is what is to be proven, then this reason—"because the cognition of anything other than *ga* cannot be defined"—would be a property of what subject? It would be a property of nothing at all.
And as for the example "like the 'going' (gati) imagined by others," showing that this too is unestablished in its locus (dharmyasiddha), he says "vāstavī" and so forth:
"All inference that is real depends upon what is established for both [parties];
therefore, because of that, the example lacks establishment in its locus."
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "example, etcetera," the inclusion of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth is intended.
Furthermore, even if not explicitly stated by the proponent, that which is made the object of his intention is precisely what is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*).
Nor is it merely the state of being "ga" (*gatva*) that you wish to establish;
rather, by this means, you intend to demonstrate the oneness of the phoneme *ga*.
And showing that in this proposition an annulment by perception and other means has been stated previously, he says: "And all this effort of yours...
All this effort of yours is for the sake of establishing the oneness of the letter *ga*.
In that case, the contradiction by direct perception has been stated as unavoidable for you.
"This" is the negation of a substratum for a distinct genus;
and by the word "and," the sublation by inference is included.
"Arising" refers to that which was described [in the verse] beginning with "pleasant" and "unpleasant."
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "But [the object] established by both," he says "of yesterday's" and so forth: "These cognitions of the letter *ga*, whether belonging to yesterday or today,
do not have a single object because they occur sequentially, just like the cognitions of taste, color, and so forth."
Therefore, this single phoneme is not established for both [parties] as something eternally existing;
rather, its eternity is merely imagined, being a conceptual construct (kalpita) that is free from fault [only from one perspective].
In the phrase "they have arisen" (*uditāḥ*), the word is also connected here by changing its gender and case-ending.

Consequently, since the distinction between individual sounds has been refuted by both perception and inference, there exists no single, dual-proven essence consisting of phonemes; rather, the eternity is merely attributed to the conceptually constructed "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), because of the determination of oneness through a cognition of uniform reflective awareness (*tulyapratyavamarśapratyaya*).
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "purified by the sound" (*nādena saṃskṛtāt*), he says: "At the time of perceiving the word," and so forth.
At the time of perceiving the word, the air-currents residing at the edge of the ear, which perform the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ, are not perceived.
When a sound is perceived through the auditory organ as refined by resonance (nāda), its cognition— due to being contiguous with that [resonance]— is sublated by direct perception (pratyakṣa).

For if the winds that refine the auditory organ were established by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it would be possible to say that "the auditory organ is refined by the sound. But these [winds] are not so established; therefore, the notion that "the perception of that sound occurs through contact with the noise" is merely a basis for conceptual construction.

Regarding what was stated, "that which is sweet appears in the form of bitter," and so forth, he says: "In the form of bitter, yellow, and so on, the cognition that operates toward [objects] such as the sweet is devoid of an object, just as the cognition of a word would be."
By this, that which was stated—that cognition regarding sound [arises] by virtue of that [external object]—is refuted;
for it is not logical that a cognition devoid of an aspect should have another thing as its object, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Now, it might be argued: "Even if the word is not the object of that cognition, how can it be without an object? To this he says: "Because of the distinctions of fast, medium, and so forth," and so on.
For no word other than those distinguished as fast, medium, and so forth appears.
And how can a cognition of something as having that nature, when it does not possess that nature, not have an object?
For cognition arises in the form of fast, medium, or slow; yet the word-sound possesses no such form of "fast," because, being eternal and all-pervasive, it is of a single uniform nature.
Nor is there any other object possessing the form of "fast" that could possibly appear [to consciousness].
Therefore, since there is no object corresponding to these forms, this [cognition] is indeed devoid of an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*).
It might be argued that the very same word, appearing both in the form of *druta* (rapid) and otherwise, will be its objective support (*ālambana*).

As it has been said: "In all cases, the external object is the support, though its nature varies according to place and time. To this, he replies with the words "or otherwise" (*anyathā vā*). To say that it perceives that very same object "otherwise" is a contradictory statement.
If there is cognition of another form, how indeed can that object be known?
Since consciousness is indeed formless, that external form must certainly belong to you;
yet since the external object is not of the same nature as it, how can it exist in that way?
Even according to the position that cognition possesses an aspect (sākārajñāna), when a manifestation arises in cognition in conformity with an external form, the object is said to be "known."
In this case, cognition does not proceed in accordance with an external object;
therefore, it is established that all mind is devoid of an objective referent and is erroneous.
"It is contradictory" means that because reality and its opposite are characterized by existing in mutual exclusion, they cannot coexist in a single substratum (*dharmin*).

Furthermore, demonstrating that everything is indeed erroneous— whether in the position of formlessness (*nirākāra*) or the position of having form (*sākāra*)— and that [cognition] is entirely without an object (*nirviṣaya*), he says "For in the case of the formless," and so forth.
For those who maintain that cognition is formless (*nirākāra-jñāna-vādin*), the form of blue and so forth is experienced as residing solely in the object.

And just as yellow and so forth appear in a mistaken cognition, the object—such as a conch shell—is not established in that way; thus, it is quite clear that this [form] lacks the status of being an object [of that cognition]. Now, if the form of yellow and so forth does not reside in the object, then it must necessarily reside in the cognition; otherwise, if it were absent in both, how could it be experienced?
Furthermore, if [the object] resides within cognition, it must be explained how consciousness can be formless (*nirākāra*).
However, having provisionally accepted the position of those who maintain that cognition is formless, this lack of an object for consciousness is stated.
But the rebuttal to this must be stated by that very same person who maintains that cognition is formless.
Even in the view that cognition possesses an aspect (sākārajñānapakṣa), the experience of an object is established through the experience of an aspect whose nature resembles the object;
however, since there is no experience of an aspect whose nature resembles the object in a mistaken cognition, it is indeed without an object.
Furthermore, there is no other mode for the apprehension of an object besides these two: possessing an aspect and being aspectless.
Therefore, it is established that all erroneous cognition is indeed devoid of an object.
And showing that no cause for error is possible here, he says: "Nor is the existence of a manifestor tenable," and so forth.
"Nor is the existence of a manifestor logical in the case of an eternal entity, especially since there are no distinctions [in it];
therefore, cognitions are not differentiated with respect to the sound (dhvani) according to its refinement."

For it is described that the difference among manifesters (*vyañjaka*) is the cause of the illusion of difference regarding the sound (*śabda*) in the form of an echo (*dhvani*). However, there can be no manifester for anything that is eternal, because such a thing cannot be affected by it; nor is it logical for something to be a manifester without producing some specific change, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), whereby anything could be the manifester of anything else. Therefore, it is not logical that distinct cognitions should arise regarding the sound in the form of an echo due to the refinement produced by its manifesters.

Regarding what was stated—that a lamp and so forth are accepted as the manifestor of a jar and so on—the author introduces the meaning of the first verse and, while refuting it with the second and subsequent verses, says: "For just as one employs a manifestation for the purpose of perceiving a jar and so forth, a sound does not likewise [manifest] in the ear for the perception of a word. "For just as one employs a manifestation for the purpose of perceiving a jar and so forth, a sound does not likewise [manifest] in the ear for the perception of a word. (1.20) Just as one directs a manifestation toward a jar and so forth for the sake of perceiving that jar and so forth, a sound does not function in the same way within the auditory organ for the sake of perceiving a word. This is because, in the case of the jar and so forth, the manifestation is something other than the object to be manifested; however, in this case, the sound itself is the very thing to be manifested. Furthermore, since the sound is not perceived prior to its manifestation, it cannot be established that it exists as a substrate for the manifestation. Therefore, the analogy is invalid. Thus, the claim that a sound is the manifestor of a word is untenable. This concludes the discussion. The term *iti* at the end indicates the conclusion of the section. This concludes the commentary on the first chapter. The second chapter begins. Now, the proponent of the theory of manifestation (*vyañjakavādin*) states: "If it is argued that the sound is the manifestor of the word, like a lamp is of a jar... and so forth. To refute this, he says: "For just as one employs a manifestation for the purpose of perceiving a jar and so forth, a sound does not likewise [manifest] in the ear for the perception of a word. Just as one employs a manifestation such as a lamp for the purpose of perceiving a jar and so forth, a sound does not perform the same function in the ear for the perception of a word. Why? Because the sound is not perceived prior to its manifestation. Since it is not perceived, it cannot be established that it exists as a substrate for the manifestation. Therefore, the analogy is invalid. Consequently, the claim that a sound is the manifestor of a word is untenable. This concludes the section. The term *iti* indicates the end of the section. This concludes the commentary on the first chapter. The second chapter begins. Now, the proponent of the theory of manifestation (*vyañjakavādin*) states: "If it is argued that the sound is the manifestor of the word, like a lamp is of a jar... and so forth. To refute this, he says: "For just as one employs a manifestation for the purpose of perceiving a jar and so forth, a sound does not likewise [manifest] in the ear for the perception of a word. Just as one employs a manifestation such as a lamp for the purpose of perceiving a jar and so forth, a sound does not perform the same function in the ear for the perception of a word. Why? Because the sound is not perceived prior to its manifestation. Since it is not perceived, it cannot be established that it exists as a substrate for the manifestation. Therefore, the analogy is invalid. Consequently, the claim that a sound is the manifestor of a word is untenable. This concludes the section. The term *iti* indicates the end of the section. To refute this, he says: "For just as one employs a manifestation for the purpose of perceiving a jar and so forth, a sound does not likewise [manifest] in the ear for the perception of a word. If sound, existing in its natural state, is capable of being perceived by the ear,
why is it not perceived even when that ear is unrefined?
Since the presence of the appropriate causes exists, perception must indeed occur;
how could it be otherwise at the time when the refined auditory faculty is present?
If it is capable [of being perceived] when there is no perception, how could it be so later on as well?
And if it possesses the capacity for existence, the word would become something else once it has been produced.
Furthermore, even subsequently, that knowledge does not arise by its own power;
rather, its production is described as resulting from hearing the conditioned teachings and so forth.

Granted that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is indeed refined (*saṃskṛta*), this must still be addressed: is sound by its very nature capable of producing a cognition of its own object, or is it incapable?
In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the object would be perceived even before the refinement of the auditory organ.
This is precisely what [the author] expresses in the passage beginning with "even when unrefined" (*asaṃskṛto 'pi*).
"Of that" means of the word;
"that" refers to [the object].

Therefore, the formal argument (*prayoga*)— beginning with "if the cause were deficient," and so forth— should be stated as before, and there would also be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra-saṃskāra*) is useless.
If, on the other hand, the second position is held, then even when the auditory organ is refined, the perception of sound would not occur, because the sound would always remain unfit for perception.
Furthermore, even on this view, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ is indeed useless.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not differ from a state incapable of producing something does not produce it; for example, a *kodrava* grain does not produce a rice sprout. And sound does not differ from its state of being incapable of producing cognition, even when the auditory organ has been refined. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), as he demonstrates with the words "the entity" (*bhāva*).
That which possesses a connection by way of fitness is "possessed of fitness" (yogyatāyogin).

Now, if the word *hi* were intended to be the cause for the production of cognition, then the dilemma regarding its being either suitable or unsuitable would apply there; however, since it is held that the auditory organ alone, when refined, is the cause for the perception of sound and not the sound itself, the aforementioned fault does not follow. Anticipating this objection and providing a rebuttal, he says "of the sound," and so forth:
"In this way, sound would simply be ungraspable, because it is of no utility toward that [cognition];
for it has no distinction whatsoever from taste and the other [objects]."
For in this way, because sound has no utility [in the cognition of taste] and so forth, it would not attain the status of being an object of knowledge for that cognition.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not function as a utility in a particular cognition is not an object of knowledge for that cognition; for example, taste and so forth in the case of auditory cognition. And sound does not function as a utility in auditory cognition; thus, there is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). This reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because if that which provides no assistance were to be an object of knowledge, there would be a lack of restriction, leading to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even taste and so forth would be cognizable by auditory consciousness.

But surely, because its own cause acts as a regulator, there will be no over-extension [of the definition]; for instance, that which arises from the conditioned auditory faculty, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), and so forth, arises specifically as a cognition of sound and not as a cognition of taste and so on, due to the specific determination of the causal capacity.

Furthermore, even if one accepts that sound is a cause, one must necessarily accept a specific restriction regarding the causal capacity [of the causes]. For instance, when the objection is raised: "Even though all [the sense organs] are equally causes, why is it that the cognition of sound has the nature of an auditory awareness alone, and not the nature of an awareness of the ear or other [senses]?"—the answer to this must be given solely by means of the specific restrictions on the causal capacities. Having considered all of this and setting aside the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), he says: "Or rather, this [cognition] is produced by them as having the nature of an auditory awareness," and so forth. "Or rather, this [cognition] is produced by them as having the nature of an auditory awareness."
Knowledge [is attained] through refined hearing and other means that are free from verbal expression and desire.
The word "nāma" indicates acceptance [of the opponent's position].
And how this position is untenable will be demonstrated later with the words beginning, "Or who [is the agent] of the cognition?
etc., by means of [the arguments concerning] hearing conditioned phenomena and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) and others is intended.

Even if sound were not the cause, there would still be a fault; for instance, there are two alternatives: is this sound by its very nature of the same essence as that cognition and its object, or is it not? Regarding the first alternative, he states the fault with the words "tajjñānajñeya" and so forth:
"Even if it continues to exist in the form of that cognition and its object," [it would follow that it is eternal].
The term "sound" would have to be understood as continuing [from the previous context], even for that cognition of yours.
Otherwise, cognition would not be recurrent; rather, it is that [object] which recurs.
If you claim that "the object of cognition is the word," then your position would be subject to a supreme contradiction.
For those two, cognition and the object of cognition, possess a nature like that of a chain;
indeed, because of their inseparable connection, the presence of one entails the presence of the second.
If sound were of the same nature as the cognition that knows it, then, because its cognizable nature would persist at all times, the cognition of it would also be eternal, just as sound itself is.

For it is not the case that when Devadatta’s nature of being connected with a staff persists, the staff itself does not persist. This is because [the cognition] follows [the object] like a chain in the intellect.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because.

Because the natures of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the knowledge (*jñāna*) are bound together as if by a chain, it is established that when one nature exists, the existence of the second necessarily follows, since there is no deviation [from this rule].

"Let it be so; what is the fault? To this he says "saṃskṛta... and so forth: "For even when there is no embellishment of the auditory organ, cognition is clearly implied as being connected precisely with the knowledge produced by hearing the articulated [word]."

The phrase "indeed, [the word] is connected only with the cognition produced by hearing the refined [sound]" (*saṃskṛtaśravaṇotpādyajñānasambaddha eva hi*) implies the ellipsis "[the word] persists" (*śabdo 'nuvartate*).

Since the word, being connected with the cognition produced by hearing the refined [sound], persists at all times, it follows that even for one whose auditory faculty is unrefined, the cognition of that [word] would occur; therefore, the refinement of the auditory faculty is useless.

Regarding the second position as well, he states the fault with the words beginning "tajjñeya": "If the word is not of the nature of that which is to be known, like taste and so forth which are not of its nature, then auditory cognition would not have that [word] as its object-essence; such being the case."
This is easily understood.

All of this has been stated while assuming that cognition, even though it does not benefit that [object], has the nature of cognizing it. Now, demonstrating that it is improper for cognition to have the nature of cognizing that [object] when no relation exists, he says: "Or what...
"What indeed is the relation of cognition with the word, by virtue of which [cognition] is held to have the form of the cognition of that word? For it cannot be identity, because they are distinct."
Nor does that [cognition] arise from that [word], because the word is not its producer;
for if it were produced by it, then by necessity, that [cognition] would exist at all times.
[678] Thus,
if it were the case that the cognition of that object would either always arise or never arise at all,
then the hypothesis of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory faculty would be useless.

For the restriction between entities is indeed of only two kinds: identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), since there is no other form of assistance (*upakāra*). Nor is a relation between that which is not assisted and that which does not assist logical, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Since this twofold restriction does not exist between word and cognition, how could a cognition whose nature is the understanding of that [object] arise when such a restriction is absent?
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the principle].
Furthermore, it might be argued that even without a necessary connection, that cognition is established as having the nature of cognizing that object because it arises in the form of that object;
but this is incorrect.
Because [the Mīmāṃsakas] accept that cognition is formless (*nirākāra-jñāna*).
Indeed, the Mīmāṃsakas do not accept that cognition possesses a form (*sākāra-jñāna*).

Or, even if that were the case, it would still be illogical because it would entail the consequence that sound is imperceptible (*parokṣa*). For in this way, sound would indeed be imperceptible and not perceptible (*pratyakṣa*); consequently, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it, the very claim that "cognition has that [sound's] form" could not be proven.
Nor is its establishment [as having the form of the object] possible through the exclusion of other effects, because we do not admit that [the cognition] is the producer [of the object].

This might be argued: even for the proponent of the theory of images (*sākāravādin*) for whom the object is indeed the producer, since the object is always imperceptible, how is it understood that the cognition possesses the form of the object?
True.

However, this is the means [for establishing it]: that another cause is determined through the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of its effect; and that [cause] is determined by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the differentiator of the various forms such as blue within cognition.

For instance, since the causes—the eye, light, and mental attention—are common to all cognitions, the differentiation of cognition into blue and so forth is not produced by them. Therefore, by implication, it is determined that this differentiation is produced by that other cause which was inferred through negative concomitance. Consequently, because it is produced by that [cause], it is established that this form is apprehended by the cognition.
But this is not even a valid means for you, because you do not admit that it [the self] is a cause.
It might be argued: "Since the eyes and other sense organs are also always imperceptible, how is it determined that they are indistinguishable across all cognitions?
This is true, provided one is considering the Vijñānavāda (Cognition-Only) perspective.

For that proponent of consciousness-only (vijñānavādin) describes the particularity of consciousness as being produced solely by the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), just as in dreams and the like,
and not as produced by an external object;
however, all this is said while assuming the existence of an external object.

Otherwise, this very point should be challenged: how could the existence of the external object be established even from the difference in the effect? Only the existence of a cause in general would be established, but not the external [object], for that cause might just as well be internal, as in the case of dreams; so enough of this digression.
Furthermore, showing that there is still a fault even if one grants that sound is a producer [of cognition], he says: "In its production," and so forth. "That" refers to that production.
He concludes with the words "In this way" and so forth.
"Not nine" refers to the position that [the causes] do not produce [the effect].
"This is the certainty" means: [it is certain that they do not produce it].
In the case of knowledge, which is eternal, the characteristics are its existence and non-existence.

Thus, having first accepted the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ, it was stated that such refinement is useless by considering whether the object possesses a nature that produces or does not produce [cognition]. Now, demonstrating that the refinement of the auditory organ itself is impossible, he says: "For if the refinement were occasional," and so forth. For if the refinement were occasional, cognition would arise only when it exists; in that case, the postulation of a refinement might be considered appropriate. "Occasionally" (*kadācit*) means at certain times.
Furthermore, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), characterized as a potency, is to be inferred from its effect, which is cognition;
and that cognition either always exists or it occurs at all times.
How indeed could that which is occasional indicate a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of it?
Therefore, the subsequent [explanation] regarding the refinement of the auditory organ has not been well elucidated.
For in this way, it is logical that consciousness, which is the effect of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), is occasional;
provided that the formative force itself is occasional.
Otherwise, while its cause remains eternally present and unimpaired, why would that effect only occasionally occur?

And showing that it is not logical for a modification (*saṃskāra*) to be occasional for an eternal auditory faculty (*śrotra*), he says: "It is to be determined by the effect, which is cognition," and so forth.

For instance, a modification of the auditory faculty and the like, being determined by the effect that is cognition, must be a modification whose nature is power (*śakti*), because it is power alone that is determined by an effect. Furthermore, that power is essentially identical with the auditory faculty and is not distinct from it; otherwise, since the effect would arise [from the power], it would follow that the auditory faculty is merely the cause.
Moreover, because no relationship [between the faculty and the power] is established, if the power were to exist, the cognition of its existence would have to occur at all times.
If, on the other hand, that [object] were non-existent, then the cognition produced by it would never occur;

consequently, the occasional nature of cognition would not exist. Therefore, how could an occasional cognition indicate a refinement characterized as a capacity belonging to the auditory organ? It certainly could not.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the inherent power [of the auditory organ] is not to be inferred from the effect of cognition.

What then? A previously non-existent, occasional power is bestowed upon the auditory organ by the sounds; that very power is what is inferred from cognition. Thus, because a previously non-existent, occasional power is bestowed [upon it], the occasional nature of consciousness is logically established as being indicated by that power. To this he says: "If a power is bestowed upon the auditory organ," and so forth. "Or if [the power] is non-different [from the organ]."
Otherwise, the eternity of space or the directions would be lost due to their being born.
There are three possible positions: that the power (śakti) is either identical with the auditory organ, distinct from it, or both distinct and non-distinct.
In the first position, the auditory organ—whether it be of one or both natures—would necessarily be impermanent, just like the nature of the power itself.
Why? Because of its birth, that is, its origination.
Now, it might be argued: "We do not accept that the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is non-different from its power (*śakti*);
rather, we hold that the power itself is non-different from the auditory faculty. Behold, this is the manifestation of great blindness!
For how could another [power], while in conjunction with one's own nature at that very same time, become distant?
Because non-difference is characterized by the mutual penetration of their own-natures,
it is quite trivial to say that water existing at a distance from milk does not experience its contact.
To show that even if this position were accepted, it would still entail a fault, he says "And because of existence," and so forth:
"Because it is not distinct from existence, conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛti) would also possess permanence;
consequently, the cognition of things would occur at all times."
Because it is non-different [from the entity], the conditioned factor (saṃskāra) would also necessarily be eternal, just like the nature of the entity itself.
Therefore, pointing out this further fault, he says "by that," and so forth.
Regarding the second position as well, he states the fault with the words "But in the case of difference," and so forth:
"But in the case of its difference, the relationship [of the power] to it is not tenable;
moreover, the ear would lack the status of being an agent, because cognition arises from the power."
If it were admitted that the capacity (śakti) is distinct from the entity possessing it, then the relationship "this is the capacity of that" would not exist;
for that which cannot be benefited by another cannot logically be dependent upon it.
Moreover, the auditory organ does not benefit the capacity, since it is accepted that only the manifesting factors, such as sound-waves (nāda), provide benefit.

Furthermore, if the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) were also something that assists [the capacity], then there would be an infinite regress, because the capacity that assists the capacity would itself have to be distinct from the auditory faculty.
Consequently, since the capacities alone would be joined together in a series and the effect would arise from the capacity itself, the auditory faculty would be a non-producer.
From that, it would follow that it lacks the status of a real entity (*avastutva*).
Now, if it is admitted that the power [of the auditory organ] is non-different from the power that assists it, then why is there such hostility toward the non-difference of the primary power?

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the power being produced eternally, because its cause—the auditory organ—is eternal; and that which cannot be assisted has no need whatsoever for auxiliary causes.
He states the third position with the words "bhedābheda," etc.: "Therefore, a separate alternative position, free from both difference and non-difference,
is stated as the answer [to the objection], because of the refinement of the auditory organ and because [the sound] is not so refined."
By this very [argument], the embellishment of both the object and the sense-faculty must be rejected;
therefore, manifestation in the case of eternal [sounds] is in every respect baseless.
Consequently, whatever distinctions such as long, short, and so forth are differentiated by relying upon individual manifestations, they are all likewise without a foundation.
"Individually" means in the examination of the person (*pudgala*) and so forth; for it is impossible to simultaneously affirm and negate a single [entity].

For instance, difference and non-difference are characterized by mutual exclusion, because the determination of one occurs precisely through the exclusion of the nature of the other. For when the nature of something is not determined without the exclusion of its own essence, it exists in exclusion of that; as, for example, either of existence or non-existence. And since those two are characterized by mutual exclusion, the negation of the nature of one is inseparable from the affirmation of the other. Thus, by the force of the negation of otherness, there is an affirmation of identity; at that very moment, the negation of that [identity] is also not tenable, because it would follow that otherness itself could not be negated. In this way, the fault must be stated for both positions.
"By this very [means]" refers to the two alternatives regarding the nature of being fit or unfit for the production of knowledge by virtue of its inherent disposition (*prakṛti*).
He concludes with the words "therefore," and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "succession and so forth," there is the inclusion of protracted vowels, acute accents, and the like.
"But for those [who hold] that this sound is perceived by the ear even when not reached, and so forth— even though there is a similarity in the mere fact of non-attainment— [it is replied:
'Even though there is a similarity in the mere fact of non-attainment, not everything is perceived, because the restriction of capacity is established, as in the case of a magnet and iron.'"
Although everything is equally unattained, nevertheless, due to the specific restriction of the powers of things, there is no grasping—that is, no apprehension—of a previous object.
Just as a stone called a magnet, while attracting iron that has not reached it, does not attract every unattained object.

Regarding the examples beginning with "the light of a magnet," he raises a doubt concerning the lack of proof for the illustration according to the opinion of Śaṅkarasvāmin: "If it is argued that there too attraction occurs through the reaching of the light of the magnet, [we reply:
surely this light is not seen; how then is it known to exist?"

For he said that even in that case, the attraction of iron occurs solely through the power of the penetration by the radiance of the magnet-stone (*ayaskāntamaṇi*); otherwise, there would be an attraction of all pieces of iron situated in every location.
Although its radiance is not perceived like the radiance of a lamp, it must nevertheless be inferred, because attraction is not observed when there is an obstruction or at a great distance.
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*).
By means of non-apprehension, [the author] negates the conventional usage of existence, thinking, "May this not be seen."

Regarding the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*) stated—that there would be the consequence of attracting all iron situated in every location—he says "Why does it not attract... and so forth to refute it:
"Why does that light not attract wood and other such things?
If you say it is because its power is restricted [to iron], then that is the same even in the case of non-contact."
Even in the case of reaching [the object], the same undesirable consequence applies: why does the light of a magnet not attract all wood and other materials that it has reached?

If it is argued that there is no over-extension because the specific nature of things (*padārtha-svabhāva*) acts as a restrictive factor, then who has removed the capacity of the nature of things to act as a regulator even in the case of non-reaching? Since that is not accepted there, the postulation of an invisible light is indeed useless.
Regarding what was stated there— that for one situated far away or nearby, perception and non-perception would be equal and there would be no sequence— it is said in response to that:
"By those situated far, in the middle, or nearby, it is perceived simultaneously."
Immediately following the application, all [cognitions] therein arise from the nature of knowledge.
The apprehension of [words] in succession is unestablished, because cognitions arise simultaneously immediately after the employment of the sounds.
Regarding what was said— that there can be no occurrence of intensity, dullness, and so forth— he replies with the verse beginning "dūrāsannādi" (due to distance, proximity, etc.):

"Just as a form is perceived clearly or unclearly through the distinction of distance, proximity, and so forth, in the same way, the distinctions of intensity, dullness, and so on would exist in sound as well."

Just as form (rūpa) is clearly perceived even when it is not reached and is non-pervasive (avyāpin), so too in the case of sound, which is non-pervasive and not reached, there will be sensations such as intense or faint.
[Objection: But for the opponent, the perception of form without reaching it is unestablished; how then can it be stated as an example?
[Response: This is not a fault.

Although it is not established merely by the word of another, nevertheless, that which is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established for both parties. What, then, is the valid means of cognition here? It is the simultaneous perception of the near and the distant. For that which possesses motion reaches what is near quickly and what is distant after a long time, as when Devadatta goes from one village to another. However, the simultaneous perception of the branch and the moon is observed immediately following the opening of the eyes; therefore, it is understood that the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakārin*).

Regarding this, Uddyotakara has said: "Because cognitions arise so rapidly that their temporal distinction is not perceived, this is a false impression, like [the perception of] piercing a hundred lotus petals.

This is incorrect; for if that were so, there would be no determination of sequence even in cases such as *saro rasaḥ*, since the rapidity of their arising is the same. Consequently, there would be no difference in their apprehension, and since all cognitions arise rapidly, there would never be a perception of sequence. This has already been examined in detail previously.
Furthermore, he himself says: "If the eye were to act without reaching its object, then there would be no efficacy for obstructions such as walls; thus, obstruction would be impossible.
Moreover, the non-perception of what is distant and the perception of what is near would not occur, because there would be no distinction [in the eye's action].
It might be argued: 'Only that object which becomes the objective range of the eye is perceived, while that which does not become so is not perceived.'"
But that is not the case;
for it is impossible for there to be the status of being an object apart from a relation.
What, then, is this so-called "status of being an object" apart from a relation?
"It is merely that what I call 'causal relation' (sambandha) is designated by you as 'the state of being an object' (viṣayībhāva); there is no difference whatsoever.
This is incorrect;
for we say that the state of being an object is the state of being a cause, not a [mere] relation.

For instance, an object such as form (*rūpa*) is said to "become an object" when it functions as a cooperative cause (*sahakāritā*) for the arising of visual consciousness, but not by being in physical contact with it.
Furthermore, the meaning of "cooperation" is twofold:

either mutual assistance, as in the case of one staying inside a room [who is aided] by the spreading of light; or the performance of a single purposeful action, as in the case of one who perceives form merely by opening their eyes.
In both cases, it is only a specific cause of consciousness that is called its "object," not something related to it.
If it is argued that this very restriction to a specific cause would not exist in the absence of a relationship, we say:
no.

Because the specific determination [of effects] is established through the power of their own causes, that very thing arises from its own cause in such a way that only a certain thing becomes a producer of cognition and not another; for all entities possess distinct intrinsic natures despite the non-difference of their causes.
And just as, according to you, although the relation is equal [in both cases], why is it that the eye perceives only form and not taste?
If you say, "It does not perceive it because there is no relation," then why should that very relation not exist, since the location is not different?

For there is no determining cause here by which the eye follows only the visible form (*rūpa*)—and not even the taste existing in that same location—and likewise does not follow a visible form situated at an extremely distant place, despite both being in the same location.

If it is argued that its own cause (*svahetu*) is the determining factor, this is equally true for the position that [the sense organ] does not reach [its object] (*aprāptipakṣa*); so enough with this elaboration.
With the words "of those appearing as distinct," etc., he anticipates the objection of the opponent:
"If cognitions appearing as distinct have a single objective basis, how is this so?
This same objection applies equally to the proponents of external objects who maintain that cognitions of form [have a common basis]."

"How could there be a single object for cognitions that appear as distinct? For in this way, the cognitions of taste, form, and so forth would have a single objective basis"—this is the opponent's intention.
He states the rebuttal with the words "equally" (*tulyam*) and so on:

"This objection applies equally even to cognitions of form—that is, to cognitions whose objects are forms—regarding how there could be a single objective basis for appearances that are clear and so forth, given the distinctions of being distant, near, and so on."
And this is an objection raised by the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*).

However, for those Vijñānavādins who describe the aspect as residing solely in the object and not in consciousness, every instance of consciousness arises as devoid of an external object, as self-cognizing, and as distinct [from one another] due to differences in aspects such as clarity and so forth; thus, this objection does not apply to them.

Even for those proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) who maintain the position that cognition possesses a form (*sākārajñāna*), since they do not admit a complete identity of form with the object, there is no contradiction in multiple cognitions appearing as distinct having a single object by virtue of their partial similarity to it; thus, this objection is not valid.

To the question, "What then is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the apprehension of sound through contact, and what is the establishing proof (*sādhaka*) for its apprehension without contact? he says, beginning with "In the case of contact," etc.
However, in the position that there is apprehension through contact, it would be like the inner part of the ear.
There would be no cognition of "uninterrupted" in the case of things such as the sound of thunderclouds.
"Like the wing inside the ear" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
The suffix *vati* is used after a word ending in the genitive case.

Just as the continuous sound of a bird's wing that relieves the itching of the ear is perceived, so too, since the sound of clouds and the like is grasped only when it has reached the region of the ear by spreading out according to the analogy of a *kadamba* flower bud, its perception would necessarily be simultaneous [with the arrival].
Nor can it be said that this illusion of separation occurs due to the influence of its own causes, conjunction, or the locus of inherence;
for these are not apprehended by the auditory organ.
Indeed, no cognition ever arises that superimposes the form of an object that has not itself become an objective datum (*viṣaya*).
For visual consciousness does not superimpose the similarity of taste.

Having thus stated the proof that contradicts the apprehension [of an object] through contact, he states the proof for its apprehension without contact, beginning with "tadvicchinna" (separated from that):
"Separated from that [object], [the ear] would be a producer of cognition, just like the mind;
otherwise, the ear would act without reaching [its object], unlike the skin and other senses."
The word "tad" means "therefore.
"Not otherwise, like the sense of touch and so forth" is an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
The meaning is that just as there is no perception through the severance of the sense organs such as the skin, so it would be here as well.
Having raised the objection that the example [of the mind] lacks the property to be proven by the words "the mind also," etc., he refutes it:
"For those who assert that the mind also acts by reaching its object, it is not logical for their mind to reach an object situated at a very distant place, because it lasts for only a single moment."

On this point, Uddyotakara, Kumārila, and others provide the following proofs: "The eyes and ears function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakārin*), because they are external sense organs (*bāhyendriya*), like the nose and other [external senses].
The inclusion of the term "external" is for the purpose of avoiding a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the internal organ, the mind (*manas*).
Likewise: "Being instruments (*karaṇa*), they do not perceive obstructed objects, like the nose and other [senses]."
The qualification "while being an instrument" (*karaṇatve sati*) is added for the purpose of excluding [the sense-objects] themselves.

Likewise, color and sound are perceived by external sense-faculties that function through direct contact (*prāpyakārin*), because they are objects of the external sense-faculties, just like odor and taste.

Similarly, the cognition of color and sound has as its objective support an object perceived by an external sense-faculty that functions through direct contact, because it has as its objective support an object of an external sense-faculty, just like the cognition of odor and taste.
Regarding this, he states the refutation beginning with "As for that which... and so forth:
