"As for the proof of reaching the object [by the sense organs] based on their being external senses and so forth—that is inconclusive because of contradiction with things of a different class possessing other properties."
This is easily understood.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Therefore, this is the view of the Vedic scholars," he says "separate" and so forth:
"Previously, they were separate and distinct from conjunction and disjunction;
and because the wind is imperceptible, it is not logical that they are non-distinct."
For this very reason, because there is no distinction [in its nature], motion is not possible for it;
and due to the absence of momentum (*vega*), it does not persist as long as that momentum lasts.

"Previously" refers to the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*). [The opponent objects: "In that case, they must be non-different [from the substance]. To this he says, "of the wind," and so forth.
For it is the very winds, as they arise in conjunction and disjunction, that are called conjunctions and disjunctions when they are non-different [from the substance].
Furthermore, it is not logical for non-momentary entities to possess a nature of conjunction even sequentially, because they are of a single, unchanging form.

Regarding what was said, "having reached the space of the ear," and so forth, he says "karṇa... and so on: If [the sound], having reached the space of the ear, produces an efficacy in the auditory organ, then why is there no perception of that [efficacy] in the cognition of sound, as in the case of the stroke of a whip?
"It is improper to say that attention to sound obstructs his sensation, for one who knows the difference between the strike of a whip and the wind [does not fail to perceive the former]."
In this regard, there are two possible positions: either this wind would have a nature that is perceptible, or it would have a nature that is imperceptible.
In the first case, at the time of perceiving sound, the movement of the wind would also be perceived, just like the stroke of a whip.

Furthermore, it might be argued that because two cognitions do not arise simultaneously, the attention directed toward sound—the perception of sound—obstructs the sensation or apprehension of this wind.
This is reasonable to say regarding the sensation of a whip-lash or another breeze produced by a fan at the time of perceiving sound;

for just as there would be an experience of another breeze made by a fan or the strike of a whip at the moment of perceiving sound, so too would there be a tactile awareness of the wind reaching the region of the ear.
By this, he states that the thesis regarding the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions contradicts direct perception.

And it has been established that the illusion of simultaneous apprehension does not arise from the force of rapid production, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Granted, there may indeed be an illusion of simultaneity caused by rapidity even in the case of successive occurrences; nevertheless, this [objection] is of no consequence here, as it is irrelevant to the subject at hand. This is what is demonstrated by the words "due to rapidity" (*lāghavāt*) and so forth: "Due to rapidity, there is an illusion of simultaneity even when there is succession."
There is nothing whatsoever here [in the body], because the wind is not apprehended in any way at all.
If it were the case that the illusion of simultaneity arises merely from the rapidity of the arising of consciousness, that might be so;
however, there is no total non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception.

For in this case, there is indeed a total non-perception of the wind reaching the region of the ear, whether by way of succession or simultaneously. Therefore, the response that "this illusion of simultaneity in consciousness is caused by rapidity" is of no consequence.
The meaning is "insubstantial."
Then, with the words "But even if," etc., he states the second position:
"Even if wind is described as being beyond the senses, as by the followers of Kaṇāda,
then for you too, what causes the attainment of touch there [in that wind]?"
The followers of Kaṇāda are the Vaiśeṣikas;
for them, air has sound as its inferential mark.

The author of the Bhāṣya, Śabara, also stated: "The conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to air are not perceived, even though they manifest from the region of the ear-cavity of the imperceptible air."
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "By what is its contact with touch produced? *Spṛṣṭi* means touch; *tasyāptiḥ* means its attainment, that is to say, its occurrence. This is what is meant:

how can there be for that air the occurrence of touch which has been asserted by the author of the Bhāṣya? For, against those authors of the *Śikṣā* who maintain that "air attains the state of sound," the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "If sound were composed of air, it would have to be a particular configuration (*saṃniveśaviśeṣa*) of air."
Furthermore, we do not recognize the presence of aerial parts within sound,
in the way that one recognizes the threads in a cloth;
yet such is not the case here.
"If it were so, we would perceive them through touch;
however, we do not feel the aerial components that have entered into the sound."

Even granting that air is beyond the senses, he states another fault with the words "Or let it be," and so forth: "Or let air be beyond the senses; however, there would be a perception of the tangible—whether hot, cold, or otherwise—belonging to that which is conjoined with it, just as in the case of fire."

"By means of this or that wind" means through the conjunction with each respective [wind]. That which belongs to the triad of elements known as water, fire, and motion is so described. "Contained therein" (tadgata) means having reached that or being dependent upon it; that is to say, it is supported by it.
This is a compound with the second case ending, according to the rule beginning with *dvitīyā-śrita*.
And this [term "feeling"] is in grammatical apposition with "of the tangible.
Thus, feeling (vit) results from that tangible which has the nature of being cold, hot, or otherwise;
"as in other cases."
It is like [the perception] of something other than that which resides in the abdominal air (koṣṭhavāyu) considered to be the manifestor of sound;
the suffix *vati* is used here after a word in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*).

Just as there is a cognition of the touch of cold and so forth belonging to the wind blowing during the winter season while carrying masses of snow, or as there is for the breeze blowing during the summer season when all quarters of space are pervaded by the rays of the young sun, so too would it be in this case for the wind existing at a time devoid of both cold and heat.
With the words "But even if," etc., he anticipates the opponent's objection:
"But even if there is no cognition because of its lack of connection with the ear-cavity..."
How is it not understood that [the sound] has not yet reached the space of the ear?
Therefore, this conception, based on the view of the Vedic scholars, is groundless;
it does not lead to the satisfaction of the wise, and thus it shines only among the Vedic scholars themselves.
"Of that" means of the wind.
"Non-connection" means...
Non-contact;
this is to be construed with "the ear-cavity.
The remainder is easily understood.

Regarding what was stated, "Or else, in accordance with the Vedas," and so forth—there, making an extension (*atideśa*) precisely to the point that "the refutation is the same," he says: "Those who assert that space is partless; against them, the faults previously mentioned should be understood as equally applicable even if the auditory organ were a single, partless direction."

Regarding the view that the auditory organ consists of partless space, the defects previously mentioned—such as the futility of refinement (*saṃskāra*) and the impossibility of refinement—are equally applicable to the view that the auditory organ is the quarters of space (*dik*); therefore, no separate refutation need be stated.
Regarding what was stated—“Even though it is all-pervading and one,” and so forth—he replies with the verse beginning “In the position that space is one and all-pervading.
In the position that space is one and all-pervading, no division can be conceived;
for that space is indeed one, being both the basis of the conditioned and otherwise.
The auditory faculty has the single space as its essence; there is no unconditioned [space] within the ear-cavity.
Therefore, the restriction of its refinement is not established by means of a distinction in its physical basis.
According to the proponent of a single sense-faculty (*ekendriyavādin*), a sense-faculty that has received its refinement at one location would become the awakener [of cognition] in all bodies.
Let it be granted that the arising of cognition occurs within specific regions of the bodies of men;
however, for you, there can be no spatial separation of the primary cause (pradhāna), because space is a single entity.
Even if it is argued that our self, though partless and possessing complete knowledge,
perceives only within the body, this too is flawed.
By this very same reason, the non-establishment of deafness and so forth [as properties of the self] follows;
for it is not logical that the very same thing should be unenjoyable by another, since there would be no distinction.
"And another" refers to that which has the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its basis.
For this division of that which is partless is not logical, because it would entail the consequence of having parts (*sāvayavatva*).

However, in the case of an imaginary division, there is a contradiction regarding the occurrence or non-occurrence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); for causal efficiencies do not conform to superimposed objects, because they are necessarily tied to real entities (*vastu*).

Consequently, if a sense faculty is refined upon one substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and that [faculty] has the nature of being a cognizer, then—since that very same [faculty] exists in its ultimate sense upon other substrata as well—it follows that it would be both refined and a cognizer everywhere.
By this, everything that was stated—beginning with "in the bodily regions of persons"—is refuted. Showing that a single entity cannot possess ultimate divisions, he says "of persons" and so forth.
"Spatial separation from the primary" (pradhānavaideśyam) means the spatial separation of the primary body, that is, its existence in different locations within space.
Even when it is stated thus, [the opponent] is at fault,
because it is impossible for one thing to be divided; hence,
there is no established order.
The absence of established order.
He shows precisely this lack of distinction with the words "for that which has not abandoned its prior form," and so forth: "For if no particularity arises,
how indeed could your ear, having not abandoned its prior form, be something not enjoyed by another?"

Furthermore, it might be argued that because [the auditory organ] is controlled by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), there is indeed a distinction; to this he says "because of its permanence," and so forth: "Because of its permanence and independence, the auditory faculty, being uncontrolled by merit and demerit, would follow as being always available for enjoyment by everyone, like space."
Eternality is the reason for independence, and likewise for the state of being uncontrolled.
Now, he asks why there is no subjugation even of that which is independent, and says: "Dharma, adharma," and so forth.
For space is never assisted by dharma or adharma;
since it is eternal, it lacks the state of being an effect—so what kind of subjugation could this be?

For by being independent (*anapekṣatva*), it is said that something is not an effect (*akārya*); and whatever is not an effect is not brought under the control of anything, such as a rabbit’s horn or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*). Since the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is not an effect, this is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*). By the phrase "because of its permanence," he refutes the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason; and by the phrase "in the absence of being an effect, what is this 'being brought under control'? he refutes its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).

But surely, the subjugation of even that which is not an effect is observed; for example, the ear, which was previously incapable of being used as an organ of hearing, later becomes capable of such use through the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth. Consequently, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To this, he states the refutation beginning with "mantra-auṣadhādi":
"And furthermore, how could it become an object of experience (*bhogya*) through the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth?
For, because it is eternal, it does not acquire any distinction (*viśeṣa*) from those [causes]."
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), scraping and so forth are included.
"How could it be?"—the ellipsis to be supplied here is: "if even in that case there were no state of being an effect" (*kāryatā*).
But surely, even for that which is not an effect, mastery will be achieved through the mere production of a specific quality; to this he replies with "Because of its permanence," and so forth.

"In that case, since the physical basis (adhiṣṭhāna) is impermanent, the mastery over the eternal auditory faculty (śrotra) will occur through the mediation of its modifications. To this he says: "But if, although the basis is impermanent, there is no momentary impermanence [of the faculty], then deafness and so forth would not be possible, because it is impossible for there to be any excellence (atiśaya) in its nature. "But if, although the basis is impermanent, there is no momentary impermanence, then deafness and so forth would not be possible, because it is impossible for there to be any excellence in its nature."
"Even in the case of what is impermanent":

because it perishes at a later time, even that [entity] does not undergo the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*), since—due to its being of a single nature—it is like something permanent for which no destruction occurs even after a day; therefore, how could there be any refinement (*saṃskāra*)?
Having conceded the excellence [of the argument], he states the fault with the words "Or let it be":
"Or let there be an excellence in that space; however, this [excellence] does not exist in it.
Nor [can it arise] from a connection with a substratum, because [space] is eternal and independent."
Therefore, deafness and the like cannot be attributed to it even through its door [of the auditory organ];
this remains the same even if space were composed of parts, provided it is eternal.
"This" refers to the excellence (*atiśaya*).

Although it does not exist [independently], he says "nor by means of the substratum," etc., meaning that even so, it will belong to that [excellence] as well due to its connection with the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Regarding what was stated, "And space is not partless," and so forth: even there, if the eternity of a space possessing parts is admitted, then all the refutations that apply to the position of an eternal, partless space are equally applicable; this he indicates by the words "of space," and so on.

Regarding what was said, namely "just as there [in that case], while existing," and so forth, he replies with "even for you who exist only there," and so forth: "Even for you who exist only there, such a removal [of the self] due to ownership is not tenable, if even that [the self] possesses momentariness."
For what excellence has arisen in it subsequently, such that—
deprived of its ownership— it would not obtain enjoyment once again?
This is easily understood.
Regarding what was stated, "For [the embellishment] of the manifesting air-currents," etc., he says there:
"And when such an embellishment is not applicable to either the auditory organ or the sound,
because the production of an embellishment is untenable through the alternatives of difference or non-difference."
For if the refinement were distinct [from the auditory organ and the sound], the ear and the sound would not be refined;
nor would there be any relationship whatsoever between the refinement and those two.
For a relationship between distinct things must be one of cause and effect;
and in that case, this [relationship] would exist at all times, because the cause is always present.
Even in the view that [the cognition] is not a different entity [from the self], it would likewise be eternal;
therefore, it could not be produced, and it follows that cognition is eternal.
Therefore, a restriction of capacity for wind and so forth is not tenable; for if there is no connection with an object to be produced, capacity itself is impossible.
"Yadā" means "from which cause"; "evam" means "in the manner just described."
Because there is no excellence (*atiśaya*) in that which is eternal, refinement (*saṃskṛti*) is not at all tenable;
therefore, the restriction of capacity for wind and so forth is not established—this is the connection with what will be said later.
Demonstrating in detail how such refinement is untenable, he says "difference and non-difference," and so forth.

Regarding the embellishment (*saṃskṛti*), there are two possible positions: it must be either distinct from or non-distinct from [the auditory organ and the sound], since no other alternative for a real entity is possible.

In the first position, the embellishment of both the auditory organ and the sound would be untenable, because it would be the production of something else; for when a jar is produced, a cloth is not said to be embellished.
Nor is a connection established between that embellishment and those two, by means of which they might both be embellished through the production of an embellishment related to them.
For, since difference is admitted, there can be no relationship characterized by identity.
And if there is a relationship between two distinct things, it must necessarily be characterized by causality, because there is no other form of assistance possible.

If that causal relationship were to exist, this mental impression (*saṃskāra*) would occur at all times, because its cause—the auditory faculty and the nature of the sound—would be present at all times.
Regarding the second position as well, he states the fault with the words "anarthāntara" and so forth. "Tadvat" means like the nature of the auditory organ and the sound.
"Asau" refers to the formative force (*saṃskāra*).
And therefore, because it is eternal, this formative force is not produced by anything.

Furthermore, if the arising of cognitions such as those of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were admitted [to proceed from that], it would follow that cognition is eternal; thus, there is the fault of [implying] eternality.
He concludes with the words "That is not so" (*tan na*) and so forth.

With the words "Therefore," and so forth, he provides the proof for the non-eternality of sound: "Therefore, because manifestation is impossible, this cognition of sound is the result [of the sound itself], just like the cognition manifesting a jar or similar object, which is invariably concomitant with the production of the apprehended object."

Therefore, since both production and manifestation are established through the presumption of an effect, there would be an equal difference in capacity everywhere, regardless of whether there is effort or a desire to speak.

The formal argument is as follows: whatever is occasional is produced by a cause that possesses origination, just like the cognition whose object is a particular jar; and the cognition of sound is occasional. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Because that [eternal] cognition is never perceived, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, because manifestation (*abhivyakti*) has been refuted, the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory.

"Having this as its result" (*idamphala*) is analyzed [as follows]: that which has this characteristic—namely, the inseparable connection with the arising of the object to be apprehended—as its result.
The remainder is easily understood.
Since the refutation has already been stated previously regarding the view that the quarters are the auditory organ, it is not stated again.
Therefore, reminding one of that very same refutation mentioned before, he says: "And whatever reasoning," and so forth.
"Whatever reasoning there may be for the refutation of [the quarters] being a portion of space..."
This entire [mandala] should also be understood by those possessed of intelligence as being located in every direction.
Regarding what was stated: "If there were an embellishment (*saṃskāra*) of the object as well, then by that [cognition] only a single [object] would be embellished," and so forth;
to that, he says "of the object" and so on:
"Even if there were an embellishment of the object, by that [cognition] only a single [object] would be embellished."
Because [the object] has not perished and because of the restriction of capacity, there is no refinement of the object from this [contact].
No;
even if there were an embellishment (*saṃskāra*) of the object, it would follow that only a single [moment] is embellished—this is not so.
Why? Because it has been refuted as being non-existent.
The word "of the impression" (saṃskārasya) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
For indeed, an impression that is either distinct or non-distinct [from the object] has already been refuted; for this reason as well, there is no impression of the object.
Why? Because of the restriction of capacity, which will be explained later.
The word "ca" (and) in the phrase "śaktiniyateśca" should be understood as having been elided in its indication.
By this, the meaning becomes:
and because of the restriction of capacity, the refinement of the object (*viṣayasaṃskāra*) is not tenable, as will be explained hereafter.
He demonstrates that very restriction of capacity with the words "In the production of cognition," and so forth:
"If [the word] were unfit for the production of cognition,
this word would never be perceived by anyone anywhere, because it would be of no use for the cognition thereof."
If, however, it possessed the capacity to produce cognition, this word would be perceived by everyone, everywhere, and at all times,
since it would remain as the cause of cognition.
There are two possible positions: whether this sound is by its very nature incapable of producing cognition at any time, or not.
In the first case, it would never be apprehended by anyone. In the second case as well, it would be apprehended by everyone at all times, because its nature is uniform.
Therefore, there is no efficacy in conditioned phenomena.
It might be argued: "Even if it is capable, it might at times fail to produce cognition due to the force of a contrary condition;
likewise, even if it is incapable, it will produce [cognition] once its capacity has been imparted by auxiliary conditions. To this, he says: "For that... and so forth. [p.692]
For whether it be capable or incapable, that [nature] resides within itself by its very essence;
what opposing factor or auxiliary cause is able to destroy its purpose?

For it is not logical that something which either destroys or does not produce an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should be either a contradictory factor or a cooperative condition, because this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If one accepts [that it both] destroys and produces, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the loss of its permanence.
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "just as when it is being produced," he says:
"And this [object] is suitable for the production of cognition for some [persons]."
Therefore, this [cognition], as it arises, is not perceived by everyone.
Alternatively, if its refinement (saṃskṛti) were to occur through sounds situated nearby,
then the word would be heard by those very [sounds], but how much more so by those situated at a distance?

This fault does not apply to the position that [the word] is produced, because it arises from its own cause as something already capable of producing a specific cognition; therefore, it is not perceived by everyone at all times.
However, this fault belongs only to one for whom the sound is modified, provided that such a modification is possible. Demonstrating this, he says "Alternatively," and so forth.

Not only is there the fault that even a distant object would be perceived if one accepts the capacity to produce cognition by nature, but there is also a fault in the position of modification; therefore, another alternative has been stated.
"But how much less so by those standing at a distance?"— this is the connection with the word "is heard.
However, he shows directly that it must indeed be heard [by them].
This very point is clarified by the passage beginning with "sāmīpye" (in proximity) and so forth:
for even in the case of proximity, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is postulated as the cause;
and that same impression is common to those [sounds] even when they are situated at a distance.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Because [the production] of sound has been refuted," he says "From a specific refinement" and so forth:
"If it is understood that the birth [of sound] from articulations is due to a specific refinement,
then the production of sound cannot be rejected by anyone."
For that specific refinement does not exist apart from the word;
otherwise, the word would become unknowable. Therefore, the word itself must also be produced.

If the refinement (*saṃskṛti*) arises, then it follows that the sound also arises, because the sound is not distinct from that refinement. Alternatively, if there is a distinction, then since cognition would arise from the refinement alone, the sound would have no causal role; consequently, it would follow that the sound is not an object of cognition (*ajñeya*).
Therefore, one must admit that the sound also comes into being.

Now, it might be argued: "Just as for you a sound arises with the capacity to produce a specific cognition, so too for us there will be a restriction of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), by which it is not perceived by those who are at a distance.
To this, he says: "And the conditioned," and so forth.
"And the conditioned sound never [produces] that nature [of being perceived by all]."
If it were always perceived, it would abandon its attachment to impermanence.
Even if it is conditioned such that it is capable of producing a cognition occurring within the continuum of a specific individual, there remains a fault nonetheless.
For instance, if it does not abandon its conditioned nature—which is fit for the production of cognition—then there follows the undesirable consequence that such a cognition would arise at all times.
On the other hand, if it does abandon it, then there follows the undesirable consequence of its impermanence.
Therefore, it must be admitted that [it] indeed arises from that.
Regarding what was stated in the passage beginning "But in the case of the two-fold impression," he says "In the case of the two," and so forth:
Even in the view that there are two impressions, it is true that the two defects [previously mentioned] exist;
however, there is no deficiency of either one, because of the persistence of the former [impression].
According to the view of those for whom there is a theory of origination, it is logical that one or the other [of the conditions] might be deficient;
however, this is not the case in the position of those who maintain the theory of conditioning (saṃskāra), because for them the nature of the previously conditioned entity always persists.

With the words "For thus," and so forth, he demonstrates that very persistence: for if those conditioned auditory organs and phonemes were not destroyed by their manifestors previously, then because they would have reached a state of non-destruction, there would consequently be hearing of everything by everyone.
"Because of the attainment of passing away" means because of the consequence of impermanence;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the thesis.
Regarding the term *sarvaśruti*: it means "hearing at all times" (*sarvasmin kāle śrutiḥ*), not the analysis [of the compound] as "the hearing of everything" (*sarvasya śrutiḥ*).
Because of the prohibition of compounding [in the rule] "and in the case of karma."

Now, it might be argued that the connection with the audition [of sound] is restricted to specific persons because the auditory organ and the phonemes are cultivated [only for them], and therefore it is not heard by everyone.
If that were so, then those who are perceivers of other phonemes would not obtain the hearing of sound at all.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "restricted" (*niyata*).
If the auditory faculty and its connection with the sound were fixed, and the letters were already perfected,
then there would be no further hearing for those who are attaining other letters.

The compound [niyatavarṇaprapannāḥ] is analyzed as "men who are fixed and capable of hearing. Alternatively, the analysis is "those others who have entered the castes" or "those who have entered other castes."

Furthermore, one might think: "There may be another refinement (saṃskāra) of the auditory faculty and the sound that makes them fit for the arising of the cognition of those other phonemes. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the verse beginning *tadvarṇa* and so forth:
"If they are refined again so as to be fit for the cognition of those phonemes and persons..."
If it were to persist only in those two, would there not indeed be a scriptural authority for those two as well?
The compound *te ca te varṇanarāś ca* means "those [colors] and those men.

Which, then, are those colors? They are those which are perceived by these practitioners (*pratipattṛbhiḥ*). And who are those men? They are the very ones who are the practitioners (*prapattāraḥ*). The compound *vijñānaṃ tatra yogyau* refers to the cognition regarding them;
the phrase *tayor eva* refers to those two alone.
"Of the previously conditioned ear and sound";
"of those two as well" refers to the previously mentioned phoneme and person.
This is what is meant:
later, when the phonemes beginning with *ka* are heard by others, they should likewise be heard by those who previously heard them,
because of the persistence of their prior nature.

Now, showing that if there were no persistence [of the same entity], it would follow that they are impermanent, he says "In the case of exclusion," and so forth: "In the case of exclusion, these auditory perceptions and phonemes are entirely different; how then could they not result in the abandonment of the hope for their permanence?"
This is easy to understand.
Regarding what was stated, "Just as [the sun], though one, [is seen] in water and so forth," he says: "In water and so forth, this sun is not seen as a single entity possessing a manifold nature,
because all cognitions of reflections remain without an objective basis."
For it has already been established without distinction that all erroneous cognition is indeed devoid of an object;
nevertheless, he now establishes this again specifically regarding cognitions of reflections, for both the positions of *sākāra* (with-form) and *nirākāra* (without-form).
With reference to the first position, he says "they are without form," and so forth.
In your position as well, all cognitions are established as being formless,
whereas the external object is admitted to possess form.
Moreover, this reflection is observed as being situated within water and other such media,
whereas the sun and other celestial bodies existing in the vault of the sky do not abide in that manner.
If it is asked why that [object] shines forth in such a way through delusion, the answer is precisely because of that;
however, it is not clearly without a basis, since it is devoid of an object possessing that form.
If the realization of that very [object] were otherwise, then this well-spoken word would be otherwise;
but if it were so, everything would be the knower of everything.
There would be the realization of that very [object] if it were perceived as existing in such a state;
but when it is apprehended in another form, how could there be a perception of it?
For even if consciousness possesses an aspect, it is not distinct from the known object;
only when an aspect exists is it logical for consciousness to be its grasper.

For you, the Mīmāṃsaka, consciousness is formless while the external object possesses form; therefore, that form which is seen within the water is not a form of cognition, since it is admitted that only the external object possesses form.
Nor is it admitted that this is a reflection existing as a separate entity, for that would entail the consequence that the sun itself is not perceived.
Nor has the sun entered into the water such that it might appear thus, because it resides in the region of space.

If it is argued that it appears as such through delusion (*bhrānti*), then in that case, the cognition would not have the sun as its objective support (*ālambana*), because that sun lacks a form existing within the water.

Consequently, since an object is devoid of the form under which it appears to a given cognition, it is established that such a cognition is without an objective support. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever does not possess the nature that appears in a particular cognition is not the object (*viṣaya*) of that cognition; for example, color-form (*rūpa*) is not the object of auditory cognition. And the sun does not possess the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that appears in the cognition of the reflection. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
The reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because the sun lacks a form existing within the water;
nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
for in such a case, anything whatsoever would become the object of perception for anyone.
Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory (*viruddha*).
Furthermore, one might argue that it is simply the same sun that is perceived differently due to a difference in location, and therefore the reason (*hetu*) is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*).
Aside from someone as audacious as you, who else could possibly assert that "it is the very same thing, yet it is otherwise"?

For instance, by the phrase "that very [thing]," its own nature is affirmed; by the phrase "otherwise," that [nature] is negated. How, then, could affirmation and negation, which are mutually contradictory, be logical in a single [entity] at one time?
If, moreover, that very same thing were to exist even while being perceived otherwise, then the entire universe would become one.
Consequently, arising and destruction would occur simultaneously, and all cognition would have a single object.

Therefore, if this object were perceived exactly as it possesses distinctions of place, time, and so forth, then it would indeed be perceived; how, then, could there be a lack of proof [for its existence]? Regarding the second position, the view that cognition possesses a form (*sākāra*), he demonstrates the lack of an external objective support (*nirālambanatā*) for cognitions that are like reflections, beginning with the words "Even in the case of having a form" (*sākāre ’pi*).

For in the theory of cognition possessing a form, even though there is the awareness of a form, an external object is said to be known because one experiences a form that is not distinct from the external object, and not because of an experience of a distinct form.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the definition].

Furthermore, in these cognitions of reflections, there is no experience of an aspect that is non-different from the aspect of the sun; for otherwise, the cognitions of reflections would be indistinguishable from non-erroneous cognitions of the sun.
Regarding what was stated, "for those who do not see the sun," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "pāramparya":
"Let it be understood that what is presented through a traditional succession is perceived by means of a downward function;
however, even though its mode of existence is upward, it is conceived as being only downward."
For it has been established that if that sun were to be conceived as being understood exactly as it is situated, it would be seen in that very way, and not otherwise.
"Let it be understood":
[this refers to] the self;
"having an upward movement": [this refers to] the breath.
The meaning is "surrounding the sun";
"it thinks" refers to the self (ātman).
This is what is meant:
if indeed the self perceives the sun situated above, which is presented through a continuous series [of reflections], why does it conceive of it as being only below and not above?
For it would be perceived exactly as it is only if it were grasped according to its actual state.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle.

Regarding what was stated as a consequence—namely, that "the face, presented by the inward-turning function [of the mirror], and so forth"—to that he replies: "Not so; by that function directed toward it... and so on.
It is not the case that the inward-turning function is presented by the function directed toward that [mirror];
rather, one who perceives the face understands it to be "inward" through delusion.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "The cognition of a reflection," and so forth.

The cognition of a reflection does not have one's own face and so on as its objective support, because it appears as something distinct from that [face], like the cognition of taste, sound, and so forth.
"Because it appears as something having different characteristics from that":
this is an indication by means of a state-characteristic (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*);
the meaning is "because of its appearing with characteristics different from that."

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition appears with a manifestation distinct from [its object] does not have that as its objective support (*ālambana*). For example, the cognition of taste and so forth does not have sound as its objective support, nor does the cognition of sound have taste as its objective support; and cognitions of reflections appear with manifestations distinct from the face and so forth. This is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Warding off the charge that this [argument] is unestablished, he says "alpīyasī" and so forth:
"For in a small mouth, what is small appears in a mirror;
and trees and the like, when submerged in water, are perceived as inverted."
The original object faces the mirror, whereas the reflection does not;
furthermore, this reflection is situated within the water and so forth, while the original object remains at a distance.
Furthermore, the reflection differs from the original object in being gross, subtle, and so forth, by way of conforming to its basis; therefore, for this reason, the [reason] is not unestablished.

In a very small mirror, even a large face appears smaller; likewise, branches and so forth that are below appear submerged in water, as do trees and the like. Similarly, a face is perceived in water and other media as facing inward and as situated at a distance, yet the reflection of the face and such things does not actually exist in that manner.

Likewise, due to the difference in the bases such as swords, a reflection appears in the form of distinctions such as length; yet the original object (bimba) does not possess those same distinctions of length and so forth. Thus, it is not unestablished that cognition manifests in a manner distinct from its object.
Avoiding the charge of inconclusiveness, he says: "Even by means of a distinct appearance," and so forth:
"If the cognition of an object were possible even through a distinct appearance, then every mind—such as that directed toward form, sound, and so on—would have all objects as its domain."
And when even a single object is seen as separate [and manifold] by the eye slightly closed with a finger, that too is considered an objectless error.
The undesirable consequence that every cognition would have everything as its object serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
As for what was stated, beginning with "when slightly closed," that too has been refuted by this very [argument], because that [cognition] likewise lacks an object.
As it was stated in the passage beginning with "and in the case of existing in multiple locations," he replies there with the words "the arising of a reflection," and so forth:
"But the arising of a reflection has already been refuted here,
because two corporeal things cannot occupy the same place simultaneously due to their mutual resistance."
For the reality of a reflection has already been refuted previously by such arguments as the impossibility of an embodied object occupying the same location [as its source].
"Let it be granted that the reflection is a real entity; nevertheless, its being apprehended by a single cognition is unproven. Demonstrating this, he says "anekadeśa," etc.:
"Or even if the reflection exists as residing in many locations, on account of the distinction [between them], such as gross and subtle, unity is simply not found."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of distinctions such as length and so forth is intended.

Now, it might be argued that even though there is a distinction such as grossness and so on, there is indeed a state of being accessible to a uniform cognition due to some commonality, such as blueness.
Even so, ultimate unity is not established.
If it were merely imagined (*kalpita*), then there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Furthermore, if ultimate unity (*pāramārthika-aikya*) were to exist even when things are perceived as distinct by way of place and so forth, then let there be unity between a Brahmin and a Caṇḍāla as well, due to their commonality of being human beings.

Likewise, by virtue of the generality of "femaleness," your mother, your own wife, and your own mouth and anus would all result in being one, because they are equally composed of earth (*pārthivatva*).
Since the entire universe would be a single entity by virtue of being a real thing, the undesirable consequence of a simultaneous great creation and destruction would indeed be unavoidable.

Regarding what was stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Furthermore, even if it were the case that the simultaneous perception of a single existent entity in multiple locations is untenable, let the 'beloved of the gods' (the fool) look at the sun; for while it is one, it is perceived as if residing in many places...
because of its distance, its location is not determined, and thus there is delusion; likewise, in the case of sound as well, there is a failure to determine its location due to delusion.
To this, he says: "Of men," and so forth.
And this determination which arises in men,
"The sun is situated above me," is certainly an error.
Because all living beings see only the single sun simultaneously, and never a second one at any time.
Since no second solar orb is observed here beyond the first,
and because it is neither seen nor unseen, the sun is therefore determined to be one alone.
Sound is by no means thus determined as a unity,
because its plurality is observed both successively and simultaneously.
For when many speakers pronounce the phonemes *ga* and so forth simultaneously,
the two differences are clearly perceived.

Because a second solar disc, which meets the conditions for perception, is not perceived, its non-existence is certain; thus, the unity [of the sun] being established, the erroneous cognition "the sun is situated above me" is determined.
However, the unity of sound is not established in this way, such that its existence in different locations and so forth would be erroneous.
For if unity were established, then its existence in such [different places] would be proven to be erroneous; but that very unity is not established—therefore, this [argument] is trivial.
Regarding the word *rāva*: this [term] ends in the suffix *aṇ*, meaning "this belongs to *ravi*.
Now, one might object that the oneness of sound is already established by the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); to this he replies with the words "But it is not so," and so forth.
The meaning is that the invalidity of recognition has already been established previously.
He demonstrates the proof of multiplicity through simultaneity with the words "for when," and so forth.
The term "clearly" [indicates this].
Because it appears through distinctions such as fast, medium, and slow [tempo].
Explaining this even in terms of sequential application, he says "But in the case of sequential application," and so forth:
"In the case of its sequential application, however, its difference is not only understood through perception,
but also through an inferential mark (liṅga) by means of the sequence of cognitions."

"Not only by means of perception" means that even then, there is an experience of a distinct manifestation through differences such as *paṅkaja* (lotus) and so forth; nor is this a difference in the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), since that has already been refuted previously.
"Also from the inferential mark (*liṅga*)" means:

The meaning is: "also by means of inference. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not exist at a certain time cannot have its causes complete at that time; for example, visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) which fails to arise when there is a deficiency of the eye, even though the collection of conditions such as form, light, and attention is present. Furthermore, at the time of the arising of a single cognition of the letter *ga*, the cognitions intended to occur subsequently do not exist. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Since the state of having complete causes is pervaded by the state of existing, and that [state of completeness] is absent here.

But is it not the case that if the probandum is the mere negation of the state of having an unimpaired cause in a general sense, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*)?
For even if an eternal sound were a cause, its opponent maintains that the non-arising of cognitions occurring at a later time is due solely to the deficiency of auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*).

If, on the other hand, the negation being proved is the state of having an unimpaired cause specifically in the form of the cause called "sound," then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, the example is deficient in the property to be proven;
for visual consciousness does not fail to arise due to a deficiency in the causes of sound,
but rather due to a deficiency in the eye.
This is not so;
the probandum is established by way of generality alone, and thus there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For that very [generality] is not possible [in the case of the particular], since it cannot be assisted by that [particular].
For that which is beneficial must be depended upon; otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the principle].

Therefore, if one accepts that a word which is not dependent [on anything else] is the cause [of cognition], then every cognition arising from it would have its cause entirely unimpaired, and thus it would always occur.
If, however, it does not occur, then the absence of that cognition would indicate a deficiency in that very word; so how can this be considered a case of proving what is already established?

Even when proving the deficiency of a cause in its specific form (*viśeṣa*), there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), nor is there a lack of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*) in the example. For this is the intended meaning here: that which does not occur even when something else is present cannot be the cause of that thing; for example, visual consciousness does not arise even when sound is present. Likewise, even though the specific nature of the sounds such as the letter *ga* exists, the cognitions intended to be produced by them do not arise. Thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). Here too, the impossibility of dependence for an eternal entity serves as the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary position.

Nor is there a deviation [from the rule] by means of a seed or the like situated in a granary, because it is impossible for that to be a primary cause with respect to the sprout; so, enough with this elaboration.

Regarding what was stated previously, beginning with "because it depends on the manifesting sounds" (*vyañjakadhvanyadhīnatvāt*), although that has already been refuted in substance, [the author] speaks again—refuting it once more with the words "vyañjaka... etc.—with the desire to proclaim that this position is indeed faulty even if there were a manifester for eternal things.
"And let its perception depend upon the manifesting sounds;
however, its apprehension must occur in the form as it actually exists."
Otherwise, this apprehension of it would not occur, because its form does not appear;
for sound does not manifest as pervading the entire expanse of space.
Why does the auditory perception conform to the different locations of those sounds?
Rather, the manifestation should appear by its own nature alone, like a jar or other objects.
All this has been stated as a mere theoretical construction,
and the incapacity of manifestors has been established both because manifestation is impossible and for the reasons already explained.
The notion that "it is indeed that very same [object] which is perceived" has already been refuted;
therefore, the fact that [the object] is distinct due to the difference in location remains uncontradicted.
For if the apprehension of sound were dependent upon its manifestor, why would it not be apprehended as long as it remains pervading space?
It has been explained previously that such apprehension of it would occur [only if it were so], otherwise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga);
yet, sound is not apprehended as far as space extends.
Therefore, it is not logical that the hearing of a word conforms to the resonance (dhvani).

What, then, is logical? It is logical that the word itself should conform to that hearing which perceives it. And in this way, the word is established by that [hearing] and not otherwise; consequently, it would manifest in its entirety, just like a jar or other objects—this is the summary of the meaning.
"Tad" means "therefore."

Regarding the phrase "and by way of succession, as in 'one [moves]' etc.," he says "by way of succession" and so forth: "And whoever moves from one distinct location by way of succession is established [as such] because of momentariness; otherwise, his movement would not occur."
Because it follows its own nature as being inseparable from its former location,
the attainment of another location is not possible for that which is stable.

For movement is simply the arising of what is impermanent in another location, but not so for what is permanent; because it is impossible for that which does not abandon its nature of abiding in one place to go to another location, and because if it were to abandon it, there would follow the consequence of losing its permanence.
This very point is shown by the passage beginning with "of that which is not separated from its former location," and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "as in the case of a large excavation," he says "of the sky" and so forth:
"Because the sky is indefinable, its manifestation cannot be conceived;
and because it is beyond the senses, this light does not exist in the sky—it is merely perceived as such."

Since the substantiality of space (*nabhas*) is not established, its manifestation is not logical; for it is designated as such merely by the absence of tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*). For instance, those who do not perceive any resistance in the dark say, "This is just space; there is nothing here. Even for those for whom space is a real entity, it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*); how then could there be a cognition of the sky? Therefore, he says: "And because it is beyond the senses."
If this is so, what is perceived when the earth is dug up? To this he says: "That light is likewise [perceived]."
Showing that manifestation is not at all tenable even if space were a real entity, he says "Furthermore," and so on:
furthermore, manifestation is not tenable in space either, just as it is not in sound.
For this manifestation, which is cognition, would be eternal because its cause is ever-present.
And just as a manifestor is in no way possible in the case of a word, so too,
when the cognition of a word occurs, the notion that it has an external adjunct is merely an error.
Therefore, it is established that length and the other qualities are not properties of all sounds;
for those [qualities] would belong [to the word] if sounds were its manifestors, and that has been refuted.
"That it should be so":
the sound of [phonemes] such as *dīrgha* (long) is their property (*dharmatva*). And "that": [refers to the aforementioned].
The capacity of sounds to manifest [meaning].
Regarding what was stated, "And there is no connection with an unperceived object," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning, "Even though these are absolutely distinct.
"Even though these are absolutely distinct, words and their objects are capable of producing a uniform conceptual reflection (*tulyapratyavamarśana*); this has been discussed repeatedly before."
Therefore, a word is not a designator by virtue of having a connection with a perceived object;
rather, it has been established that in reality, this [word] is not a designator through its own intrinsic function (*khavṛtti*).
This is the summary of the meaning here:

if you are establishing the consequence that there is an absence of a relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) for ultimate objects and words, then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For it has been refuted in detail, in the *Śabdaparīkṣā*, that universals (*jāti*), specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and so forth, possess the status of being signified or signifier.

Now, even the conventional [relation] is not free from inconclusiveness; for it has already been established in the investigation of *apoha* that certain objects, despite being absolutely distinct, may by their very nature become causes for a single-form conceptual cognition (*pratyavamarśajñāna*), thereby bringing about the conventional relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between word and object.
Therefore, all this that is being said against the Buddhists who maintain that the meaning of a word is *apoha* merely flounders due to its extreme triviality.
He states the justification for the denotative capacity [of words] from the perspective of conventional reality (saṃvṛtti) with the verse beginning "mithyāvabhāsinaḥ" and so forth:
"For these cognitions produced by words appear falsely;
this is because the relationship of denoted and denoter is established only for universals (jāti), specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa), and the like."
Due to that delusion, speakers, despite the actual difference [between individual instances],
consider with a uniform understanding that the word "cow" is indeed one and the same.
Therefore, that which has been stated by one who speaks much and incoherently—
namely, that which prioritizes a distinction between words— is entirely without foundation.

For that cognition by which the form of another is concealed by its own appearance—because it does not manifest the object as it truly is—is a conceptualizing cognition (*kalpikā buddhiḥ*), and it is called "concealment" (*saṃvṛti*). The form established by that [cognition] is said to be "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*).
That alone is conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisattva*) and not ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*), because it lacks true existence.
Furthermore, all erroneous cognition is devoid of an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*).

Furthermore, it might be asked: "In the absence of ultimate unity, how do words bring about conventional usage characterized by affirmation and negation through the power of superimposition? To this he says, "For instance," and so forth: "For instance, there is no unity in hand-gestures and the like, because they are distinct cognitions;
and their manifestation as such has been refuted due to distinctions such as fast and slow."
Furthermore, no single universal (sāmānya) is perceived therein that persists [through them];
yet, by virtue of linguistic convention (saṅketa), this [exclusion] becomes the means for understanding negation and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "trembling of the hand, etc.," the winking of the eyes and so forth are included.
The connection is with the phrase "due to the distinction between fast, slow, and so on," which refers to the distinction in cognition (*buddhi*).

Furthermore, this distinction of speed and so forth is not produced by a manifestor, because manifestation has been refuted; thus, it is "its manifestation," meaning the manifestation of that which is eternal. Nor does it serve as a factor for linguistic usage by virtue of a universal (sāmānya), because such a universal is unestablished.
It is not logical for a universal that is not apprehended to be a constituent of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), because it would follow that such usage would occur at all times.
Regarding the phrase "it is a factor for the comprehension of negation and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes affirmation, permission, entreaty, and the like.

Their "course" (gati) is cognition; its "limb" (aṅga), that is, its cause, is this [action] such as the trembling of the hand. The ellipsis is to be supplied: "In the same way, it will be so with sound as well."

Regarding what was stated—"Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning is declared to be indeed eternal"—he replies with the verse beginning with "sākṣāt": "Words do not directly [denote] external objects because of their lack of connection to them; rather, it has been said that these words indicate the speaker's intention."
Indeed, there is no real relationship between word and object such that it could be either eternal or non-eternal.
For it has already been explained in the "Examination of Words" (*Śabdaparīkṣā*) that words do not denote an external object, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between them.
Furthermore, if they were to convey [meaning] without such a connection, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If this is so, then what do they actually convey? To this he says: "They are indicators of the speaker's intention" (*vivakṣāsūcakāḥ*). Even the speaker's intention they do not convey as a denotable object (*vācyatayā*); rather, they indicate it by way of being a logical mark (*liṅgatayā*).
For this very reason, it is said that they are "indicators" (sūcaka).

To explain: from a word once uttered, there arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines the object (*artha*), not one that determines the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). And how can that which is not determined by means of a known word be the meaning of a word?

If this is so, what is the connection between those [perceptions and non-perceptions] and the intention to speak, by virtue of which the former could indicate the latter as a logical mark (*liṅga*)? To this he says, "Of that," and so forth: "For they are ascertained through perception and non-perception as being the effects of that [intention]; therefore, the relation of cause and effect is clear in this case."

Since words are ascertained through perception and non-perception within oneself as being the effects of that intention to speak, the relationship between them is characterized solely as one of cause and effect.

If that were so, then convention (*samaya*) would be useless, because the relationship of cause and effect is ascertained by perception and non-perception alone; thus he says, "And the relationship of cause and effect," and so forth:

"And the relationship of cause and effect, which has been ascertained through convention and the like—that very [relationship] one would understand from words when one intends to speak, just like a movement of the hand."

He thinks as follows: although the causal relationship between the mere intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) and [the resulting word] is certain, it is impossible to ascertain the specific intention to speak in another's mental continuum without a convention (*samaya*). Therefore, a convention is established for the sake of ascertaining that [specific intention].
But how can this [specific intention] be ascertained even through a convention?

For instance, if at the time of establishing the convention there were a means of cognition for the specific intention to speak in the other person, then that convention, once established therein, would later serve as the cause for cognizing the specific intention during the time of linguistic usage.

To the extent that there is no such means [to establish the convention], for indeed a convention cannot be established without uttering the word; and consequently, if the specific intention were understood from that very word, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

For the word indicates the specific [intention] by virtue of the convention, yet the convention cannot be established without the understanding of the specific and non-specific [meanings]; thus, the mutual dependence is evident.

This is not a fault. When it is accepted that this entire verbal convention (*śābda-vyavahāra*)—because it is erroneous—is based solely on one's own internal mental appearance (*svapratibhāsa*), like the verbal usage of two moons by a person with ophthalmia (*taimirika*), then there is no room for such criticism. Furthermore, it is not the case that in every instance the word itself is the cause for the cognition of a specific intention (*vivakṣā-viśeṣa*); for otherwise, one might establish a convention (*samaya*) by indicating a specific intention through other means, such as pointing directly to an object (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*), through context (*prakaraṇa*), or by demonstrating a specific meaning. Thus, there is no fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Furthermore, this same objection applies equally to you, the proponent of injunction (*vidhivādin*): since the cognition of another is not perceptible, how can there be certainty regarding the speaker and the listener’s apprehension of the same object? And without certainty regarding the apprehension of the same object, a convention (*samaya*) is not tenable; whatever response you have to this point will also serve as mine.
It might be argued: "Since the word is not inherent in the intention (*vivakṣā*), how can its connection with that intention be determined through convention?"
For in this case, a convention established for one purpose does not serve to indicate another meaning, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

This is not a fault; for by the term "intention to speak" (*vivakṣā*), what is intended here is either the form of an object that does not conform to that [intention], or its own nature (*svarūpa*) when it is excluded from that [intention].

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) consists in its nature as the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). It is precisely this particular intention that is intended here; and it is with respect to that alone that there is a convention (*samaya*), not with respect to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), for it is that very thing which is denoted by the word.
This is because a conceptual construction (vikalpa) bearing that form subsequently arises;
however, it has already been stated that the mere intention to speak is not expressed by the word itself.

If this is so—if the relationship of a word is indeed characterized by causality (kāryakāraṇa) with respect to the form of an object that follows upon the speaker's intention (vivakṣā)—then how is it that in various places the teachers speak of the relationship between word and meaning as being "conventional" (sāmayika) or "based on convention" (samaya)? To this he says: "By means of the object residing in the intention," and so forth. The relationship of words, which consists of the nature of cause and effect with an object residing in the intention, arises when there is a convention (samaya).
Therefore, it is called "conventional" (sāmayika) because it is illuminated by convention;
thus, their connection is also termed "convention," though not in a primary sense.

Because it arises when there is a convention (*samaya*) in the mind of the listener, it is "conventional" (*sāmayika*); the suffix *ṭhaṭ* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *adhyātma*.

Although in that context the root *bhū* is taken to signify existence (*sattā*), nevertheless, since in ultimate reality there is no difference between existence and arising, that very [arising] is intended to be expressed as existence itself.
Furthermore, because it indicates the convention within the continuum of the speaker, it is called "convention" (*samaya*) by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
Because it exists at a specific time, it is possible for it to occur at that very time.

Now, if it has been stated that from the perspective of ultimate reality there is no relation between entities, how then does the characteristic of causality come to be? To this he says, "by those which have become cause and effect," and so forth.
"Those very [entities]" means that [the relation] is not something other than the two entities that have become cause and effect.
But it is precisely those two that, being thus described, possess the relationship of cause and effect.
"Two things existing in the relation of cause and effect" means "stated as such," using the expression "the state of being cause and effect" and so forth for the sake of brevity.

If this is so, since those two [the word and the object] differ with each individual's application [of the convention], how can there be for the speaker and the listener a cognition of an identical relation?

For indeed, it occurs to the speaker thus: "I am conveying that very same object by means of that very same word which was grasped by me at the time of the convention"; and likewise, it occurs to the listener thus: "He is conveying this very same object by means of that very same [word]. Otherwise, how could there be linguistic communication between two who stand in different positions? To this, he says: "And those... and so forth.
And since those [individuals] are perceived by the dull-witted as having a single, unitary nature,
it is therefore held that they pervade the time of convention and linguistic usage.
"By the dull-witted" means by those who are deluded.
"When it has passed" means when it has been grasped.
That time which is reached and pervaded by convention and linguistic usage is described as such.
Its pervasion [is established] by means of both cause and effect and by means of uniformity; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

[705] Now, why is it not accepted that there is only one ultimate relation, such that a merely conceptual one is desired? To this he says, "But one," and so forth: "But a single, real relation is not at all tenable here;
because objects are unmixed, there would be a lack of relation in the case of difference."
A relation, if it were to exist, would have to be between things that are either distinct or non-distinct.
First, it cannot be between distinct things, because since all things abide within their own selves, there is no commingling among them.
Even in the case of non-difference, since that entity is only one, with what could there be a conjunction, and with whom? Therefore, there would be a lack of relation.

As for the refutation of the relationship characterized by convention (*samaya*)—beginning with the words "Convention [is] for every person" and so forth—he says "Convention," etc., demonstrating that therein the point is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*):
"Convention is for every person and for every utterance;
Thus and more has been said by one who does not understand the opponent's position."
For the *samaya* is not a primary relation between those two by virtue of being a property of humans;
rather, it is a relation only in the sense that it is the indicator of that [object]. It is not a primary [relation].
Furthermore, others do not accept this [eternity of the Veda] on account of its being recited anew;
for the Lord and others have been refuted, and it was not created at the beginning of creation.

For a refutation is defined as the occurrence of an undesired consequence; however, the Buddhist does not accept convention (*samaya*) as the primary relationship between word and meaning, because that is a property of persons.

Since there is no damage whatsoever to what he accepts when that [convention] is refuted, and furthermore, a property belonging to one thing cannot be the relationship of another, lest it lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

As for the two positions stated—that [the convention] is either established at every utterance or from the very beginning of the world—they are not subject to refutation simply because they are not accepted [by us]. He states this with the words "at every utterance," and so forth.
"This" refers to the convention (*samaya*).
"The others" refers to the Buddhists.
"Of Īśa and so forth" means of Īśvara, Brahmā, and the others.
Regarding what was stated previously—that "the relation may exist even with respect to each [individual]" and so forth—he replies with the verse beginning "pratyekam" (with respect to each):
The relation that exists with respect to each [individual] appears distinct due to the momentary destruction [of things];
and a uniform reflective cognition (*tulyapratyavamarśa*) is not contradicted even when there is difference.
The second position alone is the correct one here.
Nor does it entail the consequence of a cognition of difference, because there is no contradiction in [the universal] being the cause of a uniform reflective awareness even when there is difference.
Therefore, that which was stated—that if there were difference, there would be a cognition of difference—is inconclusive.

It might be argued: "This momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is not established for us; so how can it be said that [the object] is distinct from momentary destruction? To this he says "krameṇa" and so forth:
"And the cognitions having those [objects] as their content clearly arise in succession."
They also state the sequence for those [energies], for otherwise there would be no sequence.
"Of that too" means they state— that is, they demonstrate— the sequence of the relationship;
for otherwise, it would be without sequence.
The connection is with the word "of cognitions" (dhiyām).
And this is the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) regarding the contrary [case]. The formal argument (prayoga) is to be understood as before.
Regarding the argument that linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is impaired because of the difference between the cognitions of the speaker and the listener, he says "all at once" (*sakṛdeva*), etc.:
"But when a convention is established for many [people] all at once, a distinct convention is not accepted, just as in the case of a single moment of blue and so forth."
The relation is not one for the speaker in his cognition, nor another for the hearer;
and it is of a single form, since it persists for both.
In order for the listener to establish the connection [between the words and their meanings],
the speaker first resorts to that very [connection] which was previously apprehended by him.
Since his reflective cognition (pratyavamarśadhī) occurs with a single form,
he therefore determines oneness even though the word and other factors are distinct.

Just as a momentary instance such as blue is not divided even when perceived by many, so too, even though a convention is established by many, the related entity will not be divided; how much less so in the case of two?
The point is that this is because all [perceivers] abide in an identical conceptual determination (*pratyavamarśa*).
Therefore, no relation other than that between the speaker and the listener comes into being.

Regarding what was stated—"If [you say] this is the same even in the case of a jar and so forth, no, because of the established nature of the universal," and so on—he replies with the verse beginning "Even in the case of a jar and so forth":
"Even in the case of a jar and so forth, the universal has already been refuted;
for no configuration (ākṛti) is accepted that is distinct from the qualities of the elements."
Nor is its capacity for supporting [the universal] and so forth established by virtue of its form;
for even those [qualities] would be eternal if they were non-different from the form.
If there were a difference [between the word and its power], there would be the fault of a lack of relation; if, however, the power were produced from it, there would be impermanence.
Therefore, a power for lifting water and so forth is not logically possible on the basis of a generic form (*ākṛti*).
Even if power were distinct from the jar and so forth, these faults would certainly follow:
its effects, such as holding water and the like, would necessarily be eternal.
"Even more so" refers to the examination of the universal (*sāmānya*) [discussed] previously.
Furthermore, he states the refutation of this very point in brief with the words "for not," and so forth.
O Mīmāṃsaka, you maintain that for entities such as the sun-born [beings] or [the elements] such as earth and water, there exists a genus (*jāti*) distinct from their qualities such as blackness;

yet, although it is claimed to be perceptible, it is not perceived. Nor is it tenable that it is non-distinct [from them], because that would entail the consequence that those things, such as jars, would also be eternal, just like the nature of their forms (*ākṛti*).

Furthermore, if it is admitted that [the universal] is distinct [from the individuals], then there is the fault of the absence of a relation; for between distinct things, the only possible relation would be that characterized by origination from them (tadutpatti). Consequently, if such origination were to exist, it would follow that the universal is impermanent, because it possesses the property of being produced, like a jar. In some versions, however, the reading is "permanence" (nityatā); in that case, the meaning is as follows: if the production of jars and so forth from that universal is accepted, then it follows that jars and so forth are permanent, meaning that because the cause is eternally present, their production would occur eternally.

In the position that it possesses both natures, the defects inherent in both positions would follow, as well as the consequence of the loss of its unity; for it is impossible for a single entity to possess two natures.
For in this way, those two would simply be stated as two distinct entities, not as one single thing consisting of both natures.
In the case of neither alternative, there would be the consequence of losing its status as a real entity (*vastutva*),
and it would be impossible for a single thing to be both affirmed and negated;
these are the faults.
The additional fault consists of the consequence that [the relationship] would be unestablished, the consequence of [the self's] eternality and so forth,
and the consequence that effects such as the constant holding of water would occur perpetually.

Regarding what was stated— that "the relation is indeed the capacity" (*śakti*) and so forth— he replies with "And the capacity alone," etc.: "If the capacity alone is the relation, and its differentiation is not admitted..."
There would be a single power for both words and their meanings, because they are non-distinct.
Even if there were a distinction, there would be no relation whatsoever between that [universal] and those two [particulars];
if it were produced from them, it would lack permanence, and there is no other possible mode of existence for a real entity.
Nor is it "other," because the same faults previously mentioned would follow regarding the characteristics of being both or neither.
Regarding what was stated [in the verse] beginning with "at the time of explaining the relation," he says "sambandha... and so forth:
"But at the time of explaining the relation, when a word such as 'cow' (go) is uttered, some understand it for the sake of the cognition of the relation, while others do not."
Because, due to the existence of a relationship, it is manifested in such a way;
however, if the relationship were yours, everyone would ascertain the meaning.
For you maintain that the relation is indeed a potency (*śakti*) that is eternal;
and is that [potency] restricted and unlimited in its production of the cognition of an object?
If there were no fixed limit, why would everyone not perceive everything? Even if there were a limit, what would be its cause? If you say it is nature (*prakṛti*), then it must be so by itself.
Prior to the grasping of the convention, and furthermore when that [convention] is not remembered,
how could a single cognition function there as something possessing activity?
For that capacity is established as being necessarily concomitant with the arising of that cognition;
or else, it is postulated that the capacity itself is necessarily concomitant only when it is known.
If the known and the unknown are distinct, then its permanence is lost;
but if they are one, for what reason is this division described?

Since there exists a relationship of such a nature—characterized by the relation of cause and effect—it would be logical that some people understand [it], because that [relationship] stands as the producer of a determinate cognition. However, he shows that everything is untenable regarding the relationship according to your [position] with the words "tāvakīne" (in your [view]) and so forth.

For it is held that the relationship is characterized by capacity (*śakti*), and the nature that produces [an effect] is called capacity. Furthermore, this [capacity], being of an eternal and unitary nature, is restricted to the production of the cognition of the intended object. Consequently, there are two alternatives: is this [capacity], which is restricted to the cognition of the object, admitted to be universal (without limit in terms of persons), or is it not?
