In the first case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that everyone would simultaneously and in every way ascertain the object.

Even in the second position, a cause that determines the specific nature of producing a particular consciousness must be stated; for while it is logical that produced entities have their own causes and conditions as the determinants of their specific nature of producing particular effects, this is not the case for eternal things—such is the meaning.

It might be argued: "Even for eternal things, their very nature (*prakṛti*) is such that they produce only specific effects and not everything, for intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) do not admit of questioning. If that is so, then if this nature of theirs exists by itself, independent of anything else, it follows that for that very same specific cognizer who has previously grasped the convention but later forgotten it, the production of cognition would occur at all times; for the power fixed for the generation of that cognition would be constantly present.

Now, it might be argued: "Because it is the cause of knowledge, the capacity characterized as a relation produces knowledge only when it is known, not when it is unknown; therefore, the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not occur.
This is incorrect.
For if a mutual distinction between the states of being known and being unknown is admitted, then its eternity is lost.

If, on the other hand, there is no difference [between the two], then the distinction between the two natures—the known and the unknown—is untenable; for it is not possible for a single entity, with respect to a single person, to possess the two mutually contradictory natures of being both known and unknown.
Furthermore, if there were a means of practice, the capacity would indeed be known; however, thinking that such a means itself is not possible, he asks "Furthermore" and so forth:
"Moreover, by what means is the capacity intended to be cognized?"
If it is argued that this is established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), we reply that this is not so, because the following principle holds here:
In this context, one perceives through direct perception the word, the elder, and the object denoted;
and one perceives through inference the listener's comprehension.
And by means of "presumption from the impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti), one cognizes the capacity residing in both [the word and the object];
through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), they understand the relationship as being established by three means of valid cognition.
With the words "from presumptive testimony" (*arthāpatti*) and so forth, he first sets forth at length the opponent’s rejoinder.

For Kumārila has described this principle for the apprehension of the relationship as follows: first, one perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) the word, the elder who is the speaker of the word, and the object which is the thing to be expressed; thereafter, one perceives—that is, determines—through inference (*anumāna*), by means of the mark (*liṅga*) characterized by purposeful action (*ceṣṭā*), that the hearer has understood [the meaning].
Purposeful action is called an inference by treating it as an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a causal factor (*kāraka*).
And thereafter, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), one understands the capacity that rests upon both—that is, the capacity resting upon both word and meaning.

Since they are understood directly through presumptive testimony, it is said that "they are understood by means of presumptive testimony. Thus, [the relationship] is established by three means of valid cognition (*tripramāṇaka*).
He for the sake of whose realization there exist the three means of valid cognition characterized by perception, inference, and presumptive testimony is so described.
With the words "in quite another way" and so forth, he states the refutation:
"Because it is established in quite another way, the [causal] capacity cannot be understood;
for from the word, which is conventional and so on, there arises an unconfused comprehension."
By this, he states that the argument from presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is inconclusive, because it has been demonstrated that comprehension is possible even without an eternal relationship.

Showing that its postulation is not only improper due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it, but also improper because it is contradicted by valid cognition, he says: "But in the case of the permanence of power (*śakti*), it would depend on convention (*saṅketa*) and so forth; [if it did not], the comprehension of word-meanings would occur at all times. In the view that power is eternal, however, it depends upon convention and the like;
otherwise, the comprehension of the meaning of words would occur constantly, without anything [such as convention] being required.
Furthermore, when another capacity is present, as in the case of words such as *kali* or *māryā*,
the sound (*dhvani*) would not convey a different meaning, because its power is restricted.
If a single capacity is postulated for the purpose of illuminating various meanings,
or if capacities are distinct, then a single word would simultaneously be a knower of multiple meanings.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those words which reveal their meaning by depending upon convention do not possess an eternal connection, just like the words *agāvī* and so forth; and the worldly and Vedic words such as *go* and so forth reveal their meaning by depending upon convention. This is an instance of the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), because dependence is pervaded by the possession of a non-eternal connection, which is itself contradictory to the possession of an eternal connection.
And this proof will be established later.
But here, only its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.
For it is accepted that words are connected with a relation characterized by power (*śakti*), which is the cause for the comprehension of meaning, and which is an eternal connection.
And since that power is eternal, it cannot be assisted; thus, it does not depend upon anything such as convention (*saṅketa*).
Consequently, the comprehension of word-meanings resulting from that [power] would occur at all times.

Furthermore, is that power restricted to a single meaning or restricted to multiple meanings? Even regarding the position that it is restricted to multiple meanings, there are the following alternatives: is the power of a single word that illuminates multiple meanings one and the same, or is it manifold?

In that regard, concerning the first position: when a different convention is established according to differences of place, time, and so forth, the observed capacity of a sound—such as the word *kali* or *mārya*—to convey a different meaning in the Draviḍa or Āryan countries respectively (namely, denoting the end of a time-period or a calamity such as rain), would not be possible, because its power is fixed, just like the eye and other sense organs.
For the eye, by virtue of convention, cannot be directed toward the perception of taste and so forth.
Even in the second position, there would follow the undesirable consequence that all persons simultaneously apprehend the meaning of a word from a single sound.
He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "When the word is one," and so forth.

In this very context, he states another fault: "And because the capacity to illuminate the meaning," and so forth: "And since the capacity to illuminate the meaning is established at all times, the understanding of that meaning would also occur for everyone at all times."

If it is postulated that its capacity depends upon convention, then surely it would depend upon an auxiliary factor; yet that [capacity], being immovable, cannot be something that requires an auxiliary.
"In that" means in the comprehension of the meaning. "She" refers to [the word].
It is power;
it is immovable;
it is eternal.
And this is the reason for its being incapable of being assisted.

Even granting the dependence on convention (*saṅketa*), he states another fault with the words "And because of the purpose of illuminating the object," and so forth: "And because the convention, which serves as the cause for illuminating the object, depends upon humans,
there is the possibility of falsity even when the capacity [of the word] is produced by something other [than that convention]."

Thinking, "May I indeed understand the meaning without confusion," you have rejected the person as the cause of confusion; yet, just as words employed by those persons are sometimes confused, why would Vedic words—which are common to all meanings—not be confused when they are applied to specific things by them according to their own will?
This is because those persons lack knowledge of the true nature of reality.
For how could the convention established by those who do not know the truth be restricted, since it proceeds independently according to their own will?
And therefore, since even a convention (samaya) arises from independent desire, why would it—being both autonomous and hostile—not avoid a contradictory meaning?
Having accepted the position that there is a capacity to illuminate multiple meanings, he states another fault, beginning with "The capacity to illuminate multiple meanings":
"Let there indeed be a capacity in a single sound to illuminate multiple meanings;
however, not all objects such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth are useful for every [purpose]."
Since it is also possible for [words] to indicate meanings contrary to what is intended,
your postulation of an eternal relationship between words and their meanings is pointless.

Although words possess the capacity to convey multiple meanings, objects do not possess the capacity to perform all causal functions, because the relationship between cause and effect is strictly determinate.
Otherwise, nothing would be either obstructive or non-obstructive.

Therefore, when one intends to convey an object that accomplishes a specific causal function, how can it be established that the author of the convention applies a word—which is common to all objects—exclusively to the intended object?
Therefore, since falsity is possible, the postulation of an eternal relation is indeed useless.

Showing once again its lack of purpose, he says, "And in regard to convention," and so forth: "If there is dependence upon convention, why is this relationship— which is characterized by eternal capacity— being fostered without any cause?"
No one is observed to be present as an assistant to that [word] such that it has a function in making an object known other than through convention.

If the relation were the cause for the cognition of meaning merely by its existence, then it would occur even for one who is ignorant of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); therefore, its dependence upon convention must necessarily be admitted.

Consequently, if convention itself is accepted as the cause for the cognition of meaning, why is another eternal relation postulated which, being established [by nature], stands ready without any further cause?
For such is the function of the relation: the production of the cognition of meaning; if that is accomplished by convention, what is the purpose of imagining another eternal relation?
Furthermore, it has been discussed hundreds of times that there can be no dependence on anything for that [Self] which is incapable of having any excellence added to it.
Moreover, if one were to postulate causality for something whose causal capacity is unobserved, then alas, why could one not postulate that deities cause purging upon reaching the *harītakī* fruit?
With the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*) and so forth, he demonstrates that the establishment of the relationship is achieved precisely through its function:
"For indeed, this linguistic convention is not observed without a convention;
therefore, the establishment of the relationship [is possible], and thus this succession is not purposeless."
"Therefore" means from convention;
"this succession is without an object" [means it is not based on a real entity].
Because the postulation of a causal efficacy for that which has not been observed leads to the fault of infinite regress.

For instance, even when a relation has been postulated, why would another further cause with unobserved efficacy not be postulated? Since there is no distinction in terms of having unobserved efficacy, this process would continue again and again, resulting in a vast succession of undesirable consequences.

Having thus established the pervasion (vyāpti) of the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa), he concludes with the verse beginning "narecchā" what was previously demonstrated regarding the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti):
"Even from a convention arising solely from mere human desire, linguistic usage is possible; therefore, [your] connection [between word and object] is not established."
"Yoga is not accomplished"—
the word "eternally" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

And by establishing this, he shows that what was stated—namely, "because all those who lack direct perception [establish it] through a prior precedent," and so forth—is stated in a manner that is mutually contradictory, with the words: "Otherwise, it would be impossible.
It is suspected that such conventional usage would be impossible otherwise;
however, since yoga is beyond the senses, it is not understood by ordinary men.
Since all [beings] lack direct knowledge [of this], and since each preceding [cause] is not established, the connection is not proven; why, then, is it so imagined?

For if all [persons] were ignorant, how then could the establishment of a relationship [between words and meanings] occur through a succession of prior ignorance? Indeed, a lineage of the blind is not capable of instructing others regarding specific forms. As it is stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya: "In matters of this kind, the word of a person does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge, just as the word of the blind does not [attain validity] regarding specific forms."

It might be argued: "All [ancient sages] are said to be ignorant because they did not perceive [the truth] directly, but not because they lacked complete knowledge in every respect; for by the means of valid cognition known as the impossibility of otherwise accounting for verbal usage (*śābdavyavahārānyathānupapatti*), it is established that the ancient elders of the past certainly possessed such knowledge.

This is not so, because verbal usage could proceed through convention even otherwise. While this is not yet definitively demonstrated, it remains at least doubtful whether he [the creator of the convention] was eternal or non-eternal.
For this very reason, he says "it is suspected" and so forth.

The intention is as follows: by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the mere existence of a relation is established, but not its specific nature, because no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with that [specific nature] has been proven.
Therefore, there is no difference between presumptive testimony and inference.

It might be argued: "The capacity of the non-eternal to cause the comprehension of meaning has not been observed, nor is it logical," as was previously established; therefore, because of this incapacity, the eternal is proven.
To this we reply: this same argument applies equally to the eternal, and it remains unproven.
For instance:

It is equally [the case] that even for a permanent relation, the status of being a cause for the comprehension of meaning has not been observed. Since the capacity to convey meaning is observed in the case of hand gestures and the like despite their impermanence, [your claim that such a capacity is] unobserved is unestablished.
For this very reason, [our] argument that [the relation] is untenable is unestablished.
Furthermore, because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is incompatible with both succession and simultaneity for that which is permanent, the claim that it is untenable is merely trivial.

Having thus concluded that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is inconclusive, he presents the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) with the words "those [words] such as 'cow' and 'horse,'" and so forth:
"Those words such as 'cow' and 'horse' are connected with an eternal relationship,
because they depend upon convention, unlike words such as 'gāvī' and the like."
The word "tad" means "therefore"; "nityasambandhayoginaḥ" means "of that which possesses an eternal connection."
The connection is "not so";
however, the formulation of the argument has already been shown previously.
But surely, since words such as *gāvī* and the like are incorrect (*asādhu*), their status as denoters is not accepted by the opponent; thus, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).
As it has been stated by Kumārila:
"While the word *go* remains established for us, [the use of *gāvī*] arises from an incapacity for that."
Even the cognition of "cow" produced by words such as *gāvī* follows the original word.

Thus, this is its meaning: when the correct expressive word "go" exists, it is said that the cognition of a cow which arises from the use of incorrect forms such as "gāvī" does not arise from those [incorrect forms] themselves; what then is the source? It follows the primary, correct word "go," because it is produced due to an incapacity for that [correct form].

The term *gāvyādeḥ* is connected with *sāmānādhikaraṇye* (in the state of grammatical coreferentiality). When that word *go* is the correct [form], a person’s inability to utter it is "that incapacity" (*tadaśakti*). The activity of the palate and other articulatory organs arising from that is so described; the word *gāvī* and others are produced (*kārita*) by that [activity]. Thus it has been said by Bhartṛhari: "Just as a child being taught says 'gāvā' or 'aśvā'..."
It is unmanifest to those who do not know it; therefore, for those who know it, there arises certainty through its manifestation.
Thus, when a correct word ought to be employed, if an incorrect form (apabhraṃśa) is used instead, some meaning is inferred through that [incorrect form] which is mediated by the correct word.
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, this is stated: "In the word *go*, when it is present as capable [of denoting its object], because of being produced by that incapacity," and so forth.
Even the cognition of "cow" arising from words such as *gāvī* follows the original word.
He refutes that with the words "That is not so," and so forth:
"That is not so, because [words like] *śanaka* and others do not convey a refined (saṃskṛta) meaning;
how could there be a comprehension of the meaning by following the root word?"
Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning is not accepted as eternal; rather,
it is logical that it is conventional, since that is possible in every respect.
"Of Śanaka and others" refers to fishermen and the like;
by the word "etcetera," barbarians and so forth are included.

For indeed, when meaning is conveyed to them by means of refined (saṃskṛta) speech alone, only confusion arises; therefore, the comprehension of meaning is not properly achieved by following the original words.
Regarding what was stated— that dissolution may take the form of the destruction of a region or the destruction of a family, and so forth— it is said in response:
"That dissolution which takes the form of the destruction of a region or the destruction of a family,
or that which is desired by the Buddhists as being unimpeded, and which is even suspected by Brahmā and others..."

In that Veda, a supreme cognition whose root has been destroyed is possible; likewise, false conceptions arising from delusion, intoxication, and the like, as well as erroneous imaginings, are possible.
It might even be suspected that this is a different Veda altogether, having merely assumed the guise of one; such a doubt persists as long as no subverting evidence is revealed.
He thinks as follows: "We do not describe dissolution as consisting in the annihilation of sound, nor do we maintain that there is a beginningless person who acts as the creator and destroyer."
Rather, the entire world is indeed beginningless;
even linguistic convention proceeds as a verbal usage established by conceptual constructions arising from beginningless predispositions.

However, as for this dissolution described by you in the form of the destruction of countries and so forth, and that dissolution described by the Buddhists as having the nature of being consumed by fire, water, and wind—extending ultimately to the limits of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system, bounded below by the circle of wind and above, respectively, reaching up to the first, second, and third dhyānas—this [latter] is suspected even by Brahmā and others because it is uncontradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and because it cannot be refuted. Therefore, in both these two kinds of dissolution, the destruction of the Veda is possible, as is the postulation of a contrary meaning.
Thus, the suspicion that this [other] Veda has become a mere semblance or a deceptive appearance of that [original one] does not cease until you state a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
It might be argued that there is indeed a subverting proof [for the opposite view].

For instance, one might determine that "at present, it is so everywhere; it has been so, and it will be so. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even if there were a desire to produce it otherwise," and so forth.
Even if there were a desire to produce it otherwise, the sound would not persist.
In that very way, if such a desire were to arise in men, it could not be otherwise.
One might suspect that the Veda is thus not of a nature different from its text and meaning; however,
if it were produced according to one's own will, such suspicion would not cease.

For if, despite the existence of a desire to alter [the text], the sound of the Veda were not to proceed otherwise, and if such a desire to alter could not be produced, then a person’s power to effect such alteration of the Vedic recitation and so forth would be established.
Even in that case, it is not established for all persons, because mere non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*),
and because we observe extraordinary capacities among certain individuals.
To whatever extent it is possible, the recitation of Vedic passages such as "śaṃ no devīrabhiṣṭaye" could be performed otherwise, or their meaning explained otherwise;
for indeed, Mīmāṃsakas, etymologists (Niruktakāras), and others are seen to interpret the meaning of the Vedas in many different ways.
Therefore, doubt is not dispelled.
Regarding the description of the refutation beginning with "And because sequence is an effect," etc., he says there: "And not by all men is a sequence established for all accepted;
they also compose the sequence of words, sentences, and syllables independently."
Otherwise, some composed work would be the Veda for you;
thus, even in the case of a mere meaningless composition, your theory of authorship is destroyed.

"He intends to speak exactly as he has been told by others"— this lack of necessity means that there is no beginninglessness in this case, just as there is none in the case of a linguistic convention.

The term *padāni* (words), *vākyāni* (sentences), and *akṣarāṇi* (syllables) are mentioned in that order; thus, it should be analyzed as "the sequence of these. Regarding the phrase "even in the case of a mere meaningless composition" (*anarthagranthamātre’pi*): the connection is that "composition" (*kṛti*) is destroyed. A "meaningless composition" is one whose meaning (*artha*) does not exist—such as a sentence like "ten pomegranates" (*daśa dāḍimāni*) and so forth—or one whose meaning is contrary to the Veda, such as the tenets of the Buddhists and others. It is called such because it is both "meaningless" (*anartha*) and a "composition" (*grantha*).
By the word *mātra*, he demonstrates pervasion (*vyāpti*).
*Kṛti* means cause. "In that way" [is the meaning].
"Like the Vedas";
"indeterminacy" means lack of restriction.
This means that this restriction would not exist;
"tad" means "therefore."
Regarding what was stated by the opponent, namely "I speak those spoken by another," and so forth,
he replies with the verse beginning "If such an intention as 'I speak those spoken by another' were to exist":
for [the cognition] would be like a distinction of objects due to a delusion consisting in a common conceptualization.
"Like the division of karma":
the suffix *vati* is added to a word ending in the locative case (*saptamī*).
By this, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) is stated through the demonstration that the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is possible for a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*).
It might be asked: "How is the erroneous nature of this established? To this he says: "But those uttered by another," and so forth.
"But those [sounds] uttered by another are not [the same], because of their difference in pitch and other qualities.
Nor is this a property of the manifestor, since it is perceived as being of the nature of the phoneme itself."
Consequently, distinct colors are observed for each individual person, just as they are for jars and other objects;
therefore, since this difference is perfectly clear, why is its mark denied?
"By means of accents, etc.
means by means of the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth.
By the word "etc.," the inclusion of fast (*druta*), medium (*madhya*), slow (*vilambita*), and other such tempos is intended.
Nor is this property of vowels and so forth a property of the manifestor. Why?
The meaning is that [the phoneme] is established because its nature as a *varṇa* (articulate sound) is perceived in vowels and so forth. "That mark" refers to this.
The "mark" (cihna) of that distinction of color (varṇabheda) is "that mark"; by the phrase "and there is no other mark," it is being denied as to what that [mark] might be.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Just as in the case of jars and so forth by means of a genus," he says "previously" and so on:

"And previously, the indication of conventional usage for jars and so forth by means of a genus was refuted, because that [genus] does not exist and because it is incompatible with the individual. (2682)
"Previously" means in the investigation of the universal (*sāmānya*).
"By its non-existence" means...
Because that universal (jāti) is non-existent;

or even if it were existent, since it cannot be assisted by the individual (vyakti) characterized as a jar or the like, it is impossible for them to be connected, and thus it is illogical to characterize worldly convention (vyavahāra) by means of that universal.

By means of that [argument regarding] genus (*jāti*), he shows that whatever has been postulated is entirely inconsistent, starting with the words "therefore, the universals of the palate, etc. [The verse reads:
"Therefore, the universals of the palate and so forth are not established in all men;
consequently, a speaker does not emit sounds by qualifying them with those [universals]."

Regarding what was stated, “And their distinct universals (jāti) are the causes for the manifestation of sounds,” and so forth, he replies with the words beginning with “That is not so” (tan na): That is not the case; those distinct universals are not the causes for the manifestation of sounds, since either the individual instances (vyakti) or the universals inherent in them persist only as long as the phonemes (varṇa) do.
"Tad" means "therefore."

Regarding what was said there concerning the conjunction of the palate and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "tatra tālvādi" and so on: "In that case, the sequence of sounds is not preceded by the order of conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and so forth; and for you, both [the universal and the individual] would be eternal."

As for what was also stated, beginning with "just as in the case of whirling and so forth," he states there that the example is unestablished by means of the passage beginning "just as in the case of whirling and so forth":
"Just as the parts of whirling and so forth are not characterized by a genus,
so too there is no sequential continuity for the palate and other articulators that would pertain to the sounds and phonemes."
Because [the existence of] a genus has been refuted; this is the sense.
Regarding what was stated, "or [the cognition] belongs to the individuals themselves," and so forth, he says:
"Even for individuals, because of their subtlety, there is no determination of the properties of the genus;
therefore, by virtue of that, there is no perception of sequence among the phonemes, even though they are all-pervading."
Regarding what was stated as "by the power of that," he says there: "by the power of that," and so forth.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "the qualities of the sound" (*dhvaniguṇān*), it is replied there with "that is not so," and so forth: "Therefore, the phonemes (*varṇa*), following after all those qualities of the sound which are established as eternal, would not be the means for cognizing the distinction of meaning."

Regarding what was stated, "And their distinct universals (jāti) are the causes for the manifestation of sounds," and so forth, he states the refutation of the universal by way of concession, beginning with "Furthermore," etc.: "Furthermore, the distinct universals are the causes for the manifestation of sounds; they function as long as there are phonemes, or else the individuals are associated with them."
Thus, because the manifestors exist eternally, there would be the eternal perception of sound;
therefore, for you, a sequence of phonemes consisting of a sequence of manifestations is not tenable.
And this collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāya*) should be understood as introducing a statement.
The word *iti* indicates a reason. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: because the [phonetic] classes (*jāti*) remain as the causes for the manifestation of sounds, therefore...
The perception of sound would necessarily be eternal,
because there is no succession in its manifestation; therefore, it is of that nature.
It is not logical...
it is clearly indeed...
thus.

In that regard, having accepted the relationship between the universal and the individual, he states the fault with the words "of those universals whose nature consists in their connection with individuals," and so forth:
"And when there is the establishment of universals whose nature consists in their connection with individuals..."
Furthermore, the eternality of individual instances would also unavoidably follow as a consequence.
Or, if the individuals characterized by their genus and relations were to be established [as eternal],
then even you, though unwilling, would have to accept the non-eternality of the genera themselves.

Because the relation resides in both [the universal and the individual], and because the eternality of universals is admitted, it follows that the individuals—which possess the nature of that relation—must also be eternal;
for otherwise, the universals would not have that relation as their essential nature.
Likewise, because the non-eternality of individuals is admitted, it follows that the universals—which possess the nature of that relation—would also be non-eternal.
Furthermore, the impermanence of individuals would be established by their own nature only if, through that connection, the universals (jāti) were also impermanent;
for otherwise, as long as one related member remains intact, it is not logical for the other to be deficient, since that would entail the loss of the very nature of the relationship.

Warding off another objection previously stated, he says: "Because manifestation is impossible," and so forth. Since the impossibility of manifestation has already been established above, those phonemes being manifested in this manner would not be non-expressive.
"Those" refers to the end of the individual instance.
Regarding what was stated—that time is one, all-pervading, eternal, and so forth—it is said in response: "Time, too," and so on.
Time, too, as being one, all-pervading, and eternal, has already been refuted;
like the phonemes, it is not manifested by anyone within all entities.
When it is manifested through the phonemes (varṇas), this [sphoṭa] does not serve as a factor for communication;
for it is no different from other [manifested things], and its eternity is established because it exists elsewhere as well.
Therefore, the sequential order of phonemes, as well as their short, long, and protracted durations,
which are divisions of time, are not logically possible if they were merely adventitious properties of the sound-currents.
Therefore, there is no such eternal property belonging to a word;
thus, for those who maintain the non-eternality of phonemes, the non-eternality of the word is established.
Even the duty of another would not constitute a constituent part [of one's own path], like the speed of a horse and so forth,
if manifestation were to be postulated here by means of manifesting conditions.
"Already previously" refers to the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*).
"And it is not manifested by anything" means that it is not revealed by any [means].
Because of non-existence; and even if it were existent, because the manifestation of a permanent entity would be constant;
"because of non-distinction from others" means that there is no distinction from something else.
For instance, that nature of time which is manifested in seeds, sprouts, creepers, and so forth— that same nature of time being manifested in phonemes has no remaining object whatsoever;
because that single [nature] exists elsewhere as well, it is eternal.
"From [the word] *yogāt*... that; therefore. It is not logical."
Because time does not exist; and even if it did exist, its indivisibility is accepted [by you].
Regarding the passage beginning with "even in the case of another's property" (*paradharme 'pi*), he says "even in the case of another's property," and so forth.
The remainder is easily understood.
But if all [words] were eternal, the presumption [of their existence] would be refuted;
for it has been established that the nature of the cognition of meaning belongs to things that are impermanent.
When a phoneme arises from another intention produced by a speaker’s desire to speak something specific, its audition occurs immediately after that [intention].
That cognition, which arises from the preceding phonemes and is heard very rapidly,
subsequently produces a memory within itself by depending upon that [preceding] memory.
With respect to the cognitions that grasp and originate them,
this sequence among the phonemes— whether as the state of being produced or as the state of being a cause— is dependent upon the person.
Therefore, it is perfectly clear that phonemes differ at every step,
due to the distinction in their sequential order, as in the cases of *dama* and *mada*, or *latā* and *tāla*.
In such a manner, these [phonemes] establish the distinction of meaning;
for this very reason, the postulation of the *sphoṭa* here is also useless.
The argument from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has been refuted;
for, by the passage beginning with "from the trembling of the hand, etc.," both the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and the subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) have been described.
Regarding impermanent things...

Even if they were eternal, one would not perceive them as identical; for since they are distinct in every instance, it is logical that the phonemes (*varṇa*)—which are impermanent—are the cause of the difference in cognition in cases such as *sara* and *rasa*.
However, they cannot be eternal, because they would possess a single uniform nature in all instances.
And demonstrating that there is no other individual entity (*vyakti*) distinct from those [atoms] in a gradual sequence, he says: "Whoever intends to express what... and so forth.
This, first of all, is the general meaning of the passage here.

In the continuum of the speaker, for each phoneme, the cognitions that give rise to them—produced by preceding immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) through the desire to speak—come into being; from these, the phonemes arise. These [phonemes], in turn, acting as cooperative causes for the cognitions apprehending each preceding phoneme within the continuum of the listener, directly produce successive cognitions of their own respective objects. Subsequently, they indirectly produce successive recollections of their respective objects.

Furthermore, with respect to the cognitions that arise from them within the continuum of the speaker and which produce them, those [cognitions] possess the status of being produced; or, with respect to the [cognitions] that arise in the continuum of the listener, they possess the status of being causes. This very sequence is their [order], and not anything else.

Moreover, because there is a distinction between cause and effect, and because the phonemes possess distinct intrinsic natures at every step, a difference in cognition is logical in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*; but this is not the case for eternal [phonemes], since they are always and everywhere of a single uniform nature.
Nor is the sequence intended to be something distinct from those [phonemes];
the intention is that even if it were a distinct entity, its connection [to the phonemes] would not be established.
As for the meaning of the individual parts, it is connected as follows: "the phoneme arises."

In the case of "sadā smaya" and so forth, an *a*-sound and so on follows an *s*-sound and so on; [this occurs] because another intention (*vivakṣā*) arises from that which has arisen from the intention for the *s*-sound and so on. That other intention which has arisen from the intention for a particular sound—such as the *s*-sound—is what is meant by the expression "that which has arisen from that intention. This is what is being said: [The text continues: "From that [intention], another intention arises; from that [other intention], the phoneme arises; from that [phoneme], the word arises; from that [word], the sentence arises; and from that [sentence], the meaning arises. In this way, the meaning is established through a sequence of causes and effects. Therefore, it is not the case that the meaning is understood directly from the phonemes themselves. Thus, the meaning is not perceived from the phonemes alone. This is the point. Furthermore, since the phonemes are produced by an intention, they are impermanent. And because they are impermanent, they do not possess the capacity to convey meaning. Consequently, the meaning is not perceived from the phonemes. This is the conclusion. The connection with what is to be stated later is as follows: that subsequent desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), which arises from each preceding desire to speak that brings about each preceding phoneme within the continuum of the speaker, produces a memory for each subsequent phoneme that arises from it.

Thus, having first established that the phonemes existing in the continuum of the speaker are produced by the desires to speak, [the author] now establishes that they are the cause of the cognition existing in the continuum of the hearer; this refers to the word "of that" (*tasya*).
The term "ga" (or "ya," as indicated) is what is connected here.
The connection is that "hearing arises for him.
"Immediately" means without interruption.
Having thus established that [the final phoneme] is the cause of the listener's cognition, he now establishes its status as the cause of memory: "pūrva... etc.

"Pūrva-varṇānām" means of the preceding phonemes; "vit" means cognition. That which has an "anugama"—meaning a continuous experience (*saṃvit-anubhava*)—arising from that [cognition] is described in that way.
"Not with too rapid an audition" means that for one who hears too rapidly, there is no capacity for the arising of memory;
"he" refers to such a person.
Each subsequent phoneme depends upon the memory of each preceding phoneme;

[the compound] "samutthāpakāni ca grāhīṇi" (both producers and perceivers) is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound, meaning that they produce and perceive their respective objects through the assistance of that memory.
Regarding those phonemes (*varṇas*), [the compound] "those which grasp what brings them forth" (*tatsamutthāpakagrāhiṇi*)—this is either a *tatpuruṣa* or a *karmadhāraya* compound.

[The former implies: "being produced in dependence upon those which bring them forth"; [the latter implies: "being a cause in dependence upon the grasper, the existence, the memory, and the cognition of the class [of phonemes]. Thus, having rejected a sequential order as a distinct entity, and wishing to refute the *sphoṭa*—which is postulated by grammarians and others as the expressive essence of sound (*śabdātmāna*) and distinct from the phonemes—he says "for this very reason," and so forth.
For that [sphoṭa] was indeed postulated by the grammarians for the sake of understanding meaning;
yet since the phonemes themselves are capable of that, this postulation of his is purposeless.
Because this [object] is not perceived despite being perceptible, its non-existence is determined;
however, if it were imperceptible, it could not serve as a signifier, just like a logical mark (*liṅga*).
He demonstrates this with the words "of the perceptible," etc., [showing] how some Vaibhāṣika might [assert] that it is eternal.
For no such partless, eternal essence of sound (*śabdātman*), distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), is observed to appear in the auditory consciousness.
Because [the object] would exist as something characterized by perception;
on the contrary, its non-existence would be established.
Now, regarding the second position, there are further alternatives: would the reason (hetu) be a property of existence, a property of non-existence, or a property of both?

In the first alternative, the reason (hetu) would have to be either a property of the subject (dharmin) called *sphoṭa*, or a property of some other subject. In that regard, because that very subject called *sphoṭa* is unestablished (*asiddha*), a property belonging to it cannot,
for the time being, serve as the reason.
Even a property of something else is not a [valid] reason, because it lacks the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*);
for example, as when "having arms" is adduced to prove the impermanence of a jar.
Nor is it a property of non-existence.
Because that [reason] establishes the opposite;
nor is it a property of both,
because it is inconclusive.
The establishment of that [imperceptible object] must occur either through its essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) or through its effect (*kāryahetu*).
First, it is not the former position, because since that object is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), its essential nature is not established;
or, even if it were established, the search for a logical reason would be useless, because its essential nature is already proven.
Furthermore, this is because the effort [of the proponent] is directed toward that very end.
Nor is the second position tenable, because a causal relationship with something beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) cannot be established.

It might be argued: "Just as the occasional nature of auditory and other cognitions establishes their dependence on other causes, and by implication establishes the existence of the sense organs such as the ear, so too here we shall take the cognition of meaning as the subject (*dharmin*). Then, even though the phonemes (*varṇa*) are identical, since there is a difference in the cognition of meaning in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, we shall postulate another cause called *sphoṭa*."
This too is incorrect, because the non-distinctness of the phonemes (*varṇa*) is unestablished.

For it has just been demonstrated that the phonemes themselves, being distinct in every instance due to the difference between cause and effect, are capable of bringing about the cognition of meaning; thus, there is no postulation of a [separate] entity.
The intention is that such faults must be stated regarding its being an object of inference.

Now, it might be argued: "It is not an object of inference; what then? It is absolutely invisible. To this he says: "But if it were invisible, this [inference] would simply not exist. Just as a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is unknown does not become a means of cognition, so too would this [inference] be, because of its own lack of being known.
If it is argued that the cognition of that [object] occurs by its mere existence because it is established as the cause,
and that it is intended to be a cognizer [of the object], then it would have to be present at all times, like the eye.
Even when the convention [linking words to meanings] is not understood, and even when the phonemes have not been heard,
there arises cognition regarding the objects to be expressed by them, due to the presence of the efficient cause.
For this [universal] is eternally existent and has no dependence whatsoever;
nor is it manifested by sounds, conventions, or phonemes, because such manifestation is never observed.
For they say that manifestation is knowledge; yet that knowledge does not exist [in the object]. Therefore, the postulation of this manifestor is entirely purposeless.
Now, if it were the cause for the cognition of an object even when unknown— merely by its existence, like the sense organs such as the eye—
then the cognition arising from it would occur at all times;
likewise, the cognition arising from it would exist even without the grasping of linguistic conventions and so forth.
This very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "saṅketa" (convention).
Regarding this, he states the justification with "tathāhi" (for instance).

Now, it might be argued: "It is accepted that this [word] is the cause for the cognition of an object only when manifested through convention, not by its mere existence; therefore, the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not occur. To this, he replies with "dhvanisaṅketavarṇaiḥ" (by sounds, conventions, and phonemes), and so forth.
"Because of non-perception" means because of non-apprehension,
and also because it is intended to be imperceptible.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "For this knowledge... and so forth.
It might be argued that the claim "that which appears is not perceived" is unestablished;

for indeed, in a cognition where the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by each preceding phoneme have reached full maturity through repeated cultivation, the word appears as a partless whole. To this he says, "by the sound," and so forth:
"In [a cognition] in which the seeds have been sown by the sound, together with the final articulation..."
When the intellect has reached full maturation through repeated practice, the word appears [within it].
This too has been postulated by him here as being without a cause;
for even in that [conceptualization], no other word is perceived as appearing.
That cognition in which the maturation of all the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the intellect has arisen and returned [to consciousness] is described as such.

"Without signs" (*nirnimitta*) means that it is the phonemes themselves that are subsequently determined by a recollective synthetic cognition (*saṅkalanā-pratyaya*) according to how they were experienced; this is the intended meaning.
For indeed, neither do we perceive any other partless essence of sound (*śabdātman*) subsequent to the apprehension of the final phoneme, nor does the speaker himself discern such a thing.
If it were only thus—"it would be good for me if this were so"—then, deluded by the desire for what is auspicious, one dreams that the word reaches its completion at the ultimate stage of cognition.
Thus, first, the refutation regarding the position of permanence has been shown to be untenable.
Now, he states a common refutation for both the positions of permanence and impermanence with respect to the partless [word], beginning with "janyatām" and so forth:
"Whether it be produced or manifested by sounds occurring in succession..."
Even for those who maintain that the sphoṭa exists, their position regarding sequence is contradicted.
For it is not logical that the individual and the universal should occur sequentially in that which is partless;
because there is no existence outside of their single form, they would indeed exist entirely at once.
For some Vaibhāṣikas, by means of expressing the function of words, have understood the sentence-sphoṭa to be produced because it is impermanent;
"niraṃśaka" means in a reality that is partless.

"Because it does not exist outside of a single form": because the form intended as the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), whether manifest or unmanifest, does not exist apart from one known or manifested form; therefore, both that universal and that individual would belong to everything.
And consequently, the employment of the remaining phonemes and so forth would be rendered useless.
He states the refutation even regarding the position that [the sphoṭa] has parts: "Even if it has parts... etc.
Even if it has parts, just as phonemes (varṇas) are conveyors [of meaning] through a sequence, why should the parts of the sphoṭa not be likewise? Why have unseen [entities] been postulated?
For those parts of the sphoṭa must either be individually meaningless or meaningful.
In the first case, because they arise sequentially, it follows that they would fail to convey meaning— just like individual phonemes—
or else their status as signifiers would be merely conceptual, since they lack that nature [of being signifiers] while being treated as having it.

For it is said that a sentence is a single meaningful entity; its constituent parts are not themselves meaningless, yet that [unitary] essence would have to be superimposed upon them through conceptual construction, like the quality of "lion-ness" attributed to a young boy.

And if a denotative capacity must be assumed through such construction, it is better that the very portions of the phonemes (varṇabhāga) be the denoters; why then are imperceptible portions of a *sphoṭa* postulated?

If, on the other hand, they possess meaning, then the postulation of multiple [meanings] is pointless; for a sentence is defined as a form of speech whose meaning is complete. If each individual part were to possess meaning, then there would be as many sentences as there are parts, and thus a single entity consisting of multiple parts would not be established.
Furthermore, it would follow that the meaning of the sentence would be understood upon the comprehension of just a single part.
As it has been said:
Even if each [word] were individually meaningful, there would be the false assumption of multiplicity;
moreover, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning could occur through the cognition of a single constituent part.
Thus [it is said] in *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.249.

Regarding what was stated— that "the universal (jāti) and the individual (vyakti) cannot logically be manifested sequentially because they are partless"— the author here anticipates the opponent’s rebuttal with the verse beginning "In the universal," and so forth:
"If the universal and the individual have been manifested simultaneously by a single sound,
then other phonemes are employed solely for the purpose of further manifesting the individual."
Since its nature is difficult to determine,
it has been made such that it is manifested again by other phonemes belonging to the same class of articulation.

Even if the universal (*jāti*) or the individual (*vyakti*) of the *sphoṭa* is produced in its entirety by a single sound (*dhvani*), nevertheless, the employment of subsequent sounds is not useless, because their purpose is to bring about clear manifestation (*spaṣṭavyakti*). For just as a verse, when repeated again and again, becomes clearly manifest, yet it does not become so from a single utterance; nor is any further distinction added to it by repeated repetition, and yet that repetition is not useless—so too here, the subsequent sounds will not be useless. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "since" (*yataḥ*).
"Difficult to determine" means it is impossible to ascertain.
He replies with the words "of that very [entity]" and so forth:
Why does manifestation not recur again and again for that very same entity or for another single one? For, in this way, there would be no distinction between them.

The word "nanu" is used as an interrogative particle. Why is the manifestation of that very first articulated phoneme, or of some other single phoneme contained within it, not produced through repeated repetition?
For once a manifestation has been brought about by that [repetition], it cannot be said that it has not been brought about.

For indeed, the utterances of each successive phoneme have as their sole fruit the exclusion of that [particular] individual [of the word], since all phonemes possess an identical capacity. And since that exclusion can be accomplished by a single phoneme repeated again and again, the utterance of the remaining phonemes would be useless.
Nor should it be accepted that the successive phonemes possess distinct capacities;
for it is impossible to impart any further distinction to that which is partless, and if no further distinction can be produced, it follows that the postulation of distinct capacities is redundant.
And while all this might be possible if manifestation were real, that very manifestation is not possible; showing this, he says "viṣayendriya... and so forth:

"And manifestation, consisting of the refinement of the object and the sense-faculty, like [the manifestation of] phonemes, must also be denied in the case of the mind in which that [manifestation] appears."

"Like color" means that just as the manifestation of colors— whether in the form of the refinement of the object or the sense organ— is refuted by the alternative analysis of their intrinsic natures as being either capable or incapable of generating cognition, so too should it be refuted here;
this is the meaning of "even in the case of its appearance."
Even in the absence of the *sphoṭa*, this is a statement made on the basis of a hypothetical admission (*abhyupagamavāda*).

What is meant is this: if indeed another essence of sound called *sphoṭa* were to appear as distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), then its manifestation would be possible, since manifestation consists in being perceived.

However, it has already been explained that it does not so appear; even granting that it might appear, manifestation is nonetheless untenable in either case for something whose nature is inherently both perceptible and imperceptible.
Having concluded with the words "Therefore," etc., he demonstrates the sequence of the logical justification for the comprehension of meaning even without a *sphoṭa*:
"Therefore, that cognition of the entire word which occurs first through perception within the cognitions of the successive [phonemes] is the cause of the cognition of the meaning."

[Page 725] But surely, since phonemes (varṇas) occur sequentially and are experienced only in sequence, and recollection follows the manner of experience, how can a single recollective cognition—which manifests all the phonemes together—be possible without the *sphoṭa*? Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a manifestation of sequential phonemes when the cognition itself is non-sequential. Anticipating this objection, he says: "When the final phoneme is cognized," and so forth: "When the final phoneme is cognized, a recollection produced by all the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) arises simultaneously with respect to all the phonemes."

By this very [argument], he does not say that first there is experience, and then, immediately following that, the memories arise in sequence according to the experience; rather, after those memories, at a later time, another memory-based collective cognition (*samuccayajñāna*) arises simultaneously, which determines all the phonemes as a whole, because it determines the objects exactly as they were perceived.
And he shows that this is well-established for all proponents [of philosophical systems], and not merely imagined by me himself, with the words "and in all":
"And in all these cases, for all proponents,
a mental cognition of a synthesis is accepted, even though the objects exist as cognized in succession."
"This" refers to the knowledge of synthesis.
And he shows that this must necessarily be accepted because it is endowed with reasoning, by means of the passage beginning with "naced" (if not):
"If that were not accepted, then indeed, among things perceived sequentially,
the appearance of a collection in the form of 'a hundred' and so forth would never arise."

For if every recollection were to arise exactly according to the sequence of experience, then there would be no simultaneous conceptualization of a hundred and so forth among things experienced sequentially;
nor would there be any distinction among conceptualizations of a hundred, ten million, and so on, at the time of their arising.
He concludes with the word "therefore":
"Therefore, although there may be a successive cognition of the phonemes by means of the ear and the mind respectively,
subsequently, however, there occurs a simultaneous recollection."

If this were so, then the cognition of the aggregate alone would be the cause of the comprehension of the meaning, and not those phonemes (*varṇa*), because they have long since ceased; yet this is not tenable, since it is well known even among children that the comprehension of meaning occurs immediately after the word. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Mounted upon that," and so forth. "Because they are mounted upon that [cognition], those phonemes are not distant from the awakening of the meaning;
therefore, the worldly people say that the cognition arises from the word."
"Mounted upon that synthetic knowledge" means those who have ascended to it.
Regarding the term "by worldly people," this is an instance of the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) with the sense of "one's own."

One might object: "Even so, since those [past objects] have long since ceased to exist, they are absolutely non-existent; how then could there be an ascent (or apprehension) of them? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In a cognition possessing form (*ākāravat*), all of this is logical;
otherwise, how could those things that have perished appear in memory?"
He asks why it is not tenable in the case of the formless [cognition] and says, "Otherwise, indeed," and so forth.

Consequently, that collective cognition which was described by Kumārila against the proponent of *sphoṭa*—beginning with the words "for when the final phoneme is known"—is tenable only according to our own view, and not according to the view of you Mīmāṃsakas who maintain the formless [theory]; this is what is being stated.

Now, it might be argued that this is indeed consistent even for the Mīmāṃsakas, for according to their view, the phonemes (*varṇa*) have not perished such that they would fail to appear; rather, they simply exist with their manifestation concealed. Anticipating this objection with the words "Now [if] the phonemes... and so forth, he refutes it with the words "No," and so forth: "Now, if the phonemes were known previously as having their manifestation concealed..."
They are remembered as being precisely as they were when present, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence [of their appearing] with clear manifestation.

For if those very phonemes, having been previously experienced and subsequently having their manifestation obscured, were to be grasped by a cognition of synthesis, then that cognition of their synthesis would necessarily appear clearly, just like the cognition of one's own self-experience;
this is because the form resides in the external object and that form is unitary.
Furthermore, if their manifestations were obscured, how could they appear? For manifestation is, by its very nature, perception.

Furthermore, if the persistence of the past were possible, then this [objection] might hold; however, since there is no such persistence of the past, its manifestation is not tenable—this is what he shows with the words "apāstā" and so forth: "And persistence has already been refuted previously; therefore, if there were such persistence, recollection would occur at the very same time as the cognition of the experience of the phonemes, because they would share a single cause."
Regarding the word "previously":
this refers to the *Traikālyaparīkṣā*.
In this very context, he states the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) beginning with the words "in its persistence," and so forth.
The undesirable consequence that recollection would arise at the very time of the cognition experiencing the color is the subverting proof.
"From a single cause" means because of having an identical cause.

On this point, the grammarians raise an objection: "If there is no single essence of speech called *sphoṭa*, then how does the cognition of the word 'cow' (*go*) arise with a single form? To this, he says: "The fact that there is a single cognition of the word 'cow,' etc. [p.727] We certainly do not deny that there is a single cognition of the word "cow."
And due to the identity of the object grasped by those [two cognitions], there arises the notion of oneness regarding the word.
"One-minded" (*ekamati*) means having a single intention; its state is "oneness of mind" (*ekatva*).

And [it is so called] "by virtue of being grasped by that and having a single purpose. By "that" is meant the single cognition (*buddhi*); "grasped by that" (*tadgrāhya*) refers to what is apprehended by it. That which has a single purpose (*eka-artha*)—meaning a single aim—is described as such. Then, *tadgrāhya* and *ekārtha* form a copulative compound (*dvandva*); the states of these two are "being grasped by that" and "having a single purpose," and [the phrase ends] with "by those two."
This is what is meant: because it is apprehended by a single cognition and because it illuminates a single object possessing a dewlap and so forth, the word "cow" is said to be one.
And he shows that this unity of cognition is not pure in all cases with the words "due to rapidity," and so forth:
"Due to rapidity and because the difference is slight, that [unity] might occur even in the case of the word 'cow';
however, in words such as 'Devadatta,' a clear distinction is perceived."
"From swiftness" means from rapid pronunciation;
"having little interval" means having very slight separation; "that" refers to the aforementioned [state].
There is a single cognition [of the word].

However, in the case of words such as "Devadatta," since the sounds (*dhvanayaḥ*) are perceived with very clear distinctness through the capacity of each individual phoneme, the claim of a single cognition is unestablished with respect to one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*).

He establishes [the point] with the verse beginning "arising from the phonemes" (varṇotthā): "This cognition of the object arises from the phonemes, because it occurs immediately after the knowledge of them;
for whatever is such [a cognition], it indeed arises from that, just as the cognition of fire arises from smoke and so forth."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition arises immediately after a certain specific cognition is produced from that [preceding cognition] through a continuous succession, just as the cognition of the possessor of a mark (such as fire) arises from the cognition of the mark (such as smoke).
And the cognition of an object occurs immediately after the cognition of a phoneme; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Furthermore, what is being proven here is the conventional status of being an effect (*kāryatā-vyavahāra*).
Therefore, there is a distinction between the probandum and the probans.
Warding off the objection that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says:
"There exists no cognition of meaning that occurs immediately after a cognition of a word distinct from the phonemes; therefore, there is no other word that is expressive."

The cognition that has as its appearance the nature of sound (śabdātman) distinct from the phonemes does not exist immediately following that [cognition]; rather, it exists immediately after the cognition of the phonemes. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

By this, it is also shown that there is the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) due to the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).

Showing that it is also not inconclusive, he says "kāryatā" and so forth: "For in all cases, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), which are the basis for the linguistic usage of 'being an effect,' are ascertained; by that, pervasion (vyāpti) is indeed determined."

The cause is the basis for the conventional usage of "being an effect. What is that? It is positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The relationship is one of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

That which conforms solely to the positive and negative concomitance of that [cause] is the only basis for the conventional usage of "being an effect," and nothing else. Therefore, the impossibility of any other basis for the conventional usage of "being an effect" serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*); thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.

It might be argued: "Let it be that the *sphoṭa* is not the expressive agent; rather, the phonemes themselves, being eternal, will be the expressive agents, and their eternity is established through means of valid cognition such as perception. To this, he says: "In the case of the impermanent," and so forth: "When the expressiveness of the phonemes alone has been established as impermanent, and when both recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and inference (*anumāna*)—the proofs for [their] eternity—have been refuted..."
"Recognition and inference" (pratyabhijñānumāne) refers to recognition and inference.

In some places, the reading is "recognition-inference" (pratyabhijñānānumānam); in that case, it should be understood as either a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) or a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*) resulting from the elision of the word *sahita*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "and contradiction with one's own statements," he says: "Of contradictions with one's own statements, etc. The objection was raised due to ignorance of the contradictions with one's own statements and so forth; for all of those [contradictions] exist for you in the opposing position.
It has been established that, being eternal, speech cannot be the illuminator [of meaning],
because it lacks sequential order and the like, and because it is not perceived as eternal.
"All those" refers to contradictions with one's own statements and so forth. "Succession and so forth" refers to [the following].
By the word "etcetera," the Śruti and Smṛti are understood in their respective order.

For instance, because [the Veda] is eternal, there is no sequence produced by time; nor is there one produced by space, because it is all-pervading; nor is there one produced by manifestation, because manifestation has already been refuted.
Likewise, it has been demonstrated in many ways that even in the production of knowledge, there is no utility for things that are eternal.
Regarding what was stated—that which is to be said, such as "which word is the one-syllabled [monosyllabic]?
and so forth—it is replied there with the words "by means of the conceptual differentiation of the distinctness of the substratum" (*dharmibhedavikalpena*), and so on.
By means of the conceptual differentiation of the distinctness of the substratum (*dharmin*), the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is asserted.
Because, due to the knowledge of the characteristics of inference, that which appears possesses the status of being the subject (dharmin).
Whatever object, established through non-investigation, appears in cognition— of that much alone,
even for [the Mīmāṃsakas] such as Śaṅkara, there is the status of being the subject (dharmin).
For it is precisely regarding that [object] that this dispute among proponents has arisen;
however, there is no dispute for anyone concerning a distinction fabricated by mere whim.

That very subject (*dharmin*) which is established by virtue of appearing to both the proponent and the opponent is the basis for dispute regarding its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*); it is not one imagined according to one's own whim, because there is no dispute regarding such a thing. For when one imagines a specific quality in a subject fabricated by one's own whim, nothing can be prevented. "Appearing" (*bhāsita*) means that which is currently manifesting.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "an object established without investigation," and so forth;
it is easy to understand.

Showing that when a subject (dharmin) has been indicated without qualification, any conceptualization of it in terms of a specific distinction is a "futile rejoinder" (jātyuttara), he says "Therefore," and so forth:
"Therefore, when [the subject] is indicated without qualification, there is conceptualization in terms of a specific [distinction]."
It obstructs the operation of every inference whatsoever.
The cognition produced by an injunction is a valid means of knowledge because it is generated by causes free from defects; such arguments as these are also subject to analysis.
If the thesis is "the cognition produced by an injunction connected with an eternally existing object," then for an opponent,
the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi) follows.

And this [cognition] is itself eternal, being described as such because it is eternally connected with its object characterized by form; if the cognition produced by that [eternal form] is the subject (pakṣa), then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the opponent.
Regarding what was stated: "impermanence is [the state of] perishability," and so forth.
Regarding this, he says "the state of being thus" (tādavasthya), and so forth.
Being thus is permanence; its opposite is impermanence.
For if the state of being thus does not cease, what else could be admitted as persisting?
What is intended by "abiding"?
Since the state is not distinct from that which abides, when that [state] ceases, it follows by implication that the latter also ceases.
Otherwise, how could it be logical for something that does not share the same acquisition and preservation (*ekayogakṣema*) to be of the same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as it? This is the sense.

Regarding what was stated in TS 2743, beginning with "And if [the reason] were based solely on the senses," etc., he says there: "And if the reason is conceived here as being based solely on the senses," etc.
And if the reason is conceived here as being based solely on the senses...
Since the universal has already been sublated, no deviation is perceived.
"Previously" refers to the examination of the universal (*sāmānyaparīkṣā*). Regarding TS 2744:

even if there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to [the category of] genus (*jāti*), one might still suspect that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful. Anticipating this, [the author] says "svanirbhāsī" and so forth, demonstrating the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the reason, namely its being perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*).
That which is the cause of sensory cognition manifesting its own appearance would be sensory;
however, it has been established that causality does not exist in what is eternal.

An object that is the cause of sensory cognition appearing as its own likeness is called "sensory" (*aindriyaka*); and since it is established that for an eternal entity, purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is impossible through either succession or simultaneity, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is proven.
Regarding TS 2745,
"And [the reason] in 'because of being perceptible,' etc.," he says "of all," and so forth:
"And for all [of these], this status as a reason for such a meaning is well-established."
Otherwise, this same conceptual construction would apply equally everywhere, even in the case of smoke and so forth.
And it is described as "such" because its object is of this nature; "of this nature" means that which is charming only so long as it is not investigated.

Otherwise, even in the case of smoke and the like, one could raise the following doubt: "Is the smoke taken as a logical mark (liṅga) something perceived by the senses, or is it a transformation of consciousness, primordial matter (prakṛti), time, and so forth? Or is it a composite whole (avayavin) produced from atoms, or not produced at all? If such doubts were raised, there would be defects such as the failure of one or both parties to establish their position.
Regarding the argument that "cognition immediately following effort" is the proof for being produced and impermanent, he says "prayatna... and so forth:

"Furthermore, for us, the capacity to initiate an effect that is cognition immediately following effort is not established for things such as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*), which are conventional (*sāṃvrta*)."

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: the fact that cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and so forth possesses the capacity to initiate an effect that arises from knowledge subsequent to effort is not established.

For if a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is alleged on the basis of cessation through deliberation and so forth according to the Sautrāntika system, then such a deviation is not established for you, because according to their view, cessation through deliberation and the like possess only conventional existence (*saṃvṛti-sat*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is conventional (saṃvṛta) to be the initiator of any effect, because that would entail the loss of its defining characteristic.

For indeed, that alone which performs purposeful action (arthakriyākārin) is the ultimately real (paramārtha), while anything other than that is conventionally real (saṃvṛtisat); such is the definition of the ultimately real and the conventionally real.

Alternatively, there is a deviation according to the Vaibhāṣika view; for even there, the kind of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and so forth that you have described as having the nature of destruction is not accepted by the Vaibhāṣikas. This he demonstrates with the words "And not," and so on:
"And the two cessations are not admitted to have the nature of destruction, because [they are] untainted (*anāsrava*);
that which is cessation through deliberation is a disjunction (*visaṃyoga*) that is distinct for each [object]."
The other cessation, which is the absolute obstruction of arising, occurs through non-analytical means;
therefore, those who do not understand the established tenets float about as mere conceited deluders.

Regarding the phrase "from cessation" (*nirodhāt*): this refers to both analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*). To explain what kind of things these are intended to be, he says: "because [they arise] from those with outflows" (*sāśravair yataḥ*).

The distinction made regarding entities associated with afflictions is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) because it is attained by means of analytical wisdom (*pratisaṅkhyā-prajñā*). Furthermore, this cessation is distinct from the substance that constitutes the fetter; for this very reason, it is said to be "separate, separate.
This is because of the established tenet that there are as many substances of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-dravya*) as there are substances of conjunction (*saṃyoga-dravya*).

On the other hand, "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) refers to that dharma which is distinct from dissociation and which acts as an absolute obstacle to the arising of future dharmas.

And that [cessation] is not obtained through analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyā*); rather, it is due to the deficiency of conditions (*pratyayavaikalya*). Therefore, it is called "cessation not through analytical discernment" (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
As it has been said:
"Cessation through deliberation is disjunction, which is distinct for each [defilement];
cessation not through deliberation is another, which is the absolute prevention of arising."
[Thus:

"Let it be granted that [the two] lack intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*); nevertheless, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*)," showing this, he says: "Not from the absence of intrinsic nature," and so forth. "And the two [states of] self-destruction are not preceded by effort (*prayatnānantarīyaka*)."
The mass of light from skulls and so forth is likewise based on ignorance.
"Those which follow immediately after effort"— the connection is "no," because they lack intrinsic nature (asvabhāva).

For destruction is merely the negation of the existence of a thing, and space is merely the absence of the tangible; therefore, both of these, being their own destructions, are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). How, then, could there be for these two the property of following immediately upon an effort? This is because only that which possesses intrinsic nature is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). [The opponent asks: "In that case, what is the basis for the cognition of destruction and so forth? To this he says: "the shards," and so on. "A mass of light" means a collection of light.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the mass of darkness (tamas) is included.
Regarding what was stated— that even though there is no distinction, an entity is neither impermanent nor permanent, and so forth—
it is replied with the words "of one," and so on:
for a single nature of an object, duality is excluded.
Therefore, an eternal part denoted by the term "universal" is not tenable here in the case of a jar.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Impermanence is thus to be conceptualized," he says "remaining in that state" and so forth.
What is intended by impermanence is merely the negation of remaining in that same state;
in this regard, lamps and the like are clear examples as the probandum.

Impermanence is intended as the probandum merely as the negation of remaining in that same state; in that case as well, the example of a lamp exists as something possessing the property to be proven, so how can there be a deficiency of the probandum in the instance?
With the words "of the flame, etc.," he raises the objection—according to the view of others—that even the example of the lamp and so forth lacks the property to be proven (sādhyahīnatā).
