[The opponent argues: "The perishability of the flame and such is not unestablished at every moment;
rather, the light particles there move quickly to another location."
For in the region of the wick, light exists in a condensed state; as long as it moves forward [or upward], it is understood as "flame."
Even beyond that, whatever departs and moves away would be of the nature of light;
yet, because of its extreme subtlety, it is not perceived thereafter.
For in that case, the parts of the flame and so forth move very rapidly to another location, rather than being subject to disintegration at every moment.
Now, as to why they do not all spread out simultaneously, he says: "By the subsequent parts," and so forth.
When the path is obstructed by the subsequent parts, the preceding ones do not proceed;
and just as the subsequent ones release [the way], so too do the preceding ones move forward.
Now, if they possess the property of spreading, why do they not burn the grass, cotton, and so forth situated near them? To this he says:
"Even upon reaching," and so on.
Even upon reaching, the occurrence of these [fires] in grass and such is not possible.
This is merely a conceptual construction, because no means of valid cognition has been stated.
The meaning is that they possess their observed functions only in the state of aggregation, and not in the state of being dispersed.
He refutes this with the words "tadetad" and so forth.
Even if this conceptualization were accepted, the example would not be deficient in respect to the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*).
For it has been stated that what is intended as the probandum—impermanence—is merely the negation of a state of being otherwise (*tādavasthya*).
And since that state of being otherwise does not exist at all in the case of a lamp and so forth, how could there be a deficiency in the probandum?
Nevertheless, even while conceding this fault, he says "Furthermore," and so forth: "Moreover,
when [fire] comes into contact with grass, cotton, and the like whose powers are unimpeded,
this consequence of its burning activity does not cease, as before."
"Of those whose power is unimpeded" refers to the constituent parts such as flames; "as before" means because there is no difference from their state when they were combined.
Now, [the author] shows that if a distinction is admitted, then the consequence of the loss of its permanence is unavoidable, by saying "otherwise" and so forth: "Otherwise,
what kind of permanent nature would it have for you in those cases,
when a distinction between the capacities and incapacities of its own nature is established?"
This is easy to understand.

Regarding what was stated— "The eternity of the sentence must be asserted on the grounds that no connection [between word and meaning] is created"— he replies with the words beginning "And of the connection," etc.:
Since the eternity of the connection has already been refuted previously,
the eternity of the sentence is not tenable on the grounds that no connection is created.
Thinking that, according to your view, a sentence itself is not even possible—that of which you seek to establish permanence—the author, examining the sentence, says "of which," and so forth:
"And of which sentence is permanence accepted? Is it of the sequence of phonemes consisting of mere phonemes, or of something distinct from them?"
Is it that sometimes the sentence would be merely the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves without distinction;

or rather, that the sentence consists of the phonemes themselves as distinguished by their sequential occurrence; or else, that the sentence is something distinct from the phonemes called *sphoṭa*? Thus there are three positions.
Regarding that, he states the fault in the first position with the words "of phonemes," and so forth:
"Phonemes devoid of sequence possess no denotative power;
therefore, such [phonemes] do not constitute a sentence, nor does sequence exist among them."
Because these [phonemes] are all-pervasive and eternal, no sequence of space or time is possible for them,
whether like that of written letters or like the distinction between fruits, flowers, and so forth.
If these [letters] were to exist according to their own inherent sequence, the form *sara* would indeed be possible;
however, forms such as *rasa* could not occur, because that would contradict the established order.
The letter *ra* and others likewise remain established; they do not arise from air in a sequence different from their own. This is the proof for their eternity and unity.
Otherwise, recognition— which you yourself have stated to be a proof for permanence and unity— would be fallacious, because it occurs even when there is difference.
Regarding the second position as well, he says: "Even a sequence (*krama*) of these does not exist.

For indeed, there are only two kinds of sequence for entities: either one produced by space (*deśakṛta*), such as that of ants, written characters, or syllables; or one produced by time (*kālakṛta*), such as that of seeds, sprouts, stalks, flowers, fruits, and so forth. First of all, a spatial sequence is not possible for phonemes (*varṇa*). Why? Because of their pervasiveness (*vyāpti*); since phonemes are omnipresent (*sarvagata*), it is not logical for a sequence produced by spatial separation to belong to something that, like space, exists by occupying all locations. This is because all [phonemes] reside in the same location within space.
Nor is it produced by time, because all things, being eternal, would exist simultaneously.
Furthermore, the sequence must be either created by a person or inherent;
first of all, it is not accepted as created by a person, because that would entail the Veda having a human origin.

If, on the other hand, [the word] were inherent by nature (*svābhāvika*), then it would always be "sara" and never "rasa. Nor can it be accepted that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are distinct in every instance, because the permanence of phonemes is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Furthermore, it is precisely the negation of that [distinction between phonemes] which is intended to be proven; otherwise, recognition would be inconstant (*vyabhicārin*).
Now, it might be argued that the sequence of manifestation will then constitute the sentence; to this he says "And not," and so forth:
"And the sequence of manifestation is not the sentence, because manifestation is denied in the case of what is eternal.
Since the status of being a sentence is thus untenable, eternality is not possible."
By the word "ca" (and), it indicates that the sentence called *sphoṭa* is not distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*);
the implication is that this [view] has already been refuted by the Mīmāṃsakas themselves.
This is because the manifestation [of such a thing] is denied in the case of what is eternal.
The meaning is that the manifestation of an eternal entity has been refuted.
Regarding what was stated, namely "because it is a linguistic convention concerning perceptible objects" and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "Just as words such as *vṛddhi*":
"Just as words such as *vṛddhi* have meanings fashioned by mere intention,
so too can words such as *svarga* and *yāga* be conceived in that very same way."
In works such as dramas, narratives, and tales, where the subject matter is produced by the author's imagination,
no eternal, real connection between word and meaning is intended to exist.
Those for whom the meaning is constructed according to one's own will are so described.

Those dramas, narratives (*ākhyāyikā*), and the like, whose very form or nature consists of stories such as that of Mahāśvetā—which are produced by a person themselves as something entirely new—are so described.

And since no eternal relationship between word and meaning—characterized as *śakti* (expressive power)—is intended to exist in those [works], the point is that the same might be suspected to be the case with the Veda as well.
With the words "tatrāpi" and so forth, he raises an objection regarding the lack of establishment of the example according to the opponent's view:
"In that case as well, the potency is eternal while the injunction is non-eternal;
it is solely due to that [injunction] that an error arises with respect to the eternal potency."

Even in those cases such as invented stories (*utpādyakathā*), a permanent capacity (*nityā śakti*) is indeed admitted; however, the application (*niyoga*) made by persons toward an object that is non-existent is impermanent, and it is due to that very [application] that a cognitive error (*pratītivibhrama*) arises regarding the permanent capacity. Therefore, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).
He responds with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely): "But surely, since there is no individual entity (*vyakti*) there in the external world, for what object is [the word] postulated?
If it is said to be in the reflection of conceptual construction (*vikalpapratibimba*), then the same doubt may be raised regarding the Veda as well."
"External" means Mahāśvetā and so forth.

Regarding what was stated, "By whom indeed has the supersensuous connection between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth been seen? and so on, he replies with the verse beginning "atīndriyārthasambandhām":
"Who indeed can comprehend a power whose connection to its object is supersensuous?
Therefore, even the injunction (*niyoga*) in the Veda is not conceived as being dependent upon human beings."
Nor is there understanding of it from the elders, for they too remain ignorant by their own nature; however, comprehension may be expected from an explanation that relies upon human agency.
By this, you yourself have demonstrated through implication the following: namely, that whatever cognition of the meaning of the Veda arises, it arises solely from human-based exegesis.

For, by its very nature, the power [of the word] regarding supersensible objects is inherently inaccessible to the senses; consequently, no human-determined application (*niyoga*) of the word is possible with respect to that supersensible power, nor is the comprehension of it possible from elders, because all of them are equally ignorant—just as the perception of a specific color from the words of the blind is impossible.
Therefore, by implication, this comprehension of meaning rests solely upon the interpretation of a person, as there is no other possible recourse.

With the words "nanu" and so forth, the opponent raises an objection: "Is this inquiry not equally applicable to a scripture that is of human origin? For one acts toward that [scripture] either out of faith or even because of doubt regarding its meaning."
But surely this same objection applies equally to human-authored scriptures as well;

for instance, do people of the present day understand the meaning of the words of the Buddha and others—who were teachers beyond their perception—according to the intended sense, or rather the opposite?
He provides the following response, beginning with the words "Not so" (*na tatra*).
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):

it refers to that reality consisting of what is to be abandoned and so forth, along with its means, which is beneficial for human goals—whether it be a product of human effort (*pauruṣeya*) or unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*).
For in that regard, the wise followers of the Sugata proceed by adhering strictly to logic (*nyāya*) alone, and not by mere report (*pravāda*).
"By faith" means by conviction born from rational reflection; that is to say, by certainty.
This is because conviction is only appropriate regarding an object established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Not otherwise,
because doubt has not been transcended therein;
or else, because of doubt regarding the object.
In the case of an object that is absolutely beyond the senses, such as heaven, deities, or the *apūrva*, this is not so;

for in the case of a human-authored statement, since the person expresses his own intention, an unerring tradition is possible, and an uninterrupted tradition can be rightly expected through a succession of listeners.
But it is not so in the case of a non-human (authorless) [scripture], because there is no instructor therein.

Furthermore, when an instructor acts or speaks for the purpose of communicating with the world through the medium of activity, he does so by following the very conventions of the world; therefore, the establishment of that meaning could also be possible through worldly consensus.
However, this is not the case for non-human (apauruṣeya) [texts], because there is an absence of any intentional effort on the part of anyone therein.
If this is so, why do you not proceed by means of just any scripture, since doubt is equal in all cases? To refute this objection, he says "by perception," and so forth:
"When the object has been purified by perception and inference..."
For it is not so with a Vedic word, since that [Vedic word] is itself the means of cognition.

Where the existence of the intended object is not contradicted by perception and inference, one who proceeds on that basis may be considered successful even if doubt remains; however, this is not the case where there is a contrary state of affairs, because in such instances a doubt regarding an undesirable outcome arises due to its being obstructed by observed means of valid cognition.

To the objection that "if this is so, then activity toward the Veda will also occur by this very same principle," he replies with "For it is not thus," and so forth. [He explains: "one's own conviction," etc.
The meaning is that it is authoritative by its very nature.

Therefore, it is not proper to engage with it after examining it through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that would entail the consequence of its authority being extrinsic (*parataḥ*). Furthermore, the purification of its object is also not possible.

For instance, the person (*puruṣa*) is taught in the Veda as one whose prior and subsequent forms have neither fallen away nor arisen, and who is sequentially both the agent of actions and the enjoyer of their fruits;
yet it has been demonstrated in the *Ātmaparīkṣā* that this is untenable.
Likewise, the permanence of certain entities is also taught [in the Veda].
That too has been demonstrated as untenable in the *Sthirabhāvaparīkṣā*.

Likewise, universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, though not perceptible, are asserted to be perceptible; similarly, the sequential arising, abiding, and cessation of entities, though impossible, have been specified.

Likewise, the productivity of that which cannot receive any new qualification and was previously a non-agent, by depending on another, has been taught; likewise, the maintenance of an already accomplished entity as its effect, by depending on another, has also been propounded.

Likewise, many such [claims] as "destruction occurs without a cause" are found to be contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). How, then, could an intelligent person act on the basis of such a scripture?

Furthermore, he demonstrates that the other proof stated by Kumārila for establishing the eternity of the relationship is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of its similarity to dramas and the like, which consist of narratives whose content is produced; this is shown in the verse beginning with "utpādya" and so forth:
"Without considering the property of a narrative whose subject matter is produced, [the relationship] is equal in regard to the Veda."
Thus, this which has been described here by others is incoherent.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is called "utpādyārthā" because it is a narrative (kathā) whose subject matter (artha) is to be created (utpādya);
and its property (dharma) is that its subject matter is fashioned according to the author's will (icchāviracitārthatva).
To the question "What has been described there?", he says: "The beginninglessness of words and their objects," and so forth.

Apart from the beginninglessness of words and their objects, there could be no other cause for the beginninglessness of the relationship [between them]. Therefore, in the Veda, no such thing as a [newly established] relationship exists.
The inference that no connection was established due to the absence of skillful means,
as well as the inference that there was no teaching, must be contradicted by what is actually observed.

Sound has the nature of phonemes (*varṇa*), and its object is the universal (*sāmānya*); because these two are beginningless, their relationship—characterized as a power (*śakti*)—is likewise beginningless, since power is not distinct from the entity itself; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the non-creation of the relationship is inferred due to the absence of any means for creating it. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever lacks the means for producing something does not produce it, just as a potter, even when possessing the entire collection of causes such as a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, water, and thread, does not produce a jar [if he lacks the specific means]; and all persons lack the means for creating the relationship. This is an inference based on the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has been demonstrated—by the passage beginning with "To whom could the speaker resort in order to establish a connection for the listener?"—that all persons lack the means [to do so].

Anticipating the objection that "if this is so, it follows by inference that there is an absence of the communication of the connection, just as there is an absence of its cause," he says: "But as for the inference from non-communication," and so forth.
In the case of an inference based on non-communication, the reason "because of the lack of means" is unestablished (*asiddhi*).

With the words "of the elders" (*vṛddhānām*) and so forth, he demonstrates that very same lack of proof: "The repeated comprehension observed among the elders is the means; therefore, its abandonment [is required] for the realization of non-proof."

This very repeated observation of the elders' comprehension of the relationship is itself the means of communicating that relationship; for one is not able to communicate it to another without having first comprehended it oneself. "The loss of that" refers to the loss of the means.
"Avagama" means comprehension;
it refers to the understanding of the relationship [between word and meaning].
With the words "For this [would be so]," etc., he states the refutation:
"For all this would indeed be the case if the determination of the meaning of the Veda were established as non-contradictory even with respect to the elders; otherwise, there would be a failure."

Regarding what was stated—"the beginninglessness of words and their referents," and so forth—if by "beginninglessness" you intend the eternity of words and their referents, that is unproven, because the all-pervasive momentary destruction [of all things] has already been established.

If, on the other hand, you mean the beginninglessness of the causal series, then [your reason] is inconclusive and contradictory; for since a relation is not distinct from its relata, it would follow that the relation itself is non-eternal, just like them.

As for what was stated regarding the absence of a means (*upāya*), that too is unproven; for it has been established that even though there is difference, certain objects are by their very nature capable of producing a single uniform conceptual determination (*ekākāra-pratyavamarśa*), just like the eyes and other sense organs.
Therefore, the intention is this: the cognition of both speaker and listener which determines a single object is itself the means (*abhyupāya*) for its own production.

Furthermore, as for what is said regarding the observed comprehension of elders (*vṛddha*), it has already been stated therein: "And there is no understanding of that from the elders, for they too remain ignorant by their own nature."
"Otherwise, there would be a contradiction":

if it is maintained that elders, even while being themselves ignorant, nevertheless comprehend the relationship [between word and meaning], then there is a contradiction with what is perceived, just like the claim of a blind man that he sees forms; such is the meaning.
Regarding what was stated— "A proof must be asserted against such a thing as 'being a composite'"— he replies with the words beginning "siddha":
"Because it possesses a pervasion that is established through a universal application, no counter-proof whatsoever is possible against a probans such as 'being a composite'."

That whose pervasion through the inclusion of all [instances] is established is described as such; its state is its "nature" (*tattva*). By this, he demonstrates that this [inference] proceeds by the force of real entities (*vastubala*), because for any other [type of inference], pervasion through the inclusion of all instances is unestablished. Furthermore, in an inference proceeding by the force of real entities, there is no possibility of a counter-argument (*pratisādhana*), because it is impossible to alter the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things.
Nor is the occurrence of two mutually contradictory natures possible in a single [locus], because that would entail the loss of its unity. //2781//
Demonstrating that very pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a universal synthesis (*sarvopasaṃhāra*), he says "sārthakā" and so forth.

Demonstrating the establishment of pervasion through a comprehensive synthesis of all cases, he says "sārthakāḥ" and so forth: "Those very phonemes, when they are meaningful, have distinct meanings, and are joined in a specific sequence, are designated as 'words,' 'sentences,' and 'collections'— thus they are said to be."
Therefore, the pervasion— that [the Veda] possesses meaningfulness, distinct meanings, and a specific sequential arrangement— is unimpeded, as it is excluded from being of human origin.
"So be it.

It was stated [by us] that [the Veda] is produced as a composite whole; however, it has been previously demonstrated that if the phonemes were not of human origin, all of this would be untenable. Therefore, the pervasion (vyāpti) is established.

But surely, since the reason "because of being denotable by the study of the Veda" also has its pervasion (*vyāpti*) established through a universal application (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), for it is indeed the case that no author of the Vedas is ever perceived—anticipating this objection, he says "vedādhyayana... and so forth:
"In the case of being denotable by the study of the Veda, there is certainly no such ascertainment of pervasion;
therefore, in this proof, the 'doubtful exclusion' (*saṃdigdhavyatirekitva*) is evident."
"Not so," [one might object].

For instance, in the case of "being a composite" (*saṅghātatva*), the negative concomitance (*vyatirekitva*) with the opposite of the probandum is not doubtful; however, in this case, it is indeed doubtful.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "of such a kind," and so forth:
"When such a sequence [of causes] and the incapacity of humans to act have been established,
this pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot at all be ascertained here."
When all human qualities have been directly perceived, this certainty indeed arises; and this is possible for an omniscient being.
"Of such a kind" refers to [injunctions] such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma.

He shows that if the incapacity of all men to produce such a sequence of syllables were certain, then there would be certainty regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*); however, that very [incapacity] cannot be ascertained by anyone who is not omniscient, as he states in the passage beginning with "of all human attributes," and so forth.
And this [is] certainty.

Now, one might object: "Since qualities of the Veda such as the teaching of dharma and so forth, as well as its difficulty to recite, are not observed in human-authored statements, the human origin of the Veda is simply impossible; how then could there be the fallacy of being 'unproven due to doubt'? Anticipating this, he says: "The human origin of the Veda is clearly conceivable," and so on: "The human origin of the Veda is clearly conceivable, Just as are [the teachings on] sexual misconduct, the killing of living beings, and the speaking of untruth."
For qualities of the Veda such as difficulty of pronunciation, lack of acute accent, obscurity, and unpleasantness to the ear are observed even in the speech of atheists and others.
Whatever is observed, such as the removal of poison or prosperity,
is seen to be true even in the case of mantras and doctrines concerning Vainateya and others.

He thinks as follows: even if there is indeed non-perception, since mere non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), it remains doubtful and unestablished (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*). For it is possible that at some time or place there might be persons who are the authors of such Vedic dharmas;
moreover, mere non-perception is not established, because Vedic dharma—such as the instruction on sexual misconduct and so forth—is observed even in the words of atheists and others.
Sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyākriyā*) is improper sexual conduct (*kāmamithyācāra*), meaning,
for instance, approaching one's mother and so forth;
its instruction is found in rites such as the *gosava*.

As it has been said: "The sacrificer (*upahā*) sucks water, cuts grass, and approaches his mother or even a woman of another lineage," and so forth. Here, *upahā* refers to the sacrificer; this refers to the instruction for the slaughter of living beings in the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other such rites.
As it has been said:
"Many [sacrificial animals] are employed on the middle day of the Aśvamedha; according to the scriptural injunction, they are fewer than three hundred animals."
Thus,
it has been taught that untruth is false speech;
as it has been said:
"For falsehood joined with jest does not cause harm, nor among women, O King, nor at the time of marriage;
they say that these five falsehoods—when life is at stake and when all one's wealth is being seized—are not sinful."
Cf.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya p. 241.
Thus it is said.

The connection is as follows: "the designation" (abhidhā) means the naming (abhidhāna) of these [faults] such as sexual misconduct and so forth; it is observed that even the words of the Vedas, the Dharma, and the atheists are seen [to contain them].
The word "tathā" (thus) is used in the sense of conjunction.

*Durbaṇatva* (difficulty of pronunciation) is the state of being hard to articulate; *anudāttatva* (lack of accentuation) is the state of being pleasing to the mind; and *kliṣṭa* (obscured) is that which is separated [by other words], as in the example: *āmandrair indra haribhir yāhi mayūraromabhiḥ*.
For here, the particle *ā* in *ā mandraiḥ* is connected with the word *yāhi*, even though it is separated by intervening words.
The meaning is "come.

"Unpleasantness of hearing" (aśravyatā) means being disagreeable to the ear. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of [faults such as] the breaking of words (padaviccheda), protracted vowels (pluta), acute accents (udātta), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the power of removing poison and so forth": in the removal of poison, *bhūti* means capacity or efficacy—that is, *prabhāva*.
Alternatively, it is a compound consisting of "the removal of poison" (*viṣāpagama*) and "prosperity" (*bhūti*).
"Bhūti" means prosperity, "vibhūti" means manifestation, and "aiśvarya" means sovereignty;
by the word "ādi" (and so forth), possession by spirits or planets, subjugation, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and so on are included.
"Satyam" means non-contradictory.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "Vainateya, etc.," the inclusion of the mantra systems of the Buddhists and others is intended.

Regarding the objection that "the same might be the case in India as well," he says: "Furthermore, by this method, not even a single human-authored statement can be established, since Buddhist speech could likewise be inferred in this way."
Thus, the inference is as follows:

the study of the Sugata’s teaching, which was mentioned first, is preceded by a study of its own kind, because it is designated as "the study of the Sugata's [teaching]," just like the study at present.

If this is so, how then will that [teaching] of the Sugata be established? To this he says: "Because its form is manifested by that," and so forth. Because its nature is manifested by that [Buddha], it is called his;
and even in that case, the recollection of an author is based on the purpose [of the teaching].
If it is argued that others do not accept this, then why is it not accepted when the reasoning is equal?
Let it be that such is not the desire of the other; nevertheless, it is inferred to be so on the basis of logic.
That which has as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) the form manifested by that Sugata is "thus" (tathā);
the state of being so is "reality" (tattva).
Even in that regard, the recollection of the Buddha as the agent can be explained as being based on a figurative expression (arthavāda).
For why, in this case as well, is the root *kṛ* not explained as having the meaning of "remembering"?

It might be argued: "This is not accepted by the Buddhists, so how could it be established in this way? To this he says: "If the principle is the same, why is it not accepted? If this meaning were supported by logic, then why would the Buddhists not admit it? For it is not reasonable for a discerning person to refuse to accept a matter that is established by logic.
Even though a discerning Buddhist would not accept such a position, we say that it is nonetheless logically entailed for you.
Strengthening this very point by means of that statement, he says "And always," and so forth:
"And at all times, men for the most part speak untruth;
just as there is no confidence today [in their words], so too there is none when they report on past events."
Thus, by this reasoning you have stated, no author anywhere is established, even when he speaks of his own work in a certain text.
Therefore, let this hope for truth in those [scriptures] that are not of human origin be abandoned;
for meanings contrary to the Veda have been propounded in them.
Regarding the phrase "by this very [reason]," it refers to what was just stated, beginning with "and at all times," and so forth.
One might think: "Let it be that all [Vedic words] are non-human (apauruṣeya)"; to this he says, "And therefore," and so forth.
Consequently, the fact that [the Veda] is non-human in origin would not be established as having a true meaning;
the point is that this is because of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to the words of the Buddhists and others.

For instance, according to your own view, doctrines such as selflessness—which are contrary to the meaning of the Veda—are taught in those words of the Buddhists and others, even though they are not supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); likewise, it is possible that such [contrary] things might also be found within the Vedic [texts].

Thus, the inconclusiveness [of the reason] has first been demonstrated; now, demonstrating its contradictory nature because it subverts what is desired [by the opponent], he says "Moreover" (apica) and so forth:
"Moreover, in this way, beginninglessness would be established, but not dependence on various [sources].
Therefore, if [the Veda] were uncreated, any other scripture would also be uncreated."

For indeed, its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) is intended to be proven; yet that is not established. What, then, is established? Only its beginninglessness (*anāditva*), which is precisely what is undesired. It might be argued: "Once beginninglessness is established, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), its being uncreated (*akṛtakatva*) is necessarily established, for it is not logical for that which is created to be beginningless. To this, he says "Therefore," and so forth.
Therefore, if there were any state of being created despite beginninglessness, then even the linguistic usage of the Persians and others would [be considered] such.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "for instance" (tathāhi) and so forth:
"For instance, the linguistic conventions of the Persians and others depend upon others;
and the tenet of the nihilists is produced by the mental impressions of others."
"Dependent on another" means that they proceed by means of the conditioning of another person.
"Existing through the conditioning of another" means that for whom there is an existence (*bhāva*) by means of the conditioning of another; he is thus described.

Or, it has the nature of coming into being through the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) of another; thus it is "arising from the formation of another" (*parasaṃskārabhāvī*). From that [term], the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the word itself [to form *parasaṃskārabhāvika*]. For even those philosophical systems (*siddhāntas*) whose conventions are fashioned by one's own intuition proceed precisely by the power of conceptualizing the meaning as heard from others; their activity generally occurs solely through the force of another’s formation, just like worldly transactions which function according to [conventional] perception.

If it is argued, "Let there be the non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) of all [scriptures]," he says "īdṛśī" and so forth: "And even if such a state of being uncreated were established, what benefit would that be for you? For this entire effort of yours is directed toward establishing the absence of falsehood."
In such [a case], where a false meaning is possible.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the past and future times," he says "kālatva" and so forth:
"In the case of 'time-ness,' 'person-ness,' and so on, there is a doubtful negative concomitance (saṃdigdhavyatirekitā),
because— as in the previous case— there is no proof that humans lack the capacity for such instruments."
Since individuality has been refuted, the speaker must be understood as the agent alone;
thus, in both types of formulation, the illustrative example (nidarśana) is stated to be devoid of the probandum (sādhya).

For all people, the proof of the capacity for causal agency is a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the opposite of the reason; since such [a subverting proof] has not been demonstrated, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of all these reasons in the case of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) is doubtful, and thus they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
"As before" means as in the proof of [the property of] being expressible by the study of the Veda.
"The example is devoid of the probandum" refers to [the examples] "like the present time" and "like an ordinary man."
And therefore, regarding the statement "let it be understood" and so forth, he says "of a person," etc.:
Because of the dependence on human instruction and because the proof is produced [by human effort],
there is no dependence on a speaker with respect to its own object, nor with respect to the subject (*dharmin*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"In the case of the subject and the example" means: in the case of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "the cognition produced by that," he says: "Let it be so in the case of eternality," and so forth.
If the sentence were eternal, then the property of being produced from an eternal sentence would clearly be unestablished for both the subject (*dharmin*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
And thus, since the authorlessness of the Vedic injunction remains unestablished,
the fault of being "doubtfully unproven" (sandigdhāsiddhatā) applies to the latter reasons as well.
Here too, as before, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
The locative case in "of the subject and the example" (*dharmidṛṣṭāntayoḥ*) is dependent on "the state of arising from an eternal sentence" (*nityavākyodbhavatvasya*).
The genitive of relation in "of the sentence" (*vākyasya*) is dependent on "eternality" (*nityatve*).
The genitive case in "nityavākyodbhavatvasya" (of the state of being produced from eternal sentences) expresses dependence on the [logical] non-establishment [of that state].
And in the subsequent cases, such as "because they are produced by causes free from defects," and so forth, the same applies.

Showing that the two reasons—"because it is produced by speech that is unauthoritative and ill-composed" and "because it is free from sublation"—are indeed certainly unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "And it is sublated," and so forth.
"And the Veda is clearly sublated once momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has been established.
Since [the Veda] is eternal by its very nature, how could cognition produced by it [be valid]?"
For it is stated in the Śruti that the Puruṣa "is not destroyed";
thus, the sublation of that [opponent's] position has already been clearly declared, and its lack of proof is evident.

For one for whom the difference in place, time, and person is as directly perceptible as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, by that very fact the absence of sublation in that case is determined.
The connection is that "the eternal [scripture], first of all, is sublated in its own nature.
This is what is meant:

when momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga), which pervades all entities, has been established by means of inference proceeding from the power of valid reasons, then this very scripture accepted as eternal is indeed sublated; the mention of "its own nature" is for the purpose of excluding the literal meaning [of the words].
"How can there be an intellect produced by that? means "there is none at all.
By this, it is stated that the reason—"because it is produced by speech not uttered by a reliable person"—suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Demonstrating that the [reason] "because of being free from sublation" (*bādhavarjanāt*) is certainly unestablished (*asiddha*) in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), he says: "For it does not decay," and so forth.
It is recited in the Veda: "This is indestructible; for it does not decay; indeed, O Maitreyī, this Self is imperishable.
Prior to the establishment of selflessness (*nairātmya*) for that person—the Self—sublation was stated.

Therefore, its lack of establishment (*asiddhatva*) is certain. But is it not the case that, according to the statement, "An injunction (*codanā*) is said to be a word that impels one toward action," only a specific portion of the Veda is called an injunction, and not the entire Veda? Since it is the cognition produced by an injunction (*codanā*) that has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), even if other parts of the Veda having a different purpose were to be sublated, there would be no sublation of the injunction; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is indeed established.
This is not a fault. By the term *codanā*, every Vedic sentence whatsoever is sometimes intended, and not only that which is always instigating (*pravartaka*).

Otherwise, the sentence "One should not harm living beings" would not be a *codanā*, because it does not instigate action. Furthermore, what was stated in the Bhāṣya—that "here, both the beneficial and the harmful are indicated by *codanā*"—would also be contradicted; for a *codanā* does not instigate one toward what is harmful, such that the harmful could be indicated by it.

Furthermore, regarding that other point stated in the Bhāṣya— "Indeed, someone's cognition may indeed be subverted by a human utterance, but there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for concluding that a Vedic statement is false"—
since this [Veda] is eternal, its subversion would entail the possibility of subverting the *codanā* (injunction) itself, which is indeed difficult to avoid. For it has been said by Kumārila:
And by establishing the state of being authorless, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*hetutva*) will be proven;
for it is clearly observed that even the Vedic word, though authorless, is subject to sublation when its objects concern eternal entities such as the *puruṣa*.

Likewise, in such cases as "heaven results from the agnihotra," the doubt [regarding the validity of the means] is difficult to ward off; thus, the aforementioned fallacy of being "doubtfully unestablished" (sandigdhāsiddhatā) remains clear.
For this very reason, having once again set aside the state of being doubtfully established, he says "like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand," and so forth.
Regarding the word "therein":

Regarding the statement that "it does not undergo subversion in another place, at another time, or in another person, and therefore it is non-false"— that [argument] is refuted by this [following point].

Regarding what was stated [in the verse], "Therefore, like light," he says: "When the meaning of the form is not known by men, etc. Since the Veda remains as darkness when its form and meaning are unknown to men, the attachment of the dull-witted to it is like that of the Persians toward their own customs.
And those who do not understand the meaning of that [teaching], due to their connection with the outflow of evil,
likewise engage in the defilements such as the harming of living beings.

"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to its own nature (*svarūpa*), and "object" (*artha*) refers to that which is denoted (*abhidheya*). The analysis of the compound is: "those two, form and object, are unapprehended by humans. In this context, form is unapprehended because it is impossible to determine, either through itself or through another, whether this is merely a phoneme (*varṇa*), or whether it is something else—a specific sequence of phonemes—or neither. The same lack of certainty regarding the object (*artha*) should also be understood.
And because it has become shrouded in darkness due to the absence of certainty, it is as if without light;
thus, "evil" refers to the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) from the habitual practice of previous sins, which are their natural outflow (*niṣyanda*).
"In that very way" means accordingly.
As among the Persians.

Regarding what was stated previously— that those who seek dharma and adharma must necessarily rely upon *codanā* alone as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— to that he replies with the verse beginning "With regard to dharma": "With regard to dharma, the validity of *codanās* is not established either intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or from others, because their meaning is not determined by dull-witted people."
The mention of "dharma" is illustrative; "adharma" should also be understood as included.

If this is so, then who is the basis for the systematic arrangement of dharma and the rest? To this he says "jñāna" and so forth: "Therefore, let the Person, whose mass of internal darkness has been dispelled by the light of knowledge, be accepted as the teacher of the distinct meanings of the Vedas."
Thus ends the examination of scripture.
"Internal darkness" refers to afflicted and non-afflicted ignorance; he by whom the mass of internal darkness has been dispelled—that is, destroyed—by the light of knowledge is described as such.
Regarding the term "of those who are secluded":
"Of those who are blameless and wise" means of those who are pure, unstained by blemishes such as the desire to kill animals or sexual misconduct.
"Deserving of being an instructor"—
the sense is that only in this way does the postulated authorlessness of that [Veda] become meaningful.
Otherwise, if that meaning were not known, it would be entirely useless.

By this, the following is stated: your acceptance of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is not tenable without an omniscient being; therefore, he must necessarily be accepted, because it has been demonstrated that otherwise the validity [of scripture] would remain unestablished. Consequently, it is better that the very words spoken by him be the basis for dharma and other matters; what is the use of further postulating a non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) that is not supported by any means of valid cognition?

As for what was said—that even though [the Dharma and so forth] are accessible through the meditative absorption (samādhi) of a yogin, they do not exist—that too is faulty; the sense is that this will be proven later by means of inference (anumāna) for the yogin.
Thus concludes the examination of scripture.
In TS 2810,
with the words "evam" and so forth, [the author] further supports the very fact that independent revelation (svatantra-śruti) is untenable by means of another method,
once the human origin of the Vedas has been thus established.
Their intrinsic validity, too, is refuted without effort.

For instance, thinking that the authority of the Veda (*śruti*) must be established, the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas) maintain that, in general, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of all means of knowledge is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), whereas invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

They argue that if validity were indeed extrinsic, there would result the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and other defects, which would lead to the collapse of the distinction between what is a valid means of knowledge and what is not.

For instance, four positions are possible: first, that both validity and invalidity are intrinsic (*svataḥ*); second, that both are extrinsic (*parataḥ*); third, that validity is extrinsic while invalidity is intrinsic; and fourth, the reverse of this. Among these, the first position is not tenable. To explain: would those two reside in a single individual instance, or in different instances?
First of all, the two properties of validity and invalidity, which are characterized by mutual exclusion, cannot coexist in a single individual instance because they are contradictory.

Nor can they exist in different instances, because in that case there would be no basis for restriction and no possibility of a determining cause, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of an indistinct arrangement between valid and invalid cognitions.
For if both were independent, there could be no such rule as "this is indeed valid."

Furthermore, because the two are both characterized by a common sublation (*bādha*) such that their difference is obscured, and because no other cause for determination is admitted, there would be no established distinction between "this is valid cognition" and "this is non-valid cognition," due to the lack of knowledge through differentiation.

Nor is the second position tenable, because it follows that a cognition which is initially devoid of both natures would be without any nature at all. For when validity and its opposite—which are defined by mutual exclusion—are absent, no other form of this [cognition] can be determined; thus, it would undoubtedly result in the cognition being indefinable (*anupākhyatva*).
And it is said:
"First of all, duality does not exist from its own side, nor does it exist from another, due to contradiction;
for in this way, the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) follows as a consequence even in the nature of cognition."
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of the distinction between individual cognitions,
even so, since [the cognition] is independent of anything else, why and where it does not occur must be determined.
Nor is the third position tenable, because of the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus ends the thirty-seventh [verse] on the exhortation (*codanā*).
For it is thus: first of all, validity cannot be expected from another that is itself not a means of valid cognition, because that [other] is itself invalid.

Nor can it be expected from one that is a means of valid cognition, because by the same line of questioning, if one expects its validity from another, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.
Consequently, for one who follows a succession of means of valid cognition in order to establish even a single instance of a means of valid cognition, an entire human lifespan would be consumed.
Therefore, since no other alternative is possible, it should be accepted that the validity of all means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), while invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) for this is as follows: those things which are necessarily of a certain nature do not depend on anything else for that nature, just as space does not depend on anything else for its incorporeality; and cognitions (*vijñāna*) and so forth, which are the subjects of dispute, are necessarily of the nature of being valid means of knowledge. This is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Nor is this [reason] inconclusive, because a property that is impossible by its own nature cannot be produced by another, just as corporeality cannot be produced in space. As it has been said: "A power that does not exist inherently cannot be produced by another. (TS 2811–2812).
Here, with the words "by its own nature" (*svataḥ*) and so forth, [the author], while considering the thesis-meaning to be a mere void, begins the refutation by means of an investigation thereof.
Regarding the statement, "The validity of all means of valid cognition is intrinsic," what meaning is intended by you for this sentence?
In response to the question, "What is the intended meaning? the opponent says: "The capacity for the cognition of the object of knowledge, and so forth," and so on.
"Their capacity for the cognition of the object of knowledge and the like is established as inherent;
for a capacity that does not exist by itself cannot be produced by anything else."
2812 = ---V *codanā* 47cd;

PVD75b6: If cognition (*jñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then its inherent capacity (*svābhāvikī śaktiḥ*) lies in the awakening to the object of knowledge—that is, in the determination of the object of knowledge—because cognition has the nature of determining an object. Alternatively, if the eyes and so forth are [the means], then their capacity lies in the production of cognition that accords with reality. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), this is included: that the capacity of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) for the comprehension of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*) belongs to it inherently (*svata eva*).
Right here, the opponent states the argument beginning with "na hi" (for not...).
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "anapekṣatvam evaikaṃ" (only independence itself), and so forth.
Independence alone is the sole basis for validity;
for that very [validity] would be destroyed if dependence were resorted to.
"Of validity" means of the establishment of validity. "For that very [thing]" refers to that same [establishment].
Validity [is established],
because when the pervader is absent, the pervaded cannot remain.
It might be argued: "Let it be destroyed; what is the fault in that? To this he says, "For who," and so forth:
"For what proponent of logic would adopt a position that destroys its own foundation, by which even the means for establishing that [position] is destroyed by his own very statement?"

Validity is the root [of authority], and that is sublated by dependence, because dependence is contradictory to its pervader. For validity is pervaded by independence; how then could it find a footing when dependence exists, which is contradictory to its own pervader? By the words "by which," etc., he demonstrates that validity is pervaded by independence. "By which" refers to this.
The meaning is "because."
To explain how it perishes, he says: "For [validity] is dependent...
For validity is established as being dependent upon something in certain cases;
and what [cognition], having an unstable cause, will establish the probandum?
"It is not established" means that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
To the objection, "Let there be the fault of infinite regress," he replies with the words "unestablished," and so forth.
A proponent whose reason is unstable and not definitively established is described as such.

This means that a signifier makes its object—namely, the pervaded (vyāpya)—known only when it is itself known, not by its mere existence; therefore, how can a proponent who has not himself first understood [the reason] employ a proof for the sake of convincing another?
With the words "If it is thus accepted," and so forth, he begins the refutation:
"If the object is accepted in this way, yet it is not non-distinct [from the cognition]."
The potency of all things has been established previously.
For the essential nature (svarūpa) that is capable of performing its intended function is called "power" (śakti).
If that [nature] were devoid of the state of being an existent entity (bhāva), then an existent entity could not possess causal factors (kāraka).

In this regard, what is intended by the term "intrinsic" (*svābhāvikī*)? Is it intrinsic because it is eternal and causeless, or rather, even though it is impermanent, it is called intrinsic because it arises from its own causes at the very moment the nature of cognitions is established, and is not subsequently produced by another cause? Thus, there are two alternatives. Regarding these, the first alternative is not tenable; for instance, would that [nature] be distinct, non-distinct, both, or neither? These constitute four possible positions.

In this regard, it cannot be the former [the arising of power], because the connection [of power with the entity] would be unestablished and because it would follow that the entity is not an agent; for it has been demonstrated many times that the power of all entities is non-distinct from them, as if it were their very nature.
Indicating this very point, he says "iṣṭa" and so forth.

For the capacity for cause and effect is the power of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śakti*); and if that intrinsic nature were not of the essence of the entity itself, that entity could not be an agent.
And thus, the implication is that it would follow that this [object] is not a real entity.

Now, if the position is that [the capacity] is non-different [from the object], then it could not be inherent; for since the object is impermanent by virtue of being produced through the power of causes, it follows that the capacity—which is non-different from it—would also be impermanent by virtue of being produced through the power of causes.
Otherwise, because their *yogakṣema* (acquisition and preservation) would be distinct, there could be no identity [between them].
He states this very point in the passage beginning with "And that [capacity] would be impermanent in such a way," and so forth.
And since such a capacity is impermanent and arises through the power of its own causes,
how can you maintain that it is the inherent nature of the means of valid cognition?

Furthermore, demonstrating that because the capacities of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are not distinct from the [means] themselves, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that they are eternal and lack causality—just like the nature of capacity itself—he says: "For if capacity were inherent... and so forth.
For if capacity were inherent, there would be either its eternity or its lack of causality.
And because they are identical in nature to those [causes], the means of valid cognition are certainly eternal and their causality is certain.
And so, he states "always existing" and so forth to show what the fault would be:
"If there were no dependence on causes, there would either be constant existence or non-existence; therefore, an effect dependent on that [cause] which occurs only occasionally is not tenable."
Furthermore, the nature and the function of the means of valid cognition are observed to be occasional;
therefore, according to you, their power must be manifested, not inherent.
If there were no cause, there would be either constant existence or constant non-existence.
As for the case of permanence, however, constant existence is already established even without being stated; therefore, it was not mentioned.
He states another consequence with the words "hence," and so forth.
"Dependent on that" means dependent on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By this,
the contradiction of the thesis with perception and inference is shown as applicable in each case.
For indeed, the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being occasional is established by direct perception itself;
it is also inferred from the sequence of their effects. Therefore, the acceptance of their permanence is clearly contradicted by these two means of valid cognition.
With the words "of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānām*), etc., he anticipates the opponent's method for resolving the two aforementioned undesirable consequences:
"If the intrinsic nature of the means of valid cognition attains manifestation through manifestors,
and if that [nature] initiates its effect while depending on other conditions..."
For when the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is manifested by its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), then it is perceived and not otherwise.
Therefore, even though [the means of cognition] is eternal, there is no consequence of its being perceived at all times;
nor is there the consequence of the effect existing at all times, because it is admitted that the production of an effect depends upon other causes, and not upon this [eternal entity] alone.
The meaning is that, for this reason, the occasional nature of the effect arises from the presence or absence of other auxiliary causes.
He provides a rebuttal with the verse beginning "vyakti" (manifestation), etc.:
"If manifestation were dependent on other causes and distinct from the eternal entity,
then there would be the constant perception of those effects which possess that [eternal] nature."
"Manifestation and dependence on another cause" refers to manifestation and dependence on another cause.
For it was previously refuted in detail during the examination of scripture (*śruti*) that there can be manifestation of an eternal entity;
and it was established that dependence on another cause is illogical for that which cannot be assisted.

Regarding the phrase "of those whose effects are of that nature": "those" refers to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); their "effects are of that nature" means that their form (*rūpa*) is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

However, the position of being both [existent and non-existent] is not tenable because of contradiction and because it entails the faults inherent in the two aforementioned positions. Nor is the position of being neither tenable; for since mutually exclusive forms entail the affirmation of the other when one is negated, it is illogical to negate that which has just been affirmed at that very same moment, as there is a contradiction between affirmation and negation in a single locus—this is the intended meaning.
This [point] has not been stated [explicitly] because the refutation is so obvious.
Now, having accepted the final three positions, he states the refutation beginning with "pṛthaktvam" (separateness):
"Whether the power be separate or possess a dual nature, even so,
that cognition would necessarily be eternal, for it is conjoined with an eternal power."
"Distinctness" refers to the position of difference (*vyatireka*).
The mention of "possessing both natures" is an illustration; one should also understand that the acceptance of the position of "possessing neither nature" is intended.
Alternatively, since that [non-existence] also has the nature of negating both forms, it indeed possesses a dual nature.
In all three of these positions, because cognition is connected to an eternal power, it would necessarily be eternal.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Otherwise, indeed," and so forth.
Otherwise, it would not be eternal, because it would lack a constant uniformity;
for at one time it is connected with the cognition of that [object], and not at another.
For otherwise, if cognition connected with power were impermanent, then the permanence of power would not be established. Why? Because of the lack of conformity to a single form;
that is to say, because of the absence of persistence in a single nature.
He demonstrates that very lack of concomitance with a single form by means of the passage beginning with "kadācit" (at some time), and so forth.

For if consciousness were impermanent, there would result for its capacity two natures—one connected with that cognition and one unconnected; yet it is not logical for a single entity to possess two mutually contradictory natures, because that would entail the loss of its unity and lead to the collapse of all conventional usage based on difference.
With reference to the second alternative, he says "atha" and so forth: "Now, the capacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is produced from its own causes;
once produced from its own causes, it is not further endowed [with capacity] by other things."
With the words "In this regard," and so forth, he states the fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) as being a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*):
"In this matter, we have no dispute; for who could subsequently attribute a capacity to a partless entity that has arisen from its own causes?"
For that form which is subsequently attributed by others is indeed a different state of being; thus, its own intrinsic nature is not taught.

For indeed, since both types of entities—those stable and those unstable—are partless and thus fully established in their own nature, it is impossible for a power that constitutes their very essence (*ātmabhūta*) to be imparted by another cognition at a later time. If such an imparting were to occur, it would necessarily be the production of a different entity altogether, rather than the imparting of a power that is identical with the entity's own nature.
Furthermore, it has been stated that if one does not accept the power as being the very nature of the entity, it follows that the power would lack causal efficacy.

It might be argued: "Let it be that no capacity can be imparted at a later time to a partless entity; but why should this not happen to an entity with parts? To this he says: "For the connection with contradictory properties," and so forth.
"Indeed, the connection with contradictory properties is declared to be the differentiator of entities;
since [the entity] is not produced when that [property] is produced, that [differentiation] exists even in the case of a capacity."
If it were to exist,
there would follow the consequence of contradictory properties.
Regarding an unstable entity, he specifically states the refutation with the words "established," and so forth:
"Since all objects have their momentary destruction established,
nothing whatsoever has the power to impart another cognition to them."
For they do not persist beyond that point,
whereby they might acquire a capacity for some result from another condition.
"In some cases, the fruit" refers to the ascertainment of the object and so forth;
the remainder is easily understood.
It might be argued: "If you have no dispute [with us], then how is it that extrinsic validity (*parataḥprāmāṇya*) has been accepted? To this, he says: "But this much," and so forth.
"But these wise followers of the Sugata say this here:
even though this [validity] resides in some cognition, it cannot be known intrinsically (*svataḥ*)."
"To be known" means to be ascertained;
"by itself" means...
Because it consists of the very nature of consciousness as mere experience, it does not depend on corroboration by an effect that arises at a later time.
It might be argued: "Since the capacity is not distinct from consciousness, when consciousness is apprehended, that capacity is also necessarily apprehended;
so how can it not be possible to know it? To this he says, "yathāvasthita... and so forth:
[he refers to] the capacity for attaining the cognition of the object to be known as it actually exists.
Who indeed is capable of ascertaining [an object] from experience alone, since its nature is that of experience?

"Bodha" is knowledge and "āpti" is attainment; thus, "bodhāptī" refers to the knowledge and attainment of the object to be known as it actually exists. The analysis of the compound is: "the capacity with respect to that [object], i.e., its domain.
"From the mere" means from that which does not depend upon the thorough knowledge of causes such as a relationship or other qualities.
To the question "Why is it not the master [of cognition]?", he says: "Even in the case of the non-means of valid cognition," and so forth.
For even in the perception of a mass of hair and the like—which is a non-means of valid cognition—there exists the nature of experience when it appears with a clearly manifest form.
Regarding the phrase "in the perception of a mass of hair, etc.":
this refers to the perception of a tuft of hair and so forth.

By this he means that although a capacity has been experienced, it nevertheless cannot be ascertained because of the similarity [of the object] to what is not a valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), due to error—just like the potency of poison and the like.
For experience alone is not the cause of certainty, since it requires other factors such as repeated practice;
for certainty occurs only in that aspect where no further quality is superimposed by a cause of error.
From what, then, is that [cognition] to be ascertained? He says: "Therefore," and so forth.

Therefore, whether it be the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) or something else, it is required solely for the sake of ascertainment, and not for the production of that [initial cognition], as is the case with poison and the like.
"Or else" means:
it is the knowledge of the purity of the cause;
but it is not for the purpose of instilling that [knowledge].
The connection is that "it depends on something else. "Of this" refers to the capacity (śakti).

Since certainty has the person as its substratum, it stands to reason that there is a dependence on other causes for its production, but not for its implantation; for the latter is the substratum of the capacity (*śakti*), and since that capacity is already accomplished at the time of the simultaneous arising [of the cognition], the sense is that [certainty] is already established.
With the words "Just as," etc., he explains the example "like poison and so forth":
"For just as in the case of poison, liquor, and the like, because they are perceived as equal to other things,
and because there is an absence of immediate results, there is no certain determination of their nature."

Just as the identity [of a cause] with its effect is understood when the production of that result— such as fainting, perspiration, or speech— is certain, so too is the certainty regarding the capacity for that [result] understood in the case of cognition.

"Because of observing its equality with that which is other than it": the analysis of the compound is as follows: "other than that," such as poison and so forth, refers to things like *nāgarapānaka* (a medicinal drink); "equality" (*samatā*) means similarity (*sārūpya*); and "observing" (*īkṣaṇa*) refers to the act of perceiving that [similarity].
"[Because of] the absence of an immediate succession of results."

The analysis [of the compound] is: "the fruit" refers to fainting and so forth; "because of the absence of its immediate succession" means that there is no fruit immediately following it. This is what is meant by "the lack of certainty regarding this self."
"In the absence of certainty regarding the self [as consisting of] poison and so forth" means "identity with that," which is to say,
having the nature of poison and so forth.
"Ascertainment of that capacity" means the ascertainment of attaining the realization of the objects of knowledge exactly as they exist.

Pointing out the contradiction with his own statement regarding the thesis, he says "Furthermore," and so forth: "Moreover, you have stated that this validity, characterized as a capacity, is indeed beyond dispute and must be ascertained by another means of valid cognition."
"The potencies of all entities are established through the presumption based on the necessity of their effects;
thus, since they are established by presumption (arthāpatti), how could they not be established by something other [than inference]?"
"How is it not established from another?
[The answer is: "It is indeed established," because presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); such is the meaning.

Regarding what was stated—that "that very [cognition] would perish"—he says "niṣpanna... and so forth, demonstrating its inconclusiveness: "For valid cognition, which has been established as having a partless nature from its own cause, does not thus incur destruction, because it requires nothing else for its ascertainment."
Clarifying this very point, he says: "Not for the sake of establishing its own nature," and so forth.
Another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not required for the establishment of its intrinsic nature;
however, it is required in the process of comprehension for the purpose of ascertaining that form.

It might be argued as follows: "If you are establishing extrinsic validity (*parataḥprāmāṇya*) with respect to cognition, then for us as well, this is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For even cognition itself is accepted as being established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); how much more so its validity, which consists in its capacity?
However, since cognition does not depend on anything else when it must perform its own function—characterized by the ascertainment of the object—it is said to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in that regard."
This is incorrect;

for without the ascertainment of validity, the very ascertainment of its own object is impossible. Furthermore, how can that which has been made an object of doubt and so forth be independent regarding its effect? Or, if there were dependence on the apprehension by another means of valid cognition, how would there not be an infinite regress (anavasthā) in your own position? Thus, this [argument] is trivial.
With the words "Furthermore," and so forth, he demonstrates the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the reason "because [the cause] is necessarily restricted to the existence of that [effect].
Furthermore, in this way, non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇya*) would also follow as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*);
for that which does not exist intrinsically cannot possibly arise from anything whatsoever.
Or rather, it is possible to state the first [reason] in its entirety: that independence alone is the sole basis for invalidity.
Just as the capacity for non-contradiction is ascertained from another source, so too is the capacity for correspondence;
therefore, in every respect, these two are equal.
Therefore, what excellence of validity has been observed in contrast to its opposite,
such that it is held to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*), while invalidity is held to be extrinsic (*parataḥ*)?

Likewise, the capacity for corroboration is understood as "ascertainment from another"; "both are equal" refers to both the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the non-means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
"By the opposite" means by way of invalidity;
this refers even to one who thinks thus.
The powers are not considered inherent because they are eternal, nor because they arise from their own causes and subsequently do not depend on any other cause;
rather,
their inherent nature consists in the fact that the powers of entities arise with specific, determined forms by virtue of their very nature.

For indeed, whatever form exists within the causes themselves is precisely what is imparted by them to the effect; just as when a jar is being produced from potsherds, its color and other qualities are initiated through their own respective qualities, whereas the capacity to fetch water and so forth is not imparted to the jar because it does not exist within those [causes], but rather that capacity manifests for it spontaneously; likewise, in the case of cognition as well, the power to discern objects is not imparted by its causes—the sense organs and so on—because it does not exist within them, but rather it arises for it spontaneously.
Therefore, the claim that "its power is intrinsic" is merely the babbling of that [opponent] as well;

for by this same logic, it would follow that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is also intrinsic. For even that [invalidity] is characterized by the capacity to determine a contrary object and so forth, yet the eyes and other [senses] do not possess such a capacity.

Furthermore, if a form that does not exist in itself is not imparted by causes to the effect, then how is it that the sense-faculties and so forth impart to consciousness a state of possessing form—a quality that does not exist in themselves?
If they can impart that [form] even though it does not exist [in them], why would they not likewise impart the capacity for the determination of objects?
For there is nothing to obstruct them in the imparting of that [capacity].

Furthermore, if capacities (*śakti*) are admitted to be non-different from the entity (*bhāva*), then, like the very nature of the entity itself, their own existence would be dependent upon causes; how, then, could they be considered inherent?

On the other hand, if they are different, then the relationship between them and their own substrates cannot be established by the entities themselves, because those entities do not confer any benefit upon them.
And it is not logical for that which confers no benefit to be a substrate, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, if these [causes] were independent and signless (*animitta*), they would not depend on the restriction of place and time.
For instance, whatever depends on something— whether it be dependent or independent— and then dissolves,
or whatever is independent and functions autonomously, why would that ever cease at any particular place or time?
Consequently, things would not possess their own specific capacities;
otherwise, everything would be applicable to everything.
Others, however, think that this statement—"all means of valid cognition [arise] from themselves," and so forth—is made on the basis of observing those effects.

For all things whatsoever, being already existent, are produced by causes, because of the necessity of the production of effects. Indeed, non-existent things such as sky-flowers can never be produced anywhere, nor can oil be produced from sand. If an existent thing were to arise from a non-existent one, then since there would be no distinction among all non-existent things, everything would arise everywhere at all times.
This is untenable,
because it would entail the consequence that the cause is purposeless; for, according to your view, nothing is produced in that which is non-existent.
Even if [the effect] already exists, because there is no desire for anything whatsoever, there is nothing at all that needs to be done; for what could he be doing that would make him its agent?
Consequently, it follows that the relationship between cause and effect is non-existent.
If it is argued that manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is produced for that which already exists, we say no.
For that [action] as well, there is a contradiction in its production because of its being either existent or non-existent;
since even in that case, this twofold dilemma arises: is it produced while being existent, or rather while being non-existent?
Regarding the first position, it has already been stated that production is untenable due to the absence of any further excellence (*atiśaya*).
In that case as well, if one resorts to manifestation, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.
Nor is the second position tenable, because action is not admitted for that which is non-existent;
or, if it were admitted, it would follow—by way of figurative usage—that even the non-existent could be produced.
Furthermore, would manifestation be produced as something distinct from the entity, or as something non-distinct?
If it were produced as something distinct, then nothing at all would have been done to the entity;
for when one thing is produced, another is not said to be produced, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
If it is argued that manifestation is produced as something related to that [object], we say no; for since it cannot be assisted, its status as being related to that object is unestablished.
Or, if assistance is admitted, then because that [assistance] would also be a distinct entity, there would follow an infinite regress, and thus the relationship would remain unestablished.
Even if [the manifestation] were not a distinct entity from the cause, it would follow that the causes are useless.

Furthermore, since the manifestation—which has the nature of an assistance—would arise from the very existent that serves as its substratum, it would follow that the manifestation is eternal, because the nature that is the cause of manifestation exists at all times.
Moreover, it has been demonstrated in many ways that dependence on another is not logical for that which cannot be assisted.
Now, as for the position that manifestation is produced as something not distinct from the entity itself, that too is untenable because there is no excellence (atiśaya) added.
For if it is said that "that which is not distinct from the entity is produced," it amounts to saying that the very nature of the entity is being produced.
And since that [nature] exists and is entirely devoid of parts, its production is logically impossible; this is precisely what must be considered.
Furthermore, like manifestation, there would be the production of an entity that is non-existent, because there is no difference [between the two].

Alternatively, just as with the nature of an entity, it would follow that manifestation must also be produced as something already existent; yet even this is not tenable, because there is no additional excellence (*atiśaya*) [in the manifestation], and because it has already been stated that this leads to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, if the operation of causes is desired with respect to an object that already exists, it would follow that the causes never cease from producing their effects.
For what reason would the causes cease once [the effect] has been perceived?
If you say "because the existence of the effect [is already established]," no; for [the causes would still operate].
According to your view, because that [effect] exists even prior [to its production],
therefore only that which has a cause arises from non-existence,
and not things such as a sky-flower.
Because there is an absence of a cause capable of producing that [specific effect].
Therefore, due to the specific restriction of causal power, there will be a restriction of the relationship between cause and effect;
for it is not accepted that every entity is capable of producing everything.
