Because the capacity of all entities is determined by a beginningless succession of their own causes.

Furthermore, if it is argued that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is said to be "intrinsic" (*svataḥ*) because it cannot be produced by anything else if it were non-existent, then by this same logic, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) would also necessarily be intrinsic; thus, this [position] is trivial.

Moreover, as for one who thinks that what is called "validity" is the capacity of cognition to produce the determination of an object, and that since capacity resides in a momentary cognition, it does not exist intrinsically and cannot be produced—[this too is untenable].
Because its activity is untenable at any of the three times.
To explain: first of all, it is not produced prior to the arising of consciousness, because it is dependent.

For it is not logical for that which is dependent to be produced in the absence of its support, just as a painting cannot exist in the absence of a wall; otherwise, it would follow that it is non-dependent.
For this very reason, simultaneous production is also untenable because [the cognition] is dependent;
for it is not possible for a wall and a painting—the support and the supported—to be produced simultaneously.
Nor can it be produced after the cognition has already arisen, because of its momentariness.
Because there is no duration [of the cognition] for that long.

Therefore, the claim that "the intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of all means of valid cognition is asserted" is incorrect. For instance, what was stated—that validity is the capacity to produce the determination of an object—is incoherent; because the determination of an object is a synonym for cognition itself.

Furthermore, it is not logical that a power (*śakti*) residing in that very cognition should be the producer of that same cognition, for that would entail the consequence of its being non-resident; moreover, because the relationship of cause and effect is untenable between things existing at the same time.

As for what was said—that because it is resident, it cannot be produced simultaneously with or prior [to the cognition]—that too is incorrect, because since there is no distinction [between them], the status of being resident is not established.

Indeed, it is the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity that performs a specific purposeful action; when there is a desire to know merely that [nature], it is designated as "capacity" (*śakti*). It is not a separate entity.

For if it were a separate entity, it would follow that the entity itself is not the agent of action, and the relationship [between them] would be unestablished; this has been thoroughly analyzed in many ways.

Therefore, the capacity that constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of consciousness—because its acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are non-different from those of consciousness—is not different from the nature of consciousness itself; thus, it is not contradictory to say that it is produced even though it did not exist prior to the arising of consciousness.

Furthermore, it is entirely logical to say that it arises simultaneously with consciousness, because an attribute that constitutes the intrinsic nature shares the same acquisition and preservation as the entity itself.
Granted that power is non-different from the entity; nevertheless, it remains unproven that existence and non-existence are dependent [upon it].
For instance, existence does not depend on it, because, being already fully accomplished in its entire nature, it is independent.
Nor is it logical for existence to have [power] as its substratum, because [power], being non-existent, can effect nothing.
If it is argued that stability is produced by it, as the Vindhya is [distinguished] from the Himavat, we say no;
for stability is not distinct from the stable entity.
For the very nature of the endurer is expressed in that way by the exclusion of other distinctions;

yet, since the self of the endurer is not produced by that basis, [the basis] is entirely ineffective. Even if stability were distinct [from the endurer], that which establishes the stability of the endurer would likewise be entirely ineffective.
Because stability is a distinct entity, nothing is produced for one thing by the production of another;
thus, in both cases, that which causes stability is ineffective.
If it is argued that it produces stability as something related to that [entity], [we reply:]...

No, for—just as in the case of the supported and the supporter—the relationship between that which possesses duration and its duration is unestablished; furthermore, this leads to the consequence of an infinite regress. This has already been largely examined. Moreover, if it is accepted that the duration which supports an entity is a distinct thing (arthāntara), then the destruction of no entity whatsoever would ever occur, because the supporting duration would always be present.
Nor can it be said that destruction will occur by the power of a cause of destruction even while stability persists;
for since that [cause] is likewise ineffective, its status as a destroyer is untenable.
For in that case as well, this dilemma necessarily arises: does the cause of destruction produce a destruction that is a distinct entity from the thing itself, or does it produce the thing itself?
To begin with, it does not produce the entity itself, because that [entity] is already established.
And if it produces something else, nothing has been done to the entity, since it remains in its original state.
Furthermore, because there is no destruction of the entity, the cause of destruction accomplishes nothing; this has been analyzed in detail in the *Sthirabhāvaparīkṣā*.
Furthermore, by its very nature, an entity must be either unstable in essence or stable in essence.

In that regard, if an entity is produced from its own cause as being inherently unstable by nature, then it cannot possibly remain by itself after the completion of that nature; thus, both a cause of stability and a cause of destruction are ineffective for it.

Now, even if an entity (*bhāva*) is by nature stable, since its own nature cannot undergo alteration, there is no destroyer of it; and because it is itself stable, there is likewise no sustainer. Thus, in both cases, the causes of stability and destruction are ineffective.

Nor is the position tenable that [the power] resides in what is non-existent, because, being devoid of all intrinsic nature, it is impossible for it to be a substratum or to possess the activity of supporting; like the horn of a hare, the fact that power is dependent [on a substrate] is unestablished.

Or, even if [the proof] were established, there would be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), because color and other qualities, though dependent [on a substance], are seen to arise simultaneously with the jar;
and because the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow regarding invalidity as well.
For invalidity too is a capacity that produces the determination of a contrary object.

Furthermore, since the capacity residing in cognition does not arise even throughout the three periods of time, it would follow—just as with validity—that the capacity consisting of invalidity is also intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
Moreover, if the capacity of cognition does not manifest even throughout the three periods of time, then cognition would result in being devoid of all efficacy.
For how could a property belong to something if it does not arise for that thing even throughout the three periods of time? It would be like the corporeality of space.

Or from where was this most wonderful sorcery learned by the powers (*śakti*), by which these [powers], though their existence has never been attained even in the three periods of time within consciousness, nevertheless experience union with it?
If you say that they experience it because it is some great being due to its eternity, no;
[it is not so].
Because it would follow that everything possesses causal power,
and because there is no regulating factor;
for we do not perceive any cause or regulator that, being independent, determines a specific object such that these [cognitions] belong to consciousness and not to anything else.
Consequently, it has been stated that because there is no proximate cause [for restriction], these [defects] would accrue to everything.

Furthermore, it is not logical for any substratum to be of no service to them, since, due to its eternality, there is no specific nature (svabhāva-viśeṣa) to be produced by anything. Enough of this prolixity.

Furthermore, analyzing the meaning of the proposition in another way, he says "from themselves" (*svataḥ*) and so forth: "Or else, it is intended that for those [cognitions] that have arisen, their occurrence toward their own effects is 'from themselves,' because the validity of these means of valid cognition is described as being from themselves."
This is what is meant:

now, by the phrase "intrinsic validity" (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), the following sense is intended: that for cognitions already produced, their subsequent operation toward their own effects occurs intrinsically, without depending on any other cause; that is to say, they function as the cause [of their own confirmation].
Thus, the intention of the opponent is that the aforementioned faults do not apply.
In this context, the specific function of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is either the ascertainment of their own validity or the ascertainment of the object.
In performing this specific function, they do not depend upon a further cause.
From where, then, does their mutual dependence arise? To this he says: "For in the acquisition of their own nature," and so forth.
For it is accepted that entities depend upon causes for the acquisition of their own nature;
however, once they have acquired their own nature, they proceed toward their own effects by themselves alone.
Having established in general that the acquisition of their own nature by entities depends upon other causes, he applies this principle to cognition as well,
saying "in mere arising," and so forth:
"Therefore, there is dependence upon its own causes only in the case of arising."
This [capacity] belongs to cognitions with respect to their own qualities, but not toward the production of certainty.
Regarding the phrase "in their own qualities":
this is a locative of support (*adhāra-saptamī*) with respect to the arising of certainty.

This is what is meant: when the production of certainty must be effected regarding those qualities inherent in cognitions—such as their nature of non-erroneous awareness, their being produced from pure causes, and so forth—there is no dependence upon these [external factors].

If this is so, how then do they function as causes in that regard? To this he says: "For in production," and so forth. For in their production, since their validity is determined by the objects [they apprehend], their occurrence is independent of their own causes, like a jar or similar things.
"Validity" (*prāmāṇya*) and "the object" (*artha*) constitute "validity and the object"; the "ascertainment" (*viniściti*) of these two is [the compound].
The connection is that [it is] "the production of that" (*tasyā janana*).
The term "ascertainment of the object" (*arthāniściti*) is stated with reference to initial sensory perception (*ālocanā*).
Because for others [the cognition] itself consists of ascertainment;
"functioning" (vṛtti) means being the cause.
With the words "a lump of clay," etc., he explains the example "like a jar" and so forth:
a jar depends upon a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, and other such factors for its production.
However, in the matter of fetching water, he has no need for that [assistance].
Thus, validity must necessarily be intrinsic;
for if validity were dependent on something else, an infinite regress would result.

Having thus established that there is no contradiction between the thesis and its meaning, he says "and at the end, it necessarily exists," etc., in order to prove the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason "because [the effect] is necessarily determined by the existence of that [cause].
"At the end" means in the very last cognition.
"That" refers to validity (*prāmāṇya*). Why must it necessarily be accepted at the end? To this he says: "Dependent on another," and so forth.

He demonstrates this very point with the words "If it were the primary [means of knowledge]," and so forth: "If the status of being a primary means of knowledge (pramāṇatva) were to be established by another means of knowledge, then we, desiring it to be so in that case as well, would never attain a firm conclusion."
Just as the first cognition requires corroboration, so too must that corroboration itself be sought for further corroboration.
The first cognition is the root; that which arises from it is the fundamental (*maulikam*).
That is to say, it is inherent [in that cognition].

For instance, extrinsic validity (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*) might arise either from a cognition that accords with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda-jñāna*), or from the thorough knowledge of the excellence of its causes. Regarding these, he says "just as... and so forth, demonstrating that the first position is not tenable. Now, it might be argued: "The validity of the cognition that accords with purposeful action is accepted as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*); therefore, there will be no infinite regress. To this, he says "of some... and so forth.

"But if it is maintained by someone that validity belongs to [cognition] itself, then for what reason is there such hostility toward the first [cognition] being likewise? (VV 2854). Demonstrating the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) even in the second position, he says: "If [validity] were dependent on qualities," and so forth. (Bṛhaṭṭīkā; PVD 75a1; TBV 6,29–30; SVR 251,15–16).

Thus, if the status of perception and other means of valid cognition were dependent upon excellences (guṇas), and if those excellences never exist without a means of valid cognition, [then there would be no way to establish them].
Therefore, for one who desires another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to determine those qualities,
the validity of that [second cognition] would likewise depend upon qualities determined by yet another [cognition].
"Dependent on qualities" means dependent upon the thorough knowledge of the qualities of the cause.
"Validity" [is so called].
The determination of validity [is as follows]:
"they do not exist" means that they do not exist in the sense of being unfit for the conventional usage of existence.
"Of that too" refers to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which delimits qualities.
"Dependent upon qualities delimited by another" means...
The meaning is that validity depends upon the ascertainment of that quality which has been determined by another means of valid cognition.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "Just as in 'today' (adya), so too in 'another' (anya)"; thus, as before, there would be an infinite regress.
Desiring it to be so in each respective case, we would never attain a definitive conclusion.
If it is not accepted that the knowledge of qualities has its validity dependent upon those qualities,
then even the initial cognition of the object would not require the valid cognition of the qualities.
Therefore, even after reflecting at great length, it is better to rest at the very beginning on that very point where validity is necessarily to be admitted as being intrinsic in some cases.
The meaning is that just as in the first cognition validity depends upon qualities determined by another means of knowledge, so it is in other cases as well.
"As before" means like the ascertainment of validity through correspondence (*saṃvāda*).
Regarding the phrase "therein, therein": this refers to each preceding cognition of a quality (*guṇajñāna*).

Now, if it is accepted that the validity of the cognition of a quality is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) precisely to avoid the fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), then what is the aversion toward the cognition of the object (*arthavijñāna*) such that its validity is held to be extrinsic (*parataḥ*) rather than intrinsic? We perceive no reason whatsoever for this.
Therefore, when the shore is not in sight, even after a bird has flown a great distance, it must return to that very same place; thus, enough with this ill-founded and improper practice.
This very point is shown by the passage beginning with "knowledge of qualities" (*guṇajñāna*).
That whose validity (*prāmāṇya*) depends upon qualities—that is, depends upon the ascertainment of qualities—is described as such.

It might be argued that there is a distinction between the cognition of correspondence and the cognition of excellence from the root-cognition, and therefore the validity of those two is intrinsic while it is not so for the first; to this he says "saṃvāda... and so forth:

"By what additional factor would the cognition of correspondence or the cognition of excellence possess that dependence upon the first [root-cognition] by whose power [its validity] would come to be?"
Therefore, intrinsic validity is established as the general rule in all cases;
it is set aside only by the two [conditions]: the occurrence of a sublation and the cognition of defects in the cause.
Even though this [validity] is dependent on something else, an infinite regress does not result;
for this [validity] is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that [means of valid cognition] is established intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
Now, if cognition were indeed intrinsically valid (*svataḥpramāṇa*), it would follow that all cognitions are valid; therefore, he says "therefore," and so forth.

*Utsarga* is a general rule or prescription; that which arises from this is *autsargika*. *Bādhā* is the ascertainment of the object being otherwise, and the knowledge of a defect in the cause; thus, [the phrase refers to] sublation (*bādhā*) and the knowledge of a defective cause (*kāraṇadoṣajñāna*).

But surely, since validity is established as the default state, how can it ever be set aside? If invalidity were established through the two means of [cognizing] a subverting factor and the cognition of a defect in its cause, then that invalidity, being established by those two, would be extrinsic (*parataḥ*). If you say, "We indeed accept this," then in that case, just as with validity, there would be an infinite regress here as well. To this he says: "Dependent on another," and so forth. There would be an infinite regress if invalidity were established by means of what is itself invalid; however, invalidity is accepted as being derived from a source of a different nature (i.e., a valid cognition).
And since that [validity] is established through itself alone, how could there be an infinite regress?
He demonstrates this very point with the words "For a means of valid cognition," and so forth:
"For just as a means of valid cognition is not established by another means of valid cognition,
likewise invalidity is not established by means of invalidity."
For if they shared a basis of the same genus, stability would not be possible;
however, because it belongs to a different genus and has a distinct cause, it is firmly established with deep roots.
Regarding the phrase "of a different kind":
it refers to that which lacks a valid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*).
And this is connected with the expression "firmly rooted and established."
"Because it has another cause" is the statement of the reason (*hetunirdeśa*).
The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: that which has another cause characterized by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[It is said to be] "firmly established on a solid foundation."
That which is firm—unshakable by defects such as infinite regress—and whose root is well-established is "tathā"; the state of being so is "tattva" (reality).

It might be argued: "Even if a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) does not depend [on other factors] for its validity, nevertheless, only when it is itself recognized as being unsublated is it capable of establishing the invalidity of another; it cannot do so otherwise. To this he says: "The subverting cognition, first of all," and so forth. "The subverting cognition consists in the ascertainment of the object's difference [from what was previously perceived]. Because its own validity is independent, it sets aside the prior cognition."
"Apohate" means he rejects; that is to say, he refutes [it] by means of its lack of validity as a source of knowledge (pramāṇa).

It might be argued: "Even in the case of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), just as in the case of the first cognition, another subversion is indeed possible immediately after the subverting cognition; so how is the dependence on a further subversion eliminated therein, by which there could be a certainty of its being subverted? To this, he says: "In that case too," and so forth. "In that case too, however, there might occasionally be a need for a further exception (*apavāda*) for one who has developed suspicion regarding the previous [subversion]. That [need] is also removed by even a slight [further subversion]."
"In some cases there too" refers to when there is a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) characterized by the ascertainment of a different meaning. "Of one who has conceived doubt" means:
"Of the person";
"by the former" means by the first cognition.
"Even she" refers to one who relies on exceptions. "By a small [amount]" refers to...
The word "with effort" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
To the question "How does it cease?", he says: "Another sublater," and so forth.
If, while one is searching for another, a further sublater arises, then by the sublation of the intermediate one, the status of the first as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established.
Then, when a thorough investigation has been conducted with appropriate effort,
the sublater of the sublater would not be known, due to the absence of a root.
Therefore, because it is free from contradiction, that very [subsequent cognition], being more powerful, sublates the former; thus, the validity of that [former] alone is set aside.
Thus, it does not transcend the threefold knowledge of the investigator;
therefore, as long as no sublation has arisen, one need not further suspect a sublater.

If, upon investigation, another sublater arises for that very sublater, then because the middle one has been sublated by the third, the first alone would be the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If, however, no further sublater arises—due to the absence of a fundamental cause—then the first is sublated by that very second which is stronger; thus, its validity is set aside by it.
"He does not overstep" means he does not transcend; "who is this person? is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Now, why does the third cognition not likewise require a sublater, as the second cognition does, such that there would necessarily be three cognitions for an investigator? To this he says, "And therefore," and so forth:
[it refers to] that cognizer for whom no sublater has arisen—that is, has been produced.

To the question "Why should this not be suspected?", he says: "For he who, out of delusion, imagines an invalidating cognition even when none exists— he, being of a doubting nature in all worldly transactions, shall go to his ruin."
Destruction means ruin,
resulting from the loss of reality.
This very point is supported by the following scriptural teaching beginning with "And so":
"And thus, O son of Kuntī, the state of being a doubting soul has been condemned by Vāsudeva: 'Neither this world nor the next exists for one who is a doubting soul.'"
"By Vāsudeva" means by Viṣṇu.
"Kaunteya" refers to Arjuna, the offspring of Kuntī.

If this were so, then even in the first cognition, the suspicion of sublation would not arise; and consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that all cognitions possess validity. Anticipating this objection, he says: "To whatever extent a sublation is possible regarding a cognition, and to that same extent, when sought, [the sublation] does not arise within that very cognition."
Those knowers who desire their own welfare should not persist in speculating about that object with the thought, "It might perhaps exist."
Cognizing subjects who desire their own welfare should not persist in speculating about that object with the thought, "It might perhaps exist at some time. [2875]

In whatever cognition a certain degree of sublation might be suspected, when that very extent of sublation has been sought for and does not arise, it is to be understood—by supplying the ellipsis—that "it (the sublation) does not exist" in relation to that cognition itself.
Showing where the denial of efficacy (kriyā-apavāda) is possible, he says "deśa" and so forth:

"The distinctions of place, time, person, and state are indeed established through conventional usage; therefore, those [distinctions] existing in a given case must be taken into account by one who seeks to refute [the efficacy of an action]."
Place, time, person, and circumstance are what have been so described; "the distinctions of these" is the compound.

And since these various distinctions of place and so forth are obstructive only to some individuals and not to all, one should not entertain doubts about all [factors] in every case; showing this, he says "distant place," etc.:
"Due to being situated at a distant place, there may be an incorrect perception;
in that case, there might be doubt regarding something else, but merely going near [to the object] [removes it]."
The limit of sublation occurs through a change in time, person, or circumstance, but there is no dependence on such factors in that [sublation] itself,
as in the case of the cognition of a mirage and the like.
"Anyāśaṅkā" means the suspicion (*āśaṅkā*) regarding something else, such as water;
"kvacid" means in some [place].
"In the case of a mirage and so forth" means "merely approaching [the object]"; this is to be connected with the phrase "the limit of the exception.
What is meant is as follows:

Where distance alone can be the cause of error, there only the mere act of approaching is required to determine whether a sublation exists or not; one need not wait for time or other factors, because those are not causes of error in that context. He states an example for this: "like the cognition of a mirage and so forth."
The cognition of a mirage and so forth is the delusion of water and the like regarding a shimmering heat haze and such.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one should understand [other cases] such as the cognition of largeness in something small, and likewise the cognition of smallness in something large when it is at a distance, and so on;
for in those cases, there is no possibility of dependence on time and other factors for those who have approached nearby.
The same applies to time and the other factors as well.
By means of this example, he demonstrates that one should take into account only that which can possibly serve as the cause of error in a given case, and nothing else.
Regarding that, he speaks with reference to a specific time: "In such darkness," and so forth.
In such a time of deep darkness, whatever doubt there may be concerning cows, horses, and the like, or whatever erroneous determination occurs, its limit is the manifestation of light.
That time in which darkness has gathered is described as such.
With reference to a particular person, he says "tathā" and so forth:
"For instance, in cases such as [mistaken notions of] the moon, directions, the Vedas, colors, and accents,
the determination of their being otherwise occurs through inquiry of another person."

In the case of those suffering from ophthalmia and the like, when there is the cognition of two moons and so forth, the determination of its falsity occurs solely through questioning other persons; in that instance, there is no dependence on time or other such factors.

With reference to the distinction of states, he says "attachment, aversion," and so forth: "When an object is difficult to know, if it is being known by those whose faculties are impaired by attachment, aversion, intoxication, madness, hunger, thirst, and the like, there is error due to the absence of those [impairments]."
"Because of the absence of that" means because of the absence of the state of passion and so forth.
By the phrase "debt and so forth," he demonstrates through worldly convention as well that, regarding the knowledge of an investigator, there is dependence on a third [witness] alone;
for even in a transaction concerning debt and the like between two disputing parties,
there is one statement from the defendant and two statements from the plaintiff.
For fear of infinite regress, no further statement is written;
rather, the master, the witnesses, and the members of the court shall then deliver the final decision.
Thus, for all three types of knowledge, transformation is everywhere intended;
for this very reason, the "threefold truth" of the gods is also proclaimed.
Therefore, since both [validity and invalidity] are intrinsically established as valid or invalid as the case may be, there is no infinite regress for either of them.

Furthermore, even if the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of perception and other means of knowledge were established as extrinsic (*parataḥ*), while that of verbal testimony (*śābda*) were not, our position would still be proven. For this entire undertaking has the result of establishing the validity of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*). Once the intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of verbal testimony as a means of knowledge is established, the validity of the injunction is already established; therefore, what need is there for us to exert effort to prove the intrinsic validity of others? Thinking thus, and demonstrating the intrinsic validity of verbal testimony as a means of knowledge, he says "eternally" (*nityam*), and so forth.
Furthermore, whatever statement is determined to be eternal or composed by a trustworthy person is not corrupted in the slightest by either the listener or the speaker.
Those who are teachers of knowledge there, as well as fellow students, ward off destruction; such are they who are capable of protecting those like him.
Therefore, the statement is not seen to be affected by defects that are negated by its excellences;
or rather, in the absence of an author, those defects could not exist, being without a locus.
Verbal cognition as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is indeed twofold: that produced by an eternal sentence and that caused by a sentence composed by a reliable person (*āpta*).
Regarding these two types, he demonstrates the faultlessness of the cause.
For instance, in the case of an eternal sentence, no defect arising from a listener or a speaker is possible.
Because it is constantly protected by teachers of knowledge, instructors, and students;
and because, even regarding that which is spoken by a reliable authority (*āpta*), faults are excluded therein by virtues such as compassion.
Demonstrating the faultlessness of the eternal word in another manner, he says "Or rather" (*yadvā*) and so forth.
For defects such as passion and the like, being attributes of a person, reside only in an agent.
How could they persist in sentences that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) upon the cessation of their substratum, the agent?
For that would entail the consequence of them being non-resident [anywhere].
For this is the nature of a dependent phenomenon: that it conforms to its basis.

Now, one might object: "If the authority of the words of a reliable person (*āpta*) is accepted on the grounds that their virtues (*guṇa*) eliminate defects (*doṣa*), then authority would have to be admitted as arising from virtues; consequently, the fault of infinite regress (*avasthā-doṣa*) would apply here as well. Anticipating this, he says "In that case," and so forth: "In that regard, two things are observed in the speech of a reliable person: the absence of defects and the presence of virtues.
And it has already been explained how authority does not [arise] from virtues."
Therefore, because the speaker possesses excellence, defects are excluded by that;
and the sentence is inherently a means of valid cognition, characterized by the absence of defects.
That pair whose nature consists in the absence of defects and the presence of qualities is described as such.

"Thus stated" refers to what was said [in the verse] beginning with "If the status of perception and other means of valid cognition were dependent upon qualities," and so forth. "Refuted by that" means refuted by those [qualities].

The phrase "characterized by the absence of defects" implies that the intention is this: the function of qualities devoid of defects consists solely in the negation of defects, not in the production of validity.

Now, anticipating the objection of another school that even if validity is accepted as resulting from the ascertainment of the absence of defects, an infinite regress remains, he says "the absence of defects," and so forth:
"If the absence of defects in the words of a reliable person is understood through their excellences,
then the same infinite regress would occur for one who follows [the view] that [validity] is dependent upon the possession of excellences."

For instance, the absence of defects is to be ascertained through the thorough knowledge of excellences; furthermore, the validity [of that ascertainment] is to be determined from the absence of defects in the thorough knowledge of excellences. In that case too, the absence of defects is to be known from the excellences, and again in that case likewise—it is thus that very same infinite regress (anavasthā) remains, which destroys all systematic establishment.
He responds with the words "This is not a fault," and so forth:
"This is not a fault, for at that time the knowledge of qualities is not required at all;
qualities are not beneficial there by virtue of being known."
By their mere presence, they are all capable of turning away faults;
while they are present, no cognition whose object is human fault arises.
"In them existing" means in the qualities (*guṇa*).
If it is indeed not produced, then what follows? To this he says: "And by defects...
Because it is not being cognized as having defects, its validity is not sublated;
and since that [validity] is established when not sublated, it remains here too as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
The connection is that "validity is not set aside.
Why? Because it is not being cognized; and because faults are absent—since they are negated by excellences—it is for this very reason that they are not being cognized.

And as for the phrase "established as not set aside": it is established because it is not set aside; for when there is an absence of an exception to a general rule, that rule is established by its own nature.
Regarding the phrase "here too":
the word "too" (api) indicates that this applies not only to that which is non-human (apauruṣeya), but also to the words of a trustworthy person (āptavākya).
Now, one might object: even if faults are not actually perceived in some human statement, they are nonetheless possible, since they depend upon that [human agency].

Consequently, just as excellences (guṇas) are capable of excluding faults by their mere existence, so too faults are capable of excluding excellences. Therefore, why is it said that "validity is not sublated because the faults are not being perceived"? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The faults exist or do not exist," etc.
"In the case of a human statement, however, it is suspected whether faults exist or do not exist."
And because there is no author of the Veda, for us there is not even the slightest suspicion of error.
Therefore, that validity which is asserted for the Veda on account of its independence is established all the more intrinsically even in the case of what is composed by a reliable person.
He thinks as follows:

"It is not necessary for us to establish the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of human speech; rather, this entire undertaking is solely for the sake of establishing the authority of the Veda. Therefore, even if the lack of authority of human speech were to arise, there would be no harm whatsoever to the Veda, because its authority is established precisely due to the absence of any suspicion of defect. Thus, it is said [to be authoritative] because of its independence (*anapekṣatvāt*). As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Therefore, it is a means of valid knowledge because of its independence."
This being so, no other condition or another person need be expected, for this [condition] is itself a condition.

Furthermore, there are two possible positions: is it intended that there be an operation toward an object already determined by another means of valid cognition, or is it not? Regarding these, if the second position—that it is not intended—is held, then he shows that the authority of the Veda is established by its very nature with the words "vedārthe":

"Insofar as there is at all times a non-connection of the subject matter of the Veda with other means of valid cognition, by that very fact its status as a means of valid cognition is established; otherwise, it would be a mere restatement (anuvāda)."
The meaning of the Veda consists of such statements as "from the Agnihotra sacrifice, heaven results.

Regarding the phrase "by other means of valid cognition": this refers to the connection (*saṅgati*)—that is, the relationship through having a common object—with means other than the Veda, such as perception and so forth; the negation of that is "non-connection" (*asaṅgati*).
"By that very [means]" means by way of non-attachment; "of this" refers to the Veda.

Now, if the position is that the engagement [of a means of knowledge] is desired [only when the object is already known], then, because it would be apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*), the cognition occurring at a later time would not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*). Demonstrating this, he says: "Otherwise, there would be the status of a restatement (*anuvādatva*). Otherwise, if the engagement of a means of knowledge is desired even when the object has already been understood by other means of knowledge, then, because it illuminates an object already illuminated by another, it would have the status of a restatement; thus, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its invalidity, just like memory and so forth.

Therefore, the sense is that whatever is a means of valid cognition does not depend upon connection with another means of valid cognition; thus, the self-validity (svataḥprāmāṇya) of every means of valid cognition is established.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "of another as well," and so forth:
"Even if another [cognition] were a means of valid cognition, association would not be the cause;
for among cognitions of the same object, validity belongs to only one through the process of exclusion."
"Of another [means of knowledge] than the Veda" refers to perception and so forth.
"Of those having the same object" means those that operate upon a single subject matter.
"Of one alone" means of the first [member],
because the others are merely restatements (anuvāda).
Nor is it logical that the validity of the first [cognition] should depend on those subsequent cognitions, because they themselves lack validity since their objects have already been apprehended.

An objection is raised: "But surely, in a place of deep darkness and the like, even for an object already grasped by an initial cognition, there is a further determination by subsequent means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) during the state of clear illumination. Anticipating this, he says: "Even where there might be a determination again by subsequent means of valid cognition... and so forth. "Even where there might be a determination again by subsequent means of valid cognition, it is certain that in that case too, that object was not clearly ascertained by the preceding [cognition]."
The meaning is that because the object of the preceding cognition has not been definitively ascertained, it lacks validity altogether.

Furthermore, if validity were to result from the connection with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it would follow that a cognition whose object has perished immediately after arising, as well as auditory perception, would not attain validity, because no other means of valid cognition operates upon their respective objects. This is shown by the verse beginning with "sakṛt": "And there would be no validity regarding an object that has perished immediately after arising; moreover, auditory cognition would be invalid if it were not connected with [other senses] such as the eye."
"Not connected with the eye and so forth" means that there is no connection because they do not share a single object.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is independent of connection with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is valid by itself; for example, auditory cognition and a cognition that has perished after arising simultaneously. And the cognition whose object is the meaning of the Veda is independent of connection with another means of valid cognition. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
With the words beginning "If [it is argued] regarding the ear," etc., he raises the objection that the example lacks the probans (*sādhanavikalatā*):
"If its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) is due to its connection with another auditory cognition,
then it is established for the Veda as well, because of its connection with another cognition produced by it."
However, for both [parties], there is no cognition produced by another means of proof;
therefore, the corroboration of a cognition produced by a different cause is not required.

For instance, when even a single sound is being heard by many people, the validity of this auditory cognition is determined by its dependence on the connection with another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), due to the occurrence of other auditory cognitions.
He provides the rebuttal with the words "it is established even in the case of the Veda" and so forth, meaning "due to the connection with another cognition produced by that [Veda].
This refers to the relationship with another cognition generated by the Veda.
"Of both" refers to the auditory cognition and the cognition of the meaning of the Veda.

What is meant is this: in the statement "because of independence from connection with another means of valid cognition," what is intended by "another means of valid cognition" is that which is produced by a different instrument (*sādhana*), and not that which is to be accomplished by the same instrument. Therefore, since the reason is qualified, the sense is that the example is not deficient in its probans (*sādhanavikalatā*). [This refers to] "corroboration by a cognition produced by another cause."
And that knowledge is said to be "produced by another means" (hetvantara-kṛta); thus, the analysis of the compound is "the correspondence of that [knowledge]" (tasya saṃvādaḥ).

Now, if it is intended that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*) merely by the occurrence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be established by the same single means [as the first], then, considering this to be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), he says "Just as," and so forth:
"Just as the connection with another cognition dependent on the same sense organ is established as the cause for perception, so too let it be stated in the case of the Veda."
"The cause is established" means that its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is due to its connection with another auditory cognition, according to the statement [of the opponent].
To the question of how this should be explained regarding the Veda, he says: "By a single sentence alone," and so forth.
For when a correspondence with the fact is obtained through a single sentence across different places, times, and persons, no other cause need be sought.
Therefore, that cognition which has arisen firmly and is not contradicted by cognitions of other locations and so forth is undoubtedly a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
"Firmly" means because it is free from doubt and error.
"By cognitions of other locations and so forth" means...
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the cognitions of other persons and so forth.

Showing that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says "sādhyā" and so forth: "The validity (*pramāṇatā*) of words and the other [means of knowledge] is not something to be proven by inference; otherwise, let that [validity] of perception also not be [proven], since there is no distinction in its being equally something to be proven."
The sense is that the meaning of the Veda cannot first be established by perception, because it is beyond the reach of the senses;
nor can it be established by inference, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
[This applies] to words.
The word "of the Vaidikas" is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
or, the specific [subject] is understood from the context.

It might be argued: "Even for perception, its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is indeed established by inference. To this he says: "Of the means of valid cognition," and so forth. If the validity of the means of valid cognition is established by another [means], and that [other] is also established by yet another, then an infinite regress (anavasthā) would result.

If the validity of the means of cognition were established by something other [than itself], then that [validity] would likewise be established for the objects of cognition as well. Therefore, [the validity of the means of cognition] must be self-established.
If the validity of that inference were to be established by another inference, as in the case of perception, there would be an infinite regress.

Alternatively, if the validity of the means of proof called inference is not established by another, then let the validity of the things to be proven—such as perception and the like—not be established either, since there is no distinction between the two cases.
With the words beginning with "nanu," the Buddhist supports the very point that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Indeed, perception and the other means of knowledge are not apprehended as being "means of knowledge" in this manner;
and if they are not so apprehended, linguistic and practical activity (*vyavahāra*) cannot be accounted for.

If there were no dependence upon another means of valid cognition for the means of valid cognition themselves, then there would be no certainty regarding these [means], such as perception and so forth, that they are indeed "means of valid cognition.
Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total collapse of all worldly transactional activity.
He provides a rebuttal with the verse beginning "pramāṇaṃ grahaṇāt" and so forth:

"A means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is established in its own nature prior to apprehension; and being independent regarding its own object, once that object has been cognized, it is then measured by others. [2910]

This is what is meant: although a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) depends upon another means of valid cognition for the ascertainment of its own nature, nevertheless, there is no cessation of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), because it is independent of another means of valid cognition with respect to the determination of the object. If the object is determined, then by that much alone all practical activity is completed; so what is the use of investigating the certainty regarding the nature [of the cognition], since this [investigation] has the purpose of ascertaining the object? This is the summary meaning. The meaning of the individual words is now stated: "prior to the apprehension" (*grahaṇāt pūrvam*).

The meaning is "prior to the ascertainment that 'this is a valid means of cognition'. By "in its own nature" is meant "by way of the determination of the object. "Independent" means that, with respect to the determination of its own object, it does not depend upon another means of cognition.
When that [object] has been cognized by its own means of knowledge and ascertained, it is subsequently cognized by means of inference and other pramāṇas;
for as you yourselves have stated, even from us, [knowledge] is obtained only from what was previously unknown.
This is easy to understand.

If this is so, one might suspect that by this same logic, even valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would follow as being [established] only from itself; anticipating this, he says "invalid cognition" (*apramāṇa*), and so forth: "Furthermore, invalid cognition stands with respect to its own object as if it were a valid cognition; its falsity cannot be apprehended without another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)."

For that which is invalid appears as if it were valid; therefore, it does not determine its own object by its mere existence. Consequently, its falsity—that is, its character of determining a false object—cannot be apprehended without another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); thus, its status is established extrinsically (parataḥ).

But surely this is the same even for a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for that too, in some cases regarding its own object, appears as if it were not a valid cognition. To this he says: "For [there is] no alteration of the object," and so forth. For the alteration of the object was not grasped by the preceding [cognition], just as its true nature was.
Therefore, in this case as well, the cognition [of falsity] arises either when there is an alteration [of the object], or else when there is a defective cause.
And by that much alone, falsity is apprehended, not as having any other cause;
for this very state of arising is measured as being the means of valid cognition.
"By the former" means by the immeasurable. "Taken up" means...
It has been grasped.
"Like the state of being so" (*tathātva*) is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

This is what is meant: just as the state of being so is apprehended by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not the case that falsity (*mithyātva*) is [apprehended] by means of non-valid cognition; therefore, they are not the same.

For indeed, it is only while in the state of arising that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is cognized as "a means of valid cognition," and not as "not a means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*), because it always appears as a means of valid cognition; this is the intended meaning.
With the words beginning with "that" (*tad*), he concludes that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
Alternatively, the connection is with the phrase "cognition when the cause is defective" (*duṣṭakāraṇe dhīḥ*).
"And by that much alone" means:
otherwise, [the cognition would arise] through the notion of existence and through the notion of a defective cause.
This might be so.

If the correctness of these two cognitions were already apprehended, then falsity would be apprehended by them; and if there were a dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend their correctness, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, he says "at the stage of its arising," and so forth.
"This" refers to the cognition of an object otherwise than it is and the cognition of a defective cause.
Therefore, the sense is that there is no infinite regress.

Regarding the proof stated—namely, that "the Vedic word of the Buddhists and others has false meaning because it is a sentence, like the human statement 'fire is cold' and so forth"—the author says "Therefore, even where... etc., demonstrating that this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
"Therefore, even where falsity is being demonstrated to opponents, both of these [points] must be stated there, and not merely the similarity [of properties]."
"In which [case] also" refers to the initial injunction and so forth.
"These two" refers to the following pair.
The cognition of alteration and the cognition of a defective cause;
"mere similarity" means the equality with a human statement that lacks truth, by virtue of such properties as being a statement and so forth.
To provide the justification for why it should not be stated, he says "tatra" and so forth:
"In that regard, relying on some mere similarity with invalid cognition,
the unwise attempt to prove the falsity of all valid cognition."
For their own destruction, they conceive such means;
likewise, for another as well, a similar [means] arises by way of a reflection.

And because it has been refuted by that [scripture], the means of proof is not in accordance with reality; therefore, the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), being inherently authoritative, is not capable of being sublated.

If something were invalid merely by virtue of sharing a common property with what is invalid, then it would follow that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are invalid everywhere; for it is possible to state a common property such as "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) in every case—this is the summary of the meaning.
To explain how this leads to self-destruction, he says: "it arises," and so forth.
[He adds: "even for the opponent."
"Of the Mīmāṃsaka.

Regarding the phrase "by means of a reflection": just as a reflection arises immediately after an original object (*bimba*), so too does a counter-argument arise for the Mīmāṃsaka immediately after the proof (*sādhana*) presented by the Buddhist; this is the meaning.

For it can be stated as follows: "The Vedic word is non-false, because it possesses the nature of being speech and so forth, just like the human statement 'fire is hot and luminous. Since the Buddhist and others have proposed a proof for the thesis that 'the injunction (*codanā*) does not denote things as they truly are'—a proof which is thus refuted and contradicted by such a counter-proof—it is not capable of subverting the injunction. Why? Because of its intrinsic validity (*autsargika-prāmāṇya*). That whose validity is intrinsic is described as such; the state of being so is its essential nature."

To this, it is replied with the words "here it is said," and so forth; beginning from "and in the acquisition of their own nature by entities," he begins to state the refutation in due order: "To this it is replied: for those things whose persistence is desired once they have been produced, is this very arrangement not indeed well-founded?"
"With a basis" means having a real entity as its substratum; the sense is that an operation is impossible for that which is non-existent.
What, then, is this systematic arrangement? It begins with "the acquisition of self-nature" and so forth.
It is accepted that for jars and other such things, there is a dependence on causes at the time of acquiring their own nature;
however, once they have acquired their nature, their engagement in their own effects occurs by themselves alone.
Now, as to why it is not tenable even in the case of cognition, he says "But that which," and so forth:
"But as for that cognition which you also accept as unstable immediately after its birth—
since it has no self-nature once it has perished, what kind of activity could it have thereafter?"
"What kind of activity could there be for that which is non-existent?
The meaning is that there is none at all, because a non-entity is devoid of all causal capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Or, even if it were existent, no activity could be established because all entities are devoid of volitional impulse (*nirīhatva*).
Furthermore, there is no effect for cognition to exert itself toward;
if it is argued that its nature consists in the determination of its own object,
we say no.
Because this [means of knowledge] is a synonym for cognition, the claim that it "makes itself" is untenable.
If it is argued that its own function is the production of the ascertainment that "this is a valid means of knowledge," we say no;
for there is sometimes a lack of such ascertainment, and because the opposite is also observed.
By this, the contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition regarding the thesis here has also been established.

Nevertheless, through the non-perception of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility—which consists in the perception of something else—the absence of activity in a non-existent entity is ascertained by perception.
Furthermore, due to its lack of form, it is also established by inference, like a lotus in the sky.
By the phrase "this is also desired by you," he points out the contradiction with one's own statement.
He shows this very point with the two verses beginning with "the operation" (*tameva vyāpāra*).
For the operation of causes is indeed observed to be distinct from their birth;
[the author] intends to speak of "birth" so that the same [distinction] does not apply to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as well.
For that [cognition] does not remain for even a moment, nor is it produced as something non-cognitional,
such that it might subsequently function in the apprehension of an object like the sense organs and so forth.

For Kumārila has stated "activity" (*vyāpāra*) and so forth in order to demonstrate the utility of the inclusion of the term "birth" (*janman*) in this sūtra: "Perception is the arising of cognition in a person when there is contact of the sense-faculties with an existent object.
He says "for not... and so forth, in order to establish that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) belongs only to the cognition (*buddhi*) which is designated as "arising" (*jāyamāna*).
What is the reason? He says: "for not... and so forth.
"Tad" refers to cognition.
[p.771] With the words "But even if," etc., he anticipates the opponent's reply:
"But even if cognition is admitted to be non-momentary and eternal..."
This constitutes a contradiction with what has been accepted; thus, there is sublation by reasoning.
Likewise, elsewhere Kumārila has described the permanence and unity of cognitions;
as it was said: "Since cognitions also possess the nature of consciousness, their permanence and unity are therefore accepted; however, their differentiation is based on [their] objects."
In this position as well, there is a contradiction with what has been accepted (*abhyupetavirodha*) regarding the thesis, as well as a contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*).
For instance, the momentariness of cognitions has been accepted;
as it was stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "For that [cognition] is momentary; it will not persist until the time of another cognition."
Likewise, because of such statements as "it does not remain even for a single moment," there is also a contradiction with the sacred teachings (pravacana).
He demonstrates the contradiction with reasoning in the passage beginning with "sādhitvā" (having established).
For every entity has been established in detail as undergoing momentary destruction;
and since that which is eternal is not produced, what need could it have for dependence on a cause?
He demonstrates that the dependence on a cause is not logical if permanence is accepted, by means of the passage beginning with "And [if it were] permanent," and so forth.
For that which is produced depends on other causes out of a desire to attain its own existence; but as for that which is unproduced because of its permanence, what dependence could it have?
With the words "Therefore" (*ataś ca*) and so forth, he demonstrates the sublation by inference through the formulation of a formal argument (*prayoga*):
"And therefore, it can be said that valid cognition (*pramā*) does not function by itself;
subsequently, it [does not function] in its own effects because of its lack of nature (*nairūpyāt*), like a sky-lotus."
By the words "Or let it be," etc., [the author] concedes non-momentariness and demonstrates the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge:
"Or let cognition be non-momentary and proceed by itself;
if it were for the sake of determining its own validity, then why would there be doubt and so forth?"
If [a cognition] were to produce the ascertainment of its own validity by itself, then doubts and the like would not occur regarding that valid cognition.
By the word "and the like" (ādi), error, the contradiction preceded by it, contrary activity, the formulation of mutually contradictory definitions, and non-correspondence are included.

Consequently, because one experiences after a valid cognition a form of ascertainment that is the opposite of certainty—such as doubt and so forth—the absence of ascertainment is established by perception itself, just as the absence of a jar is established by the perception of a location devoid of it.
And consequently, there is a contradiction with direct perception regarding the proposition that it exists.
In TS 2928, beginning with the words *prāmāṇya*, he establishes the contradiction specifically regarding perception.
Since the ascertainment of validity occurs there by virtue of the presence of that [cognition] alone,
once it has arisen, doubt and error have no footing.
"In that" refers to the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
To the question "Why are they without a basis? he says "ascertainment," and so forth. (TS 2929)
Because there exists a relationship of sublation between certainty and the superimposing mind,
for it is only when superimposition is removed that complete certainty prevails.
Why is this so? He says: "Because of superimposition," and so forth.

For a certain cognition (*niścaya*), because its aspect is the opposite of superimposition, does not attain its own stability without first setting aside its object; just as the sensation of heat [does not coexist] with cold. Therefore, how could there be the occurrence of error regarding an object that has been apprehended by such a cognition?
Then, with the words beginning "tataś ca," he also demonstrates the contradiction with his own statement:
"And therefore, for the sake of establishing the validity of the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (codanā),
the argument that it arises from causes free from defects is pointless."
The state of being produced from a cause is "causally originated.
By the word "etcetera," [the following] is included: being produced by speech that is unerring and sublime, the absence of contradiction, and so forth.
For it is thus:

Cognition produced by an injunction is a valid means of knowledge because it is generated by causes free from defects, just like cognitions derived from logical marks, the words of a reliable person, and the senses.
---V Codanā 184:
Likewise, because it is produced by speech that is not uttered by one who is untrustworthy, and because it is free from sublation; XX ---V Codanā 185ab:
By stating this proof for the sake of establishing the validity of the cognition produced by *codanā*, it is asserted that the ascertainment of validity arises from extrinsic means (*parataḥ*).

Furthermore, for one who asserts that "the validity of all means of valid cognition is intrinsic" (YD 47ab) and "and the refutation thereof" (PVD 75b6), there is a contradiction between these two statements.
with the words beginning "siddhe," [the author] anticipates the opponent's reply:
"Once intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya) is established, [the scripture] serves to ward off exceptions."
Even if that were accepted, it would still be so, because such a doubt is impossible.
For doubt persists only so long as certainty has not arisen;
once that certainty has emerged, how can there be any room for invalidity?
By this means, one's effort toward the cessation of that [doubt] becomes purposeful;
for one who has ascertained the identity of a post does not suspect it to be otherwise.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "We do not state a proof for the sake of establishing the validity of the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*); rather, we do so to negate the invalidity that has been attributed to it by the opponent. This too is not tenable. Why? Because such a suspicion is impossible. For it has been stated: "Because there exists a relationship of sublated and sublator between the mind of certainty and the mind of superimposition," how then could this suspicion of invalidity arise once certainty has been produced?

By means of which your exertion in employing the proof (*sādhana*) for the sake of its cessation might become fruitful. Regarding this, he states the example beginning with "in the case of a post" (*sthāṇau*).
One who has understood the nature of being a post (*sthāṇutva*) as having a certain identity (*tādātmya*) is described as such.
"Alteration" refers to [the properties of] being a tree, being a person, and so forth. (TS 2934)
If this is so, how can the suspicion of invalidity be dispelled without the employment of a formal proof? To this he says: "yadrūpa... and so forth.
"When a certainty regarding a specific form arises with respect to a given object, the suspicion of its opposite is removed by that very [certainty]."
"Regarding the doubt of the opposite of that form":
this means regarding the doubt concerning a nature that is contrary to that form.
"From that very [source]" means because of the ascertainment of its form.
Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration with the words "Just as from smoke," and so forth:
"Just as when the existence of fire and such is apprehended through signs such as smoke,
the exclusion of its non-existence follows from that very same [apprehension]."
The exclusion of its non-existence means the exclusion of the non-existence of fire and so forth.
He concludes with the words beginning "apramāṇya" (non-authoritativeness): "In this way, let it be accepted that the exclusion of non-authoritativeness occurs by itself;
therefore, a formal proof for the removal of non-authoritativeness is not required."

Right here, he states the reason for the accumulation [of faults] with the words "if there were doubt regarding two types of valid cognition," and so forth: "If, however, doubt regarding two types of valid cognition were to arise in that case, there would be no ascertainment of validity, because it would have been made the object of error."
The two types of invalid cognition consist of doubt and error.

By means of the verse beginning with "ya" (who), [the author] demonstrates the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving what is pervaded by a contradictory [property], thereby establishing the contradiction with one's own words:
"That which has been made an object of cognition by doubt or erroneous cognition— just like a post— there is at that time no ascertainment of its true nature."
Because the object made the focus of doubt and error—which are contrary to certainty—is pervaded by them, there is no room for certainty regarding it.

With the verse beginning "By the cognition of the crow" (*balibhuk*), he demonstrates the contradiction with inference (*anumāna-virodha*) and the establishment of his own position (*svapakṣasiddhi*):
"Just as a post, fire, non-authoritativeness (*apramāṇa*), and so forth, are determined by others through cognitions such as the crow, smoke, the arising of causes, and defects."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those whose natures are made objects of doubt or error must have their true nature determined by another, just like a post or similar objects; and the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of certain [cognitions] is likewise made an object of doubt or error. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
"Smoke-eater" (*balibhuk*), "smoke" (*dhūma*), and "faults arising from causes" (*hetūtthadoṣa*) are mentioned thus;
the compound *teṣu pratyayāḥ* means "cognitions regarding those."
And by these [examples], the connection with the post and so forth is shown in their respective order;
and by this, the pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason is demonstrated.
Now, avoiding the charge of non-establishment by teaching that [the reason] is a property of the subject, he says: "That which has become the object of doubt or error,
let its ascertainment by another [means] be understood as the criterion for its being a valid means of knowledge."
"Yat" means "because";
"gatam" means "gone."
It is certain.
Of what? The word "of a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇasya) is to be supplied as the remainder.
For it has been established that the cognition produced by Vedic injunction (codanā) is the object of doubt and error.
"So be it.
Just as there is a determination regarding a post or similar object based on something external,
the statement beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth demonstrates the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

Regarding what was stated in TS 2941–2942—that once intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is established, there is a need for a proof to ward off exceptions—that is not tenable, as it has been demonstrated that such a suspicion is impossible. Now, even granting that a formal argument might be employed to remove the suspicion of invalidity, he says "And this... and so forth, showing that even such an argument is not tenable according to your own position:
"And this is your position: in whatever sentence the negation is not heard... [TS 2942]
In that very case, the exclusion of others is understood as its own nature in another instance.
And here, there is no formal application (prayoga) stating that "the cognition produced by an injunction is a means of valid knowledge" (pramāṇa);
therefore, there is no exclusion of invalidity (aprāmāṇya).

For you who maintain that the meaning of words is purely prescriptive (vidhi), this is your position: that in whichever sentence a negative particle (*nañ*) is employed, there the exclusion of another (*anyavyavaccheda*) is understood, whereas elsewhere it is simply a prescription.
Now, in this probative statement beginning with "not produced by an injunction" (*codanājanita*), there is no employment of a negative particle.
Therefore, how could the exclusion of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) be established by means of this?
Regarding what was stated in TS 2943— "how then [can there be] doubt and so forth?"— he shows the meaning conveyed by the word "and so forth" (ādi) with the words beginning "Furthermore," etc.:
"Furthermore, if the validity of all means of valid cognition were ascertained..."
If it were established by itself alone at that time, why would there be a difference of opinion among the proponents?
If the validity of all means of valid cognition were established through themselves alone, then there would be no difference of opinion among disputants regarding the nature of that validity.
To explain how that very [principle] is established, he says: "By which some," and so forth.

By which some [authorities], such as the Mīmāṃsakas, a restriction is loudly proclaimed that [validity] arises from itself alone; while by others, it is held that something [arises] from itself and something from another, and thus no fixed rule is accepted.
"By some" refers to the Mīmāṃsakas;
"by others" refers to the Buddhists.

By them, certain [means of valid cognition] are accepted as intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), such as self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), the cognition of a yogin, the cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyājñāna*), inference, and perception resulting from repeated practice (*abhyāsavat*).

For that [cognition] is indeed ascertained by itself (*svataḥ*), because the causes of error have been cast aside through the power of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). However, some [cognitions] are [ascertained] from another source, such as the cognition produced by a Vedic injunction (*codanā*) which is the subject of dispute, and perception in which the cause of error has not been removed, because neither repeated practice nor the cognition of successful purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) has been attained.
If this were so, then according to your view, there would be no dispute regarding inference and the like, since they would be valid by themselves (*svataḥ*).

For instance, some maintain that inference arises from a logical mark (liṅga) possessing three characteristics, some that it is born from a mark with two characteristics, and others that it originates from a mark with a single characteristic. Furthermore, the formulation of its definition would be useless.
Likewise, it is the same as saying that one need not establish its validity for the sake of the Lokāyata school, because its validity is determined intrinsically (svataḥ).

This is not a fault, because inference arises from the ascertainment of a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is constrained by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*); thus, even without a direct correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*), its non-deviation from the object is ascertained through its being produced by a causal chain ultimately dependent on such a thing. Therefore, its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is asserted.

It is only because the proponent lacks full knowledge of the nature of the logical mark as the cause for that [inference’s] production that they dispute one another while the inference has not yet arisen; once it has arisen, there is no dispute, because its nature and so forth have been ascertained.
For this very reason, the teachers, in their definition [of inference], perform only the exposition of the nature of the mark (liṅga) as the cause for the arising of that [inference].
For how indeed could the production of inference occur from the determination of the nature of a contrary mark?
Furthermore, the objection that it is unnecessary to establish the validity of inference against the Lokāyata is also untenable.
For we do not establish the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of inference; rather, we establish its conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). To explain:

the Lokāyata, deluded by hearing treatises that teach false objects, does not engage in the usage of inference even though its validity is established—just as the Sāṅkhya does not. Therefore, by demonstrating its object, the usage which possesses that object is established.
Whatever is produced from something is endowed with the capacity to bring about that [same] thing, just as perception is with respect to its own object.

And this cognition of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), which arises from the object to be inferred and arrives by way of the perception of a mark connected to that [object], is established as valid through the communication of the convention in this manner;
for, in the case of perception, he has applied the conventional usage of "validity" solely on the basis of non-deviation from the object.
And what else could its non-deviation be than its arising from that [object]?
As it has been said:
"Since there is no [cognition] in the absence of an object, even in the case of perception there is validity;
since that which possesses a nature connected [to the object] is the cause of that [cognition], both [perception and inference] are equal."

Thus, as it is said in *Pramāṇaviniścaya* 1.3: "Therefore, just as the Sāṅkhya, although determining the absence of an elephant on the tip of a blade of grass, fails to engage in the conventional usage of 'absence' due to the delusion caused by hearing [false] scriptures, so too does this Lokāyata."

Furthermore, the validity of cognition produced by *codanā* (Vedic injunction) is not established; for if it were, one could argue that its status as valid is here being proven—just as in the case of inference—through conventional usage. However, this is not the same [as the case of inference], because the necessary invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is not established there, and thus validity itself remains the thing to be proven. It might be argued: "Let there indeed be a difference of opinion; why, then, is it not consistent with the theory of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*)? To this he says: "The dispute arises from error," and so forth.
"Because the dispute arises from error, and that [error] is sublated by certain knowledge (*niścaya*)."
Having thus ascertained the reality, the disputants would no longer engage in debate.

By this, demonstrating the establishment of the absence of certainty through the perception of the effect of error—which is contrary to certainty—he shows that the proposition of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is contradicted by inference.

Furthermore, he demonstrates another perception of an effect contrary to certainty with the words "intrinsic" (*svataḥ*), etc.: "If the validity of all means of knowledge were determined intrinsically..."
Nothing whatsoever would be subject to contradiction, because it would function with certainty.
For one who acts with the notion that what is not a valid means of knowledge is a valid means of knowledge is indeed deceived;
however, through the realization of intrinsic validity, no one is ever led astray.

For non-conformity (visaṃvāda) is recognized as the effect of an error that is contrary to certainty; and that [non-conformity] would not occur if intrinsic validity were accepted, because the cause of that [error], namely the error itself, would have been removed by certainty. The term "contrary" (viparīta) refers to that which possesses non-conformity.
With the words "nanu" and so forth, the opponent objects:
"Surely, one who acts on the basis of what is not a valid means of knowledge incurs either [cognitive] failure or contradiction;
for its ascertainment is held to be extrinsic, through a sublating cognition."
But one who proceeds on the basis of a valid means of cognition does not encounter non-correspondence;
and it is precisely for this [cognition] that we maintain the ascertainment of intrinsic validity.

For one who acts on the basis of what is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), there is indeed deception; and it is already accepted that the ascertainment of that non-valid means of knowledge depends upon something else.
However, for one who acts on the basis of what is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no deception.
And since its own intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya) is accepted [by you], how can the proposition of intrinsic validity be contradicted by inference?
He replies with the words beginning "Not due to ignorance of the intention," etc.: "This is indeed what is intended here:
that the validity of all means of valid cognition is determined intrinsically (*svataḥ*)."
Since there is no determination of intrinsic validity in that case,
non-validity is understood therein by the force of elimination.
Therefore, because its lack of authority is ascertained immediately after its arising, without depending on a cognition of defects produced by a change in the object or its cause.
It is not logical to mistake that which is not a means of valid cognition for a means of valid cognition;
therefore, no one would ever act based on such [a cognition], since it does not accord with reality.
