This is what is intended here: if you accept that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possess intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), then you would have accepted that a means of valid cognition is pervaded by the arising of the ascertainment of its validity.

Consequently, wherever the ascertainment of validity—which is the pervader of the means of valid cognition—does not arise, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) necessarily follows by implication, because valid and invalid cognitions are mutually exclusive in nature.

Consequently, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) also follows by its own inherent capacity, because there is no dependence on the recognition of causes for non-correspondence; this is because invalidity is ascertained through the mere non-arising of the ascertainment of validity. Therefore, that which was stated—"its ascertainment is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), [arising] from a subsequent cognition that sublates it"—is not tenable.

This being the case, since validity and its opposite are ascertained respectively by the production or non-production of the certainty regarding validity, no activity whatsoever could possibly occur for any discerning person based on what is not a valid means of knowledge; so how could there be any possibility of non-correspondence? "From the cognition of that" means from the ascertainment of the state of being non-correspondent.

These [objections] should be regarded as defects of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) alone, because they reveal the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the reason by way of exposing defects in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*); they are not, however, defects of the thesis itself.
For otherwise, since the thesis is not a constituent part of the proof, exposing its defects would constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the opponent.
Demonstrating that the example "like a jar" and so forth is unestablished, he says: "And a time for action distinct from the time of birth does not exist;
because jars and the like are momentary, the illustration is unestablished."

But surely, jars and the like are indeed seen after their birth to perform purposeful actions such as holding honey or water without depending on potters and so forth; how then can it be said that for them there is no time distinct from their birth?
To this he says "teṣām" and so on:
"For of those [jars] which do not depend on potters and the like at a later time..."
Because it depends upon its own material cause and other factors, there is no self-initiated activity.
One's own material cause (*upādāna*) is each preceding moment of the same genus;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the person who possesses it and so forth is intended.

What is meant is this: at a later time, entirely different moments of a jar or other objects are seen existing in dependence upon their own material causes and so forth; however, the continued existence of anything after its birth is not established, because all entities are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Just as the first cognition," he says "And not... and so forth: "Nor is there the consequence of infinite regress, because [the validity] relies on another means of knowledge; therefore, the ascertainment of intrinsic validity occurs in the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*)."
The opponent objects [with the words beginning with] "nanu":
"Indeed, what excellence does that [subsequent cognition] possess over its predecessor,
such that it is not accepted as being dependent on another, just like the preceding cognition?"
He provides the formal definition with the words beginning "It is said," and so forth: "It is said that validity consists in correspondence with reality;
and for that, there is no defining characteristic other than the cognition resulting from repeated purposeful action."
And cognition appearing as purposeful action is clearly experienced;
it is also ascertained by a mental state consisting of a reflective awareness (*amarśana*) that arises from that [experience] alone.
Therefore, because its own intrinsic validity has been correctly ascertained,
no further cognition of the attainment of purposeful action need be awaited.

And since that first cognition, which manifests the object to be accomplished, possesses the nature of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the determination of its validity follows from this very reason.

This is the summary of the meaning here: valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed defined as non-contradictory knowledge, according to the statement, "Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge. And this non-contradiction is characterized solely by causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), because the investigation of valid cognition has that [efficacy] as its purpose.
A discerning person, seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), investigates whether a cognition is valid (*pramāṇa*) or invalid (*apramāṇa*), not out of mere habit.

That purposeful action is characterized by the arising of a cognition manifesting [effects] such as burning or cooking; for, precisely through the production of that [cognition], the desire of one who has engaged in activity for the sake of purposeful action is satisfied.

And that cognition of purposeful action manifests of its own accord through the direct perception of self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*); because it is a clear experience, it is subsequently ascertained by the arising of a reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*) in accordance with that experience. Thus, it is established intrinsically (*svataḥ*).

Nor is that [cognition] something to be accomplished as another fruit desired by a person, such that there would be an infinite regress for one who pursues the arising of another cognition appearing as a further purposeful action.

For in the world, fruits such as prosperity or its cessation are what is sought after, and these are fully realized simply through the manifestation of cognitions in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth; since people cease their efforts once they have attained satisfaction by this much alone, it is said that its establishment is "self-evident" (*svataḥ*).
Furthermore, that prior cognition which serves as the cause has the capacity to reach its object (*prāpaṇa-śakti*), and this is called its validity (*prāmāṇya*).

Since this capacity cannot be determined by those who have not practiced and thus do not recognize the effect, it is ascertained through the subsequent activity of the resulting cognition; therefore, the validity of the first [cognition] is said to be extrinsic (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*).
Furthermore, avoiding the charge of infinite regress in another way, he says "In the first," and so forth:
"For regarding the first object, which is a real entity, the second [cognition]— characterized by correspondence with the real entity— would not arise, because its cause would be impossible."
For indeed, in the case of one who misapprehends a cluster of *aśoka* blossoms and the like as fire,
a cognition manifesting burning and cooking never arises.
Alternatively, if it were produced from something of a different class, it would follow that it is not fire;
for fire is characterized by its connection to those specific effects.

For if the initial, first cognition had been directed toward a non-entity, then the subsequent cognition of the result would not have arisen at a later time, due to the absence of its cause; this is because the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) is necessarily bound to a real entity. Indeed, from a cognition that apprehends what is not fire—such as when one acts with the determination that it is fire upon seeing a cluster of *aśoka* blossoms—there do not arise cognitions manifesting burning, cooking, and so forth. Or, if such cognitions were indeed produced, then that [object] would simply be fire; why? Because the defining characteristic of fire (*vibhāvasu*) or heat is precisely its status as the cause for the production of effects such as burning and cooking. This is the meaning.
He concludes with the words "Therefore" and so forth:
"Therefore, as long as a cognition appearing as purposeful action has not arisen,
a doubt regarding the validity of the first [cognition] arises due to the causes of error."
Now, one might object: "Just like the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), the initial cognition is also directly produced by the object such as fire;
so why is there a suspicion of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) regarding that [initial cognition] alone, and not regarding the subsequent one? Anticipating this, he says "immediately after," and so forth:
"Immediately after, there is the non-perception of the result and the perception of similarity."
Furthermore, the mother's lack of clarity and so forth are the causes of error in this case.
But when a cognition manifesting the effect has arisen, this [uncertainty] does not exist,
because there is a direct perception of the activity that is intrinsically bound to the real entity.

For in the first cognition there exists a cause of error; namely, the non-occurrence of a result characterized by burning and so forth immediately following that [first cognition], the similarity of the cognition to an erroneous one, and the lack of proficiency in the intellect.
By the word "and so forth," disregard, lack of practice, and the like are included.
However, in the case of the cognition of the result, no cause of error whatsoever exists; therefore, its ascertainment occurs through itself (*svataḥ*).

Showing that even in the first cognition, where the cause of error has been dispelled by repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) and so forth, its validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), he says "In the case of [the cognition]... and so on:

"But when there is repeated practice, a distinction is perceived from a cognition that does not have that [object] as its domain, even though the result of that [first cognition] was already obtained."

Just as for yogins, or for those skilled in such matters, a cognition arises with a vivid appearance regarding gems, syllables, and the like—where the causes of error have been entirely removed—so too, elsewhere, through the power of practice, a cognition arises with an even more vivid appearance, free from any suspicion of delusion. Arising without interruption, it produces a reflective awareness (*parāmarśapratyaya*) that determines its own kind and excludes what is dissimilar; thus, being excluded from that which is of a different class and not its object, its validity is said to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

As for the one who thinks that even when an activity is accompanied by repeated practice, the ascertainment of validity—characterized by the capacity to reach the object—is achieved through inference alone because of the observation of a mark characterized by conformity (*tādrūpya*), and thus the determination of validity is always extrinsic (*parataḥ*) and never intrinsic (*svataḥ*);
we do not understand this.
For it must be explained from where the ascertainment of the mark, characterized by unconfounded conformity, itself arises.

If it is argued that this is due to repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), then, in that case, if a non-confused similarity (*sārūpya*) common to members of the same class is determined through the exclusion of dissimilar forms by the power of practice—since there is no cause for error—why is there such an aversion to its being a valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) that one would claim it is not determined even when it has been experienced and there is an absence of causes for error? Furthermore, what is this so-called "similarity"? If it is the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpatā*), then because that exists even in false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*).
If it is argued that [the mark] is the appearance as red, that exists in a cognition apprehending things such as a cluster of *aśoka* flowers; thus, there is indeed a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
If, on the other hand, it is the state of being an effect of an object such as fire, it must be explained how that is ascertained.
If one were to pursue another further mark to establish that, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, it might be argued that by the power of habituation alone, that [capacity] is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) even without following a logical mark (*liṅga*); it is established of its own accord.

If that is so, then if such a capacity of habituation is admitted, why is it not also admitted that the ascertainment of the [cognition's] capacity occurs through the power of habituation alone, even without following a logical mark?

Furthermore, if that status as an effect (*kāryatā*) of cognition is established, then the pursuit of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is useless; for from the very determination of its being an effect, the capacity to bring about the attainment of that object is established, just as in the case of inferential cognition (*anumāna*).

Just as inferential knowledge possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) because it arises through the power of perceiving a mark (*liṅga*) that is connected to a real entity, and thus determines—indirectly—that the object is its effect, rather than by the force of similarity (*sārūpya*);
for otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), so too here [in the case of perception], validity must be intrinsic.

For instance, where the cognition of the probandum (*sādhyārtha*) does not arise even when the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is ascertained, the cognizer must then follow the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the instance (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*).

In this case, however, since the capacity of cognition to lead one to its object is established precisely through the determination of that effect—given that it does not deviate from the object—it is not "conformity with the form" (*tādrūpya*) that serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*).

If this is so, how is it that the Teacher, concerning the Lokāyata, said: "He indeed asserts that perception alone is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not inference"? [The answer is: Having observed the correspondence and non-correspondence of certain individuals in their activity, he would state its definition through universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) for the sake of ensuring that one who acts according to the instruction is not deceived. That is to say, what is established as such through similarity to what has been perceived does not exceed the status of being an object of inference. This is not a fault; for this was stated with reference to cognitions occurring in one's own or another's continuum that have objects not [directly] experienced.
Because of the statement, "except for those [cognitions] whose objects have been previously experienced," otherwise—
if validity were determined in all cases merely through similarity (sārūpya)— then the prohibition "except for those whose objects have been previously experienced" would be purposeless.
Therefore, it is established that a cognition which arises when the causes of error have been dispelled by the force of repeated practice is valid by itself (*svataḥ*).
Regarding what was stated— "Just as the first cognition requires corroboration," and so forth— he replies with the verse beginning "vailakṣaṇya" (due to the non-perception of difference):
"But when there is no perception of a difference [from other cognitions], then due to the suspicion that the object might be of a different kind,
there can be no ascertainment of its validity without a subsequent cognition that manifests the [intended] effect."
In that case, even though its status as a means of valid cognition exists, it cannot be determined;
it is cognized solely through the subsequent knowledge of the action and so forth.
Therefore, that first cognition depends upon corroboration;
yet, in the same way, a further corroboration by means of another corroboration need not be sought.

For where validity, though experienced, cannot be ascertained due to the presence of causes for error, it is ascertained through another cognition—that of successful purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*). Since the person’s desired object is accomplished by that alone and their expectation is thereby satisfied, no further corroboration need be sought through yet another corroboration, just as in the case of the initial cognition.
Regarding the objection that "if it were desired for someone [else]," and so forth, he says "because of the cause of error," and so on:
"Because the cause of error is absent, its validity is intrinsic;
whereas for the first [cognition], if that [cause] is present, there is aversion [to its validity] because of the possibility of error."

[2946,11] But surely, a cognition whose capacity to reach an object is uncertain because its inseparable connection with that object is doubted—would that not fail to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like inference?
For it is accepted that inference lacks validity when there is doubt regarding the object's inseparable connection; likewise, it would follow that perception also lacks validity.
This is not a fault.

For perception is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it demonstrates its own nature as being inseparable from the object in the manner of inference; rather, it functions by determining the object as it appears.
Thus, that which brings about the attainment of the desired object for one seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is called a valid means of knowledge.

It does not become "that which brings about attainment" by moving the person to the location of the object, or by bringing the object to the location of the person; rather, it does so by impelling the person toward action.

And one does not set that person in motion by grasping him with the hand; rather, one indicates the object of his activity. And that indication consists in nothing other than the determination of the appearing object.
And wherever there is doubt, there necessarily exists a determination of the appearing form.
Because it is impossible to have a reflective judgment (*vimarśa*) regarding that [object] if it has not been ascertained (*anavasāya*).

Therefore, since the operation of perception is completed by this much, a subsequent doubt regarding the invariable concomitance with the object does not obstruct the operation of perception; thus, even when doubt arises, the validity of the perception remains intact.

However, that which arises being seized by a determinative judgment of a form contrary to the object appearing in it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the cognition grasping a mirage which is seized by a determinative judgment of water, because in that case the operation of the aforementioned means of valid cognition is absent.

Furthermore, that which I suspect to be the cognition of a yellow [object] when there is the luster of a gem, or the cognition of a gem when there is the luster of a gem—that too is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because in those cases there is an absence of both appearance and determination (*avasāya*) that correspond to reality.
For the apprehension or non-apprehension of perception depends upon the power of appearance, and not merely upon non-contradiction with the object.

Moreover, in this case, there is no appearance of an object as it exists in its own nature, place, and time; nor is the place and time identical to those [of the actual object], since place and time are also differentiators of the nature of an object.
Otherwise, indeed, the conventional usage of difference would be abolished.

Since inference, being conceptual in nature, has the universal as its object, the determination that it has a real entity as its object cannot be based on appearance; for the real entity does not appear [in inference], but rather [its objectivity is established] by virtue of ascertainment.
As it has been said:
"How can that form which is not ascertained by determinate cognitions (*niścaya*) be their object? (PV 1.59b–d).

Furthermore, since inference—though devoid of a fallacious appearance—arises by the power of perceiving an object that is inseparably connected [to the probandum], its validity is due to an indirect connection with the real entity; therefore, a certainty regarding the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) must necessarily be required therein.
Otherwise, the arising of inference would be impossible. Thus, perception is not equal to inference.
With the words "nanu" and so forth, the opponent points out the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) that arises when validity is established by something else:
"Now, if the validity of that [subsequent cognition] is not yet ascertained, how could a discerning person proceed toward it, since their desired goal has not been reached?"

For indeed, for one who acts with prior reflection, there must be activity once certainty regarding validity has been attained; yet, since there is certainty regarding validity only when activity exists, there is a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). Thus, how could there be activity for a discerning person when the desired object has not been ascertained?
He responds with the words beginning "It is said," etc.:
"It is said that this discerning person proceeds by means of doubt alone."
And thus, no impairment of his omniscience follows as a consequence.
For activity is of two kinds: that which aims at purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and that which aims at the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇyaniścaya*).

Regarding these, it has been demonstrated how the first kind of activity occurs even when there is doubt, because perception functions as an instigator of action merely by the determination of the object as it appears.

Therefore, in this case, no impairment of its distinctiveness follows; for it is observed that even with doubt regarding the object, people such as farmers still engage in activity—this is the intended meaning.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that the conduct of farmers and others who act without certainty regarding their means is characterized by acting with prior reflection (*prekṣāpūrvakāritā*), because a means is dependent upon its end (*upeya*); for if the end is not certain, certainty regarding the means is impossible. Showing that even the second type of activity is all the more appropriate even when there is doubt regarding validity, he says: "By doubt," and so forth.

Since its occurrence depends upon doubt, it is therefore a means of knowledge because it is a certain method for the ascertainment of validity; thus, it remains a means of knowledge even when doubt exists.

Since that person has ascertained that activity prompted by doubt is itself the means for determining validity, it is entirely appropriate for him to engage in action, given the absence of doubt regarding the means.
How is that means determined by him? He says: "If one acts with doubt," and so forth:
"If, while acting with doubt, the attainment of the result should occur for me, then the ascertainment of its validity will indeed be known right there."
"It is not otherwise," nor is such an inquiry as "Why does he abide in the means? appropriate here, for there is no other way [to attain the goal].
For no one attains the goal without the means;
thus, even one who harbors doubt does not forfeit their status as a discerning person.
"Even one who acts out of doubt" means even one who has proceeded with a doubt regarding its validity (*prāmāṇya*).
The rest is easily understood.

With the words "But surely... and so forth, the opponent demonstrates the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the determination of validity based on the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), thereby supporting his own position.
For surely, even in a dream, there exists a cognition that appears as purposeful action;
yet that [dream cognition] possesses no validity, nor does its cause—the first [waking cognition].
"Of that first cause" means of the cause of the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*). The connection is that it does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*).
He responds with the words "It is not so," and so forth:
"It is not so; for that state is indeed an error, entirely lacking any external basis. In those states, there is no correspondence with an external object."
Moreover, since they are of a nature known by themselves and are not distinct from mind and mental factors,
the difference between the two states is also clearly perceived by that [consciousness].

If, first of all, this objection is raised against a Buddhist who maintains the existence of external objects, then it has been shown by the first verse that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For in this way, that proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) maintains that validity (*prāmāṇya*) arises from correspondence with the object (*arthasaṃvāda*), and not from correspondence with the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñānasaṃvāda*). Furthermore, there is no correspondence with an object in dreams, because all dream states are erroneous and thus lack any non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) therein; since all cognitions arise even without an object, they are devoid of a real referent (*nirviṣayatva*). Therefore, the point is that since the definition of validity applies only to the cognition occurring in the waking state, it is not logical to allege a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) on account of this [dreaming].

Furthermore, in a dream, the cognition of causal efficacy is non-occurrence-based, lacks prior continuity, is unstable, and confused; whereas in the waking state, it is the opposite of that. Thus, since such [waking] cognition possesses validity, how can there be an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) based on dreams?
If this objection is raised against the Yogācāra, even then it is irrelevant to the present context.
For this definition of valid cognition pertains to the conventional level (*sāṃvyavahārika*).
"Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge" (PV 2.1ab).

In this context, non-contradiction is precisely the experience of a cognition that manifests purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), because when such [action] appears, people engage in worldly activity accordingly.
And because the engagement with objects is for that purpose;
and that conventional knowledge belongs to the waking state,
since in that very state all worldly transactions are clung to as being ultimately real.
But this is not the case in the state of dreaming;
therefore, since the qualification "while being a cognition of the waking state" has not been heard [in the definition], there is no deviation by means of the other [dream-cognition].
It might be thought that if its validity were determined by something else, it would follow that it is an object of cognition; but surely this is not contradictory.

It might be argued as follows: "If everything appears identically in all its aspects [as being produced by another], how is this distinction determined? In that case, because it is being measured by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would become an object of cognition (*prameya*); and it is not logical for the means of valid cognition itself to be the object of cognition, due to contradiction. This is the objection. The rebuttal is: "But this is not contradictory. "This" (*ada*) refers to this very point.
Due to the difference in perspective, there is no contradiction, just as in the designations of cause and effect or father and son.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "tad-grāhya" and so forth:

"For its validity is proclaimed as being dependent upon the object to be apprehended by it; since that [object] is understood through something else, its status as an object of cognition (prameyatva) is established."
And thus, due to the difference in perspective, just as in the case of cause and effect and so forth,
the established distinction between the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the status of being an object of valid cognition (*prameya*) is not contradictory.

With respect to that object which is apprehended by that cognition, it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and not the object of cognition (*prameya*); however, with respect to another establishing means of valid cognition, it is indeed the object of cognition and not the means of valid cognition. Thus, there is no fault of confusion, just as the terms "effect" and "cause" are not confused due to the difference in their mutual dependence.
He concludes with the words "Thus" and so forth:

"Thus, when the status of a means of valid cognition is ascertained through the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), there is no infinite regress, because further expectation has ceased; this is established."

Regarding the phrase "due to the cessation of further expectation" (*parākāṅkṣāvinivṛtteḥ*): the analysis of the compound is that it is both "further" (*parā*)—meaning other—and "expectation" (*ākāṅkṣā*).

Alternatively, "further expectation" (*parākāṅkṣā*) is the expectation regarding something else, namely something other than the corroboration; [the phrase means] "due to the cessation of that. This is the compound.

Furthermore, by the definition "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge," this characteristic is stated for that cognition which is the cause for attaining a result characterized by the realization of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Consequently, since this characteristic does not apply to the cognition of the result itself, how could there be any room for the objection: "How is its validity determined?
For instance, when the seed is defined as the cause of the sprout, would a question arise among the wise: "How is the sprout itself a seed? [The answer is that it would not.]

Just as the existence of a seed is understood from the observation of its sprout, so too the validity of a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is understood from the observation of its fruit, characterized by purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Furthermore, the fruit in that case is not apprehended by another means of cognition, which would lead to an infinite regress;
for the fruit, being of the nature of cognition, is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) itself.
Furthermore, error regarding the very nature of cognition is impossible;
for if that [nature] were not ascertained, it would follow that self-reflexive awareness itself does not exist—thus, this argument is trivial.

Now, having raised the prima facie objection regarding the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in the determination of validity by means of the purity of the cause— starting with the verse beginning "Even when [cognition] has arisen"— the author refutes it with the verse beginning "In this case as well. "Even when a cognition has arisen, it is not yet determined for as long as the purity of its cause has not been apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)."
Regarding this as well, the wise have said that it is called "various states" because that purity is recognized through a non-dependent, corroborative cognition.
For when an object is proximate, the purity of the causes is understood without effort simply by observing the correspondence with the resulting cognition.
For when an object is remote, the cognition arising from it is valid,
because it is produced by that [object], just like this [cognition] which has a proximate object as its domain.
For knowledge is of two kinds: that which has a proximate object and that which has a remote object.
Among these, in the case of that which has a proximate object, the determination of its validity does not arise from the ascertainment of the excellence of its causes;
rather, it arises from a cognition that accords with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

For in that case, the ascertainment of the qualities [of the cause] is not possible as long as validity is not determined through correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, once validity is established, the subsequent ascertainment of the qualities of the causes occurring at a later time is entirely irrelevant.

However, regarding knowledge whose object is a remote thing (*viprakṛṣṭārtha*), he says "for in the case of the remote," etc., demonstrating that the determination of its validity arises from the certainty of the qualities of its causes.

In the case of the cognition apprehending a golden conch-shell which has a remote object, its validity is ascertained because it is produced by that [pure cause], that is, because it is produced by a pure cause, just like the cognition apprehending a white conch-shell which has a proximate object. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: whatever is produced by a pure cause is valid, such as the consciousness apprehending a white conch-shell which has a proximate object; and this consciousness appearing as a yellow-shaped conch-shell, which has a remote object, is produced by a pure cause. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
But is it not the case that the reason is unestablished?
For indeed, the purity of the cause cannot be ascertained without correspondence with the object, because the sense faculties are beyond the reach of the senses.
And if there is dependence upon correspondence with the object, then validity itself is already determined; thus, the ascertainment of the excellence of the causes would be entirely useless.
This is because [the determination of its validity] occurs at a time subsequent to the ascertainment of its validity.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "At one time, having ascertained the possession of excellence (*guṇavattā*) through the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*) from a cognition whose object is proximate, one may later ascertain the possession of excellence—even for a cognition whose object is remote—without any correspondence, simply by virtue of that previous certainty; therefore, the ascertainment of validity will come about.
This is incorrect.

For entities that perish moment by moment, such a uniform activity is not possible, because their capacities differ at every moment due to the application of various successive conditions. Anticipating all these objections, he says: "By the attainment of the action to be accomplished, as when a white conch is situated before one," and so forth.
It is understood that the consciousness arising from eyes affected by jaundice is not [a valid perception].
Thus, when the purity of the cause has been brought about, that very same cognition which takes the form of yellow [appears] in a conch made of gold.
However, its status as a valid means of knowledge is determined by the arising of a cause of purity,
just as in the case of a conch-shell where the cognition of a white form occurs once the action has been accomplished.

By this he means the following: we do not determine the validity of a cognition—whether it pertains to a remote object or occurs at a later time—solely on the basis of the purity of its causes, such that the reason [of our argument] would be unestablished (*asiddha*), since distinct capacities arise through the application of various and successive conditions at every moment.

Rather, it is at the very moment when the purity of the cause of a cognition apprehending a nearby object—such as that which grasps a white conch—is ascertained through the attainment of the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by its whiteness, that the validity of the cognition of a golden conch located in a distant place, which arises simultaneously with a yellow appearance, is determined on the basis of the complete purity of its causes.

For it is not possible for there to be a change in the nature of the causes in that very same state, lest there be a discrepancy between the purposeful activity and the cognition whose object is the nearby thing.
Showing that this is indeed accepted by you Mīmāṃsakas, he says: "Because of the non-affliction by hunger and so forth," and so on.
By the statement regarding the non-affliction by hunger and so forth, the author of the Bhāṣya has already said this:
"Therefore, due to delusion, an infinite regress is urged here."

By this, the contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) regarding the proposition has also been demonstrated. For it has been stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "When the mind or the sense organ is afflicted by hunger and so forth, or when the external object is [afflicted] by subtlety and so forth, then there is false cognition; when they are unafflicted, there is correct cognition. Indeed, the contact of the sense organ, the mind, and the object is the cause of cognition. In its absence, there is no cognition; thus, a defect residing in that [contact] is the cause of false cognition. For when [the causes] are defective, cognition becomes false, since we observe correct apprehension upon the removal of the defect."

If it is asked, "How is it that a defect is understood? [the answer is: "If, while searching with effort, we do not perceive a defect, then, due to the absence of evidence [to the contrary], we consider it to be non-defective.
For by this passage, the author of the Bhāṣya has clearly stated that the ascertainment of validity arises from the knowledge of the purity of the causes [of cognition].
Otherwise, what would be shown by the phrase "while searching with effort"?
And consequently, there is a contradiction of the thesis that [cognition] is intrinsically valid.

Regarding what was stated: "By what is the cognition of correspondence or the cognition of excellence considered superior?"—in that regard, the matter concerning correspondence has been explained previously; now, concerning the cognition of excellence, he says "by the suspicion of being produced by a defective cause," and so forth:
[the truth] is not apprehended due to the suspicion that it is produced by a defective cause.
The knowledge of the purification of one who possesses pride and so forth is considered superior.
"Mānatā" means validity (*prāmāṇya*). "Of the first" refers to...
Of the knowledge of the meaning.
For that [knowledge] is the first because it arises prior to the knowledge of the purity of the cause;
"that" means for that reason.
With the words "In this way," etc., he demonstrates that activity is not unobserved:
"And thus, when the purity of the cause is ascertained through the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*),
the application of activity toward that which has not yet performed its purposeful action is logically established as having a referent."
"Having not performed its purposeful action" means that by which the purposeful action has not been performed; it is described as such. "Inexpressible" means:
"Inexpugnable" means "blameless";
this is because it is considered to be preceded by the ascertainment of its validity.
Therefore, regarding the statement that "self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is established as the general rule (*autsargika*) everywhere," he says, "If [validity were] from itself," and so forth:

"If self-validity were established as the general rule everywhere, It would be set aside by the two [factors]: the cognition of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) and the cognition of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*)."
Validity [of cognition] arises precisely from the absence of knowledge of sublation or of defects in its cause;
and thus, for you, the determination of validity would result from another.
For thus, this absence is a distinct means of valid cognition called "non-apprehension" (abhāva) in your view, whereas in my view, it is an inference known as "non-apprehension."
In this context, the first verse restates the opponent's position, while the second and subsequent verses provide the refutation.

For if validity were set aside by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) and so forth, then it would follow that the ascertainment of validity is admitted to occur precisely from the absence of such subverting cognitions;
consequently, validity would be declared to be extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
Since even non-existence (abhāva) is accepted as a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), [we reply:
in our position, however, because it is included within inference (anumāna) under the designation of "non-apprehension" (anupalabdhi), it is not a separate means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, since the universal rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) are constructed as having words and their meanings as their objects, they lack any standing when investigating the actual reality (*vastu*). This is because all things are established in their own respective natures and thus lack any conformity with another nature; consequently, your mere presentation of these [rules] only reveals your ignorance regarding the proper scope of universal rules and exceptions. For it is shown by the phrase "by this very [reasoning]" and so forth that, by the very same logic you have described, a universal rule and exception could just as well be postulated in the opposite manner.
By this very same reasoning, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) might also be intrinsic (*svataḥ*);
for in that case as well, it can be argued that such is the underlying principle (*nyāya*).
Therefore, the non-validity of all cognitions is established as the general rule (*autsargika*);
it is set aside only by the absence of knowledge regarding sublation, causal defects, or the defectiveness of the cause.
As for what was stated by Kumārila:
"Therefore, the validity of cognition is established by its very nature as consciousness;
it is set aside only by the knowledge of a defect in the cause or by the cognition that the object is otherwise."
Quoting the *Ślokavārttika*, he says "tathā bodhātmakatvena" and so forth, showing that it is possible to state [the same] even by this direction: "In the same way,
because its nature is cognition (*bodha*), the status of being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is attained for the intellect (*buddhi*)."
It is set aside by the knowledge of qualities arising from the cause of knowledge of things as they truly are.
If invalidity were dependent on another [means of knowledge], there would necessarily be an infinite regress;
for this [invalidity] is dependent upon a means of valid cognition, yet that [means of valid cognition] is not established intrinsically.
The term *apramāṇatā* involves the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *a*.

Furthermore, "knowledge of the object as it is" (*yathārthajñāna*) is knowledge of the correspondence with the object, and "knowledge of the qualities arising from the cause" (*hetūtthaguṇajñāna*) is knowledge of the qualities produced by the causal factors; this is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "even though that [validity] depends on another," he says:
"Non-authoritativeness," and so forth.
"For this" refers to non-authoritativeness.
"And that" refers to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To the question "In what sense is it non-abiding?", he says "For thus," and so forth.
For you state that validity arises from the absence of sublation;
yet the absence of sublation is itself accepted as another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence" (abhāva).
Its validity is asserted because there is no sublation of it;
yet, if one were to desire it to be so in every case, no fixed rule would be found.

Regarding what was stated, "the subverting cognition," and so forth, he says: "Because the status of being an independent means of valid cognition (*anapekṣapramāṇatva*) is not established in the case of a subverting cognition, therefore this [subsequent cognition] does not at all negate the preceding knowledge."
Because the means of valid cognition called non-existence (abhāva) is dependent [on other factors], its status as an independent means of valid cognition is unestablished.
With the words "But even if," and so forth, he establishes the very point of infinite regress:
"Even if validity is accepted in some cases without the absence of a sublater,
what is the cause for such hostility toward that same state in the first instance?"
If, for fear of infinite regress, validity is accepted in some cases even without the absence of a sublater, then the absence of a sublater would not need to be required even in the first cognition;
and consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that all cognitions are valid.

Regarding what was stated there— "In that case as well, there would be a dependence on a sublation," and so forth— he replies with the verse beginning "And this sublating cognition... This sublating cognition sets aside the preceding knowledge.
Since its authority is independent, what doubt could there be in this case?

Furthermore, the possibility of a subverting factor (bādhaka) that renders [the cognition] invalid is suspected here; yet such a suspicion arises only regarding what is already determined as certain. This [suspicion] is contradictory [to the claim of certainty].

If a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) were one whose status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is independent [of anything else], how could there be any suspicion of a refutation therein—such that it is said, "In that case too, there might be a dependence upon a refutation"? Consequently, this which has been stated is mutually contradictory: namely, that it possesses the status of an independent means of knowledge, while at the same time a subverting factor is suspected therein.

For it is thus: by the term "independent" (anapekṣam), that which has been made the object of a certainty is expressed; and where there is certainty, doubt is impossible, because of the relationship of sublated and sublator between certainty and superimposition, and because doubt, by virtue of resting upon two parts [of an object], proceeds in the form of a superimposition.

Regarding the passage beginning with "then, by appropriate effort," he says: "In the view that validity is intrinsic (svataḥprāmāṇya)," and so forth. Even in the view that validity is intrinsic, since [validity] is ascertained by its own inherent force (svarasena), why is effort exerted to establish the existence of a subverting factor (bādhaka)?
For instance, that in which no certainty regarding its validity arises by its own inherent force,
but which must be ascertained through effort, possesses a subverting factor by implication.
Therefore, what is said here regarding the three types of knowledge of the investigator?
Since that [object] is determined intrinsically, there is no room for even one [of those knowledges].
And if doubt arises even when there is no perception [of a sublater], because of uncertainty,
this is since non-perception is not invariably concomitant with the absence of a sublater.
This being the case, why have you found satisfaction in the triad?
For even when it is not perceived, sublation must be suspected here just as before.

As long as there is no correspondence with the practical effect (*kāryasaṃvāda*), so long does the suspicion of sublation (*bādhāśaṅkā*) not cease; therefore, the restriction regarding that triad [of conditions] is fruitless.
Therefore, even by one for whom no contradiction has yet arisen, a subverting factor must be suspected again;
for the true nature of a thing never remains established through mere deception.
Cognition that arises throughout one's life, which is free from causes of impairment,
and which appears as yellow when directed toward a conch shell, does not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If the determination of validity were intrinsic (*svataḥ*), then since validity would be pervaded by such determination, wherever there is no determination, invalidity would necessarily prevail by implication; thus, the presence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) would be established even without effort. Consequently, any effort made to establish its absence would be futile. Furthermore, in that case, there would be no possibility for even a single examination by an investigator (*parīkṣaka-jñāna*) to have any relevance, let alone three; therefore, this statement [of yours] is also inconsistent. He shows this by saying "therefore" (*ataḥ*) and so forth, demonstrating that these three examinations by an investigator do not go beyond this [consequence].

It might be argued that the absence of a subverting factor cannot be ascertained by mere non-perception alone, because even for something existent—such as that which is distant, subtle, or obstructed—there is no perception; thus, since non-perception is not pervaded by the absence of a subverting factor, an effort must be made to establish that absence.

If this is so, you must abandon the restriction to three cognitions of the investigator; for, as in the case of the first cognition, sublation may be suspected in other cases as well. Indeed, until the cognition of the result arises, by what means could the suspicion of sublation be removed, such that there would be a restriction to three? For it is not proper for those who act with discernment to have their suspicions removed merely by verbal assertion without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the investigation of the means of valid cognition is based on the actual state of things; this is not a mere practice of sophistry (*chala*) being undertaken, whereby one would examine only a few moments of cognition.

If, however, validity were established merely by the occurrence of the threefold cognition, then alas, for those whose eyes are afflicted by jaundice throughout their lives and to whom a conch shell appears only as yellow, that cognition of theirs would have to be valid!

It might be argued: "Even if it were invalid, why does no subverting cognition arise after the examination of the three types of knowledge? Since it does not arise, one concludes that it does not exist. Anticipating this doubt, he says "viśuddhi" and so forth:
"A subverting cognition would not arise due to the absence of a cause for purification, or due to some other cause; therefore, the doubt is not removed by this [mere non-arising]."
The cause of purification is the sprinkling of the sap of *droṇa* flowers and so forth;

in the absence of that, no subverting factor arises, or rather, it does not arise due to another cause. This is just as, for a person who has experienced the illusion of water in a mass of mirages in a desert, the cognition appearing as a desert region devoid of the nature of water does not arise because he does not approach [the mirage].
Regarding the passage beginning with "one might suspect" (*utprekṣeta hi*), he says: "This suspicion is indeed based on a cause, insofar as it arises from delusion;
however, when purity and consistency are observed, no suspicion would arise for the wise."
He does not become one whose nature is characterized by doubt regarding any worldly transactions;
for his intellect is free from doubt when he perceives purity and correspondence.
Furthermore, regarding this point, if some dull-witted person should again harbor doubt,
I consider that censure is directed toward him because of his state of being characterized by skepticism.
It has been established that doubt is removed by both the purity of the cause and by corroborative knowledge.
As for what was further stated, beginning with "And likewise by Vāsudeva," etc., that merely reveals one's own reliance on partisan assertions (*bhaktivāda*), not the actual state of affairs.
For the determination of the true nature of a thing cannot be known from mere words lacking logical justification to another discerning person whose mind is inclined toward investigation.
For, demonstrating that the word of Vāsudeva is not contradictory because it is established by another related [authority], he says "atrāpi" and so forth.

Here, in this demonstration of the correspondence of purity, regarding one such as you who raises a doubt—thinking that "even with respect to a correspondence, a further correspondence must be sought in the same way"—it is considered that the state of being characterized by doubt was censured by Aja, Viṣṇu.
To the objection that "as much as there is a denial, so much is it possible in the case of cognition," and so forth, he says "place," etc.:
"When the determination of validity is conceived in dependence on the distinctions of place, time, person, and state,
the determination of validity is clearly [attained] from another."

For instance, in the case of earlier cognitions, the determination of their validity is ascertained through other means of knowledge, since their absence of sublation with respect to place, time, and so forth is well-established.
By this, he demonstrates a contradiction with his own words.
For, when the ascertainment of validity is postulated as being dependent upon place, time, person, and circumstance, it is clearly stated that [validity] is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

Since the absence of sublation by another means of knowledge is ascertained regarding place, time, and so forth, how could the acceptance of the ascertainment of validity in the initial, preceding cognition not be accepted as being extrinsic?

For the absence of sublation must necessarily be ascertained through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: if intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) were admitted, it would follow that all cognitions are valid; therefore, you must necessarily state that intrinsic validity belongs only to that [cognition] for which there is no sublation, and not to any other. Furthermore, that absence of sublation cannot be ascertained by mere non-perception (*anupalambha-mātra*), because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); rather, it must be ascertained through the non-perception of something that has reached the conditions for perception (*sāmarthya-anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta-anupalambha*), since only such non-perception is invariably concomitant (*vyāpta*) with the absence of sublation.

And since this non-apprehension of what has reached the conditions for apprehensibility is not logically distinct from a corroborative cognition, it would follow that the ascertainment of validity must be accepted as arising from a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Regarding the phrase "debt and so forth" (*ṛṇādīti*) and so on, he says:

"But that legal proceeding concerning debt and so forth which is capable of being expressed in three propositions— that, being of such a nature, is not to be cited as an example when establishing valid cognition."

In that state, the plaintiff and the defendant, though repeatedly recollecting [the case], are unable to achieve a clear perception regarding that object, for they do not obtain subtle scrutiny there.

Indeed, valid cognition must be established according to the actual state of things; it cannot be established through quibbling (*chala*). Therefore, this example cited is not relevant to the subject at hand and is thus declared to be improper for the current discussion.

While the established nature of valid cognition is under discussion as being tied to the intrinsic nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*), your citation of the conventional practice of debt and so forth—which is based on conventions created by mere whim and is of a deceptive nature—only reveals your own ignorance regarding the subject at hand.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Even the triple-truth of the gods," he says "trisatyatā" and so forth:
Even the triple-truth of the gods is not at all a cause for certainty;
for if that [certainty] does not exist from the very beginning, it would certainly not arise later either.

Regarding the phrase "from the first": if the absence of certainty were due to the first statement, then that certainty would not arise at all from the two subsequent statements occurring at a later time, because there would be no distinction between them.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "tadīyam" and so forth:
"Since these two subsequent statements belong to that [same person],
what distinction is there between them and the others in the absence of a [distinctive] cognition in the first case?"
"Uttara" means occurring at a later time;
"pratyayābhāva" means the absence of conditions.
"In the absence of certainty" means "of the other two";
that is to say, of those two which occur at a later time.

For if one were to speak one statement and a second as false, why would he not speak a third as well? Who then could restrain him at that time, such that confidence could arise from a third [statement]?
Regarding the passage beginning with "therefore, intrinsic validity," he says "therefore" and so forth:
"Therefore, by the reasoning previously stated, there is an infinite regress even in your own position,
since validity and invalidity are established accordingly."
The previously mentioned reasoning is as follows:
"For it is said by you that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists because there is an absence of sublation;
yet this very absence of sublation is itself accepted as another means of valid cognition called 'non-apprehension' (*abhāva*)."
Thus it has been stated by these and other [verses].
Regarding the statement beginning with "eternal" and "composed by a reliable authority," he says "the sentence," and so forth: "An eternal sentence has already been refuted by us in detail;
moreover, in your tradition, there is no reliable authority who has exhausted all faults without exception."
But how can one whose mass of obscurations is undiminished be considered authoritative?
For it is possible that his speech might otherwise [be false] due to his defects.

Previously, in the *Śrutiparīkṣā*, it was refuted in detail that [the Vedic] word is eternal; thus, since its existence is unestablished (*asiddha*), how could there be any occasion for an investigation into its intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*)?
Furthermore, since an "authoritative person" (*āpta*) is not admitted by [the opponent] himself, even a statement composed by him remains unestablished.

For instance, only one whose defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth—the causes of falsehood—have been abandoned without remainder can rightly be called an authoritative person. Otherwise, how could the status of being an authoritative person be established for one whose mind is overwhelmed by defects such as passion, which are the causes of falsehood?

Furthermore, you do not accept any person who has abandoned the entire web of afflictions, by means of whom the word of an authoritative teacher (āpta) could constitute a valid means of knowledge for you.

Furthermore, even granting that there might be such a person as an authoritative one (āpta), he shows that his word remains nonetheless unestablished with the words beginning "Even if [an authority] were born" (jāte 'pi).
"Even if an authority were born, by whom could that flood of his qualities be known,
such that there could be a definitive determination regarding a statement composed by an authority?"
Even for one who, possessing the vision that transcends the senses, might perceive the perfection of his qualities,
what need would he have for the word composed by a trustworthy person?
For he, being independent of verbal testimony, attains the object by himself;
another, however, due to a lack of knowledge regarding a trustworthy person, does not comprehend the object from that [testimony].

For it is not possible to ascertain that "this is the statement of that person" without first ascertaining that he is an authoritative person (*āpta*); yet such ascertainment of an authoritative person is not possible. To explain: even if one who has exhausted all defects without exception and perceives supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*) were to ascertain him as authoritative, his statement would still be of no consequence at all. Since he himself perceives all objects directly, one does not act on the basis of his statement; therefore, the ascertainment of him as authoritative is useless.

Furthermore, any other person of limited vision is not capable of ascertaining that [the speaker] is trustworthy; thus, such a person does not understand the meaning from that statement on its own, because it remains uncertain.
Regarding the passage beginning with "those who are teachers of knowledge," he says:

"In the doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), since destruction is impossible for that which has arisen as an intrinsically certain cognition, for what purpose would there be any prevention?"
"From the nature of certainty" means from the arising of certainty;
otherwise, if certainty were not produced intrinsically, then the doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) would be lost.
Therefore, regarding the passage beginning with "or by those [words] where qualities are excluded," he says "not indeed" and so forth:
"The sentence is not indeed corrupted by defects that have been set aside by qualities;
however, because the qualities are not ascertained, it is impossible to determine it [as valid]."

Even if a statement is not faulty because its faults have been eliminated by its excellences, nevertheless, since the excellences residing in another person's continuum are beyond the reach of the senses, it is impossible to ascertain that the statement possesses excellences when they remain uncertain; nor can that which is not ascertained be intrinsically valid (*svataḥpramāṇa*).
Alternatively, regarding the claim that "faults would not exist due to the absence of an author," he says "of the sentence" and so forth.
The lack of an author for the sentence has already been refuted previously;
therefore, in the absence of an author, those faults cannot exist as they would be without a substratum.
The phrase "all the more so" refers to the examination of sound.
Regarding that [statement], "In the case of the word of a reliable person (āpta), two things are observed," etc., he says:
"And that the status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) arises from excellences (guṇas) has been stated as it is logically appropriate;
furthermore, if the excellences are not recognized, the absence of defects (doṣābhāva) is not perceived."
[Page 795] It is not tenable that a statement is intrinsically a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as characterized by the absence of defects;
for since the absence of defects cannot be fully cognized, it cannot serve as a defining characteristic.

Regarding the phrase "thus it has been said," the wise have stated therein [in the verse beginning with] "the wise have said," and so forth, that which was asserted—that a statement is intrinsically authoritative (*pramāṇa*) and not characterized by the absence of defects—is also untenable. This is because qualities (*guṇas*) are beyond the reach of the senses; therefore, as long as they are not cognized, it is impossible to characterize the absence of defects, which consists in the presence of those very qualities.

He says this very thing: "For the absence of defects is not a defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*). A *lakṣaṇa* is that by which something is characterized; that which is not a *lakṣaṇa* is an *alakṣaṇa*, meaning it does not serve as an indicator.
The sense is that [the absence of defects] is because it is not fully cognized.
He shows that a characteristic cannot exist if it is not cognized by saying "for indeed," and so forth.
For indeed, when a staff is not cognized, people do not perceive [the person] as "staff-bearer. And this claim that "that which is characterized is itself the means of valid cognition" is refuted.
The absence of defects is ascertained through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by means of the absence of [the presence of] valid cognition;
therefore, it is logical that the definition of a statement [is established], and thus the establishment of validity is extrinsic (parataḥ).

Furthermore, even if the absence of defects were indeed the defining characteristic, it would still be a defect itself, because it would entail a contradiction with one's own statement. For if validity is characterized by the absence of defects, then validity would clearly be extrinsic (*parataḥ*); and consequently, the statement that "validity is intrinsic" (*svataḥ*) would be contradicted.

This very point is clarified: if the absence of defects were ascertained by a means of valid cognition termed "non-existence" (abhāva), then that [absence] could serve as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), because that which is not ascertained cannot function as a defining characteristic. Furthermore, there is no other means of valid cognition that can ascertain non-existence; therefore, it would be stated even more clearly that validity is extrinsic (parataḥ), arising from that which is called the means of valid cognition of non-existence.
Regarding what was stated—that knowledge whose object is human defects does not arise when those [defects] are present—he says "nṛdoṣa... and so forth:
knowledge whose object is human defects does indeed arise even while those [defects] exist.
But if there is indeed an absence of defects, how can there be a cognition [of it] when qualities are not known?

Even if a cognition directed toward faults does not arise when virtues are present, since the virtues residing in another's continuum are beyond the reach of the senses, it follows that in their non-cognition, there can be no ascertainment of the absence of faults; for the absence of faults is of the same nature as the presence of virtues. Indeed, the absence of a jar cannot be known if the location devoid of the jar is not itself cognized.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "hatred" (dveṣa):
"Defects such as hatred and delusion are sublated by compassion, wisdom, and so forth;
for if there were no certainty regarding compassion and the like, how could their non-existence be established?"
"Of them" means of the defects.
Regarding this, Kumārila has said: "At that time, the excellences (guṇas) do not function by way of being cognized;
rather, when the absence of defects (doṣābhāva) is to be known, they are helpful merely by their existence."
Thus, with the words "this [is] that," etc., he raises an objection:
"But at that time, the excellences (guṇas) do not operate by way of being cognized;
rather, when the absence of defects (doṣābhāva) is to be known, they are helpful merely by their existence."
"Benefactors" means those who assist in the determination that there is an absence of defects.
He provides the rebuttal with the words "If it were so," and so forth:

"If it were so, there would be no doubt, nor would there be a mistaken cognition, regarding one esteemed as authoritative, [thinking] 'Does he have faults or not?'— [the thought] 'He certainly has them' would arise."
Therefore, both doubt and error may arise in someone regarding this matter,
as long as he is not understood to be a repository of virtues.

If qualities were to function toward the ascertainment of the absence of defects merely by their existence, then no one would ever experience doubt or error regarding the absence of defects in a person recognized as authoritative (*āpta*), since such [doubt and error] would have been sublated by that ascertainment. But this is not the case; therefore, as long as the ascertainment of the possession of qualities does not arise, doubt and error concerning the absence of defects certainly persist. Thus, qualities do not function by their mere existence alone.
Furthermore, even if there is an absence of defects, if there is ignorance [of them], the certainty of intrinsic validity would still not occur;
likewise, in that case, doubt regarding the speaker would remain as before.

Now, it might be argued: "Let there be no operation of the excellences (*guṇa*) for the sake of ascertaining the absence of defects; nevertheless, the ascertainment of validity will arise from the very absence of defects, even if that absence is not itself ascertained.
This too is incorrect, because, as before, it would entail the consequence that there is no disagreement regarding a speaker who is accepted as authoritative.

For once the validity of his statement is ascertained intrinsically (*svataḥ*), it is not reasonable to have such thoughts concerning that speaker as: "Is he a speaker of truth or not? or "He is certainly not."
By the word *vimati* (misconception), both doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyāsa*) are intended here;

for, since *vimati* is defined as a cognition (*mati*) having a contrary aspect (*viparītākāra*), doubt—which, by its nature of apprehending two sides, possesses the possibility of a contrary aspect—is included.
Furthermore, as for this which was stated by Kumārila:

"Therefore, because of the absence of defects due to the presence of excellences, and because of that absence, the two types of non-valid cognition do not exist; thus, the general rule remains unrefuted."
And so forth; he shows that even this is indeed untenable when there is no ascertainment of the absence of defects, by saying "of the absence of defects," etc.:
"Since the absence of defects is unknown, how can the non-existence of the two kinds of invalid cognition be cognized, by means of which there might be an ascertainment of validity?"
[Page 797] Now, even if the non-existence of the two types of invalidity is cognized,
if validity were understood as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in this way, then there would be no disagreement [regarding its nature] as there was previously.
For if knowledge were established as being free from doubt and error—which are its subverters—then it would be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Otherwise, how could a general rule (*utsarga*) apply to an object that is already overtaken by subversion?
And since those two, doubt and error, have their cause in defects (*doṣa*), it is not tenable to ascertain their absence unless there is an ascertainment of the absence of defects.
"The non-existence of the two kinds of invalid cognition" means the non-existence of doubt and error.
He demonstrates that very doubt with the words, "Is his word a means of valid cognition? and so forth:
"Is his word a means of valid cognition, or is it not?
It is indeed not a means of valid cognition for anyone, because of the certainty of intrinsic validity."

Thus, it has been demonstrated that it is not logical for the absence of defects and so forth to serve as factors for the determination of validity merely by their existence; now, demonstrating in detail these two points—that if one requires certainty regarding them, there would follow both extrinsic validity and an infinite regress—he says "doṣābhāva... and so on:
"Therefore, in all three cases—the absence of defects, the absence of non-validity, and the presence of excellences—a cognition [of them] must necessarily be admitted as a rule."
In the absence of defects and in the absence of the two types of invalidating factors, a cognition of the excellences must necessarily be admitted as a certainty;
for it has been established that otherwise the ascertainment of validity would be impossible.
If it is indeed admitted [to exist], then what follows? To this he says: "That," and so forth.
It is thus conceptualized as either a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
How could that which is a factor for the ascertainment of an object as it truly is be a non-means of valid cognition?

This very cognition regarding all three aforementioned [objects] is intended as a factor for the validity [of the means of knowledge]. There are two possible alternatives: is it non-valid or is it valid?
If it is the first alternative, then it cannot be a factor for the determination of validity, because it is itself non-valid.
For a witness who is perceived to be non-valid does not become a factor for a determination in a legal proceeding.
Since validity is established as extrinsic, how is the determination of that validity reached? Or rather, how is it understood that this cognition possesses the nature of being valid?

If it is argued that [the cognition is valid] because of the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), then the same problem recurs here once again: is that [absence of a subverting cognition] itself a means of valid cognition (*pramā*) or not? Thus, every fault follows here as well.

Now, if the second position is held, then there follows the consequence that the validity of that intended cognition would depend on something else, and there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Desiring to demonstrate that very infinite regress, he asks, "How? and so forth.
"He too" refers to the proponent of the second position.
The absence of a subverting cognition.
To explain how that same fault persists here as well, he says "In the case of validity," and so forth:
"If validity were attained from another source, then the status of the subject at hand as a means of valid cognition would be lost;
or else, how could that which is not a means of valid cognition be the cause of a cognition that accords with reality?"
It must be considered by what means the validity of this [cognition] is also understood;
otherwise, the undesirable consequence follows that it would lack validity due to the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*).
This is easily understood.
"Of this too" refers to the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*).

Furthermore, if validity were determined in all cases by the principle previously demonstrated—that "from the absence of defects [in the causes], there is the absence of faults"—then validity would have to be accepted as extrinsic (*parataḥ*) from the very beginning, and there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He shows this with the words "tasmāt" and so forth:
"Therefore, from the qualities [of the causes] comes the absence of defects; from that absence..."
Because the two types of valid cognition do not exist [for him], his general rule remains unrefuted.
If validity were thus determined in all cases, then here too that previously mentioned multitude of defects would follow, and an infinite regress would result.
Regarding the phrase "as previously stated":

since qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth residing in another continuum are beyond the senses for one who possesses the vision of the Path (*mārgadarśana*), they cannot be ascertained; and because they are not ascertained, the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) is likewise unascertained. Consequently, the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*) remains unascertained, and thus validity (*prāmāṇya*) would not be established on the basis of qualities and the like. Furthermore, if those [qualities] were to assist merely by their existence, then there would be no disagreement [regarding the validity of all cognitions]. Such a host of faults applies universally in this manner.

Furthermore, regarding that which was stated as a factor for the determination of validity—namely, the absence of defects (*doṣa*) due to the presence of excellences (*guṇa*), and so forth—there arises a twofold conceptual possibility: is this pair, consisting of the non-existence of the two types of invalidity and the absence of defects, intended as a mere absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or rather as having the nature of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*)?
Regarding the first position, he states the fault with the words "the absence of defects," and so on:
"And this negation—that when there is an absence of defects, there is the existence of valid cognition (*pramā*)."
If it were postulated as being absolute, its establishment would simply not be possible.
Its establishment through the non-perception of its absence is not tenable;
nor is it logical on account of the fault of infinite regress, because of [the resulting] non-perception.
If mere non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) alone is intended, then its establishment would not be possible at all.
For its establishment would have to occur either through itself or through another.
If it were established through itself, it would do so either by virtue of having a self-luminous nature or by producing a certainty.
There are the following positions: that [the self] might exist either because it is sometimes perceived from another source or because it is not perceived.
First of all, its establishment as having the nature of self-luminosity is not tenable, because that [self] is a non-entity, whereas the nature of luminosity is a property of entities.
For it is cognition alone that is established by self-awareness through its nature of luminosity.
However, non-existence does not have the mere negation of the intrinsic nature of a thing as its characteristic;
nor is it established by itself through the production of a certainty,
because since non-existence is characterized by the absence of all causal capacity, it is impossible for it to be a producer.
Alternatively, if it were a producer, it would follow that it must be a real entity (*vastu*);
for, since it cannot have any excellence added to it, it would be independent of auxiliary causes, and there would follow the consequence that the effect arising from it alone would never cease.

Furthermore, its establishment through perception from another [source] is not possible; why? Because of its non-existence—that is, because its nature is non-being—and because perception has existence as its object.
Nor can its establishment be through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), because that would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

For in that case, since non-apprehension itself is of the nature of an absence, how is it established? Regarding this as well, the consideration of whether it is established "by itself" or "by another" necessarily arises.
It cannot be by itself, because that would entail the same faults already mentioned.
Nor [is it produced] from another, because of the fault of infinite regress.
He demonstrates that very infinite regress with the words "the non-existence of defects and the two kinds of non-cognition," and so forth:
"The non-existence of defects and the two kinds of non-cognition is known through non-perception;
the non-existence of that perception [of non-perception] would be known by another, leading to an infinite regress."
The compound means the non-existence of both the defects and the two types of non-authoritativeness.
Regarding the second [type of negation], that which consists of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), he states the fault with the words "If that consists of exclusion," and so forth:
"If that consists of exclusion because of the perception of something else distinct [from the object],
then the non-cognition of the absence of faults would consist of the cognition of qualities."

Furthermore, it would follow that the nature of the cognition of the intended valid knowledge is [simply] the cognition of the non-existence of the two types of invalid knowledge, and that it is distinct from them.
If the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition is known either through its own nature or otherwise,
from what source does your certainty arise that the remaining one is the self as a valid cognizer?
