If it is argued that [the object] exists because it cannot be otherwise accounted for (*anyathānupapatti*), then surely it would be known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);
or else such certainty would likewise arise from inference (*anumāna*) or some other means.

For the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*), by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), would necessarily consist of the presence of excellences (*guṇa*); consequently, the cognition of that [absence] would also result in being of the nature of the cognition of excellences, which is not desired, because of the statement: "At that time, excellences do not function as something being cognized" (p. 800). Furthermore, even the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*) would, under the view of exclusion, remain nothing but the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, the cognition of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition would also result in having the very form of the intended cognition of validity, and thus—

The statement, “Because of that [cognition], the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition is established, and thus the general rule (utsarga) remains unrefuted,” is not tenable because it is ill-conceived (*duḥśliṣṭa*).

For, since that very [cognition] is ascertained as being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its status as a valid means of knowledge is then ascertained; thus, due to this relationship of cause and effect, the meaning of the sentence would be ill-conceived because there is no distinction [between the two].

Furthermore, because the cause and the effect are distinct, it would follow that the cognition of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition is distinct from the cognition of the valid means of knowledge—that is, it would be something other than that.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is of the nature of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) to be characterized by the absence of those [two].

Having accepted the establishment of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition through the statement "when [the absence] is known," he demonstrates the extrinsic validity (*parataḥprāmāṇya*) of knowledge according to the opponent's own view, by means of the principle of "presumption through the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*).
This is because there is no other possible recourse once one has set aside the intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of a cognition other than doubt and error.
Demonstrating that the logical argument stated in the passage beginning with "Therefore, from the qualities... is inconclusive, he says: "And for that very reason," and so forth.
For by that same reasoning, it is possible to assert that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is also intrinsic (*svataḥ*), because this [same logic] applies clearly to that case as well.

Therefore, because of those defects, there is an absence of excellences; due to that absence, the nature of the means of valid cognition does not exist. Consequently, the general rule remains unrefuted.
Since this state of general exclusion (utsarga) is constructed solely by the speaker's intention,
it can be clearly expressed even regarding that which lacks a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa), just as in the case of human authority (māna).
Since validity has been established for cognition that is by nature sublated,
it is set aside by the knowledge of qualities arising from causes that produce knowledge of things as they truly are.
Since its validity is not negated by the non-cognition of defects, invalidity is not set aside;
and since it has not been set aside, that [validity] also remains established as being intrinsic.
Regarding the phrase "it exists":
what can be said about that? To this he says, "Therefore," and so forth.
"Like a human being" (mānavat):
the suffix *vati* is added to a word ending in the locative case.
"That too": [refers to the same].
Invalidity.
The remainder is easily understood.
Regarding the question of whether defects exist or do not exist, he says "defects," etc.:
"Whether defects exist or do not exist is suspected in the case of human [compositions];
since an author is established even for the Veda, there is no suspicion of defects for us."

Since the author of the Veda has been established in the *Śrutiparīkṣā*, the claim that "due to the absence of an author" is unproven; therefore, for us who are discerning people, there is not a lack of suspicion regarding defects in the Veda, but rather such suspicion certainly exists.
Therefore, regarding the statement "because of independence," he says "hence" and so forth:
"Hence, that which is asserted as the authority of the Veda because of its independence is unestablished,
since even that depends upon an author."
"So too" refers to the Veda.
Regarding the passage beginning with "by other means of valid cognition regarding the meaning of the Veda," he says: "If there is a corroborating cognition...
If there is no corroborating cognition, nor is the purity of the cause ascertained, then because doubt arises, the Veda possesses no authority.

If both of these—the cognition that accords with purposeful action and the cognition of the purity of its causes—are not accepted as the grounds for determining validity in the case of the Veda, then, due to the deficiency of the causes for determination, the determination of validity in the Veda cannot be attained, because an effect is impossible without its cause.
Regarding the statement "even for another [cognition] there is validity," he says "even for another" and so forth:
Even when another [cognition] possesses validity,
such a connection alone is postulated as the cause, because certain conviction is based upon that.
"Of such a nature" means characterized by the thorough knowledge of the quality of correspondence (*saṃvāda*).

In this regard, the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) has already been refuted previously. Therefore, the claim that "whatever is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not depend upon connection with another means of valid cognition" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because another means of valid cognition is required for the sake of ascertainment (*niścaya*).

He demonstrates this very point with the words "For when it is established," and so forth: "For when its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is already established, certainty is produced by this [cognition]; however, no new status as a means of valid cognition is generated for it by this [cognition]."
By this, the following argument is also refuted: "In some cases, there may be a determination by subsequent means of valid cognition," and so forth.

For when the validity of a [subsequent] cognition is ascertained through another means, the status of the preceding cognition as a means of valid cognition—characterized by its capacity to lead to the attainment of the object—does not thereby disappear.
Regarding the objection that there can be no validity (*prāmāṇya*) with respect to an object that perishes immediately after being once produced, he says "sakṛt" and so forth:
"And validity would indeed exist with respect to an object that is once produced and does not perish;
even when [the object] is not ascertained, that validity certainly exists, for ascertainment also occurs through the process already described."
This is *seti* (lying) and *mānatā* (penance).
Demonstrating the very sequence already stated, he says: "If, because of the purity of the cause," and so forth.
If the cognition of the purity of the cause and so on constitutes certainty, and if the purposeful action—characterized by burning and the like—is directly attained; [then that cognition is valid].
Alternatively, when a state of practice that is independent of external means arises for the sake of liberation,
there is no longer any determination based on authoritative means once all such methods have been abandoned.
Therefore, although validity exists in that [cognition], it remains undetermined;
because it is as if non-existent, it is designated as "not existing at all."
And if it is argued that "if purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) has been attained,
then certainty arises from that," this connects with the subject at hand.
But surely, since the cognition of purposeful action has a different object, it is not logical for the establishment of the validity of the preceding cognition to derive from it?

For instance, since a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) is impossible, visual cognition regarding water apprehends only color-form (*rūpa*), whereas the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) such as bathing and so forth has only touch (*sparśa*) as its object. How, then, could a cognition having one basis validate the validity of a cognition having a different object? [This would lead to] an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This is not a fault.

Because two objects existing within a single continuum are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*), even a cognition having one basis will establish the validity of a cognition having a different object.
For color and touch do not exist in isolation from one another, since they depend upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

In that regard, because the preceding cognition is observed to function under the form of an object even when no actual object exists, the subsequent cognitions—which grasp the touch inseparable from that object—do not require the arising of a definitive ascertainment (*niścaya*).

[Objection: Even so, since all entities are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), the touch inseparable from the color grasped by the preceding cognition is certainly not made an object by the activity of the subsequent cognition; how, then, can there be a definitive ascertainment based on that?

This is not a fault. When there is a desire for a causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that is no different from that of the preceding moments of form and so forth grasped by the prior cognition, the subsequent moments of form and so forth are designated as "one" because they share the same *yogakṣema* (commonality of acquisition and preservation). For those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*), practical activity (*vyavahāra*) does not occur with respect to [discrete] moments. Alternatively, since the object of the subsequent cognition is invariably concomitant with the object such as form determined by the prior cognition, and because it serves as its cause, determination (*niścaya*) based upon it is not contradicted, even though there is a conventional distinction between them.
Regarding what was stated, that "auditory cognition would be invalid," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "Of auditory cognition":
Even for auditory cognition, there is a clear connection with the cognitions of the eye and the other senses;
for color, sound, and so forth, exist as dependent upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Because they are inseparable from one another and act as mutual causes within the continuum, their relationship certainly exists; thus it is perfectly clear.

For even in the cognitions of those [other persons], the auditory cognition would be valid by way of that [object], just as there is a transformation of smoke and fuel; this is because it is connected with the cognitions of others.
The lack of connection with other cognitions, such as those of the eye and so forth, is not established at all.

For instance, because the sound of a lute and its related qualities, such as color, depend upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there exists between them a relationship characterized by mutual inseparability, just like that between smoke and the transformation of fuel.

Furthermore, when considering their occurrence in a continuous series, each preceding group serves as the cause for each subsequent one; thus, there is also a relationship characterized by a direct cause-and-effect relation.
Consequently, there is also a connection, mediated by a succession [of cognitions], with the cognitions that apprehend those [objects].

Therefore, auditory cognition is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it possesses the aforementioned connection with other cognitions such as those of the eye and so forth. For instance, when a person who desires a lute hears the sound of a lute from afar, and a doubt arises due to its similarity to the sound of a flute or the like, his subsequent activity leads to the sight of the lute's form; thus, the previously arisen doubt—namely, "Is this the sound of a lute, or is it the sound of a flute, song, or the like?"—is dispelled.

And in a place where, due to hearing the echoes of drums and the like, one who has acted upon them does not achieve the attainment of that object, he understands its lack of authority because of the discrepancy.
Regarding the statement, "But there is no cognition produced by another means of proof for either [of the two]," and so forth, he says "sādhanāntara" and so on:
"But this cognition produced by another means of proof is ascertained; therefore, a correspondence with knowledge produced by another cause is desired."
"This" refers to that which perceives the form of the lute and so forth.

Just as [it was said] regarding the connection with another cognition dependent on a single sense-organ, [the author] says "in this way" and so forth: "In this way, the connection with another cognition dependent on multiple sense-organs is established as the cause for perception; however, this is not observed in the case of the Veda."
"This is not seen"— thus,
the connection with another cognition is dependent upon various sense faculties.
To explain how this is established as the cause for direct perception, he says "tathā hi" and so forth:
"For instance, first there arises a cognition of water produced by the eye;
then another [cognition] based on the tongue and the body, appearing as drinking, bathing, and so forth."
"Born of the eye" means visual consciousness whose object is form.
"Supreme" means—
Arising at a later time.
Regarding the passage beginning with "by a single sentence alone," he says "even by one," and so forth:
"But even by a single sentence, a correspondence with the fact cannot be obtained regarding place, time, persons, and so on, because doubt arises concerning everything."
"The heavenly world arises from the *agnihotra* sacrifice"—this is heard equally [in the scriptures];
yet, being devoid of the factor of certainty, it is merely the croaking of words.
By this, he states that the correspondence with the object (*arthasaṃvāda*) is unestablished (*asiddhatā*).

For, from the statement "Heaven results from the Agnihotra," doubt indeed arises in a discerning person because there is no cause for certainty; thus, correspondence regarding place, time, and so forth is not established.
Furthermore, showing that agreement is not found among all other people, he says "In heaven and so forth," etc.:
"And a difference of opinion even among Brahmins is observed regarding heaven and such;
therefore, no agreement on the meaning is found here among men and others."

For instance, the authors of the *Nirukta* and others describe heaven as a particular location such as the summit of Mount Sumeru, which is the abode of a person who excels ordinary humans, a locus of superhuman bliss, and enriched with various requisites.
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that heaven is simply a particular state of joy belonging to humans themselves. Furthermore, disagreement is observed even regarding the nature of sacrifice (*yajña*).
For it is heard that in ancient times, sacrificers sacrificed with an animal made of flour;
however, other wicked and pitiless men have described the animal as being a specific living being alone.
Therefore, he says "that which has arisen is firm," beginning with "produced by the *codanā*.
In the case of knowledge produced by the *codanā*, firmness was previously set aside;
for its being such [i.e., true] is doubtful because of the similarity of the object grasped by it to other things.
"Previously" refers to the *Śrutiparīkṣā*.
"Due to similarity with others" means:
Because it is equivalent to the cognition produced by human-authored statements such as "Heaven does not result from the Agnihotra sacrifice."

Moreover, this claim of yours—that the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction does not fail with respect to place and so forth—is mere words. He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "asarvadarśibhiḥ":
"How has this been determined by the non-omniscient Brahmins, that the cognition produced by the injunction is entirely non-deceptive?"
Regarding the passage beginning with "It is not to be established by inference," he says "ascertained" and so forth:
"The validity of perception as well is stated to be ascertained by means of the aforementioned inference;
because it is produced from pure causes, it is a valid cognition, like any other such [cognition]."

For a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is defined as the occurrence of an undesired consequence; however, it is not the case that the establishment of the validity of perception through inference is undesired, such that a *prasaṅga* could be leveled against it.
How the validity of perception is established by means of inference has already been stated previously.
He recalls that very point [with the words]: "It is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is produced from pure causes."
"Like that which is other than those" means like perception that apprehends an object in close proximity.
Regarding the passage beginning with "By what other means is the validity of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) established," he says "of all" and so forth:
And the validity of all [cognitions] is not to be established by another means of valid cognition,
because it has been proven that there is no error regarding the cognition of purposeful action (arthakriyājñāna).
And how there is no error in the cognition of causal efficacy has already been established by the passage beginning with "correspondence with the object" (*vastusaṃvāda*);
therefore, because validity arises from correspondence with the cognition of causal efficacy, there is no infinite regress.

He shows that even when the object of proof is established by inference, it is certainly not the case [that error exists], with the words beginning "ātma": "And when an inference arises from a logical mark (liṅga) called the effect of the self, which is ascertained to be non-deviant, there is no error whatsoever."

It has been stated that "self" (*ātman*) refers to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*); the analysis of the compound is: "that mark (*liṅga*) which has those [two] as its designation.

That mark whose certainty is non-deviant is described as such. What is meant is this: inference, which arises by the power of the ascertainment of marks designated as essential nature and effect—[marks] which are constrained by the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*)—is valid by itself (*svataḥ*) because there is no cause for error; thus, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "If [the object] were not established by this," he says "In some cases" and so forth: "But in some cases, the error that arises through the power of various causes of delusion is dispelled by this [means of knowledge], because there is no certainty regarding that [object]."

Because of the absence of causes for certainty such as repeated practice, error may arise in some initial perception; therefore, its status as a valid means of knowledge cannot be established through itself alone.

Regarding the statement that "the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is established in its own form prior to the apprehension [of the object]," he says "unmanifest," and so forth: "An object does not become established as manifest by virtue of having an unmanifest manifestation; therefore, like the perception of another, it must be accepted that cognition is known."
That object whose manifestation is unmanifested is described as such.
For knowledge must necessarily be known;
because if that [knowledge] were unknown, it would follow that everything is unknown.

For it is the very manifestation of the object (*arthābhivyakti*) that is called "cognition" (*jñāna*), and nothing else. And if that manifestation were imperceptible (*parokṣa*), it would follow that the object itself is also imperceptible. This is because an object that is the referent of a cognition occurring in another mental continuum (*santāna*) has an unmanifested manifestation. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever object has an unmanifested manifestation is not perceptually manifest (*pratyakṣa*) to that [subject], just as an object apprehended by a perception belonging to one person's continuum is not perceptually manifest to another. And the cognition under dispute has an unmanifested manifestation for someone; this is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Nor is the reason inconclusive, because if that object were perceptible without the production of its manifestation, it would follow that it is perceptible to everyone;
yet this is not the case.
Therefore, the opposite is true.

Regarding the phrase "and just as by those which are themselves unknown," he says "by themselves" and so forth: "But because they are insentient in nature, objects are not grasped by the sense organs such as the eye; rather, they serve as causes for the cognition of those [objects]."

Because the eyes and other [faculties] are insentient by nature like external objects, they do not possess the apprehension of objects in a primary sense; rather, their "apprehension of objects" is merely a conceptual construction based on their serving as causes for consciousness. Thus, it might be argued that objects are "apprehended" by them only in the sense that they produce the cognition of objects while remaining themselves unknown. But if this were so, what effect would consciousness have upon the object such that it could be said to "apprehend" the object—even though it is itself unknown—just as the eyes and other faculties do?
If you say that consciousness effects a manifestation [of the object], we say no.
Because they are synonyms for knowledge (*jñāna*).
Manifestation (*abhivyakti*), apprehension (*upalabdhi*), discernment (*paracchitti*), and experience (*saṃvedana*)—these and others are called synonyms; they do not denote a different entity.
Furthermore, it is not logical for something to be its own instrument (*karaṇa*).
Because there is a contradiction in an action operating upon itself,
and because of the existence or non-existence [of the object] in its states of having arisen or not yet arisen;
for instance, would cognition produce itself when it has already arisen, or when it has not yet arisen?
It is not first of all produced, because it is produced as being of one and the same fate (ekayogakṣema) as its own self.
Nor is it logical that what does not share the same fate as something else should possess that thing's intrinsic nature (svabhāva), for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, the production of an intrinsic nature that has already been produced is not logical, because there is no further excellence (atiśaya) to be added.
Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of the cessation of all causal activity;
nor is the position that [the cause] is unarisen tenable, because of its non-existence.
For the operation of a non-existent thing is not logical, since it is characterized by a total absence of any description of functional capacity.
Because if there were activity, it would follow that existence is lost;
for this alone is the definition of existence: the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
Therefore, the example is not equivalent to the subject of the argument.
Regarding the passage beginning with "therefore, in this case, being known," he says "therefore, in this case," and so forth:
"Therefore, in this case, being known constitutes validity,
because the experience of an object is never obtained if it remains unknown."

Now, one might object: "If cognition is established by itself through self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), then cognition would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by itself. Anticipating this doubt, he says "etāvat tu" and so forth: "But even if there were this much [self-awareness] here in the apprehension of self-awareness, because of the presence of causes of error, there would be no certain determination of its being such [i.e., valid]."
And at that time, even an entity is not apprehended by us as being real,
because through perception based on similarity, there is the possibility of superimposing something other than that [entity].

Indeed, it has been demonstrated in many ways that the certainty "it has been experienced" does not arise in its entirety simply because of the experience itself, since the production of certainty depends upon other causes. Therefore, although the capacity of cognition for the determination of an object is apprehended through self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), it is said to be "uncertain" because certainty does not arise due to the presence of causes of error—such as similarity with what is non-valid, lack of repetition, and so forth.
This is because there is a distinction between the experience and the certainty.
Consequently, there is no fault in maintaining that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥprāmāṇya*) by means of the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*).
As it has been said: "The cognition of its own nature is intrinsic, while its validity is established through practical efficacy (*vyavahāra*).
Thus, the term *tathātva* refers to validity.
Regarding the statement that "invalidity, moreover, [is established] in relation to its own object," and so forth, he says: "arising from practice" (*ābhyāsika*), and so on.
Just as knowledge arising from practice is understood to be valid by itself, so too some false knowledge is established as invalid by itself.
"Resulting from practice" means *ābhyāsika*.
Just as it has been stated that in some cases validity is determined by itself (*svataḥ*) through the power of practice, so too is falsity determined by itself for some.
And indeed, we observe certain people, such as those with ophthalmia, who by the power of habit determine a cognition of a mass of hair and the like to be false immediately upon its arising.
Regarding this point as well, concerning the cognition of falsity when there is a change [in the object], he says "bādhakāraṇa... and so forth:
"Even when there is knowledge of a subverting factor or of a defect in the cause, the aforementioned infinite regress occurs;
by that much alone, it is not possible to grasp its falsity."
It has been said:
"For it is stated by you that something is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) because there is no sublation;
yet the absence of sublation is itself accepted as another means of knowledge called non-apprehension (abhāva)."
By [the verse] beginning with "ityādinā" (and so forth),
[it is said]: "tad" (that).
Therefore.
Regarding the claim that "this very state of arising is what is measured as valid cognition," he says "the state of arising," and so forth:
"This very state of arising is measured as valid cognition;
[it is not so] because it is non-conceptual and because self-awareness is not accepted."
Nor can it be known by another cognition, because that other cognition is not present at that time;
for that too would be unmanifest, or else it would lead to an undesirable consequence.

Regarding the state of its arising, is it determined by itself as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or rather by another cognition occurring simultaneously, or by one occurring at a later time? These are the alternatives.
In that regard, first of all, it is untenable for it to be grasped as a means of valid cognition by itself, because all cognitions are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) with respect to themselves.
Nor is the perception of a cognition by another [cognition] accepted, because it is admitted that consciousness (*buddhi*) is eternally beyond the reach of the senses (*parokṣa*).

Nor can it be established by another cognition occurring at the same time, because two cognitions do not arise simultaneously. Nor can it be established by one occurring at a different time, because that other cognition is itself unestablished; and since its object is unestablished, the cognition that takes that object as its own is also unestablished due to its lack of manifest manifestation. If one were to require the establishment of that [second] cognition by yet another cognition, it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress.
Therefore, regarding the passage beginning with "wherever there is falsity," he says "even in the Veda" and so forth:

"Even in the Veda, a subverting means of knowledge has already been stated in the form of inference; therefore, by the exclusion of the Self and other entities asserted therein, it is not tenable as a valid authority."
Furthermore, because its human origin is established, the presence of a defective cause must be suspected;
or else, as in the case of fire, there might be an inherent capacity for false cognitions.
Therefore, knowledge arising from an injunction is suspected of having a defective cause;
and that which is suspected of having a defect because a defect has been observed does not differ from that which is suspected of having a defect [in general].
The Buddhists do not state that mere similarity [with other things] is a subverting proof against the Veda;
rather, it is because the categories such as the "self-universal" (ātmasāmānya) and so forth taught therein are subverted by valid cognition.
This has been established in the *Ātmaparīkṣā* and other works.

Furthermore, it is stated that its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) is possible because, in the *Śrutiparīkṣā*, the human origin of the Vedas has been established; or even if they were not of human origin, the possibility of causes for falsity exists—such as in the case of forest fires and the like—and thus its lack of authority is conceivable. This is not said merely on account of a formal similarity (*sādharmya*). One might object: "Even if it is indeed conceivable, how can its lack of authority be established by mere conceivability? To this he says: "And because of a perceived defect, that which has a suspected defect does not differ [from the former].
That sentence in which defects are suspected is so described.
"It is not divided" means that the validity of both is equal, because both are equally fit for the practical application of the term "existent."
He concludes with the words "Therefore" and so forth:
"Therefore, even for the Veda, intrinsic validity is not tenable;
by that [reasoning], let it be accepted that its author was one who was certain and free from defects."
The analysis of the compound is: "it has been composed and it has been explained" (*kṛtaś cāsāv ākhyātaś ca*).

"Explained" (*ākhyāta*) means "expounded. It is a third-case compound meaning "composed and explained by faultless persons" (*nirdoṣaiḥ puruṣaiḥ kṛtākhyātaḥ*). Its state is its "nature" (*tattvam*); thus the analysis is: "the state of being both ascertained and composed/explained by faultless persons" (*niścitaṃ ca tan-nirdoṣakṛtākhyātatvaṃ ca*).
This very point should be accepted; the connection is that this is for the sake of establishing the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda.
And thus, if this is accepted, there would be extrinsic validity (parataḥprāmāṇya); however, if it is not accepted, the implication is that there would simply be invalidity (aprāmāṇya).

Regarding the claim that "one should accept the fact that [the Veda] was composed by one who is certain and faultless," Kumārila offers the following reply, beginning with the words *rāga* and so forth:
"For indeed, the more that speakers are possessed of passion, hatred, and the like, the more they protect their own sacred recitation (*svādhyāya*); is this not so?"
Who has what weakness? Or who is the first reciter of which [section]?
Who would ensure the preservation of the accents, and who would corrupt a word by placing it in the wrong position?
For how could one who has enemies intent on finding his weak points not indeed recite the Veda with care so as to remain faultless?
If those men who study the Veda were pure and remained indifferent [to worldly affairs], they would have declared it thus by others: "The Veda has not been destroyed."
Then, after a long time, having been neglected and destroyed,
the Veda would become something entirely different, reduced to the state of a mere semblance.
And by those who restrain those possessed of passion, hatred, and so forth—
who are consumers of the Vedas— the Veda is always protected and shall not lose its own nature.

Whose memory, intellect, and so forth would an opponent weaken; or who, having studied from whom, could alter the weakness or the deviation of the accents such as the udātta; or who could break up what is not a word and recite it as a word? Since there are men who study the Veda, exerting themselves with aroused vigor, intent on searching for the slightest flaw in that Vedic reciter—how could such a Vedic reciter not recite the Veda with reverence?

Therefore, since there is no suspicion regarding the lack of authority of this Veda, the intention is: why should its status as being "declared by one who is established as faultless" not be accepted? For instance, if those who study the Veda, though pure-minded, were to remain indifferent while their Vedic texts were being destroyed by others and failed to declare them, then it would be possible to suspect that this Veda is something else entirely, having merely assumed the appearance [of the original].

To the extent that this Veda has always been protected by those of pure intellect—who, by obstructing and warding off men who would destroy it and whose minds are overwhelmed by passion and other afflictions—how could it ever abandon its own essential nature?

It might be argued: "Even if the Veda has been protected by them at all times, nevertheless, since it was completely destroyed during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), its alteration later on is possible. Anticipating this objection, he says: "It is accepted," and so forth. "It is accepted that the entire world was never otherwise [than as it is now];
no ultimate great dissolution is known to exist."
He refutes this with the words "This is not so," and so forth:
"Let it be granted that this is not so; for indeed, the textual reading may be identical, yet the realization of the true nature of its meaning does not occur without direct perception."
In this way, indeed, the mere equality of the textual recitation alone has been established.

But surely, it is the means for attaining the understanding of the meaning; therefore, for that purpose, its status as being composed and transmitted by one who is certainly faultless must necessarily be accepted.

Furthermore, he shows that it is not possible for one who is not omniscient to determine equality with respect to all places and times merely by the non-observation of a recitation, in the passage beginning with "And all," etc.:
"And all men, as well as all places and times,
appear clearly in the mind of the observer like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand."
He is capable of understanding the identity of the recitation; otherwise, however, how could there be disagreement due to differences in place, time, person, and circumstance?
Right here he states the proof, beginning with "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth:
if the reading were identical [in all cases], then doubt or disagreement regarding the reading among persons in certain places and so forth would not occur.
Regarding the statement "the entire world is accepted [as existent]," and so forth, he says: "The world is always thus perceived," and so on.

Even here, you have no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that the world is always thus perceived. It is not logical to establish non-existence merely through non-perception, as in the case of Saṃvarta.
There is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever to prove that the world is always exactly like this.
Furthermore, as for what is described by the Buddhists as the "eonic dissolution" (*saṃvartakalpa*)— the destruction of the receptacle world due to the impossibility of human birth—
and that which is stated by the authors of the *Smṛtis*:
"In the beginning, this was nothing but darkness, unperceived, without defining marks,
inactive, unknowable, as if entirely in deep sleep.
(Manusmṛti 1.5)
Thus, there is no subverting evidence whatsoever for either of these two types of dissolution by which the world could be established as always being exactly like this.

Furthermore, the non-existence of things is not established by mere non-perception, because even when a thing exists, it may not be perceived in certain circumstances; for the pervasion of mere perception by the absence of the thing is unproven.

Furthermore, because the Veda possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), there arises from it a constant certainty regarding the nature of its own meaning; since there is no delusion [in this regard], and because its eternity makes it impossible to alter its inherent nature, destruction is not possible in either case according to your own view. Therefore, he shows that for those who study the Veda, its preservation is entirely fruitless, with the words beginning "intrinsically" (*svataḥ*). On the view of intrinsic validity, the Veda produces certainty intrinsically regarding the nature of its own meaning; thus, there is no possibility of delusion or the like.
Therefore, while the states of ignorance, doubt, and error remain,
not even a single young bird among the twice-born would require instruction.
Furthermore, for that whose root is unknown, even destruction is not possible;
for what kind of destruction could there be of that which is eternal and surpasses even the diamond?
If it is argued that there is a change in its manifestation, that [change] has already been refuted in the case of what is eternal; therefore,
the wise consider even the preservation of such a thing to be fruitless.
"Dvijapota" means a young Brahmin.
Thus far, it has been demonstrated that its destruction is not possible due to its intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*).
Now, in order to show that it is also not possible because of its eternity (*nityatva*), he asks "Who indeed... and so forth.
"If there is a change in manifestation" means that it is connected with "destruction. "That" refers to [the destruction].
"Manifestation";
"of this" refers to the Veda.

He concludes with the verse beginning "atīndriya": Therefore, let it be accepted that there is an author who perceives objects beyond the senses, whose internal obscurations have been dispelled, and who knows the detailed classification of the meaning of the Vedas.
Thus concludes the examination of the doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*).
Internal darkness is afflicted and non-afflicted ignorance; its accumulation is its massing. One by whom that has been shaken off is so described.
"One who knows the distinctions" has been explained as the "agent."
The word "of the Veda" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Thus, it has been established that the matter asserted is in every way contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that the reason—"because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, the proof for establishing the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "those whose objects are characterized by doubt and error," and so forth; such is the meaning of the refutation.

As for the presentation of four alternatives followed by the attribution of faults to three of them, even there the Buddhist has no stake; for not even one of these four positions is accepted by the Buddhists, since they accept the position of non-restriction (*aniyama*).
Indeed, it was previously explained that both of these—some things [arise] from themselves and some from others—are [part of their view].
For this very reason, the presentation of four alternatives is also improper.
This is because even the fifth position, that of non-restriction (aniyamapakṣa), is possible.

Others, however, describe the meaning of the thesis differently: validity consists in having cognition as its very nature (*bodhātmakatva*). And this belongs to cognitions inherently (*svābhāvika*), not produced by excellences (*guṇakṛta*), since cognition as such is possible even in the absence of excellences, as in the case of erroneous cognition. Therefore, it is said that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥprāmāṇya*).

But since it is held that qualities perform nothing other than the removal of defects, validity depends upon qualities for the sake of destroying those [defects], not for the sake of its own acquisition.
This is incorrect,
because it is not logical that validity consists solely in the nature of cognition.
Since [validity] is also possible in the case of erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*),

if you argue that validity is a specific excellence of awareness (*bodhaviśeṣa*), then you should not say that it is inherent to cognitions and not produced by excellences (*guṇa*), because it exists even in erroneous cognition despite the absence of excellences.

For if validity were intended to be a specific excellence of awareness, then it would be appropriate to demonstrate a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding its being produced by excellences, but not regarding anything else.

Furthermore, by the statement "because it exists even in the case of the knowledge of the opposite (viparyayajñāna)," the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) is shown not with respect to a specific cognition (*bodhaviśeṣa*) being produced by a quality,
but rather with respect to cognition in general (*bodhasāmānya*).
Moreover, the opponent does not maintain that cognition in general is produced by a quality.
Rather, it is a specific excellence of awakening (*bodhaviśeṣa*).

Nor can it be demonstrated that there is any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in its being produced by excellences (*guṇakṛtatva*). Furthermore, we do not maintain that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥprāmāṇya*) on the grounds of its being produced by excellences, such that you would have to establish its intrinsic nature (*svataḥ*) by negating that [extrinsic production].
Rather, even though this particular cognition has been experienced, it does not produce a certainty in accordance with that experience because of the presence of some cause for error;
therefore, it is established as being "dependent on another" (*parataḥ*) for the sake of producing that certainty.
Furthermore, such a hypothesis could indeed be made even regarding invalidity.

The nature of being awareness (*bodhātmakatva*) is indeed non-validity; and that [non-validity] is inherent to cognitions and not produced by defects, because it occurs even in the case of correct cognition when there is an absence of defects. Therefore, non-validity is said to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Defects, however, perform only the sublation of excellences (*guṇa*); thus, for the sake of that sublation, non-validity depends upon defects, but not for its own acquisition. Consequently, this [argument of yours] is trivial. Uveyaka, however, says: "The nature of being awareness is not what constitutes the validity of cognitions; rather, what is it? It is non-contradiction with the object (*arthāvisaṃvāditva*)."

For instance, even when there is the nature of cognition (*bodhātmakatva*), if there is no non-contradiction with the object, there is invalidity, as in the case of the cognition of silver regarding mother-of-pearl.

Even without the nature of cognition, where there is non-contradiction with the object, there is validity, as in the case of smoke in relation to fire. Therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), it is established that validity consists precisely in non-contradiction.
And that [validity] arises from its own very cause.
It is not from another causal complex; therefore, it is said that the validity of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
Since the word *sva* signifies "one's own," the meaning is:
"from its own cause."

By the latter half of the verse beginning with "For a capacity that does not exist inherently," the reason for the denial of the existence [of validity] from another causal complex (*sāmagryantara*) is stated.
The meaning is: "Indeed, that which does not exist inherently cannot be produced by another, namely, by something other than the causal complex of cognition.

It might be argued: "Even for the causes of cognition, [the factors] are common to both valid and invalid cognitions; therefore, how could validity be restricted solely to the causes of cognition? Consequently, validity must be produced by a different causal complex, and not produced merely by the causes of cognition."
And that other causal complex is indeed accompanied by excellence (*guṇa*), and the excellences of the sense organs and so forth are its cause.

In the case of verbal testimony, it is established through common usage that the very fact of being composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) constitutes the excellence of the cause. Since this [excellence] is absent in the Veda, its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) follows as a consequence.
This is not a fault,
because it is unestablished that [validity] is produced by a different causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
For it is not possible for the operation of the excellences (*guṇa*) to be perceived as occurring toward the production of the effect called validity in a positive manner.
For it is the very nature of the sense-faculties and so forth, independent of anything else, that produces a cognition which is non-discrepant with the object.
As for collyrium and the like, their function lies in the removal of defects, not in the imparting of a quality.

Now, it might be argued: "Since the nature of the sense-faculties and so forth exists even when there is invalidity, it would follow that validity must arise in all cases, because the cause is complete."
This is not so;
for when defects are present, an effect distinct from that produced by another causal complex will arise.

It might be argued: why is the opposite not understood—that the very nature of the sense organ and so forth, independent of anything else, produces erroneous cognition, whereas a different causal complex, through the presence of excellences (*guṇa*), produces a cognition that does not deviate from the object?

This is indeed true; however, since it is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) alone produces validity in inference and the like, and since this is possible in the case of perception as well, that [three-fold nature] alone is postulated as the producer [of validity].

As for the effect consisting of erroneous cognition, since it does not arise from the mere nature of the sense organs and so forth, it leads one to postulate another causal complex (*sāmagrī*); thus, [the objection] is faultless.
But all of this is not without fault.

For instance, regarding what was stated—that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of cognition consists solely in its non-contradiction with the object, and that this arises from its own cause alone—this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). This is because we ourselves accept that "validity is a non-contradictory cognition" (*avisaṃvādivijñāna*); by this statement, the non-contradiction with the object is indeed the validity of cognition. However, since the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is specifically employed [in the definition], one might say that validity is not primarily intended for smoke and the like, which are of a non-cognitive nature; thus, validity as mere non-contradiction with the object remains unestablished [for those things].
Because knowledge alone is primary in the engagement with objects to be abandoned or accepted.

For instance, even when smoke and so forth—which are invariably concomitant with fire—are present, a person does not engage in action toward the object until the arising of cognition occurs. Therefore, since knowledge possesses an immediate causal efficacy (*avyavahita-kārakatva*) regarding engagement, it alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As it has been said: "Cognition is the means of valid cognition."

Because activity regarding objects to be abandoned or acquired is dominated by that [cognition], and because the non-contradiction of cognition— characterized by its capacity to reach the object— is simply the reaching of the object itself (since obstacles and the like are possible), and since this capacity is indeed the very nature (*ātmabhūta*) of things, who would desire its production from something else such that it would need to be negated?
For it is not logical that a property which has not been produced when [the thing] is produced should be its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And although that [validity] is the very nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the causes of error exist, it cannot be ascertained by those who have not yet realized its effect; thus, it is determined from something else, namely the effect called the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*).
Therefore, validity is said to be extrinsic (*parataḥ*) with respect to ascertainment, not with respect to its production.
Consequently, the refutation of its production from other causes is redundant, as there is no dispute on that point.

Indeed, you yourselves also accept that the determination of capacities occurs through external factors, as it has been said: "The capacities of all entities are established through the presumption of their effects.

Furthermore, the argument that is described as a reason for negating the existence of an entity from another causal complex—namely, "A capacity that does not exist inherently cannot be produced by anything else"—is equally applicable even to the case of non-existence; thus, that too would follow as being inherent.
That reason is not new, because it is inconclusive.

Furthermore, as for what was said— that the operation of excellences (*guṇa*) in the production of invalidity is not perceived to be possible through a positive formulation (*vidhimukhena*)— even this affirmative statement does not have its meaning clarified, so it is not understood.
What is this so-called "activity" (vyāpāra) by way of a positive injunction?

If it is first of all the intentional engagement for the sake of producing an effect, thinking, "I shall do this and that," then such [activity] is not possible even in the case of the sense organs and so forth. For entities possess no deliberative agency, since both volition and activity are impossible due to the momentariness of all things.
Consequently, since the operation of the sense organs and so forth could also occur by way of affirmation (*vidhimukhena*), they would not possess causality.

Now, if it is maintained that the sense organs and so forth are accepted as causes because they operate toward the production of an effect through their mere existence—even without the presence of an operation called "action"—then this is equally true for qualities (*guṇas*) as well.
For no other operation, fixed for all causes in the production of an effect, is perceived or possible apart from the proximity of their own existence.

Now, if it is argued that validity arises when defects have ceased upon the presence of excellences (*guṇa*), and therefore—because it is mediated by the cessation of defects—an operation of excellences through a direct positive formulation (*vidhimukha*) is impossible, then this is equally true for defects as well.

For instance, even when defects are present, if excellences have ceased, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) arises; thus, defects too would not have an operation toward the production of invalidity through a positive formulation.
Consequently, invalidity would also follow as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*), since there is no distinction [between the two cases].
For defects are not observed to operate directly toward invalidity by setting aside the excellences;
therefore, since no other causal relationship is possible except that which follows from the presence or absence of those [excellences], the causality of excellences is equal to that of defects.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that the very form of the sense organ and so forth, independent of anything else, produces a cognition that does not contradict the object—that too is incorrect.

Because it would follow that all cognitions are valid by virtue of having their causes complete, just like the nature of awareness (*bodharūpatā*). Just as the nature of awareness— which, though dependent upon the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), occurs in every cognition because its causes are complete even when defects and so forth are present— likewise, non-contradiction with the object (*arthāvisaṃvāditva*) would also [occur in every cognition].

It might be argued as follows: when invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) arises due to defects, validity (*prāmāṇya*), even though its causes are complete, does not arise; for it is impossible for two contradictory states, such as validity and its opposite, to coexist in a single cognition. However, the nature of awareness (*bodharūpatā*), being without opposition, certainly occurs everywhere. If this were so, then the very nature of the sense faculty would not be established as a cause independent of anything else, because even when that [faculty] is present and unimpaired, the effect called "validity" does not arise.
Indeed, it is not logical for that which is independent of anything else to ever fail to produce its effect.
Nor is it logical that something which does not arise even when another thing is present should have that as its sole cause, for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, you ought to explain this: if validity has its causes complete, why does it not arise even when defects (*doṣa*) are present?
If you say, "Because the defect, which is a cause contrary to itself, is present," [we reply: ...
The same applies to invalidity as well.

For that too, at that time, its own contradictory cause—such as the sense organs and so forth—is present; thus, let there be no production [of invalidity]. Furthermore, even if validity, fearing defects which are its contradictory causes, were to desire not to arise, why would it disregard its own cause, which exists at that time with unimpeded capacity?
For in this way, his own unimpeded power would be manifested if he were to produce his own effect by force, even though it was unwilling to arise.
An organ, its power being impaired by defects, would not produce validity; nor would it produce cognition at all due to its incapacity.
Otherwise, validity—being produced solely by the causes of cognition—would not be established, because it does not arise even when those [cognition-causes] have arisen.

For that which does not necessarily arise even when another thing arises cannot have the same cause as it, just as a rice sprout, which does not arise even when a *kodrava* sprout arises, does not share the same cause.
And since validity (*prāmāṇya*) does not necessarily arise even when cognition arises, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
Furthermore, no one could destroy a capacity that is identical in nature to the thing itself without destroying the thing's own essence.
And thus, it can also be recited as follows:
"Let it be accepted that the validity of all cognitions is intrinsic;
for a power that exists intrinsically cannot be destroyed by another."

Thus it may be argued: "It is not intended that the mere absence of defects in the sense organs is the cause of validity. Rather, it is a specific [absence]—namely, being free from defects; by means of that, the aforementioned defects do not apply."

If this is so, it follows that a different causal complex (*sāmagryantara*) alone, accompanied by excellences (*guṇa*), is the cause of the validity of the sense organs and so forth, because only that which is accompanied by excellences can possibly be free from defects (*doṣa*).
Consequently, one should not say that [the validity of cognition] is unestablished because it is not produced by a different causal complex.
If it is argued that the function of excellences lies in the removal of defects and not in the production of validity;
That is not so;
since cessation (*apagama*) is a non-entity (*avastu*), it is not logical for any activity to occur with respect to it.
For no activity whatsoever is possible regarding a non-entity, such as a rabbit's horn, which by its very nature cannot be produced.
As for what was stated—that in inference and so forth, it is observed that the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) alone produces the cognition which is the producer of validity—this too is unproven.

For it is not the three-fold character alone that produces the inference; rather, there are also qualities residing in the cognizer (*pratipattṛgata*), such as non-delusion and the presence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding memory.

For even when the three characteristics [of a logical reason] are present, inference does not arise for a cognizer who has lost the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the memory of the relationship or who has not yet perceived that relationship; therefore, it is unproven that only that which produces cognition is what produces validity, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Consequently, the opposite position remains difficult to refute.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the effect in the form of erroneous cognition does not arise from the intrinsic nature of the sense faculties and so forth, that too is sheer audacity.
For it would follow that erroneous cognition could arise even without depending on the sense faculties;
indeed, it is not logical for something to depend on that from which it does not arise, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Furthermore, the cognition of two moons and so forth produced by those with ophthalmia and other defects does not arise independently of the sense faculties.

Furthermore, if validity is described as non-contradiction with the object, then how is the non-contradiction with the object known in the case of the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*),
such that those of your school who perceive the truth would apply the designation of "validity" to it?
For it is not possible to determine the capacity for that [result] without knowing its effect, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, since this entire web of words was constructed with the hope of establishing the authority of that very Veda which [the opponent] denies, it is not established for that very [Veda]; thus, this is merely like one seeking rice who threshes the husks—enough of this digression.
Thus concludes the examination of intrinsic validity.
To him whose great compassion has become his very nature through many incalculable aeons,
the best of speakers, who proclaimed dependent origination— TS 0005cd— [to him I bow].
Having prostrated before that Omniscient One, this *Tattvasaṅgraha* is composed.

By this, he provides a mere introduction for the purpose of supporting that qualification of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) which was stated as being taught by an omniscient one, saying "In this way," and so forth:
"In this way, since the validity of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established intrinsically (*svataḥ*)."
One does not strive to establish the existence of a being who perceives objects beyond the senses.

Thus, by the reasoning just stated, it is established that the validity of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not arise from themselves alone. Consequently, a person who perceives supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*) is established without any effort; therefore, no further separate exertion is undertaken for the sake of proving him.
It might be asked: "How can this be established without effort? To this he says, "Of the Veda as well," and so forth:

Since the authority of the Veda also depends upon a person, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) resides in that [person] who possesses knowledge beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya-jña*).
Otherwise, if the person who is the agent were subject to ignorance, doubt, and error, this [scripture] would possess no authority at all, just like anything else.
Having understood the connection between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth,
he who has taught it must be accepted by others as one possessing clear knowledge that transcends the senses.
"Of him" means of the person.
"From that" means from the person who is the agent.
"In that" means in the Veda;
this is a locative case of locus (adhikaraṇa-saptamī) in relation to the word "validity" (prāmāṇyatā).
"Validity" (prāmāṇya) means the quality of establishing objects that transcend the senses without error;
and this has been stated from the perspective of the views of others.

This is what is meant: if you must necessarily accept the authority of the Veda, then its authority is logically derived from its author—such as a person—and not intrinsic (*svataḥ*), as has been established previously. Furthermore, if that author of the Veda is one who perceives supersensible objects (*atīndriyadṛk*), then it is logical for the Veda to possess authority because of that author; otherwise, if the author were possessed of erroneous knowledge, doubt, and so forth, the Veda would incur a state of non-authority, just like the speech of a madman or the like.

Therefore, that author of the Veda who was previously established in the "Examination of Revelation" (*Śrutiparīkṣā*) as a perceiver of supersensuous objects must necessarily be accepted even by the Mīmāṃsakas; thus, his rejection should not be undertaken.

For indeed, having understood that no human being possesses the vision of supersensuous objects because the eye of their intellect is impaired by the cataracts of defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like, and considering that a person seeking to understand *dharma* and *adharma* would—finding no stable basis for the validity of cognition in things perceived by the senses—rely solely upon the Veda, just as a bird [seeks safety] when it cannot see the shore; or rather, thinking that all persons are corrupted by passion and the like, as well as by ignorance (*avidyā*), due to their lack of the means to pacify those defects, and therefore that there is no one at all who perceives supersensuous objects—the followers of Jaimini, being themselves impoverished of the wealth of such qualities, reject the possibility of a seer of supersensuous objects. Thus, they maintain that *dharma* is an object characterized solely by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), and not characterized by the senses and so forth; for the Vedic injunction alone is capable of making known an object that is past, present, future, subtle, concealed, or remote, whereas no other sense organ can do so.
And they provide proof for this:

"That whose form is made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in the non-apprehension of an absence—which has as its nature the absence of the five means of valid cognition—enters exclusively into the domain of the conventional usage of 'non-existence' for the wise, just like a sky-lotus; and the person who perceives all things has a form made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in the non-apprehension of an absence. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), because what is to be proven is the fitness for conventional usage.
Non-existence, however, is established solely through the means of valid cognition consisting of non-apprehension.

Now, one might object: "Is not all that is to be known (*prameya*) merely these five objects, such as form and so forth? And people in the world who know them are already well-known. Therefore, your thesis is contradicted by common experience. Anticipating this, he says: "The negation of being a knower of Dharma," and so on.
"If only the negation of being a knower of Dharma is intended here..."
When a person understands everything else, by what can he be restrained?

For here, in establishing the authority of the Veda, what is intended to be expressed is merely the negation of [the soul's] being a knower of dharma, the self, and the universe; it is not a negation of its being a knower of everything denotable by the word "all. Therefore, we do not negate that usage of the term "omniscient" which occurs among people with respect to some person in relation to their knowledge of all things other than dharma and adharma. Thus, the meaning is that no contradiction with common experience (*pratītibādha*) is possible.

Furthermore, showing that if even for you Buddhists the status of omniscience were to be attributed to some person other than one who knows dharma and adharma, then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), he says: "And the word 'all'... and so forth.
The word "all" is everywhere intended to depend upon the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).
Therefore, since there exists an omniscient being who is the subject under discussion, what do we lose?
Furthermore, he shows what that subject under discussion is—namely, that which is called "all"—in the passage beginning with "arthe ca" and so forth:
"And because [direct perception] is impossible regarding an object, some effect is postulated even in the case of the word;
in that regard, let him who knows all words be called 'omniscient' by name."

Just as in grammar it is explained by the grammarians that when an operation such as an affix or an augment is prescribed by a rule—such as "agni-dṛk" and so forth—that which is enjoined does not apply to the meaning itself, but is understood through implication to apply to the word expressing that meaning; in the same way, if you also, on the grounds that it is impossible for anyone to know everything, rely on the fact that the word "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*) as recited in your own established doctrine emphasizes the form of the word itself, and thus define "all-knowing" as one who knows the word "all" (*sarva*), then let it be so. [This would be] merely nominal, a mere name; for there is no one who can oppose someone who assigns a name as they please, since a name arises solely from independent whim. This is the sense.
Furthermore, even if there is some other basis for [the claim], such as oil, water, ghee, and so forth—by all of that, let it be that he is omniscient; he cannot be denied [that status].

Furthermore, even if "omniscient" is intended to mean one who has as his object all things other than merit and demerit—such as oil, water, ghee, and so forth—nevertheless, this results in proving what is already established.

Furthermore, is he intended to be omniscient through a concise knowledge of the entire world in its general form, or rather through a detailed knowledge of it in its specific forms? Regarding the first position, [the author] shows that it results in proving what is already established with the words beginning "bhāvābhāva" (existence and non-existence):
"When the entire world is said to consist of the nature of existence and non-existence, by whom is a person not accepted as omniscient in respect to that summary?"
Thus, if one is omniscient by relying on the "all-encompassing nature" even through the brief summary of knowable objects and the measurable, who is able to prevent that?

For the entire world, indeed, has the nature of non-existence because its intrinsic nature consists of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and so forth; yet it has the nature of existence because it is established as having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*). Thus, this universal property (*sāmānyadharma*)—the fact that the entire world possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence—which we have described, pervades all things. If one were to establish someone as "omniscient" based on the thorough knowledge of the entire world in that form, even so, that is quite acceptable; for by this much alone, the status of being a "knower of all phenomena" (*dharmajña*) is not proven for anyone. That is what is meant by "in brief."
That very state of being both existent and non-existent is the summary of the world, in the sense that "it is summarized by this.

Thus, even when there is full comprehension through general properties such as "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Furthermore, those who have ascertained all categories (padārtha) in their entirety, to whatever extent they exist,
would all be omniscient by virtue of knowing them, provided they were acquainted with those treatises.

Furthermore, it might be argued that one is established as omniscient by knowing all those categories (padārtha) that have been determined and taught as "everything" within their respective treatises—such as the five aggregates (skandha) by the Buddhists, the six categories (padārtha) by the Vaiśeṣikas, the sixteen [topics] beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the objects of cognition (prameya) by the Naiyāyikas, and the twenty-five principles beginning with primordial nature (prakṛti) and the Great One (mahat) by the Sāṅkhyas, and so forth. If this were the case, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); for other students who understand the meaning of those texts would also consequently become omniscient.
Likewise, who indeed would not accept as omniscient even one who, by means of the six instruments of knowledge, possesses discernment regarding the six objects of knowledge?

Furthermore, it might be argued that he who thoroughly discerns the sixfold objects of these [entities] through the six means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—namely, perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, presumptive testimony, and non-apprehension—is omniscient. To this we reply: even here, you are proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).
For instance, perception, being restricted to the fivefold objects such as form and so forth, does not have dharma and adharma as its object.

Inference also does not have them as its object, because its domain consists of the probandum (liṅgin) whose connection with the mark (liṅga) has been grasped by perception; and since dharma and the like are beyond the senses (atīndriya), it is impossible for anyone to grasp their connection [with any mark].

Although all verbal cognition has as its object that which is beyond the senses, one cannot nevertheless become a seer of supersensible objects through such knowledge; for that knowledge is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) since its object is something beyond the senses.
Nor is it logical that a person who relies on non-perceptual knowledge should be a direct perceiver.
Furthermore, analogy (*upamāna*), because its object is similarity and its qualifying attributes, does not have *dharma*, *adharma*, and so forth as its object, as has been stated.

Therefore, that which is remembered is the object of knowledge for comparison (*upamāna*), as it is qualified by similarity; or rather, it is the similarity itself, which is based upon that [remembered object].
As stated in the *Ślokavārttika*:

"Presumption (*arthāpatti*) also has as its object another thing postulated because a seen or heard fact would otherwise be inexplicable; it does not have *dharma* and so forth as its domain, for there is no seen or heard fact whatsoever that is inexplicable without *dharma* and so forth."

Or, let it be granted that presumption (*arthāpatti*) has *dharma* and so forth as its object; nevertheless, because its nature is not perceptual (*apratyakṣa-svabhāva*), one who possesses it cannot be established as a direct perceiver (*sākṣāt-darśin*) of *dharma* and the like.
As for non-existence (*abhāva*), however, since its object is precisely the absence of a cognizable thing (*prameyābhāva*), it is illogical for it to have *dharma* and the like as its object.

Thus, it has first been demonstrated that in establishing an omniscient being in a concise manner, one is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Now, he states the fault in establishing omniscience through the detailed cognition of the entire world, beginning with the words "But by way of particulars" (*viśeṣeṇa*): "But for him who imagines [an omniscient being] as one who directly perceives all objects in their particularity (*viśeṣa*), that imagination of his is both futile and false."
It is futile; it is fruitless because it is of no use for the attainment of the goals of human life.
It is false; it is erroneous because its object is an impossible thing.
He demonstrates that very quality of having an inconceivable object with the words "of one alone," and so forth:
"Who is capable of knowing all the atoms within a single body, or all its hairs and body-fur?"

Indeed, even the thorough knowledge of every single atomic division within a single body is impossible for men; how much more so, then, will there be the thorough knowledge of all the subtle and other specific distinctions existing throughout the entire world?
Demonstrating the futility of conceptual construction, he says:
"The means for attaining knowledge of the detailed particulars of all constituent parts,
if undertaken like an examination of a crow’s teeth, is useless."

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "parts" refers to the hands and so forth, while "individuals" refers to the *dhava*, *khadira*, *palāśa*, and other trees; thus, they are "parts and individuals. These parts and individuals are taken collectively, and he who knows their detailed expansion—characterized by atoms, hair, leaves, and so on—is described in that way. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent, according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*;
its formation has been explained.
The meaning is that it is useless because it is impossible, and because, by not having dharma and adharma as its objects, it is of no utility toward human goals (puruṣārtha).

Establishing this very point by means of an illustration, he says "yathā" and so forth: "And just as it is fruitless to say that one knows all things with the eye, so too the proposition that [the Buddha] is an omniscient perceiver of all things is likewise fruitless."

By this, it is stated, as appropriate, that the proposition (pratijñā) suffers from the fallacies of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatva) and being contradicted by common experience (pratītibādhitatva).
However, regarding that point of dispute and the utility for human goals in its proof, he demonstrates it with the verse beginning "svadharma" (one's own dharma) and so forth:
"In the proof and refutation of one who knows only his own dharma and adharma,
the acceptability or rejectability of the scripture composed by him is indeed established."
In that regard, while establishing the knowledge of the subtle distinctions of the entire world,
people labor in vain through their zeal for composing treatises and engaging in debates.
The compound is analyzed as "one who is his own [teacher] and who knows only dharma and adharma," referred to as such; [the phrase] "his means of proof and refutations" is the analysis.
This is a locative case.
For it is the acceptability or rejectability of the scripture composed by him that is established; thus, the connection is according to the respective order.

This is what is meant: if the proponent of the proof establishes his own teacher as one who knows dharma and adharma, then once that proof has been established, the acceptability of the scripture composed by him is proven.

And if the opponent, when refuting, negates the other's accepted teacher as one who knows only his own dharma and adharma, then once that negation has been made, the rejectability of the scripture composed by that teacher whose knowledge of dharma and adharma has been refuted becomes established.

Furthermore, as for the zeal with which the Sāṅkhyas, Buddhists, and others engage in composing treatises or in debate—having abandoned the diverse [range of] objects of dharma—to establish the omniscience of one renowned to both oneself and others, who pervades the entire world, by means of proving his knowledge or ignorance regarding subtle and other distinctions: that is merely the fruit of their affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
In the phrase "for the sake of establishing the knowledge of the subtle distinctions of the entire world," the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*);
however, in the phrase "in treatises or in debate," the locative case is used in the sense of a fixed point of reference (*avadhāra-saptamī*) relative to the zeal.

This might be the case: if there were no person who fully understands dharma and so forth, then how could there be an understanding of merit and demerit in the world? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the exclusion of perception and other means connected to all cognizers," and so on. [Thus,] merit and demerit would come to be cognizable solely through scripture.
Even though the position of the Mīmāṃsakas is established by this much alone, the further effort made to refute an omniscient being is like killing what is already dead.
Even those who, because the root has been severed and the knowledge of dharma destroyed, claim that there are omniscient persons— they have merely performed the threshing of chaff.
"Being cognizable solely through scripture" means being cognizable through scripture alone.
Although the word "scripture" (āgama) is a general term, it should nevertheless be understood by implication as referring specifically to the non-human (apauruṣeya) scripture.
"By this much alone."

Even though the Mīmāṃsā position—that "Dharma is that object characterized by Vedic injunction"—is established merely by the negation of [the Buddha's] knowledge of Dharma, the further effort we shall undertake to negate an omniscient person is fruitless, like killing the already dead, because the desired result has already been achieved. Furthermore, the effort made by Buddhists and others to prove an omniscient being once the knower of Dharma has been slain by the means of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) is likewise useless due to the absence of the intended result; it is like husking chaff for one who desires rice—such husking is merely the husking of chaff. Thus, for Buddhists and others, abandoning the knower of Dharma who is the primary subject and instead attempting to prove a knower of every subtle distinction existing throughout the entire world is analogous to the husking of chaff.
Regarding the phrase "because their root is severed":
those whose root—the primary thing, which is the thorough knowledge of the reality that is the nature of phenomena—is severed, are so described.
