The state of being that is their essence (*tattva*).

He shows that for these [proponents], such as the Buddhists and others who seek to establish an omniscient being, not only is their desired goal unestablished, but there is also the occurrence of an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*), by means of the verse beginning with "directly" (*sākṣāt*): "Since he would directly perceive impurities, tastes, and so forth, they would necessarily follow as being self-cognized; who indeed would postulate such a one? [Note: This refers to the logical absurdity that if an omniscient being were to perceive all things directly, including foul odors and tastes, those objects would have to be experienced through his own sensory consciousness, which contradicts the nature of such perceptions.]

It might be argued that because the Sugata and others have taught the reality of the entire mass of categories, their omniscience is inferred; thus, the proposition is sublated by inference and the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). Anticipating this objection, he says "na ca" and so forth:

"And the teaching of the meaning of the Vedas, Upavedas, primary and secondary limbs [of the Veda], and so on, is not observed in the words of the Buddha and others. How then could he be omniscient in vain?"

The Vedas are those known as the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma*; the Upavedas are *Āyurveda*, *Dhanurveda*, and so forth; the six limbs (*aṅga*) of the Vedas are phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual science (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), prosody (*chandas*), etymology (*nirukta*), and astronomy (*jyotiṣa*); their sub-limbs (*pratyaṅga*) are their constituent parts, such as verbal roots and the like; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of their ancillaries such as commentaries (*bhāṣya*) is intended. The meaning of these is that which is expressed (*abhidheya*); the statement that conveys (*pratipādaka*) it is the means of understanding. The sense is that no such [statement] from Buddha or others is observed which propounds the subject matter taught in the Vedas and so forth.
For the composition of a treatise that expounds the entire mass of all categories is not observed in anyone, since it is seen that all treatises have distinct subject matters.

Furthermore, it might be argued that because we observe the teaching of only a limited number of topics by the Buddha and others, other matters not taught in their own works may also be inferred as being known by them, since their capacity for thorough knowledge has been demonstrated; thus, the aforementioned fault remains in place. To this, he says "svagrantha" and so forth: "If it is maintained that an object known to oneself is [inferred] even if it is not recorded in one's own works, then all poets would be omniscient simply by virtue of the composition of their own poetry."

If it is maintained that even a meaning which is not recorded in texts and not explicitly taught is understood by them through the power of inference, then poets who compose narrative works based on their own imagination would also have to be considered omniscient, since they too are seen to possess the capacity for such thorough knowledge; thus, the reason [proposed] is inconclusive due to this lack of distinction.

It might be argued that while the teaching of supersensible objects is observed in the case of the Buddhas, it is not seen in the case of poets; therefore, it is inferred that only they possess the thorough knowledge of all supersensible objects, and not others. For otherwise, if one lacks the capacity for the thorough knowledge of all supersensible objects, one would likewise lack even a limited knowledge of supersensible objects, since there is no distinction between them. Thus, because the reason is qualified by the condition "provided there is the state of being a knower of supersensible objects," there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to poets. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the case of the omniscient ones," and so forth.
And when there are many omniscient beings who teach contradictory doctrines,
and all of whom possess equal grounds for their claims, which one indeed could be definitively identified as the true one?

Among the many Sugatas, Kapilas, Kaṇabhakṣas, Akṣapādas, and others who have been designated as omniscient by their respective devotees—when these are the objects of proof—which single one among them should be determined and ascertained as omniscient? For the reason for ascertaining someone as omniscient—the teaching of supersensuous matters—is equal in the case of all of them.
Nor is it logical to determine that all of them are omniscient, because they all teach mutually contradictory doctrines.

For it is not logical that all those who provide instruction for mutual benefit should be perceivers of reality, because things possess a single nature and thus lack any association with multiple mutually contradictory intrinsic natures.
If it is argued that the Sugata alone is to be accepted as such, he says "If the Sugata," and so forth:
"If the Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not?
Or if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference in their views?"
If it is argued that both would therefore be omniscient, he says: "Now, if both," and so forth.

Furthermore, it might be argued that the non-erroneous knowledge of the reality of all things without exception can be inferred for that very person whose speech has once been observed to have true meaning; to this he says "gaṇita... and so forth:

"In respect to a single portion such as mathematics and the like, all beings—including the Victors, Buddhas, and other sentient beings—are equally speakers of truth; thus, no distinction [between them] is discerned."
For indeed, among all embodied beings such as the Jinas, Buddhas, and others, speech that is non-contradictory is observed in certain instances regarding limited portions of calculation and the like.

It is not the case that for those who chatter excessively there would be nothing at all that possesses a true meaning; as it has been said: "Among a man who speaks much, it is not the case that there is not even a single word with a true meaning.

Consequently, since the cause is equal for all and no distinction can be determined, it would follow that everyone is omniscient; yet this is not tenable, because—as previously stated—it involves the teaching of mutually contradictory meanings.

Furthermore, it might be argued that he whose speech cannot be refuted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) anywhere will indeed be omniscient; to this, the author says "by which very," and so forth:
"By whatever reason the omniscience of one person is established, that same reason applies to another as well, merely out of partiality for one's own position. [2996]
The very same refutations that the Śākyas employ with vehemence in their proof of the omniscient Jina,
those very same ones the Jainas also apply.
In that case, how can a definitive conclusion be reached by means of their unstable and divergent arguments and refutations,
which are swallowed up by the emergence of mere reflections?
For the very reason that is employed by the sons of the Sugata to establish the omniscience of the Sugata—

namely, "The Sugata directly knows the reality of all objects because he teaches objects that have not been heard or inferred and are non-erroneous, just as a person who has perceived water through direct perception teaches it"— this same reason is presented by the Digambaras to establish the omniscience of the Jina.
Consequently, the doubt remains exactly as it was before.

Similarly, when the Digambaras present a proof for the omniscience of the Jina, the Śākyas raise objections such as: "He is not omniscient because the doctrines he taught, such as *syādvāda* and so forth, are untenable. When the Śākyas present a proof for the omniscience of the Sugata, the Jainas adopt those same objections: "He is not omniscient because the principles he taught, such as momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth, are untenable."

Furthermore, just as a reflection arises immediately upon the presence of an object, so too do refutations that stand in mutual opposition to these proofs arise immediately after those proofs. Therefore, how can a determination regarding anyone’s omniscience be made by means of these unstable proofs and refutations, which are themselves swallowed up by the very emergence of counter-reflections?
It might be argued: "He alone for whom no refutation can be made by anyone in the ultimate sense shall be recognized as omniscient. To this, he says "In this way," and so forth:
"In this manner, when those who imagine themselves to be omniscient have been mutually defeated, the proponent of the Vedas will destroy all others who remain in small numbers."
Exalting himself, he says:
"Just as any medicinal herb, when touched by the tips of a mongoose's teeth,
destroys all snake venom even when applied playfully."

Whatever reasoning— whether worldly or Vedic— is present in the mouths of the proponents of the Vedas, it all serves to remove the poison of the false knowledge of the snakes that are the Śākyas and others.
What, then, is this "any reasoning" (yukti)? He says: "Of whom," and so forth:
"Who indeed would conceive of that person whose [existence] reasons are unable to refute, characterized as being knowable, cognizable, a real entity, existent, and so on?"
He who imagines that an omniscient being is known by means of only a single instrument of knowledge surely perceives all tastes and other objects with his eye alone.

For that [proponent] for whom properties such as "knowability" (jñeyatva) and so forth—being unperceived as common to both the similar and dissimilar instances—constitute subverting arguments (bādhaka), is utterly impossible and should not be accepted by a discerning person.
For it can be said: "The Sugata is not omniscient, because he is knowable, cognizable, a real entity, existent, a speaker, a human being, and so forth, like a man on the street.
And these [reasons] are not inconclusive (anaikāntika).
For it is held that one is omniscient through the knowledge of all things; and that thorough knowledge of every object must occur either through sensory cognition or through mental cognition.

First of all, it cannot be by means of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*), because that has restricted objects as its domain; thus, having all things as its domain is untenable. For instance, cognitions such as those of the eye and so forth, because they have restricted objects as their domain, cannot possibly have all things as their domain. Indeed, these cognitions of the eye and so forth are produced by their own causes—the sense organs—which act as restrictors, and thus have the very nature of apprehending only restricted objects. Consequently, since they are well-known in the world to never transcend the boundaries of their own respective objects, it is not tenable that they should apprehend all things.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the various sense faculties being redundant.

Consequently, as for that Buddhist who postulates that one knows all phenomena—including taste, form, and so forth, which are apprehended by different sense faculties—by means of a single cognition, based on the statement "one knows everything by one [cognition] and sees everything by one," it follows that this Buddhist proponent must necessarily understand all phenomena, such as taste and the rest, through a cognition that has the eye as its instrument and extends to those distant objects.
And this cannot be maintained.
Let it not be that there is a simultaneous apprehension of all objects by means of a single cognition; for it will occur by means of multiple [cognitions].

Since multiple cognitions cannot occur simultaneously—and even if they could, there would still be no apprehension of all things—because the mind of another is not an object of sensory cognition, and because an object that has reached a state beyond one's range, such as being distant, subtle, or obstructed, cannot be grasped by it.

It might be argued: "Even if the apprehension of heterogeneous objects by cognitions such as that of the eye is not observed at present, nevertheless, it is conceivable that at some other time, such an apprehension of a heterogeneous object may have occurred for someone. To this he says, "By whatever types of means of valid cognition," and so forth:
"But by whatever types of means of valid cognition there is the perception of whatever types of objects..."
This has been seen by the world at present, and likewise it was so in another time as well.

For the specific determination of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities is dependent upon causes; it is not accidental. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everything could possess the intrinsic nature of everything else. Consequently, how could a change ever be possible for that which has acquired its selfhood in dependence upon such causes? For it is not conceivable that smoke, whose very existence is tied to fire, should arise from anything other than fire—this is the intended meaning.
Nor is the position tenable that [change occurs] through mental cognition.

For although that [knowledge] has all objects as its domain, nevertheless, it does not possess an independent operation of grasping objects; otherwise, it would follow that there would be no such things as the blind or the deaf.

Furthermore, if it were dependent [on other factors], then because its object-domain would be limited to those objects already grasped by sensory cognition, it would follow that it could not discern objects such as distant, subtle, or concealed things, or the minds of others, which have not been made objects of sensory cognition.

It might be argued that because we observe differences in degrees of excellence among individuals resulting from the practice of wisdom and other qualities, an ultimate limit of perfection is also possible; to this, he says "ye 'pi" and so forth:

"Even those men who are seen to possess excellence through their wisdom, intelligence, and strength do so by way of small, incremental differences, and not by means of perceiving what is beyond the senses."
For even a wise man, though capable of perceiving subtle matters,
excels other men by not transgressing the norms of his own kind.

For it has never been observed that anyone, even through practice, attains the vision of objects beyond the senses. To illustrate: even a man of supreme intelligence, though capable of perceiving subtle objects by means of his refined intellect, is seen not to transcend the natural limitations inherent to his own species—that of being human—characterized by such traits as the lack of divine vision; he is seen to surpass other men only in these [intellectual] respects, but no one is seen to be endowed with divine vision and so forth. This is the sense.

And then, with his divine eye—utterly pure and surpassing that of humans—he sees beings going to happy destinies and going to miserable destinies, and so forth; the sense is that [the opponent thinks] what is proclaimed by the Buddhas is simply not tenable.

Granted that there may be an excellence in all cognitions due to practice and other factors, nevertheless, these [cognitions] excel only while remaining within the boundaries of their own respective objects. Demonstrating this in detail, he says: "In sounds accessible to the ear," and so forth:
"In sounds accessible to the ear, through the perception of what is distant or subtle..."
An excellence of person is not perceived through the apprehension of form and so forth.

Furthermore, even by means of the eye, the manifestation of subtle forms situated at a distance is performed through the attainment of excellence; however, there is no seeing of sound and other such objects.

"Perceptions" (*upalabdhi*) refers to cognitions (*jñāna*) regarding things that are distant or subtle; the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the phrase "by those" (*tābhiḥ*) is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, one may interpret it as "by means of the perception of the distant and subtle. Thereafter, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed in the sense of cause (*hetu*), and the suffix *tas* is prescribed because [the word] belongs to the class beginning with *vidhā*. However, the connection is not that "the seeing of sound and so forth is performed by the eye."

Thus far, the non-transgression of the limits of their respective objects by the sense-faculties and their cognitions has been demonstrated; now, he establishes that the excellence of mental consciousness is seen precisely through its non-transgression of the objects it practices, beginning with the words "In this way," and so forth:
"In this way, a great excellence is observed in the investigations of the treatises;
however, the knowledge of other treatises is not obtained by that alone."

Clarifying this very point, he says "having known," and so forth: "Having understood that the distinction between correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*) is remote, the intellect is not excelled [in its capacity] by the determination of constellations, lunar days, and planetary positions."
Even one who is distinguished as a knower of light, such as the eclipses of the moon and sun and so forth,
is not able to know the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of words beginning with "ādi."
Likewise, even one possessing a superior knowledge of the Vedas, histories, and so forth,
is not capable of directly perceiving the creation, the deities, or the past.
One who knows the luminaries (jyotis) is a jyotirvit. The analysis of the compound is: he in whom there exists an excellence (atiśaya) of those knowledges found in the Vedas, Itihāsas, and so forth.
By the word *apūrva*, dharma and adharma are expressed.

Furthermore, demonstrating that even when excellence occurs by transgressing the limits of its own object, it does not reach the state of ultimate perfection, but is instead seen to be limited by only a certain degree of distinction, he says: "One who, having leaped, traverses ten cubits of space," and so forth:
"He who, having leaped, traverses ten cubits of space, is not able to go a *yojana*, even with hundreds of practices."

For instance, even if some individuals whose bodies were thick with phlegm and were initially unable to leap even a single cubit into the air, later—through the process of practice—attain such lightness of limb as to clear a space of ten cubits in the sky, they would still remain incapable of flying even a single *yojana* along the path of the birds, even with a hundred efforts.
He concludes with the words "Therefore" and so forth:
[p.827] Therefore, even by means of superior cognitions that have reached an extreme distance,
one is able to know only something slightly more [than others], but not that which transcends the senses.
"Exalted cognitions" (*atiśayajñānāni*) means cognitions that possess excellence (*atiśaya*) or pre-eminence (*prakarṣa*).
The compound is formed by a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) even in the third [case]. The word "by them" (*taiḥ*) is used in the instrumental case to express the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Clarifying this very point, he says "one" and so forth: "The perception that arises for one situated in a single room would have its power only there, and not at all in another room."
And as for those objects separated by great distances— by lands, mountains, and oceans,
or by other continents and islands— who here could perceive them while remaining right here?
A *varṣa* is a specific region of the world;
for example, the land of Bhārata is called *Bhāratavarṣa*.
Showing that others as well have placed their own hands upon this matter, he says "Nala," and so forth:
"And while Nala and Ṛtuparṇa— both of whom were experts in the heart of horses and dice— were traveling together in a carriage, these words were spoken by Ṛtuparṇa."
No one knows everything; an omniscient being is not possible.
There is nowhere any single person in whom knowledge reaches its ultimate perfection.
Regarding the word *saṃvāha*: it means a chariot;
for it is indeed heard in tradition that there was once a king named Nala.
It is said that, being ignorant of the secret of the dice, he lost his entire kingdom through gambling.
His queen was named Damayantī;
having been deprived of his whole kingdom, he went into the forest accompanied by her alone.
Even though he had arrived there, by the power of fate he was separated from her while there;

his face clouded by the storm of grief born from the separation from his beloved, plunging into an ocean of anxiety, and wandering here and there with his physical luster utterly diminished, he somehow managed to survive for a short time by adopting the service of King Ṛtuparṇa, remaining there unrecognized. And that queen of his, after much difficulty, reached her father’s house.
Her father proclaimed Damayantī’s svayaṃvara throughout all lands so that her husband might come there.

King Ṛtuparṇa heard that there was indeed to be a svayaṃvara for Damayantī; having heard this, he set out for that place with Nala as his charioteer. Now, Ṛtuparṇa was an expert in the secret of dice, but he did not know the secret of horses.
Nala, however, knew the heart of horses but was not an expert in the heart of dice.
Ṛtuparṇa had already ascertained that he was an expert in the heart of horses;
having realized this, he said to him, "Sir, teach me the heart of horses."
Nala also said, "I shall tell you if you will likewise tell me the secret of the dice.
Then R̥tuparṇa declared, "No one knows everything," and so forth.
Thereafter, King Nala learned the secret of the dice from R̥tuparṇa, won back his kingdom once more, and brought it home; such is the story.

Furthermore, as one who is omniscient, he must necessarily know objects of the past and the future; otherwise, if he were to know only the present, he would be a knower of a limited portion (*pradeśajña*) rather than omniscient. And [the author], demonstrating that knowledge of the future and so forth is not possible [for a non-omniscient being], says "anāgate" and so on:

"And there is not even the slightest capacity for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the future; nor can there be the arising of inference (*anumāna*) and the like without signs (*liṅga*) and so forth."
Since perception arises by the power of the objective reality of a thing, and since a future thing is not yet a reality, perception has no operation upon it.
Nor does inference apply, because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
For there is no known logical mark anywhere that is connected with a future thing, because the future thing does not exist.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of examples is intended. The mention of the future is illustrative; it should be understood that the past is also included, because in that case as well, there is no operation of direct perception due to its lack of substantial reality.
Therefore, the pervasion (vyāpti) of the group of reasons, such as "being an object of cognition" (prameyatva), is established.

For this very reason, the pervasion of the previously mentioned reason—"because its form has been made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-apprehension" (abhāvapramāṇaviṣayīkṛtavigrahatvāt)—is also stated to be established.
Thus, having demonstrated the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reasons, he concludes [the point to be proven] with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), and so forth:
"Therefore, there exists no direct perceiver of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*);
rather, he who perceives through eternal speech (*vacana*) truly perceives."
It might be argued that not everyone perceives through an eternal word alone;
for instance, Śākyamuni perceives from the words composed by the sage Kanakakāśyapa and others, and others perceive even from those [words].
To this, he says "etad" and so forth.
Unable to tolerate this, whoever considers that even the Buddha and others possess knowledge of supersensible objects based on another human scripture—
Because it is equal to that very [person], the non-authoritativeness of your statement—
and indeed of the person [who made it]— must be stated by means of the very reasons previously mentioned.

Regarding this statement just mentioned—that "he who sees by means of eternal speech truly sees"—one who cannot tolerate this, such as a Buddhist or another, might think: "One does not see everything through this eternal speech, but rather through that produced by another person, such as the scripture composed by Kanakakāśyapa and others regarding Śākyamuni. For one who speaks thus, it must be stated that his speech lacks authority (*apramāṇatā*). His speech is "that speech" belonging to another person; the reason is that it is equal to the speech of any other person whose words have been observed.
The connection [of the sentence] is that it must be stated that the person who composes the scripture is not an authoritative source (*apramāṇatā*).
How so?—by means of the previously mentioned reasons, such as being an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and being an object of valid cognition (*prameya*).

[Objection: But surely the succession of Buddhas is beginningless, and thus the established doctrine (siddhānta) composed by them is also beginningless. Consequently, because these two [the Buddhist doctrine and the Veda] are likewise beginningless—just like the succession of those devoted to the Vedas and the Veda itself—they are free from fault. To this, he replies with the words "of sentences composed by an author," and so forth: "That which is called the beginninglessness of sentences composed by an author..."
That which rests upon two types of non-valid cognition cannot establish validity.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "The words of Śauddhodani [the Buddha] do not possess the status of valid cognition because they are dependent;
for Śauddhodani likewise did not perceive Dharma by himself."
Just as there is a lack of authority for Śauddhādana and his statement, so too there is a lack of authority for others such as Kanakakāśyapa and their words.
Even if one were to postulate a beginninglessness for such individuals,
it does not exceed the state of lacking authority, because they remain situated in that very condition.
Therefore, even if the beginninglessness of such individuals and their statements is postulated, it does not exceed— indeed, it remains far removed from— that lack of authority,
because they remain precisely within the state of being unauthoritative.
Therefore, those who act like Mīmāṃsakas assert a commonality of beginninglessness for the Buddhas, just as they do for those who study the Vedas.
Because it is a specific kind of ignorance, it does not attain equality with them;
for in this way, validity and invalidity would both be beginningless.

In this regard, even if the similarity between the Buddha and others on one hand and the Vedic scholars on the other is described merely by virtue of their beginninglessness, nevertheless, authority is not established by that beginninglessness alone, because there is no contradiction between being beginningless and being either authoritative or non-authoritative.

The collective meaning is simply this: while both the Vedic scholars and the Buddha and others may respectively possess beginningless authority or lack thereof, the mere fact that both are beginningless does not establish that one is authoritative and the other is non-authoritative.
Clarifying this very point with an example, he says "yaḥ" and so forth.
Indeed, those valid cognitions and their fallacies, as well as their respective merits and defects, though beginningless,
do not all become equivalent merely by virtue of being beginningless.
Gold that serves as the basis for worldly transactions is without beginning or end, existing just as it is;
since illusory gold is also like this, in what respect is it equal to that [real gold]?
The analysis of the compound is: "the qualities and defects of valid cognition and its fallacies."

Now, having avoided the charge of proving what is already established— that the body [of the Buddha] has been made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-apprehension— he states the distinction of the Veda from the Omniscient One while establishing the non-existence of the Omniscient One,

beginning with the words "Omniscience," and so forth: "Omniscience in the case of the Buddha and others, and the eternity of the Veda— those who claim these two are equal, to them the distinction is now stated."

To those who speak thus—that there is no distinction between the two because they are equal as causes for right practice, since the cognition of supersensuous objects occurs both through the eternal Veda and through the words of the Omniscient One—the specific distinction of the Veda is now stated in response to such speakers.

For indeed, the Omniscient One is not established by even a single one among the five means of valid cognition—perception, inference, verbal testimony, analogy, and presumptive testimony. Therefore, how could there be any similarity between him—who is non-existent and whose form has been swallowed up by the means of valid cognition known as non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*)—and the Veda, which is a means of valid cognition recognized even by cowherds and their wives? Thinking thus, [the author] refutes the claim that he is established by the five means of valid cognition such as perception, starting with the words "The Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*). "The Omniscient One is certainly not seen at present by people like us.
(Codanā 117ab)
And no single part or inferential mark has been perceived that could lead to an inference.
Kumārila’s *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*—; SrDS 3.076; R 29,16+26;
---V cited in: NBhū 462,14; TBV 45,8, PKM 250,4, pādas ab BSS 133,12 (v.l. *cakṣurādibhiḥ*), LSS 121,8f., (will be discussed below TS 3503f u. ...).
(Refuted together with [the previous argument])—First of all, an omniscient being is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by people like us who possess limited vision.
For the direct perception of those with limited vision is threefold: sensory cognition, mental cognition, and the self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Even this threefold [cognition] is not capable of making an omniscient being known, because it does not have that as its object.
For sensory cognition is restricted to the five objects such as form; therefore, by means of it, the mental qualities inherent in another's continuum are not made into objects.

Nor is it so by means of mental cognition (*mānasa*), because—since it perceives an object immediately following the object grasped by sensory cognition—it is restricted to objects such as form, just like sensory cognition.
Nor can they be known through self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because that has as its object only the present minds and mental factors existing within one's own continuum.
Therefore, by means of it, the mental phenomena belonging to another’s continuum, those belonging to one’s own continuum, and those that are future cannot be perceived.
Furthermore, since it is precisely the knowledge of the yogi that is the subject to be proven, the consideration of whether it is apprehended or not apprehended does not apply here.
Nor can it be established by inference, for the Buddhists maintain that inference relies upon three types of logical marks (*liṅga*).
Among these, since the present context concerns a proof by way of affirmation (*vidhi*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is the mark under consideration here.

Nor is it an effect (*kārya*), because the causal relationship is established through perception and non-perception; and since no causal relationship can be proven between anything and an omniscient being who is beyond the reach of the senses.

Even an essential nature (*svabhāva*) cannot serve as a reason to establish the existence of an omniscient being, because if that [being] is not perceived, it is impossible to apprehend an essential nature that is non-distinct from it.

Therefore, a "portion" (*ekadeśa*)—which must be observed, well-known, and function as a logical mark (*liṅga*)—that is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), does not exist when examined, such that it could lead to the inference of an omniscient being.

Furthermore, in establishing the existence of an omniscient being, every reason fails to escape the three types of fallacy: unestablishedness (*asiddhi*), contradictoriness (*viruddhatva*), and inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

For when a reason (*hetu*) is stated, it must be asserted as either a property of an existent (*bhāvadharma*), a property of a non-existent (*abhāvadharmo*), or a property of both; these are the three possible positions.

Among these, with respect to the omniscient one (*sarvajña*) as the subject (*dharmin*), a property of an existent cannot be established as being admitted by the opponent, because that very subject is unestablished (*asiddha*) since it is the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*); or, if it were established, it would follow that there is no dispute.
For how could a proponent not accept a property of an existent that he desires for that [subject], given that it is impossible to apprehend a mere property without a substratum?
Nor is a reason that is a property of non-existence suitable for establishing an omniscient being, because it is contradictory, as it proves something contrary to existence.
Nor is one that is a property of both [existence and non-existence], because it is inconclusive.

For how indeed could a property of both existence and non-existence possess the nature of a reason—characterized by non-deviation from existence—which is obtained through the exclusion of its occurrence in the counter-example called "non-existence" when proving a property of existence?

Therefore, since not even a single part of any of the three types [of evidence] functions as a probans (*liṅga*) that leads to inference, there is no establishment of an omniscient being through inference.
He shows that there is also no determination of an omniscient being from scripture (*śabda*) with the words "nor is there any scriptural rule," and so forth:
"Nor is there any scriptural rule that makes known an eternal omniscient being."
And how can he be established by means of a fabricated truth?
The cognition that arises with respect to an object not in contact with the sense organ [but] through a word is verbal (śābda).
And that is of two kinds: that produced by eternal words and that caused by human utterance.
In that regard, since there exists no eternal scripture (*āgama*) establishing an omniscient being, the first [alternative] is not possible.

Furthermore, as for what is recited in the Upaniṣads and other texts—such as, "He who is truthful in speech, truthful in resolve, and truthful in desire; he is to be sought after, he is to be known"—that too must be regarded as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

And as for the human statement that says, "That Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One," since that lacks authority (*apramāṇatva*), how could he be made known by such an untruth?
It might be argued that we do not recognize [the Buddha] as omniscient based on just any statement;
rather, it is based on what was spoken by that Blessed One himself:
"I am omniscient, I am all-seeing; there is nothing unknown to the Tathāgata," and so forth.
Therefore, he says "atha" and so forth, meaning that it is understood from his very words alone:
"Now, if the omniscient one is recognized by others solely through his own words..."
How could the establishment of those two, which are mutually dependent, be possible?
This being the case, the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) results.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because it was spoken by the Omniscient One," and so forth.
"The word is true because it was spoken by the Omniscient One; therefore, its existence [is established].
How could both of these be established without another established root source?
For instance, the validity of that statement cannot be ascertained as long as it is not understood that "this was spoken by an omniscient one.
And since the cognition of that omniscient person arises from that very statement, a clear circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is evident.
[The phrase] "established from another source" refers to a different basis.
The meaning is: "except for another determined cause."

Furthermore, it might be argued that an omniscient being is established based on the words of disciples such as Śāriputra, since he said, "This one who delights the Śākya clan is omniscient. To this, [the author] replies with the verse beginning "asarvajñapraṇītāt" and so forth: "But if those who understand an omniscient being from a statement composed by one who is not omniscient—a statement devoid of a foundation—do not likewise [understand] an omniscient being from their own words, why not?"

For there is no distinction between the statement of another and one's own statement for one who has not established the absence of valid cognition [in the former], such that we perceive no reason—other than sheer stupidity—for why Buddhists do not accept an omniscient being on the basis of their own words, yet accept it on the basis of the words of another.
Now, if it is thought that there have been and will be infinite Tathāgatas, and that therefore the omniscience of one is established by the word of another,
and that of another by the word of yet another— regarding this, he says: "Many omniscient ones would have to be postulated for the sake of establishing even a single omniscient one," and so forth.
Whoever is even a single non-omniscient person does not understand the omniscient one.

For one who follows a succession of omniscient beings in order to establish a single omniscient being, even upon the exhaustion of an entire human lifespan, it is impossible for a person of limited vision to produce a certainty regarding an omniscient being; thus, it would follow that one must postulate an infinite series of omniscient beings.

Moreover, let alone the fact that those of the present day are incapable of understanding an omniscient being who is not present; rather, even those contemporaneous with him are simply unable to know him if they are not themselves omniscient. Demonstrating this, he says:

"This one is omniscient," and so forth: "For even by those cognitions existing at that time, it is impossible to know that 'this one is omniscient,' since they are devoid of the specific cognition of his knowledge and its objects."
If an omniscient being is not understood by someone, then for that person,
the authority of his words does not exist, because their source is unknown, just like the words of others.

The knowledge of that omniscient one—that very knowledge is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the object to be discerned (*paricchedya*) for that consciousness; thus it is described as "that [consciousness] which has that [knowledge]. They are empty of, or devoid of, that.
Alternatively, they are empty of that which is to be known by his knowledge; the meaning is that they are not omniscient.
For it is not possible to conclude that someone is omniscient merely from seeing their physical body.
This is because this determination is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of a connection with a qualified cognition;
and that qualified cognition, which has all objects as its domain, is the means of proof.
Its status as having all objects as its domain cannot be determined without the apprehension of the objects to be grasped by it.
For the cognition of "the man with a staff" does not occur without the apprehension of the staff.

The formal argument is as follows: for whatever [cognition] has the apprehension of a qualifier (*upādhi*) as its condition of apprehension, there is no apprehension of that [qualified object] in the absence of the apprehension of that qualifier; just as the apprehension of "the man with a staff," which has the apprehension of the staff as its qualifier, does not occur when the form of the staff—the qualifier—is not apprehended. And for those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*), there is no apprehension of the form of the knowable (*jñeya*), which is the apprehension of the qualifier for the apprehension of the omniscient one's knowledge. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), because the apprehension of the qualified is pervaded by the apprehension of the qualifier.
And that [omniscient being] does not exist here [in this world].

Consequently, since even a non-omniscient person present at that time cannot ascertain an omniscient being, the words of an omniscient being—though they may exist—are themselves unascertained for such a person and thus lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*), because of the absence of the determination of the omniscient one's knowledge, which is the cause for ascertaining the authority of the source.
This is just like the case of other [non-omniscient] persons' words.
"Of the words of the man on the street."

Now, suppose it is thought that because he thoroughly understands the various types of mental dispositions and behaviors of his entire assembly of disciples, he wins over the minds of those to be trained through miracles such as telepathy, and thereby effortlessly demonstrates his own nature as omniscient to them. To this, he says: "Even by all the disciples," and so forth:
"Even while corroborating the objects known by all the disciples, he would not be omniscient, because of the exclusion of objects known by other worlds."
Furthermore, it is impossible for there to be a corroboration of all knowable objects known by every person,
because there is no meeting with men residing in the three worlds throughout the three periods of time.

Even if one were to know the objects known by however many people present at that time, one would still not be omniscient, because of the lack of knowledge regarding objects known by other people who are not present at that time.

For one does not become all-knowing through the knowledge of only a single part, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle. Nor is it possible for there to be a correspondence with everything known by every person present at that time.

Because there is no possibility of corroboration for those who are far away and those who do not seek [to question him], one might argue: "When all people approach the Tathāgata simultaneously and ask whatever they wish, the Blessed One answers them at that very moment; therefore, there is indeed corroboration regarding all objects of knowledge known by all men. To this, he says: "by those residing in the three times and the three worlds.

For a meeting with men existing in the past, future, and present times is nowhere possible, nor is a meeting with those residing in the three worlds consisting of heaven, the underworld, and the mortal realm.
Alternatively, the "three worlds" should be understood as consisting of the three realms: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

It might be argued: "If he did not possess the capacity to know the objects known by the entire world, then how could there even be agreement regarding only a small portion of those objects? Yet such agreement does exist; therefore, we consider that he indeed possesses the capacity to know all things. To this, the author replies with the verse beginning "Even one who knows a little," and so forth:
"For even one who knows only a little is able to delude a few people, so that they—whose minds are deluded by devotion—might accept him as omniscient."
Some, though capable of verifying what has been eaten, what was thought of, or what object is held in the fist,
are devoid of knowledge of the Dharma and other such truths due to their deceptive arts.
Likewise, some who are skilled in magic, sorcery, and the like, delude ignorant people so that they appear to be omniscient.

For the mere knowledge of a few supersensuous objects does not establish his mastery of *dharma*, *adharma*, and so forth, because this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the existence of deceptive knowers who are skilled in illusions, sorcery, and the like.

For instance, by the application of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so on, they indeed correctly identify food and condiments as they were eaten, objects as they were thought of in the mind, and substances held in the fist;
yet, by this much alone, they do not become knowers of *dharma* and the rest.

Just as some who are skilled in the arts of illusion display various gardens, celestial palaces, throngs of apsarases, sons of gods, and so forth in the sky, there is thus an inconclusiveness [in the argument].

[Objection: But surely in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, Brahmā and others are celebrated as omniscient; for it is recited therein that "the knowledge of Brahmā is unobstructed, as is his dispassion. How then is it not established through scripture that there is an omniscient being? To this, he says "itihāsa... and so forth:

"In the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, even though Brahmā and others are proclaimed to be all-knowing, and it is stated that their knowledge is unobstructed and they possess dispassion," [this does not establish an omniscient being].
That [omniscience] must also be spoken of only in a figurative sense, like the meaning of mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas);
or else, it is said to consist in the absence of obstruction regarding the knowledge of the dharmas and other matters under discussion.
Although his unimpeded knowledge pertains to all four subjects under discussion— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— that knowledge does not have all objects as its domain.
Just as there are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) in the mantras, so too in the *itihāsas* and other texts, the omniscience of Brahmā and others is to be understood from such explanatory passages.
For an explanatory passage is so called because it speaks of one matter while having another purpose.
Alternatively, since his knowledge is unimpeded regarding the four subjects under discussion—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—the unimpeded nature of this knowledge of Brahmā and others is indicated.
But it is not because of non-obstruction regarding all objects.

Now, one might object: "If the cognition of that [mind] regarding things such as dharmas were obstructed elsewhere, how could it be called 'unobstructed' (apratigha)? To this, he says "na hi" and so forth:
"For it is not because of mere non-obstruction that it is said to have a universal range;
rather, it is indeed unobstructed because it is unobstructed even with respect to its own objects."

If this is so, and if [knowledge] is called "unimpeded" because it is not obstructed by its own object, then the knowledge of all persons is indeed unobstructed with respect to its own object. What, then, is the distinction of Brahmā and others such that their knowledge alone is called "unimpeded" and not that of others? To this, he says: "And this," and so forth.
"And this knowledge that yields results extends as far as the domain of Dharma and so on;
however, there is no purpose whatsoever served by knowing all things such as trees."
To the extent that this functional knowledge is not obstructed,
it receives the designation of "unimpeded consciousness" (apratigha-vijñāna) because of that.

This explains that among those things conducive to human goals, such as dharma and so forth, the knowledge of that very Brahmā proceeds unimpeded, and not that of others. To manifest this distinction, it is stated that the knowledge of Brahmā and the rest is "unimpeded" (apratigha) because it is unobstructed regarding its own objects, whereas that of others is not.
Regarding the term *aupayikajñāna*: knowledge concerning that which is conducive (*aupayika*)—that is, dharma and so forth which are useful for human goals—is *aupayikajñāna*.
The word "yāvat" means "without distinction";
this is a qualification of the appropriate knowledge.
Alternatively, he states another position:
"Or rather, that knowledge exists within the self itself, set in motion by the practice of meditation;
it is precisely because of its lack of obstruction that the non-obstruction of knowledge is asserted."
"In the self" means in the person;
"of that very [self]" refers to that same one.
Of the knowledge whose object is the self.

But surely, ten imperishable qualities such as knowledge and the rest are recited as belonging to Īśvara; how then is it that he does not become omniscient through the connection with unmanifest knowledge? To this he says, "Knowledge," and so forth: "Even though Śaṅkara is heard of as possessing the ten imperishables—knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—he too possesses knowledge by virtue of being a knower of the Self."

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the awakening to reality; dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the turning away from sense objects; sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is eightfold, consisting of: *aṇimā* (minuteness), *laghimā* (lightness), *mahimā* (magnification), *prāpti* (attainment), *prākāmya* (efficacy), *īśitva* (lordship), *vaśitva* (control), and *yatra-kāmāvasāyitā* (the power to resolve at will). He who possesses these ten imperishable qualities beginning with knowledge is "the one of ten imperishables" (*daśāvyaya*). Among these, *aṇimā* is when, having become a minute body, one moves easily through the world, unseen by all beings.
*Laghimā* is that by which, due to lightness, one moves about like the wind.
Mastery (*mahimā*) is that by which, being honored, praised, and worshipped in all worlds, one becomes greater even than the great.
Attainment (*prāpti*) is that whatever one contemplates with the mind, that very thing one obtains.
Irresistible will (*prākāmya*) is that one’s desire becomes abundant; the meaning is that one is able to enjoy sense objects.
Sovereignty (*īśitva*) is that by which one becomes the lord of the three worlds.
Mastery (*vaśitva*) is that by which one brings under control all beings, both stationary and moving; he also becomes Indra over them.

The power of dwelling wherever one desires (*yatrakāmāvasāyitā*) is that by which one dwells in whichever place one wishes—whether among the realms of Brahmā, Prajāpati, the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pitṛs, Piśācas, humans, or in other species suitable for those [beings].
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of knowing the self":
the meaning is that he is possessed of knowledge by virtue of knowing the self, but not by virtue of possessing a complete and exhaustive understanding of all categories of objects.
But why, even when only a single portion is fully known, is Śaṅkara alone called the possessor of knowledge and no other? To this he says: "For this very thing," and so forth.
For that alone is true knowledge which is the vision of the pure Self;
whereas that which pertains to the impure and its causes is called ignorance.
It is called "thus" because it is both pure and the self; the compound [taddarśana] means "the vision of that.
Regarding the phrase "having that as its cause":
the cause of that vision of the pure self is "that-cause"; what is that? It is the self itself.
When that pure Self, which is the cause of those [qualities], exists, the impure vision of the Self that nevertheless arises is called ignorance (ajñāna), because it is contemptible.

Now, one might object: "If it is admitted that the arising of pure knowledge for Brahmā and others results from the practice of meditation, then what is the cause of such hostility toward the Buddhas and others, by which their knowledge is not also accepted as unimpeded and pure? Anticipating this doubt, the author states "But even so," etc., showing the distinction of Brahmā and the others by presenting an alternative view: "But even so, because Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara have the Veda as their body, they are omniscient through the Veda which consists of all knowledge; what then [is the use] of a human being?"
Where are mortals such as the Buddha and others, and where are the three supreme gods?
That you should, out of delusion, hold the view that they too are omniscient because of rivalry with them—how strange!
Because the Vedas have become their very self, they are called the "bodies of the Vedas.
Because they are the cause for the knowledge of all things, the Veda consists of omniscience.
What is meant by this is that the knowledge of Brahmā and the others regarding dharma and so forth does not proceed with independent obstruction.
Rather, it is by means of the Veda;
and this is not accepted by you in the case of the Buddha and others,
because their knowledge is self-dependent (*svāyatta*).
Furthermore, it is indeed logical that the arising of pure knowledge through the practice of meditation occurs for Brahmā and others, because they are gods and thus superior to all people,
and because this is recited in the Veda; however,
such capacity can never be possible for a human being, as he is the opposite of them.
Therefore, the view that humans are also omniscient is a deluded vision;
this is merely a deluded perspective on your part.
It might be argued: "If Brahmā and others are recited in the Veda, then how would it not follow that the Veda itself is non-eternal, due to its connection with non-eternal denotata?

On the other hand, if the eternity of the Vedas is maintained, then the status of Brahmā and others as denotata of the eternal Veda is contradicted, because they are non-eternal. Or, if that [status] is not contradictory, then there is no contradiction in Buddhas and others also being their denotata. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even though it is eternal," and so forth.
Furthermore, even in the eternal Vedic scripture, there is the mention of the triad beginning with Brahmā;
and because of that [triad's] eternity, the eternity of the Vedas is not impaired.
"Because of their eternity" means because those [entities], beginning with Brahmā, are eternal.
With the words "For they," and so forth, he clarifies this very point:
"For they are eternally endowed with eternal qualities and eternal actions;
because it is possible for them to be denoted by the eternal Vedas, they are not contradictory."
But for impermanent beings such as Buddhas, there can be no comprehension through an eternal scripture;
and if an eternal scripture were accepted, the postulation of an omniscient being would be futile.

It cannot be known through an eternal scripture, because that would entail the contingency of the relationship between word and meaning being non-eternal; furthermore, an eternal scripture is not accepted by others,
and even if it were accepted, it would render the postulation of an omniscient being useless.
He demonstrates this very point with the words: "Because of making him known as omniscient.

It is better for him to have an awakening to the Dharma through the knowledge of an omniscient one, rather than from a Dharma that has been obscured by the knowledge of an omniscient one as revealed in the Vedas.
Only the knowledge of dharma and so forth that is not obscured is being qualified;
thus, the status of being knowable through scripture cannot be established for an omniscient being.
It is held that the comprehension of Dharma itself is preferable to the mere indication of an omniscient being by means of an eternal scripture.
To explain how this is preferable, he says: "Revealed by the Veda," and so forth.
For knowledge of Dharma arising on the basis of the Veda remains unobscured; otherwise, since the worldly condition is uniform, such knowledge would be possible for everyone alike.
But the Dharma known by the omniscient one as revealed by the Veda is concealed once he has attained *nirvāṇa*, because it is no longer manifest.
Even during the state prior to *nirvāṇa*, there is an absence of instruction due to his lack of desire [to teach].
And even when there is instruction, there is no hearing of it by everyone, everywhere, and at all times.
He shows that the omniscient one is not to be apprehended through the means of valid cognition known as analogy by stating "someone similar to the omniscient one," and so forth:
"If someone similar to the omniscient one were seen at present,
then the existence of the omniscient one could be understood by the force of analogy."

For analogy (*upamāna*), because its object consists of similarity and its adjuncts, necessarily follows upon the apprehension of a similar thing and has as its domain an object not currently in contact [with the senses]; for example, the recollection of a cow by means of perceiving a *gavaya*. However, since no one is known to exist who is similar to an omniscient being, analogy does not function here due to the absence of the apprehension of a similar object. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: that for which there is no apprehension of a similar thing is not accessible through analogy, just like the son of a barren woman; and there is no apprehension of a similar thing in the case of an omniscient being—this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Furthermore, he demonstrates through the verse beginning with "narān" that not only is the apprehension of an omniscient being impossible by means of analogy (*upamāna*), but rather, for all men whatsoever, it is logical to ascertain their non-omniscience through analogy based on similarity:
"Having observed that all men of the present time are themselves non-omniscient,
one ascertains the non-omniscience of all remaining [men] by means of analogy based on that similarity."

Desiring to demonstrate that an omniscient being is not established even through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), he first raises the objection of the opponent's view, beginning with "For the instruction...
and so forth: "For the instruction of Buddha and others regarding the domain of dharma, adharma, and so forth, would not be possible otherwise [i.e.,] if there were no omniscient being."
Even when perception and the other means of knowledge have been refuted as establishing an omniscient being,
he who thus establishes an omniscient being solely through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)— [is as follows:]...

This instruction on dharma and so forth by the Buddha and others would not be possible otherwise if dharma and the rest were not directly known by him; therefore, even though perception and other means of knowledge have been refuted as establishing an omniscient being, one who maintains that an all-seeing person is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) maintains what is untenable, according to the reasoning to be stated hereafter—this is the sense.

Alternatively, he shows that this is indeed inference (*anumāna*) and not presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) are present, by means of the words "yadvā" and so forth.
Or rather, the proof (*sādhana*) operating here is that which is based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
Elsewhere, it is said that [the existence] of an omniscient being is asserted because [in other cases] we observe that [such status] is preceded by knowledge.
Indeed, whatever instruction there may be, it is all preceded by knowledge;
just as the instruction regarding the powers of *abhayā* and other [medicines] is of such a nature.
This instruction concerning dharma and adharma is an instruction made by him;
therefore, its being preceded by his knowledge is inferred from it.

By the term "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*), he states the impossibility of an inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭam*). For when a relationship between a specific mark (*liṅga*) and its possessor (*liṅgin*) has been perceived through direct perception, and that very same possessor is later inferred by means of that same mark for the purpose of eliminating doubt, then it is called an inference based on specific observation.

However, no relationship has ever been apprehended anywhere between the teaching of *dharma* and so forth and an omniscient being; therefore, this [inference] is only one based on general observation.

For it is observed that, in general, instruction elsewhere within one's own continuum is preceded by knowledge. Therefore, just as Devadatta’s arrival at another location is perceived to be preceded by movement, and thus the sun’s movement is inferred from its arrival at another location, so too the knowledge of the Blessed One, such as Buddha, will be inferred from his instruction on the Dharma and so forth.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is an instruction is preceded by the speaker’s knowledge, just like the instruction regarding the potency of *harītakī* and other substances; and this instruction on the Dharma and so forth by Buddha and others is an instruction—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
To this, he states the following reply, beginning with "anyathāpi" (even otherwise):
"Since it is established even otherwise, this presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not tenable;
for this very reason, this inference (*anumāna*) also does not stand as valid."
For the instruction of the Buddha and others can be accounted for otherwise [than as being based on omniscience],
due to delusion regarding what was seen in dreams and the like, or from hearing that which is untrue from the Vedas and so forth.
For since instruction can occur even otherwise through delusion and so forth, both inference and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are inconclusive.
To explain how it can occur otherwise, he says "dreams, etc.
As stated in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*: "Instruction indeed arises from delusion; even in the absence of delusion, it arises from the Veda."
In that regard, existence is seen through delusion, as in the case of an object perceived in a dream; it is not seen through the Veda, as in the case of Manu and others.

However, in the case of those such as the Sugatas who are ignorant of the Vedas, it is possible that their teaching arose from delusion or for the purpose of deceiving others; this is what is established by the passage beginning with "ye hi" [p.
"For as for those who do not know the Vedas, [their teaching] cannot possibly originate from the Veda."
[This is] due to the instruction provided by them, which arises solely from delusion.
Whether for the purpose of deluding disciples, or out of delusion itself, or by relying upon that [delusion],
the teaching of wicked instructors prevails in the world.
"Because it does not have that as its basis" means because it does not have the Vedas as its basis.
How is it understood that this instruction does not have its basis in the Vedas? To this he says: "If this [were based on the Veda]," and so forth.
"If this were rooted in the Veda, then those who uphold the Veda would themselves provide the instruction, just as Manu and others did."
However, because instruction was given by them to fools and Śūdras,
it is known that such teaching is corrupt, being merely conventional like a counterfeit coin.

For if the teaching of the Dharma and other matters by the Buddha and others were rooted in the Veda, then they would have taught it only to learned Brāhmaṇas, as Manu and others did; yet they did not teach it to Brāhmaṇas alone, but rather to dull-witted Śūdras. Therefore, it is understood that such teaching is conventional and false, like the practice of counterfeit coins and the like.

However, as for those such as Manu and others, because they were knowers of the Veda, it is shown that their instruction on dharma and so forth is rooted solely in the Veda and not independently, by means of the verse beginning with "ye tu" and so on:
"But those such as Manu and others who are established as preeminent among the knowers of the Threefold Science (trayī),
whose works are relied upon by the knowers of the Threefold Science— they are utterances originating from the Veda."
The three Vedas, known as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, are called the Trayī; those who know them are called "knowers of the Trayī" (trayīvidaḥ), referring to the Brāhmaṇas.
Those for whom the treatises on Dharmaśāstra and so forth are based upon the injunctions of the Trayī are described as such.
He states the reason for their reliance on those texts: "their utterances originate from the Vedas."
Those whose utterances originate from the Veda are described as such.
To the question of how this too is determined, he says "nādṛṣṭvā" and so forth:
"Neither without having seen the Vedic sentences, nor without having shown them to his disciples,
would the composition of a treatise or its transmission to them be possible."
"Arpaṇa" means making known.

Thus, since the omniscient being is not established by any of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is understood through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) as being non-existent (*abhāva*) alone; therefore, this reason—"because his form has been made the object of the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence"—is established. Furthermore, it was previously demonstrated that this reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); the sense is that the conventional usage of "non-existence" occurs precisely because there is no other cause for it.

Even those who think: "We do not establish an omniscient being by pointing him out specifically (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*); rather, we establish merely the possibility in a general sense—that there exists some omniscient being, or that omniscience exists somewhere—because we observe the excellence of wisdom and so forth"—to them he says this, beginning with "A man" (*nara*), etc.:
"A man who is omniscient exists, and that omniscience [exists] as well"—any proof (*sādhana*) that might be employed [in this way] is indeed deficient in its thesis (*pratijñānyūna*).
The object that one intends to establish is not denoted by this [statement];
and as for that which is indeed spoken, there is no purpose whatsoever in its establishment.
Since the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason has already been established previously, [the author] now first demonstrates the fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).
When one thing is intended to be proven, if something else is proposed as the thesis, that is a "deficient thesis" (*pratijñānyūna*), which is a fault of the thesis.
And here, what is intended to be proven is the omniscience of one's own Teacher, not omniscience in general.

For a discerning person does not seek an omniscient being out of mere addiction; rather, it is out of a desire for engagement or withdrawal, thinking, "Having learned what is dharma and what is adharma from his words, I shall engage or I shall withdraw. And even if such a person were established in a general sense, he would be of no use to a person regarding engagement, because one cannot ascertain his specific words without knowing those particulars. Therefore, since that very particularity must be established by one desiring engagement, a general proposition is indeed deficient as a proposition.
This refers to "the object which one intends to prove."
"That which is intended to be accomplished" refers to the specific object,
namely one's own Teacher.
"By this" means by the proposition;
"that which is said" refers to what follows.

Without touching upon specific particulars, someone might claim that "there exists somewhere a person who is omniscient" or that "omniscience exists"; however, even if such [an omniscient being] were established, it would serve no purpose whatsoever.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"If omniscience is asserted for the sake of establishing the truth of his scripture,
that [truth] is not obtained merely by establishing the existence of an omniscient being in general."
"Sa" means that the truth of his scripture is established.
To the question "Why is it not obtained?", he says "as long as" and so forth:
As long as the Buddha is not omniscient, his word is false;
once an omniscient being is established anywhere at all, how could that [word] not be true?

For as long as the omniscience of the Buddha is not established, there can be no certainty regarding the truth of his words; nor would the truth of the Buddha’s words be established by the mere general proof of an omniscient being, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between them.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "in another," and so forth:
"If there were another omniscient being, then the truth of one's own word [would depend] on that other;
for only through their coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) could there be a relationship of mutual dependence between the two."
He says, "For when there is co-referentiality," and so forth, to explain when indeed no obstruction exists between those two.
Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) means being dependent upon a single person.
"Between those two" refers to [the two reasons].
Between omniscience and the speech of truth,
there is the relationship of part and whole,
and the relationship of cause and fruit.
This is what is meant: when there is a single substratum, the state of being omniscient would be the cause of true speech; otherwise, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

To show that whatever proof has been formulated by others for the sake of establishing the existence of an omniscient being is also refuted by this very [argument], he says "that which is all," and so forth:
"Whatever is called 'all' in this world is indeed perceived by someone,
because it possesses the nature of being an object of cognition, a knowable thing, and a real entity, just like curd, form, taste, and so on."
Even if mere knowledge were specified, it would result in the fallacy of the thesis being deficient;
for one who is intended as "omniscient" is not established in this manner.
If there were someone other than the Buddha who had attained omniscience,
what use would that person's knowledge be for establishing the authority of the Buddha’s word?

Whatever is endowed with such properties as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) or being a real entity (*vastutva*) is directly perceived by someone, just as the color, taste, and so forth of curd; and since the entire collection of things has the nature of being objects of cognition and the like, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Here too, as before, one must state that there is a deficiency in the thesis and that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, the establishment of omniscience is not possible either through specific characteristics or through general characteristics.
Therefore, it is established that there is no omniscient being;
because of his non-existence, his word does not exist, and thus it is impossible for anyone to act on the basis of his word.

Alternatively, even granting that an omniscient person might exist, speech composed by an omniscient one is simply not possible—that is, from which your own [tradition's] activity could proceed. Demonstrating this, he says "Having reached the ten stages," and so forth:
"Having reached the ten stages and with all passion and the like extinguished, he perceives everything through a knowledge equal to pure crystal."
And one who has entered meditative absorption, while maintaining a mental retention whose object is all things,
is likewise pervaded by all objects and is thus entirely incapable of teaching.

For indeed, you describe it as follows: one established on the tenth stage, through a cognition resembling pure crystal due to the removal of the stains of all defilements such as passion, discerns the entirety of the knowable.

Consequently, while in this state, even though he maintains *dhāraṇā*—the one-pointedness of mind—he is occupied solely with the awakening to the object (*arthabodha*) and is thus unable to teach the Dharma; for no one is capable of performing so many activities at once.
If it is argued that he teaches after having emerged [from meditative absorption], the author says "And when," and so forth:
"And when he should teach some single thing like an ordinary speaker, that would be the utterance of one who knows only a portion, not the speech of an omniscient being."

For there is no engagement in speech that is devoid of discursive thought; therefore, he must teach the Dharma while remaining in a state of mind accompanied by conceptualization. Consequently, since there would be no distinction between a fool and a scholar in this state, he would not be omniscient, and what he has spoken would thus be the speech of one who is not omniscient.

It might be argued that he does not teach anything at all, because he always abides in non-conceptual meditative absorption; rather, by his sovereign power, there arise for those who are receptive mental representations appearing as the diverse teachings of the Dharma.

As it has been said: "From the night the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment until the night he passed into parinirvāṇa, in this interval the Tathāgata did not utter or pronounce even a single syllable. For what reason? Because the Tathāgata is indeed always in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*). Nevertheless, those who are to be disciplined through the teaching of syllables and sounds hear a sound issuing from the mouth, the *uṣṇīṣa*, and the *ūrṇā* of the Tathāgata," and so forth. Regarding that, it says: "While he has entered that meditative absorption," and so on; "while he is established in that meditative absorption like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*)."
Teachings issue forth at will even from walls and other such objects.
By means of them, men come to know all the matters they desire to understand,
and they swiftly attain their benefits according to their individual capacity.
Such things as this, when being proclaimed, shine forth for those who possess faith; but we are faithless, and thus we seek logical arguments.
The *cintāratna* is the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).

This is the collective meaning here: while this might appear beautiful when described as being without authoritative proof (*apramāṇaka*) to those who are merely full of faith, how could those like us—who seek only logical reasoning because they grasp matters established by valid means of knowledge—accept this as it is being stated without authoritative proof?

Furthermore, even if such a hypothesis were granted, the fact that teachings emerging from walls and the like originate through the sovereign power of an omniscient being remains precisely doubtful; thus, it is shown that it is not appropriate for discerning people to have confidence in them as authoritative by saying "of those emerging from walls and the like," and so forth:
"And for those emerging from walls and the like, there would be no status as being taught by a reliable authority."
And there would be no trust in them as to by whom these [verses] were composed.
Could these have been composed by the Buddha, or could they have been taught by deceiving brahmins playing with distant echoes?
Or perhaps they were scattered by invisible minor spirits and the like;
therefore, those who consider themselves wise should not place their trust in them.
Everything is easily understood.

This much has been stated by Kumārila as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*); now, according to the opinion of Sāmaṭa and Yaśaṭa, he again states the refutation of the omniscient one, beginning with "And this," and so forth:
"Thus, omniscience in persons is, by its very nature, without foundation;
and this is further considered: how can one be regarded as an all-seeing being?"
One who knows everything either simultaneously or in succession, or by virtue of a single nature,
or according to what is predominant, or through [inherent] capacity, would be accepted as omniscient.

The simultaneous cognition of contradictory natures, such as the pure and the impure, is not observed by a single consciousness; nor is it seen anywhere that they have entered into a distinct [single] cognition.
Who could possibly be able to understand, even in hundreds of years, each individual thing— past, present, and future— that is infinite in number?
He who perceives everything through an undifferentiated intrinsic nature does not perceive the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of all things.
What is the use of even an omniscient one being a cognizer of a universal form?
An object is not apprehended at all by a cognition that possesses a different aspect.
That consciousness of a single form must be either correct or false;
if it were correct, then all things would necessarily follow as non-dual, since such [a nature] is contradicted by what is perceived.

Furthermore, if there were a difference in nature [between you and the Omniscient One], then for you, the disciples, the Omniscient One, dharma, adharma, and their teachings would not exist, because his essential nature would be undetermined.
If the cognition of a single [entity] were false, then the omniscient one would be mistaken;
his word would not be trustworthy, like the speech of a madman or the like.
If one who knows all action together with its causes through supramundane knowledge born of meditative concentration is asserted to be omniscient, [then that is acceptable].

Whether it be perception, inference, or verbal testimony—none of these, nor anything else produced by them, exists as a means of valid cognition for its existence; therefore, such a thing does not exist.
Whether simultaneously or in succession, how can there be inference without an effect?
Furthermore, there is no such thing as "capacity" [if it were independent]; for if something were inherently capable, everything would be so.
All knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) are capable of awakening to everything;
yet, due to the failure of their means, they do not awaken to the whole.
"The claim that there exists a certain unique omniscient being who has attained an uncommon means distinct from all other persons is thus devoid of any proof."
Thus, when no omniscient person whatsoever can be established,
then human speech cannot be the cause for the realization of the Dharma.
Thus say the Mīmāṃsakas, who are devoted to independent Vedic revelation;
and the human origin of the Vedas has been established in detail.

Is he omniscient because of the simultaneous thorough knowledge of all things; or rather, by means of a sequential succession; or else, from knowing the entire world through a single form such as "eternal" and so forth; or perhaps, from understanding the primary [factor], namely, the knowledge of only that which is useful for human goals, such as karma and its fruits; or finally, is he called omniscient due to possessing the capacity for the thorough knowledge of all things, just as fire is called "all-consuming" even though it does not consume everything either sequentially or simultaneously?
Regarding that, in the first position there are two possibilities: either one would know everything simultaneously with a single cognition, or with multiple cognitions.
It cannot be with a single [cognition], because we do not observe the simultaneous apprehension by a single cognition of mutually contradictory objects such as the pure and the impure.
