To the objection that many cognitions having various contradictory objects might occur for him all at once, he says: "Or [there would be] diverse modes of movement."
The connection is made by changing the case ending of "not seen" (*na dṛṣṭaḥ*).

For it is not the case that beings with a single stream of consciousness are observed to have simultaneous movements in different directions; this is because it would be impossible to know [this] even in hundreds of years.
The mention of "hundreds of years" is illustrative; [it remains so] even in [the course of] aeons (*kalpa*).
Otherwise, his independence would be lost.
Therefore, there must exist one who directly perceives supersensuous objects.
But no one perceives [the object] by means of an eternal word, because that is impossible.
Therefore, there exists a direct seer of supersensuous objects, and not through the medium of an eternal word, because such an eternal word is impossible.
The restrictive particle *eva* ("only")—which has been placed out of its logical order—is to be understood immediately after the word *sākṣāt* ("directly").

Granted that an eternal word might exist, nevertheless, it is not logical for it to function as a cause for the cognition of supersensible objects; demonstrating this, he says "of the eternal," and so forth:

"The capacity of an eternal word does not arise either from itself or from another, because there is a contradiction between succession and simultaneity when producing the cognition of its own object."

In this context, "its own object" (*svārtha*) refers to its own denotation; alternatively, "its own" (*svaḥ*) means the self, which is the nature of the word, while "object" (*arthaḥ*) means the denotation. Thus, "its own object" (*svārthau*) refers to both the word-nature and the denotation; it is for the sake of producing knowledge of these two that the capacity of the eternal Word must exist—either intrinsically (*svataḥ*), as established by its very nature, or through some other auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇāt*).
In that regard, it cannot first be from itself. Why? Because for an eternal entity, there is a contradiction with respect to the production of an effect through either succession or simultaneity.
Indeed, no other mode besides succession and simultaneity is possible by which causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) could occur, because these two are defined by their mutual exclusion.
Thus, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is pervaded by succession and simultaneity alone.
And it is not logical for an eternal word to produce the cognition of its own object successively;

because at the time of producing the first effect, its nature—which produces the effects that are cognitions occurring at subsequent times—has not fallen away, those effects arising from that [nature] alone would necessarily occur simultaneously.

Nor is it logical [for the cause to produce effects] successively, because even at a later time, since the nature of the cause—which is capable and unimpaired in its capacity for causal efficiency—persists just as it did at the stage of producing the first effect, its failure to produce [subsequent effects] would be contradictory.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is devoid of a property that pervades another is also lacking the property pervaded by it; for example, a jar or similar object, which is devoid of the property of being a tree, is lacking the property of being a *śiṃśapā* tree, which is pervaded by "tree-ness. And the eternal speech known as the Veda is devoid of the properties of succession and simultaneity, which pervade the property of causal efficacy (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). Thus, this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) by implication. Consequently, there is no possibility of power (*śakti*) in an eternally existing word either from itself or from any other auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*), because power—which is not distinct from its own nature—cannot be produced, just like the nature itself.
It has been discussed in many ways that even if [the Veda] were a different entity, its relationship [to the truth] would still be established;
therefore, it is incorrect to claim that the thorough knowledge of supersensible objects depends upon eternal speech, because such a claim is sublated by inference.

Regarding what was said—that there is no knower of Dharma because his form has been made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa)—[the author], demonstrating by means of the opponent’s own admission that the proposition denying the existence of a knower of Dharma is sublated by the means of knowledge of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) and that the reason is unestablished (asiddha), says: "Therefore, heaven, sacrifice, and so forth... and so on.
"Therefore, heaven, sacrifice, and so forth were revealed after being known by himself;
thus, according to you as well, there exists a creator of the Veda who is a seer of supersensuous objects."
One who knows the purpose of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa), or indeed one who knows all dharmas—
if such a person were not accepted, the authority of the Veda would otherwise not exist.
However, by this acceptance of the Knower of Dharma, which is obtained through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti),
this negation of His that you have formulated at length is sublated.
"From itself" means independently; that is to say, by means of knowledge that does not depend upon the Vedas.
"Such as that" means of the kind which is being rejected by you. "Obtained through presumptive testimony" (arthāpatti) means...

[This is] obtained by the force of the acceptance of the authority of the Vedas; for this very reason, even the claim that [the Lord] has a form established as an object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa) is unproven, because he is established as an object through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
Furthermore, the objection raised by analyzing the various ways in which the term "all" (*sarva*) depends on its contextual meaning does not apply at all;
for we do not accept this position.

Indeed, we do not assert that the "Omniscient One" is one who knows every single object intended [by the word "all"] as distinct from [the specific categories such as] dharmas and so forth, such that the aforementioned objection could be leveled against him.

Rather, he is intended as omniscient whose mind—devoid of the stains of all afflictive and cognitive obstructions—illuminates the entirety of the knowable, such as the phenomena (dharma) and so forth.
And regarding that, you have not adduced any subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa).
As for what was said, "as many atoms as there are in a single body," and so forth—that is merely a thesis stated without any supporting evidence.

Furthermore, the establishment of a matter is not possible through a mere thesis devoid of logical justification, for that would entail the absurd consequence that everything could establish every possible object. Anticipating all such [objections], he says "Moreover" (*kiñca*) and so forth:
"Moreover, this which has been stated is indeed causeless, being merely a proclamation issued by your command."
Who is capable of knowing how many hairs there are on his head and body?
Since no one could have all things illuminated by a lamp of unshakable, non-conceptual knowledge, there is no contradiction in what has been stated here.
"Without cause" (*akāraṇa*) means that for which no cause—namely, the statement of a reason possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*)—is found; thus it is so described.

It is "stainless" (*nirmala*) because it is free from the stains of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*). It is "unshakable" (*akampya*) because it cannot be moved by the winds of Māra, the heretics, or [the forces of] decline. That very gnosis (*jñāna*) is itself the lamp, due to its similarity with light.
That by which every object, such as dharma and so forth, has been illuminated—that is, made an object of cognition—is described as such.
Although it is a dependent compound (*sāpekṣa*), the compound is justified because the meaning is clearly understood.
It is stated here that this does not constitute a logical flaw.
The word "valid cognition" (pramāṇa) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The sense is that not only has it not been stated, but there is also no subverting argument (bādhaka) here whatsoever.
For instance, perception (*pratyakṣa*) cannot be a sublater (*bādhaka*), because it does not have that [proposed property] as its object.
Indeed, when a thing is apprehended by perception in a certain way, if one were to accept a contrary property regarding that very thing established by perception, it would be sublated by perception;
for example, the property of being non-audible (*aśrāvaṇatva*) in the case of the subject "sound" (*śabda*) is sublated by its being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*).
But it is not the case that [omniscience] is negated simply because perception does not function there.
Furthermore, no one who is not omniscient can perceive through direct perception all the mental states existing within the continua of others;
therefore, the claim of omniscience regarding such [states] cannot be sublated by perception.
Because all [beings] are limited in their vision;
or, if [an object] were made an object of cognition, he alone would be omniscient—thus there is no refutation.
It might be argued: "We do not say that perception, while functioning, establishes non-existence."
Rather, it is that which is ceasing [to function].
For instance, when there is a cessation of perception with respect to an object, its non-existence is determined, as in the case of a rabbit's horn;
whereas where there is activity, its existence is established, as in the case of a pot and so forth.
Nor can it be said that because perception has never at any time operated upon the object of an omniscient being, the non-existence of such a being is determined from the absence of that perception;
for this is incoherent,
since the certainty that arises from the cessation of an operative perception does not itself arise from perception.
Because existence and non-existence are contradictory in one and the same place;
nor is the cessation of perception pervaded by the non-existence of an object, such that the non-existence of the object could be ascertained from it,
for we observe the cessation of perception even when an object exists, provided it is obstructed or otherwise remote.
It might be argued: "We do not say that the ascertainment of non-existence arises from the mere cessation of perception;
rather, it is the ceased perception itself that establishes non-existence.
To this we reply: you are merely changing the wording.
There is no difference in meaning.
Nor is it logical that a difference in meaning follows merely from a difference in words, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For instance, "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) is said to be the negation of the existence of a thing.
By the word "ceased" (*nivṛtta*) as well, that very same thing is denoted from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
The distinction is merely this: one [term] expresses it by excluding other differences when there is a desire to know that alone, while the other does so without such exclusion.
However, in ultimate reality, both terms establish only the non-existence of the entity.
The state of being a cause for what is non-existent is impossible, because that [non-existence] is characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity.

Therefore, whatever is the producer or the illuminator of something must possess an existent presence at the time of that thing's production or illumination; it cannot be of a nature that has already ceased, just as a seed is for a sprout or a lamp is for a form.
For those two, once they have ceased, are not capable of producing a sprout or a jar, nor of illuminating a form and so forth.
Furthermore, what is the intended meaning here when it is said that "perception, having ceased, establishes non-existence"?
If the meaning is that it has ceased from the present time-path (*adhvan*), then by implication it would mean "from the past and future states.
And it has already been established previously that past and future entities do not exist.

How, then, could the operation of a non-existent thing be established? Or, if it is argued that even a present thing is said to have ceased from a certain object when it does not arise with respect to that object—
even so, the non-existence of a real entity is not established by this, because of the lack of invariable concomitance (*vyabhicāra*).
For the mere fact that visual consciousness does not arise with respect to objects such as odors or tastes does not establish their non-existence by that alone.
Therefore, the non-existence of anything is not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If this is so, how do you explain the establishment of the non-existence of jars and the like in another location through the direct perception called "non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*)?
This is not so;
for it is not said that perception establishes non-existence by taking non-existence as its object.
Rather, it is because the establishment of one of two objects—which are both capable of being associated within a single cognition—is itself the establishment of the non-existence of the other.
For when those two [the object and the cognition] exist, a cognition restricted to a single form is not possible,

because there is no distinction in their capacity. However, in the case of omniscience, it has not been ascertained by anyone that it is associated with the knowledge of any particular true dharma, such that we could determine its non-existence upon perceiving that specific thing alone.
Because that [omniscient being] is always and absolutely beyond the range of perception,
direct perception cannot, for its part, serve as a sublater of an omniscient one.
Nor does inference establish the non-existence of an omniscient being.
This is because it is accepted as being within the scope of a formal rule (*vidhi*).
For it is precisely non-existence (*abhāva*) that is described as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) having non-existence as its object, and nothing else.
Therefore, even the three [means of knowledge] beginning with presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) lack the capacity to establish [the existence of the self].

Now, it might be argued: "We do not establish the non-existence of an omniscient being by way of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*); rather, taking all men as the subject (*pakṣa*), we establish their non-omniscience through relative negation (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*). Therefore, the operation of inference and other means of knowledge certainly occurs. Let this be so; nevertheless, inference is still not possible, because no probans (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with non-omniscience among all men has been established.

Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding [the probans] such as "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*) or "being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*), that too will be demonstrated later to be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).

Nor does presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) establish that [the Buddha] is not omniscient, because no means of valid cognition other than perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) is established as being distinct from these two.

Or, even if there were another means of valid cognition, presumptive testimony is not sufficient to prove non-omniscience; for presumptive testimony consists in the postulation of something unperceived when a perceived or heard object cannot otherwise be accounted for.

Furthermore, no object such as what is perceived and so forth among all men is inexplicable in the absence of non-omniscience, such that it would have to be postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Nor is analogy (*upamāna*) capable [of establishing this]; for it is only an object already being remembered—characterized by its similarity to a present thing, or mere similarity itself residing in the remembered object—that is cognized by analogy with the present thing.

For example, when a person who has previously experienced the perception of a cow goes to the forest and sees a *gavaya*, there arises from that sight of the *gavaya* a cognition of its similarity to the cow previously experienced.
As it has been said:

"Therefore, that which is remembered, as qualified by similarity, would be the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for analogy (*upamāna*); or else, it is the similarity itself as connected with that [remembered object]."
Thus says the *Ślokavārttika*:
"Therefore, the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is precisely the subject (*dharmī*) as it is being remembered; and only an object already experienced is made an object by memory, nothing else."

Furthermore, the minds residing in the mental continua of all persons have not been experienced by any omniscient being such that they could be made objects of memory. Nor is there a determination of a property common to all men—such as non-omniscience—with respect to an object being experienced, by virtue of which non-omniscience could be analogically attributed to all men.
Even that [property] such as existence (*sattva*) which is observed in some cases to coexist with non-omniscience is not established as a property common to non-omniscience.
Because even for an omniscient being (*sarvajña*), there is no contradiction with [the presence of] the property of being a sentient being (*sattva*) and so forth.
For it is not the case that because one observes the property of being a sentient being in a cow, the similarity of jars and other things to a *gavaya* is thereby inferred.
Granted that all men may indeed share the commonality of being sentient beings and so on, their lack of omniscience is nonetheless not established [by this].
By this very [argument], that which was stated—namely, "having seen men," and so forth—is refuted.
Furthermore, there exists no means of valid cognition called "verbal testimony" (śabda) that can subvert the existence of an omniscient being.

For as for that [testimony] which is of human origin, it is admitted by the Mīmāṃsakas themselves to be non-authoritative with respect to objects beyond the senses; and as for that which is of non-human origin, it has already been demonstrated that even that is non-authoritative.
Nor is any Vedic statement found that establishes the non-omniscience of all men;
nor does the absence of a teaching on that point prove the non-existence of such a quality, because not all things fall within the scope of scriptural instruction.
Otherwise, it would follow that even your own mother’s marriage and similar matters do not exist, simply because they are not mentioned therein.

Nor is it logical to conclude that [the omniscient being] is not mentioned anywhere simply because his mention is not seen in one particular place, for since he is heard of in hundreds of different branches (śākhās), his mention is possible elsewhere as well;
we shall demonstrate later that in another branch he is indeed clearly mentioned as "omniscient" (sarvajña).
Furthermore, the non-existence of the knower of all things is not established by the fact that he has been made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-apprehension (abhāvapramāṇa).

For if non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is described as a mere negation (*prasajya-lakṣaṇa*) consisting simply in the cessation of other means of valid cognition, then it would be neither a cognition of anything nor a cause of cognition; thus, it is not logical for it to take an object, because it is a non-entity.
Therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition.

Alternatively, if by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*) what is intended is simply another entity distinct from the entity called a "means of valid cognition," even so, its status as a means of valid cognition would not be established, since its nature consists in being excluded from the means of valid cognition.
For it is not logical that one who is other than a Brahmin could be a Brahmin.
This might be argued: "He is not described as being excluded from all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
rather, he is simply another specific type of cognition, distinct from the five intended means of valid cognition."
If this is so, it must be stated what its form is.

If you say that because he is not within the scope of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), his form is simply "this omniscient one does not exist," then if such is its form, it is not a means of valid cognition, because it is fallacious (*vyabhicāra*).

For when the five means of valid cognition—which do not possess the nature of being causes for [the existence of] an omniscient being—cease, that entity such as the omniscient one does not necessarily cease, since it is not invariably concomitant with them; therefore, this cognition would not be true.
Thus, the point is that there is no subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the existence of an omniscient being.

It might be argued: "That very non-perception (*anupalambha*) which has been described by you as being of the nature of inference (*anumāna*) will itself be the sublater of the omniscient one; what need have we here for any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
This is true: non-perception is indeed a means of valid cognition.
However, this must be considered here.
Do you intend by "non-perception" (anupalambha) for the purpose of establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being your own non-perception, or rather the non-perception by all persons?

Furthermore, is this non-perception intended to be without qualification—by not resorting to the qualification "of that which has reached the conditions of perceptibility"—or is it with qualification?

Regarding this, showing first that a non-perception without qualification is not a valid means of proof (pramāṇa) for establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being, he says: "Nor by mere non-observation," and so forth.
Nor can its non-existence be determined by mere non-perception,
because perception is neither the cause nor the pervader of things.

The inclusion of the word "mātra" (mere) is for the purpose of excluding the qualification "that which has reached the conditions for perception. "The ascertainment of its non-existence" means the ascertainment of the non-existence of an omniscient being.
Why? Because perception cannot be the cause or the pervader of things—that is, of objects.

For perception by one of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) is not a pervader of things, as the nature of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*) is of the *śiṃśapā* tree; for even when a thing exists, its non-perception is possible due to distance in space and so forth.
Nor is it the cause, as fire is of smoke, because things themselves lack the status of being causes with respect to their own perception.

Furthermore, it is not logical that the cessation of one thing should entail the cessation of another if that other is neither its cause nor its pervader, for this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Moreover, the non-perception of an effect does not indicate the absence of the cause in general;
rather, it indicates the absence of only that cause whose capacity is unimpeded.
Furthermore, for those of limited vision, there is no unimpeded capacity regarding the perception of things such that,
upon its cessation, it could establish the non-existence of those things.
If it is asked, "Even when the cause and the pervader have ceased, how can there be the cessation of the other?", he says here:
"The cessation [of the effect and the pervaded] is appropriate here in the absence of the cause and the pervader,
because the possessed-of-cause and the pervaded arise from them and exist as one with them."
Just as smoke, mangoes, and so forth cease to exist in the absence of fire or trees,
otherwise there would be no causality at all, and the consequence of manifoldness would follow.
That which has a cause is "caused" (hetumat); the meaning is "an effect.
The analysis of the compound is "that which is both caused and pervaded.
The connection with the preceding [phrase] is that the cessation of those two—the caused and the pervaded—is logical.
The reason for this is "because [the effect] arises from that and because they possess a single nature.

For when the cause ceases, that which possesses the cause necessarily ceases, since it acquires its own being by arising from that cause—just as smoke ceases when fire ceases. Likewise, when the pervader ceases, the pervaded ceases, because it has a single nature with that pervader, due to their being of one essence.
This is just as mangoes, *khadira* trees, and so forth cease when the tree ceases, since a specific type of tree is precisely what is perceived as a mango and the like.
Otherwise, if it were not to cease even when the cause has ceased, then that could not be its cause at all.
For it is not logical that something which exists even when another is absent should have that as its cause, for this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is it logical that something which does not cease when another ceases should be the very nature (*svabhāva*) of that other, just as a cow is not the nature of a *gavaya*.

Therefore, only a pervading nature (*svabhāva*) can exclude its own pervaded, and only a cause (*kāraṇa*) can exclude its effect (*kārya*), when they are absent; nothing else can do so, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
As it has been said:
"Therefore, a nature connected with that alone [excludes] the entity itself."
Or one should negate the cause by means of the effect, due to their non-deviation from one another.
Otherwise, how could the cessation of one thing result in the cessation of another?
Just because a mortal does not possess a horse, must he necessarily not possess a cow as well?
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, showing that if one accepts that one’s own apprehension (*svopalambha*) is both the cause and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) with respect to all objects, then a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) results in the thesis, he says "of one’s own apprehension," and so forth:
"And if, for the sake of determining all objects, there arises from some cognition of yours the status of being the cause and the pervader of [your] own apprehension..."
At that time, you yourself would have been established as the knower of all things without effort;
therefore, why should you harbor self-loathing toward yourself, who are by nature omniscient?
The genitive in *hetutvavyāpakatvayoḥ* is used in relation to "ascertainment" (*niścaya*).

Regarding the two genitives and locatives in *upalambhasya cārtheṣu*, they are to be applied respectively to the relationship [of cause] and the state of being an object, with reference to the phrase *hetutvavyāpakatvayoḥ*.

What is meant is this: if you have ascertained through some means of valid cognition that your own perception is the cause and the pervader with respect to all objects, then you have clearly asserted omniscience for yourself.
For the knowledge of one who is not omniscient cannot pervade the entirety of all that is knowable;
and since you employ a proof for the sake of establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being, that very [omniscience] is what is being negated—thus there is a contradiction with your own words.

Thus, first of all, a non-perception that is without qualification does not deserve to be cited to establish the non-existence of an omniscient being; nor does it do so when qualified by the phrase "because of the non-perception of one who meets the conditions for perceptibility. For if it were to be cited in that way, it would either be stated by its own word—as in the statement: "There is no jar in a certain particular place because of the non-perception of what meets the conditions for perceptibility"—and the same would apply to the proof of the non-existence of an omniscient being.
Just as the absence of another entity—which is of the nature of the cause or the pervader and meets the conditions for perception—is demonstrated by its own term, as in:
"There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire," or "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because of the absence of trees";

for it is not the case that when something else which is unconnected, being neither a cause nor a pervader, is excluded—as in "There is no sensation of cold here because of fire"—the negation of the sensation of cold occurs through the direct affirmation of the fire, which is its direct contradictory; so too it would be in the case of the negation of an omniscient being.

However, the negation of an omniscient being occurs through the affirmation of something either directly contradictory to it or, indirectly, of something contradictory to its pervader; just as the negation of the sensation of frost occurs through the affirmation of fire, which is contradictory to the cold that pervades that sensation.

Or else, it occurs through the affirmation of something contradictory to its cause; just as the negation of the bristling of hair and so forth—which are effects of cold—occurs through the affirmation of a particular fire, which is contradictory to the cold that is their cause.

This occurs either through the affirmation of an effect that is incompatible with [the object to be negated], as for example, when in a particular location the presence of smoke or the like—an effect of fire and so forth which is incompatible with cold—is affirmed, resulting in the negation of the sensation of cold;

or through the perception of an effect of something incompatible with the cause [of the object to be negated], as for example, when by pointing out smoke—the effect of fire, which is incompatible with the cold that causes goosebumps and the like—the negation of goosebumps and so forth is established:
"This place does not contain a person possessed of specific signs such as goosebumps, because of the smoke."

Or, there is a negation of something by way of enjoining that which is pervaded by its opposite; for example, because dependence—which is pervaded by non-necessity, the opposite of necessity—is enjoined, necessity is negated. All these applications of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) are impossible for the purpose of establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being, because such an all-knowing person never meets the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
And this [non-apprehension] is a specific type of non-apprehension of that which meets the conditions for apprehension; he demonstrates this with the words "for this very reason," and so forth.
For this very reason, this omniscient being is not established as perceptible for you;
for if he were perceptible, omniscience would belong to you yourself without effort.
How can he whose knowledge has all things as its object be visible to you,
if such knowledge of all objects does not belong to you as well?

For this very reason, to avoid the consequence of contradicting your own words, you must not accept that the omniscient one is personally perceived through the characteristics of perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
Otherwise, you would be admitting omniscience in yourself.
To explain how this is so, he says: "having all objects as its domain," and so forth.

For if there were also a cognition therein whose object-domain is all things, then you would indeed be omniscient, having attained the conditions for perception; otherwise, one who is not omniscient cannot have an omniscient being within the range of their perception.

It might be argued: "Let it be that for us the omniscient one does not meet the conditions for perception; nevertheless, why is it that these applications of non-perception do not succeed in establishing his non-existence? To this he says, "Therefore," and so forth: "Therefore, because [the omniscient one] is by nature of a perceptible form, the non-perception of him—which arises from a specific kind of non-observation—is not established in the case of causes, pervaders, or essential natures."

Because the omniscient one does not possess the characteristics of perceptibility for you, for that reason, the specific non-perception of those things whose nature consists of pervading the causes of omniscience—namely, the non-perception of what has reached the conditions of perceptibility—is not established.
If it is argued, "In that case, let the other remaining factors be established; nevertheless, the non-existence of the omniscient one is indeed proven," he says, "And this," and so forth.
And this threefold perception proceeds in a manifold form.
That [is established] through the application of the distinctions between non-comprehension and comprehension regarding those very [objects] that are contradictory and so forth.
When the deficiency of power in this [Māyā], which consists of the primary divisions, has been established with respect to the All-Knowing One, the others are effortlessly refuted.

This very non-perception (*adṛṣṭi*) of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and the cause (*kāraṇa*), which was just mentioned, when elaborated in three ways, is divided into nine types.
To explain how, he says: "the non-apprehension of that, its opposite, and so forth" (*tat-tadviruddhādyagati*).

By the word *tat* (that), the triad consisting of the essential nature, the pervader, and the cause under discussion is referred to. That which is opposed to that [triad] is "its opposite" (*tadviruddha*). This [opposite] is also of exactly three kinds, due to the distinction between the opposites of the essential nature, the pervader, and the cause. That which has "its opposite" as its beginning is "that, its opposite, and so forth" (*tadviruddhādi*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), three types [of evidence] are included: the contradictory effect (*viruddhakārya*), the contradictory cause (*viruddhakāraṇa*), and that which is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāpta*).
Furthermore, by the second occurrence of the word "that" (*tat*), those same three—essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth—are connected;
thus, it is "that and its contradictories, etc. (*tattadviruddhādi*).
The meaning is that their "non-going and going" (agatigatī) are respectively the non-going and going of what is contrary to them;
that is to say, the non-going of those [two] and the going of what is contrary to them and so forth.
The compound *tayor bhedas tena prayoga* means "the application by means of the distinction between those two."

In that regard, since there is no other way [to proceed], three types of non-perception have been directly indicated: the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the cause (*kāraṇa*), and the pervader (*vyāpaka*).

Since all remaining types of non-perception are indicators of these very three types of non-perception through a series of intermediate steps, this threefold non-perception constitutes their fundamental classification.

For instance, by means of perceiving what is contradictory to those [three], the perception of what is contradictory to the essential nature, the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader, and the perception of what is contradictory to the cause have been indicated.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the perception of a contradictory effect, the perception of the effect of something contradictory to the cause, and the perception of that which is pervaded by the contradictory are included.

And by these [three], the non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and the cause (*kāraṇa*) are indicated respectively as appropriate; therefore, since the incapacity of the threefold basic divisions to establish the non-existence of an omniscient being has been demonstrated, it follows that the incapacity of those [arguments] which have not become part of that treatise is established without even an effort. Thus, no separate effort need be made to demonstrate their incapacity, for when the root is cut, the branches cannot remain.

In ultimate reality, however, the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature alone is the root of all [non-apprehensions]; it is described as being threefold by way of relying on the distinctions between different objects.

It might be argued: "If the omniscient one were not perceived according to the criteria for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), then let there be no establishment of the specific non-perception of him; however, since his cause and his pervader do meet the criteria for perception, why is their specific non-observation not established? Furthermore, since things such as those contradictory to him possess a perceptible nature, why is their perception not established? To this, he says: "Causality, etc. "Causality, pervasion and the state of being pervaded, and contrariety—these are established when there is perceptibility; and so too is that self which possesses its specific qualifications."
The omniscient one is not perceived by you; therefore, these non-perceptions are incapable of refuting him, nor is there any other factor for negation.
The term *kāryakāraṇabhāva*, *vyāpyavyāpakatva*, and *virodhitā* form a copulative compound (*dvandva*).

For the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established through perception and non-perception; however, since an omniscient being and the like are invisible, the relationship of cause and effect with such a being cannot be established.
Nor can there be a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), because that too is preceded by the non-perception of something that has reached the conditions for perceptibility.

For instance, when the cessation of one thing necessarily entails the cessation of another, the latter is designated as being pervaded by the former; moreover, the establishment of such a cessation does not occur without the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
Furthermore, opposition (*virodha*) is established only between two perceptible entities, not between imperceptible ones.

Thus, opposition characterized by the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is observed in the case of one thing occurring while its cause remains unimpaired, provided that the other is absent.
Furthermore, existence and non-existence cannot be determined with respect to two things whose intrinsic natures are imperceptible.

Even contradiction, characterized by mutual exclusion, is established between two things only when the determination of one is inseparable from the exclusion of the other, as in the case of succession and simultaneity. And such determination is not possible regarding that which is invisible.
If this is so, how is the contradiction between existence, non-existence, and so forth established, since neither of the two is perceptible there?
This is not a fault.
For existence and non-existence are not first determined separately and only afterwards is their contradiction established on the basis of their relationship as the excluded and the excluder.

What then? [The contradiction exists] only between two things that are distinct and mutually exclusive. For it is established that their contradiction occurs at the same time within a single substratum (*dharmin*), and not in a different substratum.
Indeed, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the absence of a cow and the presence of a horse.

Nor is there a contradiction between those two at different times within a single substratum; for it is not the case that the subsequent existence and non-existence of what previously was non-existent, or what already existed, are impossible.

Rather, the contradiction lies in their simultaneous non-delimitation with respect to one and the same entity, and not in that very [entity] itself, because [the other] is delimited by means of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
If it is asked: "How can there be an exclusion of that which has not been delimited?"

For this very reason, it is precisely because [a property] is not delimited within that subject (*dharmī*) that its exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is possible. Otherwise, how could the exclusion of a property already delimited therein be effected?

For the exclusion of its absence is nothing other than its own delimitation; and the delimitation of the absence of others therein is nothing other than the delimitation of that [property] as distinct from others.

Therefore, that subject (*dharmin*) whose non-existence is excluded and whose existence is determined must necessarily be admitted to be perceptible; for it is not possible to determine what is imperceptible, nor is it possible to exclude a contrary property in that which has not been determined.

However, this is not possible in the case of an omniscient being, because all human beings as subjects are not perceptible to anyone, such that—by determining the property of non-omniscience in them—the exclusion of omniscience could be established.
Otherwise, it would follow that he himself is omniscient.
Therefore, the contradiction between omniscience and non-omniscience is not established with respect to a subject that is imperceptible;
however, it is established within one's own continuum.
Even there, it is not established in the future state, because at that time [the subject] is not visible.
Therefore, it is established that the relationship of cause and effect and so forth belongs only to the perceptible;
and as for the self with its qualifiers,
the connection is that "it is established."
In this context, "self" (ātman) means intrinsic nature (svabhāva). That which exists together with a qualification is "with qualification" (saviśeṣaṇa).
Here, the qualification is the state of being devoid of the three kinds of remoteness. These are the "non-visions."

The non-perceptions of cause and so forth [do not apply] to an omniscient being, because a relationship of cause and effect, contradiction, or pervaded and pervader between him and anything else is unestablished; furthermore, even when other conditions for perception are present, his perceptibility is never established at any time or place. And there is no other factor for negation apart from this specific kind of non-perception.

Furthermore, demonstrating the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of his own unqualified application of non-perception by showing it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says "If," and so forth:
"If the omniscient one were refuted merely on the basis of your non-perception of him,
then you would also have to refute your mother's marriage and other such matters."
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the marriage of one's mother, etc.," there is the inclusion of the sexual enjoyment of one's own parents and similar acts;
thus, the implication is that you would have become born of an adulterer (*jārajāta*).

As it has been said: "If the non-perception of objects by your dull eye were to invalidate their existence, then alas, you are ruined, for it would follow that even the application of the designation 'uncle' could not occur."
In this regard, he anticipates the opponent's rebuttal with the words "sutākhyetyādi":
"If the existence of that cause is understood through the observation of its effect called 'son,' then surely that effect is observed in some cases even in the absence of that [cause]."

Since that [cause], such as the mother’s marriage and so forth, is established through the means of valid cognition of inference (*anumāna*) by observing effects such as the naming of the son, its non-perception is not established; therefore, there is no consequence of its non-existence. With the words "the absence of that" and so forth, he demonstrates the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of this reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*). "The absence of that," etc. [he says].

Even in the absence of such a marriage, and likewise in the absence of sexual enjoyment with a husband who has been married, the effect known as a son is observed in the case of some wicked woman through her union with another man; let it be so. If it were thus, it would follow that [the child] belongs to the mother [alone]. This is an established inference based on the Sun. Consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that you yourself are born of an adulterer (*jāraja*) is difficult to avoid.

Since the Master Dharmakīrti also intended to demonstrate the undesirable consequence of the absence of the basis for the specific designation "father," he indeed brought forward the undesirable consequence of being born of an adulterer.

With the words "If its non-existence is not understood from the perception of another," etc., he anticipates the opponent's reply: "If its non-existence is not understood from the perception of another, then surely that perception of another must be established for you; how can it have that [non-existent thing] as its object?"
"The apprehension of other persons" means the apprehension of others;
"of that" refers to [the marriage of] one's mother and so forth.

Non-existence is not apprehended; rather, it is existence itself [that is apprehended]. In this regard, the non-establishment of the perception of another is being demonstrated, as he says: "But surely," and so forth.
Being asked "How so?", the opponent replies: "Because of [the Buddha's] teaching.
[The author asks: Is this [teaching] not found even in the case of an omniscient being? Furthermore, why is this other statement of his own not considered here?
Moreover, men are generally speakers of untruth at all times;
therefore, just as there is no confidence in present matters, so too there is none in the recounting of past events.
The word "siddha" (established) is connected with the subject under discussion.
Showing that the opponent's instruction is inconclusive by pointing out the consequence of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says: "not even in the case of an omniscient being.
This refers to [the following].
Regarding the instruction:

why should it not exist in the case of the Omniscient One? Indeed, it does exist. If the instruction concerning [the propriety of] one's mother’s marriage and so forth is accepted as authoritative, then why should this instruction of ours—that "the Omniscient One exists"—not also be accepted as authoritative? For there is no difference between them.
Furthermore, he shows by the words "And this," etc., that you have yourself stated through your own words that such an instruction lacks authority.

Thus, it has been demonstrated that the cessation of one's own perception is not a valid means of proof for establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being, because an unqualified [non-perception] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and a qualified [non-perception] is unestablished (*asiddha*). Now, demonstrating that the cessation of the perception of all persons is unestablished, and therefore cannot serve as a valid means of proof for proving the non-existence of an omniscient being, he says: "Or let it be so," and so forth. "Or let there be no such teaching, or let there be no validity for it; nevertheless, how have you reached this certainty: that an omniscient being is not perceived by anyone?"
For in this way, there would indeed be certainty regarding the perception of the self in all sentient beings;
and it has been described that by perceiving that, you have become omniscient.
Regarding the term "instruction" (upadeśa):
the ellipsis is "that which establishes the existence of the Omniscient One.
Or rather, it refers to the authority of this instruction.
Regarding the phrase "the vision of the self of all beings":
it means the vision of the intrinsic nature of all beings.
If one were to say, "We certainly possess this vision of the self of all beings," he replies with the words beginning with "that view" (taddṛṣṭi), and so forth.
In that vision, [it means] in the vision of the self of all sentient beings.
Otherwise, doubt would be appropriate even in the case of non-perception, as in the case of [the existence of] living beings;
for it is suspected that some who are omniscient might know [it].
"He sees himself by himself through himself as the light of the self"—this too is suspected; and for this reason, the non-perception of everything remains uncertain.
"Otherwise" means in the absence of the perception of a self in all sentient beings. "Like a sentient being" means:
This is like [the case of] the existence of an object remote in space and so forth, which possesses existence despite its non-perception.

What is meant is this: just as there is doubt regarding the existence of an object remote in space and so forth—even though it is not perceived, because it exists even while unperceived—so too, doubt is appropriate even when there is the perception of objects within the range of an omniscient person existing in another individual.

Alternatively, this is the meaning: just as there is doubt regarding the existence of an omniscient being even when he is not perceived, so too there is doubt regarding the perception of the object that is omniscience; for in both cases, non-perception is possible due to the remoteness of their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*).

Now, it may be argued that doubt is appropriate regarding the existence of a real entity, because since such an entity might sometimes not be perceived—even though it exists—it is a possibility that can be conceived.

However, the vision of an omniscient being is not possible for anyone of limited vision, and it is not reasonable for a discerning person to entertain doubt regarding a matter that is impossible; therefore, he says "some," etc.,
and "by themselves," which is stated because of the acceptance of the tenets established by others.
The term "by himself" (svayam eva) is explained by the word "by the self" (ātmanā).
"Self" (ātman) refers to the person (puruṣa).
It is called "light" (jyotis) because the self has the nature of luminosity due to its being of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa).
He supports this very point with the words beginning "For thus" (*tathāhi*):
"For by the word 'all,' all living beings are intended;
and since he is not excluded from 'all,' his non-perception is uncertain."
"And he" refers to the Omniscient One.

It might be argued: "Only those of limited vision (arvāgdarśin) are intended by the word 'all,' and not the omniscient one; therefore, no such doubt will arise. To this, he says "tadeka... and so forth:
"What connection could there be here [between passion and the state of being all] that would hold even when excluding that one [the omniscient person]?
For passion and the like do not cease simply because they are unknown to others."

For if the non-perception of others who possess limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*)—to the exclusion of that omniscient being—is adduced as the reason, then there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), because there is no counter-argument characterized by an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between that non-perception of one's own and the absence of an omniscient being.
With the words "for not" (*na hi*) and so forth, he establishes that very lack of a necessary connection.

Thus, the inconclusiveness and the unestablished nature of the means of valid cognition called "non-apprehension" have been demonstrated. Now, demonstrating that the reason "because its form is made the object of the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence" (*abhāvapramāṇa*) is also of doubtful establishment, he says "some," and so forth:
"Some who see only what is near also perceive [the object] through inference;
for indeed, some things are considered by some people to be subtle in certain cases."
For instance, although the proof for the momentariness of the Vedas, the earth,
and so forth was previously stated very clearly, it was not perceived by the dull-witted.
Thus, even the absence of his knowledge is not ascertained through doubt alone;
for it is those who are free from suspicion who perceive non-existence.

Since it is possible that some individuals of dull intellect, though possessing only limited vision, might at times establish the existence of an omniscient being through inference, the reason "because it is the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-apprehension" (*abhāvapramāṇa*) is subject to the fallacy of being "unestablished due to doubt" (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*).

For instance, although the momentariness and non-selfhood of the Vedic sound, the earth, mountains, bodies, thunderbolts, and so forth, are extremely clear, they were not perceived by you, the beast-like Mīmāṃsakas; yet, they have been established by us through the presentation of more robust proofs. Similarly, even if no proof for an omniscient being is currently found at this time, it remains "doubtful" because its possibility is still conceivable. Therefore, the claim that [the omniscient being] has a form made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in the absence of the five means of knowledge is unestablished, because it is itself a matter of doubt.
This is why [it is said]: "because..."
Because there is an absence of proof.
Furthermore, even if there were no inference for all those of limited vision to establish the existence of an omniscient being,
he says "even in the absence of inference," etc., demonstrating that the reason remains inconclusive:
"Even in the absence of inference, there is no certainty of non-existence from this [lack of inference]."
It is like the existence of fire and so forth, even when the effects such as smoke have not yet begun.

For it has been established previously that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is neither the cause of a thing nor its pervader; how then could the thing cease to exist upon the cessation of that [cognition]? For instance, in the case of fire within a mass of iron or similar objects that have not yet produced their effect—such as smoke—and which is situated inside the interior of a room, no inference arises due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*). Nevertheless, its existence has not ceased; thus, there is no certainty regarding its non-existence. Similarly, when there is an absence of inference to prove the non-existence of an omniscient being, there remains doubt.
"From this" means from the absence of inference.

That fire or other [cause] by which the effect, such as smoke, has not been commenced is so described; the analysis of the compound is: "that fire or other [cause] which has not commenced the effect of smoke and so forth. It is like its existence (*sattva*), as if in the presence of its being.

By stating "When an object has been perceived at some time," and so forth, the opponent demonstrates that perception is the cause of doubt, using the example of fire in an iron ball and the like; he then argues that since such perception is absent in the case of an omniscient being, doubt is untenable, thereby supporting the very point that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
"Indeed, doubt regarding an object perceived at some time is appropriate, just as in the case of a wooden post; for such doubt relies upon two alternative possibilities."
Since a post and a man have both been seen at some time or other, it is appropriate that doubt regarding their nature arises; however, an omniscient being has never been seen in such a manner.
For doubt is appropriate only regarding an object that has been previously perceived at some time, as in the case of a post and not elsewhere, because it rests upon both alternatives; otherwise,
doubt would take as its object everything unperceived,
and consequently, there would be no restriction to resting upon both alternatives.
Therefore, doubt is appropriate in cases such as a fire in a red-hot iron ball, but not in the case of an omniscient being, because such a being is never perceived at any time.
He responds with the words beginning "nanu" (surely): "Surely, O wise one, by this very same method, the non-existence of your mother’s marriage and so forth would follow for you without any doubt."

If, at some time, there were doubt regarding an object perceived and certainty of non-existence regarding another, then by this same logic, the existence of your mother’s marriage and so forth would become free from doubt for you; for you have never before perceived your mother’s marriage, such that even in this case there would not be a certainty of its non-existence for you.
And here, the remaining objection should be stated as before, with the response following the previous pattern;
the term "O wise one" is a word used in derision.

If this is so, then doubt would follow as being entirely without basis; to this he says "by us," and so forth: "But by us, doubt is described here even in the absence of valid cognition (pramā), because of the cessation of valid cognition regarding both the existence and non-existence of things."

For since the mere absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva) demonstrates both the existence and non-existence of a thing, there is a lack of determination; thus, doubt is described as arising precisely from the failure to produce a certainty regarding existence or non-existence.
As it has been said: "Doubt is a deliberation that depends on specific features [of the object], resulting from the lack of determination between perception and non-perception."
It might be argued that the cessation of valid cognition is observed in both cases—whether an object exists as a real entity or not—to which he replies with the words "of the eyes, etc.
For when there is a deficiency in the eyes and so forth, there is no valid cognition even though the object exists;
and even when those [faculties] are unimpaired, there is no [cognition] due to the absence of the object, as in the case of a jar or similar things.
Therefore, since non-apprehension alone is observed in two ways,
it is better that there be doubt regarding an omniscient being even on account of the absence of a means of valid cognition.
For instance, even when an object such as a jar exists, valid cognition does not arise for one who lacks eyes.

Furthermore, even when those [faculties] such as the eyes are unimpaired, it does not arise if the object known as the "referent" (viṣaya) is absent due to being non-proximate; this is how it connects with the present context. This is just as in the case of a jar that is not proximate in a suitable location.
"Of the solitary" means of that which is devoid of the qualification of being perceptible.
"Because of being seen in two ways" means in both existence and non-existence.
*Tat* means "therefore"; *varam* means "better."
Because it is the cause for the reconnection of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).

For indeed, regarding those whose roots of virtue have been severed by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), there is a longing for the reconnection of those roots; this junction is described by two views, according to the statement: "There is a longing through the two views.
For this very reason, in various places the masters raise a doubt, asking: "If [you ask] what is the proof for its existence, let there be doubt precisely because of that."

It might be argued: "If an omniscient being exists, why is he never perceived by anyone at any time? Even if it were granted that he is eternally unperceivable by those of limited vision, why would his effect not be apprehended by someone? For it is not the case that because the eyes and other sense organs are imperceptible, their effect—namely, cognition—must also be imperceptible. To this, he says: "For even though he exists," and so forth: "For even though he exists, he would not be seen by the dull-witted, just like the conceptualizations of others."
And like actual iron balls, coals, or fire, it does not perform any function.
Or that effect may be invisible, like the passion produced in another kalpa;
or even if the effect were visible, its concomitance with that [cause] would not be perceived.
Since the Knower of All Objects is always invisible to those of dull intellect,
his existence cannot be established through inference.
And it has been stated that a means of valid cognition which lacks both a cause and pervasion is incapable [of establishing] this entity;
furthermore, since its existence is observed even when it has ceased, there is doubt because of that as well.
It should be connected with the phrase "would not be perceived directly.

For it is not the case that everything whatsoever must be perceived all at once, such that the non-existence of an omniscient being would follow from the absence of perception; this is because the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) residing in other persons, though they exist, are not perceived by others.

Nor is it necessary that causes always be engaged in producing their effects, such that the non-existence of an omniscient being would result from the non-perception of his effects; for we observe things such as fire in a heated iron ball, which has not yet initiated its effect in the form of smoke.

Granted that causes are always possessed of their effects, nevertheless, this does not constitute a certainty regarding the absence of those effects. For it is not the case that every effect that has arisen is pervaded by perceptibility—such that the non-existence of an effect could be established through its non-perception—since even an effect that has arisen may not be perceived. This is like the passion of another person: for example, although passion arises in another person from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) at the beginning of an eon (*kalpa*), it is not perceived, yet its non-existence is not thereby established.

Or even if the effect is observed, because that cause is beyond the senses, it is possible that for a person who has not grasped its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), an inference of it will not arise; likewise, it is conceivable that even if an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) exists, his existence would not be established through inference. "For those whose vision is dull" (*jaḍadṛśām*): "vision" (*dṛk*) is simply cognition (*dhī*); thus "vision-cognition" (*dhīdṛg*). Those whose vision-cognition is dull are so described.

Furthermore, it was previously stated that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is neither the cause of a thing nor its pervader (*vyāpaka*). Therefore, the point is: how could a thing cease to exist upon the cessation of this inference, which is neither its cause nor its pervader?

It is described as being "neither its cause nor its pervader. One cannot argue that even though the means of valid cognition called inference is neither a cause nor a pervader, we nevertheless observe a thing ceasing when that inference ceases; for there is nothing impossible regarding what is observed. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even when this [inference] has ceased, the existence [of the thing] is observed."
Even when this inference has ceased, the existence of this object is still observed, as was previously stated in the case of fire in a red-hot iron ball and so forth.

Having thus demonstrated in detail the impossibility of any subverting evidence (bādhakapramāṇa) for establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being, he concludes with the words "Therefore" and so forth: "Therefore, there is no evidence whatsoever that subverts the existence of an omniscient being; rather, the proof for this will be stated in detail."
It might be argued: "Just as we have no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that sublates that [position], so too you do not have a proof for it. To this, he says: "But the proof for this..."

Regarding what was stated— that [the Buddha] is the means for attaining knowledge of the detailed expansion of all individual components and so forth— here [the author] says: "Even though the means for thoroughly knowing all objects without exception may be fruitless,
the wise followers of the Sugata exert themselves with another mind."
"With another mind" means with another intention.
To the question "Who, then, is this person?", he says "He who knows the attainment of heaven," and so forth.
It is understood that there exists one who knows the causes for attaining heaven and liberation;
not only is he perceived directly, but he is also recognized as omniscient.

For we are primarily establishing that the Blessed One possesses the means of knowledge (*sādhana*) consisting in the cognition of the causes for attaining heaven and liberation; whereas this proof of his omniscience—that he is the knower of all objects—is incidental. This is because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the operation of the Blessed One’s cognition even regarding other matters, and thus, being omniscient through the direct thorough knowledge of all objects, he cannot be contradicted by anyone. Therefore, it is not reasonable for those who are discerning (*prekṣāvat*) to reject him.
However, it is shown that for those who seek the attainment of omniscience, their engagement for that purpose is indeed appropriate.

Therefore, since there is thus an absence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) and since the proof for an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) to be described hereafter is perfectly clear, this rejection by you of an omniscient being who is the sole object of certainty—namely, that "all persons are not free from passion and the like, and are not undefiled"—is shown to arise solely from delusion (*moha*). This is what is indicated by the words beginning with "therefore" (*tataśca*). "Therefore, when there is an absence of subverting evidence and the proof is clear, why do those of dull intellect disagree regarding the omniscient one? (v. 109)

It might be argued: "We reject [the existence of such a person] because we believe there is no such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a person of that kind, and not out of delusion. To this he says, "Mābhūd vā" and so forth:

"Or let there be no proof for that; however, as long as a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) is not certain, there would be doubt. But on what basis is this certainty of theirs [regarding its non-existence] founded?"
This is stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position], for there is indeed a proof that will be stated later.
"This is the certainty" refers to the Mīmāṃsakas' conviction that "there is no omniscient being."

As for what you say— that "injunction alone is capable of making known objects such as the past, the present, the future, the subtle, and the remote, whereas no other sense organ can do so"— this too is shown by the verse beginning with *bhūtādi* to be merely a claim, proclaimed without proof and based on mere devotion:
"Injunction alone, and nothing else, is capable of making known the past and so forth"—
this restriction is indeed logical only if the non-existence of any other [means of knowledge] for that purpose has been definitively established.
"Another" refers to the direct perception of the Omniscient One and so forth.
"The non-existence of others" refers to...

It is only when the non-existence of another omniscient being has been definitively ascertained that it is proper to speak in this way, and not otherwise; for otherwise, the restriction would be purposeless.

Regarding that [objection] beginning with "the entire world is subtle," he says "pradhāna" and so forth: "In order to establish the Knower of the Purpose of Pradhāna and Puruṣa as the Knower of All Objects, that means of valid cognition was stated previously, and another will be stated later."

Therefore, in order to establish the meaning for one who knows the subtle distinctions of the entire world, people do not labor in vain through the agitation of composing treatises or engaging in debates.

We do not exert effort in proving the existence of an omniscient being by setting aside reflection upon the domain of the omniscient one itself; rather, our effort is directed solely toward proving the knower of Dharma, who is the primary subject.

Accordingly, earlier, in the proof for the knower of Dharma, you yourself stated that there is a means of valid cognition called *arthāpatti* (presumption), saying, "Thus, by accepting a knower of Dharma, he is obtained through *arthāpatti*," and later you will state the means of valid cognition called *anumāna* (inference). Therefore, people are not being troubled over an inappropriate matter, but rather on a truly appropriate one.
Regarding the passage beginning with "connected to all cognizers," he says "all" and so forth:
"Because perception and other means of knowledge connected to all cognizers are not excluded,
the state of being knowable solely through scripture is not established for merit and demerit."

Since perception and other means of knowledge—which have as their objects things such as *dharma* and are connected to all cognizers—cannot be refuted by mere non-perception (*adarśanamātra*), it follows that *dharma* and *adharma* cannot be established as being cognizable through scripture alone.
Regarding what was said, beginning with "by this much," he says "by this much" and so forth:
"And although by this much the Mīmāṃsā position remains unestablished,
the effort made by others to refute the Omniscient One is due to extreme [folly]."
"Even though it is unestablished" means that for one who knows the Dharma, it is established; "by others" refers to the Mīmāṃsakas.
Regarding the passage beginning with "But those [who say] because their root is severed," etc.,
he says: "But those who, because their root is unsevered and the knowledge of dharma remains unimpaired,
declare that there are omniscient persons— by them wisdom has been revealed."
The elision of the vowel *a* in the word *ahata* should be understood;
"by them" refers to the Buddhists.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Because he sees directly through perception," [the author] says "By means of the sense of taste," and so forth:
"If the tastes of wine, impurities, and the like were perceived by him through contact with the gustatory faculty, then at that time, he himself would be subject to censure."
By means of the mental consciousness itself, which arises from the cultivation of the true nature of reality,
even those things censured in conventional truth are experienced as if they were unattained.
Even if there were a direct perception of the taste of wine and so forth by him, there would still be no loss of his status as a knower of the Dharma.

If it is argued that he would incur blame, [the response is: one who perceives those tastes through contact with the sense-faculties such as the tongue would be blameworthy according to worldly convention; however, the Blessed One does not perceive them in that way. Rather, he perceives them with the mind, and since that [mental consciousness] does not reach its object, what is produced by it is not recognized as such in the world.
Indeed, in the ultimate sense, no one is subject to blame, because such blame is unstable.

For instance, that which is censurable for a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) is not so for one who has renounced the world (*jīrṇadvija*); however, although liquor and such things are condemned in the world according to conventional practice, even when he experiences them, the Blessed One is not subject to censure because he experiences the liquor only mentally.

This might be argued: "Just as others experience suffering and the like upon perceiving liquor and such through contact with the sense organ of taste, so too would it follow for one who perceives it even by means of the mind."
This is not so.
Taste and other objects experienced through their connection with the sense organs of taste and so forth cause benefit or harm to the organ and thus become causes of suffering and the like.
Furthermore, these appear as causes of suffering and so forth only to certain individuals whose minds are distorted by the influence of unwholesome karma and the like, and not to everyone.
For instance, just as water appears to hungry ghosts (pretas) in the form of pus and so forth, yet for the Blessed One (Bhagavat) it is not the case that everything exists [in such a manner].

This is because, since he perceives through the mind alone, there is no possibility of impairment of the sense faculties and so on; furthermore, because the Blessed One consists of the five types of activity that are untainted (anāsrava), there is no possibility of the predominance of tainted karma (sāsrava-karma). Moreover, because he perceives things in their non-erroneous, impermanent nature and so forth, there is no state of perversion (viparyasta); for this very reason, even mental suffering characterized by dejection and the like is impossible for the Blessed One, since that [suffering] is born of delusion (moha).

And all this [is so] provided that external objects exist; however, since the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is impossible [in ultimate reality], those [objects such as] the impure and so forth do not exist at all. Let it not be that they appear in the vision of those who have distanced themselves from all conceptual constructions of the impure and so forth, just as hairs and the like do not appear in the vision of those with unimpaired eyes when defects such as cataracts have been removed.
As it has been said:
"Indeed, its [the mind's] impurities, tastes, and so forth appear due to ignorance."
Therefore, they are established as non-perceptible, like the disc of a second moon.
But how could that brahmin not be censurable in this world, whose Vedic sounds—existing within his mouth, belly, and so forth—are always connected to every impure place due to their pervasive nature?
And regarding the passage beginning with "nor [is it] the Veda, the Upavedas, or the Angas," he says "precisely because" and so forth:
Precisely because the speech of the Tāyin is not seen to set forth meanings proclaimed in the Vedas and other such sources, for that very reason he is omniscient.
Indeed, it is possible that the Veda— which possesses a status unique among all non-Buddhist outsiders—
speaks falsely regarding the self and so forth, having been studied through negligence.
One becomes omniscient by knowing an object exactly as it exists, in its form of being and so forth;
however, the objects such as the self (*ātman*) and others as described in the Veda do not exist in that way, because they are sublated by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, how could one who teaches them in that same manner be a seer of reality?
Nor can it be said that these were not known by him even as false, for they were indeed known exactly as they are.

For instance, all unwholesome courses of action, such as the killing of living beings, have been taught as causes for an unhappy rebirth; likewise, by statements such as "In this world there is no sentient being or self, but these phenomena exist with their causes," the self and so forth were declared to be non-existent. Thus, the Blessed One’s lack of knowledge regarding the categories prescribed in the Vedas and other scriptures is unproven.
Regarding the passage beginning with "even though not recorded in his own treatises," he says "non-dual" and so forth:
"The non-dual gateway to Śiva, which strikes fear into those of wrong views,
was clearly taught as selflessness (nairātmya) for the benefit of those to be trained."
It is "second" because it has not been attained by other non-Buddhist teachers, for all of them are intent upon false views of a self;
and all of this qualifies the term "selflessness.
It is called "the gateway to the auspicious."
Because it serves as the means for entering nirvāṇa,
"auspicious" (śiva) refers to nirvāṇa. Regarding the phrase "of those with wrong views":
Those for whom views such as that of a self are contemptible are so described;
the meaning is that [the teaching] causes terror in foolish people who are adhered to false views,
as it has been said:
"I do not exist, I shall not be; it is not mine, it shall not be"—such is the terror of the fool; for one who has grasped [the truth], fear is destroyed.
By this [verse],
it is shown that for those who remain fixed in erroneous adherence— thinking "I do not exist"— it is not even possible to express the realization of that [reality], let alone to realize it.
Furthermore, he shows that this has never before been fully understood by anyone remaining on the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), stating:
"Unfamiliar to those in cyclic existence, once known, it turns back all misfortune;
for those engaged in its practice and so forth, it is the supreme mine of the jewels of virtue."
If even the wise know such a supreme reality,
who would not consider those who know the purpose of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa to be omniscient?
The meaning is that it is unfamiliar and unpracticed by worldly ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
To the question of how it serves for their benefit such that it was taught for that purpose, he says "known" and so forth:
when known—that is, directly realized—it becomes the cause of the cessation of the entire mass of misfortunes characterized by afflictions, birth, and so on.

Even if poets were to realize that supreme reality which is useful for the goals of man—namely, that even at a later time, when practiced, [the study of grammar] produces specific qualities such as eloquence (*rathyā*) and so forth—they too might be considered omniscient. For we do not accept omniscience as being restricted to a single individual; rather, whoever knows the reality as it has been described in this way is intended to be "all-knowing," and no one else. Since this is not the case for poets, there is no over-extension of the definition. (3323)

By this, he shows that what was stated previously—“and among the omniscient ones, there is a multiplicity,” and so forth—is also refuted, saying “And this,” etc.: “And this kind of knowledge of selflessness belonging to Vardhamāna and others does not exist at all; for all the non-Buddhist heretics have perished because of their view of a self.”

For those by whom it is asserted that the non-momentary nature [of things] is sublated by perception and other means of knowledge— just as [the non-momentary nature] of fire is illogically stated— how indeed could they be omniscient?

How can it be conceived that those who stumble regarding this perceptible object well-known even to the Vāhīkas and others could possess a clear comprehension of things beyond the reach of perception?
In this way, however, his lack of omniscience is understood even more clearly,
because of his association with false knowledge and because of his teaching of what is contrary [to reality].
Just as another person, being deluded by the perception of a post as a man, is corrected through subsequent experience,
so too [the object] is to be known through all methods of investigation based on the establishment of the logical reason (*hetu*).
And because he is omniscient due to his correct knowledge of the reality of all things,
there is no doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in this reason.
