As it has been said: if the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) were possible for Vardhamāna, Kapila, and others, then they too would possess omniscience. However, all of these are seized by the crocodile of false self-grasping (*vitathātmagraha*), which is the cause for the production of every defect; they are teachers of such things as non-momentary entities, which are sublated by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, how could the perception of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha-darśana*) enter the path of possibility for those who stumble even regarding objects that have entered the range of comprehension for the minds of children? For it is said: "What proof is there that Kapila is not [omniscient]? Indeed, this proof can be stated here quite clearly: those who are associated with false knowledge are not among the omniscient, just like a man who has conceived the delusion that a post is a person; and Vardhamāna and others are associated with false knowledge—this is the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
Because non-omniscience, which is incompatible with omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), is pervaded by the state of being accompanied by false cognition;
nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), since it has been demonstrated through all investigations that these [scriptures] reveal contrary objects;

nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its exclusion from the dissimilar class being doubtful, because omniscience is intended as the state of correctly and completely knowing all things.
Furthermore, where there is right knowledge, there is no possibility of its opposite, false knowledge.

It might be argued: "Even if these [scriptures] do indeed reveal contrary meanings, nevertheless, it cannot be concluded from this that they are associated with false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), because worldly transactions can be carried out in other ways as well, owing to the diverse intentions of persons. Therefore, the reason is 'doubtful-unestablished' (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*). Anticipating this, he says: "If these words of the *Syādvāda* and so forth were intentional... and so on. "If these words of theirs, such as the *Syādvāda*, were merely intentional, then what would be accepted as the actual nature of all things by them?"
If it is argued that they stated this—namely, that [the claim] "he is omniscient" contradicts the means of valid cognition such as *syādvāda*—with another intention in mind, let it be so;

for we do not intend to establish independently that Vardhamāna and others are non-omniscient. Rather, you, who are established in mutually contradictory views, asked: "If the Sugata is omniscient, then what is the proof that Kapila is not? To this, we state a proof by accepting the difference in their opinions according to your own view; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
For if their statements are described as being intentional (ābhiprāyika), then it must be stated what they consider to be the ultimate (pāramārthika) nature of reality.
Being questioned in this manner, the opponent says: "Because of selflessness, momentariness, and so forth.
[The author replies: If it is thus that [the Buddha knows] selflessness, momentariness, and so forth, then he is indeed all-seeing, because of his direct perception of the true nature of all things.
Let them also [be accepted], because they all abide in unanimity;
for they did not proclaim a definitive meaning that contradicts one another.
If one were to assert that he possesses a self and so forth, then a difference of opinion would indeed have been stated, and thus there would be no lack of proof (*asiddhatā*).

To this, he gives the reply beginning with "If it were so": "For we do not intend to prove that 'this one is omniscient' by pointing him out specifically like seizing a horn; rather, [we mean] in a general sense.

If it is accepted that Kapila and others possessed such thorough knowledge of reality, then you should not ask how there can be a difference of opinion between those two, since they would all stand in complete agreement."
However, that teaching among them which presents mutually contradictory meanings is established as being of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
For it is not logical that those who abide in a state of unanimous consensus would proclaim a mutually contradictory, definitive (*nītārtha*), and ultimate nature.

Therefore, one who desires to accept differences of opinion must state that their words are intentional (*ābhiprāyika*); and once these differences of opinion are admitted, one should not ask, "Who indeed is to be determined as the one [authoritative]?"—for it has already been established that the Sugata alone is determined to be omniscient by virtue of possessing the aforementioned knowledge, and no other. //3332–3333//

Furthermore, demonstrating that if one accepts the aforementioned knowledge for Kapila and others, they would necessarily attain the status of a Sugata, he says: "Of that which has been established as its nature, and which pertains to all things," and so forth.
869] Of that which has been established as its nature, and which pervades all entities...
Through the direct realization of reality, the Sugatas are all-seeing.
And for them, in such knowledge, the state of being a Sugata is not differentiated;
because of their possession of praiseworthy knowledge, this much is its defining characteristic.
That reality characterized by selflessness and so forth is so described because its form— its intrinsic nature— has been established and proven through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Of them" refers to Vardhamāna and the others.
"Thus much" means the state of possessing praiseworthy knowledge.
"Of that" refers to [the aforementioned].
Regarding the state of being a Sugata:
because one has attained the grasping of all obscurations, such as those regarding the knowable, in a praiseworthy manner through the knowledge of selflessness, one is called a Sugata.

Furthermore, he shows that even when the possibility of an omniscient being is established in a general sense, it necessarily refers to the Blessed One alone, by means of the following passage beginning with "Even though such a one is possible":
"Even though such an omniscient being has been established in a general sense,
the Sugata is specifically determined [as that person] because of the invariable concomitance with his defining characteristics."
The word "tad" means "therefore.
"Because of the inseparable connection with the characteristics" means because of the inseparable connection with the characteristics of an omniscient being.
One might object: "How can he be established without a specific designation? To this, he says: "Even though his specific qualities are not specified," and so forth.
"Even though his specific qualities are not specified, some omniscient being may exist—someone who knows the entire world exactly as it is, in its nature of selflessness and so on."

For although the definition of an omniscient being has been stated in general terms as "one who understands the entire world exactly as it is, in its nature of being selfless and so forth," the specific [subject] in whom that [definition] is found is understood by implication; thus, the explicit mention of a specific subject is redundant. The point is that this definition of omniscience is found only in the Blessed One and nowhere else, because he reveals the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the means thereto, through various skillful methods and the complete four noble truths.
For it is not possible to teach an object that is unknown in its suchness—that is, as it truly is, without error and in its entirety—as has been said:
"Indeed, it is difficult to explain that which is beyond perception, namely the goal and its cause."

It might be argued: "Even if the world is known by him in its form as being devoid of self (anātman) and so forth, how is he established as omniscient? To this he says: "When selflessness has been directly perceived," and so on.
When selflessness has been directly perceived, no fault finds a footing, because it is contradictory to that [fault], just as darkness does not persist in a brightly burning lamp.

Omniscience indeed consists in the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Among these, the afflictions themselves—namely attachment and so forth—are called the "afflictive obscuration" because they act as a hindrance to the vision of reality. Furthermore, the lack of complete knowledge regarding all aspects of the truth of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, even when that truth has been seen, as well as the inability to explain it, constitutes the "obscuration of the knowable. Therein, the abandonment of the afflictive obscuration occurs through the direct perception of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
However, the abandonment of the obscuration of the knowable occurs through the devoted, uninterrupted, and long-term cultivation of that very same vision of selflessness.

For it has been ascertained through positive and negative concomitance that these afflictions, such as attachment and the rest, are rooted in the false view of a self and do not arise by the power of external objects;
because even when an external object is present, they do not arise without improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*),
and they do arise even in the absence of an object when improper conceptualization (*ayoniśovikalpa*) is manifest.
Furthermore, it is not logical that something which does not conform to the existence or non-existence of another should be its cause, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor do these [defilements] inhere in a self imagined by others, because such a self has already been refuted. Or, even if such a self existed, it would follow that passion and the other defilements would either arise eternally or never cease at all.
Because the self, as the cause of arising and persistence, is always present in its unimpaired state;
and because it is impossible for that which cannot have any excellence added to it by others to depend upon them—this has been discussed at length.

Furthermore, since the dependence [of a cause] on either an existent or a non-existent [effect] is denied, it is illogical for these [causes] to possess inherence (*samavāya*) in anything; therefore, their own existence is not bound to an eternal cause.
Nor do they arise through the power of external objects;

rather, they are produced by the power of the vision of a non-existent self. For instance, attachment to a self does not arise in one who does not perceive "I," nor does the intense clinging to "mine" emerge toward an object that is not grasped as such, provided that object is not apprehended as being conducive to the production of one's own pleasure.
Furthermore, hatred never manifests in one who is unattached toward an object that is not apprehended as being adverse to oneself or what belongs to oneself.

Because [affection] is impossible toward that which does not obstruct one's own interests or which counteracts such obstruction; thus, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and the rest produce those two [affection for self and self-interest], and these in turn produce affection for self-interest, as well as hatred and so forth. Through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it has been established—clearly even down to cowherds and women—that the root of these [defilements] is the grasping of self and self-interest, which arises from the grasping of a self. Furthermore, the vision of selflessness (nairātmya-darśana) is the opposite of the vision of a self, because its objective support (ālambana) consists of aspects contrary to that [vision of self].

For it is contradictory for these two—the vision of selflessness and the vision of a self—to coexist or be identical within a single continuum at the same time, just as it is contradictory for a rope and a snake, or the cognition thereof, to exist together.

Therefore, because the vision of selflessness contradicts the vision of a self, it also contradicts passion and the other afflictions rooted in that [vision of self], just as a particular fire contradicts the particular physical reactions such as horripilation caused by cold.

When that vision of selflessness, which is the adversary of all defects, has been directly realized, the host of defects such as attachment, being its opposite, finds no place to abide—just as darkness cannot remain in a place pervaded by light; therefore, through the vision of selflessness, there occurs the grasping of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: wherever there is the presence of an entity that is incompatible with another, the latter does not attain its existence there; for example, darkness does not persist on the surface of the earth when it is in contact with the spreading radiance of a blazing lamp. And in a person who has directly perceived the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*), there is the presence of the vision of selflessness, which is incompatible with the multitude of afflictions (*doṣagaṇa*). This is thus the "perception of the incompatible" (*viruddhopalabdhi*).

It might be argued as follows: Just as when the mind is occupied by the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya-darśana*), there is no opportunity for the vision of self (*ātma-darśana*) to arise due to their mutual opposition, so too, because the opposition is equal, there would be no opportunity for the vision of selflessness to arise when the mind is occupied by the vision of self; consequently, since the vision of selflessness is impossible for anyone, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Or, whether the vision of selflessness is possible or not, even if there is opposition between these two, an absolute relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva*) is not established, as is the case with passion and hatred, or pleasure and pain.
Since what is intended to be established here is absolute abandonment (*atyantaprahāṇa*),
and not merely the non-manifestation for a limited time, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, the reason is inconclusive because it is observed that even in those who possess unimpaired majesty, passion (*rāga*) and other afflictions arise.
This is not so.

If the arising of the conceptualization of selflessness were impossible within the continuum of one whose afflictions consist of non-apprehension, then there would indeed be no possibility for the emergence of the vision of selflessness. However, since the manifestation of the conceptualization of selflessness is established by experience for everyone to that extent, and since that very [conceptualization] can reach a state of excellence through cultivation—just like the conceptualization of a beloved woman—it eventually attains the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of its vivid appearance and its grasping of an object cognized by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, how could the emergence of the vision of selflessness be impossible?
Moreover, just as in a place enveloped by darkness there is the possibility of an opportunity for light to arise after some time, why should that not be conceivable here as well?

Nor can it be rightly said that such a cultivation is impossible for anyone; for at the time of such direct perceptual knowledge, lack of interest on the part of all [beings] cannot be the cause, since the engagement of a discerning person is invariably concomitant with interest.

Even though there may be a desire [to attain liberation], a discerning person does not proceed [toward its cause] because of a lack of thorough knowledge regarding the nature of that which is to be abandoned, since it is impossible to abandon a fault whose nature has not been identified.

Even if there is knowledge of their nature, one does not undertake an effort to abandon faults if one perceives them as eternal, because that which is independent cannot possibly be destroyed. Or, even if they possess a cause, one does not apply oneself to cultivation (bhāvanā) due to uncertainty regarding the nature of that cause; for like a disease whose origin is unknown, that which is not understood in its root cause cannot be abandoned.

Or, let us grant that there is such a thorough knowledge of the cause; yet, having understood that cause to be eternal, why would a person acting with foresight not strive to abandon it, since it is impossible to obstruct a cause that is unimpaired?

Or, even if that cause were impermanent, why would one not exert effort after realizing that the defects are the very nature (*dharmatā*) of living beings, given that it is impossible to abandon an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Or, if the defects lack an intrinsic nature, why does one desist because a means for their destruction is impossible? For there is no attainment of the goal for one who is devoid of the means.
Furthermore, even though the means exist, because they are not fully understood, their practice would be impossible.

Since it is impossible to practice that whose true nature is not fully understood, or even if it were fully understood, one might—like jumping—fail to apply oneself because one considers the ultimate excellence of cultivation to be unattainable due to its fixed limit or the impossibility of rebirth; or, even if the destruction of defects through the arising of their opposites is possible by reaching ultimate excellence, one might still not begin the application because one suspects that defects could recur, as in the case of the hardness of copper and other metals. Therefore, in this regard, a lack of desire for liberation is not established.

For instance, those whose minds are oppressed by the sufferings of birth and so forth, and who—with minds weary of cyclic existence—seek its pacification for themselves, namely those destined for the enlightenment of Śrāvakas and others, possess precisely this fear of cyclic existence as the cause for their desire to cultivate selflessness.

However, those who—by virtue of a particular spiritual lineage (*gotra*)—are by their very nature solely devoted to bringing about the welfare of others, and who, having observed the world tormented by the three types of suffering such as that of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), become pained by the suffering of others due to being under the sway of compassion; having cast aside regard for themselves and accepted all transmigrating beings as their own self, they apply themselves to their protection—for them, compassion alone is the cause for engaging in cultivation. This is because it is difficult to explain the means and the goal when both are beyond direct perception. If it is asked, "What is the purpose for a discerning person in bringing about the welfare of others? the answer is: no [purpose].
That alone is the purpose, because it possesses the characteristic of being desired;
nor does it entail the consequence of being dependent [on something else],
since the attachment to performing what is beneficial for oneself is based on the grasping at a self that is conceptually constructed, and because this is approved by all virtuous people.

Furthermore, because the act of benefiting others is invariably followed by its own fruit, and moreover, it is precisely the impossibility of a lack of desire for engagement in cultivation that has begun to be demonstrated here; for even if he were indeed lacking in foresight (*aprekṣāvattva*), how could he be devoid of desire for engagement simply on that account? Therefore, this alone must be stated: "No one engages in benefiting others because of a lack of purpose," and it has already been said regarding that point.

Moreover, just as some are observed to be excessively habituated to cruelty, taking delight in the misfortunes of others and rejoicing in the suffering of others without any apparent cause, so too why should it not be possible that some, being habituated to compassion, take delight in the happiness of others and suffer at the suffering of others, even in the absence of any other motive?

Nor is there a lack of understanding regarding the essential nature of the defects (*doṣa*), because the hosts of afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—such as attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, intoxication, envy, and avarice—which consist in the forms of clinging, hostility, and the elevation of self and what belongs to the self, arise and pass away with their essential natures fully known.
Furthermore, they are not eternal, because they are experienced as being occasional.
For this very reason, they are not without cause; for if they were causeless, being independent of anything else, it would be impossible for them to be restricted by place, time, or intrinsic nature.

For this reason as well, their status as having permanent causes is refuted; for since a cause such as the *ātman* would always be present, and being incapable of receiving any additional excellence (*atiśaya*), it would not depend upon auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*)—it would follow that things arising from that alone would be produced simultaneously at all times. Therefore, by implication, these must have impermanent causes.

Even though their cause is impermanent, its nature is indeed known, because it has been previously established that the host of defects such as attachment and so forth have the misconception of self and what belongs to self as their cause, and because they conform to the presence and absence of that [misconception]. Nor can these [defects] be properties of a living being; they would not be properties at all.
This is merely "conditionality" (idampratyayatāmātra), because the conventional usage of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmin*) is superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Now, even if these [mental states] possess the nature of mental factors (dharmas) by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness or by arising therein, they remain unproven and inconclusive.

Furthermore, one who maintains the relationship of object and subject must admit that consciousness has the nature of apprehending an object; otherwise, there would be no relationship of object and subject between the object and the cognition.

If it is accepted that [consciousness] has the nature of apprehending an object, then it must be stated that the object is apprehended by that very part of its own self which constitutes its nature of apprehending the object.
Otherwise, how could it be apprehended?
If it were apprehended by way of a non-existent form, then there would be no relationship between object and subject.

For instance, the object is not in the same state as the cognition when the cognition makes it its object, and the cognition is not in the same state as the object when it makes that object its own; thus, cognitions would be entirely without objects.
Consequently, it would follow that all categories of objects are unestablished.
Therefore, it is established that its innate nature (*svabhāva*) is to grasp the forms of real objects (*bhūta*).
And it has already been demonstrated that the nature of a real object consists in being momentary, selfless, and so forth.
Therefore, its very nature is the apprehension of selflessness; it is not of the nature of the apprehension of a self.

Furthermore, that which appears to be otherwise is established as being due solely to the power of adventitious conditions through the force of delusion—not by way of intrinsic nature, just as the cognition of a snake in a rope.
For this very reason, even though the mass of afflictions (*kleśagaṇa*) may be extremely powerful, it is incapable of uprooting the capacity for the vision of selflessness.
Because it is produced by adventitious conditions, [the view of self] is unstable;

however, the knowledge of selflessness is powerful because it is intrinsic and because it is supported by valid cognition. Thus, although their opposition is equal, the knowledge of selflessness is established as the antidote to the view of self, whereas the view of self is not [the antidote] to that [knowledge], because it is the opposite of it.

Even for one who holds the position that no external object exists, in his view as well, cognition has the nature of grasping selflessness (*nairātmya*) alone and does not consist of the vision of a self, because that self is non-existent.

For instance, even if he does not accept cognition as having the nature of grasping an object due to the absence of such an object, he must necessarily admit that it has the nature of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*);
otherwise, there would be no establishment of cognition itself.
Furthermore, that self is to be experienced only through its existing nature as non-self, non-dual, and so forth, and not otherwise, because the same faults as previously mentioned would follow.
Therefore, it is unestablished that these [qualities] are properties of a living being.

Nor does it follow that their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is established merely by the fact that they arise therein; for if that were the case, their abandonment would be impossible, since such a conclusion is not invariably certain.
For instance, the cognition of a snake arises with respect to a rope, and yet that [cognition] ceases upon the arising of correct knowledge.
Nor is it impossible for there to be a means for its destruction,
because the practice of an entity whose nature is opposed to its own cause is possible as a means for such destruction.

For instance, those things which possess the practice of a nature contradictory to their own causes are such that an absolute severance of their continuum is possible, just as in the case of rice and so forth; and since these [afflictions] such as passion and the like are likewise, a means for their destruction certainly exists.

Nor is there a lack of thorough knowledge regarding them, because from the very knowledge of the nature of a cause, it is clearly determined that whatever entity has an object and aspect contrary to it is its antidote.
And it has already been demonstrated that the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya-darśana*) is the antidote in this case, precisely because it possesses an object and aspect contrary to it.
Nor is there a fixed limit to its excellence, as is the case with jumping and similar activities;
for that which is produced by successive prior practice becomes its very nature and does not perish, since each subsequent effort is solely intent upon imparting a new distinction,
and because it possesses a stable substratum.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated later that wisdom and the like arise from seeds of a similar kind belonging to the past, whereas jumping and such activities do not;
nor is there an impossibility of other births, since the continuity of previous lives has already been established;

nor is there the possibility of the defects arising again—like the hardness of copper and so forth—because the vision of selflessness, which is their antidote, has attained ultimate internalization and thus never departs.

For fire, which is the opponent of the hardness of copper and other metals, is only occasionally present; therefore, it is logical that when hardness and the like cease to exist due to its absence, they may arise again once that [fire] has departed.

But this is not the case for the defilements (*mala*). Alternatively, even if the Path (*mārga*) were to perish, there is no necessity for the faults (*doṣa*) to arise again, because [the destruction of the Path] is not invariably followed by their reappearance—just as with ashes and the like. To explain: when wood and such things have been reduced to ashes through contact with fire, they do not resume their former form even after that fire has departed; the same would apply to the faults, and thus the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, since the defilements (*mala*) were previously incapable [of persisting] due to their adventitious nature, how could that selflessness (*nairātmya*), once it has become naturalized, lack the power to subvert them? Indeed, an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be overturned without effort.
Nor is it appropriate for discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*) to exert effort to abandon or adopt things to be avoided or attained without first perceiving their faults or virtues.

And for a person whose mind is not inverted (*aviparīta*), it is impossible to perceive virtues in what are actually faults or to perceive faults in the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), precisely because they are free from inversion.
For those whose intellects are not inverted do not take up a faultless thing as being faulty, nor a faulty thing as being endowed with qualities;
and the vision of selflessness is never faulty,
because it possesses the quality of being free from all afflictions.
For thus, because all stains such as passion have been removed without remainder, there is no affliction consisting in the obstruction to seeing reality;
nor is there the affliction of the burning of body and mind caused by the outbursts of passion and the like;
nor is there the affliction of disease, decrepitude, and so forth bound to birth, because of the absence of the afflictions that are the cause of birth.

Nor is there the affliction of distaste as found in the enjoyment of tainted pleasure, because the flavor of the bliss of tranquility is exclusively non-distressing; therefore, it is not fitting to exert effort for its abandonment,
but rather, if it should exist, it should only be for the sake of its non-decline.
Because the intellect by its very nature leans toward virtue,
there is no effort to adopt faults, since they are defective as the locus of all calamities;
therefore, the cultivation of selflessness is possible.

And it is observed that through reaching the ultimate limit of its cultivation, this [meditative concentration] results in a cognition with a vivid manifestation, as in the case of one afflicted by passion who meditates on a beloved woman.
For indeed, in such a person, confused speech such as "Look! or "Embrace me!", as well as bodily activities corresponding to his intention, proceed based on a direct perception.

Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) possesses strength because its object is the reality of things (*bhūtārtha*), whereas the vision of a self (*ātmadarśana*) is the opposite due to being the reverse; thus, there exists the relationship of adversary and antidote (*vipakṣapratipakṣabhāva*). Furthermore, since passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) proceed by contact with the unreal grasping of a self, there is no relationship of adversary and antidote between them based on the apprehension of contradictory forms.
Nor [is there a contradiction] due to perversion (*viparyāsa*), because both [the self-grasping and the view of annihilation] are equally perverted by virtue of being produced by non-perversion.

Furthermore, a contradiction between these two is not established, because both have the same source—namely, the grasping at a self—and because they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship. For instance, when there is attachment to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), hatred arises toward that which obstructs it; it does not arise otherwise.

Furthermore, it is not logical for two things that arise from the same cause and stand in a relationship of cause and effect to possess the status of sublated and sublator, as in the case of fire and smoke both originating from the same fuel, or as in the case of the grasping of a self and attachment; this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
As for their non-simultaneous production, it is because the mind that serves as their material cause lacks the capacity to project two simultaneous cognitions of the same kind.
Nor is there mutual contradiction between pleasure and pain; for pleasure and pain are of two kinds: mental and those born of sensory objects.

In that regard, first, as for those two [views] arising in the mind, because they are associated with aversion and attachment respectively, and because they share a common destiny with passion and hatred, there is no possibility of mutual contradiction between them; for they are both equally erroneous, grasp an undifferentiated nature, have the grasping of a self as their single source, and stand in a relationship of cause and effect.
Furthermore, as for those two [views] arising from sense objects, there is likewise no contradiction, because there is no fixed determination regarding their distinct causes.
For instance, from the very same object that pleasure arises, pain also arises when it is indulged in to excess; thus, there is no fixed determination of distinct causes for the two.
But it is not so for the vision of selflessness [in relation] to the other.

Furthermore, while both of these are equal in strength because they are produced by the power of their respective objects, this is not the case for the path and the defects; for the path alone possesses strength because its object is the reality of things (*bhūtārtha*), whereas the defects do not.

Moreover, pleasure and pain are short-lived, but the vision of selflessness is not like that, because—as previously stated—it never departs due to having become one's very nature (*sātmatva*); therefore, there is no deviation [in the argument].
However, the reason why [defilements] do not arise simultaneously has already been stated.
Furthermore, it is incorrect to claim that passion and the like still arise even for those who have ascertained selflessness through the power of inference;

for it is the realization of selflessness consisting in meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*)—which, by virtue of its vivid appearance, is a non-conceptual cognition directly perceiving the reality of selflessness, and which is non-erroneous because its object is a matter established by valid cognition—that is described as the antidote to the view of self by utterly uprooting it, and not that which consists of hearing and reflection (*śrutacintāmaya*).

Because the defilements have been practiced since beginningless time and have become firmly rooted, their destruction occurs only through the gradual increase of their opposites, and not by hearing [the teaching] just once;

just as the sensation of cold is not destroyed merely by contact with the form of fire. Nor is it established that the arising of passion and so forth occurs even when the knowledge of selflessness—which is the essence of what has been heard and contemplated—is present, such that there would be a logical inconsistency.
For indeed, the followers of the Sugata simply dispel the arisen obsessions of passion and so forth by means of the power of mental attention directed toward the foul and other such objects.
For this very reason, their possession of unimpaired majesty is established;
and for this same reason, their opposition to [the afflictions] is established through the vision of selflessness.
Because they are diminished when that [knowledge] is present before one.

For those things which possess the nature of being diminished by the proximity of something else, they possess the nature of being utterly destroyed without leaving a trace when that [proximate thing] reaches its ultimate increase—just as a flame of fire is utterly extinguished upon the increase of water. And since the defects possess the nature of being diminished by the proximity of the knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*), how could they maintain their existence when that [knowledge] has reached its ultimate increase?
Therefore, the reason is not inconclusive.
And because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa), there is no contradictory nature [to the reason].

Having thus established the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), he speaks in order to demonstrate the abandonment of the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): "Because of the excellence of direct realization. And due to the excellence of direct realization, there is no defect remaining along with its latent predispositions (*savāsana*).
Therefore, omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is established through liberation from all obscurations.
[Page 876] It is understood from the context that "of what selflessness" refers to direct realization.

Its non-distinctiveness consists in the fact that, through many means in many ways over a long period of time and in every aspect, there occurs the absolute manifestation of the virtues and faults regarding that [selflessness] and its opposite.
For this very reason, even though the Śrāvakas and others possess the vision of selflessness, they do not attain omniscience.
Because there is no distinction between such [ordinary] internal states and those [of a Buddha], the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) has not been abandoned.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That cultivation which is characterized by being attentive, continuous, and long-term has as its fruit a cognition that appears as if it were grasped in the palm of one's hand; for example, the cultivation of a woman by one afflicted with passion. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has already been demonstrated that such an engagement is possible for a compassionate person due to their altruistic intent.

Nor is there any inconclusiveness [of the reason], because the subject—the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which has as its object the selflessness inherent in all phenomena—is the logical reason (*hetu*) by virtue of being touched by the cultivation endowed with the three aforementioned qualifications; and the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is its vivid manifestation.
By this property to be proven, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the aforementioned proving property (*sādhana-dharma*) is established, since vivid manifestation does not depend on any other cause.
And consequently, by implication, pervasion even with omniscience is established.
For that which is the state of the mind’s clear manifestation toward the object of selflessness and so forth as it exists in all things—that alone is its omniscience, and nothing else.

Thus, since the general pervasion of meditative cultivation by the clear manifestation of the object being cultivated is established, it is established by implication that it is also pervaded by omniscience.
Because it is impossible for this [cognition] to appear clearly with respect to a subject (dharmin) as previously described;
by this, those faults that were stated regarding the proof of existence are refuted,
since the existence of an omniscient being is not what is to be proven.

Since it is established that the subject (dharmin), the mind, possesses the property to be proven—namely, the quality of manifest appearance—in this manner, because it is established through direct realization, there is the abandonment of the latencies of defects characterized by deficiencies of body, speech, and intellect; thus, the abandonment of the two obscurations is accomplished.
Consequently, through liberation from all obscurations, omniscience is established.
It might be argued: "Granted that this is established in a general sense, yet it is not established in the case of the Sugata. To this he says, "And this," and so forth:
"And this is accepted by the Sugata because he proclaimed selflessness at the outset;
therefore, the Tathāgata stands at the head of all the founders of other schools."
Thus, as has been stated, this omniscience is accepted as established for the Sugata alone, and not for Kapila or others. Why? Because he proclaimed selflessness from the very beginning.
This is what is meant:

he by whom this selflessness (*nairātmya*) of all things was proclaimed in its entirety at the outset through the teaching that all categories of entities consist of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and so forth—he, as a distinguished person established by the logical mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅga*) due to his initial proclamation of the manifold varieties of selflessness regarding all phenomena, is called by us the "Sugata.
By means of this teaching of his, his possession of stable and complete knowledge regarding the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the means thereto, is proven.

Therefore, it is appropriate for those who desire to practice according to his teachings to establish that he is omniscient and authoritative precisely through his union with gnosis (*jñānayoga*), and not on account of his knowledge of the number of insects and such;
however, even regarding the number of insects and so forth, the possibility of his knowing them is established,
while his stable and complete knowledge of reality is established directly.

For instance, he whose knowledge of reality is established through the teaching of selflessness (*nairātmya*) that accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), possesses stable knowledge of that very selflessness because his teaching is consistent from beginning to end. This is because even within the ninefold scriptural collection (*navāṅga-śāstrapravacana*), there is a single coherent purpose (*ekavākyatva*) across all teachings—whether they concern pleasant objects or the teaching on the truths characterized by suffering and so forth. Furthermore, his omniscience (*aśeṣajñāna*) is inferred from his illumination of the Four Truths through diverse means, since he has abandoned the remaining [defects] characterized by the inability to demonstrate the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*).
For one who does not know all aspects of its virtues and defects, and who is unskilled in its exposition, cannot explain it in such a manner;
nor is it reasonable to say that he explains it after having learned it from the Veda, because the Veda has been established as being of human origin— this is the intended meaning.
Therefore, it is established that the Blessed One stands at the summit of all teachers without exception, due to his possession of the excellence of primordial wisdom.

Therefore, demonstrating that there is no equality between others and the Blessed One— who possesses the aforementioned excellence of knowledge— the author says "by him," and so forth: "Because of that [Blessed One], who is endowed with the vision of reality in accordance with valid cognition,
others who teach contradictory doctrines do not possess an equal cause."
For those whose speech is agitated by the sublation of their claims through the scope of valid cognition,
the possession of the power of suprasensory knowledge is indeed far removed.
Indeed, there is no reason whatsoever that establishes their possession of superior knowledge;
for if there were such a reason, it would have to be the very mark (liṅga) consisting of their own words.
And since those words of theirs convey meanings that contradict valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), how could one perceive their possession of superior knowledge from them?
If it is argued that even the word of the Sugata is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says "connected," and so forth:
"It is connected [to reality], possesses appropriate means, declares the goals of human endeavor,
and regarding even perceptible objects, it is not contradicted in the slightest by the two types of valid cognition."

"Connected" means that the sentences are mutually consistent through the convergence upon a single purpose, and not disconnected like the sentence "ten pomegranates," and so forth. "Concordant" refers to that in which the taught method—characterized by the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so on—is feasible because it can be practiced; it does not refer to an impossible method, such as the instruction to adorn oneself with the crest-jewel of Takṣaka to pacify poison. "Human aim" refers to the characteristics of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); [the teaching] expresses this, and not something that results in a non-aim for humans, such as an examination of a crow's teeth.
Now, one might object that all of this is also present in the statements of Kapila and others; to this he replies with the words "even when perceived," and so forth.
"Perceived" (dṛṣṭe) means intended as the object of perception and inference.
"By the two means of valid cognition" (pramāṇābhyām) refers to perception and inference.

It is "uncontradicted" because the object as it has been described exists exactly so. For instance, there is no possibility of otherwise-ness for the five aggregates—characterized by the perception of signs such as blue and so forth, or pleasure and pain, and by cognitions such as attachment—which are intended to be perceived directly; likewise, there is indeed non-perceptibility for those things intended to be non-perceptible, such as form, sound, and their configurations, as well as pleasure and so forth, substances, actions, universals, conjunctions, and so on, which are [erroneously] held by others to be perceived directly.

Likewise, for those things intended as objects of inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛttānumāna*), there is indeed their existence as such; just as it is with the four noble truths. And for those not intended as its objects, there is indeed their non-objectivity; just as it is with the self (*ātman*) and so forth, which others consider to be objects of inference by the force of real entities.
By the use of the word "api" (also), it is shown that there is no modification even in the unseen [karma].

For here, with reference to passion and so forth, or the dharma arising from them, the very vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is taught as the antidote for their abandonment—acting in opposition to the view of self (*ātmadarśana*) which is their cause—and not, like the treatises of Kapila and others, are practices such as ritual bathing or the *agnihotra* sacrifice taught as being non-contradictory to that cause.

It is for this very reason that the Blessed One said, "This should be accepted by the wise only after examination, like pure gold," and indicating this, he says: "Like gold, it is stainless when examined through heating, cutting, and rubbing; it does not undergo any alteration."

Just as pure gold, free from all defects, undergoes no transformation when examined through heating and other tests, so too the jewel of the Blessed One’s word is not altered by direct perception—which is like heating—by inference proceeding from the power of facts—which is like a touchstone—and even by scripturally dependent inference, which is indicated by the example of cutting. Therefore, the intention is that for those who act with circumspection, engagement with such a scripture alone is appropriate, and not with any other.

Demonstrating the analogy with a jewel, he says "samasta" and so forth: "The jewel of the Tathāgata’s word, which arises in accordance with the destruction of the darkness of all false doctrines, has not been obtained by those with many defilements."
Then those possessed of supreme wisdom spoke of the Sugata alone as the Omniscient One;
and they called him the best of physicians, for he knows the primary purpose of human existence.
Therefore, it is established by valid cognition that Kapila is not the omniscient Sugata;
yet this clear argument just stated has not been perceived by the deluded.
"Evil thought" is indeed the dense darkness; its "destruction" is its annihilation. That whose arising is conducive to that [destruction] is described as such.
"By those with many defilements" means by those lacking merit.
"Anantaroditā" means that which is produced from the logical mark (liṅga) consisting of the effect known as the aforementioned statement.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In certain parts such as mathematics," he says:
"From the very interval already described, the distinction is also determined:
[the superiority] of those who cause the destruction of Smara over false holy places such as Ṛṣabha."

Since it has been established that the Blessed One, the Conqueror of Māra, possesses a superiority over Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and others due to his possession of the aforementioned excellence of knowledge, it is not proper for you, who speak the truth, to say that "no distinction is perceived"; such is the overall meaning.

It might be argued that we state there is no difference between the two because they are non-contradictory regarding certain parts of subjects such as mathematics; to this he says, "For who," and so forth: "For what fool would consider one who knows the reality of the meaning of the entirety of the scriptures to be equal to one who possesses knowledge merely of common meals or who knows only the alphabet?"
Regarding the passage beginning with "by that very reason," he says "tadyena" and so forth:
"That reason by which the omniscience of one person is established does not apply to another,
because the entity that serves as that reason does not exist [in the case of the other]."
"Tad" means "therefore";
it refers to that causal entity.

Even if it were granted that there exists mere verbal expression—because [the teachings] such as Syādvāda and others are instructors whose meanings are non-erroneous and all-pervasive—nevertheless, because that causal entity which is tied to a real thing lacks the actual meaning of a reason, it does not function as a reason for another, such as Kapila. For it is the real thing itself, by virtue of being tied to a real thing, that makes a real thing known, and not mere verbal expression.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the refutations," he says:
"Those refutations, free from passion, which the Śākyas utter thus within the teaching of the omniscient Jina— these the Digambaras are unable [to refute]."
"Free from agitation" means devoid of impetuosity;
for they act solely out of compassion to benefit others, and not out of anger, pride, and so forth, as is the case with you.
"Thus" [is said] because of the demonstration that the Syādvāda and other doctrines taught by him are defective.
Regarding the passage beginning with "by those who abide therein," he says "that which," and so forth:

"That reality which has been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through a proven logical connection is established in the Buddhist system (*saugatasiddhānta*), but not so in other doctrines."
Therefore, let a definitive conclusion be sufficiently reached through those established, distinct proofs and refutations, which are like reflections that have emerged and seized the object.
"Yat" means "because";
"siddhapratibandhena" means "by means of an established connection."
The meaning is: "by means of a connection characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*), which functions through the power of real entities (*vastubala*).
"By that" means "for that reason."

Regarding the passage beginning with "of that which is knowable," he says: "But for omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), there exists no contradiction whatsoever— either directly or otherwise— with being knowable and so forth."
The state of being knowable and so forth is established through the exclusion of non-knowability and so forth;
however, that [state] does not have a fixed characteristic through the exclusion of omniscience.

One who wishes to establish the negation of one thing by means of the affirmation of another must establish that which is indeed contradictory—either directly or indirectly—not that which is non-contradictory; for otherwise, the negation of anything whatsoever would follow from the affirmation of just anything.
And there is no contradiction, either direct or indirect, between omniscience and such properties as being knowable and so forth.

For, when examined, the contradiction between entities is established as being of only two kinds: either characterized by mutual exclusion, such as that between existence and non-existence, or between succession and simultaneity;
or characterized by the impossibility of coexistence, such as that between fire and the sensation of cold.
Regarding these, he first demonstrates that omniscience cannot coexist with properties such as "knowability" and so forth, by stating "because of unknowability," and so on.

It has been stated previously that the contradiction between two things is characterized by their existing through mutual exclusion, such that the determination of one is inseparable from the exclusion of the other.
However, "knowability" and so forth do not exist through the exclusion of omniscience; rather, they exist through the exclusion of "unknowability" and so forth.
Showing that the second contradiction is also not possible, he says: "Omniscience," and so forth:
"Furthermore, this omniscience does not have its cause fully present anywhere;
once existence and the other [conditions] have arisen, what has previously occurred ceases."

For when one thing exists with its causes unimpaired, and another comes into being such that the former ceases to exist due to its presence, only between those two is there an opposition characterized by non-coexistence; however, this omniscience has not been observed to have previously functioned with its causes unimpaired, such that it could later be said to cease upon the occurrence of existence and so forth.
To the question "Why has it not arisen?", he says: "Because of the absence of intrinsic nature," and so forth.
For that [omniscience] never arises when there is no cognition of its own nature;
prior to its arising, this very omniscience would thus be established.

If you accept that omniscience ceases when the existence of sentient beings and the knowability of objects is present, then it would follow that prior to the presence of sentient beings and so forth, this [omniscience] was non-existent and unknowable even by self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*). Consequently, since it is non-existent and thus lacks intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), and since it is unknowable and thus not perceived by self-awareness, this omniscience would not arise at all; how then could it be said that what previously existed later ceases?
For the arising of that which lacks intrinsic nature is impossible.

Nor is there any basis for establishing the existence of that which is unperceived, because the establishment of the existence of a thing is dependent upon cognition. Therefore, the intention [of the opponent] is that this results in a contradiction with their own words. Furthermore, if his activity prior [to omniscience] is admitted, then omniscience would be established even without effort toward such activity; thus, its rejection is not logical, otherwise there would be a contradiction with one's own words. Demonstrating this, he says: "Prior to activity," and so forth.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "given that omniscience is admitted to exist prior to [the activity of] teaching."

Now, it might be argued: "Even if being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) and so forth are not contradictory [to omniscience], they nonetheless imply the non-existence of an omniscient being. To this he says: "And when there is the affirmation of something non-contradictory, the exclusion of another is not logical;
otherwise, from the existence of color (*rūpa*), the absence of taste (*rasa*) would also be inferred."

But as for one who thinks: "Even if being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) and so forth are not contradictory with omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), speech-actuality (*vaktṛtva*) is indeed contradictory; for, through its causal chain, this [speech] exists in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which cannot coexist with omniscience."

For it is according to the logical principle that "one does not utter speech without first applying vitarka and vicāra" that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the cause of speech. Since all conceptualizations are intertwined with verbal expression, there is no apprehension of the true nature of reality (*vastusvarūpa*), because that [true nature] is the domain of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*). Therefore, since the true nature of reality is not fully known during the state of conceptualization, omniscience does not exist [in such a state]. Thus, by the non-perception of the cause—namely, omniscience, which is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) to the property of being a speaker—the certainty of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established; hence, the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

And this reason called "being a speaker" (vaktṛtva) is indeed implied by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "whose characteristics are knowability, being an object of cognition, being a real entity, existence, etc.

Having raised this objection with the words "this very thing is implied here by the word 'etc. and so forth, [the author] refutes it here with the words "and those who [assert] the state of being a speaker" and so forth.
[The verse states: "He who fancies himself [to be a speaker] regarding that state of being a speaker which is implied here by the word 'etc.'"...
There is certainty regarding the exclusion [of one] due to their mutual contradiction.
Omniscience exists in conceptual construction, yet one is omniscient through non-conceptualization;
for an object is not apprehended by a cognition permeated by verbal expression.
In this regard as well, those who imagine that the Omniscient One possesses the status of a speaker because he conforms to discursive thought do not [understand] the possibility of his speech.
Nor is he accepted as omniscient by virtue of the operation of conceptual cognition;
for if there were conceptualization at that moment, his status as a speaker would not be established.

Some maintain that the Blessed One’s status as a speaker arises solely from the manifestation of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*); others, however, describe the Blessed One’s engagement in speech even without conceptualization, due to the force of previous [karmic] impressions alone.

Regarding these views, in the first case, if non-omniscience is being proven in the state of conceptualization, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), for those [opponents] indeed accept that the Blessed One lacks all-encompassing vision in that state. Alternatively, if it is intended to establish non-omniscience in the state of non-conceptualization—
In that case, the reason is unestablished;
for at that stage there is no occurrence of speech, because the conceptual construction that motivates it is absent at that time.

Now, one might object: "If non-omniscience is admitted during the state of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then because his words would be spoken by a non-omniscient being, they would necessarily lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The state of being composed by a non-omniscient [being], etc. "The state of being composed by a non-omniscient being is not at all applicable to him; because his omniscience is implied, there is therefore correspondence (*saṃvādana*)."
Just as someone, having experienced heat, subsequently speaks of it,
therefore there is no contradiction with the object, because [the cognition] arises from the experience of that object.
Therefore, at the time of omniscience, this reason is unestablished;
however, at the time of conventional discourse, it would be the establishment of what is already established.
Even though he was not omniscient at that particular time, this [scripture] is nonetheless not of non-omniscient origin. Why? Because it is encompassed by his omniscience.

For this very reason, since it is produced by a conceptual construction arising from the power of an omniscient one’s cognition, it possesses validity—just like an inferential conceptualization—due to its indirect connection with the real object.
In this very context, because of its connection with the real object through a succession of examples, it also possesses validity, just like an inferential conceptualization.
Right here he states an illustration, beginning with "having experienced," and so forth.
"Therefore" means:
because of the statement that [the result] exists by virtue of the power of the experience of heat.

"Because it arises from the experience of that object" means that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises indirectly from the experience of that object, namely heat. This might be argued: if an omniscient being possesses conceptual cognition, then he would be subject to error; for conceptual construction is by its very nature erroneous, since it proceeds by determining an object as being what it is not, through the appearance of its own internal representation.
This is not so.

If one were unable to distinguish between the superimposed form and the real form, then one would indeed be deluded; however, since one ascertains that which is beyond the scope of conceptual construction as having a superimposed nature, while simultaneously perceiving the external object—which is the domain of non-conceptual cognition—as being distinct and real in its true nature, how could such a person be said to be mistaken?
If it is asked: "If he is not mistaken, why does he superimpose [the unreal] during the state of conceptualization?"
No;
because he knows the means for the application of words.

Since he perceives nothing that gives rise to a word other than the superimposing conceptual construction (*āropaka-vikalpa*), nor does he find any referent of a word other than what is superimposed, he—knowing the means for the application of words and being unable to remain silent without communicating to others the reality as it has been realized out of compassion for the world—constructs, with the desire to explain it, the superimposing conceptual construction which is the means for the application of words, and the object of superimposition which is the denotation of the word.
And this objection, having been anticipated later, will be refuted;
however, we have mentioned it here because it arose in the context of the discussion.
For this very reason, the inference of passion from the state of being a speaker is also incorrect, since the production of speech is possible even otherwise.
For speech, movement, and so forth are not the effects of passion (*rāga*) alone, because they have the general desire to speak (*vaktukāmatā*) as their cause.
And since that desire to speak can also occur in one free from passion through compassion (*karuṇā*), there is a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
If it is argued that this very compassion is itself passion, [we reply:]...
No,
nothing undesirable follows from the absence of compassion.

Rather, they call "attachment" (rāga) that clinging of the mind toward objects associated with outflows (sāśrava), which is projected by the view of a permanent self, pleasure, and what belongs to a self.
Preceded by that [compassion], hatred (*dveṣa*) is the aversion toward that which obstructs the self and what belongs to the self;
and the grasping at a self and what belongs to the self is delusion (*moha*), whereas compassion is not so.
For even in the absence of grasping at a self, compassion arises solely through the power of habituation upon merely seeing a particular kind of suffering.
For it is thus described in the treatise that for those free from passion, loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] have the Dharma and so forth as their objects.

It might be argued: "Even if you were merely proving the non-manifestation of knowledge regarding all objects, there would still be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); for what you intend to prove is the incapacity to know the full extent of the reality of all things. Therefore, there is neither the fallacy of proving the already established nor the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason, because what is intended as the reason is merely the capacity for verbal expression. To this, he says: *samasta...* and so forth: "Even if you [the opponent] were to eliminate the capacity for the cognition of all things, the fact that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful remains as it was."
Even if the capacity for the activity of verbal expression is accepted as the reason [for the existence of a creator],
the fault of "uncertainty regarding the negative concomitance" (saṃdigdhavyatirekitva) persists.
In both cases, because there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the reason when its opposite of the probandum is asserted,
the reason is inconclusive due to having a doubtful negative concomitance (*saṃdigdha-vyatirekitva*).
Now, regarding the position that the Blessed One’s speech proceeds even without conceptual construction, he says "By the mechanism of the wheel's rotation," and so forth:
"Even though the Protector is free from conceptual construction, Teaching proceeds by the power of the momentum of the accumulations, through the mechanism of the wheel's rotation."
Even for those wise ones who say this, the argument is not established.

For just as a wheel continues to spin due to the force of prior momentum even when the activity of pushing the staff has ceased, so too, some wise followers of the Sugata—the Vijñānavādins—maintain that while the Blessed One remains with the entire web of conceptual construction extinguished, the teaching still proceeds by the force of the momentum from his prior accumulations of merit and knowledge. Against them, the fault of the reason being clearly unestablished (*asiddha*) is indeed recognized.

It might be argued that in this view, because for everyone there is only the experience of one's own internal appearance, in the ultimate sense no one possesses the status of a speaker; however, through the force of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), even when another person speaks, a conceit of speakership arises in the world when a cognition appearing as such is produced, with that other person standing as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). It is precisely this speakership, which is conceptually determined and conventionally recognized by the world, that is intended as the reason.

One might object: "A reason (hetu) or a property (dharma) that is established according to one's own philosophical tenets (siddhānta) is not what is being employed; rather, it is precisely that which is recognized by the world. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (asiddha). Anticipating this, he says "vaktṛtvam" and so forth:
"But as for 'speaker-ness' (vaktṛtva), which is considered by the world to be determinative..."
In such a case, there would be a doubtful exclusion of the reason from the heterologous instances (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*).
Here too, as before, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its exclusion from the heterologous class is doubtful.
With the words "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth, the opponent refutes the charge of unestablishedness (*asiddhatva*) that was raised here regarding the system of the Vijñānavādins.
But surely, in what system is there no lack of proof for this which is logically untenable?

He thinks as follows: only that which expresses what is certain for both parties is a proof (*sādhana*) or a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), and not something that is unestablished for one or the other or expresses doubt, because of the principle that [the latter] requires further proof.

How can a lack of proof be raised against this doctrine of Vijñānavāda, which is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For a refutation does not occur through the mere fabrication of proof or lack of proof according to one’s own whim; rather, it occurs when proof or lack of proof is established by the force of valid cognition. And the system of Vijñāna is not established by the force of valid cognition, since it has been refuted in detail.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said" (ucyate): "If it is held that 'being a speaker' is an independent means of proof,
then [the reason] would be either unestablished in its locus (āśrayāsiddha) or doubtful in its non-establishment (sandigdhāsiddhatā)."
Because this matter is subject to doubt, its unestablished nature due to uncertainty remains firm; therefore, you must state such a proof by way of reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅgasādhana).
And in that case, the property is revealed as established by scripture alone;
however, there exists no further means of cognition for the purpose of establishing its actual existence.
In this regard, there are two possible alternatives: either "speakership" (*vaktṛtva*) is intended as an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*), or as a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*).

Regarding the first position, because the locus (*āśraya*) is not established in its specific form, the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).

Even if the locus is intended in a general sense, as long as speakership has not been proven by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the opponent, it remains unestablished due to doubt; for according to the logical rule, only that which is expressed with certainty for both parties constitutes a proof.
The word "asya" refers to "the state of being a speaker.
Therefore, lest this fault should occur, you must accept that this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (a reductio ad absurdum).

In that case as well, regarding a *prasaṅga* proof, only that property which is established for the opponent solely through scripture that is agreeable when left unexamined should be presented as the probans in order to expose their internal contradictions; it should not, however, be established by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as that would be purposeless.
Furthermore, since "being a speaker" is not established for the opponent through scripture alone, the reason (*hetu*) possesses the character of being unestablished for both parties.
Concluding with the words "In this way," etc., he demonstrates the reversal of the meaning of what has been stated by others:
"In this way, who would not postulate that person for whom reasons characterized by being an object of cognition, substantial existence, and so forth, are powerless to refute?"
Thus, no reasoning whatsoever— whether worldly or Vedic— residing in the mouth of a proponent of the Vedas is capable of removing the poison of the knowledge of a fierce serpent.
In this world, even when merely looked upon by those with venomous eyes, a dull-witted Brahmin of meager power is unable to even draw a breath, let alone remain seated.
But even a sound argument, when residing in the mouth of a proponent of the Vedas, is ill-fated;
it is like a necklace resting on a foot, due to its placement upon an inferior locus.
"Who would not conceive of it?"—the remainder of the sense is "by way of its possibility.
The meaning is that its possibility is established precisely because no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) is perceived.

Let this matter rest for now: it is not at all surprising that an incorrect argument does not shine when placed in the mouth of a proponent of the Vedas; however, even a correct argument does not gleam when stated by you due to the defect of its locus (*āśrayadoṣa*).

To the question "How so?", he says: "The non-deviation from fire," and so forth. Even the non-deviation of smoke from fire cannot be asserted; for, according to his [the opponent's] view, that which is smoke exists elsewhere as well.
Because it has the nature of a single entity, it exists even in water;
if fire were also present there, what would be the basis for its exclusion?

For it is well known even to the intellect of a cowherd’s child that smoke has an origin dependent upon fire, and thus its non-deviation from it is self-evident. However, by you—who describe the ultimate identity of the entire world through such properties as "being an entity" (vastutva) and so forth—it is impossible to establish the non-deviation of smoke from fire; for according to your view, smoke exists ultimately in water as well, since it possesses the nature of an entity.
To this, he says “In that case also,” etc., [meaning]: “It might be argued that there is indeed non-deviation. He replies with the words beginning “In that case also.”

In that case as well, if it were admitted that fire exists within the ocean by way of identity (*tādātmya*), then water and the like would not be the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) when fire is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
Consequently, in the absence of a counter-example, what basis could there be for the exclusion of the mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke, from the counter-example?
Or else, why would the cognition of its form or its effect not occur even there [in the ocean]?
Or rather, let there be a real difference in entities within a nature that is devoid of specific characteristics.
If it is held that fire exists in the ocean in an ultimate sense, why does no cognition arise that perceives its form and manifests the effects characterized by burning, cooking, and so forth?
If it is argued that a difference in characteristics is accepted, he says: "having a different nature," and so on.
This has been examined in detail in the *Syādvādaparīkṣā*; let this matter rest for now.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "by a single means of valid cognition," he says "samasta... and so forth: "The mental cognition that is omniscient, which arises through the power of the repeated practice of the reality connected to all things, is postulated as the single means of valid cognition."
But visual consciousness and the others do not [perceive them]; therefore, why is it said that "he certainly perceives all tastes and so forth with his eye"?
And mental cognition, which consists of the experience of form and so forth, is established;
even for an opponent, there is no dispute regarding this much of an object, as it is so clear.
For it is described by him that memory has as its object form, sound, and so forth,
and that in a dream, mental cognition consists of the experience of all objects.
Furthermore, when an omniscient being is conceptualized by means of a mental [cognition] whose object is indeterminate, why would he perceive tastes and so forth with that visual faculty?
Even if that [perception] were produced by the visual faculty alone, this fault would still occur;
however, one indeed perceives taste and so forth through the mind in its collective state.
Even where an excellence is observed, it occurs without overstepping its own specific object;
thus, there may be the perception of distant or subtle things, but not the functioning of the ear with regard to visible form.
Therefore, such undesirable consequences as have been stated by others do not apply,
because an excellence in mental cognition is held to occur precisely without overstepping its own object.
Just as it is observed by people at present that perceptions of various kinds of objects arise through specific types of means of valid cognition, so it is for us in other times as well.

If the thorough cognition of all objects were admitted to belong to the cognitions of the sense faculties such as the eye, then the aforementioned fault would indeed follow. However, since omniscience is intended by means of a mental consciousness—which arises from the culmination of the excellence of practicing the reality of all things, such as their impermanence and other characteristics, which has sentient beings' welfare as its domain, and which attains the status of direct perception through its vivid appearance and non-deceptiveness—it apprehends all things simultaneously; it is not by means of the cognitions of the eye and other senses.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that mental cognition is not well-established as having all objects for its domain, since you yourself have described the memory-cognition of objects such as forms and sounds; and that is indeed mental cognition. Furthermore, since the appearance of forms and so forth in dreams is extremely well-known, its denial cannot be made.
Since excellence is desired precisely by not overstepping one's own purpose, you have not brought anything undesirable upon us.

Even for the proponent of cognition (*jñānavādin*) who maintains that an omniscient being is intended by the term "sensory cognition" (*akṣadhi*), this is also acceptable; for it is accepted that when the latent impressions of the lineage of faults (*doṣadauṣkulyavāsanā*) are abandoned, there is the attainment of mastery (*vibhutva*) over all cognitions by virtue of their functioning toward all objects.
Indeed, the latent impression of the lineage of faults is the very cause that restricts cognitions.
Thinking that once that is abandoned, how could these [cognitions] possibly have restricted objects as their domain, he says: "Or, purified," and so forth.
Or perhaps cognition may be entirely pure, having all things as its object;
for some excellence in the cause is expected to produce some excellence even in the result.
For it is not observed that *āmalaka* trees in the desert bear small fruit;
in reality, they possess that same nature everywhere else as well.
"Therefore, there is also this scriptural statement that 'snakes hear with their eyes';
for the karmic powers of sentient beings are indeed diverse and capable of producing inconceivable effects."

For since the specific nature of entities is determined by the diversity of their causes, it is impossible to ascertain that an object observed once in one place exists everywhere and at all times in that same way. Indeed, it is not reasonable for discerning persons to conclude through mere observation that *āmalaka* fruits are small simply because they were found in deserts; for even when such a cause is possible, there may still be a difference in causes in every location. Therefore, it is not contradictory that someone might perceive all objects with the eye, even when it has been opened by the probe of the power of specific yogic practice.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of whatever kind," he says "of whom" and so forth:
"For he to whom all things situated in the three times appear as having such restricted capacities is fit to speak in this manner."
Likewise, regarding the phrase "with its capacity restricted":
the connection is that every object appears with its capacity restricted to that desired form.

To explain what that [means of knowledge] is like, he says: "By whatever kinds of means of valid cognition," and so forth. "Whatever kind of perception of objects occurs for people in the world by means of whatever kinds of means of valid cognition at present, it was exactly the same in other times as well."
Even now, the power of the world cannot be known by you,
who are but a mere creature, because all powers remain undetermined.
Alas, omniscience consists in the knowledge of the capacities of all sentient beings without exception;
yet this cannot be established through inference, because of the possibility that things might be otherwise.
