It might be argued: "We do not say this on the basis of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that it was so at another time; rather, we say it on the basis of inference (*anumāna*). For whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been seen to grasp a certain class of objects, it was exactly the same at another time, because it is a means of valid cognition. To this, he replies: "And there is no establishment [of the thesis] through inference," because, as in the case of the *āmalaka* fruit and so forth, one observes a specific effect of a specific cause.
Furthermore, because it is possible for activity to occur even otherwise—by means of grasping an object of a different class—the reason is inconclusive.

Regarding the statement, "Even those who are seen to possess excellence," and so forth, he says: "Also by virtue of the knowledge of supersensible objects," and so on. Even by virtue of the knowledge of supersensible objects, men are observed to possess qualities such as wisdom through the power of learning and other such means.
There exists a well-cultivated science known as *hīkṣaṇikā* and others,
which brings about the thorough knowledge of another's mind even in this very life.
Whatever object has not been heard of, inferred, or seen in this life—
whether past, present, or future— they know it and they speak of it.
In this world, men are possessed by various powers— such as those of mantras, lordly nāgas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and so forth— and thus they manifest in a state of coherent discourse.
Even if it were not seen and so forth, there is still no subverting evidence here;
since some means of valid cognition exists, the non-existence of that [object] is not established.

[Page 889] However, the claim that "this is not due to the perception of supersensible objects" is unestablished; for indeed, through the power of sciences such as *īkṣaṇikā*, the knowledge of others' minds and the thorough cognition of past, present, and future entities is actually observed among *ḍākinīs* and others.
By the word "etcetera," those of the *gāndhārī* lineage and so forth are included.

Furthermore, since the thorough cognition of supersensible objects is seen to occur elsewhere as well—due to various spirits, seizures, and the power of possession—there is no rejection [of such cognition] in other cases either.
Or, let it be granted that there is no observation of an instance of deviation;
nevertheless, it is not logical to determine the non-existence of an omniscient being merely on the basis of non-perception.
Thus, his non-existence—that is, the non-existence of one who perceives supersensible objects—is not established.
Regarding the passage beginning with "For even a wise man," he says "And by what has been stated," and so forth:
"And since the author of the Veda has been established by the manner already explained,
you must necessarily admit a person who perceives objects beyond the senses."
Therefore, a wise man should be capable of perceiving subtle matters;
even while transcending his own kin, he shall surpass other men.
By "stated" is meant [as discussed] in the *Aśruti-parīkṣā*.
Right here he states the proof, beginning with "Just as in their own objects," and so forth:
"Just as the capacity of the ear and other [senses] is distinguished with respect to their own respective objects,
so too would it be for the mind, due to the particularity of its movement and connection."

Just as the capacity of the auditory organ and others for their respective objects is specialized by a particular mode of movement and by a particular yoga characterized by ointments and so forth, so too it is possible that the capacity of the mind is likewise specialized by a particular cause.

In this regard, he demonstrates the distinction of the ear and other senses produced by the excellence of their range with the words "For instance," and so forth: "For instance, vultures perceive a form situated at a very great distance; likewise, treasures and the like are perceived even when concealed by means of perfected ointments and such."
He also states that [the object] is "concealed" (*tiraskṛta*) and so forth, which is produced by a specific yoga.
The connection is with the phrase "by means of perfected ointments and the like," as in "it is seen."
This third case ending is used here in the sense of either cause (hetu) or instrument (karaṇa).
Having thus established that a specific mode of rebirth is the cause for a specific capacity of knowledge, he says "In this way," etc., applying it to the subject at hand: "In this way,
through a specific mode of rebirth, there occurs the perception of gods and so forth,
as well as of subtle, concealed, and other [objects], in accordance with the nature of their own birth."

"According to the conformity of their own rebirth" means that their knowledge and vision proceed downward but not upward; thus, when knowledge occurs according to the conformity of their respective rebirths, who can prevent it for the gods such as those belonging to the retinue of the Great Kings?
He also applies the distinction produced by yoga in the passage beginning with "through the practice of yoga" (*yogābhyāsa*), etc.:
"And due to the specific excellence of the practice of yoga, the mental cognition of yogins becomes preeminent; there is no sublation of this."

However, if the negation of excellence is made by demonstrating the impossibility of the causes such as the application of movement (*gati*) and conjunction (*yoga*) as previously described, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Showing this, he says:
"If there were excellence in cognition despite the deficiency of movement, conjunction, and so forth."
This is rejected, for it is improper; indeed, there can be no fruit in the absence of a cause.
Just as knowledge of other treatises is not obtained by that alone,
so too is excellence [not attained] when there is a deficiency in each subsequent cause for it.

Regarding that which was said, "in the case of those things accessible to the ear," and so forth—that too has been refuted by this very argument; the intention is that it is impossible to negate such a specific excellence (atiśaya) merely on the basis of its non-perception.

Regarding what was stated as "In this way, in the investigations of the treatises," and so forth, [the author] replies: "Nor from the knowledge of one part," and so forth. It is not claimed that the existence of omniscience follows from the knowledge of a single part, such that the direct perception of heaven and other realms would result from the knowledge of the Vedas and so on.
However, because an increase is observed through the practice of wisdom, compassion, and so forth,
another excellence is understood to arise from that which is increasing.
Because these [qualities] are mental attributes,
they can reach a limit of perfection through great practice, just as in the case of cruelty, since they result in the ultimate realization of all objects.
For wisdom, by its very definition, consists in the realization of phenomena (dharmas);
even if a single [phenomenon] remains uncomprehended, that wisdom remains incomplete.

For we do not maintain that the complete knowledge of all objects follows merely from the thorough knowledge of a single part—such that you asserted that knowledge of other treatises is obtained by that much alone.

Rather, because an excellence of wisdom is observed through the power of practice, it is possible that another distinction, consisting in the thorough knowledge of supersensible things, arises from that practice as it increases and reaches a state of superior excellence.

This has been established previously; now it is further substantiated by the following formal argument (*prayoga*): Whatever qualities belong to the mind, when there is an excellence of practice, are capable of reaching the ultimate limit of their development—just as, for example, the lack of compassion in a Vedic scholar who has mastered the *Jaimini-sūtra*. And wisdom (*prajñā*) is a quality of the mind. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

There is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) regarding this reason, because the attainment of the ultimate limit of wisdom—which is characterized by the awakening to the essential nature of things—is not possible without the thorough knowledge of all objects.
Nor is the reason unestablished due to an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), because the possibility of a particularity of practice has already been established in detail.
The word *kāṣṭhā* is a synonym for excellence (*prakarṣa*).
Or those things which proceed from prior seeds of a similar kind possess the nature of ultimate increase, due to the specific excellence of their conditioning.
Furthermore, compassion, intelligence, and other such qualities that can arise—just like [the powers of] rice and so forth—possess the aforementioned properties;
thus, when these have increased, there is omniscience.

Alternatively, those things which are produced from prior seeds of a similar kind and possess the property of undergoing absolute increase when there is a specific conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*) are possible, such as rice and the like; and compassion, wisdom, and so forth possess the aforementioned properties. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Here too, as before, there is no lack of proof or inconclusiveness.
"Mati" is synonymous with "prajñā."
"Having the properties as previously described" means that they proceed from seeds of a similar kind belonging to the preceding moment.
And those things which are subject to diminution, when in the presence of their antidote,
undergo absolute diminution, like the impurities in gold and the like.
Likewise, these afflictions, the objects of knowledge, and falsehoods are possible;
for when those factors as they have been taught are abandoned, the cognitions become stainless.
Just as these aforementioned phenomena are possible, so too is their defilement;
for likewise, there exists an antidote capable of uprooting them completely.

Alternatively, those things which are observed to possess the property of diminution in the presence of their counteragent must possess the property of potential absolute diminution when that counteragent reaches its ultimate increase, just as in the case of gold or a stain. Since passion and the like possess the property of diminution upon the manifestation of the characteristics of selflessness and so forth, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
The reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because the contradiction between the afflictions and the knowledge of selflessness has already been proven.
Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because when the counteragent has reached its ultimate increase, the persistence of the opposing factor is impossible.
Otherwise, how could that which is incapable of uprooting [an opponent] entirely bring about even a slight diminution?
For a diamond, even when situated within a mass of blazing fire with a multitude of clearly manifesting sparks, never undergoes any diminution.

Nor is there any inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) due to the impossibility of the complete increase of the counter-position, because the possibility of such complete increase has already been established in detail.

Alternatively, those factors which do not perish even in the presence of their antidotes are such that their antidotes are incapable of uprooting them completely—just as, for example, a stain on gold; and the afflictions, the cognitive obstructions, and so forth, possess the aforementioned properties. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Here too, as before, the fallacies of being unestablished (*asiddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) must be avoided.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the karmic obstructions and others is intended.
Because it is bound to the vision of reality, an absolute diminution of this internal darkness is understood to occur, just as it does for external darkness.
And when that [obscuration] has been diminished, great unimpeded knowledge would proceed independently throughout the entire sphere of the knowable.

Alternatively, those things which obstruct the vision of reality are subject to absolute diminution, just as external nocturnal darkness is; and since the afflictive and cognitive obscurations (kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa) and so forth obstruct the vision of reality, this is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
To show that this [reason] is not inconclusive (anaikāntika), he says:
"And of that," referring to that internal darkness.
Or those [qualities] which have become established in a stable substratum, even if they were somehow harmful,
do not require further effort for their continued existence, provided that no subverting factor is present.
Through the distinctions of excellence in their formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), they function up to the ultimate limit;
they clearly manifest like the purity of refined gold.
These qualities, such as intelligence and compassion, are as previously described;
and when they reach their ultimate limit, omniscience becomes radiant.
There is no deviation [of the rule] here on account of jumping and the heating of water;
for jumping does not arise from jumping alone, but rather from strength and effort.

Alternatively, those qualities which reside in a stable substrate, which once produced by some means possess a specific excellence, and which—provided there is no opposing condition—do not require further effort for their continued existence, are capable of reaching the ultimate limit of excellence through the progressive refinement of their conditioning (*saṃskāra*).
For example, the purification of gold and the like; and wisdom, compassion, and so forth possess these aforementioned characteristics. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Nor is there any deviation from this rule in the cases of jumping or the heating of water.
The intention is that [the reason] possesses a qualification (*saviśeṣaṇatva*).

For jumping and the heating of water, once initiated, do not continue without depending on further effort and so forth for their re-initiation. Nor do they have a stable substratum. Or rather, thinking that there is no deviation from the case of jumping because it requires the qualification "provided that there is the operation of seeds of the same kind," he says: "For that [jumping] does not arise from jumping alone."
Jumping does not arise merely from jumping itself.
To the question "In what case, indeed, does it arise?", he says: "Jumping [occurs] when there is strength and effort.
Jumping occurs when strength and effort are present, but not when jumping is already present.
The point is that because those two—strength and effort—possess a stable capacity, jumping also possesses a stable nature.

This might be the case if jumping occurred solely through strength and effort and not from jumping itself; for if that were so, whatever kind of jumping a person achieves through practice, they would have attained that same kind even before the practice.
This is not a fault.
Because the body was previously impaired by phlegm and other humors, fasting does not occur at first;
however, later, once the bodily impairment has been gradually removed through effort, the fasting remains exactly according to one's strength.
This must necessarily be understood in this way.
Otherwise, if jumping were to result from jumping alone, then there would be no fixed limit to the excellence of jumping.

Alternatively, he shows that there is no deviation [from the rule] by means of jumping, because even jumping, which depends on specific causes, does not establish an ultimate limit of its persistence; thus he says "yadi vā" and so forth: "Or else, even jumping would reach a state of ultimate perfection through the excellence of meditative concentration, strength, speed, and so on, arising from its own causes."
The accomplishment known as "swift as thought" is likewise heard of as a valid authority;
by it, the master goes even to a great distance merely by thinking of it.
Nor is its non-existence established by mere non-perception;
nor is the opponent able to state any subverting argument (bādhaka) in this matter.

For we certainly accept that jumping can reach an ultimate degree of excellence through the application of specific powers of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), just as the Blessed One’s accomplishment called "swift as thought" (*manojavā*) is taught; for one established in that state, there is a speed like that of the mind.
It is for this very reason that it is renowned as "swift as thought.
And there is no subverting proof against its existence.
Nor is it logical to reject something merely because it is not perceived, for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Moreover, it is indeed observed that due to a particular kind of practice conditioned by specific factors within the physical basis (*āśraya*), there occurs an absolute distinction in movement; therefore, showing that such a movement is possible for the Blessed One as well, he says: "The young royal swan," and so forth.
"The young royal swan is not even able to leave its nest, yet through the power of specialized practice, it goes even to the far shore of the ocean."
Just as its movement varies according to the differences in practice conditioned by its basis,
why should a superior movement not be possible from a similar [basis]?
For while in the stage of a bodhisattva, one is not able to attain such a state;
however, once the Sage has attained a distinguished meditative absorption, he would be able to do so.

Just as a young royal swan, though initially unable even to leave its own nest, later—once its wings have grown and it has gained some slight familiarity—flies even to the far shore of the ocean; so too, it is possible that another person may attain a distinguished state through practice conditioned by a particular excellence of support (*āśraya-viśeṣa*).
If it is argued that it is only due to the acquisition of a particular wing that the bird travels to such a distant place, and not by the power of practice, [we reply:]...

For even a young bird, though its wings have grown, is not seen to fly away all at once; rather, by practicing the movement from one branch to another in succession, it first travels a short distance, and only afterwards, having cast off all fear, does it go to a much more distant place.

Furthermore, when a specific excellence of the basis (*āśrayaviśeṣa*) is attained, just as the movement of a swan and the like—though previously incapable—is subsequently distinguished, so too for the Blessed One, though he was previously incapable during his stage as a bodhisattva, such a movement is possible once he has acquired a specific basis through the attainment of a specific meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is the ultimate point; the mention of "practice" (*abhyāsa*) is not essential.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that practice which possesses the condition of a possible specific basis is capable of resulting in extreme distance, just like the practice of a young royal swan; the practice of humans possesses the condition of a possible specific basis—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
He shows that what was stated— namely, "at a distance of ten cubits," and so forth— is refuted by the verse beginning with "ten":
"If one were to leap and go through space at a distance of ten cubits,
such a power might exist because of that cause, even for traveling a great distance."

By including the qualification "provided there is a stable substratum," he shows that [the reason] is not inconclusive due to the heating of water, as stated in the passage beginning with "being heated":
"When being led toward heat, there is the destruction of the water."
Since there is stability of the basis because of this, for whom is there excellence in what?
It might be argued: "But how is it established that wisdom and the other [virtues] have a stable basis? To this he says, "Of mental [qualities]," and so forth:
"But for mental qualities, the continuum of consciousness is the basis;
because they function through a common connection, they do not cease under any circumstances."
It is the continuity of mind; it is so called because of its occurrence through the application of a basis.
The meaning is that [the mind] proceeds by way of its connection with the support characterized as the basis of a bodhisattva;
for a distinguished support is intended here.

Thus, since the existence of other worlds has been established, and because bodhisattvas—who have made great compassion their very nature—remain until the end of saṃsāra to deliver all sentient beings without exception, the continuum of consciousness residing in that support possesses an exceedingly stable foundation.

However, that [compassion] which exists within the mental continuum of the Śrāvakas and others is not based on a stable foundation; because they attain parinirvāṇa more quickly due to their lack of compassion, they lack the effort required for its persistence—this is the intended meaning.
If it is asked how the second qualification is established, he says: "As long as," and so forth.
"To whatever extent the flood of qualities turns toward her, to that same extent she exists in an even more exceedingly radiant manner."
To explain how this very point is established, he says "luminous" and so forth:
"This mind is luminous, having the nature of seeing reality;
for it abides by its very nature [in that state], whereas the stains are considered adventitious."
And this has already been explained by us previously.

Furthermore, it has been established that these specific qualities, such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth—which consist in the vision of reality—are by their very nature the innate disposition (*svabhāva*) of the mind. Thus, it is proven that when wisdom and the other qualities are instilled once, they become the natural state (*prakṛti*) through their own inherent force.

If it is asked how the second qualification—that consciousness consists in the vision of reality—is established, he says: "If the mind were restricted to having another's cognition as its nature," and so forth: "For if the mind were restricted to having another's cognition as its nature, then, because perception would be unestablished, the cognition of an object would be impossible."
Therefore, consciousness possesses the nature of self-awareness because it is luminous;
and this self-awareness remains established as having an unimputed form.

For all proponents of philosophical views must necessarily admit that the primary nature of the mind is indeed self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); otherwise, if it were held that [the mind] is cognized by another subsequent cognition, then the cognition of objects would not be established because its own apprehension would remain unproven.
Therefore, the primary nature of consciousness is simply the illumination of itself.

And since that very self has impermanence and other such qualities as its form, it follows by implication that the mind is established as having the nature of the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*). This is the intended meaning.

It might be argued: "Let it be that the mind consists of the vision of reality; nevertheless, since even abandoned powers can arise again, it is difficult to avoid the charge that all the aforementioned reasons are inconclusive. Anticipating this, he says: "When one has attained intimacy with the path," and so forth. "Therefore, once intimacy with the path has been reached, there can be no overcoming of it by those faults such as passion and hatred, for they have already been rendered weak."
And because the path, which washes away and destroys all defects, has become second nature, there is no loss of it without effort; yet there is no effort without seeing its virtues.
Therefore, the Jina is understood to be omniscient, adorned by a multitude of stainless and unshakable qualities, his nature being impervious to the winds of defects.

Since the path has already become habitual even before [the attainment of full realization], when the stains such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth—being adventitious and weak—are unable to overcome the path, how could they possibly overcome it once the path has attained the state of being habitual?

Furthermore, it is not possible for one who has attained the state of habituation to abandon a quality of the mind without effort, just as a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) cannot abandon his natural lack of cruelty toward living beings.
Moreover, for one who perceives reality (*tattvadarśin*), no effort toward the abandonment of a thing that possesses excellence is possible.
Why? Because of seeing its virtues;
and this has already been explained previously.
*Apakṣāla* means a fault or defect.

Alternatively, in order to show that whatever has been stated by you regarding "being a real entity" (*vastutva*) is itself sufficient for proving that [the omniscient being], he first establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason "being a real entity" and so forth, saying:
"Furthermore," etc. "Furthermore, whatever things are meditated upon, those clearly appear [in the mind] when the meditation reaches its perfection, just like the objects of desire and so forth."
And all phenomena are cultivated for a long time and in many ways by the Great Intelligence in their ultimate form as empty, selfless, and so forth.
Furthermore, the reality of such forms as emptiness and selflessness has been established;
therefore, that [cognition] is considered a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) because it arises from the cultivation of the true object.
In this regard, the fundamental formal argument (*maula-prayoga*) to be stated is as follows:

Those things which possess properties such as being real entities (*vastutva*) and being cognizable (*jñeyatva*) are capable of being clearly manifested by a single cognition occurring at the limit of the intensification of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣaparyanta*); for example, a beloved woman, a son, a thief, and so forth, when cultivated by those overwhelmed by desire and the like. And all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) possess properties such as being real entities; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Nor is this [reason] inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For it is thus: if...
And establishing that this cognition of emptiness and so forth is a means of valid direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), he says "direct perception," and so on:
Direct perception is a means of valid knowledge because it manifests clearly and because it accords with the real object,
just like the appearance of blue and other colors arising from the basis of the eyes and other sense organs.
The simultaneous and clear manifestation of all phenomena is possible within a single cognition; therefore, let it be understood in this very way.
Because it is thus vividly contemplated— like a woman, a son, or a thief— even meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which manifests through the mere power of intention, is not difficult to attain.

This [cognition] is a direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), like the cognition of the eye and other senses, because it possesses vivid manifestation, is non-conceptual, and is non-erroneous due to having as its object a thing established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Consequently, once it is established that vivid manifestation occurs through mere cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is likewise established that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) manifest vividly and simultaneously within a single cognition. Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is proven: that the simultaneous, clear appearance of all phenomena in one consciousness is possible.
The formal argument is as follows: whatever is being clearly contemplated (vibhāvyate) is capable of appearing vividly in a single cognition simultaneously, just like a woman or other such objects;
and all phenomena (dharmas) are being clearly contemplated—this is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
To show that this reason should not be considered unestablished (asiddha), he says "desire" and so forth.
And since the possibility of cultivation has already been established in detail previously, the reason is not unestablished.

Having thus established the pervasion by demonstrating that vivid manifestation is invariably concomitant with mere cultivation, [the author], now showing the primary meaning of the proof, says "cultivation" and so forth: "All phenomena, such as the existence of real entities and the like, possess a vivid manifestation in a single cognition that reaches the culmination of the excellence of cultivation, just like [objects] such as a beloved person."
And thus, for whomsoever the reasons characterized by substantiality, existence, production, and so forth, are capable of providing certainty, who would not establish that [object]?
In this [system], the All-Knowing One is the perfected one, whose circle of the entire knowable is pervaded by a single moment of cognition,
and who has become the crest-jewel upon the heads of gods and asuras.

That single cognition in which the culmination of the excellence of cultivation resides is described as such. Although the terms are in different grammatical cases (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is used because it conveys the meaning.
Those things which clearly manifest in that single cognition—the culmination of the excellence of cultivation—are described as such.

And he in whose cognition those [objects] appear in such a manner—he, who has the entire circle of knowable things pervaded by a single simultaneous cognition, who has become the crest-jewel of all gods and asuras—is established as the Omniscient One.
Indeed, those [qualities] such as dharma and so forth are known by someone even without verbal communication,
because they have been taught by one whose very nature is truth, just like the purity of gold and other [precious substances].

Alternatively, those things which are taught as having a true nature are known by someone, just as the purity of gold and so forth; and since phenomena (dharmas) and so on are taught as having a true nature, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
It might be argued that since instruction is possible even after knowing [the truth] from the Veda, the proof is already established and thus redundant; to this he says, "Of the Vedas," and so forth:
"If the human origin of the Vedas is established, then the proof is established and not [merely] a means of proof."
Instruction regarding what is unknown can be true, for a person may indeed be accidental [in their discovery].
Since the human origin of the Vedas was established previously in the "Examination of Revelation" (Śrutiparīkṣā), there is no proving of what is already proven.
Furthermore, one might argue that because instruction can occur even by chance due to ignorance, the reason is inconclusive; to this he says, "of that which is unknown," and so forth.
For it is not possible to speak, as a rule and in great measure, of something unknown by chance in a manner that does not contradict the means of valid cognition.
The supersensory power inherent in mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and so forth,
[is seen] in such things as the liberation from piśācas and ḍākinīs and the removal of poison.
If the pure cognition of the Sage, Tārksya, and others were not direct knowledge— distinct from what is derived from scripture or inference— how could it have been spoken of?

Furthermore, it must be explained how that power of mantras and the like to remove poison and so forth—which is entirely beyond the senses—could have been spoken by the Buddha and others if it were not directly known by them.
If it is argued that [the Buddha] spoke after knowing [the truth] through inference, he says: "And not through inference," and so forth.
There is no knowledge of that [truth] through inference, because it has never been perceived before;
for that reason, the perception of the relationship [between the sign and the object] is impossible.

For an object whose relationship with its defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is not known cannot be the object of inference; nor can the relationship of any inferential mark (liṅga) with such an absolutely imperceptible (atyantaparokṣa) object be ascertained.
Nor was it heard from another source, because the same line of questioning would apply;
nor is such a thing produced by chance, for its nature is non-erroneous and thus cultivated.
This teaching has this very [purpose] as its ultimate aim; it is not a fabrication based on any other cause.
For if the activity were produced by some other cause, then indeed that name would be subject to doubt.
For one whose mind is agitated by thirst as he approaches a river,
such a state of chance is appropriate for the attainment of coral.

If it is argued that [the teaching] was spoken after hearing it from another, this is not so, because that other person is subject to the same inquiry. For even in that case, this investigation applies: how did that other person know it? For an instruction of such a kind is not possible without having known it oneself. If it is argued that he too knew it from yet another, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, in a succession of blind men, since none possess direct knowledge, there could be no correct instruction. As it has been said: "In matters of this nature, the word of a person does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just as the word of the blind regarding specific forms [is not authoritative]."
One might object that non-contradiction could occur by chance, like the carving of letters by a wood-boring insect; anticipating this doubt, he says "not by chance," and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is: that whose very nature is non-contradiction occurring by chance.
It is possible for one who has set out with the intention of seeking one thing to encounter a correspondence with a different object by mere coincidence.
Just as for one who has set out with the intention of approaching a riverbank, there might be an approach to the foot of a tree;

yet in this case, such an action undertaken with a different purpose is not possible. For, having made the promise, "O monks, I shall teach you the Dharma," it is determined that this teaching—which proceeds from that promise—is solely intent upon the instruction of the Dharma and so forth, and not intent upon any other purpose.
*Vāhinī* means a flowing river.
Vidruma is coral; it is either a tree or a sprout.
If it is argued that [the Veda] is inconclusive because instruction could arise even from delusion, he says "of those with distracted minds," and so forth:
"It was not spoken by those who are deluded and have distracted minds;
for this [Veda] has a fixed sequence and is a supreme means of accomplishing the fruit."

Indeed, it is not possible for those with distracted minds to speak at length a sentence that possesses a fixed sequence, is free from internal contradictions between its earlier and later parts, and accomplishes the goals of human beings.
Therefore, it is established that Dharma and the other [objects of knowledge] have been directly cognized by someone.

It might be argued: "Even if this is established in a general sense, you still wish to prove that the Sugata possesses knowledge of the Dharma; how, then, is that proven for him? Anticipating this objection, he says—proving the Blessed One’s knowledge of the Dharma—"He who reveals the truth not heard or inferred," and so forth: "He who reveals the truth not heard or inferred, being intent upon it, and whose nature [of that truth] is known through direct perception—he is such a teacher."
Just as another person who has directly perceived water and so forth might communicate it,
he has spoken for the sake of others about that truth which was neither heard nor inferred by them.
The Supreme Sage [taught] the characteristics of the mudrās, maṇḍalas, kalpas, and so forth, which transcend the senses and whose efficacy is known by others through definitive certainty.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whoever is intent upon that [teaching] and instructs others on truths not previously heard or inferred must have directly realized the reality of those meanings, just as one who has directly perceived water and the like instructs others regarding it; and such is the Blessed One. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Since the truthfulness and other qualities [of his teaching] have already been established, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*);
nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as this has already been demonstrated.

And it should be understood that because all these reasons are present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), they are not contradictory (*viruddha*). Regarding the phrase "whose efficacy is unknown to others":
that is so described whose efficacy, such as that of a seal and so forth, is unknown by others.
Regarding what was stated, "Therefore, by means of superior cognitions," and so forth, he says in response: "Therefore,
by means of superior cognitions operating through the power of skillful means,
everything— even that which is beyond the senses— can be known with certainty."

Regarding the passage beginning with "staying in a single room" (*ekāpavarakasthityādi*), he says "one" (*eka*) and so forth: "The perception that arises for one staying in a single room would have its power only in that very place, and not at all in another room."
This is appropriate for you to determine only when there is the experience of the capacity residing in all sentient beings; otherwise, what would be its basis?

This has been stated by your honor as being based merely on the authority of a formal proposition; for it is not possible for those of limited vision to determine that all persons lack the capacity to know supersensuous objects simply because such objects are not perceived by them.

It might be argued: "We do not determine incapacity merely by non-perception; rather, we do so through reasons such as 'being a person' (puruṣatva). For instance, all persons whatsoever are incapable of fully cognizing the objects of others situated at a distance and so forth, because they possess the properties of being a person, being a real entity, being knowable, and so on—just like myself. To this, he replies with the words beginning "by taking oneself as the example," and so forth.

If, by using oneself as an example, one were to determine the absence of capacity in others based on reasons such as their being human and so forth, then an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would occur regarding the effect as well.
For if your own dullness were thus established as certain, then all the wise would,
by your very example, become dull-witted.
The term "certainty" (niścaya) stands in grammatical apposition with the term "effect" (kārya).
In this regard, the reasons [adduced] are inconclusive because they lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For instance, one could also say: "All persons are of dull intellect, because they possess the nature of being persons, just like you."
But this is not the case;
for it is not possible to determine that a property not observed in one person is absent in all persons, because we observe differences among individuals.

And as for what was said by Ṛtuparṇa—that "no one knows everything," and so forth—that too is merely a thesis stated by him without any proof; demonstrating this, he says: "There is no final limit of knowledge in any single person anywhere"—this too is cited as mere words, devoid of reason.

Alternatively, showing that this statement by Ṛtuparṇa is not authoritative because it was made with reference to persons equal to himself— thus avoiding contradiction— he says "svasamān" and so forth: "Or else, such a statement was uttered by Ṛtuparṇa with reference to beings equal to himself who are dull-witted and of impure intellect."
The means of valid cognition have been explained in detail regarding the possibility of an omniscient being, and the refutations previously advanced by others against him have been rejected.
Alternatively, even if that proof of its possibility has not been stated,
its possibility is understood merely through the removal of subverting factors.
For when a sublater is perceived and a prover has not been revealed, doubt arises; by that means, it attains the status of being a possibility.
And when that [independence] is established, the restrictive rule (niyama) is thereby proven:
namely, that dharma is defined by the Veda alone, which is independent.
"Equal to oneself" means those who are the same as oneself.

Regarding the statement "it is not seen in the future" and so forth, he says "and in the future," etc.: "And with respect to a future object of cognition, the capacity of direct perception for yogins would likewise exist; this has been stated in the *Tantreṇaikālyaparīkṣaṇa*."
Regarding the "Examination of the Three Times":

for it is stated there that all entities indeed enter into the state of cause and effect either directly or indirectly. Among these, only a present entity is the effect—either directly or indirectly—of the past, and it is the cause of the future.

Experiencing all aspects exactly as they are through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yogins— by means of the subsequent pure mundane conceptualizations (*śuddhalaukika-vikalpa*) which, though ultimately devoid of an object, are non-erroneous due to their connection with the real entity (*vastu*)— take as their object the past and future continuum of phenomena (*bhāvasantati*) existing as cause and effect, and thereby establish the past and future entities. This is because [the object] has reached the state of being an effect or a cause either indirectly or directly.
Yogins discern that very nature which belongs to the present.
And subsequently, they follow after [the objects] with pure mundane cognitions whose nature is accompanied by conceptual construction, even though those objects do not exist in reality.
Based upon the actual and the future continuity of those causes and fruits,
the teachings concerning the past and the future proceed.
Thus [it is said].

And this is not accepted by the Sautrāntikas, because they maintain that the Blessed One has directly perceived everything. Therefore, demonstrating the view favored by the Sautrāntikas, he says "Or else" and so forth:

"Or else, through the power of yoga, there may arise for yogins a mental [cognition] that is vivid, resembling what has actually occurred or what is yet to be born, and which is independent of inference or scripture."

Just as the cognition of one who sees a true dream—though ultimately devoid of an external object and independent of logical marks or scripture—arises non-deceptively by the power of a particular basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa*), so too, for yogins, through the power of yoga, past and future objects arise with a vivid appearance exactly as they were or will be, independent of logical marks or scripture.
And that is accepted as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It might be argued: "Perception is held to have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, yet the past and the future do not exist by way of their particular characteristics; how, then, is it logical for them to have the particular characteristic as their object? To this he says, "Its own nature," and so forth:
"Because it is cognized as the manifestation of its own nature, its object is that particular characteristic;
and because it is experienced as a clear manifestation, it is accepted as perception."
Therefore, there exists indeed a direct perceiver of supersensuous objects;
since an eternal word does not exist, no one perceives [them] by means of it.

Even though a past or future entity does not exist by way of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no contradiction because it is designated in the treatise as having its own-characteristic as its object due to self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*).

Furthermore, because it possesses a vivid appearance, it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*); and because it is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*) insofar as it is not in disagreement with such an entity, it is established as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) since it is endowed with the definition of direct perception.
Unable to tolerate this, he says "the cognition of supersensuous objects" and so forth:
"The wise declare that the Sage’s cognition of supersensuous objects arises from the aforementioned inference, and not from any other scripture composed by him."

The wise followers of the Sugata (Saugatas) declare that the cognition of supersensuous objects—which is established by the aforementioned inference, independent of scripture, produced through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and directly perceives its object—belongs to the Blessed Sage; they do not hold it to come from any other created scripture. Therefore, since such [scripture] is not accepted [by us], there is no fault at all.

Regarding what was stated, "of [words] having an author, being artificial, and being sentences," and so forth, he says: "Of [words] having an author, being artificial, and being sentences... and so on.
An eternity without beginning (anāditā) is not asserted for those [words] having an author, being artificial, and being sentences;
for the sake of establishing their validity, since that [eternity] exists even in the case of what is non-valid.
For instance, neither the nihilists and others, nor their words,
nor even the Vedas and their expounders possess authority, despite their being beginningless.
For we do not state "beginninglessness" as a probans for the sake of establishing validity;
because it occurs even in the contrary case (the vipakṣa), it would be inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Therefore, the refutation you have stated is based on a mere attribution (adhyāropa).

Furthermore, demonstrating that all these criticisms apply even more clearly to you yourselves—who, in order to establish the authority of the Vedas, assert the beginninglessness of both the speakers of the Vedas and the Vedas—[the author] says: "Of the speakers and artificial sentences," and so forth.
Indeed, beginninglessness is asserted for the speakers and artificial sentences.
For the sake of establishing validity, we refute it out of mere rivalry.
And "speakers" and "unfabricated statements" form a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
Among these, "speakers" refers to the commentators of the Vedas.
To the question "How are they refuted?", he says "The speakers," and so forth:
"The speakers are equal to [ordinary] agents, and the authority of the Vedas depends upon them,
because the cognition of their meaning arises from explanations composed by them."
"Dependent upon that" means dependent upon the speaker.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because of the description made by him."
Because the comprehension of meaning arises from the explanations provided by those speakers, the Vedas possess authority in dependence upon them.
And so, he states "Therefore," etc., to show what the fault is:
"Therefore, the Vedic sentences possess no authority because of their dependence; nor indeed does such authority belong to those who speak of Dharma themselves without having perceived it."
Even if beginninglessness were postulated for such speakers,
it does not differ from that of atheists and others, as they likewise occupy a position of non-authoritativeness.
Because it is a specific form of ignorance, everything here attains equality;
thus, validity and invalidity would not be beginningless.
"Not at all"—this is to be connected with "validity" (*pramāṇatā*).

And since, in this way, the Vedas lack validity due to their dependence [on others], and since all those who proclaim them are like a succession of blind men who do not perceive the Dharma and thus lack authority, what was stated by the opponent—"Validity and invalidity would both be thus beginningless"—is incorrect. Demonstrating this, he says: "Validity and invalidity would not both be thus beginningless."

For if the validity of fabricated statements made by speakers were established, then the beginninglessness of that validity would follow; however, since it is not established, the sense is that it is incorrect to claim the beginninglessness of both.

Furthermore, as for this [argument] we have advanced—establishing the equality of the Buddha and his words with the Vedas and the students of the Vedas—that was done merely out of rivalry; however, there is no equality between the Blessed Ones and their words on the one hand and these [Vedas] on the other, but rather a great distinction. Showing this, he says "yadvā" and so forth:
Or rather, this very distinction indeed exists between the Sage and his words:
he personally perceived the Dharma and, being full of compassion, he taught it.
For this has been established:
that the Blessed One personally saw the Dharma and taught it. Therefore, the point that they did not themselves see the Dharma is unproven; such is the intended meaning.
It might be argued: "How is it established that he alone taught the Dharma? To this, he says:

"Because from which [source] there is the accomplishment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), and from which there is [the accomplishment] of the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*), that is called 'Dharma' by all wise men."
And "of the supreme good" (niḥśreyasa); the connection is "from which [it] arises. In that context, prosperity (abhyudaya) is happiness, and the supreme good is liberation (mokṣa).
That is called "dharma" in such a sense, because of the statement: "Dharma is that from which the attainment of worldly prosperity and the supreme good results."

Granted that *dharma* is the cause for the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), how is it established that this word of the Sugata is the cause thereof, by virtue of which he would possess knowledge of *dharma*? To this, he says:

"Because of the rules concerning the mantras, yogas, and so forth taught by him, when performed according to the prescribed method, even visible results (*dṛṣṭadharma*) such as wisdom, health, and mastery arise."
The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is that which was taught by the Bhāgavata and consists of the rules for mantra-yoga and so forth.
"Yoga" means meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of mudrās, maṇḍalas, and other such elements is intended.
Regarding the phrase "even in the present life":
by the word "even" (api), he indicates that this occurs not only in a future life, but in this very birth.

Having thus demonstrated that it is the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), he says "samasta... and so forth, showing that it is also the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*): "From the vision of the selflessness of all phenomena, as revealed by that [scripture], there occurs the cessation of the flood of afflictions arising from the view of a real effect (*satkārya*)."
The view of a self and what belongs to a self proceeds in the form of the perception of a sentient being;
and through the conceit of "I" and "mine," every affliction proceeds without exception.
And that demonstration of selflessness is the adversary to the view of a self;
when it has become habitual through practice, that [view] ceases.
And that mass of root-afflictions is understood to cease due to the absence of its cause;
when that [cause] is absent, existence, which has it as its cause, is not born again.
And liberation is proclaimed as the absolute release from that [self];
therefore, the vision of selflessness is the gate to the non-dual Śiva.
For all non-Buddhist teachers, liberation is desired through the cessation of the ego-sense; yet, as long as there exists a self, the ego-sense does not cease.
Because the efficient cause exists and because the object itself is not defective,
if that [cause] were defective, it would follow by its absence that there is a perversion [of cognition].

It is accepted that liberation for all beings is indeed the absolute cessation of the continuity of birth; and the means for its attainment is the word of the Blessed One alone, because it is precisely here, and nowhere else, that the vision of selflessness—which serves as the antidote to the afflictions that cause birth—is taught.

Furthermore, since all other non-Buddhist teachers are intent upon a false view of the self, it is therefore logical that only the word of the Blessed One possesses the characteristic of Dharma, as it constitutes the means for attaining both worldly prosperity and the supreme good, and nothing else does.
Therefore, the collective meaning is that this alone should be resorted to by those seeking the highest good, and nothing else.

As for the meaning of the individual parts, it is said: if it is asked how it is established that the flood of afflictions (*kleśaugha*) arises from the view that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryadarśana*), he replies with the words "self and what belongs to the self" (*ātmātmīya*), and so forth.
This has already been explained by us previously.

If the flood of afflictions has indeed arisen from the view that things have real existence (*satkāryadarśana*), how is it that this [flood] ceases through the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*)? To this he says, "the view of a sentient being," and so forth.
"The view of a sentient being" (*sattvadṛk*) means the perception of a sentient being;
that is to say, the view that things have real existence (*satkāryadṛṣṭi*).
Its opposite is the counteragent;
this too has already been shown previously.
Regarding the phrase "in that":
In the demonstration of selflessness,
"she" refers to the view of a sentient being.
"Rooted in that" means rooted in the view of a self-entity (*sattvadṛṣṭi*). "Due to the absence of a cause" means...
Because of the absence of the cause known as the perception of a sentient being;
"in that" refers to the mass of afflictions.
"Having that as its cause" means having the mass of afflictions as its cause. "Is not born" means...

For it is not logical for an effect to arise in the absence of a cause, as that would entail the consequence of causelessness. "Complete liberation from those" means liberation from the arising of those afflictions or of that renewed existence (*punarbhava*) once again; that is "complete liberation from those."

As they have said: "Liberation (apavarga) is the ultimate release from that [suffering]. Now, one might object: "Since the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) has been taught as the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) even in other systems, and the ten wholesome paths of action (*kuśala-karmapatha*) are taught as the causes of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), why then is it said that the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) alone is the unique door to liberation? To this, he says: "Of all," and so forth. In this regard, because the aggregates (*skandhas*) arise from the notion of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*), liberation occurs upon their cessation; thus, there is no dispute among any seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) on this point.

Furthermore, that cessation of ego-grasping (*ahaṅkāra*) is not possible for those of other schools, because they are obsessed with a false view of self, and because ego-grasping is rooted in the view of self. Therefore, how could this [ego-grasping] cease while the existence of a self and the obsession with the existence of a self remain—their causes being complete—and while its own object, the self, remains unrefuted? As it has been said: "As long as the mind possesses ego-grasping, the continuity of birth does not come to rest; and ego-grasping does not depart from the heart as long as the view of self persists."
"There is no other teacher in the world who propounds selflessness; there is no path to the method of pacification other than your teaching.
For indeed, mental phenomena are not to be extracted by being pulled out like thorns or the like;
rather, since they proceed through attachment to objects as they appear to be, they are to be eliminated by refuting their cause.
If it is argued that "the yogi indeed defiles the self," he replies with the words beginning "taddūṣaṇa" (the refutation of that).
For in that case, being defiled means it must be refuted by way of non-existence (*abhāva*), because otherwise the refutation of it would be purposeless.
To explain: if one were to adhere to the self as existing and then refute it on the grounds of its being a cause of suffering, [that would not constitute a true refutation].
In that case, the refutation would be entirely purposeless;
for that refutation is intended for the sake of relinquishment,
and since it is impossible to relinquish what is inherently eternal and constitutes its very nature, that refutation consequently becomes utterly futile.

Nor can their self be refuted by the word "non-existence," because that would entail the error of those who, while clinging to the existence or non-existence of a self within the self, fall into perversion.

Furthermore, even if there were some other refutation of that [self] by way of its being a cause of suffering and so forth, nevertheless, he says "it is not tenable" and so on, demonstrating that the cessation of the ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*), which arises solely from the view of a self, would not be logical:
"It is not tenable to say 'I am not' if indeed something called 'I' exists. Otherwise, the claim that 'the knower of reality necessarily attains nirvāṇa' would be false."
The meaning is that the view "I am not" in this way— that is, the view "I do not exist"— is not tenable. "If 'I' were to exist" means if the self were to exist.
Therefore, the claim that one who speaks in contradiction to reality attains nirvāṇa is false;

for liberation is held to result from the disappearance of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and since the ego-sense cannot logically cease while a self exists as its object, what logic is there [in your position]?
He concludes with the words "Therefore," and so forth: "Therefore,
although in other religious systems there is a slight attainment of prosperity resulting from the abandonment of the ten unwholesome actions, it is very meager."
But the attainment of liberation does not exist even in the slightest degree,
because of being characterized by the view of a self-entity (sattvadṛṣṭi), and thus the roots of affliction have not been uprooted.
Regarding "by the abandonment of the ten unwholesome [actions]":
the ten unwholesome [actions] are killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.

Alternatively, the ten unwholesome [actions] are recited as: failing to protect others, not giving, not attending [to others], falsehood, unpleasant speech, that which is harmful, lack of study, lack of faith, lack of compassion, and longing [for what is improper].
The ten wholesome [actions] are the opposite of those.

The diminution of those unwholesome actions means, in effect, abstaining from them and practicing the ten wholesome ones. It is called "lighter" because it is preceded by a lack of perversion; thus, one falls away from it more quickly.
The root of the afflictions is precisely the view of a self-entity.
He also demonstrates a specific teaching of the Blessed One regarding the cause of higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*), beginning with the words "ten," and so forth:
"Furthermore, those ten wholesome paths of action which were proclaimed by the Protector—
when embraced by right view, they become exceedingly powerful."
"They are powerful" because they possess stable and sublime fruits.
He asks why the others are not powerful, and says "sattva" and so forth:
"But those [paths] are enveloped by the view of a self (sattvadṛṣṭi) due to their association with error;
therefore, being impure, a pure fruit does not arise from them."
Thus, when the Supreme Sage is the teacher of the reality of phenomena,
what person of sound intellect would say that he does not perceive the Dharma himself?
For indeed, from a perfectly pure cause alone does a perfectly pure fruit arise, not from an impure one.

"The best of sages" (*munisattama*) means that among sages—both those outside [the Buddhist fold] and those in training or beyond training—he is the most excellent (*sattama*), the beautiful (*śobhana*); thus, he is the "best of sages."

Regarding what was said— that they speak of the omniscience of the Buddha and others as being equal to the eternity of the Veda, and so forth— it is replied with the words "of the Protector" (*tāyinaḥ*), etc.: "The omniscience of the Protector and the eternity of the Veda..."
The wise do not speak of them as being equal, because permanence is impossible.
For its sublation has been declared on account of the contradiction between succession and simultaneity;
it is not in any way logical that consciousness and the like should be its effect.
Regarding the term "tāyinaḥ":
it refers to the Blessed Buddha.
For if the eternity of this Veda were possible, then one might say, "And that which is the eternity of the Veda"; however, since that very [eternity] is not established, [it cannot be said].

This has already been established by the presentation of the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*); and he now recalls that very same subverting proof with the words "due to the contradiction between succession and simultaneity" (*kramākramavirodhataḥ*). This, moreover, has already been explained previously.
Regarding what was stated [in TS 3186ab]: "An omniscient being is not seen at present by people such as ourselves," he replies with the words beginning "is seen" (*dṛśyate*).
Is it you who say, "An omniscient being is not seen now," or do you mean "by everyone"? The refutation of this has been set forth here in detail.
For your non-apprehension alone is subject to deviation;
however, the exclusion of all other observers is doubtful, and thus it is not a valid means of proof.
And this further point was stated by Kumārila: "The conceptualization that 'it did not exist' cannot be [established] as easily as its negation. To that, he says "nirākaraṇa" and so forth:
"The conceptualization that 'it did not exist' cannot be [established] as easily as its negation; this is incorrect, because even regarding the past, such a negation is impossible."

The claim that just as a refutation of an omniscient being can be made regarding the past—namely, that "he was omniscient"—such a conceptualization cannot be established, is improper; for even in the past, his refutation is impossible.

By the use of the word "api" (even), he shows that it is likewise impossible in the present and future times; for, as previously stated, the absence of something cannot be understood from mere non-perception.
With the words "It might be thought," and so forth, he anticipates the proof proposed by the opponent:
"It might be thought that the past time is empty for you, the all-seeing one."
Because it is time, just as the present time is perceived.
Because its negative concomitance is doubtful, this is not a valid proof;
for it has not been ascertained that this present time is devoid of it.

The formal argument is as follows: this past time is devoid of an omniscient being, because it is time, like the present time. Since no subverting proof has been presented against the opposite of the probandum (i.e., that the past was not devoid of an omniscient being), there is uncertainty regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka); therefore, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Furthermore, the example is unestablished (asiddha) because its possession of the property to be proven is itself doubtful.
Or, let it be granted that the example is established; even so, he says "because of the cause," etc., showing that it is not proper to establish what is desired merely by observation:
"And because of the absence of the causal complex, that which is called 'past' does not exist now;
but why should it not be possible in past time, as in the case of Rāma and others?"
What, then, is the obstacle here [to the following inference]: "That which does not exist now did not exist in past time either"?
For it is not possible to infer that because Rāma, Bharata, and others do not exist now, they did not exist in past time either.
Therefore, the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to the counter-examples of Rāma and the others.
Regarding what was stated [in TS 3186cd]: "And no part is perceived that could serve as a logical mark," to this he replies with the words beginning "of wisdom and so forth":
"Having taken wisdom and the rest as the subject (*dharmin*), the logical mark has been proclaimed;
yet no such mark is perceived, nor is existence being proven."

By the passage beginning with "those which are of a different class," the status of wisdom and the other qualities as the subject (*dharmin*) is established, and thus the logical mark (*liṅga*) has been stated; therefore, the claim that "the logical mark does not exist" is unproven.

Nor is mere existence (*sattā*) being proven; rather, what is proven is a quality of wisdom and the others known as "absolute excellence," and that itself is omniscience. Consequently, whatever faults there might be in proving mere existence do not apply here at all.
Regarding the passage beginning with "And there is no scriptural rule," he says "But by scripture," and so forth:
"We do not establish the omniscient one by means of scripture;
for when the previously mentioned inferential mark exists, who indeed would speak of him through scripture?"

For when an inference functioning by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta*) is possible, no one would seek to establish a real entity based on a statement that merely follows one's own whim.
Therefore, we do not establish the existence of an omniscient being through scripture;
rather, we do so through inference.
And that is exactly as previously stated.

Furthermore, demonstrating that this is not established and that there is no scriptural rule which eternally reveals an omniscient being, he says "But rather," and so forth: "But rather, if you accept the Veda as a means of valid cognition,
then why, O fools, is the Blessed One's omniscience not understood from it?"
O Brāhmaṇa, it is clearly recited by the wise in another branch of the Veda that the Blessed One, the omniscient and most excellent of sages, is named Nimitta.

For there exists another branch [of the Veda] called the *Nimitta*, in which this very Blessed One Śākyamuni is clearly recited as omniscient; why, then, is he rejected by you, who yourselves accept the Veda as authoritative, yet remain so deluded?
Showing how he is recited there, he says "yo 'sau" and so forth: "He who, having manifested himself in a dream as a six-tusked white elephant, was born as the Bodhisattva, an ocean of virtues."
He will be one whose fame is proclaimed everywhere, omniscient, and compassionate;
he will have attained the state of immortality, pure, and indeed the father of all the world.
"One whose fame is proclaimed" means one whose renown is celebrated throughout the entire world.

"One who has attained the state of immortality" means one who has attained the state of *nirvāṇa*, characterized by the cessation of all afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*).
"Pure" means consisting of the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
By this much, the Blessed One’s perfection of his own welfare (*svārthasaṃpat*), characterized by the abandonment of ignorance, has been elucidated.
Illuminating the perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpat*), he says: "the father of all the world."
He is the father and the teacher,
because he establishes the entire world in the three types of knowledge and in the happy realms.
With the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's reply:
"Now, if it is maintained that this other recension (*śākhāntara*) is not included within the Veda,
then no reason for this can be determined here except for your own prejudice."
Furthermore, those properties such as accent and so forth, which are well-known to arise from the Vedic revelation,
can be produced here as well, since they originate solely from human will.
"This" refers to another branch known as the *Nimitta*;
he refutes it with the words "In this case," and so forth.
With the words "nanu" and so forth, the author anticipates the opponent's reply:
"But surely, such an eternal scripture cannot be found here by anyone else."
If [the Veda] were eternal, it would be a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda); if its purpose were that [eternity], there would be non-eternality.
"Thus, 'intent on that' means intent on establishing the Omniscient One.
To the question 'How is it not possible to attain [him]?', he says: 'And because he is eternal,' and so forth."

If this scripture, which is intent upon establishing the existence of the Omniscient One, were eternal, then it would necessarily be regarded as having the status of an *arthavāda* (a commendatory or explanatory passage) or serving another purpose.
On the other hand, if its status as an *arthavāda* is not accepted, then its non-eternality would necessarily follow.

But why does [the author] say that if [the Veda] were eternal, it would result in its being merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda)? He says: "And if the eternity of the scripture were established," and so forth: "If the eternity of the scripture were established, the postulation of that [Vedic injunction] would be useless;
for from that [scripture], people will understand dharma itself."
"That conceptual construction" refers to the conceptual construction of an omniscient being.
To the question "Why is it useless?", he says "Since," and so forth.
"From that" means from an eternal scripture.
He provides a rebuttal with the words "Certainly not" and so forth: "Indeed, even though this Veda is well-known, it possesses no eternality;
for its fruit consists of cognitions that arise immediately after effort and cognitions that occur in a temporal sequence."
However, if you accept the validity of this well-known [Veda],
then its validity would necessarily follow for other branches as well, since they too possess the nature of the Veda.
Although this Veda, consisting of the Ṛgveda and so forth, is extremely well-known in its essential form, nevertheless its eternity is unproven.
To the question "How so? he says: "That which..."

For this reason: whatever cognition arises immediately after an effort, or whose fruit is successive cognition, is impermanent, just like a jar or similar objects; and the Veda is likewise [such]. This is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).
Furthermore, its lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) and other defects have been refuted in detail in the *Śrutiparīkṣā*, so they are not stated here.
"Of this" refers to the Veda.

If it is argued that the status of other branches as Veda is unestablished, he says "jñāpanīyam" and so forth: "Either the non-Vedic status must certainly be made known by you through reasoning; otherwise, for you, its not being stated in scripture would remain doubtful."

"Otherwise" means that if its non-Vedic nature is not made known, then that which you have stated regarding the Omniscient One—that he is not mentioned in the Śruti, the Veda—would be "doubtfully unestablished" (sandigdhāsiddha).
Regarding what was said—that there would be impermanence if [the Veda] were directed toward another—he replies with "And let there be eternality," and so forth:
"And let there be eternality for the Veda, and let it be directed toward that [supreme goal];
yet why would there be impermanence in that which is directed toward the supreme? Because it is connected to the meaning of destruction."
When asked "Why?", the opponent replies: "Because of the connection with a perishable object.
That is to say, impermanence follows as a consequence because of the connection—that is, the relation—with a perishable entity.
With the words "If this were so," and so forth, he demonstrates the lack of necessity [in the opponent's argument]:
"If this were so, how could clarified butter, wild millet, gold, matted hair, and the like—
which exist as eternal entities— be said to be impermanent?"
*Ājya* is clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
*Nīvāra* is a specific variety of grain.
*Cāmīkarajaṭa* is fire.
"By that" means by the Veda.

With the words "jāti" and so forth, the author anticipates the opponent's reply: "If the universal (jāti) is also eternal in that case, has it not already been refuted? Furthermore, if the word denotes only that [universal], there would be no cognition of 'ghee' and the like."
In his case as well, why would the eternity of speech not be lost? Or rather, let there be a form even in the Omniscient One; by that, its eternal nature remains intact.

In that regard, it might be argued that since a universal (jāti) exists in things such as clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth, and that [universal] is what is denoted by the word, there will be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This, however, is incorrect;
for the universal has already been refuted at length during the examination of the general property (*sāmānya*).

Or, let there be a universal (jāti); even so, from words such as *ājya* (clarified butter) which denote the universal alone, the cognition of the individual (vyakti) would not follow. Consequently, for one who seeks an object to be accomplished by means of the individual, the denotation of the universal would be entirely useless.
If it is argued that the individual is understood through necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatayā*), we say no.
Because there is no remoteness in cognition:

for it is not the case that immediately after the word, the cognition first arises regarding the universal, and only subsequently does the cognition of the individual arise as its necessary concomitant. Rather, in the world, from the word there arises a determination of the object capable of causal efficiency without any intervening interval.
And it is precisely with the desire to convey that [universal] that one employs the word;
therefore, it is not correct to say that the cognition of the individual does not arise from the word.
Moreover, if the word were to denote only the universal and not the individual, [the following would occur].
Likewise, having understood that [the word] expresses something unrelated—like an injunction to milk a bull—a discerning person would certainly not proceed toward the individual based on the word.

Now, if it is accepted that the individual, in the form of its manifestation (*abhivyakti*), is denoted by the word so that this undesirable consequence does not arise, then how could the loss of the eternity of the Veda not follow?

Furthermore, even if it were granted that words primarily denote the universal (*jāti*) and that the denotation of the individual follows as a necessary concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*), he shows that even so, the eternity of the entire other tradition (*āgama*) is not contradicted, with the words beginning "even if [he were] omniscient" (*sarvajñe 'pi*).

For even in the case of a single omniscient being, it is logically possible for him to be denoted by a generic term due to the multiplicity imagined through the difference of his states; how much more so, then, in the case of an immeasurable succession of beginningless omniscient beings?

Furthermore, even if you do not accept the *Nimitta* as a separate branch (*śākhāntara*) of the Veda, the fact that it is not mentioned in the [other] Śruti remains doubtful; demonstrating this very point, he says "And then," and so forth:
"And then, the determination of the meaning of Vedic sentences would depend on independence—either from the Veda itself or from another person whose mind is overcome by delusion and the like."

Since there is the Vedic revelation stating, "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," what proof is there that the meaning of the statement "the Jina is omniscient" is not likewise [authoritative]?
For since the Vedic sentences possess independence due to their eternity, no ascertainment of the Vedic meaning arises from them; for this Veda does not cry out, "This is my meaning, and not another.
Nor does the ascertainer reach a determination of the meaning from himself or from another commentator, because according to your own view, all people are corrupted by delusion and other defects.
Consequently, even the meaning that "the Blessed One is omniscient" could very well be inferred from such sentences as those concerning the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
What is "pramā"? It is nothing at all.
Regarding that which was further stated— that it is impossible for there to be a correspondence with the knowledge and objects of all men— he replies with the verse beginning "svarga," etc.:
"Because he has clearly taught only heaven and liberation,
and because of his thorough knowledge of the primary goal, he is understood to be omniscient."
Of what use is the knowledge of the number of grains of sand in the oceans?
What is the point for us in this, other than the mere awareness of that knowledge?
Regarding what was stated—that "it must be spoken of as being merely figurative"—he says [in response]: "gauṇatvena" and so forth.

This restriction—that even he who knows the meaning of the mantras and the arthavādas must speak of [the omniscient one] only as figurative—would be established only if an omniscient being were refuted.
But once it has been established in detail that the previously mentioned sublation is untenable,
the restriction to a secondary sense remains doubtful, because the primary meaning is also possible.

For if an omniscient being were refuted by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then, by the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), its figurative meaning would necessarily follow; it would not be so otherwise, since its primary meaning is also possible. Furthermore, it is not logical for an eternal word to be an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), for an eulogy consists of a teaching intended with a specific purpose (*abhiprāya*). And that [purpose] is not possible in a word devoid of intention, in the absence of a desire to speak (*vivakṣā*).
Alternatively, regarding the passage beginning with "from the knowledge of the dharmas and so forth under discussion," he says "dharmādi" and so on:
"If there were non-obstruction merely by means of the knowledge whose object is the dharmas and so forth..."
When that is clearly described as fruitful, then the world has been conquered by the Buddhas.
To explain how [the goal] has been won, he says "because," and so forth:
because in both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and liberation (*mokṣa*),
they have previously established an unimpeded knowledge that is unique to them and exceedingly clear.
