For since it was previously established that the Blessed One’s knowledge of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) is unimpeded, the Blessed One’s own words would imply that his knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth is unique and uncommon; thus, he would not have accepted [the status of] being omniscient.

Regarding what was said—that consciousness exists in the self alone—even there, since such knowledge is possible only in the Blessed One, nothing undesirable has been entailed; demonstrating this, he says: "And that which is consciousness in the self alone," and so forth.
"And that which is consciousness in the self alone, set in motion by the practice of meditation—its non-obstructed nature has already been established for them."
"Of that too" means of the knowledge of the self. "Of them" means...
"Of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
previously" refers to the passage beginning with "Insofar as the flood of qualities is in this [earth]," and so forth.

But has it not been described there that self-knowledge consists of self-awareness (*svavedana*), and not the knowledge of an internal agent (*antarvyāpārapuruṣa*)? How then can this be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*)? To this he says: "For this alone," and so forth.
For this very thing is that knowledge, namely, the vision of the pure self.
Because of the realization that there is nothing but mind, which is free from adventitious defilements.
If it is asked how the experience of mind-only is established, he says: "unperceived object," and so forth.
It has been previously demonstrated that cognition is devoid of the forms of the perceived object and the perceiving subject;
and it has been revealed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones to be empty of the affliction of duality.
By that [knowledge], those of great intelligence became perfected, possessing wisdom unaccustomed to cyclic existence;
for even today, teachings continue to shine forth through their sovereign power.
"Previously" refers to the *Bahirarthaparīkṣā* (Examination of External Objects). Those for whom cognition is unsuitable and unfavorable to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) are described as such.
What, then, are those teachings heard to exist under his sovereignty? He says: "By nature luminous," and so forth.
"In the mind which is by nature luminous and unstained by the forms of duality, how could one whose self is undeluded regarding the forms of duality have a contrary notion?"

And upon awakening to the selflessness of both [person and phenomena], the defects such as attachment and aversion— which arise from conceptual constructions regarding women and so forth— are completely exhausted without effort.
This is that supreme reality which the speaker of truth has proclaimed;
it bestows all prosperity and is beyond the reach of Keśava and others.
"One whose self is undeluded regarding the two aspects" means one who has abandoned the adherence to the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*).
"Awakening to the selflessness of the two" refers to awakening to the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "the two" are the apprehended and the apprehender; their "selflessness" is their lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*).
"Beyond the range of Keśava and others": Keśava is Hari; by the word "and others" (ādi), Īśvara and so forth are included.
Now, as to why a pure vision of the self is not accepted even by Keśava and others, he says: "For [the self] is known," and so forth.
"For the stable self is known by others as resembling a pure crystal;
yet that [notion] of theirs is an error, because of the refutation of an eternal self."
If consciousness that grasps a self were to arise from a self,
then it would follow that consciousness of all selves arises simultaneously.
Furthermore, if it were not produced from that [object], or if it were admitted to be eternal,
then it would not have that as its object, just like the mind of another person.
"By others" refers to Keśava and his followers.

Since the self has been refuted in the *Ātmaparīkṣā*, knowledge concerning it is impure because it is erroneous. Furthermore, regarding this knowledge of theirs which is described as having an eternal self as its object, there are two alternatives: does that knowledge arise from that self, or does it not? In the first case, all knowledge concerning that [self] would arise simultaneously, since its cause would be unimpaired. If the second case is held, then even there, that [knowledge] must be either eternal or non-eternal.
In either case, because it would have to conform to that [past] self by means of that very nature, it would not attain the status of having that as its object, just like any other mind.

Regarding what was stated— that "this very thing is that knowledge which is the vision of the pure self"— he replies with the verse beginning "grāhya" (the object of apprehension), etc.: "If the vision of the pure self were indeed that [ultimate] knowledge, it would not be so, because [the self] lacks the characteristics of an object of apprehension, as has been established in detail."
Furthermore, even if it is admitted that the self has the nature of cognition,
there can still be no such apprehension because of the existence of a distinction between the seen and the seer.
If it is maintained that this cognition possesses the nature of self-luminosity,
then self-awareness (svasaṃvitti) follows as a consequence, and cognition would thereby become perceptible (pratyakṣa).

If, first of all, the self (*ātman*) is admitted to be insentient (*jaḍa*) by nature, then the cognition having that as its object would necessarily be impure by its very nature; for it has been established in the *Bahirarthaparīkṣā* that all cognitions are devoid of the relationship between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). Alternatively, if the position is that the self is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), even then, because there is no difference between the seen and the seeing, the state of being grasped and grasper is untenable, and thus there could be no cognition "having that as its object. For the relationship of object and subject can only exist when there is a distinction between the object and the subject.

Now, if it is accepted that this [cognition] has itself as its object by virtue of being luminous like a lamp, then there would follow the undesirable consequence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), and the intended imperceptibility of cognition would be contradicted. He demonstrates this with the words: "And the intellect would be perceptible."
Regarding what was stated, namely, "Moreover, because [the Veda] has the Veda as its body," and so forth, he says: "And there is no connection whatsoever between Brahmā and the others and the Veda;
because of their difference, because of its eternity, and because of the absence of dependence, just like anything else."
Consequently, it is inconsistent for Brahmā and the others to have the Veda as their body,
and it is likewise inconsistent for the Veda to consist of all-encompassing knowledge, because its meaning is not definitively ascertained.
Furthermore, the Fully Awakened One is established as omniscient by virtue of his own independence;
he is not, like Brahmā and others, postulated as such merely because he has the Veda as his body.

If a relationship existed, Brahman and the others would possess the Veda as their body; however, no relationship exists between the Veda and Brahman and so forth. For it has been established that the relationship between entities is of only two kinds, characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination therefrom (*tadutpatti*). In this regard, since difference is admitted, there is no relationship of identity.
Nor is there a relationship of origination, because since both are eternal, they cannot be assisted by one another, and thus there is an absence of mutual dependence.
And as for the claim that the Veda consists of all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvajñānamayatva*), why is this? Because its meaning is not certain.

For it is only when the meaning is definitively ascertained that it is reasonable to postulate that the Veda consists of all-encompassing knowledge; yet, as has already been demonstrated, such ascertainment is impossible according to your own view.
Furthermore, we do not accept that the Blessed One is omniscient by way of the Vedas as you do;
rather, it has been established that the Blessed One is himself omniscient because his knowledge is self-arisen (*svayambhū*).

Regarding what was said— that the Buddhas and others are mortals— the author, demonstrating that the Blessed One’s mortality is unestablished, says "five," and so forth: "Because he exists outside the cycle of existence consisting of the five realms of rebirth, there is no mortality."
We maintain that the emanation of the Buddhas is understood by us to be just like that.
Samsara consists of five destinies, distinguished as those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, gods, and humans; and since the Blessed Ones are outside of that, their mortality is unestablished.
To the question, "How then is it heard that they were born into families such as that of Śuddhodana?", he says: "That is considered to be an emanation."
Corroborating this very point with scripture, he says "In Akaniṣṭha," and so forth:
"In the delightful city of Akaniṣṭha, which is devoid of the Śuddhāvāsa [heavens], the perfectly awakened Buddhas attain enlightenment there; however, it is an emanation that awakens here."
There are gods named Akaniṣṭha; in one part of their realm are the gods known as Śuddhāvāsakāyika.

For it is here that only the pure noble ones (ārya) dwell. Above them is the place called Māheśvarabhavana. There, only those bodhisattvas who are in their final existence and established on the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are born.
But in this case, the scripture states that such a manifestation is perceived through its sovereign power.
If it is argued that "this is not established for us," he replies with the words "by independence" and so forth:
"But how is mortality determined by you independently?
Not through the gateway of another's scripture, because that [scripture] is not established as such."
Nor do we assert that they are omniscient out of rivalry with them;
for who would conceive a rivalry between sky-flowers and things that truly exist?
For if you assert mortality as being independent [of scripture], then there is the fallacy of the "unestablished due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*).

Indeed, you possess no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the Lord's mortality by which such independent mortality could be proven; therefore, you must state his mortality by way of another person’s scripture.
And since that other person’s scripture stands in the form already described, their mortality remains unestablished.
To the question, "How is it established that these [entities] are like flowers in the sky? he says: "By the absence of all causal capacities," and so forth.
For it has been proven that eternal things are devoid of form due to their lack of all causal capacities; therefore, the Śiva (Tryambaka) and others desired by our opponents do not exist.
For Śaṅkara and others are asserted by opponents to be eternal;

and since it has been established that for eternal things there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—whether occurring successively or simultaneously—and that the absence of all capacity is the definition of non-existence, it follows that the three-eyed Lord (Tryambaka) and others, who are desired by opponents to be eternal, do not exist at all. Thus, their resemblance to a flower in the sky is indeed proven.
Tryambaka is Śaṅkara.

Furthermore, even granting that Tryambaka and others exist, we do not engage in rivalry with those venerable ones because of their extreme inferiority; demonstrating this, he says "Furthermore" and so forth.
Moreover, their knowledge is perverted due to their view of a self and other such [entities].
But for the Buddhas, it is non-erroneous, as has been established in detail.
Therefore, no competition is entered into with them because of the vast difference between us;
for who would compete with those suffering from cataracts against a man with healthy vision?
This is easily understood.
Regarding what was stated—that even though the *āgama* is eternal, it is called "Veda"—he says "guṇakarma... and so forth:
[The status of] qualities, actions, Īśvara, and so on, as well as of the Vedas, has been cast aside.
And because of that eternality, we do not accept the scripture as eternal.
Since momentary destruction pervading all things has been established, nothing whatsoever possesses permanence; therefore, all that you have said is inconsistent.
Regarding what was stated, namely "similar to an omniscient being" and so forth, he says: "By means of analogy," etc.

The existence of an omniscient being is not established by means of analogy, because it has been taught that [analogy] is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); therefore, existence is not established from it either.
For when existence is well-known, similarity is understood from that;
for instance, when the locus (dharmin) such as a cow is well-known, only its similarity to a gavaya and so forth is established by it.
Furthermore, the subject (*dharmī*) "the omniscient one" is not established, because according to your own view, that very person is the object to be proven (*sādhya*).

Therefore, since the existence of an omniscient being is under discussion as the *sādhya* according to your position, there is no possibility for an application of analogy (*upamāna*); thus, its refutation is useless, because there is no prior attainment [of the object] to be negated.
The point is that a negation must be preceded by a prior attainment.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Having seen men who are not omniscient," he says: "Men have been seen to be non-omniscient," and so forth.
For if all men indeed have been seen by you, then there is a contradiction with your own words in your denial of an omniscient being.

This is because, by admitting the perception of all men—however distant or hidden—and by admitting the ascertainment of the power of cognition associated with other mental continua, one would clearly be admitting omniscience for oneself, since this entails the admission of perceiving objects that are remote in space, time, and nature.
For such thorough knowledge is not possible for one who is not omniscient;

and since you employ a proof (*sādhana*) in order to negate that [omniscience], it is that very [proof] which is being negated—thus there is a contradiction with your own words (*svavacanavyāghāta*), just as if one were to say, "My mother is barren."
Showing that the reason is unestablished (*asiddhatā*), he says: "Even when a person stands before you, how could you have the certainty,
'This one is not omniscient,' since you yourself are one who perceives what is beyond the senses (*atīndriyavid*)?"
If one holds the view that the self is not omniscient while being certain that all others are omniscient,
there would be an over-extension [of the argument], because even those such as Ajita and others would be determined to be omniscient.
If it is argued that certainty regarding all phenomena is not accepted because sublation is not observed,
then surely the suspicion of sublation does not differ from the non-observation of sublation even when [the cognition] has been stated.

For instance, when a person stands before one, it is impossible for a non-omniscient person to ascertain that "this man is not omniscient" based merely on seeing his body; how much more so in the case of a person situated in a different time and place?
This refers to the impossibility of such a certainty as "this [person] is not omniscient.

Now, if—lest the reason be unestablished—it is accepted that by the non-omniscience of oneself there is an ascertainment of the non-omniscience of all others, then, demonstrating that this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and thus results in the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "In the perception of one's own non-omniscience," and so forth.

The analysis of the compound is: "the view of non-omniscience in oneself. It might be argued: "When the proof for [one's own] omniscience regarding all phenomena is being formulated, it is sublated by what is perceived, namely the distinctions in wisdom and so forth; therefore, a proof for that [omniscience] is being provided. Since the omniscience regarding reality (*tattva*) being established is not sublated by anything, there will be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."
This is incorrect.

Just as a reason does not prove a thesis that is contradicted by perception, so too it does not prove one where contradiction is suspected; therefore, the suspicion of contradiction is not distinct from actual contradiction. Consequently, even the proof of non-omniscience should not be accepted, because its contradiction is suspected.

Regarding what was said—that the teaching of the Buddha and others could be explained otherwise—he says "svarga... and so forth: "Who other than a dull-witted person would, out of delusion, deny that faultless teaching of the Buddhas which establishes the path to heaven and liberation?"
The claim that the teaching is based on something other [than valid cognition] is unproven;

for a faultless teaching regarding the path to heaven and liberation cannot arise from delusion. Furthermore, the faultlessness of the Blessed One’s word has been established by all forms of investigation.
"From the dull-witted" refers to Kumārila.
The meaning is: "if he himself considers that [to be] supreme."
Regarding the phrase "or for the purpose of deluding the disciples," he says "even when seen," and so forth:
"Even when seen, [it brings about] prosperity as well as the supreme pacification of the defects of the mind."
And then, by that [means], he caused supreme delusion to befall those who were attaining [the goal].
"Seen" means in this very life;
"prosperity" is characterized by constant health, sovereignty, and so forth.
The connection is with the words "attaining";
and "the pacification of faults" means the subsiding of defects such as passion and the like.

Therefore, this is a hyperbolic statement (atiśayokti) to the effect that a supreme delusion was produced for those disciples who, through the instruction on the mantra, meditation, and ritual observance, and by performing the practice exactly as prescribed, were [supposedly] attaining [the goal].
If you consider such a delusion to be [genuine], then you yourself would be the deluded one, since you perceive what is not a delusion at all to be a delusion.
If it were argued that this [teaching] is rooted in the Veda, he says:
"And this teaching of the Buddhas is not rooted in the Veda at all;
for that which has been proclaimed by them is stainless, whereas in the Śruti it is stained."
For it is not logical that a stainless teaching should have its root in something stained.
Regarding the point that [the teaching] is for fools and Śūdras, he says "for the sake of accomplishing their own welfare" and so forth:
"For the sake of accomplishing their own welfare, the instruction given to them is not of such a kind;
rather, this entire undertaking is of such a nature as to be performed for the sake of others."
Therefore, those whose nature is compassion and who are consecrated to establishing the welfare of the world,
because they are kinsmen without a bond, declare that state to exist in all beings.
"Footstep" (pada) refers to the path to higher rebirth and the supreme good, used in the sense of being the foundation for the perfection of all virtues.

He shows that it is possible that those very [teachers] such as Manu and others, who provided instruction only to the proponents of the Vedas, did so for the sake of deluding them, by means of the passage beginning with "For those who... and so forth:
"For those who are overcome by greed, fear, hatred, envy, and the like—their teaching would be partial, belonging to those whose natures are devoid of compassion."

Furthermore, he shows that whatever teaching the Blessed Ones gave, even to children, manifests their very greatness, by saying "compassion," and so forth: "But those who are dependent on compassion, who clearly perceive reality, and who are free from fear of any denial, have given teachings everywhere."
To whatever extent a person is seen to be afflicted by defects such as folly,
to that same extent does the compassion of the Protectors flow forth toward them.
For they do not desire any relationship such as marriage or alliance; rather, they must perform acts of service.
Therefore, this is what is sung by the virtuous: [p.920] "No connection such as marriage or wedding is desired by them;
indeed, a beneficial service must be rendered. Thus it is from this that the song of the righteous arises.
The arrival of a married woman at her husband's house is called *āvāha*.
To the question "What is that song? he says:
"In one perfected in knowledge and conduct, in a Brahmin, in a cow, in an elephant, and even in a dog or an outcaste, the wise perceive the same."

Moreover, by you yourself, O fool, speaking with a mind so excessively arrogant due to pride in a false caste— saying "from the ignorant Śūdras"— you have most clearly manifested your own great stupidity here in this assembly of learned men. For instance, the venerable Brahmins carry themselves with the swelling pride of arrogance by postulating that there exists some distinct entity called the universal (sāmānya) known as "Brahminhood," or else by observing their own state of being consecrated through the *jātakarman* and other rites.
Regarding the claim that he was born from a Brahmin mother to a Brahmin father, based on his birth from the womb of a Brahmin woman:
in the first case, [the author] shows that this is merely a decoration of the sky-lotus by saying "in hundreds" and so forth.
For when birth has been refuted in hundreds of ways, what is the point of pride in birth?
If no excellence superior to that [of other things] is established, how can that [consciousness] be considered "distinguished"?

All those who possess qualities such as mastery, whose defilements are entirely exhausted, are without distinction in this regard; and when united with that [state], they are of a different nature [from their previous condition].
If they were to be established, then those depending upon them would be distinguished;
otherwise, there would be no distinction at all, just as in the case of the hunter and the twice-born caste.

Moreover, let us grant that such a caste exists; nevertheless, if a specific excellence (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the physical basis (*āśraya*) produced by it were perceived, then your pride might be justified. However, since we do not observe any such superiority, he demonstrates this with the words beginning "tadanya... and so forth. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "other than those Brāhmaṇas" is *tadanya*; "one whose basis is other than that" is *tadanyāśraya*; and "the non-establishment of that" is *tasyāsiddhiḥ*. Thus, [the basis] of the Śūdra and others is not established [as distinct].

For we do not perceive any superiority in Brahmins over Śūdras and others in terms of wisdom, intelligence, and so forth, nor in terms of feces, urine, flesh, blood, and the like. Since such a superiority is unestablished, how could that caste (*jāti*), which would have to be its substratum, be distinguished?

For if that were the case, you—who are puffed up with the arrogance of the doctrine of caste—could rightly say: "They should grant it [the Veda] only to those who profess the Vedas, just as Manu and others did."

If, however, by virtue of belonging to the Brahmin caste, you were by nature the very repositories of a multitude of qualities such as self-mastery (*vaśitva*), lordship (*īśitva*), the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*), and compassion, and were free from all defects, then your distinction might be established; otherwise, how could your distinction be proven, given that even a Brahmin who is like a hunter, a fisherman, or a leather-worker possesses the Brahmin caste? //3575//
Regarding the second position as well, he states the fault with the words "the birth-rites and so forth," and so on: "Those rites such as the birth-ceremony that are well-known are like other things;
for those conventional practices would indeed exist even in the case of artificial beings."
"Like others besides them" means like those who are considered Brāhmaṇas by convention (*kṛtrima*). "Conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*) means...
Like the naming ceremony and other such rites, these are merely conventional.

Even in the third position, intoxication is not justified; for it has already been stated that there is no distinction whatsoever between the bodies of a Brāhmaṇa and a Brāhmaṇī and those of Śūdras and others, insofar as they are all composed of impure substances such as semen and blood.
Moreover, since your status as having a Brahmin father is indeed doubtful, pride is likewise unjustified; demonstrating this, he says "And the past," and so forth:
"And a great deal of time has passed, and women are exceedingly fickle;
therefore, even in your own case, it is impossible to determine your Brahminhood."
Indeed, there exists no one among you who knows supersensuous objects;
nor has even the eternal Veda declared the purity of your lineage.
At some point in time, since birth can occur even in one who does not belong to the Brāhmaṇa lineage, it is also possible that a Brāhmaṇa is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).
Even if you were previously a Brāhmaṇa, it is certainly possible that you were born of adultery due to the fault of your mother’s conduct;
for generally, women afflicted by passion and fickle-minded are found to exist even by transgressing the boundaries of their family vows.
Nor do you accept any person who perceives supersensuous objects, from whom certainty might arise;
nor does the Veda declare the purity of your lineage.

Furthermore, not only is it improper for you—who have not ascertained your own status as Brahmins—to be stained by pride regarding caste; moreover, it shows that even Manu and others, whose own caste-status was unknown, gave instruction to those of the twice-born only out of delusion. This is shown in the passage beginning with "Therefore," etc.: "Therefore, Manu and others, whose [own] twice-born status was unrecognized, would not have given instruction to the twice-born, because of their uncertainty regarding it."
Those whose twice-born status is unperceived and undetermined are described as such;
"on account of that uncertainty" means on account of the lack of certainty regarding those twice-born ones.

Furthermore, showing that the fact that Manu and others have given instruction to us alone is not a cause for your greatness, but rather indicates nothing but dullness, he says "niryuktikatvam" and so forth:
"The lack of reasoning regarding the meaning of the Veda is an incapacity within oneself to make it known."
"Brahmins who have become dull-witted from the mere recitation of the Vedas are not capable of critical examination."
I suspect that for some reason, Manu and the others certainly received their instruction from the Vedas and other sources from the Brahmins themselves.
"Stupefied by the study of the Vedas": those who have become dull-witted (*jaḍa*) through the study of the Vedas are "stupefied by the study of the Vedas" (*vedādhītijaḍa*).
This means that by means of Vedic study, their capacity for understanding reality has been cast far away.
"From somewhere" means from a cause.

For this very reason, having understood that the Vedas and other such works lack logical consistency, [the author] shows that Manu and others declared their own words to be established by authority (*ājñāsiddha*) in the passage beginning with "The Purāṇa... and so forth:
"The Purāṇa, the Dharma of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs, and medical science—"
These four, established by authoritative tradition, must not be undermined by logical arguments.
I think that this very threat was given by them to the dull-witted;
for otherwise, what else could their "attainment through command" be but mere words?
The Purāṇa is a scripture;
the Dharma of Manu is that which was composed by Manu.

"Veda with its limbs" (sāṅgo veda): it is "with its limbs" because it exists together with the six limbs, beginning with grammar (vyākaraṇa). "Medical science" (cikitsitam): [it is so called because it treats].
The science of medicine;
"by that very [reason]" means by that cause.
That is to say, having ascertained the lack of logical justification for these Purāṇas and the like, as well as the dullness of you yourselves.
"By those," and so forth: furthermore,
by those great-souled ones who have clearly ascertained the logical consistency of their own statements, and who possess the capacity to communicate that [consistency] to others.
Thus, having cast off all fear, they roar their lion’s roar, which brings about the exhaustion of the rut of the intoxicated elephants that are the false teachers.
"Kutīrthyāḥ" refers to the false teachers who are like rutting elephants; "siṃhanāda" is that whose nature it is to bring about the exhaustion of their rut.
"Evam" refers to what is about to be stated.
What, then, is this "lion's roar"? He says:
"Like gold, O monks, my word should be accepted by the wise after examination through heating, cutting, and rubbing on a touchstone, and not out of reverence."
Moreover, he says "And those who... and so forth, to show that the instruction was given by the Blessed Ones themselves to the ultimate Brahmins, and not by Manu and others:
"And those who, because they have cast off all evil, are the ultimate Brahmins."
They have practiced the stainless selflessness found only in the teaching of the Sage.
For this very reason, the ascetics are proclaimed to be of four kinds;
indeed, the doctrines of others are empty of true ascetics and brahmins.
The etymological derivation of "brāhmaṇa" is from having "washed away" (*vāhita*) unwholesome qualities (*pāpadharma*).

And these [true brāhmaṇas] exist only here, within the teaching of the Blessed One, the Sage, because of the instruction on the practice of selflessness (*nairātmya*); they do not exist elsewhere, because other systems lack the means for the destruction of evil.
For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Only here is there a śramaṇa; only here is there a brāhmaṇa. The doctrines of others are empty of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."
In this context, there are four types of *śramaṇas* established in the fruits, beginning with the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*);
likewise, there are exactly four types of *brāhmaṇas* who maintain those [fruits].
Regarding the verse beginning with "Is there any man... (3580), he says "man," and so forth:
It has also been established that such statements as "there exists an omniscient person" do not constitute a valid proof,
because they are seen to suffer from the fault of a deficient thesis (*pratijñānyūnatā*).

He states by which text this is established: "Even though the means for the thorough knowledge of all objects is fruitless," and so forth, as previously stated: "The wise followers of the Sugata nevertheless exert effort... and so on.
Furthermore, we do not establish the existence of an omniscient being for the sake of practicing what he has spoken after having understood that he is omniscient.
Rather, for those who desire to attain the state of omniscience, the destruction of faults and the excellence of qualities are established for that purpose;

for it is by means of inference functioning through the power of real entities (*vastubalapravṛttānumāna*) alone that the followers of the Sugata apply themselves toward human goals, and not merely on the basis of hearsay.
Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated how properties such as "knowability" (prameyatva) can function as a means of proof (sādhana).
As for what you said—that [the Buddha] has reached the ten stages (daśabhūmi)—that too was stated by you without understanding our established doctrine (siddhānta);
for the Blessed One is not held to have reached the ten stages.
Rather, it is maintained that up to the stage of the bodhisattva through the ten stages (daśabhūmi), and beyond that, the stage of a Buddha (buddhabhūmi) is attained.

Showing that even the argument previously stated—that "what is sung by one who knows only a single part cannot be the speech of an omniscient being"—has already been refuted, he says "ekadeśa... and so forth:
"But that which is sung by one who knows only a single part could not be the speech of an omniscient being;
regarding this point as well, it was previously stated [in the verse] that 'it follows from the connection with the omniscient ones.'"
Explaining this very point once more, he says "Just as," and so forth:
Just as one of limited vision, having experienced objects such as sacrifices and the like,
subsequently projects them onto the mind and speaks of them based on that experience.
And that statement of his is not produced without the knowledge of that object;
thus would the speech of an omniscient being be, yet it differs because of a difference in its causes.
"One of limited vision" means one who perceives only what is proximate, that is to say, one who is not omniscient;
"the arising of knowledge regarding that object" refers to this.
The cognition of that object, such as heat and so forth, is its experience; "cognition of that object" refers to that speech whose birth or production arises from it.
By the double negation "not not," he shows that it is indeed born from the cognition of that object.
"In this way" means that even that [speech] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being born from the cognition of that object.
If this is so, one might ask: what is the distinction between the words of those with limited vision and the words of the Buddha? To this he says: "But it differs because of the difference in cause."
He clarifies this very point with the verse beginning "samasta" and so forth:
"The cognition of all things has become the cause for this [omniscience],
whereas the cognition of only a few objects remains its [ordinary] condition."
"Of this" refers to the word of the Buddha;
"of that, however" refers to [the following].
Of the statement of one who knows only a single part.
With the words beginning "vikalpa," the opponent raises an objection:

"In the absence of conceptual construction (vikalpa), what indeed could his intention to speak (vivakṣā) be? For, because he has abandoned all conduct, conceptual construction no longer occurs for him."
For the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is not possible for one in whom conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is absent, since that intention is a specific kind of conceptual construction.
Therefore, being pervaded by conceptual construction, how could it maintain its existence in the absence of the latter?
Indeed, there is no possibility of a *śiṃśapā* tree existing in the absence of trees.

Furthermore, conceptual construction is impossible for the Omniscient One, because he has abandoned all obscurations such as the afflictions and the cognitive veils; and since conceptual construction is by its very nature erroneous, if it were to manifest in him, the All-Knowing One would become an errant being.
He replies with the words "not so," and so forth:

"It is not so; for his volition is not afflicted, since he possesses neither obscuration nor [mental] exhaustion. But who could ward off that which is wholesome and conducive to the welfare of the world?"
For conceptualization is of two kinds: it is afflicted because it is conducive to affliction and so forth;
it is wholesome because it arises from association with non-attachment and so forth.
Among these, that which is afflicted does not exist at all for those who have abandoned the obscurations of the afflictions and so forth, due to the absence of its cause.

But that which is wholesome is not in contradiction even with one whose obscurations have been abandoned; therefore, by whom can that wholesome conceptualization—which has been set in motion through the Blessed Ones' practice of compassion and is conducive to the arising of the world's welfare—be prevented from becoming manifest?

It might be argued that since every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is by its very nature erroneous—because it functions by determining its own internal appearance, which is not an actual object, to be an actual object—the manifestation of such a construction is indeed contradictory for one who has abandoned the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "And he does not determine that conceptual construction to possess an object," and so forth.
For he knows that it is without a basis (*nirālamba*); indeed, he is like a magician.
Just as a certain magician knows that his mind, which takes horses and other things as its determined objects, is actually without an external object, he does not become deluded because of it.

For if he were to grasp that conceptual construction—which is itself objectless—as having an object, then he would be deluded; however, since, like a magician, he understands it precisely as the object of that cognition, how could he be deluded?
Regarding the statement "that which was said," etc., and the claim that "what is being proclaimed shines among those who have faith," he says "ityādi" (and so forth):

"That which was said, 'what is being proclaimed shines among those who have faith,' was spoken by the twice-born [Vasiṣṭha] in accordance with the subject at hand; this [present case] is not like that."

How so? What is that which is under discussion? He says that this [argument] does not correspond to it: "And thus unperceived by all objects, it is not at all capable of being demonstrated. For this is indeed what is under discussion here; regarding that, the great-minded ones have said: "Furthermore, since the nature of the object is not perceived, there is no means of knowing it. Therefore, because the object is not established, its capacity is also not established. (PV 1.6) If one asks, "What is the meaning of 'not perceived'?"—it means that the nature of the object is not apprehended. And if the nature of the object is not apprehended, how can its capacity be known? For capacity is understood through the perception of the nature of the object. Thus, since the object is not established, its capacity is likewise not established. This is the point. Furthermore, they have said: "If the object were established by another cognition, then that [second] cognition would also require another [cognition], leading to an infinite regress. If it were established by itself, then the object too would be established by itself. (PV 1.7) If the object were established by another cognition, then that second cognition would also require another, resulting in an infinite regress. If it were established by itself, then the object would also be established by itself. This is the meaning. Furthermore: "The capacity of the sense organs is inferred from the effect, but the capacity of the mind is not so inferred. Therefore, the capacity of the mind is not established. (PV 1.26) The capacity of the sense organs is inferred from the effect,
If he were to lack the capacity for instruction, what would happen then? You must therefore state that there would be no scripture.
Regarding this, they say: "Let it be so; but have you seen him speaking?
If this undesirable consequence is urged by means of a *prasaṅga-sādhana*," [then we reply: "No."
If speakerhood were not admitted, there would be no acceptance of scripture;
but if a composer is accepted for the scriptures, then his speakerhood must also be admitted.

Thinking that the opponent will say, "I have stated this as a *prasaṅga*-proof (reductio ad absurdum), not as an independent argument," and thus [the opponent] will express himself through his own words, [the author], wishing first to establish the nature of this present *prasaṅga*-proof, says "And regarding that, they say," and so forth.

As for what was said by you—that there is no capacity for teaching that which is excluded from all objects—first, you must be asked: "Let there be no capacity for its teaching; what fault ensues here? Having been asked this, the opponent reveals his own answer:
"From that," and so forth.

To this it is replied: even so, there is indeed an absence of scripture; what contradiction is there here? For you have not perceived him speaking such that there would be a contradiction based on the fact that he was seen. Thus questioned, you must state by implication: "I do not establish his status as the speaker by having myself perceived that the scripture was composed by him; rather, it is you yourselves who accept that the scripture was composed by him, and that acceptance of yours is untenable if his status as the speaker is not accepted."

Therefore, by those who necessarily desire that the scripture was composed by him, his status as a speaker must also be accepted; thus, this undesirable consequence is established through a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga).

Having thus established that this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (a reductio ad absurdum), he now says "If it is so," etc., in order to apply the point that [the opponent] has failed to state what is consistent with the subject at hand: "If such a principle is well-known among those who speak according to logic,
then in a *prasaṅga*-proof, the property [of the probandum] is accepted by the opponents based on mere faith."
And if [the reason] were established through logic, it would be an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*);
and such a thing is what is desired by the opponent—that scripture was composed by him.
Due to the momentum of his accumulated provisions, teachings issue forth from even walls and other such objects at will, like those from a wish-fulfilling gem for that person.
Therefore, he is designated as the "author" by virtue of his sovereign mastery and his engagement [with the teaching];
it does not follow that his status as a speaker is merely a consequence of following conceptual construction.
"But as for us, who lack faith and yet seek logical arguments— it was with this in mind that I spoke those words, not knowing the full context."
For it is a logical principle that whatever property has been accepted by the opponent based solely on scripture is precisely what is stated in a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) argument.

In this case, if the opponent had intended that the scripture was composed by [the Buddha] because of his status as its speaker, then there would indeed follow the consequence that, due to the absence of such speakership, the scripture is not composed by him; however, he has accepted him as the author of that scripture merely by virtue of his sovereign authority (*adhipatya*), and not because of an acceptance of his being the speaker.
Therefore, your attempt to establish speakership by accepting the scripture as composed by him was stated by you without understanding the meaning of a *prasaṅga*.
Regarding that which was stated, "of those [sounds] emerging from walls and so forth," and so on,
he says "walls and so forth" etc.:
"And why is there no status as being taught by a reliable person (āpta) for those [sounds] emerging from walls and so forth?"
When their manifestation occurs through the state of that sovereign power, [it is so called].
For if those teachings did not proceed by virtue of his sovereignty, then they would not possess the quality of being taught by an authoritative person (āpta).
But since it is accepted that they proceed by virtue of his sovereignty, why then should they not be considered taught by him?

Regarding what was said— that there can be no trust in them— he replies with the verse beginning "sambhinna" and so forth: "How could those [Vedas] have been composed by playful beings such as Piśācas, since they are devoid of base matters such as incoherent talk and violence?"
In those [realms], there is no teaching of base matters such as frivolous speech, violence,
and so forth, nor any activity such as that of playful piśācas and the like.
That [scripture] is held to be in agreement with the two means of valid cognition regarding its entire subject matter,
wherein not even the slightest sublation by those two means of valid cognition is observed.

And that which, although entirely beyond the senses, is not contradicted by what precedes or follows it, and which impels all persons toward the arising of qualities such as compassion; [that is the means of valid cognition].
Endowed with all excellent qualities, it establishes the practice of the virtuous life and brings about various forms of prosperity for fortunate beings both in this world and the next.
It expresses the antidote to the entire mass of latent tendencies and breaks open the gates and doors of the city of Nirvana.
If that [teaching] were the word of playful Rākṣasas,
let them alone be the perfectly awakened ones (sambuddhas), since it stands possessed of all those characteristics.
Indeed, by the assignment of another name, the nature of the thing does not cease to exist;
however, one who applies a name to something that is not qualified would be censured by the virtuous.

For if there were an instruction therein regarding dancing, singing, violence, sexual misconduct, and so forth as things to be performed, then—given that we observe the activities of Piśācas and others who delight in such play—it might be conceivable that those [scriptures] were composed by them.

However, it has already been established that this word of the Blessed One is consistent with valid cognition, free from internal contradictions, appropriate for noble persons, enjoining virtues such as compassion, and bringing about the fruits of heaven and liberation.
How, then, could such a thing be attributed to a playful Piśāca or similar being?
If you give even human beings the name "piśāca" (demon), let it be so;
for there is no loss of a thing's essential nature in the mere assigning of a name.
However, the summarized meaning is this: by applying the conduct of the uncivilized toward the distinguished Blessed One, you alone would become an object of reproach for the virtuous.
The meaning of the individual components is now stated: frivolous talk refers to instruction in singing and the like;
violence refers to the killing of living beings; and base matters refer to sexual misconduct and so forth.

"Consistent with the two means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇadvayasaṃvādī*) means that there are two means of valid cognition, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); "consistency" (*saṃvāda*) with these two refers to having an object that is not contradicted by them. That which possesses this is so described.
It is "regarded" (*matam*).

"Certainly" means that it is "entire" regarding its object; that is to say, it is connected with the phrase "in agreement with the two means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) regarding the objects of those two means of valid cognition.

The holy life (*brahmacarya*), which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end, is the complete collection of all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—the flood of afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through vision and cultivation.
"Abiding in that characteristic" means abiding in the characteristic of a Perfectly Awakened One (*sambuddha*).
As it has been said: [3612]...
"Since that which was to be known through higher knowledge has been known, that which was to be cultivated has been cultivated,
and that which was to be abandoned has been abandoned, one is therefore called 'Awakened' (buddha). Thus,
it is reasonable to consider that the Veda itself was composed by playful spirits, *piśācas*, and the like.

Demonstrating that by which unseemly practices such as sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached in the Gosava sacrifice and others were proclaimed, he says "kāma" and so forth: "By whom unrefined actions, characterized by sexual misconduct, wrong conduct, violence toward living beings, and the like, were proclaimed through his speech."
It is suspected that this was composed by serpent-demons (bhujaṅga-piśāca) and the like;
for such speech is indeed conceivable from those who delight in their activities.
A serpent is a rogue.
Regarding what was said, namely "simultaneously pure, impure, and so forth," he replies with the verse beginning "simultaneously" (*yugapat*), etc.:
"Of those contradictory natures such as the pure and the impure, simultaneously..."
Knowledge perceived by a single cognition is not contradictory for you, for your awareness is indeed such.
Although some entities are mutually contradictory, they are nonetheless not contradictory with respect to awareness— that is, with respect to knowledge—
since it is observed that even by a single cognition, multiple contradictory objects can be apprehended simultaneously.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "By way of mutual exclusion," and so forth. "Alternatively, because their characteristics exist through mutual exclusion, there can be contradiction among them in that they do not coexist in a single locus."
There is illumination by a single cognition, yet there is no contradiction among them, because pure and impure things, snakes and peacocks, and so forth, are perceived simultaneously by the eye.
For the contradiction between entities is indeed of two kinds: that characterized by existing through mutual exclusion, and that characterized by non-coexistence.
Among these, for those things whose nature consists in existing through mutual exclusion, their identity is contradictory;
whereas for those things that cannot coexist, their existence in the same location is contradictory.
Nor does the fault of appearing within a single cognition entail their identity or their occupying the same location;
therefore, there is no contradiction among them on account of appearing in a single cognition.
Furthermore, it is observed that even things which are contradictory appear together within a single cognition.

Just as there is the simultaneous apprehension of the pure and the impure—such as a snake and a peacock—which possess characteristics established through mutual exclusion by means of visual cognition;
and by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of shadow, sunlight, and so forth.
If, then, even for contradictory things, their appearance in a single cognition is not contradictory...
Anticipating the objection that, this being the case, pleasure and pain, or attachment and aversion, would necessarily appear simultaneously in a single cognition, he says "pleasure" and so forth:

"But as for the fact that there is no simultaneous perception of the distinctions such as pleasure and pain, that is not contradictory; it should be understood as resulting from the absence of the cause and from non-proximity."

"That is to be known" means that the simultaneous non-perception of pleasure and the other [feelings] is to be understood as being due to their non-existence because they do not arise in the absence of their causes, and not because of mutual contradiction; this is the sense.
What is meant is this: in that case, the cause for their non-presence is the deficiency of their respective causes, not mutual contradiction.

He shows that even for those things whose opposition is real— and not merely conceptual, like the case of the pure and the impure— there is a simultaneous appearance within a single cognition, by means of the passage beginning with "blue, yellow," and so on: "Because blue, yellow, white, and other distinct forms, despite differences in location and nature, are seen simultaneously without contradiction."
The connection is that [things] are "contradictory" by way of difference of place and difference of nature (*prakṛti*).
In this context, "difference of place" means being in that place or not being in that place;
"difference of nature" means having a nature such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
Or rather, it is the state of being the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) of blue and so forth.

Regarding what was stated—that [the omniscient one] is past, present, future, and so forth—it is said in reply: "The all-knowing one has indeed been established as one whose entire circle of objects of knowledge is pervaded by a single moment of cognition; therefore, a sequential process is not resorted to."

On this point, some of our own fellow-schoolmen (*svayūthya*), supporting the position of the Vijñānavādins, raise an objection: "If the entire circle of objects of knowledge (*jñeyamaṇḍala*) were pervaded by a single momentary cognition (*ekajñānakṣaṇa*) simultaneously, then the infinity [of things]—which is established through the determination of the limits of entities (*bhāva*) and their efforts (*yatna*)—would be contradicted.
For, when entities are determined such that there is no entity other than those mounted upon a single cognition, how could they not be finite?
And it has been said:
"There is no other entity whatsoever that is not mounted upon a single cognition;
since they are cognized as being 'this many,' how could they not be finite?
Therefore, whatever fault there is in the position of successive [cognitions] applies equally to the position of simultaneous cognition.
This is without substance.
If the objection is raised based on the view of those who maintain that consciousness is formless (*nirākāra-vijñānavādin*), then everything is incoherent.
For instance, whatever object of knowledge exists, it experiences its own being.

Because that [omniscient mind] delimits all of that [the universe] by its mere existence, it is designated as "pervading" it; however, this is not a pervasion in the sense of spatial extension, as when jars are pervaded by a cloth.

Nor does the mere fact that things are delimited by a single cognition entail a loss of their own essential nature (*ātmasvabhāva*), such that they would abandon their infinite nature simply by virtue of being delimited by a single cognition.

For numerous entities such as blue, yellow, and so forth, when their forms are apprehended simultaneously in a single moment of cognition— as in the case of a variegated sun and other such objects— do not abandon their plurality,
nor do they mutually interpenetrate; rather,
they are determined by cognition exactly as they exist.
Not in any other form.
Likewise, the world of sentient beings is also apprehended by the mind of the Omniscient One exactly as it experiences existence.

Since the world of sentient beings and so forth is situated without limit in the cardinal and intermediate directions, its apprehension is by way of being limitless, and not by way of being limited; how, then, could there be the consequence of its being finite?
It might be argued: "If the apprehension of the whole is accepted, how could there not be an apprehension of the limits?
This is not so;
for what necessary connection is there here such that wherever there is an apprehension of the whole, there must necessarily be an apprehension of the limits?
For indeed, among all those entities that exist, not even a single one experiences existence with a nature unknown to the cognition of the Omniscient One.

Rather, every single one arises and passes away with its nature known precisely by the mind of the Omniscient One; not even one is excluded. This is the meaning of the term "all" (sakala). And this alone constitutes their pervasion by a single cognition.
Otherwise, one would have to deny that they are expressible by all words as well, lest there be the consequence of their being finite; thus, this [argument] is trivial.
As for what was said—that because of the delimitation "there is nothing other than the entity mounted upon a single cognition," how could they not be finite?—that too is incorrect.
For in the view of those who maintain that cognition is formless (*nirākāra-jñāna-vāda*), there is no mounting of entities within the nature of cognition.
Rather, they are indicated by that [cognition] merely by virtue of their existence.

Nor is it accepted that things are infinite because their nature is such that they cannot be delimited by cognition—which would entail the consequence that they have a finite end simply by being known.
Instead, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is infinite due to the boundlessness of its spatial extension.
The world of sentient beings, moreover, is [incomprehensible] even by way of its being beyond enumeration.

Nor does there exist any contradiction with its being an object of cognition (*grāhya*) simply because it lacks spatial limitation; for if it were limited, there would be some contradiction with its being an object of cognition such that it could not be apprehended.
If it is asked, "If he does not comprehend it as having limits, how can he be omniscient?"—it is precisely for this reason.
Precisely because he does not grasp that [reality] as having a limit, he is omniscient;
otherwise, grasping an infinite object as finite, he would be mistaken.
For it is said that one who grasps what exists as existing and what does not exist as non-existing is called "all-knowing."
Furthermore, there is no limit to the world of sentient beings and the receptacle-world.

Therefore, how could one be called "non-omniscient" when, by perceiving the limit consisting in the non-existence of a limit produced by movement as being non-existent, one perceives the existing limit produced by the delimitation of omniscient knowledge as being existent?
It might be argued that on the view of formless cognition (*nirākārajñāna*), the apprehension of objects is untenable because such cognition is undifferentiated with respect to all things.
Because, for that reason, the distinction between individual cognitions would be untenable, the position of formlessness (*nirākārapakṣa*) should not even be proposed,
since it is always subject to refutation.
This, however, is incorrect.

For no division according to each respective object (*pratikarmapanna*) is admitted for the cognition of the Omniscient One, because that [cognition] has all things as its object; since it is accepted that this is not the perception of blue alone or yellow alone, but rather of everything.

For one whose vision is limited (*arvāgdarśana*), whose cognition has restricted objects as its domain, the impossibility of establishing a division [of objects] is stated to be a fault under the theory of formless cognition (*nirākārajñānapakṣa*), because there would be no distinction in every case.
For instance, because there would be no restriction such as "this is the cognition of blue, not of yellow," it would follow that every ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is omniscient;
however, since that is precisely what is accepted by the Omniscient One, what undesirable consequence could possibly befall whom?
Therefore, in the state of omniscience, it is entirely non-contradictory for [cognition] to arise through the power of yoga without a mental aspect (*nirākāra*).
If it is argued that there would be no thorough knowledge of things to be abandoned and things to be adopted through differentiation, we say:
no.

For if there were a contradiction in the manifestation of the objects to be abandoned and those to be adopted when infinite objects appear simultaneously; or if, in the absence of such contradiction, that object to be abandoned or adopted appearing along with others were to lose its true nature; or even if, having lost its true nature, it did not manifest through differentiation; or finally, if—even though it manifests distinctly—a subsequent pure worldly reflective cognition (*vimarśapratyaya*) that delimits it does not arise—then all this might be said.

To whatever extent the entire world appears, even that object—whether to be rejected or accepted—appears precisely as it is defined: with a non-contradictory manifestation and without its own essential nature being lost.

Furthermore, it is indeed determined subsequently by a pure worldly reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśa*) produced through the power of omniscient knowledge. Thus, how could there be any lack of full comprehension regarding it through such a distinction?
In this way, it has been demonstrated that this objection does not apply to the position that knowledge is formless (*nirākāra*).
Now, an objection is raised regarding the position of those who maintain that cognition possesses a form (*sākārajñānavāda*).
Even in that case, there is indeed no contradiction.

For instance, just as that infinite reality experiences its own existence by following after infinite forms, so too it is entirely consistent that the omniscient mind arises by grasping the forms residing in immeasurable things.
This is because there is no contradiction in a single cognition arising by assuming the forms of multiple objects.
If it is argued that there is indeed a contradiction for a single [cognition] to possess multiple forms, we say no; for those forms are unreal.

For if the forms were ultimately real for a single [consciousness], then there would be a contradiction with its manifold nature; however, it is accepted that these forms are indeed devoid of intrinsic nature (*asvabhūta*).
If it is argued that, because he is associated with erroneous cognition, the Omniscient One would consequently be mistaken, we say no;
this fault does not apply because his knowledge is a thorough comprehension of things as they truly are.
For if one were to grasp the unreal as being real, then one would be deluded; however, when one knows unreal aspects (ākāras) precisely as unreal, how could one be deluded?

If it is argued that one is deluded because one engages in worldly conventions such as "seen" with respect to objects while grasping aspects mounted upon a non-distinct cognition, we say no, because of the thorough knowledge of the correct means.
For if one were to discard the appropriate means of apprehension and grasp an object by some other, non-primary means, then one would be mistaken.

However, in the position of those who maintain that cognition possesses an aspect (sākārajñānavāda), there is no operation of grasping an object for cognition other than the experience of its own aspect. Therefore, how could one be mistaken while grasping an object through its appropriate mode of apprehension?
Therefore, just as with the objects of knowledge, because even a single cognition arises by apprehending the forms of infinite entities, it is said that infinite reality is pervaded by it.

Furthermore, by whichever nature entities ascend into the self of cognition, by that very same nature they are determined by the subsequent reflective consciousness (*parāmarśacetas*). However, entities do not ascend into the omniscient mind following limited distinctions;
rather, whatever exists in its entirety, all of that ascends [into it].

Because the material cause of all cognition possesses an unimpeded capacity with respect to its status as an objective support for everything, and because mental consciousness has all things as its object, it is therefore impossible for an omniscient mind to grasp only a limited number of entities and their forms. Furthermore, since the subsequent pure mundane reflective cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-śuddhalaukika-parāmarśapratyaya*) does not delimit [reality] by being restricted to a specific location, how could there be a delimitation such that one could say, "It is only this much," which would imply finitude? Thus, there can be no end.
Even if a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) has arisen that there is nothing other than what is appearing, there is still no consequence of [the world] being finite.

For if that which is appearing were indeed finite within the non-conceptual mind of the Omniscient One due to its appearance, then its infinitude would be delimited by the reflective awareness-mind obtained subsequent to it;
and from that delimitation, the loss of infinity would follow.

To the extent that an object appearing [to cognition] appears as infinite within the mind of an omniscient one—because his power is unimpeded with respect to everything—therefore, whatever else does not so appear is indeed finite.

And since the exclusion of that very [finite object] is performed by the conceptualizing mind (*parāmarśacetas*), you have all the more established the infinitude of entities; thus, this [objection of yours] is trivial.

Furthermore, as for those who maintain that all yogic cognition is indeed without an external object (*anālambana*), yet is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it accords with reality—just like the perception of a true dream—for them, the objection regarding its having limits has no room at all; so, enough of this prolixity.
Demonstrating that this [position] is not contradicted even by the view of those who describe him as omniscient according to his own will, he says "whatever...":
"Whatever he wishes to know, he knows that necessarily;
such is his power, for he has abandoned all defilements."
Having attained knowledge, the Lord indeed practices according to his own will, either simultaneously or in succession, through the moments beginning with the "seated" (sitta) and so forth.

With the words "syād vā" and so forth, he states that there is no contradiction even in the view that knowledge occurs sequentially: "Alternatively, one who knows all that is to be known through sixteen moments of consciousness, in the nature of the Four Truths, in succession, is therefore called 'all-knowing' (sarvavid)."
In such a state of consciousness, O Lord, even a mere moment (lava) need not be waited for; how much less so a period of a hundred years?
"By means of sixteen moments of mind" refers to the patiences (*kṣānti*) and the knowledges (*jñāna*).

There are eight patiences, beginning with the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*), and eight knowledges, beginning with the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*); for it is stated that "this clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) is distinguished by these sixteen."
"Even a mere lava" refers to the following convention:
a *kṣaṇa* is the ultimate limit of time; one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*; and sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*.
"Aṅga" is used as a form of address.
"Abda" is a synonym for "saṃvatsara" (year).
Regarding the passage beginning with "by means of an undivided nature," he says "svabhāvena" and so forth:
"He who perceives everything by means of an undivided nature..."
He perceives the very intrinsic natures of all phenomena.

[Objection: But surely, in the treatises, the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of yogins is described as having only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, and not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). How then can the very natures of things be cognized by a yogic consciousness that has the universal as its object? To this, he says: "That which is excluded from what is non-self, non-momentary, and so forth," and so on. [The particular characteristic is that which is excluded from those things that are non-self, non-momentary, etc.]
Because it is the cause for the conceptualization of tranquility, it is here called a "universal."

And the consciousness that apprehends that [object], which arises through the power of cultivation and is manifested for the lords of yogins, has the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as its object.

For that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), when excluded from what is of a different class, is called a "universal characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) in the treatise because it serves as the cause for a cognition of a non-differentiated form. Therefore, it is not at all contradictory that the yogic cognition which grasps it—arising with a clear manifestation through the power of meditative cultivation—has the particular characteristic alone as its object. How could that which has the universal as its object not be a grasper of the particular characteristic?

Furthermore, whatever was said regarding "that cognition of a single form" and so forth, all of that is refuted by this very point, since the yogic cognition has the particular characteristic as its objective domain.

Now, as for that universal which we have described as being inexpressible through such forms as identity or difference and so forth—being merely conventional (sāṃvṛta)—and which is imagined by other outsiders (tīrthika) to be ultimately real (pāramārthika): the claim that the cognition of a yogin has the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as its object on the grounds that it grasps that [universal] is unestablished. Demonstrating this, he says "identity, difference," and so forth: "That universal which is inexpressible as identical or different and so forth, and which is imagined by others—that is not grasped by the yogi’s mind through this [cognition]."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it should be understood that [the object] is indefinable by means of such qualities as permanence and so forth.
Why is it that there is no apprehension of that [object] by means of that [consciousness]? He says: "non-conceptual," and so forth:
"The mind of the Lord of Yogis is non-conceptual and non-erroneous."
And it follows that [the cognition] would be overcome by conceptual construction and error in its apprehension of that [object].
The cognition of a yogin is accepted as a valid means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) because it is non-conceptual and non-erroneous.

If, however, that [cognition] were to have the aforementioned universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, then, because its object would be a conventional reality, it would follow that it is beset by conceptual construction.
Furthermore, because its object would be a false universal imagined by others, it would entail that it is beset by delusion.
Alternatively, if each were to have both as its object, two faults would ensue.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that because its object is an unreal thing superimposed [upon reality], it follows that it is overcome by conceptual construction and error.
Furthermore, demonstrating by another method that the grasper of that [universal] follows as being overcome by conceptual construction and error, he says:
"And the universal which is proclaimed to be of the nature of conceptual construction and inexpressible," and so forth.
That which has the nature of constant persistence is established as being formless.

Since it has been proclaimed— that is, established— in the context of *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of others) that this aforementioned universal (*sāmānya*), which is inexpressible and indefinable as being either identical to or different [from particulars], is the very nature (*ātman*) of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it follows— this is the connection with the subject at hand—
that upon the apprehension of that [universal], one falls into the error of conceptual construction. For,
because the universal would have conceptual construction as its nature, the yogic cognition that apprehends it would likewise necessarily be of the nature of conceptual construction.

Because that [universal] is apprehended precisely as being identical [to the particular], and because conceptual construction by its very nature functions—through the determination of a non-object as an object—within its own internal appearance, it follows that it possesses the nature of error; thus, it would necessarily be overcome by delusion.

Furthermore, as for the universal imagined by others in the form of an eternal, pervasive entity, that too has been demonstrated in the "Examination of the Universal" (*Sāmānyaparīkṣā*) to be entirely devoid of any real nature; therefore, if that were apprehended, it would most clearly entail being overcome by the delusion of conceptual construction.
Regarding what was stated, "action together with its cause and its fruit," and so forth, he says "with its cause," etc.:
He who knows action together with its cause and its fruit through supramundane knowledge born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is designated as omniscient.
Previously, its existence was established through inference;
there exists such a [cognition] which serves as the means of valid knowledge for its presence.
Regarding the passage beginning with "simultaneously or in succession," he says "simultaneously" and so forth:
"Whether simultaneously or in succession, knowledge [of the capacity] exists from the manifested effect;
that capacity also exists when he performs the teaching."
This is easily understood.
Regarding the statement "having obtained the means for non-common [attainment]," and so forth, he says: "One who has well-practiced the selflessness of phenomena," and so on.
This stainless teaching, whose selflessness of phenomena has been well-practiced, has been established by him through all the treatises and remains uncontradicted by any means of valid cognition.
She, whose knowledge is unattainable by those in cyclic existence and who is beyond the reach of Keśava and others,
is worshipped with their heads according to their capacity by the most wise.
It brings about the destruction of the entire host of enemies that are misfortunes,
and it is the cause for the attainment of various prosperities and nirvāṇa.
"He who has attained the uncommon means, who is the distinguished [characteristic] of all persons without exception,
he alone is the omniscient Lord"— this is established by valid proof.
"By the entire treatise" means by this *Tattvasaṃgraha* in its entirety.
"Knowledge unsuitable for those in saṃsāra" means...
"Unfamiliar to those in saṃsāra" means not innate to them; that teaching in which such knowledge [is present] is described as such.
The phrase "beyond the scope of Keśava and others" is coreferential with the teaching itself by virtue of its own grammatical gender.
Regarding the phrase "bestowing the destruction of the entire host of enemies that are misfortunes":
the analysis of the compound is as follows: misfortunes themselves are the enemies; their "host" is a collection; and its nature is to effect their "destruction.
Regarding the phrase "the cause for the accomplishment of various prosperities and the attainment of nirvāṇa," the word "cause" (kāraṇa) is to be connected with each [term] individually.
The meaning is that it is the cause for the accomplishment of various forms of prosperity and the cause for the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the phrase "when it is thus," he says "it is thus," and so forth:
"And when, in this way, some omniscient being indeed arises as the cause for the realization of Dharma and so on, then human speech [becomes authoritative]."
"Only someone" means only the Sugata, not Kapila or others;
this is the intended meaning, as was stated previously.
And as for the fault that was stated regarding the conceptual distinction between cognition with form and cognition without form, we have already provided a rebuttal to that as well.
And it has been said therein:
"Others [hold that cognition] is with appearance, without appearance, or indeed only with appearance."
They do not cognize any object whatsoever as being external to consciousness.
Thus [it is said].
Anticipating the objection, "How can it be said that there is no consequence of error even when resorting to both positions? he says:
"The consideration of whether [the Buddha] is formless (*nirākāra*) and so forth is not applicable to the Omniscient One;
for just as your own cognition [is directed] toward some object, so too is the [Omniscient One's] supreme [cognition]."
Thus concludes the examination of the person who perceives that which transcends the senses.
The *Tattvasaṃgraha*, composed by Śāntarakṣita, is completed.

[936] This reflection on formlessness (*nirākāra*) which was previously undertaken by us while remaining within the position of those who maintain that consciousness alone exists (*vijñānavāda*), is now—when we are establishing the existence of an omniscient being while provisionally accepting external objects for the sake of you Mīmāṃsakas who are attached to external objects—not at all applicable to you proponents of external objects (*bahirarthavādin*).
Why is this? He says: "For as... and so forth.
For you must necessarily describe the apprehension of an external object by a cognition as being either with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*nirākāra*).
Otherwise, there would be the total abolition of external objects.

Consequently, just as and in whatever manner your cognition operates with respect to some object, in that very same form will the supreme, most excellent—that is, the omniscient—operate; thus, this [objection] is not to be raised.
Thus, whatever abundant and pure merit I have acquired, may it,
possessing radiant splendor, eternally delight the minds of all beings by attaining the state of being the abode of the incomparable glory of the Jina.
By that [merit], may the entire world become like the lotus-feet of the Sugata.
Thus concludes the examination of the person who perceives that which is beyond the senses.
The Pañjikā composed by Kamalaśīla is completed.
